## Volume front matter

### Series title page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions produced over the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes for each volume and for each author of some importance who follows; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture.

An exceedingly accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Exposition of the Gospel of Matthew (G, S)*

## Book One

### Chapter One

[Column 0009A]

“Book of the generation.” It is indeed the custom of the sacred Scriptures to give a name to the subject of a book’s exposition, just as Genesis is so called because it begins by discussing the nature and origin of created things. For this reason Matthew gave this title to his Gospel, since at its beginning he recorded the genealogy of Christ’s humanity, although in what follows he also made mention of his teaching and miracles.

“Of Jesus Christ.” Jesus is the proper name of the flesh assumed; in Latin it is interpreted as “Savior.” Christ is the name of his dignity; in Latin it is called “anointed.” Under the ancient law, priests and kings were anointed, and this man is rightly called anointed, since he is the true priest, offering himself for our sins, [Column 0009B] and the king of all kings, at whose name every knee bends, and who, according to the testimony of the Psalmist, was anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit above his companions.

“Son of David, son of Abraham.” It is asked why he named David before Abraham, or why he mentioned only these men, leaving out so many fathers. But, as Jerome says, the order is reversed, though necessarily altered; otherwise, after naming Abraham and then David, he would have had to name Abraham again in order to show that David was his son. It should also be noted that he named these men because Christ was promised to be born from their offspring. Thus to Abraham it was said: “In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12)—and that seed is Christ. To David it was said: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne” (Ps. 131 [132]:11).

“Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar.” It is asked why he named only Tamar and Rahab, foreigners and sinners, in Christ’s genealogy. The evangelist did this, however, to show that Christ is the Savior not only of the Jews but also of the nations. Tamar is interpreted as “bitterness” or “palm,” and signifies the Church, which was bitter in sins but was sweetened through Christ’s grace. The name “palm” also seems appropriate to her because of victory in struggles and the crown of heavenly rewards.

Rahab is interpreted as “breadth,” and likewise seems fittingly to signify the Church, enlarged throughout the whole world, as it is written: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your dwellings; do not spare” (Isa. 54:2).

Ruth is interpreted as “seeing”; she signifies the Church, which sees God through purity of mind, or as “determining,” because the Church has firmly resolved to persevere in the faith of Christ. Thus the Apostle says: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor an angel nor a principality, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38).

“David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife.” It is asked why he gave the name of Uriah while passing over the name of Bathsheba. The answer is that he inserted the name of Uriah as the name of a righteous man, whereas he passed over Bathsheba’s name because of the monstrous crime of adultery and murder committed on her account.

“Joram begot Uzziah.” We read that Ahaziah was born from Joram; Ahaziah begot Joash, whose son Amaziah succeeded him, and after him came Azariah, who is also called Uzziah. The names of three kings are omitted from the Savior’s genealogy because Joram joined himself to the most impious house of Jezebel, and also so that, according to the predetermined arrangement, the three sets of fourteen generations might be completed.

“Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian deportation.” Jerome related that this passage had been confused through a scribal error between the Greeks and Latins. He maintained that the father, called Jehoiakim in Hebrew, was not led away into Chaldea but died in his own land, and that his son Jehoiachin, returning from captivity, begot Shealtiel.

Augustine, however, related that this was done for the sake of a mystery, so that Jeconiah—whose name is interpreted as “preparation of God”—might be counted twice, being placed at the end of the earlier catalogue and at the beginning of the following one. He thus signifies Christ, the cornerstone, in whom God the Father prepared to join two peoples, like walls, into one house.

“Jacob begot Joseph.” It is commonly asked how Matthew said that Joseph had Jacob as his father, whereas Luke named Heli. The answer is that Jacob and Heli were brothers, born at different times and from different lines, and that they appear to have been Joseph’s grandfathers. Mathan, who traced his descent through Solomon, had by one and the same wife, named Esai, a son Jacob; and Mathat, who traced his descent through Nathan from the same tribe, though not through the same line, after Mathan’s death had a son Heli. Thus Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers through different paternal lines. One of them, namely Jacob, took the wife of his deceased brother Heli and begot Joseph according to natural descent; but according to the command of the law, Joseph was the son of his brother.

“Her husband.” That is, Mary’s servant. Do not let the idea of marriage occur to you here; remember that in Scripture betrothed women are called wives.

“From whom Jesus Christ was born.” He fittingly says not “from whom,” in the plural, but “from whom,” in the singular—that is, from the virgin alone, without male seed.

Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations. The first set of fourteen, beginning with Abraham and ending with David, terminates with David himself. The second, beginning with Solomon after David, ends with the first Jeconiah, that is, the father who is called Jehoiakim among the Hebrews. The third begins with the second Jeconiah, that is, the son of Jehoiakim, who is called Jochin in Hebrew, and extends to Christ, so that Christ himself is included in the count.

This number of fourteen, set down three times, historically displays the threefold division of the Israelite people. The first existed under patriarchs, priests, and judges before the kings; the second under kings, prophets, and priests; the third under governors, prophets, and priests after the kings.

Mystically, ten refers to the Decalogue, four to the Gospels, and three to faith in the Trinity, because through the harmony of the Law and the Gospel the faith of the Holy Trinity is proclaimed. The number forty appears to signify the type of the present age, since the years proceed in fourfold cycles and the world is bounded by four regions. Ten multiplied by four produces forty, and two has rightly been added because it signifies the two Testaments, through which Christ governs the universal Church and has disclosed what pleases him in goodness and what displeases him in evil. Alternatively, the number itself signifies the two commandments of love, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

The number forty may also be understood in another way: seven times six make forty-two. Just as the Israelite people, liberated from Egyptian slavery, measured out their encampments through forty-two very difficult stages in the desert—seven times six—and, after receiving Joshua as leader, crossed the opened Jordan and entered the promised settlements after defeating their enemies, so the Lord Jesus, in the forty-second generation, came in the flesh and descended to share our mortality, at the time when Abraham’s faith dispersed the world’s darkness of blindness.

Through so many men, as though through dwellings corresponding to that number, one reaches the intelligible Jordan—that is, the Virgin Mary, filled with the flood of the Holy Spirit—with Jesus Christ as leader. Set there as though a hook, he killed by being killed the coiled dragon caught on the hook.

Matthew, beginning with Abraham and descending to Joseph, expounded Christ’s genealogy. Luke, beginning with Christ and ascending to the Lord himself, enumerated seventy-seven generations. In the descent Christ’s humility is signified, for, according to the Apostle, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). In the ascent our exaltation is signified, because Christ was humbled for this purpose: to exalt us.

Moreover, that mystical number signifies the complete forgiveness of sins. Hence the Gospel says: “I do not say to you, up to seven times,” and so forth (Matt. 8:22).

“Now the generation of Christ was as follows.” If you wish to attach this sentence to what precedes, it refers to the ancestors already named; if to what follows, it shows that the generation began to take place in this manner.

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.” It is commonly asked why Christ wished to be born from a virgin who was nevertheless betrothed. We believe that this happened for four reasons: so that, when Mary fled into Egypt, Joseph might provide the assistance of his service; so that she would not be stoned as an adulteress; so that Christ would not be despised as the son of fornication; and so that Christ’s lineage might be demonstrated through Joseph.

“Who was related to Mary.” Since it was not customary for historians to include women in genealogies, and so that the devil might remain unaware of Christ’s birth, thinking that Christ had been born from Joseph’s seed—otherwise he would not have dared to lay hands on him.

“She was found to have conceived in the womb by the Holy Spirit.” He says that Joseph found her to be pregnant. Although he speaks, as it were, specifically of the Holy Spirit, we must nevertheless believe that the man Jesus was formed in the Virgin’s womb not by the Holy Spirit alone but by the whole Trinity. He speaks particularly of the Holy Spirit because the triune God formed him in the Virgin; and by his coming he abundantly bestowed upon believers the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.”

He was righteous in that he mercifully sought to care for his relative, of whom Scripture said: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matt. 12:7), not righteous in the manner of the proud scribes and Pharisees, who considered themselves righteous imitators of the Law while cruelly shedding the blood of their neighbors on account of transgressions of a law which they themselves by no means observed.

“He himself will save his people from their sins.” Certainly the people of whom it is said in the Gospel, “But as many as received him,” and so forth (John 11:12); not the people of whom it is said: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11).

“And he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son.” This does not mean, as some wrongly suppose, that Mary bore other sons from Joseph after Christ, who are called the Lord’s brothers. Here “until” is used for an indefinite period, as it is said in the Psalms: “Until I make your enemies your footstool” (Ps. 109 [110]:1). It should also be noted that all only-begotten sons may be called firstborn. But not every firstborn son can be so called when others follow him. He is rightly called firstborn because, among many brothers, he rose first after conquering death and gave them an example of rising again.

## Chapter Two

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea.” He names it to distinguish it from the other Bethlehem, which is in the tribe of Zebulun.

“Behold, Magi from the East,” and so forth: “We have come to worship him.” They are not called Magi because of magical art, but because of a certain philosophy. They are believed to have been successors of Balaam and, stirred by his prophecy, sought the king who had been born after seeing a new star. According to their divine prophecy, he would shatter all the leaders of foreign peoples.

“And gathering together all the chief priests,” and so forth, “in Bethlehem of Judaea.” The star did not appear to the Magi at that time because it had previously led them. This occurred for the condemnation of the Jews, so that, when questioned by Herod, they might disclose the place of Christ’s birth and have no excuse for ignorance after neglecting the faith. Before his birth, they had shown not only that he would be born but also where he would be born.

Mystically, the three Magi signify the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—or the human race, which took its origin from the three sons of Noah.

[Column 0013B]

“And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them,” and so forth, “until it came and stood over where the child was.” This star signifies prophecy, which, from the beginning of the promised blessing to Abraham’s seed, promised, as it passed onward, that Christ would come, until it showed him born in the fullness of time.

“When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” That is, understanding that prophecy had reached its fulfillment, they rejoice with inexpressible joy—those who come from the three parts of the world to the faith of Christ.

“And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” That is, entering the Church through faith, they found Christ with the primitive Church, which had been converted from the Israelite people to his faith.

“And going forward, they worshiped him.” They would certainly not have worshiped him if they had not believed him to be the Lord. Mystically, the peoples of believers went forward and worshiped with true faith and pure confession.

“And opening their treasures,” and so forth. In gold the royal dignity of Christ is shown; in frankincense, his true priesthood; in myrrh, the mortality of his flesh. In another interpretation, gold signifies spiritual understanding, frankincense the fragrance of virtues, and myrrh the mortification of the body. All these things are offered daily to the Lord by this Church, dispersed throughout the three parts of the world.

Others wish to understand in these gifts the three kinds of philosophy: physics, ethics, and logic, which the world offered after the faith for the praise of God, although previously it had devoted them to empty study. Others say that allegory is indicated by gold, history by myrrh, and anagogy by frankincense.

“And having received an answer,” and so forth, “they returned to their own country by another way.” Our country is paradise, to which the human race must return through obedience, having been expelled from it through disobedience. Herod signifies the devil, to whom we are forbidden to return after receiving the faith.

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared,” and so forth, “and withdrew into Egypt.” Joseph signifies the teachers, Mary the Church, and Egypt—which is interpreted as “darkness”—signifies the Gentile world. This figure of Christ’s journey into Egypt signifies his passage with his Church from the Israelite people to the nations through preachers.

Herod signifies the hatred of the Jews, who desired to erase Christ’s name and destroy those who believed in him, [Column 0014A] or the heretics who sought to kill Christ—some in his humanity, others in his divinity, and likewise in his members. Night signifies the ignorance in which the Jews were left in their error when the apostles were announcing the light of faith to the Gentiles.

“And he was there,” and so forth, “until I called my son out of Egypt.” Herod’s death signifies the end of Jewish hatred, when, before the day of judgment, Christ will return to the Jews through the teachers of the final age. He will not abandon the Gentiles but will reign in both peoples.

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi.” It is plausible that, after the Magi reported nothing to Herod, he thought they had been deceived by the appearance of a false star and, failing to find the newborn king, had been ashamed to return to him. Thus, once his fear had been removed, he rested for a time from pursuing the child.

Later, when the events performed and spoken in the temple by Simeon and Anna became known, he realized that he had been deceived by the Magi. Then, desiring to reach Christ’s death, he killed not only in Bethlehem but throughout all the surrounding districts, showing no restraint. He killed all the children from one a night old to one two years old.

The wicked king reckoned, according to the time he had learned from the Magi, that the newborn God-King, whom the stars of heaven served, might appear to human eyes at the weaker age of one or two years. Alternatively, if he wished to conceal his age by the smallness of his body, it is unclear whether he would complete this slaughter after one year from the Lord’s birth or after two—unless perhaps we say that, after one year had elapsed, he ordered the infants of the four days belonging to the following year to be killed, at which point the day of their passion is venerated by the Catholic Church.

“Then was fulfilled,” and so forth, “she refused to be comforted, because they are not.” It is asked how Rachel could weep for the sons of Judah—that is, Bethlehem—as though they were her own, since she was the mother of the sons of Benjamin.

The answer is either that she was buried in Bethlehem and therefore received the name of mother there, or that the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were joined on the occasion of the slaughter of the children. Thus, beyond the borders of Judah, the persecution raged also in the territory of Benjamin.

Ramah is the name of a place near Gibeah, but it is interpreted as “exalted” and signifies that the lamentation over the slaughter was dispersed far and wide.

According to the allegory, Rachel—whose name is interpreted as “sheep of God” or “seeing God”—signifies the Church, which desires to see God with the whole intention of her mind. She is also the hundredth sheep whom the good shepherd sought on earth after leaving the ninety-nine sheep, that is, the orders of angels in heaven.

The killing of the children signifies the slaughter of Christ’s martyrs. The weeping Church does not wish to receive temporal consolation, because those who have once been crowned with Christ will not return to this age. Alternatively, she mourns the killers of the martyrs, whom she had first desired to have as children.

“And they are not”—that is, they are not destined for life but are proceeding toward eternal damnation.

## Chapter Three

“In those days John the Baptist came,” and so forth, “for the kingdom of heaven is near.” He says “in the wilderness of Judaea” because, just as it had previously been prophesied to them, “Behold, your house will be left desolate,” so in John’s days Judaea was largely desolate.

Shortly before, the Jews had returned from the captivity that occurred under Zerubbabel. Many, however, having taken wives and children in captivity, were unwilling to return to their own land and remained in exile.

Mystically, John signifies the Savior, who preached to desolate Judaea—that is, to Judaea abandoned by God because of its transgression of the Law—and announced that the kingdom had drawn near. The one who opened the way into the heavenly kingdom for human beings was drawing near. Alternatively, he proclaimed that the future Church was at hand, since in Scripture it is very often designated by the name “the kingdom of heaven.”

“For this is he of whom it was spoken through the prophet Isaiah, saying: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness.’” He is called “voice” because he went before the Word; “of one crying,” that is, of the Lord speaking through him. “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40:3). The voice went before the Word for this purpose: to make smooth the Lord’s way to our heart through faith in preaching.

“Make his paths straight.” He makes paths for the Lord who comes to him when he places no obstacle in the Lord’s way to impede the journey of the one hastening toward him.

“John himself had a garment of camel’s hair.” He displayed austerity of clothing because he preached repentance, since repentance is to be practiced in sackcloth and ashes.

“And a leather belt around his waist.” The leather belt indicates that penitents must mortify the flesh and restrain lust.

“His food was locusts and wild honey.” The locust is about the length of a finger and is good to eat. It has a lively flight but quickly falls. This shows that John’s teaching is good for those who obey it and complete it in their works, but that they must fear the more excellent teaching of Christ, which soon arrives.

Wild honey consists of the leaves of a tree of remarkable sweetness, and it shows the excessive sweetness of John’s teaching.

Mystically, however, John signifies Christ, who had assumed the garment of flesh from the Jews, who were weighed down by the certainty of a corrupted Law and by the burden of sins.

The leather belt signifies the mortality of the assumed flesh. In another sense, John’s garment of camel’s hair signifies the Church which Christ put on, converted from the Gentiles to his faith. Previously it stank through the worship of idols and the foulness of life.

The leather belt signifies the mortification of the members that are upon the earth. Locusts, which usually remain in coastal regions but are carried by the wind and scattered across the fields, devouring crops, signify believers in Christ. Snatched from unbelief by the wind of the Holy Spirit, they are cast into the field of the Scriptures; there, after consuming the grain of spiritual meanings and the sweetness of allegories, they leave to the Jews only the straw of carnal observance.

“Seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming,” and so forth. Pharisees is interpreted as “divided,” because they claimed for themselves, above all others, a special knowledge of the Law and observance of God’s commandments.

Sadducees is interpreted as “righteous.” They boasted that they were more righteous than the others. They refused to accept the prophecies, the ministries of angels, or the resurrection, accepting only the five books of the Law, as though they had been dictated by the Lord himself to Moses. A certain Sadoc is shown to have been the founder of this heresy; its followers derive their name from him.

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” The viper is a deadly animal. The male is accustomed to sow its seed through death, inserting its head into the female’s throat; when she bites it off, she receives the seed of deadly offspring. At the time of birth, the young burst forth after eating through their mother’s womb.

So the Pharisees and Sadducees, when they were generating sons of perdition through perverse doctrine, first destroyed themselves through the guilt of their own deception.

“Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance.” That is, strive to amend your life according to the measure of your fault. And do not wish to say, “We have Abraham as our father.” Do not glory in the patriarch’s carnal ancestry, because “those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God”; rather, those who strive to imitate him in faith and works are reckoned as belonging to the seed.

“But I say to you that God is able from these stones,” and so forth. He calls the Gentiles stones because they worshiped insensible creatures instead of the Creator and possessed in their hearts the hardness of stones, without devotion. From them God raised up Abraham’s spiritual seed through faith.

“Already the axe has been laid at the root of the trees.” That is, the sentence of the Judge. Just as iron, which cuts, is held by means of a handle, so the divinity appearing in judgment is laid not at the branches but at the root and cuts off the wicked person’s opportunity to sin any longer.

“Therefore every tree,” and so forth, “will be thrown into the fire.” That is, every will which now refuses the fruit of good action will then be cut down by the sentence of the just Judge in the fire of eternal damnation and will feel punishment.

“I baptize you in water,” and so forth, “he is mightier than I.” He says that he baptizes into repentance, since he did not have the power to forgive sins. Nevertheless, John’s baptism, received with faith, was beneficial because it prepared those who received it for Christ’s subsequent baptism.

“He who is to come after me is mightier than I.” He who is God and man is mightier in forgiving sins than I, who am merely a human being.

“Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” That is, I am not worthy to claim his heavenly birth, since I was born from male seed.

Another evangelist says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.” It was customary among the Hebrews that, if a man wished to take the wife of a deceased relative, he who yielded to another by right of kinship had to remove a sandal from one foot; and the house of the barefooted man was customarily called “the house of the barefooted one.”

But John, whom the Jews considered to be the Christ, claimed neither falsely for himself the name of bridegroom, which did not belong to him, nor the bride who was owed to another, lest he lose what was his.

In another interpretation, the tied strap signifies the unfathomable mystery of Christ’s birth, according to the prophetic saying: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). John confessed himself unworthy to loosen it.

“He will baptize you in the Spirit and fire.” That is, in the grace of the Holy Spirit and in the forgiveness of sins. Alternatively, by “fire” he means the tribulation of the flesh, because sins committed after baptism are forgiven through the breaking down of the flesh.

“His winnowing fork,” and so forth, “but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.” The hand signifies Christ’s power, in which is the winnowing fork—that is, the discernment of judgment—and he thoroughly cleanses the floor of the Church. “He will burn the chaff,” that is, he will send the frivolous and unstable into eternal damnation.

“Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.” This shows that the time of John’s baptism was in the Savior’s thirtieth year. Accordingly, that age seems appropriate for preaching or receiving the priesthood. At that age David received the kingship, and Ezekiel earned the gifts of prophecy.

Some ask why the Savior received John’s baptism, since he was entirely free from the contagion of sin. The answer is either that he first received in himself whatever he would give to the human race for salvation; or that he might prove John’s baptism to be from God; or that, by receiving the waters in himself, he might sanctify them for washing away the filth of our crimes.

“John tried to prevent him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?’” He was frightened that the one who had taken away the sin of the whole world by the grace of his Spirit had come to him. John himself needed to be cleansed by Christ from the contagion of original sin, since, being born from a woman, he was not free from the stain of fault, as it is written: “What is man, that he should be undefiled, and that one born of woman should appear clean?” (Job 25:4).

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Allow it for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness’; then he allowed him.” It was as though he had said: “First baptize me in water, as I have commanded; afterward you will be baptized in the Spirit, as you ask. For thus it is fitting that we set forth the example of fulfilling all righteousness, so that the faithful may learn that no one is perfectly righteous without baptism. They must not disdain to see my powerful ones baptized by the humble, when they remember that I, who forgive sins, submitted my head to a servant’s hands for baptism.”

“After he had been baptized, Jesus immediately came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.” These mysteries must therefore be celebrated by us. Just as he consecrated baptism for us through the immersion of his body, so he also showed us that after baptism the Holy Spirit is given to us and that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened. He also made clear that the flaming sword by which the guardian cherub first closed the way is extinguished in the second baptism.

The Holy Spirit fittingly appeared over Christ in the form of a dove, to show the simplicity of his nature and to demonstrate the innocence of our life after baptism. A dove is alien to the malice of gall; likewise, all bitterness, anger, indignation, and every form of malice must be removed from us.

The dove harms no one with its beak or claws. We too must see to it that we do not consume one another by biting one another, and that we restrain our hands from thefts.

It is said to sit upon the waters so that, foreseeing the hawk’s attack, it may avoid its shadow in the water. In the same way, it is fitting for us to sit beside the streams of the Scriptures. In their mirrors we may learn how to guard against the snares of the ancient enemy.

The dove is also said to nourish the young of others as though they were its own. Thus the Christian ought to seek not only what belongs to himself but also what belongs to others.

For this reason the Holy Spirit appeared over the Savior in the form of a dove: he did not come to punish sins through jealousy but to endure them for a time through gentleness. He appeared in fire over ordinary human beings so that spiritual fervor might kindle them to punish sins in themselves—sins which God, in his gentleness, would otherwise spare from vengeance.

“And behold, a voice from heaven saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’” It was as though it said: “In you I have established my good pleasure,” that is, the salvation of the human race, in which I am well pleased.

The mystery of the Holy Trinity is revealed in baptism: the Son of God is baptized in human form; the Spirit of God descends in the form of a dove; God the Father resounds in the voice. Thus it is shown that believers are to be baptized in the name of the Father, [Column 0018D] and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter Four

“Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil.” Christ enters the wilderness, the place of struggle, by the will of his own Spirit. This admonishes us that, after receiving the forgiveness of sins in baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we should gird ourselves against the snares of the ancient enemy. By abandoning the world in our minds, as though we were in the desert of manna, we should learn to hunger only for the joys of eternal life.

And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. We read that this forty-day fast had previously been observed by Moses and Elijah, and through it it is shown that the Gospel does not differ from the Law and the prophets; moreover, by this fast we are reminded that after baptism we ought to live soberly throughout the whole time of the present age, fasting from vices and from friendship with the world. Furthermore, the Lord’s fasting before his Passion signifies our labor in him, while his refreshment after his resurrection signifies consolation in us. Mystically, however, the Lord’s hunger signifies his desire for our salvation.

And the tempter came and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” He approached in an assumed appearance, by permission to tempt, though in the purpose of his malice he was far removed from him. For he did not disdain to be tempted who had come to be killed, and the pleasure of sin did not sting his mind. Therefore that entire diabolical temptation was not within, but without. He fittingly suggested making bread from stones, so that, being hard in mind, he might display hardness in his speech. “Command,” he said, not “make,” because he knew what had been written: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.”

But he answered: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone.’” Just as the body lives by earthly food, so the soul lives by the word of God that proceeds from his mouth, whenever he wishes to reveal to our weakness the counsel of his will through the Holy Scriptures. By answering the devil, when tempted, with words from the Scriptures, he gave us an example of humility, so that whenever we suffer something from wicked people, we may be stirred more toward instruction than toward vengeance.

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple. This taking did not arise from any weakness of the Savior, but from the pride of the enemy, because he mistook the Savior’s will for necessity. The holy city is Jerusalem, where the worship of the one God and the observance of the Law of Moses were practiced. The pinnacle, however, is the summit of the temple, which above was level, as was customary in Egypt and Palestine when building houses.

And he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” In all his temptations the devil is trying to discover whether he is the Son of God; but the Lord shapes his answer in such a way as to leave him uncertain. For here it is shown that the devil, who wants everyone to fall, can persuade but cannot hurl anyone down. And just as the Lord was willing to be placed upon the pinnacle but unwilling to be thrown down at his command, so it is fitting that, if someone urges us to ascend the way of truth, we should obey; but if he wishes to hurl us from the height of the virtues into the depths, we should not listen to him.

“For it is written that he will command his angels concerning him,” and so forth. This prophecy concerns a righteous man, but the devil interprets the Scriptures wrongly when he speaks to Christ of the help of angels as though Christ were weak, while he is silent about what the Scripture says concerning himself: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk” (Psalm 90:13).

Jesus said to him: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” It should be noted that he brought forth necessary testimonies only from Deuteronomy, in order to point to the mysteries of the second Law. He provided an example of this both here in words and afterward in deeds, when he avoided the Jews raging against him by fleeing and hiding, so that human weakness might learn not to dare to test God when it has the means to do what is necessary to escape what must be avoided.

Again the devil took him up onto an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Mystically, this mountain signifies the devil’s pride, by which he himself was deceived and through which he desires to deceive others; and he showed him all the kingdoms of the world. He could not therefore enlarge his vision or show him something unknown, but only the vanity of worldly pomp, which he himself loved as though it were beautiful, and which he therefore desired to make Christ love. Alternatively, “he showed him all the kingdoms of the world” means the people of this age: some deceived through fornication, others through avarice, and ruled by the devil in the world.

And he said to him: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.” The ancient enemy rose up against the first man through three temptations—namely, gluttony, vainglory, and avarice—and attempted to conquer the Second Man through the same vices: gluttony when he said, “Command that these stones become loaves of bread”; vainglory when he said, “Throw yourself down”; avarice when he said, “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.” But he was defeated by the Second Man in the very manner in which he boasted of having conquered the first.

Then Jesus said to him: “Go, Satan.” This is understood to mean “go into eternal damnation.” If, however, someone wishes to read according to another copy, “Go behind me, Satan,” he can understand it in this way: “Look back toward the earlier times in which the devil held the world guilty before him,” as though the Lord were saying: “Look back to when you deceived the first man and deluded his descendants through various forms of idolatrous worship, and let this be enough for you up to this point. Now you will not only be unable to overthrow me, but through me you will be cast out from the power you proudly claimed to possess.” Satan is interpreted as “adversary” or “transgressor,” and rightly he goes backward, because he is the enemy of truth and the transgressor of every form of righteousness.

For it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.” Perhaps someone asks why it is commanded here that one serve God alone, when the Apostle says, “Through charity serve one another” (Galatians 5:13). The answer is readily apparent: in the Greek language, service is customarily called by two terms with different meanings. *Dulia*—δουλεία—is service common to God or a human being, or to any created nature; *latria*—λατρεία—is the service owed exclusively to the worship of the Divinity and not to be shared with any creature. We are commanded to serve one another through charity, which is called *duleum* in Greek; we are commanded to serve the one God, which is *latreum* in Greek.

Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him. The devil tempts so that human weakness may be revealed; the angels minister so that the victor’s divinity may be confirmed. Let us therefore recognize our own condition in him, because unless the devil had perceived him to be human, he would not have tempted him. Let us venerate his divinity in him, because unless he were God above all things, angels would in no way minister to him.

[Col. 0021A]

When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. Mark says: “After John had been handed over” (to prison), Jesus came into Galilee. Luke, however, said nothing about John’s being handed over, but joined his narrative in this way: “When the temptation had ended, the devil departed from him until an appointed time,” and Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee. Yet according to the evangelist John this is shown not to have happened immediately, since he says that Jesus went into Galilee before John the Baptist had been sent into prison; and that afterward, following the wine made from water, he went down to Capernaum with his mother and disciples, and then went up to Jerusalem, and later baptized at Aenon. From this it is clear that the four evangelists did not narrate events contrary to John’s Gospel, but omitted his first arrival in Galilee after his baptism, when he made wine there from water.

And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali. Nazareth is a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor, and hence our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene. Capernaum, however, is a town beside Lake Gennesaret in Galilee of the Gentiles, in the territory of Zebulun. Mystically, the fact that Jesus begins to preach after John has been handed over signifies that, when the Law ceases, the Gospel consequently arises. Nazareth is interpreted as “his shoot” or “flower,” and signifies the flower of the figures that remained imperfect under the Law. Leaving these behind, Jesus Christ passes over to Capernaum, which is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” or “field of fatness,” or “village of consolation.” He thus teaches us to pass over to the fruit of spiritual teaching, which is found in the Gospel. For in the holy Church—which is a most beautiful village in the splendor of the virtues, a field of fatness in the abundance of good works and the fullness of charity, and a village of consolation in the comfort of the Holy Scriptures and hope for the future—the Savior preaches the Gospel daily through his teachers.

It is rightly called maritime because, situated beside the sea of the world, it is battered by the waves of persecutions; nevertheless, it does not cease to free those submerged in the waves of pleasures through the nets of the Gospel. It is situated in the territories of Zebulun, which means “dwelling of strength,” and of Naphtali, which means “expansion”; in the midst of the Gentiles it stands to extend the word of God courageously and offers the refuge of protection to believers.

So that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali,” and so forth, “a light has arisen for them.” There are two Galilees: one beyond the Jordan, in which Solomon gave Hiram, king of the Tyrians, twenty cities from the tribe of Naphtali; the other beside Lake Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun, around Tiberias. To distinguish it from the former, he says “Galilee of the Gentiles” beyond the Jordan, and so forth.

“The people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” The holy Church, taken away from its former errors, became a spiritual Galilee—that is, a migration or passing over. Previously it had lived according to pagan custom in the shadow of death, that is, in carnal luxury; when Christ came, it received the light of the Gospel.

From that time Jesus began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” By preaching the same things that John had previously proclaimed, he showed them that he was the Son of God, whose prophet John had been.

As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. This means that the Lord became incarnate in the sea of this world. He saw spiritual fishermen whom, before the foundation of the world, he had foreknown as suited to the work of preaching. Simon is interpreted as “obedient”; Peter, “recognizing”; Andrew, “manly.” This appropriately applies to the person of teachers, because only those are suited to the work of teaching who are illumined by the light of wisdom for understanding, obey God’s commands through good works, and courageously urge others to know and do these things.

And he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” According to the Evangelist John, Andrew is said to have followed the Lord near the Jordan at the testimony of John the Baptist, while Peter received his name and Philip was called. The other three evangelists say that they were called from fishing. This should be understood to mean that they did not immediately cling to him inseparably, but only came to recognize who he was; then, admiring him, they returned to their own affairs.

And immediately they left their nets and followed him. Perhaps someone says: “What did each fisherman leave, since he possessed almost nothing?” But we must consider that the one who rejects the desire to possess has left much.

And going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with their father Zebedee, repairing their nets, and he called them. It may be asked how he first called two and shortly afterward another two, as Matthew and Mark relate, when Luke says that the sons of Zebedee were Peter’s partners and were called by him to help draw out the nets after they had filled their little boats in the very catch of fish, and that the Lord said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5:10). Luke then says that they brought the boats to land and followed the Lord together. Therefore we should understand that what Luke indicates happened first. At that time they were not called by the Lord, but only the prediction was made to Peter that he would catch men; afterward what Matthew and Mark narrate took place: they were called two by two to follow the Lord.

But they immediately left their nets and their father and followed him. These four disciples signify two peoples, called by God’s grace from the love and anxieties of this age to spiritual devotion. Peter and James signify the faithful Jews, recognizing the Lord and overthrowing vices; Andrew and John signify the Gentiles, believing in Christ courageously and saved by God’s grace. The two boats signify the two Churches called from circumcision and uncircumcision; the nets, the preaching of the Gospel; the sea, the world; the fish, human beings submerged in worldly pleasures and devoted to carnal wisdom; the harbors, the end of the present life. Zebedee is interpreted as “flowing,” and signifies the instability of passing things.

Morally, however, each believer can bear four names within himself if he strives to display them in the four virtues. He is Simon Peter when, through prudence, he recognizes his sins and, having destroyed them through strong obedience to God’s commands, escapes the injury of punishments. He is Andrew when, through temperance, he courageously endures temptations. He is rightly called Jacob, that is, “supplanter,” when through fortitude he conquers vices by overthrowing them. And he may fittingly be called John, that is, “the grace of God,” when he fulfills the Creator’s commands through justice and nevertheless attributes nothing of this to himself, but everything to God.

And Jesus went around all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people. He did this to teach by his example that teachers ought to be diligent and tireless, and that they should minister the word of God without regard to persons. “In their synagogues” means that in the gatherings of many they should preach not empty tales, but what benefits their hearers. He healed every disease of the body and every infirmity of the soul, giving us an example so that we might be ready to offer consolation to our neighbors in spiritual and bodily matters alike.

And his reputation spread throughout all Syria. Syria is generally said to comprise the entire region from the Euphrates River to the Great Sea, and from Cappadocia and Armenia to Egypt. It contains three very large provinces: Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, in which the Jewish people dwell.

And they brought to him all who were sick with various diseases, and so forth, including the lunatics and the paralytics, and he healed them. Lunatics are those whose suffering increased during the moon’s rising—not because it truly arose from that, but through the deception of demons, so that the disgrace of the creature might rebound into blasphemy against the Creator. Paralytics are those deprived of bodily strength, for *paralysis* in Greek means “dissolution” in Latin.

Mystically, Galilee, which is interpreted as “rolling” or “wheel,” and Syria, which signifies “height,” signify this world. Although it raises itself up on high, it nevertheless inclines toward decline and rolls down into the depths. His fame has been spread throughout the whole world, as it says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Romans 10:18). At that time the demon-possessed were also healed—that is, the Gentiles, converted to the faith, abandoned their idols. Likewise, the lunatics and paralytics were healed: that is, the unstable and those wavering amid various errors were strengthened. Hence it follows:

And great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, and so forth. The Decapolis is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, toward the east, around Hippos. They are rightly said to have followed him in crowds, because once knowledge of his name reached the ends of the earth, a crowd of believers from every nation followed the path of his commandments.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0024A]

When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. Opening his mouth, he taught them, saying, and so forth. For Luke relates that he went up onto the mountain and spent the night there in prayer; and when day had come, he chose twelve of his disciples, whom he also called apostles. After descending from the mountain, he preached to the crowds while standing in a level place. This can be understood to mean that he was first in some higher part of the mountain with the twelve chosen disciples, and afterward descended with them—not from the mountain itself, but from its elevation—into a level place, as though onto the side of the mountain. There he stood until the crowds gathered around him; then he sat down, and when the disciples approached and the crowds were present, he delivered one sermon, which Matthew and Luke narrated.

Mystically, he went up onto the mountain because he wished to commend the greater commandments of righteousness. When he sat down, he had evidently appeared in the form of a servant. The disciples approached with devotion of mind and piety of faith, so that they might receive the eternal mountains’ righteousness of peace to offer to the people. The opening of his mouth indicates the length of the sermon or the manifestation of his teaching.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” That is, those who are humble through voluntary poverty. Isaiah enumerated these beatitudes in another order but with the same meaning. The Spirit of fear, according to Isaiah, corresponds to this one, because the kingdom is acquired through humility, whereas it seemed to have been forfeited through pride.

“Blessed are the meek.” That is, those who yield before the bitterness of wickedness. They will possess the earth—not one that produces the thorn of a curse, but one that nourishes the soul without defect. The Spirit of piety corresponds to them, because they conform themselves to the divine Scriptures through obedience.

“Blessed are those who mourn.” Clearly, not with the ordinary mourning of worldly sadness, but through repentance for sins inspired by God, or through fear of eternal damnation, or through love and desire for heavenly things, or through compassion for their neighbors, because they will be consoled with eternal joy. There are tears distinguished according to these four kinds: some are moist, for washing away sins and restoring lost baptism; some are salty and bitter, for restraining the lust of the flesh; some are hot, against the coldness of unbelief and for kindling the ardor of charity; some are pure, for restoring purity of life. The Spirit of knowledge belongs to these tears, and rightly so, because through the Holy Scriptures they have learned that they themselves are to be mourned.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” That is, those who desire with their whole mind to be filled with the nourishment of righteousness and thirst through their determination to persevere in it. They will be satisfied with a refreshment that does not grow weary. The spirit of fortitude corresponds to them—that is, the spirit that performs good works without laziness or failure.

“Blessed are the merciful.” The merciful are those who benefit themselves by doing good and devote care to correcting their neighbors, so that they may obtain eternal mercy from the merciful Judge. The spirit of counsel belongs to them, through which they do not cease to counsel themselves and others.

“Blessed are the pure in heart.” That is, those who seek God simply, harbor no bitterness, are entirely free from vanity, and contemplate God with sincere love. The spirit of understanding belongs to them, because the treasury of wisdom lies open to their gaze.

“Blessed are the peacemakers.” That is, those whose flesh does not lust against the spirit, and who, by making peace among others, desire even to have peace with those who hate peace. Thus they will rightly be called sons of God, in whom nothing contrary to God is found. The spirit of wisdom is referred to them, because everything obeys their reason, and reason itself is subjected to God. This is the eighth pronouncement, which says:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution.” This appears to pertain to the Lord’s resurrection, because when the seventh day—that is, the Sabbath—had passed, and the eighth day returned as the head of the days, the Head of the Church rose, having conquered the labor of persecution. For when the number seven is multiplied sevenfold, it produces forty-nine; when the eighth, together with the head of the days of the age, is added to that one, the result is fifty. Hence, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, we are brought into the kingdom of heaven, where we receive an inheritance, are consoled and nourished, obtain mercy, are cleansed, and are reconciled to peace, so that after the week of this age has passed, we may enter the future life by rising again. Thus it comes about that the day which was first in the passing life then becomes the first day of eternity.

“Blessed are you when people curse you,” and so forth, “uttering lies because of me.” Up to the eighth beatitude he had arranged the preceding pronouncements generally. From this point he began to speak to those present, addressing them directly. Yet these things do not pertain only to those who were present and hearing them, but also to those who were absent or would exist later, just as the preceding statements do. In those he did not say, “The kingdom of heaven is yours,” or “You will possess,” but they applied only to those to whom he was speaking in person. He addresses these words especially to those present because he wished to declare their dignity by predicting the sufferings they would endure for his name.

“Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is abundant in heaven.” One who pursues empty glory cannot fulfill this command, namely, to rejoice in the Lord when torn apart by the insults of disgrace. As it is written: “Do not seek glory, and you will not grieve when you have been without glory.” We ought to rejoice so that a reward may be prepared for us in the heavenly places.

“For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.” He rightly encouraged them by the example of the prophets, who did not withdraw from preaching the truth through fear of persecution.

“You are the salt of the earth.” In “earth,” human nature is signified; in “salt,” the wisdom of the word. For the nature of salt makes the earth barren. Thus we read that certain cities were sown with salt in the anger of their conquerors. This suits apostolic teaching: the salt of wisdom should restrain the luxury of the age in the earth of human flesh, or prevent the ugliness of vices from germinating.

“But if the salt has lost its taste, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled under people’s feet.” That is: If you, through whom the peoples are to be seasoned, lose the kingdom of heaven through fear of persecution or through error, then, placed outside the Church, you will doubtless endure the reproaches of your enemies.

“You are the light of the world.” That is: Since you have been illumined by the true light, you ought to be a light to those who are in the world. “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden,” that is, apostolic teaching founded upon Christ, or the Church constructed upon Christ from many nations through the unity of faith and joined together by the cement of charity. It becomes secure for those entering it and difficult to approach for those who labor against it; it guards its inhabitants and excludes all enemies.

“Nor do they light a lamp,” and so forth. Therefore whoever obscures and conceals the light of teaching beneath a measure is one who hides it beneath temporal advantages. Whoever places it upon a lampstand subjects himself so entirely to God’s service that the teaching of truth stands above bodily service.

Alternatively, the Savior lights the lamp when he fills the earthen vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity and places it upon the lampstand—that is, the Church—because he fixed the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads. This lamp could not be placed beneath a measure, that is, confined within the measure of the Law, nor did it shine in Judea alone, but throughout the whole world.

“Let your light shine before people,” and so forth. For it is beneficial for each person to please God through good works and not to rejoice in the false favor of human beings.

“Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.” He came to fulfill what had been imperfect: removing anger, excluding retaliation, and prohibiting the hidden desire of the mind.

“Amen, I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to be.” These things pass away when they are changed for the better. The iota, which is smaller than the other letters, and the stroke, which is its smallest portion, show that even the least commandments of the Law are brought to perfection, and that all the mysteries of the Law are full of spiritual meaning. Appropriately he used the Greek *iota*, not the Hebrew *yod*, because *iota* expresses the number ten and enumerates the Decalogue of the Law, whose stroke and perfection is the Gospel.

“Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth. The least thing is the death of the cross. Whoever teaches others according to what he has abolished, and not according to what he has found and read, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; or perhaps he will not be there, since only the great can exist there. It may also be understood morally: although Scripture itself cannot be abolished, whoever does not fulfill God’s commandment within himself abolishes it and becomes utterly despised in the Church of the saints.

“For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” and so forth. That is: Unless you fulfill not only those least commandments of the Law—which is the righteousness of the Pharisees, so that they do not kill—but also those that I add, which is the righteousness of those who are going to enter the kingdom of God, so that they do not become angry, you are not fit to enter the heavenly kingdom.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill,’” and so forth. In some copies the text is added in this form: “Whoever is angry without cause.” But this must be deleted, because “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.”

“But whoever says ‘Raca’ will be liable to the council.” *Raca* is a Hebrew word meaning “empty” or “hollow,” and it is interpreted as *kenos*—κενός—which we may call, in ordinary abuse, “brainless.” By what charge of folly, then, can one be branded who faithfully believes in God and knows Christ, the wisdom of God?

“But whoever says ‘Fool’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” It is the danger of a grave offense to insult the one whom God has called “salt,” and whose understanding is made penetrating like salt, or to provoke him with a curse of stupidity by an enfeebled understanding. Such a person will therefore be fuel for eternal fire.

There are consequently degrees in these sins, from the lighter to the more serious, until one reaches the fire of Gehenna. For in the judgment there is still an opportunity for defense, while the emotion conceived in the heart is still being restrained. But in the council, once the voice of indignation has burst forth, the question is no longer debated with the accused whether he should be condemned; rather, the judges deliberate what punishment should condemn the guilty person. Gehenna, however, is certain condemnation and the punishment of the condemned. Who can say in what ways these degrees are invisibly displayed according to the merits of souls? They think that the name Gehenna was derived from a valley consecrated to idols beside the wall of Jerusalem, once filled with the corpses of the dead; the Book of Kings also records that King Josiah defiled it.

“Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar,” and so forth. Literally, this can be done if a brother who has something against us is present—that is, someone whom we have injured. We have something against him if he has injured us; in that case there is no need to seek forgiveness from the person committing the injury, but only to forgive, just as you desire that the offenses committed to you by God be forgiven.

Spiritually, however, we are compelled to understand the altar in the temple of God as faith, and the temple as ourselves. Upon this altar a spiritual gift—whether prophecy, prayer, or anything else that can be acceptably offered to God—will not be accepted unless it is supported by the purity of faith. If it comes to mind that we have something against a brother, it is necessary to return to that brother before God with a loving thought and the swiftest affection of charity; then, withdrawing our attention from that matter, we should complete the offering we have begun.

“Be in agreement with your adversary,” and so forth, “until you pay the last quadrans.” Understand Christ as the judge, the angel as the minister, and the prison as the punishments of darkness. In another passage the *quadrans* is two small coins—not because the Gospels disagree, but because one quadrans consists of two small coins. A portion of the members distinguished within this world is found to be earthly; therefore he says “the last quadrans,” that is, earthly sins. “Until you pay” is used for an indefinite duration, as elsewhere: “Until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Psalm 109).

As for the adversary with whom we are commanded to agree, some have understood him to be the devil, others the flesh, others God, and others the commandment of God—not meaning that we ought to obey the persuasions of the devil or the flesh, which we renounce in baptism, but that we are commanded to oppose them, lest by obeying we heap upon them the vengeance due for their deception.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery,’” and so forth, “he has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Among the ancients there is this difference between *passion* and *propasion*: whoever sees a woman and has his soul titillated by her has been struck by *propasion*—a preliminary movement of passion. But whoever gives consent to the pleasure passes from *propasion* to passion. Thus sin is reached through three stages: suggestion, pleasure, and consent.

This sin likewise has three forms: in the heart, in the deed, and in habit, like three deaths. One occurs within the house, when the heart consents to lust; another, as though already carried outside the gate, when consent proceeds into action; the third occurs when, through the force of a wicked habit, the mind is pressed down as though beneath an earthly weight.

“But if your right eye causes you to stumble,” and so forth, “than for your whole body to go into Gehenna.” The right eye can appropriately be understood as a beloved friend and counselor in divine matters. One must not spare him or refuse to cast him away if, by causing us to stumble, he wishes to lead us into heresy.

“And if your right hand causes you to stumble,” and so forth. By the right hand is understood a beloved helper and minister in divine works; by the left are understood the things necessary for the body. For just as contemplation is signified by the eye, action is signified by the hand. We can also understand by the right eye and right hand any relatives who are likewise to be cut off if they are a cause of stumbling.

“It was also said: ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of dismissal.’” In the later passage the Savior himself explains that Moses did this because of their hardness of heart—not in order to permit separation, but to remove murder.

“But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” Here fornication is not understood only as sexual intercourse committed with other men or women, but also as every desire, avarice, or idolatry that causes a person to stray from the Law of God. If, therefore, a wife compels a man to do something of this kind, the man who dismisses such a wife dismisses her for the cause of fornication—not only hers, but also his own, lest he commit fornication.

“Again you have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely,’” and so forth, “you cannot make a single hair white or black.” The Jews were permitted to swear by God—not because they were acting rightly, but because it is better to render this honor to God than to demons or other creatures. For one who swears either venerates or loves the one by whom he swears; and whoever does not swear cannot commit perjury. Therefore let us use an oath rarely and only from necessity, when we see people slow to believe, as the Apostle says: “What I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Galatians 1).

The throne signifies the judgment of God, who is said to sit in heaven—not because he has limbs arranged as ours are, but because, within the whole body of the world, heaven possesses the greatest beauty and earth the least. As though the divine power were more present to the eminent beauty, while it orders the least thing in the lowest places, he is said to sit in heaven and to tread upon the earth. Spiritually, however, “heaven” signifies holy souls and “earth” sinful ones. The spiritual one who judges all things and is judged by no one is appropriately called the throne of God. The sinner to whom it is said, “You are earth, and into earth you will go,” is ordered into the lowest places by the justice that assigns to each one according to his merits.

“Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil.” It is as though he said: Let what is be enough to say “yes,” and what is not be enough to say “no.” Or the words “yes, yes” and “no, no” are repeated so that what you affirm with your mouth you may prove by your works, and what you deny in words you may not confirm by your deeds. He did not say, “Whatever is more is evil,” but “is from evil”—namely, from the weakness of the person who compels you to swear. This weakness is evil; but you do well when you make proper use of an oath in order to persuade another of what you are usefully urging.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, do not resist evil.” In the Law, guilt is corrected; in the Gospel, the beginnings of sins are removed. In the Law four degrees of vengeance appear. The first is that the injured person should not avenge himself more severely. The second is the one established by the Law: “An eye for an eye,” so that vengeance does not exceed the injury. This is the beginning of peace; two degrees still remain for attaining it: that one should repay not as much, but less—for example, one blow for two—and then reach the third degree by returning no evil, indeed good for evil. Yet even there the command “Do not resist evil” has not been reached. That means not only that you should not repay the evil inflicted, but also that you should not resist when another evil is inflicted. He explains this further by saying:

“But if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.” For he does not say, “Do not strike,” but rather, “Prepare yourself to be struck again.” The physician of souls teaches that those whose salvation they wish to promote should endure their weaknesses with an even temper.

Mystically, we are commanded to offer the right cheek to the one who strikes, not the left, which the righteous person does not possess. That is: if a heretic strikes us in debate and wounds the right doctrine, let right things be set against him until the enemy, overcome, grows weary.

And to the one who wishes to bring a lawsuit against you and take your tunic [Col. 0030A], let him have your cloak as well. Luke placed this passage in reverse order, saying: “From the one who takes away your garment, do not withhold your tunic also.” What is said about the garment and tunic is to be done with regard to everything that we claim, by some temporal right, to be ours. The tunic, which is the inner garment, signifies necessities; and if it is fitting to disregard these, how much more the superfluous things signified morally by the cloak, which is the outer garment. Spiritually, every teacher takes away someone’s tunic when he demands that he confess the sins hidden in his soul, such as envy, pride, and similar things. He himself leaves the cloak behind when he is not ashamed to confess at the same time the outward crimes committed by his body.

[Col. 0030B] And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him another two. By this testimony he plainly commands an attitude of compassion and urges the provision of assistance to one who asks it of you—indeed, he indicates that you ought to wish to go beyond your strength. In another sense, if someone wishing to believe asks you what God is, hasten to show him not only the Father, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you. We understand this as having been said not only about almsgiving—since even the rich become poor if they are always giving—but also as an instruction to teachers to give freely what they have received freely, because money of this kind never runs out. Thus you will give to everyone who asks, although you will not always give what he asks for, since, by indicating righteousness, you do not send him away empty-handed, even though he may not ask for [Col. 0030C] what you will give. Moreover, the spiritual teacher ought to adapt the word of God to his hearers, so that he may receive from them the repayment of a good work.

You have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy”; but I say to you: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,” and so forth. We must therefore understand that Christ commands the love of enemies not as something impossible, as some think, but as something perfect—such as David showed toward Saul, and the martyr Stephen when he prayed for his persecutors. Here, then, a difficult question arises for those who understand less well: in the prophets there are found imprecations against enemies, which are thought to be curses, as in: “Let their table become …” (Ps. LXVIII), and so forth. But the prophet said this not as one wishing it by his own desire, [Col. 0030D] but as one foreseeing it by the Spirit. And the Lord said: “Woe to you, Capernaum” (Matt. XI). He did not wish this out of malice, but saw that it would happen to it on account of the merit of its unbelief. Again, another question arises because the Lord commands us to pray for our enemies, while John says not to pray for those who sin unto death. This is because among the brethren there are certain sins more grievous than the persecution of enemies. I think that sin unto death is to attack the brotherhood after the knowledge of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and to be driven by the fires of envy against that very grace; whereas sin not unto death occurs when someone, through some weakness of spirit, has failed to render the duties owed to the brotherhood.

So that you may be sons of your Father … “who makes his sun rise on the just [Col. 0031A] and the unjust.” He does not say: “Do these things, you who are sons of God,” but: “So that you may be sons of God.” There is one who is naturally the Son of God; but we, having received the power, insofar as we fulfill what he commands, become sons of God. He calls the sun’s rising upon the good and the evil Christ, the sun of righteousness, and the rain the teaching of truth, because Christ appeared to good and evil alike, and Christ has been proclaimed in the Gospel.

For if you love those who love you … “Do not even the tax collectors do this?”

Among them, the *publicani*—tax collectors—are called the Roman officials who pursue the revenues or public profits of the world; for ἔθνος means “nation” or “people” in Greek, and in Latin it is *gens*. Therefore the Gentiles are called *ethnici*, because they are such as they were born to be. The sense of this statement is therefore as follows: If the Gentiles and tax collectors, guided by nature, are beneficent toward those who love them, how much more ought you, being broader in love, to embrace even those who do not love you? For those whose rank of profession is more distinguished must necessarily have a more abundant concern for virtue.

Be perfect, then, as your heavenly Father is perfect. Without the love of enemies, who can fulfill what was said above? The perfection of mercy—which provides the greatest assistance to the suffering soul—cannot extend beyond the love of an enemy; and therefore the passage concludes: “Be perfect,” and so forth. This must nevertheless be understood in such a way that God is perfect as God, and the soul is perfect as a soul. Someone therefore ascends a certain degree when he loves his neighbor, but he will perfect his benevolence when he brings it, by the commandment, to the love of an enemy. For what is written in the Law—“You shall hate your enemy”—is not to be understood as the voice of one commanding the righteous, but of one permitting the weak.

## CHAPTER VI

Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, so that you may be seen by them.

It is as though he said: Beware of seeking praise from people, and thereby depriving yourselves of the reward’s fruit. Hence what follows:

Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven. For whoever pursues the empty favor of the crowd will have this counted as his reward; and for this reason he is driven away from the wedding of the eternal King when he knocks at the doors, because he is not shown to have loved him here.

Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet, and so forth. It is clear that hypocrites are those who pretend to be righteous but do not display righteousness; and consequently they receive from God, who examines the heart, nothing other than the punishment of deceit.

But when you give alms … “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

The pleasure of human praise seems to be signified by the left hand, and the intention of fulfilling the divine commandments by the right. And what is almsgiving in secret except a good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes and which is produced by a good will, even when there is no money to give? For in such matters the left hand usually acts when a person performs them not inwardly but outwardly.

[Col. 0032A] And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites … “They have received their reward.” The corners of the streets are places where one road runs across another and forms a crossroads. It is not wrong for you to be seen praying somewhere by people, but it is wrong to do this so that you may appear worthy of praise from people.

But when you pray, enter your room … “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

That is: Return from visible things to the pure conscience of your heart in order to pray to the invisible Lord, and close the door against carnal thoughts and fantasies. Resist the crowds that make noise in your thoughts, so that a spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father from the innermost heart.

When you pray, do not use many words … “Do not therefore be like them.” The Gentiles, then, think that God, like a human judge, is drawn by words into giving a verdict; and therefore they suppose that they will be heard because of their many words.

For your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Here a certain heresy of the philosophers arises, who say: “If God knows what we need before we ask, we speak to one who already knows in vain.” To them it must be answered that we are not narrators but petitioners. It is one thing to narrate, and another to implore one who knows, with humble entreaty.

Our Father, who are in heaven. That is, in the holy and righteous, to whom it is said: “You are God’s holy temple.”

Hallowed be your name. How do we ask that the Lord’s name be hallowed by human beings, when it is always holy? We ask that the Lord’s holy name be shown in this world, so that we who have been sanctified in baptism may persevere in it. And this is a daily task: we must implore sanctification, since we sin every day.

Your kingdom come. For when does God not reign, or when does that which always was and never ceases to be begin with him? We ask God for the kingdom promised to us and acquired through Christ’s passion, so that we who previously served in the world may afterward reign with Christ as ruler: “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth. That is: As your will is done among the angels who are in heaven, so let it be done among human beings who are on earth, so that, with no misery obstructing it, they may acquire the same blessedness with you.
