In another sense: As the righteous do your will, so may sinners also be converted to you. Or we understand heaven and earth as body and soul.

Your will be done. In this sense: Just as, in our heart, we delight together with the law of God according to the inner person, so may the body, unchanged by any earthly pleasures, not oppose this delight.

Give us this day our daily bread. “Daily bread” has either been said of all the necessities of this life, or of the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily. And lest some raise the question—those who do not receive Christ’s sacrament daily—we must understand daily bread [Col. 0033A] as the divine commandments, which we ought daily to meditate upon and practice.

And forgive us … and so forth. We are healthfully reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for our sins. The one who taught us to pray concerning our debts and sins promised paternal mercy and added that forgiveness would follow, binding us by a firm pledge not to ask forgiveness from God, to whom we are debtors, in any other way than as we forgive our debtors. If we lie in this agreement, there is no fruit from the whole prayer.

And do not lead us into temptation. For God does not himself lead us into it, but permits the one whom he has abandoned without his help to be led into it. Therefore the prayer is not that we should not be tempted, but that we should not be brought into temptation. [Col. 0033B] For it is one thing to be led into temptation and another to be tempted. No one can be approved without temptation. Therefore the one who must be tested by fire does not pray that he may not be touched by fire, but that he may not be consumed.

But deliver us from evil. That is, so that we may stand secure and safe from everything that the devil and the world do. But that no temptation whatsoever should be feared cannot be hoped for here in the present, because this blessedness begins here and will be perfected in the future. “Amen,” which is written at the end, is the seal of the Lord’s Prayer, which Aquila translated faithfully. We too may truly say that it signifies the purest truth of this entire prayer, and that everything which they rightly ask is undoubtedly granted to them by the Lord, if they do not neglect to keep the covenant of the final condition.

For if you forgive people their sins … “Neither will your Father forgive you your sins.”

He says, “If you do not forgive people,” as though those who forgive were not human beings—that is, not human or earthly. Hence it is written: “I said: You are gods,” and so forth. “But you shall die like human beings.” This is said to those who, because of their sins, have deserved to be human beings rather than gods.

When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.

By these words we are taught to direct our intention toward inward joys, lest, by seeking our reward outwardly, we conform ourselves to this world. What he calls “disfigure” is not a customary expression in Scripture. Exiles are also called *exterminati*, because they are sent outside their boundaries. Therefore we usually understand this expression to mean “demolish,” which is what hypocrites are accustomed to do: they feign sadness and mourning in their countenance while their resolute spirit rejoices. From this passage it is understood that ostentation can be found not only in the splendor of the world but also in mournful squalor.

But when you fast, anoint your head with oil and wash your face … “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.”

The Palestinians, whose custom he is describing, are accustomed to anoint their heads with oil on feast days. He therefore commands us, while practicing virtues, to show ourselves festive not with the oil of the sinner but with the oil of gladness, and to anoint the ruling part of our heart with spiritual oil.

Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth … “Where thieves do not break through and steal.”

Through three forms of adversity—rust, moth, and thieves—he forbids and censures every kind of avarice. Some things are darkened or consumed by rust, such as gold, silver, and other metals. Others are destroyed by worms or decay, such as clothing and wooden vessels, which perish through rot. Others are carried away by thieves, such as gems and precious stones, although they cannot be consumed by any other defilement. Thus no thing can remain forever unharmed. Hence it is said: “Every excellent work will be justified, and whoever does it will be honored in it; but every corruptible work will fail at the end, and whoever does it will perish with it.” Allegorically, rust signifies pride. Wherever it is present, it disperses the treasure of spiritual gifts and obscures the beauty of virtues. The moth signifies envy, which, gnawing secretly at good endeavor, does not cease to destroy the bond of unity. Thieves are demons and heretics, always intent on plundering those who possess spiritual treasures and stripping those laden with the adornments of virtues. In another sense, every thing becomes dirty when it is mixed with an inferior nature. Thus our mind becomes dirty through desire for earthly things, although earth is pure in its own order; but in the desire for spiritual things it remains pure, because whatever things are heavenly are pure.

Where your treasure is, there also is your heart.

[Col. 0034C] This must be understood not only of money but also of every passion: the games of the licentious, the lust of the lover, and the belly of the glutton are each a god. Each person serves the thing by which he is conquered.

The lamp of your body is your eye … “Your whole body will be full of darkness.”

The eye is the intention of the mind. If this goes before in a perverse direction, every work that follows is evil, even if it appears to be upright. For by the body are signified the works that appear to everyone; and if someone performs them with a right intention, even if they seem to human beings to possess some imperfection, all things work together for good.

Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be? If the intention of your heart is blinded in you by desire for temporal things, how much more has the deed itself become dark? And it will profit nothing, because what is imputed to you is how you performed it, not how it turned out for the one who received it.

No one can serve two masters … “And he will despise the other.” Clearly, the one who loves God hates the devil. For no knowledge can endure hating God; therefore the one who does not fear him despises him by failing to keep his commandments.

You cannot serve God and Mammon. Let the avaricious person hear this, and let him strive to use the riches called *mammon* in the Syriac language more as a master who distributes them than as a servant who guards them.

[Col. 0035A] Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, and so forth.

When he says “Therefore I tell you,” he refers back to what precedes: do not be convicted of storing up treasures, through anxiety about temporal things, with the rich of this world. We should understand that we ought not to be anxious about bodily food and clothing, but that we ought always to be anxious about spiritual food and clothing.

Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? In this statement he urges us to remember that God, who made and formed us, has given us much more than any food or covering. At this point it is customary to ask whether this bodily food pertains to the soul, since the soul itself is incorporeal, or not. But let us recognize that here “soul” refers to this present life, whose support is this bodily nourishment.

Look at the birds of the air … “Your Father feeds them.” That is: If birds, whose soul is mortal, are nourished by God’s providence, how much more human beings, to whom eternity is promised.

Are you not worth more than they? That is, are you not more valuable than irrational creatures, such as birds?

And which of you, by being anxious, can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing?

It is as though he said: Leave to them, then, the care of covering the body, whose care you see was responsible for your having a body of such stature.

Consider the lilies of the field, and so forth. These examples of birds and lilies are not presented allegorically, but so that greater things might be persuaded from lesser ones.

But I tell you that not even Solomon … Truly, what silk or purple of kings can be compared with flowers? What is as red as the rose, or as white as the lily? This is more a judgment of the eyes than of words.

And if the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, God so clothes … “Tomorrow” is used for a future time. The meaning is: If the craftsman of all things adorns with such beauty things that quickly fall and are consumed by fire, how much more will he provide for you what is necessary, since you belong to an eternal inheritance?

[Col. 0035D] Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or What shall we drink? or With what shall we be clothed?

It should be noted that he does not say: “Do not seek food,” and so forth. Rather, he says: “What you shall eat,” and so forth. Here I think he reproves those who, having rejected the common way of life, seek more luxurious or more austere foods or clothing for themselves than those with whom they live.

The Gentiles seek all these things. That is, they are concerned not with the future; they have become like foolish beasts of burden and have been made like them.

For your Father knows … “And all these things will be added to you.” Seek the kingdom of God, which is the good thing to be desired, and the necessities without which this life cannot be carried on. He did not say that these things would be given to us, but that they would be added, because eternity ought to be our intention, while temporality is to be used [Col. 0036A] in practice: the former as a good, the latter as a necessity.

Do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Since the earth produces annual fruits, he granted that we should be concerned about the present, while forbidding us to think about the future, which “tomorrow” signifies.

Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. Let the concern of the present time therefore be sufficient for us, and let us leave the care of the future, which is uncertain. I think that he called this care “trouble” for the following reason: it is punitive and belongs to the mortality that we deserved through sinning. One must beware of judging someone who provides the necessities entrusted to him so that they do not fail, since the Lord himself graciously consented to have a money box.

## CHAPTER VII

Do not judge, so that you may not be judged … “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

Here, I think, the command is that we interpret in the better sense those actions about which it is uncertain with what intention they were done, because it is uncertain with what intention something was done or what sort of person the one who now appears good or evil will eventually become. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time” (1 Cor. IV). Concerning manifest acts, which cannot be done with a good intention, it is said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII). But what he says—“For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged”—may cause difficulty. Will God judge us rashly in the same way that we judge others? Or, “With whatever measure, it will be measured back”: this cannot in any way be so with God. Rather, it is said to show how the very rashness by which you punish another must punish you [Col. 0036C]. Hence it is said: “Everyone who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI)—not by the sword of iron, but by the sword of sin.

Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye … “but do not see the beam in your own eye”?

Many people, forestalled by pride and hatred, sharply correct those whom they see disturbed by sudden anger, as though a splinter had invaded the eye of their mind and changed it from its customary state of purity. From this they are more eager to blame them than to amend them. Therefore it is said to be impossible for them to remove the splinter from their brother’s eye when they carry a beam in their own. How can it happen that, if you are angry with a person, you want him to be corrected? But if you hate him, you cannot want him to be corrected. As great as the difference between a beam and a splinter is, so great is the difference between hatred and anger.

Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see to remove … and so forth.

First drive hatred away from yourself; afterward you will be able to correct the one whom you love.

Do not give what is holy to dogs … “and, turning, they may tear you apart.” We understand dogs and pigs as contemptuous people. It is therefore not fitting to spread the evangelical pearl before such pigs who remain in the mud of unbelief, or before heretics, or before people who return to the vomit of their sins. Otherwise they may trample it—that is, despise it—and, turning, begin to tear you apart.

Ask, and it will be given to you, and so forth. Asking pertains to obtaining health and strength of soul, so that we may be able to fulfill what is commanded. Seeking pertains to finding the truth. When someone has found the true way, he will arrive at the possession itself, which nevertheless will be opened to the one who knocks.

For everyone who asks receives … and so forth. Perseverance is therefore necessary, so that we may receive what we ask for, find what we seek, and have what we knock for opened to us.

Or which of you is there who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?

Bread is understood as love, without which all other things are nothing, just as without bread a table appears poor. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compares to a stone.

Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Fish signifies faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism, or because it is caught from invisible things, or because [Col. 0037B] it is not broken by the waves of this world. He set the serpent against it because of the poisons of deceit that it sowed in the first human being. In the Gospel according to Luke, the comparison of the egg and the scorpion follows these two. The egg indicates hope, since the embryo in it is not yet perfected but is hoped for through incubation; or it indicates that the opposite of hope is looking backward, whereas hope stretches itself toward the things that lie ahead. Therefore he set the scorpion against it, whose poisonous sting must be feared from behind, because deadly despair is to be dreaded at the end.

Therefore, if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children … “to those who ask him.”

He calls lovers of this world evil. In the order of nature, the things they give are good, although they are temporal, because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII). In another sense, the Apostles, who had surpassed the goodness of the human race by the merit of their election, are nevertheless called evil in view of the supreme goodness, because nothing is immutable or good in itself except the Godhead alone. But when Luke says, “He will give the good Spirit,” he shows that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s good gifts.

Enter through the narrow gate … “and there are few who find it.”

The broad way is the one that leads to the pleasures of the world. No searching or finding is needed for it, because it offers itself spontaneously. Everyone finds the narrow way, but those who find it do not immediately enter by it, since many, captured by the pleasures of the world, turn back from the middle of the journey of truth [Col. 0037D].

Beware of false prophets … “but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.”

This is said especially about heretics, who appear to surround themselves with restraint, chastity, and fasting, as though with a certain garment of piety, but because of the intention of their poisoned mind and their predatory snares they are compared to wolves.

In another sense, examine more cautiously those who attempt to deceive you under the Christian name, bringing scandal through sweet words. But he shows how such people are to be recognized:

You will know them by their fruits. That is: Do not pay attention to their appearance, but to their works. For, if not in words, they blaspheme in their conduct.

Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? [Col. 0038A] No wise person will be able to find from heretics or unbelievers the ardor of holiness or the sweetness of truth. In another sense, I think that thorns and thistles can signify the cares of the world and the pricks of vices, as in: “Your land will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). Figs and grapes, however, signify the sweetness of a new way of life, which the Lord hungers for in us, and the fervor of love, which gladdens the human heart.

Thus every good tree bears good fruits, but the bad tree bears bad fruits, and so forth.

By the tree we understand either a good or a bad will. By fruits, however, we understand works. The works of a good will cannot be evil, nor can the works of an evil will be good; yet the will becomes good when it is converted to the highest and immutable good and filled with good, so that it produces good fruit. Hence he is called the author of all good things—that is, of both a good nature and a good will.

Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. For everyone who is not found to have produced the fruit of good works here will be thrown into the fire of Gehenna by the forceful sentence of judgment.

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, and so forth.

Both things are necessary for the servants of God: the deed must be confirmed by speech, and speech by deeds.

Many will say to me on that day: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons?” and so forth.

[Col. 0038C] It is not the merit of the one who does such things, but the invocation of Christ’s name, that accomplishes this—whether for the condemnation of those who invoke it or for the benefit of those who hear and see.

And then I will confess to them: “I never knew you,” and so forth. He significantly said “I will confess,” because they had been pretending to say such things long before. “I never knew you” means: “I do not approve of you,” because God in no way approves one whom the piety of faith does not commend.

Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. If the rock is Christ, as many testimonies of Scripture proclaim, then the one who does what he hears from Christ has built upon Christ.

[Col. 0038D] And the rain descended, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and so forth.

The rain, because it attempts to overthrow the house, is also the devil; the rivers are the Antichrist; the winds are spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. But whoever not only hears the words of God but firmly does them fears none of these things, because he has built his house upon a rock.

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like the one who built his house upon sand.

Our Lord Jesus Christ is the stable and firm foundation upon which the catholic Church is founded. But upon sand, which is fluid and cannot be brought into a single bond, every statement of the heretics is built for the purpose of collapsing.

And the rain descended … “and it fell.” What else did he wish to be understood by the rain except the devil’s manifold temptations, by the rivers manifest persecutions, and by the winds the evil spirits? No one can withstand these unless he remains steadfast with his hope fixed upon God. The danger of the final judgment may also be understood through the force of the river, when, after both houses have been completed, “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII).

And its fall was great. For it has no support from one who raises it up; instead they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

[Col. 0040A] And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds were amazed, and so forth.

By “crowds” he means unbelievers, who were astonished without believing; or he indicates everyone generally who revered such great wisdom in him. The scribes taught what had been written in Moses and the prophets; but Jesus, as Lord of Moses himself, in the freedom of his will either added what seemed to be lacking in the Law or preached it in a changed form to the people, as we read above.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0039]

## CHAPTER VIII

When he had come down from the mountain … “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.”

This miracle may be understood as having taken place after both of the Lord’s discourses—not only the one Matthew includes, but also the one Luke inserts—although Luke and Mark recorded it in another place. Mystically, the Lord’s descent from the mountain signifies his incarnation. After this, great crowds followed him, because, after the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I), the one previously known only in Judea became renowned throughout the whole world.

“If you will,” he said, “you can cleanse me.” He did not doubt the Lord’s will as an unbeliever would, but, conscious of his own defilement, he did not presume upon it.

[Col. 0039C] And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: “I will; be cleansed.” He stretched out the hand of healing, extending the affection of his mercy. He touched the sick man because he possessed the effect of health in his power. He said, “I will; be cleansed.” In “I will” he displayed the gentleness of his compassion; in “be cleansed,” the power of his majesty, because “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII). It should not be joined and read, as some think, “I will cleanse,” but separately, so that he first says “I will” and then commands “be cleansed.” He says “I will” because of Photinus, commands because of Arius, and touches because of Mani.

And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one.” And indeed, what need was there to proclaim verbally what he displayed in the body, unless to teach us not only to refrain from seeking monetary reward but also from seeking credit—

[Col. 0039D] But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.

He sent him to the priests for three reasons: first, because the Law commanded that those cleansed of leprosy offer gifts to the priests; then, so that they might see the leper cleansed and be saved by believing, or, if they did not believe, be without excuse; and so that he would not appear to violate the Law. If anyone is troubled by how the Lord seems to approve the Mosaic sacrifice, although the Church has not accepted it, let him remember that the sacred sacrifice of his body had not yet been offered on the altar of the cross, nor had it been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles and the faith of believers. Mystically, this man signifies the human race weakened by sins [Col. 0040B]. It was cleansed from the variety of its ancient error by the Savior’s outstretched hand—that is, by the Word of God becoming incarnate and touching human nature—and it was shown to the priest of whom it is said: “You are a priest forever” (Ps. CLIX). To him they offer their bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice to God (Rom. XII).

When he had entered Capernaum … “and he is grievously tormented.” The question is how Matthew’s statement that the centurion himself approached the Lord agrees with Luke’s account that he sent messengers to him. But it becomes clear to those who inquire reverently that Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that the man himself approached, since his will was conveyed to the Lord even though others acted as bearers. Just as the woman with the hemorrhage, because she believed, touched the Lord more truly than did the crowds pressing around her, so the more the centurion believed, the more truly he approached.

Lord, my boy is lying here. He is pitiable not only in one respect, because he is lying there, but also in a second, because he is paralyzed, and in a third, because he is grievously tormented. He said this to demonstrate the distress of his soul and to invite the Lord’s goodwill. Thus it is fitting for those in authority to have compassion on their subjects.

And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.” Great is the sublimity of the Lord, but greater still his humility: although he was able to heal by a word alone, he did not disdain to visit a suffering servant.

And the centurion answered and said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Because of his conscience regarding his life, the Gentile did not dare to have Christ as his guest, although he possessed faith; nevertheless, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments.

But say only a word, and my boy will be healed. Great was the centurion’s faith, by which he confessed that the work could be accomplished in Christ through a word.

For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me. He calls himself a man subject to authority, yet says that he can command those beneath him, so that the following may be understood: How much more can almighty God, who is above all, say through the angelic host to sickness that it should depart, and it departs; and to health that it should come, and it comes. Hence it follows:

And I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; [Col. 0041A] and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it. He wishes to show that God can accomplish whatever he wills not only by the arrival of his body but also through the ministries of angels.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. He marvels at the understanding of his own majesty, signifying that we too should marvel at it. When such emotions are attributed to God, they are not signs of a disturbed mind but of a teacher instructing.

And to those who followed him he said: “I have not found such faith in Israel.” He is not speaking of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times, but of all the people of the present age, who, although instructed by the Law, did not believe. The centurion, without being instructed by Christ, believed, signifying the spontaneous faith of the Gentiles.

I tell you that many will come from the East, and so forth. That is, from all the nations, just as the Gospel ought to be preached; or from the East, those who, immediately enlightened, pass onward, and from the West, those who endured sufferings for the faith unto death. They will recline, not lying down bodily, but resting spiritually.

The sons of the kingdom will be cast out, and there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. By “the sons of the kingdom” he means the Jews, among whom God formerly reigned. The gnashing of teeth and weeping of the eyes demonstrate the true resurrection of the members of the body. He also speaks of “the inner darkness,” meaning blindness of heart, and of “the outer darkness,” meaning the night of eternal damnation, where a twofold Gehenna is shown: that of excessive cold, through the gnashing of teeth, and that of intolerable heat, through the weeping of the eyes, as blessed Job says: “They pass from snow waters to excessive heat” (Job 24).

And Jesus said to the centurion, … and the boy was healed from that hour [Col. 0041C]. Faith in the Lord is proved, and the servant’s health is strengthened. Mystically, the centurion represents the elect from the nations, who, as though surrounded by a hundred soldiers, are exalted by the perfection of spiritual virtues.

And when Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever, … and she rose and ministered to them. Peter’s house is the circumcision, which had been entrusted to his apostleship; his mother-in-law, however, is the Synagogue, because in a certain sense she is the mother of the Church, which is commended in this way to Peter by the true Bridegroom: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). Peter’s mother-in-law was feverish in the Synagogue because, persecuting the Church, she was consumed by the fires of envy. Hence it is said: “The sons of my mother have fought against me” [Col. 0041D] (Song of Songs 1). The Lord touched her hand because he converted her carnal works to spiritual use; she rose and ministered to them because, now believing in the Lord, she ministers daily through spiritual service.

Morally, every soul that serves the desires of the flesh burns as though with a fever. But when it recovers through the touch of divine mercy, it restrains the flesh’s wantonness with the reins of continence and makes those very members by which it had served impurity unto iniquity serve righteousness unto eternal life.

When evening came, they brought him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were ill. All are not healed in the morning or at midday, but toward evening, when the true Sun had set—the one who said, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” [Col. 0042A] (John 9). At his setting more sick people are healed than before, because while living in the flesh he taught only a few Jews; afterward, once the nations had been set free throughout the world, he bestowed gifts upon them.

When Jesus saw the great crowds around him, he ordered his disciples to go to the other side of the lake. Jesus’ exhortation is always that we cross the bitter waves of the world in an untroubled vessel of faith, until, with him as our helmsman, we reach the shore of paradise.

And a certain scribe approached and said to him: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” The fact that Matthew says this occurred when he ordered them to depart, whereas Luke says, “As they were traveling along the road” (Luke 9), is not contradictory, since they were indeed traveling in order to come to the lake. If this scribe had said, “Lord, I will follow you,” he would not have been rejected. But since he regarded him as merely one teacher among many, and was learned in letters but not a spiritual hearer, he therefore has no place where Jesus may recline his head.

Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head,” and so forth. It was as though he had said: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of the world’s riches, when I am so poor that I do not even use a roof of my own?” In accordance with allegory, we may understand the foxes as signifying heretics, who trust not at all in Christ’s virtues but in their own cunning and, like a crafty fox, strive to lead people astray. By the birds we may understand the evil spirits, who have dwelling places in the hearts of the Jews, where Christ God finds no habitation.

[Col. 0042C] But another of his disciples said to him: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” He does not reject discipleship, but desires first to fulfill the pious duty of his father’s funeral and then to pursue this calling more freely. In this man also the Son of Man reclines his head, because divinity rests in a certain familiar dwelling within his humble breast.

But Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” To bury the dead means to cherish sinners in their sins. This is what those do who justify the wicked for gifts and bless those who commit iniquity.

And when he had embarked in the boat, his disciples followed him. The sea that the Lord desires to cross with his own is understood as the dark turmoil of the present age. The boat they board is best understood as the tree of the Lord’s Passion, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Mark 8).

And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. That storm did not arise of itself, but obeyed the authority of the one who commanded, so that he might show all that he is Lord of earth and sea.

But he was sleeping. O wondrous event! He who never sleeps slept. He slept in body in order to make the apostles keep watch, and especially so that we might never sleep in spirit.

And they approached and awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” They awaken the Lord lest they perish in the violence of the waves, because, having seen his death, they sought his resurrection with their greatest desires, lest, through his carnal death, their minds should perish forever in spiritual death.

And Jesus said to them: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” Mark says, “Do you not yet have faith?” (Mark 4); Luke, “Where is your faith?” (Luke 8). That is: If you believe that I am powerful on earth, why did you not at the same time receive me as truly God and Creator of all things on the sea? Why do you not believe that all things made by me are in my power? Why do you doubt, you of little faith? Those who are weak in faith are rebuked; those altogether alien to faith are punished, as are the Jews and heretics.

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. By rising he rebuked the wind [Col. 0043B], for through his resurrection he struck down the devil’s pride. He caused the storm of the water to cease when, by rising from the tomb, he weakened the fury of the Jews.

But the men were amazed, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”

It was not the disciples but the sailors who said: “Who is this man who appears as a human being and displays power as God?” Some wish to understand this boat allegorically as signifying the present Church, the winds as evil spirits, and the men as wicked people who desire the Church to be submerged by waves and afflictions. Yet although Jesus may seem to sleep for a time by withdrawing his help, when awakened by worthy prayers he causes the incitement of evil spirits to cease, tempers the threats of persecutors, and, with the breeze of the Holy Spirit blowing, leads the Church all the way to the gate of eternal rest.

Morally, each of us, imbued with the catholic faith, boards the ship and attempts to cross the sea with Jesus. He seems to sleep among the roar of the waters when, as the assault of filthy spirits or wicked people grows stronger, the splendor of faith becomes dark amid the very efforts of virtue and the height of hope wastes away. Yet amid such storms we must diligently awaken him, so that he himself, as pilot, may grant us the shore of salvation; then, delivered from the turmoil, we may admire his kindness toward us and, in our wonder, give thanks.

And when he had come to the other side of the lake, into the region of the Gerasenes. Gerasa is a city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, joined to Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh possessed, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the pigs were driven headlong. It signifies the nations that, after the Lord’s sleep of Passion and the glory of his resurrection, he deigned to visit through preachers. Accordingly, Gerasa is aptly interpreted as “expelling the settler” or “the approaching stranger.”

Two men possessed by demons met him. The fact that Mark and Luke mention one should be understood as referring to one of greater renown, whom that region especially mourned. But allegorically, just as there was one man possessed by a demon, so the two pagan poles, occupied by idols, not inappropriately express the type.

Coming out of the tombs, exceedingly savage. These two men, who were tormented by demons, appropriately represented the figure of two peoples: the Gentile [Col. 0044A], who, deceived by diabolical doctrines, worshiped idols in place of God; and the Jewish people, who had always been contemptuous of the divine law. They did not live in a house—that is, in their own conscience—but in tombs, that is, they delighted in dead works. For what are bodies except tombs of the dead? They were exceedingly savage because they regarded divine and human laws as nothing; these laws are signified by the chains.

So that no one could pass along that road. Before the Savior’s coming, the Gentile world was an impassable road for prophets and holy preachers, because in the savagery of its fury it refused to obey anyone. It broke fetters and chains—that is, human laws—and, as Luke writes, was driven by a demon in the desert. Having transgressed the laws, it had already gone beyond ordinary custom through the crimes of its desires.

And they cried out, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” This is not a confession of the will, since no reward follows the one who confesses, but an extortion compelled by necessity, like that of a runaway slave. If, after a long time, they see their lord, they ask for nothing except to be spared blows. So the demons, seeing the Lord moving about on earth, believed that he had come to judge them.

“You came before the time to torture us.” The devil knew that a certain condemnation awaited him in God’s judgment, to whom it is said through Isaiah: “Woe to you who plunder; will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isaiah 33). But he could not know the dispensation of the divine plan that was to be revealed to us. Therefore, fearing the power of the Lord’s coming, he thought that it was leading toward his own condemnation.

There was not far from them a herd of pigs, … “Send us into the herd of pigs.” Mark says that the herd of pigs was near the mountain (Mark 5), which does not conflict with Luke’s statement that it was on the mountain (Luke 8). The herd was so large that some were on the mountain and others around the mountain.

And Jesus said: “Go.” Let the Manichaean be ashamed, since he says that human and animal substance is one, while, for the salvation of one man, two thousand pigs, as Mark reports, are drowned. In their destruction, however, unclean people are indicated. The devil cannot receive power against anyone in order to destroy him except one who has lived in the manner of a pig and grazes upon the mountain of pride.

[Col. 0044D] But when they had gone out, they entered the pigs, … and they died in the waters. Those who do not wish to believe in Christ practice their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, once the Church has been freed from the dominion of demons. It should also be noted that demons cannot harm even animals, much less human beings, unless power is granted by God. The good God can grant this power over us according to hidden justice; he cannot grant it unjustly.

But the swineherds fled, and when they came into the city, they reported everything, including what had happened to those who had been possessed by demons. The fact that the swineherds, fleeing, announce these things signifies that some leading men even among the impious, although they flee Christian law, nevertheless do not cease to proclaim its power among the nations with amazement and wonder.

And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they asked him to depart from their boundaries. As some judge, they did this not through pride but through humility, conscious of their weakness and judging themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence, as we read happened also to Peter when he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5).

Mystically, however, the fact that the Gerasenes found the man clothed and sitting in his right mind at Jesus’ feet, as Luke says, and, recognizing what had happened, asked Jesus to depart from them (Luke 8), signifies that the ancient multitude honored its former way of life and was unwilling, and unable, to endure or fulfill Christian law. Yet they marveled at the faithful people healed of their former and ruined way of life.

## CHAPTER IX

And he embarked in the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city. Here a question arises, because Mark says that this happened in Capernaum. It would be more difficult to resolve if Matthew had named Nazareth. But now, since he came into Galilee, it is rightly said that he came into his own city, whatever town of Galilee he was in, especially since Capernaum itself so excelled in Galilee that it was regarded as a kind of metropolis.

Behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. The healing of this paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul sighing for Christ after the merit of the flesh. It first needs ministers—that is, good teachers—to bring it to Christ. Appropriately, four are found, as Mark relates, either because the entire strength of preachers is established by the four books of the Gospel, or because confidence of mind is raised by four virtues to obtain healing: sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage. Nothing is more useful than these in human life.

And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” Luke says, “Man” (Luke 5). If this troubles anyone, let him know that both expressions can be spoken at once: “Take courage, son,” and “Your sins are forgiven you, man.”

And behold, certain scribes said within themselves: “This man blasphemes.” Mark explains what they meant by blasphemy in what follows, saying: “Who, they say, can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2). In saying this, they thought he was only a man. Although they did not know the truth, they were saying: “No one can forgive sins except God alone, and those to whom he himself gives the authority to forgive.” Thus Christ is proved to be true God, forgiving sins as God.

And when Jesus saw their thoughts, and so forth. In this also he showed himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart. Remaining silent, he speaks in this way: “While I observe your thoughts, understand from them what the paralytic is obtaining. Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the one who rose and by those who saw him [Col. 0046A]. Therefore a bodily sign is performed so that the spiritual reality may be proved, and it is made clear that bodily weaknesses come upon us because of sins. For this reason the sins are forgiven first, so that health may be restored.

There are indeed five kinds of causes for which we are afflicted in this life with bodily troubles: either to increase merits through patience, as in the case of blessed Job; or to preserve virtues, as when the apostle Paul was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations; or to correct sins, as when Mary, the sister of Aaron, was struck with leprosy because of her rash words; or for the glory of God, as when Lazarus’s illness was not for death but for the glory of God; or as the beginning of eternal damnation, which is characteristic of the reprobate, as Antiochus and Herod showed to all by their present misery what they were destined to suffer forever in Gehenna. Hence it is said: “With a double destruction destroy them” (Jeremiah 17).

But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he then said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.”

“Take up your bed,” he said, so that what had been a testimony of weakness might become proof of health. “Go to your house,” lest, having been healed by Christian faith, you should now linger on the paths of Jewish faithlessness. Spiritually healthy, the one who had been ill carries the bed home when, having received forgiveness of sins, the soul returns with the body itself to the inward guardianship of itself, lest after pardon it commit anything for which it may again justly be struck.

When the crowds saw this, they were afraid, and so forth. How astonishing is the power of divine might, where salvation follows so swiftly, without any intervening delay.

And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew, and he said to him: “Follow me.”

That is, he looked upon one devoted to human pursuits and longing for temporal profits with the gaze of mercy, just as he looked upon Peter so that he might recognize the guilt of his denial. For *telos* is Greek and is translated into Latin as *vectigal*, “tax” or “tribute.” Matthew is said in Hebrew to mean “given” in Latin, and not without reason, because he received so great a gift of heavenly grace. The other evangelists, out of respect for him, did not wish to call him by his familiar name but called him Levi. He himself, however, names himself Matthew and tax collector, in accordance with Solomon’s instruction: “The righteous man is the first to accuse himself” (Proverbs 18).

At the beginning he says this in order to show in his own person that no one ought to despair of salvation, since a tax collector himself was transformed into an apostle. Here Levi signifies “added,” or “taken up,” because he was taken up by the Lord through election and added to the number of the apostles.

And he rose and followed him. Luke says: “Leaving everything, he followed him” (Luke 5). To follow is to imitate. He followed appropriately, since he abandoned what belonged to him, having been accustomed to seize what belonged to others; and he taught how one ought to follow, for, scorning human business, he became a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

And it happened, while he was reclining at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners, and so forth.

[Col. 0047A] Luke says that a great banquet took place for him in the house of Levi. This signifies that Christ reclines in the affection of believers in order to enjoy the spiritual banquet of good things, at which the rich are in need while the poor feast.

And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” The Pharisees were held by a twofold error: in the arrogance of pride they had gone far from righteousness, and they disparaged the teacher of truth for receiving sinners.

Mystically, however, through Matthew’s election and calling, the faith of the nations is expressed. Formerly they longed for the profits of the world; now, with the Lord, they are refreshed by the banquets of love and by diligent devotion to good works. This implies the haughtiness of the scribes and the envy of the Jews, by which they are tormented over the salvation of the nations. While the tax collectors feast with the Lord, the Pharisees murmur about fasting and boast of it, because those who follow the law suffer eternal hunger; but those who have received the Word within their souls, restored by the abundance of heavenly nourishment, cannot hunger or thirst.

But Jesus, hearing this, said: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill.” He calls himself the physician, by whose blood we have been healed. He calls “healthy” and “righteous” those who, trusting in themselves under his law, do not seek the grace of the Gospel; and he calls “ill” those who, conscious of their weakness, submit their necks in repentance to the grace of Christ.

“Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy [Col. 0047C], and not sacrifice.’” Let some learn through works of mercy the lesson of foolish reproach, so that they may obtain for themselves the rewards of heavenly mercy.

“For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” That is, I have not come to exalt those who falsely justify themselves through empty approval, but mercifully to gather those who repent.

Then the disciples of John approached him, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, while your disciples do not fast?” Mark and Luke narrate this as though some others had put the question to him. From this it must be inferred that the question was presented to the Lord by many different people.

Spiritually, those people were fasting who, abstaining from spiritual goods, were wasting away with fasting hearts as they followed human traditions. But those who are incorporated into Christ through love cannot fast, because they feast upon his blood and flesh.

And Jesus said to them: “Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?” and so forth. Christ is therefore the Bridegroom and the Church the bride. From this spiritual marriage the apostles were born; they cannot mourn or fast while they see the Bridegroom with the bride in the bridal chamber. But when the wedding had passed and the time of the Passion and resurrection had arrived, then they fasted.

For this mourning, celebrated in the longing of the saints before the Savior’s coming, is also not now absent, until the Bridegroom comes to judge the living and the dead. Tropologically, we are in joy as long as the Bridegroom is with us. But when he has flown away on account of our sins [Col. 0048A], then fasting must be proclaimed and mourning must be taken up.

No one puts a patch of unprocessed cloth on an old garment, for it takes away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear results. By this response the Lord teaches that the apostles, not yet strengthened by firm faith in his Passion and resurrection, could not bear the stricter commands of fasting and continence. Since they were still devoted to their old custom, a new patch is improperly sewn onto them—that is, some portion of the teaching belonging to the moderation of the new life. If this is done, the teaching itself is in a certain sense torn, because the portion concerning abstinence from food is handed on inappropriately, when the teaching prescribes a general fast not merely from the desire for food, but [Col. 0048B] from every delight in temporal pleasures.

Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, and so forth. The apostles were old wineskins before the infusion of the Holy Spirit. But after the triumph of the resurrection and the glory of the ascension had strengthened them, they became new wineskins for new wine, when the fervor of the Holy Spirit filled their hearts.

Alternatively, the garment signifies the good works we perform outwardly and by which we shine before human beings; the new wine signifies the fervor of faith, hope, and charity, by which we are reformed into the newness of our understanding.

While he was saying these things to them, behold, a certain ruler approached, … “Lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” Mark and Luke say that this man was the ruler of the synagogue and that his name was Jairus. They report that he announced to the Lord not that she was dead, but that she was near death. Matthew, however, for the sake of brevity, attends not to the father’s words but to his intention: for he did not believe that he could find alive the daughter for whom he had pleaded.

Mystically, Jairus, whose name is interpreted as “illumined” or “illumining,” is understood as Moses, who, illumined by the Holy Spirit, had received words of life so that through them he might illumine others. For what is meant by the feet of Jesus except his humanity? According to the other evangelists, the lawgiver fell down before them with the whole succession of the fathers, recognizing that the Mediator between God and human beings was far superior to him in the glory of dignity.

The daughter is the Synagogue, who was Moses’ only daughter and whom the father laments as having died at about twelve years of age. After the lawgiver’s education and the instruction of the prophets, when the mind had reached an age capable of understanding and ought to have produced a spiritual sun, she was overwhelmed by the sickness of error and extinguished by death. But the coming Redeemer restored her to life by the right hand of his power.

And Jesus rose and followed him, together with his disciples. Wherever Jesus’ coming approaches with teachers, immediately the exit from death and the entrance into life are opened.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment. This woman flowing with blood, but healed by the Lord, is the Church gathered from the nations.

It should be noted that the ruler of the synagogue had a twelve-year-old daughter, while this woman had been flowing with blood for twelve years [Col. 0049A]. That is, at the same time when the one was born, the other began to suffer. In nearly one age of this world, the Synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, and the foreign nation began to be defiled throughout the world by idolatry.

She approached from behind, or alongside: either in accordance with what he himself says, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26), or because, through faith, she had already begun to follow him after the transaction of the Incarnation’s mystery.

For she said within herself: “If I touch only the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.” That is: “If I receive faith in his Incarnation, I shall be cleansed from all the iniquity of my sins.” She believed, she spoke, she touched. In these three forms every healing is obtained: by faith, word, and deed.

But Jesus turned and saw her and said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.” He turned from the severity of just judgment to the abundance of his mercy. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3).

“He saw her and said” means: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined, he also called” (Romans 8:30). “Take courage, daughter”: she already had faith, but he was asking from her the perseverance of faith.

And the woman was saved from that hour. From the hour of the Lord’s coming, therefore, people are converted to faith, and by the Lord, who saves them, they are increased daily in the same state.

And when Jesus had come into the ruler’s house and had seen the flute players and the crowd making a tumult, he said: “Withdraw, flute players.” They are teachers singing a mournful song. The Synagogue, which through the merit of its faithlessness lost the joy of the Lord’s indwelling, lies dead in the ruler’s house, as though amid mourners and wailers, even to this day. Yet it has not been utterly abandoned by the Lord; toward the end of the age it will be restored to salvation. Hence what follows appropriately:

“The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” Allegorically, when the soul has sinned and seems to us to be dead, it is nevertheless not improperly called alive by the one who restores it to life.

And they laughed at him. This properly displays the faithlessness and blasphemy of the Jews, and demonstrates the childishness of their understanding and the wantonness of their conduct. Hence it is said: “They tested me and mocked me.”

And when the crowd had been put outside, he entered. Morally, the soul that lies dead within will not rise unless first the intrusive multitude of worldly thoughts is expelled from the innermost chambers of the heart.

And he took her hand, and the girl rose. Unless the hands of the Jews, full of blood, have first been cleansed, their dead Synagogue does not rise. It rises and walks appropriately at the touch of divine mercy, because it not only rises from the filth of crimes but immediately advances in good works.

And this report spread throughout that whole land. For “the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.” Morally, the three dead whom the Lord raised signify the three kinds of resurrection of souls, as we showed above.

And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, … and when he had come into the house, the blind men approached him [Col. 0050A]. Jesus’ house is the heavenly Jerusalem. The two blind men are the two peoples, blinded by observance of the letter and by the Gentile rite, ignorant of future things.

As the Lord passed through this world and desired to return to his own house, two blind men followed him. For when the Gospel was preached through the apostles, many from Jews and Gentiles began to follow the Redeemer, asking him to have mercy on them so that they might obtain the light of faith and good works.

And Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I am able to do this for you?” Knowing their faith himself, he asks so that confession may bring their faith forth, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes, saying, and so forth. This means that, since faith already illumines your minds, faith itself should restore the light of your eyes.

[Col. 0050B] And Jesus sternly warned them, saying: “See that no one knows.” But when they went out, and so forth, they could not remain silent because of the memory of the grace and benefit they had received.

When they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man, and so forth. This man signifies the Gentile people, who did not possess a confession of true faith and were devoted to idolatry. But when he was led to the Savior by preachers, he was healed.

And the crowds marveled, saying: “This has never appeared in Israel,” and so forth. In the crowd there is the confession of the nations. The Pharisees, however, demonstrate the faithlessness of the Jews.

Matthew alone records this incident of the two blind men and the mute man possessed by a demon. These two blind men, whom the others do not report, are narrated by Matthew; nevertheless, a similar event occurred. We often find similar events, with some difference in them that cannot be reconciled, so that we may understand that it was not the same event but another, similar one, or one that occurred in a similar manner.

And Jesus went around the cities and villages, … healing every illness. He preached the Gospel in cities and villages—that is, among the great and the small—without considering the power of the noble but the salvation of believers.

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were troubled, and so forth. Jesus looked upon the human race, afflicted by the devil through various errors, with the gaze of his mercy and had compassion on them, appointing shepherds—namely, teachers—to lead them onto the way of truth.

Then he said to his disciples: “The harvest is indeed plentiful,” and so forth. The plentiful harvest is the whole crowd of believers; the few workers are the apostles and their imitators, who are sent to the harvest.

## CHAPTER X

And having summoned his disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and so forth. It is rightly by divine grace that twelve are summoned to the apostleship, so that the salvation they would preach by word might be commended by their number. Groups of three and four were sent to preach, so that they might baptize throughout the four regions of the square-shaped world in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

For these are the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem: three each from the East, the North, the South, and the West. Likewise, because through their preaching all the nations of the world would enter the Church, in the mystery of this arrangement the three tribes of the sons of Israel encamped on every side of the Tabernacle.

Now these are the names of the twelve apostles. The catalogue is placed in the Gospel so that false apostles may be excluded.

First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. Peter is called so to distinguish him from the other Simon. In Latin, then, Peter is the same as Cephas in Syriac, and in both languages the name is derived from *petra*, “rock.” Concerning this rock Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Andrew is Greek, and from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός*—that is, “from the man”—he is called manly. Simon is interpreted as “placing,” “remembering,” or “hearing sorrow.” This suits the time when he laid aside the grief of the Lord’s death or of his own denial. But immediately afterward he heard the sorrow of his own death, when the Lord said: “When you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands,” and so forth (John 21:18).

James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, were called and surnamed by the Lord “sons of thunder,” that is, *Boanerges*, or, as it is more correctly written, *Boneregesch*, because of their exceptional cultivation of virtue, as it is written in the Gospel of Mark.

Nor was it without reason: one of them, thundering from the heavenly heights, uttered that theological voice which no one before had known how to proclaim: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth (John 1:1). Both of them also deserved to be led apart by the Lord onto the mountain and at one point to hear a terrifying sound from the cloud.

Philip and Bartholomew. Philip is interpreted as “the mouth of a lamp,” and rightly so: when he was called by the Lord, he immediately preached to Nathanael, whom he had found, the light he had recognized, saying: “The one whom Moses wrote about in the Law,” and so forth.

Bartholomew is Syriac and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends waters,” that is, son of God, who suspends the minds of his preachers so that they may contemplate heavenly things, in order that he may intoxicate earthly hearts with drops of their words.

Thomas and Matthew the tax collector. Thomas means “abyss” or “twin,” and hence in Greek he is also called *Didymus*, “Twin,” because the longer he doubted in comparison with the others, the more profoundly he learned the truth of the Lord’s resurrection.

Matthew is said to mean “given,” namely because, through the Lord’s great gift, he was transferred from being a tax collector to the office of apostle and evangelist.

[Col. 0051D] James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus. James the son of Alphaeus is the one who is called the brother of the Lord, because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of the Lord’s mother; John the evangelist calls this Mary “of Cleophas.” Alternatively, it is because Alphaeus was called Cleophas, or because, after Alphaeus’s death and after the birth of James, Mary married Cleophas, to whom ecclesiastical history says she bore Simeon as a son, making him the Lord’s cousin.

James is rightly written as the son of Alphaeus, that is, of the “learned,” whose life was of such austerity that he was truly one who overthrew carnal desire. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no meat, was never shorn, and never used baths.

Thaddaeus, whom Luke calls Judas of James and elsewhere calls Lebbaeus, is said to mean “a circle,” that is, “a cultivator of the heart.” We should believe that he had three names. For he was the brother of James, the brother of the Lord, as he himself writes in his Epistle; hence he too was called the Lord’s brother.

Simon the Cananaean and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. He added the designations to these names in order to distinguish Simon from Simon Peter and Judas from Judas of James.

Simon the Cananaean receives his surname from Cana, a village of Galilee, and is called the Zealot—that is, “the rival” or “the ardent one.” Judas Iscariot took the name Scarioth either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. Issachar, which is said to mean “reward,” indicates the price of betrayal and foreshadows his condemnation. Scarioth is said to mean “memory of death.” Hence it is argued that he did not fall under persuasion suddenly, but committed the crime of betraying the Lord after meditating on it for a long time.

[Col. 0052B] Jesus sent these twelve, commanding and saying to them. We should understand that he did not call only these twelve apostles “disciples,” but all who believed in his teaching, from among whom he chose these twelve, whom he also named apostles, as Luke records. The Lord Jesus sent these twelve to preach because, through many indications in figures, they had previously been foretold as those who would administer the divine mysteries. These are the twelve true sons of Jacob; these are the twelve springs at Elim; these are the twelve scouts sent by Moses; these are the twelve stones raised from the Jordan; these are the twelve lion cubs on Solomon’s throne; and other things of the same kind.

Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles, [Col. 0052C] and so forth, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel. This is not contrary to the passage where it is said, “Go and teach all nations,” and what follows (Matthew 28:19). Rather, it was necessary that preaching first be offered to the Jews, lest they excuse themselves as though justly, saying that they had rejected the Lord because he had sent his apostles to foreigners. In the tropological sense, however, we are commanded not to walk in the error of heretics, but, having withdrawn from the household of the Church through grave sin, to return there again through repentance.

As you go, preach, saying: For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Not through any movement of the elements, but through faith established within us; hence it is said: “The kingdom of God is among you.”

Heal the sick, and so forth, “You received without payment; give without payment.” He gave them this power while they promised the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of the signs might confirm the greatness of the promises. The holy Church does this daily when, through exhortation, it heals the sick in good works; through repentance, recalls those dead in unbelief or sins; heals lepers by correcting them from the various stains of error; and drives demons out of people through the grace of exorcism.

Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; the worker is worthy of his food. Gold may be understood as the understanding of secular wisdom; silver, as the eloquence of rhetorical art; while money enclosed in belts is hidden wisdom. Hence it is said: “What benefit is there in hidden wisdom and concealed treasure?” (Ecclesiasticus 20:32). In the two tunics let us understand the double soul; in the bag, the burdens of the world; in the staff, the protection of the flesh; and what is signified by sandals except examples of dead works?

Whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you leave. This must therefore be understood in relation to the reputation of the people, lest the dignity of preaching be disturbed by the disgrace of its recipient.

And remain there until you leave. He gives a general command of steadfastness, so that they may preserve the rights of hospitable obligation.

When you enter a house, greet it, saying, and so forth, “May your peace return to you.” What in Greek is χαῖρε (*chaire*), and in Latin *ave*, is called in the Hebrew language *Salom* [*shalom*]. What he commands means this: If contradiction should arise, you will nevertheless receive your reward for the peace you offered; they will possess the warfare they chose to have.

And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you leave the house or city, shake the dust from your feet. The dust is shaken off as testimony to your labor and to their condemnation, so that they may be without excuse, since the preaching of the Gospel reached them.

Amen, I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city. They despised only one law, namely, the law of nature; but the Jews despised at once the law of nature and the written law, and moreover the sayings of the prophets and apostles. For Lot, righteous in sight and hearing, is said to have taught them something, but he is not reported to have performed any signs there. Therefore, “from the one to whom much has been given, much will be demanded” (Luke 12:48).

Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves. By saying “Behold, I,” he expresses the authority and strength of the Godhead; and because you are my sheep, I send you. I wish you to possess gentleness and humility, so that, because of the wolves—that is, persecutors—you do not lose your patience and steadfastness.

Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Let them avoid snares through innocence, not create them. The serpent’s wisdom consists in placing one ear against a rock and closing the other with its tail, so that it does not hear the enchanters who seek poisons in its heads for use as medicines. Thus the apostolic man directs his whole life toward the governing part of the soul, so that it may remain unharmed with Christ’s help, Christ being the rock; and, being imbued with the subtle instruction of the holy Scriptures—which the tail signifies—he takes the greatest care not to hear the enchanters, that is, those who soften the vigor of the mind. Again, when the serpent enters through a narrow opening among the rocks, it strips off its old scales. So the Christian ought, through the strictness of repentance, to put off the old man with his deeds, so that he may put on the new man, who was created according to God.

Beware of men. These men are the same as the wolves: they are sinners and weak, but nevertheless fierce.

For they will hand you over to councils, and so forth, as a testimony [Col. 0054A] to them and to the Gentiles. Luke says: “This will happen to you as a testimony.” He indicates that, through persecution for the name of Christ, testimony to innocence is given not only to the Jews and Gentiles concerning their wickedness, but also to the apostles themselves.

When they hand you over, do not be anxious, and so forth, but the Spirit of your Father is the one who speaks in you. It is as though he were saying plainly to his weakened members: “Do not be frightened. You approach the contest, but I do the fighting; you utter the words, but I am the one who speaks.”

Brother will hand over brother to death, and father his son, and so forth: you will be hated by all because of my name. There is no faithful affection among those whose faith is different. He therefore foretold the disturbance that would come upon them, so that, having known it beforehand, they might bear it more lightly.

But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. [Col. 0054B] Patience, which guards the virtues, teaches that virtue consists not in beginning or even in doing, but in bringing to completion.

When they persecute you in one city, flee to another. This is not out of fear of suffering, but in order to avoid it, so that the occasion of tribulation might become a seedbed for the Gospel.

Amen, I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. That is, you will not bring them to faith before the resurrection has taken place and authority to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world has been granted. Spiritually, however, we flee from city to city when we run from one testimony of Scripture to other books, so that the Savior’s protection may come before victory is granted to his adversaries.

A disciple is not above his teacher, and so forth, and “the servant as his lord.” It is as though he were saying: “If I, the Lord and teacher, suffer, it is necessary that you, disciples and mere human beings, follow this rule of perfection.”

If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household members. He calls himself the master of the household and calls the disciples household members, promising them the kingdom of heaven. The Jews, driven by the same impulse of malice, slander them.

Therefore do not fear them. For a vain thing quickly falls away.

For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. The meaning is: Do not fear the rage of blasphemers, because the day of judgment will come, [Col. 0054D] on which both our virtue and their wickedness will be revealed.

What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in your ear, preach upon the rooftops. What you have learned mystically and secretly, speak publicly; and what I taught in a small place in Judaea, proclaim boldly throughout the world. He teaches preaching from the rooftops, raised high according to Palestinian custom; they themselves make them level, not according to our custom but in a flat design.

Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. The Savior is the first to use the name “Gehenna.” For we read that the idol of Baal was located near Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where the Siloam flows. This valley, well watered and wooded, had a grove consecrated to the idol, where the people burned their sons to the demon. That grove is called *Gehennon*, that is, “the valley of the sons of Hinnom.” The Lord threatens that he will fill the place itself with the corpses of the dead, so that it will no longer be called Topheth and Baal, but *polyandrium*, that is, “a tomb of the dead.” Thus, by the name of this place, a double punishment of fire and cold is indicated.

Are not two sparrows sold for an *as* [a small coin], and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father? The meaning is this: If small and worthless animals do not fall without God as their author, and providence is present in everything, you, who are eternal, ought not to fear that you live without God’s providence. Someone may ask how the Apostle can say, “Is God concerned with oxen?” when an ox is certainly more valuable. But concern is one thing, providence another.

But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. In fact, this numbering is not a matter of actual counting, but of the capacity of knowledge.

Therefore do not fear: you are more valuable than many sparrows. He says “more valuable” because you are rational and were created in the image of God.

Therefore everyone who acknowledges me before men, and so forth, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. The Son acknowledges him before the Father, since through the Son he has access to the Father. The good Christian acknowledges the Lord with the faith that works through love; and the Lord acknowledges him before his Father, rewarding him with eternal blessedness. To deny Christ before men is to refuse to obey his commandments. The Lord denies him before his Father because he judges him unworthy of his vision.

Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. Because every household contained both unbelievers and believers, a good war was brought about by the sword of preaching, so that evil peace might be separated: some fighting against the faith, others for the faith.

I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be his household members. Luke says: “For there will be five in one house divided: three against two and two against three,” and yet they agree, [Col. 0055D] because the woman who is the mother of the son is also the mother-in-law of his wife. Therefore she is said to be divided both against her daughter and against her daughter-in-law. Allegorically, the three pertain to those who preserve faith in the supreme Trinity; the two correspond to those who disagree in the unity of faith. The father is the devil, whose sons we were—not by creation, but by imitation. The mother and mother-in-law are the Synagogue, which is divided against daughter and daughter-in-law, because the carnal Synagogue does not cease persecuting the Church of Christ.

Whoever loves father or mother, and so forth, is not worthy of me. Love your father after God; love your mother. But if both cannot be preserved, hatred must be directed toward one’s own and devotion toward the Lord.

Whoever does not accept his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. To accept the cross and go after the Lord is to offer abstinence from the flesh or compassion toward one’s neighbor in pursuit of eternal blessedness.

Whoever finds his life will lose it, and what follows. By “life” he means the present life. Whoever denies it in persecution prepares it for eternal destruction; whoever throughout the whole day hands it over to be put to death for Christ will make it alive there.

Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. He teaches that the office of mediator is also present in himself: God has been poured into us through him. For it is evident that the apostles have received none other than God, since Christ dwells in them and God in Christ.

Whoever receives a prophet, and so forth, will receive the reward of a righteous person. He does not say that persons are to be received, but names: although the one received may be unworthy, those who receive him nevertheless do not lose their reward before God.

And whoever gives one of these least ones a drink, even a cup of cold water, in the name of a disciple, amen, I say to you, will not lose his reward. By a very light command he removed the vice of inhospitality, urging people to give cold water, so that poverty might not even be sought as an excuse for heating it with wood. The meaning is: “You make a needless appeal to poverty when your conscience knows otherwise, and you cannot deceive the company; but I know that whatever you sow, you will also reap.”

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0056C] And it happened that when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he crossed over from there to teach in their cities. Now the good teacher fulfills by deeds what he had previously promised in words. He therefore crossed over and preached in the cities of the Jews, so as to give them an opportunity for belief; and if they rejected the gift of heavenly grace when it was offered, they would be without excuse.

When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and so forth, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” He does not ask as one ignorant, since he himself had pointed out the Lamb of God with his finger to those who were ignorant. Rather, as he was to be killed by Herod, he sends disciples to the Savior so that, on the occasion of seeing the signs, they might believe in him. The meaning of this statement may be as follows: “Send word to me,” he says. “I am about to descend to the underworld. Should I announce you to the dead, as I announced you to the living, or is it unfitting for the Son of God to taste death, and will you send another for the sake of these mysteries?”

And Jesus answered and said to them: Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me. “Go,” he says, “and tell John the signs you see: the blind seeing, and so forth—and what is no less than these, the poor evangelizing.” These things prove the rigor of the master and the truth of the teacher, since among noble and ignoble alike all are equal before the one who can save. When he says, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me,” he meanwhile strikes at the messengers, as will be shown in what follows.
