When they had departed, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John, and so forth: “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.” Because the crowd thought that John was asking about Christ not on behalf of his disciples but on his own, as one doubting, he says: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed? Surely you did not go out for this purpose—to see a man like a reed, carried about by every wind—and to doubt the one whom he had previously preached? Or did one who, forced by the goads of envy against me, sought earthly profit through his preaching, feed on delicacies? Yet he feeds on locusts and wears camel’s hair. Such food and clothing are received in the lodging of a prison, for such is the dwelling place of the preaching of truth. Those who preach falsely, however, are flatterers; they abound in delicacies and wear soft clothing in kings’ houses.”

But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. John is greater than the other prophets in this respect: the one whom they preached as coming, he pointed out as present with his finger.

Amen, I say to you, among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist. He is therefore preferred to human beings who are born of women and from the intercourse of man, but not to the one born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. He did not place John above all human beings, patriarchs and prophets, but made the others equal to John, so that he might have equality with the other saints.

But the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. Many wish this to be understood of the Savior, namely, that the one who is later in time is greater in dignity. We, however, should understand it simply: every saint who is with God is already greater than the one who still remains in the struggle.

From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. What is the kingdom of heaven except the place of the righteous? When someone swollen with pride or polluted by a deed of the flesh returns to repentance, which John preached, and receives eternal life, the sinner enters, as it were, into a place that belongs to another. For it is a great violence that we, born on earth, are able through virtue to possess the kingdom of heaven, which we cannot possess by nature.

For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. He does not exclude the prophets after John; rather, the time of the Lord himself is being indicated, because John showed that the one whom they said would come had come.

And if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. By saying “whoever has ears,” he shows that what he says is mystical. There was one measure of austerity and severity in the lives of both: both were in the desert, and both contended against an unjust king and queen. John is the herald of the Redeemer; Elijah, according to Malachi, will be the herald of the Judge.

To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace who call to their companions, saying: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn.” The Lord’s marketplace is the Synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, where the Jewish people once sat and received the prophets. In the language of their homeland, they are rightly reproached every day because they were unwilling to respond either to the psalms that first attracted them, the psalms of David, or to the prophetic laments by which they were later corrected.

For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and so forth. As he said then, so also now: “You have rejected both paths of salvation. With John lamenting and preaching repentance, you were unwilling to humble yourselves; and with Christ, who, by eating and drinking with others, prefigured the joy of the kingdom, you refused to rejoice.”

And wisdom was justified by her children. He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness consists neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity in enduring poverty and in temperance, so as not to be corrupted by abundance, because the kingdom of God is not food, and so forth.

Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented. He reproaches these cities because, after so many mighty works and signs had been performed, they did not repent.

Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida. Chorazin, which is interpreted as “my mystery,” and Bethsaida, which is called “house of fruits” or “house of hunters,” [Col. 0058C] are cities of Galilee and Tiberias, situated beside the lake of Gennesaret, which is formed by the Jordan flowing through it and is called by the Evangelist the Sea of Galilee and of Tiberias. The Lord therefore mourns the cities that once possessed God’s mystery and ought to have produced the fruit of virtue, cities to which spiritual hunters were also sent. After so many miracles, they became worse than the Gentiles and did not fear to spurn God’s grace despite being ungrateful.

For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth signifies the harshness of sin, which the left side will behold on the day of judgment; ashes signify death, through which the whole mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust. Why it was preached to those who were unwilling, and not to those who once wished to believe, is known to the one whose every way is mercy and truth. It should also be noted that Tyre is the metropolis of Phoenicia, in the tribe of Naphtali. Once it stood far out in the sea, but now it is joined to the land, and its name is interpreted as “narrowness.” Sidon, a city of Phoenicia, was formerly the boundary of the Canaanites, facing north, and later of the region of Judaea. It fell to the lot of the tribe of Asher, but that tribe did not possess it because it was entirely unable to drive out the enemies. Sidon means “hunting.” These two names signify the two peoples whom the devil, the hunter, captured in the narrowness of sin, but whom the Savior Jesus freed through the Gospel.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? Or will you descend to the underworld? [Col. 0059A] In another exemplar we find: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, you will descend to the underworld.” There is a twofold interpretation: either you will descend to the underworld because you resisted my preaching with the utmost pride; or, because you were exalted to heaven by my hospitality and my signs, you will be punished with greater penalties because you were unwilling to believe even these things. In Capernaum, which is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” unbelieving Jerusalem is condemned. Of it Ezekiel says: “Your sister Sodom was justified,” and so forth. Hence what follows is added.

For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained until this day. Jerusalem is charged with greater injustice, since Sodom was not corrected by the example of Lot, whereas Jerusalem was always ungrateful for the words and miracles of the Son of God and persecuted all the saints, as well as the Savior himself.

Nevertheless, I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you. Their punishment will therefore be more bearable, since their guilt is less.

At that time Jesus answered and said: I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Acknowledgment does not always signify repentance, but also thanksgiving. Let those who slander the Savior as created rather than born be confounded, since he calls God his Father and the Lord of heaven and earth.

Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. He gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he has opened to the apostles the mysteries of his coming, [Col. 0059C] which the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed wise to themselves, did not know.

Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing before you. From these words of the Lord we learn examples of humility, so that we do not rashly presume to investigate the reasons for the calling of some and the rejection of others. Although he had introduced both matters, he did not immediately give an explanation, but said that it was thus pleasing, showing this in particular: what pleased the just one cannot be unjust.

Everything has been handed over to me by my Father. It is possible to understand mystically both the Father who hands over and the Son who receives. Otherwise, when the one who receives begins to have, the one who gives will begin not to have. When you read “everything,” you acknowledge the omnipotent Father; when you read “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom, by the nature of one substance, all things properly belong—not bestowed by grace as a gift. By “handed over” he does not mean the visible elements, which he himself created, but those who were formerly rebellious and now, through the Son, have access to the Father. The things handed over are none other than those known only to the Father in the Son; and what belongs to the Father is known only to the Son.

And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. We should understand both that the Father and the Son himself are revealed through the Son, who is the light of our mind; for the Father declares himself through his Word. Let Eunomius be ashamed of claiming for himself such knowledge of the Father and Son as they possess through the equality of their nature.

Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and [Col. 0060A] I will refresh you. The Savior invites those oppressed by the heavy burden of sins to the grace of the Gospel, or those subjected to the very heavy yoke of the law; hence it also follows:

Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and what follows.

For the yoke of Christ is the Gospel, which joins Jews and Gentiles in the unity of faith.

## CHAPTER XII

Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. This movement signifies his incarnation, as he lived among human beings. The grainfields signify peoples; and appropriately on the Sabbath, because at that time one had to abstain from vices and remain by faith in contemplation of him.

His disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat them. According to another Evangelist, [Col. 0060B] “They rubbed them in their hands and ate.” For they were hungry for the salvation of the human race, and they began by their teaching to separate people from vices through examples of good works and to convert them into the inward parts of the Church.

When the Pharisees saw this, they said to him: Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths. The Jews were always jealous both of the apostles’ teaching and of the salvation of the Gentiles. They reproached Christ as a transgressor of the law.

But he said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him? To those who reproached him for transgressing the law, Christ opposed testimony from the Scriptures and an outstanding prophecy, as though he were saying: If the typological David is read as having broken the precepts of the law because of necessity, how much more may the true David provide for the necessity of his own.

Or have you not read in the law, and so forth, because this is greater than the temple. This is an adverb of place, and the meaning is: If, because of the necessity of sacrifices, the Sabbath is violated without guilt by priests, how much more, in my presence, may my disciples, who are suffering necessity, fail to observe the Sabbaths without guilt, since I hold priests and Sabbaths under my power.

If you had known what this means, “I desire mercy,” and not sacrifice, you would never have condemned the innocent. If you had wished to understand that God chose to show mercy to the human race more through the apostles than to have the legal sacrifices observed by you carnally, you would in no way have taken pleasure in disparaging them over trifles.

The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. And when he had crossed over from there, he came into their synagogue. Because he is both the Son of Man and the Son of God, he is lord not only of priests but also of Sabbaths.

And behold, there was a man with a withered hand. This man signifies the Gentile people, who, according to Luke, had a withered right hand and a healthy left: he did not extend his right hand to the poor, and while laboring in earthly matters, he was idle in divine ones.

And they questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbaths?—in order to accuse him. They intended to accuse him of transgressing the law if he said that it was lawful to heal on the Sabbaths; but if he denied it, they wished to call him unmerciful because he prohibited an act of mercy.

But he said to them: Which of you will be a man who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbaths, [Col. 0061A] will not take hold of it, and so forth? He set before both their avarice and their greed a fitting example: they certainly did not observe Sabbath rest with regard to earthly property, being inflamed by the jaws of avarice, although they disparaged his showing mercy to human beings.

Then he said to the man: Stretch out your hand. And he stretched it out. Through the preachers he was urging the Gentiles to fulfill faith through works.

And it was restored to health like the other. Just as earlier he had cared only for the body, so afterward he hastened to care for the soul by giving generously in almsgiving.

But the Pharisees went out, and so forth, to discover how they might destroy him. They are rightly said to go out because they separated themselves from the faith of Christ and withdrew from the fellowship of those to whom the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him,” and so forth. They were thinking of killing Christ as a transgressor of the law because he had commanded the man to stretch out his hand, as though they themselves at least did not extend their hands in taking food.

But Jesus, knowing this, and so forth, healed them all. Because he was God, he knew the secret wickedness of their hearts; avoiding the crowds of unbelievers, he chose the fellowship of the faithful and healed them not only from bodily infirmity but also from infirmity of heart.

And he charged them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying, and so forth. He commanded them not to make him known not out of fear of suffering, but so that they would not have an opportunity to destroy themselves.

Behold, my servant whom I have chosen. According to his humanity, he is servant and chosen; according to his divinity, he is God who chooses.

In whom my soul has been well pleased. It was well pleased because no deceit was found in his mouth—not that God has a soul, so that God and his soul would be different things, but this was said on account of human weakness, so that you might understand and hope in the help of divine mercy. For visible things must lead to invisible things, as the Psalmist says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:8).

I will place my Spirit upon him. Insofar as he is human, I place it upon him; insofar as he is God, he has always possessed it.

And he announced judgment to the Gentiles. Although he announces that judgment to come threatens everyone, he is nevertheless said to have announced it to the Gentiles because they especially determined to receive the ministry of this announcement with believing hearts.

Nor will anyone hear his voice in the street. That is, they strive to hear his voice with the ears of the heart not because they walk on the broad way, but because they strive to enter through the narrow gate.

He will not break the bruised reed. He calls the Israelite people, although it is one kingdom, a bruised reed because they neglected to preserve among themselves the foundation of faith and the bond of charity. He did not wish to break it because he delayed giving them the occasion of their destruction in their killing. In another sense, he will break the bruised reed because now, in the Church, anyone who denies a sinner the help he needs—whether in teaching, examples, or anything else—breaks him.

[Col. 0062A] And he will not extinguish the smoldering flax. That is, he will not cause the Gentile people to give off the bitterest smoke of error; but now, in the Church, he will extinguish the smoldering flax because he sees some good in a poor and despised person that could have benefited him. Yet he spurned this because he either considers the person a sinner or sees him as poor.

Until he brings judgment to victory. And in his name the Gentiles will hope. He brought judgment to victory, with respect to his condemnation, when he rose after overcoming death; and he will still bring it to victory on the day of the dreadful examination, when he will thrust all his adversaries into eternal condemnation.

Then a demon-possessed man was brought to him, blind and mute, and he healed him. This man signifies the Gentile people, brought to faith through preachers of Christ; blind because he did not know the way of truth; mute because he did not open his mouth in praise of the Creator; and demon-possessed because through idolatry he served demons. Every day the Church continues to offer people devoted to this kind of ignorance to the Lord through devout prayers, teachings, and examples.

And all the crowds were astonished, and so forth: “Is this not the Son of David?” They were astonished when they saw the sign because they believed him to be an ordinary man born from David’s seed, and they called him the son of David because they saw that he was merciful, since they knew that David, being merciful, had learned compassionately to spare a captured persecutor.

But when the Pharisees heard this, they said: This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: What they could not deny they interpreted wrongly, because they attributed the work of the Holy Spirit to an unclean spirit. Baal himself is Beel; *zebub* means “fly.” Because flies observed the rotting flesh and blood of the victims there, he was called Beelzebul, meaning “the man of flies” or “the one who has flies.”

Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand? The meaning is: If I, according to your opinion, cast out demons by the prince of demons, you may at least infer from this that my kingdom is stable and firmly established in power, since you see that I, together with the Father, possess such power over him.

Therefore they themselves will be your judges. If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, the one by whom your exorcists cast them out—or your apostles, who do not possess such power [possibly: “who do possess such power”] over the devil—then, because they attribute their work to God and not to the devil, they show that you are condemnable, since you ascribe the work of the Holy Spirit to an unclean spirit.

But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. If I cast out demons through the Holy Spirit, know that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom has been opened to believers. Or he called the Church, or the holy Scripture, the kingdom of God, as he says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is among you”; and again: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you,” and what follows (Matthew 21:43).

Or how can anyone, and so forth, then plunder his house? The house signifies the world; the strong man, the devil; the vessels are the hearts of wicked people. Christ was plundering these vessels after binding the devil when he rose, having destroyed death, and gave us the hope of rising again and reaching the heavenly kingdom.

Whoever is not with me is against me. The devil is not with Christ but against Christ: Christ is humble and kind, while the devil is proud and envious and seeks to take away from us the happiness offered by Christ.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. Christ gathers by preaching virtues, through which people may ascend and reach the vision of divine power; the devil scatters by dragging them toward vices.

Every sin, and so forth, the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven. He said that all sins could be forgiven through repentance, but denied that the blasphemy of the Spirit could be forgiven, because they were conscious of their own wickedness and, envying the salvation of others, said that the work of the Holy Spirit belonged to the prince of demons.

And whoever says a word against the Son of Man, [and so on], “neither in this age nor in the age to come.” Whoever, because of the visible weakness of the flesh, refuses to believe in my divinity can receive forgiveness through repentance; but whoever, out of despair, says that the Holy Spirit cannot forgive sins in baptism, or that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, once received, can confer no benefit of forgiveness and contributes nothing more than other foods, will receive forgiveness neither in this age nor in the age to come. And because he denies forgiveness to the despairing both here and in the future, he plainly indicates that some sins are forgiven in the future: such are idle words and superfluous thoughts, if one strives to do good and desires to correct his evil deeds before the day of death.

“Either make,” [and so on], “the tree is known by its fruit.” The good tree is Christ, producing salvation; the evil tree is the devil, producing destruction for those who agree with him. Alternatively, the Jews are rightly called an evil tree, since they attributed the fruit of good works to the evil tree, that is, to the devil. Therefore he rebukes them with a fitting reprimand, saying:

“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” That is: words of blasphemy proceed from the wickedness of your hearts.

“But I say to you,” [and so on], “they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.” It is as though he had said: If an account must be given even for superfluous speech, how much more will your criminal blasphemy produce eternal condemnation.

“For by your words,” [and so on], “you will be condemned.” That is: you will be crowned for good speech, but for evil speech you will be condemned.

Then they answered him, [and so on], “To see a sign.” Luke says that they desired to see a sign from heaven. Finally, they wanted to have a sign of his divinity like that which occurred under the prophet Elijah, when fire came down from heaven and consumed two commanders of fifty.

But he answered, [and so on], “No sign except that of the prophet Jonah.” He calls it an evil generation because of its transgression of God’s commandments; adulterous, because, having abandoned the true God, it served the idols of various peoples. “To it,” he says, “I do not wish to show a sign of my divinity from heaven, but from earth I will show an example of my passion.”

“For just as Jonah was,” [and so on]. For if you count Friday together with the preceding night, the Sabbath together with its night, and the Lord’s night with the following day, you will find three days. Moreover, he called the tomb “the heart of the earth.” Jonah, because his name is interpreted as “dove” or “mourning,” signifies Christ, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove; for he bore our sorrows in his body upon the wood. Nineveh is interpreted as “beautiful”; it signifies the Church adorned with the beauty of virtues. That Christ had lain in the tomb for two nights and one complete day signifies that by the single death of his body he destroyed the double death of body and soul.

“The men of Nineveh,” [and so on], “more than Jonah is here.” Not in a judgment of authority, but in the correction of life. The Ninevites show that the Jewish people are condemnable, because Jonah preached only briefly and with words, whereas Christ taught for a much longer time both by words and by signs of divine power.

“The queen of the South,” [and so on], “more than Jonah is here.” She shows that the Jewish people are worthy of condemnation, because she came from the ends of the earth to learn wisdom from Solomon. The Jews, however, refused to learn wisdom from Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, dwelling in their midst. The queen of the South and the men of Nineveh signify the whole company of the saints, because the saints strive to correct their offenses through repentance, or take precautions lest they sin through wisdom.

“But when the unclean spirit has gone out of a person.” At the time when the law was given, the unclean spirit was driven out by the Jews; now, in baptism, it is compelled to depart from each of the faithful.

“He wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” The dry places are the hearts of believers, which lack the moisture of lust. Wandering around in them, he will not find consent to his wicked suggestion.

“Then he says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when he comes, he finds it empty, swept clean, and adorned.” He will find the empty house—that is, a person sluggish in good works—adorned with the pretense of virtues through hypocrisy.

Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there. He takes the seven principal vices, from which the seed of every kind of wickedness sprouts; he himself is the eighth.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. So will it be with this most evil generation.” The condition of the Israelite people after the law had been corrupted was worse than it had been in Egypt before the law; and for every person it is better not to recognize the way of truth than, having recognized it, to turn back from it.

While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. Someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.” He did not report this simply, as it might seem, but deceitfully: he wished to test whether he would place maternal affection before the duty of preaching.

But he answered, [and said], “My brother, sister, and mother.” He did not ask as though he were ignorant, nor did the mother thoughtlessly despise her children, since the law commanded that father and mother be honored. Rather, he wished to show that spiritual kinship is greater than physical kinship, as he said elsewhere to his disciples: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Mystically, however, the mother is the Synagogue, and the Jews are said to stand outside because they were unable to enter the faith of Christ together with the believing Gentiles. But someone may ask how the Gentile people, doing the Father’s will, can become the mother of Christ. Since by believing they become brothers and sisters, she undoubtedly becomes a mother by preaching, when she gives birth to others for God through instruction and brings them to faith.

## Chapter XIII

At that time Jesus went out of the house. That is, from the Israelite people, among whom he had taken flesh from a virgin.

He sat beside the sea. That is, through the apostles he was preached throughout the world to the various nations.

And great crowds gathered around him. Through preachers, crowds of believers were gathered to Christ.

So that he entered a small boat, [and spoke] in parables. The small boat signifies the Church, which in the world is surrounded by the waves of persecutions. Those who stand on the shore, however, are touched neither by the waves of the sea nor able to enter the boat, yet are not without the word of God. They signify those who, newly coming to the faith, have been stripped of the error of unbelief but have not yet entered the Church through the washing of baptism. Alternatively, the crowd standing on the shore signifies those who persevere here in the firmness of faith, are not touched by the error of unbelief, and yet are not permitted to enter the gate of paradise.

“Behold, a sower went out to sow his seed.” Christ went out from the bosom of the Father into the world to scatter the seed of his teaching, both through himself and through his preachers, so that the fruit of good works might grow in the hearts of believers.

Some fell beside the road, and the birds ate them. The seed falls beside the road when the heart of the hearer tramples underfoot the preaching it has heard through wicked thoughts, and unclean spirits remove it from the memory.

Others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil; and immediately they sprang up, and so forth. The rocky places signify hardness of heart, where there is no depth of soil—that is, no devotion to discipline. When the sun of persecution rises, or when hidden temptation comes, the word of God received in the heart with joy dries up, because it lacks the root of charity.

Others fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. The thorns signify riches, which pierce the heart with pains, preventing those who seek them from finding them; and, once they have been found, preventing them from being preserved. They wound the purpose of the possessor and drag it toward eternal condemnation.

But others fell on good soil, [and so on], another thirtyfold. The good soil signifies perfect hearts. In one person the word of God produces faith in the Trinity, which is signified by the number thirty; in another, the perfection of good works, represented by sixty; in another, perseverance, which leads to eternal reward, represented by the number one hundred. Some have understood the thirtyfold as married persons, the sixtyfold as widows, and the hundredfold as virgins.

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Whoever has the will should understand with the ears of the heart.

The disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” and so on. As Mark says, “To these it has not been given”; but “to those,” because they are very strong, everything is presented in parables. Those who strive to enter the sanctuary of God will understand the final things of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. And rightly they hear in parables, because they do not wish to recognize the truth with the senses of their hearts closed.

“Whoever has, to him more will be given, and he will abound; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” Whoever possesses love of the word will be given the understanding to comprehend what he loves. But whoever does not possess love of hearing—even if he appears to possess something through natural intelligence or literary training—will lose even this, so that he may rejoice in no sweetness of true wisdom.

Although this may seem to have been said especially about the apostles, to whom it was given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God through charity and faith, and about the Jews, who, seeing in parables, did not see, and hearing, did not understand, and who were about to lose the letter of the law, it can nevertheless be understood generally. Often an able teacher deprives himself of wisdom by neglecting it, while the simple and diligent person tastes it through labor. For this reason, at times the diligent person permits slowness of understanding, so that he may find the greater rewards of recompense the more he labors in the effort of discovery.

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.”

Now he explains to the apostles that he spoke to the crowds in parables because they arrogantly considered themselves to be seeing and hearing. For this reason they were unwilling to submit themselves to heavenly instruction, so that, while the simple and humble came to know the heavenly mysteries, they themselves would remain empty of spiritual understanding.

It is not unreasonable to say that the Jews were blinded so that they would not understand what the Lord spoke in parables, in order that, when their faith in him had been provoked, they might crucify him; and afterward, terrified by the miracles performed in his name after the resurrection, they might be humbled all the more by the guilt of the Lord’s death and love him more intensely, rejoicing that so great a crime had been forgiven them. Their pride was so great that it had to be cast down by such humiliation.

“So that the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled in them, saying: ‘You will hear with hearing and will not understand; and seeing, you will see, and will not see.’” This concerns the crowds, who possess bodily sight and hearing outwardly but have deprived themselves of sight and hearing inwardly, in body and heart.

“For the heart of this people has grown dull.” He says that the heart of the Jews has grown dull through the grossness of wickedness and the abundance of sin.

“They have heard heavily with their ears.” Because they received the Lord’s word ungratefully, closed their eyes, and did not deserve salvation afterward. They are blind not by nature but by will.

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. For truly I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.” The prophets Abraham, Isaiah, and Micah saw, but they looked from afar and greeted salvation as in a mirror and in an enigma. The apostles, however, had the Lord present among them and did not need to be taught through angels or through various forms of visions.

Those whom Matthew calls prophets and righteous people, Luke called prophets and kings. For they are truly great kings, who know how to rule and prevail rather than succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations.

He presented them with another parable, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.” He is rightly called “like” something when he is found to be entirely suited to it. Thus he sows good seed in the field of his body, because he strives to bring the seed of good will to the perfection of works.

“But while people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and went away.” This statement urges us to be watchful, lest, while we grow sluggish through idleness, the devil scatter the filth of vices over the seed of good will.

“But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared. The servants of the master of the household came and said to him, ‘Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field?’” and so forth. Here an example of patience is given to us, so that, just as the master of the household was patient with the enemy’s deceit, so we may not immediately resort to revenge when we suffer some injury, but rather to endurance.

The servants said to him, [and so on], “lest, while you uproot them, you also uproot the wheat with them.” Here we have an example of discernment and of tolerating the wicked, lest, if by taking revenge we repay evil with retaliation, we provide the good with a scandalous example to imitate.

“Let both grow until the harvest,” [and so on], “but gather the wheat into my barn.” From this we learn the long-suffering of patience, so that through long-suffering we may meditate upon justice and not neglect patience in judgment.

He presented them with another parable, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches.”

The mustard seed is the preaching of the Gospel and knowledge of the Scriptures, which leads to life. The one who sows is our understanding and spirit, which, receiving the seed of preaching and nourishing it with the moisture of faith, makes it sprout in the field of its breast.

It is the smallest of all disciplines because, at the beginning of its teaching, it is not regarded as credible: it preaches that the God who is the author of life died, and it proclaims the scandal of the cross. Compared with the doctrines of the philosophers it seems much smaller. But because their teachings, softened like vegetables, quickly grow and collapse, this smallest seed, when it has been preached in the soul of a believer or throughout the whole world, grows not into a vegetable but into a tree, so that souls may rest in its branches—that is, in the diversity of its doctrines.

The mustard seed can also signify the humility of the Lord’s incarnation. A man, Joseph, took it and buried it in a garden; it grew into a tree because, rising, it ascended into heaven. It spread out its branches, that is, its preachers, in whom all the faithful might rest from the weariness of this life.

He spoke another parable to them: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened.”

This woman is the apostolic preaching mentioned above, or the Church gathered from the various nations. She took the leaven—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures—and hid it in three measures of flour, so that spirit, soul, and body might not differ among themselves, but, agreeing as one, might obtain whatever they asked of the Father.

Alternatively, the woman is the Church, which, among the branches of the sons of Noah, brings people through the leaven of faith not to a threefold division but to the unity of divinity. And according to Plato, we unite the three passions of the human soul through leaven when, from the rational faculty—which he thought to be in the brain—we possess prudence; in the irascible faculty—which he thought to be in the gall—we maintain firmness against vices; and in the concupiscible faculty—which he regarded as being in the liver—we take up the desire for virtues.

A *satum* is a measure among the Palestinians, containing one and a half *modii*.

Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the crowds, and he spoke nothing without a parable. For he continues to speak in parables to the unbelieving crowds up to the present. The disciples—that is, believers—ask him at home, so that they may know the hidden mysteries.

“I will open my mouth in parables,” and so on. This testimony is taken from the Seventieth Psalm and is spoken in the person of the Lord. For no one was found in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth who was worthy to open the book and break its seals.

Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house, and his disciples approached him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” Having dismissed the Jewish crowds, he enters the Church of the Gentiles, and there, while the faithful disciples learn devoutly, he explains the divine mysteries.

What, then, has been explained by the Lord—we ought to accept with faith. But what has been left unspoken and entrusted to us, let us touch on briefly. The people sleeping are the teachers of the Church; the servants are the angels, who daily see the face of the Father. The teachers must therefore remain watchful, lest the enemy—that is, the devil—sow weeds, namely, the doctrines of heretics.

In the statement, “Let both grow,” a place is given for repentance, so that we may not cut off a brother too quickly. The Apostle’s statement seems contrary to this: “With such a person do not even eat.” But between wheat and weeds, so long as they are still grass, the distinction is either nonexistent or difficult. Here the Lord warns us that, whenever something is ambiguous, we should not quickly pronounce judgment, but reserve the outcome for God the judge.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” [and so on], “and he bought that field.” The hidden treasure is the desire for heaven; the field is the discipline of heavenly study, in which the treasure is hidden from human praise so that it may be kept safe from unclean spirits.

He certainly buys this field by selling everything who tramples all earthly desires under the guardianship of heavenly desire. Alternatively, the treasure in the field is the two Testaments. Perceiving that much lies hidden in them, a person gains leisure for himself by despising temporal things, so that he may be rich in the knowledge of God. Envy does not conceal this treasure; rather, it is hidden so that it may not be lost.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls,” and so on. Having found one precious pearl, he sold everything he possessed, because, compared with heavenly life, everything one possesses becomes worthless.

If you wish to examine holy people, you will find one Jesus Christ, who is without fault, better than them all. If you seek understanding, you will find that he alone surpasses the rest: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). And among all commandments, charity is likewise the most excellent, in which all things are restored; and among the other books, the Gospel is shown to be the strongest.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” [and so on], “but the bad they threw outside.” The net signifies the Church, which invites everyone alike to the forgiveness of sins. It is drawn to the shore—that is, to the end of the age—through the teaching of preachers; at the end of the age, the righteous are received into heavenly dwellings, while the impious are sent into the outer darkness.

Jesus said to them: “Therefore every scribe who has been instructed,” [and so on], “new and old.” He admonishes the apostles that whatever they preached in the Gospel they should confirm by the words of the law and the prophets. It is as though he had said plainly: In the holy Church, the learned preacher is the one who knows how to bring forth new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and old things concerning the terror of punishment.

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, [and so on], “this wisdom and these mighty works.”

There is a difference between the Synagogue, which is interpreted as “assembly,” and the Church, which is interpreted as “calling.” Animals and inanimate things can be assembled, but only beings possessing reason can be called together. Therefore the ecclesiastical writers rightly preferred to call the people of the new grace, summoned as rational beings into the unity of faith, the Church rather than the Synagogue, as though it were an assembly of irrational beings.

“Is this not the carpenter’s son,” [and so on], “and they were scandalized because of him.” The error of the Jews is the salvation of the Gentiles. It was certainly not without the cause of a definite mystery that Christ, appearing in the flesh, wished to be called the carpenter’s son. His father is truly a carpenter, since he fashioned from nothing all that is in heaven and on earth; and even now he daily fashions vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy.

Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country.” Not only he himself, the head of the prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and all the lesser prophets were held in less esteem in their own cities than in foreign ones, because it is almost natural for fellow citizens to envy one another. Thus the Jews considered not the presence of his works but the weakness of his human nature.

And he did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief. He did not wish to reveal to them many miracles of his divinity, lest, the more clearly they saw the power of his divinity shining forth, the more culpable they would become by despising the truth.

# Book Three

## Chapter XIV

At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus. And he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are performed through him.” Herod, thinking correctly about the resurrection of the dead, in every way declared to his servants that the saints would rise again with greater power, because he thought that John, who had performed no signs, had risen from death. The Jews, however, believed that Christ had not risen but had been taken away by his disciples. By saying that John performed mighty works because he had risen from death, this foreigner showed a readier disposition toward faith than that of the Jews.

For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother. For John had said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her,” and so on. Ancient history relates that Philip, the son of Herod the Great, under whom Christ fled into Egypt, had taken the daughter of King Aretas as his wife. But when disputes arose between the father-in-law and son-in-law, and also between the brothers, Aretas took his daughter away from Philip and gave her to Herod, the enemy of Philip, to increase the insult.

But when John rebuked Herod because he had taken the wife of his living brother, Herod, loving his wife more than God’s commandments, wanted to kill John. Fearing the people, however, who had been baptized by John, he found in an oath a means of carrying out the crime he had conceived, as the following events make clear.

On Herod’s birthday the daughter of Herodias danced, [and so on], and because of those who were reclining with him, he ordered it to be given. Two mortals, we read, celebrated their birthdays, but both polluted them with blood. They warn us that we should fear the day of death more than celebrate the day of birth with indulgence.

Herod cannot be excused for the murder, since he had sworn for the purpose of preparing a trap for the opportunity that would come. Herodias feared that the unlawful marriage might be dissolved; therefore she instructed her daughter to ask for John’s head, so that she might have control of the tongue that she knew wished to forbid the incest.

Herod was not truly saddened by such a request. Rather, it is the custom of historians to narrate events as they appeared to those present at the time. He was pretending sadness on his face while rejoicing in his mind.

He sent and beheaded John in prison, [and so on], and it was taken to her mother. John’s beheading signifies that the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the prophets. John was diminished by the loss of his head, while Christ was exalted on the cross, because Christ had to increase and John to diminish.

His disciples approached, [took his body], and came and told Jesus. Those who buried him and reported the matter appear to signify those who, after the law had been extinguished for them in a carnal sense, passed over to the grace of the Savior, because John’s burial signifies the abolition of the law.

When Jesus heard this, he withdrew, [and went] to a deserted place apart. Not through fear of death, but out of mercy toward his enemies, lest they add murder to murder. Alternatively, after John’s head had been cut off—that is, after the prophetic oracle of the Jews had been lost—Christ withdrew into the desert of the Church, which previously had no husband.

When the crowds heard this, they followed him on foot from the cities. The crowds of the Gentiles, converted from their former errors to faith in Christ, followed him through their own labor.

When he went out, he saw a great crowd, and had compassion on them, and healed their sick. So that complete faith might immediately obtain its reward, Jesus went out. This signifies that the crowds had the will to go but not the strength to precede him; therefore he goes out to have mercy.

When evening came, the disciples approached him, saying, “The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed; send the crowds away,” and so on. That evening, when the true sun had set as the end of the age approached, signifies that the Jews murmured against the Gentiles, who were more suited to seek food for themselves in the gatherings of heretics than to make use of the nourishment of the divine books.

But Jesus said to them, “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat.” He urges them to break the bread so that, when they testified that they did not have enough, the manifestation of the sign might become clearer. At the same time he suggests that our hearts are to be nourished by those whose examples have awakened them to love heavenly things.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that John says the Lord tested Philip to discover where food might be found for the crowds, while the other evangelists report that the disciples said to the Lord, “Send the crowds away,” and so on, to which he replied, according to Matthew, “They do not need to go away,” it may be understood that after these words the Lord looked upon Philip and said what John records. Then, what John records as answered by Philip, Mark records as answered by the disciples, wishing it to be understood that Philip spoke on behalf of the others.

They answered him, “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.” The five loaves signify the five books of the law of Moses; the two fish signify prophecy and the Psalms. The Old Testament teaches this threefold distinction when Scripture says: “Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

He said to them, “Bring them here to me.” Hear, Marcion; hear, Manichaeus: he commands that these things be sanctified and multiplied. The eyes of all hope in him, for he fills every living creature with blessing and gives food to everyone.

And when he had ordered the crowd to recline on the grass. To recline on the grass means to trample, with contempt of the mind, the flowers and pleasures of this age and the allurements of the flesh. Alternatively, according to another evangelist, he had them recline on the ground by fifties and hundreds, because through the repentance signified by fifty one ascends to the perfection signified by one hundred. The different arrangements of those reclining are the different gatherings of the Churches.

Having taken the five loaves and the two fish, he took them into his hands, because he himself completed everything by his work.

Looking up toward heaven. Because he taught us to hope for help from there.

He blessed and broke them. Because he showed what holiness the law and the prophets possessed.

And he gave the loaves to the disciples, [and so on], and they were satisfied. The Lord first disclosed the mysteries of the Old Testament through his distribution to the preachers of the Gospel; then they provided nourishment and spiritual refreshment from them to the crowds of all nations.

And they gathered the leftovers, twelve full baskets of fragments. The twelve baskets are the twelve apostles, who gathered the mysteries from those fragments, because what cannot be understood by the uneducated must be sought out by the perfect.

The number of those who ate was five thousand men, besides women and children. This multitude had not yet reached the number seven. The four thousand who eat and the five fish signify those who, still placed in a worldly condition, know how to make good use of outward things. The four thousand and the seven loaves signify those who, instructed inwardly by sublime spiritual grace, are greater. The women and children signify the weaker sex and fragile age, who are not yet worthy of the gift.

Immediately Jesus ordered the disciples to get into the small boat and go ahead of him across the strait, until he had dismissed the crowds. John alone reveals why he sent the disciples away and went up the mountain to pray: he says that Jesus withdrew because they wanted to make him king. Here we are taught to avoid seeking human favor as a reward for the good things we do.

Mark says that the Lord compelled his disciples to cross over and go ahead to Bethsaida, which is a city in Galilee belonging to Andrew and Peter. What Luke says—“Jesus withdrew to a deserted place which is Bethsaida,” and so on—may, unless I am mistaken, be understood from the fact that he does not say “which is Bethsaida” but “who is.” He therefore may not have intended the city itself, but the deserted place belonging to its boundaries.

After dismissing the crowd, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. He teaches us to advance beyond earthly things and ascend to the summit of a higher concern.

When evening came, he was there alone. But the boat was being tossed about in the middle of the sea, for the wind was contrary. This labor signifies the adversities of the present age and the blasts of unclean spirits that confront those striving to reach the shore of the heavenly homeland.

In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. The last watch shows that divine mercy offers help to those who, under pressure, consider human weakness and the feebleness of their own strength.

When they saw him, [and so on], “It is a phantom.” O Marcion and Manichaeus, if the Lord was not born of a virgin but appeared in a phantom, how is it that the apostles now fear seeing a phantom?

And they cried out from fear. Confused shouting and an uncertain voice are the judgment of great fear; but, according to the Psalmist, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.”

“Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” He heals what was troubling them first by saying, “Take courage.” Then he says, “It is I,” without adding what he is, so that they might recognize him by his familiar voice; or so that they might understand that he was the very one whom they knew had spoken to Moses: “You shall say this to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you.’”

Peter answered and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the water.” And he said, “Come.” In every passage Peter is found to possess the most ardent faith. With that same ardor of faith he says here, as it were openly, “You command, and suddenly the waters become solid.” Thus a body that is heavy by itself becomes light.

And Peter came down from the boat to go to Jesus. Let those who say that the true flesh of Christ did not walk upon the waters explain how Peter walked, since they will not deny that Peter was a real human being.

But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me.” He is left for a little while so that his faith may be strengthened and he may understand that he was preserved not by the ease of his request but by the Lord’s power.

Immediately stretching out his hand, he took hold of him and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” The one whom elsewhere he saw denying him, here he extended his hand to prevent him from sinking into the depths. If Peter, whom we said above possessed the most ardent faith, is rebuked in this way, what must be said of us, who do not possess even the smallest portion of such little faith?

Mystically, Peter signifies the Church journeying toward the heavenly homeland and treading upon the waves of this age with the straight step of faith and the practice of good works. When he turns back even slightly from the course of faith and, terrified in the storm, begins to sink beneath the waves, he represents the weaker members of the Church, whom the storm of temptations frightens. The right hand of divine protection pulls them out so that they do not sink completely.

And when he had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased. For into whatever heart God comes through the grace of his love, all the battles of the world, of vices, and of evil spirits are immediately suppressed and grow quiet.

And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. The land is called Gennesaret because it lies beside the lake of Gennesaret. Likewise, Tiberias is named after the nearby city that was called Cenereth but, after being restored by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was called Tiberias.

Gennesaret is therefore interpreted as “the beginning of rising.” Then full tranquility will be restored to us, when through Christ the inheritance of paradise is restored to us.

When the men of that place recognized him, they sent word throughout the whole region and brought to him all who were ill. They begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were made well.

This act signifies the firm faith of the Gentiles. Not content with the salvation of those who are present, they invite those deceived by various errors throughout the surrounding regions to run to the true physician. Understand the fringe as the smallest commandment, which may not be transgressed; or as the assumption of flesh, through which we come to the Word of God.

## Chapter XV

For God said: “Honor your father and your mother”; and, “Whoever curses father or mother,” and so on. Honor is indicated by providing the necessities of life, and cursing by withholding them. The scribes and Pharisees overturned this law and taught the most wicked children to say to their parents: “The gift that comes from me will benefit you.” Thus, fearing to accept what they had seen dedicated to God, the parents would choose to lead a life of poverty rather than eat from the consecrated offerings.

“Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying:” It was not because the saying prophesied concerning their wickedness was good, but because it corresponded well to their character. For they honored him with their lips when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth; and you do not care about anyone, for you do not regard a person’s status” (Matt. 22). But their heart was far from him, when they wished to trap him in his speech, as Luke testifies, saying that they asked: “Is it lawful to pay the tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 22).

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth.” The foods prohibited in the Law, and those eaten by the Gentiles, the Jews call common, and they think that the person who eats them is defiled. But the Savior shows that all things are clean when they are received with a clean conscience. If this is so, how can what Paul says stand: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10)? It must therefore be understood that these things are clean in themselves, as creatures of God; but the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

[Col. 0075A] “You know that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying.” You know that in this discourse every superstitious Jewish observance is destroyed, since they think that their religion consists in consuming some foods and abominating others.

“Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” If this is so, what of Paul’s statement: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. 3)? The question is resolved by what he says: “But God gave the growth.” God plants, and no one can uproot that planting unless it has turned toward an improper understanding. Hence it is said in Isaiah: “I planted you as a vineyard; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

“Leave them; they both fall into the pit.” He commands that the Pharisees be left to their own judgment, just as the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition.” They are rightly called blind guides of the blind: they not only fail to take care that they themselves do not fall into the snare, but also drag those who follow them with them into the precipice of death.

“Are you still without understanding?” The Lord rebukes the apostles because, in a matter that is clear, they seek a mystical interpretation.

“But what proceeds from the mouth comes out of the heart, and these things defile a person.” Therefore the governing faculty of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. Hence the devil can be the assistant and instigator of evil thoughts, but not their author. For he does not know how to probe the hidden recesses of the heart; rather, from a person’s bodily appearance [Col. 0075C] he judges what we are occupied with inwardly. When he sees someone intent upon a particular vice, he entices him and hastens to lead him astray.

“And Jesus, departing from there, withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.” At last, leaving his slanderers behind, he withdraws into the territory of foreign peoples.

“And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those regions and cried, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” This woman signifies the Church coming to the Lord from the dwelling-place of its former empty way of life.

“My daughter is grievously vexed by a demon.” That is, the Church, already believing on behalf of its peoples so that they too may be saved from error, implores divine mercy. Likewise, this daughter is any soul enslaved in the Church to the deceptions of evil spirits, for whom Mother Church [Col. 0075D] anxiously entreats the Lord, so that, while the soul itself is unable to accomplish anything by its own efforts, he may inwardly awaken it by inspiring it with knowledge of the true light.

In the tropological sense, the daughter vexed by a demon is the conscience of any person polluted by the filth of vices; its correction must be continually demanded from the merciful Creator with lamentation.

“But he did not answer her a word.” He did not wish to answer, lest he seem to contradict his own statement: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10), and thereby give his slanderers an opportunity. Mystically, however, if the Lord does not grant the requests of the Church’s first tears, he must be approached repeatedly with persistent crying; the intercession of his saints must be sought, so that they themselves [Col. 0076A] may plead with the Lord that the Church be heard. Thus, if she does not change her mind from her purpose, she will in no way be deprived of the fruit of her petition.

“Send her away, because she cries out after us.” The disciples did this because they did not yet understand the Lord’s mysteries, whether moved by compassion for the Syrophoenician woman or wishing to be rid of her persistence, lest she continually cry out to them as though they were an unmerciful physician. Mark says that this woman came to the Lord in the house, while Matthew depicts her as crying out behind him as he walked. This is to be understood as follows: the woman first came to Jesus while he was in the house, but, having failed to obtain an answer there, she followed him as he went out until she deserved to hear what follows:

“I was sent only to the sheep that have perished of the house [Col. 0076B] of Israel.” This does not mean that he was not sent to the Gentiles, but that he was sent first to Israel, so that, when they did not receive the Gospel, his transfer to the Gentiles might rightly take place.

“It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Under the person of the woman, the faith, patience, and humility of the Church are wonderfully proclaimed. Faith, because she believed that her daughter could be saved. Patience, because, though so often rejected, she persevered in prayer. Humility, because she compared herself not with dogs but with puppies. The table too is holy Scripture, from which puppies do not eat the children’s bread-crusts, but crumbs. For those who have turned to the faith, though formerly despised among the Gentiles, seek in the Scriptures not the surface of the letter but the spiritual meaning by which they may advance. And this takes place beneath the table [Col. 0076C], because they place the functions of their heart and body beneath the fulfillment of the divine commandments.

“O woman, great is your faith,” and so forth. In this woman the faith of the Gentiles is praised, which, immediately upon the apostles’ preaching, obtained complete salvation for itself and its people.

“And her daughter was healed from that hour.” Because of the mother’s humble and faithful speech, the demon left the daughter. This makes clear that through confession in baptism little ones are freed from the devil, although they are not yet able by themselves to do anything good or evil.

“And when Jesus had crossed over from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee, and, going up onto the mountain, he sat there.” That is, having completed the dispensation of salvation for the Gentiles, he returns to Judaea through preachers [Col. 0076D]. He goes up the mountain, calling us toward heavenly things; and he sits there, showing that rest must be sought in heaven.

“And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, and so forth.” With the Lord therefore seated on the mountain—that is, reigning gloriously in the citadel of heaven—the faithful crowds approach with devoted minds. They bring with them those who are mute in confessing the faith, blind through the error of unbelief, deaf and disobedient to the commands of their superiors, lame in wicked works, and weak under the burden of sins. They cast them all at Jesus’ feet through the teachings of the Gospel, because they submit them to his humanity to be healed.

“Then Jesus called his disciples and said: I have compassion on the crowd,” and so forth, “lest they faint on the way.” Here affection and compassion for human weakness are expressed, and an example is offered to teachers: they should share their counsels with their disciples. The crowd that has followed him for three days—that is, persevered with him in the faith of the Holy Trinity, or before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—the Lord does not wish to send away fasting from the nourishment of sacred instruction, lest, growing weary on the journey of this life, it fail to reach its desired lodging-place.

“But they said: Seven loaves and a few small fish.” The seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in which we find the feast of our minds through the grace of the Holy Spirit. By the small fish we understand the saints, through whom this same Scripture is seasoned.

“And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground.” At the feeding with five loaves, the crowd reclined on hay [Col. 0077B]; here, however, on the earth, because under the Law we are commanded to trample down the desires of the flesh, whereas in the New Testament we are to abandon temporal possessions themselves.

“And Jesus took the seven loaves and the fish,” and so forth. The breaking of the loaves signifies the opening of the sacraments, by which the world was to be nourished through the apostles’ distribution. By giving thanks, he showed his joy at the salvation of the human race and instructed us to give thanks to God in all things.

“And they all ate and were satisfied.” They are satisfied who commit to memory the nourishment of inward sweetness, so that they may find it again.

“And they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets full.” The basket, woven from rush and [Col. 0077C] palm, signifies the saints and all the perfected in the Church. Through the freshness of faith and the height of their hope for heavenly rewards, they are capable of receiving the higher commandments and counsels, because they surpass the general way of life of God’s people in the loftiness of mind and deed.

“And those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.” They are rightly said to have numbered four thousand, so that by this number he might teach that they were fed with the nourishment of the Gospel, or refreshed by the four virtues: prudence, in which knowledge of what should be sought and avoided is found; temperance, in which earthly desire is restrained; fortitude, in which firmness of spirit exists against temporal troubles; and justice, which is diffused through all the others [Col. 0077D] by love of God and neighbor. In the women and children we understand the weak and those easily led astray.

“And having dismissed the crowd, he went up into the boat and came to the region of Magadan.” Although Mark called this place Dalmanutha, there is nevertheless no doubt that the two names designate one place. For Magada is interpreted as “its fruits” or “messenger,” signifying a garden. Of this it is said: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride” (Song 4). There the fruits of virtue are produced, and from the guardians of the walls the Lord’s name is proclaimed with praise all day and night.

## CHAPTER XVI

“And the Pharisees came to him,” and so forth, “to show them a sign from heaven.” After the meals just mentioned, with manna sent everywhere from heaven, they wished to be fed for a long time, after the example of Moses.

“But he answered and said: In the evening,” and so forth. From the elements, rainy and clear days can be predicted; but the teachers of the Law were unable to understand the Savior’s coming from the prophets’ predictions. Spiritually, however, when evening has come, you say: “It will be clear, for the sky is red.” This signifies that through the blood of Christ’s Passion forgiveness of sins is granted at his first coming.

“And in the morning: Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy.” This signifies that at his second coming he will come with fire going before him.

“And he left them and departed.” He rightly departed, leaving the adulterers behind, because, according to the Apostle, “there is no fellowship between light and darkness” (2 Cor. 6).

“And when his disciples had come across the lake, they had forgotten to take bread.” This forgetfulness shows that the apostles had very little concern for the flesh: they possessed the bread of life, the Lord, by which they were nourished in their hearts.

“He said to them: Look out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Mark adds here: “and the leaven of Herod” (Mark 8). The leaven of the Pharisees is to preach the Law in words while attacking it by one’s deeds. The leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, and—what is the source of crimes—hatred and persecution directed against Christ and his saints.

[Col. 0078C] “Then Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi.” This city, restored by the tetrarch Philip and named in honor of Tiberius Caesar, is now called Paneas. It lies in the province of Phoenicia, at the foot of Lebanon, where the two springs of the Jordan and Dan arise.

“Then he questioned his disciples, saying: Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He asks appropriately, not “Who do they say that I am?” but “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” For those who speak of the Son of Man are people. But those who understand his divinity are called gods.

“But who do you say that I am?” He does not ask because he is ignorant of the disciples’ and outsiders’ opinions, but so that he may reward their confession of faith with a worthy recompense.

“Peter answered and said: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He calls God “living,” expressing both the name and the nature, in contrast with the false gods of whom we sing: “They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes,” and so forth (Ps. 113).

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.” Bar-Jonah in Syriac is rendered in Latin as “son of the dove.” Here Peter’s simplicity is shown: he is called the son of spiritual grace.

“For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you.” That is, human beings puffed up with carnal wisdom have not revealed it.

“And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Metaphorically he says to him: “Upon this rock”—that is, upon the Savior whom you have confessed—the Church is built. He has granted the faithful confessor a share in his name.

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” He calls heretical perversity the gates of hell, or vices and sins, from which death comes to the soul.

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” That is, the knowledge and power of discernment by which you should admit the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy.

“And whatever you bind,” and so forth. This power is undoubtedly given to all the apostles, to whom after the resurrection he says generally: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and so forth (John 20). The same office is also entrusted to bishops, presbyters, and the whole Church, although some of them, misunderstanding it, suppose that they can condemn the innocent and absolve the guilty. They can do no such thing; rather, by attempting this, they deprive themselves of the power granted to them.

“And Jesus commanded his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.” He explains the reasons for the prohibition of preaching at that time when he adds:

“From that time Jesus began to show his disciples,” and so forth, “and rise again on the third day.” The meaning is: Preach me at the time when I have suffered these things. For it is not now useful to preach Christ and proclaim his majesty when, shortly afterward, they will see him scourged and crucified.

“And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” Or, as it is better expressed in Greek: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen.” He took him aside so that, in the presence of his fellow disciples, he would not seem to rebuke his teacher. He began to rebuke him out of the affection of one who loved him, as if to say: “My ears cannot accept this, nor can it happen that the Son of God should be killed.”

“But he turned and said to Peter: Get behind me, Satan.” Satan is interpreted as “adversary.” Because, he says, you speak against my will, you are called Satan; but follow me by turning your will toward my will.

“You are a stumbling-block to me.” Because you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings. It is my will to die for the salvation of humanity; but you, desiring your own will, do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may bear much fruit.

“Then Jesus said to his disciples: If anyone wishes to come after me.” Having revealed the mystery of his Passion, he exhorts them, and at the same time all people, to follow the example of his Passion, promising the future salvation of souls.

“Let him deny himself.” We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through our old condition and strive toward what we are called to be through the new.

“And let him take up his cross and follow me.” Another Evangelist says that the cross must be carried daily, because the cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the spirit is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor, as the Apostle says: “I chastise my body,” and so forth (1 Cor. 9); and again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0080A] “For whoever wishes to save his life,” and so forth, “will find it.” The Church has one time of persecution and another of peace. In a time of persecution, the soul must be laid down; in a time of peace, earthly desires must be broken. Therefore blessed are those who hate their life by guarding it, lest they lose it by loving it.

“For what will it profit a person if he gains the whole world,” and so forth? Nothing profits us in a time of peace if we gain perishable things only to lose the eternal. He adds:

“Or what will a person give in exchange for his soul?” For Israel, Egypt and Ethiopia will be given; but for the human soul, only what the Psalmist sings: “I will take the cup of salvation,” and so forth.

“For the Son of Man is going to come,” and so forth, “with his angels.” After the terror he adds something joyful, as if to say: You fear death, but hear of the glory of the triumphant one and the ministry of the angels. For he who is lesser than the Father in his humanity is equal in majesty.

“Amen I say to you, there are some of those standing here,” and so forth. In this passage the Church is called the kingdom of God. He promised that some of his disciples would live in the body until they saw the Church of God raised up against the glory of this world: “when the Son of Man comes in his kingdom,” that is, when he extends his power. If, however, we wish to understand the kingdom of God here as heavenly blessedness, some of those standing there also saw this on the mountain.

## CHAPTER XVII

“And after six days Jesus took Peter,” and so forth. It is asked why Matthew and Mark testify that Jesus took the disciples with him after six days. Luke says: “About eight days later” (Luke 9). The answer is easy: here the intervening days are counted; there, the first day, on which he made this promise, and the final day, on which he fulfilled it. In the mystical sense, after the six ages of the world the saints are to rest from all labor; here, however, the eighth time signifies that they are to rise again. He takes only three with him either because “many are called, but few are chosen,” or because those who are now imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity will then deserve to rejoice in his eternal vision. He rightly adds “apart,” because then the righteous will be separated from the wicked, whose vices now oppress them, even though they are separated from them in the intention of faith.

“And he was transfigured before them.” He did not lose the substance of his true flesh, but showed the glory of his future resurrection [Col. 0080D], his own and ours. For as he then appeared to the apostles, so he will appear after the judgment to all the elect. At the very time of judgment, however, he will be seen by the good and the wicked in the form of a servant, so that the perverse may be able to understand that he is the judge whom they formerly rejected.

“And his face shone like the sun, and his garments,” and so forth. Since we know nothing brighter to look upon than the sun, not only the Lord’s glory but also that of the saints in the resurrection is compared with the sight of the sun. The Lord’s garments are understood as his saints, who before the ascent of the mountain seemed despised, because, according to the Apostle, “it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3). Mark says that they were white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can make. That is, the Savior does not wish to give his faithful on earth the brightness reserved for them in heaven; nor can a teacher of souls, or an outstanding cleanser of his own body, produce such purity as the Lord, who cleanses his Church from every defilement of flesh and spirit.

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” Luke writes more explicitly here, saying: “Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke of his departure.” Moses and Elijah signify the oracles of the Law and the prophets. These have been fulfilled in the Lord, are now open to the learned, and will be revealed more clearly in the future to the elect.
