In Moses, who died, those who are to be raised from the dead before the day of judgment are signified; in Elijah, who has not yet died, those who will be found alive are signified, because together they will be snatched up to meet the Lord in the air and will be led to eternal life.

“Peter said to him: Lord, it is good for us to be here,” and so forth. As another Evangelist testifies, blessed Peter did not know what he was saying: while placed on earth, he hoped that the heavenly promises would be granted to him; he thought that tabernacles should be fixed in the heavenly state, where no breath of adversity would remain; and he thought that the prophets and the Law should be separated from the Gospel, although they had been its ministers, so to speak. Yet he knew what he was saying when he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here,” because truly the only good of humanity is to enter into the joy of its Lord and stand in contemplation of him.

“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.” [Col. 0081C] From this let the one who sought a material tabernacle learn that in the resurrection the saints will be protected not by the covering of buildings but by the glory of the Holy Spirit.

“And behold, a voice from the cloud saying,” and so forth. It should be noted that just as the mystery of the Trinity was declared when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, so it was declared when he was glorified on the mountain. For the one whom we confess in baptism we will praise together in the resurrection. Here the Holy Spirit is in a bright cloud, there in a dove: the one who now keeps with a simple heart the faith he receives will then contemplate in open light what he had believed.

“And when the disciples saw this, they fell,” and so forth. They were afraid because they recognized that they had gone astray, either when they saw the cloud or when they heard the voice.

“And Jesus came and,” and so forth, “Do not be afraid.” For he mercifully touched them, so that, once fear had been removed, their minds might admit the sound of the speaker’s words.

“But when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one,” and so forth. Only Jesus is seen, the cloud, Moses, and Elijah having been removed, lest the Father’s testimony seem uncertain; or, in Christ, the veiled mysteries of the Law and the prophets are disclosed as fulfilled.

“And as they were descending from the mountain,” and so forth. He does not wish these things to be preached, lest after such great glory the cross become a stumbling-block.

“Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” This is the Pharisees’ tradition, according to Malachi: that Elijah will come before Christ’s advent and restore everything to its ancient condition. It is as though he were saying: [Col. 0082A] “If you have already come in glory, why does your precursor not appear?”

“But he answered and said to them: Elijah will indeed come,” and so forth. Elijah is promised as one who will come before the great day of the Lord, restoring everything, so that he may turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children—that is, so that they may believe in Christ, resist Antichrist, and restore what is subject to death.

“I tell you that Elijah has already come.” He says this about John, who was Elijah in spirit.

“And they did not recognize him,” and so forth. That is, they despised him and beheaded him.

“So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.” For Herod and Herodias, mocking him and sending him back to Pilate’s tribunal, consented to his crucifixion, although they themselves did not kill him.

[Col. 0082B] “And when he had come to the crowd, a man approached him,” and so forth. Matthew calls this man lunatic according to the popular report, while Mark describes him as deaf and mute—not because the moon serves demons, but because the demon, observing its course, attacks people, so that, if possible, through the creature it may disgrace the Creator. Tropologically, the lunatic, who does not persist in what he has begun, signifies those who are now carried into the fire of lust and now into the water of greed. The apostles are accused of being unable to heal him, not because this is attributed to their weakness, but to the unbelief of those who must be healed.

“O unbelieving generation,” and so forth. He says this not because he has been overcome by weariness, but as a compassionate physician who is angry not with the person but with the vice.

“And Jesus rebuked him.” From his previous sins it is understood that the demon had invaded this lunatic, since it is the person himself, not the demon, who is rebuked by the Lord.

“And the demon went out from him.” According to Mark, it went out crying loudly and tearing him; either to inspire hatred of the power or to avenge the injury of its expulsion.

“I also say to you: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed,” and so forth. Faith is not compared, as some think, with a small grain of mustard seed, but with a great one; nor is the moving of the mountain physical, but [it is] that of the man whom the Lord had transferred from being a lunatic.

“But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” Here he instructs not only the apostles but everyone for life, so that we may know that greater temptations must be overcome by this remedy.

[Col. 0082D] “And when he had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached,” and so forth. After Augustus Caesar, Judaea became tributary. Hence Joseph too departed for Bethlehem and was brought up in Nazareth, which is a town of Galilee, and Capernaum a city, where the tax collectors who demanded tribute did not dare to approach the Lord himself because of the greatness of his signs, but approached his disciple; or they questioned him maliciously, as elsewhere.

“And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying.” The Lord anticipated him so that the disciples would not be scandalized by the demand for tribute, since they saw that he knew what had happened in his absence.

“What do you think, Simon?” Since he had been born the Son of the king according to both substances, he ought not to pay tribute. Yet, through the humanity he assumed, just as he endured the cross for us, so he also paid the tribute.

“Go to the sea and cast a hook,” and so forth. Mystically, the fish that was caught first was in the depths of the sea—that is, the first Adam—so that through the second Adam the first might be liberated. The stater, that is, confession, contains two didrachmas; and rightly so, because it was paid for the sinner and the righteous, and the price was divided.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” After the tribute had been paid for Peter and the Lord, they supposed that he had been set above all the apostles. Therefore they ask who is greater in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the Church.

“And Jesus called a little child,” and so forth. Either he showed them simply a child in age, to demonstrate the likeness of innocence [Col. 0083B], or he showed them himself, who had come to minister rather than to be ministered to, in order to give them an example of humility.

“Unless you turn,” and so forth. He urges them to preserve, after the likeness of childhood, simplicity without arrogance.

“Therefore whoever humbles himself like this child,” and so forth. Whoever, like a child, does not remember an injury, does not take pleasure in looking at a woman, and humbles himself as an example of me—he will enter the kingdom of heaven.

“But whoever causes scandal,” and so forth. It is far better for a harmful person, even by the most atrocious temporal punishment, to end his bodily life than, by injuring his brother, to incur the eternal death of the soul.

“Woe to the world because of scandals.” Since scandals must exist in this world, woe to the one who, through his own fault, leaves himself open to scandals [Col. 0083C]. By this general judgment Judas is struck, for he had prepared his heart for betrayal.

“But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble,” and so forth. By the hand he warns us to exclude friends necessary for work; by the foot, those necessary for the business of traveling about, if they cannot be corrected and injure the soul.

“And if your eye causes you to stumble,” and so forth. “Scandal” is a Greek word that we render as “stumbling-block” or “striking of the foot.” If someone whose assistance we need tries to turn us aside onto the path of error, we must entirely abandon his company.

“I tell you that their angels,” and so forth. The angels of the little ones—that is, of the humble—enjoy constant contemplation of God. He also uses “face,” in human fashion, to mean certain vision and knowledge.

“For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.” That is, to restore what had been crushed and cast away; therefore do not destroy what has been saved by him.

“What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep,” and so forth. By means of this parable he teaches the same thing that he had previously taught in words: through the good shepherd he brings back the little sheep, carried on his shoulders because of its great weakness—that is, the human race, redeemed by his blood—and joins it to the number of the angels.

“But if your brother sins against you,” and so forth. If our brother sins against us, we have the power to forgive; but the brother must be rebuked privately, so that he does not remain in sin. If he listens, we gain his soul, and through the remedy given to another salvation is also acquired for us [Col. 0084A]. He therefore indicates the order by which we can avoid scandals: if we watch ourselves so that we injure no one, if we rebuke the sinner out of zeal for justice, and if from the heart we open the inward resources of mercy and compassion for repentance.

“But if he does not listen to you,” and so forth. Finally, many must be told to regard him as an object of detestation, so that one who could not be saved by shame may be saved by reproach. When it is said, “Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18), it is shown that the one who acts under the name of a believer while doing the deeds of unbelievers is more detestable than those who are wholly Gentiles.

“Whatever you bind,” and so forth. He grants the apostles authority, so that those condemned by such judgments may know that a human sentence is strengthened by divine authority.

[Col. 0084B] “For if two of you agree,” and so forth. We can also understand this spiritually: where spirit, soul, and body agree, they will obtain from the Father whatever they ask. There can be no doubt that the petition concerns good things when the body wishes to possess what the spirit desires.

“Then Peter came to him and said: Lord, how often will my brother sin against me,” and so forth? When asked how he should forgive a sinning brother, he replied: four hundred and ninety times, so that he should forgive a brother who sinned that many times in one day, provided that he repented from the heart—however many times he could not sin.

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven is likened to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,” and so forth. In accordance with the custom of the Syrians, and especially the Palestinians, he presents a parable in order to indicate what is conveyed by the comparison [Col. 0084C]. The one who settled accounts with his servants is understood better than anyone as our Redeemer, of whom the Psalmist says: “O God, give your judgment to the king,” and so forth (Ps. 71).

“And when he began to settle accounts.” This servant who owed ten talents is the Jewish people, bound by the Ten Commandments of the Law and liable for the debts of many transgressions. His master ordered him to be sold with everything he possessed, because, on account of the magnitude of his offenses, he handed him over to the foreign power of the nations, so that what they had refused to pay voluntarily they would be compelled to pay under punishment.

“But that servant fell down,” and so forth. When the people subject to the Law felt themselves hemmed in, they turned to prayers and promised that they would do under compulsion what they had previously refused of their own accord. To the repentant person Isaiah says: “I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. 44). But let us hear what this ungrateful servant did afterward.

“But when that servant went out,” and so forth. Once liberated from captivity, the Jewish people not only gave no thanks to their Redeemer, but, adding new sins to their former ones, did not cease, in contempt of their master, to harass their fellow servant—that is, the Gentile people—as though it were subject to them.

“When his fellow servants saw what was happening,” and so forth. Who are these fellow servants except the apostles and preachers of the Gospel, who daily implore the Lord for the salvation of believers against the deceit of persecutors, as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And now, Lord, look upon their threats,” and so forth?

“Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt,” and so forth. Once freed from their distress, they afterward showed no compassion toward their poorer neighbors, but savagely demanded payment from their debtors.

“And his master, being angry, handed him over to the torturers,” and so forth. That is, he handed the blasphemous people over to the Romans; or to evil spirits, who would punish their incorrigible soul and wickedness with endless torments without end.

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you,” and so forth. From these words it is clear that, if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, what we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance will again be demanded of us.

## CHAPTER XIX

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings,” and so forth. From this point he begins to narrate what the Lord did, taught, or suffered in Judaea. First, beyond the Jordan to the east; afterward, also on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, Bethphage, and Jerusalem. For although the whole province of the Jews is generally called Judaea in distinction from other nations, more particularly its southern region is called Judaea, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, the Decapolis, and the other regions within the same province.

“And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.” He heals Galileans in the borders of Judaea, so that the sins of the Gentiles might be admitted into the forgiveness that was being prepared for Judaea.

“Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any reason?” They ask this so that, whatever he answers, they may hold him as though caught in a syllogism. If he said that she should be dismissed and another taken, the preacher of chastity would seem to teach this against himself; if he answered that she should not be dismissed, they would accuse him as a sacrilegious opponent of the teaching of Moses and, through Moses, of God. But the Lord brings Scripture forward as a witness, so that he may escape their trap, opposing the natural law and God’s first judgment to the later concession, which was granted not by God’s will but by the necessity created by sinners.

“For the one who made them from the beginning made them male and female,” and so forth. He uses the singular number so that the union of one married couple might be established [Col. 0085D]. The reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit.

“Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.” What God joined by making one flesh cannot be separated by a human being, unless perhaps by God alone. A human being separates them when, because of the desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first.

“How then did Moses permit you to dismiss your wives because of the hardness of your hearts,” and so forth? It was not God but Moses who permitted it, seeing the desire for second marriages. He preferred to indulge discord rather than allow hatred and murder to continue, so that, according to the Apostle, it might be the counsel of a human being, not the command of God.

“For whoever dismisses his wife,” and so forth. There is therefore only one carnal cause—that is, fornication—and one spiritual cause—that is, fear of the Lord—for dismissing a wife, as many are recorded to have done for the sake of religion.

The disciples said to him: “If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” That is, if the yoke of wives is so burdensome, it is not expedient voluntarily to subject oneself to servitude, when one will have to endure a greedy, abusive, and wandering woman.

He said to them: “Not everyone grasps this saying,” etc. That is, it has been given to those who have sought virginity and have labored to obtain it, not to those upon whom necessity was imposed by accident and fortune.

“For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb,” etc. Thus there are two carnal kinds of eunuchs, [Col. 0086B] and a third, spiritual kind, to which a reward is promised, because for Christ’s sake, although they could be men, they make themselves eunuchs. Nothing at all is owed to the others, for whom chastity is a necessity rather than a choice.

“Whoever can grasp it, let him grasp it.” This is the voice of one encouraging and rousing his soldiers to the reward of modesty, as though he were saying: “Whoever can fight, let him fight, overcome, and triumph.”

Then little children were brought to him, so that he might lay hands on them and pray. For they thought that the Lord praised only those who were physically pure, and not also those who were pure in will, not knowing that the Lord did not bless those eunuchs whom the necessity of childhood makes chaste, but the virtue of self-restraint.

But the disciples rebuked them. Since they did not yet possess fully complete faith, they thought that he might grow weary, like other people who offer things, because of the importunity of those presenting them. [Col. 0086C]

But Jesus said to them: “Let the little children come to me,” etc. Significantly, he said “of such,” not “of these,” to show that it is not age but character that reigns.

And when he had laid his hands upon them, he departed from there. The Lord therefore lays hands upon little children when, granting humble people the grace of his help, he directs them according to his will, so that they may be able to obey his commands.

And behold, someone approached him and said: “Good Teacher,” etc. I believe he had heard only that those who wished to be like little children were worthy of entering the kingdom of heaven; therefore he desired to have explained to him not in parables but openly by what merits of works he could attain eternal life.

[Col. 0086D] “Why do you question me about goodness? God alone is good.” He does not reject testimony to goodness, but excludes the error of treating a teacher as existing apart from God, in comparison with whom no one is good.

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” etc. We can prove that this young man was a tempter from the fact that he deceitfully asks what those commandments are, as though he himself had not read them, or as though the Lord could command things contrary to God.

“I have kept all these things,” etc. The young man is lying if he had fulfilled in practice what was set forth in the commandments.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He would certainly not have gone away sad if he had heard that his possessions had to be sold and distributed to the poor.

[Col. 0087A] “If you wish to be perfect, go,” etc. For a bag is more easily despised than the will. Many abandon riches but do not follow the Lord, although to follow him is to imitate him. In the legal commandments the active life was commended; but the Savior led the man who gloried in its perfection onward to the beauty of evangelical contemplation, saying: “Go, sell,” etc.

“Amen I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.” He does not say, “It is impossible,” but “with difficulty,” because it requires the greatest labor for those who trust in money to enter the court of the heavenly kingdom. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever loves riches will not gain fruit from them.”

“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle,” etc. Understanding this, the Psalmist says: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). And concerning himself he says: “For I am alone and poor” (Ps. XXIV). In a higher sense, it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. For he wished to be understood by the name “camel,” because, having voluntarily humbled himself, he bore the burdens of our weakness.

When the disciples heard this, etc. What does this response pertain to, unless it is that they understood that all who love riches—even if they are unable to acquire them—are reckoned among the rich?

“With human beings this is impossible,” etc. That is, it is possible for God to turn them, through the Word, from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things. In this rich man we may understand the Jewish people, falsely glorying in observance of the Law and scorning evangelical perfection; to whom, deservedly, the camel—that is, the Gentile people—is preferred, since they more easily chose to enter upon the arduous way of God’s commandments. Thus we read in Isaiah that the camels of Midian and Ephah enter the gates of Jerusalem with gifts and offerings.

Then Peter answered, etc. As though he were saying: “We have done what you commanded; what reward will you give us?”

“Amen I say to you, you who have followed me,” etc. Since the number twelve often signifies totality, through the twelve seats of the apostles the total number of those judging is shown, and through the twelve tribes of Israel the totality of those who are to be judged is indicated.

“And everyone who has left house,” etc. The meaning is: Whoever has abandoned carnal things for the Savior will receive spiritual things, [Col. 0087D] which, in comparison and by virtue of their worth, will be as though a hundred were compared with a small number.

“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” This is fulfilled in Judas and in the thief, and likewise every day, because some complete in the flesh what they begin in the spirit, while others begin late but bring it to completion with a good ending.

## CHAPTER XX

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder,” etc. Our Creator is the householder who sent into his vineyard—that is, the Church—as many saints as he brought forth from righteous Abel to the last saint who will come at the end of the world, sending them like so many branches.

“And having made an agreement with the laborers,” etc. The denarius bears the image of the king, and everyone who approaches the Church ought in Christ to receive the image of the Godhead, which he had lost in paradise through the serpent’s envy. The laborers of this vineyard were first the patriarchs, then the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally the apostles; they cultivated within it the beauty of sacred conduct according as the time ordained.

“And going out about the third hour,” etc. From the beginning to the end of this world the Lord does not cease to send preachers to instruct the people of the faithful. Its morning extended from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth hour to Moses; and the ninth from Moses to the Lord’s coming. During these periods that ancient people, while striving to worship God in right faith, labored as though in the cultivation of a vineyard. The eleventh hour extends from the Lord’s coming to the end of the world. At that time the Gentiles, who previously stood idle, are called to the Lord’s vineyard through the apostolic laborers. They said: “Because no one has hired us,” that is, no one has opened to us the ways of life. We may also distinguish these differences of hours in each individual according to the stages of life, since one person is led to a good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in extreme old age.

“When evening had come,” etc. By means of a likeness he explains in past time the arrangement of the future, when Christ, the governor and ruler of the whole creation, will restore the reward to all, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body. He will begin with the last and proceed to the first, either because those who come late are often rewarded first, since they leave the body for the kingdom sooner, or because they receive an equal share in the recompense of eternal life.

“When those who had gone out about the eleventh hour came,” etc. Thus, as though after murmuring, they received the denarius—those who after long periods in hell reached the joys of the kingdom—whereas we receive it, as it were, without murmuring after the Mediator’s coming, because as soon as we leave the body we receive it without delay.

“But he answered one of them,” etc. This friend who is rebuked can signify the first-formed man and those who believed in that time. He is told: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” that is, did you not receive the reward I promised you, namely, my image and likeness? What more do you seek—not so much to receive more yourself as to desire that no one else receive anything?

“But I wish to give to this last one also,” etc. The Jews truly, having a wicked eye—that is, a corrupt intention—complained against God’s goodness, foolishly doing so, since the bestowal of the kingdom is not a matter of human merit or dignity but of the divine generosity.

“So the last will be first, and the first last.” That is, the Jews will be turned from head to tail, and the Gentiles will be changed from tail to head.

“For many are called,” etc. For many come to the faith, but few are brought to the heavenly kingdom.

“And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the Twelve,” [Col. 0089A] etc. He had often said this very thing to the disciples, but because what they had heard could slip from their memory amid the many intervening events, he now repeats it as he is about to go up to Jerusalem, preparing them for the trial, lest, when the persecution and disgrace of the cross came, they should be scandalized as insufficiently fortified.

“Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him,” etc. From what, when he was announcing the disgrace of his Passion, did she derive her expectation of the kingdom, except from the Lord’s words: “And on the third day he will rise”? She thought that immediately after the resurrection he would reign, and in a womanly error and with an affectionate intention she made her request, not knowing what she was asking—just as Peter did when he thought that three tents ought to be erected.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “You do not know what you are asking.” The mother makes the request, but the Lord speaks to the disciples, understanding that her prayers arose from the wishes of her sons. The desire was good, but the request was ill-considered; for that reason she is not put to shame, since it arose from love of the Lord. He therefore blamed neither their will nor their purpose, but only their ignorance.

“Can you drink the cup,” etc. By the name of the cup, or of baptism, he signifies the suffering of martyrdom, by which it was fitting that both he and they should be brought to completion. James received it from Herod, and John from Domitian, by whom he was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil and also exiled to the island of Patmos. From this we shall see that he did not lack the spirit of martyrdom, although he did not shed blood before his persecutor.

“But to sit at my right hand,” etc. This means: “It is not mine to give to the proud. For you are still proud. But if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are: it has been prepared for others, so become others, and it has been prepared for you.” What does “become others” mean? First humble yourselves, you who already wish to be exalted.

When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers. It is understood either from the Lord’s response or from the apostles’ indignation that the sons, without their mother’s knowledge, inflamed by immoderate desire, sent her to make great requests.

But Jesus called them to himself and said, etc. The gentle teacher rebukes neither the two for their desire nor the ten for their indignation and envy. Rather, by his example he teaches that the greater is the one who has become lesser; and, if they disregarded his words, they would blush at his deeds.

“And as they were going out from Jericho,” etc. Mark records this as having happened to one blind man. The question is resolved in the same way as the earlier question concerning the two men who suffered from a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes. Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” signifies the decline of our mutability and mortality. As Christ returned from it to the heavenly Jerusalem, a great crowd of believers followed. Many interpret the two blind men as the Pharisees and Sadducees; others as the two peoples of the Old and New Testaments, who were not yet able to say: “In your light we shall see light.” He says that they were beside the way because they seemed to possess knowledge but did not know the way, which is Christ. One followed the written Law and the other natural law, [Col. 0090A] but both were blind without Christ. When the Lord ascended to heaven, because they could not see by themselves, they heard the proclamation of the Savior, confessed him as the Son of David, and strove to maintain hope of their salvation and illumination, investigating and seeking to discover what true religious worship was.

“But the crowd rebuked them,” etc. At first many Jews, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, and afterward also Gentiles, repeatedly pressed them with harsher and stronger persecution, lest the world, which was to be enlightened, should invoke Christ. Yet the mad fury of the attackers could not deprive those predestined to eternal life of the salvation prepared for them. Morally, we can interpret the rebuking crowd as the tumult of carnal thoughts and cares resisting our spiritual devotion and prayer, which must be overcome with firm constancy of mind.

“And Jesus stood and called them,” etc. For it is characteristic of God to arrange all mutable things with unchangeable purpose. Although for our sake he endured temporal things, he nevertheless gives us light from the place that knows no passage into mutability.

“Moved with compassion for them,” etc. The touch of mercy grants what nature or weakness had taken away. Thereafter they follow Jesus not so much with their feet as with their virtues: the one who does the good he understands both sees and follows him.

## CHAPTER XXI

“And when they had drawn near to Jerusalem,” etc. Bethphage was a village of priests on the Mount of Olives, and is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “house of the jaws.” Bethany, which Luke joins to it, is a little village or town situated on the side of the same mountain, and is called “house of obedience.” As he was coming to Jerusalem, he exalted both by his presence, because before his Passion, through teaching many, he filled them with the gifts of devout confession and spiritual obedience. They are beautifully described as towns situated on the Mount of Olives, that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us with the anointing of spiritual gifts.

“Then Jesus sent two disciples,” etc. That is, teachers who, by preaching the Gospel, would penetrate the unlearned shores of the whole world like the walls of an opposing fortress. Some have interpreted these two apostles as Peter and Philip, who, first crossing the boundaries of the Jews, led the Gentiles to Christ. Philip presented Samaria, as it were the she-ass; Peter presented Cornelius, as it were the foal of the she-ass.

“And immediately you will find a she-ass tied,” etc. The she-ass demonstrates the Synagogue, which had borne the yoke of the Law; the foal of the she-ass demonstrates the wanton and free people of the nations. Entering the world, the preachers found both bound by the chains of unbelief and the cords of sins, as the Apostle says: “For all have sinned,” etc. (Rom. III). Matthew alone, therefore, who wrote the Gospel in the Hebrew language, mentions that the she-ass was brought to the Lord; the other three mention the foal, to show that salvation for the Synagogue also should not be doubted if it repented. Moreover, the two disciples show the twofold order of preachers, directed toward circumcision and uncircumcision, or the mystery of the twofold commandment of love.

“And if anyone says anything to you,” etc. Teachers are commanded not to cease preaching because of opposing adversity, since even among such people, although they are sinners, some are appointed to life.

“Now all this happened,” etc. This testimony is written in Zechariah. But it must be understood that, according to the literal sense, the Lord could not sit upon both animals within so short a stretch of road. Therefore, since the historical account contains either an impossibility or something shameful, let us seek higher meanings. The daughter of Zion is the city of Jerusalem and signifies the Church of the faithful, which is the daughter of the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all. Jesus sat upon it, having been brought from uncircumcision and circumcision through the preachers, because he dwells in their hearts, saying to them: “Learn from me, for I am gentle,” etc. (Matt. XI).

“And they placed their garments upon them,” etc. The apostolic garment may be understood as instruction in the virtues, eloquence of the Scriptures, or the variety of ecclesiastical doctrines. Unless the soul has been instructed and adorned with these, it does not deserve to have God as its rider.

“Very many in the crowd spread out,” etc. While the ass bears the Lord, many spread their garments on the road, because the holy martyrs, stripping themselves of the clothing of their own flesh, prepare the way with their blood for God’s simpler servants, so that with an unhindered step of the mind they may proceed toward the walls of the heavenly city, where Jesus leads. Morally, Jesus travels toward Jerusalem seated upon the ass when every believer, governing his soul—that is, his own beast of burden—leads it toward the innermost vision of peace. They spread garments on the road who discipline their bodies, preparing a path for him to the mind, or offering good examples to those who follow.

“But others cut branches,” etc. They cut branches from the trees who extract the judgments of the Fathers from the teaching of truth and, in the way of God, submit them through humble preaching to the mind of the hearer who is approaching.

“But the crowds that went before,” etc. The people of the Jews went before in faith, and the multitude of the Gentiles follows in the same faith. With one voice they all cried “Hosanna,” a Hebrew word that sounds in Latin as “Save,” because they recognized that Christ is the salvation of the world. They added “in the highest,” because his coming is not only the salvation of human beings but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly things, so that every knee—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—might bend before him.

“And Jesus entered the temple of God.” After entering the city, he first went to the temple, instructing us also to place the devotion of divine worship and prayer before all earthly affairs in every place. On the tenth day of the month Moses therefore commanded that a lamb be taken and kept until the fourteenth day, prefiguring this coming of the Lord. After the meal held in Bethany, he entered the city on the tenth day of the month, five days before Passover, and remained there until, on the fourteenth day of the month, having received the Mosaic lamb, he went out with the disciples to the place of prayer, where he was seized and bound by the Jews and began the mysteries of his own sacrifice.

“And he drove out all those who were selling,” etc. The priests devised this plunder from the people, so that various sacrificial victims might be sold to those coming from far away, for the priests themselves to receive again what had been purchased. So that the poverty of those who came would not disrupt this trick of theirs, they appointed moneychangers who, under this pretext, would lend money. But because the Law prohibited taking interest, and money lent at interest could not be profitable if nothing useful was received in return, they devised another scheme: instead of moneychangers they appointed *collybistae*, who accepted *collyba*—what we call delicacies or cheap little gifts—such as raisins and various kinds of fruit, in return for lending money, so that they might exact in these things, which are bought with money, what was not permitted in coin. In this way the robbers had turned the temple of God into a den of robbers, pursuing profits from religion.

Mystically, Jesus enters the temple of the Father, that is, the Church, to drive out from it bishops and the whole crowd who pursue avarice. Observe that, because of the avarice of the priests, God’s altars are called the tables of moneychangers: they sell the grace of the Holy Spirit and do everything to devour the peoples subject to them. Of such people it is said: “They devour my people,” etc. (Ps. LII). Morally, too, in our mind, which ought to be the temple of God, whenever it produces thoughts that injure its neighbor, robbers—as it were—sit in a cave, killing those who walk in simplicity.

[Col. 0092C] “The blind and the lame approached him,” etc. He healed the blind, so that the bodily illumination of these people might also become a spiritual lamp for the hearts of their slanderers. He cured the lame, so that those who limped in faith might acquire better feet by running toward Christ.

“When the chief priests saw,” etc. What madness on the part of the priests! They were looking, as it seems to me, at the greatest of all the signs the Lord displayed: that a man, and in their eyes a contemptible one, while scribes and Pharisees raged against him and watched their profits being destroyed, could with the blows of a single whip drive out such a multitude and do other things that an innumerable army could not have done. For something fiery and star-like radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity shone upon his face. Although they did not dare lay hands upon him, they nevertheless slandered his deeds and turned the testimony of the people and children who cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” into a charge, since, evidently, this could be said only to the Son of God.

But Jesus said to them: “Certainly. Have you never read,” etc.? How moderately he tempers his response! He did not say what the scribes wanted to hear: “The children are doing well to bear witness to me.” Nor, on the other hand, did he say: “The children are mistaken; you ought to pardon their age.” Instead, he brings forward an example from Psalm VIII, so that, while the Lord remained silent, the testimony of the Scriptures might confirm the children’s words.

“And leaving them, he went away,” etc. In that departure he prefigured the calling of the Gentiles and the fact that he could not remain in Israel. It should also be understood that he was so poor and flattered no one that in the greatest city he found neither a host nor a lodging; rather, he lived in a small rural place with Lazarus and his sisters.

“But returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry,” etc. When the darkness of night had been dispelled and noon was near—the hour at which the Lord was about to illumine the world through his Passion—he became hungry as he returned to the city, either demonstrating the truth of his human flesh or burning with concern for the salvation of believers and the faith of Israel. He saw a tree with leaves only, that is, the Synagogue, standing immobile with the superstitions of the Pharisees and the ornament of words but without any fruit of truth. The fig tree withered because, while the Lord was hungry, it did not possess the food he desired. Its leaves withered and its branches broke, but its root will live; from it, at the end of time, if they wish to believe, shoots of faith may sprout, and the Scripture will be fulfilled that says: “There is hope for a tree.”

“When the disciples saw this, they marveled, saying,” etc. Since he was soon to suffer, he ought to mark the disciples’ minds beforehand by this miracle. The Savior could therefore have withered his enemies also by the same power, had he not awaited their salvation through patience.

But Jesus answered and said to them, etc. Mystically, the devil is represented on account of his pride. When teachers preach the Word, he is driven from the hearts of those who are foreordained to life, but he is permitted to exercise the madness of his tyranny in the turbulent and bitter minds of unbelievers. He rages against them all the more fiercely the more deeply he grieves that he has been driven away from harming the godly.

“And whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.” Here the question is raised why Paul, who asked the Lord three times that the angel of Satan might depart from him, could not obtain this. But the difficulty of this question has already been resolved by the ancient explanation of the Fathers, who rightly understood that only those ask in the Savior’s name who ask for what pertains to eternal salvation. Often, when we ask for things that concern true salvation, we ourselves, by living badly, turn away from us the hearing of the just Judge. And when we pray beneficially for sinners so that they may repent, and through our own merit we are worthy to be heard, their perversity nevertheless stands in the way, preventing us from obtaining what we ask. Yet here we should hope that, although we may be unable to obtain their salvation, we will by no means be deprived of the fruit of our prayer, because we will be rewarded for the love we have shown them. It also sometimes happens that, if we do not immediately obtain what we have piously asked for here, we possess it in the future, increased by delay.

“And when he had come into the temple,” etc. They slander the authority whose divine origin they doubt, and imply that what he does belongs to the devil, adding: “Who gave you this authority?” They most plainly deny that he is the Son of God, supposing that he displays signs by alien powers.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “I will ask you,” etc. He questions them so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their own judgment.

[Col. 0094A] But they were reasoning, etc. If they had answered that John’s baptism was from heaven, the inevitable response would have been: “Why, then, were you not baptized by him?” But if they wished to say that it had been contrived through human deception, they feared the people, who had received baptism from him in crowds and regarded him as a prophet.

And answering Jesus, they said, etc. He does not say that he does not know what logically followed, because truth cannot lie; rather, he says that he is unwilling to reveal it to those who concealed beneath a lie what they knew. And the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” that is, John, “and I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Ps. XIII).

“But what do you think?” etc. This man is God the Father, who loves all the human beings he created with paternal affection. His elder son is the Gentile people, brought forth from the time of Noah, who, according to Luke, is described in the same parable as harsh and dissolute. Therefore, when the Father commanded through knowledge of the natural law, “Go, work in the vineyard”—that is, “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV)—he proudly answered, “I will not.” Later, however, at the Savior’s coming, he worked in God’s vineyard, because through repentance he corrected the insolence of his words by labor. The second people are the Jews, who answered Moses: “Everything whatsoever you have said, we will do.” Yet they did not go into the vineyard.

“For John came in the way of righteousness,” etc. John came preaching the way of righteousness because he pointed out with his finger that Christ, who is the consummation of the Law and the prophets, was present. Moreover, the kingdom of God may be understood as the Gospel of God, in which the Gentiles precede the Jews because they believed more quickly.

“Hear another parable. There was a householder who planted a vineyard,” etc. God the Father planted a vineyard because, after expelling the nations, he settled his people in the land of promise. He surrounded it with a hedge, either the wall of the city or the protection of angels. “And he dug a winepress in it,” either altars or those things whose titles prefix three Psalms. “And he built a tower,” that is, the temple. Concerning it Micah says: “And the tower of the cloud” (Mic. IV). “And he leased it to farmers,” whom elsewhere he calls hired laborers. He is said to have gone away not by a change of place, but to show that he left the vintners free to exercise their own judgment in their work.

“When the season of fruits drew near,” etc. [Col. 0094D] The servants who were sent first can be understood as Moses and Aaron, whom they beat with a scourge and sent away empty-handed. Moses was harassed on their account, etc. They also cast out David himself, the servant of the supreme householder, covered with insults or wounded in the head, as Mark’s Gospel relates, saying: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings XII). They changed both his kingdom, transferring it to one of low birth, and his religion, replacing it with impiety.

“Again he sent other servants,” etc. Understand these servants as the choir of the prophets. But which of them did they not persecute? They killed those who proclaimed the coming of the Lord Savior. As for what he says—“They beat one, killed another, and stoned another”—let us read Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, and from it we shall learn fully what sufferings each of God’s servants endured.

“Finally he sent his son to them,” etc. When he says, “They will respect my son,” this does not arise from ignorance. Rather, God is always said to be in doubt so that human free will may be preserved; and even after so many crimes he still reserved for them a place of mercy.

“But when the farmers saw the son,” etc. The Lord proves most clearly that the rulers of the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. They understood that this was the one about whom it had been said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” etc. (Ps. II), when they were saying: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII). They claimed his inheritance for themselves, because, after killing him, they tried to extinguish the faith that comes through him, to prefer their own righteousness, which comes from the Law, and to implant it among the Gentiles whom they were seeking to instruct. That he was killed outside the vineyard signifies either that he suffered outside the gate or that, first rejected by the hearts of unbelievers, he was then condemned to the cross.

“When the lord of the vineyard comes,” etc. They ask this not because he does not know what they will answer, but so that they may be condemned by their own response.

Jesus said to them: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which,’” etc.? How, he says, will this prophecy be fulfilled except because Christ, rejected and killed by you, will be preached to the Gentiles, who will believe, so that, like a cornerstone, he may build for himself from both peoples one city of the faithful?

[Col. 0095C] “Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you,” etc. By the kingdom of God he meant the sacred Scriptures, taken away from the Jews and handed over to us, so that we might produce their fruits.

“And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken,” etc. Whoever offends Christ through evil works will indeed be broken, but through God’s patience is nevertheless preserved for salvation. Whoever, however, utterly denies Christ, when the stone falls upon him it will crush him, so that not even a potsherd will remain with which to draw a little water. In another sense: Here it strikes sinners; in the judgment it will come upon them with the punishment of destruction.

## CHAPTER XXII

“And Jesus answered and again spoke in parables,” etc. He calls the Church of the righteous the kingdom of heaven, [Col. 0095D] and says that it is like a king—namely, the one of whom it is said: “Give the king your judgments,” etc. (Ps. LXXI). He made a wedding feast for his son because, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the holy Church to him.

“And he sent his servants,” etc. He sent the prophets as preachers of the Lord’s Incarnation, whom he later mentions under the name of slaughtered bulls, because according to the Law they exercised vengeance upon enemies. Again he sent the apostles, represented under the name of fattened animals, because of the grace of inward richness or the desires of sublime contemplation. The prophets announced that this feast would come; the apostles announced that it had already come.

“But they neglected it,” etc. To go to the farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labor; to go to business is to long for the profits of worldly activities, through which someone pretends not to live according to the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation.

“But the others seized his servants,” etc. Having sent armies of angels or Roman commanders, he destroyed the proud persecutors of the martyrs and burned their city, because not only their souls but also the flesh in which they had dwelt will be tormented by the flame of Gehenna. What follows speaks most openly of the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles.

“And his servants went out into the roads,” etc. The roads are understood as the doctrines and errors of the Gentiles. From all these, however, they came to the wedding—that is, they believed in Christ—and the very condition of those attending the feast clearly shows [Col. 0096B] that the present Church is signified by this royal wedding, in which the wicked are gathered together with the good.

“But the king entered to see,” etc. The king’s entrance shows the Lord’s coming on the day of judgment, when he comes to distinguish the faith and merits of each person. Moreover, the one who is said not to have been found wearing a wedding garment represents all those who are joined in wickedness. The wedding garment consists of the Lord’s commandments and the works fulfilled from the Law and the Gospel, which make the clothing of the new person. He calls him “friend” because he was invited to the wedding; he accuses him of shamelessness because, wearing a filthy garment, he has polluted the purity of the wedding. But he was silent, because then every argument of excuse ceases, when the one who accuses outwardly is the same as the witness who inwardly accuses the conscience.

[Col. 0096C] “Then the king said to the attendants,” etc. Then the feet and hands are bound by the severity of the sentence—those who were unwilling to be bound by evil works in the present life. We call the inner darkness the blindness of the heart; the outer darkness, the eternal night of damnation. Into it the person is then unwillingly thrown who now willingly fell into blindness of heart. There, it is said, teeth gnash and eyes weep, so that each limb may be subjected to punishment, each having here served as a slave to its particular vices.

“Then the Pharisees went away,” etc. Caesar Augustus had appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, king over the Jews, so that he might preside over the tributes and obey the Roman empire. The Pharisees therefore sent their disciples, as people less known and less suspect, with the soldiers of Herod—either mocking him because they paid tribute to the Romans and were not devoted solely to divine worship, or so that they might deceive him secretly and easily, or so that, if discovered, they would suffer less embarrassment before him. For when an evil plot is exposed, the less shame arises in proportion to the baseness of the person involved.

“Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” etc. They call him teacher and truthful so that, as a respected and praised man, he might supposedly open to them the mystery of his heart plainly. They deceitfully provoke him so that, fearing the Lord more than Caesar, he might say that tribute ought not to be paid, and so the Herodians, hearing it, could immediately seize him as a leader of sedition against the Romans.

But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, etc. He did not answer them gently and peacefully according to their words, but spoke harshly according to their conscience, because God often speaks to the soul rather than to the body and responds to the will rather than to words.

“Show me the coin of the tribute,” etc. Wisdom acts wisely, so that the tempters themselves may confess through their own words; and he asks this in order to answer their words appropriately.

They said to him: “Caesar’s,” etc. Here we should understand that Caesar means Tiberius, the stepson of his stepfather, who had preceded him in that office, under whom the Lord also suffered.

“Give back,” he says, “to Caesar what belongs to Caesar”—the coin, the tribute, and the money—and “to God what belongs to God”—tithes and firstfruits. Alternatively: just as Caesar demands from you the impression of his image, so also does God, so that just as the coin is returned to him, so the soul, illumined and marked by the light of his countenance, may be returned to God.

On that day the Sadducees approached him, etc. Since they believe that souls perish together with bodies, they rightly invent this sort of tale, which exposes as delirious those who affirm the resurrection of bodies. It is possible, however, that something of this kind once happened among their people.

“In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife of the seven will she be?” etc. They set obscenity against the tale in order to deny the truth of the resurrection. But mystically these seven brothers who died without children [Col. 0097C] correspond to all the reprobate, who throughout the whole course of this age—which revolves through seven days—remain barren of good works. When these men have each been snatched away by a wretched death, even worldly existence itself, which they had spent without the fruit of a living work, will finally pass away like a barren wife.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “You are mistaken,” etc. Since Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom, let us understand the statement simply: *nubere* (“to marry”) is written of men, and *nubi* (“to be given in marriage”) of wives. They are like angels in heaven, without any fear of death or stain of corruption, and they enjoy the perpetual vision of God without any earthly act of guilt.

“But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read?” etc. He brings forward testimony from the five books of Moses to prove the eternity of souls, for the sake of the Sadducees, who accept only those books. It would have been foolish to produce testimonies from the prophets, whose authority they did not follow.

“He is not God of the dead,” etc. After proving that God cannot be the God of souls unless they persevere, he consequently introduces the resurrection of bodies, with which they performed good or evil deeds together.

But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced them, etc. They gathered together and said among themselves: “Let one of us speak for all, so that, if he wins, we may all seem to be victors; but if he is defeated, he alone may appear confounded.” And he asks what the great commandment is, so that whatever the man answers, there may be an opportunity for accusing him by asserting that another commandment among the many is great.

Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. The first and greatest commandment of all, therefore, is knowledge and confession of the divine unity, together with the performance of good works. Good works, moreover, are fulfilled in love of God and of one’s neighbor.

When the Pharisees had gathered, Jesus questioned them, etc. They are not reproved for saying that he is the son of David, but for not believing that he is the Son of God. For he is David’s Lord, remaining God before the ages, and David’s son, becoming man in time.

And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare, etc. Since they could not find a word that would expose him to their ambushes, they no longer question him after being refuted, but hand him over, once openly seized, to the Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but are difficult to quiet. Let us therefore approach him whom the devices of the wicked could not overcome with a simple heart and devout dedication, as the author of salvation, so that we may be illumined and our faces may not be ashamed, because he is found by those who do not tempt him and appears to those who have faith in him.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0097]

[Col. 0097D] After the tempters had been deservedly confounded and rejected, Jesus turned his discourse to his own people, so that the confusion of the former might become instruction for the latter. For discourse is fruitless if, when one person is confounded, another is not thereby instructed.

# CHAPTER XXIII

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds, up to “For they say and do not do,” etc. By the “chair of Moses” he indicates the authority of the law, and because of the dignity of their priesthood and name he urges the peoples to submit to them, considering not their works but their teaching. In the Church today there are examples of such men who teach their subjects what they themselves avoid fulfilling, or who increase the burden of repentance upon sinners, so that either the sinner necessarily rejects repentance or, having undertaken it and being unable to bear it, sins more grievously after taking offense—although it is surely better to give an account because of mercy than because of cruelty. Of such men he rightly added that they would not touch the burdens themselves with even one finger: that is, they did not carry out even in the smallest matters what they presumptuously undertook, without faith and the grace of Jesus Christ, both to observe and to hand down for observance, contrary to the custom of their fathers.

“For they enlarge their phylacteries,” etc. They called the little cases containing the Decalogue *phylacteries*; they wore them on the forehead as though for their protection and defense, failing to understand that the Lord’s commandments are to be carried in the heart through constant meditation, not on the body. There was also a small and short fringe placed at the four corners of their cloak to distinguish their clothing, just as circumcision was placed in the flesh according to the commandment of the law. The woman who suffered from a flow of blood touched this fringe on the Lord’s cloak, but she was not pierced by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees.

“But do not be called Rabbi,” etc. Many raise questions here about the calling of fathers and teachers, but they are easily resolved. Just as the fact that by nature there is one God and one Son does not prevent others from being called gods by adoption, so also one Father and one Teacher does not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an extended sense.

“Whoever is greatest among you will be your servant.” As though he said: Whoever wishes to precede his brother in ruling must first precede him in serving. Hence the Apostle says: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Romans 12); let him surpass him in acts of service, so that he may be able to surpass him in holiness.

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled,” etc. Everyone who heedlessly exalts himself on account of his merits will at least in the future, if he persists, be humbled by the Lord; and whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good deeds will be exalted by him.

“Woe to you, scribes,” up to “nor do you allow those entering to enter.” As though he said: Woe to you who know that my bodily coming was proclaimed by the prophets, yet neither believe yourselves nor allow others to take notice through the pretense of your teaching. Morally, this sentence also condemns every teacher who, through evil deeds, closes before his disciples the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0099C] “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees,” etc. He shows that they sought various profits both from disciples and from outsiders whom they mixed into the people of God, as well as through the appearance of holiness. One who had once been a son of Gehenna, seeing the vices of his teachers and understanding that by their deeds they were destroying what they taught in words, returned to the vomit of his paganism and, as a transgressor, proved worthy of a greater punishment.

“Woe to you, blind guides,” etc. He accuses the inventors and teachers of this device of greed and impiety: no one held a person who swore by the temple or by the altar guilty of perjury; but anyone who swore by the gold in which they themselves delighted, or by the gift on which they fed, they immediately compelled, as guilty of perjury, to pay what he had sworn by [Col. 0099D]. These things were therefore called more sacred so that people might be made readier to offer gifts than to pour out prayers in the temple. Spiritually, however, the temple and altar signify Christ himself; the gold and gift signify the praises and sacrifices of prayers that we offer in him and through him. For it is not he who is sanctified by these things, but they by him.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint,” etc. He accuses them of greed because, for the support of the priests and Levites, among whose number the Lord’s portion was included, they zealously demanded tithes even of insignificant herbs, for the support of the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord, while neglecting judgment in the examination of cases, mercy toward the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God, which are the weightier matters.

[Col. 0100A] “Blind guides, who strain out a gnat,” and the rest. Just as then, so now, contrary to God’s commandment, we swallow and neglect what is worthy—such as judgment and the matters he listed above—and display our diligence in small things that bring profit, thereby preserving the appearance of religion. Allegorically, these matters can also be referred to the Jews, who released Barabbas, who had not broken the Sabbath, which they observed with great diligence; but they killed the Lord, who spiritually signified the Sabbath through judgment, mercy, and faith, which they especially despised. And the name of the gnat appropriately represents a seditious and murderous man, because this animal both disturbs by its buzzing and delights in blood. By the name of the camel, because of its humility in bending down to carry burdens despite its great size, the Lord is appropriately understood [Col. 0100B].

“You cleanse what is outside the cup,” and the rest. They are accused of pretense and falsehood: outwardly, in their dress, they displayed holiness, but inwardly they were full of the filth of vices.

“First cleanse what is inside the cup,” and the rest. That is: First cleanse the heart and conscience from lust and evil desires, from fraud and deceit; then outwardly, through your works, you will truthfully display holiness. This applies against those who detest bodily sins—fornication, theft, and similar acts—as though they were the gravest offenses, but regard spiritual sins, which the Apostle condemns no less—that is, bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, pride, and the rest—as trivial.

[Col. 0100C] “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites,” etc. Just as tombs are outwardly decorated with whitewash, marble, and gold, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead, so wicked teachers, because they teach one thing and do another, display cleanliness of clothing and humility of speech, but inwardly are full of every impurity and iniquity.

“You build the tombs of the prophets,” etc. They pretended, in order to win the favor of the crowd, to abhor the treachery of their fathers, magnificently decorating the memorials of the prophets whom their fathers had killed. But by the very act they testify how much they consent to their fathers’ wickedness: they kill the Lord, who had been foretold by those same prophets, by treating him with insults.

“And you, fill up the measure of your fathers.” That is: Complete what was lacking in them: they killed servants; you crucify the Lord. He did not say this as a command, but by showing what they were going to do.

“Serpents and brood of vipers.” That is: Just as vipers are born from vipers, so you were born as murderers from murderers.

“How will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” Will you escape it by building the tombs of the saints, or rather by cleansing your hearts from wickedness?

“Therefore, behold, I send you prophets,” up to “from city to city.” That is: The Son of God himself sent the apostles, just as he had previously sent the prophets. At the same time, observe, in accordance with the Apostle’s writing to the Corinthians, that Christ’s disciples possess various gifts: some are prophets, who proclaim things to come; others are wise, who know when they ought to deliver a discourse; others are scribes, thoroughly learned in the law. Among these were Stephen, Peter, and Paul, who were killed, and many others who, during the persecution, were driven from Judea and migrated to the people of the nations.

“So that all the righteous blood may come upon you,” and the rest. How is blood demanded from the Jews which they themselves did not shed? Because it is the custom of Scripture often to reckon two generations of people, namely, the good and the wicked.

“From the blood of righteous Abel,” and the rest. Why did he wish to mention Abel, who was the first, and Zechariah, who was by no means the last? Perhaps because, through Abel the shepherd, who was killed in the field, and Zechariah the priest, who was killed in the temple court, he wished to indicate under their names that martyrs of both ranks must be understood: those from the laity and those devoted to the service of the altar [Col. 0101B]. There has been much dispute about which Zechariah this was; but we think he was the one who was killed by King Joash of Judah between the temple and the altar. Yet it is asked why he is called the son of Barachiah here, when the history of Kings asserts that he was the son of Jehoiada. *Barachiah* in our language means “blessed of the Lord,” while the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is expressed by his Hebrew name, and the Nazarenes sometimes use this form in the Gospel. In place of “son of Barachiah,” Jerome testifies that he found “son of Jehoiada” written.

“How often I wanted to gather your children,” and the rest. He uses the likeness of a living creature that has so great an affection for its offspring that, affected by their weakness, it too becomes weak. And, something you will find more difficult among other creatures, while protecting its young with its wings it fights against the kite. So also our mother, the wisdom of God, which was weakened through assuming flesh, protects our weakness and resists the devil lest he snatch us away. What the bird attempts out of affection against the kite, wisdom accomplishes against the devil by its power.

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” He foretold that, once the heir had been killed, the Romans would come; and, as though plundering an empty nest, they took away their place, nation, and kingdom.

“For I say to you: You will not see me,” and the rest. We are compelled to understand this mystically of that coming of his when he will come in glory. Alternatively, the Jews have been given a time for repentance: let them confess the blessed one who comes in the name of the Lord, and they will behold the face of Christ.

# CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0101D]

And Jesus went out from the temple, up to “not one stone will be left upon another.” According to the historical sense, the meaning is clear; mystically, however, the Lord, taking account of our weakness, caused all those things to be overthrown, so that, when shadow and type had ceased, the reality itself, now proclaimed throughout the world, might hold the palm of victory.

As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, up to “and the consummation of the age.” Mystically, this signifies that, remaining in repose among the holy, the Lord detests the madness of the proud, and delights always to inhabit the fruitful height of the holy Church.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “See that no one leads you astray,” and the rest. There have been many whom the Savior foretold here, who falsely claimed for themselves the name of Christ [Col. 0102A]. Among them was Simon Magus in Samaria, who even claimed to be the great power of God. He also left these words, among others, written in his books: “I am the Beautiful One, I am the Paraclete, I am the Almighty, I am everything belonging to God.”

“For you will hear of wars and reports of wars,” and the rest. They are warned not immediately to think, when the disturbance of wars becomes widespread, that the devastation of the province and the final destruction of the city and temple were imminent, but rather that these things should be delayed for forty years.

“For nation will rise against nation,” and the rest. In the literal sense, it is clear that these things preceded the destruction of the city. Mystically, however, one may understand kingdom against kingdom; pestilence, meaning those whose speech spreads like cancer; a famine of hearing the word of God; the shaking of the whole earth; and separation from the true faith among heretical teachers, who, fighting against one another, bring victory to the Church.

“They will hand you over to tribulation,” and the rest. It should be noted that this saying of the Lord applies partly to the Jewish captivity brought about by the Romans and partly to the day of judgment. Through the apostles, the person of all believers is represented: toward the end of the world, those who follow the apostolic faith must be tested through tribulations.

“And then many will be scandalized,” and the rest. What we read happened at the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel and is carried out in stages; but it will occur most fully when the Antichrist comes at the end of the age, when many will be scandalized by the overwhelming severity of torments and by prodigious signs.

“And many false prophets will arise,” and the rest. Those, therefore, who remained during the siege of the city, and those besieging it, alienated from Christ, are, we think, better understood as heretics who come against the Church and falsely claim to be christs. Their first was Simon Magus; their last, and greater than the others, is the Antichrist.

“And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached,” up to “and then the end will come.” He clearly signifies that the end of the world will not come before the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world. The appropriate time for that end will be when the Gospel has been preached to all nations: for the help and salvation of those who believe, but for testimony and condemnation of those who do not believe [Col. 0102D].

“Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation,” etc. These words may be understood of the coming of the Antichrist, as the Apostle Paul preached most plainly. They may also be understood simply either of Christ, or of the image of Caesar that Pilate placed in the temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood in that very holy place down to the present day. According to the true usage of Scripture, an idol is also called an abomination.

“Then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains,” up to “Let him not turn back to take his cloak.” It is established that these things happened according to the historical sense. According to the spiritual meanings, however, when we see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not—that is, when heresies and crimes reign among those who seemed consecrated to heavenly mysteries, and when those who practice iniquity disturb the peace of the faithful—then we who are in Judea, that is, who persist in the confession of the true faith, must ascend to the summit of the virtues. Then the one who is on the roof, that is, who spiritually lives by rising above carnal concerns, must not descend to the lowly acts of his former way of life, nor resume the desires of the world or of the flesh that he had abandoned. For our house must be understood either as this world or as our own flesh in which we dwell. And the one who is in the field, that is, in the Church, must not look back to worldly affairs or to the restraints of the passing life from which he has renounced himself.

“Woe to those who are pregnant,” etc. This too can be said according to the historical sense: during the persecution of the Antichrist [Col. 0103B], or the Roman captivity, pregnant women and nursing mothers, weighed down by the burden of children, could not make an unencumbered flight. Spiritually, the soul that is found occupied by carnal desires during that final persecution is compelled, oppressed, to undergo eternal woe.

“But pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.” In winter, the harshness of the cold prevents people from going into solitude and hiding in the mountains and deserts. On the Sabbath, it would be a transgression of the law if they wished to flee, or imminent death if they remained. If the passage is understood of the consummation, it commands that our faith and love for Christ not grow cold, and that we not grow sluggish, idle in God’s work, on the Sabbath of the virtues.

“And unless those days had been shortened,” and the rest. This tribulation, the heavier its burden in comparison with others, will be moderated by the shorter duration of its time [Col. 0103C]. It is believed that it will attack the Church for three and a half years, as can be known from the prophecy of Daniel and the Apocalypse of Saint John.

“If they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’” and the rest. If someone promises you that Christ dwells in the wilderness of pagan and philosophical doctrine, or in the inner chambers of heretics, who claim to know the secrets of God, do not give your faith to them, lest they find an opportunity to deceive.

“For just as lightning comes out from the east,” and the rest. His statement that his coming would reach from east to west applies against those who locate Christ in particular regions of the earth and say that he is with them. His comparison with lightning applies against those who gather secretly, as though in inner chambers, and with only a few, as though in a wilderness. The name “lightning” also concerns the manifestation and splendor of the Church, signifying likewise the night or clouds of this age; for then the brilliance of lightning appears.

“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” That is, into heaven, where he lifted from here the body he assumed in manhood. According to the Apostle: “We will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4). He also suggests the zeal of the saints: the eagle, surpassing other birds in flight, rejoices to fix its eyes upon the very rays of the sun. He also alludes to the fact that the eagle customarily brings into its nest a stone that resists poisons—the one “cut from the mountain without hands” that overthrew the kingdom of the devil [Col. 0104A].

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days,” up to “and the stars will fall from heaven.” The heavenly bodies will be seen to grow dark on the day of judgment, not because their own light is diminished, but because the brightness of the true light comes upon them. When he says, “The stars of heaven will be falling,” this means that they will be deprived of their own light.

“And the powers of heaven will be shaken.” That is, the angelic powers will tremble. Mystically, however, the Church is the sun, moon, and stars, to which it was said: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song of Songs 6), because then she will not appear to the wicked persecutors who rage beyond measure.

“Then the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.” For many who seemed to shine with grace will fall when the wicked persecute them, and even the faithful and the strongest will be shaken [Col. 0104B].

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Here we should understand either the sign of the cross, so that the Jews may see the one whom they pierced, or the victorious banner of the triumphant one.

“And then all the tribes of the earth will beat their breasts.” Namely, those born on earth who did not understand their honor, but were compared to foolish beasts and became like them (Psalm 48).

“And he will send his angels with a trumpet,” and the rest. The Apostle speaks of this trumpet, which resounds with the sublime mysteries of divine praise.

“And they will gather his elect from the four winds,” and the rest. That is, from the four regions of the world—and not only this, but from the end of the earth to the end of heaven: from the farthest boundaries of the earth in a straight line up to the furthest limits of heaven, where, to those watching from afar, the circle of heaven appears to rest upon the earth [Col. 0104C].

“Learn a parable from the fig tree,” up to “Know that he is near, at the gates.” As though he said: Just as you recognize the coming of summer and the entrance of the west wind and spring, so, when you see all these things that have been written, do not think that the consummation of the world is already present, but understand that they come as certain preludes and forerunners, to show that it is near, at the gates. Mystically: When you see the Synagogue bringing forth the fruit of righteousness—which the Lord, on coming to it, did not find—do not doubt that the day of the final crisis and the summer of true peace and light are near.

“Heaven and earth will pass away,” and the rest. Heaven and earth will pass away through a transformation into renewal [Col. 0104D], but the word of the Lord will in no way pass away without the effect of its fulfillment. Hence the prophet also says in the person of the Lord: “My word that goes forth from my mouth will not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55).

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows,” etc. Therefore, when the apostles asked more explicitly about the day of judgment after the resurrection, he answered: “It is not for you to know the times” (Acts 1), and the rest.
