From this it is clear that he himself knows; but he is said not to know because he makes those who do not know, that is, he does not disclose to them what they would know uselessly, so that, uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on the following day.

“For just as in the days of Noah,” and the rest. He confirms by many examples that the day of his coming will be sudden, comparing it with the days of Noah and Lot, when sudden destruction overtook mortals [Col. 0105A].

“For just as they were in those days,” up to “marrying and giving in marriage.” Marcion’s and Manichaeus’s doctrine does not condemn marriages or food here; rather, it condemns the immoderate use of lawful things. Since wars, famine, and the other future events were mentioned above, he now mentions things that are signs of peace. We should understand, according to the Apostle, that after struggles and dissensions a brief peace will follow, so that the faith of believers may be tested and, from the evils already endured, they may hope that the Judge is coming.

“Until the day on which Noah entered the ark.” Mystically, he enters the ark perfectly when, on the day of judgment, the Lord illumines the Church, his eternal dwelling, by the presence of his vision [Col. 0105B]. And those who here insult the saints while indulging themselves will there be punished with eternal condemnation when the saints have been crowned.

“Then two will be in the field,” and the rest. He signifies those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field. The one will be taken who does not adulterate the word of God, but speaks in Christ as from God and before God; the one who proclaims Christ not chastely but out of rivalry will be left behind.

“Two will be grinding at the mill,” and the rest. He calls “grinding” those who, established among the peoples, are governed by teachers amid the whirl and cycle of temporal affairs. He signifies them under the name of women because it is advantageous for them to be governed by the counsels of the knowledgeable. The part that has entered marriage solely for the love of continuing the race and has distributed earthly substance in order to acquire heavenly things will be taken; the other will be left behind [Col. 0105C].

“Two will be in bed,” and the rest. These are those who choose the leisure and repose of monastic life; the two are said to be from two kinds of disposition. Whoever has devoted himself to continence for the Lord, so that, living without anxiety, he may consider the things of God, will be taken by God. Whoever does so for any other reason will be left behind. Jeremiah, describing the fall of any sinful soul under the figure of Judah, says: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lamentations 1). These three classes of people are the three men whom the prophet Ezekiel saw being delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah raised the ark upon the waters, and therefore represented rulers [Col. 0105D]. Daniel signified the life of the continent, since he devoted himself to abstinence even in the royal court. Job, living in marriage and managing the affairs of his own household, pleased God; through him the order of good married people is rightly represented.

“Therefore keep watch,” up to “because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come.” While the master of the household is unaware, the thief breaks into the house, when the spirit has grown sluggish in guarding itself; unexpected death bursts into the dwelling of the flesh and carries off the master of the house, unaware, to punishment.

“Whom do you think is the faithful servant?” and the rest. He shows the difficulty, not the impossibility, of accomplishing virtue. The Lord Christ appointed apostles and their successors over the household—that is, the Church—which he redeemed from the hand of the enemy with his own blood. One of them said: “Let a man regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the ministries of God” (1 Corinthians 4). The servant must be faithful in devoutly distributing his master’s money and not hiding it; he must be prudent in carefully discerning the capacity of each servant.

“To give them food at the proper time,” and the rest. That is, so that, at the proper time, they may serve their fellow servants the nourishment of teachings in the hope of rewards. Luke says, “a measure of wheat” (Luke 12), showing that the discourse of teachers must be formed according to the quality of the hearers, so that it may suit each person individually and yet never depart from the summit of common edification.

“Blessed is that servant,” up to “he will set him over all his goods.” That is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0106B], not necessarily so that they alone possess dominion over these things, but so that they may enjoy eternal possession of them more abundantly than the other saints, as the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor,” etc. (1 Timothy 5).

“But if that evil servant should say,” up to “and he eats and drinks with the drunkards.” Just as, in the case of one faithful steward, the whole order of good rulers is taught—how they should live and how they should be rewarded—so, in this most wicked servant, the work deserving condemnation and the eternal condemnation of all bad prelates are narrated together. Neglecting love of the Lord, they not only devote themselves to luxury but also provoke their subjects through injuries. Figuratively, however, “striking fellow servants” may be understood as corrupting the hearts of the weak, who have not yet been made firm in faith, hope, and love, by displaying an example of wicked action or speech [Col. 0106C].

“The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him,” and the rest. This very point he teaches: they should know that the master will come precisely when he is not expected. “He will cut him in two,” that is, separate him from the company of the saints, “and appoint his portion with the hypocrites”—namely, with those who were in the field and those who were grinding, yet were nevertheless left behind. When he says that there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, he expresses the twofold punishment of Gehenna: fire and cold. Hence it is also written in Job: “He passes from waters of snow to excessive heat.”

# CHAPTER XXV

“Then,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” up to “and five were wise.” He called the Church the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0106D]. The five-number doubled completes the ten; and because a multitude of the faithful is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is declared to resemble ten virgins. Since the wicked are mixed with the good and the reprobate with the elect, she is rightly said to resemble both wise and foolish virgins. As for his saying that the virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, I think it should be understood in this way: the one called the bride consists of those very virgins—just as, when all Christians run together into the Church, the children are said to run to their mother, although the one called the mother consists of those children gathered together. It seems to me, therefore, that the five virgins signify continence divided according to the five objects of enticement: the appetite of the soul must be restrained from the pleasures of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch [Col. 0107A].

“But the five foolish, having taken their lamps,” and the rest. Oil expresses gladness of mind. Whoever does not rejoice because he is pleasing to God inwardly does not have oil with him. The wise, however, took oil with them in their vessels, together with their lamps; that is, they placed the joy of good works in their heart and conscience. As the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.”

“But while the bridegroom was delayed,” etc. To sleep means to die; but to doze before sleep means, before death, to reach the sleep of death through the weight of illness.

[Col. 0107B] “But at midnight there was a cry,” etc. Suddenly, as though in the deepest night, the day of judgment steals upon us, because it cannot at all be foreseen when it will come. While everyone is secure, the cry of the angels and the trumpet of the powers that precede him will resound the coming of Christ.

“Then all those virgins arose,” etc. That is, the elect and the reprobate alike, awakened from the sleep of death, count the works they have with them, on account of which they will receive their recompense.

“But the foolish said to the wise,” and the rest. Then they seek outside themselves, and in vain, a testimony to their works, whose reward they now lose because of their love of empty praise.

“Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you,” etc. They answer not out of greed but out of fear. The testimony of each person scarcely suffices for himself; how much less for himself and his neighbor [Col. 0107C].

“Go instead to those who sell,” etc. They should not be thought to have given advice; rather, they recalled their guilt indirectly, as though they were saying: “Let us now see how those who used to sell you praises and lead you into error will help you—those who made you seek glory not before God but from human beings.”

“But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came,” and the rest. That is, while they bent down toward the things that are outside, the one who judges came. Those who were ready—that is, those whose conscience gave a good testimony before God—entered with him into the wedding feast, that is, into the place where the pure soul is joined to the clean and perfect word of God and made fruitful. And the door was shut, that is, the entrance to the kingdom of heaven; for after the judgment there is no place for prayers or merits [Col. 0107D].

“Finally the other virgins also came,” up to “I do not know you.” Behold, they cry out for the door to be opened, and, compelled by the pain of their rejection, they repeatedly invoke the title of their lord. They offer prayers, but they are not known, because then God abandons as strangers those whom now, on account of the merit of their life, he does not recognize as his own.

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” A general exhortation to the disciples follows, because we must always fear the final day, which we can never foresee.

“For just as when someone goes abroad,” and the rest. The proper place of the flesh is the earth, from which it is led as though into a foreign land when, through our Redeemer, it is placed in heaven [Col. 0108A]. Yet, when departing, he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful.

“And to one he gave five talents,” and the rest. The five talents, therefore, express the gift of the five senses; the two signify understanding and action; and by the name of one talent understanding alone is signified.

“To each according to his own ability,” and the rest. Therefore he gave not according to generosity or parsimony, but according to the capacities of those receiving. Finally, the one who had made ten from five talents and the one who had made four from two receive a similar joy, because the rewarder does not consider the size of the profit but the willingness of the effort. It is rightly reported that another five or another two came as profit, because, when preaching is devoted to both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled [Col. 0108B].

“But the one who had received one,” and the rest. To hide one’s talent in the earth, therefore, is to entangle the received ability in earthly actions, not to seek spiritual profit, and never to lift the heart above earthly thoughts.

“After a long time,” and the rest. The long time is the period between the Savior’s ascension and his second coming. Let each person consider what he has received and what profit he brings back from what was entrusted to him, because the one who now gives generously in piety will then strictly demand an account of his merits in judgment.

And the one with five talents came forward, up to, “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Through the word “Well done” also the Lord intimates his joy, inviting the servant who has labored well to eternal joy. “Well done” is also an interjection of one rejoicing; and the Lord, rejoicing well, commands the good and faithful servant to enter into his joy, because he alone is the one to whom the Prophet says: “You will make us rejoice with the joy of your presence,” and so forth. And he invites him to many good things, because in comparison with future things, which endure, present things, which pass away, seem to be almost few.

But the one who had received the single talent came forward, [saying] up to, “Look, you have what is yours.” Truly, what is written—“to make excuses for sins”—befell this man, so that the crime of pride might be added to sloth and negligence. He ought simply to have entreated the one whom he instead slanders, and he says that he acted according to prudent counsel, lest, while seeking profits from the money, he should also suffer loss of the principal—that is, lest I should be compelled vainly to render an account for other things. It is enough for each person to render an account for himself.

“Wicked and lazy servant,” up to, “with interest.” He is called wicked because he makes a slanderous accusation against the Lord; lazy because he was unwilling to double the talent, so that in the one respect he might be condemned for pride, and in the other for negligence. “If,” he says, “you knew me to be harsh and cruel, and to pursue what belongs to others, reaping everywhere that I had not sown”—alternatively, “to reap where I had not sown” means also to declare guilty of impiety those in whom the word of the Law or the Gospel had not been ministered—“why did no such thought arouse love in you? You should have known that I would seek my own more diligently, and you should have given my money to the money-changers, or bankers”—that is, the preaching of the Gospel to the other teachers, [Col. 0109A] as the apostles did when they appointed presbyters and bishops throughout the individual provinces—or to all believers, so that whatever they said in speech they might fulfill in deed.

“Therefore take the talent from him,” and so forth. We see this happening daily in the holy Church: for many, while they minister well, are led by the added grace of what they receive externally also to a mystical understanding.

“For to everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound,” and so forth. Whoever has faith and good will in the Lord, even if as a human being he has something lacking in his works, will receive it from the good Judge. But whoever does not have faith loses even the other virtues that he seemed naturally to possess. These words can be interpreted in many ways concerning charity, natural ability, and knowledge. [Col. 0109B]

“But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty,” and so forth. The same one who is the Son of God and also the Son of Man will then come in his majesty to judge—the one who is now. It is as though he says: The one who is soon to come came in his humility to be judged; then the Lord will sit upon the throne of his majesty—that is, he reigns over his holy and glorious Church, concerning which it is written: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”

“And all the nations will be gathered before him,” and so forth. There are therefore two classes of people gathered for judgment, although they will be divided into four. There are two classes of the perfected: one, those who will judge with the Lord and will not themselves be judged, concerning whom the Lord says: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matthew 19:28); the other, those to whom it will be said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:25). These will be judged, and they will reign. Likewise, there are two classes of the reprobate: one, those who will be found outside the Church; they will not be judged, but will perish, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The impious do not rise in the judgment” (Psalm 1:5). Alternatively, the other class of the reprobate consists of those who will be judged and will perish; to them it is said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25), and so forth.

“And he will place the sheep at his right hand,” and so forth. Understand “right” and “left” according to what you read elsewhere: “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left” (Ecclesiastes 10:2).

“Then the King will say to those who are at his right hand,” up to, “and you came to me.” In the historical sense, these words concern the reception of the kingdom and the generosity of benevolence by which bodily needs are supplied to the needy. According to the higher understanding, however, they display the perfection of charity: the one who hungers and thirsts for righteousness is refreshed by the bread of the word and the drink of divine wisdom; the one who has strayed from the way of truth is brought through repentance into the lodging of Mother Church; the one who is weak in faith is taken up; and the one placed in the prison of anguish, tribulation, and sorrow is lifted up by the aid of consolation.

“Lord, when did we see you hungry?” and so forth. Either they say this in wonder at Christ’s glory, or because, in view of the magnitude of their fear and the abundance of their reward, everything good that they had done then seemed small to them.

[Col. 0110A] “As long as you did it for one of these my brothers,” and so forth. He seems to have said this concerning the poor in spirit, toward whom he had extended his hand when he said: “These are my brothers and my mother, those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

“And these will go into eternal punishment.” Origen vainly promises, after many cycles of years, liberation from hell for the impious and even for the devil, since the Lord proclaimed that the punishment is eternal.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place.”

After all the sayings that he had completed from the beginning of his Gospel up to the time of the Passion, speaking and preaching in the hearing of the disciples or the crowds—that is, from the day on which he came to Bethany and the event concerning the ointment took place, up to the day on which all these things were done and said—we understand, although the Evangelists do not mention it, that four days had elapsed, so that the day might arrive which Matthew and Mark defined as two days before the Passover. Mystically, after two days of the most brilliant light of the Old and New Testaments, the true Passover is celebrated for the world. The Passover, which in Hebrew is called *Pasche*, is named from “passing over,” because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over them; or for this reason the day of this solemnity was mystically called a “passing over” through the Law: because on it the Lamb of God was to pass from this world—or was himself about to pass over—or was about to lead us, through a saving passage, as though from Egyptian slavery. [Col. 0110B]

“And the Son of Man,” he says, “will be handed over to be crucified.” Let those be ashamed who think that the Savior feared the death of the Passion: he foresaw it, yet did not avoid the ambush; he was neither terrified nor did he flee. Indeed, while the others were unwilling to go, he proceeded fearlessly, when Thomas said: “Let us go, and let us also die with him.”

“Then the chief priests gathered together,” and so forth. They gather to enter into counsel about how they might kill the Lord, not fearing an uprising, as the simple wording shows, but taking care lest he be taken from their hands by the aid of the people.

“But when Jesus was in Bethany,” and so forth. By recapitulation Matthew and Mark return to that day in Bethany which was six days before the Passover, and they recount what John relates concerning the supper and the ointment. From there Jesus was going to come to Jerusalem; thus they return to the point from which they had digressed, to the Lord’s discourse, which he delivered two days before the Passover. And the account of Judas is joined to the counsel of the priests, which they held while deliberating about the Lord’s death.

The Lord remains in Bethany—that is, in the house of obedience—which once belonged to Simon, formerly a leper but already healed by the Lord, his former name remaining so that the power of the healer might be evident. Some wish to understand Simon the leper as a part of the people that believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon also means “obedient.”

[Col. 0111A] “A woman came to him,” and so forth. This woman was Mary Magdalene, who elsewhere, while still a sinner, wet his feet; now, however, justified, she poured holy oil upon his head. Alabaster is a kind of very white marble, streaked with various colors, in which they are said to preserve ointments especially well and without spoilage. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, whiter than elsewhere, while the most highly prized variety is found in India.

Moreover, according to the other Evangelists, Mary’s ointment is said to have been made from nard, the principal plant used in ointments, and to have been *pisticum*, that is, “faithful,” because some physicians are accustomed to adulterate ointments with similar herbs. For *pistis* in Greek means “faith,” from which *pisticum* is derived. Mark says that it was “spiked,” meaning that not only the root of nard but also, to make it more precious, the addition of its spikes and leaves had increased the abundance of its fragrance and power.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary signifies the faith of the holy Church, which anoints the Savior’s head with holy ointment when it confesses and proclaims the power of his divine virtue with worthy reverence. But when it receives the mysteries of his assumed humanity with unworthy reverence, the ointment of *pisticum* nard—that is, faithful and true ointment—is poured upon the Lord’s feet. [Col. 0111B]

“But when the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying: Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” Matthew and Mark use synecdoche here, placing the part in the name of the whole. John, speaking more precisely, testifies that Judas said this, wishing to disclose on this occasion his habit of stealing; the others, however, spoke out of concern for the poor.

“But Jesus, knowing,” and so forth. He said that he would not always remain with the apostles in bodily presence, although by the power of his divinity he never abandoned them, as he testifies elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you,” and so forth.

“For by pouring this ointment,” and so forth. What you think is the destruction of the ointment is an act of preparation for burial.

“Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world,” and so forth. Attend not so much to her preparing the Savior for burial by anointing his head, as to his foreknowledge of future events: though he was to suffer and die after two days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole [Col. 0111D] world.

“Then one of the Twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests,” and so forth. This sentence should be joined to the passage above in which he reported the priests’ counsel concerning Christ’s execution. By saying, “One of the Twelve went,” he shows that Judas was neither invited nor compelled by any necessity, but entered into the counsel of his own accord, prompted by his criminal mind.

“And from then on he sought an opportunity,” and so forth. Many people today abhor Judas’s unspeakable crime, yet do not take care when, on behalf of women, they give false testimony against anyone. Certainly those who deny the truth for money sell the Lord for money; for he himself said: “I am the truth.” When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord, they betray God, since God is charity.

[Col. 0112A] “Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread,” and so forth. They call the fourteenth day, on which they were accustomed to kill the lamb, the first day of Unleavened Bread, although it ought properly to have been called Passover. On that day, when he was seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of the sacrifice itself, although he was crucified on the following day.

“Go into the city to a certain man,” and so forth. The names have deliberately been omitted—whether of the water-carrier, whom the other Evangelists mention, or of the master of the house—so that an opportunity might be indicated for all who desire to celebrate the true Passover, that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments, and who seek either to receive him as a guest in the lodging of their mind.

[Col. 0112B] “And the disciples did,” and so forth. In another Gospel it is written: “They found a large upper room furnished,” and so forth. The large upper room is the spiritual Law, emerging from the narrowness of the letter; in a lofty place it receives the Savior. The water-carrier is a herald of grace. Whoever follows him into the house of the Church prepares refreshment for Christ in the high chamber of the mind, by transcending through the enlightening Spirit the surface of the letter, because he recognizes that all the mysteries of the Passover, as well as the other ordinances of the Law, are Christ’s sacraments.

“When evening had come,” and so forth. Evening came then when the light of the world—that is, the true Sun—was hastening toward the setting of death. Then the Lord reclined with the disciples, for whom he prepared eternal rest.

[Col. 0112C] “Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me.” He foretells the betrayer, yet does not identify him specifically, lest, being openly charged, he become still more shameless. He casts the crime into the group, so that the guilty man might repent; and those who feared their own frailty believed the Teacher more than themselves.

“Surely it is not I, Lord?” They ask sadly about a sin of which they had no consciousness.

“He who dips his hand with me in the dish,” and so forth. While the other disciples were saddened, withdrawing their hands and restraining food from their mouths, Judas, with the recklessness and shamelessness with which he was about to betray him, also put his hand into the dish with the Teacher, so that his boldness might counterfeit a good conscience.

A *paropsis*, as some say, is a square food vessel, so called because it has equal sides—that is, equal dimensions. In its place Mark uses “dish,” a clay vessel suitable for holding liquid. It could have happened that on the same table a square clay vessel contained a sauce into which the disciple could put his hand with the Teacher, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The man of my peace,” and so forth.

“The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written concerning him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed.” Punishment is foretold, so that the one whom shame had not overcome might be corrected by the announced penalties. Morally, however, woe today to the man who, with ambushes placed in his mind, approaches the table wickedly and does not fear to participate in the most holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries, betraying the Son of Man not to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinful members—that is, to his own.

[Col. 0113A] “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” He is not therefore to be thought to have existed before he was born, since no one can fare well unless he exists; rather, it is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist wickedly.

“But Judas, who betrayed him, answering said: Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” He asks lest, by remaining silent, he seem to betray himself. Unlike the others, he calls him not “Lord” but “Teacher,” as though he would have an excuse if, after denying the Lord, he had at least betrayed a teacher.

“You have said so.” It is as though he says: “Because I did not say it.”

[Col. 0113B] “While they were dining, Jesus took bread,” up to, “This is my body.” When the solemn rites of the former Passover had been completed—the rites celebrated in remembrance of the ancient liberation of God’s people from Egypt—he passed to the new Passover, which he wished the Church to observe in remembrance of his redemption, substituting the sacrament of his body and blood for the flesh and blood of the lamb.

He blessed the bread and broke it, because he deigned to subject the humanity he had assumed to death in such a way as to demonstrate that the power of divine immortality truly dwelt in it; and thus he taught that it would be raised from death more quickly.

“And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you.” He gives thanks to show what each person ought to do under the chastisement of his own fault, if he himself bears with equanimity the chastisements caused by another’s fault; and what a subordinate should do when corrected: the equal gives thanks to the Father.

“For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” Since bread strengthens the flesh, while wine produces blood in the flesh, the former is mystically referred to the body of Christ and the latter to true blood, because Christ must remain in us and we in Christ. Water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup; for, as John bears witness, the waters are the peoples.

[Col. 0113D] “But I say to you, I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine,” and so forth. That is, I will no longer take pleasure in the carnal ceremonies of the Synagogue, which is called Christ’s vine or vineyard; among these rites, the sacred observance of this Paschal lamb also held the chief place. The time of my resurrection will come; that day will come when, placed with him in the kingdom of God—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—I will be filled with new joy with you from the fountain of grace, for the salvation of that same people, regenerated by spiritual grace.

Alternatively, we should understand the old wine as the body he received from Adam’s stock, and the new wine as the immortality of renewed bodies. When he says, “I will drink the new wine with you,” he also promises them resurrection, so that they may put on mortality.

“And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” Beautifully, he leads the disciples, who have been imbued with the sacraments of his body and blood and commended to the Father through a hymn of pious intercession, onto the mountain. He does this typologically to signify that through the practice of his sacraments and through the aid of his intercession we ought to ascend to the higher gifts of virtue and the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which we may be anointed in our hearts. [Col. 0114A]

“Then Jesus says to them: You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.” He foretells what they are about to suffer, so that when they have suffered it they will not despair of salvation but will be freed through repentance. He significantly added, “On this night you will be scandalized,” because those who suffer scandal endure it in night and darkness. Let us instead say: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

“For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah. The good Shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and so that from many wandering flocks there may become one flock and one shepherd.

“But Peter, answering, said to him: Even if all are scandalized because of you,” and so forth. This is neither recklessness nor a lie; it is the faith of the apostle Peter and his burning affection for the Lord and Savior. He was carried away by such affection and love that, because of the weakness of his flesh, he did not consider the truth of God’s words, as though what the Lord had said did not have to come to pass.

“Jesus said to him: Amen I say to you, on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Mark, however, said: “Before the cock gives voice twice, you will deny me three times.” It is evident that the threefold denial began before the first crowing and was completed before the second crowing. It does not matter at what intervals the three denials were spoken, since his heart was so possessed by fear before the first crowing that, when questioned, he could deny the Lord not only once but a second and a third time.

“Peter said to him: Even if I must die with you,” and so forth. “Love is strong as death.” Through the love of the mind they did not fear the loss of life, but human presumption without divine protection was vain, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “Unless the Lord guards the city,” and so forth (Psalm 126:1).

[Col. 0114D] “Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane.” This is not contrary to the fact that Luke says Jesus went out to the Mount of Olives, while John says that he went out into a garden. To this day the place of Gethsemane is shown at the foot of the Mount of Olives, where we understand that it was the garden about which John narrated. Nor is it established that a church was built above it.

When the Lord prays on the mountain, he silently admonishes us that we ought to pray only for heavenly goods. But when he prays in the valley—and in the valley of the fruitful land, or of richness, which is what *Gethsemane* means—he likewise intimates to us his humility, teaching that the richness of love must always be preserved in our prayers and inwardly. Alternatively, as death approached, the Lord prayed in the valley of richness, openly indicating that he underwent death for us through the valley of humility and the richness of charity.

“And Jesus said to his disciples: Sit here,” and so forth. [Col. 0115A] In the house where they had eaten the Passover, he ordered the disciples to wait a little while for his return, showing that his prayer alone is the redemption of us all.

“And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled.” He began to be sorrowful to prove the truth of the humanity he had assumed, and that he was truly sorrowful. Yet, so that suffering would not dominate his soul, he began to be sorrowful through suffering. For it is one thing to be sorrowful and another to begin to be sorrowful. He was sorrowful not from fear of suffering, but because of the most wretched Judas, the scandal of all the apostles, the rejection of the Jewish people, and the destruction of miserable Jerusalem.

“Then he said to them: My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” [Col. 0115B] The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, since it was the condition of bodily feeling, not fear of death, that affected him. For the one who assumed a body had to undergo everything that belongs to a body: to hunger, thirst, be distressed, and be sorrowful. Divinity does not know how to be changed by these emotions.

“Remain here and keep watch with me.” He does not forbid sleep, since the time for sleep had not arrived while danger was imminent, but he forbids the sleep of their own unbelief and the torpor of their mind. For he knew that, with the devil pressing upon them, their faith would be overcome by sleep. He commands them to keep watch with him, since the same suffering was impending for them.

“And going forward a little, he fell on his face, praying and saying: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He falls upon his face to show the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh. He asks that, if possible, the cup pass from him—not out of fear of suffering, but out of mercy for the former people, lest he drink the cup proffered by them. Hence he expressly did not say, “Let the cup pass from me,” but “this cup,” that is, the cup of the Jewish people, who cannot have the excuse of ignorance if they kill me, since they possess the Law and the Prophets, who daily prophesy concerning me.

“Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” “Let not,” he says, “what I speak from human feeling come to pass, but let what I descended to earth by your will come to pass.”

“And he came to his disciples and found them sleeping; and he said to Peter: So you could not keep watch with me for one hour?” He rebukes Peter separately from the others because, more than the others, he had boasted that he would never be scandalized; now, because of the magnitude of his sorrow, he had been unable to drive away sleep.

“Keep watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.” That is: Pray lest the final temptation overcome you and hold you within its falls.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” He shows two wills in himself: the human will, which belongs to the flesh, and the divine will, which belongs to the Godhead. To fear in the Passion belongs to human weakness; to accept the dispensation of the Passion belongs to the divine will and power.

Alternatively, these words are addressed to those who had promised that they would never deny him. Their spirit was willing, but their flesh was weak, because they had not yet put on power from on high.

[Col. 0116A] “Again, a second time he went away,” up to, “Your will be done.” He prays a second time that, if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd withers, the Father’s will may be done—a will that is not contrary to the Son’s will, since he himself says through the Prophet: “My God has willed that I should do your will” (Psalm 29:9).

“And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.” The Lord alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all. The apostles’ eyes were weakening and oppressed because denial was near.

“And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words.” Just as the temptation of desire is threefold, so the temptation of death is threefold. Opposed to the desire that exists in curiosity is the fear of death: for just as in the former there is eagerness to know things, so in the latter there is fear of losing such knowledge. Opposed to the desire for honors or praise is fear of disgrace and insults; opposed to the desire for pleasure is fear of pain. It is therefore not unreasonable to understand that the Lord prayed three times, because of the threefold temptation of the Passion, that the cup might pass from him, but in such a way that the Father’s will might rather be fulfilled.

“Then he came to his disciples,” up to, “Behold, the one who will betray me is approaching.” It is understood that, after saying to them, “Sleep and rest,” the Lord lingered a little while, so that what he had foretold might happen, and then added: “Behold, the hour has drawn near.” For this reason, according to Mark, the word “Enough” is placed after those words—that is, “you have rested.”

But the reason that, when he returned to them and found them sleeping, he rebuked them the first time, remained silent the second time, and ordered them to rest the third time is this: first, after the resurrection, he rebuked them when they were scattered, distrustful, and trembling. Second, after sending the Paraclete Spirit, he visited their burdened eyes so that they might continue in the freedom of the Gospel. Third—that is, upon his return in glory—he will restore them to security and rest. [Col. 0116C]

“While he was still speaking, behold, Judas,” up to, “sent by the chief priests and elders of the people.” Judas’s action corresponds to the change in his mind: having abandoned the weapons of life, he proceeds against his Teacher with clubs; he approaches the author of life with death in mind.

“Now the one who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying,” [Col. 0116D] and so forth. The wretched man thought that the signs he had seen the Savior perform were done not by divine majesty but by magical arts. And since he may have heard that the Savior had been transfigured on the mountain, he feared that through a similar transformation he might slip from the hands of the attendants. Therefore he gives them a sign, so that they may know that the one whom he would indicate with a kiss was the same man.

“Hail, Rabbi,” and he kissed him. The Lord accepts the betrayer’s kiss, not to teach us to pretend, but lest he appear to flee the betrayal; at the same time he fulfills the saying of David: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119:7).

“Friend, why have you come?” The word “friend” (*amice*) is to be understood *κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν*—ironically—or certainly according to what we read above: “Friend, how did you come in here?”

[Col. 0117A] “And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand,” and so forth. This was certainly Peter, with the same ardor of mind with which he did the other things. For he knew how Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious people, had received the reward of righteousness and perpetual priesthood.

According to allegory, the savage servant is the Jewish people, enslaved to the chief priests in an obligation of obedience, because in the Lord’s Passion it lost the right ear—that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law. Nevertheless, it remained content with the left ear, that is, with the usefulness of the letter, which was the ear severed by Peter’s sword. This does not mean that Peter took away the capacity for understanding from those who heard, but that he disclosed that it had been removed by divine judgment from those who were negligent.

Yet, according to Luke, the same right ear was restored by divine mercy to its former function in those of the same people who chose to believe.

Alternatively, the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signifies hearing renewed after the oldness has been removed, so that it may exist in newness of spirit and not in oldness of the letter. Whoever receives this from Christ will also receive from Christ the power to reign with Christ. This is signified by the name of the servant, Malchus, which is interpreted as “king” or “one who will reign.” [Col. 0117B]

“Then Jesus said to him: Put your sword back,” and so forth. That is: Let vengeance cease; let forgiveness be granted.

“For all who take up the sword,” and so forth. That is: Those who desire to avenge themselves in the present through retaliation die by the very sin of their souls.

“Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father?” and so forth. It is as though he says: “I do not need the aid of twelve apostles, even if all of them were defending me, for I can have twelve legions of the angelic army.”

Alternatively, this number signifies every kind of people under the Roman Empire. These are the angels of God who carried out God’s judgment when, after the Lord’s resurrection, they were sent by him in the forty-second year and destroyed the wicked city.

“In that hour Jesus said to the crowds,” and so forth. It is foolish, he says, to seek one who offers himself willingly with swords and to investigate him through a betrayer at night, as though he were hiding, when he teaches daily in the Temple. But for this reason you gather against me in darkness: because your power is in darkness.

“But all this happened,” and so forth. The words are therefore those of the prophets’ Scripture: “They pierced my hands,” and so forth (Psalm 21:17).

[Col. 0117D] “Then the disciples, leaving him, fled.” Mystically, just as Peter—who washed away the guilt of his denial with tears and completely eradicated it through his confession of love for the Lord—shows the restoration of those who fall in martyrdom, so the other disciples, who forestalled the moment of arrest by fleeing, teach those who feel themselves less capable of enduring punishments that it is much safer for them to seek the protection of hiding places than to expose themselves to the danger of combat.

“But Peter followed him from a distance,” and so forth. He is worthy of wonder and yet of reverence: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. That he fears belongs to nature; that he follows belongs to devotion; that he denies belongs to an unexpected attack; that he repents belongs to faith.

Mystically, Peter’s following the same Lord from a distance to the Passion signified that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s sufferings, but in a very different way: the Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffered for the Church. [Col. 0118A]

“And entering inside,” and so forth. How Peter was able to enter, John makes clear: either because of his love for the Teacher or because of human curiosity, wishing to know what judgment the high priest would make concerning the Lord—whether he would hand him over to death or dismiss him after having him scourged.

“But the chief priest,” up to, “with many others,” and so forth. The name of the high priest appropriately corresponds to the vigor of his action. For *Caiaphas* is interpreted as “investigator,” or “shrewd,” or “vomiting from the mouth.” He was shrewd in carrying out the wickedness of his deceit, but shameless in uttering a lie. And the Scripture was fulfilled: “They searched out iniquity; they failed while searching with searching; the arrows of children became their wounds” (Psalm 63:7).

“Finally two false witnesses came,” and so forth. The false witnesses slander him either because they did not understand his words in the sense in which they had been spoken, or because, after adding or changing a few things, they made what they said seem like a just accusation. They alter the words and say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” But the Savior said: “You destroy it,” not “I,” because it is unlawful for us to inflict death upon ourselves.

Then they alter the words again: “And after three days I will build another not made with hands,” so that he might seem to have spoken specifically about the Jewish Temple. But the Lord, to show that it was a living and breathing temple, had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another. [Col. 0118C]

“And the chief priest, rising,” and so forth. Impetuous and impatient anger, finding no place for an accusation, throws the high priest from his seat, so that he might demonstrate the madness of his mind through the movement of his body.

“And the chief priest said to him: I adjure you by the living God,” and so forth. In adjuring him, he is shown to condemn one who is silent, because he was unwilling to believe the one who confessed.

“Jesus said to him: You have said so.” He used a similar answer against Pilate, so that they might be condemned by their own judgment. Mark wrote, “I am,” to show that Jesus’ words, “You have said so,” have as much force as if he had said, “I am.”

“Nevertheless I say to you,” up to, “coming in the clouds of heaven.” That is: You will prove that the one whom you now judge unjustly, while he is in weakness, reigns in perpetual happiness and will come in majesty to judge with equity.

[Col. 0118D] “Then the chief priest,” and so forth. It is a Jewish custom, whenever they hear something blasphemous and apparently directed against God, to tear their garments; we read that Paul and Barnabas did this. Mystically, however, in the Lord’s Passion the high priest himself tore his garments, to show that the Jews had lost the priestly glory of the high priesthood because of their crimes and that the high priests possessed an empty seat.

But the fact that the Lord’s tunic could be torn neither by those who crucified him nor by the soldiers signifies that the solidity of the holy and universal Church—which is customarily called the garment of its Redeemer—can never be torn apart by any disturbance.

“But others struck him in the face with their palms,” and so forth. The one who was then struck by the Jews is now also struck by the blasphemies of false Christians. He is struck with blows by those who prefer their own honors to his. They spit in his face who reject the grace of his presence. They strike him in the face who, blinded by unbelief, assert that he did not come, as though they were banishing and repelling his presence.

The error of heretics concerning Christ is defined in three ways: they are mistaken either about his divinity, or about his humanity, or about both.

[Col. 0119A] “But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard.” He did not approach Jesus’ attendants, lest any suspicion arise.

“And one maidservant came to him, saying: You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” A woman is the first to betray him, so that it might appear that this sex too had sinned toward the Lord’s death and might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion. Hence it receives the first mystery of the resurrection, so that the ancient error of transgression might be abolished.

“But as he was going out through the doorway.” He therefore went out into the forecourt after the first denial, and immediately the cock crowed, as Mark records. When he returned again to the courtyard, what follows took place.

“Another maidservant saw him,” and so forth. Here he was addressed by two people: by a maidservant, whom Matthew and Mark mention, and by another person, whom Luke mentions. After the first denial, therefore, he returned to the courtyard and, according to John, stood by the fire. The maidservant noticed him when he rose to go out, and said to those who were inside in the courtyard near the fire: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.” But the one who had gone outside, hearing this, returned and swore to them, while they protested, that he did not know the man.

And after a little while those who were standing there came up, etc. Matthew and Mark speak in the plural of those who were saying this with Peter; Luke and John, however, use the singular. We should understand either that they used the plural instead of the singular as a customary manner of speaking, or that one person in particular, as though he knew and had seen him, made the assertion, while the others, following his conviction, joined in accusing Peter.

For your speech makes you manifest. Not because the Galileans spoke another language, but because every province and region has its own distinctive features and cannot avoid the native sound of its speech.

And immediately the cock crowed. The fact that Peter denied him before the first cockcrow signifies those who, before the resurrection, did not think Christ to be God, having been shaken by his death. But because he denied him twice before the second cockcrow, he is to be understood as signifying those who now err concerning him in either substance—either according to his humanity or according to his divinity—and therefore deny the truth. For the first cockcrow is the resurrection of the Head, that is, of the Lord himself. The second is his resurrection, but in the body of the universal Church. Morally, however, the cock signifies one of the teachers, if by the succession of times you wish to understand the merit of the matters in question.

And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, etc. In another Evangelist we read, “The Lord looked upon Peter.” It seems to me that that look was divinely directed, so that he might remember how often he had already denied him and what the Lord had foretold. And so, when the Lord mercifully looked upon him, he might repent and be restored to salvation, just as every day, when we are placed in some danger or labor, we say, “Lord, look upon me,” etc.

And Peter went out and wept bitterly. He goes outside so that, separated from the council of the impious, he might wash away the filth of his fearful denial with unrestricted tears. Thus, every day, penitents ought to separate themselves from the company of the wicked.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0120B]

And they brought him bound, etc. John explains that, immediately after seizing him during the night, they bound him and brought him first to Annas, then to Caiaphas, afterward to Pilate, and also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death was delivered over to be led away bound.

Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing this. “What is that to us?” they say. “You accepted the price; you see to it yourself as you wish.” The wicked betrayer gained nothing from having repented, since by his repentance he could not correct his crime. If at some time a brother sins against his brother in such a way that he is able to amend what he has done, the sin can be forgiven him. But if the deeds remain, repentance is taken up in vain in words, as is said in the Psalm concerning this most wretched Judas: “And let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108:7)—so that he not only could not amend the wickedness of his betrayal, but also added to his former crime the guilt of his own murder.

And after taking counsel, they bought from them the potter’s field, etc. The field, in the Lord’s interpretation, is called the world; the potter, however, is our Christ, who first created us from the clay of the earth and again recreated us through an earthly body. The price of whose blood was given for the burial of strangers, because we, who were strangers to the Law and the Prophets, take up their misguided pursuits for salvation and possess eternal rest at the price of his blood.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah, etc. This testimony is not found in Jeremiah, although something similar is found in Zechariah; and although the meaning does not differ greatly, the order and the words are different. In Jeremiah it is stated that he bought a field from the sons of his brother and gave him silver—not, indeed, under the designation of the price that appears in Zechariah as thirty pieces of silver; nevertheless, the purchase of the field is not found in Zechariah. We must unquestionably accept that whatever the Holy Spirit spoke through them belongs individually to all and wholly to each. Therefore, since the things spoken through Jeremiah belong as much to Zechariah as to Jeremiah, and those spoken through Zechariah belong as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah, what need was there for Matthew to correct himself when, encountering one name in place of another, he had read what he himself had written? Why did he not rather follow the authority of the Holy Spirit, by whom he surely felt that his mind was governed more than ours?

[Col. 0121A]

Now Jesus stood before the governor, etc. Luke explains this passage concerning their accusations more clearly. The Jews are convicted of impiety because, although they accuse the Savior, they cannot find even any plausible false charge that they can bring against him; and therefore, as Mark says, their testimonies were not in agreement.

Jesus says to him, “You say so.” He so moderates his answer that he both speaks the truth and does not expose his speech to slander.

Then Pilate says to him, etc. The one who condemns Jesus is indeed a Gentile, but he refers the responsibility to the Jewish people. Consider how many things they bring against you. Jesus, however, did not wish to answer anything, lest, by dispelling the accusation, he should be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be postponed.

But on the solemn day, etc. This was the custom of one who took pleasure in pleasing a foreign people by such actions.

Now he had at that time a notorious prisoner, etc. Luke reports that Barabbas, the son of their teacher, had been sent to prison because of an insurrection that had occurred in the city and because of murder. A person is called the son of the one by whom he is conquered.

But while he was seated on the tribunal, etc. In the woman there is represented the figure of the Gentile people, which, already believing, summons to faith in Christ the unbelieving people with whom she was conversing. Because she herself had suffered greatly and was destined, for Christ’s sake, to enter the same glory, she makes him with whom she was conversing known. At this moment, and not before, the devil understood that through Christ’s death he would be stripped and would lose the spoils of the human race, whether in the world or in Tartarus. Therefore he strove through the woman, through whom he had seized the spoils of death, to rescue Christ from the hands of the Jews, lest through his death he himself should lose dominion over death. Moreover, the tribunal is the seat of judges; the throne, of kings; the chair, of teachers.

But they said, “Barabbas.” The Jews’ request clings to them even today: in place of the Savior they chose a murderer; in place of the giver of life, one who took it away. Thus they have not deserved to recover the freedom of soul or body that they sold.

[Col. 0121D]

They all say, “Let him be crucified.” What great cruelty on the part of the faithless, who desire to kill an innocent man by what seemed to them the worst kind of death! Yet the cross had been chosen by the Lord: he was to have the cross itself as his sign and, after conquering the devil, to place it like a trophy upon the foreheads of the faithful.

But when Pilate saw this, until you see to it, etc. Pilate took water, in accordance with the prophetic saying, “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Psalm 25:6), so that, in the washing of his hands, the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed and he might separate us from the impiety of the Jews who cried, “Crucify him.”

“I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.” The judge who is compelled to pronounce sentence against the Lord does not condemn the one brought before him, but reproves those who brought him, declaring that the one who is to be crucified is righteous. “You see to it,” he says; “I am the servant of your laws; you are shedding the blood.”

Then he released Barabbas to them. It is no wonder that the Jews cannot possess peace, since the author of sedition was released to them—that is, the devil, who long ago, because of the fault of pride, was driven from his homeland of light and sent into the prison of darkness. Since Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the father,” or “son of their teacher,” he can bear the type of Antichrist, whom those to whom it is said, “You are of your father the devil,” will prefer to the Son of God.

But after he had scourged Jesus, etc. Pilate first scourged him himself and afterward handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked, so that the Jews, satisfied with his punishments and insults, would cease thirsting for his death. Mystically, however, Pilate, whose name is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammerer,” signifies the devil, who, according to the Prophet, is the hammer of the whole earth. Through him the Lord strikes his vessels, which are to be fashioned for the use of ministry, when he permits his chosen ones to be tested by various temptations.

Then the soldiers of the governor, until “Hail, King of the Jews.” Whatever the soldiers did, they nevertheless bestowed mysteries upon us who believe. In the scarlet cloak, which Mark calls purple, because one kind of purple is red and very similar to scarlet, he sustains the bloody deeds of those who carried them out, or indicates his flesh, which he exposed to sufferings. In the crown of thorns he removes the ancient curse, or displays the assumption of our sins, for which he deigned to become mortal. With the reed he kills poisonous animals, or he held the reed in his hand so as to write the sacrilege of the Jews. In both aspects of the Lord’s clothing—shameful according to the judgment of his enemies, but most glorious by the Lord’s own choice—the whole multitude of his elect is clearly represented, divided into the venerable martyrs and the rest of the faithful people. According to Luke, he is clothed in a white garment when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous. He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he glories in the triumph of victorious martyrs.

And spitting upon him, and the rest. Pagans and heretics, the soldiers of the devil, continue to do these things even today. They strike Christ’s head, as though with a reed, when, contradicting his divinity, they attempt to confirm their error by the authority of sacred Scripture. For Scripture is commonly written with a reed. They spit in his face who reject the presence of his grace with accursed words conceived from the inner madness of a blind mind, and deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

And after they had mocked him, and the rest. When Jesus is scourged, spat upon, and mocked, he does not have his own garments, but those which he had assumed on account of our sins. But when he was crucified, and the spectacle of mockery and derision had passed away, then he received his former garments and assumed his proper adornment.

But as they went out, they found a Cyrenian man, etc. [Col. 0123A] At first, according to John, he carried the cross himself; afterward it was laid upon Simon, whose name is interpreted as “obedient,” who came from the city of Cyrene in Libya, which is interpreted as “heir.” This is because Christ suffered for us, providing believers with an example so that they might follow in his footsteps. Simon, coming out from the village, carries the cross behind Jesus when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s passion.

And they came to a place called Golgotha, etc. Golgotha is a Syriac name and is interpreted as “Place of the Skull.” That place was then outside the city in Aelia, on the northern side of Mount Zion. It is called the Place of the Skull not because of the baldness of the first man, whom some misguided people vainly suppose was buried there, but because of the beheading of criminals and condemned persons. For this reason the Lord was crucified there: where formerly there had been an area for the condemned, there the standards of martyrdom might be raised. The Apostle also describes the moral figure of the cross when he says, “Rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints,” etc. (Ephesians 3:17–18).

And they gave him wine to drink, etc. The bitter vine produced bitter wine, which they offered to the Lord Jesus, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22). The statement, “When he had tasted it, he would not drink,” indicates that he tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day. Mark, however, omitted the fact that he tasted it; what he refused, he made clear by saying, “He did not accept it”—the wine which Mark calls “myrrh-flavored.” He put gall for bitterness, and wine flavored with myrrh is extremely bitter, although it is possible that both gall and myrrh made the wine exceedingly bitter.

After they had crucified him, etc. John explains more distinctly how this was done. The Lord’s four-part garment represented his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world, that is, throughout the four regions of the earth, and distributed harmoniously among all those regions. But that tunic, for which they cast lots, signifies the unity of all the parts. Since unity is held together by the bond of love—which is the more excellent way and is above all commandments—it is rightly said to be a garment woven from above. What is commended by the lot, which is granted not according to a person or merits but by the hidden judgment of God, except the grace of God, which comes to all in unity?

And sitting down, they kept watch over him. The diligence of the soldiers and priests benefits us, so that the greater and clearer might be the power of the one who rose again.

And they placed above his head, etc. Beautifully, the title that testifies that Christ is king is placed not beneath but above the cross. Although on the cross he suffered in the weakness of his humanity for our sake, above the cross he shone with the majesty of a king. Appropriately also, because he is both king and priest, when he offered to the Father the pre-eminent sacrifice of his own flesh upon the altar of the cross, he also displayed the dignity of a king, since he bore the title. Thus it might be known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross he had not lost his dominion, but rather confirmed and strengthened it. As far as the literal sense is concerned, these three languages predominated there above the others: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the learned among the nations; and Latin, because of the Romans, who by then ruled almost all nations. Thus, whether they wish it or not, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of the divine Law testify that Jesus is King of the Jews—that is, the ruler and God of those who believe and confess.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, etc. The robbers crucified on either side of the Lord signify those who, under the faith and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any discipline of stricter continence. But whoever does these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory is clearly represented by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those, however, who renounce the world either with a view to human praise or with some other less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and actions of the blasphemer.

Likewise the chief priests, etc. Therefore, in confessing these things, they condemn themselves by their own sentence. For the one who saved others could certainly have saved himself, if he had wished.

“If you are the King of Israel,” etc. A deceitful promise. “He has risen, then”; even if he comes down from the cross, you will likewise not believe.

The robbers also said the same thing, and the rest. Since according to Luke one of them did this, while the other rebuked him with a deserved reprimand and entreated the Lord with faithful supplication, the matter could be signified in the plural by the customary manner of speaking. We see this happening in the Church even today, when true and false Christians alike are touched by worldly afflictions. Those who bear the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a deceitful mind desire to be freed by the Lord for the joys of the present life. But those who with simple intention glory, with the Apostle, in the cross of our Lord desire to be rescued from present troubles in such a way that they commend their spirit into the hands of their Creator. In the two robbers both peoples may also be represented, because both blasphemed when together they consented to the Lord’s death. But one, terrified by the greatness of the signs, repented, and even to this day rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the land, etc. Mark, in recapitulating, specifies the hour at which the Jews cried out most insistently that the Lord should be crucified. What they emphatically appeared unwilling to have done, he shows that they did at the third hour. He indicates most truthfully that the Jews’ tongue, rather than the soldiers’ hands, was more responsible for killing the Lord, although the soldiers crucified him at the sixth hour. Therefore the order of reason—or rather of divine mercy—required that at the same hour when he had once closed the gate of paradise against Adam in his transgression, the Lord should open the gate of paradise to the repentant robber; and that at the hour when the first Adam introduced death into this world by sinning, the second Adam should destroy death by dying.

And about the ninth hour, etc. He laments the misery of those whose nature he assumed. For the very nature that he had assumed had been abandoned by the Father on account of sin, not the Son, who is one with the Father. He shows how greatly those who sin ought to weep, since the one who never sinned wept in this way; and he shows how patient and hopeful sinners ought to be amid scourging, since he passed to immortality only through death.

But some of those standing there, etc. I think they were Roman soldiers who did not understand the particular character of the Hebrew language. If, however, you wish to understand them as Jews who said this, they do this in their customary manner: they slander the Lord on account of weakness, as though he were imploring the aid of another.

And immediately one of them ran, etc. After they had completed everything, they gave him what they were. The Jews themselves were also vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the Prophets and Patriarchs, as though, from a full vessel, they had been filled with the iniquity of this world; their heart was like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and twisted hiding places. Since hyssop, around which they placed the sponge, is a low-growing herb that cleanses the breast, we appropriately understand it as Christ’s humility, which they surrounded and thought they had ensnared. Hence the Psalm says, “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50:9). Through the reed upon which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, which was fulfilled by this deed.

But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit. After receiving the vinegar, he said, “It is finished”; he uttered this with a loud voice. Luke clearly identifies what he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” The statement that he “gave up his spirit” shows that the giving up of the spirit belongs to divine power, as he himself had also said: “No one can take away the soul,” etc.

And behold, the veil of the temple was torn, etc. Josephus also reports that the angelic powers, once guardians of the temple, then cried out together, “Let us depart from these dwelling places.” Mystically, the veil of the temple is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the Law that had been concealed might appear and pass over to the people of the nations.

And the earth was shaken, etc. The literal meaning of the greatness of the signs is beyond doubt: heaven and earth, and all things, were to show that their Lord had been crucified. But it seems to me that the earthquake and the rest bear the type of the nations: after the former vices of error and the hardness of their hearts had been softened, those who had previously been like tombs of the dead recognized the Creator.

And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose, etc. The bodies of the saints rose so as to show the Lord rising; and when the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. By the holy city in which those who rose were seen, we may understand either the heavenly Jerusalem or this earthly city, which had formerly been called holy because of the temple and the Holy of Holies, in distinction from the other cities in which idols were worshiped.

Now the centurion and those who were with him, guarding Jesus. It was not the centurion alone who glorified God, but also the soldiers. How great, then, was the blindness of the Jews, who refused to believe despite the many mighty deeds performed by the Lord and the great signs that appeared at his death! Therefore the faith of the Church is rightly represented by the centurion. Once the veil of the heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death, the Church immediately confirms Jesus, both as truly a righteous man and as truly the Son of God, while the Synagogue remains silent. Indeed, the very number one hundred, which in the bending of the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, corresponds most clearly to the mystery and faith of the Church: in place of the Law, the Gospel has been entrusted to her; in place of the riches of the earth, the heavenly kingdom has been promised.

Now many women were there, watching from a distance, who had followed, etc. They ministered to the Lord from their own possessions, so that he might reap their material things while they reaped spiritual things—not because the Lord of creatures needed food, but to present a type of teachers, who ought to be content with food and clothing from their disciples.

When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea came, etc. He is called rich not because the writer boasts in reporting that this noble and very wealthy man was a disciple of Jesus, but to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate. Arimathea itself is Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Thamnitica near Diospolis.

And Joseph, having taken the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth. The Lord’s simple burial condemns the ostentation of the rich, who cannot be without riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding, we can take this to mean that the Lord’s body ought to be wrapped not in gold, gems, and silk, but in pure linen. Yet it also signifies that the one who wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth is the person who receives him with a pure mind.

And he placed it in a new tomb, etc. He is placed in a new tomb so that no one might invent that, after the resurrection, another body had risen while the other bodies remained. The new tomb can also signify the womb of the virgin Mary; and the stone placed against the entrance can indicate the great stone by which the tomb could not have been opened without the assistance of many people. Those who have come from Jerusalem in our own time report that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber cut out beneath an overlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch the roof with an outstretched hand. It has an entrance from the east, to which that great stone was rolled and placed. In the northern part of the tomb is the burial chamber itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock. It is seven feet long and rises three palms above the rest of the pavement. This place is open not from above but along the entire southern side, through which the body was brought in. The color of the tomb and burial chamber is said to be mixed red and white.

Now Mary Magdalene was there, etc. When everyone else returned to their own homes, only the women, who loved him more closely, followed the funeral and took care to observe how he was laid, so that at the proper time they might offer him the gift of their devotion. Even to this day holy women do the same on the day of preparation, when humble souls—burning with a love of the Savior proportionate to their greater awareness of their own frailty—carefully attend in this world upon the traces of his passion, in which the future rest is being prepared. If they are perhaps able to imitate it, they examine with pious attentiveness the manner in which that passion was completed.

On the next day, which is after the day of preparation. Since humanity was created on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—for which reason he also wished it to be called the Sabbath, that is, rest—the Savior rightly completed the mystery of human restoration by being crucified on that same sixth day. Resting in the tomb on the Sabbath, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. In this there shines forth an example both of our devotion and of blessed recompense: in this sixth age of the world we must suffer for the Lord and, as it were, be crucified to the world. In the seventh age—that is, when a person pays the debt owed to death—we ought to rest after good works, with our bodies indeed in the tombs but our souls dwelling with the Lord in hidden peace, until at last, when the eighth age comes, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive together with their souls the incorruption of the eternal inheritance.

The chief priests assembled, etc. In the name of the deceiver and in the theft of the disciples, they prophesy the truth, although they do not understand it. Christ was indeed a deceiver—not as they think, sending people from truth into error, but sending them from falsehood into truth. For just as the devil is a mediator who deceives people into death, so Christ is the mediator of life, reconciling the world to God. The Savior’s disciples were also spiritual thieves, because, through a just judgment, they transferred the Scripture of the New and Old Testaments, taken away from despisers and ingrates, for the use of the Church; and while those people slept at night—that is, while they languished in unbelief—they withheld from them the Savior who had been promised and sent to them, and entrusted him to be believed in by the nations. Their unbelief regarding the resurrection was worse for them than the cruelty of the cross.

But they went away and, together with the guards, sealed the stone. As far as they could, they would have laid a hand upon the one who was rising, so that their diligence might benefit our faith; for the more carefully he was guarded, the more clearly the power of his resurrection was displayed.

But in the evening of the Sabbath, until they came to see the tomb. They began to come on the evening of the Sabbath, but at daybreak on the first day of the week they arrived at the tomb. That is, in the evening they prepared the spices, but in the morning they carried the prepared spices to the tomb. Matthew, for the sake of brevity, stated this somewhat obscurely, but the other Evangelists show more clearly the order in which it happened. After the Lord was buried on Friday, the women returned from the tomb and prepared spices and ointments for as long as it was permissible to work; on the Sabbath they remained silent according to the commandment, as Luke clearly indicates. When the Sabbath had passed and, with evening approaching, the time for work had returned, they promptly bought the spices they had not adequately prepared, as Mark records, so that when they came they might anoint him.

And very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb. But it is asked how the Evangelist can say, “In the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the week,” when the customary order of times has evening becoming darker toward night rather than brightening toward day. Speaking mystically, the Evangelist sought to indicate how much dignity this most sacred night received from the glory of death’s defeat. From the beginning of the world until then, the course of times had been ordered so that day preceded night, in accordance with the order of the first creation. On this night, however, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of times was changed. For he who rose from the dead during the night showed the effect of that resurrection to his disciples on the following day; most rightly, therefore, that night was joined to the light of the following day, and the order of times was established so that day should follow night. Formerly, night appropriately followed day, because humanity, having fallen by sin from the light of paradise, descended into the darkness of this age. Now day most appropriately follows night, when through faith in the resurrection, by Christ’s gift, we are led back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life.
