The two women of the same name and of the same love and devotion, who came to see the Lord’s tomb, signify the two peoples of the faithful—the Jewish and the Gentile—who desire with one and the same zeal to celebrate the passion and resurrection of their Redeemer.

And behold, a great earthquake occurred. The earthquake signifies that the hearts of the carnal are to be shaken by faith in the passion and resurrection toward repentance, and, moved by a most salutary fear, raised to everlasting life.

For an angel of the Lord, until “And he sat upon it.” The angel came to discharge the service owed to the Lord. He rolled away the stone so that it might provide human beings with evidence that the Lord had already gone out. The angel who proclaimed the Lord’s coming into the world appeared standing, thereby indicating that the one he proclaimed was coming to conquer the ruler of the world. This angel sat, so that by sitting he might also signify that, after conquering the author of death, the Lord had already ascended to the seat of an everlasting kingdom. He sat upon the stone that closed the entrance of the tomb, to teach that by his own power he had overcome the barriers of hell and cast them down.

His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing [Col. 0129A] was like snow. Thus, by his appearance and expression as well, he signified that the one who announced the glory of the resurrection would be both terrible in condemning the reprobate and kind and gentle in comforting the elect.

But the angel answered and said to the women, “Do not be afraid, you.” It is as though he openly says: “Let those who do not love the coming of the citizens of heaven be afraid—those who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to reach their society—not you, who see your fellow citizens.”

“For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified,” etc. “I know,” he says, “that you have come to honor the Savior’s burial as an act of love; but you cannot see him present here, for he has already risen by his own power, although you will never experience him as absent in his majesty. And if you do not believe my words, test the truth of the resurrection at least by the empty tomb.” He added:

“And going quickly,” until “There you will see him; behold, I have told you beforehand.” Blessed women, who, instructed by the angelic oracle, were worthy to announce to the world the triumph of the resurrection and to proclaim that the dominion of death, which Eve had introduced when she was seduced by the serpent’s breath, had been overthrown!

“He will go before you into Galilee.” That is, into the rolling-place of the nations, where formerly there was error and where no one set a firm foot upon unstable ground. For Galilee is interpreted as “rolling,” or “wheel,” or “transmigration.” Morally, it is recognized in the mortification of the flesh and seen in the transmigration of the mind.

And they went out quickly from the tomb with great fear, [Col. 0129C] etc. It is rightly asked how Mark can write, “They said nothing to anyone,” when Luke, agreeing with Matthew, says, “Returning from the tomb, they reported all these things,” etc. We must understand either that they did not dare say anything to anyone about the angels themselves—that is, that they did not answer what they had heard from them—or perhaps that they said nothing to the guards, whom they saw lying there.

And behold, Jesus met them, saying, “Hail.” They deserved to hear the greeting of the Lord, the first to rise, so that Eve’s curse might be removed from women. Morally, Jesus meets with a greeting all who begin the path of virtue, offering assistance so that they may reach everlasting salvation.

But they approached, etc. These women approach and take hold of his feet because they worshiped him. But the woman who was seeking the living among the dead, and did not yet know that the Son of God had risen, rightly hears, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

Then he says to them, “Do not be afraid.” In both the Old and the New Testament this must always be observed: whenever a more troubling vision appears, fear is first driven away, so that afterward what is said may be heard with a tranquil mind.

“Go, announce to my brothers that they should go into Galilee; there they will see me.” Since this promise of the Lord’s appearance was fulfilled for many, it should be understood as spoken prophetically. Galilee is interpreted either as “transmigration” or as “revelation.” For the grace of Christ had migrated from the people of Israel to the nations, so that, as the Apostles preached the Gospel, it might prepare a way in human hearts.

“There they will see me.” That is, there they find my members and recognize the living body in those who receive them. According to the interpretation of Galilee as “revelation,” this is not to be understood as referring to the form of a servant, but to that form in which he is equal to the Father. There will be revelation as the true Galilee when we are made like him and see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

When they had gone, behold, some of the guards, until “and we will make you secure.” Therefore all who misuse the temple’s offerings and the things contributed for the uses of the Church for evil purposes by which they satisfy their own pleasure are like the scribes and priests who purchase a lie and the Savior’s blood.

The eleven disciples went into Galilee, etc. Why, then, does Jesus go before the disciples into Galilee so that he may be seen by them? They follow him so that, when they see him, they may worship him. The reason is that Christ rose from the dead as the firstfruits of those who sleep; those who belong to Christ follow him, and in their own order they pass from death into life. There, seeing him, they worship, because, contemplating him in the form of his divinity, they praise him without end. To this vision corresponds the statement, “Then, with unveiled face,” as the Apostle testifies, “beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18)—all who now reveal our way to him and follow his footsteps with sincere faith.

But some doubted. Thus they recognize the Lord, whom they worship with their faces bowed toward the earth; yet a doubt not to be dismissed remained in their minds, because they thought that they were seeing not the body in which he had suffered raised again, but only the spirit that he had surrendered when his passion was completed.

And Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” He speaks here of the humanity he assumed, by assuming which he was made for a little while lower than the angels, and in which, rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor (Hebrews 1:9) and set over the works of the Father’s hands, with all things subjected beneath his feet. Among all these things, even death itself was subjected beneath his feet, although for a time it appeared to prevail over him.

Therefore go and teach all nations, etc. First, then, he commands that the nations be taught—that is, instructed in the knowledge of the truth—and thus baptized, because without faith it is impossible to please God; and: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Finally he adds: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you,” because just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

“And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” Mark says: “And the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God.” Because he is himself both God and man, he was taken up into heaven and sat there in respect of his humanity, which he had assumed from the earth; in respect of his divinity, by which he fills earth and heaven alike, he remains with the saints on earth. Meanwhile, it should be noted that the divine majesty, which is present everywhere, is present in one way to its elect and in another to the reprobate. It is present to the reprobate through the incomprehensible power of nature, by which it knows all things, the latest and the earliest, understands thoughts from afar, and foresees the ways of each individual. It is present to the elect through the grace of loving protection, by which, through his presence, he disciplines them specially with gifts or punishments, as a father teaches his children, and by teaching advances them toward possession of the inheritance to come.

# EXPLANATION OF THE LORD’S PRAYER

[Col. 0131]

“Our Father, who are in heaven.” In the evangelist Matthew, the prayer appears to contain seven petitions, three of which ask for eternal things and the remaining four for temporal things—though these temporal things are necessary for attaining the eternal. For when we say:

“Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” some have rightly understood these words as referring to spirit and body. They must be retained altogether without end, and they begin here. However much we advance, they increase within us; but when perfected—which is to be hoped for in the other life—they will always be possessed.

When, however, we say:

“Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation; but deliver us from evil,” who does not see that these petitions concern the needs of the present life? In that eternal life, then, where we always hope to be, both the sanctification of God’s name, his kingdom, and his will will remain perfectly and immortally in our spirit and body. Daily bread is so called because it is necessary here, in whatever quantity must be supplied to soul and body, whether it is understood spiritually, bodily, or in both ways. Here also is the forgiveness that we seek, where sins are remitted. Here are the temptations that either entice or drive us to sin. Here, finally, is the evil from which we desire to be delivered; there, none of these things exists.

The evangelist Luke, in the Lord’s Prayer, embraces not seven petitions but five, and yet does not differ from this account. By the very brevity of his version, he has indicated how the seven are to be understood. God’s name is sanctified in the spirit, whereas God’s kingdom will come in the resurrection of the flesh. By showing that the third petition is in a certain sense a repetition of the preceding two, Luke made this understood more clearly by omitting it. Then he adds the three petitions concerning daily bread, the remission of sins, and the avoidance of temptation. But what Matthew placed last—“But deliver us from evil”—Luke did not include, so that we might understand it as belonging to the earlier statement about temptation. For this reason he says, “But deliver,” and does not say, “and deliver,” thereby showing that it is one petition: not this, but that. Thus each person may know that he is delivered from evil when he is not led into temptation.

[Col. 0131]

# EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (C, S)

# LETTER TO ACCA

[Col. 0131D] As we are about to write an exposition of the Gospel according to Mark, with the help of the grace contained in the Gospel itself, we have thought it necessary first to indicate briefly what occasion led Mark to write his Gospel. When the bright light of the true God had arisen over the city of Rome through the preaching of the blessed apostle Peter, the word of truth so illumined the minds of all who gladly heard it that those who listened daily could never become satiated. Therefore hearing alone did not suffice for them; they earnestly begged Mark, his disciple, with every kind of entreaty, to commit to writing for their perpetual instruction the things that Peter preached orally, so that at home and abroad they might remain occupied in meditating on such teaching. They did not cease their entreaties until they obtained what they had requested.

When Peter learned, through the Holy Spirit, that he had been deprived by this devout theft, he was pleased. Considering their faith and devotion in this matter, he confirmed what had been done and entrusted the written work to the churches to be read perpetually. Clement, in the sixth book of his *Dispositions*, records that these events took place in this way. The bishop of Hierapolis, Papias by name, also gives similar testimony. He says as well that Peter mentioned Mark in his first letter, which he wrote from the city of Rome, naming Rome figuratively as Babylon when he says: “The church that is chosen in Babylon greets you, and Mark, my son.”

Having taken up the Gospel that he himself had composed, Mark went to Egypt. First announcing Christ at Alexandria, he established a church with such teaching and moral discipline that he compelled all Christ’s followers to conform to his example. Finally, Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, seeing that the first church at Alexandria was still practicing Judaism, wrote a book, as though in praise of his nation, concerning their way of life. And just as Luke relates that the believers at Jerusalem held everything in common, so Philo committed to memory what he observed taking place at Alexandria under Mark’s instruction.

They report that Mark was of Israelite nationality and descended from a priestly lineage. After the passion and resurrection of the Lord and Savior, he was instructed in evangelical faith and the sacraments through the apostles’ preaching, and belonged to the number of those of whom Luke writes: “A great many of the priests were obedient to the faith” (Acts 6). Therefore, being thoroughly trained in the precepts of the Law, he set before the people whom he was calling to the faith an excellent order of life in every respect. He also demonstrated the canonical observance of Easter, which was to be imitated by all the churches of Christ.

At the prompting and urging of you, dearest bishop Acca, and of many other brothers, we are about to write an exposition of his Gospel. As the Lord grants, we shall take care to insert here and there what we have found collected in the examples of venerable Fathers. We shall also interpose some material of our own, modeled upon their understanding, wherever it seems appropriate. I humbly beg the reader that, if he considers these little works worthy of transcription, he preserve with careful writing the annotation of the names set above, just as is known to have been done in the exposition of the Gospel of the blessed Luke, which we composed many years ago with the help of God’s grace.

May heavenly grace always protect your holiness as you pray for us. Above all, I beseech in the Lord all who may happen to read these works to deign to become intercessors before the merciful Judge for my weaknesses of both body and soul.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0133]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0133B]

“The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,” etc. “As it is written in Isaiah the prophet.” This beginning of Mark’s Gospel should be compared with the beginning of Matthew, which says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David,” etc. From both accounts, our one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man, is to be understood. Appropriately, the first evangelist calls him the Son of Man, while the second calls him the Son of God, so that our understanding might gradually rise from lesser things to greater and, through faith and the sacraments of the humanity he assumed, ascend to knowledge of the divine eternity.

Appropriately, the evangelist who was going to describe his human generation began with the Son of Man, namely David or Abraham, from whose stock he assumed the substance of flesh. Appropriately, the one who began his book with the beginning of evangelical preaching preferred to call our Lord Jesus Christ more particularly the Son of God, since he was both of human nature, receiving the reality of flesh from the line of patriarchs or kings, and of divine power, preaching the Gospel to the world.

“Gospel” means “good news.” What news is better than this: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matthew 3)? To be born humanly belongs to man; to preach the entrance into the heavenly kingdom to those who repent belongs to God. Thus Matthew rightly calls him the Son of David, whom he affirms came in the flesh. Mark rightly calls him the Son of God, whom at the very front of his book he designates as the author of the Gospel and the guarantor of the eternal kingdom.

Here it should be noted that the holy evangelists who left us a written account of the Lord’s incarnation approached the task of writing, indeed, inspired by one Spirit, but each established a different beginning and a different endpoint for his narrative. Matthew, beginning with the Lord’s birth, carried the sequence of his narrative forward to the time of the Lord’s resurrection. Mark, beginning with the commencement of evangelical preaching, continued to the time of the Lord’s ascension and the preaching of his disciples to all the nations throughout the world. Luke, beginning with the birth of the forerunner, brought his Gospel to its conclusion at the Lord’s ascension, when the disciples, returning to Jerusalem, awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit in divine praises. John, taking his beginning from the eternity of the Word of God, through whom all things were made, likewise reached in his evangelizing as far as the time of the Lord’s resurrection.

As Mark was therefore about to write his Gospel, he appropriately placed first of all the testimonies of the prophets who had foretold long ago what was to come. In this way he made clear that what he was writing was to be received by all as true and without any hesitation or doubt, since it had previously been foreknown and foretold by prophets filled with the Holy Spirit. At the same time, by this single beginning of his Gospel, he instructed both the Jews, who had accepted the Law and the Prophets, to receive also the sacraments of the Gospel that their own prophets had foretold, and the Gentiles, who had come to the Lord through all the proclamations of the Gospel, to accept and revere as well the authority of the Law and the Prophets. Otherwise, if anyone, following the heretics, accepted only the Old Testament or only the New, he would remain alien to God’s covenant.

“Behold, I send my angel,” etc. John is called an angel, not by a community of nature, as Origen’s heresy holds, but by the dignity of his office. For *angelos* in Greek means “messenger” in Latin. This name could rightly be given to the man who was sent by God to bear witness concerning the light (John 1) and to announce to the world the Lord who was coming in the flesh.

Nor is it surprising that he is mystically called an angel, though among those born of women no one has arisen greater than he (Matthew 11), since it is clear that all who properly carry out the office of the priesthood can be called angels because of their duty to evangelize. The prophet says: “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

“A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” etc. It is established that the only-begotten Son is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). From our own speech we understand that the voice sounds first, so that afterward the word may be heard. John, therefore, is called “voice” by the prophet because he precedes the Word. Since he preceded the Lord’s coming, he is called the voice, because through his ministry the Word of the Father was heard by human beings.

He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of redemption to Judea, which had been abandoned and left destitute. What he was to cry out is revealed when it follows: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Everyone who preaches right faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the coming Lord into the hearts of his hearers, so that the force of grace may penetrate, the light of truth may illumine, and he may make straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

It should certainly be noted that of the prophetic testimonies Mark has placed here, one is found in Isaiah alone, while the other is found in Malachi. Yet the evangelist should not be thought either to have been deceived or to have deceived others by saying that a text was written in Isaiah which Isaiah did not write. Rather, it should be understood that although the words he included from Malachi are not found in Isaiah, their meaning is found in Isaiah and in several other places, and more clearly in what he himself adds here: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

Who does not see how great the agreement is between the two statements? For what Malachi said—that an angel was to be sent before the Lord’s face to prepare his way—is precisely what Isaiah said: that the voice of one crying in the wilderness was to be heard, saying, “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Just as John could rightly be called an angel because he preceded the Lord’s face by evangelizing, so he could rightly be called a voice because he went before the Word of God by sounding it forth, as was said above. In both statements the preparation of the Lord’s way is similarly preached.

Therefore the evangelist is not mistaken when he writes that this was said by Isaiah. Although he did not find it written by Isaiah in the same words, he found it written by him in the same meaning. It could have happened that, as Mark was composing his Gospel in his mind, Isaiah came to him instead of Malachi, as often happens. Yet he would certainly have corrected this without any doubt, at least after being warned by others who could have read it while he was still alive, unless he thought that the name of one prophet had come to his memory in place of another not without reason, because the Lord had ordained that it be written in this way.

Why the Lord ordained this should be understood first and foremost as having been most usefully indicated in this manner: namely, that all the holy prophets spoke with one Spirit and were joined by such marvelous agreement that this is something far greater than if everything said by all the prophets had been spoken through the mouth of one man. Therefore whatever the Holy Spirit said through them must be accepted without hesitation; each individual statement belongs to all, and all belong to each individual.

Since, then, what was said through Isaiah belongs as much to Malachi as to Isaiah, and what was said through Malachi belongs as much to Isaiah as to Malachi, why should Mark have corrected the text when he found that one prophetic name had occurred to him in place of another and had been written by him? Why should he not rather have followed the authority of the Holy Spirit, who—as he himself certainly felt more strongly than we do—ruled his mind, and left the text written in this way? For in this manner the Lord had arranged to instruct us that there is such great agreement among the prophets in their words that we may not absurdly, but most fittingly, attribute to Isaiah what we find spoken through Malachi.

“John was in the wilderness baptizing,” etc. It is clear to all nations that John not only preached the baptism of repentance but also administered it to some. Nevertheless, he could not give baptism for the remission of sins. The remission of sins is granted to us only in the baptism of Christ.

It should therefore be noted that he is said to have preached “a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” Since he could not give a baptism that would release sins, he preached it, so that just as he preceded the incarnate Word of the Father with the word of preaching, so he might precede with his own baptism the baptism of repentance by which sins are released, though his baptism itself could not release sins.

“And they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.” An example of confessing sins and promising a better life is given to those who desire to receive baptism. Likewise, when Paul was preaching at Ephesus, many believers came confessing and declaring their deeds, so that, renouncing their former life, they might deserve to be renewed in Christ.

For this reason, too, when various kinds of living creatures were shown to the blessed Peter in a heavenly sheet, he was told: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). This means plainly: Kill unbelievers with respect to what they previously were, through renunciation of crimes and the promise of devout religion; then, having been instructed in the sacraments of the Christian faith, transform them into members of the holy Church.

“And John was clothed in camel’s hair,” etc. He says “clothed in hair,” not wool. The former is a sign of austere clothing; the latter, of softer luxury. The leather belt with which he was girded, as Elijah also was, is a sign of mortification.

Then follows: “And he ate locusts and wild honey.” This is fitting for an inhabitant of the wilderness, who did not satisfy himself with the delicacies of food but only the necessity of human flesh. His clothing and food can also, by way of symbolism, suitably express the quality of his inner way of life.

He used harsher clothing, just as the Lord also testified in his praise when he said to the Jews: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who dress in soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matthew 11). For John did not indulge the life of sinners with flattering words but rebuked it with the force of harsh denunciation, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 23).

He had a leather belt around his loins because he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires; we have learned from the Apostle that this is characteristic of those who belong to Jesus Christ. He ate locusts and wild honey because his preaching tasted sweet to the crowds. The people thought, and all were considering in their hearts concerning him, whether perhaps he might be the Christ. But that opinion soon reached its end when his hearers understood that he was not himself the Christ but Christ’s forerunner and prophet. In honey there is sweetness; in locusts, a lively flight—but one that soon falls.

[Col. 0137B] “And he preached, saying: One mightier will come,” etc. Among the ancients it was customary that if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who was destined for him, the man who was to become her bridegroom by right of kinship would loosen his sandal. What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, if not the bridegroom of the holy Church? John himself says of him: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3).

But because people thought John was the Christ—a claim John himself denies—he rightly declares himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal. It is as though he were plainly saying: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s footprints, because I do not presumptuously claim for myself the name of bridegroom.”

This can nevertheless be understood in another way. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? The incarnate Lord, coming among us, appeared as though wearing sandals, for in his divinity he assumed the dead matter of our corruption. But the mystery of this incarnation is not within the reach of the human eye. It cannot be investigated at all: how the Word becomes embodied; how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is ensouled within the mother’s womb; how the one who has no beginning is conceived and comes into existence.

The strap of the sandal, therefore, is the bond of the mystery. John cannot loosen the strap of his sandal because he himself is not sufficient to investigate the mystery of the incarnation, although he recognized it through the spirit of prophecy.

“I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” John does not yet openly preach that the Lord is God or the Son of God, but only that he is a man stronger than himself. For his hearers were still inexperienced and could not grasp the profound mystery: that the eternal Son of God, having assumed a human being from the Virgin, had been born anew into the world. They had to be introduced gradually, through recognition of his glorified humanity, to faith in his divine eternity.

Yet he declares somewhat secretly and in veiled speech that this man is truly God, when he affirms that he will baptize with the Holy Spirit. For who could doubt that no one other than God can give the grace of the Holy Spirit?

As time passed, when he saw that these same hearers of his had become more capable of understanding, he openly preached him as the Son of God, saying: “But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. And I saw and bore witness that he is the Son of God.”

We are baptized by the Lord in the Holy Spirit not only when, on the day of baptism, we are washed in the font of life for the remission of sins, but also every day, when by the grace of that same Spirit we are kindled to do what pleases God.

“And it happened in those days,” etc. The Savior received baptism from John for three reasons. First, because he had been born human, so that he might fulfill all the righteousness and humility of the Law. Second, so that by his own baptism he might confirm John’s baptism. Third, so that, sanctifying the water of the Jordan, he might show through the descent of the dove—the Holy Spirit—the Spirit’s coming into the baptismal washing of believers.

[Col. 0138B] “And immediately, as he was coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened,” etc. The mystery of the Trinity is demonstrated in the Lord’s baptism. The Lord is baptized, the Spirit descends in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice, bearing witness to the Son, is heard.

The heavens are opened not by the elements being physically unsealed, but to spiritual eyes, just as Ezekiel also recalls at the beginning of his book that they were opened. The dove also rested upon Jesus’ head, lest anyone think that the Father’s voice had been addressed to John rather than to the Lord.

Beautifully, after saying, “And the Spirit descending like a dove,” he added, “and remaining in him.” This was a special gift bestowed upon the Mediator of God and human beings: once the Holy Spirit had filled him, the Spirit never departed but remained perpetually in him.

For his faithful, however, the grace of the Spirit is sometimes bestowed and sometimes withdrawn for the performance of extraordinary virtues and miracles. Yet for the work of piety and justice, and for preserving love of God and neighbor, the grace of the Spirit is never absent from them. Hence the Lord promises this Spirit when he says to them: “You will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John 14).

In the Lord, however, the Spirit remains especially—not as in his elect, according to the measure of faith, but as John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1). The Spirit remains in him not only from the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, but rather from the time when he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb.

The fact that the Spirit appeared to descend upon him when he was baptized was a sign of the spiritual grace to be given to us in baptism. After we have been regenerated from water and the Spirit for the remission of sins, the fuller grace of that same Spirit is customarily given to us from heaven through the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

Likewise, the fact that he saw the heavens opened after the baptism happened for our sake. Through the washing of the regenerating water, the door of the heavenly kingdom is opened to us—the door that, when the first-formed humans sinned and were expelled from paradise, was closed to the whole human race by the interposition of cherubim and a flaming sword.

This flame is extinguished for each believer when he is immersed in the waters of life. He is reconciled with the angelic spirits when he returns to the peace of his Creator, so that, if he preserves the sacraments of faith with a pure heart and body, he may soon, once freed from the flesh, enter the heavenly kingdom.

Otherwise, how would the heavens then be opened to the Lord, when, by becoming human and dwelling with us on earth, he was at the same time containing heaven and earth by his divine power?

The paternal voice that was made known from heaven—“You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased”—did not teach the Son something he did not know; rather, it showed us what we ought to believe: namely, that the one who came with the others to John to be baptized as a man was truly the Son of God, not only the Lord of John himself but also of the entire world, and therefore truly able to baptize in the Holy Spirit.

That same voice also taught us that through the water of cleansing and the Spirit of sanctification we can become children of God. “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1).

The Holy Spirit rightly descended in the form of a dove, an exceedingly gentle animal, free from the bitterness of gall, to signify figuratively that he seeks simple hearts and does not deign to dwell in impure minds, such as that of Simon, to whom Peter said: “You have neither part nor share in this matter; for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8).

“And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness,” etc. Matthew likewise, after describing the Lord’s baptism and the voice from heaven saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” immediately adds: “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4).

But lest anyone doubt which spirit they meant when they said that he was led or driven into the wilderness, Luke wisely first wrote that “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan,” and then added: “And he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness.” Thus no one might think that the unclean spirit had been able to accomplish anything against him, since, full of the Holy Spirit, he went wherever he wished and did whatever he wished.

The forty days and forty nights during which he is tempted signify the entire period of this age, during which he never ceases to tempt his members—that is, the holy Church. The world in which we serve the Lord is divided into four parts. There are also ten commandments, by observing which we serve the Lord and struggle against the malice of the tireless enemy. Ten multiplied by four makes forty. Therefore the entire period of our service is aptly encompassed by the number forty, in days and nights.

After being baptized, then, the Lord is driven by the Spirit into the wilderness and tempted by Satan, so that he might offer his faithful an example of life: after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, they must gird themselves not only to practice works of virtue but also to endure persecution for the sake of justice.

He withdraws into the wilderness to teach us that, after abandoning the world’s enticements and the company of the wicked, we must serve the divine commandments in all things. He is tempted alone by the devil to signify to us that all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution, and that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

He is tempted for forty days and forty nights to indicate that, as long as we live here and serve the Lord—whether prosperity flatters us, which pertains to the days, or adversity strikes us, which corresponds to the symbolism of night—the adversary is always present throughout the world to those walking in the law of the Lord, and does not cease trying to hinder our journey.

“And he was with the beasts, and the angels ministered to him.” He dwells among beasts as a human being, but receives angelic service as God. And when, in the wilderness of holy conduct, we endure the beastly ways of human beings with an undefiled mind, we deserve the ministry of angels, by whom, once freed from the body, we may be transferred to eternal joys in heaven.

“After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God,” etc. Once John had been handed over, Jesus himself rightly begins to preach. When the Law ceases, the Gospel consequently arises. If the Savior preaches the same things that John the Baptist had previously preached, he shows that he is the Son of the same God whose prophet John is.

No one should suppose that John’s being handed over to prison occurred immediately after the Lord’s forty-day fast and temptation. Whoever reads John’s Gospel will find that before John was handed over, the Lord had already taught many things and performed many miracles. Indeed, his Gospel says: “This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee” (John 2). It also says: “For John had not yet been sent into prison” (John 3).

They report that when John had read the books of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he approved the historical account and affirmed that they had spoken the truth, but that they had composed the history of only one year—the year in which the Lord also suffered—after John’s imprisonment.

John therefore passed over that year, whose events had been set forth by the three, and narrated what had happened in the earlier period, before John was confined in prison. This will be evident to those who carefully read all four volumes of the Gospels. This circumstance also removes the apparent disagreement between John and the others.

When Mark had said that Jesus came into Galilee preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, he added: “And saying: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near. Repent and believe in the Gospel.”

“The time is fulfilled,” he says—the time of which the Apostle speaks: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4).

Therefore the times are fulfilled: repent. How long ago this has been proclaimed! Would that it might at last be heard: “The times are fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near! Repent and believe in the Gospel.” Renounce dead works; believe in the living God. What benefit is there in believing without good works? The merit of good works did not bring you to faith; rather, faith begins so that good works may follow.

“And passing along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew,” etc. These were the first called to follow the Lord. Fishermen and uneducated men are sent to preach, lest the faith of believers be thought to rest not on the power of God but on eloquence and learning.

It may be asked how he called two pairs of fishermen from their boats: first Peter and Andrew, then, having gone a little farther, two other sons of Zebedee, as Matthew and Mark relate. Luke, however, says that both their boats were filled with the great catch of fish, and mentions Peter’s companions, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were called to help when they could not draw in the full nets. At the same time, they marveled at the great quantity of fish that had been caught, and he said only to Peter: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching human beings” (Luke 5). Yet he also says that they followed him after bringing the boats to land.

From this it is to be understood that what Luke indicates happened first. At that time they were not called by the Lord; only Peter was told that he would catch human beings. This was not said as though he would never again catch fish. For we read that after the Lord’s resurrection they went fishing.

Thus he said that thereafter Peter would catch human beings; he did not say that he would no longer catch fish. From Luke’s account, therefore, it can be understood that they returned, as was customary, to the fishing catch, so that afterward what Matthew and Mark relate might take place: when he called them two by two and himself commanded them to follow him—first the two, Peter and Andrew, and then the other two sons of Zebedee.

At that time they followed him not after bringing the boats to land as though intending to return, but as people following one who was calling and commanding them to follow.

“And they enter Capernaum, and immediately, on the sabbath, entering the synagogue, he taught them.” He especially makes frequent use of the gifts of his healing and teaching on the sabbaths, showing that he is not under the Law but above the Law, since he came to fulfill that same Law, not to abolish it.

He does not choose the Jewish sabbath, on which it is forbidden either to light a fire or to move hand or foot, but the true sabbath. The rest beloved by the Lord is found when, striving for the salvation of souls, we abstain from servile work—that is, from everything unlawful.

“And they were astonished at his teaching,” etc. Those teachers taught the peoples what had been written in Moses and the Prophets. Jesus, however, as God and Lord of Moses himself, by the freedom of his will either added to the Law what seemed lacking or preached it to the peoples in altered form, as we read in Matthew: “It was said to the ancients, but I say to you” (Matthew 5).

And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, etc. This is not a voluntary confession, which is followed by the reward of confession, but an extortion of necessity, which compels the unwilling to confess. Just as runaway slaves, after a long time, when they see their master, ask for nothing except mercy from the blows, so the demons, seeing the Lord suddenly present on earth, believed that he had come to judge them. The Savior’s presence is the demons’ torment.

And Jesus threatened him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of the man.” Since “through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. XII), the remedy of salvation first had to operate against the author of death himself: first the serpent’s tongue had to be closed, lest it spread its venom any further; then the woman who was first deceived had to be cured of the fever of carnal desire; third, the man who had listened to the words of his ill-advising wife had to be cleansed from the leprosy of his error. Thus the order of restoration in the Lord was to be the same as the order of the fall in the first parents.

“And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.” Luke says of the unclean spirit that it came out of the man in such a way that it harmed him not at all. It may therefore seem contradictory: how, according to Mark, did it convulse him—or, as some manuscripts read, “throw him into convulsions”—when according to Luke it harmed him nothing? But Luke himself says: “And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, it came out of him and harmed him nothing” (Luke IV). Hence it is understood that Mark’s expression, “throwing him into convulsions” or “convulsing him,” corresponds to Luke’s “when it had thrown him down in their midst”; and what Luke adds, “and it harmed him nothing,” means that this tossing and agitation of his limbs did not weaken him, as demons sometimes depart only after certain members have been cut off or torn away.

And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, etc. Having witnessed the power of the miracle, they marvel at the novelty of the Lord’s teaching, and through what they saw they were stirred to inquire into what they had heard. For surely the signs were performed for this purpose—whether the Lord himself performed them in the man he had assumed, or whether he granted his disciples power to perform them—so that through them the Gospel of the kingdom of God that was being preached might be believed more surely. Those who promised heavenly joys to earthly beings displayed heavenly things and divine works on earth. The disciples, indeed, performed everything as pure human beings, by the Lord’s gift. But the Lord himself, by the singular power of his might, worked healings and miracles, and spoke in the world what he heard from the Father. For earlier also, as the Gospel testifies, he was teaching them “as one having authority, and not as the scribes” (Matt. VII). And now, with the crowd bearing witness, he commands the unclean spirits with authority, and they obey him (Mark I).

And immediately, leaving the synagogue, they came into the house of Simon, etc. If we say that the man freed from the demon morally signifies a mind cleansed from unclean thought, then, correspondingly, the woman afflicted with fever but cured at the Lord’s command displays the flesh restrained from the heat of its desire by the precepts of continence. For “all bitterness, and anger, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy” (Eph. IV) are the fury of an unclean spirit. But understand “fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed—which is the service of idols” (Eph. V)—as the fever of seductive flesh.

“And immediately they tell him about her, and he came and raised her up, taking her by the hand.” In Luke’s Gospel it is written that they pleaded with him for her, and that, standing over her, he commanded the fever. At one time the Savior cures the sick when asked; at another he does so spontaneously. In this he shows that, against the passions of vices also, he always responds to the prayers of the faithful, and sometimes grants things which they themselves scarcely understand in themselves, either giving them understanding of what they ought to understand or, in answer to their pious requests, forgiving what they do not understand, in accordance with what the Psalmist asks: “Who understands his sins? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. XVIII).

And immediately the fever left her, and she ministered to them. It is natural for those suffering from fever, when health begins, to grow weak and to feel the discomfort of their illness. But the health bestowed by the Lord’s command returns all at once. Nor does it merely return: it is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to minister to those who had helped her. In accordance with the laws of tropology, the members that had served uncleanness in order to produce fruit for death now serve righteousness unto eternal life.

When evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him, etc. The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of him who said, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John IX). When the sun had set, more demoniacs than before and more sick people were healed, because the one who, while living temporally in the flesh, taught only a few Jews transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world after trampling down the kingdom of death. Of his ministers, as heralds of life and light, the Psalmist sings: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. LXVII). The Lord ascended above the setting because from the place where he set in his passion he revealed his greater glory by rising again.

And he cast out many demons, etc. Luke writes of these things more explicitly: “Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (Luke IV). The demons therefore confessed the Son of God, and they knew that he was the Christ because the devil had recognized him as a man when he was wearied by a forty-day fast, yet through temptation had not been able to discover whether he was also the Son of God. Now, through the power of his signs, he either understood—or rather suspected—that he was the Son of God.

He therefore did not persuade the Jews to crucify him because he thought him not to be the Christ or the Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by his death. For the Apostle truly says concerning this mystery, hidden from the ages, that “none of the rulers of this age knew it; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II).

Why, then, does the Lord forbid the demons to speak? The Psalmist makes this clear when he says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my justifications and take my covenant upon your mouth? Yet you have hated discipline” (Ps. XLIX), and so forth. This is so that no one, while hearing someone preach, may follow one who is in error. For the devil is a wicked teacher, who often mingles falsehoods with truths, so that under the appearance of truth he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

And rising very early, he went out and departed into a deserted place, etc. If the Savior’s death is expressed by the setting of the sun, why should his resurrection not be signified by the return of dawn? When its light was revealed, he went into the desert of the nations, and there he prayed in his faithful, because he stirred their hearts by the grace of his Spirit toward the power of prayer. “And he was preaching in their synagogues and throughout all Galilee, and casting out demons.” In this preaching, which is said to have taken place throughout all Galilee, that discourse delivered on the mountain is also understood, of which Matthew makes mention. For Mark continues in this way:

And a leper came to him, beseeching him, etc. He connects this account of the cleansed leper so that he may be understood as the one whom Matthew mentions as being cleansed when the Lord descended from the mountain after that discourse. For Matthew says: “And when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him” (Matt. VIII). “And behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” etc.

Since the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it” (Matt. V), the man who was excluded by the law, presuming that he could be cleansed by the Lord’s power, judged that grace—which could wash away the leper’s stain—was not under the law but above the law. Yet, just as the authority of power is displayed in the Lord, so the constancy of faith is displayed in the leper. He fell on his face, which expresses humility and shame, so that each person may blush for the stains of his own life; but shame did not suppress his confession. He displayed his wound and asked for a remedy, and this was a confession full of both religious devotion and faith.

“If you will,” he said, “you can cleanse me.” He attributed the power to the Lord’s will. In speaking of the Lord’s will, he did not doubt it as one distrustful of his compassion, but, conscious of his own pollution, he did not presume. Jesus, moved with pity for him, stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him: “I will; be cleansed.” And when he had spoken, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was cleansed.

There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is present in the command. “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII). Do you see, then, that it cannot be doubted that God’s will is power? If his will is power, those who assert one will necessarily assert one power. Thus, as one possessing the power to heal and the authority to command, he did not shrink from providing testimony through his work. He says, “I will,” because of Photinus; he commands, because of Arius; he touches, because of Manichaeus. The law indeed forbids touching lepers; but because he is Lord of the law, he does not obey the law—he makes the law.

He therefore did not touch him because the man could not be cleansed without touch, but to prove that he was not subject to the law. He did not fear contagion as human beings do; rather, because the one who freed others could not be contaminated, the leprosy that was accustomed to contaminate the one who touched it was driven away by the Lord’s touch.

At the same time, there is this remarkable feature: he healed him in the manner in which he had been entreated. “If you will, you can cleanse me.” “I will,” he said, “be cleansed.” You have the will, and you also have the effect of compassion. Therefore, contrary to what most Latins think, the words should not be joined and read, “I will cleanse,” but separated, so that he first says, “I will,” and then commands, “Be cleansed.”

And he sternly charged him at once and sent him away, etc. Why is he commanded to tell no one? So that he might say that our benefits should not be publicized but kept hidden, and that we should abstain not only from monetary reward but also from praise.

But go, show yourself to the chief priest, etc. He is commanded to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been cured not according to the order of the law but by God’s grace, above the law. He is commanded to offer a sacrifice so that the Lord might show that he was not abolishing the law but fulfilling it: walking according to the law, yet healing above the law those whom the remedies of the law had not healed.

And he rightly added, “for a testimony to them”—that is, if they believe in God, if the leprosy of impiety departs. If anyone is troubled by the fact that the Lord appears to approve the Mosaic sacrifice, although the Church has not retained it, let him remember that the holy sacrifice of holies, which is his body, had not yet begun. He had not yet offered his own holocaust in his passion. The symbolic sacrifices ought not to be removed before the thing symbolized had been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles who preached it and by the faith of the believing peoples.

Since this man typologically signifies the human race sick with sins, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but, according to Luke’s Gospel, as full of leprosy. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Rom. III). They are cleansed when the Savior stretches out his hand—that is, when the Word of God becomes incarnate and touches human nature—so that they may be purified from the manifold error of the past and may hear with the apostles: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV).

Those who had long been abominable and separated from the people of God and from the camp may now at last be restored to the temple and offered to the priest, namely to him of whom it is said, “You are a priest forever” (Ps. CIX). They hear from the Apostle: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. III), and they offer for their cleansing, as Moses commanded, that is, they present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (Rom. XII).

But he, when he had gone out, began to preach and spread the report, so that he could no longer openly enter a city, but remained outside in deserted places; and they came to him from every direction. The perfect salvation of one person draws many crowds to the Lord. For, since he had taught by his own inward and outward condition that he had been healed, he did not keep silent about the benefit he had received, as the one from whom he had received it had commanded. Rather, immediately upon leaving, he began to preach and spread the report, acting as an evangelist.

It is therefore rightly asked what it means that the Lord commanded some things he had done to be concealed, yet they could not be concealed even for an hour. Did the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, will something in this matter that he was unable to accomplish? We must observe, however, that through his mortal body our Redeemer offered us an example in everything he did. When performing a miracle, he both commanded silence and yet could not be kept silent about it. In this way he showed that his elect, following the example of his teaching, should indeed wish to remain hidden in the great things they do; yet, so that they may benefit others, they should be revealed against their will. Thus it is an expression of great humility that they desire their works to remain unspoken, and of great exaltation that their works cannot remain unspoken.

The Lord therefore did not will something that he was unable to accomplish. Rather, by the instruction of his teaching, he gave an example of what his members ought to will and of what happens to them even when they do not wish it.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0146A]

And again he entered Capernaum, etc. The Savior, God of all, visits all things with a saving progress. At one time in the deserts, now in the city, now beside the sea, he ministers to the crowds the gifts of heavenly teaching and virtues. At one time he prays alone on the mountain; at another he helps those labouring at sea, lest they perish. Everywhere he bestows the gifts of salvation, showing that every rank and condition belongs to his grace.

According to the mystical meaning, after performing a miracle in the city he withdraws into the desert, and there he receives the crowds gathering to him with kindly compassion, showing that he loves a life more peaceful and withdrawn from the cares of the world, and that, because of the desire for it, he applies himself to healing bodies.

In human fashion, as though avoiding the crowds of those who sought him, he did not wish to enter the city openly. But allegorically he teaches that Truth does not display the open manifestation of itself to minds agitated by the tumult of the flesh; rather, to all whom it sees separated from the allurements of temporal things, it pours out the light of its gifts more abundantly.

Yet because heavenly compassion does not abandon the carnal—even granting them the grace of its visitation, through which they too may become spiritual—the Lord returns from the desert to the city. Many gather there, and he speaks the word to them; then, by healing the paralytic, he gives many an opportunity for the inward healing that is found in faith.

But the fact that, while the Lord was teaching, so many gathered in the house that they could not fit there, not even at the door, signifies our salvation in particular—our salvation, who came from the nations to faith. When the Lord was preaching in Judea, we were not yet able to enter to hear him. Yet, although we were outside, he caused the words of his teaching to reach us, because he himself gathered us through the mouths of holy preachers and, although we were found outside the synagogue in which he preached, made us participants in his Gospel.

And they came, bringing a paralytic to him, because four men carried him. The healing of this paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul that, after a long lethargy of carnal allurements, sighs for Christ. First of all, it needs ministers who will lift it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good teachers who will suggest the hope of healing and the help of intercession.

They are rightly said to have been four, either because all the power and speech of preachers are established upon the four books of the holy Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the mind is raised in confidence to obtain health. Of these it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom: “For she teaches sobriety and wisdom and justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wis. VIII). Some call these by different names: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

And when they could not bring him to him because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where he was. They desire to bring the paralytic to Christ, but the intervening crowd shuts them off on every side. For often, when the soul comes to its senses after the lethargy of a weakened body and desires to be renewed by the remedy of heavenly grace, it is held back by the obstacle of its former habit.

Often, amid the very sweetness of secret prayer and what is like a pleasant conversation with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts intervenes and prevents the mind’s vision from seeing Christ. What, then, should be done? Certainly one must not remain below, outside, where the crowds are in turmoil; rather, one must climb the roof of the house in which Christ teaches. That is, one must seek the sublimity of sacred Scripture and meditate on the law of the Lord day and night with the Psalmist. “How does a young man correct his way?” “By keeping your words,” he says (Ps. CXVIII).

And having opened it, they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic was lying. Once the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because when the mysteries of Scripture are unlocked one arrives at knowledge of Christ—that is, one descends to his humility through the devotion of faith.

The house of Jesus is rightly found, according to the account of another evangelist, to be covered with tiles, because beneath the contemptible covering of letters, if someone is present to unlock the divine things, the power of spiritual grace will be discovered. The uncovering of the tiles in Jesus’ house is the opening, within the lowliness of the letter, of the spiritual sense and heavenly mysteries.

The fact that the sick man is lowered with his pallet signifies that Christ must be known by a human being who is still established in this flesh.

When Jesus saw their faith, etc. As the Lord was about to cure the man of paralysis, he first loosened the bonds of his sins, showing that he had been condemned to the dissolution of his limbs because of the bonds of his faults, and that he could not be healed by the restoration of his members unless those bonds had first been released.

Thus also, to the paralytic who had long waited in vain for the movement of the water beside the Sheep Pool, the Lord said after healing him: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John XIV).

“Son,” he said, “your sins are forgiven you.” O wondrous humility! He calls “son” one who is despised, weak, and loosened in all the joints of his limbs—one whom the priests would not have considered worthy to touch. Or he rightly calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven.

We should indeed consider how great each person’s own faith is with God, since another’s faith had such power that the whole man suddenly rose up already saved, outwardly and inwardly, and the faults of some were forgiven because of the merit of others.

But some of the scribes were sitting there and reasoning in their hearts, etc. The scribes speak truly when they say that no one can forgive sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. Christ is therefore proved truly to be God, because he can forgive sins as God.

Yet they give testimony to God while going astray by denying the person of Christ. Thus the Jews err: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ. But the Arians err far more foolishly. Though, overcome by the words of the Gospel, they do not dare deny that Jesus is Christ and can forgive sins, they nevertheless are not afraid to deny that he is God.

But, desiring to save the faithless, he manifested that he is God both by his knowledge of hidden things and by the power of his works. For it follows: “Immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they reasoned thus among themselves, says to them: Why do you reason about these things in your hearts?” He shows himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart.

In a certain way, while remaining silent, he says: “By the same majesty and power by which I see your thoughts, I can also forgive sins to human beings. From yourselves understand what the paralytic is receiving.”

“Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your pallet, and walk’?” There is a great difference between saying and doing. Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But “Rise and walk” could be approved both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rising.

A bodily sign is therefore performed so that the spiritual reality may be proved, although it is the same power that forgives the faults of body and soul. We are also given the understanding that many bodily weaknesses occur because of sins. Perhaps for this reason sins are forgiven first: so that, once the causes of weakness have been removed, health may be restored.

There are, in fact, five kinds of causes for which we are afflicted by bodily troubles in this life. Either we are burdened by bodily illness through patience in order to increase our merits, as were the blessed fathers Job and Tobias and countless martyrs in both Testaments; or we are afflicted for the preservation of virtues already received, lest they perish when pride brings temptation, as with the Apostle Paul, to whom, lest he be exalted by the greatness of revelations, “a thorn in his flesh was given, an angel of Satan to buffet him.”

Or we suffer in order to understand and correct our sins, as Mary, the sister of Aaron, was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of words of rashness and pride. Or, like the paralytic of whom we are speaking, we are afflicted because we cannot be healed from illness until our sins have first been forgiven.

Or we suffer for the glory of God who saves, either through himself or through his servants, as the man born blind in the Gospel, who had sinned neither himself nor his parents, but was afflicted so that the works of God might be manifested in him; or as Lazarus, whose illness was not unto death but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God might be glorified through it.

Or we suffer as the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is the condition proper to the reprobate, as with Antiochus and Herod. Each of them, in his own time resisting God, showed to all by his present wretched afflictions what torments he would suffer perpetually in Gehenna. To them applies the prophet’s saying: “With double destruction destroy them.”

Therefore, in all the temporal adversities we suffer, we must give thanks to the Lord with humility and, conscious of our weakness, rejoice in the remedies granted to us. We must return to our conscience, carefully examine both our works and our thoughts, and cleanse by worthy correction whatever we discover that we have done wrong. Whatever we find has perished in us through the fault of self-exaltation, even among the things we believed we had done rightly, we must also punish with humble satisfaction. This is often the cause of our scourging.

For the innocent and just to be scourged for the increase of their rewards belongs to the perfect and is a special gift of the virtuous. But to be driven by temporal blows toward eternal torments is the punishment of the unrepentant reprobate.

But so that you may know that the Son of Man has power, etc. If, according to the Psalmist, he is also God—the one who has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east is from the west—and if the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, then he is himself both God and Son of Man. Thus Christ as man can forgive sins through the power of his divinity, and Christ as God can die for sinners through the weakness of his humanity.

Spiritually, to rise from the pallet is for the soul to withdraw itself from carnal desires, in which it lay sick. To take up the pallet is to separate even the flesh itself, restrained by the reins of continence, from earthly pleasures through hope of heavenly rewards.

To take up the pallet and go home is to return to paradise. For this is truly our home, which first received the human being—lost not by right but by fraud, and at last restored through him who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy.

Alternatively, the man who had been sick carries the pallet home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, returns with the body itself to the inward guardianship of the self, lest after pardon it admit anything for which it might justly be struck again.

And immediately he rose, took up the pallet, and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this.” How wondrous is the power of divine might, where, without any intervening delay of time, swift health accompanies the Savior’s command! Those who were present rightly turn their astonished hearts, after rejecting the darts of blasphemy, toward the praise of such great majesty.

And he went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd came to him, and he taught them. While teaching in Capernaum, the Lord commended the heavenly power of his teaching by the healing of the paralytic. Having done this, he went out to the sea, so that he might not only establish human civic life in the way of truth, but also preach the Gospel of the kingdom to the inhabitants of the sea, teaching them to despise the wandering movements of passing things and to overcome them by the firmness of faith.

Finally, he teaches the very large crowd that came to him there. There he calls the tax collector from the customs booth and makes him an apostle and evangelist. There he makes many sinners, corrected through repentance, worthy of his supper and, by hearing him, worthy of his mysteries. He draws them away from the swelling waves and the whales of deceptive desires and leads them toward the solid ground of a peaceful way of life, which consists in hope of heavenly goods. For it follows:

And as he passed by, he saw Levi of Alphaeus, etc. “To the customs booth” refers to the administration and collection of taxes. For *telos* (τέλος) in Greek is called *vectigal* in Latin, “tax.” Levi is the same person as Matthew. But Luke and Mark, out of modesty and respect for the evangelist, did not wish to give the name by which he was commonly known.

Matthew himself, in accordance with what is written—that the righteous person is his own accuser—at the beginning of his account calls himself Matthew and a tax collector, so that he might show his readers that no converted person ought to despair of salvation, since he himself was suddenly changed from a tax collector into an apostle and from a customs official into an evangelist.

And rising, he followed him. In Luke’s Gospel it is written more fully: “And leaving everything, he rose and followed him” (Luke V). Understanding, therefore, what it truly means to follow the Lord, Matthew follows him after leaving everything. For to follow is to imitate. Thus, so that he might pursue poor Christ not so much in his steps as in his affection, he who had been accustomed to seize what belonged to others left what belonged to himself.

Giving us a perfect model of renouncing the world, he left not only the profits of tax collecting but also disregarded the danger that might come from the rulers of the world because he had left the accounts of the taxes unfinished and unarranged. He was led by so great a desire to follow the Lord that he reserved for himself absolutely no regard or thought for anything in this present life.

Indeed, the Lord himself, who outwardly called him through human speech to follow him, inwardly kindled him through divine inspiration so that he would immediately follow the one calling him. Invisibly, the Lord taught him how he ought to follow. Therefore, by the merit of his obedience, as he abandoned worldly business with contempt, he became a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

And it came to pass, while he was reclining in his house, that many tax collectors, etc. The evangelist Luke writes that Levi held a great banquet for him in his house, a detail that aptly corresponds to the figures of the mysteries. Whoever receives Christ into the inner dwelling is nourished by the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. Thus the Lord willingly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who believes.

This is the spiritual banquet of good works, at which the rich people need and the poor feast. Tax collectors, as their name also shows, are those who collect public taxes, or those who lease the revenues of the treasury or of public affairs; those who pursue the profits of this world through business are likewise included under the same designation.

The tax collectors had therefore seen that one of their number had turned from sins to better things and found a place for repentance, and for this reason they too did not despair of salvation. Nor did tax collectors who remained in their former vices come to Jesus, as the Pharisees and scribes did when they murmured; they came in repentance, as the evangelist’s following words signify: “For there were many who also followed him.”

The Lord went to the banquets of sinners so that he might have an opportunity to teach and provide spiritual food to those who invited him. Finally, although he is frequently described as going to a banquet, nothing else is reported except what he did and taught there. Thus both the Lord’s humility in going to sinners and the power of his teaching in converting penitents are demonstrated.

And the scribes and Pharisees, seeing that he ate with sinners, etc. If the election and calling of Matthew expresses the faith of the nations, who previously longed for the profit of the world but now are refreshed with the Lord at the banquets of charity and with the diligent devotion of good works, then surely the haughtiness of the scribes and Pharisees signifies the envy of the Jews, who are tormented by the salvation of the nations. To them he himself says: “Amen, I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

When Jesus heard this, he said to them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. For I have not come to call the righteous but sinners.” He reproves the scribes and Pharisees, who, thinking themselves righteous, avoided the company of sinners. He calls himself a physician, who, in a wondrous manner of healing, was wounded for our iniquities, “and by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. LIII).

He calls “well” and “righteous” those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X), those who, presuming upon the law, do not seek the grace of the Gospel. But he calls “sick” and “sinners” those who, overcome by consciousness of their weakness and seeing that they cannot be justified through the law, submit their necks in repentance to the grace of Christ.

[Col. 0151B]

And the disciples of John, etc. Other evangelists report that the Pharisees themselves and John’s disciples pressed the Lord with this question. Here, however, the Gospel seems to sound as though some others, moved by concern over this matter, had put the question to him.

We should therefore conclude that this question was raised with the Lord by several groups: by the Pharisees, certainly; by John’s disciples; and by the guests or by any others who were troubled by the question of why John’s disciples and the Pharisees fasted, while the Savior’s disciples did not fast.

In the mystical sense it may be explained as follows: John’s disciples and the Pharisees fast, while Christ’s disciples do not, because everyone who either boasts of the works of the law without faith, or—what is more serious—follows human traditions, or even receives Christ’s own proclamation only with the bodily ear and not with the faith of the heart, wastes away with a fasting heart while abstaining from spiritual goods.

But whoever is incorporated into Christ’s members by faithful love cannot fast, since he feasts upon his flesh and blood.

Alternatively, John does not drink wine or strong drink, while the Lord eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners, because abstinence increases the merit of the one to whom no power over nature is given. But the Lord, to whom the power of forgiving sins naturally belonged, why would he avoid those whom he could make purer through abstinence?

Christ also fasted, so that you would not evade the commandment; he ate with sinners, so that you would perceive grace and recognize power.

And Jesus said to them: “Can the sons of the wedding feast fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast on that day.”

In Matthew it is written: “Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. IX). The bridegroom, therefore, is Christ; the bride is the Church. From this holy and spiritual marriage the apostles were born. They cannot mourn or fast as long as they see the bridegroom in the bridal chamber and know that the bridegroom is with the bride.

But when the wedding has passed and the time of the passion and resurrection has arrived, then the sons of the bridegroom will fast. According to the laws of tropology, it must be understood that as long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when, because of sins, he has withdrawn and flown away from us, then fasting must be prescribed, and then mourning must be taken up.

No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the new patch tears away from the old, and a greater tear is made. When the Lord was asked why his disciples did not fast, he replied that those who were still carnal and not yet made firm by faith in his passion and resurrection could not sustain the stricter fasts and precepts of continence. Otherwise, through excessive austerity, they might lose even the faith they seemed to possess.

He therefore calls the disciples themselves still old garments, to which a new patch is unsuitably sewn—that is, some small portion of teaching belonging to the moderation of the new life. If this is done, the teaching itself is in a certain way torn, because the portion concerning abstinence from food is applied inopportunely, when that teaching prescribes a general fast not merely from desire for food but from every joy of temporal pleasures.

He says that a patch of this sort—that is, a portion relating to food—ought not to be given to people still devoted to their old habit, because a kind of tearing seems to result from that side as well, and it is not suited to their old condition.

And no one puts wine, etc. He also compares these same people to old wineskins, which, he says, are more easily burst by new wine—that is, by spiritual precepts—than able to contain it. But they had already become new wineskins when, after the Lord’s ascension, they were renewed by praying and hoping in their desire for his consolation. For then they received the Holy Spirit, and when, filled with him, they spoke in every language, the Jews who did not understand them nevertheless bore true witness by saying: “For these men are full of new wine” (Acts 2). For new wine had already come to new wineskins: that is, the fervor of the Holy Spirit had filled spiritual hearts.

Alternatively: The teacher must beware lest he entrust the secrets of the new mysteries to a soul not yet renewed but persisting in the oldness of malice.
