If anyone asks what, mystically, is the difference between new wine and the new garment, it is readily apparent: by wine we are inwardly refreshed and made drunk, whereas with a garment we are clothed outwardly. Since both, however, pertain to the meaning of spiritual life, the garment plainly signifies our good works, which we perform outwardly and by which we shine before human beings. But new wine expresses the fervor of faith, hope, and charity, by which, in the presence of our Creator, we ourselves are inwardly reformed in the newness of our understanding.

And it happened again on the Sabbaths, etc. We read below that many people were coming and going, and that they did not even have time to eat; consequently, like human beings, they were hungry. Their rubbing the ears of grain in their hands and relieving their hunger indicates a stricter way of life: they sought not prepared dishes but simple foods. But the Pharisees said to him: “Look, why are your disciples doing what is not lawful on the Sabbaths?” Observe that the first apostles of the Savior destroy the letter of the Sabbath against the Ebionites, who accept the other apostles but reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

Mystically, however, the disciples pass through the grainfields—namely, those of which the Lord says: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest. And the one who reaps receives a reward” (John 4). This occurs when holy teachers, with the care of pious solicitude, observe those whom they seek to instruct in the faith of truth, and with attentive consideration weigh how, and in what order, they ought to draw each one toward salvation. Thus they are understood to hunger for nothing more than the salvation of human beings. The first of the reapers himself once hungered for this salvation amid his prayers; then, when those whom he desired had been offered to him as food, he heard: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10).

And there is a remarkable agreement in the mystery: there, too, animals sent from heaven are commanded to be slaughtered and eaten; here, the disciples are said to have plucked the ears of grain consecrated by the Lord’s passing over them and, according to the account of the other evangelists, to have rubbed them with their hands and eaten them. For this is what the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, and strip off the old man with his deeds” (Col. 3). For no one passes into the body of Christ, nor does anyone feed the teacher with the fruits of his progress, except by rejecting old desires and becoming a new person through the new commandment of love.

To pluck the ears of grain, therefore, is to uproot human beings from their earthly preoccupation, in which they had fixed the root of their mind, so to speak, upon earth alone. To rub them with the hands is, by examples of virtue, to strip the purity of the mind even from the desire of the flesh, as though from the husks and coverings of the awns. To eat the grains is for each person, cleansed from the filth of vices, to be incorporated through the mouths of preachers into the members of the Church.

And it is fittingly remembered that the disciples did these things as they went before the Lord, because the teacher’s word must precede, and then the grace of heavenly visitation must enlighten the heart of the hearer who follows. Fittingly, too, they did so on the Sabbaths, because holy teachers themselves labor in preaching for the hope of future rest, and likewise admonish their hearers not to devote themselves to useless business for love of the world, but rather to toil at good works for eternal rest.

Again, those who strive to obey the divine commands walk through the grainfields with the Lord when they delight in diligently meditating upon the sacred words. They hunger in the grainfields when, in those same sacred words through which they pass by reading, they desire to find the bread of life—that is, when they take care to reach those words by which they may kindle within themselves a greater love for their Creator. And this occurs on the Sabbaths when, with their minds quieted and free from turbulent thoughts, they rejoice to be at leisure and to see “how sweet the Lord is, and how blessed is the one who hopes in him” (Ps. 33). Assuming the attitude of piety and humility, they strive to attain the rest of their souls.

They pluck the ears that happen to present themselves, and turn them over in their hands and cleanse them after crushing them until they reach food, when they take up the testimonies of Scripture to which they come in reading through meditation, and examine them with diligent scrutiny until, finding and drawing out in them the marrow of love that seemed to lie hidden, they reach it. For just as wheat grains that refresh us are concealed beneath the harshness of the awns, which bristle, so divine gifts of love are often hidden beneath what appeared to be the usefulness of the letter, feeding minds that hunger and thirst for righteousness with the food of inward sweetness.

This refreshment of minds displeases foolish defenders of the Sabbath, but it is approved by the Lord of the Sabbath, because those who follow only the surface of the letter neither know the true refreshment of minds nor know how to reach the inward rest of souls. Thus their rashness is rightly confounded by the mouth of Truth, when it is added:

And he said to them: “Have you never read, etc.?” To refute the Pharisees’ accusation, he recalls the ancient history of when David, fleeing from Saul, came to Nob and, received by Abimelech the priest, asked for food (1 Sam. 21). Since he had no ordinary bread, Abimelech gave him consecrated bread, which it was lawful for no one to eat except the priests and Levites. He asked only whether the young men were pure from women; and when David answered that they had been so since yesterday and the day before, he did not hesitate to give him the bread, judging it better—according to the prophet’s saying, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6)—to free people from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God. For the salvation of human beings is an offering pleasing to God.

The Lord therefore brings this forward and says: If David is holy, and Abimelech the high priest is not reproached by you, but both transgressed the commandment of the Law with a defensible excuse, and hunger was the reason, why do you not approve in the apostles the same hunger that you approve in others? Although there is also a considerable difference here. These men rub ears of grain with their hands on the Sabbath; those men ate Levitical bread. There, the days of the new moons were also approaching the solemnity of the Sabbath, when he who had been sought at the banquet fled from the royal court.

Figuratively, when it says that David and his young men received consecrated bread, it shows that priestly food would pass over into the use of the peoples—either because we must all imitate the priestly life, or because all the children of the Church are priests. For we are anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices. Of this entire history, according to our capacity, we have spoken more fully in the exposition of the Book of Kings; and concerning the table and the bread of the Presence, in the book of the exposition of the tabernacle and its vessels.

But as for the Lord’s calling Abiathar the chief priest instead of Abimelech, there is no discrepancy. Both of them were there when David came and asked for and received the bread: Abimelech, namely, the chief priest, and Abiathar, his son. After Abimelech was killed by Saul, together with eighty-five men of his priestly family, Abiathar fled to David and became his companion throughout his entire exile. Later, when David was reigning, Abiathar also received the rank of high priest; he remained in that office throughout the whole period of David’s reign and became a man of much greater distinction than his father. Therefore he was worthy for the Lord, even while his father was alive, to treat his memory as that of the chief priest.

And he said to them: “The Sabbath was made for human beings, and not human beings for the Sabbath.” Greater concern must be shown for a person’s health and life than for observance of the Sabbath. For the Sabbath was commanded to be kept in such a way that, if necessity arose, the one who violated the Sabbath would nevertheless not be guilty. For this reason circumcision was not prohibited on the Sabbath, because it was necessary for it to be performed. Joshua also marched around the walls of Jericho with his army for seven days. And when necessity arose, the Maccabees fought on the Sabbath. Hence, when the disciples were hungry, what was not lawful according to the Law became lawful because of the necessity of hunger.

The case is like that which applies today to the prescribed fasts: if a sick person breaks the fast, he is in no way held guilty. Therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. If, he says, King David, nourished with priestly food, is excusable, and, according to the account of another evangelist, priests who violate the Sabbath through the temple service are free from guilt, how much more is the Son of Man, who is true king and true priest and therefore Lord of the Sabbath, not held guilty of the offense of plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath?

## CHAPTER III

And he entered the synagogue again, etc. The man who has a withered hand signifies the human race, dried up in the fruitfulness of good works but healed by the Lord’s mercy. His right hand, which had withered in our first parent when he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree, was restored to the health of good works through the grace of the Redeemer, when he stretched out innocent hands upon the tree of the cross.

And rightly was the hand withered in the synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the danger of inexcusable guilt is more serious. And they watched him to see whether he would heal on the Sabbaths, so that they might accuse him. Since the master had excused by a defensible example the destruction of the Sabbath that they had condemned in the disciples, they now wished, by watching the master himself, to slander him: if he healed on the Sabbath, they would accuse him of transgression; if he did not heal, they would accuse him of cruelty or weakness.

And he said to the man who had the withered hand: “Stand up in the middle.” And he said to them: “Is it lawful on the Sabbaths to do good or to do evil?” The Lord anticipated the accusation that the Jews had prepared for him in their treacherous minds. He reproved them because they violated the commandments of the Law by a perverse interpretation, thinking that on the Sabbath one must abstain even from good works, although the Law commands abstention from evil, saying: “You shall do no servile work on it”—that is, sin. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

By this commandment he also foreshadows in the present age the form of the age to come, in which those who have done good throughout the six ages of this world will, in the seventh age, have a holiday from evils alone, but not from good works as well. For although worldly works cease, the activity of good works is not idle when it rests in the praises of God.

“Should one save a soul, or destroy it?” That is: should one heal a human being, or not? It means the same as what he had said before: “To do good, or to do evil?” This does not mean that God, who is supremely good, can be the author of evil or destruction for us, but that in the customary language of Scripture, his not saving is called destroying. Thus Scripture says that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not because he hardened what was soft, but because, in his mercy, he did not soften what had been hardened by preceding merits.

And when we pray, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6), immediately adding, “But deliver us from evil,” we are plainly taught that his leading us into temptation means nothing other than his not delivering us from evil, and that his destroying a soul means his not saving it from destruction.

If anyone is troubled by the question why, when the Lord was about to heal the body, he asked about the salvation of the soul, let him understand either that “soul” is used, in the manner of Scripture, for the human being, as it says: “These are the souls who came out from the thigh of Jacob” (Exod. 1); or that he performed those miracles for the salvation of the soul; or that the healing of the hand itself signified the salvation of the soul, which, by ceasing from good works—as I said above—seemed to possess a withered right hand, so to speak.

But they were silent. And looking around at them with anger, grieved at the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored. The withered hand is commanded to be stretched out for healing, because the unfruitful weakness of the soul is healed by nothing more effectively than by the generosity of almsgiving.

Therefore John the Baptist, when the crowds asked what they should do so that they might not, like withered trees, be sent into the fire, gave this sole command: “The one who has two tunics should give to the one who has none. And the one who has food should do likewise” (Luke 3). And it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “My son, do not let your hand be stretched out to receive and contracted when it comes to giving” (Ecclus. 4). For the one who does not extend his hands to the widow asking him, in order to bestow a kindness, spreads them in vain toward God when asking forgiveness for his sins.

But the Pharisees went out and immediately took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him. By the Herodians he means the ministers of Herod the tetrarch. Because of the enmity that their lord exercised against John, they also pursued with plots and hatred the Savior whom John preached.

It was great folly for people who themselves had such great need of salvation to deliberate about the Savior’s death. How greatly they devoted themselves to wickedness is shown by the fact that they counted it as a crime that, at his word, the sufferer stretched out his right hand restored to health—as though each of them had not done greater things on the Sabbaths by carrying food, handing over a cup, and performing the other tasks necessary for nourishment. For he who spoke, and they came to be, could not be convicted of having labored on the Sabbath.

And Jesus withdrew with his disciples toward the sea. He withdrew like a human being fleeing the plots of his pursuers, because the hour of his passion had not yet come, nor was the place of his passion outside Jerusalem. He withdrew, fleeing those who pursued him in hatred; but he went there where he found many who followed him in love.

For it follows: And a great crowd from Galilee and Judea followed him, and from Jerusalem and Idumea, and from beyond the Jordan, and those around Tyre and Sidon—a great multitude—hearing what he was doing, came to him. Behold: the Pharisees and the Herodians, that is, the teachers of the people and the king’s ministers, seek to destroy the Lord by unanimous counsel. But the unlearned crowd and the common people gathered from every direction follow him with unanimous love.

They, seeing his works of power and hearing the words of his teaching, wished to learn nothing more than how to persecute him. These others, led only by the reputation of his mighty works, come in a very great multitude to hear him and to implore the help of salvation. Thus they immediately deserve to obtain the result of their will and desire, since, as we read below, many are healed by the Lord.

Here he also gave his followers an example that, if they suffered persecution in one city, they should flee to another. Thus Paul, taught by the Lord’s example and command alike, fled from Damascus, where the wicked were lying in wait for him. After departing from there, he found elsewhere innumerable peoples who followed him in piety.

According to the laws of allegory, however, the Lord, in that he went out from the synagogue and withdrew toward the sea, receiving everywhere the very great multitude of people who came to him in order to be healed and taught, clearly prefigured our salvation: he deigned to come to us through faith after Judea had been abandoned because of its unbelief.

For it is rightly the nations, long unfaithful and tossed about through the winding paths of various errors, that are compared with the instability, bitterness, and darkness of the tossing sea. But the Lord came to the sea with his disciples, and a great crowd from various provinces followed him, because, through the preaching of the apostles, he entered the hearts of the nations.

And after, in his mercy, he consecrated in them a dwelling beloved by him, he kindly received many who came to him and granted them possession of the salvation they desired. To these things what follows aptly corresponds:

And he told his disciples to have a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they should press upon him. For he healed many, so that they rushed upon him in order to touch him. The small boat that serves the Lord on the sea is the Church, gathered from the nations and crossing the waves of the passing world by the strength of a free mind.

The more widely it expands the bosom of its heart to receive the grace of its Creator, the more sublimely it assails all the tumbling movements of passing things—as a small boat driven by favorable winds assails the waves of a seething sea.

There is, however, a difference between pressing upon the Lord and touching him. The one touches him who receives his faith and love with a true heart.

They press upon him who disturb, by carnal thoughts or even by deeds, the peace of those in whom truth was accustomed to dwell. Hence those who touched him are aptly said to have been saved, because true faith and love habitually produce eternal salvation.

Because of the crowd, lest it should press upon him, the Lord entered the small boat, for, fleeing the turbulent minds of the carnal, he rejoices to come instead to those who have learned to despise both the fleeting glory and the abasement of the world, and to make his dwelling among them.

And as many as had afflictions, when the unclean spirits saw him, fell down before him. Both groups did indeed fall before the Lord: those who had the afflictions of bodily illnesses, and those who were tormented by unclean spirits. But the sick fell with the simple intention of obtaining salvation, whereas the demon-possessed—or rather, the demons dwelling in them—were compelled by the force of divine fear, not only to fall before him but also to confess his majesty.

Struck by the presence of his power and exceedingly terrified, they could by no means conceal the one whom they already knew to be the Son of God. Here one must marvel—or rather grieve—at the blindness of the Arians, who, after the glory of his resurrection and ascension, after the faith of the Gospel had spread throughout the world, after churches had been built among all nations and the name of the Lord and Savior had been praised in them from the rising of the sun to its setting, suddenly deny that he is the Son of God—the one whom demons, while he was still clothed in mortal flesh, openly confessed to be the Son of God.

For it follows: And they cried out, saying: “You are the Son of God.” And he sternly warned them not to reveal him. Why he forbids unclean spirits to speak about him, the Psalmist makes clear when he says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49).

The sinner is therefore forbidden to preach the Lord, lest anyone, while following the preacher, follow one who is wandering. For the devil is a wicked teacher, who often mixes falsehoods with truths, so that under the appearance of truth he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

Moreover, it was not only the demons, who confessed unwillingly, who were ordered to keep silent willingly about Christ, but also those who had been healed by him and wanted of their own accord to confess him. Indeed, even the apostles themselves, who after the resurrection were to preach him throughout the whole world, are commanded to remain entirely silent about him before his passion, lest, if the divine majesty were preached, the dispensation of the passion be delayed and, if the passion were postponed, the salvation of the world that was to come through it be denied.

And ascending the mountain, he called to himself those whom he himself wished; and they came to him. And he made twelve to be with him. The mountain on which the Lord chose the apostles signifies the height of righteousness in which they were to be instructed and which they were to preach to human beings. Since he was about to send them to preach the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, he rightly wished, through the elevation of the place in which they were chosen, to admonish them that they must not dissolve their minds in low desires, but must always raise them to desire and seek heavenly things.

So also, when he was about to give the Law to his former people, he appeared on a mountain and thundered from the mountain what ought to be done. But because the time had not yet come for it to be said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4), and only this was being said: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land that the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. 20)—although these same words typologically promise us the eternal kingdom, which is in the land of the living—the people could not approach the Lord speaking on the mountain.

They heard from below what was to be said, because they did not yet know how to ascend with a mind capable of understanding the mysteries that were being spoken. Moses alone, because he had learned to hear the Law spiritually, climbed to the summit of the mountain on which God was.

It is rightly said that, ascending the mountain, the Lord called to himself those whom he himself wished. For it was not through their own choice and endeavor, but through divine condescension and grace, that they were called to the apostolate. Hence elsewhere he says to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15).

And he made twelve to be with him. This was certainly through the grace of a definite mystery, so that they might commend by their number also the salvation of the world that they were to preach by their word. For three times four makes twelve. And the apostles were sent to preach three times four, so that throughout all the regions of the four-sided world they might baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Hence it is also written concerning the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven from God that it had three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west (Rev. 21). Figuratively, this shows that, through the preaching of the apostles and their successors, all the nations throughout the world would enter the Church in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

In this same mystery the children of Israel once encamped around the tabernacle in such a way that on every side, in a square arrangement, three tribes remained (Num. 1). For the primitive Church, which was in Judea, was about to establish spiritual camps for God in the faith and confession of the Holy Trinity, while believing nations from throughout the world stood around it on every side.

And that he might send them to preach the Gospel. And he gave them authority to heal diseases and to cast out demons. After forbidding wicked spirits to preach about him, he chose holy men who would both cast out unclean spirits and preach the Gospel with a pure mind and tongue. He also granted them the power to heal other diseases and even to raise the dead, as the evangelist Matthew records, so that the greatness of their deeds might bear witness to the greatness of the heavenly promises, power displayed might give credibility to their words, and those who preached new things might perform new deeds.

Hence even now, when the number of believers has grown, there are many within the holy Church who follow the way of virtues but do not possess signs of virtues.

For a miracle is displayed outwardly in vain if that which should operate inwardly is absent. For, according to the saying of the teacher of the nations, “tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14).

And he gave Simon the name Peter. He did not give Simon the name Peter for the first time here; rather, long before this, when he saw him brought to him by his brother Andrew, he said: “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as Peter (John 1).

But when the evangelist wished to enumerate the names of the twelve apostles and necessarily had to call him Peter, he briefly indicated that he was not called this beforehand, but that the Lord had given him this surname, although not at that moment, but when John recorded the Lord’s own words, thereby making his hearers attentive.

For if he had been called this beforehand, you would not see the mystery of the rock in the same way, thinking that he was called this by chance and not by God’s providence. Therefore he wished him first to have another name, so that through the very change of name the vitality of the mystery might be commended.

Thus Peter in Greek or Latin is the same as Cephas in Syriac. In both languages the name is derived from “rock”—without doubt from that of which Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). For just as Christ, the true light, granted the apostles that they should be called the light of the world, so also he granted Simon, who believed in Christ the rock, the name Peter.

Alluding elsewhere to the etymology, he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). But as for the interpretation of Simon as “putting away sorrow” or “hearing sadness,” it corresponds to that time when, after the resurrection, on seeing the Lord, he put away the sorrow either of his death or of his own denial. Yet immediately he heard the sadness of his own death, when the Lord said: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

And James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James—“he called them to himself,” understood from what precedes, when he ascended the mountain. And he gave them the names Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder.”

They were aptly surnamed sons of thunder, since one of them, thundering from heaven, uttered that theological voice which no one had previously known how to produce: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” etc. (John 1). He left these words pregnant with such weight of power that, if he had ever wished to thunder more loudly, the world itself could not have contained him.

Both of them also deserved frequently to be taken apart by the Lord and up the mountain, and sometimes to hear a terrifying sound from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Mark 9).

They also bore ancient names most appropriate to their merits. For James means “supplanter”; John means “in whom there is grace,” or “the grace of the Lord.” The former, when the Lord called him, supplanted the care of the flesh, and, when Herod slaughtered him, rejoiced to despise the flesh itself. The latter, because of the special grace of love that he had merited through virginal glory, reclined upon the breast of his Redeemer at the supper.

And Andrew and Philip and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas. Andrew is a Greek name, and it is interpreted as “manly,” from the Greek word for “man,” Ἀνήρ (*anēr*). This name most aptly adorns the one who, at John’s preaching, immediately took care to follow, see, and hear the Lamb of God, and afterward did not delay to follow the one who called him, leaving everything, and to cling to him continually.

Philip is interpreted as “mouth of a lamp” or “of lamps.” And rightly so, because, when called by the Lord, he received the light of grace with which he himself was kindled and illumined in his heart, and immediately strove, through the service of his mouth, to offer it to his brother whom he had found, saying: “We have found the one of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote, Jesus the son of Joseph from Nazareth” (John 1).

Bartholomew is Syriac, not Hebrew, and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends the waters.” This clearly signifies the Son of God, who suspends the minds of his preachers for the contemplation of heavenly things, so that, the more freely they soar toward lofty realities, the more fruitfully they may soak the hearts of earthly people with the drops of their words.

Matthew is said to mean “given,” namely because, by the great gift of the Lord, he was transferred from the tax office and public service to the office of apostle and evangelist.

Thomas means “abyss” or “twin,” which in Greek is Δίδυμος (*Didymos*). Both interpretations suit his condition. He could rightly be called Didymus because of his hesitant heart in believing the reality of the Lord’s resurrection. He could likewise rightly be called an abyss, when with firm faith he penetrated the depth of the Lord’s power manifested in the resurrection.

It should certainly be noted that, when the evangelist Matthew lists the names of the apostles, he writes: “Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas, and Matthew the tax collector.” The other evangelists therefore place Matthew first in the conjunction of the names and Thomas afterward, and they do not identify him as a tax collector, lest, by recalling his former way of life, they should seem to reproach the evangelist. But Matthew himself places Thomas before him and calls himself a tax collector, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Rom. 5).

And James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. He identifies James by adding his father’s name in order to distinguish him from James the son of Zebedee. He is the one who is called the Lord’s brother in the Gospels and in the Epistle to the Galatians, because Mary the wife of Alphaeus was the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother, whom the evangelist John calls Mary of Clopas—perhaps because Alphaeus was also called Clopas, or because, after Alphaeus died following the birth of James, Mary married Clopas.

That James was rightly surnamed the son of Alphaeus, that is, “of the learned one,” is testified by the apostles themselves, who immediately after the Lord’s passion appointed him to govern the Church of Jerusalem.

Thaddaeus is the one whom Luke, both in his Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, calls Judas of James. For he was the brother of James, the Lord’s brother, as he himself writes in his Epistle. Hence he too was called the Lord’s brother, as his fellow citizens testify, saying in their astonishment at his mighty works: “Is this not the carpenter’s son and Mary’s, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon?” (Matt. 13).

And Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him. He includes these names with additions in order to distinguish Simon from Peter and Judas from James.

Simon the Cananaean received his surname from Cana, a village of Galilee, which the evangelist Luke rendered with its interpretation, “Simon the Zealot.” For *Cana* means “zeal.” He is called Cananaean, or Zealot, that is, “an emulator.”

But Judas Iscariot took his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, as a foretelling of his condemnation. For Issachar, which means “reward,” signifies the price of betrayal. Iscariot, however, which is interpreted as “memory of death,” shows that he did not commit the crime of the Lord’s betrayal after being suddenly persuaded, but after meditating upon it for a long time.

He was chosen among the apostles not through imprudence but through providence. How great is the truth, which even an adversary serving it does not weaken! How great is the Lord’s moral teaching, who preferred to let his judgment be endangered among us rather than his affection! For he had taken upon himself human frailty, and therefore did not refuse even these aspects of human weakness.

He wished to be abandoned; he wished to be betrayed; he wished to be handed over by his own apostle, so that you, abandoned by a companion and betrayed by a companion, might bear with moderation the fact that your judgment had gone astray and your benefit had perished.

After the apostles had been appointed on the mountain, to be sent to preach the Gospel, it is fittingly added:

And they come to the house. Having chosen the apostles on the mountain, he leads them back to the house, as though silently admonishing them that, after receiving the rank of the apostolate, they should return to their own conscience; and that, the greater the care of instructing peoples they had undertaken, the more diligently they should themselves enter, by examining it, into the dwelling places of their minds. They should search carefully to ensure that nothing might be found there that would offend the eyes of the hidden examiner.

For each person rightly governs another in this way, if he first carefully investigates and purges from his own heart whatever depravity it contained.

And the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. O how blessed an occupation for the Savior, how blessed the multitude that streamed together, whose zeal for hearing the word of God and concern for obtaining salvation were so great that not even an hour for eating remained free for the author of salvation and those who were with him, because he was devoting himself to bringing comfort to the wretched!

Would that, Lord Jesus, in our own age as well, you might grant such grace to your faithful, so that by their constant eagerness to learn they might keep their teachers not only from the appetite for carnal pleasures, but sometimes even from the taking of daily bread itself.

But while the crowd from outside throngs around him, let us see how highly his relatives esteem him. It follows:

And when his own people heard, they went out to seize him, for they were saying that he had lost his mind. Truly, as he himself says elsewhere: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.” The one whom others desire to approach, see, and hear as the author of life and the wisdom of God, his relatives decide must be restrained as though he were incapable of controlling his mind.

Because they could not grasp the height of the wisdom they heard, they believed that he was speaking as one out of his senses—like those who, unable to endure the mystery of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, said: “This is a hard saying. Who can hear it?” And for this reason they went back and no longer walked with him.

Allegorically, however, in the fact that the crowd gathers densely around him while he is despised by his own as a madman, the salvation of believers from the nations is approved, and the envy and unbelief of the Jews are marked. Concerning them John says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1).

There is indeed a great difference between those who do not understand the word of God because of slowness of mind and those who deliberately blaspheme and persecute what they understand. For the former still retain some hope of salvation, if perhaps they should come to understand; but what hope of salvation remains for those who refuse to understand so that they may do good, and who devise iniquity upon their beds, when they strive, through detestation and hatred, to reject even what they rightly understood for the salvation of their souls?

For see what follows.

And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He has Beelzebub,” and, “By the prince of demons he casts out demons.” Nor is it without reason that those who inflicted so great a blasphemy upon the Lord are said to have come down from Jerusalem; rather, they were surely foreshadowing that he would be persecuted unto death by the citizens of that city. We read above, indeed, that a great crowd followed him from Galilee, and from Jerusalem, and from Idumaea, and from across the Jordan, and that those around Tyre and Sidon—a great multitude—hearing what he was doing, came to him. Thus the crowd coming from Jerusalem followed the Lord, just as did those from the other regions of the Jews and even from the Gentiles. For who does not know that Idumaea, Tyre, and Sidon were provinces or cities of the Gentiles? But the scribes descending from Jerusalem pursued him with dreadful blasphemies, because it was plainly destined to happen at the time of his Passion that the crowd of the Jewish people would lead him into Jerusalem with palms and praises, while the Gentiles would desire to see him, but the scribes and elders of the people would deliberate about his death. Thus, while the crowds, who seemed less instructed, were always marvelling at the Lord’s deeds, those men, on the contrary, laboured either to deny them or, when they could not deny them, to distort them by a sinister interpretation—as though these were not works of divinity but works of the most unclean spirit, that is, of Beelzebub, who was the god of Accaron. For *Beel* itself is *Baal*, while *Zebub* is called “fly.” And, contrary to certain corrupt copies, the name is not to be read with the letter *k* or *d* at the end, but with *b*. Beelzebub, therefore, is interpreted as “Baal of flies,” that is, “the man of flies,” or “the one having flies,” evidently because of the filth of sacrificial blood; from that most unclean rite or name they designated the prince of demons.

And summoning them, he spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan cast out Satan? And if a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. A kingdom and a city divided against themselves cannot endure.” But just as small things grow through concord, so great things collapse through discord (Sallust).

If, then, Satan fights against himself, and a demon is the enemy of a demon, the consummation of the world ought already to have come, so that the opposing powers, whose warfare among themselves is the peace of human beings, might no longer have a place in it. But if you think, O scribes and Pharisees, that the departure of demons is obedience to their prince, by which they deceive ignorant people through fraudulent pretence, what can you say about the healings of bodies that the Lord performed? It is another matter if you also attribute the weaknesses of the limbs and the marks of spiritual powers to demons. And if Satan has risen up against himself, he is divided and will not be able to stand, but has an end. By saying this, he wished it to be understood from their own confession that, by not believing in him, they had chosen to be in the devil’s kingdom—a kingdom that, being divided against itself, certainly could not stand. Let the Pharisees choose what they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they will have been unable to find anything to say against the Lord. But if he can, let them take much greater care for themselves and depart from his kingdom, which, being divided against itself, cannot stand.

[Col. 0164A] No one, having entered the strong man’s house, can plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house.

He calls the devil “the strong man”; his goods, human beings deceived by him; and his house, the world that lies in wickedness. In it, until the coming of the Saviour, he possessed his dominion, though it was badly pacified, because he rested without opposition in the hearts of unbelievers. But the Lord bound the strong man—that is, he restrained the devil from deceiving the elect—and then plundered his house, because he united to the members of his Church those whom he had foreseen as having been rescued from the devil’s snares and arranged them within it according to the distinct dignities of various ranks.

Or certainly he plundered his house because he divided among the successors of the apostles all the regions of the world over which the ancient enemy once ruled, so that each in his own province might convert to the way of life the peoples recalled from error.

Thus, through a parable—but one already exceedingly clear—the Lord shows that he liberated human beings from demons not by a deceitful operation in agreement with demons, as they charged, but by a power wholly different and opposed to them, namely, the power of divinity. Therefore they were committing a great crime when they proclaimed that what they had recognized as belonging to God belonged to the devil.

[Col. 0164B] “Amen, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of men, and the blasphemies with which they have blasphemed.”

Not all sins and blasphemies are indiscriminately forgiven all human beings, but only those who in this life have performed worthy repentance for their errors. Nor does the perverse assertion of Novatian have any place here, when he denies that forgiveness ought to be granted to penitents who fell during martyrdom; nor that of Origen, when he asserts that, after the universal judgment, even after countless ages have passed, all sinners and blasphemers will obtain forgiveness of their sins and be led into the heavenly kingdom. The Lord’s following words also refute his error, when it is added:

[Col. 0164C] “But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

Whoever, therefore, clearly understands the works of God, and, unable to deny their power, nevertheless slanders them, driven by envy, and says that Christ, the word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub’s—this person “will not be forgiven, neither in the present age nor in the age to come.” This is not because we deny that, if he should wish to repent, he could be forgiven by the one who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; rather, because we believe in that judge and giver of forgiveness, who says both that he will always accept repentance and that this blasphemy will never be forgiven, we believe that this blasphemer, because of the demands of his merits, will reach neither forgiveness nor even the fruits of worthy repentance.

In accordance with this, the evangelist John wrote most truthfully about certain people blinded on account of the merit of their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I should heal them’” (John XII).

[Col. 0164D] Therefore only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, by which a person, in the likeness of the devil and his angels, does not hesitate to attack the majesty of the Godhead against his own conscience, “has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal sin,” as the evangelist plainly declares when, after setting down this testimony of the Lord, he adds and says:

[Col. 0165A] “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’”

For neither those who do not believe that the Holy Spirit exists, nor those who believe and confess that he exists but is not God, nor those who believe that he is indeed God but is lesser than the Father and the Son, are held by the crime of unforgivable blasphemy, since they do this not from diabolical envy but under the influence of human ignorance. This is the blasphemy by which the leaders of the Jews in particular, and all who are corrupted by a similar plague of envy, blaspheme the majesty and will perish without end.

What is said according to Matthew—that the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, or speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, has no forgiveness either in this age or in the age to come—allows us to understand that certain faults are loosed in this age and certain others in the age to come. For when this is denied of one fault, the corresponding implication is evident: it is granted of certain others. Nevertheless, we should believe that this can happen only with the smallest and least serious sins, such as habitual idle talk, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in attending to one’s household affairs—things scarcely done without fault even by one who knows how such fault ought to be avoided—or sins arising from ignorance and error that are not grave. All these continue to weigh upon a person after death if they have not been released while he still remained in this life.

[Col. 0165B] Yet this must be understood: even there, concerning the least matters, no one will obtain any purification unless, while still living in this life, he has earned by good deeds the privilege of obtaining it there.

And his mother and brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him, calling him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and so forth.

The Lord’s brothers are not to be thought, according to Helvidius, the sons of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, nor, according to certain others, the sons of Joseph by another wife; rather, they are to be understood as his relatives. Certainly, when the Lord is asked about his mother and brothers, and appears to refrain from leaving his ministry of the word, he does not reject the duties of maternal affection, whose commandment is, “Honour your father and your mother.” Instead, he shows that he owes himself more fully to the mysteries of the Father than to the affections of a mother, commending the same principle to us by his example as well as by his word, when he says, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X). He does not contemptuously despise his brothers; rather, by preferring spiritual work to kinship according to the flesh, he teaches that the bond of hearts is more religious than that of bodies.

Mystically, however, the mother and brothers of Jesus are the Synagogue, from whose flesh he was born, and the people of the Jews, who, while the Saviour teaches within, come but are unable to enter, neglecting spiritually to understand what he says. For the crowd, arriving beforehand, enters his house in order to listen to his words, as the evangelist Matthew makes clear: when Judaea delayed, the Gentiles hastened together to Christ and, being nearer in faith and therefore more receptive in mind, drank in the inward mysteries of life.

In accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII).

[Col. 0166A] And they say to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.” And answering them he says: “Who is my mother and my brothers?”

The word is within; the light is within. Hence elsewhere he says, “So that, entering, they may see the light” (Luke VIII). If, then, his relatives are standing outside and are not themselves recognized—and perhaps are not recognized for our example—how will we be recognized if we stand outside? For his relatives, standing outside, do not wish to see the Lord, since the Jews, not seeking the spiritual meaning in the Law, have fixed themselves outside in the observance of the letter. They compel Christ, as it were, to come out rather to teach carnal things, instead of consenting to enter in themselves to learn spiritual things.

[Col. 0166B] And looking around at those who were sitting around him, he says: “Behold my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”

When one who does the will of God is called the Lord’s sister and brother, on account of both sexes being gathered into the faith, this is not surprising. But it is exceedingly surprising how such a person can also be called a mother. For he deigned to call his faithful disciples brothers, saying, “Go, announce it to my brothers.” Therefore, since someone can become the Lord’s brother by coming to the faith, we must ask how he can also become a mother.

But we should know that the one who is Jesus’ brother and sister by believing becomes his mother by preaching. For he gives birth, as it were, to the Lord when he pours him into the heart of the hearer. And he becomes his mother if, through his voice, the love of the Lord is generated in the mind of his neighbour.

[Col. 0166C] CHAPTER IV

And again he began to teach beside the sea.

If we examine the Gospel of Matthew, it is plainly evident that the Lord delivered this teaching beside the sea on the same day on which he had given the preceding discourse in the house. For when that discourse had ended, Matthew immediately added, saying: “On that day, going out of the house, he sat beside the sea, and great crowds gathered to him,” and so forth (Matthew XIII).

Not only the Lord’s deeds and words, but also the journeys and places in which he performs miracles and preaches, are filled with heavenly mysteries. After the discourse delivered in the house, where in a shameful blasphemy he was said to have a demon, he went out and began to teach beside the sea, to show that, having abandoned Judaea because of the guilt of unbelief, he would pass over to save the Gentiles.

For the proud and unbelieving hearts of the Gentiles are rightly likened for a long time to the swollen and bitter waves of the sea. And who does not know that the Lord’s house was the faithless Judaea? But, having left the house in which he had endured the blasphemies of the impious, he began to teach beside the sea, because, after abandoning the Synagogue on account of its unbelief, he came to gather through the apostles the multitude of the Gentile people.

[Col. 0166D] Hence it is appropriately stated beforehand that, while he was preaching in the house, his mother and brothers stood outside, as though they were not recognized by him; and that, thus leaving the house, he passed over to teach beside the sea. For after the Synagogue had fixed itself outside in the observance of the letter and preferred the figures of the Law to the inner mysteries of the Lord’s faith, the Lord bestowed upon the nations throughout the world the mysteries of salvation that it had rejected.

And a great crowd gathered to him, so that, going up into a boat, he sat on the sea; and the entire crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he taught them many things in parables.

The great crowd that gathered to the Lord as he taught beside the sea signifies the multitude of peoples flowing to the faith of truth when the apostles preach. But the fact that he himself went up into a boat and sat on the sea prefigured the Church that was to be built in the midst of nations that did not believe and contradicted the faith. The Lord sits, as it were, in the boat placed in the middle of the sea when he illumines with the grace of his visitation the minds of the faithful dwelling among the faithful and consecrates in them a dwelling beloved by him.

[Col. 0167A] Moreover, the crowd situated around the sea on the land, listening to the Lord’s words without being touched by the waves of the sea or sitting with him in the boat after crossing the waves, most aptly represents those who had recently gathered to hear the word. Indeed, through the devotion of their hearts they are separated from the bitterness, darkness, and instability of the reprobate; but they have not yet been instructed in the heavenly mysteries that they desire.

And he said to them in his teaching: “Listen. Behold, the sower went out to sow.”

In what follows, the Lord himself explains this parable, affirming that the seed is the word of God and that the sower is himself. But when he says that the sower went out to sow, he leaves us to inquire into its meaning.

The sower therefore went out to sow because the Lord, going forth from the bosom of the Father, came into the world and sowed among the human race the word of truth that he had seen with the Father, either through himself or through those whom he himself appointed. In accordance with this, Habakkuk says in his praises: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Habakkuk III)—that is, those whom you deign to consecrate with the anointing of your Spirit and make participants in your holy name.

Or certainly he went out to sow when, after calling the chosen portion of the Synagogue to his faith, he also poured out the gifts of his grace for the gathering of the Gentiles. He signified this very thing by his journey when, after the preaching delivered in the house, he went out to teach beside the sea.

[Col. 0167B] Finally, while preaching in the house, he abandoned some because of the unforgivable crime of their blasphemy; while, because of the devotion of their piety, he called others his mother and brothers. This clearly expresses the distinction within the Jewish people, among whom many are rebellious against the Lord, while some are worthy of divine adoption.

And as he sowed, some seed fell beside the road, and the birds came and ate it.

In Luke’s Gospel it is written concerning this seed: “Other seed fell beside the road, and was trampled, and the birds of heaven ate it.” Therefore, whatever the Lord deigned to explain in this parable should be received with devout faith. What he left unspoken for our understanding should likewise be investigated and briefly touched upon with devout intention.

The seed that fell beside the road perished through a double injury: it was trampled by those passing along and snatched away by birds. The road, therefore, is the mind worn down and dried out by the continual passage of evil thoughts, so that it is unable to receive and germinate the seed of the word. Consequently, whatever good seed happens to fall near such a road perishes, because, trampled by the wicked passage of evil thought, it is snatched away by demons. They are rightly called “birds of heaven,” either because they are heavenly and spiritual in nature or because they fly through the air.

[Col. 0168A] But other seed fell upon rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, because it did not have the depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered.

The Lord also explains the mystery of this seed. In this explanation we learn that the same things are not always placed allegorically with one and the same meaning. For he calls the rock the hardness of a proud mind, the soil the gentleness of an obedient soul, and the sun the heat of raging persecution. Elsewhere, however, he uses the sun in a good sense, saying that the righteous will shine in the future like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. And when teaching the construction of the spiritual house, he instructs us to dig down deeply, remove the soil, and place the rock in the foundation—that is, he warns us to purge earthly thoughts from the innermost recesses of the heart and, in their place, to lay the strength of unconquered faith in the foundation of good works.

In this passage, therefore, the depth of soil that should properly, when cultivated, receive the seed of the word is the uprightness of a spirit trained in heavenly disciplines and regularly formed to listen and obey the divine utterances. The rocky places, covered with a thin layer of turf, which can quickly cause the received seed to germinate but have no power to fix its root, are plainly those hearts that have been educated by no exercises of discipline and softened by no trials of temptation. They are pleased for a time merely by the sweetness of the word they have heard and by heavenly promises, but withdraw at the time of temptation. For when they display the momentary sweetness of the heavenly oracle before their innate austerity, they cover a great heap of stones with a small amount of earth, as though the place had been assigned to holy seed. They therefore cannot reach the fruit of righteousness, because they possess little salutary desire to conceive the seed of life and much harmful hardness to obstruct the fruit of salvation.

[Col. 0168B] And he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Whenever this admonition is inserted either in the Gospel or in John’s Apocalypse, it indicates that what is being said is mystical and salutary for hearing and learning. The ears for hearing are the ears of the heart and the inner senses—the ears for obeying and doing what has been commanded.

But for those who are outside, everything is done in parables, “so that seeing they may see and not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest at some time they be converted and their sins be forgiven.”

It should be noted in these words of the Lord that not only what he said but also what he did were parables—that is, signs of mystical realities—since those for whom everything was done in parables are said to have been unable to bring to understanding either what they saw or what they heard. What would have prevented those who were looking from understanding his deeds or journeys, if he had not wished them to be understood spiritually as revealing something more than what was apparent to the eyes of the flesh?

[Col. 0168C] For those who are outside and do not approach the Lord’s feet in order to receive his teaching, everything is done in parables, both the deeds and the words of the Saviour, because they are unable to recognize him as God either in the powers he performed or in the mysteries he preached. Therefore they do not deserve to attain forgiveness of sins, which is to be obtained through the grace of his faith.

These are those beside the road, where the word is sown. “And when they have heard, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts,” and so forth.

In this explanation by the Lord, the whole range of those who were able to hear the words of salvation but are unable to reach salvation is comprehended. There are some who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, any understanding, or even any opportunity to test its usefulness. In their undisciplined and hardened hearts the word that has been planted is immediately snatched away by unclean spirits, like birds from a well-trodden road.

There are others who approve the usefulness of the word they have heard and taste its desirability, but, lest they reach what they approve, some are held back by the terrors of adversity along this road, while others are delayed by the allurements of prosperity. The Lord compares the former to rocky ground and the latter to the thorny ground.

The Gentiles, who are not even deemed worthy to hear the words of life, are excluded. Nor should it seem strange that the Lord compared riches to thorns, since thorns wound while riches delight. They are rightly called thorns because, by the prickings of their thoughts, they lacerate the mind. And when they drag it as far as sin, they make it bleed as though from an inflicted wound.

[Col. 0169A] Apart from the prickings of vices, however, the desire for riches greatly devastates the mind and does not allow it to be secure. For when someone anxiously keeps watch over the manner or means by which he may acquire what he does not yet possess, over the foresight by which he may preserve what he has already acquired, and finally over the glory and dignity with which he may enjoy the abundance of his acquisitions, by how many goads of care must the wretched mind be ulcerated hour by hour?

Hence, appropriately, when explaining the thorns, the Lord, about to call riches by that name, first mentioned hardships, saying: “And there are others who are sown among thorns; these are those who hear the word, and the hardships of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and desires concerning other things entering in, choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.”

“The hardships,” he says, “of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches.” For anyone whom the superfluous desire for riches deceives must immediately be afflicted by the hardship of continual cares accompanying or even preceding it. What is more wretched than those who, the more they possess, the more they need, and the less they seem to themselves to have?

In accordance with this, one of the poets, mocking the lovers of money, says:

“The love of money grows as the money itself grows.” (Juvenal)

How much happier are those who confess themselves truly to be “as having nothing, yet possessing everything,” not only through their desire for true riches but also through their very contempt for false ones?

[Col. 0169B] After saying, “the hardships of the world and the deceitfulness of riches,” he appropriately added, “and desires concerning other things.” For Scripture commands: “If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and God will provide it for you.” And again it says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly desires his commandments” (Psalm CXI).

But the person who, neglecting wisdom and despising the Lord’s commandments, wanders in desire for other things can receive neither the fruit of wisdom nor attain the joy of true blessedness. Such desires choke the word because, through their intrusive thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind. And by not allowing a good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of the vital breath.

By a just judgment, therefore, it happens that the more a person desires other things, the farther he is from that poverty of spirit and desire by which they long to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians I). Rather, the wretched person fears what will truly happen to him: to be dissolved from this life and to be with the devil.

And these are those sown upon good soil, who hear the word, receive it, and bear fruit—one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.

Good soil—that is, the faithful conscience of the elect—acts contrary to all the worthless produce of the earth, because it willingly receives the seed of the word entrusted to it and, once received, preserves it steadfastly through adversity and prosperity until the season of fruit.

It bears fruit and produces one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold. Thirtyfold, when it instils faith in the holy Trinity into the hearts of the elect. Sixtyfold, when it teaches the perfection of good works. Since the adornment of the world was completed in the number six, good works are rightly signified by it. A hundredfold, when it shows that in all we do we ought to seek the rewards prepared in the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0169C] For the hundred, which in counting is transferred to the right hand, is rightly used as a sign of perpetual blessedness. Thirty and sixty, indeed, are still held in the left hand, while a hundred passes over to the right. Although the faith that reveals to us knowledge of our Creator is great, and great are the works by which faith is perfected so that it is not idle, both are necessary in this life; but the reward of faith and of works performed through love is to be hoped for in the life to come.

And he said to them: “Does a lamp come in order to be put under a bushel or under a bed? Is it not to be put upon a lampstand?”

Because above he had said to the apostles and those who were with them, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but for those who are outside everything is done in parables,” he now shows that through them the same mystery would at some time be revealed to the others as well, and that the breast of all who were to enter the house of God would be illumined by the flames of faith.

Through these words he also teaches, figuratively, confidence in preaching, so that no one, through fear of bodily disadvantages, may conceal the light of knowledge that he knows. By the name of the bushel and the bed he designates this present life and the flesh in which we live; by the lamp, the word by which we are illumined.

[Col. 0170A] Since the time of our life is contained within the fixed measure of divine providence, it is rightly compared to a bushel. Who does not see that the bed can rightly be called the body in which the soul, dwelling temporarily, rests? Hence it is said to a certain man who had been healed: “Rise, take up your bed, and go into your house” (Matthew IX). This is plainly to say: Rise from the body of negligence; and diligently raise up for the practice of good works the body in whose desires you had lain for so long. Thus enter the house of eternal dwelling, destined to receive the rewards of good works.

Whoever, therefore, out of love for this temporal life and its carnal allurements, hides the word of God covers the lamp with a bushel or a bed, as it were, because he places the desires of the flesh before the manifestation of the truth, which he fears to preach.

But he places the lamp upon a lampstand who subjects his body to the service of God, so that the preaching of truth may be higher and the service of the body lower. Nevertheless, through that very service of the body, the teaching shines more brightly: through bodily offices—that is, through the voice, the tongue, and the other movements of the body—it is conveyed to those learning in good works.

[Col. 0170B] He therefore places the lamp upon a lampstand when the Apostle says: “I do not fight as though beating the air, but I discipline my body and subject it to servitude, lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians IX).

For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest; nor has anything been concealed except so that it may come into the open.

“Do not,” he says, “be ashamed of the Gospel of God, but amid the darkness of persecutors raise the light of the word upon the lampstand of your body, holding fixed in your mind the day of final retribution, when the Lord will illumine the hidden things of darkness and disclose the thoughts of hearts.” Then praise from God will await you, while eternal punishment will await the adversaries of truth.

If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.

If anyone has the understanding to grasp the word of God, let him not withdraw, let him not turn his hearing toward fables, but let him diligently apply his ear to examining what the truth has said, his hands to fulfilling what he has already understood, and his tongue to preaching it in season and out of season.

And he said to them: “Pay attention to what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you.”

“If,” he says, “you diligently strive to do all the good you can and to make it known to your neighbours, divine mercy will be present to grant you, in the present, the capacity to grasp higher things and the ability to accomplish better things; and in the future it will truly add to you gifts of eternal recompense beyond what you know how to hope for.”

[Col. 0170C] For whoever has, it will be given to him. And whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.

“Devote yourselves,” he says, “with your whole attention to the word you hear, remembering it and examining it, because whoever possesses love for the word will also be given the understanding of what he loves. But whoever does not have love for hearing the word, even if he seems to possess skill through natural intelligence or through practice in letters, will enjoy none of the sweetness of true wisdom.”

Although this appears to have been said specifically about the apostles, who were given knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of God through charity and faith, and about the faithless Jews, who, seeing in parables, did not see, and hearing, did not understand—and who were consequently to lose the letter of the Law in which they gloried—it can nevertheless also be understood generally: sometimes an intelligent reader deprives himself through negligence of the wisdom that a person slow in intellect but diligent savours through labour.

And he said to them: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed upon the earth and sleep, and rise night and day, while the seed germinates and grows, though he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit has appeared, he immediately sends the sickle, because the harvest has arrived.”

A man casts seed upon the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart. After he has cast the seed, he sleeps because he now rests in the hope of a good work. He rises night and day because he advances amid adversity and prosperity. The seed germinates and grows while he does not know how, because, even when he is still unable to measure his progress, the virtue once conceived is led onward to advancement.

[Col. 0170D] The earth bears fruit of itself because, with grace going before it, the human mind rises spontaneously toward the fruit of good work. But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

To produce the blade is to possess, in the beginning, the still-tender growth of goodness. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward toward the progress of good work. It produces full grain in the ear when the virtue advances so far that it is capable of being a strong and perfect work.

And when the fruit has appeared, he immediately sends the sickle, because the harvest has arrived. For almighty God sends the sickle when the fruit has been produced and cuts down his harvest, because, when he has brought each person to perfect works, he cuts short his temporal life by a sentence issued, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses.

[Col. 0171A] When, therefore, we conceive good desires, we cast seed upon the earth. When we begin to do what is right, we are the blade. When we grow toward the perfection of good work, we reach the ear. When we are made firm in the perfection of that work, we produce full grain in the ear. Thus no one is seen to be still in the tender state of mind with regard to a good resolve, because God’s grain begins with the blade in order to become grain.

And he said: “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or to what parable shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it has been sown in the earth, is smaller than all the seeds that are in the earth.”

The kingdom of God is the preaching of the Gospel and the knowledge of the Scriptures that leads to life, concerning which it is said to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

This kingdom, therefore, is like a grain of mustard seed which, according to Matthew’s Gospel, a man took and sowed in his field (Matthew XIII). The man who sows is understood by most to be the Saviour, who sows in the souls of believers. Others understand the man himself sowing in the earth or in his field—that is, in himself and in his own heart.

[Col. 0171B] Who is this sower if not our understanding and spirit? Receiving the grain of preaching and nourishing the seed with the moisture of faith, it makes it sprout in the field of its breast.

“When it has been sown,” he says, “in the earth, it is smaller than all the seeds that are in the earth. And when it has been sown, it rises up and becomes greater than all the garden plants, and produces great branches, so that the birds of heaven can dwell under its shade.”

The preaching of the Gospel is the smallest among all disciplines.

For at first hearing, this teaching has no credibility of truth, proclaiming the Lord God as a man who died and the scandal of the cross. Compare this kind of teaching with the doctrines of the philosophers, their books, the splendor of their eloquence, and the composition of their speeches, and you will see how much smaller the seed of the Gospel is than all the other seeds. But when those have grown, they display nothing biting, nothing vigorous, nothing life-giving. Everything weak and withered boils forth into vegetables and herbs, which dry up and fall away. This preaching, however, which seemed small at the beginning—whether when it was sown in the soul of a believer or when it was sown throughout the whole world—does not rise into vegetables but grows into a tree, as is stated most clearly in the other Evangelists. Thus the mustard seed sown in the earth, or in the Lord’s field, rises and is changed from a vegetable into a tree, whose nature is to surpass the nature of all herbs in height, breadth, and longevity. [Col. 0173B–0174A]

For great is the height of this tree, because the preaching of the Gospel lifts the minds of its hearers toward desiring heavenly things. It is spread out in branches, because through preachers arising from it, it has occupied the boundaries of the whole world. It excels in duration, because the truth which it proclaims will never be destroyed by any end. Under its shade the birds of the air dwell, because the souls of the faithful, accustomed to fly toward heavenly things through desire and, having neglected the cravings of temporal matters, to keep their hearts above, “will hope in the protection of the Lord’s wings” (Ps. 90). Hence also the bride in the Song of Songs—that is, the holy Church gathered from many souls—glories and says: “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2). This is plainly to say: “Under the protection of him whom I desired to see, I placed myself, deprived of the comfort of others; and the joy of seeing him and his presence, sweet to my heart, compelled me to despise—or rather, to loathe—whatever is outside him.” [Col. 0174A–B]

And with many such parables he spoke the word to them, according as they were able to hear. But without a parable he did not speak to them. Privately, however, he explained everything to his disciples. This is not said as though he had never spoken openly to the crowds and had spoken to them only in parables; rather, it is because scarcely any speech of his is found in which something of the parables is not interwoven.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0173]

[Col. 0173C] And he said to them on that day, when evening had come: “Let us cross to the other side.” And leaving the crowd, they take him just as he was in the boat; and there were other boats with him. In this voyage the Lord deigns to show both natures of his one and the same person: he himself, who sleeps in the boat as a man, restrains the fury of the sea by his word as God.

Moreover, according to the allegory, the sea which he wishes to cross with his companions signifies the dark and bitter turmoil of the present age. The boat which he entered is understood, better than anything else, as the wood of his most sacred Passion. By its benefit, all the faithful who are assisted cross the waves of the world and arrive at the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland, as though at the security of a stable shore.

The other boats which are said to have been with the Lord, yet are not reported to have been taken out into the deep or to have endured any storm, signify those who have been so imbued with faith in the Lord’s cross that, not yet battered by the whirlwind of tribulations, they preserve the mysteries of the faith they received in the peace of the Church; or certainly those who, after frequent storms of temptations, enjoy for a time the somewhat clear calm of the peace that has been granted. For it is uncertain whether those boats had recently been built and brought into port, or whether, after experiencing the dangers of the sea, they had been brought back to port. Thus they can rightly designate both groups: those who have not yet been tested by temptations and those who, after frequent examination through tribulations for Christ, have gained some tranquility of circumstances with their temptations quieted for a while. [Col. 0173C–D; 0174C]

And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were cast into the boat, so that the boat was being filled. And he himself was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion. Christ fell asleep while the disciples were sailing, because, when the faithful were trampling upon the world and meditating in their hearts upon the rest of the future kingdom, and were eagerly casting behind them the treacherous vanities of the world, either by the favorable breath of the Holy Spirit or by the rowing of their own effort, the time of the Lord’s Passion suddenly arrived.

Thus it is rightly reported to have happened when evening had come, so that the setting of the true Sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the hour of the departing light. When he ascended the stern of the cross, in which he was to undergo the sleep of death, the waves of blaspheming persecutors, stirred up by demonic storms, rose up. Yet his own patience is not disturbed by them; rather, the weakness of the disciples is shaken, trembles, and is endangered. [Col. 0174C–D]

And they awaken him and say to him: “Teacher, does it not concern you that we are perishing?” The disciples awaken the Lord so that, while he slept, they might not perish through the violence of the waves, because, having seen his death, they sought his resurrection with the greatest longing, lest, if he remained longer asleep in the death of the flesh, their mind should perish forever in spiritual death. Hence it follows appropriately:

And rising, he rebuked the wind and said to the sea: “Be silent; be quiet.” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. He rebuked the wind as he rose, because, when the resurrection had been accomplished, he overthrew the devil’s pride, destroying through death him who held the power of death. He also commanded the sea to be silent and restored calm, because by conquering death and rising from the tomb he cast down the mad fury of the Jews, who had cried while shaking their head: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27).

Here it should be noted, according to the literal sense, that all creatures perceive the Creator. Those creatures to whom rebuke and commands are given perceive the one who commands them—not through the error of heretics, who think that all living things possess souls, but through the majesty of the Creator. For things that are insensible to us are sensible to him. [Col. 0175A]

And he said to them: “Why are you afraid? Do you still have no faith?” They are rightly rebuked, since they were afraid while Christ was present, although whoever clings to him cannot perish. Something similar occurred after the sleep of death, when, appearing to the disciples, he reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart because they did not believe those who had seen him risen (Mark, final chapter). Again he said to them: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke, final chapter).
