It is as though he were saying through the metaphor of the ship: Was it not necessary for Christ to fall asleep while waves swept over the boat in which he slept, and, awakened in this way, to make the power of his divinity manifest to all by immediately calming the swollen surges of the waters?

And they were afraid with a great fear, and said to one another: “Who, then, is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” Matthew writes it this way: “The men were amazed, saying: ‘What sort of man is this?’” and so forth. Therefore it was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who were amazed and were in doubt about the person of him whom the wind and the sea obeyed. But if anyone obstinately wishes those who were amazed to have been the disciples, we shall reply that they were rightly called “men,” because they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

And we too, each of us imbued with the sign of the Lord’s cross, when we intend to leave the world, certainly climb into the boat with Jesus and attempt to cross the sea. Yet he who neither sleeps nor slumbers, who always guards Israel, nevertheless seems often to fall asleep while we are sailing, as though amid the roar of the sea, whenever, while the effort of virtues is increasing, the splendor of faith is darkened by the assault either of unclean spirits, or of a few human beings, or of our own thoughts; the loftiness of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold.

In such storms, however, we must run to that helmsman and diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. He will soon restrain the storms, pour back tranquility, and grant the harbor of salvation. [Col. 0175B–D]

## CHAPTER V

And they came across the strait of the sea into the region of the Gerasenes. Gerasa is a notable city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh possessed, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the pigs were hurled. It signifies the nation of the Gentiles, which, after the sleep of the Passion and the glory of his resurrection, the Savior deigned to visit by sending preachers.

Hence Gerasa—or Gergeseni, as some read it—is appropriately interpreted as “driving out the settler” or “the stranger drawing near”: namely, it indicates that the people of the Gentiles both drove from their heart the enemy by whom they had been wickedly inhabited and that the one who had been far away became near through the blood of Christ. [Col. 0175D–0176A]

And when he had come out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit met him from the tombs, who had his dwelling among the tombs. This man, who was tormented by an unclean spirit and was raging against the Lord, yet came to him in order to be cured shortly afterward, represents the people of the Gentiles, who until the time of the Lord’s incarnation, deceived by demonic teachings, worshiped idols instead of God.

He had his dwelling among the tombs because he delighted in dead works, that is, in sins. For what are the bodies of the unbelieving except certain tombs of the dead, in which the word of God does not dwell but a soul dead through sins is confined? [Col. 0176A–B]

And no one could now bind him, not even with chains, because he had often broken chains and shackles when bound with them. And no one could subdue him. The chains and shackles signify the harsh and severe laws of the Gentiles, by which sins are restrained even in their commonwealth. After breaking the chains—as Luke writes—he was driven by the demon into the desert; even after transgressing those laws, he was led by desire toward crimes that exceeded ordinary custom. [Col. 0176B–C]

And he was always, night and day, in the tombs and in the mountains, crying out and cutting himself with stones. The demoniac raged continually, night and day, because whether the Gentile world suffered under adverse circumstances or some peace and prosperity from a flattering world smiled upon it, it knew no way to shake the neck of its mind free from the service of evil spirits.

Through the ugliness of its deeds it lay, as it were, in the tombs; through the act of pride it wandered on the ridges of the mountains; through words of the harshest unbelief, it cut itself, as though, in its fury, it had seized rocks. But, as John the Baptist bears witness, the Lord raised up children for Abraham from stones, when he converted the hard hearts of unbelievers to the grace of devotion. [Col. 0176C]

But when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and worshiped him, and crying out with a loud voice said: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” How great is Arius’s madness in believing Jesus to be a creature and not God, when demons believe him to be the Son of the Most High and tremble! What impiety of the Jews—to say that he cast out demons by the prince of demons, when the demons themselves confess that they have nothing in common with him! They did not cease afterward, in the shrines of idols, to say and confess this very thing which they had then cried out in the frenzy of the demoniac: namely, that Jesus is Christ, the Son of the Most High, and that they themselves have no peace or fellowship with him.

“I adjure you by God: do not torture me.” For he was saying to him: “Come out, unclean spirit, from the man.” The enemy of human salvation considers it no small torment to cease from harming a human being; and the longer he has usually possessed someone, the more reluctantly he consents to leave him. [Col. 0176D–0177A]

Therefore we must strive with the utmost care so that, even if at some time, as human beings, we are overcome by the devil, we may immediately hasten to avoid his snares, lest, if resistance is offered to his powers somewhat too late, he should eventually be driven out with greater difficulty.

And he questioned him: “What is your name?” And he says to him: “My name is Legion, because we are many.” He does not ask the name as one who is ignorant, but so that, once the plague which the madman endured had been publicly confessed, the power of the healer might shine forth more graciously.

The priests of our own time who know how to cast out demons through the grace of exorcism also commonly say that sufferers cannot otherwise be cured unless, insofar as they are able to understand, they openly disclose by confession everything they have endured from unclean spirits, whether awake or asleep, through sight, hearing, taste, touch, or any other bodily or mental sense.

But the spirit’s statement, “My name is Legion, because we are many,” signifies that the people of the Gentiles were enslaved not to any one form of worship but to countless and diverse cults of idolatry. [Col. 0177A–B]

Against this it is written that the heart of the multitude of believers was one, and their soul was one (Acts 4). Hence, appropriately, the unity of languages that was divided at the building of Babylon through the spirit of pride was joined together at Jerusalem through the grace of the Holy Spirit in the diversity of languages.

The former is interpreted as confusion, the latter as a vision of peace, because one faith and devotion brings peace throughout the whole world and confirms the elect in many languages and nations; but among the reprobate, sects more numerous than languages separate and confuse them. [Col. 0177B–C]

And he begged him earnestly not to drive him outside the region. In Luke’s Gospel it is written: “And they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss.” The demons therefore knew that at some future time, through the Lord’s coming, they would be sent into the abyss—not because they themselves foretold the future, but because they remembered what the prophets had said about them. Therefore they feared that the glory of the Lord’s coming, which they marveled at, would tend toward their own condemnation. [Col. 0177C–D]

Now there was there, near the mountain, a large herd of pigs feeding. And the spirits begged him, saying: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.” And Jesus immediately granted their request. He permitted the demons what they asked so that, through the destruction of the pigs, an opportunity for human salvation might be provided. For when the swineherds saw these things, they immediately reported them to the city.

Let Manichaeus be ashamed. If the souls of human beings and beasts are of the same substance and from the same author, how is it that two thousand pigs are drowned for the salvation of one human being? Yet in their destruction unclean human beings are judged figuratively—people without voice and reason, who, feeding on the mountain of pride, delight in filthy deeds. Demons can dominate such people through the worship of idols. For unless someone has lived like a pig, the devil will not be given power over him—or he will be given it only for testing, not also for destruction. [Col. 0177D–0178A]

And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and with a great rush the herd was driven down into the sea, about two thousand of them, and they were drowned in the sea. This signifies that, once the Church had been glorified and the people of the Gentiles had been freed from the domination of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ carry out their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, submerged in blind and profound curiosity.

It should be noted that the unclean spirits would have gone into the pigs only because the merciful Savior himself granted this to them when they asked—although he could certainly have banished them into the abyss. He wished to teach us a necessary lesson: namely, that we should know that those spirits have far less power to harm human beings by their own authority, since they could not harm even animals of whatever kind. The good God can grant us this power through hidden justice; he cannot grant it through injustice. [Col. 0178A–B]

But those who were feeding them fled and reported it in the city and in the countryside. The fact that the swineherds fled and reported these things signifies that certain leaders even among the ungodly, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim its power among the nations with astonishment and wonder.

And they went out to see what had happened. And they come to Jesus and see the man who had been tormented by the demon sitting, clothed, and of sound mind, and they were afraid, and so forth. In Luke’s Gospel it is written: “Sitting at his feet.”

This signifies that the multitude, delighted with its former way of life, honors the Christian law but does not wish to endure it, saying that it cannot fulfill it, while nevertheless admiring the faithful people healed from their former and ruined manner of life.

To sit at the Lord’s feet is for those from whom the demons have departed, corrected from their sins, to observe with fixed attention the footsteps of their Savior, so that they may follow them. To resume clothing is to receive again, now with a sound mind, the pursuit of virtues which the mad had lost.

The Lord’s parable of the prodigal and wasteful son aptly corresponds to this figure: when he returns to his father, he is immediately clothed in the first robe and given a ring, clearly indicating that whoever truly repents from the heart of what was lost can, by the grace of Christ, recover with the ring of unviolated faith the first works of righteousness from which he had fallen. [Col. 0178B–C]

And they began to ask him to depart from their borders. The Gerasenes, conscious of their weakness, judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence; they did not understand the word of God and, with minds still weak, were unable to bear the weight of wisdom.

The same thing is recorded to have happened to Peter when he saw the miracle of the fish. And the widow of Sarepta, blessed by the hospitality of the blessed Elijah and aware that she had received a blessing through his lodging, nevertheless thought herself burdened by his presence, saying: “What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son might die” (1 Kings 17). [Col. 0178D]

And as he was climbing into the boat, the man who had been tormented by the demon began to beg him that he might be with him. But he did not admit him and said to him: “Go to your house and to your people, and announce to them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.”

These words can rightly be understood in light of the Apostle’s statement: “I long to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1). Thus each person should understand that, after the remission of sins, he must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others also, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. He must not, because he prematurely wishes to be with Christ, neglect the ministry of preaching that is directed toward the redemption of his brothers and sisters.

As for Matthew’s saying that two men were cured from the legion of demons, while Mark and Luke mention one, understand that one of them was a person of greater distinction and renown, whom that region especially mourned and for whose salvation it labored greatly. The two Evangelists, wishing to signify this, judged that only the one should be mentioned whose fame in connection with the event had spread more widely and more gloriously. [Col. 0178D–0179B]

The general allegory also agrees, because just as one person possessed by a demon, so also two persons suitably express the type of the Gentile peoples. For when Noah fathered three sons, the family of only one was adopted into the possession of God; from the other two were produced the peoples of various nations who were enslaved to idols.

And one of the rulers of the synagogue named Jairus came, and seeing him, fell at his feet, and so forth. In this reading, when the ruler of the synagogue asks the Lord to save his daughter, but while the Lord is going to his house the woman with the flow of blood anticipates him and seizes healing, and afterward the ruler’s daughter reaches the desired healing—or rather, is recalled from death to life—the salvation of the human race is revealed. When the Lord came in the flesh, it was arranged that first certain people from Israel should come to faith, then the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved. [Col. 0179B–C]

Who, then, is this ruler of the synagogue who comes to ask the Lord on behalf of his daughter, if not Moses himself? Hence he is appropriately called Jairus, that is, “giving light” or “enlightened,” because he received the words of life to give to us and through them enlightens others; and he himself was enlightened by the Holy Spirit, by whom he could write or teach life-giving admonitions.

Seeing Jesus, he fell at his feet, because, foreseeing in the spirit the Lord who was to come in the flesh, he submitted with a humble heart to his power. He knew that the Lord would become man toward the end of the age, yet he did not doubt that he existed as eternal God before every age.

If God is the head of Christ, what should his feet be understood as more fittingly than the humanity he assumed, by which he touched the earth of our mortality? And for the ruler of the synagogue to fall at the feet of Jesus is for the lawgiver, together with the whole succession of the patriarchal fathers, to recognize that the Mediator of God and human beings far surpasses him in the glory of dignity, and to confess with the Apostle that “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1). [Col. 0179C–D]

And he begged him earnestly, saying: “My daughter is at the point of death. Come, lay your hands upon her, so that she may be saved and live.” In Luke’s Gospel it is written that she was his only daughter, about twelve years old, and that she was dying.

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is therefore the Synagogue itself, which, formed solely by the legal institution, was born, as it were, as Moses’ only daughter. And she, like a twelve-year-old girl—that is, as she approached the time of puberty—was dying. For nobly raised by the prophets, after she had reached the age of understanding, after she ought to have begun to produce spiritual offspring for God, she was suddenly struck down by the sickness of error and abandoned, in utter despair, the paths of spiritual life. Had Christ not come to her aid, she would have utterly fallen into a terrible death. [Col. 0179D–0180A]

And he went with him, and a large crowd followed him and pressed around him. As the Lord goes to heal the girl, he is pressed by the crowd, because, while offering the Jewish people salutary admonitions by which he might raise up its conscience, sick with vices, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples. [Col. 0180A–B]

And there was a woman with a flow of blood for twelve years. The woman suffering from the flow of blood, yet healed by the Lord, is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Polluted by the inborn flow of carnal pleasures and already separated from the assembly of the faithful, while the word of God was determined to save Judea, she seized for herself, with confident hope, the salvation already prepared and promised to others.

It should be noted that the ruler’s daughter was twelve years old and that this woman had suffered from the flow of blood for twelve years—that is, at the very time when the girl was born, the woman began to be afflicted. [Col. 0180B–C]

For it was at almost the same age of this present world that the Synagogue began to be born among the patriarchs and the nation of the foreign Gentiles began throughout the world to be defiled by the filth of idolatry. The flow of blood can rightly be understood in two ways: both as the pollution of idolatry and as the things carried out through the pleasure of flesh and blood.

And she had suffered much from many physicians and had spent all that she possessed, gaining nothing but becoming worse. By physicians understand either false theologians, or philosophers and teachers of secular laws, who, discussing virtues and vices with great subtlety, promised that they were giving mortals useful rules for living and believing; or certainly understand the unclean spirits themselves, who, as though advising human beings, thrust themselves forward to be worshiped as gods.

The more eagerly the Gentile world listened to these voices and expended the powers of its natural ingenuity, the less it was able to be cleansed from the filth of its iniquity. But when it learned that the Jewish people was sick and that the true physician from heaven was present, it too began both to hope for and to seek the remedy for its illness. [Col. 0180C–D]

When she had heard about Jesus, she came in the crowd from behind and touched his garment. For she said: “If I touch his garment, I shall be saved.” And immediately the fountain of her blood was dried up.

The Church comes and touches the Lord when it approaches him through the truth of faith. It comes from behind, either in accordance with what he himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12), and with the command given elsewhere: “You shall walk after the Lord your God”; or because, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, it reaches the grace of faith and knowledge of him after the mysteries of his incarnation have already been accomplished.

Thus, when it merited salvation from sins through participation in his sacraments, it dried up the fountain of its blood, as though by touching his garments. [Col. 0180D–0181A]

The fountain of blood is the origin of sin. Each person’s fountain of blood is the beginning of an unclean thought, from which every sin is born. But the Lord, through the words of the Gospel, took care not only to restrain evil deeds and words but also to uproot the root of wicked thoughts, when he granted that both might be cleansed through the sacraments of the Gospel, as though he had placed in his garments the power to dry up the obscene fountain. [Col. 0181A–B]

And immediately Jesus, recognizing in himself the power that had gone out from him, turned toward the crowd and said: “Who touched my garments?” He does not ask in order to be taught what he does not know, but so that the power which he knew well—or rather, which he himself had given—might be manifested in the woman, and so that, once the power of faith had been manifested and acknowledged, many might attain salvation.

And his disciples were saying to him: “You see the crowd pressing around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” The crowd accompanying him on every side presses around him, but one believing woman touches the Lord, because the person who is burdened by the various and disorderly masses of heresies or by perverse conduct nevertheless venerates Christ with the faithful heart of the Catholic Church alone.

For just as there are some who see but do not see, and hear but do not hear, so also there are those who touch but do not touch: those who touch Christ not with a simple heart but with a doubtful or pretended one. Hence he says to someone who loved him but did not yet fully believe: “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). He plainly indicates what it means truly to touch him: namely, to believe that he is equal to the Father. [Col. 0181B–C]

And he looked around to see her who had done this. The Lord does not forget his faithful, nor does he cease to look upon those who hope in him; rather, he judges all who deserve to be saved worthy of his regard and compassion. “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.”

[Col. 0181D] But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell before him and told him the whole truth. Behold the purpose of the Lord’s questioning: namely, that when the woman openly confessed the truth of her long illness, her sudden faith, the divine mercy, and the healing granted to her, she herself might be more firmly confirmed in faith, and might offer to many an example of salvation and life. Finally, it follows:

But he said: “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace and be healed from your affliction.” He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you.” For in the very fact that you believed, you have already been saved.

While he was still speaking, people come to the ruler of the synagogue, saying: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” Immediately after the woman was healed from the flow of blood, the ruler’s daughter is reported dead, because, when the Church had been cleansed from the stain of vices and had been called “daughter” on account of the merit of faith, the Synagogue was immediately dissolved in the mourning of both unbelief and envy.

Of unbelief, because it refused to believe in Christ; of envy, because it grieved that the Church believed. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was being spoken by Paul, reviling him” (Acts 13).

And what the messengers said to the ruler of the synagogue—“Why trouble the Teacher any further?”—is still said today by those who see the condition of the synagogue so destitute that they do not believe it can be restored, and therefore do not think that prayers should be offered for its resurrection. But “what is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Mark 10); hence it appropriately follows: [Col. 0181D–0182B]

But Jesus, hearing the word that had been spoken, said to the ruler of the synagogue: “Do not fear; only believe.” The ruler of the synagogue is understood as the assembly of the teachers of the law, about whom the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses” (Matt. 23). If he himself is willing to believe, the Synagogue subject to him will also be saved.

And they come to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and they see the commotion, and people weeping and wailing greatly. “Let all who hope in you rejoice,” he says, “they will exult forever, and you will dwell in them.” But because the Synagogue lost this joy of the Lord’s indwelling through the merit of its unbelief, it lies dead, as it were, among those who weep and wail.

Yet heavenly mercy does not allow it to perish completely. Rather, toward the end of the age it restores its remnant, according to the election of grace, to salvation and life. Hence it is appropriately added: [Col. 0182B–C]

And entering, he said to them: “Why are you disturbed and weeping? The girl is not dead but sleeping.” To human beings, who were unable to raise her, she was dead; to God she was sleeping, since, by his disposition, her soul, having been received, lived, and her flesh rested in anticipation of resurrection.

Hence Christian usage has prevailed that the dead who are believed without doubt to be destined for resurrection should be called “sleeping,” as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4).

In the allegorical sense also, since the soul that sins itself dies, nevertheless the soul which the Lord foresees will be raised and will come to eternal life may rightly be said by us to have been dead, but to him to have fallen asleep. [Col. 0182C–D]

And they mocked him. But he, having put everyone out, takes the girl’s father and mother, and so forth. Because they preferred to mock the word of the one raising the dead rather than believe it, they are rightly excluded outside, as unworthy to see the power of the one who raises and the mystery of resurrection.

The crowd is likewise expelled outside so that the girl may be raised, because if the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is not first driven from the more secret parts of the heart, the soul lying dead within will not rise. For while it scatters itself through countless thoughts of earthly desires, it does not gather itself together at all for consideration of itself. [Col. 0182D–0183A]

And taking the girl’s hand, he said to her: “Tabatha cumi,” which is translated: “Girl, I say to you, arise.” Let the diligent reader ask why the truthful Evangelist, explaining the Savior’s words, inserted from himself “I say to you,” when in the Syriac speech which he recorded nothing more is said than “Girl, arise.”

Unless perhaps he thought this should be done in order to express the force of the Lord’s command, taking care to convey to his readers the speaker’s meaning more than the actual words.

For it is also well known that the Evangelists and Apostles, when they take testimonies from the Old Testament, take greater care to present the prophetic sense than the words. And the Lord, taking the girl’s hand, raised her, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their synagogue will not rise from death. [Col. 0183A–B]

And immediately the girl rose and walked. Well said: she rose and walked. For whoever has died through sins and is touched by the hand of heavenly mercy in order to be raised must not only rise from the filth and lethargy of crimes but must also immediately advance in good works—namely, according to the Psalmist, walking without blemish and practicing works of righteousness.

And they were utterly astonished. And he strictly ordered them that no one should know of it. And he commanded that she be given something to eat. As testimony to the girl’s true restoration to life, he commanded that she be given food, lest unbelievers think that what had appeared was not reality but a phantom. But if anyone has risen from spiritual death, he must likewise soon be filled with heavenly bread, becoming a participant, that is, in the divine word and in the most holy altar.

According to the moral interpretation, those three dead whom the Savior raised bodily signify three kinds of resurrection of souls. Some, by consenting to evil pleasure, bring death upon themselves through the hidden thought of sin alone. Signifying that he gives life to such people, the Savior raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who had not yet been carried outside but was dead in the house—as though she were secretly nurturing vice in her heart.

Others not only consent to harmful pleasure but also carry out the very evil in which they delight; they carry their dead person, as it were, outside the gates. Demonstrating that such people too, if they repent, are to be raised, he raised the widow’s young son, carried outside the city gates, and restored him to his mother, because he restores the soul that has turned back from the darkness of sin to unity with the Church.

Some, however, corrupt themselves not only by thinking or doing what is unlawful, but also by burying themselves, as it were, in the very habit of sinning. Yet the Savior’s power and grace are not too weak to raise even these, provided that there are vigilant thoughts watching over their salvation like sisters devoted to Christ. To signify this, he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb and, as his sister testified, already stank, since an evil reputation commonly accompanies wicked deeds.

It should also be noted that the more grievous the death of the soul has become, the more fervently the penitent must strive, if he is to deserve to rise again. Lighter and daily faults can be healed by the remedy of lighter penance. The Lord, wishing to show this secretly, raises the dead girl lying in a room with the easiest and briefest word, saying: “Girl, arise.” Indeed, because of the ease of raising her, he had denied that she was already dead. But when the dead young man had been carried outside, he strengthens him with more words so that he may come back to life, saying: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” But when the dead man had been four days in the tomb, so that he might escape the long confinement of the pressing grave, Jesus groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, groaned again, and cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come outside.” Thus at last the man whose case seemed hopeless, having shaken off the burden of darkness, is restored to life and light.

It should also be noted that, because public guilt requires a public remedy, while lesser sins can be erased by lighter and private penance, the girl lying in the house rises before only a few witnesses, and these are strictly commanded to tell no one. The young man is raised outside the gate, with a large crowd accompanying and watching. Lazarus, called from the tomb, became so well known to the crowds that, because of the testimony of those who saw him, very many crowds went out to meet the Lord with palm branches; and many of the Jews went away because of him and believed in Jesus.

But when the Lord heard a report of a fourth dead man from a disciple, since there were no living people to pray for his restoration, he said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9), that is, let evil people burden evil people with harmful praises; and because there is no righteous person present to rebuke them in mercy, “let the oil of the sinner fatten their heads.”

## CHAPTER VI

And he departed from there and went to his native place, and his disciples followed him; and when the Sabbath had come, he began to teach in the synagogue. And many who heard him were astonished at his teaching, saying: “From where has this man got all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such mighty works that are performed by his hands?”

He calls his native place Nazareth, where he had been brought up. But how great was the blindness of the Nazarenes, who, if their minds had not been foolish, could have recognized Christ in his words and deeds, yet despised him solely because they knew his human lineage. They refer “wisdom” to his teaching and “power” to the healings and miracles that he performed. The Apostle recalls this distinction with skill and beauty, saying: “Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to the nations. But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). In this statement, he referred power to signs because of the Jews, but wisdom to teaching because of the Greeks, that is, the nations.

“Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.

The offense and error of the Jews is our salvation and the condemnation of heretics. For they perceived Jesus Christ so much as a human being that they called him this carpenter and, according to another Evangelist, the carpenter’s son; they also testified that his brothers and sisters were with them. Yet these are not to be thought, as the heretics hold, to have been the actual children of Joseph or Mary. Rather, according to the usage of sacred Scripture, they are to be understood as their relatives, just as Abraham and Lot are called brothers, although Lot was Abraham’s nephew. There are many examples of this kind.

The Lord, appearing in the flesh, did not wish to be regarded and called a carpenter and the carpenter’s son without a sure sacramental purpose. Rather, through this also he taught that he was, before the ages, the Son of the one who in the beginning created heaven and earth, the maker of all things (John 1). For although human things are not to be compared with divine things, the type is nevertheless complete, because Christ’s Father works through fire and spirit. Hence his forerunner, speaking of him as the son of a carpenter, said: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matthew 3). In the great house of this world he fashions vessels of various kinds—or rather, by softening vessels of wrath in the fire of his spirit, he changes them into vessels of mercy. But the Jews, ignorant of this sacrament, despise the works of divine power because they look only upon his carnal ancestry.

And Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his native place, among his relatives, and in his own house.”

That the Lord Jesus Christ is called a prophet in the Scriptures is also attested by Moses, who, foretelling his future incarnation to the children of Israel, said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.” Not only he who is the head and Lord of the prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were held in less esteem in their native places than in foreign cities, because it is almost natural for citizens always to envy their fellow citizens. They do not consider the present works of the man but remember his fragile childhood, as though they themselves had not passed through the same stages of life to reach maturity.

And he could perform no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief.

This does not mean that he could not perform many miracles even among those unbelievers, but that, if he performed many, he would condemn the unbelieving citizens. It can also be understood in another way: Jesus is despised in his house and native place—that is, among the Jewish people—and therefore performed few signs there, lest they become completely without excuse.

But he performs greater signs daily among the nations through the apostles, not so much in the healing of bodies as in the salvation of souls. When the Lord is said to marvel at their unbelief, he does not marvel as though it were unexpected or unforeseen, since he knows everything before it happens. Nor did he then begin to marvel at the centurion’s faith as something new and previously unknown when, hearing the words of his pious confession, he said: “I have not found such faith even in Israel” (Luke 7). Rather, he who knows the secrets of the heart wishes to show people what is marvelous, and therefore displays himself as marveling before them.

The faith of the centurion was indeed marvelous. Without a human teacher, without the language of the Scriptures, and without angelic oracles, he recognized—with a natural understanding divinely enlightened—that through miracles the one whom, on account of the weakness of human frailty, he had known to be truly human was also truly God. On the other hand, the unbelief of the Nazarenes was no less marvelous: although they abounded in teachers and in the divine words in which Christ’s coming was proclaimed, and although they had Christ himself present, impressing knowledge of himself upon them through words and signs, they nevertheless remained obstinately unbelieving.

In the one case, the astonishing blindness of the Jews is pointed out: they were unwilling either to believe their own prophets concerning Christ or to believe Christ, who had been born among them. In the other, the faith of the nations is crowned: they deserved to receive, together with the sacred oracles, the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, who was born among the Jews but rejected by them.

And he went around the villages in the surrounding region, teaching. And he called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over unclean spirits.

The kind and merciful Lord and teacher does not begrudge servants and disciples a share in his powers. Just as he himself had healed every disease and every infirmity, so he also gave his apostles authority to heal every infirmity and every disease. But there is a great difference between possessing and granting, between giving and receiving. Whatever he does, he does by the Lord’s authority; if they do anything, they confess both their own weakness and the Lord’s power, saying, as Peter did: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk” (Acts 3).

And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff. No bag, no bread, and no copper in their belt, but to wear sandals and not to put on two tunics.

A preacher must have such confidence in God that, even if he does not provide for the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that these will not be lacking for him. Otherwise, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he will provide less adequately for others concerning eternal things.

It is customary to ask how Matthew and Luke could have recorded that the Lord told the disciples not even to carry a staff, when Mark says: “And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff.” The matter is resolved by understanding that “staff” is used in one sense for the staff that, according to Mark, is to be carried, and in another sense for the staff that, according to Matthew and Luke, is not to be carried. The same distinction applies to the word “temptation”: it is said, “God tempts no one,” and elsewhere, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.” The former is seduction; the latter is testing.

Both statements, therefore, are to be accepted as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles: both that they should not carry a staff and that they should carry nothing except a staff. For when, according to Matthew, he said to them: “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth, he immediately added: “For the laborer is worthy of his food.” This clearly shows why he did not wish them to possess or carry these things. It was not because they were unnecessary for the support of this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to demonstrate that these things were owed to them by those to whom they proclaimed the Gospel and who believed it.

It is clear that the Lord did not command these things as though the Evangelists ought to live from no source other than those who provided for them as they proclaimed the Gospel. Otherwise the Apostle would have acted contrary to this command when he supported himself by the labor of his own hands, so as to be a burden to no one. Rather, he gave them the authority by which they would know that these things were owed to them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is the fault of disobedience. But when authority is granted, each person may choose not to use it and may surrender what is, as it were, his own right. Thus, in arranging what the Apostle says he arranged—that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—the Lord was telling the apostles that, securely trusting in this authority, they should neither possess nor carry the necessities of this life, whether great or small.

For this reason he added, “Nor a staff,” showing that everything is owed by the faithful to the ministers of the Lord, who seek nothing superfluous. By adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” he completely disclosed and clarified why he had said all these things. Thus he signified this authority under the name of “staff” when he said that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff, so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord—which is signified by the staff—even what is not carried will not be lacking.

The same is to be understood concerning the two tunics: they were not to think that they should carry another besides the one they were wearing, anxiously worrying that another might be needed, since they could receive one through that authority. Therefore, when Mark says that they were to wear sandals or soles, he indicates that this footwear has a mystical significance: the foot should be neither covered nor bare on the ground—that is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rest upon earthly advantages.

And when he prohibits them not merely from carrying or possessing two tunics but, more expressly, from putting on two tunics, saying, “and not to put on two tunics,” what does he admonish them except to walk not in duplicity but in simplicity?

Alternatively, it seems to me that by “two tunics” he indicates a double garment—not that in regions of Scythia, stiff with icy snow, one ought to be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunic” we should understand clothing, so that we do not wear one garment while storing another for ourselves out of fear of the future.

Allegorically, the bag signifies the burdens of the world, bread temporal pleasures, and the copper in the belt the concealment of wisdom.

For whoever possesses the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor keeps it, as it were, like money shut up in a belt. It is written: “Wisdom hidden and treasure concealed—what use are either of them?” (Sirach 41). Therefore the apostles must carry neither a bag, nor bread, nor copper in their belts, because whoever has received the office of teacher ought neither to be weighed down by the burdens of worldly business, nor be weakened by carnal desires, nor hide the talent of the word entrusted to him beneath the idleness of sluggish torpor.

And he said to them: “Wherever you enter a house, remain there until you depart from that place.”

In Matthew it is written as follows: “Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart” (Matthew 10). He gives a general command of constancy, so that they may observe the rights of hospitality, asserting that it is unfitting for a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run from house to house and violate the inviolable rights of hospitality. Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles are to enter is to be chosen, so that there may be no opportunity to change their lodging and violate the obligations of hospitality.

“And whoever does not receive you or hear you, as you leave that place, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.”

The dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: they had entered the city, and the apostolic preaching had reached the people there. Or the dust is shaken off so that they may accept nothing from them—not even what is necessary for food—because they rejected the Gospel.

And going out, they preached that people should repent, and they cast out many demons, and so forth.

The Apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5). Hence it is clear that this custom of the holy Church was handed down by the apostles themselves: those possessed by unclean spirits, or any other sick persons, are to be anointed with oil consecrated by episcopal blessing.

And King Herod heard—for his name had become known—and they were saying: “John the Baptist has risen from the dead.”

How great was the envy of the Jews, and how savage the fury of their malice against the Lord, we learn from almost every passage of the Gospel. For here they believed, without anyone bearing witness, that John—of whom it had been said that he performed no sign—could rise from the dead. But Jesus, a man attested by God through mighty works and signs (Acts 2), at whose death the elements trembled, and whose resurrection and ascension angels, apostles, men, and women eagerly proclaimed—they preferred to believe had not risen but had been secretly taken away.

When they said that John had risen from the dead and that therefore unexpected powers had become active or been performed in him, they correctly understood the power of the resurrection in every respect: the saints, when they rise from the dead, will possess greater power than they had while still burdened by the weakness of the flesh.

They also showed that the miracle of resurrection itself was not unbelievable, because they spontaneously believed it without anyone teaching them. Yet, through the blindness and envy that deservedly belonged to them, they proved that they themselves had not believed the credible reality in the Lord.

When Herod heard this, he said: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead.”

Luke wrote about this as follows: “Herod the tetrarch heard all that was happening through him, and he was perplexed, because some were saying that John had risen from the dead, but others that Elijah had appeared,” and so forth (Luke 9). It must therefore be understood either that, after this perplexity, he confirmed in his own mind what the others were saying when he declared, “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead,” or that these words should be pronounced in such a way as to show that he was still uncertain.

If he had said, “Is this perhaps John the Baptist?” there would be no need to say anything about the manner of pronunciation, since his doubt and perplexity would be evident. But since those words are absent, the statement may be pronounced in either way: we may understand that he said it believing, confirmed by the words of the others, or that he was still perplexed, as Luke records.

For Herod himself had sent for John and seized him and bound him in prison because of Herodias.

An ancient account relates that Philip, the son of Herod the elder, under whom the Lord fled into Egypt, and brother of Herod, under whom Christ suffered, had married Herodias, the daughter of King Aretas. Later, after certain quarrels had arisen against his son-in-law, her father-in-law took away his own daughter and, to the grief of her former husband, joined her in marriage to his enemy.

Which Philip this was, the Evangelist Luke explains more fully: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis” (Luke 3).

Therefore John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, rebuked Herod and Herodias with the same authority by which Elijah had rebuked Ahab and Jezebel, because they had contracted an unlawful marriage. He declared that it was not lawful, while the brother was alive, to take his wife, preferring to endanger himself before the king rather than, out of flattery, forget the commandments of God.

And when a suitable day came, Herod held a banquet on his birthday for his nobles, and so forth.

Among mortals, only Herod and Pharaoh are read to have celebrated their birthdays with festive rejoicing. Yet both kings, under an evil omen, stained their festivities with blood. Herod, however, acted with the greater impiety, since he killed a holy and innocent teacher of truth and herald of life and the heavenly kingdom, and did so at the request and according to the desire of a dancing girl; nor was he ashamed to bring the head of the murdered man before his guests.

Pharaoh, on the other hand, is not reported to have committed such madness, but only ordered the eunuch who had offended him to be deprived of life. Thus, although he strayed farther from the true worship of religion, he sinned less grievously in violating his celebration. Nevertheless, the example of both proves that it is more useful for us to recall often, by fearing the day of our future death and living chastely, than to celebrate the day of our birth through luxury. For “a human being is born to labor in the world” (Job 5), while the elect pass from the world through death into rest.

And when the daughter of Herodias herself had entered, danced, and pleased Herod, Herod is not excused on the ground that, unwillingly and reluctantly because of his oath, he committed murder. Perhaps he swore precisely in order to prepare the machinery of the future killing. Otherwise, if he says that he acted because of his oath, if she had asked for the death of her father or mother, would he have done it or not? What he would have rejected in his own case, he ought to have rejected—and especially in the case of a prophet.

When she had gone out, she said to her mother: “What shall I ask for?” And she said: “The head of John the Baptist,” and so forth.

Herodias feared that Herod might at some point come to his senses, become friendly with his brother Philip, and dissolve the unlawful marriage by repudiating her. She therefore instructed her daughter to ask, in the very midst of the banquet, for John’s head—a reward worthy of her dancing, a blood-price worthy of her request!

And the king was grieved, but because of his oath and because of those reclining with him, he did not wish to disappoint her. So he sent an executioner and commanded that his head be brought on a platter, and so forth.

It is customary in the Scriptures for the historian to narrate the opinion of many people in the manner in which it was believed by everyone at the time. Thus Joseph is called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself; so now Herod is said to have been grieved because that is what those reclining at table thought. In reality, a dissembler and contriver of murder, he displayed sorrow on his face while holding joy in his heart. He excused his crime by an oath, so that under the pretext of piety he might become impious. By adding, “and because of those reclining with him,” he wishes all of them to be partners in his crime, so that bloody dishes might be served at a luxurious and impure banquet.

And he brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.

Taken literally, this happened as described. But even to this day we see that, in the person of John the prophet, the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the prophets.

Alternatively, John’s beheading signifies the diminution of the reputation by which the people believed Christ to be John, just as the exaltation of the Lord Savior on the cross signified the progress of faith. For at first the crowds considered him a prophet, but the Lord of the prophets was recognized by all the faithful as the Son of God.

Thus John was diminished in his head, while the Lord was exalted on the cross, because, as John himself said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” It was fitting that the one who was regarded as a prophet should be recognized as Christ, and that the one who, because of his mighty works, was thought to be Christ should be understood to be Christ’s prophet and forerunner.

This too was clearly signified by the distinction in the time at which the two were born. John, who had to decrease, was born when the divine light begins to diminish. But the Lord, who is the true light of the world, at that time of year when the days begin to grow, displayed to us the light-bearing gifts of his birth.

When his disciples heard this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

Josephus relates that John, after being bound, was taken to the fortress of Machaerus and beheaded there. Ecclesiastical History relates that he was buried in Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria. But in the time of the emperor Julian, pagans, envious of the Christians who frequented his tomb with devout concern, attacked the monument, scattered the bones through the fields, and then gathered them again, burned them in a fire, and scattered them once more across the countryside.

At that time monks from Jerusalem were present there. Mingling with the pagans who were gathering the bones, they collected most of them and carried them to Jerusalem to their father Philip. He sent them to blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and they were preserved there until the time of Theophilus, bishop of that same city, when, by order of the emperor Theodosius, all the temples of the nations were destroyed. Then, after the temple of Serapis had been cleansed of its filth, the bones were brought there, and a basilica was consecrated in honor of Saint John in place of the shrine of Serapis. Read the eleventh book of Ecclesiastical History.

And the apostles gathered together to Jesus and reported to him everything they had done and taught.

The apostles reported to the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John had suffered while they were occupied in teaching; this was reported either by their own disciples or by John’s disciples, as Matthew describes. Hence what follows:

And he said to them: “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a little,” and so forth.

The reason was not only their need for rest but also the grace of a mystical signification. For Judea, having refused to believe, had removed from itself the head of prophecy; and in the desert of the Church, which had not possessed a husband, he was about to provide believers with the food of the word, distributing, as it were, a banquet of loaves and fish.

There the holy preachers, who for a time had been weighed down by a heavy burden of tribulations among unbelieving and contradictory Judea, found rest through the grace of faith bestowed upon the nations. The necessity of granting rest to the disciples is shown subsequently, when it says:

For many were coming and going, and they had no time even to eat.

Here the great blessedness of that time is shown in the labor of the teachers and the eagerness of the learners alike. Would that it might return in our own age, so that such a multitude of faithful hearers might press upon the ministers of the word that they would not even allow them free time to care for the body. For if they are denied the necessary hour for caring for the body, how much less opportunity is there for them to devote themselves to the pleasures of soul or flesh? Rather, those from whom the word of faith and the ministry of salvation are demanded at suitable and unsuitable times are consequently inflamed in spirit always to do and contemplate heavenly things, lest they oppose in their actions what they teach in words.

And they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

It was not the disciples alone who went up into the boat; they took the Lord with them and sought a deserted place, as the Evangelist Matthew clearly demonstrates.

And many saw them going and recognized them, and, on foot, from all [places] to him, and so forth.

When they are said to have arrived on foot before them, it is shown that the disciples and the Lord did not sail to another shore of the sea or of the Jordan. Rather, after the boat had crossed some narrow channel or pool, they went to nearby places in the same region, which the local inhabitants could also reach on foot.

And when he came out, Jesus saw a large crowd and had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.

Matthew explains more fully how he had compassion on them, saying: “And he had compassion on them, and he healed their sick.” To have true compassion on the poor and those without a shepherd is to open the way of truth to them by teaching; to remove bodily distress by healing; and also, by feeding the hungry, to encourage them to give thanks for heavenly generosity. The continuation of this reading recalls that he did this as well.

He tests the faith of the crowds and rewards the faith he finds worthy. By asking for solitude, he investigates whether they are willing to follow him. By following, and by setting out into the desert through the labor of their own feet rather than on animals or in various vehicles, they show how great is their concern for their salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, and refreshing the hungry, he reveals, as a powerful, compassionate Savior and physician, how much he delights in the devotion of believers.

According to the laws of allegory, Christ, who seeks the desert of the nations, is followed by many companies of believers. They have abandoned the walls of their former way of life and neglected the protection of various doctrines. The God who was first known in Judea, after the teeth of the Jews became weapons and arrows and their tongue a sharp sword (Psalm 56), was exalted above the heavens, and his glory is over all the earth.

And when it had already become a late hour, his disciples approached him, saying: “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late. Dismiss them, so that they may go to the nearby farms and villages and buy food for themselves to eat.”

By “a late hour” he means the evening, as Luke testifies, saying: “The day had begun to decline, and the Twelve approached and said to him: ‘Dismiss the crowds,’” and so forth (Luke 9). When the day had declined, the Savior refreshes the crowds, because either, as the end of the ages approaches, or when the sun of righteousness set for us, we were rescued from the long corruption of spiritual hunger.

And he answered and said to them: “Give them something to eat,” and so forth.

He urges the apostles to break the bread, so that, when they testify that they do not possess any, the greatness of the sign may become more evident. At the same time, he indicates that our hungry hearts must daily be fed through them, namely, when we are stirred to love heavenly things either by their examples or by their writings.

It should be noted that when the Evangelist John was about to write this miracle of the loaves, he first stated that the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near. Matthew and Mark, however, recall that this occurred immediately after John’s death. From this it is inferred that John was beheaded when that same Paschal festival was approaching, and that the following year, when the Paschal season returned, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was completed.

Therefore, because in the Book of Sacraments his feast is marked on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and because in the Martyrology bearing the names of Eusebius and Jerome it is read: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Edessa in the province of Phoenicia, the birth of John the Baptist, on the day on which he was beheaded,” this does not designate specifically the day of his beheading but rather the day on which his head was found in that same city of Edessa and buried in a church.

For, as the Chronicle of Marcellinus the Count testifies, in the time of the emperor Marcian two eastern monks came to worship in Jerusalem and to see the holy places. The Lord’s forerunner, appearing to them in a revelation, ordered them to go to the former dwelling of King Herod, search there for his head, and, when they had found it, bury it again with due honor.

They found and took it from there, but not long afterward it was lost through negligence. It was carried by others to Edessa and buried for a considerable time in an urn beneath the earth, in a certain cave, without honor. Then John once more revealed himself and his head to a certain religious abbot and presbyter named Marcellus, while he was living in that same cave.

That head is reported to have been found by the aforementioned presbyter and given to Julioramus, the bishop of that city [the name is uncertain in the transmitted text]. From that time the beheading of the blessed forerunner began to be celebrated in that city, on the very day, as we believe, on which the head was found or raised. You will find a fuller account of these events in the aforementioned book of the Chronicles.

And he said to them: “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said: “Five, and two fish.”

The whole of the writing of the Old Testament is signified by the five loaves of the apostles and the two fish. The five loaves signify the five books of the Mosaic Law, through which the knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the passing age, and the true worship of God were made known to the human race.

The two fish signify the Psalms and the Prophets, which fed the people instructed in God’s law with the new sweetness of grace concerning the promise of the Lord’s incarnation. We are taught by the Lord’s authority that the entire sequence of the Old Testament is contained in this threefold division of sacred Scripture.

For after his resurrection the Lord himself appeared to his disciples and said that it was necessary for everything written about him “in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” to be fulfilled (Luke 24). And when he opened their understanding so that they might comprehend the Scriptures and, having understood them, hand them on spiritually to faithful hearers, he was like one blessing the apostolic loaves and fish, multiplying them by the gift of inward sweetness and commanding that they be distributed to the crowds.

It is rightly reported, according to the Gospel of John, that the loaves signifying the Law were barley loaves. Barley is chiefly the food of beasts and rustic servants, because harsher and, as it were, coarser commandments are to be entrusted to beginning hearers who are not yet perfect. “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

And therefore the Lord, granting gifts to each according to his strength and always calling them toward more perfect things, first feeds five thousand with five loaves; second, four thousand people with seven loaves; third, entrusts to the disciples the mystery of his flesh and blood; and finally, as a great gift, gives the elect to eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.

And he commanded them to have everyone recline in groups upon the green grass. And they reclined in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.

The different arrangements of the reclining guests signify the distinct gatherings of the churches throughout the world, which together form one Catholic Church. The Lord rightly commanded them to recline in groups of fifty or one hundred, so that the crowd of believers might receive its food both with its members distinguished by their places and united in conduct.

The rest of the Jubilee is contained in the mystical meaning of the number fifty, and fifty is taken twice to arrive at one hundred. Since one first rests from evil action, so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some recline in groups of fifty, while others recline in groups of one hundred. For there are some who have rest from wicked deeds in their actions, and there are some who already have rest from perverse thoughts in their minds.

They also rightly reclined upon green grass. For it is written: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40). Those who recline upon green grass and are nourished by the Lord’s food are the people who, through the discipline of self-restraint, have trampled underfoot the allurements of carnal desires and devote themselves to hearing and fulfilling the words of God.

And after taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all. To the hungry crowds the Savior does not create new kinds of food, but, taking what the disciples had, he blesses it. For, coming in the flesh, he preached nothing other than what had been foretold; rather, he demonstrated how deeply the writings of the Law and the Prophets are laden with the mysteries of grace. He looks up to heaven to teach that the gaze of the mind must be directed there, and that the light of knowledge must be sought there. He breaks the loaves and distributes them to the disciples to place before the crowds, because he disclosed the mysteries of prophecy to the holy teachers who would preach them throughout the world.

And they all ate and were satisfied, and they took up the remnants of the fragments—twelve baskets full—and also of the fish. What remains over for the crowds is gathered up by the disciples, because the more sacred mysteries, which the unlearned cannot grasp, are not to be carelessly neglected but sought out by the mature. For by the twelve baskets the apostles are signified, and by the apostles all the choirs of teachers who follow them: outwardly despised by men, but inwardly filled with the remnants of saving food, by which to nourish the hearts of the humble. Indeed, it is well known that baskets are ordinarily used for servile tasks; yet he filled the baskets with fragments of bread, the one who chose the weak things of this world in order to confound the strong.

[Col. 0194C]

Now those who had eaten were five thousand men. Since the outer person has five senses, the five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who, while still living in a worldly condition, know how to use well the outward things they possess. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because such people must still be instructed by the precepts of the Law. Those, however, who renounce the world completely number four thousand and are nourished with seven loaves—that is, they are exalted by evangelical perfection and inwardly instructed by spiritual grace.

[Col. 0194D]

And immediately he compelled his disciples to embark in the boat and go ahead of him across the strait to Bethsaida, while he himself dismissed the people, and so forth. Why he compelled the disciples to embark, and then, after dismissing the people, immediately went up the mountain to pray, John clearly explains. After completing that heavenly feeding, he added at once: “Jesus therefore, when he realized that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, fled again to the mountain, alone” (John VI). Here he shows us a necessary example for living: in the good works we do, we must avoid the repayment of human favor, and the exercise of spiritual virtues must not turn us toward the desire for temporal pleasures. For it has happened to some that, while they were admirable in character and worthy of praise because of the merit of a more exalted life, and were rightly thought deserving of honor, they lost the beginnings of their justice after receiving money or estates. Carelessly corrupting themselves through carnal allurements and greed, they came to be regarded by those who had honored them for their good deeds not merely with distaste but even with hatred on account of their subsequent evil actions. It is much less dangerous to be wearied by the wickedness of those who oppose us in the things we do rightly than to be caressed by the favor of those who honor us. The latter often corrupts the soul by making it feel secure; the former always renders it watchful and cautious. Thus, when the Lord was beginning for us the way of life that we should follow, and those who admired his virtues wanted to make him king, he fled to the mountain to pray. But when those who envied his virtues were preparing to hand him over to death, he went to meet them willingly and offered himself to the enraged men to be bound and crucified. By this clear example he teaches us to be ready to endure the adversities of the world and cautious in avoiding its flatteries whenever they happen to smile upon us; and we should beseech the Lord in frequent prayers that the prosperity of the world may not overwhelm us and deceive us by softening us.

[Col. 0195A–B]

The disciples were going ahead of the Lord across the strait to Bethsaida, which, as we find in books concerning these places, is a city in Galilee belonging to the apostles Andrew, Peter, and Philip, near the lake of Gennesareth. Here he rightly raises the question of how Mark can say that, after the miracle of the loaves had been performed, the disciples came across the strait to Bethsaida, when Luke seems to say that that memorable miracle and heavenly feeding took place in the region of Bethsaida. For he says: “Taking them with him, he withdrew privately to a deserted place, which is Bethsaida. When the crowds learned this, they followed him, and he welcomed them,” and so forth, through the completion of the account of the sacred feeding (Luke IX). Unless perhaps we understand Luke’s words—“to a deserted place, which is Bethsaida”—to designate not the vicinity of the city itself but the deserted places belonging to it. For Mark plainly says that they were to go ahead of him to Bethsaida, where the boundaries of the city itself are evidently indicated. Luke, however, does not say “to a deserted place which is Bethsaida,” but “which is Bethsaida.” This can, if I am not mistaken, rightly be understood to mean that he did not intend the city itself, but its deserted place—that is, the place belonging to its borders. The Evangelist John, meanwhile, reports that the crowds ate bread near Tiberias and that the disciples, after embarking in the boat, came across the sea to Capernaum. Both are cities in Galilee beside the lake of Gennesareth, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.

[Col. 0195C–D]

And after he had dismissed them, he went up the mountain to pray. Not everyone who prays ascends a mountain, for there is a kind of prayer that produces sin. But the person who prays well, who seeks God through prayer, advances from earthly things to higher ones and climbs to the summit of a more elevated concern. The one who pleads anxiously about riches, worldly honor, or even the death of an enemy lies in the lowest places and sends worthless prayers to God. The Lord prays, not that he may plead for himself, but that he may obtain something for me. For although he has placed all things in the power of the Son, the Son nevertheless, in order to fulfill the form of a human being, considers that he must plead with the Father on our behalf, because he is our advocate. “We have an advocate,” the Apostle says, “with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John II). If he is an advocate, he must intercede for my sins. He therefore pleads not as one weak, but as one compassionate. Do you wish to know that he can do everything he wills? He is both advocate and judge: in the one role is the duty of compassion; in the other, the distinction of power.

[Col. 0196A–B]

And when evening had come, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land. And seeing them laboring at the oars—for the wind was against them—the disciples’ labor at the oars and the opposing wind signify the various labors of the holy Church. Amid the waves of the hostile world and the blasts of unclean spirits, she strives to reach the rest of the heavenly homeland, as though it were a secure anchorage on the shore. It is rightly said here that the boat was in the middle of the sea, while he was alone on the land. For at times the Church has been so afflicted and even defiled by the pressures of the nations that, if such a thing were possible, her Redeemer might seem for a while to have abandoned her altogether. Hence comes her voice, caught amid the waves and storms of sweeping temptations and seeking the help of his protection with a groaning cry: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn so far? Why do you overlook us in times of need, in tribulation?” (Psalm IX). She likewise explains the voice of the pursuing enemy by adding what follows in the psalm: “For he said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so as not to see to the end’” (ibid.). Yet he does not forget the prayer of the poor, nor does he turn his face away from those who hope in him. Rather, he helps those who struggle with their enemies so that they may conquer, and crowns the victors forever. Hence here too it is plainly said that he saw them laboring at the oars. The Lord saw them laboring on the sea, although he himself was on land, because even if he seems to delay for a time in bringing help to the afflicted, he nevertheless strengthens them, through regard for his compassion, so that they do not fail amid their troubles; and sometimes, by manifest assistance, he also frees them after their adversities have been defeated—as though the surging waves had been trampled down and stilled. This is also indicated in what follows:

[Col. 0196C–D]

And about the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking on the sea. Military stations and watches are divided into periods of three hours. Therefore, when it says that the Lord came to them during the fourth watch of the night, it shows that they had been in danger throughout the entire night and that help was given to them at the final part of the night.

They labor, then, throughout the dark hours of night; but as dawn approaches, and the morning star (*Lucifer*) promises the rising of the sun and the day, the Lord comes and, walking upon it, presses down the swelling back of the sea. For when human frailty, weighed down by troubles, considers the weakness of its powers, it sees nothing around it but the darkness of distress and the heat of enemies engaged in conflict. But when it raises its mind toward the light of heavenly protection and the gifts of eternal reward, it suddenly sees the morning star rising amid the shadows of night, announcing the coming day. For the morning star is said to illuminate for as much as three hours of the night—namely, the whole morning watch.

And the Lord will be present, granting, once the dangers of temptation have been put to rest, the full confidence of freedom through his protection. The text continues:

And he wanted to pass them by. But when they saw him walking upon the sea, they thought it was a phantom, and they cried out. For they all saw him and were troubled. Even now heretics think that the Lord was a phantom and did not truly assume flesh from the Virgin. Theodore, formerly bishop of Pharan, finally wrote in these terms: that the Lord, according to the flesh, had no bodily weight, but walked upon the sea without weight or body. Against this, the Catholic faith proclaims that he possessed weight according to the flesh and bodily substance, and that he walked upon the waters with weight and bodily burden, without his feet being immersed. For Dionysius, an outstanding ecclesiastical writer, speaks in this manner in his works *On the Divine Names*: “For we do not know how he was formed from virginal blood by another law beyond nature, nor how, with his feet immersed, he who possessed bodily weight and material burden walked upon the wet and unstable substance.” Why, however, did the Lord wish to pass them by as though they were strangers, when he had come to rescue them from the danger of shipwreck? It was so that, after being troubled and afraid for a moment but immediately delivered, they might be more astonished at the miracle of their rescue and render greater thanks to their rescuer. For amid the storms of suffering inflicted by the faithless against those steadfast in faith, such providence is sometimes shown by God. Often heavenly compassion has seemed to abandon the faithful placed in tribulation, so that Jesus might be thought to have wished to pass by the disciples laboring on the sea. Hence there is also that statement in the Psalmist, spoken by the Church laboring in the contest of martyrdom: “Why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me? Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? While all my bones are crushed,” and so forth. But the enemies say, terrifying them, “Where is their God?” (Psalm XLII), as though threatening the apostles exhausted by shipwreck. Their God himself says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you. When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you” (Isaiah XLIII). Hence here too it is rightly added:

[Col. 0197A–D]

And immediately he spoke to them and said: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.” And he went up to them into the boat, and the wind ceased. The first help given to those who tremble and are in danger is to drive fear from their hearts. The second is to restrain the fury of the storms by the power of his presence. Nor is it surprising that, when the Lord went up into the boat, the wind ceased. For in whatever heart God is present through the grace of his love, all the battles of vices, of the hostile world, and of evil spirits at once subside, held in check.

And they were exceedingly astonished within themselves. For they had not understood concerning the loaves, because their heart was blinded. The Lord showed, in the miracle of the loaves, that he was the Creator of all things; in walking upon the waves, he taught that he possessed a body free from every burden of sin; and in calming the winds and stilling the fury of the waves, he demonstrated that he ruled the elements. Yet the chief disciples still do not recognize him to be God. They were indeed astonished at the greatness of his works, but they were not yet able to recognize in him the truth of divine majesty.

[Col. 0198A–B]

When they had disembarked, they immediately recognized him. And running through that whole region, they began to carry on beds those who were ill to wherever they heard that he was. They recognized him by report, not by his face—or perhaps, because of the greatness of the signs he performed among the people, he was known by his appearance even to many. And see how great was the faith of the people of the land of Gennesareth: they were not content with the healing of those present alone, but sent to the neighboring cities around them, so that all might run to the physician.

And wherever he entered villages, hamlets, or cities, they placed the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched him were saved. Those who are ill do not touch Jesus’ body, nor his whole garment, but only its outermost fringe. And whoever touches it will be healed.
