Understand the fringe of his garment as the least commandment: whoever transgresses it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Or understand it as the assumption of flesh, through which we come to the Word of God and afterward enjoy his majesty.

## CHAPTER VII

And the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around him. And when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with common hands—that is, unwashed hands—they found fault with them. How true was that confession of the Lord to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.” The people of the land of Gennesareth, who seemed less educated, not only came themselves but also brought their sick—or rather, carried them—to the Lord, so that they might be deemed worthy to touch even his fringe and thereby be saved. Thus they immediately obtained the reward of the healing they desired. But the Pharisees and scribes, who ought to have been teachers of the people, did not come to hear the Word or seek healing, but only to stir up battles of disputation; and they found fault with the Lord’s disciples for having unwashed bodily hands, although they could find no defiling impurity in the works performed by their hands or by the other members of their bodies. They ought rather to have blamed themselves, for although they had washed their hands with water, they carried consciences stained with malice. “For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of the elders; and when they return from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they have washed.”

[Col. 0198C–D; 0199A]

The human tradition of washing repeatedly, for eating bread, hands that have already been washed once, and of not eating after returning from the marketplace unless one has washed, is superstitious. But necessary is the teaching of truth, which commands those who desire to share in the bread of life descending from heaven to cleanse their works through the frequent washing of almsgiving, tears, and other fruits of righteousness, so that with chaste heart and body they may be able to participate in heavenly mysteries. Anyone who has contracted defilements from the concerns of temporal business must cleanse them through the subsequent persistence of good thoughts and actions, if he wishes to enjoy the banquets of inward refreshment. But the Pharisees, interpreting the spiritual words of the Prophets according to the flesh—words in which they commanded purification of heart and conduct, saying, “Wash yourselves, be clean, and purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah I)—observed them only with regard to washing the body.

[Col. 0199B–C]

In vain, then, do the Pharisees, and in vain do all the Jews, wash their hands and wash themselves after returning from the marketplace, so long as they refuse to be cleansed in the Savior’s font. They preserve the washings of vessels to no purpose, while neglecting to wash away the filth of their hearts and bodies. For it is certain that Moses and the Prophets, whenever and for whatever reason they commanded the vessels of the people of God to be washed with water, purified with fire, or sanctified with oil, intended to command us not the cleansing of material things but rather the purification and holiness of minds and works, and the salvation of souls.

[Col. 0199C]

And the Pharisees and scribes questioned him: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with common hands?” Wonderful is the folly of the Pharisees and scribes: they accuse the Son of God because he does not observe human traditions and precepts. But the hands—that is, the works—not bodily hands, of course, but those of the soul, must be washed, so that the word of God may be accomplished in them.

And he said to them: “You splendidly set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your own tradition.” He refutes a false accusation with a true answer. “When you,” he says, “neglect the Lord’s commandments on account of human tradition, why do you think my disciples should be blamed because they hold the elders’ commands of little account in order to preserve God’s decrees?”

Moses said: “Honor your father and your mother. And whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.” In Scripture, honor is understood not so much in greetings and the rendering of services as in almsgiving and the bestowal of gifts.

“Honor,” the Apostle says, “widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy V). Here honor means a gift. And elsewhere: “Presbyters are to be honored with double honor, especially those who labor in the word and teaching of the Lord” (ibid.). Through this command we are also ordered not to muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, so that the laborer may be worthy of his reward (ibid.).

But you say: “If a man says to his father or mother, ‘Corban’”—which means “a gift”—“whatever of mine might have benefited you,” and you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, and so forth. The Lord, taking into account the weakness, age, or poverty of parents, had commanded that children honor their parents even by providing them with life’s necessities. Wishing to overturn this most provident law of God and to cloak impiety under the name of piety, the scribes and Pharisees taught wicked children that, if anyone wished to vow to God—who is the true Father—the things that ought to be offered to parents, the offering to the Lord should take precedence over gifts to parents. Or else the parents themselves, avoiding the consecrated things lest they incur the charge of sacrilege, were worn down by poverty. Thus it happened that the children’s offering, under the pretext of the temple and God, passed into the profits of the priests. This wicked custom of the Pharisees arose from such an occasion. They had many people bound by debts and unwilling to repay what had been lent to them, and they assigned the debt to the priests so that, once the money had been collected, it might serve the temple services and their own needs. This passage may also have the following brief meaning: “Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you.” “You compel,” he says, “children to say to their parents: ‘Whatever gift I was going to offer to God, I am spending on your food; it benefits you, father and mother.’” Thus the parents, fearing to receive what they saw had been dedicated to God, would prefer to lead a needy life rather than eat what had been consecrated.

[Col. 0200A–B]

And again summoning the crowd, he said to them: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand: Nothing entering a person from outside can defile him. But the things that proceed from a person are what defile a person.” The verb “defile” (*communicat*) is properly scriptural and is commonly used in public speech. The Jewish people, boasting that they are God’s portion, call “common” the foods used by all human beings—for example, pork, oysters, hares, and animals of that kind, which neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud, as well as fish without scales. Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X). What is common, therefore—what is open to other human beings and is, as it were, not part of God’s portion—is called unclean. “Nothing,” he says, “entering a person from outside can defile him. But the things that proceed from a person are what defile a person.” Let the discerning reader object and say: If what enters the mouth does not defile a person, why do we not eat food offered to idols? And the Apostle writes: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Corinthians X). We must therefore understand that the foods themselves, as God’s creatures, are clean in themselves; but the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

[Col. 0200C–D]

And when he had entered the house away from the crowd, his disciples questioned him about the parable. And he said to them: “Are you also so lacking in understanding?” What had been stated openly and was clear to the hearing, the apostles thought had been spoken as a parable, and in a manifest matter they sought a hidden meaning. The Lord rebukes them for thinking that something he had spoken plainly was expressed parabolically. From this we learn that the hearer is defective who wishes to understand what is clear obscurely, or what is obscure plainly.

[Col. 0201A]

“Do you not understand that everything external which enters a person cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his stomach, and is discharged into the sewer, purging all foods?” Among heretics and perverse people, all the passages of the Gospels are filled with scandals. From this little statement some slander the Lord, claiming that, ignorant of physical discussion, he thought that all foods go into the stomach and are digested in the sewer, although food immediately spreads through the limbs, veins, marrow, and nerves. Thus we see many people who, because of a stomach disorder, suffer continual vomiting: after dinners and meals they immediately vomit what they have taken in, and yet they are corpulent, because at the first contact liquid food and drink spread through the body. But people of this sort, while wishing to criticize another’s ignorance, display their own. For even the thinnest liquid and the most fluid food, once it has been concocted and digested in the veins and limbs, descends through the body’s hidden passages—which the Greeks call *porous* (πόρους), “passages”—to the lower regions and enters the sewer.

But he was saying that the things which proceed from a person are what defile a person. “For from within, from the heart of human beings, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, and the rest.” “From the heart,” he says, “evil thoughts proceed.” Therefore, according to Plato, the governing faculty of the soul is not in the brain but, according to Christ, in the heart. From this statement those who think that thoughts are injected by the devil are also to be refuted, since they do not wish them to arise from the will itself. The devil can be an assistant and inciter of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. But if, always lying in wait, he inflames the slightest spark of our thoughts with his kindling, we must not suppose that he also probes the hidden recesses of the heart; rather, he infers from the body’s posture and gestures what we are turning over inwardly. For example, if he frequently sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love.

[Col. 0201B–C]

And rising from there, he went away into the regions of Tyre and Sidon. Leaving behind the scribes and Pharisees, his accusers, he crossed over into the territory of Tyre and Sidon in order to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians.

And entering a house, he wanted no one to know it, yet he could not remain hidden. It is rightly asked how it can be said that the Lord did not want anyone to know his journey, and yet that he could not remain hidden. For what could he not do who, even while temporally present among human beings, invisibly arranged within himself and with the Father everything that was being done outwardly? Or for what reason should he be thought to have entered the borders of Tyre and Sidon except to free the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman from a demon and, through the faith of a Gentile woman, to rebuke the unbelief of the scribes and Pharisees? But we must think of this faithfully and devoutly: in this matter nothing happened contrary to his will; rather, a lesson was shown to the faithful who followed his journey concerning what they ought chiefly to will in the good works they perform. For after entering the house, he instructed the disciples not to reveal to anyone in that unfamiliar region who he was.

[Col. 0201D–0202A]

Nevertheless, he himself prudently made that entry known to the Gentile woman and to whomever else he wished; he himself kindled her heart by an invisible prompting to seek salvation from him. Thus, by her example, those to whom he would grant the grace of healing the sick through the display of miracles might learn to avoid, as far as possible, the glory of human favor, yet not cease from the compassionate work of virtue whenever the faith of the good rightly deserved that these things be done or the unbelief of the wicked necessarily compelled them.

“And he could not,” he says, “remain hidden.” For as soon as the woman heard about him—her daughter had an unclean spirit—she entered and fell at his feet. The woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. Figuratively, this Gentile woman who comes to the Lord with faith signifies the Church gathered from the nations. She begs the Lord on behalf of her demon-possessed daughter, when she pleads with heavenly mercy on behalf of her peoples, who do not yet believe, so that they too may be released from the devil’s deceptions. According to Matthew, she is rightly reported to have gone out from her borders, while in this Evangelist she is said to have entered to the Lord and fallen at his feet, so that from the testimony of both accounts it may be understood that only those pray faithfully and rightly for the erring who leave behind the former dwelling places of their unbelief and transfer themselves with devout dedication into the Lord’s house—that is, the Church.

[Col. 0202A–B]

“And she begged him,” he says, “to cast the demon out of her daughter.” And he said to her: “Let the children first be satisfied.” It is as though he were saying more plainly: “It remains that you too, who are from the nations, will attain salvation; but first the Jews, who by the merit of their ancient election are accustomed to be called the children of God, must be nourished with heavenly bread, and only then is the food of life to be supplied to the nations.”

[Col. 0202B–C]

“For it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she answered and said to him: “Yes, Lord. For even the little dogs eat from the children’s crumbs.” The faith, patience, and humility of the Church are wonderfully praised under the person of the Canaanite woman. Her faith lay in believing that her daughter could be healed; her patience in persevering in prayer although repeatedly rejected, as Matthew writes; her humility in comparing herself not to dogs but to little dogs. “I know,” she says, “that I do not deserve the children’s bread, nor can I receive whole pieces of food or sit at table with the father. But I am content with the little dogs’ leftovers, so that by the humility of crumbs I may come to the greatness of the whole loaf.”

What a wonderful reversal of circumstances! Israel, once a son, becomes dogs; according to the difference of faith, the order of names is changed. Of them it is later said: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Psalm XXI); and: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Philippians III). Of us, turned from the barking of blasphemous contradiction to the grace of devotion, he says elsewhere: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice” (John X).

It should also be noted that the woman who believed from the nations speaks mystically, saying that the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs. The table is the holy Scripture, which supplies us with the bread of life. Hence the Church says: “You have prepared a table before me in the sight of those who afflict me” (Psalm XXII). The children’s crumbs are the inner mysteries of the Scriptures, by which the hearts of the humble are accustomed to be refreshed. Of these the Prophet elsewhere makes a promise to the holy Church concerning the Lord: “He has established your borders in peace and satisfies you with the fat of grain” (Psalm CXLVII).

The little dogs therefore eat not crusts but crumbs from the children’s bread, because those who have been converted to the faith, once despised among the nations, seek in the Scriptures not the surface of the letter but the marrow of spiritual meanings, by which they may progress in good works. And they do so under the table of their lords: humbly subject to the word of sacred eloquence, they submit all the faculties of their heart and body to fulfilling what has been commanded, so that through the merit of their due humility they may rightly raise themselves to hope for the rewards promised by the Lord in heaven.

[Col. 0202C–0203B]

And he said to her: “Because of this saying, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.” Because of the mother’s humble and faithful speech, the demon left the daughter. Here an example is given for catechizing and baptizing infants: namely, that through the faith and confession of their parents at baptism, little children are freed from the devil, since they are not yet able by themselves to understand or to do anything good or evil.

And again, departing from the regions of Tyre, he came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the borders of the Decapolis. The Decapolis is—as the name itself shows—a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. Therefore, when it is said that the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee between the borders of the Decapolis, this does not mean that he entered the actual borders of the Decapolis. For it is not said that he crossed the sea by boat, but rather that he came as far as the sea and reached the place itself that looked toward the central region of the Decapolis, situated far away across the sea.

[Col. 0203B–C]

And they bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him. The deaf and mute person is one who neither opens his ears to hear God’s words nor his mouth to proclaim them. Such people those who, through long practice, have already learned to speak and hear divine utterances must offer to the Lord for healing, so that he himself may save by the right hand of his grace those whom human frailty cannot save.

And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears. The first door of salvation is for the Lord to take the sick person and lead him away from the crowd. He takes the sick person aside when, illuminating the mind weakened by sins through a visitation of his compassion, he calls it away from the habits of human society and summons it to follow the paths of his commandments. He puts his fingers into the man’s ears when, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he opens the ears of the heart to understand and receive the words of salvation. For the Lord himself testifies that the Spirit is called the finger of God when he says to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke II, as printed). Another Evangelist, explaining this, says: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew XII).

By this finger the magicians in Egypt were also defeated by Moses, when they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus VIII). And the Law was written on tablets of stone, because through the gift of the Holy Spirit we are defended from the snares of human beings and of evil spirits, and instructed in the knowledge of the divine will. The fingers of God, therefore, placed in the ears of the one who was to be healed, are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which he opens hearts that had strayed from the way of truth to hear and learn the knowledge of salvation. And because confession ought to follow the light of truth once it has been recognized, the text appropriately continues:

[Col. 0203C–0204A]

And having spat, he touched his tongue. The Lord, having spat, touches the sick man’s tongue when he trains the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith. The Lord’s spittle signifies the flavor of wisdom, which, as the wise man testifies, says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High as the firstborn” (Sirach XXIV). Elsewhere too, by his spittle mixed with earth, the man born blind is given sight. The spittle that descends from the Lord’s head signifies his divine nature, which is from God; the portion of earth with which he mixed that spittle signifies his human nature, assumed from human beings. And by the medicine composed of his spittle and earth he opened the eyes of the man born blind, because through confession of both his natures he rescued the human race from the inborn darkness of its errors. Therefore, having spat, the Lord touches the mute man’s tongue so that he may speak, when by the touch of his compassion he trains mouths that have long been speechless to utter words of wisdom. The text appropriately adds:

[Col. 0204A–B]

And looking up to heaven, he groaned, and said to him: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.” He looked up to heaven to teach that from there speech is to be sought for the mute, hearing for the deaf, and healing for every infirmity. He groaned, not because he himself needed to ask the Father for anything with a groan—he who, together with the Father, grants all things to those who ask—but in order to give us an example of groaning when we invoke the support of heavenly compassion either for our own errors or for those of our neighbors. When he says “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened,” this properly concerns the ears. The ears must be opened for hearing, while the tongue had to be released from the restraints of its slowness so that it could speak. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0204B–C]

And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly. Here the two natures of the one Mediator between God and human beings are manifestly distinguished. For, looking up to heaven like a human being about to pray to God, he groaned; but immediately, with a single word, as one powerful in divine majesty, he healed him. It is rightly said of the man whose ears the Lord opened and whose tongue’s bond he released that he spoke correctly. For only the person speaks correctly—whether confessing God or preaching to others—whose hearing divine grace unlocks so that he can listen to and obey heavenly commands, and whose tongue the Lord trains to speak by the touch of wisdom, which is himself. Such a person can rightly say with the Psalmist: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Psalm L). And with Isaiah: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word. Morning by morning he awakens; morning by morning he opens my ear, that I may hear as though listening to a master” (Isaiah L).

[Col. 0204D–0205A]

And he commanded them not to tell anyone. But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it, and all the more they marveled, saying: “He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.” If he knew that they would proclaim it all the more the more he commanded them not to proclaim it—he who knew both the present and future wills of human beings—why did he give this command, unless he wished to show the sluggish how much more diligently and fervently they ought to proclaim him, when he commands them to proclaim him, since those who were forbidden to speak could not remain silent?

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0205B] In those days, when there was again a great crowd and they had nothing to eat, having summoned his disciples, he said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd, because for three days now they have remained with me and have nothing to eat,” and so forth. In this reading, too, we must consider the distinct operation of divinity and humanity in one and the same Redeemer of ours; and the error of Eutyches, who dares to assert that there is only one operation in Christ, must be driven far from Christian territory. For who does not see that the Lord’s compassion for the crowd, lest they should fail either from hunger or from the labor of a longer journey, is an affection and compassion belonging to human weakness? But that he filled four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish—who does not see that this is the work of divine power? [Col. 0205C]

Mystically, this miracle signifies that we cannot pass safely through the way of the present age unless the grace of our Redeemer refreshes us with the nourishment of his word. Typologically, the difference between this feeding and that of the five loaves and two fish is that there the letter of the Old Testament is signified as being full of spiritual grace, whereas here the truth and grace of the New Testament are shown to be administered to the faithful. Certainly, both feedings took place on a mountain, as the account of the other evangelists makes clear, because the rightly understood Scripture of both Testaments commends to us the height both of heavenly commandments and of heavenly rewards. With harmonious voice, both proclaim the height of Christ, who is the mountain of the house of the Lord at the summit of the mountains. Whoever builds upon himself the city or house of the Lord—that is, the Church—raises it up on high through good works and displays it openly to all the nations; having drawn it away from the lowest pleasures, he refreshes it with the bread of heaven and kindles it toward a desire for heavenly sweetness by the pledge of spiritual food.

“I have compassion,” he says, “on the crowd, because for three days now they have remained with me and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way.” Why the crowd remained with the Lord for three days, Matthew explains more fully when he says: “And going up onto the mountain, he sat there. And great crowds came to him, having with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the weak, and many others; and they cast them at his feet, and he healed them” (Matt. XV). [Col. 0206A] The crowd therefore remains with the Lord for three days because of the healing of its sick, when each of the elect, enlightened by faith in the Holy Trinity, perseveringly and earnestly implores the Lord for his own sins and those of his people—that is, for the illnesses of their souls.

Likewise, the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, turns to the Lord in deed, word, and thought. The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners faint on the road of the present life if they are sent away within their own conscience without the nourishment of holy teaching. Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred admonition. The pious statement that proceeded from the mouth of Truth deserves very careful consideration; it says:

[Col. 0206B] “For some of them have come from far away.” There is one who, having experienced no fraud and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from far away, because through incorruption and innocence he was near. Another, stained by no impurity and no crimes, but having experienced only marriage, turned to spiritual service. He too did not come from far away, because, having used the permitted union, he did not go astray through unlawful practices.

Others return to repentance after sexual crimes, others after false testimonies, others after committed thefts, others after inflicted injuries and acts of violence, others after perpetrated murders; and they turn to the service of almighty God. These, clearly, come to the Lord from far away. For the more each person has gone astray in evil work, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God. Let nourishment therefore be given even to those who come from far away, because the food of holy teaching must be offered to converted sinners, so that they may restore in God the strength they lost in their crimes.

Likewise, whichever Jews believed in Christ came to him from nearby, because they had been instructed about him by the letters of the Law and the Prophets. Believers from the Gentiles, however, certainly came to Christ from far away, because they had not been forewarned about faith in him by any records of the sacred writings.

“And he asked them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ They said: ‘Seven.’” The seven loaves are rightly placed as a mystery of the New Testament, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is more fully revealed to all the faithful, both for belief and as something bestowed upon those who believe. They are not reported to have been barley loaves, [Col. 0206D] as were the five loaves by which five thousand people were filled, lest once again, as under the Law, the life-giving nourishment of the soul should be concealed beneath bodily sacraments. For the kernel of barley is covered by an exceedingly tenacious husk.

“And he commanded the crowd to sit down upon the ground.” Earlier, at the feeding with the five loaves, the crowd sat down upon green grass. Now, where it is to be refreshed with seven loaves, it is commanded to sit down upon the ground, because through the Scripture of the Law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (1 Pet. I). In the New Testament, however, we are commanded to leave behind even the earth itself and temporal possessions.

Or certainly, because the mountain on which the crowd was refreshed with the Lord’s loaves signifies, as we said above, the height of our Redeemer, there the crowd is refreshed upon grass, here upon the ground. There, the height of Christ is covered by carnal hope and desire on account of carnal people and earthly Jerusalem; here, with every carnal desire removed, the guests of the New Testament were held by the foundation of enduring hope, like the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass placed between them.

“And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd.” The Lord took the loaves and gave them to the disciples, so that they might set before the crowd what they had received, because, granting the apostles the gifts of spiritual knowledge, he wished the nourishment of life to be distributed throughout the world to his Church through their ministry. [Col. 0207B]

That he broke the loaves which he was to give to the disciples signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the world was to be nourished for everlasting salvation. For when the Lord himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI), what else did he demonstrate but that the bread of life must be opened to us by him, since we could not ourselves penetrate to see its interior?

In contrast, the prophet, lamenting the pitiable hunger of certain people, said to him: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV). This is to say in other words: The unlearned sought the nourishment of the word of God, by which they might be refreshed and strengthened for the virtue of good action, but, with teachers failing, there was no one to disclose to them the secrets of the Scriptures [Col. 0207C] and instruct them in the way of truth.

After taking the loaves to be broken, the Lord gives thanks, both to show how much he rejoices in the salvation of the human race and to instruct us always to give thanks to God, whether we refresh the flesh with earthly bread or the soul with heavenly grace generously bestowed.

“And they had a few small fish; and he blessed these also and commanded them to be set before the people.” If the seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in whose reading we find, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, inward feasts for our minds, whom should we understand by the small fish, which the Lord likewise blessed and commanded to be set before the crowd, except the holy people of the time when that Scripture was composed, or those whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture contains? [Col. 0207D] Rescued from the turbulent waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing, they offered us inward refreshment, lest we should fail amid the passage of this transitory world, through the example either of their life or of their death.

“And they ate and were satisfied.” They eat of the Lord’s loaves and fish and are satisfied who, hearing the words of God and looking upon examples, hasten to be stirred and rise toward progress in a more upright life. The Psalmist’s words aptly apply to them: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him. Their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. XXI). This is plainly to say: The humble will hear the word of God and do it, and they will refer everything they do well not to their own praise but to that of the heavenly giver. [Col. 0208A] Hence, suitably satisfied with the bread of life, they will reach the eternal life of the inner person.

In contrast, the prophet reproaches sluggish hearers: “You ate, and you were not satisfied.” For they eat and are not satisfied who taste the bread of God’s word by hearing it, but, because they do not do what they hear, receive none of its inner sweetness within the belly of memory, by which their hearts might be strengthened.

“And they gathered up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets.” What remained after the crowds had been satisfied the apostles gathered up and filled seven baskets, because there are higher commandments of perfection—or rather, exhortations and counsels—which the general multitude of the faithful cannot attain by observing and fulfilling them. Their execution properly belongs to those who, filled with a greater grace of the Holy Spirit, surpass the general conversion of God’s people in loftiness of mind and deed. To such people it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have” (Matt. XIX), and so forth.

Hence the baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food were stored are rightly said to have been seven, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Since baskets are customarily woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are suitably employed as a symbol of the saints. The rush, indeed, commonly grows upon the waters, while the palm adorns the victorious hand. The elect are rightly compared with vessels of rushes when they place the root of their heart at the very source of life, lest it dry up through lack of love for eternity. They are also likened to things woven from palm leaves when they retain in a pure heart the memory of the unfailing eternal reward.

[Col. 0208C] And it is rightly related that although the crowd could not contain the remnants of the Lord’s meal, it nevertheless ate and was satisfied. For there are some who, although they cannot leave all their possessions behind or fulfill what is said concerning virgins—“Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX)—and other things of this kind, are nevertheless satisfied when they hunger and thirst for righteousness, since, by hearing the commandments of God’s Law, they reach eternal life.

“Now those who had eaten were about four thousand, and he sent them away.” The number four thousand is fitting, so that by that number itself they might be shown to have been fed with evangelical food.

“And immediately, going up into a boat with his disciples, he came into the region of Dalmanutha.” For this we read in Matthew: “And having sent the crowd away, he went up into the boat and came into the region of Magedan” (Matt. XV). There is no doubt that the same place is meant under both names. For many manuscripts, even according to Mark, have only “Magedan.”

“And the Pharisees went out and began to dispute with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, testing him.” They seek a sign as though the things they had seen had not been signs. But what they seek is shown when it says: “Seeking from him a sign from heaven.” Either they desired fire to come down from above, after the manner of Elijah, or, in the likeness of Samuel, thunder to roar, lightning to flash, and rains to pour down in the summer, as though they could not slander even these things and say that they had occurred through hidden and varied disturbances of the air.

But you who slander what you see with your eyes, hold with your hand, and experience through its usefulness—what will you do with things that come from heaven? Certainly you will reply that the magicians in Egypt performed many signs from heaven. Or surely they seek a sign from heaven so that the one who had recently satisfied many thousands of people with a few loaves might now, following the example of Moses, send manna from heaven and scatter it everywhere, refreshing the entire people for a long time.

We read in the Gospel according to John that after the distribution of the loaves the crowds asked this of him, saying: “What sign, then, do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness” (John VI), as it is written: “He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (ibid.).

“And groaning in spirit, he said: ‘Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.’” The one who above was giving thanks because he would refresh the believing crowd with a heavenly gift now groans and is saddened at the foolish request of the unbelieving and testing Pharisees, because, bearing the true nature of a human being and the true affections of human nature, he rejoices over the salvation of human beings just as he grieves and groans over their errors.

Thus elsewhere, when many had been led to salvation through the preaching of the apostles, it is written of him: “At that hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones’” (Luke X). And when he was about to rebuke Judas’s crime, he was troubled in spirit, as John writes, and testified, saying: “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray me” (John XIII).

By saying, “If a sign will be given to this generation,” he signifies that none will be given, according to the psalm’s statement: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I should lie to David” (Ps. LXXXVIII)—that is, “I will not lie to David.” Finally, Saint Augustine, speaking about the agreement of the evangelists, testifies that Mark has it written thus: “And no sign will be given to it.” Therefore no sign will be given to that generation—that is, to those who test the Lord and resist his words. It will not be the kind of sign the testers were seeking, namely, one from heaven.

Nevertheless, he gave that generation many heavenly signs on earth. To the generation of those seeking the gift and desiring to behold the face of the God of Jacob, he displayed a sign from heaven when, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended into heaven; when, having sent the Spirit from above, he filled the primitive Church; and when, through the laying on of the apostles’ hands in Samaria, Caesarea, Ephesus, and many other cities and places, he supplied believing people with the grace of the Holy Spirit from heaven.

“And leaving them, he went up into the boat again and departed across the strait. And they had forgotten to take bread, and they had no more than one loaf with them in the boat.” Someone might ask and say: How did they have no bread, when, immediately after the seven baskets had been filled, they went up into the boat and came into the region of Magedan, where they heard, while sailing, that they ought to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees? But Scripture testifies that they had forgotten to take it with them.

That, as they were about to sail across the strait, they had forgotten to take provisions with them indicates how little care they had for the flesh in other matters, since the very necessity of refreshing the body—which is naturally present in all mortals—had slipped from their minds because of their attention to accompanying the Lord. The one loaf that they had with them in the boat mystically signifies the bread of life itself, namely, the Lord and Savior. Because they were always inwardly refreshed in their hearts by love for him, they cared less for earthly bread, by which the body is ordinarily nourished.

“And he commanded them, saying: ‘See and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.’” The leaven of the Pharisees is to place the decrees of the divine Law after human traditions, or certainly to preach the Law in words while attacking it by one’s deeds. Their leaven is to test the Lord and believe neither his teaching nor his works, but, by insulting him, to demand other things in which they ought to believe.

The leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, rashness in swearing oaths, religious pretense, and—what is the head and origin of every crime—hatred and persecution directed against Christ and against his precursor, the first herald of the heavenly kingdom. The Apostle, likewise forbidding both kinds of leaven, says: “Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. V).

“And they discussed among themselves, saying: ‘Because we have no bread.’ Knowing this, Jesus said to them: ‘Why are you discussing that you have no bread? Do you not yet know or understand? Do you still have your heart blinded? [Col. 0210C] Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets of fragments you gathered?’” and so forth.

Taking the occasion of the command by which the Savior had ordered them, saying, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod,” he teaches them what the five and seven loaves signify, and likewise the small fish, or the five thousand and four thousand who were fed in the wilderness. Although the magnitude of the signs is evident, something else is demonstrated by spiritual understanding.

For if the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees and the leaven of Herod signify not bodily bread but perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, why should the foods by which the people of God were nourished not signify true and complete doctrine? Marcion and Valentinus, and all heretics, possessed leaven of this kind, which must be avoided in every way. Leaven has this effect: when it is mixed with flour, what seemed small grows larger and draws the whole mass into its own character. So too, if heretical teaching casts even a small spark into your breast, a great flame will quickly grow and draw the whole possession of the human being toward itself. This is what the Apostle also speaks about: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. V).

“And they come to Bethsaida, and they bring a blind man to him, and they begged him to touch him.” All the illnesses healed by the Lord are signs of spiritual illnesses, by which the soul approaches eternal death through sin. [Col. 0211A] Just as the healing of the deaf and mute man by the Lord signifies the healing of minds that had known neither how to hear the word of God nor how to speak, and as the sweetness by which he commonly nourishes the hearts of those who love and seek him is represented shortly afterward in the feeding of the hungry crowd that had followed the Lord, so in this blind man, gradually healed by the Lord, the illumination of the hearts of fools who have wandered far from the way of truth is signified.

They begged him to touch him, knowing that the Lord’s touch could cleanse a leper and also illuminate a blind man. We touch the Lord when we cling to him with complete and sincere faith. We learn from the example of the woman who, with blessed boldness, touched the fringe of his garment that this touch is most salutary for us. The Lord touches us when he enlightens our mind through the breath of his Spirit and kindles us toward recognition of our own weakness and devotion to good action.

“And taking the blind man by the hand, he led him outside the village.” He took the blind man by the hand in order to strengthen him for the performance of good action, which, because of the long darkness of his heart, he had not known. He led him outside the village so that, separated from ordinary life, he might search more freely and earnestly in his heart for the will of his Creator, by which he might deserve to be enlightened. For whoever desires to see the light of eternity must always follow not the examples of the crowds but the guidance of his Redeemer.

“And spitting into his eyes and laying his hands upon him, he asked him whether he saw anything. And looking up, he said: ‘I see people like trees walking.’ Then again he laid his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see, and he was restored so that he saw everything clearly.”

The Lord heals this man gradually and not immediately, although he could have healed him at once with a single word if he had wished, in order to show the greatness of human blindness, which ordinarily reaches the light of divine vision step by step and through certain stages of progress; or so that he might give us frequent signs of his grace, by which he assists each increase of our perfection, enabling us to make progress in something and not fall away.

It has often been said that the spittle of the Lord’s mouth signifies the grace of his Spirit. No one doubts that the touch of his hands signifies the power of his help. For spittle proceeds from within, from the Lord’s head, whereas hands are members of the body placed on the outside. Therefore the Lord, spitting into the blind man’s eyes and laying his hands upon him so that he might see, wiped away the blindness of the human race both through the invisible gifts of divine mercy and through the outwardly displayed sacraments of the humanity he assumed.

At first, the man being healed saw people like walking trees: he perceived the form of bodies amid shadows, but, while his sight was still dim, he was unable to distinguish the outlines of their limbs. Such is how densely clustered trees appear to those looking from a distance, or how they sometimes appear in the light of night, so that it is not easy to discern whether what is seen is a tree or a human being.

For the first entrance of each person into virtue is, evidently, to observe the life and conduct of other people, so that whatever good he sees anywhere he may imitate, and whatever is evil he may avoid and detest. But whoever is so foolish and so weighed down by the darkness of a long period that he still does not know how to distinguish between good and evil, faith and faithlessness, sincere works of piety and the pretense of righteousness, sees people walking like trees, because he sees the deeds of the multitude without the light of discernment.

And what remains for such people except that divine condescension, which has granted them the ability to observe human conduct, should also grant the gift of discerning whose life among human beings ought especially to be followed and whose teaching ought to be heard? Hence it is appropriately said that, at the second laying on of his hands, the Lord restored to him the light by which he clearly saw everything.

For the one who was blind sees everything clearly when the person who has deserved to be inwardly illuminated has plainly learned how one must believe, how one must live, and what rewards are to be hoped for in the future on account of faith in the truth and the practice of righteousness.

“And he sent him to his house, saying: ‘Go to your house; and if you enter the village, tell no one.’” By commanding him to go to his house, he mystically admonishes all who are enlightened by the recognition of truth to return to their own heart, carefully consider how much has been given to them, and respond to the benefits conferred upon them with the fitting performance of good works. By ordering him, as he had ordered many others whom he healed, to conceal his healing in silence, he gives his followers an example: they should not seek the favor of the crowd for the things they do, but be content to please only the divine gaze, where the reward of their works remains.

[Col. 0212C] “And Jesus and his disciples went out into the villages of Caesarea Philippi.” This Philip is the brother of Herod, whom we mentioned above, tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. In honor of Tiberius Caesar he named Caesarea Philippi—which is now called Paneas—and it is in the province of Phoenicia. He imitated his father Herod, who in honor of Augustus Caesar named Caesarea, formerly called the Tower of Strato, and built Libyades beyond the Jordan after the name of his daughter.

This is the location of Caesarea Philippi, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon and has two sources, one called Jor and the other Dan; when mingled together, they form the name Jordan.

“And on the way he questioned his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say that I am?’ They answered him, saying: [Col. 0212D] ‘Some say John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.’”

The Lord, wishing to test the faith of the disciples, first fittingly asks the opinion of the people, lest their confession should appear to be based not on a tested recognition of the truth but on the opinion of the crowd, and lest they should seem to believe what they had discovered rather than, like Herod, to hesitate over what they had heard.

Hence, according to Matthew, he says to Peter when he confesses him as Christ: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. XVI)—that is, human teaching did not teach you the truth of faith. It is also fitting that those who give different opinions about the Lord are designated by the name “people.” For those who faithfully and piously recognize the truth of his power deserve to be called not human beings but gods. The Lord shows that the apostles were such by his second question. For it follows:

“Then he says to them: ‘But you—who do you say that I am?’” Observe, prudent reader, that from what follows and from the wording of the passage the apostles are called not human beings but gods. For after saying, “Who do people say that I am?” he added: “But you—who do you say that I am?” To those who, because they are human beings, hold human opinions: you, who are gods, whom do you consider me to be?

Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ.” Although the other apostles knew it, Peter answered before the others. He embraced everything, expressing both the nature and the name in which the fullness of virtues resides.

Are we also to debate the generation of God? Since Paul declared that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, and Peter thought that nothing more than Christ the Son of God should be confessed, we investigate when and how he was born, and how great he is, by contemplating human weakness. The end, therefore, of my faith is Christ; the end of my faith is the Son. I am not permitted to know the sequence of his generation, yet I must not fail to know the faith of his generation.

“And he sternly warned them not to tell anyone about him. And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and by the chief priests,” and so forth.

For this reason he did not wish to be proclaimed before his passion and resurrection, so that afterward, when the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he might more appropriately say to the apostles: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” For it would not have benefited him to be publicly proclaimed and his majesty spread among the peoples when shortly afterward they would see him scourged and crucified, suffering many things at the hands of the elders, scribes, and chief priests.

It should also be noted that he calls the one who must suffer many things, be killed, and rise again “the Son of Man,” because, while Christ suffered in the flesh, he remained impassible in his divinity.

“And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.” Matthew explains more clearly how he rebuked him, saying: “And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: ‘Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you’” (Matt. XVI).

We have often said that Peter possessed exceedingly great zeal and the greatest love for the Lord and Savior. After his confession, in which he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and after receiving the Savior’s reward, when, according to Matthew, he heard: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI), he suddenly hears from the Lord that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things there at the hands of the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day.

He does not want his confession destroyed, nor does he think it possible for the Son of God to be killed. He therefore takes him aside according to his own affection, or leads him away privately, lest he should appear to rebuke his teacher in the presence of his fellow disciples. He began to rebuke him out of loving affection, expressing his wish: “Far be it from you, Lord”; or, as it is better rendered in Greek, “Have mercy on yourself, Lord; this shall not happen.” That is: It cannot happen; my ears cannot accept that the Son of God is to be killed.

“When he had turned and seen his disciples, he rebuked Peter, saying: ‘Get behind me, Satan.’” Satan is interpreted as “adversary” or “opponent.” “Because,” he says, “you speak contrary to my will, you ought to be called an adversary.”

Many think that it was not Peter who was rebuked, but the adversarial spirit that was suggesting these words to the apostle. But to me, the apostolic error, arising from an affection of piety, will never appear to be an incentive of the devil. “Get behind me, Satan” is said to the devil: “Get behind me.” Peter hears: “Get behind me,” that is, “Follow my judgment.”

“For you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings.” It is my will, and that of the Father, whose will I came to do, that I should die for the salvation of human beings. You, considering only your own will, do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may bear much fruit.

“And calling the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,’” and so forth.

After revealing to the disciples the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he exhorts them, together with the crowd, to follow the example of his passion. He promises the future salvation of their souls to all who suffer tribulation for his sake; but he disclosed how much he himself would suffer and that he would rise from the dead not to all, but to the more perfect.

Here he established a model of teaching for ministers of the word, so that, considering the capacity of their hearers, they may remember to instruct each person according to that person’s measure, and not entrust higher mysteries to weak hearers than they are able to grasp.

“If anyone,” he says, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through oldness and strive toward that to which we are called through newness. Let us consider how Paul had denied himself when he said: “I live, yet it is no longer I” (Gal. II). That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live. For if he were still himself, he certainly would not be devout.

But if he denies that he lives, let him say from where it comes that he cries out holy words through the teaching of truth. He immediately adds: “But Christ lives in me” (ibid.). It is as though he plainly said: I have indeed been extinguished with respect to myself, because I do not live according to the flesh; yet I have not died in substance, since I live spiritually in Christ.

Let Truth therefore speak; let it speak: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For unless someone abandons himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him. Nor can he grasp what lies beyond himself if he does not know how to put to death what he is.

But once someone has denied himself with respect to vices, he must seek the virtues in which he may grow. For when it was said, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” it is immediately added:

“And let him take up his cross and follow me.” The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the spirit is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor.

Let us consider how Paul carried his cross in both ways. He said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. IX). Here we have heard of the cross of the flesh in the affliction of the body; now let us hear of the cross of the mind in compassion for one’s neighbor. He says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. XI).

The perfect preacher carried the cross in his body in order to provide an example of abstinence. And because he drew into himself the losses caused by another’s weakness, he carried the cross in his heart.

“For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it. But whoever loses his soul for my sake and for the Gospel will save it.” Thus it is said to the faithful: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it. But whoever loses his soul for my sake and for the Gospel will save it.” It is as though one were saying to a farmer: “If you preserve the grain, you destroy it; if you sow it, you renew it.” For who does not know that when grain is placed in the seed, it disappears from sight and perishes in the earth? Yet from the place where it rots in the dust, it grows green again in renewal.

Because the holy Church has one period of persecution and another of peace, our Redeemer indicated these periods in his commandments. In a time of persecution, the soul must be surrendered. In a time of peace, earthly desires that are able to dominate us more powerfully must be broken. Hence it is now said:

“For what will it profit a person if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a person give in exchange for his soul?”

When persecution from adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with far greater vigilance. For in a time of peace, since it is permitted to live, it is also permitted to pursue honors. Often we overcome greed as well, but what still obstructs us is that we hold to the ways of righteousness with too little vigilance, and therefore fall short of perfection.

For often we despise all possessions, yet we are still hindered by the habit of human shame, so that we are not yet able to express in our voice the righteousness we preserve in our mind. And we neglect the face of God in defense of righteousness to the same degree that we fear human faces when they stand against righteousness.

But an appropriate remedy for this wound, too, is added when the Lord says:

For whoever confesses me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also confess him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

But behold, people now say to themselves: “We are no longer ashamed of the Lord and his words, because we confess him openly.” To these I reply that among this Christian people there are some who confess Christ for no other reason than that they see everyone else being Christians. Therefore the voice of profession is not sufficient as proof of faith when a general profession shields it from shame. Yet each person should question himself, so as to prove whether he truly confesses Christ: whether he is no longer ashamed of his name, and whether he has fully subjected human embarrassment to the strength of his mind.

Certainly, in a time of persecution the faithful could be ashamed to be stripped of their possessions, cast down from their dignities, and afflicted with beatings. In a time of peace, however, since these things are absent from the persecutions we face, there is another situation in which we are exposed to ourselves. We are often afraid of being despised by those closest to us, and disdain enduring verbal insults. If an argument happens to arise with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make amends. For the carnal heart, while it seeks the glory of this life, rejects humility.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0215]

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0215C]

“And he was saying to them: ‘Amen I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until, etc.’”

In this passage the present Church is called the kingdom of God. Since some of the disciples were destined to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God established and raised up against the glory of this world, he now says, by way of a consoling promise: “There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power.”

But when the Lord was giving such extensive commands concerning the death he would have to undergo, why was it necessary for him suddenly to turn to this promise? If we attend to the matter carefully, we will recognize with what gracious providence it was arranged. Something concerning the present life had to be promised even to the disciples in their immaturity, so that they might be strengthened more firmly for the future life. Thus, when the Israelite people were being liberated from the land of Egypt, the land of promise was promised to them, so that, when they were to be called to heavenly gifts, they might be persuaded by earthly promises. Hence the Psalmist rightly says:

“He gave them the territories of the nations,  
and they possessed the labors of the peoples,  
so that they might keep his ordinances  
and seek his law” (Psalm 104).

Thus, in this passage, Truth speaks to the immature disciples and promises that they will see the kingdom of God on earth, so that they may presume upon it more faithfully in heaven. If, however, we wish to understand the kingdom of God in this saying as the future blessedness of heaven, some of those standing there saw it on the mountain a few days later. This was certainly done by a merciful providence, so that, through contemplation of the joy that always remains—even though they tasted it only briefly and for a moment—they might endure more steadfastly the adversities of the passing age.

With a most fitting expression, therefore, he testifies that the saints “taste” death, since they taste the death of the body, as it were by sampling it, while they truly possess the life of the soul.

“And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John and led them up a high mountain, apart, by themselves; and he was transfigured before them.”

In the Gospel of Luke it is written:

“Now it happened, after these words, about eight days later, that he took Peter, James, and John and went up the mountain to pray” (Luke 9).

And so forth. On the eighth day the Lord reveals to the disciples the glory of the blessedness he has promised, so that, by displaying the sweetness of heavenly life, he may refresh the hearts of all who can hear these things, and by the number eight teach that the joy of the true resurrection is to come.

For on the eighth day itself—that is, after the sixth day of the Sabbath, when he ascended the cross, and the seventh day of the Sabbath, when he rested in the tomb—he rose from the dead. Likewise, after the six ages of this world, during which we rejoice to suffer and labor for the Lord, and after the seventh age of souls, which meanwhile is lived out in the other life, we will certainly rise in the eighth age.

Matthew and Mark say that the Lord was transfigured after six days. This does not differ from Luke either in chronological order or in the meaning of the mystery, though Luke speaks of eight days, because the former mention only the intervening days; hence they simply record that it happened after six days. Luke adds both the first day on which the Lord made this promise and the last day on which he fulfilled his promise. For that reason he more moderately says, “about eight days.”

In the mystical interpretation, there the saints are to rest from all labor after the six ages of the world, while here the eighth time signifies that they are to rise. Hence, beautifully, the sixth psalm is entitled “For the Eighth,” and it begins: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” For throughout the six ages in which it is permitted to work, we must persist in prayers, lest in the eighth age of retribution we be rebuked by an angry Judge.

The Lord also wished to teach us this in the present passage by showing the example of his prayer. Of him Luke says that “he went up the mountain to pray.” He went up the mountain to pray and was transfigured there, showing that those who await the fruit of the resurrection and desire to see the King in his beauty must dwell in the heights of their minds and devote themselves to continual prayers.

He takes only three disciples with him, either because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20), or because those who now preserve with an undivided mind the faith with which they have been imbued—the faith of the holy Trinity—will then deserve to rejoice in its eternal vision.

“And he was transfigured,” he says, “before them, and his garments became shining, exceedingly white, like snow.”

The transfigured Savior did not lose the substance of true flesh; rather, he displayed the glory of the future resurrection, whether his own or ours. As he then appeared to the apostles, so he will appear after the judgment to all the elect. At the very time of judgment he will be seen by good and wicked alike in the form of a servant, so that the impious may recognize the one they despised, the Jews the one they denied, the soldiers the one they crucified, and Pilate and Herod the one they judged.

The Lord’s garments are rightly understood as his saints, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3). These garments, while the Lord remained on earth, appeared contemptible and like those of everyone else; but when he ascends the mountain, they shine with a new brightness, because “we are now children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Thus it is rightly added concerning these same garments: “Such as no fuller on earth can make white.” The fuller to be understood here is the one whom the repentant Psalmist entreats:

“Wash me more fully from my iniquity,  
and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 50).

For he cannot give his faithful on earth the brightness that awaits them, preserved for them in heaven.

“And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus.”

Moses and Elijah—one of whom we read died, while the other was taken up into heaven—appeared with the Lord in glory, as Luke writes, signifying the future glory of all the saints in him. At the time of judgment they will either be found alive in the flesh, or, having once tasted death, be raised, and together reign with him.

The Apostle bears witness:

“The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4).

Alternatively: Moses and Elijah—that is, the lawgiver and the foremost of the prophets—appear and speak with the Lord as he comes in the flesh, to show that he is the one whom all the oracles of the Law and the Prophets promised.

They appear with him not in low places but on the mountain, because only those who in their minds transcend earthly desires perceive the majesty of Holy Scripture fulfilled in the Lord. The children of Israel saw Moses, but they were not worthy to follow him when he climbed into the mountain toward God; and when he returned to them, they saw him only with a veil. They knew Elijah, but only Elisha, together with the sons of the prophets, contemplated the triumph of the one ascending.

Many of us read the words of Scripture here and there, but very few of the more perfect understand how lofty it shines in the mysteries of Christ.

“And Peter answered and said: ‘Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’ For he did not know what he was saying, since they were terrified by fear.”

O what great happiness it is to be perpetually present amid the choirs of angels in the vision of the Godhead, if the sight of Christ’s humanity transfigured, together with the company of two saints, gives such delight even when seen only for an instant that Peter wishes to detain them by his service so that they will not depart! Though, in the astonishment of human weakness, he does not know what he is saying, he nevertheless reveals the affection implanted within him.

He did not know what he was saying because he had forgotten that the Lord promised the saints the kingdom of God not somewhere on earth but in heaven. Nor did he remember that he and his fellow apostles, still enclosed in mortal flesh, could not yet enter the state of immortal life, which his mind had transcended; nor that in the Father’s house, which is in heaven, there is necessarily no house made by human hands.

Even to this day, anyone who wishes to make three tabernacles for the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels is marked by ignorance, since these cannot in any way be separated from one another: they have one tabernacle, namely, the Church of God.

“And a cloud came, overshadowing them.”

The one who sought a material tabernacle received the shadowing of a cloud, so that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this the Psalmist says:

“But the children of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Psalm 35).

And John says in his Apocalypse:

“And I saw no temple in it” (Revelation 21); “the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb.”

“And a voice came from the cloud, saying: ‘This is my most beloved Son; listen to him.’”

Because they had asked imprudently, they did not deserve a response from the Lord; but the Father answers on behalf of the Son, so that the Lord’s word might be fulfilled:

“I do not bear witness concerning myself, but the Father who sent me himself bears witness concerning me” (John 5).

A voice from heaven is also heard—the voice of the Father speaking—to bear witness concerning the Son and, once Peter’s error has been removed, to teach the truth, or rather, through Peter, to teach the other apostles as well.

“This,” he says, “is my most beloved Son. For him the tabernacle must be fixed; he must be obeyed. He is the Son; Moses and Elijah are servants. They too, together with you, must prepare a tabernacle for the Lord in the innermost chambers of their hearts.”

This passage of the Gospel agrees with the words of Moses, who, bearing witness to the Lord’s incarnation, said:

“The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me, in accordance with everything he says to you. But every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people” (Deuteronomy 18).

The one whom Moses foretold would come in the flesh and must be heard by every soul wishing to be saved, God the Father now points out to the disciples as the one who has come in the flesh and marks him as his Son with a heavenly voice.

And as though making the faith of his coming clearer to them, he says: “This man—this is the one whom Moses here promised to you would be born into the world so many times. In accordance with Moses’ own command, listen to his words, and command all true lovers of him to listen.”

It should also be noted that, just as when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, so when he was glorified on the mountain, the mystery of the entire holy Trinity is revealed. For the glory that we confess in faith at baptism, we will praise together when we see it in the resurrection.

Nor is it without reason that the Holy Spirit appeared here in a bright cloud, as another evangelist records, while there he appeared in a dove. For the one who now preserves with a simple heart the faith he has received will then contemplate in the clear light of vision what he had believed, and will be protected forever by the very grace by which he is illumined.

“And immediately, looking around, they saw no one any longer except Jesus alone with them.”

When the Son began to be designated, the servants immediately departed, lest anyone think that the Father’s voice had been directed toward them. Alternatively, when the voice was made concerning the Son, he alone was found, because when he reveals himself to the elect, God will be “all in all.” Indeed, Christ himself, together with his own, will shine as one in every respect—that is, the head together with the body.

For the sake of this unity he said elsewhere:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

“And as they were coming down from the mountain, he commanded them not to tell anyone what they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead.”

The foretaste of the coming kingdom and the glory of the triumphant one had been displayed on the mountain. He therefore does not want this proclaimed among the people, lest, on account of the greatness of the event, it seem unbelievable, and lest, after such glory, the cross that followed should cause scandal in their minds.

“And they questioned him, saying: ‘Why then do the Pharisees and scribes say that Elijah must come first?’”

It is the tradition of the Pharisees, based on the prophet Malachi, the last of the Twelve, that Elijah will come before the Savior’s arrival, turn the heart of the fathers toward the children and the heart of the children toward their fathers, and restore everything to its former state.

The disciples therefore think that the transformation of glory is what they had seen on the mountain, and they say: “If you have already come in glory, how is it that your forerunner has not appeared?” Especially since they had seen Elijah depart.

When they add “the scribes,” saying, “that Elijah must come first,” by saying “first” they show that unless Elijah has come, the Savior’s second coming has not occurred.

“He answered and said to them: ‘Elijah, when he comes, will first restore everything.’”

He will restore everything—namely, those things which the prophet mentioned beforehand when he said:

“Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the heart of the fathers toward the children, and the heart of the children toward their fathers” (Malachi 4).

He will also restore what is owed to death, which he has postponed by living for a long time. The Lord also intimated this here when he immediately added:

“And how is it written concerning the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be despised?”

That is: just as the prophets wrote many things in various ways about Christ’s passion, so Elijah, when he comes, will suffer many things and be despised by the wicked.

He will therefore restore everything: first, the hearts of the people of that age, instructing them to believe in Christ and resist the faithlessness of the Antichrist; then he will lay down his own soul through the martyrdom of faith in Christ. This is narrated more fully in the Apocalypse in mystical language.

“But I say to you that Elijah has also come, and they did to him whatever they wished, as it is written concerning him.”

The one who is to come at the Savior’s second advent according to the reality of the body has now come in John, in power and spirit. “They did to him whatever they wished”—that is, they despised him and beheaded him.

“And coming to his disciples, he saw a great crowd around them, and scribes disputing with them. And immediately, when all the people saw him, they were astonished and terrified. And running up, they greeted him.”

The difference between the disposition of the scribes and that of the crowd should be noted in every passage. The crowd was with the disciples, and the scribes were there as well; but when the Lord arrived, the whole crowd was immediately astonished and terrified, and ran to greet him. The scribes, however, are not said to have shown him any devotion, faith, humility, or reverence.

The evangelist does not say what the crowd or the scribes were disputing with the Lord’s disciples about. But, unless I am mistaken, it can appropriately be understood that the question concerned why the disciples, since they were the Savior’s disciples, could not save the demoniac who had been placed among them. This may be inferred from the words that follow in the Gospel:

“And he asked them: ‘What are you disputing about among yourselves?’ And one of the crowd answered: ‘Teacher, I brought my son to you; he has a mute spirit. Wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams, gnashes his teeth, and wastes away. And I told your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.’”

It should be observed that places always correspond to events. On the mountain the Lord prays, is transfigured, and opens to his disciples the secrets of his majesty. Descending to the lower places, he is met by the crowd and pressed by the weeping of the wretched. Above, he discloses the mysteries of the kingdom to his disciples; below, he reproaches the crowds for the sins of their unbelief. Above, he reveals the Father’s voice to those who were able to follow him; below, he drives evil spirits from those who were afflicted.

Even now, according to the quality of people’s merits, he does not cease either to ascend for some or to descend for others. For those who are still carnal and beginners, he strengthens, teaches, and chastises them, as though seeking the lowest places. But those whose way of life is in heaven he glorifies by lifting them higher, instructs them more freely concerning eternal things, and often teaches them what the crowds cannot even hear.

Mark records that this demoniac, whom the Lord healed as he came down from the mountain, was deaf and mute; Matthew records that he was a lunatic. He signifies those of whom it is written: “The fool is changed like the moon.” They never remain in the same state; changed now toward these vices, now toward those, they wax and wane.

They are mute because they do not confess the faith; deaf because they do not listen in any way even to the word of truth. They foam when they waste away in folly. For it belongs to fools, the sick, and the dull-witted to discharge saliva as foam from their mouths. They gnash their teeth when they burn with the fury of anger.
