They waste away when they grow languid through sluggish idleness and, strengthened by no energetic pursuit of virtue, live feebly.

When he says, “And I told your disciples to cast it out, but they could not,” he covertly accuses the apostles, since the inability to heal sometimes refers not to the weakness of those who heal but to the faith of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matthew 2).

“He answered them and said: ‘O unbelieving generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I endure you?’”

This does not mean that he had been overcome by weariness. He was gentle and meek; he did not open his mouth like a lamb before its shearer, nor did he break out into words of anger. Rather, he spoke in the manner of a physician who, seeing a sick person act against his instructions, might say: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste the skill of my art, when I command one thing and you do another?”

He was not angry with the person but with the vice. And he reproved the Jews for their unbelief through one man, so that he immediately added:

“Bring him to me.” And they brought him.

“And when he saw him, immediately the spirit convulsed him; and thrown to the ground, he rolled about foaming.”

When the boy was brought to the Lord, the spirit convulsed and threw him down, because often, when we try to turn to the Lord after our sins, we are assaulted by greater and new forms of the ancient enemy’s ambushes. The crafty adversary does this either to instill hatred of virtue or to avenge the injury of his expulsion.

This is why—moving from the particular to the general—he used to inflict so many grievous struggles of persecution upon the beginnings of the holy Church: he grieved that the loss of souls had suddenly been brought into his kingdom.

“And he asked his father: ‘How long has it been since this happened to him?’ He said: ‘From childhood. And often he has thrown him into fire and into water, to destroy him.’”

Let Julian be ashamed, since he dares to say that all human beings are born in the flesh without any contamination of sin, and are altogether as innocent as Adam was when he was created. For what did this boy possess that he should have been afflicted by a most cruel demon from childhood, if he was not held by any bond of original sin, when it is clear that he could not yet have possessed any personal sin?

Let the Catholic confess that no one is born free from the guilt of the first transgression, and let him invoke the grace of God, by which he may be delivered from the body of death through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Let the learned scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven understand that in this demoniac healed by the Lord the salvation of all the faithful is signified: they come into the world bound by the guilt of original sin and are saved only through the faith and grace of the one Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

When it is said, “And often he has thrown him into fire and into water,” the greatest crimes of human madness are signified. The heat of fire should be referred to the fervor of anger; water to the pleasures of the flesh, which commonly dissolve the mind through sensual delights.

Or certainly the demoniac is thrown into the fire with which the hearts of adulterers are inflamed, and into the waters that customarily extinguish charity.

“But if you can do anything, help us and have mercy on us.”

Jesus said to him: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.”

The Lord gives an answer suited to the petitioner. The man himself had said: “If you can do anything, help us.” And the Lord replies: “If you can believe, I can help you by having mercy, because an unfabricated faith deserves to obtain everything it asks for beneficially.”

By contrast, the leper who cried out faithfully, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Luke 5), received an answer suited to his faith: “I will; be cleansed” (ibid.).

“And immediately the boy’s father cried out with tears and said: ‘I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.’”

No one suddenly becomes perfect. In a good way of life, each person begins with small things in order to reach great ones. For the beginnings of virtue are one thing, progress another, and perfection another.

If faith itself were not led to its perfection by certain steps, this man, when asked whether he believed, would not have answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe?

Yet because, through the hidden inspiration of grace, faith grows according to the stages of its merits, at one and the same time the man who had not yet believed perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

“And when Jesus saw the crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: ‘Deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him, and do not enter him again.’”

The Lord’s rebuke is the power of divine authority. He did not rebuke the boy, who was suffering the violence, but the demon who inflicted it. Whoever desires to correct a sinner must certainly exterminate the vice by reproving and condemning it, while restoring the person through love.

The Lord rightly commands that the unclean spirit, once driven from the man, should not enter him again. For the person is truly freed from demonic domination who avoids returning through evil living to the sins from which he was once cleansed by repentance.

“And crying out and violently convulsing him, it came out of him.”

As the unclean spirit was coming out of the man, it convulsed him and terrified those watching with a furious cry. For often, when the devil is expelled from the heart, he produces temptations in it more severe than those he had previously stirred up when he possessed it quietly.

“And he became like a dead man, so that many said, ‘He is dead.’ But Jesus, taking him by the hand, raised him, and he arose.”

The impious enemy, compelled to flee, had already thrown him down and made him resemble a dead man. The merciful Savior raised him by the gentle touch of his right hand. Just as he showed himself to be truly God through the power of saving, so he also demonstrated through human touch that he truly possessed the nature of flesh.

For the madman Manichaeus denies that Christ was truly clothed in flesh. But Christ himself, by his touch, raised, cleansed, and enlightened so many who were suffering; and before Manichaeus’s heresy was even born, he condemned it.

“And when he had entered the house, his disciples questioned him privately: ‘Why could we not cast it out?’ And he said to them: ‘This kind can come out by nothing except prayer and fasting.’”

While teaching the apostles how the most wicked demon must be expelled, he instructs everyone in the way of life, so that we may know that the gravest temptations, whether of unclean spirits or of human beings, must be overcome by fasts and prayers.

The Lord’s anger also, when it has been kindled in punishment for our crimes, can be appeased by this singular remedy. Fasting, in general, means abstaining not only from food but also from every carnal allurements—indeed, restraining oneself from every passion of vice.

Prayer, likewise, in its general sense consists not only in the words by which we invoke divine mercy, but also in everything we do in the devoted faith of service to our Creator, as the Apostle bears witness:

“Always rejoice; pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5).

For how can anyone invoke God with words at every hour and moment without ceasing? We pray without ceasing when we perform only those works that commend us to the devotion of our Author.

By this fasting and this prayer, with the Lord’s help, we will conquer and drive away all the ambushes of the ancient enemy.

## CHAPTER IX

“And setting out from there, they passed through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know. He was teaching his disciples and saying to them: ‘The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And after he has been killed, he will rise on the third day.’”

He always mixes sad things with prosperous ones, so that when the sad things suddenly arrive they will not terrify the apostles, but will meet minds already prepared. For if the fact that he is to be killed saddens them, the fact that he will rise on the third day ought to make them rejoice.

“But they did not understand this saying, and they were afraid to question him.”

This ignorance of the disciples arose not so much from slowness of understanding as from their love for the Savior. They were still carnal and ignorant of the mystery of the cross; they could not believe that the true God whom they had recognized would die.

And because they were accustomed to hearing him speak in figures, they were horrified by the prospect of his death and wanted even in the things he spoke openly about his betrayal and passion for some other figurative meaning to be intended.

“And they came to Capernaum. When they were in the house, he questioned them: ‘What were you discussing on the way?’ But they were silent.”

For on the way they had argued among themselves about which of them was the greater. Their dispute about primacy seems to have arisen because they had seen Peter, James, and John led apart onto the mountain and believed that some secret had been entrusted to them there.

Moreover, as Matthew relates above, the keys of the kingdom of heaven had been promised to Peter, and the Lord’s Church was to be built upon the rock of the faith from which Peter himself had received his name. They were therefore disputing either that those three were preferred to the others, or that Peter was preferred to all the apostles.

[Col. 0224C]

“And he sat down, called the Twelve, and said to them: ‘If anyone wishes to be first among you, he will be last of all and servant of all.’ And taking a child, he placed him in their midst. Having embraced him, he said to them: ‘Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me.’”

Seeing the disciples’ thoughts, the Lord cures their desire for glory by healing it through a contest of humility. He teaches that primacy is not to be sought: first by a simple command concerning humility, and then by the example of a child’s innocence.

When he says, “Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me,” he either shows that the poor of Christ are to be received, for his honor, by those who wish to be great, or he certainly urges that they themselves should be little in wickedness, so that, in imitation of a child’s age, they may preserve simplicity without arrogance, charity without envy, and devotion without anger.

By embracing the child, he signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace and love. When such people fulfill what he commands—“Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11)—they may rightly glory and say:

“His left hand is under my head,  
and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs 2).

When he had said, “Whoever receives one of these children,” he rightly added, “in my name,” so that they might follow, for Christ’s name, with the help of rational discipline, the form of virtue that a child observes under the guidance of nature.

But because he was teaching that he himself is received in children—namely, as the head in his members—lest anyone think that this was all that was meant, he added:

“And whoever receives me does not receive me, but the one who sent me.”

He wishes himself to be believed to be such and so great as the Father is. Indeed, he says, there is so little difference between me and him that whoever receives me receives the one who sent me as well.

“John answered him, saying: ‘Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and he does not follow us, and we forbade him.’”

John, loving the Lord with exceptional devotion and therefore worthy of being loved in return, thought that the man who did not exercise the office should be excluded from the benefit. But he is taught that no one is to be kept away from the good he possesses in part; rather, he should be urged toward what he does not yet have.

For it follows:

“But Jesus said: ‘Do not forbid him. For there is no one who performs a mighty deed in my name and can soon speak evil of me. For whoever is not against you is for you.’”

Instructed by this saying, the Apostle says:

“Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and I will also rejoice” (Philippians 1).

Although he rejoices even over those who proclaim Christ insincerely, and although such people, at times performing signs in Christ’s name for the salvation of others, are judged not to be prohibited, their own conscience is not thereby made secure through such signs. Rather, on that day, when they say:

“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” (Matthew 7),

they will receive the answer:

“I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (ibid.).

Therefore, in heretics and wicked Catholics we must detest and forbid not the sacraments they share with us, by which they are not against us, but the divisions contrary to the peace of the truth, by which they are against us and do not follow the Lord together with us.

“For whoever gives you a cup of cold water in my name, because you are Christ’s, amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Psalm 140).

We read in the prophet David:

“Making excuses for sins,”

because many sinners put forward what seemed to be justifications for their sins, so that although they transgressed by their will, they might appear to sin by necessity.

The Lord, who searches the heart and kidneys and observes the future thoughts of each person, had said: “Whoever receives one little child in my name receives me.” Someone could make an excuse and say: “Poverty prevents me; my lack keeps me from being hospitable.”

He dissolves this excuse by the lightest command, so that we may offer a cup of water—and, according to Matthew, cold water—with our whole heart. He says “cold water,” not hot water, lest someone seek an excuse in the need for fuel amid poverty and want.

The Apostle likewise commands something of this kind to the Galatians:

“Let the one who is catechized share all good things with the one who catechizes him” (Galatians 6).

He urges disciples to provide refreshment for their teachers. And because anyone could plead poverty and evade the command, he resolves the impending question before proposing it, saying:

“Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (ibid.).

And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. Although this may be understood as a general statement against all who cause anyone to stumble, nevertheless, in keeping with the sequence of the discourse, it can also be understood as spoken against the apostles, who, while arguing among themselves about which of them was the greater, seemed to be contending with one another over rank. If they had persisted in this fault, they could have destroyed by their scandal those whom they were calling to the faith, when these people saw the apostles fighting among themselves for honor.

[Col. 0226B]

When he said, “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck,” he spoke according to the custom of the region, by which, among the ancient Jews, the punishment for greater crimes was that the condemned were thrown into the depths with a stone fastened to them. And truly, it is better for an innocent person to end bodily life through a temporal punishment, however atrocious, than, by injuring a brother, to merit the perpetual death of the soul.

Properly, the one who can be caused to stumble is called “little.” For whoever is great does not depart from the faith, whatever he may see or suffer. But whoever is small and little in spirit looks for opportunities to be scandalized. Therefore, we ought especially to take care of those who are little in faith, lest they be offended by something on our account, withdraw from the faith, and fall away from salvation.

It should certainly be noted that, in our good works, we must sometimes guard against causing our neighbor to stumble, but at other times disregard it as nothing. Insofar as we can avoid causing our neighbors to stumble without sin, we ought to do so. But if scandal arises from the truth, it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.

[Col. 0226C]

Likewise, by the millstone is expressed the cycle and labor of secular life, and by the depth of the sea is signified final condemnation. Therefore, if someone who has been led to the appearance of holiness destroys others either by word or by example, it would certainly have been better for him to have been bound to death under the outward appearance of earthly affairs than to display sacred offices in guilt as something others might imitate. For if he fell alone, even though the punishment of hell would torment him, it would nevertheless be more bearable.

And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. [Col. 0226D] It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire. Since above he had taught us not to cause those who believe in him to stumble, he now consequently warns us how greatly we must beware of those who strive to cause us to stumble—that is, to drive us toward the ruin of sin by their word or example.

He calls our hand a necessary friend, whose work and assistance we need daily. But if such a person wishes to injure us in the matter of the soul, he must be excluded from our fellowship, lest, if we wish to share in this life with one who is lost, we perish with him in the life to come. What follows is:

“Where their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.” By the worm he signifies the corruption of Gehenna, just as by the fire [Col. 0227A] he signifies its burning; or by “worm” he means the delayed repentance for crimes, which will never cease to gnaw the conscience of those afflicted in the torments, so that the fire is the punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is the pain accusing inwardly.

And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into the Gehenna of unquenchable fire, and so forth. In the foot, as also in the hand, he teaches that beloved but incorrigible people must be separated from us, lest, through the impurity of those whom we cannot correct, we ourselves also become defiled and perish. But “hands” are so called because of the necessary work they perform for us; “feet,” because of the service and movement suited to our needs.

[Col. 0227B]

And if your eye causes you to stumble, cast it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna. In the eye also, which must be plucked out because of the scandal, are signified the same people who are our friends according to the flesh but adversaries according to the spirit. Yet when we need their counsel and provision, while they seek to deceive us by evil advice and turn us aside onto the path of error, we must wholly abandon their company. For “scandal” is a Greek word; we may call it an offense, or a ruin caused by a tripped foot. Some call it *scandalum* (Greek *skandalon*) in Greek, and *scrupulum* in Latin. Thus, the one who causes his brother to stumble is the one who gives him an occasion for ruin through a less-than-upright word or deed.

[Col. 0227C]

It may also be understood simply in this way: If someone seems so necessary to us as a hand, foot, or eye—useful, attentive, and sharp in perception—but causes us to stumble and, through a disharmony of conduct, drags us into Gehenna, then even so we must not use or enjoy his temporal advantages at the risk of our souls.

Since the Lord mentioned the eternal worm and fire three times, it remains to explain how we can avoid the torment of the worm’s stench and of the fire. It follows:

“For everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted with salt.” The stench of worms usually arises from the corruption of flesh and blood. Therefore fresh meat is seasoned with salt, so that, once its bloody moisture has been dried out, worms cannot breed in it. Flesh and blood therefore create worms, because carnal pleasure, which is not resisted by the seasoning of self-restraint, generates eternal punishment for the lustful. [Col. 0227D] Whoever desires to avoid its stench should strive to restrain his body with the salt of self-restraint and his mind with the seasoning of wisdom, keeping them from the pollution of error and vices.

It is wonderfully said: “Everyone will be salted with fire.” What is salted with salt keeps away the decay caused by worms. But what is salted with fire—that is, seasoned by fires sprinkled with salt—not only drives far away every contagion of worms, but also consumes the very flesh that is salted in this way. The ordinances of the divine law declare that this was customarily done with the offerings burned on the altar, where salt was commanded to be offered with every victim and sacrifice.

Salt therefore signifies the sweetness of wisdom, and fire the grace of the Holy Spirit. “Everyone will be salted with fire,” because every elect person must be cleansed by spiritual wisdom from the corruption of carnal desire, so that he may become a sacrifice fit for the divine altars. [Col. 0228A]

Hence, after saying, “Everyone will be salted with fire,” he rightly added, “And every sacrifice will be salted with salt.” For that person truly exists as the Lord’s sacrifice who, cleansing his body and soul from vices through the love of the Holy Spirit, consecrates himself to God.

Such a sacrifice is not only sprinkled with salt but also consumed by fire, when not only the contagion of sin is driven away, but even the pleasure of the present life that exists in the flesh is removed from the minds of the elect, and they sigh with focused desire for the conduct of the future life. Was not that person a victim seasoned with sacred fire who said, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III)? Hence, “we also await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (ibid.).

[Col. 0228B]

Those who, with the most certain hope of future immortality, regarded the body of their frailty as though it had already been reformed in the likeness of the Lord’s resurrection lived even in the present as a sacrifice consecrated to God by spiritual fire, in accordance with the same apostle’s words: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XV).

We may also rightly understand the saying, “Everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted with salt” (Marc. IX), in this way: the altar of God is the heart of the elect, while the sacrifices to be offered upon this altar are the good works of the faithful. Salt must be offered in all sacrifices, because there is no good work that is not cleansed by the salt of wisdom from every corruption of vain praise and from other evil or superfluous thoughts. [Col. 0228C] For the discipline of self-restraint chastises carnal allurements.

The fire that consumes sacrifices on the altar is certainly the fire of which John says, “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (ibid. III). Through it our good works are assisted, so that they may either be begun or brought to completion; or else it is the fire of tribulation by which the patience of the faithful is exercised, so that they may possess a perfected work.

Everyone, therefore, will be salted with fire, and the sacrifice will be salted with salt (ibid. IX), because every faithful person who wishes to avoid the worm of eternal torment must be chastised either by the fire of spiritual grace or by external tribulations that befall him, so that he may become a sacrifice worthy of God.

This passage refers back to what was said above, where the offending members were commanded to be torn away. For this too is to be salted with fire—that is, to be exercised by temptations: to deny, for the love of Christ, those who are near and dear to us.

[Col. 0228D]

“Salt is good. But if the salt has become tasteless, with what will you season it?” It is good to hear the word of God frequently, to season the hidden places of the heart with the salt of spiritual wisdom, and, indeed, to become with the apostles the salt of the earth itself—that is, to be sufficient for instructing the minds even of those who still savor earthly things.

But if someone, once refreshed by the seasoning of truth, returns to apostasy, by what other teacher can he be corrected—someone who rejects the sweetness of wisdom that he himself has tasted, whether frightened away by the world or enticed by its prosperity? To him aptly applies the saying of the wise man: “Who will heal an enchanter bitten by a serpent?”

By this statement, it is reasonably believed that Judas Iscariot’s associates and Judas himself are specially indicated, [Col. 0229A] for, corrupted by love of money, he did not hesitate both to lose the rank of apostleship and to betray the Lord.

Yet because there are some whom greater knowledge lifts up, separating them from the fellowship of others, so that the more they know, the more they lose sound judgment and stray from the virtue of concord, it is rightly added:

“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” By salt, the wisdom of the word is signified. Whoever therefore strives to speak wisely must greatly fear lest the unity of his hearers be confused by his eloquence. Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but an increase of condemnation. For the better someone understands, the worse he sins. And therefore he will deservedly suffer punishment without excuse, since, if he had wished, he could prudently have avoided sin.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0229B]

“And rising from there, he came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.” Up to this point, the evangelist Mark has related what the Lord did and taught in Galilee. Here he begins to relate what he did and taught in Judea, or what he suffered there. First, he went across the Jordan toward the east, and afterward also to the region on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, Bethany, and Jerusalem.

For although the entire province of the Jews was generally called Judea, to distinguish it from other nations, more specifically its southern region is called Judea, to distinguish it from Samaria, Galilee, the Decapolis, and the other regions within the same province.

“And crowds again came together to him, and, as was his custom, he again taught them. And Pharisees came to him and asked him whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife, testing him.”

Here the difference in disposition between the crowds and the Pharisees should be noted. The crowds came together to be taught and to have their sick healed, as the evangelist Matthew explicitly records. The others approached in order to test and entrap the Savior and teacher of truth. Nor is this surprising. The former were brought by devoted piety; the latter by the goad of envy.

They therefore ask whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason, so that they might hold him as if by a horned syllogism and leave him open to entrapment whatever he answered. If he said that a wife could be divorced for any reason and another married, he would seem, as a preacher of chastity, to teach the opposite. But if he answered that she ought not to be divorced for every reason, he would be held guilty, as though of sacrilege, of acting against the teaching of Moses and, through Moses, of God.

The Lord therefore moderates his answer so that he may pass beyond the trap, bringing Holy Scripture forward as testimony and setting against it the natural law and God’s first judgment—something conceded not by God’s will but by the necessity of sinners.

“What,” he says, “did Moses command you?” They said, “Moses permitted a writ of divorce to be written and the wife to be dismissed.” In response Jesus said to them, “Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote for you,” and so forth.

What he says means this: Can God be contrary to himself, having commanded one thing earlier and then broken his own judgment by a new decree? This must not be supposed. [Col. 0230A]

But when Moses saw that, because of the desire for second wives—who might be richer, younger, or more beautiful—the first wives were being killed or forced to lead wretched lives, he preferred to permit discord rather than allow hatred and murder to continue and be carried out.

At the same time, consider that he did not say, “Because of the hardness of your heart God permitted you,” but “Moses,” so that, in accordance with the Apostle, this might be the counsel of a human being, not the command of God.

“But from the beginning of creation God made them male and female.” This is written at the beginning of Genesis. By saying “male and female,” he shows that second marriages are to be avoided. For he did not say “male and females,” which would have been sought on the basis of the earlier divorce, but “male and female,” so that they might be bound together in the companionship of one spouse.

“For this reason a man will leave his father and mother [Col. 0230B] and cling to his wife.” Likewise, he says, “He will cling to his wife,” not “to wives.”

“And the two will be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh.” The reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit.

“Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.” What God joined together by making the flesh of man and woman one, a human being cannot separate—unless perhaps God alone can do so. A human being separates them when, because of the desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates them—he who had also joined them—when, by mutual consent for the service of God, because the time is short, “we have wives as though we had none.”

“And again in the house his disciples asked him about this.” [Col. 0230C] And he said to them: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. And if a wife divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.”

In Matthew it is written more fully: “Whoever divorces his wife except on account of fornication and marries another commits adultery” (Matt. V). There is therefore only one carnal cause: fornication; and one spiritual cause for a wife to be dismissed: fear of God, as many are recorded to have done for the sake of religion. But no cause is prescribed in God’s law for marrying another while the woman who has been left is still alive.

“And they were bringing little children to him so that he might touch them. But the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.” Not because they did not want the Savior to bless them by voice and hand, but because, not yet possessing fully developed faith, they thought that he, like other human beings, might be wearied by the persistence of those bringing them.

[Col. 0230D]

When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them: “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” Significantly, he said “such as these,” not “these,” to show that it is not age but character that reigns, and that the reward is promised to those who possess a similar innocence and simplicity.

The Apostle agrees with this meaning: “Brothers, do not become children in your thinking; rather, be infants in evil, but be mature in your thinking.”

“Amen, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will not enter it.” Just as a child does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, is not captivated when he sees a beautiful woman, and does not think one thing while saying another, so you too will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven unless you possess such innocence and purity of spirit.

[Col. 0231A]

In another sense, we are commanded to receive the kingdom of God—that is, the teaching of the Gospel—like little children, because a child, when learning, does not contradict his teachers, nor construct arguments and words to resist them. Instead, he faithfully receives what is taught and obeys and remains quiet with fear. So we too must obey the Lord’s words simply and without any resistance.

“And embracing them and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.” By embracing the little children, he blessed them, signifying that those who are humble in spirit are worthy of his blessing, grace, and love.

[Col. 0231B]

“And when he had gone out onto the road, a certain man ran up and knelt before him, asking him, and saying,” and so forth. I believe that this seeker of eternal life had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to be like little children were worthy to enter the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, desiring more certain instruction, he sought to have it explained to him—not through parables but openly—by what merits of conduct he could attain eternal life.

Jesus said to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God.” Because he had called him “good teacher” but had not confessed him to be God or the Son of God, he learns that, in comparison with God, even a holy human being is not good. Of God it is said: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CV).

But “one God” who is good is not to be understood as the Father alone, but also the Son, [Col. 0231C] who says, “I am the good shepherd” (John X), and also the Holy Spirit, because “the Father from heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke XI). That is, the one and undivided Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is the one and only God who is good.

The Lord therefore does not deny that he is good, but signifies that he is God. He does not deny that he is a good teacher, but testifies that no teacher apart from God is good.

This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is proposed for our imitation if we wish to enter the kingdom of God. It should certainly be noted that the justice of the Law, observed in its own time, bestowed not only the good things of the earth but also eternal life upon those who practiced it.

[Col. 0231D]

“And he answered and said to him, ‘Teacher, I have kept all these things from my youth,’” and so forth. This man should not be thought to have questioned the Lord with the intention of testing him, as some have supposed, or to have lied about his life when he said that he had kept the commandments of the Law. Rather, he simply confessed how he had lived.

For if he had been held guilty of the fault of lying or pretense, Jesus would certainly not be said to have loved him after looking into the secrets of his heart. The Lord loves those who keep the commandments of the Law, even the lesser ones. Nevertheless, he shows those who desire to be perfect what was lacking in the Law, because he did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them. To this fulfillment plainly belongs what is added here:

“Go, sell whatever you have and give,” and so forth. Whoever wishes to be perfect must sell what he has, [Col. 0232A] and not sell only part, as Ananias and Sapphira did, but sell everything. Having sold it, he must give it all to the poor and thus prepare a treasure for himself in the kingdom of heaven.

Nor is this sufficient for perfection unless, after despising riches, he follows the Savior—that is, having abandoned evil things, he must do good. For a purse is more easily despised than the will. Many leave their riches but do not follow the Lord. The one who follows the Lord is his imitator and walks in his footsteps. Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked.

“But he was saddened by the saying and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.” This is the sadness that leads to death. The cause of his sadness is given: he had many possessions—that is, thorns and briers growing up and choking the Lord’s seed.

[Col. 0232B]

“And looking around, Jesus said to his disciples, ‘How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom,’” and so forth. It is clear that those who devote themselves here to multiplying riches disdain seeking the joys of the other life. But there is a great difference between possessing money and loving money. Many who possess it do not love it; many who do not possess it love it. Others both possess and love it. Others rejoice neither to possess nor to love the riches of the world. Their condition is safer, because they can say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. V).

Thus Solomon did not say, “He who has riches,” but “He who loves riches will receive no fruit from them” (Eccles. V). And the Lord himself, explaining this saying to the disciples who were astonished at it, added:

[Col. 0232C]

“Children, how difficult it is for those who trust in money to enter the kingdom of God.” Here it should be noted that he did not say “how impossible,” but “how difficult.” What is impossible cannot happen at all; what is difficult can happen with effort.

It can indeed happen, though with the greatest difficulty and with the help of God’s grace, that those who possess money or trust in money, once stripped of the bonds of love of money, enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye,” and so forth (Matt. XIX). If it is easier for a camel, enormous in its bodily members, to pass through the narrow opening of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, then no rich person will enter the kingdom of God. How, then, did Matthew, Zacchaeus, and Joseph enter the kingdom of God in the Gospel, or so many rich people in the Old Testament? [Col. 0232D] Unless, perhaps, they learned, through the Lord’s inspiration, either to regard riches as nothing or to abandon them wholeheartedly.

For was David trusting in the riches of his kingdom? He sings of himself: “For I am solitary and poor” (Ps. XXIV), and he exhorts others: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). I believe he did not dare to say, “Do not accept them.”

Is it believable that Abraham preferred possessions to the Lord, for whose sake he did not hesitate to strike down his only heir?

In a deeper sense, it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. By the name of “camel” he wished himself to be understood, since of his own will he took upon himself the burdens of our weakness in humility.

[Col. 0233A]

For in whom is what is written more clearly understood than in him: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III)? By the needle he signifies punctures, and by the punctures the pains endured in the Passion. He therefore calls the eye of the needle the narrow straits of the Passion. Once the garment of our nature had been torn, he deigned in a certain manner to mend it—that is, to restore it—so that, reformed for the better after the fall, we might rejoice in testimony to the Apostle’s words: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

“But they were even more astonished, saying to one another, ‘Who then can be saved?’” What does this response concern, when the multitude of the poor is incomparably greater and could be saved after the rich have been lost? It concerns this: they understood that all who love riches, even if they are unable to acquire them, are counted among the rich.

[Col. 0233B]

“And looking at them, Jesus said: ‘With human beings it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.’” This should not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud, signified by the name of that rich man, will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride. Rather, it is possible for God, through his word—as we see has happened and happens every day—to convert people from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to saving humility.

Peter began to say to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” Great was Peter’s confidence. He was a fisherman, not a rich man; he sought his food by hand and by skill. [Col. 0233C]

Yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because it is not enough merely to leave things, he adds what is perfect: “And we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give us?

Jesus answered: “Amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time—houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life.”

Some people, taking this saying as an occasion, teach the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the righteous, when everything we have left for God’s sake will be repaid to us with multiplied interest, together with the gift of eternal life. In their foolishness they do not see that, even if the promise is fitting in other respects, the mention of wives would appear shameful according to the other evangelists, [Col. 0233D]

especially since the Lord testifies that there will be no marrying in the resurrection and asserts that what has been left for his sake will be received in this time together with persecutions.

Those millenarians, however, maintain that persecutions, as well as all other contrary circumstances, will be entirely absent during their thousand years.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever has left carnal things for the sake of Christ’s Gospel will receive spiritual goods, which, in comparison and according to their worth, will be as though the number one hundred were compared with a small number. For from brothers and companions in his purpose, who are bound to him by a spiritual bond, he will receive even in this life a much more gracious love.

Read the Acts of the Apostles: the multitude of believers [Col. 0234A] had one heart and one soul, everything was held in common among them, and no one among them was in need (Acts IV)—those who had left their possessions for the Lord. Of them the Apostle also says: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Cor. VI).

This saying, “He will receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, with persecutions” (Marc. X), can certainly be understood more profoundly through symbolism. The number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, although in the bending of the fingers it seems to retain the same shape that the number ten had on the left, nevertheless grows enormously in magnitude.

[Col. 0234B]

For all who despise temporal things for the sake of the kingdom of God taste with certain faith the joy of that kingdom even in this life, which is full of persecutions, and, in expectation of the heavenly homeland—rightly signified by the right hand—enjoy the sincere love of all the elect alike.

But because many do not complete their pursuit of virtue with the same pious intention with which they began it—either growing lukewarm after receiving the love of virtue or falling back entirely into the mire of crimes—a terrifying judgment is immediately added:

“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” See Judas changed from an apostle into an apostate, and say that many who are first will be last. See the thief on the cross become a confessor, rejoicing with Christ in paradise on the very day on which he was crucified for his sins, and say that the last will also be first.

[Col. 0234C]

Every day we also see many people in the lay state excel in the great merits of their lives, while others, fervent in spiritual devotion from their earliest age, grow slack at the end through idleness and, in inert foolishness, complete in the flesh what they had begun in the spirit.

They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were astonished, and those following were afraid. The disciples traveling with the Lord toward Jerusalem were astonished and afraid because they remembered his saying that he would suffer many things from the chief priests and scribes and be killed. They feared that either they themselves would be killed with him or, at least, that he whose life and teaching they enjoyed would fall into the hands of his enemies.

[Col. 0234D]

And taking the Twelve again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. They will mock him, spit upon him, scourge him, and kill him; and on the third day he will rise.”

Our Redeemer, foreseeing that his disciples’ minds would be disturbed by his Passion, foretells to them long beforehand both the suffering of that Passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that, when they saw him dying, as had been predicted, they would not doubt that he would also rise. Here he also most openly refutes the madness of the pagans, who customarily mock his cross, since, as one who knew the future, he indicates the time of his approaching Passion and, fearless, goes to the place of his death.

[Col. 0235A]

And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him, saying: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask.” But he said to them: “What do you want me to do for you?” They said: “Grant that we may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your glory.”

Matthew writes that the mother of the sons of Zebedee made this request to the Lord on their behalf. But Mark, wishing to disclose their desire and purpose to his readers, says nothing about their mother’s intervention and instead says that they themselves asked for what he knew had been requested through their mother at their urging. Finally, the Lord, according to both evangelists, answered not the mother but them:

“You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” They said to him: “We can.”

They do not know what they are asking who seek from the Lord a seat of glory that they had not yet deserved. The height of honor already delighted them, but [Col. 0235B] first they had to undertake the path of labor. They desired to reign sublimely with Christ, but first they had to suffer humbly for Christ.

By the name of the cup or baptism he signifies the passion of martyrdom, by which both he and they were destined to be brought to completion. Hence elsewhere he speaks of his Passion: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished” (Luke XII). And as he approached that Passion, he prayed, saying: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (Marc. XIV).

Jesus said to them: “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized you will be baptized.” [Col. 0235C]

It is asked how the sons of Zebedee—James and John—drank the cup of martyrdom, or how they were baptized with the Lord’s baptism, when Scripture relates that the apostle James alone was beheaded by Herod, while John ended his life by a natural death.

But if we read the ecclesiastical histories, in which it is reported that John too was sent on account of martyrdom into a vessel of boiling oil, and that from there he emerged as Christ’s athlete to receive the crown, and was immediately banished into exile on the island of Patmos, we will see that he did not lack the spirit of martyrdom and that John drank the cup of confession, which the three youths also drank in the furnace of fire, even though the persecutor did not shed his blood.

As for what he adds:

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, except to those for whom it has been prepared”—[Col. 0235D]

this should be understood as follows: the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the giver but to the receiver. For “there is no partiality with God” (Rom. II); whoever makes himself such that he is worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive what has been prepared not for a person but for a life.

If, therefore, you are such as to attain the kingdom of heaven, which my Father has prepared for those who triumph and conquer, you too will receive it.

Again: “It is not mine to give, except to those for whom it has been prepared.” It is not mine to give it to the proud, for that is what they still were. But if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are. It has been prepared for others; become other people, and it will be prepared for you. What does “become other people” mean? First humble yourselves, you who already wish to be exalted.

[Col. 0236A]

When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant with James and John. The ten apostles were not indignant with the mother of the sons of Zebedee, nor did they attribute the audacity of the request to the woman, but to the sons, who, ignorant of their own measure, had been inflamed by immoderate desire. The Lord had also said to them: “You do not know what you are asking.”

Jesus called them and said to them: “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their leaders exercise authority over them. But it is not so among you,” and so forth.

The humble and gentle teacher neither rebuked the two who made the excessive request for their immoderate desire nor reproached the other ten for their indignation and envy. Instead, he offers an example by which he teaches that the greater person is the one who has become lesser, and that the one who is servant of all becomes their lord.

Therefore, both the former asked immoderately in vain and the latter grieved needlessly over their companions’ desire, since the summit of virtues is reached not through power but through humility.

Finally, he sets forth his own example, so that, if they paid little attention to his words, they might feel shame before his deeds. And he says:

“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many.” [Col. 0236B]

Note what we have often said: the one who served is called the Son of Man, and he gave his life as a redemption for many when he took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world.

He did not say, “to give his life as a redemption for all,” but “for many”—that is, for those who were willing to believe.

And they come to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho, with his disciples and a very large crowd, Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, a blind man, was sitting beside the road begging. When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out, etc.

Matthew says that at this point two blind men sitting beside the road and crying out to the Lord were given sight. Luke, however, says that as he approached Jericho, a blind man was given sight by him in the same sequence of events. No sensible person should suppose that the Evangelists wrote things contrary to one another; rather, one wrote more fully what the other omitted. The reason why, according to Matthew, the Lord gave sight to two blind men, whereas Mark preferred to mention one who received sight—without denying that another was present—is to be understood as follows: one of them was particularly well known. This is also sufficiently clear from the fact that Mark mentioned both his name and his father’s name, something that does not readily occur among the many whom the Lord healed earlier, except when he also specified by name Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, whose daughter Jesus raised. In this case too the same meaning becomes even more apparent, because that ruler of the synagogue was certainly a distinguished man in that place.

Without doubt, therefore, this Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, having been cast down from some great prosperity, was a man of exceptionally notorious and famous misery: he was not only blind but also sat begging. This is why Mark wished to mention him alone: his restoration of sight gave this miracle a reputation as prominent as the calamity for which he was known.

The blind men whom the Lord gave sight to when they cried out to him are therefore people ignorant of the true light—which is Christ—but, by his gift, pierced with compunction so as to recognize and confess their blindness and to ask for the light of truth. Jericho, moreover, which is said to be interpreted as “moon,” signifies the decline of our mutability and mortality. This was made especially clear by that Gospel parable in which a man descending from Jerusalem fell among robbers in Jericho and, after being wounded and stripped by them, was restored to safety through the compassionate diligence of the Samaritan. For plainly the human race, falling from the vision of supreme peace into the desires of this world through a deadly stain, is brought back by the Lord Savior to the life it had lost through wandering.

As the Lord approached Jericho, therefore, he restored light to the blind man, because, coming in the flesh and drawing near to his Passion, he led many to faith and to the confession of knowledge of God. He did not offer the ministry of the word, by which the world would be enlightened, at the beginning of his incarnation, but a few years before he suffered—that is, after he had begun to be thirty years old.

But as he was leaving Jericho, he also gave sight to blind men, because, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles and scattered them throughout the world for the enlightenment of all peoples. The fact that, as he approached Jericho, he gave sight to one man, but as he was leaving Jericho, to two, figuratively indicated that before his Passion he preached to one people only, the Jewish people; whereas after his Resurrection and Ascension, through the apostles, he disclosed more openly to both Jews and Gentiles the mysteries both of his eternal divinity and of the humanity he had assumed.

The fact that Mark writes of one man receiving sight refers especially to the salvation of the Gentiles, who had been altogether deprived of the light of truth. Therefore, just as their blindness was notorious because of their famous unbelief, so the grace of the Savior who enlightened them became famous. Mark, who wrote his Gospel among the Gentiles, appropriately says that one man received sight, so that the figure of those whom he was instructing might correspond to their salvation. Matthew, however, who wrote his Gospel for believers from the Hebrews, though it was also to reach the knowledge of the Gentiles, rightly says that two received sight, teaching that the one and same grace of faith belonged to both peoples.

The same Evangelical Scripture also took care to preserve this meaning in the following passage concerning the donkey on which the Lord deigned to sit. Matthew, who evangelized the faithful from the Jews, reports that both a she-donkey and a colt were brought to the Lord. The other three Evangelists, however, who wrote for the Church gathered from the nations, mention only that a colt was brought to the Lord and say nothing at all about its mother. They simply signify the faith of the Gentiles; Matthew, on the other hand, took care, in the immediate sequence of his narrative, to indicate the faithful people of the Gentiles as born from the faithful synagogue.

As the Lord, his disciples, and the very large crowd were leaving Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road begging. For when the Lord had ascended into heaven, and many of the faithful were following him—indeed, when all the elect from the beginning of the world were entering with him through the gate of the heavenly kingdom—the people of the Gentiles, long blind through unbelief, immediately began, on hearing of the Savior’s coming, to have hope for their own salvation and enlightenment.

It is rightly said of him that he was sitting beside the road begging. He sits begging beside the road who, not yet entering upon the way of truth and not yet possessing knowledge, strives through attentive earnestness and the searching of a salutary desire to attain it, and persists in investigating what true religious worship may be. This was especially made clear in the history of Cornelius the centurion, who prayed frequently to the God whom he worshiped, asking that he might deign to enlighten him.

What does it mean that he heard while passing by and restored light while standing, except that he had mercy through his humanity, while through the power of his divinity he expelled the darkness of our minds? Jesus, who was born and suffered for us, who rose again and ascended into heaven, may be said to have passed by, because this activity is temporal. Yet he gave sight to the blind man while standing, because, unlike that temporal dispensation, the eternity of the Word does not pass away; remaining in itself, it renews all things. For God’s “standing” means arranging all mutable things in unchangeable thought.

Thus, when passing by, he heard the petitioner’s cries, and while standing he restored his light. Although he endured temporal things for our sake, he nevertheless granted us light from that which knows nothing of the passing away that belongs to mutability.

But he prayed frequently to the God whom he worshiped, asking that he might deign to enlighten him.

When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” And many rebuked him so that he would be silent. But he cried out all the more loudly: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

The blind man hears of Jesus, asks him to have mercy on him, and does not cease crying out, although many try to stop him. When the people of the Gentiles learned the famous reputation of Christ’s name, they sought to become participants in him. Many opposed them: first the Jews, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; then the Gentiles also frequently pressed them with fiercer and more powerful persecution, so that the world, which was to be enlightened and healed, would not invoke Christ. Yet the mad fury of those who attacked them could not deprive those who had been predestined to life of the salvation prepared for them.

And Jesus, standing still, commanded him to be called.

Behold, he stands who had previously been passing by. In this matter the Lord intimates something to us that may profitably be understood of his humanity and divinity. For while passing by he heard the blind man crying out, but while standing he performed the miracle of enlightenment.

And they call the blind man, saying to him: “Take heart; rise, he is calling you.”

The Lord calls the blind man who cries out to him when he entrusts the word of faith, through holy preachers, to the people of the Gentiles who desire knowledge of the truth. These men who call the blind man command him to take heart, to rise, and to come to the Lord when, by preaching the word to the unlearned, they instruct them to have hope of salvation, to rise from the torpor of their vices, and to devote themselves to the pursuit of virtues by which they may deserve to be enlightened. They say with the prophet: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33); and again: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5).

And because the primitive Church from the Gentiles burned with such a longing for the promised light in Christ that many, abandoning the possessions of the world, followed the Gospel life naked, so that they might deserve to possess an eternal treasure in heaven, the following is rightly added concerning the blind man who was to be enlightened:

And throwing aside his garment, he sprang up and came to him.

He springs up after throwing aside his garment so that, coming to Christ, he may be enlightened: having cast away the restraints of the world, he hastens with an unencumbered step of mind toward the giver of eternal light.

And Jesus, answering, said to him: “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him: “Rabboni [my master], that I may see.”

Did the one who could restore light not know what the blind man wanted? Rather, he wished him to ask for what he already knew both that we should ask and that he would grant. For he urgently urges us to prayer, saying: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6). He asks, therefore, in order that the request may be made; he asks in order to stir the heart to prayer.

Thus the blind man immediately adds: “Rabboni, that I may see.” Behold, the blind man asks the Lord not for gold but for light. He considers it of little account to seek anything outside the light, because although a blind man may possess various things, without light he cannot see what he possesses.

Let us therefore imitate the man whom we have heard was saved both in body and in mind. Let us seek from the Lord neither false riches, nor earthly gifts, nor fleeting honors, but light—the light that we can see together with the angels, which has no beginning to initiate it and no end to confine it. Faith is plainly the way to that light. Therefore the Lord rightly answers the blind man immediately:

“Go; your faith has saved you.” And immediately, he says, “he saw, and followed him on the road.”

He sees and follows who does the good that he understands. He sees but does not follow who indeed understands the good but scorns to do good. For he follows Jesus the Lord who imitates him. Hence he says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12).

Let us therefore consider by what path he walks, so that we may deserve to follow him. Behold, although he is Lord and creator of the angels, he came into the womb of a virgin to assume the nature he had created. Yet he did not wish to be born into this world through the rich; he chose poor parents. Consequently, the mother found no lamb to offer for him but brought young pigeons and a pair of turtledoves for the sacrifice. He did not wish to prosper in this world; he endured insults and mockery, and bore spittle, scourges, blows, a crown of thorns, and the cross. And because through the delight of bodily things we have fallen from inward joy, he showed with what bitterness one returns there.

## CHAPTER XI

And when they were approaching Jerusalem, Bethany, and the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples and said to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you.”

Bethany is a small village or town on the side of the Mount of Olives, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as the evangelist John makes clear. Lazarus was raised from the dead there, and the church now built in that place displays his tomb. Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.”

Appropriately, then, as the Lord was about to come to Jerusalem and redeem the world by his blood, he first exalted Bethany by the favor of his presence. There a devout woman anointed him with mystical chrism, because, by teaching many before his Passion, he made them a house of obedience for himself, in which he would dwell through the Spirit of grace. Delighted by their pious action, he himself was, as it were, steeped in fragrant ointment.

This city is said to have been situated on the Mount of Olives in order to signify that the Church is to be saved by the grace of its founder, who sustains us with the anointing of spiritual gifts and with the perpetual light of knowledge and piety. Thus elsewhere, after saying, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden,” he immediately added: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a measure” (Matthew 5). The same Mount of Olives—that is, the supreme distributor of spiritual graces—exalts its city so that it may stand out, and fattens it with the oil of gladness so that it may shine and not fail.

And because he did not wish that this same light should be placed under a measure, he sent the disciples into the village that was opposite them. That is, he sent teachers to penetrate by evangelizing the ignorant and barbarous regions of the whole world, as though they were the walls of a village set opposite them.

Two are rightly sent, either on account of knowledge of the truth and purity of action, or to proclaim throughout the whole world the mystery of the twofold love: love of God and love of neighbor.

And immediately, when they entered it, you will find a colt tied, on which no one among humankind has yet sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone says to you, “Why are you doing this?” say: “The Lord needs it,” and immediately he will send it back here.

As they entered the world, the holy preachers found the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of unbelief. Each person was bound by the cords of his sins—and not only among the nations but also among the Jews. For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3).

Thus, appropriately, in Matthew a she-donkey is also found tied together with the colt. The she-donkey, which was subject to the yoke and tamed, signifies the synagogue that bore the yoke of the Law; the wild and free young donkey signifies the people of the nations. No one had yet sat upon it, because none of the rational teachers had previously brought to the people of the Gentiles, through useful exhortation, either the bridle of correction by which they might restrain their tongue from evil or be compelled to walk along the narrow path of life, or garments of salvation by which they might be spiritually warmed. A human being would sit upon it if someone using reason corrected it by suppressing its folly.

Therefore the two disciples sent to bring the animals to the Lord may appropriately be understood as the two orders of preachers: one sent to the Gentiles, the other to the circumcision.

And they went away and found the colt tied outside, before the door, at a crossroads, and they untied it.

The colt is rightly found outside, before the door, at a crossroads. For the door itself is the one who says: “I am the door of the sheep. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture.” This colt—that is, the people of the Gentiles—lacked these pastures of life while it still stood tied outside this door at a crossroads. And rightly at a crossroads, because, uncertain of one fixed way of life and faith, it wandered after the many doubtful paths of different sects.

And some of those standing there said to them: “What are you doing, untying the colt?”

In Luke’s Gospel it is written this way: “Those who had been sent went away and found the colt standing, just as he had told them. As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: ‘Why are you untying the colt?’” And this is entirely appropriate. For it had many owners, because, devoted to no single doctrine or superstition, it was miserably dragged about at the whim of unclean spirits into various and differing errors, walking toward mute images wherever it was led.

Indeed, in a certain vernacular usage of Scripture, what is unclean is said to be “common.” Thus the voice from heaven says to Peter: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10). For whoever is holy belongs to God alone and is common to no one. Whoever, however, is a sinner and unclean belongs to many. Many demons possess him, and therefore he is called common.

They told them what Jesus had commanded, and they let them go and led the colt to Jesus.

Those who had opposed the untying of the colt fall silent when they hear the Lord’s name. The teachers of error, who resisted when teachers came for the salvation of the Gentiles, were able to defend their darkness only until the power of the true possessor and Lord shone forth, attested by miracles. But after the power of the Lord’s faith appeared, the complaints of the adversaries yielded everywhere, and the gathering of believers was freely led to the God whom it carried in its heart.

And they placed their garments upon it, and he sat upon it.

The apostles’ garments may be understood either as the teaching of virtues, the exposition of the Scriptures, or certainly the various forms of ecclesiastical doctrine. These garments cover human hearts, previously naked and cold, so that they may become worthy of Christ as their rider.

Many spread their garments on the road.

As the donkey carried the Lord, many spread their garments on the road, because the holy martyrs, stripping themselves of the covering of their own flesh, prepare the way with their blood for the simpler servants of God, so that with unhindered steps of mind they may walk toward the walls of the heavenly city, where Jesus leads them.

Likewise, our Savior proceeds toward Jerusalem seated upon the colt when, governing the soul of each believer—his own beast, so to speak—he leads it to the innermost vision of peace. He also sits upon the beast when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

Many spread their garments on the road because they tame their bodies through abstinence, preparing a path for him to the mind or offering good examples to those who follow.

Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Both those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

Those who cut leaves or branches from the trees are the ones who extract words and sayings of the Fathers from their discourse in the teaching of truth, and submit these on the road of God through humble preaching to the mind of the hearer who is coming.

But those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna.” The Jewish people went before; the Gentile people followed. And because all the elect—whether they could be found in Judea or now exist in the Church—believed and believe in the Mediator between God and human beings, both those who went before and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna.”

“Hosanna” is said in Latin to mean “save us.” From him both those who came before sought salvation and those who are present seek it. They confess him who comes in the name of the Lord to be blessed, because there is one hope and one faith of the peoples who precede and those who follow. For just as the former were healed when they witnessed his Passion and Resurrection, so we are saved by his past Passion and his Resurrection, which endures forever. The one whom our predecessors from the Jewish people believed in and loved as the one who was to come, we believe and love as the one who has come; and we are inflamed by desire for him so that we may behold him face to face.

“Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes; hosanna in the highest.”

And he entered Jerusalem, into the temple, etc.

We read in the Gospel of John that the crowds, after being refreshed by the five loaves and two fish, wanted to seize Jesus and make him king; but, so that they could not accomplish this, he withdrew by fleeing into the mountain. Now, however, when he comes to Jerusalem to suffer, he does not avoid those who make him king. They lead him into the royal city in a glorious procession with hymns worthy of the Son of God and King. He does not restrain their voices as they sing that the kingdom of the patriarch David is to be restored in him and the gifts of the ancient blessing recovered.

Why, then, does he now willingly embrace what he previously avoided by fleeing, and accept the kingdom which, while he still had to live in the world, he had refused to receive, but which, as he was about to depart through the Passion of the cross, he did not refuse to accept? Surely it was to teach openly that he was not the temporal and earthly King of an empire, but the eternal King in heaven. To this kingdom he would attain through contempt of death, the glory of the Resurrection, and the triumph of the Ascension.

For this reason, appearing to his disciples after the Resurrection, he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” and the rest of that passage.

It should certainly be noted how great is the harmony between the crowd’s praise of the Lord and the voice of Gabriel, who evangelized the virgin mother and said: “For he will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1).

The Lord received David’s throne, or kingdom, so that he might call to the heavenly and immortal kingdom the people to whom David once provided both the governance of a temporal kingdom and examples of justice, and whom he used to kindle, through the melodies of spiritual hymns, to faith in and love of their Creator. He would summon them by words, gifts, deeds, and promises worthy of so great a Mediator between God and human beings, and introduce them into the very vision of God the Father.

To this is joined: “Hosanna in the highest,” that is, “salvation.” This clearly shows that Christ’s coming is not merely the salvation of human beings but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly things, so that “every knee should bow” to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

It should certainly be noted that “hosanna” is a Hebrew word composed of two elements, one altered and one intact. Among them, *osi* means “save” or “save us,” while *anna* is the interjection of one who pleads. Among the Latins, similarly, *heu* is the interjection of one who grieves, and *papae* the interjection of one who marvels.

Finally, in Psalm 117, where the Seventy Translators rendered “O Lord, save me,” the Hebrew reads: “Anna Adonai, osi anna.” Our translator Jerome, elucidating this more carefully, rendered it: “I beseech you, Lord; save, I beseech you.” “O Lord,” expressed through the interjection of one who pleads, means the same as “I beseech you, Lord,” expressed through the very word of supplication.

Thus *hosanna* means “save, I beseech you.” The vowel *i*, which ends the preceding word when it is fully pronounced as *osi*, is elided through the force of the vowel with which the following word, *anna*, begins. Grammarians call this *synaloepha* when scanning verses, although in that practice they pass over a written letter in scanning. In the word *hosanna*, however, the letter *i* is not even written; while the meaning intended by the speakers remains intact, it is completely suppressed.

And he entered Jerusalem, into the temple.

By entering the city and going first to the temple, he set before us a pattern of religion that we should follow. Whenever, perhaps, we enter a village, town, or any other place where there is a house of prayer consecrated to God, we should first turn aside to it. After commending ourselves to the Lord through diligent prayer, we should then withdraw to the temporal business for which we came.

As the time of his Passion approached, the Lord wished to draw near to the place of his Passion and remain nearby, so that, when the time established and predetermined before the ages arrived, he could be found there by those through whom that Passion was to be completed. By this he also made clear to all who heard that he would undergo death not unwillingly, as the impious have thought, but of his own accord. As the hour approached, he fearlessly went to the place where he had long before foretold, both by himself and through the mouths of his prophets, that he would suffer.

It should be noted that this entry of his into Jerusalem took place five days before Passover, in which he had determined to fulfill the mystery of his most holy Passion. For John relates that he came to Bethany six days before Passover, where a supper was prepared for him, and, while many were reclining at table, Mary, the sister of Lazarus, poured mystical ointment over him. On the following day, seated upon a donkey and met by a very large crowd with palm branches, he came to Jerusalem.

Here the harmony not only of events but also of times between the Old and New Testaments, between shadow and truth, and between the Law and the Gospel should not be passed over in silence. For it is written in the Law, when the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month, let each one take a lamb for his families and households.” And shortly afterward: “You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening” (Exodus 12).

On the tenth day of the first month, therefore, the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be brought into the house, because on the tenth day of that same month—that is, five days before Passover—the Lord was to enter the city in which he would suffer. And just as the lamb, chosen from the whole flock, awaited the appointed day of its sacrifice, so the Lord, while the entire council of elders and rulers conspired against him, awaited with certainty the hour at which he would offer himself to God as an offering and sacrifice for the salvation of the world, as a pleasing fragrance.

The lamb was sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth day of the first month; and at that same hour the Lord ate the lamb with his disciples. Having fulfilled the decrees of the legal Passover, he immediately went out with them to the place of prayer, where he was seized and bound by the Jews and began already the rites of his blessed sacrifice.

And after looking around at everything, since it was already the hour of evening, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

He did not do this only once. Rather, throughout all five days from the time he had gone up to Jerusalem until the time of his Passion, he used to do the same: by day he taught in the temple, while at night he went out and stayed on the Mount of Olives, as we read in Luke.

By teaching unbelievers, he diligently performed the duty of correction. By staying among the faithful, he graciously displayed to them the favor of his kindness. It is rightly said that, after looking around at everything, he went out to Bethany. The inward Judge examines the hearts of all, and when he finds nowhere to lay his head among those who contradict and resist the truth, he withdraws to the faithful and rejoices to make his dwelling with the Father among those who obey the word. For Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.”

It should also be understood that the Lord was so poor, and flattered no one to such an extent, that in the greatest city he found neither a host nor a lodging, but stayed in a small village with Lazarus and his sisters. Their village was Bethany.

And on the following day, as they were going out from Bethany, he was hungry.
