He was hungry either to demonstrate the truth of his human flesh or because he hungered for the salvation of believers and burned with zeal against Israel’s unbelief.

And when he saw from a distance a fig tree with leaves, he came to see whether he might perhaps find something on it. And when he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And Jesus, answering, said to it: “May no one ever again eat fruit from you.”

Just as the Lord often spoke many things in parables, so he also used to do certain things in parables. What reason could there have been for him, when hungry, to seek fruit from a fig tree whose season any person knew had not yet arrived, and to condemn a tree that had no fruit at that time with a curse of eternal barrenness, except that by this deed he also terrified the people whom he taught by word? He warned that anyone who had leaves but no fruit—that is, who displayed words of righteousness without works—might deserve to be cut down and cast into the fire.

For every tree is known not by its flowers or leaves but by its fruit. That is, every person is proved not by the estimation of reputation or the pomp of speech but by the testimony of his actions.

Hungry, therefore, the Lord saw a fig tree with leaves and came to seek fruit on it, but found none. For desiring the salvation of the human race, he saw Judea possessing the words of the Law and the Prophets, and he came to test, by teaching, reproving, and performing miracles, whether he might perhaps find in their hearts some fruit of faith and life.

But because the fig tree was found to have leaves without fruit, it was condemned, because Judea, which uttered the words of Scripture without works, deserved to be punished. I say this not because the whole synagogue was rejected, since the primitive Church was certainly established from it. Rather, that portion of the synagogue deserved condemnation which refused to nourish Christ when he was hungry by doing good, and which preferred to be shaded by the leaves of spiritual words rather than adorned with the fruits of the Spirit.

To them he says elsewhere: “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin” (John 5).

This passage appropriately corresponds to that parable of his in which he says: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and did not find any. And he said to the vine-dresser: ‘Behold, it is three years since I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down, then; why should it even occupy the ground?’ But he answered and said to him: ‘Lord, leave it this year also, until I dig around it and apply manure. And if indeed it bears fruit—otherwise, afterward you shall cut it down’” (Luke 13).

The vine-dresser is the order of the apostles and spiritual teachers, who diligently strove to call the synagogue to repentance so that it would not perish and to plead with the Lord for its salvation. Chief among them was James, the brother of the Lord, who was placed over the governance of the Church of Jerusalem.

But because it consented to bear no fruit of obedience—neither in the legal decrees, nor in the prophetic testimonies, nor in the very grace of the radiant Gospel—it was cast away by the Lord, remaining like a barren fig tree for three years, and was overthrown by an eternal curse. For it was not only rejected from the lot of the elect; it was also cut away from the very ground that it occupied uselessly.

But you too, if you do not wish to hear Christ say at the judgment, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, because I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25), beware of being a barren tree in this life. Rather, offer to poor and hungry Christ the fruit of piety that he needs.

And they come to Jerusalem. And when he had entered the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in the temple; and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves.

What the Lord did figuratively by cursing the fruitless fig tree, he immediately made clearer by driving the wicked from the temple. The tree had committed no sin by having no fruit when the Lord was hungry, since its season had not yet arrived. But the priests sinned by conducting worldly business in the house of the Lord and by ceasing to bear the fruit of piety that they ought to have borne and for which the Lord hungered in them.

The Lord withered the tree by his curse so that people, seeing or hearing these things, might understand all the more that they would be condemned by divine judgment if, without the fruit of works, they relied solely on the applause of religious speech, or, like the sound and covering of flourishing leaves, sought to flatter themselves.

But because they did not understand, he consequently exercised against them the severity of deserved punishment. He expelled the business of human commerce from the house in which only divine matters were commanded to be conducted: sacrifices and prayers were to be offered to God, and the word of God read, heard, and sung.

It must indeed be believed that he found only those things being sold or bought in the temple which were necessary for the service of that temple, in accordance with what we read happened elsewhere, when he entered the same temple and found people selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves there. Clearly, these things were acquired from the local inhabitants by those who had come from far away solely so that they might be offered in the house of the Lord.

If, then, the Lord did not want even those things to be sold in the temple which he wanted to be offered in the temple, because of the greed or fraud that is ordinarily the characteristic crime of merchants, with what severity do you think he would punish anyone he found there occupied with laughter or idle talk, or enslaved to any other vice? If the Lord does not permit temporal business to be conducted in his house, although it could lawfully be conducted elsewhere, how much more do those things that are permitted nowhere deserve heavenly wrath when they are done in buildings consecrated to God?

Since the Holy Spirit appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove, doves rightly signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Who, then, are those who today sell doves in the temple of God, except those who in the Church accept a price for the laying on of hands—the laying on by which the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? A dove is sold when a price is demanded for the laying on of hands through which the Holy Spirit is received.

Our Redeemer, however, overturns the seats of those who sell doves, because he destroys the priesthood of such merchants. Hence the sacred canons condemn the heresy of simony and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. The seats of those who sell doves are overturned because those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood either in the eyes of human beings or before the eyes of God.

And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.

He speaks of the vessels that they brought in for the sake of trading. But far be it from us to suppose that the Lord would cast sacred vessels out of the temple or forbid them to be brought into the temple, where he set forth an example signifying his future judgment. Rather, he removes unclean and profane vessels from the temple and forbids them to be brought in again, when he not only drives all the reprobate away from the Church but also restrains them with an eternal scourge so that they may not enter again to disturb the Church.

And even now this is the true house of the Lord: the purification of the hearts of the faithful. It is such that divine compunction not only removes the sins that were present but also that the grace of God, persevering within them, helps them not to return to those sins.

And he was teaching, saying to them: “Is it not written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’?”—for all nations, he says, not for the one Jewish nation, nor in one place within the city of Jerusalem, and certainly not a house of bulls, goats, and rams, but of prayer.

But you have made it a den of robbers. There can be no doubt that those who sat in the temple to receive gifts sought injuries against certain people who did not give them. Thus the house of prayer had become a den of robbers, because they knew how to station themselves in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did. The temple, moreover, and the house of God is the mind and conscience of the faithful themselves. Whenever it brings forth perverse thoughts in order to injure a neighbor, it is as though it were sitting in a den of robbers. They kill those who walk innocently and straightforwardly when they drive the swords of injury into people who are guilty of nothing. The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of robbers when, having abandoned the innocence and simplicity of holiness, it tries to do what may enable it to harm its neighbors.

And as they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree dried up from its roots. Not merely the branches or trunks of the fruitless fig tree, but even its root, by drying up, displayed the divine sentence of rejection passed upon it. And John says that the axe has been laid at the root of the trees (Matthew III). The fig tree was therefore dried up from its roots, so that it might be shown that the impious nation was not to be chastised for a time or in part by external attacks and then, when the Lord showed mercy, restored after repentance to its former freedom—as sacred history often records—but was rather to be struck by eternal condemnation. It was dried up from its roots to make clear that the wicked people were to be utterly deprived not only of human glory outwardly but also of divine favor inwardly. For it lost both the salvation and life that it could have received in heaven, and the homeland that it had already possessed on earth.

And Jesus answered and said to them: Have faith in God. Amen, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, “Be taken up and cast into the sea,” and does not hesitate in his heart, but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him. Pagans who have written insults against the Church commonly reproach us, saying that we have not had complete faith in God, because we have never been able to move mountains. We must answer them that not everything done in the Church has been written down, just as our Scripture itself bears witness concerning the deeds of Christ himself, our God and Lord. Hence this too could have happened: if necessity had demanded it, a mountain could have been removed from the earth and cast into the sea. We read that something similar happened through the prayers of the blessed father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man distinguished for his merits and virtues: a mountain gave way on the earth by as much space as the inhabitants of the city needed. For when he wished to build a church in a suitable place and saw that the site was narrower than the project required, since it was confined on one side by a sea-cliff and on the other by a nearby mountain, he came to the place by night and, bending his knees, reminded the Lord of his promise, asking him, in accordance with the faith of the petitioner, to move the mountain farther away. When morning came, he returned and found that the mountain had left the builders of the church precisely as much space as they needed. Thus he—or some other man of equal merit—could, if circumstances had required it, have obtained from the Lord, by the merit of faith, that a mountain actually be taken up and cast into the sea.

Yet because the name “mountain” sometimes signifies the devil—on account, evidently, of the pride by which he raises himself against God and wishes to be like the Most High—the mountain is taken up from the earth at the command of those who are strong in faith and cast into the sea when, through holy teachers preaching the word, the unclean spirit is driven from the hearts of those predestined to life and is permitted to exercise the madness of his tyranny in the troubled and bitter minds of unbelievers. This does not mean that he had not previously possessed a seat and kingdom there, but that he rages all the more fiercely against those whom he is allowed to torment because he is more deeply grieved to have been driven away from harming the godly. Something similar appears in the Apocalypse: “And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and behold, a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea” (Apocalypse VIII). When the angel sounded the trumpet, the burning mountain was cast into the sea because, when the teacher of truth preaches the word, the ancient enemy, kindled by the flames of envy, approaches to corrupt the minds of the perverse more grievously, so that he may avenge upon the faithless the pain of his expulsion from the faithful.

And whenever you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins, etc. A distinction among those who pray must be noted. Whoever possesses perfect faith, which works through love, can, by praying or even by commanding, move spiritual mountains. Thus Paul acted with Elymas the magician, depriving him both of sight and of his wicked art. Thus he acted with the pythoness at Philippi, from whom he expelled the evil spirit—that is, the exceedingly proud mountain. But when this mountain was cast into the sea, the persecution of the Gentiles which immediately followed taught how much the raging fire had inflicted upon him. Those, however, who are not yet able to climb to such a summit of perfection should ask that their sins be forgiven, so that they may deserve to enter into eternal life. Without doubt they will obtain what they ask, provided that they themselves first forgive those who sin against them. But if they disdain to do this, they can neither perform miracles by praying nor obtain forgiveness for their own sins.

And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders came to him and said: By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority to do them? They construct, in different forms, the same accusation with which they had earlier charged him when they said: “By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons.” For when they say, “By what authority do you do these things?” they doubt God’s authority and wish it to be understood that what he does belongs to the devil. By adding, “Who gave you this authority?” they most plainly deny that he is the Son of God, believing that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another.

But Jesus answered and said: I will ask you one question, and answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from human beings? Answer me. The Lord could have refuted the accusers’ charge by an open answer, but he wisely questions them, so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their judgment.

But they were reasoning among themselves, saying: If we say, “From heaven,” he will say to us, “Why then did you not believe him?” For the one whom you confess to have received prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things.

But if we say, “From human beings”—we fear the people. For everyone held John to be truly a prophet. They therefore saw that whichever of these answers they gave, they would fall into a snare, fearing stoning, but fearing still more the confession of the truth.

And answering, they said to Jesus: We do not know. And Jesus answered and said to them: Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things. I do not tell you what I know, because you do not wish to admit what you know. Justly repelled and thoroughly confounded, they departed. And what God the Father says through the prophet in the psalm was fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” that is, John himself. “I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Psalm CXXXI). It should be noted, moreover, that knowledge of the truth is chiefly to be withheld from those who ask for two reasons: when the one who asks is either less capable of understanding what he asks, or is unworthy, through hatred or contempt of the truth itself, to have what he asks revealed to him. Regarding the first, the Lord says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” Regarding the second, he commanded his disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

## CHAPTER XII

And he began to speak to them in parables: A man planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress, and built a tower. This man who planted the vineyard is the same one who, in another parable, hired laborers for his vineyard. He planted the vineyard about which Isaiah speaks most fully in a song, concluding: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” And in the psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt,” he says; “you drove out the nations and planted it.” He surrounded it with a hedge, either the wall of the city or the assistance of angels. And he dug in it a winepress—or an altar, or those winepresses whose titles head three psalms: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. And he built a tower, plainly the temple, of which it is said through Micah: “And you, tower of the clouded daughter of Zion.”

And he leased it to tenants. Elsewhere he called these the laborers of the vineyard, who had been hired at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours. And he went away to a distant place—not by a change of location. For where can God be absent, when all things are filled by him? And does not the Lord say through Jeremiah: “I am God who is near, and not far away”? Yet he appears to leave the vineyard so as to leave the vintners free discretion to work.

And at the proper time he sent a servant to the tenants, so that he might receive from the tenants some of the vineyard’s fruit. But they seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed. He rightly says “the time of fruits,” not “the produce.” For no fruit came from the obstinate people; no produce of this vineyard, although it was sought frequently and diligently, was found. The servant who was sent first is therefore understood to be Moses, the lawgiver, who for forty continuous years sought from the cultivators some fruit of the law he had given, but they beat him and sent him away empty-handed. For they provoked Moses in the camp and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit. And he himself openly declares in a song what he thinks of the fruit of this vineyard, saying: “For their vine is from Sodom, and their vine-shoot from Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of gall, and their clusters are bitterness in them; the wine of dragons is their wine, and the venom of incurable asps” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

And again he sent another servant to them, and they wounded him in the head and treated him with insults. The other servant signifies King David the prophet and the other psalmists, who were sent after Moses so that, after the legal commandments, they might rouse the tenants to the practice of good works by the melody of psalmody and the sweetness of the lyre. David himself, who would lift the heart of the people toward heavenly desires, also ordained that continuous praises of the Lord should be sung with sweet melody amid the rites of bodily sacrifices. But they treated this servant with insults and wounded him in the head because, thinking little of the psalmists’ songs that called them to praise the Lord, they rejected David himself, who had shone as the head and fountain of psalmody in the Holy Spirit. For by saying, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (III Kings XII), they exchanged both his kingdom, because of his lowly lineage, and religion, through impiety. Nevertheless, he prayed for this vineyard, which, having been brought out of Egypt, had sheltered the mountains of Palestine beneath its shade, so that it might not be uprooted: “Lord God of hosts, turn now; look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vineyard, and direct it, which your right hand planted” (Psalm LXXIX). Here he likewise explained who the man was who planted this vineyard: namely, the Lord God of hosts.

And again he sent another, and they killed him, along with many others, beating some and killing others. Understand the third servant, together with his companions, as the choir of the prophets, who repeatedly confronted the people and foretold the evils that were about to come upon this vineyard. But which of the prophets did they not persecute? “And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Lord Savior” (Acts VII). All these men spoke much about the barrenness of this vineyard, but it is enough to cite the lament of one—Jeremiah: “I had planted you as a choice vine, wholly genuine seed; how have you turned into the degeneracy of a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah II). That the three ranks of servants can encompass the figure of all the teachers under the law, the Lord plainly declares elsewhere, saying: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

He still had one beloved son, and he sent him to them last, saying: “They will respect my son.” What he says—“They will respect my son”—does not arise from ignorance. For what could the master of the household not know, when here the Father God is understood? Yet God is always said to be uncertain so that human free will may be preserved. Let us question Arius and Eunomius. Behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he moderates his judgment; and, insofar as it depends on us, he is shown to have lied. Whatever they answer concerning the Father, let them understand the same concerning the Son, who says that he does not know the day of consummation.

But the tenants said to one another: This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. The Lord most clearly proves that the leaders of the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood that he was the one to whom it had been said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II). And therefore, as though consulting their own interests, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him. And if we let him go on this way, everyone will believe in him” (John XII). The Son’s inheritance, therefore, is the Church, given to him from all the nations. His Father did not leave it to him by dying; rather, he wondrously acquired it by his own death and possessed it by rising again. After he had been killed, the evil tenants tried to seize it, when the Jews, by crucifying him, attempted to extinguish the faith that comes through him and to exalt their own righteousness, which comes from the law, and to plant it among the nations who were to be instructed.

And seizing him, they killed him and cast him out of the vineyard. He marks the obstinate wickedness of those who, even after the Lord had been crucified and raised from the dead, were unwilling to believe the preaching of the apostles, but cast him away like a worthless corpse. For, as far as they were able, by excluding him from their own boundaries, they handed him over to the nations to receive.

What, then, will the lord of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants, and give the vineyard to others. The Lord himself immediately explained this verse in Matthew, saying: “Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew XXI). He had also shown figuratively that this would happen when, as an example of the unbelieving Jews, he cursed the fruitless fig tree. By contrast, he later compared those who believed, whether Jews or Gentiles, to a fruitful and excellent tree, saying: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” (John XV). When he had said that the lord of the vineyard would come after the destruction of the evil cultivators and give the vineyard to others, he immediately confirmed by a prophetic example that this had been divinely arranged, adding:

Have you not read this Scripture: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes”? How, he says, could this prophecy be fulfilled—which says that the stone rejected by the builders is to be placed as the cornerstone—unless Christ, rejected and killed by you, is to be preached to the Gentiles who would believe, so that, like a cornerstone, he might join two peoples in himself and build for himself from both peoples one city of the faithful, one temple? The same teachers of the synagogue whom he earlier called tenants he now calls builders. For those who had been commanded to cultivate the people subject to them, like a vineyard, so that it might bear the fruits of life, were also commanded to construct and adorn them, as a house worthy of God as its inhabitant. Hence the Apostle, writing to the faithful, says: “You are God’s cultivated field, God’s building” (I Corinthians III). But the same men who, like the worst tenants, refused to return the fruit of God’s vineyard to the great master of the household, like wicked masons, labored to remove from God’s house the precious and chosen stone that was to be placed either in its foundations or at the corner—that is, they tried to take away from their hearers faith in Christ.

[Col. 0252B] And they sought to seize him, but they feared the crowd. For they recognized that he had spoken this parable against them, and, leaving him, they went away. The chief priests and scribes sought to kill the Lord, as though he were lying against them. But by seeking to do this, they showed that what he had said was true. For he is the heir whose unjust death, he had said, would be avenged by the father. Those wicked tenants could be restrained from killing the Son of God for a short time by human fear, until his hour came, but they could never be restrained by divine love.

In the moral sense, whenever the mystery of baptism, which is to be exercised through works, is entrusted to a member of the faithful, a vineyard is leased to him, as it were, for cultivation. One servant, another, and a third are sent to receive the fruit when the law, psalmody, and prophecy are read, and their admonition is followed by good conduct. But the servant who is sent is treated with insults or beaten and cast out when the word that has been heard is despised or, worse still, blasphemed. He kills the heir sent to him, insofar as it lies within him, when he tramples upon the Son of God and insults the Spirit of grace by which he was sanctified. When the wicked cultivator has been destroyed, the vineyard is given to another, when some humble person is enriched with the gift of grace that the proud person scorned. But the fact that the chief priests, scribes, and elders, seeking to lay hands on Jesus, are restrained by fear of the crowd also happens daily in the Church: whenever someone who is a brother in name only, and does not love the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace, is ashamed or afraid to attack it because of the multitude of good brothers living alongside him. Yet, as the Lord says concerning the exceedingly foolish bird, the ostrich, when the time comes he raises his wings on high, because he will rejoice to persecute the Church, as though he could hand the Lord over to the cross and take pleasure in making a spectacle of him.

And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and Herodians, to trap him in his speech. By “Herodians” he means the soldiers of Herod the tetrarch, who was himself at that time in Jerusalem and, as the evangelist Luke testifies, agreed with Pilate and the Jews in scorning and ridiculing the Lord. The chief priests, scribes, and elders, therefore, seeking to seize the Lord, feared the crowd. And because they could not accomplish this themselves, they tried to bring it about through the hands of earthly authority, so that they might appear to be free from responsibility for his death. For Judaea had recently been subjected to the Romans under Caesar Augustus, when the census was celebrated throughout the world; it had become a tributary province, and there was great sedition among the people. Some said that taxes ought to be paid for the sake of the security and peace for which the Romans fought on behalf of all; but the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for their righteousness, strove in the opposite direction, saying that the people of God, who paid tithes, offered first fruits, and gave the other things written in the law, ought not to be subject to human laws. The fuel of this sedition grew so strong that after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Romans pressed them, the people preferred to lose their homeland, nation, kingdom, that august temple with its religion, and even the light itself rather than pay taxes.

They came and said to him: Teacher, we know that you are truthful and care about no one. For you do not look at a person’s face, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or shall we not pay it? This flattering and deceitful question sought to provoke the respondent into fearing God more than Caesar and saying that taxes ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians, hearing it at once, might seize him as the author of sedition against the Romans.

But knowing their cunning, he said to them: Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius, so that I may see it. And they brought one to him. This is a kind of coin that was reckoned as ten units of currency and bore the image of Caesar. Wisdom always acts wisely, so that the tempters may be refuted by their own words: “Bring me,” he says, “a denarius.”

[Col. 0253C] And he said to them: Whose image and inscription is this? Those who think that the Savior’s question expresses ignorance rather than providence should learn from this passage that Jesus certainly could have known whose image was on the coin; but he asks so that he may answer their words appropriately.

They said to him: Caesar’s. Then Jesus answered and said to them: Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. By “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” let us understand the coin, the tribute, and money; and by “to God the things that are God’s,” tithes, first fruits, offerings, and sacrifices. In this way he himself paid tribute for himself and Peter, while rendering to God what belongs to God by doing the will of the Father.

Alternatively: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. Just as Caesar demands from us the impression of his image, so God demands that, just as the coin is returned to Caesar, the soul marked and illumined by the light of his countenance be returned to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV).

This light is the whole human being and the true good, which is perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. He said “marked upon us,” as a denarius is marked with the image of the king. For the human being was made in the image and likeness of God, which he corrupted by sinning. His true and eternal good, therefore, is to be marked anew through rebirth.

And they marveled at him. They ought to have believed because of such great wisdom, but they marveled because their cunning attempt to lay a trap had found no opening. And, as Matthew writes, they left him and went away, carrying back unbelief together with their amazement.

And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. There were two heresies among the Jews: one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees placed before everything else the justice of traditions and observances, which they call *deuterosis* (“second tradition”); hence they were also called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “just,” claimed this title for themselves although they were not just. While the former believed in the resurrection of both body and soul and confessed the existence of angels and spirits, the latter, according to the Acts of the Apostles, denied everything.

And they questioned him, saying: Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if someone’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, his brother should take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died, leaving no offspring, etc. Those who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies, judging that souls perished together with bodies, rightly invent a story of this kind, which would expose as madness the claims of those who asserted the resurrection of bodies. It is possible, however, that something of this sort really happened among their people at some time.

At the resurrection, then, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife. They oppose the absurdity of the story to deny the truth of the resurrection. Mystically, however, these seven brothers who died without children correspond to all the reprobate, who throughout the whole course of this age—which revolves through seven days—remain sterile in good works. When these men have been individually carried off by wretched death, worldly life itself, which they spent without the fruit of a living work, will finally pass away like an unfruitful wife.

And Jesus answered and said to them: Is this not why you go astray, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? They go astray because they do not know the Scriptures. And because they are ignorant of the Scriptures, they consequently do not know the power of God—that is, Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Corinthians I).

For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. Women are properly said to marry, while men are said to take wives. But let us understand the statement simply, as though “marry” were said of men and “be given in marriage” of women. If in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, then bodies capable of marrying and being given in marriage will rise. No one says of a stone or a tree, or of things that have no sexual organs, that they neither marry nor are given in marriage; the statement concerns those who, although capable of marrying, nevertheless do not marry for some reason. What follows—“But they are like angels in heaven”—promises a spiritual way of life. They are like angels in heaven who, renewed by the glory of the resurrection, enjoy the perpetual vision of God without any fear of death, without any stain of corruption, and without any activity belonging to an earthly condition. Whoever desires to rise to this equality with the angelic rank must now stoop in acts of devotion to the least of his brothers.

[Col. 0255A] But concerning the dead, that they rise, have you not read in the book of Moses, at the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? To prove the truth of the resurrection, he could have used many other and clearer examples, among them: “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will arise.” And elsewhere: “Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, some to eternal life, and others to reproach and eternal confusion” (Daniel XII). The question therefore arises what the Lord intended by producing this testimony, which appears ambiguous or does not sufficiently pertain to the truth of the resurrection. We said above that the Sadducees, confessing neither angels, nor spirit, nor the resurrection of bodies, also preached the destruction of souls. They accepted only the five books of Moses and rejected the prophecies of the prophets. It would therefore have been foolish to produce testimonies whose authority they did not follow. Moreover, to prove the immortality of souls he gives the example: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Immediately he adds:

He is not the God of the dead but of the living. Once he has proved that souls remain after death—for he could not be the God of those who did not in any way continue to exist—the resurrection of bodies follows, since bodies, together with souls, have done either good or evil.

And one of the scribes approached; he had heard them disputing. Seeing that he had answered them well, he asked him which commandment was first of all. Jesus answered him that the first of all the commandments is: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

He calls this the first and greatest commandment: before all else, each person must establish it deeply in the heart as the sole foundation of devotion. He demonstrated this more clearly in his conclusion when he said: “There is no other commandment greater than these.” The first and greatest commandment, therefore, is knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the practice of good works. Good works are perfected in love of God and neighbor. The Apostle commends this briefly in other words, saying: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians V).

And the scribe said to him: Well said, teacher; you have spoken the truth, for there is one God, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart, with all the understanding, with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. This response of the scribe shows that a serious question was often debated among the scribes and Pharisees: which commandment of the divine law was first or greatest. Some praised victims and sacrifices, while others, with greater authority, preferred works of faith and love, since many of the fathers before the law pleased God solely through faith—which works through love—without any practice of victims or sacrifices, and held the highest place with him. No one, however, is ever found to have pleased God through burnt offerings and sacrifices alone, without faith and love. The scribe declared that he too held this position.

But Jesus, seeing that he had answered wisely, said to him: You are not far from the kingdom of God. He was not far from the kingdom of God because he proved to be a supporter of the position proper to the New Testament and to evangelical perfection. Hence we must inquire more carefully how Matthew says that this scribe, or doctor of the law—as Matthew himself calls him—tested the Lord by asking about the first or greatest commandment, while according to this evangelist the Lord declares that he is not far from the kingdom of God. For it is clear that those who seek wisdom by testing cannot find it, and therefore cannot approach the gates of the heavenly kingdom, which is opened only to the wise. Scripture says: “Seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him” (Wisdom I). Unless perhaps we say that although he approached the Lord intending to test him, after hearing his answer he was corrected and immediately returned to the grace of devotion; and that the one whom he had previously thought should be deceived by testing, he later recognized as one to be embraced and followed. Or perhaps we should not understand the testing as evil, like that of an enemy wishing to deceive, but rather as cautious, like that of one wishing to examine someone unknown. For it was not written without reason: “Whoever is quick to believe will be diminished in heart” (Ecclesiasticus XIX).

And no one dared to question him any longer. The Pharisees, Sadducees, and the other leaders of the Jews, seeking an opportunity for accusation and trying to find some word that could be used against him, had been refuted in their arguments. They no longer questioned him but openly handed him over, once he had been seized, to the Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but are slow to cease.

And Jesus answered and said, while teaching in the temple: How do the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David? For David himself says in the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.’” David himself calls him Lord; how then is he his son? Jesus’ question benefits us even today in argument against the Jews. Those who confess that Christ is to come also assert that he is merely a holy human being descended from David. Let us therefore ask them, taught by the Lord: if he is merely a human being and only David’s son, how does David call him his Lord—not through an uncertain error or by his own will, but in the Holy Spirit? They are not reproved for calling him David’s son, but because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. For he is both David’s Lord, remaining God before all ages, and David’s son, born as a human being at the end of time. The fact that the enemies are subjected to him by the Father signifies not the Son’s weakness but the unity of nature, because one acts in the other. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father on earth.

And in his teaching he said to them: Beware of the scribes who wish to walk about in robes, to be greeted in the marketplace, to sit in the first seats in the synagogues, and to have the places of honor at banquets. To walk about in robes means to appear in public dressed in more splendid garments. Among others, the rich man who feasted splendidly every day is described as having sinned in this way. It should be noted that he does not forbid those to be greeted in the marketplace or to sit or recline first whose official position entitles them to such honors. Rather, he teaches the faithful to beware as wicked those who improperly love these things, whether they possess them or do not possess them, reproving the mind—not the rank—with just severity. Yet it is also blameworthy if those who wish to be called teachers of the synagogue on the chair of Moses take part in lawsuits in the marketplace. For two reasons, indeed, we are commanded to be attentive to those who desire empty glory: we must judge the good things they do to be worth doing, or else be inflamed by rivalry and rejoice in vain to be praised for the good things they only pretend to do.

They devour widows’ houses under the pretext of lengthy prayer; these will receive a more lengthy judgment. He does not merely say, “They will receive judgment,” but adds “more lengthy,” indicating that even those who pray standing in the corners so as to be seen by people deserve condemnation, while those who pursue these practices more extensively, acting as though they were more religious, and seek not only praise from people but also money, are to be punished by a more severe judgment. There are people who pretend to be righteous and highly esteemed by God and do not hesitate to accept money from the lowliest people, troubled by the awareness of their sins, as though they were going to be their patrons in judgment. Although prayers ordinarily help a poor person with an outstretched hand, these men spend the night in prayer chiefly for this purpose: to take money from the poor. The curse of Judas rightly applies to them: “When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin” (Psalm CVIII). He goes out condemned when he is judged, and turns his prayer into sin when the man who is now held in high esteem by people discovers then, in the divine judgment, that he can neither intervene for others nor even rely upon his own merits; indeed, he pays the penalty among his crimes for the very prayers by which he had deceived human judgment.

And Jesus, sitting opposite the treasury, watched how the crowd was throwing copper coins into the treasury. Since in Greek the word φυλάττειν means “to guard,” and *gaza* in the Persian language means “wealth,” the treasury is ordinarily called the place where wealth is guarded. By this name they also called both the chest into which the people’s offerings were collected for the temple’s necessary uses and the porticoes in which they were kept. You have an example concerning the porticoes in the Gospel: “Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple” (John 8). You have an example concerning the chest in the Book of Kings: “Jehoiada the high priest took one treasury chest, opened an opening in its top, and placed it beside the altar, on the right as one enters the house of the Lord. The priests who guarded the doors put into it all the money that was brought to the temple of the Lord. When they saw that there was a great deal of money in the treasury, the king’s scribe and the high priest came up, poured it out, and counted the money found in the house of the Lord” (2 Kings 12). Thus the Lord, who had warned that seekers after precedence and empty glory were to be avoided, and who had foretold that a greater judgment would be rendered for feigned prayers, also distinguishes with exact judgment those who bring gifts into the house of the Lord, so that he may repay each according to their heart and works, because the same internal judge never ceases to act in the same way in the Church.

And many rich people were throwing in large amounts. But when one poor widow came, she put in two small coins, which is a quadrans. Calculators call a quadrans the fourth part of any thing—whether of a place, a period of time, or money. Perhaps, therefore, in this passage it signifies a fourth part of a shekel, that is, five obols.

And calling his disciples, he said to them: “Amen I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who put into the treasury.” This passage teaches us morally that whatever we offer with a good intention is acceptable to God. He weighs not the substance of those who offer, but their conscience; he does not consider how much is in his sacrifice, but from how much it is offered. According to the laws of allegory, however, the rich who were putting gifts into the treasury represent the Jews, uplifted by the righteousness of the Law; while the poor widow represents the simplicity of the Church. She is rightly called poor because she has cast away the spirit of pride and the desires for temporal things, as though they were the riches of the world. She is a widow because her husband endured death for her and now, hidden from her eyes in the inner chambers of heaven, lives as if in a part of another region. She puts in two small coins into the treasury because she brings before the sight of the divine Majesty either the gifts of love of God and neighbor or those of her faith and prayer. In that treasury the offerings of our devoted activity are preserved, recorded and sealed as though in an exact account. These offerings, small when her own frailty is considered but accepted because of the merit of her devout intention, surpass all the works of the proud Jews.

“For all of them put in out of what abounded to them. But she, out of her want, put in all that she had, her whole livelihood.”

The Jew puts into God’s gifts out of abundance when, presuming upon his own righteousness, he prays thus within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of mankind—robbers, unjust persons, etc.” (Luke 18). But the Church puts her whole livelihood into God’s gifts, because she understands that all that she lives by is not due to her own merit but to God’s gift, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid.). And again: “I will keep my strength for you, because you, O God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58).

**BOOK FOUR**

**CHAPTER XIII**

And as he was leaving the temple, one of his disciples said to him: “Teacher, look at the kind of stones and the kind of buildings!” And Jesus answered him: “Do you see all these great buildings? Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

According to the historical sense, the meaning is clear. When the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures of the Law and the arrangement of its commandments were so destroyed that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews; and once the head had been removed, all the members fought against one another. Since, moreover, when faith had been established among the nations and the Church of Christ had been founded, Judaea was destined to pay the penalties deserved by its faithlessness, the Lord appropriately leaves the temple after praising the Church’s devotion in the poor widow, and foretells that its future ruin and its buildings, then objects of admiration, would shortly afterward be leveled. Divine providence arranged that, once the grace of evangelical faith had been revealed throughout the world, the temple itself, formerly august, should be removed together with its ceremonies. Otherwise someone still immature and infantile in faith, seeing those things remain which had been established by the holy prophets and instituted by the Lord, might gradually slip from the sincerity of faith that is in Christ Jesus into carnal Judaism through admiration for a holy worldly institution. Thus God, providing for our weakness and desiring his Church to multiply, caused all those things to be overturned and utterly removed, so that when shadow and type had ceased, the truth itself, now declared throughout the world, might hold the more genuine palm of victory.

And as he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew questioned him privately: “Tell us, when will these things happen, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to reach their fulfillment?”

Because some had praised the temple’s buildings, the Lord had openly answered that all these things would be destroyed; the disciples therefore privately ask about the time and signs of the destruction foretold. The Lord sits on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple when he discusses the temple’s ruin and the destruction of the nation, so that even the position of his body may correspond to the words he speaks. Mystically, he signifies that, remaining at rest among the holy, he detests the madness of the proud. For who does not see that the Mount of Olives designates the fruitful height of the holy Church, in which the Lord always delights to dwell? That mountain bore not unfruitful trees and a sterile forest, but olives, whose oil nourishes light to dispel the darkness of night, heals infirmities, and grants rest to the weary. The Church itself proves that all these things occur especially in her when it says: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, will hope in the mercy of my God” (Psalm 51).

And Jesus answered and began to say to them: “See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will deceive many.”

As the destruction of Jerusalem approached, many leaders arose who claimed to be christs and reported that the time of freedom was already, almost at that very moment, approaching. In the Church itself, during the times of the apostles, many heresiarchs appeared who, among their many other teachings contrary to the truth, proclaimed that the day of the Lord was imminent. The Apostle condemns them in his Letter to the Thessalonians. Many Antichrists came in Christ’s name; the first of them was Simon Magus. As we read in the Acts of the Apostles, everyone in Samaria, from the least to the greatest, listened to him, saying: “This man is the power of God that is called Great,” because he had bewildered them for a long time by his magical arts (Acts 8).

“But when you hear of wars and reports of wars, do not be afraid. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet.”

Wars concern enemies, but seditions concern citizens. It is abundantly clear that both of these had prevailed among the Jewish people from the time of the Lord’s passion onward—the people who chose a seditious robber instead of Christ the Savior. But as these events approach, the apostles are warned not to be frightened and not to abandon Jerusalem and Judaea, because the end—namely, the desolation of the province—would not immediately follow; rather, it would be delayed for forty years, after which would come the final destruction of the city and temple.

“For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines. These things are the beginning of sorrows.”

In the Gospel of Luke it is written: “There will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines” (Luke 21). It is clear that these events literally occurred before the final and most grievous sufferings, by which the whole province was devastated—indeed, wiped out—namely, during the Jewish revolt. But “kingdom against kingdom,” the pestilence of those whose speech spreads like cancer, famine for hearing the word of God, the shaking of the whole earth, and separation from the true faith may be understood more appropriately of heretics, who fight against one another and thereby create victory for the Church.

That so many adversities were deservedly to be poured out upon Jerusalem and the entire province of the Jews, the Lord makes clear by adding:

“But take heed to yourselves, for they will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before kings and governors because of me, as a testimony to them.”

This was either the sole or the principal cause of the Jewish nation’s destruction: after the murder of the Lord and Savior, it also persecuted the heralds and confessors of his name and faith with impious cruelty.

“And the Gospel of God must first be preached among all the nations.”

That this was fulfilled is attested by ecclesiastical histories, which report that all the apostles, long before the destruction of the province of Judaea, were dispersed throughout the entire world to preach the Gospel, with the exception of James the son of Zebedee and James the brother of the Lord, who had earlier shed their blood in Judaea for the word of the Gospel. Since the Lord knew that the hearts of the disciples would be distressed by the destruction and ruin of their nation, he lifts them up with this consolation: they were to know that, even though the Jews had been rejected, they would not lack companions in joy and the heavenly kingdom. Indeed, far more people than would perish from Judaea would be gathered from all the nations throughout the world.

“And when they lead you away and hand you over, do not prepare beforehand what you should say; but whatever is given to you in that hour, say it. For it is not you who are speaking, but the Holy Spirit.”

When we are led before judges because of Christ, we ought to express only our own will on Christ’s behalf. As for the rest, Christ himself, who dwells in us, speaks, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is supplied in our reply.

“Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his child, and children will rise up against their parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name. But whoever…” etc.

We have often seen this happen during persecutions, and there is no faithful affection among those whose faith is divided.

“But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—let the reader understand.”

For what Mark says, “standing where it ought not to be,” Matthew has written, “standing in the holy place” (Matthew 24). In every respect the two expressions signify the same thing, since the abomination of desolation ought not to stand in a holy place. When we are summoned to understanding, it is shown that the saying has a mystical meaning. In a simple sense it may refer either to the Antichrist, or to the image of Caesar that Pilate placed in the temple, or to the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood for a long time in the very place of the Holy of Holies. According to the ancient Scripture, an idol is also called an “abomination.” Hence “of desolation” is added, because an idol was placed in the desolated and deserted temple.

“Then let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down into the house, nor enter to take anything from his house. And let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his garment.”

It is clear that these things were fulfilled literally. When the Roman war and the extermination of the Jewish nation were approaching, all the Christians in the province, warned by an oracle, withdrew farther away, as ecclesiastical history relates. Settling beyond the Jordan, they remained for a time in the city of Pella under the protection of Agrippa, king of the Jews, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles and who, with that part of the Jews that wished to obey him, always remained subject to Roman rule.

According to the spiritual meanings, when we see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—that is, when we perceive heresies and crimes reigning among those who seemed to have been consecrated to heavenly mysteries; when we see those who practice iniquity and speak lies, men of blood and deceit, whom the Lord abhors, disturbing the peace of the faithful—then all of us who are in Judaea, that is, who persist in confessing the true faith, must not be enslaved to earthly and weak actions. Rather, we must ascend to the summit of virtues all the higher as we see more people following the broad and wandering paths of vice.

Then the one who is on the housetop—that is, the one who has risen above carnal things in mind and lives spiritually as if in the free air—must not descend to the lowly actions of his former way of life, nor return to the desires of the world or the flesh that he had abandoned. Our house is to be understood either as this world or as our own flesh, in which we dwell. Concerning it the Apostle says: “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God” (1 Corinthians 5).

And the one who works in the Church, planting and watering like Paul and Apollos (1 Corinthians 3), must not look back toward the worldly hope to which he renounced himself, nor rashly presume to resume the bonds of this transitory life, which he had already stripped off in order to follow Christ naked.

“But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in those days.”

Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing during the captivity then present, since the burdens of their wombs or the hands of their children greatly impede the necessity of flight. Read the history in the Book of Kings, where Jonathan’s wife, attempting to avoid the evil of captivity by a hasty flight, fell and received her son into her lap, leaving him permanently lame.

“But pray that it may not happen in winter.”

Matthew has written: “Pray, however, that your flight may not happen in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24). If we understand this of the captivity of Jerusalem, when it was captured by Titus and Vespasian, they ought to pray that their flight not take place in winter or on the Sabbath. In the one case, the harshness of the cold prevents them from going into solitude and hiding in the mountains and deserted places; in the other, either fleeing would be a transgression of the Law, or remaining would mean imminent death.

But if it is understood of the consummation of the world, this commands that our faith and love for Christ not grow cold, and that we not grow sluggish in idleness on the Sabbath of virtues, that is, in the work of God. This saying of the Lord therefore refers partly to the Jewish captivity brought about by the Romans and partly to the day of judgment. For in Matthew, too, the disciples are read to have asked the Lord, when he was about to say these things: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?”

“For those days will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, nor will there be.”

These words properly apply to the time of the Antichrist, when not only more frequent torments than previously customary will be inflicted upon the faithful, but—what is more grievous—the working of signs will also accompany those who inflict the torments. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “His coming is according to the working of Satan, with every deception, signs, and false wonders” (2 Thessalonians 2).

How many miracles and how many acts of power the holy martyrs often performed before their persecutors, and yet those persecutors neither wished to believe nor to cease persecuting! Who, then, would convert an unbeliever to faith, when the faith of one who already believes would not be terrified and shaken, if the persecutor of piety were also to become a worker of wonders—if the very person who rages with torments so that Christ may be denied were to provoke belief in the Antichrist through miracles?

What refuge, then, what hope will remain for the elect amid these things, unless the heavenly grace that grants the righteous the power of endurance should quickly take away from the wicked the power to persecute and afflict? Therefore, with provident compassion, he adds:

“And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days.”

This tribulation will be all the more moderate in the brevity of its duration as it is more severe than the other pressures that preceded it in the weight of its suffering. For it is believed, insofar as one may infer from the prophecy of Daniel and the Apocalypse of Saint John, that it will attack the Church throughout the world for three and a half years.

“And then, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ! Look, there!’ do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and portents in order to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.”

Some refer these words to the time of the Jewish captivity, when many who claimed to be christs drew behind them crowds of deceived people. But it should be noted that during the miserable siege of that wretched city there was no faithful person to whom the divine exhortation not to follow perverse teachers would need to be given. Rather, all alike—the lesser and the greater, the besieged and the besiegers—remained estranged from Christ. It is therefore better understood of heretics, who come against the Church falsely claiming to be christs. The first of these was Simon Magus; the last, and greater than the others, is the Antichrist.

“But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars of heaven will be falling.”

The heavenly bodies will appear dark on the day of judgment, not because their light has diminished, but because the brightness of the true light—the supreme Judge—will have come upon them when he appears in his majesty, and in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels. Nothing, however, prevents us from understanding this literally: the sun and moon, together with the other stars, may then for a time be deprived of their light, just as the sun is known to have been during the Lord’s passion. At that time the moon, being full, lay hidden beneath the obscuring earth. Hence the prophecy of Joel remains incomplete to this day. After saying, “The sun will be turned into darkness,” he added, “and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2).

Likewise Isaiah, speaking of the day of judgment, says: “The moon will be ashamed and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the presence of his elders” (Isaiah 24).

But after the day of judgment has been completed and the glory of the future life has begun to shine, when there is a new heaven and a new earth, what the same prophet says elsewhere will take place: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days.”

“And the powers that are in the heavens will be shaken.”

What wonder that human beings, who are earthly both by nature and by perception, should be disturbed by this judgment, when even the powers of heaven themselves—that is, the angelic powers—tremble at its sight? Blessed Job also bears witness to this, saying: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command” (Job 26). What, then, will the boards do when the pillars tremble? What will the reed of the desert suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

“And then he will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.”

By “the four winds” he means the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. And lest anyone suppose that the elect will be gathered only from the four quarters of the earth, rather than from all its extremities together with its inland regions, he appropriately adds: “From the end of the earth to the end of heaven”—that is, directly from the furthest boundaries of the earth to its farthest limits, where, to those looking from a distance, the circle of heaven appears to touch the earth.

No elect person, therefore, will remain on that day who does not meet the Lord as he comes to judgment in the air, whether found still living in the body or already raised from death to life. The reprobate, too, come to judgment: some are found living in the body, others are raised from death to life. But there is this difference: the righteous are gathered into the joy of their Lord, whereas his enemies, once judgment has been completed, will be scattered and perish from the presence of God.

“From the fig tree learn the parable: when its branch has already become tender and its leaves have appeared, you know that summer is near. So also you…” etc.

By the example of a tree he taught about the coming of the consummation. “Just as,” he says, “when the shoots of the fig tree have become tender, a bud bursts into flower, and the bark gives birth to leaves, you understand that summer is coming and that the west wind and spring are entering, so, when you see all these things that have been written, do not suppose that the consummation of the world has already arrived. Rather, understand that they come as preambles and forerunners, showing that it is near and at the doors.”

According to mystical meanings, however, this fruitfulness of the fig tree can be understood more deeply, namely, of the state of the synagogue. Once, when the Lord came to it, because it had no fruit of righteousness, it was condemned to eternal barrenness in those who were then unbelieving. But since the Apostle said that “a hardening has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11), when the time arrives for the long blindness of faithlessness to be removed and for all Israel to receive light and salvation, what will the formerly barren fig tree do except return the fruit it had refused to yield?

This accords with blessed Job: “A tree has hope: if it has been cut down, it will flourish again, and its branches will sprout. If its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and produce a crown of foliage, as when it was first planted.” When you see this happen, you will not doubt that the day of the final judgment and the summer of true peace and light are near.

“Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.”

By “generation” he means either the entire human race or, specifically, the Jews.

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

The heaven that will pass away should be understood not as the ethereal or starry heaven, but as the aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven and the clouds of heaven receive their names. Peter bears witness to this when he says: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed was destroyed, being flooded with water. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people” (2 Peter 3). He clearly teaches that the heavens destined to perish by fire are none other than those destroyed by water—that is, these empty and cloudy expanses of the windy air. The water of the flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain peaks, should not be believed to have reached beyond the boundaries of the air and the ether. Wherever the floodwater could reach, there, in accordance with the blessed Peter’s statement cited above, the fire of judgment will also reach.

But if heaven and earth will pass away, one may ask how Ecclesiastes can say: “One generation passes away and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1). The clear answer is that heaven and earth pass away with respect to the form they now have, yet in their essence they continue without end. “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7). And the angel says to John: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21). These will not be newly created as different things, but these same things will be renewed.

Heaven and earth, therefore, both pass away and will remain, because they are cleansed by fire from the form they now possess, yet are preserved always in their own nature. Hence the Psalmist also says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101). The final change of these things is now announced to us by the very alternations through which they continually vary for our use. The earth, deprived of its winter appearance by dryness, grows green through the moisture of spring. The heaven is daily covered with the darkness of night and renewed by divine brightness. From this, then, let every faithful person understand that these things both perish and are nevertheless restored through renewal, since they are constantly repaired as though from a state of decline.

“But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.”

Arius and Eunomius rejoice, as though the teacher’s ignorance were the disciples’ glory, and they say: “The one who knows cannot be equal to the one who is ignorant.” Yet Jesus—the Word of God—made all times, for “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Since the day of judgment is included among all times, how can he be ignorant of a part whose whole he knows?

The reason must therefore be given why he is said to be ignorant. The Apostle wrote concerning the Savior: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2). Why are they hidden? After his resurrection, when the apostles questioned him about the day of judgment, he answered more clearly: “It is not for you to know the times and moments that the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1). When he says, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows, but that it is not beneficial for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on that day. Finally, what follows in the Gospel also compels us to understand the matter in this way. In teaching that the Father alone knows, he includes the Son in the Father. For “Father” is, in every case, a name that implies a Son.

“See, keep watch, and pray. For you do not know when the time will be. It is like a man who has gone on a journey and left his house and given authority to his servants,” etc.

The Lord clearly shows why he said: “Concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.” It is not beneficial for the apostles to know, so that, suspended in uncertain expectation, they may always believe that the one whose coming they do not know is about to come. He did not say, “We do not know at what hour the Lord will come,” but, “You do not know.” After giving the example of the master of the household, he teaches more plainly why he keeps the day of the consummation secret, saying:

“Keep watch, therefore; for you do not know when the Lord of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning. Otherwise, coming suddenly, he may find you sleeping.”

The man who went on a journey and left his house is undoubtedly Christ. After his resurrection he ascended victoriously to the Father and left the Church bodily, yet he never deprived her of the protection of his divine presence, remaining in her all the days until the consummation of the age. The proper place of the flesh is the earth, but it was led, as it were, to a foreign place when, through our Redeemer, it was established in heaven.

He gave his servants authority for every task because, having granted his faithful the grace of the Holy Spirit, he gave them the ability to serve through good works. He also commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch, because he orders the order of pastors and spiritual leaders to devote themselves to the care of the Church entrusted to them with vigilant attention.

“And what I say to you I say to all: Keep watch.”

We are commanded to keep watch not only by the apostles and their successors, the leaders of the Church, but by all of us. We are all commanded continually to guard the doors of our hearts, lest the ancient enemy break in by suggesting evil. Each of us must take diligent precautions so that the Lord, when he comes, does not find us sleeping. For each person will give an account to God for himself.

The one who keeps watch maintains the eyes of the mind open for the sight of the true light. The one who keeps watch preserves through action what he believes. The one who keeps watch drives from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence. Hence Paul says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15). Again he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13).

**CHAPTER XIV**

It was Passover, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread was two days away.

Passover, called *phase* in Hebrew, is named not from *passio*, “passion,” as most people think, but from “passing over,” because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not strike them; or because the Lord himself, offering help to his people, passed over them from above. Evangelist John, expounding the sacramental meaning of the word more profoundly, says: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). He plainly declares that the day of this solemnity was mystically called “the Passover” because the Lamb of God, who would take away the sins of the world, was to pass from this world—either passing over himself or leading us through a saving passage, as though from Egyptian slavery.

According to the text of the Old Testament, there is this distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover is the name of the single day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, namely, the fourteenth day of the first month. On the fifteenth day, when they departed from Egypt, the festival of Unleavened Bread followed; it was established as a solemnity lasting seven days, that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month.

The evangelists, however, customarily use the terms interchangeably, calling both the day of Unleavened Bread “Passover” and the Feast of Unleavened Bread “Passover.” Mark says: “It was Passover and Unleavened Bread, two days away” (Mark 14). Luke says: “The feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover” (Luke 22). Likewise John, when the matter was taking place on the first day of Unleavened Bread, that is, on the fifteenth day, says: “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled but might eat the Passover” (John 18).

They did this because the day of Passover was also commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread, and because, as though celebrating a perpetual Passover, we are commanded always to pass from this world. One day saw the lamb sacrificed in the evening; seven days of Unleavened Bread follow in order, because Christ Jesus, having suffered once in the flesh for us in the fullness of time, commanded us to live throughout the whole period of this age—which is reckoned in seven days—in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5). With every effort, he admonishes us to flee earthly desires as though they were the bonds of Egypt and, as if withdrawing from worldly conduct, to undertake the secluded journey of the virtues.

And the chief priests and scribes were seeking how they might seize and kill him by deceit. But they were saying: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps there be a disturbance among the people.”

They ought to have prepared victims for the approaching Passover, smoothed the walls of the temple, swept the floors, cleansed the vessels, and purified themselves according to the rite of the Law so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb. Instead, they gathered and began plotting how to kill the Lord. As the simple wording shows, they were not afraid of sedition; they feared that, with the people’s help, he might be taken from their hands.

And when he was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, and reclining at table.

About to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations by his blood, he stays in Bethany, the house of obedience, which had once belonged to Simon the leper—not because he remained leprous at that time, but because he had formerly been a leper and was afterward cleansed by the Savior, while his former name remained, so that the power of the healer might be displayed. Thus, too, in the catalogue of the apostles, Matthew is called a publican by his former vice and occupation, although he had certainly ceased to be a publican. Some wish to understand Simon the leper as the portion of the people that believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon also means “obedient.”

[Col. 0268A] A woman came with an alabaster vessel of costly ointment of spikenard; and, breaking the alabaster, she poured it over his head. This woman was Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, whom Jesus raised from the dead, as John explicitly records.
