He also testifies that this event took place six days before Passover, on the day before Jesus came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, amid palms and the acclamation of the crowds.

She was the same woman, and not another, who formerly—as Luke writes—while still a sinner, came and bathed the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance, anointed them with the ointment of pious confession, and, because she loved greatly, obtained from the merciful Judge forgiveness for her many sins. But now, justified and made familiar to the Lord, she poured holy oil not only on his feet—as John likewise relates—but also on his head, as Matthew and Mark testify.

Alabaster is a kind of white marble interspersed with various spots, from which ointment vessels are customarily carved, since it is said to preserve their contents most effectively and keep them unspoiled. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, where it is whiter than elsewhere; the finest, however, is found in India.

Nard is an aromatic shrub with, they say, a strong and thick root, though it is short, black, brittle, and yet oily, having a scent like *sinum* [reading uncertain] or cypress; it has a harsh taste and a small, dense leaf whose tips spread into spikes. For this reason perfumers celebrate both the spikes and the leaves of nard as possessing a double endowment. This is what Mark means when he says, “costly ointment of spikenard.” For the ointment that Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard; to make it more precious, the fragrance and potency of its spikes and leaves were also added, increasing its excellence.

Natural philosophers report concerning nard that it holds the chief place among ointments. Hence it was fittingly offered for anointing the Lord’s head and feet. There are indeed many varieties of it, but all are less effective than the Indian variety, which is more precious.

[Col. 0268C] Mystically, this devotion of Mary ministering to the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks in the Song of Love, saying: “While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song of Songs 1). These words she fulfilled once, literally, by Mary’s hands; and she does not cease fulfilling them spiritually every day in all her members, who glory as they are spread throughout the whole world and say: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2).

When the Church acknowledges, praises, and proclaims with fitting reverence the power of his divine nature, which he possesses together with the Father, she surely pours precious ointment upon his head. But when she regards with equally fitting reverence the mysteries of his assumed humanity, she pours upon the Lord’s feet the ointment of spikenard, *pisticum*, that is, faithful and true. For she commends by her pious preaching and venerates with devoted service that nature of his by which he deigned to touch the earth—that is, to dwell among human beings.

There were some who were indignant within themselves and said: “Why has this ointment been wasted? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” Mark too, like Matthew, speaks here by synecdoche (*synecdōchicōs*), using the plural number for the singular. For John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this, because of his greed: he had been a thief, and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it.

It can also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded of it when Judas said it, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of them all in their words. But Judas is so identified because he was a thief, whereas the others acted from concern for the poor [alternative reading: “rejoiced” (*laetari*)]. John, however, wished to record this only of the one whose habit of stealing he believed should be disclosed on this occasion.

What follows is:

“And they were indignant against her.”

I do not believe that this was said of the good apostles who loved Christ and were diligent in his service, but rather of that one, mentioned under a plural number, who was shown to have adhered faithfully neither to the Lord nor to his disciples, and to have had no concern for the poor.

But Jesus said: “Let her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has performed a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me.” Another question arises: why did Jesus say to the disciples after his resurrection, “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28), while here he says, “You will not always have me”? It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence, since after the resurrection he would not be with them in the same way as he was then, in constant companionship and familiarity. Remembering this, the Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him thus no longer” (2 Corinthians 5).

“What she had, she did; she went beforehand to anoint my body for burial.” What you consider the waste of the ointment is an act of preparation for burial. Nor is it surprising that she gave me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

“Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” Consider his knowledge of the future: although he was to suffer after only a few days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world.

It should be noted that, just as Mary obtained glory throughout the world, wherever the holy Church has been spread, because of the service of pious devotion that she offered to the Lord, so, conversely, the man who did not fear to disparage her service with a reckless tongue became widely infamous for the mark of treachery and rightly hateful both to God and to human beings. But the Lord, rewarding the good with praise that it deserved, passed over in silence the future insults of the ungodly.

And [Col. 0269D] Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went away to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. Wretched Judas! He believed that he had suffered a loss from the pouring out of the ointment, and he wished to compensate for it with the price of his Master. He no longer demanded a fixed sum, so that his betrayal might at least appear profitable; rather, as though he were selling a worthless slave, he left the amount in the power of the buyers, to give whatever they wished.

When he said, “He went to the chief priest to betray him to them,” he showed that Judas had not been invited by the rulers, nor constrained by any necessity, but had voluntarily undertaken the plan in accordance with his criminal mind.

When they heard this, they rejoiced and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might betray him at a convenient opportunity.

Many people today recoil from Judas’s crime—that he sold the Lord, his Master and his God, for money—as monstrous and abominable, yet they do not guard themselves against committing the same offense. When, for bribes, they give false testimony against anyone, they plainly sell God for money, because he himself said: “I am the truth.” When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because “God is love.”

Therefore those who despise the commands of love and truth certainly betray God, who is love and truth—especially when they do not sin through weakness or ignorance, but, like Judas, seek an opportunity to exchange truth for lies and virtue for crime when witnesses are absent.

And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they were sacrificing the Passover, the disciples said to him: “Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

He calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when, having discarded the leaven, they customarily sacrificed the Passover—that is, killed the lamb—in the evening. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5). Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon, nevertheless on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he both handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated and, when he was seized and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of that sacrifice—that is, of his Passion.

And he sent two of his disciples and said to them: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.” This is indeed a sign of his foreknowing divinity, since, speaking with the disciples, he knew what would happen elsewhere. Fittingly, as the disciples prepared the Passover, a man carrying a jar—or, according to another evangelist, an amphora—of water met them, to show that the mystery of this Passover was to be celebrated for the complete cleansing of the whole world.

Water signifies the bath of grace; the jar signifies the frailty of those through whom that same grace was to be ministered to the world. Hence they say: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4). The disciples therefore prepare the Passover where a jar of water is being carried in, to indicate that the time has come when the blood of the typological Passover is to be removed from the threshold and doorposts of the true worshipers, and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is to be consecrated for removing the sins of the world.

Follow him, and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: “The Teacher says: Where is my dining room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?” Deliberately, the names both of the water-carrier and of the master of the house have been omitted, so that it may be indicated that the opportunity is given to all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments and to receive him as a guest into the lodging of their minds.

And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us, and so forth. The large upper room is the spiritual law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in an elevated place. For whoever still observes the letter that kills, whoever understands nothing more in the lamb than an animal, plainly celebrates the Passover in a lesser way, because he has not yet learned to grasp the majesty of the Spirit in the words of God.

But whoever has followed the water-carrier—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, transcends the surface of the letter through the illuminating Spirit and prepares a meal for Christ in the lofty chamber of the mind. For he recognizes that all the mysteries of the Passover, as well as the other decrees of the law, are his mysteries.

When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve. And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said: “Amen, I say to you: one of you will betray me—the one who is eating with me.” He who had foretold his Passion now foretells the betrayer, leaving room for repentance, so that when Judas realized that his thoughts and the secrets of his conscience were known, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, openly exposed, he become more shameless. He casts the crime into the midst of the group, so that the guilty man might repent.

They began to be distressed and to say to him one by one: “Surely, I am not the one?” The eleven apostles certainly knew that they were thinking nothing of the sort against the Lord, but they trusted their Master more than themselves. Fearing their own frailty, they sadly asked about a sin of which they had no consciousness.

He said to them: “It is one of the Twelve, the one who is dipping his hand with me in the dish.” O wondrous power of the Lord! He had first said, “One of you will betray me.” The betrayer persists in evil; he is accused more clearly, yet his name is still not given. While the others were distressed, withdrawing their hands and forbidding food to their mouths, Judas, in the recklessness and shamelessness with which he was about to betray his Master, also puts his hand into the dish with him, so that audacity might counterfeit a good conscience.

And indeed the Son of Man goes, as it is written concerning him. But woe to that man by whom the Son of Man will be betrayed! Corrected neither the first nor the second time, he does not withdraw his foot from betrayal. Rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. He foretells the punishment, so that the announced torments might correct one whom shame had not overcome.

Even today, and forever, woe to that person who approaches the Lord’s table with an evil mind, with plots concealed in his thoughts, and with a heart polluted by some crime, yet does not fear to participate in the most holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries. For he too, after the example of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely, to his members, whom he dares to profane by presuming upon that immeasurable and inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. He sells God who, neglecting fear and love of him, is shown to love and pursue earthly and perishable things in his place—even criminal things.

“It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” This does not mean that he is to be thought to have existed before he was born, because no one could be well off unless he had existed. It is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist wickedly.

And while they were eating, Jesus took bread, and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, saying: “Take; this is my body.”

When the celebrations of the former Passover had ended—the celebrations held in remembrance of the ancient liberation of God’s people from Egypt—he passed over to the new Passover, which he wished the Church to observe in memory of its redemption. Thus, in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb, he substituted the sacrament of his own body and blood, and showed that he himself was the one of whom it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109).

He himself breaks the bread that he offers to the disciples, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will and arrangement. As he says elsewhere, he has authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again.

For the sake of the sacrament, he first blessed this bread before breaking it, because he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, filled with the grace of divine power the human nature that he had assumed and was about to suffer in. He blessed the bread and broke it because he deigned to subject the assumed human being to death in such a way that he demonstrated that the power of divine immortality truly existed in him, and therefore taught that he would be raised from death all the more swiftly.

And taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. When he is said to have been approaching his Passion, he is reported to have taken bread and given thanks. Thus he gives thanks who receives the scourges of another’s iniquity. He who had done nothing deserving punishment humbly blesses while being punished, so that he might show what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own guilt, if he himself bears patiently the scourges of another’s guilt; and so that he might show what a subject should do when corrected, if, placed under the scourge, he gives equal thanks to his father.

And he said to them: [Col. 0272C] “This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many.” Because bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood in the flesh, the former is mystically referred to the body of Christ and the latter to his blood. But because Christ must also remain in us and we in Christ, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s chalice. For, as John testifies, the waters signify the peoples.

Nor is it permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as a grain of wheat alone, without the addition and preparation of water, cannot become bread. Such an offering would signify that the head should be separated from the members, and it might suggest either that Christ could have suffered without the love of our redemption, or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his Passion.

When he says, “This is my blood of the new covenant” (Matthew 26), he refers to the distinction from the old covenant, which was dedicated by the blood of goats and calves. As the lawgiver said while sprinkling it: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you” (Hebrews 9). For it is necessary that the copies of the true things be cleansed with these offerings, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better sacrifices than these. The Apostle declares this beautifully and fully throughout his Epistle to the Hebrews, distinguishing between the law and the Gospel.

“Amen, I say to you: I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

That the Synagogue is called the Lord’s vine or vineyard is attested both throughout Scripture in various places and more explicitly by Isaiah in the song he sang about it: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5).

From this vineyard the Lord had drunk for a long time, although many of its branches had been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine. For although many in that people strayed from the straight path of faith, there were nevertheless many throughout the whole period of the law whose pious thoughts and supreme virtues delighted God.

But once the Lord had suffered in the flesh and risen from the dead, the time had come for that legal and figurative observance to cease, and for the things performed according to the letter, transferred into a spiritual meaning, to be observed more perfectly in the new covenant with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, as he was going to his Passion, the Lord said: “I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” It is as though he said openly: “I will no longer take pleasure in the carnal ceremonies of the Synagogue, in which even these sacred rites of the paschal lamb held the chief place. The time of my resurrection will come; that day will come when, established in the kingdom of God—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—I will be filled with new joy with you from the fountain of grace, through the salvation of that same people regenerated by the Spirit.”

And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. This is what we read in the Psalm: “The poor will eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him will praise the Lord” (Psalm 21). The hymn may also be understood as that hymn which, according to John, the Lord sang while giving thanks to the Father, in which, raising his eyes upward, he prayed for himself, for the disciples, and for those who would believe through their words.

Fittingly, after imbuing the disciples with the sacraments of his body and blood and commending them to the Father in a devout hymn of intercession, he leads them up to the Mount of Olives, symbolically indicating that through receiving his sacraments and through the help of his intercession, we ought to ascend to higher gifts of virtue and to the charisms of the Holy Spirit, by which we are anointed in the heart.

And Jesus said to them: [Col. 0273D] “You will all be scandalized on this night.” He foretells what they are to suffer, so that when they have suffered it they will not despair of salvation, but may be freed through repentance. He significantly added, “You will be scandalized on this night,” because just as those who become drunk become drunk at night, so those who suffer scandal endure it in night and darkness. But let us say: “The night is far gone; the day is near” (Romans 13).

Because it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah; and, unless I am mistaken, it is said from the prophet’s person to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13). The sixty-eighth Psalm, which is sung entirely by the Lord, also agrees with this meaning: “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued.” The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and from many wandering flocks there may be one flock and one shepherd.

But [Col. 0274A] Peter said to him: “Even if all are scandalized, yet I will not be.” This was neither recklessness nor a lie, but the faith of the apostle Peter and his ardent affection for the Lord and Savior.

And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you: today, on this very night, before the rooster gives its second call, you will deny me three times.” Peter made his promise out of the ardor of faith, while the Savior, as God, knew the future. Note that Peter denies at night, and denies three times. But after the rooster crowed, and as the darkness diminished and the approaching light was announced, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the filth of his threefold denial with tears.

It should certainly not be considered contradictory that, while Mark says, “Before the rooster gives its second call, you will deny me three times,” the other evangelists simply say, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter’s entire denial was a threefold denial. For he remained in the same denial, in the intention and purpose of lying, until, reminded of what had been foretold to him, he was healed by bitter weeping and sorrow of heart.

If this entire denial—that is, the threefold denial—had begun only after the first crowing of the rooster, the three who said that the Lord had foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed would appear to have spoken falsely. Conversely, if he had completed the whole threefold denial before the rooster began to crow, Mark would be found to have reported superfluously, in the Lord’s own words: “Amen, I say to you: tonight, before the rooster gives its second call, you will deny me three times.”

But because that threefold denial began before the first crowing of the rooster, those three evangelists considered not when Peter would complete it, but how great it would be and when it would begin—that is, the threefold denial that would occur before the rooster crowed, although in his mind the whole denial may be understood as present even before the first crowing.

For although the whole threefold denial began in the words of the denier before the first crowing and was completed before the second crowing, nevertheless, in the disposition of Peter’s mind and in his fear, it was conceived in its entirety before the first crowing. It makes no difference over how many intervals of time the three denials were uttered, since his heart possessed the whole denial even before the first crowing, having been filled with such great fear that, when questioned, he could deny the Lord not once only, but a second and a third time.

Thus, for those who attend more correctly and carefully, just as the man who has seen a woman for the purpose of lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart, so whenever Peter expressed in words the fear that he had conceived so vehemently in his mind that it could persist until the third denial of the Lord, the entire threefold denial must be assigned to the moment when a fear sufficient for the threefold denial seized him.

And they come to an estate called Gethsemane. The place of Gethsemane, where the Lord prayed, is shown even today at the foot of the Mount of Olives, with a church now built above it. Gethsemane is interpreted as “valley of the fat ones” or “of fatness.”

Since not only the words and deeds of our Savior, but also the places and times in which he acts and speaks, are—as has often been said—full of mystical figures, when the Lord prays on the mountain he silently admonishes us that we ought to seek only sublime things in prayer and to plead for heavenly goods. But when he prays in a valley, and in the valley of the fat ones or of fatness, he equally intimates that humility must always be preserved in our prayers, together with the inward fatness of love.

Thus no one, while praying to God, should dare to parade his merits after the example of the proud Pharisee, but should rather proclaim with humble voice and mind: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). Nor should anyone whose heart is dry of love for his neighbor kneel to appease the Creator’s favor, like the man who, unwilling to remit to his brother the hundred denarii he owed him, vainly begged his lord to forgive him ten thousand talents.

Nor should anyone whose breast is starved of love for the Creator seek in prayer any temporal thing rather than the vision of God, so as to be numbered among those of whom he himself says: “They have received their reward” (Matthew 6). For what else is it to place one’s thought below than a certain dryness of mind? But those who already, through holy desires, feed upon the food of inward delight by understanding heavenly things grow fat, as it were, on richer nourishment.

The Psalmist desired to be fattened with this fatness when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Psalm 62). As far as the dispensation of the Lord’s Passion itself is concerned, the Lord, aptly approaching death, prayed in the valley of fatness, because through the valley of humility and the fatness of charity he underwent death for us. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Philippians 2). And “greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

And he takes Peter, James, and John with him, and begins to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he says to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Christ fears, while Peter does not fear. Christ fears; Peter says: “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13). Christ says: “My soul is troubled.” Both are true, and both are full of reason, because the one who is inferior does not fear, while the one who is superior assumes the disposition of one who fears.

The former, as a human being, does not understand the force of death. The latter, as God established in a body, displays the frailty of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who deny the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded. Finally, he said this, yet Manichaeus did not believe it, Valentinus denied it, and Marcion judged it a phantom. He so conformed the human being whom he demonstrated by the truth of his body to the corresponding affection that he said: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matthew 26).

He therefore assumed my will; he assumed my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow, because I proclaim the cross. It is my will, which he called his own. Because as a human being he assumed my sorrow, as a human being he spoke …

And therefore he says: “Not what I will, but what you will” (ibid.). It is my sorrow that he assumed with my human affection. Therefore he grieved for me, who had nothing for which to grieve on his own account. And, with the delight of eternal divinity set aside, he is affected by the weariness of my weakness.

“My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death.” The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, since it was the condition of bodily feeling, not fear of death, that troubled him. For he who assumed a body had to undergo all that belongs to a body, so that he might hunger, thirst, be angered, and be saddened. Divinity, however, does not know change through such affections.

“Remain here and keep watch.” And when he had gone forward a little, he fell upon the ground. When he commands, “Remain here and keep watch,” he does not prohibit sleep, whose time had not yet come in the face of the impending danger, but the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of the mind. After giving them the command to remain and keep watch with him, he went forward a little, fell upon his face, and displayed the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh.

And he prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him, and said: “Abba,” and so forth. What was that voice except the sound of our weakness? Many who are still weak are troubled by the death that lies ahead. But let them have a right heart and avoid death as far as they can; and if they cannot, let them say what the Lord himself said—not for his own sake, but for ours. What did he say? “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Behold, you have the human will expressed. Now look at the right heart.

“But not what I will, but what you will.” “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5). He called his own the will that he had assumed temporally from the Virgin; but the will of him who sent him was that will which, as the eternal one, he possessed timelessly in common with the Father.

He prays that the cup may pass, to show truly that he was also human. But remembering why he was sent, he completes the dispensation for which he was sent, and cries: “But not what I will, but what you will.” “If death is to die without my dying,” that is, according to the flesh, “let this cup pass,” he says. But because this will not happen otherwise, he says: “Not what I will, but what you will.”

When he invokes the Father by the twofold name “Abba, Father,” he shows that he is the God and Savior of both peoples, namely, the Jewish and the Gentile. For *abba* likewise signifies “father.” But *abba* is Hebrew, *pater* Greek and Latin. Therefore, to teach that both peoples would believe in him and that he must be invoked by both, he himself first invokes him in both languages. For he is the good shepherd who, by laying down his life for his sheep, makes one sheepfold from two flocks.

Therefore, in the voice of both flocks, he asks the Father’s help, so that we, instructed by his example, whenever we sense adversity approaching, may invoke God the Father—those of Hebrew origin saying *Abba*, and we who have come from the nations to faith in Christ saying “Father”—and may seek heavenly protection with one devotion of faith and charity.

Hence the eminent teacher, taking from the Lord the form of instruction, addresses his hearers in this way: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8). “Abba” for those who come from the people of Israel; “Father” for us who have come from the nations to faith in Christ.

And he comes and finds them sleeping, and says to Peter: “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not keep watch for one hour?” He who had said above, “Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized,” is now unable to overcome sleep because of the magnitude of his sorrow.

“Keep watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “And do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6)—that is, temptation which we cannot bear. We do not reject temptation altogether, but pray for the strength to endure temptations.

Therefore, at present he does not say, “Keep watch and pray, lest you be tempted,” but “lest you enter into temptation.” That is, lest temptation finally overcome you and hold you within its snares. For example, a martyr who sheds his blood in confession of the Lord is indeed tempted, but is not bound in the nets of temptation. Whoever denies, however, falls into the wounds of temptation.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” This was said against the presumptuous, who think that whatever they believe they can accomplish. Therefore, as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, so much must we fear the frailty of the flesh. Yet, according to the Apostle, let us put to death the works of the flesh by the Spirit.

This passage also stands against the Eutychians, who say that in the mediator between God and human beings, our Lord and Savior, there was one operation and one will. For when he says, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” he shows two wills: the human, which belongs to the flesh, and the divine, which belongs to the Godhead. Here the human will, because of the weakness of the flesh, refuses Passion; the divine will, however, is most ready. For to fear in the Passion belongs to human weakness; to undertake the dispensation of the Passion belongs to divine will and power.

And again, going away, he prayed, saying the same words; and returning once more, he found them sleeping. He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all. The eyes of the apostles were growing weak and were weighed down by sleep, with denial near at hand.

And he comes a third time and says to them: “Sleep now and rest; it is enough,” and so forth. When he had said, “Sleep now and rest,” and added, “It is enough,” and then continued, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be betrayed,” and so forth, it is certainly understood that after saying to them, “Sleep and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a while, allowing what he had announced to occur, and then added: “Behold, the hour is near,” or, “The hour has come.”

For this reason *sufficit*—“it is enough”—was placed after those words: that is, “It is enough that you have rested now.” But because the Lord’s intervening silence has not itself been recorded, the passage constrains the understanding, so that another punctuation or delivery must be sought in those words.

[Col. 0278A] “Rise; let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me is near.” After praying three times and commanding that the apostles’ fear be corrected through the repentance that would follow, he proceeds confidently toward his persecutors, willingly presenting himself to be killed, and says to the disciples: “Rise; let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me is near.” Let him not find us as though we were afraid and drawing back; let us go willingly to death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of those who are to suffer.

[Col. 0278B] The betrayer had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss,” and so forth. It was shameless and criminal presumption to call him “Master” and to offer a kiss to the one he was betraying. Yet he still retains something of a disciple’s modesty, since he did not openly hand him over to the persecutors, but did so by the sign of a kiss.

The Lord accepted the betrayer’s kiss, not to teach us to pretend, but lest he appear to flee from the betrayer, and at the same time fulfilling the saying of David: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119).

But one of those standing nearby drew a sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. Peter did this, as the evangelist John makes clear, with the same ardor of mind with which he had done the other things. For he knew how Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious men, had received the reward of justice, an everlasting priesthood.

Luke adds that the Lord touched the servant’s ear and healed him. The Lord therefore never forgets his compassion: he does not permit even his enemies to be wounded. They inflict death upon the righteous man; he heals the wounds of his persecutors. Mystically, he teaches that even those who, by consenting to his death, had contracted a wound of soul could, if they produced worthy fruits of repentance, merit salvation.

[Col. 0278C] And Jesus answered and said to them: “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to seize me?” and so forth. “It is foolish,” he says, “to seek with swords and clubs one who willingly hands himself over to your hands; and, as though I were hiding at night and avoiding your eyes, to investigate through a betrayer one who taught daily in the temple. But for this reason you gather against me in darkness: because your power is in darkness.”

Then his disciples, leaving him, all fled. The Lord’s saying is fulfilled, that all the disciples would be scandalized in him on that very night. For although they fled at the Lord’s request, as John writes, they nevertheless displayed the fear and timidity of their minds, since they proved more ready to seek the protection of flight than to trustingly suffer with Christ.

A certain young man was following him, clothed in a linen garment over his naked body, and they seized him. But he, abandoning the linen garment, fled from them naked. By the words “clothed in a linen garment over his naked body,” the body is understood—that is, over a naked body—because he had no other clothing than the linen garment alone. The evangelist does not say who this young man was. Whoever he was, he proves that the Lord’s love remained greater in him than in the others: when they had already fled, he himself, held fast by the bond of love until he was seized by the enemies, did not cease to follow him. Yet he did not possess perfect love, since, when seized, he was able to flee from the Savior’s company. For just as perfect love casts out fear (1 John IV), so fear besieging the mind shows love to be imperfect.

But we should examine more carefully what the evangelist writes about this young man. He does not say that he fled from the company, or that he fled from following the Lord; rather, he says: “Abandoning the linen garment, he fled from them naked.” He fled from the enemies, whose presence and deeds he detested; he did not flee from the Lord his Savior and Teacher, whose love he preserved fixed in his heart even while absent in body. Nor does anything prevent us from understanding that this young man was John, the disciple loved by the Teacher above the others. The fact that he was still a young man at that time is indicated by his long life afterward in the flesh. It could have happened that, having slipped from the hands of those who were holding him for a moment, he soon recovered his garment and returned, mingling with the crowd leading Jesus as if he were one of them, until he reached the high priest’s courtyard, where he was known. He himself recalls this in his Gospel.

Just as Peter—who washed away the guilt of his denial with penitential tears and utterly uprooted it by confessing his love for the Lord—shows the restoration of those who stumble in martyrdom, so the other disciples, who by fleeing anticipated the moment of the arrest, teach those who feel themselves less capable of enduring punishments the prudence of flight. It is much safer for such people to seek the protection of hiding places than to expose themselves to the danger of combat. Thus this young man also, who, abandoning the linen garment, fled naked from the impious, signifies both the deed and the intention of those who, in order to become safer from the attacks of enemies, cast away whatever they seem to possess in this world and learn to serve the Lord naked rather than, by clinging to worldly possessions, give their adversaries material for tempting them and calling them back from God—following the example of blessed Joseph, who, leaving his cloak in the adulteress’s hands, sprang outside, preferring to serve God naked rather than, clothed in worldly desires, serve the prostitute.

And they led Jesus to the high priest. The high priest is Caiaphas, who—as the evangelist John writes—was the high priest of that year. Josephus bears corresponding witness about him, saying that he had purchased the high-priesthood for himself from the Roman ruler without possessing the merit of the office. It is therefore no wonder if an unjust high priest judges unjustly.

But Peter followed him from a distance, and so forth. He rightly followed from a distance, since he was already about to deny him at close range. For he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Yet in this he is especially worthy of our admiration: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. That he is afraid belongs to nature; that he follows belongs to devotion; that he denies belongs to sudden weakness; that he repents belongs to faith.

Alternatively: Peter’s following the same Lord from a distance toward the Passion signified that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s Passion, but in a very different way. The Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffered for the Church.

And he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself by the fire. There is the fire of love, and there is also the fire of desire. Of the former it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it should burn?” (Luke XII). Of the latter: “All of them are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea VII). The former, descending upon the believers in the upper room of Zion, taught them to praise God in various tongues. The latter, kindled in Caiaphas’s courtyard by the prompting of the evil spirit, armed the harmful tongues of the faithless to deny and blaspheme the Lord. What the wicked council was doing inside the high priest’s house, the fire materially kindled outside in the courtyard amid the night’s cold prefigured typologically.

Therefore, whoever extinguishes within himself the vicious and harmful fire can say with the prophet to the Lord: “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your justifications” (Psalm CXVIII). But those in whom turbid rivers of vice have overwhelmed the flame of love hear from the Lord: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV). Numb with this cold for a time, the apostle Peter wished to be warmed, as it were, by the coals of Caiaphas’s attendants, because he sought the comfort of temporal advantage in the company of the faithless. But soon, when the Lord looked upon him, he left behind both the physical fire of the wicked and the unbelief in his heart. After the Lord’s resurrection, restored by the holy fire, he completely cleansed the fault of his threefold denial by a threefold confession of love. For after that memorable catch of fish, when he came to the Lord with his fellow disciples and immediately saw the coals laid out, with a fish placed upon them, and bread, he kindled the hidden recesses of his heart with the coals of love.

And certain men rose up and bore false witness against him, saying: “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands.’” How are they false witnesses if they say what we read that the Lord said? A false witness is one who understands words in a sense other than that in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken about the temple of his body. But they also slander him in the very words, and, adding or changing a few things, pretend to make a legitimate accusation. The Savior had said: “Destroy this temple.” They change it and say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” “You,” he says, “destroy it, not I,” because it is unlawful for us to inflict death upon ourselves. Then they alter it to: “And after three days I will build another not made with hands,” so that he seems to have spoken specifically about the Jewish temple. But the Lord, to show that it was a living and breathing temple, had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

And the high priest rose and came forward, and questioned Jesus, saying: “Do you answer nothing to what these men are accusing you of?” But he remained silent and answered nothing. Impetuous and impatient anger, finding no place for accusation, shakes the high priest from his seat, so that by the movement of his body he might display the insanity of his mind. The more Jesus remained silent before the false witnesses and wicked priests, who were unworthy of an answer, the more the high priest, overcome by fury, provoked him to respond, so that he might find an opportunity for accusation in anything he said. Nevertheless, Jesus remained silent. For as God, he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted into a calumny.

[Col. 0281A] Again the high priest questioned him and said to him: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” But Jesus said to him: “I am.” In Matthew it is written that when the high priest questioned and adjured him whether he was the Christ, he answered: “You have said so” (Matthew XXVI). In place of this Mark wrote: “I am,” evidently showing that what Jesus says to him—“You have said so”—has the same force as if he had said: “I am.”

“And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” Therefore, if for you, O Jew, pagan, and heretic, contempt, weakness, and the cross are disgrace in Christ, see that through these things the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of God the Father, and that he who was born human from a virgin will come in his heavenly majesty with the clouds. Hence the Apostle, after describing the abasement of the cross—saying that “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross”—adds and says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II).

But the high priest, tearing his garments, said: “What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy.” The fury that had shaken him from the priestly seat now provokes the same madness to tear his garments. He tears his garments to show that the Jews have lost their priestly glory and possess an empty high-priestly seat. But it is also Jewish custom, whenever they hear something blasphemous and apparently directed against God, to tear their garments. We read that Paul and Barnabas did the same when they were being honored in Lycaonia with the worship given to gods. Herod, however, because he did not give glory to God but consented to the people’s excessive praise, was immediately struck by an angel.

In a deeper mystery, it happened that during the Lord’s Passion the Jewish high priest himself tore his garments, while the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. It was signified that the priesthood of the Jews, because of the crimes of their priests, was to be torn apart and entirely removed from its state of integrity; but the solidity of the holy universal Church, which is customarily called the garment of its Redeemer, would never be torn apart. Rather, even if Jews, Gentiles, heretics, or bad Catholics despise the humility of the Lord and Savior, the Church’s chastity will nevertheless remain inviolate until the consummation of the age in those whom he finds outside among the elect.

And some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with blows, and to say to him: “Prophesy.” And the attendants struck him with slaps. Here the prophecy was fulfilled that says: “I gave my cheeks to those who struck me, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah L). But he who was then struck with the blows and slaps of the Jews is also struck now by the blasphemies of false Christians.

He who was then spat upon with the saliva of unbelievers is now dishonored and provoked by insults from those who are mad, though faithful in name only. They covered his face, not so that he would not see their crimes, but so that, as they had once done to Moses, they might hide from themselves the grace of knowing him. For if they believed Moses, they would perhaps also believe the Lord. That veil remains to this day, unrevealed over their heart. But for us who believe in Christ it has been removed. For it was not without reason that, when he died, the veil of the temple was torn in the middle, and the holy mysteries of the Holy of Holies, which had remained hidden throughout the whole period of the Law and concealed from carnal Israel, were disclosed to the worshipers of the New Testament.

When they say to him, “Prophesy,” and, according to the other evangelists, “Prophesy: Who is it that struck you?”, they say this as an insult to one who had wished to be regarded by the peoples as a prophet. But because he himself ordered what he suffered, everything happens for our sake, just as Peter exhorts us: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, let us arm ourselves with the same thought,” and prepare ourselves to endure reproaches and insults for his name.

And while Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came. When she saw Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene,” and so forth. What does it mean that a servant girl is the first to expose him, when men could surely have recognized him more easily? Could it be that this sex also might appear to have sinned in the Lord’s death, and that this sex might also be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion? For this reason a woman first receives the mystery of the resurrection and guards the commandments, so that the ancient error of transgression might be erased.

And he went outside before the courtyard, and the rooster crowed. The other evangelists are silent about this crowing of the rooster, but they do not deny that it happened, just as elsewhere one evangelist passes over in silence many things that another recounts.

Again, when the servant girl saw him, she began to say to those standing around: “This man is one of them.” But he denied it again. We should not think that this was the same woman who had accused him earlier. Matthew says very plainly: “As he went out through the gate, another woman saw him and said to those who were there” (Matthew XXVI), and so forth. In this denial of Peter we learn that Christ is denied not only by one who says that he is not the Christ, but also by one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is one. The Lord did not say to Peter: “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but: “You will deny me.” He therefore denied him when he denied that he was his disciple.

And after a little while, those standing there again said to Peter: “Surely you are one of them. For you are also a Galilean.” This does not mean that the Galileans spoke a different language from the people of Jerusalem, since both were Hebrews, but that each province and region has its own characteristics and cannot avoid its native manner of speech. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles, when those upon whom the Holy Spirit had come were speaking in the languages of all nations, among the others who had come from different parts of the world, even those who lived in Judaea are reported to have said: “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we each hear our own language in which we were born?” (Acts II). And Peter, speaking to the brothers in Jerusalem, says: “It has become known to all who live in Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Haceldama” (Acts I). Why “in their language,” unless the same name was pronounced one way by those in Jerusalem and another way by the Galileans?

But he began to curse and swear: “I do not know this man whom you are talking about.” And immediately the rooster crowed again. Scripture often signifies the mystery of events by the arrangement of times. Hence Peter, who denied him in the middle of the night, repented at the crowing of the rooster. After the Lord’s resurrection, in the light of day, he likewise professed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times. For the error he had made in the darkness of forgetfulness, he corrected by recalling the light already hoped for; and, having attained the presence of that same true light, he fully restored whatever had wavered.

I think this rooster should be understood as one of the teachers who, awakening us as we lie asleep and rebuking the drowsy, says: “Awake, righteous ones, and do not sin.”

And Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he began to weep. How harmful are the conversations of the wicked! Peter himself, among unbelievers, denied knowing a man whom among his fellow disciples he had already confessed to be the Son of God. But while he remained in Caiaphas’s courtyard he could not perform repentance. He went outside, as the other evangelists relate, so that, withdrawn from the council of the impious, he might wash away the filth of his fearful denial with free-flowing tears.

## CHAPTER XV

And immediately, in the morning, the chief priests, with the elders and scribes and the whole council, made a plan; they bound Jesus, led him away, and delivered him to Pilate. He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. Observe the priests’ diligence in evil: they stayed awake all night in order to commit murder, and they delivered him bound to Pilate. For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death, they handed over bound to the judge. Nevertheless, it should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then. Rather, immediately after he was seized in the garden at night, they bound him, as John makes clear, and thus led him first to Annas.

And Pilate questioned him: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Since Pilate asked him about no other charge except whether he was the King of the Jews, the impiety of the Jews is exposed: they could not find even a false accusation to bring against the Savior.

But he answered him: “You say so.” He answered in such a way that he spoke the truth while leaving his words inaccessible to accusation. Notice that he gave some answer to Pilate, who was unwillingly passing sentence, but refused to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his speech.

Pilate again questioned him, saying: “Do you answer nothing? See how many charges they bring against you.” But Jesus still answered nothing. The one who condemns Jesus is indeed a Gentile, but he refers the matter back to the Jewish people: “See how many charges they bring against you.” Jesus did not wish to answer anything, lest, by clearing away the charge, he be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be postponed.

But the chief priests stirred up the crowd so that he would release Barabbas to them instead. The petition they obtained with such effort remains with the Jews to this day. For when they were given a choice, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and one who took life instead of the giver of life. They therefore deservedly lost salvation and life, and subjected themselves so completely to robberies and seditions that they lost both their country and their kingdom, which they loved more than Christ; nor have they deserved to recover, up to the present, the freedom either of soul or of body that they sold.

Pilate again answered them: “What then do you want me to do with the King of the Jews?” But they cried out again: “Crucify him.” Pilate said to them: “Why, what evil has he done?” Pilate offered many opportunities for freeing the Savior: first by contrasting the robber with the righteous man, then by asking: “What then do you want me to do with the King of the Jews?” When they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately consent. Rather, following the suggestion of his wife, who had sent him word, as Matthew writes, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matthew XXVII), he himself answered earnestly [or: “also”]: “Why, what evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus.

But they cried out still more: “Crucify him.” Thus was fulfilled what he had said in the twenty-first Psalm: “Many dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me” (Psalm XXI); and what Jeremiah says: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jeremiah XII). Isaiah also agrees with this sentence: “I expected them to do justice, but they did iniquity and not justice, only a cry” (Isaiah V).

But Pilate, wishing to satisfy the people, released Barabbas to them and handed Jesus over, after he had been scourged, to be crucified. Jesus must be understood to have been scourged not by someone other than Pilate himself. For John writes plainly: “Again they all cried out, saying, ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber. Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him” (John XVIII). He then adds: “And the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head,” and so forth (John XIX). He is believed to have done this, and to have handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked, so that, satisfied with his punishments and insults, they would cease to thirst eagerly for his death.

This happened so that, since it was written, “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Psalm XXXI), when he was scourged we might be freed from blows, as Scripture says: “The scourge will not come near your dwelling” (Psalm XC).

And the soldiers led him into the courtyard of the praetorium, summoned the whole cohort, clothed him in purple, placed upon him a crown of thorns that they had woven, and began to salute him: “Hail, King of the Jews.” Because he had been called King of the Jews, and because the scribes and priests had brought against him the charge that he was usurping rule over the people of Israel, the soldiers did these things in mockery: they stripped him of his former garments and clothed him in purple, which ancient kings used; they placed a crown of thorns on him instead of a diadem; they gave him a reed for a royal scepter, as Matthew writes; and they worshiped him as though he were a king.

We should understand all these things mystically. Just as Caiaphas said, “It is necessary that one man die for all” (John XVIII), without knowing what he was saying (Luke IX), so whatever these men did, although they acted with a different intention, nevertheless bestowed mysteries upon us who believe.

It should be noted that where Mark says, “They clothed him in purple,” Matthew says: “They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him” (Matthew XXVII). It is understood that what Matthew says—“They put a scarlet cloak around him”—is what Mark expressed by “clothed in purple.” For that scarlet cloak was used by the mockers in place of royal purple; it was a kind of red purple very similar to scarlet. It may also be that Mark mentioned purple because of the color of the cloak, even though it was scarlet.

Mystically, therefore, the purple in which the Lord was clothed signifies his flesh, which he exposed to sufferings. Concerning it the preceding prophecy had said: “Why then are your garments red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isaiah LXIII). In the crown that he wore, made of thorns, is shown the taking upon himself of our sins, for which he deigned to become mortal. Accordingly, his forerunner testified about him: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). The Lord himself testifies that thorns are customarily used as a sign of sins, when he said to the first-formed man after his fall into sin: “Your earth will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis III). This plainly means: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and stings of vices.”

According to Luke’s Gospel, the Lord is clothed by Herod in a white garment, whereas in the other evangelists he is said to have been mocked by Pilate’s soldiers under a scarlet or purple garment. When the two accounts are compared, the one expresses the innocence and purity of the humanity he assumed, while the other expresses the truth of the Passion by which he was to reach the glory of the immortal kingdom. For just as purple imitates the color of the blood poured out for us, so it also indicates the garment of the kingdom that he entered after the Passion and opened for us to enter.

But since the Apostle says, “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III), and Isaiah says to the Lord concerning all the elect, “With these you will clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isaiah XLIX [the printed citation reads “XIL”]), the two garments of the Lord—disgraceful according to the judgment of his enemies but most glorious according to the Lord’s own choice—can aptly signify the whole multitude of his elect, distinguished into venerable martyrs and the rest of the faithful.

He is clothed in a white garment when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous.

He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he rejoices in the triumph of victorious martyrs.

And they struck his head with a reed and spat upon him. And kneeling, they worshiped him. The soldiers of Pilate did these things then; heretics and pagans, the soldiers of the devil, do them even now. Since God is the head of Christ, those strike his head who deny that he is truly God. And since Scripture is customarily written with a reed, those strike Christ’s head as with a reed who, contradicting his divinity, attempt to confirm their error by the authority of sacred Scripture. They spit in his face who, out of the insanity of an inwardly blind mind, reject his presence with words conceived for cursing and deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

The soldiers mocked him and worshiped him as though he had falsely claimed to be God. But today there are people—an even graver madness—who worship him with firm faith as the true God, yet immediately despise his words as though they were fables by their perverse actions, and put the promises of his kingdom far below temporal pleasures.

And they lead him out to crucify him. And they compel a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. This Simon appears to have been a man of considerable reputation at that time, since his sons too are identified by name as though already known to everyone. But we must beware of thinking that there is a contradiction between this and what John writes, namely, that the Lord himself carried his cross, whereas the other evangelists report that this Simon of Cyrene carried it.

At first the Lord carried it; afterward it was placed upon Simon to carry, when they happened to encounter him as they went out. This accords very well with the order of the mystery. For he himself suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps.

And because this Simon is said to have been not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian—for Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles—the peoples of the Gentiles are rightly signified through him. Once strangers and foreigners to the covenants, they are now, through obedience, fellow citizens and members of God’s household, and, as it is said elsewhere, “heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans VIII). Accordingly, Simon is aptly interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.”

Nor should we pass over the fact that this same Simon is said to have come from the countryside. In Greek, the countryside is called πάγος (*pagos*). Hence we call pagans those whom we see as alienated from the city of God and, as it were, lacking the civilized manner of life. But Simon, coming out from the countryside, carries the cross after Jesus when the peoples of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion.

And they bring him to Golgotha, a place which is interpreted as “Place of the Skull.” Outside the city gate are places where the heads of the condemned are cut off, and so they received the name “Calvaries,” that is, of the beheaded. The Lord was crucified there so that where previously there had been a place for the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised.

And just as for our sake he was made the curse of the cross, scourged and crucified, so for the salvation of all he is crucified as though he were guilty among the guilty.

And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he did not accept it. God says to Jerusalem: “I planted you as my true vine; how have you become a bitter, foreign vine?” (Jeremiah II). A bitter vine produced bitter wine, which was offered to the Lord Jesus, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII). When it says, “He did not accept it,” or, according to Matthew, “When he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matthew XXVII), this indicates that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day.

When Mark says, “He did not accept it,” this is understood as “he did not accept it in order to drink it.” He tasted it, as Matthew testifies, so that what Matthew says—“He would not drink”—is what Mark expressed by “He did not accept,” while Mark omitted the fact that he tasted it. And when Mark says “wine mixed with myrrh,” we should understand Matthew to have said “mixed with gall” (Matthew XXVII). For he used gall as a representation of bitterness. Wine mixed with myrrh is extremely bitter, although it is also possible that wine was made extremely bitter with both gall and myrrh.

And when they crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots for them to determine what each should take. The evangelist John explains this more fully: the soldiers divided the other garments into four parts, according to their number, but cast lots for the tunic, which was seamless, woven from the top throughout.

The Lord’s four-part garment signified his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those regions. That tunic, assigned by lot, signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of love. For if love, according to the Apostle, is the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and stands above all commandments, it is rightly said that the garment signifying it was woven from the top throughout.

What else is commended by the casting of lots except the grace of God? Thus it reaches all through one thing when the lot pleases everyone, because God’s grace also reaches all through unity. And when a lot is cast, the matter is entrusted not to the person or merits of anyone but to God’s hidden judgment.

And because, as the Apostle says, “our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer serve sin” (Romans VI), as long as our works are directed toward the destruction of the body of sin, and as long as the outward man is corrupted so that the inward man may be renewed day by day, it is the time of the cross. These are indeed good works, but they are still laborious, and their reward is rest. For this reason it is said, “Rejoicing in hope” (Romans XII), so that with gladness we may carry out our work amid labors, in expectation of future rest.

This gladness is signified by the breadth of the cross in the transverse beam where the hands are fastened. By the hands we understand works; by the breadth, the gladness of the one who works, because sadness causes narrowness. By the height, to which the head is attached, we understand the expectation of reward from the exalted justice of God, who will render to each according to his works (Matthew XVI): to those who seek eternal life through perseverance in good work, glory and honor and incorruption. Thus the length, by which the whole body is extended, signifies perseverance itself; hence those who endure are called long-suffering.

The depth, which is fixed in the earth, prefigures the hiddenness of the mystery. You remember, unless I am mistaken, how the Apostle’s words are explained through this representation of the cross, where he says: “Rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Ephesians III).

Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him. Some think that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, and that darkness began from the sixth hour until the ninth, so that the three hours from his crucifixion until the darkness began may be understood as having elapsed. This could indeed be understood quite correctly, unless John said that at about the sixth hour Pilate sat on the tribunal at the place called the Stone Pavement, but in Hebrew Gabbatha (John XIX). He continues: “It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour.” And he says to the Jews: “Behold your king,” and so forth.

If, then, at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, he was handed over to the Jews to be crucified, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have thought because they did not understand Mark’s words? Mark had already said: “And when they crucified him, they divided his garments.” If he had wished to mention the time when the deed occurred, it would have been enough to say: “It was the third hour.” Why did he add, “And they crucified him,” unless he wished, by recapitulation, to signify something that would be discovered when the Scripture was read at a time when the hour at which the Lord was hung upon the wood was known to the whole Church, so that either this error could be corrected or this falsehood refuted?

But because he knew that the Lord was crucified by the soldiers, not by the Jews, he wished secretly to show that those who cried out for him to be crucified crucified him more truly than those who, in accordance with their office, performed their service to their ruler. It is therefore understood that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out for the Lord to be crucified. It is shown with complete truth that they crucified him when they cried out, especially since they did not wish it to appear that they themselves had done this and therefore handed him over to Pilate, as their words sufficiently indicate according to John.

Thus what they especially did not wish to appear to have done, Mark shows that they did at the third hour, indicating most truthfully that the Jews’ murderous tongue, rather than the soldiers’ hands, was responsible for the Lord’s death.

And there was an inscription bearing the charge against him: “The King of the Jews.” The inscription placed above his cross, on which was written “The King of the Jews,” showed that even by killing him they could not bring it about that they would not have him as their king—the one who will render to them according to their deeds with the clearest and most exalted power. Hence the Psalm sings: “Yet I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm II).

And because he is both king and priest, when he offered to the Father the outstanding sacrifice of his flesh upon the altar of the cross, he also displayed in the inscription the royal dignity with which he was endowed, so that he might make known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross’s instrument of execution he had not lost his kingdom but rather confirmed and strengthened it.

And they crucify with him two robbers, one on his right and the other on his left. The robbers crucified on either side with the Lord signify those who, under the faith and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any discipline of stricter continence. But all who do these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory are clearly represented by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those, however, who renounce the world either for the sake of human praise or with some other less worthy intention, rightly imitate the mind and actions of the blaspheming robber on the left.

Concerning such people the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, if I give all my possessions for the food of the poor, if I seem to perform many other works of piety or to have received gifts of spiritual grace, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII). Blessed are those who leave what is theirs for the Lord and for the Gospel. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew V).

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him among themselves with the scribes, were saying: “He saved others,” and so forth. Even unwillingly, the scribes and priests confess that he saved others. Thus your own judgment condemns you. For the one who saved others could certainly have saved himself if he had wished.

“Let Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” A fraudulent promise! What is greater: to descend alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and you do not believe; therefore, even if he descended from the cross, you likewise would not believe.

And those who were crucified with him reviled him. How could those who were crucified with him revile him, when, according to Luke’s testimony, one of them reviled him, while the other rebuked him and believed in God? Unless we understand Matthew and Mark, briefly touching on the matter, to have used the plural number here for the singular, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read the plural expression, “They shut the mouths of lions” (Heb. XI), although Daniel alone is understood; and the plural expression, “They were sawn in pieces” (ibid.), although tradition tells this of Isaiah alone. What, for example, is more commonplace than for someone to say, “The peasants are insulting me,” even if only one is insulting him? What Luke revealed concerning one would be contradictory only if they had said that both robbers reviled the Lord, since one person could not then be understood under a plural number. But when it is said “robbers,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and “both” is not added, this can be said not only if both had done it, but also because, since one did it, he could be signified, according to ordinary usage, by the plural number.

But since, as Luke testifies, one robber blasphemed the Lord, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us” (Luke XXIII), while the other rebuked him with a fitting reprimand and entreated the Lord in faithful supplication, saying, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (ibid.), we see this happening in the Church even to the present day. When Christians, both true and false, are touched by worldly afflictions, those who carry the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a feigned mind desire to be delivered by the Lord into the joys of the present life. But those who, with sincere intention, glory with the Apostle in nothing except the cross of our Lord, desire rather to be rescued from present troubles in such a way that they commend their spirit into the hands of their Author and long to share with him in the kingdom of heaven. Hence, rightly, the man who prayed to the Lord with doubtful faith was utterly rejected by the Lord and deemed unworthy of any answer. But the prayers of the one who sought eternal salvation for himself the Lord soon graciously deigned to receive. For whoever, placed amid tribulations, seeks from the Lord only temporal consolations, deprives himself alike of temporal and eternal joys. But those who truly sigh for the good things of their heavenly homeland reach them without any doubt, through Christ’s mercy.

And when the sixth hour had come, darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour. The most brilliant light of the world withdrew its rays, lest it either see the Lord hanging there or allow the impious blasphemers to enjoy its light. It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was about to withdraw from the center of the world—but at dawn, that is, when the sun of his resurrection had already risen, he celebrated the mysteries of his resurrection. By the timing he signified what he displayed by the effect of his work: he died for our sins and rose again for our justification.

For it is also written concerning Adam when he sinned that he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the afternoon breeze (Gen. III). “In the afternoon,” namely, when the light of faith had declined; “in the breeze,” when the fervor of charity had cooled. He was heard walking because he had withdrawn from the sinful human being. Therefore the order of reason—or rather, of divine compassion—required that at the same hour at which he had then closed the gate against Adam’s transgression, the Lord should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant robber; and at the hour at which the first Adam, by sinning, had brought death into this world, the second Adam should at that same hour destroy death by dying.

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Heloi, Heloi, lama sabachthani,” which is translated, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He used the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. The words that are read in the middle of the verse, “Look upon me,” are superfluous. For in Hebrew it reads, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Nor should you be surprised at the lowliness of the words or the complaints of one forsaken when, knowing the form of a servant, you see the scandal of the cross. Just as hunger, thirst, and weariness were not proper to divinity but bodily sufferings, so also the saying, “Why have you forsaken me?” was proper to the bodily voice, because according to nature the body in no way wishes to be deprived of the life joined to it. Although the Savior himself said this, he was properly displaying the frailty of the body while remaining the power and wisdom of God. As a human being, therefore, he speaks, carrying our own experiences: that in dangers we think we have been abandoned by God. As a human being he is troubled, as a human being he weeps, as a human being he is crucified.

And some of those standing nearby, hearing this, said: “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” Not all of them, but some. I think they were Roman soldiers, who did not understand the particular character of the Hebrew speech but, from his saying “Heloi, Heloi,” thought that Elijah was being invoked by him. But if you wish to understand them as Jews who said this, they are likewise acting according to their customary practice, slandering the Lord in his weakness by claiming that he was imploring Elijah’s help.

But one man ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him, saying: “Let be; let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” John explains more fully why vinegar was given the Lord to drink, saying: “Afterward, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been accomplished, in order that Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ Now a vessel had been placed there full of vinegar. So they put a sponge full of vinegar on hyssop and brought it to his mouth.” He saw, therefore, that everything that had to happen before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit had been accomplished; and in order that this too might be fulfilled—“And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. CXVIII)—he said, “I thirst.” It was as though he were saying: “You have left this undone; give what you are.”
