For the Jews themselves were the vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. As though from a full vessel filled with the iniquity of this world, they had hearts like a sponge, fraudulent through hidden recesses that were, in a manner of speaking, cavernous and twisted. Since hyssop, around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar, is a lowly herb that purifies animals, we fittingly understand it as the humility of Christ, which they surrounded and thought they had outwitted. Hence the Psalm says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Ps. L). We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II), his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

By the reed on which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, for this act fulfilled it. Just as a language is called Greek, Latin, or any other language, signifying the sound produced by the tongue, so a reed can be called the letter written with a reed. But we very commonly call the sounds of the human voice “tongues”; to call Scripture a “reed” is less customary and therefore more richly figurative in the mystical sense.

But Jesus, uttering a loud cry, breathed his last. What the Lord said with this loud voice Luke clearly indicates, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” And when he had said this, he expired (Luke XXIII). But what John writes—that when Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (John XIX)—means that between the words “It is finished” and “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit,” that loud cry was uttered which John omitted, while the other three evangelists recorded it.

And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The veil of the temple is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the law that had been covered might appear and pass over to the people of the nations. For previously it had been said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXVI). But now: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory,” he says, “over all the earth” (Ps. LXVI). And in the Gospel he had first said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X). But after his passion: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

Now when the centurion who stood facing him saw that he had expired after crying out in this way, he said: “Truly this man was the Son of God.” The clear reason for the centurion’s wonder is explained: seeing the Lord expire in this manner—that is, give up his spirit—he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” For no one has the power to give up his spirit except the one who is the Creator of souls. It should also be considered that the centurion, standing before the cross in the very scandal of the passion, confessed him to be truly the Son of God, while Arius preached a creature in the Church. Therefore, appropriately, the faith of the Church is signified by the centurion. Once the veil of heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death, she immediately affirms Jesus, both truly a just human being and truly the Son of God, while the Synagogue remains silent.

There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him. By James the younger he means James the son of Alphaeus, who was also called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt. John mentions her in his Gospel, saying: “Now standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas” (John XIX). Mary of Clopas seems to be called so from her father or from her kinship.

James was called the younger to distinguish him from James the elder, namely the son of Zebedee, who was called among the first of the apostles and chosen by the Lord. It was customary among the Jews—and according to the ancient practice of the nations it was not considered blameworthy—for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Paul recalls that he renounced this practice, which could cause scandal among the nations: “Do we not have the right to take along believing women, as do the other apostles?” (I Cor. IX). They ministered to the Lord from their possessions, so that he might reap their material things, while they reaped spiritual things. This was not because the Lord, the Creator of creatures, needed food, but so that he might provide an example for teachers: that they ought to be content with food and clothing from their disciples.

But let us see what kind of companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; Mary the mother of James and Joses, his maternal aunt; and the others whom we read of in the other Gospels.

[Col. 0293A] And when evening had already come, since it was the Preparation, which is before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a noble councillor, came. He is called a councillor because he belonged to the order of the curia and administered the office of the curia. He is also commonly called a *curialis*, from the management of civic duties. Arimathea itself is Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel in the region of Thamnitica, near Diospolis.

*Paraskeuē* (Παρασκευή) is called *praeparatio* in Latin, “preparation.” By this name the Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week, because on it they customarily prepared the things necessary for the Sabbath rest. This accords with the command once given concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” and so forth. Since, therefore, the human being was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—whence he also wished this day to be called Sabbath, that is, rest—the Savior was rightly crucified on that same sixth day and fulfilled the mystery of humanity’s restoration.

Therefore, when he had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished”—that is, the work of the sixth day, which I undertook for the world’s renewal, is now entirely completed. On the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the event of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. Here an example shines before us both of our devotion and of our blessed reward: in this sixth age of the world we must suffer for the Lord and, as it were, be crucified to the world; but in the seventh age—that is, when a person has paid the debt of death—our bodies must remain in the tombs, our souls in hidden peace with the Lord, and we must rest from good works until, at last, when the eighth age arrives, those very bodies, glorified by the resurrection, receive together with their souls the incorruption of the eternal inheritance.

“He came,” it says, “Joseph of Arimathea, a noble councillor, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God. And he boldly went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.” This Joseph is praised as having been a man of great dignity in the world, but of still greater merit before God. For it was fitting that the man who would bury the Lord’s body should be such a person—worthy of that ministry through the justice of his merits and able, through the nobility of his secular power, to obtain the opportunity to perform it. For no unknown or ordinary person could approach the governor and obtain the body of one who had been crucified.

Joseph bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth. The simplicity of the Lord’s burial condemns the extravagance of the rich, who cannot be without their riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding, we may also take this to mean that the Lord’s body should be wrapped not in gold, gems, or silk, but in pure linen. Yet this too signifies that the person who wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth is the one who receives him with a pure mind.

Hence the custom has arisen in the Church that the altar sacrifice should be celebrated not in silk or dyed cloth, but in earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean linen cloth. We read that this was established in the records of the bishops by blessed Pope Sylvester.

And he placed him in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock, and rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Those who in our time came from Jerusalem to Britain report concerning the Lord’s tomb that it was a round chamber hewn out of the underlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch the ceiling with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance from the east, against which that great stone was rolled and set.

In the northern part of this tomb was the sepulchre itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and rose three palms above the rest of the pavement. This place was open not from above but entirely from the southern side, through which the body was brought in. The color of the same tomb and burial chamber is said to be a mixture of red and white.

Now Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was placed. In Luke we read that all his acquaintances stood at a distance, as did the women who had followed him. After his body had been laid away, these acquaintances of Jesus returned to their homes; only the women, who loved him more closely, followed the funeral and took care to observe how he was placed, so that at the proper time they might offer him the service of their devotion.

Even to the present day, holy women do the same on the day of Preparation, that is, the day of preparation. Humble souls, the more conscious they are of their own frailty and the more fervently they burn with love for the Savior, diligently attend in this world upon the traces of his passion, in which the future rest is being prepared; and, if they can perhaps imitate it, they carefully consider in what order that same passion was completed, with devout attentiveness.

## CHAPTER XVI

And when the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus. In Luke’s Gospel it is written that, returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath they rested because of the commandment. The commandment of the law, therefore, was that Sabbath silence should be observed from evening to evening. Thus the devout women, after the Lord had been buried, were occupied in preparing ointments for as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset—as Luke writes.

And because at that time, owing to the shortness of the time, they could not complete the task, they hastened immediately after the Sabbath had passed—that is, after the sun had set, when permission to work had returned—to buy spices, as Mark reports, so that they might come in the morning and anoint his body. For they did not wish to approach the tomb when the evening of the Sabbath had already been overtaken by the hours of night.

And very early, on one day of the Sabbaths, they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen. “The first day of the Sabbaths” is the first day from the day of Sabbaths—that is, of rests—which ecclesiastical custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the resurrection of the Lord Savior. The same meaning is conveyed when we read “one day of the Sabbath,” or “one day of the Sabbaths”: namely, one day from the day of Sabbaths, that is, of rests observed on the Sabbaths.

The holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices, and showed the service of human devotion even to him whom they had loved while alive, now that he was dead. And so, if we believe in the one who died and, filled with the fragrance of virtues, seek the Lord with the reputation of good works, we surely come with spices to his tomb.

The fact that the women came to the tomb very early, after the sun had risen—that is, when the sky was already growing white in the eastern part, which does not happen except through the nearness of the rising sun—shows, according to the historical sense, the great fervor of charity in seeking and finding the Lord. According to the mystical understanding, it gives us an example of offering the Lord the fragrance of good works and the sweetness of prayers, with our countenance enlightened and the darkness of vices dispersed.

And they said to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. For it was very large. Matthew sufficiently explains how the stone was rolled away by the angel. But the rolling away of the stone mystically signifies the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been covered by the veil of the letter of the law. The law had been written on stone; when its covering was removed, the glory of the resurrection was revealed, the abolition of ancient death and the hope of perpetual life for us began to be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished. Entering from the east into that round chamber hewn in the rock, they saw an angel sitting on the southern side of the place where Jesus’ body had been laid—for this was on the right. Since the body, lying on its back with its head toward the west, necessarily had its right side toward the south.

Matthew writes that the angel who rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb was first seen sitting upon the stone itself, and that he ordered them to enter the place where the Lord had been laid and to see that he had already risen from the dead. Luke writes that, when they entered the tomb, they found two angels standing there.

Those women, therefore, who came with spices see angels, because those minds behold the citizens above who advance toward God through holy desires accompanied by virtues. We should also note what it means that the angel is seen sitting on the right. What is signified by the left except the present life? And what by the right except perpetual life? Hence it is written: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II).

The Church has placed the left hand of God—that is, the prosperity of the present life—under her head, pressing it down with the intention of supreme love. But God’s right hand embraces her, because she is held entirely within his eternal blessedness. Since, therefore, our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel who had come to announce his unending life rightly sat on the right.

He appeared clothed in a white robe because he announced the joys of our festival. The whiteness of the garment proclaims the splendor of our festivity. Shall we say “our,” or “his”? To speak more truthfully, let us say both his and ours. The resurrection of our Redeemer was our festival, because it restored us to immortality; and it was the festival of the angels, because, by restoring us to heavenly things, it filled their number. At his and our festival, therefore, the angel appeared in white garments, because while we are restored through the Lord’s resurrection to the things above, the losses of the heavenly homeland are repaired.

But now let us hear what the angel said to the women as they approached.

“Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him.” “Do not,” he says, “be afraid.” As though he were saying openly: Let those who do not love the coming of the citizens above be afraid. Let those who, pressed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to reach their fellowship fear. But why are you afraid, when you see your fellow citizens?

Thus Matthew, describing the angel’s appearance, says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. XXVIII). In lightning there is the terror of fear; in snow there is the gentle appeal of whiteness. Since almighty God is terrible to sinners and gentle to the just, the angel who bears witness to his resurrection is rightly shown both with a face like lightning and with clothing white as snow, so that by his very appearance he might terrify the reprobate and soothe the devout.

“You seek Jesus of Nazareth.” In Latin speech, *Jesus* is interpreted as “salutary,” that is, “savior.” But at that time many could be called by this name, not substantially but nominally. Therefore the place-name is added, so that it may be clear of which Jesus the statement is made: “of Nazareth.” Immediately the cause is added: “crucified”; and then: “he has risen; he is not here.” “He is not here” is said in respect of the presence of his flesh, although he was nowhere absent in the presence of his majesty.

“But go and tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee.” We should ask why Peter is designated by name among the disciples. If the angel had not expressly named him, the man who had denied his Master would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial.

In this matter we should consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he had determined to place above the whole Church to fear the voice of a servant-girl and deny himself. We understand that this was done through a dispensation of great compassion, so that the one who was to become the shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to have mercy on others. He first revealed him to himself, and then placed him over the others, so that from his own weakness he might recognize how mercifully he should endure the weaknesses of others.

It is rightly said of our Redeemer: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you.” For Galilee is interpreted as “made migration.” Our Redeemer had already migrated from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. He is first seen by the disciples in Galilee after the resurrection because we shall see the glory of his resurrection with joy if we now migrate from vices to the heights of virtues. He who is announced in the tomb is shown in migration, because the one recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the migration of the mind.

But they went out and fled from the tomb—for trembling and fear had seized them—and they said nothing to anyone. For they were afraid. It is rightly puzzling how Mark can write, “They said nothing to anyone,” when Luke says: “Returning from the tomb, they announced all these things to the eleven and to all the others.” Similarly Matthew says: “They went out quickly from the tomb, with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples” (Matt. XXVIII).

Unless we understand that they did not dare say anything to the angels themselves—that is, to respond to what they had heard from them—or perhaps to the guards whom they had seen lying there. The joy that Matthew mentions does not conflict with the fear of which Mark speaks. We should understand both emotions as having occurred in their minds, even if Matthew himself had not mentioned the fear.

Now Jesus, rising early on the first day after the Sabbath, appeared first to Mary Magdalene. John teaches most fully how and where this appearance of the Lord took place. The Lord rose early from the tomb in which he had been laid when evening had already come, so that the Psalmist’s saying might be fulfilled: “In the evening weeping shall remain, and in the morning joy” (Ps. XXIX).

Buried, therefore, on the sixth day, which is called the Preparation, around the evening hour, he remained in the tomb during the following night and the Sabbath day, together with the following night, and thus rose on the third day—that is, in the morning of the first day after the Sabbath. It is not without reason that he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights: he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death.

For he came to us, who were held in the death of both spirit and flesh. He brought to us one death of his own—that is, the death of the flesh—and dissolved the two deaths of ours that he found. If he himself had taken on both, he would have freed us from neither. But he mercifully accepted one and justly condemned both. He brought his single death to our double death, and by dying subdued our double death.

“He appeared,” it says, “first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.” She went and announced it to those who had been with him, mourning and weeping. Just as at the beginning the woman was the author of guilt for the man, while the man carried out the error, so now the woman who had first brought and tasted death first saw the resurrection. And lest she endure among men the reproach of perpetual guilt, she who had transmitted guilt to the man also transmitted grace to him.

Therefore this woman, who was the first to announce the joy of the Lord’s resurrection to the mourning and weeping men, is rightly said to have been healed of seven demons, so that it might be signified that she had been full of every vice but cleansed from all of them by divine gift; and that where sin abounded, grace had abounded still more. The number seven is customarily set mystically for universality.

She who had been healed of seven demons—that is, freed from every crime—was the first to see the Lord rising from the dead, so that no truly repentant person might despair of pardon for sins committed, when he sees that the woman who had once been subject to so many and such great vices was suddenly raised, through the merit of faith and love, to such a height that she was the first to proclaim to Christ’s evangelists and apostles the miracle of his accomplished resurrection.

And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. The disciples’ slowness in believing the Lord’s resurrection was not so much their weakness as—so to speak—our future firmness. For that resurrection was demonstrated to them, while they doubted, by many proofs; and when we recognize these proofs as we read them, what else do we do but become strengthened by their doubt? Mary Magdalene, who believed more quickly, did less for me than Thomas, who doubted for a long time. By doubting, he touched the scars of the wounds and cut away the wound of doubt from our hearts.

After this he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking and going into the countryside. And they went and reported it to the others, but they did not believe them. Luke explains more fully how this happened. When Mark says that he appeared “in another form,” Luke states this more clearly: their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him, until, when they came with him to the village to which they were going, they set a table for him as for a stranger and finally recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke XXIV).

As the same Luke adds immediately afterward, they rose at that very hour and returned to Jerusalem. They found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon. They themselves then related what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread (ibid.).

When Mark says that they announced it to the others, or that the others did not believe them, while Luke says that those others were already saying that he had truly risen and appeared to Simon, what are we to understand except that some who were there did not wish to believe this? Who does not see that Mark omitted what Luke explained in his narrative? Namely, what Jesus had said to them before they recognized him, and how they recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

For when Mark immediately says that he appeared in another form to those going into the countryside, he at once adds: “And they went and announced it to the others, but they did not believe them.” As though they could announce someone whom they had not recognized, or recognize one who had appeared to them in another form. How, then, they recognized him so that they could make their announcement, Mark undoubtedly omitted. This should be committed to memory so that we may become accustomed to observing the manner of the Evangelists: they omit what they do not recount and join together what they do recount in such a way that, for those who lack experience in this matter, error arises from nowhere else more readily than from the belief that the Evangelists do not agree with one another.

Finally, while the eleven were reclining at table, he appeared and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen from the dead. How is it “finally,” as though they were not to see him afterward? For this was the last occasion on which the Apostles saw the Lord on earth, when he ascended into heaven, which occurred forty days after his resurrection.

Was he then going to reproach them because they had not believed those who had seen him risen, when they themselves had already seen him so many times after the resurrection? Let us therefore understand that, after the many demonstrations by which he had presented himself to his disciples over forty days, he appeared to them once more, finally, while they were reclining—that is, on the fortieth day itself.

And because he was then about to ascend from them into heaven, let us understand that on that day he especially wished to reproach them because, before they themselves saw him, they had not believed those who had seen him risen, even though after his ascension the nations, which had not seen him, were to believe when the Apostles preached the Gospel.

After this reproach, Mark continues:

And he said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

Since they were going to preach that whoever did not believe would be condemned—and since such a person would not have believed what he had not seen—were they not themselves first to be rebuked because, before they had seen the Lord, they had not believed those to whom the Lord had appeared?

But when he said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature,” was the holy Gospel to be preached to senseless things or irrational animals, so that the disciples would be told, “Preach to every creature”? By the name “every creature,” every nation of the Gentiles can be signified.

Previously it had been said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” But now it is said: “Preach to every creature,” so that the preaching rejected by Judea might then become our aid, when Judea had proudly rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Perhaps each person may say to himself: “I have already believed; I shall be saved.” This is true if he holds faith through his works. For true faith is that which is not contradicted in conduct by what it says in words.

Hence Paul says concerning certain false believers: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I). John says here: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (I John II).

But when it is said, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned,” what are we to say here about little children, who because of their age are not yet able to believe? There is no question concerning adults. In the Church, therefore, little children believe in the Savior through others, just as from others they contracted those sins that are remitted to them in baptism.

The signs that will accompany those who believe are these: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.

Does this mean that, because we do not perform these signs, we do not believe at all? These signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For, so that faith might grow, it had to be nourished by miracles. When we plant young trees, we pour water over them for as long as it takes to see that they have become firmly established in the soil. But once they have taken root, the watering ceases. This is why Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. XIV).

Or do we not possess signs and powers of another kind that we ought to consider more subtly? Holy Church indeed performs spiritually every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. When her priests, by the grace of exorcism, lay hands on believers and forbid the evil spirit to dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons? And when the faithful abandon the secular speech of their former life and proclaim the holy mysteries, declaring, as far as they can, the praises and power of their Creator, what else do they do but speak in new tongues?

When, through their good exhortations, they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they pick up serpents. And when they hear deadly suggestions but are not at all drawn into evil action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it will not harm them. Whenever they see their neighbors weakened in good works, they come to their aid with all their strength and, by the example of their own conduct, strengthen the lives of those who falter in their own actions. What else do they do but lay hands on the sick, so that they may be well?

These miracles are certainly greater in proportion as they are more spiritual. They are greater in proportion as through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

[Col. 0300C] After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. We must consider what Mark means when he says, “He sits at the right hand of God,” while Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts VII). Why does Mark testify that he saw him sitting, whereas Stephen says that he saw him standing?

We know that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who fights or gives assistance. Since our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the end as judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his assumption, because after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge at the end. Stephen, however, engaged in the struggle of his suffering, saw him standing, because he had him as his helper. Thus, while Stephen was overcoming on earth the unbelief of his persecutors, Christ fought for him from heaven by his grace.

The text continues:

But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed. What should we consider in this, what should we commit to memory, except that obedience followed the command, and signs followed obedience? Among other things, we should note that the later Mark began his Gospel than the others, the farther forward in time he extended it in writing. For he records nothing about the Lord’s birth or that of his precursor, nothing about the infancy or childhood of either of them, and, apart from naming him at the beginning of his Gospel as the Son of God, he does not write at greater length about the Savior’s birth. He began with the commencement of the evangelical preaching, which took place through John, and by his narrative reached the time when the apostles spread the same word of the Gospel by preaching it throughout the world.

A substantial question nevertheless remains: how could this same evangelist have written that the angel said to the women, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter: He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” and yet have reported nowhere afterward in his Gospel that the Lord was seen there by the disciples?

Matthew indeed says that the disciples went into Galilee, saw the Lord there, worshiped him, and received from him the command to go, teach, and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Yet, when the writings of the other evangelists are examined, they show that he had already appeared to the disciples several times—especially on the day of his resurrection itself, in Jerusalem and at the village of Emmaus.

Why, then, did he specifically foretell that he would go before them into Galilee and would be seen there by the disciples, when he was seen neither only there nor there first? Let us therefore see for what mystery he commanded, according to Matthew and Mark, after rising: “I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me.” This was indeed fulfilled, but it was fulfilled after many other events, although the command is phrased in such a way—without prejudice to necessity—that one might expect either this alone or this first to have been destined to occur.

Beyond doubt, therefore, since this is not the voice of an evangelist narrating that the event happened in this way, but the voice of the angel speaking by the Lord’s command, and of the Lord himself, which the evangelist reports as having been spoken by the angel and by the Lord, the saying must be understood as prophetic. For “Galilee” is interpreted either as “transmigration” or as “revelation.”

First, then, according to the meaning “transmigration,” what else should be understood by “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” except that Christ’s grace was destined to pass over from the people of Israel to the Gentiles? The apostles would in no way have been believed by them as they preached the Gospel unless the Lord himself had first prepared the way for them in human hearts.

This is what we understand by “He will go before you into Galilee.” But when, rejoicing, they marvel that difficulties have been broken through and overcome and that a door has been opened for them in the Lord through the illumination of the faithful, this is understood by “There you will see him”: that is, there you will find his members. There you will recognize his living body in those who receive you.

According to the interpretation of “Galilee” as “revelation,” however, this must no longer be understood in the form of a servant, but in that form in which he is equal to the Father—the form he promised his lovers through John when he said: “I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John XIV). This is not according to what they were already seeing, which, even after his resurrection, he later displayed with his scars not only to be seen but also to be touched. Rather, it is according to that ineffable light with which he enlightens every person coming into this world; according to which “he shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend him” (ibid.).

He went before us there, from where, when coming to us, he did not go before us; and, going before us to that place, he did not abandon us. That will be the revelation, the true Galilee, when we shall be like him and see him as he is. It will also be the more blessed transmigration from this world into that eternity, if we embrace his commands in such a way that we may deserve to be gathered at his right hand.

Then those on the left will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life. From here they will pass over there, and there they will see him in a manner in which the ungodly do not see him. For the ungodly will be taken away so that they may not see the glory of the Lord, and the wicked will not see the light. “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (ibid. XVII), as he is known in that eternity to which he will lead his own through the form of a servant, so that, set free, they may behold him in the form of the Lord.

[Col. 0301]

EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE. (C)

[Col. 0301]

LETTER OF EXHORTATION FROM ACCA, BISHOP, TO BEDA THE PRIEST

[Col. 0301D] To the most reverend brother in Christ and fellow priest, Beda the presbyter, Acca sends perpetual greetings in the Lord.

I have often urged your holy brotherhood, both by writing in your absence and by speaking with you in person, to undertake writing on the Gospel of Luke after your exposition of the Acts of the Apostles. Until now, you have preferred to postpone this through a modest excuse, testifying that you were deterred from attempting the work chiefly for two reasons: namely, that the work itself is arduous and that it has already been undertaken by the most holy and learned bishop Ambrose.

You did not dare to undertake a task exceeding your strength—or rather, you thought that there was no need for anyone to repeat a work that had plainly been completed so well by the greatest intellect. After the powerful statements of so great a man, you feared that either to say the same things differently would make you appear a compiler, or to set weaker things beneath them would make you seem less learned. You were also very much afraid that you might be thought to be composing new works in criticism of the studies of the ancients, and that the old proverb might be applied to you:

Why pour fish into the sea, or water into the rivers?

But pour abundant gifts into places in need.

I answer this objection of yours briefly: according to the comic poet, “Let nothing be said that has not been said before”; and charity bears all things. It has never been the custom of the saints to envy or provoke one another, but each has offered what he could, according to his abilities, in adorning the house of the Lord.

For neither did blessed Pope Gregory fear offending the Fathers whose many Gospel readings he himself revised in his homilies; nor did Augustine, or any other expositor among the Fathers who came before him, withdraw his hand through fear of their authority, whether from explaining the psalms or anything else requested of him, or from writing whatever seemed appropriate to him.

Indeed, as Augustine himself says, it is necessary for many books to be produced by many people in different styles, though not with a different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach the greatest number: to some in one way, and to others in another.

There are, however, certain passages in blessed Ambrose’s exposition of Luke that are at once so eloquent and so lofty—as I do not doubt your holiness has also observed—that they can be understood only by learned people. By uneducated or fastidious readers, of whom you will find many in the present age, they cannot even be sought, because of the difficulty either of grasping what is eloquent or of comprehending what is profound; such readers may think that what is higher than they are is not to be investigated, or that what is stronger than they are is not to be examined.

The most learned father Augustine also showed no small judgment. When writing to Paulina, God’s servant, about seeing God, he thought that no testimonies of blessed Ambrose should be used more than those taken from this little work; and he judged that these should not merely be set forth simply, but also expounded. Thus, by reconsidering a very few statements of that expositor, he composed a considerable volume.

I have thought this worth mentioning so that both your holy brotherhood and those who read may recognize it together. For when, with God’s help, you have completed the work I request, I want this letter to be placed at its beginning, so that it may be known that you were asked to write on Luke for no other reason than fraternal condescension: namely, so that those who, because of the weakness of their understanding, cannot grasp lofty or difficult matters may more easily apprehend them when they are explained in a simpler style.

Therefore, dearest brother, devote yourself diligently to the work I have mentioned and expound blessed Luke in a polished discourse. Since Saint Ambrose passed over certain matters without discussion because, as a man of supreme learning, he considered them plain and unworthy of inquiry, take care to explain these also more carefully, consulting the little works of the other Fathers and using either your own words or theirs.

I also believe that through your most vigilant study—you who spend days and nights awake in meditation on God’s law—the Author of light will reveal in some places what should be understood concerning matters they left untouched. For it is entirely just and fitting to the governance of heavenly piety and equity that you, who have pursued with tireless mind the eternal and true light of wisdom, setting aside all the affairs of the world entirely, should both here obtain the fruit of a purer understanding and, in the future, behold with a pure heart the King in his beauty, the very one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

I considered it necessary to inform your holiness that some people are troubled by the fact that, in your exposition of the Apocalypse, when you came to the four living creatures, you said in a new interpretation that Matthew is represented by the lion and Mark by the man. Some others, by contrast, assign the man to Matthew because he begins by writing about the Lord as a human being, and the lion to Mark, in whom the voice of one crying in the wilderness is heard.

I ask you to indicate more fully in this work what seems truer to you concerning these matters. May the God of love and peace preserve your holy brotherhood in remembrance of us and deign always to enlighten you for considering the wonders of his law.

LETTER OF RESPONSE FROM THE VENERABLE BEDA TO ACCA, BISHOP

[Col. 0303]

[Col. 0303C] To the most blessed and greatly desired lord, Acca, bishop, Beda, humble presbyter, sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

Truly marvelous, and marvelously true, is the statement of the outstanding teacher: “Charity believes all things, hopes all things” (1 Cor. XIII).

In letters sent to me, you say that you ask me to write something for you; yet, while asking, and before receiving my reply of agreement, you prepare the seal of a preface for the little works you have requested as though they had already been obtained and perfectly completed. Before the foundation has been laid, before even the materials have been brought, you yourself, as though the building of so great a labor had already been completed, send the keys by which its entrance is to be secured. Thus I am ashamed not to undertake quickly a work which your friendly faith presumes should be undertaken quickly and completed even more quickly.

This is certainly caused by nothing other than the unquestioning confidence of mutual love, which, from a friend’s heart, as has been said, believes and hopes everything that can be done.

And so, as soon as I had read the pages of your most sweet holiness, I submitted myself to the labor of the work imposed upon me. To pass over the countless restraints of monastic service, I was myself at once its dictating author, its notary, and its copyist. Having gathered from here and there, as though they were the most distinguished and worthy craftsmen of so great a task, the little works of the Fathers, I diligently examined what blessed Ambrose, what Augustine, what, finally, the most vigilant Gregory—according to his name, the apostle of our people—what Jerome, the interpreter of sacred history, and what the other Fathers had understood and said concerning the words of Luke.

As you commanded, I immediately set this down on sheets, either in their own words or, for the sake of brevity, in my own wording, as seemed appropriate. Since it would have been laborious to insert their names at every point and identify by name what had been said by each author, I thought it convenient to print, at a distance in the margin, the initial letters of their names. Through these letters I indicate individually where each Father’s material begins and where the discourse I have transferred ends, taking every care that I not be accused of stealing the statements of my predecessors and presenting them as my own.

I earnestly beg—and through the Lord I entreat those who read—that if anyone should judge these little works of ours, whatever their quality, worthy of copying, they should remember also to attach the aforementioned signs of the names exactly as they find them in our exemplar.

I have also added, wherever it seemed appropriate, certain matters that—as I may use the words of your holiness—the Author of light opened to me, as indications of my own labor. Although I am not able, as you wrote, to spend days and nights awake in meditation on divine law, I do not doubt that I have devoted no small amount of study to the Scriptures. Nor do I doubt that I have been able to see, in this little work and indeed in every reading, only those things that the Author of light has deigned to reveal to me—that is, to discern them by thinking rightly.

But when you say that some are troubled by why, in the Apocalypse, I assigned the lion to Matthew and the man to Mark in a new interpretation, whoever is troubled by this ought to have observed that I said this was not my new interpretation, but an ancient explanation of the Fathers. I did not arrive at this view by myself; rather, I recalled that it had been expounded in this way by blessed Augustine, and I added briefly the reasons for which he affirmed it.

It is not irrelevant, therefore, to set down Augustine’s own words and show what he thought about the evangelists and the living creatures that signify them. In this way our work will be protected from unjust criticism, and the present discussion will be strengthened by the authority of so great a teacher.

After introducing many beautiful and excellent observations about the evangelists in the first book of his work On the Harmony of the Gospels, he continues among other things as follows:

“Although each of them appears to have maintained a certain order of narration of his own, nevertheless none of them is found to have wished to write as though ignorant of the preceding writer, or to have omitted matters unknown to him that another is found to have written. Rather, as each was inspired, he added a contribution of his own labor that was not superfluous.

Matthew, then, is understood to have undertaken the incarnation of the Lord according to his royal descent, and many of his deeds and sayings according to the present life of human beings. Mark, following him like an attendant and abridger, appears to be his companion. With John alone he said nothing; by himself he said very little; with Luke alone he said less; but with Matthew he shares very many passages, almost as many words as Matthew himself, whether in agreement with Matthew alone or with the others as well.

Luke, however, appears to be more concerned with the Lord’s priestly descent and person. For he also traces his genealogy back to David not through the royal line, but through those who were not kings, arriving at Nathan, son of David, who himself was not a king. This is unlike Matthew, who descends through King Solomon and then follows the other kings in order, preserving in them the mystical number about which we shall speak later.

The Lord Jesus Christ, the one true King and the one true Priest, showed that he bore in himself the figure of these two persons, separately commended among the fathers: the former for ruling us, the latter for making expiation for us.

And a little later:

“According to his humanity, Christ,” he says, “became both king and priest. God gave him the throne of David his father, so that his kingdom would have no end, and so that the human being Christ Jesus might be mediator between God and human beings, to intercede for us.

Luke did not have a companion joined to him as an abridger, as Mark was joined to Matthew—and this perhaps not without some mystery, because kings are not without the service of attendants. Therefore, the one who undertook to narrate the royal person of Christ had joined to him, as a companion, one who in some manner followed in his footsteps.

But because the priest alone entered the Holy of Holies, Luke—whose concern was with Christ’s priesthood—did not have a companion following him who might in some manner abridge his narrative.

These three evangelists, however, differ most in those matters that Christ carried out temporally through human flesh. John, on the other hand, chiefly contemplated the very divinity of the Lord, by which he is equal to the Father, and took particular care to commend it in his Gospel to the extent he believed sufficient for human beings.

Thus he is carried far above these three, so that you may see these three, in a certain manner, dwelling on earth with Christ as a human being, while John has transcended the cloud that covers the whole earth and reached the clear heaven. There, with the sharpest and firmest vision of mind, he saw ‘in the beginning the Word’ of the Lord ‘with God,’ through whom all things were made, and recognized that the Word himself became flesh so that he might dwell among us.

Again, after some further discussion:

“Therefore, it seems to me that those who have interpreted the four living creatures in the Apocalypse as representing the four evangelists have attended more plausibly to the view that understood the lion in Matthew, the man in Mark, the calf in Luke, and the eagle in John than to the view that assigned the man to Matthew, the eagle to Mark, and the lion to John.

They wished to derive a conjecture from the beginnings of the books, not from the entire purpose of the evangelists, which ought to have been examined more carefully. For it is much more fitting that the one who most especially commended the royal person of Christ should be understood through the lion. Hence, in the Apocalypse, the lion is mentioned together with the royal tribe, where it is said: ‘The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered’ (Rev. V).

According to Matthew, magi are also said to have come from the East to seek and worship the king who appeared to them, having been born under a star; and King Herod himself feared the infant Christ as king and killed so many children in order that he might be able to kill him.

No one has doubted that Luke is signified by the calf because of the great sacrifice of the priest. For there the narrative begins with the priest Zechariah. There the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth is recalled. There the mysteries of the first priesthood are narrated as fulfilled in the infant Christ. And there are many other matters that can be carefully observed, by which it becomes clear that Luke’s concern was with the person of the priest.

Mark, however, who chose to narrate neither a royal nor a priestly lineage, nor kinship or consecration, and who nevertheless is shown to have been occupied with those things that Christ as a human being performed, appears to signify only the figure of a man among those four living creatures.

These three creatures—the lion, the man, and the calf—walk upon the earth. Hence these three evangelists are occupied chiefly with what Christ performed in the flesh and with the commands he gave to those bearing mortal flesh for the conduct of mortal life.

But John, like an eagle, flies above the clouds of human weakness and beholds the light of unchangeable truth with the sharpest and firmest eyes of the heart.”

I have inserted these few testimonies, excerpted from many others of blessed Augustine, into the prefatory letter in order to repel the slander of complainers. As has been said, they may provide protection for our earlier work and affix to the present work a seal of no small distinction.

May the grace of heavenly assistance preserve your holy fatherhood, which prays for us, and always strengthen you for the defense of his holy Church.

BOOK ONE

[Col. 0307]

[Col. 0307A] Blessed Luke the evangelist, intending to speak about everything that Jesus began to do and teach until the day on which he was taken up, first took care to rebuke the audacity of those who had written falsely about him. He silently admonishes the reader that one must follow not only what he himself proclaims, but must recognize as utterly detestable whatever has a different sound. And lest an occasion for error arise among the weak, the reading of those who write superfluously here and there should be completely rejected.

For the statement, “If they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them” (Mark XVI), could not have been made about everyone generally, but only about certain people endowed with a special strength of faith or knowledge.

Thus Luke begins:

PROLOGUE

Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed everything from the beginning carefully, to write it out for you in order, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of those words in which you have been instructed.

In this most explicit prologue he indicates that his chief reason for writing the Gospel was to prevent the false evangelists from having the opportunity to preach falsehood. Their surviving writings testify that, under the name of the apostles, they attempted to introduce sects of unbelief. Thus some are found to have falsely placed their writings under the name of Thomas, others of Bartholomew, some of Matthias, and others even under the title of the twelve apostles.

Basilides and Apelles also—one of whom taught, among other abominable doctrines, that there were 365 heavens, and the other that there were two mutually opposed gods—left behind Gospels defiled by the error of their names.

Among these matters it should be noted that the Gospel called “according to the Hebrews” is to be counted not among the apocryphal writings but among ecclesiastical histories. For even Jerome, the interpreter of sacred Scripture, appears to have drawn many testimonies from it and to have translated it into Latin and Greek.

Luke immediately refutes the false Gospels in his preface. “Since many,” he says, “have undertaken to set in order a narrative.” By “many” he counts them not so much according to their number as according to the manifold diversity of their heresy. They were not endowed with the gift of the Holy Spirit; rather, in empty labor, they attempted to arrange a narrative instead of weaving together the truth of history. Consequently, they left to others the completion of a work over which they had labored in vain.

He refers, of course, to those who, although there are four of them, produced not so much four Gospels as one Gospel, harmonized through the most beautiful variety of four accounts. They produced them just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word had delivered them.

By this statement not only Luke and Mark are designated—neither of whom had seen the Lord present in the flesh and therefore had to learn by hearing what they were to write—but also the apostles Matthew and John. They too had to hear from those who had been able to know his infancy, childhood, and genealogy and to be present at his deeds many things that they were to write.

When he says that it seemed good to him also to write, he does not mean that it seemed good to him by his own judgment, but that, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, it seemed good to him as well. In accordance with this, the apostles say in their letter: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” Through this grace, what is good comes to seem good to us also.

He says that he had followed not merely a few things but all things. Yet, having followed all things, he thought it good to write not everything, but about all the matters that he believed suitable for confirming the faith of the readers, since the world itself could not contain everything if it were written down (John XXI).

For this reason he deliberately passed over certain things that had been said by others, so that grace in the Gospel might shine forth in manifold ways and so that the individual books might stand out through certain distinctive mysteries of events and miracles.

“Theophilus” is interpreted as “one who loves God” or “one loved by God.” Therefore, whoever loves God, or desires to be loved by God, should consider the Gospel written for him and preserve it as a gift given and a pledge entrusted to him. Otherwise the money of the word that he has received may be destroyed either by the moth of heretical corruption or by the rust of sordid greed.

What is promised to this same Theophilus is not an explanation of every new and unknown matter, but the expression of the truth of those words in which he has been instructed. This is so that he may be able to recognize in what order each thing was done or said concerning the Lord or by the Lord.

For one who desires to be perfect must not merely believe in Christ; he must also know the order both of his perpetual divinity and of his temporal dispensation.

CHAPTER ONE

There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, whose name was Elizabeth.

The most sacred nobility of the Lord’s precursor descended in glory not only from his parents but also from his ancestors, so that the faith in his coming might be proclaimed more freely—not as something conceived through a sudden inspiration, but as something received through ancestral succession.

Since the dignity of Aaron, the first high priest under the Law, is known to all, a few words should be said about Abijah. When King and prophet David, with great devotion, sought to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob, while the Lord determined that this should be done instead by Solomon, David therefore prepared for Solomon everything needed for the expenses of the house and provided measurements and descriptions for every part of the building. Thus, as the external structure of the worship increased, the inner height of devotion might also grow.

He likewise distributed the divisions of the priestly and Levitical ranks among all the works of the house of the Lord. There were princes of the sanctuary and princes of God—that is, high priests—from both the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar. He divided their courses according to their ministries, so that they might enter the house of God, into twenty-four lots. In these, the lot of the eighth course fell to the family of Abijah, from which Zechariah arose.

He divided the two families among themselves by lot: one house, Eleazar, presided over the others, while the other house, Ithamar, had the rest under it. Read the book of Chronicles, and also the seventh book of Josephus’s Antiquities, where he reports that it was established that each lineage should minister to God according to the order of the lot for eight days, from Sabbath to Sabbath. There he also asserts that twenty-four divisions were made from the tribe of the Levites, so that they too, chosen by lot in the same way, might minister for eight-day periods according to the custom of the priests.

It was not without reason that the first herald of the New Testament was born in the course of the eighth lot. For just as the Old Testament is often expressed by the number seven because of the Sabbath, so the New Testament is sometimes expressed by the number eight because of the mystery either of the Lord’s resurrection or of ours.

Therefore, because the heavenly kingdom is entered only through observance of both Testaments, it is rightly related that in Solomon’s temple there was a mystical ascent of fifteen steps. The one who cries out to the Lord in tribulation and is heard is likewise led upward by psalms of the same number of steps. At last, placed in the courts of the house of God, he can hear: “May the Lord bless you from Zion” (Ps. CXXXIII).

The time of Herod, a foreign king, also bears witness to the Lord’s coming. For it had been foretold: “The prince shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX).

From the time when the ancestors came out of Egypt, they were ruled by judges of their own nation until the prophet Samuel, and afterward by kings until the Babylonian exile. After the return from Babylon, supreme authority was exercised by the priests, until Hyrcanus, at once king and priest, was afflicted by many calamities through the envy of his brother and was finally killed by Herod through a fraudulent plot. Hyrcanus himself had raised Herod’s father from an ignoble foreigner—an Idumean by birth—to a position of distinction and citizenship.

Then, by the order of Caesar Augustus, the kingdom of Judea was entrusted to Herod to govern. In the thirty-first year of Herod, in accordance with the prophecy just mentioned, he who was to be sent came.

[Col. 0310A] Now both were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.

“Righteous before God” is well said. Not everyone who is righteous before human beings is righteous before God. Human beings see one way; God sees another. Human beings look at the face, God at the heart. Therefore it can happen that someone appears righteous to me because of a goodness deliberately fashioned for popular approval, yet is not righteous before God, if his righteousness is not formed from simplicity of mind but is merely counterfeited through flattery.

Blessed, however, is the one who is righteous in God’s sight. Blessed is the one of whom the Lord deigns to say: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” For the true Israelite is one who sees God, knows that he is seen by the Lord, and displays to him the hidden things of his heart.

“Walking,” he says, “in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.” First comes the commandment; second, the ordinance. When we obey the heavenly commandments, we walk in the Lord’s commandments. When we judge, and judge rightly, we seem to hold to the Lord’s ordinances.

The praise is therefore complete, since it encompasses lineage, conduct, office, deed, and judgment: lineage in one’s ancestors, conduct in righteousness, office in the priesthood, deed in obedience to the commandment, and judgment in the ordinance.

What he added—“blamelessly”—is what the Apostle says: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. XII). Ecclesiastes likewise says: “Do not be exceedingly righteous” (Eccl. VII). For righteousness that is generally too severe provokes the complaint of human beings. But righteousness that is tempered avoids, through the very sweetness of its moderation, even the complaint of envy.

[Col. 0310C] And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.

It was divinely arranged that John should be born to parents advanced in age and long deprived of the fruit of marriage, so that the unexpected birth of a child might make the gift more gracious to them and prepare the others, through their astonishment at the miracle, to hear the future prophet.

Accordingly, all who heard it kept it in their hearts, saying: “What, do you suppose, will this child be?”

Now it happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood—

Through Moses the Lord had indeed established one high priest, and when he died had commanded that one successor should follow him in order. This was preserved until the time of David, by whom it was decreed—through the Lord’s agency, as we have said—that there should be several, who would minister in turn during their assigned periods, each devoting himself to chastity and not approaching his own household at all.

Thus Zechariah is now affirmed to have exercised the priesthood in the order of his division.

By lot he was chosen to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord; and the whole multitude of the people was praying outside, at the hour of incense. He was not now chosen by lot, when the incense was to be burned, but had long before been selected by lot, when, as the first in the order of his priesthood, he succeeded to the course of Abijah. It had been commanded that the incense be carried into the Holy of Holies by the high priest, while all the people waited outside the temple, on the tenth day of the seventh month. This day, called the Day of Expiation or Atonement, falls among us—because of the varying course of the moon from which the Hebrews calculate their months—sometimes in September and sometimes in October. For the month in which Passover is celebrated holds the first place in the year both by the order of creation and by the decree of the Law, as the Lord says to Moses: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. On the tenth day of this month, let each man take a lamb,” and so forth (Exod. XII). Writing to the Hebrews, the Apostle thus recalls this day: “Into the first tabernacle the priests always entered, completing the duties of the sacrifices; but into the second the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offers,” and so forth (Hebr. IX). Unfolding the mystery of this day, he shows that Jesus is the true high priest. When the days of his office had been completed—that is, when the dispensation of the flesh had been fulfilled in his own blood—he entered the hidden places of heaven, to make the Father propitious toward us and to intercede for the sins of those who still wait praying before the doors and love his coming. Beautifully, therefore, his descent is announced by the angel on the day on which his ascent was prefigured by the Law. For “he who descended is himself also the one who ascended” (Ephes. IV); and, as the Psalm says, “his going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit” (Psal. XVIII).

[Col. 0311A] Now an angel appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. The angel appropriately appears both in the temple and beside the altar and on the right, because he proclaims the coming of the true priest, the mystery of the universal sacrifice, and the joy of the heavenly gift. For just as present things are often signified by the left, so eternal blessings are often foretold by the right. Accordingly, in the praise of Wisdom it is sung: “Length of days are in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory.”

And Zacharias was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him, and so forth. The angel strengthens trembling Zacharias, because, just as it belongs to human frailty to be troubled by the sight of a spiritual creature, so it belongs to angelic kindness at once to comfort mortals who are afraid at the sight of them by speaking gently to them. In contrast, it belongs to demonic savagery always to shake with greater terror those whom it perceives to have been frightened by its presence; and this is overcome by no better means than steadfast faith.

And your wife Elisabeth will bear you a son, and you will call his name John. Having said that the prayer had been heard, he immediately promises the birth of a son to his wife. This does not mean that the man who had entered to offer sacrifice for the people could have abandoned the public prayers in order to pray for the reception of children, especially since no one prays for what he despairs of receiving. Indeed, he was so mindful of his own age and of his unfruitful wife, and so despaired of children being born to him, that he did not believe the angel promising this. Rather, when he says, “Your prayer has been heard,” he signifies redemption for the people; and when he adds, “Your wife will bear you a son,” he discloses the order of that same redemption: namely, that Zacharias’s son, once born, would go before the Redeemer of that people by proclaiming him.

An indication of singular merit is given whenever a name is imposed or changed by God for human beings. Thus Abram, because he was to become the father of many nations, was called Abraham. Thus Jacob, because he saw God, deserved to be called Israel. Thus King Josiah, because of the summit of his outstanding virtue, was named by God long before he was born. John, therefore, is interpreted as “in whom there is grace,” or “the grace of the Lord.” By this name it is declared, first, that grace was granted to his parents, to whom a son was born in their old age; then, to John himself, who would be great before the Lord and would still be enriched with the gift of the Holy Spirit while in his mother’s womb; and finally, also to the children of Israel, whom he was to turn toward the Lord their God.

And he will be joy and exultation to you, and many will rejoice at his birth. The father rightly rejoices because he has received a son either born in his old age or endowed with such grace. Others also rejoice, those to whom he will announce, for the first time, the entrance of the kingdom of heaven. It should be noted that many rejoice at the birth of the Forerunner, whereas, at the birth of the Lord, the angel announces “great joy that will be for all the people.” For the one was to preach salvation to many, while the other came to grant it to all who were willing to receive it.

[Col. 0312A] For he will be great before the Lord, and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. It is a sign of great virtue before the Lord when one who preaches heavenly joys in the wilderness completely rejects earthly delights. Yet this also stands out as great before the Lord, although it may seem contemptible to human beings: that the man greater than anyone born of women was beheaded because of the amusement of a dancing girl. The angel who made the promise himself explains the order of his greatness in what follows: “And he will drink neither wine,” he says, “nor strong drink.” *Sicera* is interpreted as “intoxication”; by this term the Hebrews signify every drink capable of causing drunkenness, whether made from fruits, grains, or any other substance. It was characteristic of the law of the Nazirites to abstain from wine and strong drink during the time of their consecration. Hence John, Samson, Jeremiah, and others of this kind, so that they might remain Nazirites—that is, holy—always strive to abstain from these things.

For it is fitting that a vessel dedicated to heavenly grace be disciplined away from the enticements of the world, and that one who desires to be filled with the new wine of the Holy Spirit not be drunk with wine, in which there is excess. Thus rightly, when the drunkenness of wine is removed from someone, the grace of the Spirit is increased in him. John showed that he was filled with this grace, as had been foretold, when the blessed Mary entered and he leaped in his mother’s womb, recognizing the duty of his forerunning and, insofar as he was then able, proclaiming the coming of the Lord.

[Col. 0312D] And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah. When John, bearing witness to Christ and baptizing peoples in faith in him, is said to have turned the children of Israel to the Lord their God, it is plainly evident that Christ is the Lord God of Israel. If Christ is—and indeed because Christ is—the Lord God of Israel, let the Arians cease denying that Christ is Lord God. Let the Photinians be ashamed to give Christ a beginning from the Virgin. Let the Manichaeans cease believing that the people of Israel have one God and Christians another.

And because John is said to go before him, let them see that the eternal God, existing before the ages, was born as a human being within the ages, and therefore was called by his forerunner sometimes a man who would come after him, and sometimes the Son of God. He is rightly said to go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, because just as Elijah was the herald of the Judge who was to come, so John became the herald of the Redeemer. Hence, also, both followed the wilderness in an entirely similar way of life: they had frugal food, rough clothing, and despised belts. Both endured the madness of a king and queen. Both embraced the wilderness, were frugal in food, rough in clothing, and contemptible in girding. Elijah divided the Jordan as he sought heaven; John turned people toward the saving washing by which heaven is sought. John lived with the Lord on earth; Elijah was revealed with him in glory.

[Col. 0313A] And he will turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children, and the disobedient, and so forth. To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children is to pour into the peoples, by preaching, the spiritual knowledge of the ancient saints. The prudence of the righteous is not to presume upon righteousness from works of the Law, but to seek salvation through faith. Thus, although they live under the Law and fulfill the commandments of the Law, they understand that they are to be saved by the grace of God through Christ. “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. I). And Peter says concerning the yoke of the Law: “Neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear it, but through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they also were” (Acts XV).

Because the unbelieving are to be instructed in this prudence both by John and by Elijah, this sentence spoken by the angel about John is rightly foretold concerning Elijah by Malachi in almost the same words: “Prepare,” he says, “a perfect people for the Lord.” For because he had said that Zacharias, praying on behalf of the people, had been heard, he teaches in what manner that same people must be saved and perfected—namely, by repenting at the preaching of John and believing in Christ.

And Zacharias said to the angel: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.” Hesitating because of the greatness of the promises, he asks for a sign by which he may be able to believe, although the angel’s very appearance or address ought to have been sufficient for him as a sign. Thus he paid the deserved penalty for his distrust by remaining silent; that same silence became both the sign of faith that he had sought and the penalty for unbelief that he had deserved.

And the angel answered and said to him: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to announce these good things to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place,” and so forth. He wishes it to be understood that, if a human being made such promises, it would be permissible to demand a sign with impunity; but when an angel makes the promise, there ought no longer to be any doubt. He gives the sign that is requested, so that the man who spoke in disbelief may now learn to believe by remaining silent.

Here it should be noted that the angel testifies both that he stands before God and that he has been sent to announce good news to Zacharias. For when angels come to us, they outwardly fulfill their ministry in such a way that they nevertheless never cease inwardly through contemplation. They are therefore both sent and stand before him, because although an angelic spirit is circumscribed, the highest Spirit, who is God himself, is not circumscribed. Thus angels are sent and yet are before him, because wherever they are sent they move within him.

[Col. 0314A] And the people were waiting for Zacharias, and they wondered that he was delaying in the temple. When he came out, he could not speak to them. And they understood that he had seen a vision in the temple; and he himself was making signs to them, and remained mute. And when the days of his service had been completed, he went to his house.

This is what I said: during the time of their course, the high priests, devoted only to the duties of the temple, abstained not only from embracing their wives but also from entering their own homes. Here an example is given to the priests of our time, who are commanded always to serve at the altar, that chastity must be preserved perpetually. For at that time succession in the priesthood from the stock of Aaron was being sought, and therefore time had necessarily to be provided for the begetting of offspring. But because now it is not carnal succession but spiritual perfection that is sought, priests are consequently commanded, so that they may always be able to stand before the altar, always to abstain from their wives and always to observe chastity.

After these days his wife Elisabeth conceived. That is, after the days of Zacharias’s service had been completed. John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, mentioning this most sacred conception, says: “These things took place in the month of September, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, when the eleventh moon was beginning, at the time when the Jews ought to celebrate the fast of the Feast of Tabernacles.” It was found that that very eighth day before the Kalends of October was the equinox, in which the beginning of the night is longer than that of the light. “He must increase,” he says, “but I must decrease” (John III).

For the light had been diminished by darkness when the Jews, according to the Law and the prophecy, offered sacrifices to God; and it was then that John was conceived. These were the offerings previously made for the sins of the people, and they had to cease when John, that is, the Baptizer, was conceived. Therefore his father Zacharias, the priest of the Jews, became mute, because their sacrifices, which were offered for the sins of the people, already had to cease and fall silent. For the one priest was coming who would offer to God, from his own sacrificed lamb, a sacrifice for the sins of all.

By these words of blessed John we are taught that immediately on the day after the Day of Expiation the change of the priestly course was then celebrated, and that therefore this took place at the conception of the Lord’s Forerunner. It is not without reason that this is foretold as a day of fasting and affliction by the angel, because through him the affliction of repentance was to be preached to human beings.

[Col. 0314D] And she kept herself hidden for five months, saying: “Thus the Lord has dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among human beings.” Elisabeth shows how great is the concern of the saints that they admit nothing shameful for which they ought to blush. She is ashamed even of the gifts she had longed to receive; and although she rejoices that the reproach of barrenness has been removed, she is nevertheless embarrassed by giving birth in old age. Yet she is ashamed of the burden of motherhood only as long as the honor of her offspring remains hidden. For she who hid herself because she had conceived a son began to exult loudly when the blessed Mother of God entered, because she was going to bear a prophet.
