Allegorically, Zacharias can signify the Jewish priesthood, and Elisabeth the Law itself. Exercised by the teachings of the priests and, as it were, supported by male assistance, the Law ought to have borne spiritual children, but, as though suffering the injury of barrenness, it was entirely unable to do so. This was not because there were not many people of exceedingly perfect life both before the Law and under the Law, but because the Law brought no one to perfection; and it could not open the kingdom of heaven unless Christ went before it.

It is rightly said that both were righteous before God, because just as the Law is good and the commandment holy, just, and good, so also the legal priesthood, in accordance with the dispensation of that time, was holy, good, and just. What follows—that they were both advanced in their days—can thus be explained: the devotion of the Law, like its adolescence or youth, flourished in the times of Moses and thereafter; but as the Savior’s advent approached, a grievous old age bent it down. At that time the order of the priesthood was confused by the ambitions and rivalries of the high priests, and the Law itself was torn apart by the traditions of the Pharisees, becoming less capable of bringing forth children for God.

Zacharias therefore enters the temple, because it belongs to priests to enter the sanctuary of God and to understand the final mysteries of heavenly things. The multitude prays outside, because those who cannot ascend into the secrets and mysteries must necessarily attend humbly to the instructions of their teachers. But while Zacharias places incense on the altar, he learns that John will be born; for while teachers burn with a greater flame of divine reading, they discover that God’s grace is to come through Jesus Christ and that, from the inner marrow of the letters, as from the womb of Elisabeth, it is to emerge.

This is rightly done through an angel, because the Law was ordained through angels in the hand of the Mediator. But the one who delays believing what he has heard is punished with the penalty of silence, because the person who does not understand that a spiritual meaning lies within the letters is mute. Such a man no longer knows how to speak words to the people as a teacher, but, deprived—as I may say—of word and reason, communicates by silent signs.

Such was the Jewish priesthood at that time, when it did not even care to know either the meaning of the sacrifices or the sayings of the Prophets. Thus, while Zacharias remains mute, Elisabeth conceives John: although the high priests do not understand the distinction of faith, and the Pharisees and scribes lose it, so that they neither enter themselves nor permit their hearers to enter, the inner parts of the Law nevertheless abound in the sacraments of Christ.

Elisabeth rightly conceals her conception for five months, either because Moses, the lawgiver himself, sets forth the mysteries of Christ figuratively in five books, or because the entire sequence of the Old Testament prefigures that same dispensation of Christ, through the deeds and words of the saints, in the five ages of the world. And because the incarnation of Christ was to occur in the sixth age of the world, or was to serve for the fulfillment of the Law, the angel sent to Mary rightly announces in the sixth month of John’s conception that the Savior would be born, as the reading that follows demonstrates.

In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth. Angels are designated by personal names so that their power in their work may also be signified through their names. They do not receive proper names in that holy city which the complete knowledge of the Almighty has perfected through vision, as though their persons could not be known without names. Rather, when they come to us to administer something, they also derive names among us from their ministries.

Gabriel, therefore, is sent to the Virgin Mary; his name is interpreted as “the strength of God.” He was coming to announce the one who deigned to appear humbly in order to conquer the powers of the air. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psal. XXIII). And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (ibid.). Through the strength of God, therefore, the one was to be announced who is the Lord of virtues and mighty in battle, and who was coming to war against the powers of the air.

Understand the sixth month as March, on whose twenty-fifth day our Lord is handed down as both conceived and suffering, just as he was born on the twenty-fifth day of December. Whether we believe that the spring equinox occurs on this day—as some think—or that the winter solstice occurs on that day, it is altogether fitting that he who enlightens every human being coming into the world should be conceived or born with the increase of light.

But if anyone argues that before the time of the Lord’s birth and conception the light either increased or overcame the darkness, we reply that John then proclaimed the kingdom of heaven before his coming, and that preachers are now also commanded: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Psal. LXVII). But why John was conceived around the autumnal equinox and born around the summer solstice is explained by the one who speaks either in his own person or, as many believe, in the person of the Old Testament: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III).

To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. For many reasons the Savior wished to be born not from an unmarried virgin but from a betrothed woman. First, so that through the genealogy of Joseph, whose relative Mary was, Mary’s origin might also be known. For it is not customary for Scripture to trace the genealogy of women. The statement that they were “of the house of David” can indeed be understood of both.

Second, it was so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress, since he preferred that some should doubt his parentage rather than her chastity. At the same time he removed any occasion for impure-minded women to defame the Savior’s mother with false suspicions. Third, so that, when she fled into Egypt and returned from there, she would have the support of a husband who would be both guardian and witness of her completely undefiled virginity. Fourth, so that her childbirth would not be exposed to the devil; for if he had recognized that he was born of a virgin, he might perhaps have feared to hand him over to death as one more outstanding than other human beings.

Now Mary in Hebrew means “star of the sea,” while in Syriac she is called “lady”; and rightly so, because she was worthy to bring forth both the Lord of the whole world and the everlasting light for the ages.

And the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” She is rightly called “full of grace,” for she obtains the grace that no other woman had deserved: namely, to conceive and bear the very author of grace.

[Col. 0317A] When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying and considered what kind of greeting this might be. Learn from her the conduct of a virgin; learn from her modesty; learn from her proclamation; learn from her mystery. It belongs to virgins to tremble and to be afraid at every entrance of a man, and to regard every word spoken by a man with reverence. Let women learn to imitate her purpose of modesty.

The angel found her alone in her inner chamber, where no man could see her; she was alone, without a companion, alone, without a witness, so that no degraded affection might corrupt her. She was greeted by an angel. Learn, virgin, to avoid wantonness in speech. Mary herself was wary even of an angel’s greeting. Yet, he says, she was considering what kind of greeting this was. And therefore she did so with modesty, because she was afraid; with prudence, because she was astonished at the novelty of the blessing’s formula, which had nowhere been read and had nowhere previously been encountered.

[Col. 0317B] And the angel said to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God.” Seeing her troubled by an unusual greeting, one reserved for her alone, he calls her by name as a familiar acquaintance and orders her not to be afraid. And because he had called her full of grace, he both establishes and explains that same grace more fully, saying:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus.” Jesus is interpreted as “Savior” or “saving one.” The angel, addressing Joseph, explained the mystery of this name: “For he himself,” he said, “will save his people from their sins.” He did not say “the people of Israel,” but “his people”—that is, those called from uncircumcision and circumcision into the unity of faith, so that, gathered from their different sides, they might become one shepherd and one fold.

He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father. It was also said of John that he would be great, but John would be great as a human being, whereas Jesus would be great as God. John was great before the Lord; of Jesus, however, it says: “He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.”

Therefore the one who was conceived and born in the Virgin’s womb is the same Son of the Most High. He is the same human being, created in time from his mother, who is God, born before time from the Father. If the same one is human who is God, let Nestorius cease to say that only a human being was born from the Virgin, and that this human being was received by the Word of God not into unity of person but into inseparable fellowship. Otherwise he is convicted of asserting not one Christ, true God and human being, but two—which it is impious to say—and consequently of proclaiming not a Trinity but a quaternity.

The Catholic faith, however, just as it most rightly confesses one human being composed of flesh and soul, so also confesses one Christ composed of the human being and the Word. This accords with the words of the angels, who asserted that the throne of David his father would be given to him. For by declaring that the very one whom he says will be called the Son of the Most High would have David himself as his father, the angel demonstrates one person of Christ in two natures.

He received the throne of David so that he might call to an everlasting kingdom the people to whom David and his sons once provided the governance of a temporal kingdom—the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

[Col. 0318A] And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. Isaiah also says: “His government will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and justice” (Isa. IX). He did not say in the acquisition of glory and earthly treasures, nor in victory over many nations and the destruction of proud cities, but “in judgment and justice.” Through these things the kingdom of Christ is both multiplied and strengthened in each individual believer and throughout the universal Church in the world.

By the house of Jacob he means the whole Church, which was either born from a good root or, although it was a wild olive tree, was nevertheless grafted by the merit of faith into a good olive tree. Addressing it after the triumph of his Passion, the Savior says: “You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him” (Psal. XXI).

Jesus is not asserted, in the words of the future tense, to be destined to become great, to be called the Son of the Most High, to receive David’s scepter, and to reign in the house of Jacob because, according to the thinking of heretics who have departed from the truth, Christ did not exist before Mary. Rather, it is because, as they maintain, a human being assumed into God was glorified with the glory that the Word of God had before the world existed with the Father—that is, so that a human being together with God, full of grace and truth, might receive the same name of Son and the same person of Christ.

Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” She reverently disclosed the purpose of her mind: namely, that she had resolved to lead a virginal life. Because she was the first among women to devote herself to so great a virtue, she rightly deserved to excel the other women by a unique blessedness.

“How,” she says, “will this happen?” She did not say, “How shall I know this?” but, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” She was inquiring about the manner of the obedience to which she was to submit, not demanding a sign by which she might believe. For it was not fitting that the virgin chosen to bear God should be doubtful through distrust; she was cautious through prudence, because a human being could not easily know the mystery that had remained hidden in God throughout the ages.

Since she had read, “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son,” but had not read how this could happen, she rightly believed what she had read and asked the angel about what she had not found in the Prophet (Isa. VII).

And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” It is not through the seed of a man, he says—something you do not know—but through the work of the Holy Spirit, with which you are filled, that you will conceive. There will be conception in you, but no lust. There will be no heat of desire where the Holy Spirit casts his shadow.

Yet in the words “the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” the twofold nature of the incarnate Savior may also be signified. A shadow is usually formed both by light and by a body. The one over whom it is cast is refreshed by as much of the sun’s light or heat as is sufficient, but the sun’s own burning intensity is moderated, so that it can be endured, by the interposition of a slight cloud or some other body.

Thus, because the blessed Virgin, being a pure human being, could not bodily receive the entire fullness of divinity, the power of the Most High overshadowed her—that is, the incorporeal light of divinity assumed a human body in her. Concerning this the Prophet beautifully says: “Behold, the Lord,” he says, “ascends upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX). This means: Behold, the Word of God, coeternal with the Father, light from light, born before the ages, will at the end of the ages assume flesh and a soul unburdened by any weight of sin, and from the Virgin’s womb, like a bridegroom from his chamber (Psal. XVIII), will proceed into the world.

And therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God. To distinguish him from our holiness, Jesus, who is uniquely holy, is asserted to be destined to be born. We, even if we are made holy, are not nevertheless born holy, because we are constrained by the very condition of corruptible nature. Thus each of us rightly says with the Prophet in lamentation: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother brought me forth in sins” (Psal. L).

He alone is truly holy who, in order to conquer the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived from the mingling of carnal intercourse. “He will be called,” he says, “the Son of God.” What do you say here, Nestorian, who, by denying that blessed Mary is the Mother of God, strive to oppose the manifest truth? Behold, he said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. How, then, is the Son of God not God? Or how can she who gave birth to God not be Θεοτόκος—that is, “Mother of God”?

And behold, Elisabeth your relative has also conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word is impossible with God. So that the Virgin would not distrust her ability to give birth, she receives the example of an aged barren woman who was to bear, so that she might learn that all things are possible for God, even those that appear contrary to the order of nature.

If anyone is troubled by the statement that Elisabeth was the blessed Mary’s relative, since one derived her origin from the house of David and the other from the daughters of Aaron, let him observe that their ancestors, by giving their children in marriage to one another, could have joined the two tribes. If this explanation should not satisfy someone who presses the objection contentiously, as though such a union could not have occurred contrary to the prohibition of the Law, let him read Exodus, where it is written: “Aaron took as his wife Elisabeth, daughter of Aminadab, sister of Naasson, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (Exod. VI).

Let him see that, before the decree of the Law, the priestly and royal lines had already been joined together by heavenly providence. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ, who was to be the true King and Priest according to the flesh, would also receive his flesh from both lines, namely from the stock of David and of Aaron. Hence in both these tribes the mystical anointing was celebrated according to the Law, as a prophecy alike of Christ’s name and of his generation.

David himself, entering the house of God, received the holy bread and the sword as both king and priest. He was prefiguring the one who would come from his seed, who would both fight for our freedom by royal right and offer, for our absolution, the bread of his flesh.

Mary said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord. Let it be done to me according to your word.” What devoted humility this is: she both desires the angel’s promise to be fulfilled and calls herself, the one chosen to be a mother, a handmaid. She most clearly indicates how little merit she claims for herself in obeying the Lord’s commands.

“Let it be done,” she says: let the holy one be conceived in a virgin without the seed of a man, be born from the Holy Spirit with unimpaired flesh, be born from a woman as mother without a human father, and be called the Son of God.

And the angel departed from her. Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, to a city of Judah. Having received the Virgin’s consent, the angel immediately returned to heaven, while she sought the hill country. She hastened to visit Elisabeth, not as one who disbelieved the proclamation or was doubtful about the sign, but as one joyful because of her desire and devout because of her duty.

At the same time she provides a typological example: every soul that has conceived the word of God in its mind should immediately ascend, by the steps of love, the lofty summits of virtue, so that it may enter the citadel of the city of Judah—that is, of confession and praise—and be able to dwell there for about three months, until it reaches the perfection of faith, hope, and charity.

And she entered the house of Zacharias and greeted Elisabeth. Learn from Mary, Virgin, humility, so that you may be chaste in body and devout in heart. The younger visits the elder; the virgin greets the married woman. For the more chaste a virgin is, the more humble she ought to be; and by showing deference to her elders, she should commend the character of chastity through the praise of humility.

Alternatively: Mary comes to Elisabeth; the Lord comes to John. Mary comes so that Elisabeth may be filled with the Holy Spirit; the Lord comes so that John’s baptism may be consecrated. The humbling of the greater is, of course, the exaltation of the lesser. Finally, the text continues:

And it happened that, when Elisabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. Observe the distinction and the particular force of each word. Elisabeth first heard the voice, but John first sensed the grace. She heard according to the order of nature; he leaped according to the reason of the mystery. She sensed Mary’s arrival; he sensed the Lord’s.

The women speak of grace; the infants inwardly experience its workings, and they begin the mystery of piety through their mothers’ acts of progress. Through a twofold miracle, the mothers prophesy by the spirit of the infants. The infant leaped, and the mother was filled. The mother was not filled before the son; rather, when the son had been filled with the Holy Spirit, he also filled his mother.

And she cried out with a loud voice and said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” It should be noted that the prophecy previously spoken concerning Christ is fulfilled not only by the miracles of events but also by the precise force of the words. For this is the fruit promised under oath to the patriarch David: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon my throne” (Psal. CXXXI). At the same time, it should be observed that Mary is blessed by Elisabeth with the same voice by which she was blessed by Gabriel, so that she might be shown to be worthy of reverence both among angels and among human beings, and rightly preferred to all women.

And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? She does not inquire as one ignorant of what she recognizes to be the work of the Holy Spirit—namely, that she is visited by the Lord’s mother for the benefit of her own offspring—but, struck by the novelty of the miracle, she confesses that this is not the result of her own merit but of a divine gift.

For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb. Elisabeth was ashamed of the burden of giving birth as long as she did not know the mystery of faith. But she who hid herself because she had conceived a son began to boast because she was bringing forth a prophet. She who had previously been ashamed now blesses, and she who had previously doubted is now strengthened.

“For behold,” she says, “as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb.” Therefore she cried out with a loud voice when she sensed the Lord’s arrival, because she believed that the birth was holy. There was no cause for shame where the birth of a prophet could establish the credibility of a generation granted, not contrived.

And blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord will be fulfilled. You see that Mary did not doubt but believed, and therefore obtained the fruit of faith. “Blessed,” he says, “is she who believed.” And truly blessed is she who was superior to the priest. When the priest had denied, the virgin corrected the error. Nor is it surprising that the Lord, about to redeem the world, began his work with his mother, so that she through whom salvation was being prepared for all might be the first to draw the fruit of salvation from the pledge. At the same time, one should note how greatly grace enriched Elizabeth’s soul when Mary entered, illuminating it through the spirit of prophecy concerning the past, the present, and the future alike. For when she said, “Blessed are you who believed,” she plainly indicated that she had recognized through the Spirit the angel’s words that had been spoken to Mary [Col. 0321C]. And when she added, “The things that were spoken to you by the Lord will be fulfilled,” she foresaw those things that would also follow her in the future. By calling her “the mother of her Lord,” she showed that she understood that she was carrying in her womb the Redeemer of the human race.

And Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.” “The Lord,” she says, “has exalted me with so great and unheard-of a gift that it cannot be explained by any service of the tongue, but can scarcely be grasped even by the inmost feeling of the heart. Therefore I offer all the powers of my soul in hymns of thanksgiving. Whatever I live, perceive, and discern, I gladly devote to contemplating the greatness of him whose end there is none, because my spirit rejoices in the eternal divinity of that same Jesus—that is, Savior—by whose temporal conception my flesh is made pregnant.” To this the Psalmist’s statement is similar: “But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation” (Ps. XXXIV). For he too revered the Father and the Son with equal love.

Because he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid. “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.” She rejoices that the one whose lowliness is regarded is rightly to be called blessed by all, just as, conversely, the one whose pride is condemned with contempt wastes away, punished by the name Eve—that is, “woe,” or calamity. For it was fitting that, just as death entered the world through the pride of our first mother, so the entrance to life should again be opened through Mary’s humility.

[Col. 0322A] Because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. He looks back to the beginning of the hymn, where it was said: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” That soul to which the Lord deigns to do great things is accustomed to magnify him with worthy praises, and by exhortation can say to those who share the same desire and purpose: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. XXXIII). For whoever, having come to know the Lord, refuses insofar as he can to magnify him and sanctify his name will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.

His name is called holy because, by the summit of his unique power, he transcends every creature and is set far apart from all that he has made. This is better understood in the Greek expression, in which the very word ἅγιον, “holy,” signifies, as it were, being outside the earth. In imitation of him, we too are commanded, according to our capacity, to be set apart from all who are not holy and are not devoted to God. For the Lord says: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. XI). Whoever consecrates himself will rightly be seen as being outside the earth and outside the world. For he too can say: “Although we walk upon the earth, our manner of life is in heaven.”

And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him. Turning from particular gifts to the general judgments of God, she describes the condition of the whole human race and explains in alternating verses what the proud and the humble deserve, what the children of Adam possess through free choice, and what the children of God are through grace. “Therefore,” she says, “it is not only to me that he who is mighty has done great things, but in every nation and generation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.”

He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts. By “his arm” she means the very Son of God. This does not mean that God the Father is defined by the form of human flesh and that the Son clings to him like a bodily limb; rather, because all things were made through him, he is called the arm of the Lord. Just as your arm is that through which you work, so God’s Word is called his arm, because through the Word he worked the world. Why does a human being extend an arm in order to accomplish something, unless it is because what he says is immediately brought about? If he possessed such power that what he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm. Therefore, when we hear that the Son of God is the arm of God the Father, let carnal habit not obstruct us; instead, insofar as he grants us the ability, let us contemplate the power and wisdom of God through which all things were made.

He has cast down the powerful from their throne, and has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, and has sent the rich away empty. What he said about his arm, and what he promised concerning generation after generation, must also be attached to these verses, *apo koinou* (“in common”), through the individual clauses. For throughout all the generations of the age, the proud continue to perish and the humble to be exalted by the pious and just dispensation of divine power.

He has helped Israel, his servant, remembering his mercy. Beautifully he calls Israel the Lord’s servant, since Israel has been taken up by him for salvation: obedient, that is, and humble, in accordance with what Hosea says: “Because Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hos. XI). For whoever refuses to humble himself cannot possibly be saved, nor can he say with the Prophet: “For behold, God is my helper, and the Lord is the upholder of my soul” (Ps. LIII). “Whoever humbles himself like a little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed forever. By the seed of Abraham he means not a carnal but a spiritual seed—that is, not merely those descended from him in the flesh, but those who, whether in circumcision or in uncircumcision, followed the traces of his faith. For while still in uncircumcision he himself believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness. He then received circumcision as the seal of that same faith [Col. 0323B], so that by faith he might become the father of both peoples, as the Apostle fully explained in his Epistle to the Romans. The coming of the Savior, therefore, was promised forever to Abraham and to his seed—that is, to the children of promise, to whom it is said: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III).

The mothers fittingly prophetically anticipate the birth either of the Lord or of John, so that, just as sin began through women, good things may also begin through women, and life, which perished through one woman’s deception, may be restored to the world while two women proclaim in rivalry.

But Mary remained with her for about three months, and returned to her own house. Mary remained until Elizabeth, when the time of childbirth had been completed, saw the birth of the precursor of her Lord, for whose sake above all she had come. It was stated above that every chaste soul which has conceived a spiritual desire for the Word must immediately take upon itself the lofty yokes of heavenly discipline; and, having remained there, as it were, for the days of three months, it must not cease to persevere until it shines with the perfect light of the chief virtues. Describing these months of complete radiance, the Apostle says: “But now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three. But the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. XIII).

Now the time for Elizabeth to give birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. Holy Scripture is accustomed to use the word “fulfillment” only concerning the origin, condition, or action of good things, signifying that their life possesses the fullness of perfection. Thus the time for Elizabeth to give birth was fulfilled. “The days of Mary were fulfilled, that she should give birth” (Luke II). “Solomon completed building the house of the Lord” (2 Chron. III). Abraham, or some other patriarch, died old and full of days. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV). In contrast, the days of the impious are empty and void. “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV).

And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her. The birth of the saints brings joy to many because it is a common good. For righteousness is a common virtue. Therefore, at the birth of a righteous person, the distinction of the life to come is foreshadowed, and the grace of the virtue that will follow is marked out by the joy of the neighbors [Col. 0324A].

And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. But his mother answered and said: “By no means; he shall be called John.” The holy Evangelist wonderfully thought it worth mentioning beforehand that many supposed the infant should be called Zacharias, after his father, so that you might understand that it was not some unsuitable name that displeased his mother, but that she had received through the Holy Spirit the name which had previously been announced by the angel to Zacharias. The mute father, indeed, could not communicate the child’s name to his wife, but Elizabeth learned the prophecy, which she had not learned from her husband.

And they said to her: “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.” But they were making signs to his father [Col. 0324B], and so forth. “John,” he says, “is his name”—that is, we are not giving a name to one who has already received a name from God. He has a name of his own, which we have recognized, not one that we have chosen. Nor should you be surprised that the woman asserted a name she had not heard, since the Holy Spirit, who had entrusted it to the angel, revealed it to her. She who had prophesied Christ could not have been unaware of the Lord’s forerunner. It is appropriately added that no one among his relatives was called by this name, so that you may understand that the name belonged not to the family but to the prophet.

Immediately his mouth and his tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God. And fear came upon all their neighbors. Since the voice of one crying in the wilderness had been born, it was fitting that the parent’s tongue should be loosed. For it was not fitting that the father should remain silent in praise, when he rejoiced that the herald of the Word had been born to him. His lips, which unbelief had bound, faith had now released.

If anyone wishes to examine this also allegorically, the celebrated birth of John signifies the beginning of the exaltation of the grace of the New Testament. His neighbors and relatives preferred to give the father’s name rather than John’s because the Jews, who were joined to the law by a kind of kinship through its observance, wished rather to pursue the righteousness that comes from the law than to receive the grace of faith. But the mother strives to communicate the name John—that is, “the grace of God”—by words, and the father by letters, because the law itself, together with the Psalms and the Prophets, openly proclaims the grace of Christ in its statements, while that old priesthood bears witness to the same grace through the figurative shadows of its ceremonies and sacrifices.

Zacharias appropriately speaks on the eighth day after the child’s birth [Col. 0324D], because through the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath—the hidden mysteries of the legal priesthood were revealed, and the tongue of the Jewish priests, which the bonds of disbelief had tightened, was released by the voice of rational understanding.

And throughout all the hill country of Judea all these things were being spoken of. And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: “What, then, will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes” (Ps. CX).

Behold, the one silence of Zacharias benefits not only himself—when it is imposed as the punishment of unbelief and as a sign for believing—but also, when it is removed, it astonishes all his neighbors with wonder and fear. The entire surrounding hill country is filled with the report of the prophet’s birth. All who could hear are prompted to investigate more carefully the circumstances and condition of the child who has been born, so that this future prophet of Christ may be commended by such omens and by others like them, and may provide, so to speak, preceding signs for the precursor who runs before the Truth.

And Zacharias, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.” How great is the abundance of heavenly grace, if the devotion of our faith is ready to receive it! Behold, the speech that alone had been taken from the unbeliever was restored, together with the spirit of prophecy, to the believer.

The Lord visited his people, wasting away as though from a long illness, and, as though sold under sin, he redeemed them by the blood of his only Son. Because blessed Zacharias knew that this was about to happen, he narrates it in prophetic fashion as though it had already happened. It should also be noted that he is said to have visited and redeemed his people, not because he found them to be his when he came, but because by visiting them he made them his. Similar is what is sung about the same people at the end of Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI). For he did not find that same woman—the strong woman, namely, the Church, devoted in faith—but by betrothing her to himself he made her strong, because he perfected her through the excellence of her faith.

And he has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant. He calls the firm height of salvation the “horn of salvation.” All bones, indeed, are enclosed by flesh, but the horn projects beyond the flesh; therefore the horn of salvation is called the kingdom of Christ the Savior, by which a height of the spirit that surpasses the joys of the flesh is proclaimed to the world. As a figure of this, David and Solomon were consecrated to the glory of kingship with a horn of oil.

As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old. “From of old,” he says, because the whole Scripture of the Old Testament proceeded as prophecy concerning Christ. It was not only Jeremiah, Daniel, Isaiah, and others of their kind—those specifically called prophets and who spoke openly of his coming—but also Adam the father himself, Abel, Enoch, and the other patriarchs, each by his own deeds, who bore witness to his dispensation. Hence, rebuking the hardness of the Jews, the Lord himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also. For he wrote about me” (John V).

Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us. This should be joined to the preceding verse: “He has raised up for us”—that is, “he has raised up salvation for us from our enemies.” After first stating briefly, “And he has raised up for us a horn of salvation,” he immediately explains more clearly what he had said: “Salvation,” he says, “from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.” By “all who hate us” he means either perverse human beings or unclean spirits. From their hand we have meanwhile been saved in hope, and in the future we will be saved in reality.

To show mercy to our fathers and to remember his covenant: “The oath that he swore to Abraham our father,” and so forth. He had said that the Lord would be born in the house of David, in accordance with the words of the prophets; he now says that the same Lord would free us in order to fulfill the covenant he established with Abraham. For it was chiefly to those patriarchs that either the gathering of the nations or the incarnation of Christ from their seed was promised.

Matthew also wished to convey this briefly, beginning his Gospel in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” Here it should be noted that in both Evangelists David is placed before Abraham. For although David is later in the order of time, he is greater in the gift of the promise. To Abraham, who, while still in uncircumcision, left his own country, came to know God, and earned the testimony of faith, only the faith of the nations and the most holy assembly of the Church was promised, when the Lord said to him: “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVIII).

But David heard, through a more exalted oracle, that Christ would be born from him according to the flesh: “And when you have completed your days,” he says, “so that you may go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will make his throne firm forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (1 Chron. XVII).

In holiness and righteousness before him, all our days. He plainly and briefly indicates how the Lord must be served: in holiness and righteousness, before him, and for all our days. For whoever departs from his service before death, or stains the purity of his faith by any uncleanness or injustice, or strives to remain holy only before human beings and not also before the Lord, serves the Lord without yet having been perfectly freed from the hand of spiritual enemies; like the Samaritans of old, he attempts to serve both the gods of the nations and the Lord.

And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High. For you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways. Beautifully, while speaking about the Lord, he suddenly turns his words to the prophet, so that this too might be shown to be a gift of the Lord. But the question arises: how does he address an infant eight days old? Yet how could one who was born fail to hear his father’s voice, when, still enclosed in the womb, he heard Mary’s greeting? Unless perhaps Zacharias should be understood to have wished, chiefly for those who were present, to proclaim the future gifts of his son—which he had learned earlier through the angel—as soon as he was able to speak.

Let the Arians hear and be ashamed; let the meek hear and rejoice: Christ the Lord, whom John preceded by prophesying, is called the Most High. In accordance with this, the Psalmist, praising God and the perfect man in one person, says: “Mother Zion will say: A man, and a man was born in her; and he himself, the Most High, founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). He calls the one who was made and who founded her the same man whom he names the Most High.

To give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins. As though wishing to explain and commend more carefully the name Jesus—that is, “Savior”—he repeatedly mentions salvation, recalling that the horn of salvation is to be raised up, that salvation will come from enemies, and that knowledge of salvation is to be given to the people. But lest you suppose that temporal and carnal salvation is being promised, he adds: “for the forgiveness of their sins.” The Jews, however, prefer for this reason not to receive Christ Jesus but to await the Antichrist: they desire to be saved outwardly rather than inwardly, and to be freed not from the dominion of sin but from the yoke of human servitude.

Through the tender mercies of our God, by which the dawn from on high has visited us. And the prophet, speaking of the Lord, says: “Behold, the man whose name is Dawn” (Zech. VI). He is rightly called “Dawn” because, opening for us the rising of the true light, he made children of light out of children of night and darkness, as blessed Zacharias next explains, saying:

To illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace. For the Lord to illuminate those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death means to pour the rays of the knowledge and love of himself into those who have lived in sins and in the blindness of ignorance. To such people the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” Our feet are directed into the way of peace when the course of all our actions accords with the grace of our Redeemer and Illuminator.

He fittingly testifies, in the proper order, that hearts must first be illuminated and afterward deeds directed, because no one can practice a peace he has not first learned. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII). This means: “You who sat in darkness, be illuminated, and enter the way of peace from which you had long been exiled.”

Now the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel. Since he was to become a preacher of repentance, it was appropriate and just that he should follow the hardships of solitude; and so that, as a young man, he might raise his hearers more freely by teaching them to reject the allurements of the world, he himself should also spend his early life in the deserts, in austerity.

CHAPTER II

Now it happened in those days that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. Since the Son of God was to be born in the flesh, he chose for himself the parents he wished and the place of birth he wished; he brought them to that place before he was born in whatever way he wished. So too, at the time he wished—or rather, at the time which he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, had ordained from eternity and foretold through the mouths of the prophets—he entered the world to save it.

For just as, being born of a virgin mother, he showed that the glory of virginity and the angelic honor of chastity were especially pleasing to him, so also, being born in a time of profound peace, he taught that he greatly sought and loved peace, and indicated that he would always deign to visit those who pursue peace and charity. In accordance with this, he promises the faithful: “For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII).

What greater sign could there have been of a most tranquil kingdom and of peace—as far as human beings are concerned—than for the whole world to be enclosed in a single enrollment, and for all the far-flung boundaries of the world to be included under the same census coinage? Augustus, its author and governor, reigned, according to the reliability of historical accounts, in such peace for twelve years around the time of the Lord’s birth that, with both foreign and civil wars quieted throughout the whole world, the prophet’s spiritual foreknowledge seems to have been fulfilled even literally.

That prophet, proclaiming in mystical language the dispensation of Christ, says: “And it shall be in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Mic. IV). A little later he also took care to describe the condition of that most sacred time: “And they shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for war. House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord” (ibid.).

This new enrollment of the world not only bore witness to the coming of that supreme King, who would enroll his elect, gathered from every region of the world, in the register of eternal blessedness; it also assisted the leaders of that same kingdom through the peaceful stability of its administration. For when all the nations had been restrained by the tumult of wars, the shadow—terrible at that time, so to speak—of the Roman name protected the disciples of Christ, who were about to preach to the world, from the heat of the rebellions that arose wherever they wished to go for the sake of the Word.

Thus an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should declare its census, because the edict of Christ the King was imminent, through which the whole world would attain salvation. He perfectly fulfills the meaning of the name Augustus, since he both desires his own people to increase and is himself sufficient to increase them; and he commands that those subject to the registrars of his mission be marked not by the payment of money but by the offering of faith. “Go,” he says, “into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

This was the first enrollment made by Quirinus, governor of Syria. And all went to be enrolled, each to his own city. The enrollment conducted in the time of Quirinus is also recorded by Josephus, the distinguished historian of the Hebrews, in the eighteenth book of his *Antiquities*, in these words:

“Quirinus, a man who, by the agreement of the Roman senate, had risen through the several magistracies to the rank of consul, and who was also honorable in his other offices, came with a few companions to Syria, having been sent by Caesar to administer justice among the nations and also to become the assessor of their property.”

Therefore, when it says, “This was the first enrollment made by Quirinus, governor of Syria,” it means either that this enrollment was the first of those that encompassed the whole world—for many parts of the earth are often recorded as having already been enrolled—or certainly that it then began, when Quirinus was sent to Syria.

And just as at that time, under Augustus as emperor and Quirinus as governor, all went to be enrolled, each to his own city, so now, under the governors of the Church—that is, its teachers—or rather at the urging of Christ, who promises rewards, let us all go, with no one excluded from the census of righteousness. Let us come to him, we who labor and are burdened, and he will refresh us. Let us take his yoke upon us and learn from him, because he is gentle and humble of heart, and we shall find rest for our souls (Matt. XI).

For this is our city and homeland: namely, the blessed and heavenly rest of souls, to which we were created by God Christ at the beginning of the world’s birth and to which we have been recreated by the man Christ at the end of the ages. To go to this city of peace and rest and to carry devoted treasures to our King means, through the daily growth of virtue and faith, to contemplate what joys of the heavenly light are eternal; to despise both the favorable and unfavorable things of the world in order to acquire them; and, once they have been acquired, to offer ourselves to God as a gift more precious than gold, cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit (2 Cor. VII).

If we examine more carefully the kind of coinage that was paid to Caesar, we shall find that it too is capable of cleansing us—not insignificantly in devotion. We can seek and find this nowhere better than in the Gospel itself, where, when the Lord was being tested concerning the payment of tribute to Caesar, he said: “Show me the coin of the census.” “And they,” he says, “offered him a denarius. And Jesus said to them: Whose image and inscription is this? They said to him: Caesar’s. Then he said to them: Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke XX).

Here one should first note that the denarius paid to Caesar, which contained ten *nummi*—as its name also indicates—was marked with his image and inscription. Then one should infer that, since the Lord commands that Caesar’s things be rendered to Caesar and God’s things to God, we too are carefully instructed to offer to God our King, in the likeness of the royal denarius, the tenfold law: that is, the love of God and of neighbor, one of which, received in three commandments, embraces the other seven, and which must be preserved with an undivided heart.

In this denarius of sacred Scripture, stamped with the ten heavenly commandments as though with an equal number of golden coins, whoever knows how to contemplate the face and name of the eternal King will find the knowledge of the divine will. Each person inscribes it perfectly upon the tablets of his heart with the pen of diligent correction, believing, hoping, and loving.

We carry this denarius with us on the road as though enclosed in a purse when we know how to say with the Psalmist: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. IV). Nevertheless, while God is witness, we keep this seal of faith and this joy of hope and charity hidden away in the meditation of our conscience.

But when we reach our homeland, we shall bring forth to our King, whose vision we thirst for and toward whom we hasten with every effort of virtue and with the whole attention of our minds, the gifts of our good conduct that had been hidden on earth and are to be crowned in heaven. Then what we have said in darkness will be spoken in the light, and what we have spoken in the ear in private rooms will be proclaimed upon the housetops (Matt. X).

And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, and so forth. By a heavenly dispensation the enrollment was arranged so that each person was commanded to go to his own homeland. This occurred not only because of the mystery we have mentioned, but also so that the Lord, conceived in one place and born in another, might more easily escape the fury of the plotting Herod.

If he had been born to parents from Bethlehem, the shrewd investigator might have suspected their sudden flight, especially since everyone knew that they traced their ancestry to the line of David, from which Christ was to come. David himself bears witness to him by his name, his homeland, and his occupation. For David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” He received the name, indeed, because he struck down the giant with strength and was handsome in appearance and beautiful of face; but, in a higher mystery, he prefigured the one who would be born from his house and family, who alone would overcome the ruler of the world, being “beautiful above the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV), born himself in Bethlehem and the shepherd of intellectual sheep—that is, the ruler of simple souls.

One must also contemplate the immense and most gracious humility of this one. He not only deigned to become incarnate for us, but also to become incarnate at a time when he would immediately be entered on Caesar’s census and, for our liberation, would himself be subjected to servitude. Peter points out to us the path of his humility—which he came not to change conditions but dispositions—to us: “Be subject,” he says, “to every human creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Pet. II). His fellow Apostle Paul likewise says: “Render to all their due: tribute to whom tribute is due; taxes to whom taxes are due; fear to whom fear is due; honor to whom honor is due. Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. XIII).

Now it happened, while they were there, that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and so forth. The Lord is rightly born in Bethlehem not only because of the indication of his royal lineage but also because of the mystery of the name. For Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.” He himself is the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). The place in which the Lord was to be born was therefore previously called “house of bread,” because it was surely destined that he should appear there in the substance of flesh, the one who would refresh the minds of the elect with inward nourishment.

Even to this day, and until the consummation of the age, the Lord does not cease to be conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem, whenever any hearer, having received the flower of the Word, makes himself a house of eternal bread. Each day he is conceived through faith in the virginal womb—that is, in the mind of believers—and each day he is brought forth through baptism.

Each day the Church, mother of God, accompanied by her teacher, ascends from the wheel of worldly conduct—what Galilee signifies—to the city of Judah, namely, of confession and praise, and pays the census of her devotion to the eternal King. In imitation of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, she is at once married and undefiled: as a virgin she conceives us from the Spirit, as a virgin she gives birth to us without pain; and, betrothed, so to speak, to one, but made fertile by another, she is visibly joined in each of her parts—which together constitute the one catholic Church—to the bishop set over her, while she is filled by the invisible power of the Holy Spirit.

Hence Joseph is also rightly interpreted as “increased.” This name indicates that the persistence of the teacher who speaks is of no value unless it receives an increase of heavenly assistance so that it may be heard.

But when Mary is described as having given birth to her firstborn son, this must not be understood, in accordance with the view of the Helvidians, as meaning that she also produced other sons—as though one could not be called firstborn unless he had brothers, just as one is ordinarily called only-begotten only if he has no brothers. Both the testimony of the law and clear reasoning show that all only-begotten sons can also be called firstborn, but not all firstborn sons can be called only-begotten. The term means not only the firstborn after whom others follow, but also the one before whom no other has emerged from the womb.

Indeed, because it is prescribed that every male who opens the womb is to be called holy to the Lord (here, below), whether brothers follow or do not follow, whatever first emerges from the womb is by right to be consecrated as firstborn.

But in a higher sense, the Son of God, appearing in the flesh, is both Only-begotten of the Father according to the excellence of his divinity and Firstborn of every creature according to his fraternal fellowship. Of the latter it is said: “For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the Firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII). Of the former: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John I). He is therefore Only-begotten in the substance of the Godhead, Firstborn in the assumption of humanity; Firstborn in grace, Only-begotten in nature. Hence he is called both brother and Lord: brother because he is Firstborn, Lord because he is Only-begotten.

[Col. 0331C] And she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.

“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Isa. IX). What is greater than every praise? “A little one has been born for us, so that we might be able to become perfect adults.” He who clothes the whole world in varied adornment is wrapped in humble swaddling clothes, so that we may be able to receive the first robe. Through him all things were made, yet his hands and feet are bound in a cradle, so that our hands may be extended toward good works and our feet directed into the way of peace. He for whom heaven is a seat is confined within the narrowness of a hard manger, so that he may enlarge us through the joys of the heavenly kingdom. He who is the bread of angels is laid in a manger, so that, like holy animals, he may refresh us with the grain of his flesh. He who sits at the right hand of the Father lacks a place in the inn, so that he might prepare many dwelling places for us in his Father’s house.

Yet the fact that he is born not in his parents’ house but in an inn and on the road can be understood more profoundly through its symbolism. For he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Therefore, while he remains truth and life through the essence of his divinity, through the mystery of the Incarnation he became the way by which he might lead us to our homeland, where we would enjoy truth and life.

And there were shepherds in that same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them.

With excellent propriety, when the Lord has been born, the shepherds keep watch and defend their flock by guarding it against the snares of the night. This was intended to show, among other things, that the time had come which the true and only good Shepherd had once promised, saying: “Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock, and I will deliver them from all the places in which they were scattered on the day of cloud and darkness.” And shortly afterward: “And I will raise up over them one shepherd who will feed them, my servant David, and I will cause the most wicked beasts to cease from the land” (Ezek. XXXIV), etc. What the prophet wonderfully foretold, we see fulfilled still more wonderfully by the Lord.

The prophet Micah also recalls this place and time, saying: “And you, misty Tower of the Flock, unto you shall come the daughters of Zion, and the first power shall come, the kingdom of the daughter of Zion” (Mic. IV). The Tower of the Flock, which in Hebrew is called the Tower of Eder, lies approximately one thousand paces east of the city of Bethlehem [Col. 0332B]. By the prophecy contained in its name, it had long before pointed to these shepherds; to it the daughters of Zion—that is, the angelic powers—came when they appeared to the shepherds.

Therefore, when the Lord has been born, let the shepherds keep watch over their flock of sheep, signifying that, once his dispensation has been revealed, the shepherds of chaste souls will keep watch in the Church. To them it is said: “Feed the flock of God that is among you” (I Pet. V). It is fitting, moreover, that an angel appears to the shepherds while they are keeping watch, and that the glory of God shines around them, because those who know how to preside diligently over faithful flocks deserve, more than others, to see heavenly things. While they themselves piously keep watch over the flock, divine grace flashes more abundantly over them.

In another way: an angel instructs Mary, an angel Joseph, and an angel the shepherds. The citizens of heaven bear witness that the Lord is to be conceived, has been conceived, and has been born, so that they may adequately instruct mortals and continually render service to their Creator. For in what follows, too, they are said always to be present with him when he is tempted, suffers, rises again, and ascends into heaven.

And they were afraid with great fear. And the angel said to them: “Do not be afraid. For behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people.”

Not for all the Jewish people, many of whom proved rebellious, but for the whole faithful people, gathered from every tribe, nation, and language into the one Church of Christ, eternal and great joy is proclaimed.

“For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.” This is the first power, this is the kingdom of the daughter of Zion, which, according to the testimony of the prophet mentioned above [Col. 0332D], was promised as coming at the Tower of the Flock.

Here it should be carefully noted that the angel who addresses the shepherds during the watches of the night does not say, “Tonight,” but, “Today a Savior has been born for you.” This is clearly for no other reason than that he had come to proclaim great joy. For wherever the sadness of events done or to be done at night is signified, “night” is often added, or is even mentioned alone. Thus: “All of you will be scandalized because of me on this night” (Matt. XXVI). And elsewhere: “Amen I say to you, today, on this night, before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark XIV).

Nor did the angel, surrounded by such great light, appear without purpose, so that the glory of God is said to have shone around the shepherds—that is, to have scattered rays of light over them on every side—a detail never added throughout the whole series of the Old Testament, despite the frequent appearances of angels there. Rather, he mystically announced beforehand what the Apostle later taught openly, saying: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII).

“And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.”

The Savior’s infancy has been impressed upon us repeatedly both by the proclamations of angels and by the testimonies of the evangelists, so that what he became for us may be fixed more deeply in our hearts. For, as the prophet says, “He was wounded because of our iniquities and weakened because of our sins” (Isa. LIII).

It should be observed with particular care that the sign given of the Savior’s birth is that the infant will be found not clothed in Tyrian purple, but wrapped in filthy rags, and not lying on couches adorned with gold, but in mangers. This means that for our sake he assumed not only the appearance of humility and mortality, but also of poverty. “Although he was rich, he became poor for us, so that by his poverty we might be enriched” (II Cor. VIII). Though he was Lord of heaven, he became poor on earth, to teach earthly beings that through poverty of spirit they can acquire the kingdom of heaven.

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

When one messenger had announced that God had been born in the flesh, a multitude of the heavenly army immediately flew in and burst forth with united voice in praise of the Creator, both to offer Christ the devotion of their service, as they always do, and to instruct us by their example. Whenever one of the brethren resounds with words of sacred instruction, or whenever we ourselves recall to mind what we have read or heard that pertains to piety, we should immediately return praises to God with mouth, heart, and deed.

It is fitting, too, that the approaching choir of angels receives the designation “the heavenly army.” It humbly obeys that powerful leader in battle who appeared to overthrow the aerial powers, and itself vigorously drives away those opposing powers with heavenly weapons, lest they be able to tempt mortals as much as they wish. For just as, by the foresight of an excellent emperor, all places are fortified by military forces against the arrival of the enemy, so God, because unclean spirits are everywhere active in the overthrow of peace, has established armies of angels for our protection. By their presence the boldness of demons is broken, and the grace of peace is supplied to us.

Since God is born both God and man, peace is rightly sung for human beings and glory for God. The angels glorify God incarnate for our redemption because, when they see us being received, they rejoice that their own number is being filled. They desire peace for human beings because those whom they had previously despised as weak and rejected now, with the Lord born in the flesh, they honor as their companions.

When they ask peace for human beings, they explain for whom it is intended: for those of good will—that is, for those who receive the Christ who has been born—not for Herod, the chief priests, and the Pharisees, or the other antichrists, who were troubled when they heard of his birth and pursued him with swords as far as they were able. “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.” But: “Great peace for those who love your name, Lord, and there is no stumbling block in them” (Isa. XLVIII).

The following also most appropriately applies to them: “I awaited your salvation, Lord” (Ps. CXVIII)—that is, I sighed with a long anticipation of my desire for Christ’s coming advent.

And it happened that, when the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has accomplished and shown to us.”

Examine carefully how reasonable the shepherds’ words are and how worthy of the shepherds of the Church. For, as though they were truly keeping watch, they did not say, “Let us see the child,” or, “Let us see what is being spoken of,” but, “Let us see the word that has come to pass”: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word became flesh” (John I). Let us see how the Word that always existed was made for us—what the Lord accomplished and showed to us.

This Word made itself; for this very Word is the Lord. Let us therefore see how this very Word—that is, the Lord himself—made himself and showed us his flesh. What we could not see while he was the Word, let us see now that he has become flesh.

This resembles what John says: “What was from the beginning, what we heard, what we saw with our eyes, what we looked upon, and what our hands touched, concerning the word of life—and the life was manifested, and we saw it, and bear witness, and proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us” (I John I).

And they came in haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger. When they saw him, they recognized the word that had been spoken to them about this child.

The shepherds hasten to see Christ, whom they have come to know, desiring with the full attention of their minds to behold his coming. Christ’s presence must not be sought with sluggishness. Perhaps this is why some who seek do not deserve to find him: they seek Christ lazily.

These shepherds found him without delay because they ran to him with sincere faith. To go to him in haste does not mean to quicken the steps of one’s feet, but always to advance in faith and virtue. “They found,” he says, “Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger.”

The shepherds of the Lord’s flock, too, are raised more frequently and more sweetly by heavenly revelation amid the darkness of this life; and so, with greater fervor, they enter by contemplation the gates of Bethlehem—that is, the sublime life of the fathers who preceded them, in which the bread of life is always both preserved and nourishing. There they find, at their first vision, nothing else in Scripture than the virgin beauty of the Catholic Church, represented by Mary; the manly assembly of spiritual teachers, represented by Joseph; and the humble coming of the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, inserted in the pages of sacred Scripture like an infant placed in a manger.

From this manger of the holy Scriptures that outstanding animal, most suited to sacred sacrifices, was fed; it proclaimed with rejoicing: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a pastureland” (Ps. XXII). And shortly afterward: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me” (ibid.).

“When they saw,” he says, “they recognized the word that had been spoken to them about this child,” because it is the proper order of things that, once the incarnation of the Word has been known, loved, and celebrated with due honor, one should eventually reach, through long practice and the sharpening of the mind, the contemplation of the glory of the Word with greater capacity.

And all who heard it marveled at what had been told them by the shepherds.

The people are compelled to reverence for God by the shepherds. Let this not seem to you an insignificant example of faith, nor the person of the shepherds contemptible. Certainly, the more lowly they were in worldly understanding, the more precious they were in faith.

The Lord chose not the wise but the simple as heralds of himself—people who would not know how to falsify what they had heard—and he sent not rhetoricians but fishermen to preach the gospel.

Finally, in the Old Testament also, he appointed shepherds as the principal messengers of his dispensation. Abel, the first martyr, who consecrated the blameless conduct of his pastoral office with his own blood—and whose blood, as a figure of the Lord’s passion, cries from the earth—like a most learned and first shepherd, devotedly offered the first fruits of his flocks to the Lord.

Abraham, the father of faith, who rejoiced to see Christ’s day, saw it and was glad, is described as seeking not veins of gold from which to procure ornaments for his own adornment, but springs of water from which to water his cattle, digging for them in the veins of the earth.

Jacob, the father of the twelve tribes, was scorched by heat and frost for twenty years while tending sheep. As a figure of the true Shepherd, by displaying the variety of his virtues among the waters of saving instruction, he endowed them with a more exalted condition.

Moses, the lawgiver, who first, as a type of the sevenfold Church, defended seven sisters who were feeding their flocks from the violence of invading shepherds until they could water their sheep, later deserved to see and address the Lord amid the pastures of the desert, to perform signs with his shepherd’s staff, and to free the people of God.

David himself, whose son our Lord deigned to be called and to be, rescued his father’s ram from the hand of a bear or lion. He showed that the Lord would be born from David’s lineage and city—the one like whom there is none—rescuing the needy from the hand of one stronger than he, and the poor from those who seized them.

For this reason, the testimony of the shepherds should not be considered insignificant. They deserved to keep watch and hear the hymn of angelic rejoicing at the time when the Good Shepherd appeared, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert to seek the hundredth sheep.

The entire faithful flock continually longs for and implores his coming: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord” (Ps. CXVIII).

But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.

What does the phrase “pondering” mean? He ought to have said, “She considered them in her heart” and “She preserved them in her heart.” But because she had read the holy Scriptures and knew the prophets, she compared what had happened to her concerning the Lord with what she knew had been written by the prophets concerning the Lord. When these things were compared with one another, she recognized a harmony resembling that of the heavenly cherubim, with their faces joined in shared light.

Gabriel had said: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son” (Luke I). Isaiah had foretold: “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII). Micah had foretold that the daughters of Zion would come to the Tower of the Flock and that the first power would then come.

The shepherds said that companies of the heavenly city had appeared to them at the Tower of the Flock, singing of the Christ who had been born. Mary had read: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I). She saw the Son of God crying in the manger, the one who saves human beings and animals. In each of these things and in others like them, she compared what she had read with what she heard and saw.

And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen, just as it had been told to them.

The shepherds glorify and praise God for everything they had heard from the angels and seen in Bethlehem, just as it had been told to them—that is, they glorify him because, when they came, they found nothing other than what had been told to them. Or else, just as it had been told to them, they offer glory and praise to God.

Indeed, the angels had told them to do this—not by commanding them in words, but by offering them the pattern of their devotion, when they resounded with united rejoicing, “Glory to God in the highest.” For the one who says, “I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people” (here above), certainly urges them to glorify and praise God.

Likewise, the teachers of spiritual flocks sometimes, while the others sleep, ascend through contemplation to heavenly things; sometimes they go around inspecting the camps of the faithful and seeking examples of uprightness; sometimes they return to the public duties of their pastoral office by teaching, so that they may pour forth in preaching to their neighbors the memory of the abundance of God’s sweetness, which they had tasted while swiftly contemplating it (Ps. CXLV).

And when the eight days had been completed for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

The rite and religion of circumcision took its beginning from the blessed patriarch Abraham. Although he was still in his foreskin, he had believed God perfectly, and it had been reckoned to him as righteousness. He received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith that existed while he was uncircumcised.

From him also arose the practice of assigning names to infants on the day of circumcision. For when he received from God the covenant of circumcision, on that same day he also, together with his wife, received an enlargement of his name. Until then he had been called Abram—that is, “exalted father”; thereafter, on account of the merit of his faith, he was called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations.” Sarai, likewise, was called Sarah.

Circumcision had many types and figures. It was, as has been said, the seal of the righteousness of faith for Abraham and his offspring; an indication that those who belonged to this offspring and this faith were to be chastened from every pollution of flesh and spirit; and a prophecy of the Savior who would be born from this offspring. Through baptism he would cleanse us in the present from every pollution of deadly action, and in the future, through the resurrection, free us forever from every corruption of death itself.

Above all, it pleased the giver of grace and of the law that, at that time, the gift of forgiveness should be administered through circumcision—a gift that would release human beings from the sin of Adam’s transgression. The one who now says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III), was himself then saying: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. XVII).

The covenant in question was not specifically the covenant of circumcision, which could not be broken by an infant who was not yet able to discern, but by elders who knew, could, and ought to have observed it. Rather, it was the covenant that God made with the first human being, a covenant which everyone who has lived even a single day on earth is shown to have transgressed, and therefore is known to need some remedy of salvation.

For those who were faithful either before the time of circumcision or, after circumcision had been given, from the nations outside Israel—such as Job, that exemplar of patience, and his friends and children—saved themselves and their own from original sin either through sacrificial offerings or certainly through faith alone, because “the righteous one lives by faith” (Rom. I), and “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI).

But those who have been propagated from the stock of sin, conceived in iniquities and born in pleasures, need these and similar remedies.

Our Redeemer, however, came into the world without sin in order to take away the sins of the world. Just as through his baptism he provided remedies for us—that is, by undergoing the baths of water he consecrated them for the washing away of our crimes—so also, through the circumcision he received, he cleansed not sins of his own, for he had committed none, but taught that the oldness of our nature in him was to be renewed.
