He thereby signified that it is now to be cleansed through him from the stain of vices and, on the last day, to be completely restored from the manifold plague of mortality and death itself.

Accordingly, Jesus is fittingly said to have been circumcised on the eighth day. We do not easily read of this having been done to anyone in the Old Testament, although it was very frequently commanded for everyone, except only Isaac, who, as the first son of promise, is said to have received circumcision on the eighth day.

Jesus, I say, is rightly circumcised on the eighth day, because both of the renewals of ours that we have mentioned—the present and the future, of spirit and of flesh—were prefigured in his resurrection and are to be perfected in ours.

Concerning our first resurrection, which meanwhile is celebrated through the amendment of life and faith, the Apostle says: “For all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

Concerning the second, which is hoped for at the end, he says: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (I Thess. IV).

Almost everyone recognizes that the number eight corresponds to the glory of the resurrection. For the Lord also rose on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath. And we too, after the six ages of this world and the seventh age, the Sabbath of souls, which is now meanwhile being lived in the other life, will rise as though in an eighth age. Then we shall be truly circumcised—that is, stripped of all the vices and corruptions of carnal desire, in which lust especially reigns—and our foreskin will truly have been cut away.

For, as the Lord says: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; nor can they die any longer, for they are equal to the angels and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke XX).

“His name was called,” he says, “Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.”

Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” The faithful and all the elect rejoice to share in this name through both circumcisions of their own, about which enough has been said, so that just as they are called Christians from Christ, they may also be called saved from the Savior—now saved in hope through faith, but then saved in reality through the vision of the glory that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

This name was assigned to them by God not only before they were conceived in the womb of the Church through faith, but even before the ages of the world.

Not only the etymology of this most holy name, but also the number represented by its letters gives off the fragrance of the mysteries of our perpetual salvation. Among the Greeks, Jesus is written with six letters, Ἰησοῦς—namely, ι, η, σ, ο, υ, ς—whose numerical values are 10, 8, 200, 70, 400, and 200, which together make 888.

That number, because it rejoices in the figure of the resurrection, has already been sufficiently discussed above. For what eight signifies when set down simply is also signified when it is multiplied by ten or by one hundred. Or certainly, the accumulation of perfect numbers should be understood as an indication of firmness.

We may also say that the Savior’s name contains eight in its completed form, because by rising on the eighth day he provided mortals with an example of resurrection. It contains eight multiplied by ten, because by the figures of his resurrection the Decalogue of the law both instructed us how it ought to be fulfilled and assisted us in fulfilling it.

Thus, just as he rose from the dead and no longer dies—“death will no longer rule over him”—so we too should consider ourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus (Rom. VI).

The name also contains eight multiplied by one hundred, because, by displaying the glory of his resurrection, it indicated the reward that will follow us in the future. The number one hundred, which, after the entire course of the numbers on the left, is the first to turn toward the right, most suitably corresponds to the joys of that age, when “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (I Cor. XV), when “we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with those who have risen, in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV).

Accordingly, as a figure of all the elect, the first son of promise, born to and circumcised by a father who was one hundred years old, was appropriately called Isaac, a name that signifies “laughter” or “joy.” In every respect he prefigured the happiness of that future age directed toward the right, concerning which the Lord says: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

But since the subject is circumcision, it is worth asking why Moses himself—who reports that the law of circumcision was given by God to the patriarchs and repeatedly impressed upon him—did not have anyone circumcised throughout the whole period of his leadership, except only one son of his, whom his mother circumcised with a very sharp stone lest the Lord strike him, but left all those who were born in the wilderness to be circumcised by Joshua. Thus he interrupted for forty continuous years a divinely commanded custom that had been observed for four hundred and six years and handed down to him by ancestral succession.

I would not believe that this was done without reason, but rather with a great mystery. Without prejudice to the understanding of our predecessors, I shall briefly state what I myself think.

Moses proclaims circumcision, but Joshua accomplishes it, because “the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). The letter that commands is of no benefit unless assisting grace is present.

While Moses proclaims it, the foreskin grows, because, as the Apostle says, “by works of the law no flesh will be justified before him. For through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. III). And elsewhere: “Until the law, sin was in the world. But sin is not counted where there is no law” (Rom. V). And again: “The law entered so that the trespass might increase. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness” (Rom. VII).

But after Joshua had led the people into the promised land, he cut away with stone knives the foreskin that had grown during Moses’ lifetime. For “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V).

Why Joshua used stone knives for circumcision is understood by the one who reads that “the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X), and, “Upon this rock,” he says, “I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

What was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh, God accomplished by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and, because of sin, condemning sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit (Rom. VIII).

This grace of Christ justifies not only the faithful of the New Testament. Whoever was perfect under the law was saved through faith, not by works of the law, but by this same grace of Christ who was to come in the flesh.

The people circumcised by Joshua represent those who were perfect under the law; Moses’ son represents those who, compelled by the strictness of the law, learned to plead for Christ’s grace and avoided the circumcision of the rock as though it were the Lord’s threatening sword hanging over them. Peter bears witness to this when, speaking of the yoke of the law, he says: “Neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear it, but we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they also were” (Acts XV).

And the Psalmist, enclosed as though in the prison of the law and finding no way of escape except in Christ’s grace, cries out: “When my heart was in distress, you lifted me up upon the rock. You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX).

Certainly, when circumcision is proclaimed, no one should suppose that only the restraint of one bodily member is commanded—as though it were enough to be safe from fornication, or to use marriage temperately, or to glory in virginity, without adding the other virtues. Rather, the circumcision of all the senses that we carry in heart or body is commanded.

Moses, receiving the purest words of God, complained that he was uncircumcised in lips. Stephen likewise said to unbelieving Jews: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII).

Therefore, the person has been cleansed by true circumcision who stops his ears so that he does not hear bloodshed (Isa. XXXIII), closes his eyes so that he does not see evil, guards his ways so that he does not sin with his tongue (Ps. XXXVIII), and takes care lest his heart be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness (Luke XXI).

He is the one who, while breath remains in him and the Spirit of God is in his nostrils (Job XXVII), does not speak iniquity with his lips (ibid.); who washes his hands among the innocent (Ps. XXV) and keeps his feet from every evil way (Ps. CXVIII); who disciplines his body above all and brings it into subjection (I Cor. IX); and who guards his heart with every vigilance, because from it life proceeds (Prov. IV).

After circumcision, that person was brought to Jerusalem and presented to the Lord who, in accordance with the one who says, “Turn away from evil and do good” (I Pet. III), after ceasing from sins, began to abound in good works.

He can say: “My eyes are always toward the Lord,” and, “I will go around your altar, Lord, that I may hear the voice of your praise” (Ps. XXV). He says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II), and, “I lifted up my hands to your commandments, and I turned my feet toward your testimonies” (Ps. CXVIII).

Whether he eats, drinks, or does anything else, he does everything for the glory of God (I Cor. X), and says: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate” (Ps. CXVIII); and finally: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Even the good action itself, when it is hidden, needs circumcision no less, so that when I fast, pray, or give alms, I seek inward glory. For if I stand at the street corners, disfigure my face, and sound a trumpet before me so that I may be seen and praised by people (Matt. VI), I appear circumcised outwardly, but remain unclean in heart and incur the penalties of simulated holiness as well.

This is exemplified by the people of Shechem. Although they seemed to imitate the circumcision of the patriarchs, they did it not for the Lord’s covenant but for the sake of lust. They acquired no reward; indeed, on the third day, when the pain of wounds is most severe, they perished amid the ruins of their city.

Such people, having forgotten the prophet’s warning, “Circumcise yourselves for the Lord and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jer. IV), will be sent into eternal death when the time of resurrection arrives, their supposed virtues emptied of the trust they had placed in them.

Therefore the Apostle diligently commends circumcision hidden in the heart, “whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. II).

[Col. 0341A] And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord.

The decree of the law was that a child should be brought to the temple of the Lord on the thirty-third day after circumcision, and that an offering should be given for him; the firstborn male, however, was to be made holy to the Lord.

Mystically, as we have said, this indicates that no one who has not been circumcised from vices is worthy of the Lord’s presence, and that no one who has not been released from the bonds of mortality can perfectly enter the joys of the heavenly city. For it says: “The wicked will not dwell near you, nor will the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. V). And the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption” (I Cor. XV).

But if you examine the words of the law itself more carefully, you will certainly find that not only was the incarnate Lord free from the contagion of sin, but he was also free from the obligation of the law. For this reason he more willingly submitted to it: to prove that it was holy, just, and good, and to free us from its servitude and fear through the grace of faith.

The Mother of God herself was likewise free both from sexual intercourse and from the legal obligation. For Moses says: “If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean for seven days, as during the days of the separation of her menstruation; and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised. She herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch nothing holy, nor enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification have been completed,” and so forth (Lev. XII), as the regulations concerning a woman who has given birth continue.

Note, therefore, that it is not every woman who gives birth, but she who has given birth after receiving seed, who is designated unclean and taught by the rite of the law to require cleansing. This distinguishes her from the woman who, while a virgin, conceived and bore a son and called his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us” (Isa. VI).

Therefore neither the Son, who is God with human beings, nor the mother who gave birth through the working of the Holy Spirit, needed the sacrifices of victims for purification. Rather, just as the Lord Christ did, so also the blessed ever-virgin Mary voluntarily subjected herself to the law so that we might be released from the bond of the law.

As it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

The phrase “every male opening the womb” signifies the firstborn of both human beings and animals. It was commanded that both should be called holy to the Lord and therefore belong to the priest. This was subject to the provision that he was to receive a price for a human firstborn and have every unclean animal redeemed. “Its redemption,” it says, “shall be after one month, at five shekels of silver” (Lev. XXVII).

Without entering into a more subtle treatment, it should be stated briefly that all those firstborn were either figures of the one who, although he was the only-begotten Son of God, deigned to become the firstborn of all creation—truly and uniquely holy to the Lord, because he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (Isa. LIII)—or else indications of our devotion.

We ought to assign to the Lord’s grace all the beginnings of good action that we, as it were, bring forth from the heart, and redeem evil deeds by offering worthy fruits of repentance for each of the five senses of body or soul.

Thus, when he says “opening the womb,” he speaks according to the customary manner of birth. It does not mean that our Lord, having entered and sanctified the lodging of the sacred womb, should be believed to have violated its virginity when he emerged. This is the view of heretics, who say that the blessed Mary was a virgin until childbirth but was not a virgin after childbirth. Rather, according to the Catholic faith, with the virgin’s womb closed, he proceeded from his bridal chamber like a bridegroom.

The Prophet beautifully speaks of this: “He turned me toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary that looked eastward, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall remain closed to the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord’” (Ezek. XLIV).

It may also be mystically signified that no one except the Lord can open the womb of the virgin Church through water and the Holy Spirit to beget children for God. For this reason, this male is called holy to the Lord with incomparable dignity.

And to offer a sacrifice, as it is prescribed in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. It was prescribed in the law that, for a child, if male—as I said—on the fortieth day, and if female, on the eightieth day after birth, a yearling lamb without blemish should be offered as a burnt offering, and a turtledove or young pigeon as a sin offering: “But if her hand does not find the means,” it says, “and she is unable to offer a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a burnt offering and the other as a sin offering” (Leviticus 12). Therefore the Lord Christ Jesus, although he was rich, became poor for our sake, and willed that a poor offering be made for him. Thus, by his own poverty, he might make us rich here in faith and there heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him.

In the moral sense, whether someone produces strong works or weak ones—for these are distinguished by the terms “male” and “female”—in order that they may legitimately be consecrated to the Lord, he must offer both a sheep of innocence and a turtledove or pigeon of compunction. For since these birds have groaning instead of song, they rightly signify the tears of the humble, which we greatly need even in good works. For although we know that what we do is good, we do not know with what strictness it will be examined by the Lord, nor with what perseverance it must be brought to completion by us.

But whoever, lacking the riches of virtues about which the Apostle says to the Corinthians, “In everything you have been enriched in him, in all speech and in all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1), does not find a lamb of innocent life in the flock of his deeds, should at least offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons—that is, he should flee to seek the assistance of tears. And rightly two: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering (Leviticus 12). For a burnt offering is called that which is wholly burned, because there are plainly two kinds of compunction. The soul that thirsts for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. First it afflicts itself with tears, because, as it recalls its sins, it fears that it may suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by a long anxiety of sorrow, a certain security born of hope for pardon arises, and the spirit is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. For the mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are, what the fellowship of the blessed spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it laments more deeply because it is absent from everlasting blessings than it previously wept when it feared eternal evils. Thus, whoever first offered a turtledove as a sin offering, weeping lest he be led to punishment, makes the other a burnt offering when afterward he begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

[Col. 0343A] He offers a pigeon as a sin offering who “labors in his groaning” and “washes his bed every night” (Psalm 6): that is, through each night of guilt that strikes him, he does not cease to wash with tears his good works, in which he ought to rest. They bring young pigeons as a burnt offering who, mourning the absence of their heavenly homeland, say: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered you, Zion” (Psalm 136). For just as pigeons delight in resting above streams, so that they may foresee the hawk’s approach by its shadow moving across the waters and at the same time escape it, so indeed the souls of the poor in spirit, rising above the waves of the world in their minds, observe the examples of the malicious enemy all the more frequently in this Babylon, by whose groanings they are nourished; and therefore they lift the wings of their desire toward eternal things all the more often.

There is this difference, certainly, between the significance of the turtledove and that of the pigeon: the pigeon, which is accustomed to live, fly, and mourn in a flock, signifies the activity of the active life. Of this it is said: “The multitude of believers were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was common among them” (Acts 4). The turtledove, however, which delights in solitude—to such a degree that, if it happens to lose its mate, it remains alone thereafter—proclaims the heights of the contemplative life, because this virtue belongs to few and is allotted to them individually.

Isaiah alone sees the Lord of hosts and contemplates the praises of the Seraphim; and because he has kept silent wrongly, he groans like a solitary turtledove. Moses alone, while the people remain fearfully at a distance, ascends to the Lord and, by tearful prayers, obtains that the same people not be struck down. Daniel alone remains among the angels while his companions flee. Ezekiel alone marvels at the chariots of the Cherubim and the lofty buildings of the heavenly city. Paul alone is caught up to the delights of paradise and to behold the secrets of the third heaven.

Again, when I enter my chamber and pray to the Father in secret with the door shut, I offer a turtledove. But when I seek companions in the same work and, singing with the Prophet, say, “Come, let us adore and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94), I bring pigeons to the altar. And because both offerings are equally acceptable to the Creator, Luke wisely did not say whether turtledoves or young pigeons were offered for the Lord, lest he prefer one manner of life to the other, but so that he might teach that both should be followed and both offered in divine worship.

Therefore, since the discussion of purification has been prolonged, what mystery is contained in the number of the days of purification itself, and why the same number was ordered to be doubled in the purification of a woman who has given birth, will be more appropriately explained in Leviticus.

[Col. 0344A] And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. When the Lord was born in the flesh, not only the angels from heaven but every age of mortal humanity and both sexes bear witness. For it was fitting that the Savior of all, just as his coming in the flesh had been foretold by the deeds and words of all the faithful throughout the whole course of the world, should likewise, when he came, be proclaimed with the common praise of all. Thus the prophecy was fulfilled that says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (Psalm 148), and so on, until it says: “Young men and virgins, old men together with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord, because his name alone is exalted. His praise is above heaven and earth.”

“Righteous,” he says, “and God-fearing” (ibid.), because justice is difficult to preserve without fear. I do not mean that fear which, under the threat of punishment, dreads the loss of temporal goods—a fear which perfect love customarily casts out—but the holy fear of the Lord, which endures forever and ever. By this fear, the more ardently the righteous person loves his God, the more carefully he avoids offending him.

And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ; and he came by the Spirit into the temple. Observe the expressions of Scripture: he said that he would see death. How is death seen, and with what eyes, when by coming it closes those very eyes so that they see nothing? But “to see death” signifies to experience it. Very blessed is the one who will see the death of the flesh if he has first striven to see the Lord’s Christ with the eyes of his heart—living in the heavenly Jerusalem, frequenting the thresholds of God’s temple; that is, following the pious examples of the saints in whom the Lord dwells, and sighing with the Psalmist: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the will of the Lord” (Psalm 26).

Thus he too will deserve to receive the Word of God in his hands and to embrace him in the arms of his faith and love. But when it says, “And he came by the Spirit into the temple,” it signifies that, by the same grace of the Spirit through which he had formerly foreknown that he would come, he now recognized the Savior as coming and as about to be seen by him.

And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he himself took him into his arms. Great indeed is the Lord’s power, but no less clearly does his humility shine forth: he whom heaven and earth cannot contain is carried wholly in the arms of an old man.

In a figurative sense also, Simeon, an old man, receives Christ, an infant, to teach us to put off the old man, who is corrupted with his deeds, and, renewed in the spirit of our mind, to put on him who has been created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth (Ephesians 4). That is, having put away falsehood, we should speak the truth and fulfill with mouth, heart, and deed the other things belonging to the condition of the new man.

[Col. 0345A] The righteous and devout elder, according to the law, takes the child Jesus into his arms, to signify that the righteousness of works which came from the law—for who does not know that works are commonly represented by hands and arms—must be changed by the humble yet saving grace of evangelical faith. The elder receives the infant Christ to indicate that this world, as though already worn out by old age and a long life, will return to the innocence and, so to speak, infancy of Christian conduct, and that its youth will be renewed like that of the eagle.

And he blessed God and said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.” You see that not only the righteous of the New Testament but also those of the Old Testament desired the hope of future life: they wished to be released from the body and even regarded laying down the burden of earthly life as the way of peace, since they did not doubt that they would possess perpetual rest in the bosom of Abraham.

Indeed, Jeduthun—that is, “the one who leaps over worldly desires”—after silently contemplating for a long time the many evils of the world, grew fervent through inward meditation of the heart. At last he spoke with his tongue and revealed what he had been doing within: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me. Behold, you have made my days old” (Psalm 38). In these words he plainly reveals how great a consolation he hopes to receive at the end of his present miseries, whose arrival he desires while he waits.

“Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples.” Blessed are the eyes that see what Simeon saw; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20). “That very thing,” he says, “which you prepared to be seen afterward by all nations, peoples, and languages in mind and faith, and which you foresaw as something to be sought with hope and love, I now contemplate as your salvation, long desired, with both the eyes of my flesh and those of my heart.”

“A light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.” Christ, the salvation of God, is prepared by God the Father as a light for both peoples. He is called especially the glory of Israel, to whom he was long hoped for and whose coming was announced beforehand; but he is called the revelation of the Gentiles, whose eyes of the mind, already sunk in deep blindness and lifted by no hope of the Lord’s coming, he deigned to visit, reveal, and enlighten at once.

And rightly is the revelation of the Gentiles placed before the glory of Israel, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” Thus the Psalmist, when he said, “The Lord has made his salvation known; before the sight of the Gentiles he has revealed his righteousness” (Psalm 89), added: “He remembered his mercy to Jacob and his truth to the house of Israel” (Psalm 97).

[Col. 0345D] And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were being said about him, and Simeon blessed them. He calls Joseph the Savior’s father, not because, according to the Photinians, he was truly his father, but because, for the sake of preserving Mary’s reputation, he was regarded by everyone as his father. The Evangelist had not forgotten that she had conceived by the Holy Spirit and given birth as a virgin; rather, expressing the opinion of the people—which is the true law of historical narrative—he calls Joseph Christ’s father.

Although he may also rightly be called Christ’s father in the sense in which he is rightly understood to be Mary’s husband without bodily union, through the bond of marriage—indeed, much more closely joined to him than if he had adopted him from elsewhere. For Joseph was not for that reason to be called Christ’s father because no one had begotten him through intercourse, since he would rightly have been his father even if he had adopted elsewhere a child not begotten by his own wife.

And he said to Mary his mother: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed.” He is rightly appointed for resurrection, because he is light, because he is the glory of the people of Israel, because he says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11).

But how is he appointed for downfall, unless because he is also a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense—that is, a downfall for those who take offense at the word and do not believe? Of these he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 22). He has been appointed for downfall not only in himself but also in those who preach him, as the Apostle testifies: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Corinthians 2). Whoever, when the Apostle preaches, follows the word he hears with love rises and is saved by the good odor. Whoever pursues it with hatred falls and dies by that same odor.

As for “a sign that will be opposed,” understand this as the faith of the Lord’s cross. Concerning it the Jews say to the Apostle Paul: “For as regards this sect, it is known to us that it is opposed everywhere” (Acts 28). And the Apostle himself says: “We preach Christ Jesus crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1).

“And a sword will pierce your own soul.” No historical account teaches that the blessed Mary departed this life by the stroke of a sword, especially since it is not the soul but the body that is customarily killed by iron. It therefore remains to be understood that the sword of which it is said, “Their sword is in their lips” (Psalm 58)—that is, the grief of the Lord’s passion—pierced her soul.

Although she did not doubt that Christ, as the Son of God, would willingly die and would have avoided death itself, nevertheless she could not see him, born from her own flesh, crucified without feeling pain. For the iron that is said to have pierced Joseph’s soul is best understood as the harsh tribulation of the mind.

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” It was once uncertain which of the Jews would receive the grace of Christ, which they certainly knew was to come, and which would prefer to reject it. But when his birth was heard of, the thoughts of hearts were immediately revealed: King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. The shepherds, with fear and joy, resound with praise to God and proclaim to human beings the message of peace.

When his teaching and power had become widely known, some flocked to him as a teacher of truth, while others fled from him as from a deceiver. When the sign of his cross was raised, some, as though he had justly been put to death, mocked him with blasphemies; others, as though he were the author of life, grieved bitterly that he should die.

Even to this day, and until the consummation of the present age, the sword of the harshest tribulation does not cease to pierce the soul of the Church, as the sign of faith is opposed by the wicked, and as, when the word of God is heard, it mournfully observes many rising with Christ through belief, but more falling from faith. When the thoughts of many hearts are revealed, wherever the excellent seed of the Gospel has been sown, there it sees the weeds of vices either prevail more than they ought or—even more grievously to say—alone sprout and reign.

And there was Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher; she had advanced in many days, and so forth. According to the historical sense, Anna is shown to have been devoted in conduct, venerable in age, and in every respect worthy to bear witness to the incarnate Lord.

[Col. 0347B] According to the mystical interpretation, because she signifies the Church, which in the present is widowed by the death of her bridegroom and Lord, the number of the years of her widowhood also signifies the time of the Church: the period during which, established in the body, she is away from the Lord, and, preserving the thresholds of the heavenly temple with great devotion, awaits that daily coming of the Lord of which he says: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

For seven times twelve makes eighty-four. The seven refer to the course of this age, which revolves through seven days; the twelve refer to the perfection of apostolic teaching. Therefore, whether it is the universal Church or any faithful soul that strives to dedicate the whole of its life to apostolic ordinances, it is praised as multiplying seven by twelve and serving the Lord through the symbolic eighty-four years.

Likewise, the period of seven years during which she had remained with her husband most fittingly corresponds to the time of the Lord’s incarnation. For, as I said, perfection of time is commonly indicated by the number seven. But there, on account of the privilege of the Lord’s majesty, by which he taught while dwelling in the flesh, the simple number of seven years is expressed. Here, on account of the height of apostolic dignity, seven years are multiplied by twelve.

The mysteries concerning Anna also harmonize with the fact that her name is interpreted as “grace,” and that she is the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “the face of God,” while she sings with the Psalmist: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4). And she descends from the tribe of Asher—that is, “blessed”—who is eighth in birth-order among the twelve patriarchs. It has been repeatedly emphasized that this number is sacred in the New Testament.

And she herself, coming up at that moment, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem.

[Simeon prophesied; the married woman had prophesied; the virgin had prophesied; the widow too had to prophesy, so that neither any condition nor either sex might be lacking. Therefore Anna is introduced as one who, both in the service of widowhood and in her conduct, is such that she may plainly be believed worthy to announce to all that the Redeemer had come.]

And when they had fulfilled everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. At this point Luke passed over what he knew Matthew had sufficiently explained: namely, that after these events, so that he would not be found and killed by Herod, the Lord was carried by his parents into Egypt; and that, after Herod’s death, he finally returned to Galilee and began to dwell in his own city, Nazareth.

For the Evangelists commonly omit certain things in such a way that, whether they have seen them mentioned by others or foreseen in the Spirit that they would be mentioned by others, they seem, through the continuous sequence of their own narrative, to have omitted nothing. Nevertheless, when the attentive reader considers the writing of another Evangelist, he finds at what point the matters passed over have been inserted.

But the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him. The distinction of the words must be noted. The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he was a child—that is, insofar as he had assumed the condition of human weakness—had to grow and become strong. But insofar as he was also the Word of God and eternal God, he neither needed to become strong nor could he increase. Hence he is most rightly described as full of wisdom and grace.

He was full of wisdom because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. He was full of grace because the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, was granted great grace: from the moment he began to be man, he was perfect both as man and as God. The same is implied by what John writes, that he was full of grace and truth, commending under the name of truth the same excellence of divinity that Luke commends under the name of wisdom.

And his parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover. You see that this Evangelist was not without reason compared among the four living creatures to a calf, an animal assigned to sacrifices, since his narrative proceeds chiefly around the temple and Jerusalem.

At the beginning he places a priest praying at the altar; he presents the multitude of the people in the temple courts; soon after Mary, having conceived the Lord, he sends to Jerusalem; he brings her into the house of the high priest. There he reports the birth of John the Baptist and, immediately after the birth, transfers the Lord with an offering. Each year he brings him there with his parents and inserts him, at the age of twelve, among the choirs of teachers in the temple. There, among other things astonishing to the wise, he says: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father” (Luke 2). And after other matters of this kind, he concludes his Gospel with the disciples praising God in the temple.

And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast; when the days had been completed and they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem. He had been shown from his birth—or rather, from his conception—to be God by clear signs of miracles. Now, as soon as the appropriate time of life had arrived, he also began reverently to disclose and reveal each of his two substances, showing what he owed to the Father according to the truth of divine majesty and what he owed to his mother according to the weakness of the humanity he had assumed.

Nor was it without providence that he revealed the first beginnings of his faith at the age of twelve, since these were destined to be revealed and elucidated throughout the world through the ministry of the twelve apostles. We may also say that, just as by the number seven, so by the number twelve—which is formed by multiplying the parts of seven among themselves—the universality and perfection of things or times are signified.

[Col. 0349A] And therefore, since all places and times ought fittingly to be occupied, it is right that the radiance should take its beginning from the number twelve. Thus he is not said idly to have shown himself forgetful of his parents, but to instruct us that he exists not only before those parents themselves, but even before Abraham came to be; and that he takes pleasure in remaining in the city and temple of God, as though by paternal right.

And his parents did not know it. But supposing him to be in the company, they traveled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances. When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem looking for him.

Someone may ask how the Son of God, raised with such care by his parents, could have been left behind through forgetfulness when they departed. The answer is that it was customary among the children of Israel, when they gathered in Jerusalem for the festivals or returned to their own homes, for the men and women to travel in separate groups, while infants and children could go indifferently with either parent. Therefore the blessed Mary and Joseph may each have supposed that the child Jesus, whom they did not see accompanying them, had returned with the other parent.

And it happened that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them. He sits in the midst of the teachers like a fountain of wisdom, but as an example of humility he seeks first to hear and question the teachers before instructing the unlearned. So that children may not be ashamed to learn from their elders, God himself, in keeping with the condition of human age, is not ashamed to listen to human beings. So that no weak person may dare to teach, that child wished to be taught by questioning, although through the power of his divinity he supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers.

But all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers, and when they saw him they were amazed. Note the distinction of the words, and carefully contemplate the mysteries of your salvation and faith: “They were astonished who heard him, and when they saw him they were amazed.” They were astonished all the more at the wisdom of his answers because, when they saw him, they despised the smallness of his years. His tongue revealed divine wisdom, but his age displayed human weakness.

Let the Jewish teachers, therefore, be astonished at these things as though they were new, and let them be troubled by doubtful amazement between the lofty matters they hear and the weakness they see. But we, knowing that this is the one over whom the Prophet once exulted with joyful rejoicing, saying, “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9), should by no means marvel that he became man so small that nevertheless he remained what he had always been, God and mighty. At one time he gave those whom he wished to instruct signs of his divinity; at another, signs of his humanity. Rather, with faith, hope, and love worthy of him, let us give thanks because he who was great and greatly to be praised—but whom we did not know—was born as a child for us, so that by growing and advancing among children he might gradually lead them toward grasping the mysteries of his power and greatness.

And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you treated us in this way? Behold, your father and I, grieving, have been looking for you.” And he said to them: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

He does not deny that Joseph is his parent—Joseph who contributed nothing to his generation except service and affection, and who therefore is called his father both by the Evangelist and by Mary herself. Rather, simply and openly he makes known to them and to us who his true Father is. He does not reproach them for seeking him as though he were their son; he makes them raise the eyes of their minds to what they owe him whose Son he is eternally.

Because he is God and man, at one time he places before them the lofty things of divinity, and at another the lowly things of human weakness. As man, he questions his elders; as God, he answers with things that the elders and teachers marvel at. As the Son of God, he remains in the temple of God; as the son of man, he returns with his parents wherever they command.

[Col. 0350B] And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. What an example at once of piety and humility in the Lord! His parents do not understand the word he speaks to them about his divinity, and yet he is not ungrateful for the human attentiveness they show toward him: he goes down wherever they instruct him and is subject to them.

For what else would the teacher of virtue do except fulfill the duty of piety? What else among us would he do than what he wished to be done by us? He showed deference to a human being; he showed deference to a servant woman. For she herself says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). He showed deference to his supposed father; he showed deference to God the true Father. And certainly he had preserved his mother, a virgin, in chastity; certainly he did not differ from the Father in will, action, or time. Thus, warned by his examples, we may recognize what we owe to parents who endure so much for our sake.

The Arians, however, are accustomed to say that the Son is imperfect because he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). But what is surprising if, on account of the humanity he assumed, he asserts that he is less than the Father in heaven, since on account of that same humanity he was also subject to his parents on earth?

And his mother kept all these words in her heart. Whether she understood them or was not yet able to understand the words of the Gospel, she stored them all alike in her heart, as though to ruminate on them and examine them more carefully. Let us therefore learn from the holy virgin chastity in all things. She, no less modest in speech than in body, preserved the proofs of faith in her heart. And if she remains silent before the apostolic commandments, why do you, after the apostolic commandments, desire more to teach than to learn?

And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace with God and human beings. This passage refutes both the Manichaeans and the Apollinarians, showing that the Lord possessed true flesh and also a true soul. For just as age belongs to the flesh, so advancement in wisdom and grace belongs to the soul.

Yet he could in no way advance in wisdom if he did not possess the natural understanding granted to human beings for the sake of reason. This was not because God, who assumed him, needed it—especially since above he is described as a child full of wisdom—but because, for the remedy of our salvation, he chose this effect of his merciful assumption: that, while flesh and a rational soul were assumed by God, both might likewise be saved.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0351A]

Now, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, who ruled Judaea together with the Roman governor Pilate, were sons of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. Among them, their brother Archelaus also reigned for ten years. The Jews accused him before Augustus because of his intolerable savagery of spirit, and he perished in perpetual exile at Vienne.

To prevent the kingdom of Judaea from becoming too powerful, Augustus arranged for it to be divided into tetrarchies. Pilate, for his part, was sent into Judaea in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, assumed the governorship of the nation, and remained there for ten continuous years, almost until the very end of Tiberius’s reign.

Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness. Both of them—Annas and Caiaphas—were high priests when John began his preaching. But Annas administered the office during one year, and Caiaphas during the year in which the Lord ascended the cross; in between, three others had also held the high priesthood, but the Evangelist mentions especially those connected with the Lord’s passion.

For when legal observances had been set aside by force and ambition, the honor of the high priesthood was bestowed on no one because of the merit of his life or lineage. Rather, by Roman authority, the highest priesthood was conferred now on one man and then on another.

Josephus, accordingly, reports the matter in this way: “Valerius Gratus, having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ishmael, son of Bassi, as high priest. But not long afterward, removing him also, he substituted Eleazar, son of the high priest Ananias, in the high priesthood. After a year, he likewise removed him from office and entrusted the high priesthood to a certain Simon, son of Camythus. He too held the office for no more than a year, after which he received Joseph, also called Caiaphas, as his successor.”

Thus the entire period during which our Lord is described as having taught on earth is confined within the space of four years. Within it, the four successions of high priests mentioned by Josephus are described, each having scarcely served for a single year.

Therefore, because John was coming to preach the one who would redeem some from Judaea and many from the Gentiles, the times of his preaching are indicated by the king of the Gentiles and the princes of the Jews. But because the Gentiles were to be gathered and Judaea scattered on account of its guilt of unbelief, the very description of the earthly government also shows this: in the Roman state one ruler is described as presiding, while in the kingdom of Judaea many ruled by its fourth part.

For the voice of our Redeemer says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Matthew 12). It is therefore clear that the kingdom of Judaea had reached its end, since it lay subject to so many divided rulers. It is also fitting that not only the rulers but also the priests under whom these events took place are identified. Since John the Baptist was preaching the one who would exist as both king and priest, the Evangelist Luke marked the time of his preaching by both kingdom and priesthood.

And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. It is clear to all readers that John not only preached a baptism of repentance but also gave it to some; nevertheless, he could not give his baptism for the forgiveness of sins. For the forgiveness of sins is granted to us only in the baptism of Christ.

It must therefore be noted that he is said to be “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,” because, since he could not give the baptism that would release sins, he preached it. Just as he preceded the incarnate Word of the Father with the word of his preaching, so he preceded with his baptism the baptism of repentance through which sins are released, although his own baptism could not release sins.

As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice,” and so forth. When John the Baptist was asked who he was, he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” He is therefore called “a voice” by the Prophet because he went before the Word. He cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of redemption to Judaea, which had been abandoned and left desolate.

What he was to cry out is made clear when it follows: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Everyone who preaches the right faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the coming Lord into the hearts of those who hear. Thus the power of grace may penetrate and the light of truth may shine forth; thus he makes straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

“Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low.” What is signified here by the name of valleys except the humble, and by mountains and hills except proud people? At the coming of the Redeemer, therefore, the valleys were filled, while the mountains and hills were brought low. For in accordance with his saying, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14). A valley that is filled rises; a mountain or hill that is humbled decreases.

For in the faith of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, the Gentiles received the fullness of grace, while Judaea, through the error of unbelief, lost what had made it swell with pride.

“Crooked things shall become straight, and rough ways shall become smooth.” Crooked things become straight when the hearts of the wicked, twisted by injustice, are directed toward the rule of justice. Rough ways are changed into smooth paths when harsh and angry minds, through the infusion of heavenly grace, return to the gentleness of meekness.

When the word of truth is not received by an angry mind, the roughness of the road, as it were, repels the step of the traveler. But when an angry mind receives the word of correction or exhortation through the grace of meekness, the preacher finds a smooth path where previously, because of the roughness of the road, he could not advance—that is, could not set down the step of his preaching.

And every flesh shall see the salvation of God. Since “every flesh” means every human being, no human being in this life could see the salvation of God—namely, Christ. Where, then, does the prophet direct the eye of prophecy in this statement, if not toward the day of the final judgment? When Christ appears with the heavens opened, the angels ministering, and the Apostles seated upon the throne of his majesty, all alike—even the reprobate—will see him, so that the righteous may rejoice forever in the gift of their reward, while the wicked may groan eternally under the punishment of retribution. Since this statement clearly intends that he will be seen by all flesh at the final examination, it is rightly followed by:

He was saying, therefore, to the crowds who were going out to be baptized by him: Broods of vipers, etc. For the coming wrath is the final execution of vengeance. The sinner cannot then flee it if he does not now return to the lamentation of repentance. It should also be noted that evil offspring, imitating the deeds of evil parents, are called “broods of vipers.” Because they envy the good and persecute them, repay certain people with evil, and seek to injure their neighbors, and because in all these things they follow the ways of their former carnal ancestors, they are like poisonous children born of poisonous parents. But since we have already sinned, since we are entangled in the habit of evil custom, let him tell us what we must do so that we may escape the coming wrath.

Therefore, produce fruits worthy of repentance. In these words it should be noted that he does not merely urge the production of fruits of repentance, but of fruits worthy of repentance. For it is one thing to produce the fruit of repentance and another to produce what is worthy of repentance. The fruit of a good work ought not to be equal in the case of one who has sinned less and one who has sinned more, nor in the case of one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into some. Therefore, by saying, “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” each person is confronted by his own conscience, so that through repentance he may seek profits from good works proportionate to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through sin.

But the Jews, glorying in the nobility of their lineage, were unwilling to acknowledge themselves sinners because they had descended from the stock of Abraham. To them it is rightly said:

And do not begin to say, “We have Abraham as our father.” For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. For what are the stones except the hearts of the Gentiles, insensible to the understanding of almighty God? Thus it is said to certain Jews: “I will take the heart of stone from your flesh” (Ezekiel 36). Nor is it without reason that the nations are signified by the name “stones,” since they worshiped stones. Hence it is written: “Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them” (Psalm 113). From these stones, then, children were raised up for Abraham. For when the hard hearts of the Gentiles believed in the seed of Abraham—that is, in Christ—they became children of the one whose seed they had joined themselves to. Hence the distinguished preacher also says to those same Gentiles: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3). If, therefore, through faith in Christ we are now Abraham’s seed, the Jews, because of their unbelief, have ceased to be Abraham’s children.

For the axe has already been placed at the root of the trees. The tree of this world is the entire human race. The axe, however, is our Redeemer, who is held, as it were, by its handle and iron through his humanity, but cuts through his divinity. This axe has already been placed at the root of the tree, because, although he waits patiently, what he is going to do is nevertheless apparent.

Therefore every tree that does not produce fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. For every perverse person who scorns to produce the fruit of good works here finds the burning of Gehenna prepared and ready. It should be noted that he says the axe is placed not beside the branches but at the root. When the children of the wicked are removed, what else are they than the branches of a fruitless tree being cut off? But when the entire offspring is removed together with its parent, the fruitless tree has been cut down at the root, so that nothing remains from which a perverse offspring might grow again.

In these words of John the Baptist it is evident that the hearts of his hearers were troubled, since the text immediately adds:

And the crowds questioned him, saying, “What then shall we do?” They had been struck with terror and were seeking counsel.

But he answered and said to them: Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise. Because a tunic is more necessary for our use than a cloak, this belongs to producing fruit worthy of repentance: we must share with our neighbors not only external possessions and things of lesser necessity, but the very things that are greatly necessary to us—namely, the food by which we live bodily and the tunic with which we are clothed. Since it is written in the Law, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12), the person who does not share with his neighbor, in that neighbor’s need, even what is necessary to himself is shown to love him less.

For this reason the command is given concerning the sharing of two tunics with one’s neighbor, since it could not have been given concerning one: if one is divided, no one is clothed. In half a tunic, both the one who receives and the one who gives remain naked. Meanwhile, we should understand how effective works of mercy are, since they are commanded above all else as fruits worthy of repentance. Hence Truth itself also says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” But he said to them: “Do nothing more than what has been prescribed for you.” How great the power of the blessed Baptist’s preaching was, and how deeply it shook the minds of his hearers, is demonstrated by the fact that it compelled even tax collectors and soldiers to seek advice for their salvation. To them, just as to the crowds, he urges the practice of mercy in a manner appropriate to their circumstances. He therefore commands the tax collectors not to exact more than was prescribed.

Tax collectors, as their very name shows, are those who collect public taxes, or those who lease the revenues of the treasury or of public institutions. Those also who pursue the profits of this world through business are counted under the same designation. He restrains all of them, each according to his own station, from practicing fraud, so that, by first restraining themselves from desiring what belongs to others, they may finally reach the point of sharing their own possessions with their neighbors.

The soldiers also questioned him, saying, “And what shall we do?” And he said to them: “Do violence to no one,” etc. With the most just moderation, the excellent teacher warns them not to seek plunder through false accusation from those whom, as soldiers, they ought to have benefited. He teaches that military pay was established so that, while a soldier seeks his livelihood, he may not range about as a brigand. No office, no category of people, is excluded from the practice of mercy, which is the fullness of the virtues and alone frees from death and bestows eternal life. The Judge himself bears witness to this when he promises that he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom. For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc.

Now, while the people were expecting, and all were considering in their hearts concerning John, whether perhaps he himself was the Christ, John answered by saying to everyone: How did he answer those who were expecting something concerning him and were secretly thinking in their hearts that he was the Christ? Clearly, they were not merely thinking this; as another Evangelist explains, they sent priests and Levites to him to inquire whether he was the Christ. Thus it is evident that the Jews at that time knew very well, according to the Scriptures, that the time of the Lord’s incarnation had arrived. Yet what extraordinary blindness: they readily believed this of John, but would not believe it of the Savior, who had been confirmed by so many signs and virtues, and even by John himself.

I indeed baptize you with water. But one mightier than I will come, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie. John baptizes not with the Spirit but with water, because, being unable to release sins, he washes the bodies of those baptized with water but does not wash their minds through forgiveness.

Why, then, does he baptize if he does not remit sins through baptism? It is so that, preserving the order of his forerunning role, he who had preceded the Lord’s birth by his own birth might also precede the Lord who was to baptize by baptizing himself; and he who had become Christ’s forerunner by preaching might also become his forerunner through baptism, in imitation of the sacrament.

Among the ancients it was customary that, if a man did not wish to take as his wife the woman whom he ought to marry, the man who came to her as bridegroom by right of kinship would remove his sandal. What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, if not the Bridegroom of the holy Church? Of him the same John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). But because people thought John was the Christ—a claim that John himself denies—he rightly declares that he is unworthy to untie the strap of Christ’s sandal. It is as though he openly said: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not presume, undeservedly, to take the name of bridegroom.”

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? The incarnate Lord, when he came, appeared as though shod, for in his divinity he assumed the dead things of our corruption. But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation. It cannot in any way investigate how the Word became embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit was conceived within the womb of his mother, or how the one who has no beginning both exists and is conceived. The sandal strap, therefore, is the bond of the mystery. John cannot untie the strap of his sandal because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. That is, both with the cleansing of sanctification and with the testing of tribulation. The same Holy Spirit may also be understood to be signified by the name “fire,” because he kindles hearts through love and illuminates them through the wisdom with which he fills them. Hence those to whom it was said, “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 11), receive this same baptism of the Spirit in the appearance of fire.

Some interpret this to mean that in the present we are baptized in the Spirit, and in the future we will be baptized in fire. Just as now we are reborn from water and the Spirit for the remission of all sins, so then, before the final judgment, we will be cleansed by the baptism of purgatorial fire from certain lesser sins that cling to us as we depart this life. The Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will be revealed for what it is, and the fire will test it. If anyone’s work remains which he built upon it, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss. He himself, however, will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3).

Although this may also be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, if anyone takes it to refer to the fire of future purification, it must be carefully considered that he says the one who can be saved through fire is not the person who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon Christ’s foundation—that is, major and hardened sins, already incapable of being dissolved—but the one who builds wood, hay, and straw—that is, minor and very light sins, which the fire can easily consume. It must nevertheless be understood that no one there will obtain purification even from minor sins unless, while still living in this life, he has earned it through good works.

Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor. By the winnowing fan—that is, the shovel—is signified the discernment of a just examination; by the threshing floor, the present Church. In it, undoubtedly—and this is sufficiently grievous—“many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20): few grains destined to be received into the dwellings above, compared with the chaff that is to be consigned to everlasting flames.

The cleansing of this threshing floor is carried out even now, individually, when each perverse person is either expelled from the Church through priestly correction for manifest sins or condemned after death by divine severity for hidden ones. It will be completed universally at the end, when the Son of Man sends his angels and they gather from his kingdom all stumbling blocks. The Lord therefore has the winnowing fan in his hand—that is, he possesses the power to distinguish in judgment—because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.

And he will gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. The Lord himself concluded the parable of the good seed, upon which the enemy sowed weeds, in this way: “At harvest time I will say to my reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my granary” (Matthew 13). He thereby teaches that the impious and sinners will be handed over to the fire of Gehenna, while the holy will be crowned with heavenly glory.

There is, however, this difference between chaff and weeds: chaff comes forth from the same seed as wheat, although it degenerates from the nobility of its good root. Weeds, by contrast, differ not only in the merit of their fruit but are produced from an entirely different origin. The chaff consists of those who are instructed in the same mysteries of faith as the elect but differ from their solid perfection either through the shallowness of their works or through the emptiness of their unbelief. The weeds, however, are those who do not even deign to hear the words of faith and are therefore separated from the lot of the good both in conduct and in profession.

Thus, in the field of this world, there is one fruit belonging to the elect and two belonging to the reprobate. Everything the enemy sows is subject to the flames, and, what is more grievous, many things sown by the good sower perish—either snatched away by birds, dried up by the sun, choked by thorns, or at any rate turned into chaff. Only the wheat that has sprung from good soil and been proved worthy through patience will be stored in the granary of the elect’s heavenly life.

As in another parable, not only do the fish that avoid the nets of apostolic faith dwell hidden in the depths of the waters of sin, but many that have been drawn ashore among the good, all the way to the point of final separation, then deserve, because of the guilt of their wickedness, to be cast into the outer darkness.

He calls the fire of Gehenna unquenchable in a twofold sense: because it can never be extinguished, and because it will never cease tormenting those whom it afflicts, but will punish them with, so to speak, immortal death. This distinguishes it from that most sacred fire with which he had previously said that Christ’s elect would be baptized. Of this the Psalmist also says: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire” (Psalm 65). And shortly afterward: “We did not remain forever; rather, we passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. I will enter your house with burnt offerings” (ibid.)—that is, once the anguish of our trials has been overcome, I will enter the courts of your heavenly kingdom in thanksgiving.

But Herod the tetrarch, when he was reproved by him concerning Herodias, the wife of his brother, and concerning all the evils that Herod had done, added this above all: he shut John up in prison. These events are recalled more fully by Matthew and Mark: John was not only bound through the plots of Herodias but also beheaded. It should be understood that this did not happen at this time, but, according to John’s Gospel, after the Lord had performed several signs and his baptism had already become widely known. This Evangelist, however, mentions it in advance in order to emphasize Herod’s wickedness. For while the unlearned populace flocked to John’s preaching, soldiers believed, tax collectors repented, and the whole people together received baptism, Herod, by contrast, did not hesitate not only to despise him but also to kill him.

In accordance with a higher mystery, John the Evangelist undertook the task of writing about Christ’s divinity, while the other three undertook that of writing about his humanity. John the Baptist, meanwhile, bears the type of the old Law, which is the forerunner of grace. Thus, beautifully, while John the Evangelist was still preaching and the Lord’s forerunner was baptizing, he testifies that the Lord himself was making and baptizing more disciples. He teaches mystically that, before he was born in the flesh, the one who is eternally God through the ages was the teacher of the peoples instructed through the Law.

It is also fitting that the other Evangelists begin the Lord’s preaching after John has been handed over to prison. Their office was, after the Law had been corrupted by the Jews and defiled, as though by the darkness of a prison, through blind ignorance and savage tradition, to unfold the heavenly teaching of the Lord appearing in the flesh and working through the flesh, as though he were coming into Galilee.

Now, when all the people were being baptized, and Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened. The Lord was baptized not because he himself wished to be cleansed by the waters, but because he wished to cleanse the waters themselves. Washed through his flesh, which knew no sin, the waters of baptism were to receive authority, and what the innumerable baptisms under the Law could not do against the evil of transgression was to conceive the power of regenerative sanctification.

Thus, when he said that all the people had been baptized, he added nothing remarkable. But when Jesus had been baptized and was praying, he said, heaven was opened. For when the Lord entered the waters of the Jordan in the humility of his body, he opened for us the gates of heaven through the power of his divinity. While innocent flesh was immersed in the chilly waters, the fiery sword once opposed to the guilty was extinguished.

For was heaven then opened to him whose eyes saw the interior depths of heaven? No; rather, the power of baptism was displayed there: when each person emerges from it, the gate of the heavenly kingdom is made known to him. Likewise, the fact that Jesus—whose are all the things that belong to the Father—is remembered as having prayed after being baptized was undoubtedly done to instruct us. After the washing of baptism, if the hall of heaven is to be opened to us, we must not live idly but must devote ourselves to fasts, prayers, and almsgiving.

For although all sins have been loosened in baptism, the frailty of the flesh has not yet been made firm. We rejoice, as it were, that the Egyptians have been slain after crossing the Red Sea, but in the desert of worldly existence other enemies meet us, whom we must overcome through our own labor, with the grace of Christ as our leader and helper, until we reach the homeland of eternal life that has been promised.

And the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form, like a dove. “In bodily form” is fitting, because the Spirit could not be seen by mortals in the nature of his divinity. “Like a dove” is fitting, because “the Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” and will not dwell in a body subject to sins. Those who, like Simon, persist in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity can have neither lot nor share in him.

Hence, when the crimes of the world were once cleansed by the flood as a figure of baptism, it was not a raven but a dove that carried an olive branch in its beak and announced that peace had been restored to the world. Mystically, this teaches that the anointing of the Holy Spirit will be present only with those who have been baptized in simplicity of heart.

Let no one suppose that the Lord was first anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit after baptism, or that he underwent some development in the divine nature over time. Let him rather know that from the first moment of human conception he existed as truly human and at the same time truly God. The coming of the dove demonstrated that those who are baptized receive the Holy Spirit especially in his body—that is, the Church.

And a voice came from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased.” John rightly has no equal among those born of women, since Christ presents himself to be baptized by him, the invisible Spirit makes himself visible, and the Father commends his Son from heaven. This was not announced to the Son himself, who knew it perfectly, but either to John or to the others who were present, so that they might know it.

It should therefore be noted that the same John, who until then had preached that he was a man stronger than himself and that Christ was coming, thereafter, instructed either by the descent of the Spirit or by the Father’s testimony, openly proclaimed him to be the Son of God: “This is he,” he says, “of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who has been placed before me, because he was before me, and I did not know him’” (John 1). Likewise, concerning the dove: “I saw, and I have testified that this is the Son of God” (ibid.).

Thus the mystery of the Trinity is displayed in the Savior’s baptism, so that we too may be taught to be baptized in his name. As for the words, “In you I have been well pleased,” they mean: “In you I have established my pleasure,” that is, “through you I will accomplish what pleases me.”

The wording found in Matthew, “In whom I have been well pleased” (Matthew 3), is explained in this way: whenever someone corrects through repentance something he has done, by the very fact that he repents he indicates that he has displeased himself, since he amends what he did. Since almighty Father spoke in a human manner, as far as human beings could understand, about sinners when he said, “I regret that I made human beings upon the earth” (Genesis 6), he appeared, as it were, to have been displeased with himself in the sinners he had created.

But in our one and only-begotten Lord Jesus Christ he was well pleased. For he did not regret creating him as a human being among human beings, since he found no sin in him at all. Thus the Psalmist says of him: “The Lord has sworn and will not regret it: ‘You are a priest forever’” (Psalm 109).

And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being regarded as the son of Joseph. Jesus was baptized at the age of thirty, and only then began to perform signs and to teach, thereby indicating the lawful and mature time of life to those who think that every age is suitable either for the priesthood or for teaching.

As was read above, at the age of twelve he also wished to be found sitting in the temple among the teachers—not teaching, but asking questions. So that human beings would not dare to preach while still of tender age, he who through his divinity always teaches the angels in heaven questioned human beings on earth at the age of twelve.

No one should be troubled by the fact that Jeremiah and Daniel received the spirit of prophecy as boys, because miracles should not be taken as examples for ordinary practice. Almighty God makes even the tongues of infants eloquent and perfects praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children. But what we say through the ordinary practice of instruction is one thing; what we know from a miracle is another.

The Savior’s age of thirty at baptism can also disclose a mystery of our baptism, on account of faith in the holy Trinity and the fulfillment of the legal Decalogue. When the Decalogue is understood more sublimely through the revealed grace of faith, it is fulfilled with greater devotion.

He taught that those to be baptized should have, as it were, a sacred threefold measure when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). He commanded that this same threefold measure be multiplied by ten when he added: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid.).

As a figure of this, the bronze sea in which the priests washed before entering the temple is said to have been surrounded externally by a cord thirty cubits long and to have held three thousand measures within. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” This interpretation is supported by the fact that, after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Apostles first baptized three thousand souls.
