Since mention has been made of the bronze sea, it is pleasing to inquire how its other features correspond to the rule of baptism. “From lip,” it says, “to lip, ten cubits” (1 Kings 7), because we ought not to be constricted by earthly anxiety but enlarged by expectation of the heavenly tenfold reward.

Its lip was like the lip of a cup or like the leaf of an expanded lily. The first expresses the cup of the Lord’s passion; the second, the revealed glory of his resurrection. For the Apostle’s words, “As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6), refer to the lip of the cup. But what he adds—“so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (ibid.)—refers to the flower of the expanded lily.

Its thickness was three inches, so that all the strength of the baptized might be made firm through the perfection of faith, hope, and love. It was five cubits high, because whatever is committed by sight, hearing, taste, smell, or touch is entirely washed away by the water of regeneration.

The oxen that carried it looked toward each quarter of heaven, three to each, so that the whole world might be baptized in faith in the holy Trinity. It stood on the right side of the priests’ court, facing east, toward the south, because, while the grace of the New Testament stood firm, this was given through him “who visited us, the Dawn from on high” (Luke 1).

The number thirty is also found in countless places in Holy Scripture adapted to the mysteries of Christ and the Church. Joseph, who, as a figure of the resurrection and the New Testament, protected the Egyptians from famine for eighty years, assumed the government of the kingdom at thirty after washing away the filth of the prison. David began, at the same age, the kingdom that he would complete at seventy—that is, at the age worthy of perpetual rest. Ezekiel, at thirty years of age, with the heavens opened to him, earned the gifts of prophecy.

And because through faith we must endure adversity with patience and hope confidently for exalted rewards, the height of the ark and of the temple, and the length of the tabernacle, are also measured at thirty cubits.

“Being regarded,” he says, “as the son of Joseph.” He inserted this expression on account of those who thought that he had been born from Joseph in the same way as other human beings are generated. If anyone is troubled by the fact that, although Mary bore Christ from the Holy Spirit and Joseph is called his father not truly but in appearance, the genealogy is described through Joseph rather than through Mary, who seemed to have no connection with him, let him know first that it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave the line of women into genealogies.

Furthermore, Joseph and Mary were from one tribe, and therefore the Law compelled him to take her as a relative. They are also counted together in Bethlehem, evidently as born from the same stock and therefore so that Mary’s origin might be displayed through Joseph’s genealogy.

Luke very beautifully, when about to recount Christ’s genealogy, first set before it the Father speaking: “You are my beloved Son” (Mark 1). Thus, by divine testimony, he confirmed the same person as the true Son of God whom the order of human succession proved to be the true son of man.

Who was Heli, who was Matthat, who was Levi, who was Melchi, etc. It is rightly asked how Joseph could have had two fathers coming from different ancestral lines—one mentioned by Luke and the other by Matthew. Matthew says: “Matthan begot Jacob. Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary.” But Africanus, writing on the harmony of the Gospels, solves the difficulty of this question with complete clarity.

“Matthan,” he says, “and Matthat, at different times, each had a son by the same wife, named Estha. Matthan, who descended through Solomon, had first taken her as his wife and, leaving one son named Jacob, died. After his death, since the Law does not forbid a widow to marry another man, Matthat, who traced his lineage through Nathan and belonged to the same tribe but not the same family, took the widow as his wife. By her he too had a son named Heli. Thus Jacob and Heli became brothers, though they came from different paternal lines.

“One of them, Jacob, took the wife of his brother Heli, who had died childless, in accordance with the command of the Law, and fathered Joseph. By natural generation he was Jacob’s own son, which is why it is written, ‘Jacob begot Joseph.’ According to the precept of the Law, however, he became the son of Heli, whose brother Jacob had taken the wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother.

“Thus both genealogies are found to be valid and intact: the one enumerated by Matthew, who says, ‘Jacob begot Joseph,’ and the one designated with appropriate care by Luke, who says, ‘Who was regarded as the son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli.’ Luke also indicated this same distinction by saying that Joseph was regarded as the son of Heli, who had been the son of Matthat, because he showed sufficiently by this indication that this legal succession—which exists, as it were, through a kind of adoption on behalf of the dead—was concerned more with legal succession than with natural descent. The Evangelist carefully avoided saying in such successions that anyone had begotten another, and thus, by a fitting distinction, he proceeded not downward but upward, all the way to Adam and ultimately to God.”

These things were not suddenly discovered by us, nor composed without any authorities. Rather, they were handed down by the relatives of our Savior according to the flesh, either out of zeal to demonstrate so great a lineage or to teach what truly happened.

Africanus reports these matters in these very words, except that instead of Matthat he wrote Melchi, perhaps because his copy had it that way, or because in the history from which he learned these things he found that the same Matthat had a double name.

Since Matthew undertook to present the Lord’s royal person and Luke his priestly person—hence, in the fourfold form of the cherubim, the one is represented by the strongest of beasts, the lion, and the other by the calf, the sacrificial victim of the priests—each preserved the same purpose in composing the Savior’s genealogy as in the rest of his work.

For it has been keenly observed that Matthew, who had established the royal person of Christ as his subject, named forty men in the succession of generations, apart from Christ himself. This number signifies the period during which, in this world and upon this earth, we must be ruled by Christ according to the arduous discipline by which God chastises every son whom he receives, as it is written (Hebrews 12).

There are not forty-two generations, which would result from three times fourteen, but forty-one, because Jechoniah is counted twice, if Christ himself is also counted. He presides over the regulation of our temporal and earthly life, as it were, according to the number forty.

Since the number forty is the mystery of this laborious period in which, under the discipline of Christ the King, we fight against the devil, this is also shown by the fact that he consecrated a fast of forty days—that is, the humbling of the soul. The Law and the Prophets, through Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days, and the Gospel, through the Lord’s own fast, during which he was also tempted by the devil for forty days, prefigure nothing other than our temptation throughout the whole period of this world, in his flesh—which he deigned to assume from our mortality.

This number signifies temporal and earthly life because the seasons run through four divisions, and the world itself is bounded by four regions. Forty contains four tens, while the ten itself is completed by the number progressing from one through four.

Since Matthew wished to signify Christ’s descent in order to share our mortal condition, he therefore recounted the generations from Abraham down to Joseph and to Christ’s own birth, descending from the beginning of his Gospel. Luke, however, recounts the generations not from the beginning of his Gospel but from Christ’s baptism, and not by descending but by ascending. He thereby presents Christ more as a priest engaged in the expiation of sins: at his baptism the voice from heaven declared him, and John himself bore witness, saying, “Behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world.”

By ascending, Luke passes to Abraham and reaches God, to whom we are reconciled once cleansed and purified. It was right that he should also take up the origin of adoption, because through adoption we become children of God by believing in the Son of God. Through carnal generation, however, the Son of God rather became the son of man.

He clearly demonstrated that he did not call Joseph the son of Heli because Joseph had been begotten by Heli, but because he had been adopted by him, since he also called Adam the son of God, although Adam had been made by God and had been established in paradise as a son through the grace that he later lost by sinning.

Therefore, in Matthew’s genealogies is signified the Lord Christ’s assumption of our sins; in Luke’s genealogies is signified the Lord Christ’s abolition of our sins. For that reason Matthew recounts them while descending, and Luke while ascending. The Apostle’s statement, “He sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8), refers to the assumption of sins. What he adds—“in order to condemn sin in the flesh on account of sin”—refers to the expiation of sins.

Accordingly, Matthew descends from David through Solomon, with whose mother David sinned. Luke, however, ascends to David through Nathan, whose namesake, the prophet Nathan, was the means by which God expiated David’s sin.

Who was, he says, Matthan, who was David, who was Jesse. This number, which Luke continues, most certainly indicates the abolition of sins; you will see about it in its proper place. Nor should you be surprised that Luke lists more successions from David to Christ and Matthew fewer—that is, Luke lists forty-three and Matthew twenty-eight—since you acknowledge that the genealogy proceeded through other persons.

It can happen that some lived long lives, while men of another generation died prematurely, since we see many old men living with their grandchildren, while other men die immediately after their sons have been born.

Who was Shelah, who was Cainan, who was Arphaxad. The name and genealogy of Cainan, according to the Hebrew truth, is found neither in Genesis nor in the Books of Chronicles; rather, Arphaxad is said to have begotten Shelah, or Sale, as his son, with no one intervening between them. Thus you find: “Now Arphaxad lived thirty years, and begot Sale” (Gen. XI). Likewise in Chronicles: “Arphaxad begot Sala, who himself also begot Heber” (I Chron. I).

Know, therefore, that blessed Luke took this genealogy from the edition of the Seventy translators, where it is written that Arphaxad, being one hundred thirty-five years old, begot Cainan, and that Cainan himself, when he was one hundred thirty years old, begot Shelah. But which of these accounts is more accurate, or whether both can be true, God knows. We simply point out to the reader that there is such a great discrepancy between the two texts in the sequence of the years that, from the Flood to Abraham’s birth, the Hebrew text contains 292 years, whereas the translation of the Seventy is found to contain 1,077 years. And certain chronographers, following a middle course between these accounts, have removed only the generation of Cainan, without correcting the remaining years according to the Hebrew exemplar, and describe that same period as 942 years.

Who was Methuselah, who was Enoch. Beautifully, the order of the generations, ascending from the baptized Son of God to God the Father, has Enoch at the seventieth degree. He was transferred to paradise after his death was postponed, signifying that those who are regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit into the grace of adoption as sons will, after the dissolution of the body, be received into eternal rest. Indeed, the number seventy, because of the seventh day of the Sabbath, most aptly signifies the rest of those who, with the help of Christ’s grace, have fulfilled the Decalogue of the Law. At the time of the resurrection, it also shows that they will be joined forever to the contemplation of God’s unchanging wisdom.

Who was Seth, who was Adam, who was of God. Since no iniquity of Christ—for he had none—was joined to the iniquities of human beings, which he took upon himself in his flesh, the number in Matthew, Christ excepted, is forty. But because he joins us, cleansed and purified from every sin, to his own righteousness and that of the Father, so that what the Apostle says may come to pass, “He who adheres to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI), therefore, in the number given by Luke, Christ himself, from whom the enumeration begins, and God, to whom it reaches, are both counted, and the number becomes seventy-eight. By this number the complete remission and abolition of all sins is signified.

The Lord also mentioned this number when Peter asked him about forgiving a brother’s sins. For he said that forgiveness should be granted not merely seven times, but seventy-seven times (Matt. XVIII). Hence it is rightly believed that, by recalling this number, he commanded every sin to be forgiven. Nor did the Lord come, without reason or in vain, in the seventieth and seventh generation to abolish all sins, unless something lies hidden in that number pertaining to the signification of all sins.

This must be considered in the number eleven and in the number seven. Multiplied by one another, these numbers reach that total. For eleven times seven, or seven times eleven, makes seventy-seven. Eleven signifies the transgression of ten. But if ten signifies the perfection of blessedness—for this is also why all who were hired for the vineyard are rewarded with a denarius (Matt. XX)—and if this perfection is produced when the sevenfold creation is joined to the Trinity of the Creator, it is clear that the transgression of ten signifies sin: the sin of one who, through pride, desires to possess something more and loses integrity and perfection.

This transgression is multiplied by seven in order to signify that it was effected through the movement of the human being. For the incorporeal part of the human being is signified by the number three. Hence we are commanded to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Mark XII). The body, however, is signified by four, since bodily nature is found to be divided into four in many ways. Therefore, a human being, constituted from these elements joined together, is not improperly signified by the number seven.

Movement is not expressed in numbers when we say one, two, three, four, and so forth, but when we say once, twice, three times, four times. Therefore, as I have said, it is not seven and eleven, but seven times eleven, that signifies the transgression effected through the movement of the sinful human being—that is, of one who transgresses the stability of his perfection through the desire to possess something more.

Accordingly, when eleven is multiplied by seven, all sins reach the number seventy-seven. In this number there is also complete remission of sins: our priest’s flesh expiates us, from whom this number now begins, and he reconciles us to God, to whom this number now reaches, through the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove at this baptism, where this number is commemorated.

But if anyone wishes to object to the explanation given above by saying that Matthew set down not forty-one but forty-two generations, because, according to the account in Chronicles, Jeconiah ought to be counted as two persons, namely father and son, let him understand that this same number nevertheless indicates the present time of the Church, which, with the Lord’s help, labors in hope of the future Sabbath. For seven times six makes forty-two. Few would doubt that six pertains to works, while seven pertains to the signification of rest.

Thus the people saved from the land of Egypt remain in the desert for forty years; but because they are diligently exercised in hope of entering rest, they camp along the very narrow road in six sevens—that is, forty-two stages. At the end of these, when they receive Jesus as their leader, the Jordan is immediately opened, and, after their enemies have been conquered, they enter the dwellings promised long ago.

So also the Lord Jesus, coming in the forty-second generation after Abraham’s faith dispelled the ancient darkness of the world’s blindness, opened the gates of heaven for us through the washing of baptism, when he came in the flesh. And we, after completing the course of virtues, in which we await with patience what we do not see (Rom. VIII), shall, under the mystery of this same number, cross the river dried up under Christ’s leadership and joyfully reach the kingdoms of our promised heavenly homeland.

Because he began his baptism when he was thirty years old, and was going to cleanse the whole Church’s stains, the mystical relationship of these numbers also reveals this. For thirty, calculated through its aliquot parts, produces twelve more—the number of the patriarchs and apostles—and thus makes forty-two. Its parts are: a thirtieth, one; a fifteenth, two; a tenth, three; a sixth, five; a fifth, six; a third, ten; and a half, fifteen. Joined together, these total forty-two.

Here, as we have said, it is mystically indicated that the whole perfection of the Church consists in the faith and grace of Christ, which was first recognized by the patriarchs and then spread more widely through the voice of the apostles. Nor is there any other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts IV), just as in forty-two there is no part that is not contained among the aliquot parts of the number thirty. Thus the number thirty, through its parts, completes the forty-second, because through the mysteries of his baptism the Lord both protects the Church while it labors temporally and, when its labors are finished, brings it eternally into rest.

## CHAPTER IV

“Now Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the desert for forty days.”

Matthew and Mark indicate that these things happened immediately after the Lord’s baptism. One of them, having described his baptism, added at once: “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. IV). The other says: “And immediately the Spirit drove him into the desert, and he was there forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan” (Mark I).

But lest anyone wonder by what spirit they said he was led or driven into the desert, Luke deliberately first stated that Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and then added, “and was led by the Spirit into the desert,” so that no one might suppose that the unclean spirit had any power against him. Full of the Holy Spirit, he walked wherever he wished and did whatever he wished.

Further on, where he is plainly said to have been taken up or set upon a place by the devil, it is not his weakness but the pride of the enemy that is exposed—the enemy who considers the Savior’s will to be necessity. Jesus, therefore, is not led into the desert by the power of an evil spirit, but by the will of his own good Spirit he enters the place of combat, certain of victory, in order to overthrow his adversary.

Here he also rightly sets before us the order of proper conduct: after receiving remission of sins in baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we must gird ourselves more tightly against the new ambushes of the ancient enemy, abandon the world in mind, and learn to hunger for the joys of eternal life alone, as for the manna of the desert.

“And he ate nothing during those days, and when they were completed, he was hungry.”

The forty-day fast has authority both from the ancient books—from the fasts of Moses and Elijah—and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days, showing that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets. In the person of Moses, the Law is understood; in the person of Elijah, the Prophets. He appeared gloriously between them on the mountain, so that it might become more evident what the Apostle says about him: “Having testimony from the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. III).

At what other time of year could the observance of the forty days have been established more suitably than adjacent and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For in it this laborious life is signified, a life that requires self-restraint, so that we may fast from friendship with the world itself.

Alternatively: The Lord fasted when he was tempted before his death, while he still needed food. But he ate and drank when he was glorified after the resurrection, when he no longer needed food. In the former he displayed our labor; in the latter, our consolation. He defined both by periods of forty days.

By this number, the forty-day period seems to signify the course of this age in those who are called by grace to him who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). There are ten commandments of the Law; grace has now been spread throughout the world; and the world is divided into four parts. Ten multiplied by four makes forty. For “those whom the Lord redeemed he gathered from the regions: from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the sea.”

Thus, fasting for forty days before the death of the flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Abstain from the desires of this age” (I Pet. II). Eating and drinking for forty days after the resurrection of the flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Fasting belongs to the tribulation of combat, because one who is in the contest abstains from everything. Food, however, belongs to the hope of peace, which will not be perfect until our body, whose redemption we await, has put on immortality. We do not yet possess it so as to glory in it, but by hoping for it we are already nourished.

The Apostle shows that we perform both things together when he says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII)—as though the former belonged to food and the latter to fasting. For as we travel along the Lord’s way, we both fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future: here we do not set our heart upon earthly things; there we feed the heart above.

But the Lord became hungry when the days of his fast were completed, although nothing similar is written of Moses or Elijah when they fasted, so that the enemy might not flee in fearful sadness from tempting one whom he would see proclaimed by so many heavenly signs and also made equal to the most excellent men in abstinence. God the man became hungry in humility, so that the exalted man who is God might not be recognized by the enemy.

“And the devil said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.’”

The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his conqueror, had come into the world. Hence, through the possessed man, he also said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII).

Yet when he saw him subject to suffering, when he saw that his humanity could endure mortal things, everything he had suspected concerning his divinity was thrown into doubt by the arrogance of his pride. For, knowing nothing but pride, he doubted that this man was God when he saw him humble. Therefore he turned to the arguments of temptation.

But the soul of our Redeemer was not shaken by the necessity of temptation in the way that we, who are merely human beings, are often disturbed when temptation rushes upon us. Our enemy—even when he was permitted to take him up onto a high mountain, even when he claimed that he would give him the kingdoms of the world, even when he showed him stones as though they could be turned into bread—could not shake the mind of the Mediator between God and human beings by temptation.

He graciously accepted all these things outwardly, while inwardly his mind remained unshaken, clinging to his divinity. Even when he is said to have been troubled in spirit and to have groaned, he himself divinely ordered the extent to which he would be troubled in his humanity.

“And Jesus answered him: ‘It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’”

The Lord answered in this way because his purpose was to conquer the devil through humility, not through power. At the same time, we must observe that, unless the Lord had begun to fast, the devil would not have had an opportunity to tempt him. As it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II).

The Savior’s own response also indicates that the one who was tempted was a human being: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” Therefore, if anyone does not feed on the word of God, that person does not live.

Alternatively: The more our enemy sees us placed in this life rebelling against him, the more fiercely he strives to conquer us. He neglects to strike those whom he believes himself to possess by quiet right. Against us, however, he is stirred with greater violence insofar as he is expelled from our heart as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord represented this in himself under a certain dispensation. He permitted the devil to tempt him only after his baptism, in order to indicate to us a sign of the future manner of life: his members, after advancing toward God, would then endure more severe attacks of temptation.

“And the devil led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time.”

When the God-man is said to have been led by the devil, the mind recoils and human ears are afraid to hear it. Yet we know that these things are not incredible if we consider other things that happened in him. Certainly, the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. What, then, is surprising if he permitted himself to be led by that one onto a mountain, when he also endured being crucified by that one’s members?

It is therefore not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. For it was just that he should conquer our temptations by his temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.

It is well that worldly and temporal things are shown “in a moment of time.” For this does not indicate so much the speed of the sight as it expresses the fragility of transitory power. In a moment all those things pass away, and worldly honor has often departed before it has arrived. For what can be lasting in this world, when the ages themselves are not lasting?

“And he said: ‘I will give you all this power and their glory, because it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you fall down and worship me, all will be yours.’”

Arrogant and proud, he says this boastfully—not because the devil has power throughout the whole world, so that he could give all kingdoms, since we know that many holy men have been made kings by God. “If,” he says, “you fall down and worship me.” Therefore, the one who is going to worship the devil falls first.

“And Jesus answered and said to him: ‘It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.’”

When the devil says to the Savior, “If you fall down and worship me,” he hears, conversely, that he himself ought rather to worship him as his Lord and God.

Someone may ask how the command given here—that one must serve the Lord alone—agrees with the Apostle’s statement: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. V). The origin of the Greek language, from which Scripture was translated, easily resolves this question. In Greek, service is customarily designated in two ways and with different meanings. One word is λατρεία (*latreia*), and another is δουλεία (*douleia*).

*Dulia* is understood as common service, that is, service rendered either to God or to any being within the order of nature. From this the Greek word δοῦλος (*doulos*), meaning “servant” or “slave,” also takes its name. *Latria*, however, is the service owed exclusively to the worship of the Divinity and not to be shared with any creature. Hence those who offer idols the vows, prayers, and sacrifices that ought to have been offered to the one God are called idolaters.

We are therefore commanded to serve one another through charity—what in Greek is δουλεύειν (*douleuein*). We are commanded to serve the one God—what in Greek is λατρεύειν (*latreuein*). Hence the phrase “and him alone you shall serve” is, in Greek, λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*). Likewise: “For we are the circumcision, serving the Spirit of God” (Phil. III), which in Greek is λατρεύοντες (*latreuontes*).

“And he led him to Jerusalem and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple.”

He tests with vainglory the one whom he could not overcome with gluttony or greed, to see whether perhaps he might cast him down by the very boastfulness of his victory.

“And he said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here.’”

In all temptations the devil is trying to determine whether he is the Son of God. But the Lord so frames his response that he leaves him uncertain. “Throw yourself down.” This is the devil’s voice, by which he always desires everyone to fall downward. “Throw yourself,” he says: he can persuade, but he cannot cast down.

“For it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you, and that they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”

We read this in Psalm 90. But there the prophecy concerns not Christ but a holy man. The devil therefore interprets Scripture badly. Certainly, if he truly knew that this had been written about the Savior, he ought also to have said what follows in the same psalm against himself: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC).

He speaks of the angels’ help as though addressing one who is weak; but, like a deceiver, he is silent about his own trampling.

“And Jesus answered and said to him: ‘It is said: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

He breaks the devil’s false arrows from Scripture with the true shields of Scripture. It should be noted that he brought forward the necessary testimonies only from Deuteronomy, in order to display the mysteries of the second Law.

“You shall not tempt,” he says, “the Lord your God.” The suggestion was made to him as a human being that he should test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he had with God. Such a thing is done wrongly when it is done. It belongs to sound doctrine that, whenever a human being has something he can do, he should not tempt the Lord his God.

For the Savior himself was able to protect his disciples, yet he said to them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X). He first provided an example of this himself. For although he had power to lay down his life, and would not lay it down unless he wished, nevertheless, as an infant, he fled to Egypt when his parents carried him there. He also went up to the feast not openly but secretly, although at other times he spoke publicly to the Jews who were angry and listened with the most hostile intent; yet they could not lay hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

Thus, by teaching and rebuking openly, while not allowing the fury of his enemies to have any power over him, he demonstrated God’s power. Yet, by fleeing and hiding, he instructed us in human weakness, so that no one should dare to tempt God when he has something he can do in order to escape what must be avoided.

“And when every temptation was completed, the devil departed from him until an opportune time.”

You see that the devil is not persistent in his efforts but usually yields to virtue. Although he does not cease to envy, he fears to persist, because he more often withdraws than be defeated. Having heard the name of God, “he departed,” it says, “until an opportune time.” Later he came not to tempt him but to fight openly.

Often, however, after the ancient enemy has inflicted the battle of temptations upon our minds, he withdraws from the struggle for a time—not to put an end to the malice he has inflicted, but so that, after making hearts secure through repose, he may return suddenly and break in more easily because he is unexpected.

It should also be noted that, after setting forth only three deceits of the tempter, he says that every temptation was completed. These three embrace the origins and sources of all vices, as John testifies when he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II).

In the Gospel parable, three kinds of rejected business alone exclude people from the banquet of eternal life. The first, it says, said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it.” Another said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them.” Another said: “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”

The desire for a wife, like gluttony, belongs to the desire of the flesh. The purchase of a farm, which is not free from greed, looks to the pride of life. The testing of five yoke of oxen—that is, curiosity about bodily things, which is vainglory—relates to the desire of the eyes. Curiosity is especially powerful through the eyes.

The Lord is tempted face to face by these things as though by a stronger opponent. But when we ourselves, having received the grace of the Spirit through baptism, enter the desert of virtues, when we undertake the forty-day fast—that is, when we resolve to abstain from worldly allurements throughout the whole course of our lives—we are attacked either by hidden ambushes or, sometimes, by more direct assaults.

When he says flatteringly, “You are a strong man; eat and drink and remain as you are,” we must take care lest, unknowingly, he offer us the poisons of the ancient serpent. We must reply: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

Many, however, after conquering the desire of the flesh, are immediately attacked by greed and are sometimes even defeated by it, so that they do not fear to worship the devil in exchange for gifts that have been offered. When many praise their self-restraint, when important persons honor them and give them gifts, it happens that those who have conquered pleasures are conquered by love of money. As their madness increases with time, they not only curse and rebuke the rich whom they recognize as filled with demons through their manifest crimes, but also bow their necks, worship them, and receive them.

Hence the Apostle says that greed is the service of idols. If they also triumph over this, following the Savior’s example by worshiping the Lord their God and serving him alone in exchange for eternal joys, then the third plague, vainglory, will arise. It exalts those who have conquered the preceding vices through their own strength, so that, as though placed on the summit of virtues, they presume that they can no longer fall.

To tempt God with curious eyes is precisely this: for someone to boast of his own merits. Against this, the Lord himself, strengthening the faith of his disciples, says: “When you have done everything that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke XVII).

When elsewhere he commanded us not to perform our righteousness before human beings, in defining this he added only fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. Thus he set three weapons of defense against the enemy’s threefold weapon, so that desire of the flesh might be driven away by fasting, greed by almsgiving, and boastfulness about one’s merits by prayers.

Let what we have said in this one book about the beginnings of the Gospel dispensation suffice. But the deeds and words of the Savior that follow we shall consider from another beginning, attending not only to our own repose but also to the benefit of the readers. For, as Augustine says, the reader’s attention is refreshed at the end of a book in the same way that a traveler’s labor is refreshed by an inn.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371A] Ecclesiastical history relates that the most blessed apostle John preached the Gospel almost until the very end of his life without the aid of any written text. But when, it says, knowledge of the three Gospels had also reached him, he is said to have approved the faith and truth of what they contained, yet he saw that certain things were lacking, especially those that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching.

For it is certain that the first three Evangelists seem to contain only those events that took place in the year during which John the Baptist was either imprisoned or punished. Indeed, if you observe the beginnings of their narratives, after Matthew reports the forty-day fast and the Lord’s temptation, he immediately adds: “Now when he heard that John the Baptist had been handed over, he withdrew from Judea and came into Galilee” (Matt. III). Mark likewise says: “After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee” (Mark I).

Luke, even before he begins to report anything about Jesus’ deeds, says that Herod “added this also to all the evils that he had done, and shut John up in prison” (Luke III). Since, I say, these matters seemed to have been omitted by them, the apostle John is said to have been asked to describe what the earlier writers had passed over—events that the Savior had performed before John’s arrest.

Therefore he says in the Gospel: “This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs” (John II). And again, elsewhere, he indicates this by saying: “For John had not yet been sent into prison” (John III). It is therefore clear that he describes what Jesus had done before John was handed over.

We have thought it right to place these words of the history just mentioned at the beginning of this work—our second little book on Luke—so that none of the readers might suppose that the events which are to be explained in sequence happened immediately after the eleven-day fast, but might instead understand that they followed after several miracles had been performed by the Lord, whether in Judea or in Galilee.

“And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report about him went out through the whole region; and he himself taught in their synagogues, and was glorified by everyone.”

He calls “the power of the Spirit” the signs of miracles, just as the Jews elsewhere marvel and ask: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these powers?” (Matt. XIII). They refer wisdom, evidently, to teaching, and power to deeds. Both are joined together in this passage, since Jesus is said both to have entered in the power of the Spirit and to have taught in their synagogues.

Hence he is rightly said to have been glorified by those present and to have become known by report among those who were absent. This could not have happened without the evidence of deeds or words performed in the presence of people. Anyone who seeks the time and order of these events will find them in John’s Gospel, as has been said.

I shall pass over the rest and offer only one testimony. “When he came,” it says, “into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he had done in Jerusalem on the feast day” (John IV).

It should indeed be noted that he first records Jesus as having displayed the power of the Spirit and afterward having ministered the grace of teaching; first, a report of his powers went forth, and then his teaching was glorified. This follows the order that he also took care briefly to commend in the Acts of the Apostles: “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). He put “to do” first and “to teach” afterward, so that no teacher might presume to command his hearers to do what he himself had not yet accomplished in deeds.

“And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entered the synagogue according to his custom on the Sabbath day.”

*Synagogue* is a Greek word which in Latin is called *congregatio*, “assembly.” By this name they customarily designated not only the gathering of large crowds but also the building where the Jews assembled to hear or speak the word of God.

Thus the Lord says to the high priest Annas: “I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together.” In the same way we call both the churches of the faithful and their places and choirs by that name.

There is, however, a difference between *synagogue*, which is interpreted as “assembly,” and *church*, which is interpreted as “convocation” or “calling together.” The people of the Old Testament are designated by both terms, but those of the New Testament are called only the Church. For animals and all kinds of inanimate things can be gathered together, but only beings endowed with reason can be summoned or called together.

Therefore, it seemed more appropriate to the apostolic writers and teachers to call the people of the new grace, as possessing greater dignity, “called together” into the unity of faith rather than “assembled”—that is, to call it the Church rather than the synagogue.

On the Sabbath day they assembled in the synagogues so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLVI), they might set aside the business of the world and sit with quiet hearts to meditate on the precepts of the Law.

An indication of the devotion owed on that day still endures in the Church. In some places, as a memorial of the ancient religion, it is customary to recite on the Sabbath the song of Deuteronomy, which contains the entire condition of the ancient people—what they deserved when God was offended and what they deserved when he was propitious. Otherwise it would be out of order for the song of Moses to be recited last, after the songs taken from the prophets on the earlier days of the week.

Jesus therefore entered the synagogue on the Sabbath in order to fulfill the rite of the Mosaic Law with the fullness of heavenly grace.

“And he rose to read, and the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him.”

This is certainly an indication of the profound humility of the dispensation by which God came among human beings to serve, not to be served; he did not disdain even to undertake the office of reader.

But with a deeper providence, Luke began his account of the Lord’s deeds with the reading and explanation of the prophet, because the whole text of prophecy, reaching all the way to him, was to be opened to us through him and fulfilled in him.

Hence he explains both matters more clearly at the end of his Gospel. First he records the Savior’s saying: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV); immediately afterward he adds: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (ibid.).

Jesus therefore rose to read, so that those whom the new working of signs had not converted might at least be corrected by the testimony of the prophetic reading.

“And when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written.”

Beautifully, he receives the prophet’s book closed but reads it after unrolling it, because he first undertook to display to mortals the mystery of his Incarnation, which had been prescribed through the voice of the prophets, and afterward opened it to their understanding.

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to evangelize the poor,” and so forth.

Above, through the prophet, the Savior was speaking about the calling of the Gentiles and the confirmation of the Church. Among other things, he said: “I, the Lord, will suddenly do this in its time” (Isa. LX). Immediately he added what is read here: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.”

This does not mean that the Lord God has a Lord God, but that, according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, he speaks of things that are humble. The Psalmist had already said to him: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

When companions are mentioned, understand the nature of the flesh, through which God has us as companions of his substance. And because the anointing was spiritual and not at all anointing of a human body, as it was among the priests of the Jews, he is remembered as anointed above his companions—that is, above the other saints.

His anointing was completed at the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained in him. He was therefore anointed with spiritual oil and heavenly power, so that he might water the poverty of human condition with the eternal treasure of the resurrection, remove the captivity of the mind, and illuminate the blindness of souls.

“Blessed are the poor,” he said, “for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke VI). And again: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII). And again: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (ibid.).

To release the broken into remission; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution. “The sacrifice acceptable to God,” he says, “is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50). And therefore he says that he was sent, or anointed, to heal the broken—or those broken in heart—according to what the Psalmist also says of him: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Ps. 146).

Or certainly, “to release the broken into remission” means to raise up those who had been weighed down by the heavy and unbearable burden of the Law, and to admit them into the remission of spiritual grace. And this itself is to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord. For then the true year of Jubilee—that is, the year of freedom—was at hand: namely, the time of the Church, during which, while she remains in the body, she is a pilgrim away from the Lord. Of this the Psalmist sings: “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness” (Ps. 64). For it was not only that year in which the Lord preached that was acceptable, but also this one in which the Apostle preaches, saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). After proclaiming the acceptable year of the Lord, he also proclaims the final day of retribution, saying: “For the Son of Man is going to come in his glory with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his work” (Matt. 16). Thus he says that he was sent to proclaim all these things because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.

[Col. 0374A]

And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the attendant and sat down. The Lord read the book aloud in the hearing of all who were present, and after reading it he returned it to the attendant. For, as he himself testifies elsewhere, while he was in the world he spoke openly to the world, always teaching in the synagogue and in the Temple, where all the Jews habitually assembled. But as he was about to return to heaven, he entrusted the office of evangelization to those who had seen him from the beginning and had been ministers of the word.

And appropriately he read while standing, but after returning the book he sat down. Standing signifies one who is working; sitting, one who is resting or judging. For the Lord Jesus Christ, in order to open for us the path of knowledge that had been written concerning him, graciously undertook to work for a time in the flesh. When the duty of his holy dispensation had been completed, he chose disciples to follow his teaching and restored himself to the throne of heavenly rest, from which even now he orders all things by hidden judgment and at the end of the whole age will appear as the manifest Judge.

At the same time he mystically sets forth an example, so that every preacher of the word may also be a doer of it. Let him rise, read, and sit down: that is, let him work, preach, and in this way await the rewards of rest.

[Col. 0374B]

And it should be noted that he himself read the book opened out, but returned it to the attendant folded. For he taught his Church, through the Spirit of truth sent by the Father, all truth; yet he warned beforehand by his own example that not everything should be said to everyone, but that the teacher must distribute the word according to the capacity of his hearers, when he said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him. Then he began to say to them: Because today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. It was fulfilled in him, certainly, because, just as that Scripture had foretold, “he did great things, and the Lord proclaimed still greater things.” What greater testimony, then, can we seek than that he himself, in his own voice, marked himself out as the one who had spoken through the prophets?

[Col. 0374C]

Thus he removes the sacrilegious errors of unbelievers, who say that the God of the Old Testament is one and the God of the New Testament another, or who say that Christ began with the Virgin. For how could he have begun from the Virgin who was speaking before the Virgin?

And all bore witness to him and marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth. They bore witness to him by affirming that he truly was, as he had said, the one of whom the prophets had sung; that he had truly been anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit; and that they themselves—poor, blind, captive, and broken—truly needed his gifts in every respect.

And they were saying: Is this not Joseph’s son? How great was the blindness of the Nazarenes, who despised the one whom they recognized as Christ in his words and deeds merely because they knew his family background. Yet their error is our salvation and the condemnation of heretics. For they saw Jesus Christ so entirely as a man that they called him Joseph’s son and, according to the other evangelists, a craftsman, or the son of a craftsman.

[Col. 0375A]

In this connection, we should consider why Christ, appearing in the flesh, wished to be called the son of a craftsman—indeed, the craftsman himself. We should understand soundly that by this too he taught that he was, before the ages, the Son of the one who in the beginning created heaven and earth, God the maker of all things. For although human realities must not be compared with divine ones, the type is nevertheless complete, because the Father of Christ works with fire and spirit. Hence also his forerunner, speaking of him as of a craftsman’s son, says: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3). In the great house of this world he fashions vessels of various kinds. Indeed, by softening the vessels of wrath with the fire of the Spirit, he changes them into vessels of mercy.

Thus Malachi, speaking in the person of the Father, rightly said: “Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and suddenly the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple.” Shortly afterward he added: “And he will sit refining and purifying silver; he will cleanse the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and like silver.”

[Col. 0375B]

But the Jews, ignorant of this mystery, despise the works of divine power by contemplating carnal ancestry, as is apparent not only from what precedes in their case but also from the Lord’s subsequent words, when he adds:

And he said to them: Surely you will say to me this proverb: “Physician, heal yourself”; whatever else follows. Their insane unbelief, though unknowingly, confesses the sound faith that calls the Lord Christ both craftsman and physician. For he is truly a craftsman, because all things were made through him. He is a physician, because through him all things in heaven and on earth have been restored.

And as he himself testifies: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2). And because we have said what instrument he uses for making, let us also say what kind of method he uses for healing. Passing by, he saw a man blind from birth; he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, spread it over his eyes, and said to him: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam,” which means “SENT.” He went, therefore, and washed, and came back seeing (John 9).

[Col. 0375C]

Recognize, then, the manner of this great medicine, and rejoice that through it you have deserved to be enlightened. The clay made from the earth is Christ’s flesh. The spittle from his mouth is his divinity, because God is the head of Christ. The spittle mixed with clay enlightens us when, baptized in the pool of Siloam, we are enlightened, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory” (John 1), which previously, with darkness shutting it out, we could not comprehend.

Through Christ the craftsman you were created so that you might exist. Through Christ the physician you were recreated so that, after your wounds, you might be healthy. When his fellow citizens mocked him and urged him to heal himself—that is, to perform miracles in his own country—another Evangelist nevertheless does not excuse him without reason, saying that he could do no miracle there, except that he healed a few sick people by laying on his hands. And he marveled because of their unbelief.

This was so that no one might perhaps think that affection for one’s country ought to be held in lesser regard. He loved his fellow citizens, therefore, but they deprived themselves of their country’s love through their own envy.

[Col. 0375D]

And he said: Amen, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his own country. That the Lord Christ is called a prophet in the Scriptures is also attested by Moses, who says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me” (Deut. 18). But not only he, who is the head and Lord of the prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets, were held in less esteem in their own country than in distant cities. For it is almost natural that citizens should always envy their fellow citizens. They do not consider a man’s present works, but remember his fragile childhood, as though they themselves had not passed through the same stages of life to reach maturity.

In truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut up for three years, and so forth. He means: It does not conflict with the deeds of the prophets that I withdraw divine benefits from citizens who disdain them. For just as, when famine once oppressed the whole land, no one in Judea was found worthy to offer Elijah hospitality, but a widow of a foreign nation was sought out, who because of her faith deserved to be visited by so great a prophet; and just as, though there were many lepers there, only Naaman the Syrian, because he had devoutly sought healing, deserved to be cured by the prophet Elisha—so here he will deprive you of the heavenly gift for no other reason than envy and unbelief.

[Col. 0376A]

And if you examine the deeds of the prophets allegorically as well, you will certainly find that the Lord, by the unbelief of his own country, which did not receive him, pointed out the pride of the Jews. By the name Capernaum, however, which is interpreted as “field of consolation,” he proclaimed the salvation of the nations, where greater signs are performed daily through the apostles and their successors, not so much in the healing of bodies as in that of souls.

The widow, therefore, to whom Elijah was sent signifies the Church of the nations. Abandoned for a long time by her creator, she nourished a people ignorant of the true faith like a poor son with scanty alms—that is, she instructed them with the word lacking fruit—until the prophetic word came. In Judea, Israel’s fleece having been dried up, as though the gate of heaven were shut, it was endangered by famine; but there the prophetic word was both nourished and nourished others: received by believers and itself refreshing believers.

[Col. 0376B]

Accordingly, this same widow is rightly said to have lived at Zarephath of Sidon. Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting,” while Zarephath means “fire” or “distress of bread.” For “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5). Where care was spent, as though on hunting birds, in acquiring superfluous things; where the burning of terrible thirst and the distress of spiritual bread had previously arisen—there, through the prophetic mouth, flour and oil were blessed. That is, the fruit and gladness of charity, or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism, were made fruitful through the unfailing gift of the heavenly word.

To this day the oil of spiritual joy and the flour of blessing do not fail in her vessels, while the other nations that do not believe suffer the misery of want of divine bread and devote themselves to useless hunting. And this widow herself most beautifully declares that, before she died, she wished to make mystical bread for herself and would gather two pieces of wood—not merely by the name “wood,” but also by the number of the pieces of wood expressing the sign of the cross, by which the bread of eternal life was prepared for us.

[Col. 0376C]

And there were many lepers in Israel under the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian. Since the historical account is well known, it is necessary to touch briefly on the mystery. This Syrian Naaman, whose name is interpreted as “beauty,” represents the people of the nations, once stained by the leprosy of unbelief and crimes, but cleansed through the sacrament of baptism from every foulness of mind and body.

At the advice of the captive girl—that is, through the grace of heavenly inspiration, which the Jews were unable to preserve and which the nations seized—he was urged to hope for salvation and commanded to wash seven times. For plainly only that kind of baptism which regenerates through the Holy Spirit saves.

Hence his flesh is rightly said to have appeared after the washing like the flesh of a little child. Either because grace, the mother who gives birth to all baptized in Christ, brings them into one infancy; or, rather, that child is to be understood of whom it was said: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). The whole offspring of believers is joined to his body through baptism.

[Col. 0376D]

And so that you might know that all the sacraments of baptism had been prefigured here—in baptism we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess the faith—Naaman declares that he will no longer sacrifice to foreign gods, but will serve the Lord alone in every respect. He also rejoices to take a portion of the holy land with him, because those who have been baptized ought also to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.

Naaman, therefore, is rightly preferred: while water washes his body, faith washes his heart—that is, the people of the nations are preferred to the Jews, who are filthy with the leprosy of obstinacy. Likewise the widow of Zarephath—that is, the Church—desiring to be refreshed by the wood of the cross, is restored, while the Jews perish from hunger for the word, by the bread of the most holy body and the anointing of the life-giving Spirit.

It is thus proved that the Lord denied the gifts of his powers to his fellow citizens not because of his own inability but because of their envy; and by this example he finally showed that the whole nation was abandoned by him—not because it was not loved, but because it did not wish itself to be loved—while teachers were scattered from there throughout the world for the salvation of the nations. But what the Lord testifies in words about the Jews, the Jews themselves testify by their deed about him. For it follows:

[Col. 0377A]

And all in the synagogue were filled with anger when they heard this; and they rose up and drove him outside the city. The sacrileges of the Jews, which the Lord had foretold long before through the prophet, saying, “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34), are shown in the Gospel to have been fulfilled. For while he himself spread benefits among the peoples, they inflicted injuries upon him. It is no wonder that they lost salvation, since they drove the Savior from their territory.

For the Lord is accommodating, and by his example taught his apostles to become all things to all people: he neither rejects those who are unwilling nor binds those who are unwilling; he does not resist those who drive him out, nor is he absent from those who ask him. Thus elsewhere, when the Gerasenes could not endure his miracles, he left them as though they were weak and ungrateful.

At the same time understand that his bodily passion was not imposed by necessity but was voluntary; he was not seized by the Jews but offered himself. For when he wishes, he is seized; when he wishes, he slips away; when he wishes, he is hung up; when he wishes, he is not held.

And they led him, he says, as far as the brow of the hill on which their city had been built, in order to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went on. O inheritance of disciples worse than their teacher! The devil tempts the Lord by a word; the Jews, by a deed. He says, “Throw yourself down”; they attack him in order to throw him down.

[Col. 0377B]

Indeed, the Lord had climbed the brow of the hill to be thrown down, but he descended through their midst when the minds of the raging crowd were suddenly changed or stunned. He preferred still to heal them rather than destroy them, so that, seeing the failure of their attempted wickedness, they might thereafter desist from seeking his death.

For the hour of his passion had not yet come—an hour destined to occur not on an ordinary Sabbath but on the Friday of Passover. Nor had he yet approached the place of his passion, which was symbolized not in Nazareth but in Jerusalem by the blood of sacrifices. Nor had he chosen the kind of death, since the world had proclaimed that he would be crucified.

He therefore did not wish to be thrown down by the Nazarenes, stoned by the Jerusalemites, killed by Herod among the children of Bethlehem, or brought to completion by any other death. For what sign of royal power would stand out in such a death, by which the brow of the faithful might be armed? Only the standard of the cross was awaited. Its figure could be drawn both by the swift movement of the right hand against the assaults of the wicked enemy and, no less, could be regarded as a type of the unique monarchy.

[Col. 0377C]

Thus the Apostle, explaining the triumph of the cross, says: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2). For this is what the upper points of the cross signify: they reach toward heaven; its lower part seeks the underworld; its arms cover the earth.

And he descended to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and there he taught them on the Sabbath. See the clemency of the Lord and Savior: moved neither by indignation, offended by crime, nor violated by injury, he does not abandon Judea. Indeed, forgetful of the injury but mindful of clemency, now teaching, now liberating, now healing, he soothes the hearts of the people in faith.

But because he especially performed the gifts of his healing and teaching on Sabbaths, he shows that he came not under the Law but above the Law—having come to fulfill the same Law, not to abolish it. Nor did he choose the Jewish Sabbath, on which it was not permitted even to kindle a fire or move hand or foot; rather, the true Sabbath and rest beloved by the Lord is this: if, while devoted to the salvation of souls, we abstain from servile work, that is, from every unlawful act.

[Col. 0377D]

And they were astonished at his teaching, because his word was with authority. The word of a teacher is authoritative when he does what he teaches. For one who destroys his own sayings by his deeds is despised. In contrast, the Apostle, instructing a teacher, says: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4).

But the Lord alone, uniquely and principally, spoke with good authority, because he committed no evil through weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he ministered to us through the innocence of his humanity.

His word was authoritative in another sense as well—or, as another Evangelist says, he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. For the scribes gave the peoples the commandments they had learned through the Law. But he, as the author and fulfiller of the Law, freely substituted other commands, either changing or enlarging what seemed incomplete.

And in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean demon. It was fitting that a man who possessed an unclean spirit was in the synagogue, because he had lost the Holy Spirit. The devil had entered where Christ had departed. So even now some say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.

And he cried out with a loud voice, saying: Let us alone; what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? He means: “Cease for a little while from tormenting me, since there is no fellowship between you and our deceit.” And truly: “What partnership has light with darkness? What communion has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6).

[Col. 0378A]

Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God. This is not a confession of the will, followed by the reward of confessing, but an extorted confession of necessity, compelling unwilling speakers. As fugitive slaves, after a long time, might see their master and ask for nothing except reprieve from blows, so the demons, seeing the Lord suddenly present on earth, believed that he had come to judge them. The presence of the Savior is the torment of demons.

And Jesus rebuked him, saying: Be silent and come out of him. Because “through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2), the medicine of salvation first had to operate against the author of death himself: first the serpent’s tongue had to be closed, lest it spread its venom any further; then the woman who had first been deceived had to be healed from the fever of carnal desire; third, the man who had listened to the words of his misleading wife had to be chastened for the leprosy of his error. Thus, in this Evangelist, the order of restoration corresponds to the order of the fall.

And when the demon had thrown him into the midst of them, it came out of him and did him no harm. By divine permission, the man who was to be freed from the demon is thrown into the midst, so that the Savior’s revealed power might invite more people to faith and the way of salvation.

[Col. 0378B]

But the statement, “and it did him no harm,” seems to conflict with Mark, who says: “And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him” (Mark 1). Unless we understand Mark’s “convulsing him” to mean what Luke says, “when it had thrown him into the midst,” so that the following words, “and it did him no harm,” may be understood to mean that the violent tossing and agitation of his limbs did not weaken him, as demons sometimes depart from certain people only after limbs have been cut off or torn away.

Therefore, because the restoration of health was so complete, those who were present, though frightened and not yet believing, rightly said to one another:

Because he commands the unclean spirits with authority and power, and they come out. Holy men also cast out demons, but they can do so by the word of God; the Word of God himself, however, performs miracles by his own authority.

[Col. 0378C]

And rising from the synagogue, he entered the house of Simon. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever. If we say that the man freed from the demon morally signifies a mind cleansed from unclean thought, then, correspondingly, the woman afflicted by fever but healed at the Lord’s command represents the flesh restrained from the heat of its own desire through the precepts of self-control.

For every bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy is the fury of an unclean spirit. But understand fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed—which is the service of idols (Eph. 4)—as the fever of seductive flesh.

And they appealed to him on her behalf. And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her. At one time the Savior heals the sick when asked; at another he heals them unbidden. He shows that, against the passions of sins as well, he always responds to the prayers of the faithful, and that he either grants what they scarcely understand in themselves to be understood, or removes what they do not understand.

[Col. 0378D]

In accordance with the Psalmist’s petition: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18).

And immediately she rose and ministered to them. It is natural for those suffering from fever, when health begins, to remain weak and to feel the discomfort of their illness. But the health bestowed at the Lord’s command returns all at once in its entirety. It not only returns, but is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to minister to those who had helped her.

And, according to the laws of tropology, the members that had served impurity in order to bear fruit for iniquity unto death should serve righteousness unto eternal life (Rom. 6).

When the sun had set, all who had the sick with various diseases brought them to him. But he laid his hands on each one and healed them. The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of the one who said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When the sun sets, more demoniacs than before and more sick people are healed. For the one who, while living temporarily in the flesh, taught a few Jews, after trampling down the kingdom of death, transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world.

[Col. 0379A]

Of his ministers, as heralds of life and light, the Psalmist sings: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Ps. 67). The Lord ascended above the setting sun because from the place where he set in his passion, from that same place he revealed his greater glory by rising again.

Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying: You are the Son of God. And rebuking them, he would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. The demons confessed the Son of God and, as the Evangelist attests, knew that he was the Christ.

For the devil had recognized as a man the one whom he had wearied with forty days of fasting, but, unable to test by temptation whether he was also the Son of God, he now either understood—or rather suspected through the power of the signs—that he was the Son of God.

He therefore did not persuade the Jews to crucify him because he thought that he was not the Christ or the Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by his death. Truly, concerning this mystery hidden from the ages, the Apostle says: “None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

[Col. 0379B]

But why the Lord forbids the demons to speak about him, the Psalmist makes clear when he says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” (Ps. 49), and what follows—lest someone, while listening to one who preaches, follow one who is wandering from the way. For the devil is an evil teacher, who often mingles falsehoods with truths, so that under the appearance of truth he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

Elsewhere, however, not only the demons, who confessed unwillingly, are ordered to keep silent about Christ, but also those who had been healed by him and wished to confess him voluntarily. Indeed, even the apostles, who after the resurrection were destined to preach him throughout the whole world, are commanded before his passion to remain entirely silent about him, lest, when the divine majesty had been proclaimed, the dispensation of his passion should be delayed and, with the passion delayed, the salvation of the world that was to come through it should be denied.

When it was day, he went out and departed to a deserted place. The crowds sought him, and they came all the way to him. If the Lord’s death is signified by the setting of the sun, why should his resurrection not be indicated by the return of day? Once its light had been revealed, he was sought by crowds of believers; and, found in the desert of the nations, he was detained lest he depart. Especially since this departure, search, and finding occurred on the first day of the week, on which the resurrection was celebrated.

## CHAPTER V

Now it happened that, while the crowds were pressing upon him to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret. They say that the lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee, or the Sea of Tiberias. It was called the Sea of Galilee from the neighboring province, and the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city, which was formerly called Chinnereth but, rebuilt by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was called Tiberias.

Moreover, Gennesar is said, from the nature of the lake itself—for it is reputed to raise a breeze from itself by means of its rippling waters—to be called in Greek, as it were, “generating a breeze for itself.” For the water does not lie spread out like an ordinary lake, but is stirred by frequent winds blowing over it; its water is sweet to drink and suitable for drinking. But according to the custom of the Hebrew language, every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called “sea.”

This lake, with the Jordan flowing through it, extends for 140 stadia in length and 40 in breadth. Since, therefore, the present age is signified by the lake or sea, the Lord stands beside the sea after conquering the mortality of transient life and entering, in the flesh in which he suffered, the stability of everlasting rest. The gathering of the crowds around him is a type of the nations running together to him in faith. Concerning them Isaiah says: “All nations will flow to him, and many peoples will go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2).

[Col. 0380A]

And he saw two boats standing beside the lake. The two boats placed beside the lake signify circumcision and uncircumcision. Jesus is rightly said to have seen them, because the Lord knows his own in both peoples. By living—that is, by avoiding worldly things mercifully—they bring their hearts from the waves of this age to the tranquility of the future life, as though to the firmness of the shore.

The fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets. The fishermen are the teachers of the Church. Having been caught in the net of faith and lifted from the depths into the light, we are brought by them to the shore, like fish, and so to the land of the living. The sayings of preachers are like fishermen’s nets, which hold fast those whom they have begun to catch in the faith and do not let them go. Hence the nets are called nets, as it were, because they retain.

But these nets are sometimes let down for a catch and sometimes washed and folded, because not every time is suitable for teaching. At one time the teacher’s tongue must be exercised; at another, he must attend to himself.

[Col. 0380B]

And getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat. Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, concerning which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also through me among the nations” (Gal. 2). It is rightly called one, because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts 4). From this boat he taught the crowds, because to this day he teaches the nations from the authority of the Church.

When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch. His first request that Simon put the boat out a little from the land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, so that neither earthly things are commanded to them nor are they withdrawn so far from earthly things into the depths of the mysteries that they understand nothing at all; or that he should first preach in the neighboring regions to the nations, so that what he then says to Peter, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch,” might refer to the more distant nations to whom the preaching later extended.

[Col. 0380C]

And Simon answered and said to him: Master, having labored all night, we caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the net. “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126). Unless the Lord illumines the hearts of hearers, the teacher labors in the night. Unless the instruments of discourse are let down in the word of heavenly grace, the preacher casts the dart of his voice in vain. For the faith of the peoples arises not from the wisdom of composed speech but from the gift of the divine calling.

[Col. 0380D]

And when he had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. Their net was breaking. The net was breaking because of the multitude of fish: now, together with the elect, so many reprobates enter into the confession of the faith that they even tear the Church itself apart through heresies. The net is torn, but the fish does not fall away, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals of their persecutors.

And they beckoned to their partners who were in the other boat to come and help them. The other boat, as we said above, is the Church from the nations. Even it is filled with the chosen fish, since one boat is not sufficient; the Lord knows who are his, and the number of his chosen is certain with him.

[Col. 0381A]

And because he does not find as many in Judea who will believe as he knows have been predestined to faith and eternal life, the other boat, as though seeking receptacles for its own fish, also fills the hearts of the nations with the grace of faith.

The companion boat is rightly summoned when the net has broken, because before this Judas the betrayer, Simon Magus, those most wicked fish, had been caught; before this Ananias and Sapphira were stealthily attempting to enter the net of faith; before this, as John testifies, many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him (John 6). Then Barnabas and Paul were set apart for the apostleship among the nations (Acts 13).

And they came and filled both boats, so that they were sinking. The filling of these boats increases until the end of the age.
