But the fact that, once filled, they sink—that is, are weighed down in submersion (for they are not actually submerged, but nevertheless are endangered)—is explained by the Apostle, who says: “In the last days there will be perilous times, and people will be lovers of themselves,” and so forth (2 Tim. 3).

[Col. 0381B]

For the sinking of the boats means that people, after being raised by faith from the age, fall back into it through the perversity of their conduct. Peter himself, while still placed in weakness, displays such people in this passage. Hence it follows:

When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man. Carnal people in the Church, when they see the governance of spiritual men—especially those in whom the person of Christ is conspicuous—somehow drive it away from themselves.

They do not say this with the voice of their tongue to God’s good ministers in order to repel them; rather, by the voice of their behavior and actions they urge them to withdraw, so that they may not be governed by good men. And the more they honor them, the more insistently they admonish them by their deeds to depart from them. Peter signifies their honor by falling at the Lord’s feet; their conduct, however, by saying: “Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.”

[Col. 0381C]

Yet because the Lord did not do this—for he did not withdraw from them but brought the boats to the shore after drawing them in—it signifies that good and spiritual men ought not to have the desire to abandon their ecclesiastical office because they are disturbed by the sins of the crowds and wish to live, as it were, more safely and peacefully.

And Jesus said to Simon: Do not be afraid. The Lord strengthens the fear of the carnal and the spirits of the weak. By consoling them he raises them up, lest anyone, trembling either from awareness of his own guilt or astonished at the innocence of others, fear to undertake the path of holiness.

And what follows—

From now on you will be catching people—pertains especially to Peter. For the Lord explains to him what this catch of fish signifies: namely, that just as he now catches fish by means of nets, so one day he will catch people by means of words. The entire sequence of this event shows what is daily carried on in the Church, whose type Peter himself represents.

[Col. 0381D]

But what is added—

And when they had brought the boats to land, leaving everything, they followed him—may signify the end of time, when those who have clung to Christ will depart completely from this kind of sea.

It should be understood, however, that this is not the same calling narrated by Matthew and Mark, in which the Lord called two pairs of fishermen from their boats: first Peter and Andrew, then the sons of Zebedee. For Luke does not now indicate that they were called by the Lord, but only that it was foretold to Peter that he would catch people.

This was not said as though he would never again catch fish. For we also read that after the Lord’s resurrection they went fishing. Hence it may be understood that they had returned, as usual, to catching fish, so that afterward what Matthew and Mark narrate might take place, when he called them in pairs.

[Col. 0382A]

For at that time they did not bring the boats to land as though they intended to return, but followed him in such a way as to show that they were following one who called and commanded them to follow.

And it happened, when he was in one of the towns, that there was a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” [Col. 0384C] It is fitting that, where the leper is cleansed, no definite place is specified, so that it may be shown that not merely the people of one particular town, but peoples everywhere, were healed. And because the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5), the man who was excluded by the Law, presuming that he could be purified by the Lord’s power, judged that the grace able to wash away the leper’s stain came not from the Law but stood above the Law.

Yet just as the authority of power is revealed in the Lord, so the steadfastness of faith is revealed in the man. He fell on his face, which is a gesture of humility and shame, so that each person may be ashamed of the stains of his own life. But shame did not suppress his confession: he displayed his wound and requested a remedy. And this confession itself is full of religious devotion and faith. “If you will,” he says, “you can cleanse me.” He attributes the power to the Lord’s will. He did not doubt the Lord’s will as though he were distrustful of his compassion; rather, conscious of his own defilement, he did not presume.

And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying, “I will; be cleansed.” And immediately the leprosy departed from him. There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is present in the command. Indeed, “he spoke, and they were made.” You see, therefore, that there can be no doubt that God’s will is power. If his will is power, then those who assert one will necessarily assert one power. Thus, as one possessing the power to heal and the authority to command, he did not avoid giving testimony through his deed. He says, “I will,” because of Photinus; he commands, because of Arius; he touches, because of Manichaeus. And [Col. 0385A] although the Law forbids touching lepers, he who is Lord of the Law does not submit to the Law but makes the Law. He did not touch him because he was unable to cleanse him without touching him, but in order to show that he was not subject to the Law and did not fear contagion as human beings do; rather, because the one who freed others could not be contaminated, the leprosy that usually contaminated the one who touched it was driven away by the Lord’s touch.

There is also this marvel: he healed him in the very manner in which he had been entreated: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” “I will,” he says, “be cleansed.” You have the will; you also have the effect of compassion.

And he ordered him to tell no one. Why was he ordered to tell no one, except to teach that our benefactions should not be publicized but kept hidden?—that we should abstain not only from receiving money as a reward, but also from receiving praise.

[Col. 0385B] “Go and show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them,” and so forth. He is ordered to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not according to the order of the Law but by God’s grace above the Law. He is ordered to offer a sacrifice so that the Lord might show that he was not abolishing the Law but fulfilling it: walking according to the Law, he healed above the Law those whom the remedies of the Law had not healed. And he appropriately added, “as a testimony to them”—that is, if they believe in God, if the leprosy of impiety departs.

If anyone is troubled by how the Lord appears to approve the Mosaic sacrifice, although the Church has not retained it, let him remember that the holy sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is his body, had not yet begun. For he had not yet offered his holocaust in his passion. [Col. 0385C] The symbolic sacrifices ought not to be removed before what they signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles who preached it and of the peoples who believed.

Since this man figuratively signifies the human race weakened by sins, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but as full of leprosy. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3). That is, when the Savior stretches out his hand—meaning the Word of God made flesh—and touches human nature, they may be cleansed from the manifold error of the past and may hear with the apostles, “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15). Those who had long been kept apart as abominable from the camps of God’s people may at last be restored to the temple [Col. 0385D] and presented to the priest—to the one of whom it is said, “You are a priest forever” (Ps. 109)—hearing from the Apostle, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3). And they may offer for their cleansing as Moses commanded: that is, they may present their bodies as “a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12).

But the report about him spread more widely, and large crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses. The complete salvation of one person draws many crowds to the Lord. For, so that he might show himself to have been healed outwardly as well as inwardly, he did not at all keep silent about the benefit he had received, even though the one from whom he had received it had ordered him to do so. Rather, as Mark relates, immediately after going out he began to preach and spread the report [Col. 0386A] of what had happened, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly but remained outside in deserted places, while people came to him from everywhere (Mark 1).

Hence it is rightly asked what it means that the Lord ordered some things he had done to be concealed, although they could not be concealed even for an hour. Did the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, wish in this matter to do something he could not accomplish? We must observe, however, that through his mortal body our Redeemer offered us an example in everything he did. When he performed a miracle, he ordered it to be kept quiet, and yet it could not be kept quiet. In this way he showed that his chosen ones, following the examples of his teaching, should indeed wish their great deeds to remain hidden, but that, in order to benefit others, those deeds should be disclosed against their will. Thus it is an indication of great humility that they desire their works to be kept silent, while it is an indication of great exaltation that their works cannot be kept silent. The Lord did not wish something to happen and then prove unable to accomplish it; rather, he gave, through the authority of his teaching, an example of what his members ought to wish and of what happens to them even when they do not wish it.

But he withdrew into the wilderness and prayed. Do not attribute his withdrawal to pray to that nature which says, “I will; be cleansed,” and heals illnesses, but to that nature which, stretching out its hand, touched the leper—not, in accordance with Nestorius, because the Son has two persons, but because the same person has two operations just as he has two natures.

Alternatively: by performing miracles in the city, but spending the night in prayer in the wilderness or on the mountain, as is read below, he sets before us the pattern of both lives, active and [Col. 0386C] contemplative. Thus no one should neglect concern for his neighbors through devotion to contemplation, nor, being excessively bound by concern for his neighbors, abandon the pursuits of contemplation. The love of God should not impede love of one’s neighbor, nor should the love of God reject love of one’s neighbor because it surpasses it.

To pray on the mountain means, having left behind the cares of weak thoughts, to hasten with one’s whole mind toward the joys of eternal, heavenly contemplation. To withdraw into the wilderness and pray means to suppress the inward clamor of earthly desires as they arise and to seek within oneself a kind of secret place with the Lord, where, when the outward tumult has ceased, one may speak silently with him through inward desires.

[Col. 0386D] And it happened on one of the days that he was sitting and teaching, and Pharisees were sitting there, and so forth. Where the Lord taught while sitting, when the scribes and Pharisees were seated with him and he healed the paralytic, Luke omits this for the sake of brevity; but Matthew and Mark, who relate it, appear to raise a question. Matthew testifies that he did this in his own city, while Mark says it happened in Capernaum. The question would be harder to resolve if Matthew had also named Nazareth. But now either Galilee itself, in which Nazareth was located, should be understood as being called Christ’s city, in distinction from the region of the Gerasenes across the sea, from which, as Matthew writes, he crossed over and came to Galilee; or certainly Capernaum itself is called Christ’s city, which he made his own not by being born there but by illuminating it with his miracles.

[Col. 0387A] And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and place him before Jesus. The healing of this paralytic indicates the salvation of the soul that, after a long period of sluggishness in carnal allurements, sighs for Christ. First of all, it needs attendants to lift it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good teachers who offer hope of healing and the assistance of intercession.

According to Mark, there were four of them. This may be because the whole power of preachers and the whole of their message is established upon the four books of the Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised toward obtaining well-being. Of these it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom: “She teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wis. 8). Some, changing the names, call these prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

And since they could not find by which way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof through the tiles. They desire to offer the paralytic to Christ, but because the crowd intervenes, they are shut out on every side. For often the soul, recovering for God after the sluggishness of the lowly body and desiring to be renewed by the remedy of heavenly grace, is held back by the obstacle of its former habits. Often, even amid the sweetness of secret prayer and what seems like a pleasant conversation with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts intervenes and blocks the mind’s vision, so that Christ cannot be seen.

And what should be done in these circumstances? Certainly one should not remain below, outside, where the crowds are making their tumult. Rather, one must climb onto the roof of the house in which Christ teaches, [Col. 0387C] that is, one must desire the sublimity of sacred Scripture and meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord with the Psalmist: “By what means does a young man correct his way? By guarding your words,” he says (Ps. 118).

And they lowered him with his bed into the middle, before Jesus. When the roof had been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because through the mysteries of Scripture, once they have been unlocked, one arrives at knowledge of Christ—that is, through the devotion of faith one descends to his humility. And the house of Jesus is appropriately described as covered with tiles, because beneath the contemptible covering of the letter, if there is a teacher who unlocks it, the divine power of spiritual grace will be found. The fact that he is lowered with his bed signifies that Christ must be known by a person who is still established in this flesh.

[Col. 0387D] When he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” As the Lord was about to heal the man from paralysis, he first dissolved the bonds of his sins, to show that he was condemned to the dissolution of his limbs because of the bonds of his faults, and that he could be restored to health in his limbs only after those bonds had been released. So also, after healing the paralytic who had long waited in vain for the movement of the water beside the Sheep Pool, the Lord says to him, “See, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5).

And rightly the one whose sins were being forgiven is called “man.” Since he was a man, he could not say, “I have not sinned”; at the same time, the one who forgave the man was understood to be God. We should carefully consider how greatly each person’s faith counts with God, since another’s faith counted for so much that the whole man was suddenly saved, outwardly and inwardly—that is, fully—and the faults of some were forgiven through the merit of others.

And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?” The scribes speak truly, because no one can forgive sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. Thus Christ is proved truly to be God, because he can forgive sins as God. They give true testimony to God, but they err by denying Christ’s person. The Jews therefore err: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ.

But the Arians err far more foolishly. Though defeated by the words of the Gospel, they dare not deny that Jesus is the Christ and that he can forgive sins, yet they nevertheless are not afraid to deny that he is God. But he, desiring to save the impious, reveals himself to be God both through his knowledge of hidden things and through the power of his works.

And answering, he said to them, “What are you thinking in your hearts?” To the same God who says, “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. 43), the wisest of orators says, “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings” (1 Kings 8). Therefore, he says, by the same majesty and power by which I perceive your thoughts, I can also forgive sins to human beings. From what happens to the paralytic, understand what he receives.

Which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rise. A bodily sign is therefore performed so that a spiritual reality may be proved.

But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—if he is also God, in accordance with the testimony of Isaiah, who blots out our iniquities (Ps. 50), and the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (Matt. 9), then this same person is both God and the Son of Man. Thus Christ as man can forgive sins through the power of his divinity, and the same Christ as God can die for sinners through the weakness of his humanity.

He said to the paralytic, “I say to you, rise; take up your bed [Col. 0388D] and go to your house.” Spiritually, to rise from one’s bed means for the soul to withdraw itself from carnal desires, in which it lay sick and at rest. To take up the bed means also to restrain the flesh itself by the reins of self-control and to deprive it of earthly delights in hope of heavenly rewards. This is the bed which David washes every night: that is, he chastises it for the stains of each offense with a fitting stream of repentance.

To take up the bed and go home means to return to paradise. For that is the true home which first received the human being—not lost by right but through deceit, and finally restored by the one who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy.

Alternatively: the one who had been sick carries his bed home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, brings itself back, together with the body, to inward watchfulness over itself, lest after pardon it commit something for which it may again justly be struck.

And immediately he rose before them, took up the bed on which he had lain, and went to his house, glorifying God, and so forth. Wonderful is the power of divine authority, where salvation swiftly accompanies the Savior’s command without any intervening delay. Rightly, those who were present, renouncing the weapons of blasphemy, turn their astonished hearts to the praise of such great majesty.

And after this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” Levi is the same person as Matthew, but Luke and Mark, out of respect and honor for the evangelist, did not wish to give the name by which he was commonly known. Matthew himself, in accordance with what is written, “The righteous man is his own accuser” (Prov. 18), names himself Matthew and a tax collector at the beginning of his account, to show readers that no convert should despair of salvation, since he himself was suddenly changed from a tax collector into an apostle and from a revenue officer into an evangelist.

And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. Matthew understood what it truly means to follow the Lord, and so he followed him after leaving everything behind. To follow is to imitate. Therefore, so that he might pursue the poor Christ not so much in bodily steps as in affection, he who had been accustomed to seize what belonged to others left his own possessions. Giving us a perfect model of renouncing the world, he not only abandoned the profits of tax collection but also disregarded the danger that could come from the rulers of the world because he had left the accounts of the taxes unfinished and disordered. He was led by so great a desire to follow the Lord that he reserved for himself absolutely no regard or thought for this life. Therefore, as a just reward for diligently abandoning human business, he deserved to become a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

And Levi made him a great feast in his house. Whoever receives Christ into the inner dwelling of the heart is nourished by the greatest delights of surpassing pleasures. Thus the Lord gladly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who believes; and this is the spiritual banquet of good works, at which the rich are in need while the poor feast.

And there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining at table with them. They had seen a tax collector turned from sins to better things and find a place for repentance, and for that reason they too did not despair of salvation.

[Col. 0389D] And the Pharisees and their scribes were murmuring, saying to his disciples, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” While the tax collectors were feasting with the Lord, the Pharisees, murmuring about fasting, boast of their own fasting. Here, first, the great difference between the Law and grace is made clear. Those who follow the Law suffer the eternal hunger of a fasting mind. But those who have received the Word within their souls as food, and have been refreshed by the abundance of the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst.

Next, the form of the future recompense is foreshadowed, when, while the elect feast with Christ, the faithlessness of the proud will be tormented by fasting. To them it is said, “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21). If the election of Matthew expresses the faith of the nations, which formerly longed for the profits of the world but now are continually nourished by devoted participation in Christ’s body, then surely the Pharisees’ arrogance signifies the envy of the Jews, who are tormented by the salvation of the nations.

And Jesus answered and said to them, “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” He rebukes the scribes and Pharisees, who, thinking themselves righteous, avoided the company of sinners. For he calls himself a physician who, in a wondrous manner of healing, was wounded for our iniquities, and “by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. 53).

He calls “well” and “righteous” those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness; those who, presuming upon the Law, do not seek the grace of the Gospel. But he calls “sick” and “sinners” those who, overcome by awareness of their own weakness and seeing that they cannot be justified through the Law, submit themselves in repentance to the grace of Christ.

Here it is shown at the same time that the tax collectors did not come to Jesus while remaining in their former vices, as the Pharisees and scribes were murmuring, but came in repentance. Jesus himself also deigned to attend sinners’ banquets so that he might have an opportunity to teach and might offer spiritual food to those who invited him. Indeed, although he is frequently described as going to a banquet, nothing else is reported except what he did and taught there, so that both the Lord’s humility in going to sinners and the power of his teaching in converting the penitent might be demonstrated.

But they said to him, “Why do the disciples of John fast frequently and offer prayers, and likewise those of the Pharisees, while yours eat and drink?” Matthew reports that the disciples of John themselves said this to the Savior; from this it is clear that both groups joined together in pressing him with this question. The disciples of John especially deserve criticism not only for boasting of their fasting but also because they were bringing a charge against one whom they knew their teacher had proclaimed, and were joining themselves to the Pharisees, whom they knew had been condemned by him.

Spiritually, the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but Christ’s disciples eat and drink, because whether someone follows the works of the Law or human traditions, or even receives Christ’s proclamation only with the bodily ear, such a person, abstaining from spiritual goods, wastes away with a fasting heart. But whoever is incorporated into Christ’s members by faithful love cannot fast, because he feasts on his flesh and blood.

Alternatively: John did not drink wine or strong drink, while the Lord ate and drank with tax collectors and sinners, because he increased his merit through abstinence, he who possessed no power by nature; but why would the Lord, who naturally possessed the power to forgive sins, avoid those whom he could make purer through abstinence? Yet Christ also fasted, so that you would not evade the commandment. He ate with sinners, so that you would perceive grace and recognize power.

To them he said, “Can you make the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them; then they will fast in those days.” Christ is the bridegroom, and the Church is the bride. The apostles were created from this holy and spiritual marriage. Hence Mark the evangelist appropriately calls them the sons of the wedding—not only of the bridegroom but also of the bride—wishing it to be understood that through the washing of regeneration they were adopted into the right of divine generation.

They cannot fast or mourn as long as they see the bridegroom in the bridal chamber and know that he is with the bride. But when the wedding has passed and the time of the passion and resurrection has arrived, then the sons of the bridegroom will fast. Luke, however, does not say, as the others do, “Can the sons of the bridegroom or of the wedding fast or mourn?” but, “Can you make the sons of the bridegroom fast?” (Luke 5). He elegantly indicated that the very people who were speaking would cause the sons of the bridegroom to fast in mourning, since they themselves would kill the bridegroom.

[Col. 0391B] It should be noted, moreover, that this mourning for the bridegroom’s absence was observed not only now—that is, after the bridegroom’s death and resurrection—but also before his incarnation, throughout the whole period of this world. For the earliest times of the Church, before the Virgin gave birth, had holy people who desired the coming of Christ’s incarnation. The present times, since he ascended into heaven, have holy people who desire his manifestation to judge the living and the dead. Nor did this desirable mourning of the Church cease for any length of time except while he lived here in the flesh with his disciples.

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, it should be understood that as long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he has withdrawn and flown away from us because of our sins, then fasting must be proclaimed; then mourning must be taken up.

And he also told them a parable: “No one puts a patch from a new garment onto an old garment. Otherwise, he tears the new garment, and the patch from the new does not match the old.” When the Lord was asked why his disciples did not fast, he replied that those who were still carnal and not yet established in faith in his passion and resurrection could not endure more severe fasts and precepts of self-restraint, lest through excessive austerity they lose even the faith they seemed to possess.

He therefore calls those same disciples still like old garments, to which a new patch is improperly sewn—that is, some portion of teaching belonging to the moderation of the new life. For if this is done, the teaching itself is somehow torn, since the portion of it that applies to abstinence from food is offered inopportunely. That teaching commands a general fast not merely from the desire for food but from every pleasure in temporal delights. He says that something like a patch—a portion relating to food—should not be imparted to people who are still devoted to their old habits. For there also appears to be a kind of tearing, and it does not suit their oldness.

And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the new wine bursts the wineskins, and it is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. But new wine must be put into new wineskins, and both are preserved. He likewise compares the same people to old wineskins, saying that they would be more easily burst by new wine—that is, spiritual precepts—than able to contain it.

They will be new wineskins when, after the Lord’s ascension, they are renewed by praying and hoping in their desire for his consolation. Then they received the Holy Spirit; filled with him, they spoke in all languages, and the Jews, though ignorant of what they were saying, nevertheless bore true witness when they said, “These men are full of new wine.” For the new wine had already found new wineskins: the fervor of the Holy Spirit had filled the hearts of spiritual people.

Alternatively: the teacher must beware of entrusting the secrets of new mysteries to a soul that has not yet been renewed but continues in the oldness of malice.

And no one who has been drinking old wine immediately wants new wine, for he says, “The old is better.” He signifies the Jews, whose lives had been steeped in the savor of the old life, so that the commands of the new grace seemed offensive. For, thoroughly stained by the traditions of their ancestors, they were entirely unable to perceive the sweetness of spiritual words.

## CHAPTER VI

Now it happened on the second-first Sabbath that, as he passed through the grainfields, his disciples were plucking ears of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands. This is what Mark says: because of the excessive pressure of those who came to be healed, the disciples did not even have time to eat, and therefore they were hungry like other human beings.

The fact that they rub the ears of grain in their hands and relieve their hunger indicates a more austere way of life: they seek not prepared banquets but simple foods. And observe that the Savior’s first apostles destroy the literal observance of the Sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, although they accept the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

Luke therefore appropriately calls the day on which the letter of the Sabbath began to be dissolved δευτερόπρωτον—“second-first”—Sabbath. He wished to indicate that the observance of the legal Sabbath ought no longer to continue, and that the freedom of the natural Sabbath, which until the time of Moses had been like that of the other days, ought to be restored.

Just as the Church is saved not by circumcision or the ceremonies of the Law but by Abraham’s faith, through which he was justified while uncircumcised, working through love, so also may it be commended to God by nothing other than the spiritual Sabbath, on which Abraham himself was always free from servile—that is, sinful—action, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

He therefore calls this Sabbath “second-first” to distinguish it from the Jewish Sabbath, on which it was not permitted to travel, gather wood, or perform other necessary activities, although on this Sabbath, as on the other days, it is permitted to perform useful works. He calls it “first” as preferred to the second, either in the order of time, because throughout countless ages before the Law the fathers practiced what is now practiced, or certainly as a sign of grace, so that “second-first” may mean nothing other than that the higher Sabbath is superior to the lower.

For the first man was earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. Nor does one err who wishes to call the Lord Jesus Christ the “second-first Adam,” since in merit and grace—not in the order of human birth—he preceded Adam, in accordance with what his forerunner said of him: “He who comes after me has been made before me, because he was before me” (John 1).

The phrase “on the second-first Sabbath” may also be understood to mean that the one and the same Sabbath of the New Testament is both second and first. It is second because it is observed by us after the legal Sabbath; it is first because it was observed by the righteous of old even before the decrees of the Law.

Mystically, the disciples pass through the grainfields—those of which the Lord says, “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest, and the one who harvests receives a reward” (John 4). Thus they are understood to hunger for nothing better than the salvation of human beings. The first reaper himself, once hungering amid his prayers, soon after the meal he desired had been shown to him heard: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10).

There is a remarkable agreement in the mystery: there the animals are ordered to be killed and eaten, and here the ears of grain are likewise said to be rubbed and eaten. This means: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, and strip off the old man with his deeds” (Col. 3). For no one otherwise passes into the body of Christ, and no one otherwise nourishes the teacher with the fruits of his progress.

To pluck the ears of grain, therefore, is to pull human beings out of their earthly concerns, in which they had fixed the root of their mind, as it were. To rub them with the hands is, through examples of virtue, to strip the purity of the mind even from carnal desire, as from the husks and coverings of the awns. For the grains to be eaten means that each person, cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit, is incorporated into the members of the Church through the mouths of preachers.

And it is fitting that Mark reports the disciples doing these things while going before the Lord, because the teacher’s word must go before, and thus the hearer’s heart is illumined by the grace of heavenly visitation.

But some of the Pharisees said to them, “Why are you doing what is not permitted on the Sabbaths?” Other evangelists relate that these words were directed more directly against the Lord himself. But whether they were spoken to him, to his disciples, or to both groups by several people making accusations here and there—for no evangelist could have written anything false—nevertheless, because whatever is done by the disciples refers to the one whose teaching they follow in their actions, he immediately, in accordance with what Isaiah says, “He will judge the poor of the earth with equity” (Isa. 11), defeats the false defenders of the Law by the true examples of the saints. For he says:

[Col. 0393D] “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God, took the bread of the Presence, ate it, and gave it to those who were with him, although it is not permitted for anyone to eat it except the priests?”

The history of the Books of Kings relates that blessed David, while avoiding Saul’s ambushes, came to the priest Abimelech at Nob and asked for food for himself and his men. The priest did not have ordinary bread; but after first learning that the young men had been clean from women since the day before yesterday, he did not hesitate to give him the consecrated loaves. He judged it better, as the prophet says, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9), to free human beings from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God. For the sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings.

The Lord therefore confronts the Pharisees’ accusations and says: If David is holy and Abimelech the high priest is not reproached by you, but both transgressed the commandment of the Law with an acceptable justification, and hunger was the reason, why do you not approve the same hunger in the apostles that you approve in others?

Nevertheless, there is also a great difference here. These men rub ears of grain by hand on the Sabbath; those men ate Levitical bread and were approaching the solemnity of the Sabbath. For the bread of the Presence was baked before the Sabbath, and on the Sabbath morning it was offered and placed upon the sacred table: twelve loaves arranged in pairs, with two golden dishes filled with incense placed above them. They remained until the next Sabbath, when other loaves were brought in their place, while the former loaves were presented to the priests.

When the incense had been burned in the sacred fire on which all holocausts were customarily made, other incense was added over the twelve loaves. When David arrived at that hour and received the consecrated loaves, he showed figuratively that priestly food was destined to pass into the use of the peoples. This may mean either that we must all imitate the priestly life, or that all the children of the Church are priests. For we are anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.

And he said to them, “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” If, he says, King David is excusable when nourished by priestly food, and, according to the testimony of the other Gospel, priests who violate the Sabbath through the service of the temple are free from guilt, how much more is the Son of Man, who is true king and true priest and therefore Lord [Col. 0394C] of the Sabbath, not held guilty for plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath?

Now it happened on another Sabbath that he entered the synagogue and taught. And there was a man whose right hand was withered. The Lord teaches and performs miracles especially in the synagogues on the Sabbaths, not only to suggest the spiritual Sabbath but also because the people gathered there in greater numbers on that day. According to the ancient institution of the fathers, it was their custom, since the Law commanded them to abstain from labor, to devote themselves to reading and hearing the Scriptures.

This agrees with what James says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Moses has had people proclaiming him from ancient generations in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath.” For just as those skilled in hunting, once they learn where wild animals, fish, and [Col. 0394D] birds are abundant, spread their nets there above all, so the Lord always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gathered, wishing everyone to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth.

The man whose hand was withered clearly signifies the human race, dried up through its unfruitfulness in good works, but healed by the Lord’s compassion. His right hand, which had withered in our first parent when he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree, was restored to the health of good works through the grace of the Redeemer, when he stretched out innocent hands upon the tree of the cross. And appropriately the hand was withered in the synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the danger of inexcusable guilt is more serious.

But the scribes and Pharisees were watching to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, [Col. 0395A] in order to find a charge against him. Since the teacher had defended the destruction of the Sabbath that they had accused the disciples of by a persuasive example, they now wished, by watching the teacher himself, to bring an accusation against him: if he healed on the Sabbath, they would accuse him of transgression; if he did not heal, they would accuse him of cruelty or weakness.

He himself, however, knew their thoughts, etc. This is what we read: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Psalm 93). And what follows: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law” (ibid.). This was said of those who have learned that the law, fulfilled through Christ, commands for us not a carnal Sabbath through it, but a spiritual one.

Then Jesus said to them: “I ask you: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil?” The Lord, anticipating the Jews’ slander, which they had prepared for him with treacherous intent, rebukes them because they had violated the precepts of the law through a perverse interpretation, judging that on the Sabbath one must abstain even from good works, although the law commands abstention from evil, saying: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Leviticus 23)—that is, sin; for “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). Through the same commandment he also sketches, in present things, the form of the future age: those who have done good through the six ages of this world will have rest in the seventh from evils alone, but not from good works as well. For although worldly activities will cease, the activity of good work is not idle when it rests in the praise of God.

“To save a life, or to destroy it?” That is, to heal a person, or not. This is the same as what he had said beforehand: “to do good, or to do evil.” This does not mean that God, supremely good, can be the author of evil or destruction for us, but that, according to the usage of Scripture, his not saving someone is called “destroying” that person. Thus Scripture says that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not that he made soft what was hard, but that, because it had been hardened by preceding merits, he mercifully refused to soften it. And when we pray, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6), immediately adding, “But deliver us from evil” (ibid.), we are plainly taught that his not leading us into temptation is nothing other than delivering us from evil; his destroying a soul means not saving it from destruction.

If anyone is troubled by the question why, when the Lord was going to heal the body, he asked about the salvation of the soul, let him understand either that “soul” is used for “person” in the manner of Scripture, as it says: “These are the souls who went out from Jacob’s thigh” (Exodus 1); or that he performed those miracles for the salvation of the soul; or that the healing of the hand itself signified the salvation of the soul, which, ceasing—as I have said—from good works, seemed in a certain way to have a withered right hand.

“And looking around at them all, he said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored.” The withered hand is ordered to be stretched out for healing, because the weakness of an unfruitful soul is cured by no better means than by the generosity of almsgiving. Hence, when the crowds asked John the Baptist what they should do so that they would not be thrown into the fire like withered trees, he gave this sole command: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3). And in Ecclesiasticus it is said: “My son, do not let your hand be extended to receive and drawn back when it is time to give” (Ecclesiasticus 4). For in vain does one stretch out one’s hands to God to plead for sins, if one has not stretched them out to bring a benefit to a widow who asks.

But they were filled with folly and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. Great indeed was their folly: those who most needed healing were deliberating about the death of the Savior. How eagerly they pursued wickedness is shown by the fact that they counted it as a crime even that, at his word, the man who was suffering had stretched out his right hand whole. As though each of them had not done greater things on the Sabbath—carrying food, offering a cup, and performing the other tasks necessary for sustenance. For the one who spoke and they came to be could not be convicted of having labored on the Sabbath.

Now it happened in those days that he went out onto the mountain to pray. Not everyone who prays ascends a mountain. There is, after all, a kind of prayer that commits sin. But whoever prays well, whoever seeks God by praying, progresses from earthly things to higher ones and ascends the summit of a more elevated concern. Whoever, however, pleads anxiously for riches, worldly honor, or even the death of an enemy lies in the lowest places and sends contemptible prayers to God.

The Lord prays, not to plead for himself, but to obtain something for me. For although the Father has placed everything in the power of the Son, the Son nevertheless, in order to fulfill the role of a human being, considers that the Father must be entreated on our behalf, because he is our advocate: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2). If he is an advocate, he ought to intercede for my sins. He therefore pleads, not as one who is weak, but as one who is loving. Do you wish to know how he can do everything he wills? He is both advocate and judge. In the one role there is the duty of compassion; in the other, the mark of power.

“And he spent the night in prayer to God.” A model is prescribed for you, one that you ought to imitate. What ought you to do for your salvation, when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What should you do when you wish to undertake some work of devotion, when Christ took care to pray before sending out the apostles? Do you wish to know that he prayed for me, not for himself?

“And when day came,” he says, “he called his disciples and chose twelve of them.” Here it should be noted that evangelical and apostolic Scripture calls not only those twelve Christ’s disciples, but also all who, believing in him, were instructed by his teaching for the kingdom of heaven. They are called disciples from learning; from their multitude he chose those whom he himself wished.

“Whom he also named apostles.” *Apostles* is Greek; in Latin they are called *sent ones*. Explaining the meaning of the name, the evangelist Mark says: “And he made twelve, to be with him and to send them out to preach the Gospel.” The Lord himself also says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” They were rightly chosen as twelve, so that the salvation of the world, which they would preach in words, might also be mystically commended by their number. Three times four: a double honor [the text reads *decus dipondium*, apparently corrupt or uncertain].

This is why I also said above that, when Solomon was building the temple for the Lord as a type of the Church, he made a bronze sea in which the priests would wash, and set it upon the backs of twelve oxen: three facing north, three west, three south, and three east. He was figuratively indicating that the apostles and the successors of the apostles would cleanse all the regions of the square-shaped world from the stain of sins through faith and confession of the holy Trinity.

“Simon, whom he surnamed Peter, and Andrew his brother.” He did not now give Simon the surname Peter for the first time. Long before, when he saw him brought to him by his brother Andrew, he said: “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter” (John 1). But when Luke wished to enumerate the names of the twelve apostles, he necessarily had to mention Peter and wished briefly to indicate that he had not previously been called by this name, but that the Lord had given him this surname—although not at that time, but when John recorded those very words of the Lord, thereby making his hearers attentive. For if he had been called this beforehand, you would not perceive so clearly the mystery of the rock, thinking that he was called this by chance rather than by God’s providence. Therefore he first wished him to be called by another name, so that through the change of name itself the vitality of the mystery might be commended.

Thus *Peter* in Latin is the same as *Cephas* in Syriac, and in both languages the name is derived from *rock*—undoubtedly that rock of which Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). For just as Christ, the true light, granted the apostles that they should be called “the light of the world,” so also he bestowed the name Peter upon Simon, who believed in Christ the rock. Alluding elsewhere to the same etymology, he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

Some people therefore, violently seeking a Hebrew etymology for a Latin or Greek name, say that *Peter* means “one who dissolves,” or “one who removes sandals,” or “one who recognizes.” But both the explanation of the evangelist John, which I mentioned, and the Hebrew language itself—which does not pronounce the letter *P* at all—testify that this is not a Hebrew name. For, writing *Fetrum* instead of *Petrum*, just as they write *Faulum* instead of *Paulum* and *Filatum* instead of *Pilatum*, they forcibly attach a false interpretation to a fictitious name.

*Simon*, however, is interpreted as “obedient.” *Andrew* is a Greek name, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός—that is, from “man”—and is called “manly.” The first of the apostles are appropriately adorned with these names: they immediately recognized the Lamb of God through John and took care to see and hear him.

The fact that *Simon* is interpreted as “one who lays down sorrow” or “one who hears grief” suits the time when, after seeing the Lord following the resurrection, he laid aside the sorrow of either his death or his own denial, but immediately heard the grief of his own death, when the Lord said: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

“James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Matthew and Thomas.” Luke appropriately and reverently preferred, in the catalogue of the apostles, to call Matthew by his customary name, whereas in the first account of his calling from the tax booth, as I noted above, he chose to call him Levi. Matthew himself, in accordance with what is written—“Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified”—plainly identifies himself as Matthew, called from the tax booth, and in the order of the apostles calls himself a tax collector. Yet, although he is placed before his companion Thomas by the other evangelists, he places himself after Thomas in the list.

James and John, on account of the exceptional greatness of their virtue and spirit, were surnamed by the Lord “sons of thunder,” that is, βοανεργεῖς, or, as it is more correctly written, *banereem*. Not without reason. One of them, thundering forth from heavenly heights, uttered that theological voice which no one had previously known how to produce: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and so forth (John 1). He left this pregnant with such power that, if he had wished to thunder somewhat more loudly, the world itself could not have contained it.

Both of them also deserved on several occasions to be led apart by the Lord onto the mountain and at one point to hear the terrifying sound from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son.” They bore also their ancient names, names most suited to their merits. For *James* means “supplanter.” *John*, in whom there is grace, or “the grace of the Lord,” is so called. The former, when the Lord called him, trampled underfoot care for the flesh, and, when Herod slaughtered it, rejoiced to despise the flesh itself. The latter, on account of the special grace of love that he had earned through virginal glory, reclined upon the breast of his Redeemer at the supper.

*Philip* is interpreted as “mouth of a lamp.” And rightly so, because, immediately after being called by the Lord, he preached to Nathanael the light he had recognized when he said: “We have found the one of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth” (John 1). Later, he humbly asked about what he felt he knew less fully concerning the light: “Lord,” he said, “show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

*Bartholomew* is Syriac, not Hebrew, and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends the waters,” that is, “Son of God.” He suspends the minds of his preachers toward contemplation of heavenly things, so that, the more freely they fly through the heights, the more fruitfully they may intoxicate earthly hearts with the drops of their words.

Hence Moses, speaking mystically about the Church, appropriately says: “For the land into which you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you came out, where, after the seed is sown, water is brought in to irrigate it as in a garden; but it is a land awaiting the rains of heaven, which the Lord your God visits continually.” For worldly wisdom creeps along the ground like a serpent, whereas divine wisdom thunders from heavenly places.

*Matthew* is said to mean “given,” because by the great gift of the Lord he was transferred from being a tax-collecting publican to the office of apostle and evangelist.

*Thomas* means “abyss” or “twin.” Hence he is also called *Didymus* in Greek, because, the longer he doubted in comparison with the others, the more deeply he learned the truth of the Lord’s resurrection. Concerning him Paulinus, bishop of Nola, sang beautifully:

> Here Thomas, doubtful as a twin, called Didymus, lies;  
> Christ allowed him to doubt, through the hesitation of his fearful mind,  
> for the sake of our faith, so that we too,  
> strengthened by this guide and trembling before the Lord and God,  
> might confess that Jesus truly lives after death,  
> displaying in his living body the wounds of his flesh.

“James of Alphaeus, and Simon who is called the Zealot.” He added these designations to distinguish James from James of Zebedee and Simon from Peter, or also from Judas the betrayer. John shows that this man too was called Simon when he says: “And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.”

James of Alphaeus is the one who is called the Lord’s brother in the Gospel, because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord, whom the evangelist John calls Mary of Clopas. Perhaps the same Alphaeus was also called Clopas; or perhaps, after Alphaeus died following the birth of James, Mary married Clopas. Ecclesiastical history relates that she bore him Simeon as a son and that, because Clopas was the brother of Joseph, Simeon, being the Lord’s cousin, ruled the Church at Jerusalem after James—whether this apostle Simon or some other Simeon is intended.

The apostles themselves testify that James was rightly surnamed “son of Alphaeus,” that is, “of the learned,” since immediately after the Lord’s Passion they appointed him bishop of Jerusalem. Hegesippus, a historian who lived close to the times of the apostles, testifies that even before the shedding of blood he was truly a supplanter of carnal desire. He says:

> James, the brother of the Lord, surnamed Just, received the Church of Jerusalem after the apostles. Many are called James, but this man was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no flesh, was never shorn, was never anointed with oil, and never used a bath. It was customary for him to enter the Holy of Holies. He did not wear woolen garments but linen ones, and he alone entered the temple and knelt to pray for the people. To such an extent that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels.

Simon the Zealot is also Simon the Cananaean, from the Galilean village of Cana, where the Lord changed water into wine. For *Cana* means “zeal,” and *Cananaean* means “Zealot.”

“Judas of James, and Judas Iscariot, who was the betrayer.” For the sake of distinguishing them, he repeated the name Judas. One of them, as he himself writes in the catholic Epistle, is the brother of James and was also called Thaddaeus. The other derived the name that foretold his condemnation either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. For *Issachar*, which means “reward,” indicates the price of betrayal. *Iscariot*, interpreted as “memory of death,” shows that he did not undertake the crime of handing over the Lord under a sudden persuasion, but after meditating on it for a long time.

He was chosen among the apostles not through ignorance but through providence. How great is the truth, which even an adversarial minister does not weaken! How great the Lord’s moral wisdom, who preferred that his judgment rather than his affection should be placed in danger among us! For he had assumed human frailty and therefore did not refuse even these aspects of human weakness. He wished to be abandoned; he wished to be betrayed; he wished to be handed over by his own apostle, so that when you are abandoned by a companion and betrayed by a companion, you may bear with moderation the error of your judgment and the loss of your benefit.

“And coming down with them, he stood on a level place, together with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people.” The Lord went up into the mountains when he was about to choose the apostles, but, when he was about to teach the crowds, he returned to the level places, because crowds are capable of seeing Christ only in a lowly place.

For this is the rule followed by the Apostle when he says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, not even now are you able” (1 Corinthians 3). According to Matthew, however, the apostles themselves, as being more mature, are said to have been taught both on the mountain and from the open mouth of the Savior.

If one examines both evangelists more carefully, it can be understood that, when he chose the twelve disciples from among the many on the mountain and called them apostles—a detail Matthew omitted—he then delivered the discourse that Matthew inserted and Luke omitted, namely, the discourse on the mountain. Then, after he had descended, he delivered another similar discourse in a level place, which Matthew omits but Luke does not; and the two discourses were concluded in the same way.

“From all Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coastal region, and from Tyre and Sidon,” and so forth. I think that the “coastal region” is named not from the nearby Sea of Galilee—for he would not have placed this in a passage concerned with a miracle—but from the Great Sea, in which Tyre and Sidon could also be included. Yet, because they are cities of the Gentiles, assigned by lot to the Jews but not possessed by them, since they were unable to drive out their inhabitants, they are deliberately mentioned by name, so that the fame and power of the Savior might be made known: it summoned even foreign cities to seek healing and instruction.

Here it should be noted that, although the Lord took pity on Gentiles who came to him—for he also healed the centurion’s servant and the daughter of the Canaanite woman after approving the faith of those who asked—he is nevertheless not found to have entered their cities. He did this so as not to give the Jews, who were eager to slander him, an opportunity for complaint; rather, he reserved the complete salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his Passion and resurrection. As that time approached, when Gentiles were seeking to see him, he said: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much fruit” (John 12).

“And the whole crowd was seeking to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.” Above, the leper is cleansed when the Lord touches him; here, the whole crowd that was able to touch him is healed by the power of his spirit. The Savior’s touch, therefore, is the work of salvation. To touch him is to believe faithfully in him. To be touched by him is to be strengthened by his gift.

But each person abounds in his own understanding. The crowds that come together from far away to hear are healed by the touch of the Lord as he descends into the plain. The disciples, who have already been instructed in lesser matters, are advanced to greater things on the summit of the mountain. From among them, some are also chosen to behold him transfigured in secret on the mountain. One above all the others, as though he were to be intoxicated from the fountain of a more sublime wisdom, reclines upon the breast of the Teacher.

Rarely anywhere will you find either crowds following the Lord to higher places or a weak person being healed on the mountain. Rather, when the fever of lusts has been extinguished and the light of knowledge kindled, each person gradually ascends toward the summit of the virtues.

In the Old Testament as well, when Moses alone, together with Joshua, ascended the mountain of God, he appointed Aaron and Hur to govern the people on the plain until they returned. *Aaron*, which is interpreted as “mountain of strength,” signifies the singular excellence of the Lord’s Incarnation. *Hur*, which means “fire,” indicates the gift of the Holy Spirit. For there are many children in the Church who, although they cannot accompany their teachers in penetrating the mysteries of the supreme Divinity, can nevertheless be redeemed by the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation and marked by the ardor of the Holy Spirit.

“And he, lifting his eyes toward his disciples, said: ‘Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.’” Although he speaks generally to everyone, the Savior nevertheless lifts his eyes more particularly toward the disciples, so that he may open more widely the light of inner understanding to those who receive the word with the attentive ear of the heart.

This is similar to what Matthew says: “And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit’” (Matthew 5). To those for whom he opens his mouth while seated on the mountain, so that they may hear great things sublimely, he directs his eyes while standing on the plain, so that they may understand openly what they have heard.

“Blessed, therefore, are the poor.” Not all poor people, certainly, but only those who regard every height of the present age, however lofty it may seem, as nothing. They are rightly declared worthy of the gift of the heavenly kingdom, because they have been shown to be stripped of the desire for human pleasure.

King David declares what poverty he endured when he says: “But I am needy and poor.” And elsewhere, thinking little not only of earthly things but even of heavenly things above, and saying, “For what remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72), he immediately reveals where he had fixed the anchor of his hope by adding: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.”

Otherwise, some people, in the most wretched condition of poverty, lack both the joys of this world here because of their want of possessions and the kingdom of God there because of their wickedness of merit.

“Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be satisfied.” What it means to hunger in blessedness, and what they ought to thirst for, Matthew explains: righteousness. He teaches us most plainly that we must never consider ourselves sufficiently righteous, but must always love—indeed, burn with desire for—the daily progress of righteousness.

The Psalmist, burning with desire for heavenly things, shows that its perfect satisfaction cannot come in this age but in the future, when he says: “But I shall appear in righteousness before your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16).

The saying can also be understood simply: “Blessed are you who are hungry now”—you who chastise your body and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9), who devote yourselves to the word amid hunger and thirst (2 Corinthians 11)—because then you will enjoy the abundance of heavenly joys.

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Those who weep not over the loss of temporal advantages but over the diminution of spiritual virtues will be comforted with eternal blessedness. Here we are commanded to mourn not only our own sins but also those of our neighbor. If we love that person as ourselves, then we must necessarily rejoice in his progress and grieve over his failure—and not merely grieve, but be moved even to tears.

Thus Samuel and David mourned Saul’s sin and destruction. Thus the Lord himself wept over the sinful city; and, moved with compassion for the grieving sisters, he first wept with human pity for Lazarus, whom he was about to raise by his divine majesty. Mystically, he signified that those who are lulled by the death of sin must be mourned by their neighbors so that they may be able to live again.

When he promises that those who weep now will laugh, this must not be understood childishly. Rather, in the manner of Scripture, the name “laughter” signifies an exultation of the mind and a certain more joyful affection. Thus Sarah says: “God has made laughter for me” (Genesis 21). And it is said in Job: “The mouths of the truthful will be filled with laughter.” Through these expressions, as I said, the inward joy of the soul is represented.

“Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they exclude you and reproach you.” Whoever desires to endure weeping, hunger, and poverty for the riches of Christ’s inheritance among the saints, for the bread of eternal life, and for the hope of heavenly joys is blessed. Much more blessed is the one who does not fear to preserve these virtues amid adversity.

For however wickedly people may hate them in their hearts, they cannot injure the heart beloved by Christ. Let them exclude him and drive him from the synagogue: Christ finds and strengthens him. Let them reproach the name of the Crucified One: he raises those who have died with him and makes them sit with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2).

“And when they cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man.” When he says “your name,” he means the name “Christians,” which, so far as the Gentiles and Jews were concerned, was very often erased from memory and cast out by human beings. No reason for hatred remained except the Son of Man, because believers wished to make the name of Christ their own surname. Therefore the persecutors of the supreme name are rightly branded with the name “human beings.”

“You will be blessed,” he says, teaching that they will be persecuted by human beings but blessed beyond the human condition.

“Rejoice on that day and leap for joy. For behold, your reward is great in heaven.” This command can be fulfilled not by just any sufferer, but by one who suffers with a view solely to the reward above: so that amid hatred in the heart, insults on the lips, and even the hands of persecutors, one may remain with an equal—or rather, an even more joyful—heart.

Those who resemble us cannot achieve this, but those can who “went forth rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Therefore whoever endures many adversities on earth for Christ will receive many gifts from Christ in heaven.

But how many darts of words did the false prophets endure from Elijah, who mocked them by saying: “Cry out with a louder voice! For he is a god: perhaps he is speaking, or is in an inn, or on a journey, or certainly asleep, so that he may be awakened” (1 Kings 18). What a slaughter those men caused, when eight hundred and fifty were killed together! But because Baal, and not Christ, was at issue, they neither rejoiced at being mocked nor earned the crown by being killed; they deserved everlasting punishment.

“For their fathers did the same to the prophets.” He has rightly encouraged them by example, because those who speak the truth usually suffer persecution. Nevertheless, the ancient prophets did not, through fear of persecution, desist from preaching the truth.

It should be noted that, just as Matthew, through the eight beatitudes he gives, indicates the eighth perfection of our hope, which is dedicated to the glory of the resurrection, so Luke embraces the four cardinal virtues.

Blessed are the poor, who through temperance are restrained from the allurements of the world. Blessed are those who hunger, who, reminded by their own hunger, understand that the hungry must be shown mercy, and who themselves show mercy as far as they are able through justice. That almsgiving is rightly called justice—by which we do not give Christ what is ours but return what is his—the Psalmist testifies when he says: “He distributed to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Psalm 111).

For justice is that by which we give each person what belongs to him, owing no one anything except to love one another. Blessed are those who through prudence, discerning between good and evil, know how to mourn what passes away and yearn for eternal things. Blessed are those who through the strength of faith are able to endure every painful thing.

Therefore those who are not yet able to climb the citadel of perfected virtue must meanwhile be nourished by the blessedness of a general perfection, so that, progressing little by little from good things to better things, while they gladly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may at some time ascend sublimely to him seated on the mountain.

For those whose hearts he is still laboring to subdue and instruct he addresses as one standing—the posture of one who labors. But those whom he finds already prepared and teachable through long practice in spiritual study he addresses with the freedom and dignity of a teacher, as the tranquil Savior, seated, reveals to them mysteries concerning things above.

This difference among spiritual advances is expressed most beautifully in figures drawn from the condition of the Israelite people. The entire populace, wearing whatever garments they wished, was commanded to make for itself blue fringes on the four corners of its cloaks. The priests were to have four garments, distinguished by four symbolic colors in wondrous variety. The high priests were to wear both those garments belonging to the priests and four additional kinds of clothing, of the same colors but with the more elevated grace of their dignity, gleaming with inlaid gold and adorned with the name of the patriarchs and of the Lord himself. To explain these matters individually, or merely to set them forth, belongs to the diligence of a separate work.

“Nevertheless, woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation.” What woe is destined for the rich is better understood by contrast, where it is said that the kingdom of God belongs to the poor. Those who seek consolation here alienate themselves from that kingdom in every way, and will hear from the just judge: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16).

Here it should be noted that it is not riches so much as the love of riches that is at fault. For it is not everyone who possesses riches, but, as Ecclesiastes says, “Those who love riches will take no fruit from them” (Ecclesiastes 5). Whoever does not know how either to despise temporal possessions in the heart or to distribute them to the poor enjoys their use for the present, but in the future will lack the fruit that he could have acquired by giving.

Elsewhere we read: “Blessed is the rich person who is found without blemish, who has not gone after gold and has not hoped in money and treasures” (Ecclesiasticus 31).

“Woe to you who are satisfied, for you will hunger” (Luke 16). That rich man was satisfied when he feasted splendidly every day, but he endured a dreadful woe when he was hungry and sought from Lazarus, whom he had despised, a drop of water on his finger.

Alternatively: if those who always hunger for works of righteousness are blessed, then those who please themselves in their desires and suffer no hunger for true and steadfast goodness must be judged unhappy. They consider themselves blessed enough if they are not deprived, even temporarily, of their own pleasure.

“Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.” Solomon also says: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs 14). And again: “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Ecclesiastes 7). He plainly teaches that folly must be assigned to those who laugh, and prudence—as we have shown above—to those who weep.

“Woe when all people speak well of you.” This is what the Psalmist laments: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm 10 according to the Hebrew numbering). It is no small part of punishment when one’s crimes are not merely left unrebuked but are praised as though they had been well done.

Therefore the Lord, with foresight, does not say, “Woe, because people speak well of you,” as though guilt were followed by punishment after some interval of time; rather, he says, “Woe when all people speak well of you.” For flattery itself is the nurse of sin. As oil supplies fuel to flames, so flattery habitually supplies nourishment to those burning in guilt, and is therefore itself a very great punishment for sinners.

For just as it is fitting that the poor, hungry, and weeping should be tested by the wickedness of evildoers, so those who devote themselves to riches, banquets, and laughter are, through the anger of the strict judge, nourished toward greater punishment by the patronage of those who obey them badly.

“For their fathers did the same to the prophets.” He means the false prophets, who themselves are often called prophets in Holy Scripture because they attempt to foretell, that is, to proclaim beforehand, future things in order to win the favor of the crowd. Hence Ezekiel says: “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing. Like foxes in the desert, your prophets, Israel” (Ezekiel 13).

Thus on the mountain the Lord describes only the beatitudes of the righteous, but on the plain also the woes of the reprobate. For inexperienced hearers must be compelled to good things by threats and terrors, whereas it is enough for the perfected to be invited by rewards.

“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.” Since above he had said what they might suffer from their enemies, he now shows how they themselves ought to act toward those same enemies.

Many people think it is sufficient not to hate one’s enemies, but that loving them is commanded beyond what human nature can endure. They do not see that Moses, Samuel, and Stephen prayed for their enemies, and that David mourned his dead enemies. The Lord would not command what is impossible, but what is perfect.

Therefore, while we have the opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

Bless those who curse you; pray for those who slander you. The Apostle testifies that he and those like him did this when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless. We are reviled, and we entreat” (1 Cor. 4). But here a difficulty rightly arises: how is it not contrary to this command of the Lord that many imprecations against enemies are also found in the prophets, which are thought to be curses, such as: “Let their table before them become a snare,” and the other words spoken there? The apostle John says: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and life will be given him who sins not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” Here we must first observe that the prophets, by means of imprecation, foretold what would happen—not by the wish of one who desires it, but by the Spirit’s foreknowledge. They commonly proclaim future events in the form of an imprecation, just as they often sing in the form of past time things that were going to come.

Next, in the Apostle’s words we must understand that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray, even though the Lord commands us to pray for our persecutors. This question cannot be resolved unless we acknowledge that certain sins among brothers are more grievous than the persecution of enemies. That “brothers” signifies Christians can be proved by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures. I therefore think that a brother’s sin unto death occurs when, after coming to know God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is driven by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God. A sin not unto death occurs when someone has not alienated love from a brother, but through some weakness of spirit has failed to show the duties owed by brotherhood.

Therefore the Lord also says on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). For they had not yet become participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit or entered into the fellowship of holy brotherhood. Blessed Stephen also prays for those by whom he is stoned, because they had not yet believed in Christ and were not fighting against that common grace. And I think that the apostle Paul does not pray for Alexander for this reason: he was already a brother, and had sinned unto death—that is, unto envy—by attacking the brotherhood. But for those who had not broken off love, but had succumbed through fear, he prays that they may be forgiven. For he says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words” (2 Tim. 4). Then he adds, concerning those for whom he prays: “At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them” (ibid.). This distinction between sins separates Judas, who betrayed, from Peter, who denied.

If someone strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. He does not say, “Do not strike back at the one who strikes you”—although this too is a great command—but he says: “Prepare yourself to be struck again.” Those who serve their beloved ones as sons, or any of their dearest people when they are sick, understand especially that this pertains to mercy; so too those who serve children or the deranged, from whom they often suffer much. If the well-being of such persons requires it, they even offer themselves to suffer more, until either the weakness of age or of illness passes away.
