Since, then, the Lord, the physician of souls, was instructing them in the care of their neighbors, what else could he teach them except to endure with equanimity the weaknesses of those whose well-being they wished to promote? For every wickedness proceeds from weakness of spirit, since no one is more innocent than the person who is perfect in virtue.

Many know how to offer the other cheek, but do not know how to love the one by whom they are struck. Yet the Lord himself, who certainly first fulfilled the commands he taught, did not offer the other cheek to the servant of the high priest when he struck him on the cheek; instead he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18). Nevertheless, his heart was not unprepared—not only to be struck on the other cheek for the salvation of all, but also to be crucified in his whole body.

And from the one who takes your garment, do not withhold your tunic also. What is said concerning a garment and a tunic is to be done not only with these, but with everything that we say is temporally ours by some right. For if this is commanded concerning necessities, how much more fitting is it to despise superfluities?

Give to everyone who asks you. He says, “to everyone who asks,” not “everything that he asks,” so that you give what you can give honorably and justly. For what if he asks for money with which he intends to oppress an innocent person? What if, finally, he asks for sexual immorality? But, not to pursue the many matters that are innumerable, one must certainly give what, as far as a human being can know or believe, harms neither you nor another. And to the person to whom you have justly denied what he asks, you should make the justice of your refusal known, so that you do not send him away empty-handed. Thus you will give to everyone who asks you, although you will not always give him what he asks. Sometimes you will give something better, when you correct the person asking for what is unjust.

And from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back. He is speaking of clothing, a house, a field, an animal, and, generally, of every kind of money. Whether this should also be understood of slaves is a major question. For it is not proper for a Christian to possess a slave in the same way as a horse or silver, even though it may happen that a horse is worth more than a slave, and something made of gold or silver much more. But if that slave is educated or governed by you, his master, more rightly, honorably, and suitably for the worship of God than he could be by the person who wants to take him away, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that he ought to be despised like a garment. For a human being ought to love another human being as himself, since he is commanded by the Lord of all to love even his enemies.

And just as you want people to treat you, you also treat them in the same way. Because love is patient and kind, it not only bears the injuries of an enemy with the greatest strength, but also most graciously anticipates the favor of a friend. Nature has taught everyone to return love to one who loves. But only Christ’s teaching has instructed the perfect to compel the person who does not love them to love by means of benefits. When he commanded us to do to others first what we would want done to us, he immediately strengthened the same idea by developing it more fully, saying:

And if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them, and so forth. If even sinners, tax collectors, and Gentiles know by nature’s guidance how to be kind toward those who love them, how much more ought you—he says—who have been assigned a higher rank of profession and therefore must have a richer concern for virtue—to embrace even those who do not love you with a wider bosom of love?

It therefore seems worth asking how it is that, when the Lord testifies that those who love only those who love them, who do good to those who do good to them, and who lend to their friends do not merely fail to possess perfect love but are even compared with sinners, the one who reclined on the Lord’s breast, in bringing his Epistle concerning love of God and neighbor to completion, nowhere admonishes us to love enemies, but simply says: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and the love of God is perfected in us” (1 John 4).

If this troubles anyone, let him understand that John did not remain silent about the love of enemies, but included them also under the name of brothers, teaching that they should be loved with regard to brotherly love and commanding that we pray for them. This is so that they may not always remain enemies, but may repent from the snares of the devil and be joined to us in a brotherly covenant. Nor should it seem harsh that we say those who do not yet believe can nevertheless be called brothers because of the hope that they will believe. For the same John is also read to call them children of God. “For Jesus,” he says, “was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11). As long as they are scattered, they are not yet children of God; but by coming together into one, they already become children.

Nevertheless, love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. Since he had condemned the mutual love and benefits of sinners as unfruitful, he now shows how these things ought to be performed fruitfully by the faithful. Everyone who receives a loan borrows, even if he himself will not be the one to repay it. For since God restores more to the merciful, everyone who provides a benefit lends at interest. Or, if one does not wish to call the lender only the person who gives to someone who will repay, one should understand the Lord to have included these two kinds of giving. For either we give what we give benevolently, or we lend to someone who will repay.

Because many, as it is written, regarded interest as a source of gain and imposed a burden on those who had helped them, many did not lend—not because of wickedness, but because they feared being defrauded of what they had given freely. Divine authority also heals this weakness when it says: “And lend, expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6). That is, do not fix your hope of repayment upon a human being. Whether the person repays what you lent, God too will repay what you did at his command; whether he does not repay, your inheritance will be eternal. “The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous person is merciful and lends” (Ps. 111). “For those who bless him shall possess the land” (Ps. 36). And elsewhere, when he had said, “The man is joyful who shows mercy and lends,” he immediately added: “The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. 111).

And your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High. No greater reward can exist than that earthly human beings become sons of the Most High, who is in heaven. Therefore what he says, “and you will be sons of the Most High,” is to be understood according to the principle by which John also says: “He gave them power to become children of God.” For there is one natural Son, who is wholly incapable of sinning. We, however, become sons by receiving power, insofar as we fulfill what he commands. Hence apostolic teaching calls this adoption, by which we are called to an eternal inheritance so that we may be fellow heirs.

Thus he does not say, “Do these things because you are sons,” but, “Do these things, and you will be sons.” When he calls us to this through the Only-Begotten, he calls us to his likeness.

For he himself is kind, he says, toward the ungrateful and the wicked, and so forth. God is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked, either through his manifold mercy, by which he even saves animals while bestowing temporal goods, or through that singular grace by which, by inspiration, he glorifies only the elect with heavenly gifts. But whether you understand it in one way or the other, or in both ways, it is accomplished by God’s great goodness, which we are commanded to imitate if we wish to be God’s sons.

Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. In this passage, I think that nothing else is commanded us except that we interpret actions whose motive is uncertain in the better sense. For what is written, “You will know them by their fruits,” is said of manifest things that cannot be done with a good motive, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and things of that kind—things concerning which we are permitted to judge.

Regarding kinds of food, however, since any human food can be consumed without the fault of sinful desire, with a good motive and a simple heart, the Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to be judged by those who abstained from such foods. “Let the one who eats,” he says, “not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. 14). The same applies to what he says elsewhere: “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (1 Cor. 4).

There are therefore certain intermediate actions whose motive we do not know, which can be done either well or badly; it is rash to judge them, especially in order to condemn. Their time of judgment will come when the Lord brings to light the hidden things of darkness and discloses the purposes of hearts (ibid.). There are two circumstances in which we must guard against rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what motive something was done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person someone who now appears either evil or good will prove to be.

Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you. He commands us to forgive injuries and to give benefits, so that our sins may be forgiven and eternal life given to us. In this brief but remarkable saying he gathers together and concludes everything he had commanded at length concerning conduct toward enemies.

A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will they give into your lap. This resembles what he says elsewhere: “So that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). It is not the poor themselves, but Christ who will repay the reward to those who have given alms. Yet they are said to give it into their lap because they furnished the opportunity of earning it: whether pitiably needy or wickedly raging, they have been endured by the patience of the stronger, supported by their generosity, and sometimes drawn to the faith itself by sweet grace.

For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you. The Apostle also, exhorting the Corinthians to almsgiving, says among other things: “The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings” (2 Cor. 9). This can also be understood of everything we do in mind, hand, and tongue. “For you will repay each one,” he says, “according to his works.”

He also told them a parable: Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit? The meaning of this saying depends on what comes before, where we are commanded to give alms and forgive injuries. If anger against a violent person, he says, and love of money toward a petitioner have blinded you, can you cure his defect with your own mind corrupted by defect? Or will only the person who inflicted the injury be held guilty, and not you also, who did not know how to bear it?

But if the wickedness of that person finds you gentle and tranquil in heart, he will be moved to repentance, and you will be rewarded for your patience, because, with a seeing eye—that is, with a serene heart—you took care to lead a blind person toward the light.

A disciple is not above his teacher. But everyone who is perfect will be like his teacher. If the teacher, who as God certainly had the power not to avenge his own injuries, preferred instead to make his persecutors gentler by enduring them, then disciples, who are merely pure human beings, must necessarily follow the same rule of perfection.

Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye? This too refers to what comes before, where he warned that a blind person cannot be led by a blind person—that is, that a sinner cannot be corrected by a sinner. For many, overtaken by pride, hatred, love of money, greed, or some other crime, judge these matters to be slight or nonexistent and sharply rebuke those whom they see disturbed by sudden anger, as though the eye of the mind had been altered from its customary purity by an invading speck. Forgetful of the Lord’s command, “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke 6), they prefer to criticize and condemn rather than amend and correct.

How can you say to your brother, “Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,” while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? You do this to your brother if, for example, you rebuke in hatred what he has done in anger. As great as the difference between a speck and a beam is, so great is the difference between anger and hatred. Hatred is longstanding anger, which through the passage of time has acquired such magnitude that it is rightly called a beam. It can happen that, if you are angry with someone, you still want him to be corrected. But if you hate someone, you cannot want him to be corrected. Therefore it is said to be impossible for the person who carries a beam in his own eye to remove the speck from his brother’s eye.

Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye. That is: first drive hatred away from yourself, and afterward you will be able to correct the person whom you love. The kind of hypocrites—that is, pretenders—is truly dangerous and burdensome: while they receive accusations of every vice with hatred and envy, they also want to appear to be giving advice.

Therefore we must watch over ourselves piously and carefully. Whenever necessity begins to require that we criticize or rebuke someone, we should first consider whether the vice is one we have never had, or one from which we have already been free. If we have never had it, let us consider that we too are human beings and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes our criticism or rebuke.

Then, whether our words prove useful for his correction, which is why we speak, or for his corruption—for the outcome is uncertain—we shall nevertheless be secure in the simplicity of our own eye. But if, on examining ourselves, we discover that we are subject to the same vice as the person whom we were preparing to rebuke, let us not criticize or reprimand him. Instead, let us groan together with him, and invite him not to obey us but to strive alongside us.

Rebukes should therefore be used rarely and only in great necessity. Even then, we must strive not to serve ourselves but God. For this is the goal: that we do nothing with a double heart, removing from our own eye the beam of envy, malice, or hypocrisy, so that we may see how to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

For no good tree produces bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit. He continues the argument he had begun against the hypocrite. If you wish, he says, to possess a true and unfeigned righteousness, take care to match the righteousness you display in words with your deeds, so that, being a good tree, you may be adorned with good fruits. For even if a hypocrite pretends, he is not good if he performs evil works. And if he rebukes an innocent person, the one who performs good works is not thereby evil.

For every tree is known by its own fruit. The Apostle shows what fruit distinguishes a good tree from a bad one when he says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I warn you of, as I warned you before: those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. 5).

Almsgiving, prayer, and fasting, moreover, are indeed properly the fruits of the good, but they are sometimes practiced hypocritically even by the wicked. Concerning them the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6). And elsewhere: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7).

But the sheep should not therefore hate their clothing, because wolves often conceal themselves in it: they display one thing in order to deceive, and bring forth another in order to plunder or kill those who, under this sheep’s clothing, cannot see the wolves. This, then, is not the fruit by which he warns us that the tree is to be known, but the fruit described above.

For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they harvest grapes from a bramble. I think that the thorns and the bramble signify the cares of the world and the prickings of vices, concerning which it was said to sinful humanity: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). The fig and the grape signify the sweetness of a new way of life, for which the Lord hungers in us, and the fervor of love that gladdens the human heart. Concerning these, while the Gospel shines forth, the voice of the turtledove resounds far and wide throughout the earth: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs; the blossoming vines have given their fragrance” (Song 2).

A fig is not gathered from thorns, nor a grape from a bramble. For a mind still weighed down by the habits of the old person can pretend, but it cannot bear the fruit of the new person. If someone should object and say that Moses also harvested grapes from a bramble when he received useful advice from his gentile kinsman, or that those gathered figs from thorns to whom it was said concerning the Pharisees, “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23), let him know that, just as a genuine vine sometimes lies wrapped in a hedge and, while bearing fruit, does not preserve its thorn for human use, so the words or deeds of the wicked, when they benefit the good, are not made beneficial by the wicked themselves; rather, this happens through the providential plan of the One above.

The good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure. The treasure of the heart is the same as the root of the tree. What is brought forth from the heart is the same as the fruit of the tree. Therefore the person who keeps in his heart a treasure of patience and perfect love, pouring forth excellent fruits, loves his enemy, does good to the one who hates him, blesses the one who curses him, prays for the one who slanders him, does not resist the one who strikes or strips him, gives to everyone who asks, does not demand back what has been taken from him, does not wish to judge or condemn, and corrects the person who has gone astray with patience and love, along with the other things that the Savior taught above.

But the one who keeps a wicked treasure in his heart hates his friend, curses the one who loves him, curses the one who blesses him, and performs the other acts contrary to the good treasure that the Lord’s word condemns. So that he would not flatter himself in vain because of what follows:

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. As though not the fruit of the tree, but its leaves—that is, words alone and not deeds—were being sought in either the true Christian or the hypocrite, the Lord appropriately adds:

Why do you call me “Lord, Lord,” and do not do what I say? It is as though he were saying in other words: Why do you boast that you are putting forth the leaves of a right confession, when you display no fruits of good works? Therefore the Apostle, about to separate the precious from the worthless—that is, the good treasure from the bad, the good tree from the bad, the perfect disciple of the good teacher from the hypocrite, and the seeing guide from the blind—says: “I will come to you, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4).

By the speech of the mouth, therefore, the Lord indicates everything that we bring forth from the heart in deed, word, or thought—things that are naked and open to his eyes even more than to human beings. For it is also customary in the Scriptures to put words in place of things. Hence the Psalmist says: “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Ps. 34). And Hezekiah says: “There was no word that I did not show them” (Isa. 39)—although he had revealed to the Chaldeans the secrets of things, not of words. Likewise the Apostle says: “No one says, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12), meaning that no one recognizes Jesus as Lord with understanding, and no one embraces him by the will, except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house. Having discussed above many things openly concerning the good and the evil, and many things concerning those who are truly or falsely good—through these three persons, I think, encompassing the entire human race—he concludes his whole discourse with a parable at once terrifying and loving. In it he compares some hearers of the word to the devil and others to Christ; each of these never ceases throughout the whole time of this age to build his own house in the subjection of human beings.

Therefore the person who hears Christ’s words and does them will be compared with Christ. For just as Christ builds, teaches, and governs one catholic Church for himself out of various kinds of human beings, intending at last to dedicate it to eternal life, so the useful hearer, progressing toward heavenly things according to his own measure through various pursuits of virtue, builds for himself a dwelling of perpetual habitation. In the present he labors to square, polish, and join its stones with the cement of love; in the future he will rejoice with Christ at its dedication.

Who digs deeply and lays his foundations upon rock. When foundations are mentioned in the plural in the mystery of the Church, they signify the teachers, concerning whom it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86). When the foundation is mentioned in the singular, however, Christ is expressed as the teacher of teachers and the foundation of foundations. Concerning him it is said: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

The wise architect therefore placed these foundations not upon the earth but upon rock, because Christ establishes the minds of exalted men not in earthly desires but in his unconquerable faith, hope, and love. “The rock,” he says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). He digs deeply because, through the commands of humility, he removes all earthly things from the hearts of the faithful, so that they may not serve God for the sake of anything lowly or temporal.

In the moral sense, the foundations of the house are the intentions of a good way of life. The perfect hearer of the word, having removed through Christian humility the rubble of empty and fragile thoughts, firmly inserts these intentions into the fulfillment of Christ’s commands. In this he does within himself, with Christ’s particular assistance, what Christ does generally in the universal Church. He rejoices with the Psalmist: “He brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mire of filth; he set my feet upon a rock,” and so forth (Ps. 39).

When a flood arose, the river struck against that house but could not shake it, because it had been founded upon rock. The river’s flood—which elsewhere he calls the gates of hell when he says, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. 16)—is the same as the flood he mentioned above: “Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil” (Luke 6). It was able to rush upon the firm corners of the Church, but not to overthrow them.

For they rejoiced on that day and exulted, encouraging one another against the fury of the waves: “Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord” (James 5). And again: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his dwelling. God is in its midst; it will not be moved” (Ps. 45).

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, each of our houses is also struck daily either by unclean spirits, by wicked people, or by the restlessness of its own mind or flesh; and to the extent that they trust in their own strength, they are inclined to fall. But to the extent that they cling to that unconquerable rock, they cannot be shaken.

But the one who hears and does not do is like a man building his house upon the earth without a foundation. The devil’s house—the world that lies in wickedness—is called a house not because of the Creator’s dignity but because of the magnitude of the delinquent. He builds it upon the earth because he drags those who obey him down from heaven to earthly things. He builds without a foundation because sin has no foundation, since it does not subsist from its own nature. Evil is without substance, although, whatever it is, it grows together within the nature of the good.

Since “foundation” derives from “bottom,” we can also appropriately understand “foundation” as standing for “bottom.” The same is true of the word “hearing,” which derives from “ear,” although the ear itself is often designated by the name “hearing.” Just as a person who is plunged into a well is held by the bottom of the well, so a falling soul would settle as though in a kind of bottom, if, once fallen, it remained fixed at some measure of sin. But since it cannot be satisfied with the sin into which it has fallen, and is daily cast down into worse things, it does not find a bottom in the well into which it has fallen—this is what the figure signifies.

Hence it is rightly said elsewhere: “When the wicked comes into the depths of evils, he despises them” (Prov. 18). He declines to return because he despairs that mercy can be shown him. But when, in despair, he sins still further, he removes the bottom from his own well, so that he cannot find a place where he might be held. Therefore the one who hears Christ’s words and does not do them—whether initiated into Christ’s mysteries or entirely alien from Christ—is like a foolish man who builds himself badly, of whom it is said: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. 13).

Against which the river struck, and immediately it fell. And the ruin of that house was great. It is clear that, when any temptation comes upon them, both those who are truly evil and those who are falsely good immediately become worse, until at last they fall into everlasting punishment.

In the moral sense, however, it must be said that each person is tempted by his own desire, being drawn away and enticed. Then desire, when it has begun, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, generates death. The rush of the river can also be understood as the ordeal of the final judgment, when both houses have been completed: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted. Then the wicked—not only human beings but also the angels who belonged to the devil’s house—will go into eternal punishment, while the righteous will go into eternal life (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER VII

When he had finished all his words in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Here it must be understood that Christ entered Capernaum after he had indeed finished all his words in the hearing of the people. That is, he did not enter before he had finished these words; but the length of time that elapsed between the end of these discourses and his entry into Capernaum is not stated. During that interval the leper was cleansed, whom Matthew inserts in his proper place, whereas this evangelist anticipates him earlier.

A certain centurion’s servant, who was ill, was at the point of death, and he was precious to him. Perhaps someone asks this either out of piety, in order to find an answer, or out of impiety, in order to find fault: why did the evangelist say that the servant was at the point of death, when he is subsequently shown not to have died but to have been healed? The brief answer is that he truly was at the point of death; if he had not been restored to life by the faith of his master, who pleaded for him, and by the compassion of Christ, he would have died.

King Hezekiah likewise, according to a certain condition of human nature, was at the point of death when he heard from the words of the truthful prophet: “Set your house in order, for you will die and not live” (2 Kings 20). But by the hidden judgment of divine providence—which has ordered all things by measure, number, and weight—he was destined to obtain fifteen additional years of life through tears and prayers.

When he heard about Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him, asking him to come and save his servant. By a heavenly dispensation it happened that Jewish elders were sent to the Lord and that, while they were present, the sick man was healed, so that they would have no excuse if they did not believe although a Gentile believed.

But it is asked how Luke’s account—that the centurion sent messengers—agrees with Matthew’s, which says that he himself approached the Lord. To those who inquire piously, the answer is readily apparent: Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that the centurion himself approached, because his desire and will were truly conveyed to the Lord, even though others carried his message. Mystically, he was also commending to us what is written: “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33).

Because the Lord praised the centurion’s faith—the faith by which one truly approaches Jesus—to such an extent that he said, “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8), the discerning evangelist preferred to say that the centurion himself approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words. Luke, however, disclosed the whole manner in which the event occurred, so that from this we might be compelled to understand how the other evangelist said that the centurion approached, even though he could not have lied.

Just as the woman who suffered from a flow of blood, although she touched the fringe of his garment, nevertheless touched the Lord more because she believed than did the crowds by which she was pressed, so the centurion approached the Lord more the more greatly he believed.

For he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us. Those who report that the centurion built the synagogue for himself clearly show that, just as we customarily call the Church by that name, so they too called the synagogue not only the gathering of the faithful but also the place where they gathered, as we have taught above.

Jesus was going with them. Great was the Lord’s sublimity: he was able to heal by a word alone. But no less was his humility, by which he deemed it worthy to visit a sick servant. For, as one powerful and kind, and asked to save him, he went on his way; and in the middle of the journey, when asked, he saved him by a word, lest anyone should think that he went bodily because of weakness of power rather than as an example of humility.

Elsewhere he wished to come to heal the ruler’s son, lest he should seem to have honored riches. Here, lest he should seem to have despised a servant’s condition, he immediately consented to go to the centurion’s servant.

And when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: “Lord, do not trouble yourself. For I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Because of his awareness of his Gentile way of life, he thought that the Lord’s condescension would burden him more than assist him, and that he could not have Christ as his guest, since, although endowed with faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments. But because divine grace knows how to give what our weakness does not presume to receive, and because another centurion—who, like this one, prefigures the believing people from the Gentiles—received the gift of the Holy Spirit, on account of his great faith and righteousness, before he was baptized, this man too, though not yet catechized, merited both that his faith should be praised by the Lord and that his servant should be saved. Concerning him it is beautifully said allegorically that Jesus was not far from the house, although he did not dare invite him under his roof, because his salvation is near to those who fear him. And whoever makes proper use of the natural law, doing the good things he knows, thereby approaches him who is truly good. But those who have joined crimes to the error of paganism may appropriately be compared with those of whom the Lord says elsewhere, when the crowds were flocking to him: “For some of these have come from far away.”

For this reason I did not consider myself worthy to come to you. And we who believe from the Gentiles cannot ourselves come to the Lord, whom we are now utterly unable to see in the flesh. But all who have recognized the sufferings of our servitude ought already, through faith, to approach him who sits at the right hand of the Father; already we ought to send the elders of the Jews—that is, the leading men of the Church, who have gone before us to the Lord—and, by humbly entreating them, acquire advocates who, bearing witness on our behalf that we love the Church and, insofar as we are able, take care to build it up, may intercede with the Lord for our sins and those of our people.

But say the word, and my servant will be healed. Great was the centurion’s faith, by which he confessed the effective power of the word in Christ, and which is suited to the mysteries of our healing: although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer (II Corinthians 5).

[Col. 0416B] For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me. He says that he is a man subject to authority, whether that of a tribune or a governor, yet able to command those beneath him. We are therefore to understand that he who is God and powerful over all possesses a countless host of angelic powers obedient to his commands.

And I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it. He wishes to show that the Lord can accomplish whatever he wills not only through the presence of his bodily form but also through the ministry of angels. For bodily illnesses and hostile powers, by which man is often reduced to weakness, had to be driven away both by the Lord’s word and by the ministries of angels. Another interpretation: the soldiers and servants who obey the centurion are natural powers. Many who come to the Lord bring with them a considerable supply of these powers. Concerning such a man, in praise of the centurion Cornelius, it is said: “For he was a righteous man, fearing God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always entreating God” (Acts 10).

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. He marveled because he saw that the centurion understood his majesty. But who had produced that faith or understanding in him except the very one who marveled at it? And if another had produced it, why would he marvel, since he knew it beforehand? We must therefore note that when the Lord marvels at something, he signifies that it ought to be marveled at by us, who still need to be instructed in this way. For all such motions, when they are attributed to God, are not signs of a troubled mind but of a teacher instructing his pupils.

And turning to the crowds that followed him, he said: “Amen, I tell you, I have found no such faith even in Israel.” He is not speaking of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times but of the people of the present age. The centurion’s faith is preferred to theirs because they had been instructed by the admonitions of the Law and the Prophets, whereas this man believed spontaneously, without anyone teaching him.

And those who had been sent, returning to the house, found the servant who had been ill healthy. The faith of the master is proved, and the health of the servant is confirmed. Thus the merit of a master can also benefit servants—not only through the merit of faith but also through devotion to discipline. Matthew explains this more fully: when the Lord said to the centurion, “Go, and as you have believed, so let it be for you” (Matthew 8), the servant was healed from that hour. But blessed Luke has the custom of shortening what he sees fully explained by the other evangelists, or even deliberately passing it over; what they omitted or treated briefly he more carefully clarifies.

Mystically, as I said, the centurion, whose faith is preferred to that of Israel, plainly represents the elect from the Gentiles. Like men supported by a hundred soldiers, they are exalted by the perfection of spiritual virtues, and they ask nothing earthly from the Lord for themselves or their own people, but only the joys of eternal salvation. The number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, is customarily used as a sign of heavenly life. Hence Noah’s ark was constructed over one hundred years; Abraham, at the age of one hundred, received the son of promise; Isaac sowed and in that same year found a hundredfold harvest; the court of the Tabernacle is one hundred cubits long; in the hundredth psalm, mercy and judgment are sung to the Lord; and there are other examples of this kind. Men of such merit must therefore plead with the Lord for those who are still oppressed by the spirit of servitude in fear, so that, as they are gradually raised to higher things, perfect love may cast out fear (I John 4).

And it happened afterward that he went to a city called Nain. Nain is a city of Galilee, two miles south of Mount Tabor, near Endor, which is a large village four miles south of the same mountain.

And his disciples and a great crowd were going with him. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother. This dead man, who was carried out beyond the gate of the city while many looked on, signifies a person lulled into sleep by the deadly funeral of his crimes, and also bearing the death of his soul—not yet concealing it in the bedchamber of his heart, but exposing it to the knowledge of many through the evidence of his speech or actions, as though through the gates of his city. He is rightly said to have been his mother’s only son, because although the mother Church is one perfect and immaculate virgin, gathered from many persons, each individual believer nevertheless rightly confesses himself to be a child of the universal Church. Indeed, every elect person is a son when he is instructed in the faith, and a mother when he instructs others. Did he not act with maternal affection toward little ones who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4)?

The gate of the city through which the dead man was being carried out, I think, signifies one of the bodily senses. Whoever sows discord among brothers, whoever speaks iniquity arrogantly, is carried out dead through the gate of the mouth. Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her (Matthew 5) displays the signs of his death through the gate of the eyes. Whoever willingly opens his ear to idle stories, obscene songs, or slander makes this the gate of death for his soul; and whoever does not guard the other senses likewise makes them entrances of death for himself.

I beseech you, Lord Jesus, make all the gates of my city gates of righteousness, so that, entering through them, I may confess your name (Psalm 117), and so that, when your majesty visits it frequently with the heavenly ministers, it may not be met by the stench of a carried-out corpse, but salvation may occupy its walls and praise its gates.

And she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her. Every soul that remembers that it was redeemed by the death of its bridegroom and lord recognizes that the Church is a widow. By divine providence, a large crowd accompanied the Lord, and a large crowd accompanied the widow, so that, having witnessed so great a miracle, many might become witnesses and many praisers of God.

When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: “Do not weep.” He said, in effect: “Stop weeping for one whom you will soon see rise alive from the dead.” Mystically, the teaching of Novatian is confounded here. Novatian, boasting proudly of his own purity, attempts to nullify the humble cleansing of penitents and denies that the true mother Church, weeping over the spiritual extinction of those she has reborn, ought to be consoled by the hope of restoring them to life. Beautifully, the evangelist testifies first that the Lord was moved with compassion for the mother, and then that he raised her son, so that in one case he might show us an example of the piety we should imitate, and in the other establish faith in the power we should marvel at.

And he came near and touched the bier. Those who were carrying it stood still. The bier on which the dead man is carried out is the complacently secure conscience of a despairing sinner. Those who carry him to burial are either impure desires, which snatch a person away to destruction, or the poisonous flatteries of companions who indulge him. By lifting up sins with their favors, they heap them up, and by treating sinners with contempt they bury them, as though beneath a mound of earth. Of these it is said elsewhere: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8). The dead bury the dead when sinners flatter others like themselves with harmful favor and, piling upon them the mass of the worst flattery, crush them so that they may never attain any hope of rising again.

Therefore, when the Lord touched the bier, the bearers of the funeral stood still, because when a conscience is struck by fear of heavenly judgment, restraining both the abundance of carnal pleasures and the crowd of those who praise unjustly, it returns to itself and hastens to answer the Savior who calls it to life. Hence it rightly follows:

And he said: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. The dead man sits up when a sinner comes back to life through inward compunction. He begins to speak when he shows to all who had mourned his sin the signs of restored life. He is returned to his mother when, by the decrees of sacerdotal judgment, he is joined to the communion of the Church.

Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: “A great prophet has arisen among us.” The more hopeless the death of a soul that is recalled to life, the more people are corrected by the same example. Look at the prophet David; look at the apostle Peter. The higher their rank, the more serious their fall. The more serious the fall, the more pleasing is the mercy of the one who raises them up. And the more clearly the Lord’s mercy appeared in them, the more certain the hope of salvation appeared to all penitents, so that all who hear may rightly say:

“God has visited his people.” Not only by once taking on flesh as his Word, but also by continually sending this word into our hearts, so that we may be raised up.

And his disciples reported all these things to John. In my opinion, they did not do so with a simple heart but with one provoked by envy: John’s disciples told him of Christ’s powers and miracles. Elsewhere, too, they are shown to have complained to him in this way: “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3). John then answered them: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven,” and so forth. In this way he plainly declares both that he is a mere human being and that Christ is the Son of God. But because envy and ill will remained and could not be driven out, observe what the excellent teacher did for their correction.

[Col. 0419B] And John summoned two of his disciples and sent them to the Lord, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Clearly, he did this so that, at least on this occasion, by seeing the signs he performed, they might believe in him and, while their teacher asked the question, learn for themselves. He therefore does not say, “Are you the one who came?” but, “Are you the one who is to come?” The meaning is: “Tell me, since I am about to be killed by Herod and descend to the underworld: should I announce you there also, as I announced you in the regions above, or is it unfitting for the Son of God to taste death, and are you going to send another for these mysteries?”

At that very hour he cured many of their diseases and afflictions and evil spirits, and he gave sight to many who were blind. John had asked through his disciples: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Christ displays signs, not answering the question he had been asked, but addressing the stumbling of the messengers.

“Go,” he says, “and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and—something no less important than these—the poor have the gospel preached to them.” The poor may mean the poor in spirit, or certainly those poor in material wealth, so that in preaching there may be no distinction between noble and obscure, rich and needy. These things demonstrate the sternness of the teacher; these things prove the truth of the instructor, since for him everyone who can be saved is equal. But when he says:

“And blessed is whoever is not scandalized by me,” he chastises John’s messengers, who had not believed that he was the Christ, for the scandal of their faithlessness, and he explains to John what he had asked, namely, that God saves and that the Lord undergoes death (Psalm 67). After seeing so many signs and such great powers, anyone could have avoided scandal and instead marveled. But the minds of unbelievers suffered a grave scandal in him when they saw him dying after so many miracles. What, then, does it mean to say, “Blessed is whoever is not scandalized by me,” except openly to signify the lowliness and humility of his death? It is as though he plainly said: “I indeed perform marvelous things, but I do not disdain to endure what is lowly. Since I follow you even in dying, people must be very careful not to despise death in me while venerating my signs.”

[Col. 0420A] When John’s messengers had departed, he began to speak about John to the crowds. Since the surrounding crowd did not know the mystery of the question and thought that John doubted concerning Christ, whom he himself had pointed out, the Lord heaps fitting praise upon him, so that they might understand that John had asked not for himself but for his disciples.

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” He introduced this not by asserting it but by denying it. A reed, as soon as a breeze touches it, bends in whatever direction. What is signified by the reed except the carnal mind, which, as soon as it is touched by favor or slander, inclines in any direction? If the breeze of favor blows from a human mouth, it grows cheerful, is exalted, and bends itself entirely toward pleasing that person. But if the wind of slander bursts forth from the same place from which the breeze of praise came, it immediately inclines this mind, as though toward the opposite side, under the force of anger. John, however, was not a reed shaken by the wind: favor did not make him weak, nor did anyone’s anger make him harsh; prosperity could not lift him up, nor adversity bend him.

But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are in splendid clothing and luxury are in royal houses. John, we are told, was clothed in camel’s hair. Those who flee harshness for God’s sake, he says, serve not a heavenly kingdom but an earthly one; devoted only to outward things, they seek the softness and pleasure of the present life. Let no one therefore suppose that sin is absent from luxury and an excessive concern with clothing. If this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the harshness of his clothing. Nevertheless, the statement that John was not dressed in soft clothing may be understood symbolically in another way. He was not dressed in softness because he did not nurture the life of sinners with flatteries but rebuked it with the force of severe denunciation, saying: “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 3).

But what did you go out to see—a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. The role of a prophet is to announce what is to come, but not also to point it out. John, therefore, is more than a prophet because he announced by pointing out the one whom he had prophesied by going before.

[Col. 0420D] This is the one about whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.” What is called angelos in Greek is called nuntius, “messenger,” in Latin. Rightly, therefore, the one sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that the name may preserve the dignity of the office he fulfills by his work. It is a lofty name, but his life is not inferior to the name.

Moreover, all who are counted as belonging to the priesthood are called angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2). Indeed, every believer, insofar as he is able and insofar as he receives the breath of heavenly grace, becomes an angel if he recalls his neighbor from wickedness, if he takes care to exhort him to good works, or if he announces eternal kingdom or punishment to one who has gone astray. Whenever he offers words of holy proclamation, he truly exists as an angel.

For I tell you: among those born of women, no prophet is greater than John the Baptist. He says, “among those born of women.” He is therefore preferred to people who are born of women and from the union of man, but not to him who was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. Yet in this statement he did not prefer John to the other prophets, patriarchs, and all human beings, but made all the others equal to John. For it does not immediately follow that, if no others are greater than he, he is greater than the others; rather, he is equal to the other holy ones.

But the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. This saying can be understood in two ways. Either he called “the kingdom of God” that which we have not yet received and in which we are not yet present, concerning which he will say at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25). There, any one of the holy angels, even the least among them, is certainly greater than any holy and righteous person who bears a body that is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9).

Or, if he intended the Church of the present age to be understood as the kingdom of God—whose children include all the righteous and holy who have been able to exist from the beginning of the human race—then the Lord plainly signified himself: he was less than John in the time of his birth, but greater in the eternity of his divinity and in his lordly power. Accordingly, under the first interpretation the punctuation is: “But the one who is least in the kingdom of God”—and then follows—“is greater than he.” Under the second it is: “But the one who is least”—and then follows—“in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

And all the people who heard him, including the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism. God himself is justified through baptism, when people, confessing their own sins, justify themselves, as it is written: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.” He is justified in this respect because he is not rejected through defiance, but God’s gift is acknowledged through righteousness. “For the Lord is just, and he has loved righteousness” (Psalm 10). The justification of God therefore consists in this: that he is seen to have transferred his gifts not to the unworthy and guilty but to those made innocent and righteous through cleansing.

David also says: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 50). Therefore, the one who sins and confesses his sin to God justifies God, yielding to him who conquers and hoping for grace from him. God is therefore justified in baptism, in which there is both confession and forgiveness of sins.

But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves by refusing to be baptized by him. The phrase “for themselves,” or “against themselves,” signifies that whoever rejects God’s grace acts against himself. Alternatively, it may mean that these foolish and ungrateful people are blamed for refusing to receive God’s purpose, which had been sent to them. God’s purpose, then, is the decision by which he determined to save the world through the passion and death of the Lord Jesus. But the Pharisees and lawyers rejected it, spurning the hidden and saving mystery whose beginnings had preceded it in John’s preaching and baptism. Yet, unknowingly and unwillingly, they served that same purpose, in accordance with what the apostle Peter said about the Lord: “This man, handed over according to the determined purpose and foreknowledge of God, you afflicted through the hands of lawless men and killed” (Acts 2).

To whom, then, shall I compare the people of this generation, and to whom are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, saying: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance. We mourned, and you did not weep.” The generation of the Jews is compared to children sitting in the marketplace because formerly it received the prophets as teachers. Concerning these it is said: “From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8). And elsewhere: “The declaration of your words enlightens me and gives understanding to the simple” (Psalm 118)—that is, to the humble in spirit.

The Lord’s marketplace—whether the synagogue or Jerusalem itself—was the place in which the laws of heavenly commands were established. There these children spoke to one another, or, according to Matthew, to their peers, because they used daily, in the native language of their people and nation, to reproach the crowds of their own race for refusing to heed either the prophetic psalms of David or the prophetic laments by which they were later corrected. Whenever victory over an enemy was either foretold or recalled as already accomplished, they did not consent to rise to works of virtue. For the word “dancing” signifies not the twisting of a body swaying in theatrical movements but the energetic devotion of the heart and the religious agility of the limbs.

Whenever the laments of the prophets resounded over destructions either inflicted by the enemy or still to come, they nevertheless did not take care to flee to the remedies of repentance. The Psalmist sings: “Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob; take up the psalm and give the tambourine” (Psalm 80), and so forth. But what follows? “And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me” (ibid.).

The prophet cries out: “Thus says the Lord: Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). And again: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain; the senses of my heart are troubled within me. I will not be silent, because my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle” (Jeremiah 4). A little later: “For my foolish people did not know me; they are senseless children, without understanding” (ibid.).

For John the Baptist came, neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say: “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came, eating and drinking, and you say: “Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” As then, he says, so now you will accept neither path of salvation. For when he says, “We mourned, and you did not weep,” this pertains to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But when he says, “We played the flute, and you did not dance,” this pertains to the Lord himself, who, by eating and drinking with others, symbolized the joy of the kingdom.

But they were unwilling either to humble themselves with John or to rejoice with Christ. They said that the former had a demon and called the latter a glutton, a drunkard, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners. When he adds:

“And wisdom is justified by all her children,” he shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness does not consist either in abstaining or in eating, but in the even-tempered endurance of want, in temperance that does not corrupt itself through abundance, and in taking—or not taking—at the proper time those things whose use is not blameworthy but whose desire is. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy. And because people are accustomed to rejoice greatly in bodily feasts, he added: “in the Holy Spirit.”

Another interpretation: “Wisdom is justified by all her children,” that is, God’s dispensation and teaching, which resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4), has been proved by its faithful ones to have acted justly. Among them are those of whom it was said above: “And all the people who heard him, including the tax collectors, justified God.” Amen.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423A] The most holy history of Mary the penitent, which forms the twenty-eighth chapter of our third book on Luke, although it begins anew in order to lessen the labor of readers, nevertheless looks back in its subject matter to the conclusion of the second book. For above, whether spoken in the person of the evangelist or of the Lord and Savior—as some have preferred it—this had been said: “And all the people who heard him, including the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism.” If you interpret this as spoken by the Lord, the people who heard John are understood to be designated. If it was inserted by the evangelist, those who heard the Lord disputing about John’s greatness are understood to remain in view.

“But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves, refusing to be baptized by him.” The same evangelist proceeds to establish by deeds what he had set forth in words, proving by a most fitting example that wisdom was justified by all her children—that is, both by the righteous and by those who repent after unrighteousness.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Now,” he says, “a certain one of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him. And he entered the house of the Pharisee and reclined at table. And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment.”

Alabaster is a kind of white marble streaked with various colors, which they customarily hollow out for ointment vessels, since it is said to preserve their contents unspoiled especially well. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria; it is whiter than other varieties, and the most highly prized kind is found in India.

Some say that this was not the same woman who, shortly before the Lord’s passion, poured ointment over his head and feet, because this woman washed his feet with tears and wiped them with her hair and is explicitly called a sinner, whereas nothing of this kind is written about the other woman, nor could a prostitute suddenly have become worthy to anoint the Lord’s head.

But those who investigate more carefully discover that it was the same woman—namely Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus—and that, as John relates, she performed the same service twice. Once, indeed, here, when she first approached with humility and tears and merited forgiveness of sins. John too, although he does not narrate how it happened as Luke does, nevertheless mentioned it while commending Mary herself, when he began to speak of her brother after he had been raised:

“Now there was a certain man who was ill, Lazarus from Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister. (Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair [John 11].)”

The second time was in Bethany—for the first event occurred in Galilee—when she is found to have anointed not only his feet but also his head, no longer as a sinful woman but as a chaste, holy, and devoted woman of Christ.

This also accords beautifully with the principles of allegory. Every faithful soul first humbles itself at the Lord’s feet and bends down to be absolved from sins; then, as its merits increase over time, the ardor of its joyful faith pours fragrance upon the Lord’s head, as it were, with the scent of spices.

The universal Church of Christ likewise, in the present age, celebrates the mysteries of his incarnation—signified by the name “feet”—and renders devoted service to her Redeemer. In the future, however, contemplating at once the glory of his humanity and the eternity of his divinity, since God is the head of Christ, she glorifies him with everlasting praises of confession, as though with costly spikenard.

“Therefore,” he says, “she brought an alabaster jar of ointment.”

And standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head. She kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment. It is clear to everyone that the woman, previously devoted to illicit acts, had used the ointment for the fragrance of her own flesh. What she had shamefully offered to herself, she now laudably offered to God. With her eyes she had desired earthly things, but now, crushing them through repentance, she wept. She had displayed her hair for the adornment of her face, but now she wiped away tears with her hair. With her mouth she had spoken proudly, but by kissing the Lord’s feet she fixed that mouth upon the footsteps of her Redeemer.

As many forms of pleasure as she had possessed in herself, so many sacrifices did she discover within herself. She converted the number of her crimes into a number of virtues, so that everything by which she had despised God in guilt might serve God wholly in repentance.

But when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, because she is a sinner.” Behold the Pharisee: truly proud within himself, falsely righteous, he rebukes the sick woman for her sickness and the physician for his aid, while he himself was sick from the wound of pride and did not know it.

Therefore, whenever we see sinners, we must always first mourn for ourselves in their calamity. For perhaps we have fallen into similar things, or may fall, if we have not already fallen. And although the authority of teaching must always pursue vices with the strength of discipline, we must nevertheless carefully distinguish between them: to vices we owe strictness, but to nature compassion. Let us now hear by what judgment this proud and arrogant man is convicted.

“There were,” he says, “two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both their debts. Which of them, then, will love him more?” Simon answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.”

In this matter we must note that, while the Pharisee is convicted by his own judgment, he carries, like a madman, the rope by which he is to be bound. The woman’s good deeds are enumerated, as are the evils of the false righteous man, when he says:

“I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet. But she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not give me a kiss. But she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil. But she has anointed my feet with ointment.”

After the enumeration, the judgment follows:

“Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” What do we believe love to be except fire, and faults except rust? Hence it is said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” It is as though it were said openly: “She has completely burned away the rust of sin, because she burns fiercely with the fire of love.” For the more powerfully the sinner’s heart is consumed by the great fire of charity, the more completely the rust of sin is destroyed.

Behold, the woman who had come to the physician sick has been healed; but others are still sick over her healing. For it follows:

“And those who were reclining with him began to say to themselves: ‘Who is this, who even forgives sins?’” But the heavenly physician does not regard the sick whom he sees becoming worse even because of the medicine. He confirms the woman whom he had healed by the sentence of his mercy, saying:

Your faith has saved you; go in peace. For faith saved her, because she did not doubt that she could receive what she had asked for, but had already received from him the very certainty of hope from whom, through hope, she was also seeking salvation. She is commanded to go in peace so that she may not thereafter turn aside from the path of truth into the way of scandal.

These things have been said by way of historical exposition; now let us examine the secrets of the mystical meaning. Whom, then, does the Pharisee presuming upon false righteousness signify, if not the Jewish people? And whom does the sinful woman, coming and weeping at the Lord’s feet, signify, if not the converted Gentile people? The Pharisee asked the Lord to eat with him, because that same people, which refused to believe that he had come, did not cease hoping that he would come; indeed, in prayerful petitions it expressed its desire that he should come, saying: “Stir up your power, and come, that you may save us” (Psalm 79).

For the Lord’s eating with the Pharisee means receiving the joys of the mind from the devotion of the believing people. Hence elsewhere he says to the disciples concerning Samaria, which was to believe: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4). When they hesitated about what he meant, he explained: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work” (ibid.). “And entering,” he says, “the house of the Pharisee, he reclined.” The Pharisee’s house is the very guardianship of the Law and the Prophets, in which the Jewish people gloried in having its dwelling through the continuous practice of its way of life. The Lord entered it because, appearing in the flesh in time, he came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them. He reclined because he who could not be understood in the sublimity of his majesty assumed the humility of a servant’s form, in which he could be seen.

Therefore the woman who was a sinner in the city learned that he had reclined in the Pharisee’s house, because the Gentile people, previously bound by unclean deeds to the life of this world, learned through the report of apostolic preaching that “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4). And in the Pharisee’s house it is not the Pharisee but she who is justified, since the Jewish people follows only the letter of the Law, whereas we follow in the Law both the grace of the Spirit and the letter. He thinks that Jesus is not a prophet because he receives sinners; but we recognize him also as the true God, who is able to justify sinners.

The woman brought an alabaster jar of ointment. What is expressed by ointment if not the good fragrance of reputation? Hence Paul also says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2). If, therefore, we perform upright works by which we sprinkle the Church with the fragrance of a good reputation, what do we pour upon the Lord’s body except ointment?

But the woman stood behind his feet. We stood behind the Lord’s feet when, placed in sins, we were held back from his paths. But if, after our sins, we turn to true repentance, we now stand behind his feet, because we follow his footprints, which we had attacked.

The woman wets his feet with her tears. We too do this truly if, through compassionate affection, we bow before any of the Lord’s least members; if we sympathize with his holy ones in tribulation; if we regard their sorrow as our own.

The woman wiped with her hair the feet she had wetted. Hair is something superfluous to the body. And what does earthly substance in abundance resemble, if not hair? When it is superfluous to the necessities of use, it feels no loss even when cut off. We therefore wipe the Lord’s feet with our hair when we have compassion, out of charity, on his holy ones with what is superfluous to us, so that the mind may grieve through compassion in such a way that a generous hand also displays the effect of its grief.

The woman kisses the feet she wipes. We too do this fully if we diligently love those whom we support through our generosity, so that our neighbor’s need may not be burdensome to us, nor the very poverty that is being relieved become oppressive, and so that, while the hand supplies what is necessary, the spirit may not grow sluggish in love.

The feet may also be understood as the very mystery of his incarnation, by which the divinity touched the earth because he assumed flesh. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). We therefore kiss the Redeemer’s feet when we love the mystery of his incarnation with our whole heart. We anoint his feet with ointment when we proclaim, with the good reputation of sacred discourse, the very power of his humanity.

But the Pharisee sees this and is envious. For when the Jewish people sees the Gentile people proclaiming God, it wastes away inwardly through its own wickedness. Our Redeemer, however, recounts to it the woman’s deeds as a catalogue of the Gentiles’ virtues, so that it may recognize the evil in which it lies.

“I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet. But she has wetted my feet with her tears.” Water is outside us, whereas the moisture of tears is within us. For that unbelieving people never gave the Lord even what was outside itself; but the converted Gentile people poured out for him not only its possessions but also its blood.

“You gave me no kiss. But she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet.” A kiss is a sign of love. That unbelieving people did not give God a kiss because it did not wish to love God out of charity, though it served him out of fear. But the Gentile people, once called, does not cease kissing the footprints of its Redeemer, because it continually sighs in his love.

“You did not anoint my head with oil.” If we understand the Lord’s feet as the mystery of his incarnation, his head is appropriately understood as his divinity. Hence the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11). The Jewish people professed that it believed in God, and not in itself as though in a human being. Yet the Pharisee is told: “You did not anoint my head with oil,” because he neglected to proclaim with worthy praise that very power of the divinity in which the Jewish people professed that it believed.

“But she has anointed my feet with ointment.” Because, when the Gentile people believed in the mystery of his incarnation, it also proclaimed with the highest praise his lowest manifestation.

The two debtors, about whom the parable of Simon is set forth, signify both peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—who owed one lender, that is, their Creator, not material money but the coin of their own salvation. For our Maker, having created those whom he made in his own image and likeness, exalted them, as though by a loan, with a denarius entrusted for safekeeping. A denarius is ordinarily fashioned with the image and name of a king.

“To everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required of him. And from the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more.” The debt of both peoples is indeed multiplied by the number five. For there are five senses, which we use in this life, and through which we ought to cultivate the image of our Creator that we have received. But the people to whom the Law’s Decalogue was given through a servant owes less; more does the people to whom the grace of eternal life was entrusted through the Son. Therefore interest is accumulated for the latter through the number ten, and for the former through the number one hundred. No one doubts that the one-hundredfold pertains to the signification of the heavenly kingdom, which will be given to those on the right. For it is not without reason that it is represented by the same bending of the fingers by which the ten is represented on the left, while this is represented on the right.

This is because, both now, faith perfects the works of the Decalogue that the letter could not perfect, and in the future it will repay each according to his works: eternal life to those who seek glory, honor, and incorruption through perseverance in good work.

But because neither people has been saved by its own strength, but by his grace through faith, it is rightly said: “Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both.” And certainly the one loves more to whom more is forgiven; but the one to whom less is forgiven loves less. Whether you understand this of the good works required to perfect the knowledge we have received, or of the ignorance we have incurred and must avoid, much more has been given to the Church than to the Synagogue. The Church was once corrupted by the filth of idolatry, which was more shameful because no teacher had forbidden it; but “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5), and now it has been raised to the greater height of evangelical perfection. To it is said: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matthew 13).

The account in Numbers also aptly corresponds to this passage: when the spoils of the slain Midianites were divided equally, those who had come from the battle gave the Lord one part in five hundred from their share, while the others gave one in fifty. For the person who preserves himself safe from the enemy’s attack by exercising virtue in the camp makes a great offering; but the one who brandishes the sword of the word and lays low the innumerable forces of the adversary makes a greater one.

## CHAPTER VIII

“And it happened afterward that he himself went through city and village, preaching and proclaiming the kingdom of God, and the Twelve were with him.”

We see fulfilled in Christ’s disciples what we read was said concerning that ancient people of the Hebrews. Nor is this surprising, because the one God of both Testaments, who gave the Law through a servant, will give blessing through the Son. “As,” he says, “an eagle provoking its young to fly, and hovering over them, spread its wings, took him up, and carried him upon its shoulders” (Deuteronomy 32).

For just as newly born young birds cannot rise through the air by flying until they grow feathers, so all the faithful, if they are to become capable of flying toward heavenly things, must first clothe themselves in the feather of virtues in the nest of faith. Thus the apostles, the teachers of the faithful, gradually ascend to higher things, so that they may also be placed in charge of instructing others.

First, the Lord teaches in the synagogues, performs miracles, spreads his reputation everywhere, receives the crowds who gather to him, heals them, and instructs them. Then he makes disciples, refreshes them at the bridegroom’s wedding, leads them through the fields, and, like an eagle bringing an eagle-stone [aetite; the reading is uncertain] to defend its tender young from serpent bites, protects them from the slanders of the Pharisees. From among them he chooses the Twelve, whom he calls apostles. But at first he teaches these also in the presence of the crowd; when the crowd threatens them with him, he gives them the customary benefits bestowed on the needy. Later, as has now been read, preaching through cities and villages, he keeps only those with him who may listen to him more intimately; to them alone he explains the mysteries of the kingdom of God that he had spoken to the others in parables. Finally, as though strengthening them by the protection of his wings through the display of his virtues, he gives them power to heal and sends them to preach the kingdom of God.

“And some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, who is called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.”

Mary Magdalene is the woman whose repentance the following passage recounts without mentioning her name. The evangelist rightly and reverently makes her known by her familiar name when he recalls that she traveled with the Lord and ministered to him from her possessions. But when he describes her as a sinful yet repentant woman, he calls her simply “a woman,” lest a name of such renown—by which she is now honored throughout all the churches—should be darkened by the stain of her former error.

Seven demons are said to have gone out from her, to show that she had been full of countless, indeed of all, vices. Since the ages of the world run through seven days, Scripture often uses the number seven to signify universality. Hence the prophet also embraces the grace of the Holy Spirit under a distinction of seven virtues.

“And Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward.”

If Mary signifies the Church from the Gentiles cleansed from the filth of vices, why should Joanna not also signify that same Church, once subject to the worship of idols but now redeemed by the compassion of Christ? For every evil spirit, ready to deceive the human race, while working on behalf of the devil’s kingdom, is like a steward of the most impious Herod.
