“And Susanna, and many others, who ministered to him from their possessions.”

It was a custom among the Jews, and according to the ancient practice of that people it was not considered blameworthy, for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own substance. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul recalls that he had set the practice aside: “Do we not have the right to take believing women along with us, as the other apostles also do?” (1 Corinthians 9).

They ministered to the Lord from their possessions so that he might reap their material goods, while they reaped spiritual things. This was not because the Lord of creatures needed food, but so that he might provide a model for teachers: they ought to be content with food and clothing supplied by their disciples.

Susanna is interpreted as “lily,” or “his grace.” But I think it better, if the feminine name is figured from the lily, to understand it as referring to the fragrant brightness of heavenly faith and the golden ardor of inward love. Joanna means “the Lord is her grace,” or “the merciful Lord,” since everything by which we live belongs to him. Maria means “bitter sea,” certainly because of the inborn groaning of repentance, by which either Mary herself or each of us mourns our former vices, so that we may deserve to reach eternal grace and splendor. Magdalene means “tower”; but, just as one who comes from a mountain is called “mountain-born,” so she may better be called “tower-born” from a tower. She is the one to whom the Psalmist sings: “You have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60).

“When a very large crowd was gathering, and people were hurrying to him from the cities, he said by way of a parable: ‘The sower went out to sow his seed.’”

The Lord deigned to explain this parable himself so that he might make known that he was speaking figuratively and teach that the meanings of things must be sought even in those matters which he did not wish to explain himself. But since the Lord himself disclosed that the seed is the word of God and the varied soil signifies the differing hearts of hearers, we can understand the sower whom he left for us to seek as none other than the Son of God. He went out to sow his seed because, coming forth from the bosom of the Father, to which no creature had access, he came into the world for this purpose: to bear witness to the truth.

Hence, according to the other evangelists, when he is about to speak this parable, he is said to have gone out from the house, approached the sea, and entered a boat, indicating by the position of his body what he was conveying through the progression of his speech.

“And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it.”

The things the Lord explained should be received with devout faith. What he left unspoken for our understanding should be touched upon briefly. The seed that fell beside the road perished through a double injury: it was trampled by passersby and snatched away by birds. The road, therefore, is the heart worn down and dried out by the constant passage of evil thoughts, so that it is unable to receive and germinate the seed of the word. Consequently, whatever good seed comes near such a road is trampled by the course of evil thought and carried off by demons. They are called “birds of the sky” either because they are heavenly and spiritual in nature, or because they fly through the air.

“And some fell upon the rock, and when it had grown, it withered because it had no moisture.”

Here he rightly calls “rock” a hard and untamed heart, penetrated by no plow of true faith. The moisture at the root of the seed is, according to another parable, the oil for nourishing the virgins’ lamps—that is, love and perseverance in virtue.

“And some fell into good soil, and when it had grown, it produced fruit a hundredfold.”

By “a hundredfold fruit” he means perfect fruit. The number ten is always taken as signifying perfection, because the keeping of the Law is contained in its ten commandments. The active and contemplative life are joined together in the commandments of the Decalogue, since in it we are commanded both to love God and to love our neighbor. Love of God belongs to the contemplative life, whereas love of neighbor belongs to the active life.

The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence great perfection is rightly signified by one hundred, as it is said of the one who leaves earthly things for the Lord: “He will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19). Whoever for God’s name despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind even in this life, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life. Thus good soil is made fertile with a hundredfold fruit when a teachable heart is endowed with the perfection of spiritual virtues.

“When he had said this, he cried out: ‘Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.’”

Whenever this little admonition is inserted either in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it shows that what is being said is mystical and that we must seek it with greater attentiveness.

“His disciples asked him what this parable meant.” No one should suppose that the disciples asked the Savior this immediately after the parable had ended. Rather, as Mark says, when he was alone, the Twelve who were with him questioned him about the parables.

“And he said to them: ‘To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. But to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’”

Mark says: “But for those who are outside, everything is done in parables” (Mark 4). Therefore let us also enter with Christ’s disciples into the sanctuary of God, so that we may understand the mysteries of the kingdom of God in the last things. Those who draw near to his feet will receive his teaching, saying with the Psalmist: “Open our eyes, and we shall consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118). Rightly, then, those whose hearts’ senses are closed hear in parables and riddles; they neither enter nor care to know the truth, having forgotten the Lord’s command: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11).

“Those beside the road are the ones who hear. Then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, so that they may not believe and be saved.”

Concerning this seed Mark writes: “These are the ones beside the road, where the word is sown. And when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes it away.” Matthew says: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown.”

From this it is plainly taught that those sown beside the road are people who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, any understanding, or even the slightest opportunity for usefulness arising from temptation. Those sown upon rocky ground and among thorns, as the Lord explains, are those who approve the usefulness of the word they have heard and taste its desire, but are prevented from attaining what they approve: the adversities of this life frighten them, while its prosperities flatter them.

Against both these kinds of loss, the one who said, “With the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Corinthians 6), took care to protect the seed he had received.

Know, then, that these three kinds of soil designate all who do not put into practice the word they have heard. Whoever preserves the seed received is good soil, in contrast to all of them. The Jews and the Gentiles, who do not even deserve to hear, are excepted.

“But the seed that fell among thorns represents those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked by anxieties, riches, and pleasures of life, and they do not bear fruit.”

It is surprising that the Lord interpreted thorns as riches, since thorns pierce, whereas riches delight. Yet they are thorns because they tear the mind with the pricks of their thoughts; and when they drag it as far as sin, they make it bleed as though from an inflicted wound. As another evangelist testifies, the Lord rightly calls them not simply riches but deceitful riches.

They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long. They are deceitful because they do not dispel the poverty of our mind. The only true riches are those that make us rich in virtues.

It should also be noted that, in explaining this, the Lord says that anxieties, pleasures, and riches choke. They choke because, through their unwelcome thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind; and by not allowing a good desire to enter the heart, they kill the passage of the vital breath. It should further be noted that he joins two things to riches—anxieties and pleasures—because they oppress the mind through care and dissolve it through abundance. Through things that are contrary, they make their possessors both afflicted and morally unstable. But because pleasure cannot coexist with affliction, at one time they afflict them through the anxiety of guarding their possessions, and at another they soften them into pleasures through abundance.

“But the seed in the good soil represents those who, hearing the word with a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit with patience.”

Good soil, as we said above, is opposed to all three wicked varieties of soil: it gladly receives the seed of the word and preserves what it receives patiently through adversity and prosperity until the time of fruit.

Alternatively: good soil produces fruit through patience, because none of the good things we do are good if we do not also endure the evils of our neighbors with equanimity. The higher someone advances, the more he finds in this world that he must bear harshly. For as our mind’s love for the present age diminishes, the adversity of that same age increases.

Thus we see many people doing good things and yet laboring under the heavy burden of tribulations. But, in accordance with the Lord’s word, they bear fruit through patience. When they humbly receive the scourges, after the scourges they are exalted and received into rest.

According to Matthew it is said: “And it bears fruit, producing in one case a hundred, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” Thirty refers to marriage, for the joining of the fingers themselves, as though embracing and binding itself by a gentle kiss, depicts husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation. Hence they are represented by the upper finger being pressed downward. The greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward.

As for the number one hundred, reader, attend carefully: it is transferred from the left hand to the right. With the same fingers, but not the same hand by which married women and widows are signified in the left hand, it forms a circle and expresses the crown of virginity.

Alternatively: the thirtieth fruit is produced by the word that builds faith in the Holy Trinity. The sixtieth is produced by the word that teaches perfection of work, because there are six days in which one ought to work. The hundredth is produced by the word that proclaims the eternal life of the kingdom on the right.

“No one who lights a lamp covers it with a vessel or places it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.”

Above he had said to the apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God.” Now he shows that through them this same mystery is at some time to be revealed also to others, and that the breast of all who are to enter the house of God is to be illuminated by the flames of faith.

By these words he also teaches figuratively the boldness required for preaching, so that no one, through fear of bodily hardships, may hide the light of knowledge he possesses. By the name of the vessel and the bed he signifies the flesh; by the lamp, the word. Whoever conceals the word out of fear of bodily hardships, as I have said, places the flesh above the manifestation of truth and, as it were, covers with it the word he is afraid to preach.

He places the lamp on the lampstand who subjects his body to the service of God, so that the preaching of truth may be above and the service of the body below. Yet through that very service of the body the teaching shines more brightly, being conveyed to those who learn through bodily functions—that is, through voice, tongue, and the other movements of the body—in good works.

He therefore places the lamp on the lampstand when the Apostle says: “I do not fight as though beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9).

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor concealed that will not be known and come into the open.”

“Do not,” he says, “be ashamed of the Gospel of God. In the darkness of persecutors, raise the light of the word upon the lampstand of your body, holding firmly in your mind that final day of retribution on which God will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4). For then praise from God will await you, and eternal punishment will await the adversary of truth.

“See, therefore, how you hear.”

He urgently teaches us to listen to the word, so that we may be capable both of continually chewing it over in our own breast and of bringing it forth again for another’s hearing.

“For whoever has, to him it will be given. And whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.”

“Apply yourselves,” he says, “with complete attention to the word you hear. For whoever possesses love of the word will also receive from it the understanding of what he loves. But whoever does not possess love for the word he hears, even if he thinks himself skilled by natural intelligence or literary training, will enjoy none of the sweetness of true wisdom.”

Although this may seem to have been said specifically about the apostles, who, possessing charity and faith, were given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, and about the unbelieving Jews, who, seeing in parables, did not see, and hearing, did not understand—that is, who were destined to lose the letter of the Law in which they gloried—it can nevertheless be understood generally. Often an intelligent reader deprives himself through neglect of the wisdom that a simple but diligent reader tastes through labor.

For this reason the lazy person is sometimes given intelligence, so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence: he scorns to learn what he could have attained without labor. And for this reason the diligent person is sometimes burdened by slowness of understanding, so that he may find greater rewards in the recompense, in proportion as he labors more earnestly in the work of discovery.

“His mother and his brothers came to him, and they could not reach him because of the crowd.”

The Lord’s brothers should not be thought, with Helvidius, to have been sons of the ever-virgin blessed Mary, nor, according to some, sons of Joseph by another wife. Rather, they should be understood to have been his relatives, as we discussed above.

Certainly, when the Lord, being summoned by his mother and brothers, appears reluctant to leave the ministry of the word, he does not reject the duties of filial devotion, for the commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20). Rather, he shows that he owes himself more to the mysteries of his Father than to maternal affections, commending the same lesson to us by his example as well as by his word: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

He does not contemptuously disregard his brothers; instead, preferring spiritual work to bodily kinship, he teaches that the bond of hearts is more religious than that of bodies.

Mystically, this passage agrees with what precedes, where it is said of the Jews who look only upon the letter of the Law: “Whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.” The mother and brothers of Jesus signify the Synagogue, from whose flesh he was born, and the Jewish people. While the Savior teaches within, they come but cannot enter, because they neglect to understand his words spiritually.

The crowd, however, having arrived first, enters his house. For while Judea delays, the Gentile people has flowed together to Christ and, the nearer it is in faith, the more capacious it has been in mind to drink in the inner mysteries of life. As the Psalm says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33).

“And it was reported to him: ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wishing to see you.’”

Within is the word; within is the light. Hence above: “So that those who enter may see the light.” If, then, those standing outside are not themselves recognized as relatives—and perhaps are not recognized for our example—how will we be recognized if we stand outside?

Those stand outside wishing to see the Lord who, without seeking the spiritual meaning in the Law, have fixed themselves outside in the observance of the letter. They are like people who compel Christ to go out to teach carnal things rather than consenting to enter in order to learn spiritual things.

“He answered and said to them: ‘My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.’”

The whole perfection of heavenly life is comprehended in these two things: hearing the word of God and doing it. Hence above, when explaining the parable of the seed, the Lord said that those who had received the word only by hearing were rejected soil; but that those were good soil who retained the word they heard in a good and excellent heart and bore fruit with patience.

They are called the Lord’s mothers because each day, either by example or by speech, they give birth to him in the minds of their neighbors. They are also his brothers when they themselves do the will of his Father who is in heaven.

“Now it happened on one of those days that he himself got into a boat, and his disciples, and said to them: ‘Let us cross over the lake.’ And they embarked.”

In this voyage the Lord deigns to show both natures of his one and the same person: he who sleeps in the boat as a human being restrains the fury of the sea by his word as God.

According to the allegory, the sea or lake that he desires to cross with his followers signifies the dark and bitter turmoil of the present age. The boat into which they embark is best understood as the wood of the Lord’s Passion. Aided by it, the faithful, having traversed the waves of the world, obtain the dwelling of their heavenly homeland, like the security of a stable shore.

That the Savior himself embarked with his disciples in one boat, he explains elsewhere, when, after announcing the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection, he immediately said to everyone: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.”

“As they were sailing, he fell asleep.”

Christ fell asleep while the disciples were sailing because, while the faithful were trampling upon the world and meditating in spirit on the rest of the future kingdom, and while they were eagerly casting behind them the faithless arrogance of the world, whether by the favorable breath of the Holy Spirit or by the rowing of their own effort, the time of the Lord’s Passion suddenly arrived.

Hence Mark rightly reports that this occurred as night was approaching, so that the setting of the true Sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the very hour of the departing light.

“And a storm of wind descended upon the lake, and they were being filled with water and were in danger.”

When the Lord ascended the stern of the cross, on which he was to undergo the sleep of death, the waves of blaspheming persecutors, stirred up by demonic counsels, rose high. Yet the Lord’s own patience was not disturbed by them; rather, the weakness of the disciples was shaken, trembled, and was endangered.

“They approached and awakened him, saying: ‘Master, we are perishing.’”

The disciples awaken the Lord so that, while he sleeps, they may not perish through the violence of the waves. For they had seen his death and were seeking his resurrection with the greatest longing, lest, if he remained asleep in the death of the flesh for too long, their mind should perish forever in spiritual death. Hence it rightly follows:

“But he rose, rebuked the wind and the storm of the water, and it ceased, and there was calm.”

He rebuked the wind when he rose, because, after the Resurrection had been celebrated, he cast down the devil’s pride, destroying through death the one who held the power of death.

He also caused the storm of the water to cease when he rose, because by rising from the tomb he shook the mad fury of the Jews, which had shouted while shaking its head: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him.”

Here, according to the literal sense, it should be noted that all creatures perceive their Creator. Those to whom he issues rebukes and commands perceive the one who commands—not through the error of heretics, who think that all things are animate, but through the majesty of the Creator, to whom things that are insensible among us are sensible.

“And he said to them: ‘Where is your faith?’”

Rightly are those rebuked who were afraid while Christ was present, since whoever clings to him cannot perish. The same is shown when, after the sleep of death, he appeared to the disciples and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen.

He likewise said to them: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24).

It was as though he said metaphorically through the image of the ship: “Was it not necessary for Christ to fall asleep, while waves swept back and forth over the boat in which he was resting, and, once the swelling heaps of the waters had immediately been stilled, to reveal to all the power of his divinity?”

Those who feared were astonished, saying to one another: “Who, do you suppose, is this, that he commands even the winds and the sea, and they obey him?” Matthew writes it thus: “Then the men were astonished, saying, ‘What sort of man is this?’” and so forth. Therefore it was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who were astonished. But if someone quarrelsomely insists that those who were astonished were the disciples, we shall rightly answer that they are called “men” because they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

We too, each one of us, when marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross, prepare to leave the world and surely go aboard the boat with Jesus, attempting to cross the lake. Yet although he neither slumbers nor sleeps who always keeps watch over Israel (Ps. 120), while we are often sailing he seems to sleep amid the roaring of the sea, whenever, as either unclean spirits, wicked people, or the very force of our thoughts grows more intense amid our efforts after virtue, the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold. In such storms, however, we must hasten to that helmsman and diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. Immediately he will restrain the storms, restore tranquility, and grant us the harbor of salvation.

Amid these brief observations on the varying course of the apostolic vessel, it is pleasing to contemplate how it assists the good in their own secrecy and how the mixture of the wicked disturbs them. For behold, beginning with those who are more perfect: after celebrating the solemn rites of the Lord’s resurrection, seven chosen disciples board a boat to fish. Since they were not far from the shore of perpetual rest, but only about two hundred cubits away—that is, since they had applied as much of their mind to the world as their twofold love required—Peter having stripped himself of worldly business, they are deemed worthy to see the Lord already standing on the shore of mortality, to feast with him, and, as the morning of the light from above dawns, to receive their nets filled with the mystical number of great fish, yet not torn, and to draw them out from the lowest waves of the world.

Elsewhere, as was read above, at the Lord’s command Peter lets down the nets for a catch and gathers a very large multitude of fish. But because he was still weak in spirit, so that he tremblingly said to Christ, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5), the nets were then torn, and, if his companions had not helped, the boats too would have sunk beneath the waters.

Likewise, in this passage the disciples board the boat with the Lord and go out upon the sea. But because Judas was also present, and because the Lord is said to have slept in the stern, which was the place of the helmsman, while the wind and sea raged outside, this is reported. For although many merits of the disciples were sailing there, the treachery of the betrayer still drove the vessel at that time; and those who were firm through their own merits were disturbed by the merits—or rather demerits—of another.

Likewise, when Paul was sailing with the brothers to Jerusalem and hastening to celebrate there the day of Pentecost and the joys of the Holy Spirit, he completes everything on a direct course. But when he is sent into exile from Jerusalem to Rome, because he travels with unbelievers, the sea rages, the winds oppose him, rain threatens, cold exhausts him, the stars are obscured, the land is denied to them, wheat is thrown into the sea, the ship’s equipment is removed, and finally the ship itself is shattered after striking the sands. They seek by swimming the land of a nature they do not recognize. Those who had entered the waves of the world weighed down by their desires scarcely escape from that same hostile world naked. In accordance with what the same Apostle says: “He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3).

And they sailed to the region of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. Gerasa is a prominent city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh possessed, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the pigs were driven headlong. It signifies the nation of the Gentiles, which, after the sleep of the Savior’s passion and the glory of his resurrection, he deigned to visit by sending preachers. Hence Gerasa, or Gergesa—as some read it—is suitably interpreted as “driving out the settler” or “approaching the stranger.” This indicates that the people of the Gentiles both expelled from their hearts the enemy by whom they had been wickedly inhabited and that the people who had been far away became near through the blood of Christ.

And when he had gone ashore, a certain man who had a demon met him; he had been afflicted for a long time. This man represents the Gentile people, who for many ages—that is, almost from the very beginning of the world’s birth—were tormented by a mad frenzy.

And he wore no clothing. For he had lost the covering of his nature and virtue. Our first parents are said to have been stripped of this garment of faith and charity after they sinned. The prodigal son was clothed in this first robe after he returned repentant to his father.

He did not remain in a house but among the tombs. For he did not rest in his conscience but took delight in dead works, that is, in sins. For what are the bodies of unbelievers but certain tombs of the dead, in which the word of God does not dwell, but a soul dead through sins is shut away?

When he saw Jesus, he fell down before him. And crying out in a loud voice, he said: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” What madness of Arius—to believe Jesus a creature and not God, when the demons believe him to be the Son of the Most High God and tremble! What impiety of the Jews—to say that he cast out demons by the prince of demons, when the demons themselves confess that they have nothing in common with him! Indeed, even now, after the demons’ cry of that time, they do not cease saying and confessing in the shrines of idols that Jesus is Christ, the Son of the Most High God, and that they have no peace or fellowship with him.

“I beg you, do not torment me.” For he was commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. It had seized him for many years. The enemy of human salvation considers it no small torment to cease harming a human being; and the longer it has been accustomed to possess someone, the more reluctantly it consents to release him. Therefore we must strive with the utmost care so that, even if at some time we human beings are overcome by the devil, we may immediately endeavor to avoid his snares, lest, if resistance to his claim is delayed, he should eventually be driven out with greater difficulty.

And he was bound with chains and kept under guard with fetters. The chains and fetters signify the harsh and severe laws of the Gentiles, by which sins were restrained even in their commonwealth.

And when the bonds had been broken, he was driven by the demon into the wilderness. For even after transgressing those laws, he was led by desire to crimes that exceeded ordinary custom.

Jesus asked him, saying: “What is your name?” But he said: “Legion,” because many demons had entered him. He does not inquire after the name as one who is ignorant, but so that, once confessed before a witness what the madman was suffering [or: struggling with], the power of the healer might shine forth more gratefully.

Even the priests of our own time, who know how to cast out demons through the grace of exorcism, commonly say that sufferers cannot otherwise be healed unless they openly disclose by confession everything they have endured from unclean spirits—whether awake or asleep—through sight, hearing, taste, touch, or any other sense of body or soul. They especially require this when demons—whom the Gauls call *Dusii*—appear to men in female form or to women in male guise and, by an unspeakable marvel, pretend that incorporeal spirits seek and perform intercourse with a human body. They command that the demon’s name, by which it said it was known, and the methods of swearing by which the two parties had mutually pledged their pact of love, be revealed.

This matter resembles a lie, but is so true and so well known through the testimony of many that a neighboring presbyter once told me that he had begun to cure a certain consecrated woman of a demon, but, as long as the matter remained hidden, had been unable to accomplish anything with her. Once she confessed the apparition by which she was troubled, he immediately drove it away through prayers and the other kinds of purification that were required. He also treated the woman’s body for the ulcers she had contracted through the demon’s touch, applying medical care together with blessed salt.

But when he was entirely unable to cover one of the ulcers, which he had found embedded more deeply in her side and which continually opened, he received from the very woman whom he wished to heal advice about how she might be cured. “If,” she said, “you sprinkle consecrated oil for the sick upon that same medicine and then anoint me with it, I shall immediately be restored to health. For once, through the spirit, I saw in a distant city—a city I had never seen with bodily eyes—a girl suffering from the same affliction, and she was healed in this way by a priest.” He did as she had suggested, and immediately the ulcer consented to receive the remedy it had previously rejected.

I have explained these matters briefly against the deceits of demons so that you may understand why the Lord did not ask in vain the name of the spirit he was about to expel. As for the report that many demons had entered the man, it signifies that the people of the Gentiles were enslaved not to any one particular form but to countless and diverse practices of idolatry. In contrast, it is written that “the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one” (Acts 4). Thus, appropriately, the unity of languages was divided in Babylonia, while in Jerusalem the diversity of languages was brought together. The former is interpreted as confusion, the latter as vision of peace: for one faith and piety confirms the elect in peace among many languages and nations, while many sects—more numerous than the languages themselves—separate and confound the reprobate.

And they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss. The demons knew that at some future time, through the Lord’s coming, they would be sent into the abyss—not because they themselves foresaw the future, but because they remembered what the prophets had said about them. Therefore they thought that the Lord’s coming, whose glory they marveled at, was moving toward their destruction.

There was a herd of many pigs feeding on the mountain, and they begged him to allow them to enter them; and he allowed them. He allowed the demons what they requested so that, through the destruction of the pigs, an opportunity for human salvation might be provided. For when the swineherds saw these things, they immediately reported them to the city.

Let the Manichaean be ashamed. If the souls of human beings and beasts are of the same substance and from the same creator, how is it that, for the salvation of one human being, two thousand pigs are drowned? Yet in their destruction, figuratively, unclean people—without voice and reason—are indicated: people who feed on the mountain of pride and delight in filthy deeds. Demons can dominate such people through the worship of idols. For unless someone has lived in the manner of a pig, the devil will never receive power over him—or, if he receives it, it will be only to test, not to destroy him.

So the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed headlong into the lake and was drowned. This signifies that, once the Church had been glorified and the Gentile people freed from the domination of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ practice their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, submerged in blind and profound curiosity.

It should also be noted that the unclean spirits would not have entered the pigs unless the merciful Savior himself had granted their request—although he could certainly have banished them into the abyss. He wished to teach us a necessary lesson: namely, that we should know that they have still less power of their own to harm human beings, since they were unable even to harm animals of whatever kind. God, who is good, can give us this power through hidden justice; he cannot give an unjust power.

When those who were tending them saw what had happened, they fled and reported it in the city and the villages. That the swineherds, fleeing, reported these things signifies that some leaders of the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim its power among the nations with astonishment and wonder.

They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting, clothed and in his right mind, at his feet; and they were afraid, and so forth. This signifies that a multitude delighted in its ancient pleasure may indeed honor it, but refuses to endure the Christian law, saying that it cannot fulfill it, while nevertheless marveling at the faithful people healed of their former, ruined way of life. To sit at the Lord’s feet is, relying upon the rational examination of the mind, to contemplate the Savior’s footsteps so as to follow them. To resume clothing is to be adorned with the pursuit of the virtues that the deceived man had lost.

And the entire multitude of the region of the Gerasenes begged him to depart from them, because they were gripped by great fear. Conscious of their weakness, the Gerasenes judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence. They did not understand the word of God and, with minds still weak, were unable to bear the weight of wisdom. The same is recorded as having happened to Peter when he saw the miracle of the fish, and likewise to the widow of Sarepta, who, although she felt herself blessed by the hospitality of blessed Elijah, nevertheless thought that his presence burdened her. “What have I to do with you, man of God?” she said. “You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son might be killed” (1 Kings 17).

But he boarded the boat and returned. Above, it was said that the Lord, after leaving his parents, boarded the boat, and that, when he had calmed the waves together with the wind, he immediately went ashore and healed the demoniac who met him. By this we explained that, after leaving the peoples of Judea, from whom he derived the origin of his flesh, and after the storm of his passion had passed, he secured the salvation of the Gentiles.

After these events he returns to his homeland, because “a partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter,” and thus “all Israel would be saved” (Rom. 11). He boards the boat, but neither is he himself oppressed by sleep nor is the boat struck by a storm, because “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Yet the trophy of his passion will be made known to the tribes of Judea who are to believe through the glory of his resurrection. When among the Hebrews belief in the preacher of his death begins—in the banner by which he conquered death—he will return to his homeland as though in the boat in which he had slept, now taken up again.

And the man from whom the demons had gone out begged him to remain with him. But Jesus dismissed him, saying: “Return to your house and tell how much God has done for you.” These words can rightly be understood in light of the Apostle’s statement: “To depart and be with Christ is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1). Thus each person should understand that, after the remission of sins, he must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others as well, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. He must not, in his premature desire to be with Christ, neglect the ministry of preaching, which is devoted to the redemption of his brothers.

As for Matthew’s statement that two men were healed from the legion of demons, whereas Mark and Luke mention one, understand that one of them was a person of greater distinction and fame, whom that region especially mourned and whose salvation it sought with particular concern. The two Evangelists, wishing to indicate this, judged that only the one should be mentioned, since the fame of the event concerning him had spread more widely and more brilliantly.

The general meaning of the allegory also agrees with this, because just as one demon-possessed man represents the Jews, so two appropriately express the type of the Gentile peoples. For although Noah fathered three sons, only one family was called into the possession of God; from the other two were born peoples of different nations, who were enslaved to idols.

And it happened that when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. Above I said that at the end of the world the Lord would return mercifully to the Jews and would gladly be welcomed by them through their confession of faith. For the fact that they were all waiting for him clearly corresponds to what he says through the prophet to that same synagogue: “For many days you shall wait for me, and you shall not prostitute yourself, and you shall not be subject to a husband [*vire*, possibly an OCR form of *viro*]” (Hos. 3). For now, neither subject to Christ the husband nor prostituted with idols, it awaits, after a very long expectation, the embrace of its former bridegroom—that is, the Lord Christ—who will one day come through grace.

And behold, a man came whose name was Jairus, and he was ruler of the synagogue. To the preceding reading, in which we interpreted the rejection of the synagogue, the faith of the Church, and then the restoration of the synagogue, the dying daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is appropriately added. While the Lord hastens to raise her, the woman with the hemorrhage forestalls her, seizes health before her, and thus, by arriving first, gains the first share in salvation. “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. 68). “And when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

The ruler of the synagogue is best understood as Moses himself. Hence he is appropriately called Jairus, that is, “illuminating” or “illumined,” because the one who receives the words of life to give to us, and through them illuminates others, is himself illumined by the Holy Spirit, so that he may write or teach life-giving admonitions.

And he fell at Jesus’ feet, begging him to enter his house. If God is the head of Christ, then the feet should consequently be understood as the incarnation, through which he touched the earth of our mortality. The ruler of the synagogue therefore fell at Jesus’ feet because the lawgiver, together with the whole succession of the fathers, recognized that Christ appearing in the flesh was far superior to him in the glory of dignity. He diligently proclaimed what the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1).

He begged him to enter his house because he desired to see his coming with continual vows of joy. “My soul,” says the Prophet, “shall rejoice in the Lord and delight in his Jesus. All my bones shall say, ‘Lord, who is like you?’” (Ps. 35). This too is to fall at Jesus’ feet: to confess in devout faith that he alone is uniquely great above all.

For he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. This is the synagogue itself, formed solely by legal instruction, as though born as Moses’ only daughter. At about the twelfth year of her age—that is, as the time of puberty approached—she was dying. Nobly raised by the prophets, after she had reached the age of understanding, after she ought to have produced spiritual fruits for God, she was suddenly overwhelmed by the sickness of error and hopelessly ceased to enter the paths of spiritual life. Unless Christ had come to her aid, she would have fallen utterly into a dreadful death.

And it happened that, as he went, he was pressed by the crowd. As the Lord went to heal the girl, he was pressed by the crowd, because, while offering the Jewish people saving admonitions by which he might raise its conscience, sick with its vices, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

And there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. The woman suffering from the flow of blood is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Polluted by the congenital flow of carnal pleasures, she had already been separated from the assembly of the faithful. But when the Word of God resolved to save Judea, she seized the salvation already prepared and promised to others through confident hope.

It should be noted that the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was twelve years old and that this woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years: that is, at the very time when the one was born, the other began to be ill. At almost one and the same age of this world, the synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, while the nation of the Gentiles began throughout the world to be defiled by the corruption of idolatry.

The twofold flow of blood may also be understood as referring both to prostitution through idolatry and to the deeds performed for the delight of flesh and blood. Hence sacred history beautifully reports that, when David was still a boy and struck down the giant Goliath, the Philistines were encamped in the territory of Dommim—that is, “of bloods.” For when the Lord appeared in humility to overthrow the ruler of the world, he found the Gentile peoples devoted not only to fruitless works but also to the most polluted religion.

Therefore, as long as the synagogue flourished, the Church suffered. Its decline is the Church’s strength, because through their offense salvation came to the Gentiles.

She had spent all her resources on physicians, and no one could cure her. The physicians signify either false theologians, or philosophers and teachers of secular laws, who, discoursing with great subtlety about virtues and vices, promised that they could give mortals useful rules for seeing and believing; or, certainly, they signify the unclean spirits themselves, who, as though offering counsel to human beings, thrust themselves forward to be worshiped in place of God. The more the Gentiles exhausted the powers of their natural ingenuity in listening to these teachers one after another, the less were they able to be healed of the filth of their iniquity.

Thus Mark, writing about this woman, says: “She had suffered much from many physicians and had spent all that she had, and had gained nothing, but rather had grown worse.” But when this woman recognized that the Jewish people was sick and that the true physician had come from heaven, she too began both to hope for and to seek a remedy for her illness.

She approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped. The Church approaches and touches the Lord, drawing near to him through the truth of faith. She approaches from behind, either in accordance with what he himself says, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12), and with the command elsewhere, “You shall walk after the Lord your God”; or because, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, after the mysteries of his temporal dispensation had been accomplished, she began already through faith to follow his footsteps.

She touches the fringe of his garment and stops the flow of blood, because blessed—and truly in need of cleansing—is the person who touches even the outermost part of the word with the hand of faith. For very few are worthy either to recline upon his breast or to anoint his head with pure nard, although great was the one who considered himself unworthy to carry his sandals, and great also was the woman who was deemed worthy to anoint his feet and wipe them with her hair.

And Jesus said: “Who touched me?” He does not ask in order to be taught what he does not know, but so that the power of the faith he knew—indeed, the faith he himself had given—might be declared in the woman.

But when all denied it, Peter and those who were with him said: “Master, the crowds press upon you and distress you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” While crowds accompanying him indiscriminately press upon him, one believing woman touches the Lord. For the one who is afflicted by the various, disorderly masses of heresies seeks him with the faithful heart of the Catholic Church alone.

For just as some see without seeing and hear without hearing, so too some touch without touching: those who do not touch Christ faithfully. Hence he says to a certain person who loved him but did not yet fully believe: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20), openly teaching what it means to touch him truly—namely, to believe that he is equal to the Father.

And Jesus said: “Someone touched me. For I know that power has gone out from me,” and so forth. Let Pelagius say, if he wishes, that he is saved by his own effort. But let us say that “human salvation is vain; in God we shall exercise power.” For he himself knows that the power that propitiates all our iniquities and heals all our illnesses goes forth not from us but from him. Therefore the one who has touched the fringe—that is, the mysteries of the incarnation—does not remain hidden from him, until he advances to grasp greater things and believes by loving perfectly.

But he said to her: “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace.” He calls her “daughter” because her faith has saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you.” In the very act of believing, you have already been saved.

While he was still speaking, someone came to the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him: “Your daughter has died; do not trouble him.” After the woman was saved from the flow of blood, the ruler’s daughter was immediately announced to have died, because, while the Church was cleansed from the stain of vices and called “daughter” on account of the merit of faith, the synagogue was immediately released from the law of both unbelief and envy. From unbelief, because it refused to believe in Christ; from envy, because it was grieved that the Church had believed.

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was spoken by Paul, reviling the way before the multitude” (Acts 13).

“Do not trouble him” is still said today by those who see the condition of the synagogue so abandoned that they do not believe it can be restored, and therefore do not think that one should pray for its resurrection. But “the things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God” (Luke 18). Hence it follows:

But when Jesus heard this word, he answered the girl’s father: “Do not fear. Only believe, and she will be saved.” The girl’s father is understood as the assembly of teachers of the law, of whom the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23). If he himself wishes to believe, the synagogue subject to him will also be saved.

And when he had entered the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter, James, and John, and the girl’s father and mother. Above, the son of the widow is raised publicly; here, many witnesses are excluded. I think, therefore, that the Lord’s compassion is also shown in this: because the widowed mother of an only son could not bear delay, haste was added so that she would not suffer longer.

It is also a figure of wisdom: the Church would believe quickly in the widow’s son, whereas in the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter the Jews would indeed believe, but fewer of them.

And all were weeping and mourning for her. “Can the children of the bridegroom,” he says, “mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” Thus the synagogue, because it lost the joy of the bridegroom by which it could live, lies as though dead among mourners, without even understanding the reason for which it is mourned.

But he said: “Do not weep. She is not dead, but sleeping.” Dead to human beings, who could not raise her, she was sleeping to God, in whose power her soul lived after being received, and her flesh rested, awaiting resurrection. Hence Christian usage has established that the dead, who are not doubted to be destined for resurrection, should be called “sleeping,” as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4).

In the allegorical sense as well, although “the soul that sins shall itself die,” the soul that has deserved to be raised by Christ may be said to have been dead to us but to have fallen asleep for him.

And they mocked him, knowing that she was dead. Because they preferred to mock the word of the one raising her rather than believe it, they are rightly excluded outside, unworthy to see the miracle of the one rising.

But he took her by the hand and cried out, saying: “Girl, arise.” In Mark it is written: “He said to her, ‘Talitha cumi,’ which is translated, ‘Girl, I say to you, arise’; and immediately the girl arose” (Mark 5). Here the attentive reader may ask why the truthful Evangelist, explaining the Savior’s words, inserted “I say to you” on his own authority, when in the Syriac expression he included there it says no more than “Girl, arise.”

Jesus therefore took the girl by the hand and healed her, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their dead synagogue will not rise.

And her spirit returned, and she immediately arose. Mark says: “Immediately the girl arose and walked.” Spiritually, he indicates that whoever recovers from the death of the soul, with Christ strengthening him by his hand, must not only rise from the filth of vices but also immediately advance in good works.

And he ordered that she be given something to eat. As evidence that she had truly been restored to life, he ordered her to eat, so that she would be believed to be not a phantom but a reality. Likewise, if someone has risen from spiritual death, he must immediately be satisfied with heavenly bread, becoming a participant both in the divine word and in the most holy altar.

According to the moral interpretation, those three dead whom the Savior raised in their bodies signify three kinds of resurrection of souls. Some bring death upon themselves by consenting to an evil pleasure while the thought of sin remains hidden. To signify that he gives life to such people, the Savior raised the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, who had not yet been carried outside but had died in the house—as though she concealed the vice secretly in her heart.

Others not only consent to a harmful pleasure but also perform the very evil in which they delight, carrying forth their dead self as though outside the gates. To show that such people are restored through repentance, he raised the widow’s young son, who had been carried outside the gates, and returned him to his mother. For he restores the soul recovering from the darkness of sin to the unity of the Church, as we have also taught above.

Others corrupt themselves not only by thinking or doing what is unlawful but also by burying themselves, as it were, in the very habit of sinning. Yet the Savior’s power and grace are no less effective in raising these, provided that attentive thoughts are present, keeping watch over their salvation like sisters devoted to Christ.

To indicate this, he raised Lazarus, who had already been four days in the tomb and, as his sister testified, already stank. For a very bad reputation commonly accompanies harmful acts.

It should be noted that the heavier the death of the soul that has descended upon it, the more intensely the penitent’s fervor must necessarily persist if the soul is to deserve to rise. Wishing secretly to show this, the Lord raises the dead girl lying in a chamber with a moderate and gentle voice, saying: “Girl, arise.” And, because of the ease of raising her, he had denied that she was already dead.

But when the young man had been carried outside, he strengthens him with more words, so that he might rise again, saying: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” But when the dead man had lain for four days, so that he might cast off the long barriers of the oppressive tomb, Jesus groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, groaned again, and cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11). Thus at last the one who had been despaired of is restored to life and light after the weight of darkness has been shaken off.

It should also be noted that, because public wrongdoing requires a public remedy, while lesser sins can be erased by a lesser and private penance, the girl lying in the house rises before a few witnesses, and those same witnesses are commanded not to spread the miracle.

And, he says, her parents were astonished, and he commanded them to tell no one what had happened. The young man is raised outside the gate, with a large crowd accompanying and watching. Lazarus, called from the tomb, became so well known among the people that, because of the testimony of those who had seen him, very large crowds came to meet the Lord with palms, and many of the Jews departed because of him and believed in Jesus.

The fourth dead man the Lord recognizes when a disciple reports him; but because there were no living people to pray to the Lord for his rescue, he says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8)—that is, let the wicked burden the wicked with harmful praises; and, because there is no righteous person present to rebuke them mercifully, let the sinner’s oil make their head fat.

## CHAPTER 9

When Jesus had called together the twelve apostles, he gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure illnesses. And he sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.

Having first granted them the power to perform signs, he sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of their deeds might also testify to the greatness of the promises, the power displayed might lend credibility to their words, and those who proclaimed new things might perform new things.

Hence even now, although the number of the faithful has grown, there are many within the holy Church who possess a virtuous life but do not possess signs of virtue. For a miracle is displayed outwardly in vain if there is nothing working inwardly. For, according to the voice of the teacher of the nations, tongues are “a sign not for believers but for unbelievers.”

And he said to them: “Take nothing for the journey—neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.” It is often asked how Matthew and Luke can have reported that the Lord told the disciples not even to carry a staff, when Mark says, “He commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff” [Col. 0446B]. [Col. 0446C] This is resolved by understanding that the staff which, according to Mark, is to be carried has one meaning, while the staff which, according to Matthew and Luke, is not to be carried has another. So too “temptation” has one meaning in the statement, “God tempts no one,” and another in the statement, “The Lord your God is tempting you, to know whether you love him.” The former is seduction; the latter is testing.

Both statements, therefore, are to be understood as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles: that they should carry no staff, and that they should carry nothing except a staff. For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matt. 10), and so forth, he immediately added, “For the laborer is worthy of his food” (ibid.). Thus he plainly showed why he did not want them to possess and carry these things. It was not because they are unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to show that these things were owed them by those to whom they proclaimed the Gospel and who believed it.

It is clear that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought to live from no other source than what those to whom they proclaim the Gospel provide. Otherwise the Apostle would have acted against this command when he supported himself by the labor of his hands, so as to be a burden to no one. Rather, the Lord gave them authority by which they might know that these things were owed them. When something is commanded by the master, failure to do it is the fault of disobedience. But when authority is granted, anyone may choose not to use it and may, as it were, relinquish what is his own right.

Thus, when the Lord established—as the Apostle says he established—that [Col. 0446D] those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel, he was telling the apostles that they should confidently possess or carry none of the necessities of this life, whether great or small. Therefore he added, “Nor a staff,” showing that everything is owed by the faithful to his ministers, who demand nothing superfluous. By adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10), he completely disclosed and clarified the reason for all that he was saying.

He therefore signified this authority by the name “staff” when he said that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff. This is to be understood as meaning that, through the authority received from the Lord and signified by the name “staff,” even what is not carried will not be lacking. The same is to be understood concerning two tunics: none of them should think that, besides the one he was wearing, he needed to carry another, anxious that one might be necessary, since he could receive it by virtue of that authority.

[Col. 0447A] But when, according to Mark, he forbids not merely carrying or having two tunics but more expressly wearing them, saying, “And that they should not put on two tunics” (Mark 6), what does he urge them to do except to walk not in duplicity but simply? Alternatively: by “two tunics” he seems to me to indicate a double garment. This does not mean that in the regions of Scythia and places stiff with icy snow one ought to be content with a single tunic; rather, by “tunic” we are to understand clothing, so that, being clothed in one garment, we do not keep another for fear of the future.

“And into whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not depart from it.” He gives a general command of steadfastness, so that they may preserve the rights of hospitality, asserting that it is alien to a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to hurry from house to house and change the inviolable obligations of lodging. Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles enter is determined for them, so that there may be no opportunity to change their lodging and violate the obligations of hospitality [Col. 0447A].

“And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” Dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: that they entered the city and that the apostolic preaching reached those people. Or the dust is shaken off so that they may receive nothing from them—not even what is necessary for food—because they rejected the Gospel.

Allegorically, those who listen humbly to the word, if they have been obscured by the stains of earthly frivolity, are cleansed by the traces of evangelical preaching that they soon receive. But those who contemptuously reject it through unbelief, negligence, or even deliberate intent are judged to be avoided in fellowship; their synagogue is to be shunned, and the dust of the feet shaken off, lest the pure trace of the mind be polluted by deeds committed with the hands and comparable to dust.

Having gone out, they traveled through the villages, evangelizing and healing everywhere. What the apostles proclaimed and how they healed, Mark explains more fully. “They preached,” he says, “that they should repent; and they anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.” James also says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (Mark 6) [Col. 0447B–D].

From this it is clear that this custom of the holy Church was handed down by the apostles themselves: that the sick should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing. They preached that people should repent. Earlier he says, “He sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). For, following the example of John the Baptist and of the Savior himself, they preached both: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3). To draw near to the gates of the kingdom of heaven is to repent of those five things by which one had departed from him.

Now Herod the tetrarch heard everything that was happening, and he was perplexed because some people were saying that John had risen from the dead. How great was the envy of the Jews, and what fury of malice arose against the Lord, we learn from almost every part of the Gospel. They believed, without any witness, that John—of whom it had been said that he performed no sign—could rise from the dead. Yet they preferred to believe that Jesus, a man approved by God through powers and signs, whose death had made the elements tremble and whose resurrection and ascension angels, apostles, men, and women proclaimed eagerly, had not risen but had been secretly removed.

It should not be thought contradictory that Luke says Herod was perplexed because some people were saying that John had risen from the dead, while Matthew and Mark report that Herod himself, having heard the report about Jesus, said to his attendants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore the powers are at work in him” (Matt. 14). We should understand that after this perplexity he confirmed in his mind what others were saying [Col. 0448A–B].

And Herod said: “John I beheaded. Who, then, is this man about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. These are the words of Herod in his perplexity, mentioned above. Because he had learned from the report that this man was great, he also desired to see him, in case he might recognize whether he was John himself.

The other Evangelists describe the sequence and cause of John’s beheading in full. Luke, in his usual manner, preferred to mention it in order to indicate the state of the times, rather than repeat what he saw had already been sufficiently stated. Yet since John’s beheading is mentioned, we should note that John and the Lord each declared his own status and destiny both in the order of their births and in the order of their passion. John was beheaded, while the Lord was exalted upon the cross. John was born when the days began to grow shorter; the Lord when they began to grow longer. Thus it might also appear through these events what is meant by, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3): the one who was thought to be a prophet must be recognized as the Christ, and I, who was thought to be the Christ, must be understood to be his precursor [Col. 0448C].

When the apostles returned, they reported to him everything they had done. They told the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John had suffered while they were occupied in teaching; or Christ himself, or the disciples of that same John, reported this to him, as Matthew indicates. Hence what follows:

“And taking them with him, he withdrew privately to a deserted place, which is Bethsaida.” He did not do this out of fear of death, as some think, but out of mercy toward his enemies, lest they add one murder to another, while at the same time awaiting the appropriate time for his own passion. Anyone who reads the Gospels carefully will find that John’s passion and the Lord’s were separated by more than a year.

Indeed, the Lord performed the miracle of the loaves, as the three agreeing Evangelists testify, after John’s beheading. In describing the miracle, John first stated that the Passover, the Jewish feast, was near; afterward he said that Jesus went up to their feast of Booths. When they sought to seize him as he taught in the temple, he says, “No one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come” (John 7); and then, at the time of the following Passover, he completed the triumph of the cross.

After John had been killed, therefore, the Lord awaited the appointed time and withdrew privately to a deserted place, Bethsaida. Mystically, he was teaching that, after Judah had been abandoned—the Judah that, by refusing to believe the prophecy, had removed its head—he would bestow the nourishment of the word in the desert of the Church, which had no husband. Thus Bethsaida is fittingly interpreted as “house of fruits.” It is the place of which Isaiah says: “The deserted and impassable land shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult, and shall blossom like a lily” (Isa. 35); and shortly afterward: “They shall see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God” (ibid.).

Bethsaida is a city in Galilee, the city of the apostles Andrew, Peter, and Philip, near Lake Gennesaret, as we find in books on places [Col. 0448D–0449A].

When the crowds learned this, they followed him. He received them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and he healed those who needed healing. The Lord tests the faith of the crowds and rewards tested faith with a fitting recompense. By seeking solitude, he tests whether they will take care to follow him. By following—not on different animals or vehicles, but, as the other Evangelists report, by undertaking the journey through the wilderness through the labor of their own feet—they show how great is their concern for their salvation.

In turn, by receiving the weary as a powerful and compassionate Savior and physician, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, and refreshing the hungry, he indicates how much he delights in the devotion of believers. According to the laws of allegory, great companies of the faithful, having left the walls of their former way of life and neglected the defenses of various doctrines, follow Christ as he seeks the deserts of the nations. The God who was formerly known in Judah, after the teeth of the Jews became weapons and arrows and their tongue a sharp sword against him, says: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. 56) [Col. 0449B–C].

The day had begun to decline. The Twelve approached and said to him: “Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go into the surrounding villages and farms, find lodging, and obtain food.” As the day declined, the Savior refreshes the crowds, because either, as the end of the ages approaches, or when the Sun of righteousness set for us, we have been saved from the long wasting of spiritual hunger.

But he said to them: “You give them something to eat.” He urges the apostles to break the bread, so that when they testify that they do not have enough, the greatness of the sign may become more evident. At the same time he intimates that through them our hungry hearts must be fed every day.

For what does Peter do when he speaks through his Epistles except satisfy our grievously hungry hearts with the nourishment of the word? What do Paul and John accomplish when they speak through their Epistles except enable our minds to receive heavenly food and overcome the disgust of the hunger by which they were dying?

But they said: “We have no more than five loaves and two fish.” As yet the apostles had no more than the five loaves of the Mosaic Law and the two fish of the two Testaments, which, because of the mystery of hidden things concealed for a long time, were covered and nourished, as it were, beneath the waters of the abyss.

According to John’s Gospel, the loaves are said to have been barley loaves, which are chiefly the food of beasts and rustic servants, because harsher and, as it were, coarser commandments are to be entrusted to beginners and to hearers not yet perfected. “The natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore the Lord, giving gifts to each according to his strength and always urging them toward greater perfection, first feeds five thousand with five loaves, then four thousand with seven loaves. Third, he entrusts to the disciples the mystery of his flesh and blood. Finally, as a great gift, he grants the elect that they may eat and drink at his table in the kingdom [Col. 0449D–0450A].

Now there were about five thousand men. Because the outward person has five senses, the five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who, still situated in a worldly manner of life, know how to use well the external things they possess. They are rightly nourished with five loaves, because such people must still be instructed by the commandments of the Law.

But those who completely renounce the world are four thousand and are refreshed with seven loaves—that is, they are both exalted by evangelical refreshment and instructed by spiritual grace. I think that this difference is mystically signified by the fact that at the entrance of the tabernacle five gilded columns were ordered to be made, but before the sanctuary—that is, the Holy of Holies—four were ordered. Beginners are chastened through the Law so that they may not sin; the perfect, through grace, are admonished to live more devotedly for God [Col. 0450B].

Then he said to his disciples: “Have them sit down in groups of fifty.” And they did so. The various arrangements of the diners signify the various gatherings throughout the world of the Churches that constitute one catholic Church. They sat down not only in groups of fifty, but, as Mark attests, also in groups of one hundred.

Since the fiftieth psalm is the psalm of repentance, while the number one hundred passes from the left to the right, those who still remain in repentance for their sins sit down at the Lord’s banquet in groups of fifty and receive the hearing of the word. Those in groups of one hundred already sigh with the sole desire for eternal life, having presumed the hope of forgiveness.

Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and distributed them to his disciples to set before the crowds. When the crowds were hungry, the Savior did not create new food, but, taking what the disciples had, he blessed it. For when he came in the flesh, he preached nothing other than what had been foretold; rather, he showed that the sayings of prophecy were filled with the mysteries of grace.

He looks up to heaven to teach that the eye of the mind must be directed there, and that the light of knowledge must be sought there. He breaks the loaves and distributes them through the disciples to be set before the crowds, because he discloses to those who preach throughout the world the mysteries of the Law and the prophets, which had been closed [Col. 0450C–D].

And what remained over from the fragments was gathered up: twelve baskets. What remains for the crowds is gathered up by the disciples, because the more sacred mysteries, which cannot be grasped by the untrained, are not to be carelessly neglected but are to be sought by the perfect.

Through the twelve baskets the apostles are represented, and through the apostles all the choirs of succeeding teachers: outwardly despised by men, but inwardly filled with the remnants of saving food for nourishing the hearts of the humble. It is well known that baskets are ordinarily used for servile work; yet he filled the baskets with fragments of bread—the one who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong [Col. 0451A].

And it happened that, while he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. The disciples were present with the Lord and followed him on the way, as Mark indicates, but he prayed to the Father alone. The saints can be joined to the Lord through the fellowship of faith and love; they can behold him as distinguished from other mortals by the majesty of divine glory; and they can follow, with the steps of humility, the way he taught while living in the flesh. But the Son alone knows how to penetrate the incomprehensible secrets of the Father’s purpose.

For nowhere, if I am not mistaken, is he found praying with the disciples; everywhere he entreats alone, because human prayers do not grasp God’s plan, and no one can share with Christ in the inner things [Col. 0451B].

And he asked them, saying: “Who do the crowds say that I am?” They answered and said: “John the Baptist; but others say Elijah; and others that one of the ancient prophets has risen.”

Beautifully, wishing to test the faith of the disciples, the Lord first asks the opinion of the crowds, lest their confession seem to have been confirmed not by recognition of the truth but by popular opinion, and lest they appear to believe what they had discovered but, like Herod, to be perplexed by what they had heard.

Hence, too, when Peter confesses him as the Christ, he says according to Matthew: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. 16)—that is, human teaching did not teach you the truth of faith.

It is also fitting that those who express different opinions about the Lord are designated by the name “crowds,” whose sense and speech are always uncertain, unstable, and wandering. To distinguish his disciples from them, he immediately adds:

“But you—who do you say that I am?” The disciples of Christ are not from the crowd. Those who walk alone with the Lord are not from the crowd; nor are those who are found worthy to see him praying more privately. Yet if someone from the crowd believes in Christ, he immediately ceases to be from the crowd [Col. 0451C].

Simon Peter answered and said: “The Christ of God.” Although the other apostles knew it, Peter answered before the others. He embraced everything, expressing both nature and name, in which the sum of the virtues is found.

Are we still to raise questions about the generation of God? When Paul judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2), and Peter thought that nothing more than the confession of the Son of God should be made, are we to investigate when and how he was born and how great he is through contemplation shaped by human weakness?

The end of my faith, therefore, is Christ; the end of my faith is the Son of God. I am not permitted to know the sequence of his generation, yet I am not permitted to be ignorant of the faith of his generation [Col. 0451D].

But he rebuked them and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying that the Son of Man must suffer many things, and so forth. For this reason he did not wish to be preached before his passion and resurrection, so that, after the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he might more appropriately say to the apostles: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

It would not have profited him to be publicly preached, nor his majesty to be proclaimed among the peoples, when shortly afterward they would see him scourged and crucified, suffering many things at the hands of the elders, scribes, and chief priests.

It should also be noted that he calls the one who must suffer many things, be killed, and rise again “the Son of Man,” because, while Christ suffered in the flesh, his divinity remained incapable of suffering. It should further be noted that he himself confesses that he is the Son of Man, while Peter confesses him as the Christ, the Son of God, so that from both confessions he may be proved true God and true man [Col. 0452A].

And he said to all: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” He fittingly said, “to all,” because he had dealt with the preceding matters concerning faith in the Lord’s birth and passion privately with the disciples alone.

We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through our former state and strive toward what we are called to be through renewal. Let Truth therefore speak—let Truth speak: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” Unless someone falls away from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him. Nor can he grasp what lies beyond him if he does not know how to destroy what he is.
