But once someone has denied himself with regard to vices, he must seek the virtues in which he may grow. For it immediately follows:

“And let him take up his cross daily and follow me.” The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor.

Let us consider how Paul carried his cross in both ways. He said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified” (1 Cor. 9). There we heard the cross of the flesh in the affliction of the body; now let us hear the cross of the mind in compassion for one’s neighbor. He says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11).

In both forms of bearing the cross, however, we must note that we are commanded to take it up daily and, having taken it up, to follow the Lord [Col. 0452B–C].

“For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.” This is said to the faithful: “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will save it”—as though one were saying to a farmer: “If you preserve the grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it.”

Who does not know that when grain is cast into the seed, it disappears from sight and perishes in the earth? Yet from the place where it rots in the dust, it becomes green through renewal.

Since the holy Church has one time of persecution and another of peace, our Redeemer designated these different times in his commandments. In a time of persecution, one’s life must be laid down; in a time of peace, the earthly desires that are able to dominate us must be broken. Hence it is now said:

“For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but loses or harms himself?” When persecution from adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with far greater vigilance. In a time of peace, because it is permitted to live, it is also permitted to pursue ambitions.

Often we despise all passing things, yet we are still hindered by the habits of human shame, so that we are not yet able to express in speech the uprightness we preserve in the mind. But an appropriate remedy is added for this wound when the Lord says:

“For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his own majesty, and in that of the Father and of the holy angels.”

But people now say among themselves: “We are no longer ashamed of the Lord and his words, because we confess him openly.” To them I answer that among this Christian people there are some who confess Christ for this reason: they see that everyone is Christian.

The voice of confession is therefore not sufficient as proof of faith when a general profession protects it from shame. Yet each person has a place where he must examine himself, so as to prove himself truthful in confessing Christ.

Certainly, in a time of persecution, the faithful could be ashamed of being stripped of their possessions, thrown down from their dignities, and afflicted with blows. But in a time of peace, since persecution from our enemies is absent, there is another place where we may be exposed to ourselves.

We are often afraid of being despised by those close to us and disdain to endure verbal insults. If a quarrel perhaps arises with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make amends. The carnal heart, while seeking the glory of this life, rejects humility [Col. 0452D–0453B].

“But I tell you truly: there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” In this passage the present Church is called the kingdom of God. Since some of the disciples were to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God built and raised up against the glory of this world, the following consoling promise is now made: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

But since the Lord had given so many commands concerning the death they would have to undergo, why was it necessary for him suddenly to come to this promise? It was because something also had to be promised to the inexperienced disciples concerning the present life, so that they might be strengthened more firmly for the future. He promises them that they will see the kingdom of God on earth, so that they may anticipate it more confidently in heaven.

If, however, in this saying we wish to understand the kingdom of God as the future blessedness of heaven, then some of those standing there saw it on the mountain not many days later. They saw it so that, through contemplation of the abiding joy—although they tasted it only briefly—they might endure more calmly the adversities of the passing age.

With very appropriate language he testifies that the saints taste death, since they taste bodily death, as it were, by taking a sip, but possess the life of the soul [Col. 0453C–D].

Now about eight days after these sayings, he took Peter, James, and John. On the eighth day the Lord reveals to the disciples the glory that promises future blessedness, so that, by displaying the sweetness of heavenly life, he might refresh the hearts of all who could hear these things, and teach through the number eight that the true joy of the resurrection would come.

He himself also rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the sixth day of the week, on which he ascended the cross, and the seventh day of the week, on which he rested in the tomb. We too, after the six ages of this world, during which we rejoice to suffer and labor for the Lord, and after the seventh age of the repose of souls that meanwhile takes place in another life, will rise as though in an eighth age.

Matthew and Mark say that the Lord was transfigured after six days, but this does not conflict either with the order of time or with the reasoning of the mystery. They count only the intervening days and therefore simply say, “after six days.” Here the first and last days are also included, and therefore he more moderately mentions approximately eight days.

The former passage signifies that, after the six ages of the world, the saints will rest from their labor; this passage signifies that they will rise in the eighth time. Hence the sixth psalm is beautifully titled “For the Eighth,” and begins: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” For after the six ages in which it is permitted to work, we must persist in prayer, lest in the eighth time—the time of retribution—we be rebuked by an angry judge. The Lord himself wished to teach us this in the present passage by displaying the example of his prayer, as follows [Col. 0454A–B]:

“And he went up the mountain to pray.” He went up the mountain to pray and then to be transfigured, showing that those who await the fruit of the resurrection and desire to see the King in his beauty must dwell in the heights of the mind and devote themselves to continual prayers.

He takes only three disciples with him because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). Those who here preserve with an incorrupt mind the faith with which they have been imbued in the holy Trinity will there be found worthy to rejoice in its eternal vision.

And it happened that, while he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing was white and radiant. The transfigured Savior did not lose the substance of true flesh; rather, he displayed the glory of the future resurrection, whether his own or ours. As he appeared then to the apostles, so after the judgment he will appear to all the elect.

At the very time of judgment he will be seen by both the good and the wicked in the form of a servant, so that the impious who rejected him, the Jews who denied him, the soldiers who crucified him, and Pilate and Herod who judged him may recognize the judge.

The Lord’s clothing is understood as the choir of his saints, concerning which the Apostle says in glorification: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). This garment, while the Lord remained on earth, appeared despised and like that of others; but when he ascends the mountain, it shines with new brightness, because “now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Mark, describing these garments, therefore says: “Such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark 9). For the fuller to be understood here is the one whom the repentant Psalmist implores: “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. 50). He cannot give his faithful on earth the brightness that awaits them, preserved for them in heaven [Col. 0454C–D].

And behold, two men were speaking with him. They were Moses and Elijah. We read that one died and that the other was taken up into heaven; do they not signify, in majesty with the Lord, the future glory of all the saints, who at the time of judgment will reign with him together, whether they are found alive in the flesh or raised after having long ago tasted death?

For the Apostle testifies: “The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

Alternatively: Moses and Elijah—that is, the lawgiver and the greatest of the prophets—appear and speak with the Lord to show that he is the one whom all the writings of the Law and the prophets promised.

They appear not in the low places but on the mountain with him, because only those who seek the heights with their minds will perceive the majesty of Holy Scripture, which has been fulfilled in the Lord.

Indeed, the Jews also saw Moses, but were not found worthy to follow him as he ascended into the mountain toward God. They saw him even when he returned to them, but not without a veil. They knew Elijah, but only Elisha, with the sons of the prophets, contemplated the triumph of the one ascending. We read the words of Scripture in many places, but very few understand how brightly it shines in the mysteries of Christ [Col. 0455A–B].

And they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. Even to this day the Law and the prophets, wherever they find people at the summit of true faith, teach with mutually agreeing voices the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation.

But Peter and those who were with him were weighed down by sleep. When they awoke, they saw his majesty and the two men standing with him. The disciples were not weighed down by sleep through accidental circumstance, but for the sake of the mystery, so that after the repose of the body they might see an image of the resurrection.

When the saints are awakened to glory, they will see the Lord’s majesty all the more truly because they will also rejoice in the immortality of their own flesh, in which they conquered death. Then they will behold Moses and Elijah in glory, because they will understand more fully how not one iota or one stroke has passed from the Law, and that the Lord did not come to destroy the Law or the prophets but to fulfill them (Matt. 5) [Col. 0455C].

And it happened that, as they were departing from him, Peter said to Jesus: “Teacher, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he was saying.

O how great the happiness of remaining forever among the choirs of angels in the vision of the Godhead, if the sight of Christ’s humanity transformed, together with the company of two saints, delights us for even a moment so greatly that Peter wishes to keep them from departing even by an act of service!

Although, in accordance with human limitation, he does not know what he is saying, he nevertheless reveals the ardor implanted within him. He did not know what he was saying because he had forgotten that the Lord had promised the kingdom to the saints not in some earthly place but in heaven; that he and his fellow apostles, still weighed down by mortal flesh, could not enter the condition of immortal life; and that in that age a house made by human hands would not be necessary.

Even now the same ignorance is noted in anyone who wishes to make three tents for the Law, the prophets, and the Gospel, although these cannot in any way be separated from one another, since they have one tent—that is, the Church of God [Col. 0455D–0456A].

While he was saying this, a cloud came and overshadowed them. The one who sought a material tent receives the shelter of a cloud, so that he may learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the covering of buildings but by the glory of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The children of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Ps. 56). And John says in his Apocalypse: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

And they were afraid when they entered the cloud; and a voice came from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” Human frailty cannot endure the sight of a greater glory, and, trembling in soul and body, falls to the ground. The more someone seeks what is lofty, the more he collapses into lower things if he does not know his own measure.

The voice of the Father speaking from heaven is clearly heard, bearing witness to the Son and, after removing Peter’s error, teaching the truth—in Peter, indeed, teaching the other apostles as well.

“This is my beloved Son,” it says. “A tent is to be made for him; he is to be obeyed. He is the Son; Moses and Elijah are servants. They too, together with you, must prepare a tent for the Lord in the innermost chambers of their hearts.”

Observe also that, just as when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, so when he was glorified on the mountain, the mystery of the entire Trinity is declared. The glory that we confess in baptism we shall see in the resurrection.

Nor does the Holy Spirit appear here without purpose in a luminous cloud and there in a dove. Whoever now preserves with a simple heart the faith he receives will then contemplate in the clear light of vision what he believed, and will be protected forever by the very grace by which he will be illumined [Col. 0456B–C].

And when the voice had come, Jesus was found alone. When the Son began to be designated, the servants immediately departed, lest the Father’s voice be thought to have been addressed to them.

Alternatively: when the voice came concerning the Son, he alone was found, because when he manifests himself to the elect, “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15); indeed, Christ himself with his own will be one in every respect—the head shining together with the body.

It is on account of this unity that he said elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. The future kingdom had been anticipated, and the glory of the triumphant one displayed, on the mountain. The disciples therefore remained silent and, at the Lord’s command, told no one about the vision until the Son of Man should rise from the dead, lest its greatness make it seem unbelievable and, after so great a glory, the cross that followed should cause scandal in inexperienced minds [Col. 0456D].

And it came to pass on the following day, as they were coming down from the mountain, that a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, saying: “Teacher, I beg you, look upon my son, because he is my only child.” The setting corresponds to the events: on the mountain the Lord prays, is transformed, and opens to the disciples the mysteries of his majesty; descending to the lower places, he is received by the encounter with the crowd and assailed by the weeping of the afflicted. Above, he discloses the mysteries of the kingdom to the disciples; below, he reproves the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he reveals the Father’s voice to those who were able to follow him; below, he drives evil spirits out of those who were tormented. Even now he does not cease, according to the quality of their merits, to cause some to ascend and others to descend. For those who are still earthly and at the beginning, as though seeking the lowest places, he strengthens, teaches, and chastises; but those who are perfect, whose way of life is in heaven, he glorifies by raising them to a higher place, instructs them more freely concerning eternal things, and often teaches them what the crowds are not even permitted to hear.

And behold, the spirit seized him, and suddenly cried out, and threw him down and convulsed him with foam; and only with difficulty did it depart from him, after rending him. Matthew describes this demoniac, whom the Lord healed when he came down from the mountain, as a lunatic; Mark describes him as deaf and mute. He signifies those of whom it is written: “A fool is changed like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:11)—those who, never remaining in the same condition, are changed now toward these, now toward those vices, and increase and decrease; mute because they do not confess the faith, and deaf because they do not in any way hear even the word of faith itself.

“And I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.” By these words he secretly accuses the apostles, since the inability to heal sometimes relates not to the weakness of the healers but to the faith of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

But Jesus answered and said: “O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and endure you?” This does not mean that the gentle and mild one was overcome by weariness—he who did not open his mouth, like a lamb before its shearer (Isa. 53:7)—nor that he broke out into words of fury. Rather, it is as when a physician, seeing a sick person behaving contrary to his instructions, might say: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste the diligence of my art, while I command one thing and you do another?” Yet he was not angry with the man but with the vice; and through one man he rebuked the Jews for their unbelief, so that he immediately added:

“Bring your son here.” And as he approached, the demon threw him down and convulsed him. For as Jesus drew near, the demon threw the boy down and convulsed him, because often, after turning to God from our sins, we are assaulted by the ancient enemy with greater and new ambushes—he acts, namely, either to inflict hatred of virtue or to avenge the injury of his expulsion. Hence it is—as we pass from the particular to the general—that in the beginnings of the Church he brought about so many grievous conflicts, because he grieved at the sudden losses inflicted upon his kingdom.

And Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and returned him to his father. He rebukes not the boy, who was suffering the violence, but the demon, who was inflicting it. For one who desires to correct a sinner must indeed drive out the vice by reproving and hating it, but must restore the person by loving him, until, once healed, he can return him to the spiritual fathers of the Church.

While everyone was marveling at all the things he was doing, he said to his disciples: “Put these words into your hearts: the Son of Man is destined to be handed over into the hands of men.” Amid the great deeds of divine power he more frequently impresses and repeats the humiliation of his human passion, so that, when it came suddenly, it would not terrify them, but that they might receive it with a mind prepared beforehand. Indeed, when he says, “Put these words into your hearts,” the word “you” should be read with greater emphasis and force: you who cling more intimately to my discipleship, to whom I have disclosed more clearly the uncertain and hidden things of my wisdom (Ps. 50), while the others merely marvel at the divine deeds—store in your minds also the event of the precious blood by which the world is to be redeemed.

But they did not understand this saying. This ignorance of the disciples arose not so much from slowness as from love. They were still carnal and ignorant of the mystery of the cross, and, although they had come to know him as the true God, they could not believe that he would die. And because they were accustomed to hearing him speak through figures, they thought that what he said about his being handed over signified something else figuratively.

Then a thought entered them: which of them was the greater? Because they had seen Peter, James, and John led apart onto the mountain, and some secret matter entrusted to them there, and because the keys of the kingdom of heaven had earlier been promised to Peter and the Church was to be built upon him, they supposed either that those three were preferred to the others or that Peter was preferred to all the apostles. Some think that this thought was stirred in the disciples by the fact that, according to Matthew, the Lord gave the stater taken from the fish’s mouth to those who collected the tax, for himself and Peter—as though Peter were more prominent than the others—inasmuch as he was associated with the Lord himself in the payment of the tax. But a careful reader will find that this question had already been debated among them before the payment of the didrachma. Finally, Matthew records that this took place at Capernaum. Mark says: “And they came to Capernaum. When they were in the house, he questioned them: ‘What were you discussing on the way?’ But they were silent. For they had argued with one another on the way about which of them was the greater” (Mark 9:33–34). Whether, then, they were prompted by this occasion, or by that one, or by both, Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the causes of their error, wishes to heal their desire for glory through the practice of humility.

“Taking a child,” he says, “he set him beside himself and said to them: ‘Whoever receives this child in my name receives me.’” Either he teaches in a simple sense that Christ’s poor are to be received, for his honor, by those who wish to be greater; or certainly he urges them to be children in malice, so that, in imitation of the innocence of children, they may preserve simplicity without arrogance, charity without envy, and devotion without anger. Thus, when he said, “Whoever receives this child,” he rightly added, “in my name.” In other words, they are to follow, for the sake of Christ’s name and with the help of rational diligence, the pattern of virtue that a child observes under the guidance of nature. But because he taught that he himself was received in the child—namely, because he too was born as a child for us—lest he be thought to be only what he appeared to be, he added and said:

“And whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” He wished himself to be believed to be such and so great as the Father is. For, he says, there is no difference at all between him and me, so that whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

But John answered and said: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow us.” John, loving the Lord with exceptional devotion, and therefore worthy of being loved in return, thought that one who did not employ the service of obedience should be excluded from the benefit. But he is taught that no one should be kept away from the good that he possesses in part; rather, he should be invited to what he does not yet possess.

And Jesus said to him: “Do not forbid him. For whoever is not against you is for you.” Taught by this saying, the Apostle says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice” (Phil. 1:18). Yet although he rejoices even over those who proclaim Christ insincerely, and although such people, sometimes performing signs in Christ’s name, are judged not to be forbidden for the sake of the salvation of others, their own conscience is not thereby made secure through such signs. Rather, on that day, when they say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” they will receive the answer: “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23). Therefore, in heretics and evil Catholics we must detest and forbid not the common sacraments—which are with us and are not against us—but the division contrary to peace and truth, by which they are against us [the transmitted *non* is evidently corrupt], and by which they do not follow the Lord with us.

[Col. 0459C] It came to pass, when the days of his assumption were being fulfilled, that he firmly set his face to go to Jerusalem. By “the day of his assumption” he means the time of his passion, as its approach gradually brings him to Jerusalem. Let the pagans, therefore, cease mocking the crucified one as though he were merely a man: it is established that he foresaw the time of his crucifixion as God and, as one who was to be crucified willingly, sought the place where he was to be crucified with a firm face—that is, with a resolute and undaunted mind.

And they did not receive him, because his face was turned toward Jerusalem. Because the Samaritans saw that the Lord was going to Jerusalem, they did not receive him. For Jews do not associate with Samaritans, as the Evangelist John shows.

When his disciples James and John saw this, they said: “Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” But he turned and rebuked them, and said: “You do not know of what spirit you are.” Great and holy men, who already knew very well that this death, which separates the soul from the body, was not to be feared, nevertheless, in accordance with the disposition of those who feared it, punished certain sins with death. Thus a useful fear would be instilled in the living, while for those who were punished by death it would not be death itself but sin that caused harm; and they did not recklessly judge that sin might increase if such people continued to live—those to whom God had granted this kind of judgment. Hence Elijah put many to death, both by his own hand and by fire obtained from God. When the apostles, following his example, wished to call down fire from heaven to consume those who had refused them lodging, the Lord rebuked in them not the example of the holy prophet but their ignorance in seeking vengeance. He perceived that they desired retribution not out of love for correction but out of hatred. Therefore, after he taught them what it meant to love their neighbor as themselves, and after the Holy Spirit had also been infused into them, such acts of vengeance did not disappear entirely, though they occurred much more rarely than in the Old Testament. There, for the most part, people were servants and were constrained by fear; here, they were chiefly nourished in freedom through love. For, at the words of the apostle Peter, Ananias and his wife fell dead, and were not raised again but buried; and Paul says of a certain sinner: “I have handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his soul may be saved” (1 Cor. 5:5).

[Col. 0460B] “The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them.” And so, he says, you too should follow the deeds of him by whose spirit you are marked: now offering compassionate care, but judging justly in anger.

As they were traveling along the road, someone said to him: “I will follow you wherever you go,” and so forth. Wonderful and fearful alike is the just dispensation of the hidden judgment. The Samaritans are sought as people who might receive the Lord, and, because they refuse, they are forbidden to be struck down. This man promises to follow him and is sent away; another first desires to bury his father and is compelled to evangelize. Another, intending to follow the Lord, wishes first to announce this very thing at home, and is not permitted. Someone who does not follow Christ performs mighty works in Christ’s name and is ordered not to be forbidden. In all these individual cases we must say with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). And with Samuel: “Man sees what is outward, but the Lord looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7).

And Jesus said to them: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” From the Lord’s words it is shown that the one who promised service was rejected because, seeing the greatness of the signs, he wished to follow the Savior in order to seek profit from miraculous works, desiring the very thing that Simon Magus had wished to buy from Peter. Such faith is therefore rightly condemned by the Lord’s sentence, and he is told: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of riches and worldly profits, when I am so poor that I do not even have a little lodging and do not use a roof of my own?” Alternatively, he may be understood to have been moved by the Lord’s miracles and to have wished to follow him for empty boasting, which the birds signify. His profession of discipleship, however, was feigned; this pretense is signified by the name of foxes. By the laying down of his head he signified his humility, which had no place in that pretender and proud man.

But he said to another: “Follow me.” And he said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” He does not reject discipleship, but, wishing first to fulfill the pious duty of his father’s funeral and then to follow Christ more freely, he appears in every respect worthy for the Son of Man to lay his head upon—that is, for divinity to rest in a familiar dwelling within his humble breast.

And Jesus said to him: “Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and announce the kingdom of God.” It should be noted in this saying that sometimes lesser goods must be set aside in our actions for the sake of the usefulness of greater ones. For who does not know that burying the dead is the merit of a good work? And yet the man who had asked to be released in order to bury his father was told: “Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and announce the kingdom of God.” The service of this duty had to be postponed to the ministry of preaching: by the one, a dead man would bury the dead in the earth according to the flesh; by the other, he would raise the dead in soul to life. But how can the dead bury the dead unless one understands a twofold death? One is the death of nature, the other of guilt; one by which the soul is separated from the flesh, the other by which God is separated from the soul. Or perhaps he calls those who do not believe “the dead,” and “their own dead” those who would nevertheless leave the body without faith.

And another said: “I will follow you, Lord, but first permit me to announce this to those who are at home.” If a disciple who is going to follow the Lord is rebuked because he wishes merely to announce this even at home, what will become of those who, with no useful purpose and no intention of building up faith, do not fear to revisit repeatedly the homes of their relatives whom they left behind in the world?

And Jesus said to him: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” To put one’s hand to the plow is, as though with an instrument of compunction, to wear down the hardness of one’s heart with the wood and iron of the Lord’s passion and to open it for bringing forth the fruits of good works. If someone, beginning to cultivate it, takes pleasure in looking back with Lot’s wife toward the vices he had left behind, he is already deprived of the gift of the coming kingdom.

# CHAPTER X

After this the Lord appointed another seventy-two. Just as no one doubts that the twelve apostles both exhibit and prefigure the model of bishops, so it must be understood that these seventy-two bore the figure of presbyters, that is, priests of the second order. Although in the earliest times of the Church, as apostolic Scripture testifies, both groups were called presbyters and both were called bishops. One of these numbers signifies maturity of wisdom, the other diligence in pastoral care.

It is fitting that seventy-two are sent. Either because the Gospel had to be preached to that many peoples of the world, so that, just as there were twelve tribes of Israel, these too might be appointed for the instruction of foreign peoples; or because, by the very number of those preaching, it was indicated that the whole world was to be illumined through the Gospel of the highest and indivisible Trinity. It is established that the sun habitually pours the circuit of its light over the world through seventy-two hours, that is, three days. The Lord himself calls himself the day and his apostles the hours, saying: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble” (John 11:9). And in the Psalms it is rightly commanded: “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2), that is, “Light from Light, true God from true God” (John 1:9; cf. the Creed).

In many passages of Holy Scripture as well, the mystery of the Trinity is displayed through three days, especially because the Lord rose from the dead on the third day. In the Old Testament too, when the people reached Mount Sinai, they received the law on the third day. Likewise, he crossed the Jordan River—through which the grace of baptism was commended—on the third day after he had approached it.

And he sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come. Because there are two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—and because charity cannot exist with fewer than two (for no one is properly said to have charity toward himself, but through love he reaches toward another so that charity may exist), the Lord sends the disciples to preach two by two. Through this he silently indicates that one who does not have charity toward another must in no way undertake the office of preaching.

It is rightly said that he sent them ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come. For the Lord follows his preachers: preaching goes before him, and then the Lord comes to the dwelling place of our mind. Words of exhortation run ahead, and through them truth is received into the mind.

And he said to them: “The harvest is indeed great, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest.” The great harvest signifies the multitude of peoples; the few workers signify the scarcity of teachers. These are the workers of whom the Psalmist speaks: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:5–6). To speak more plainly, the great harvest is the whole crowd of believers; the few workers are the apostles and their imitators who are sent into the harvest.

“Go; behold, I am sending you like lambs among wolves.” He calls the scribes and Pharisees wolves; they are the clerics of the Jews.

“Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals, and greet no one on the road.” A preacher ought to have such confidence in God that, although he does not foresee the expenses of the present life, he knows with complete certainty that these will not be lacking to him. Otherwise, while his mind is occupied with temporal things, he will provide less carefully for the eternal needs of others.

He is also forbidden to greet anyone on the road, so that the great haste with which he must proceed on the journey of preaching may be shown. If anyone wishes to understand these words allegorically as well, money is enclosed in a purse. Enclosed money signifies hidden wisdom. Therefore, whoever has the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor holds it like money tied up in a purse. And it is written: “Hidden wisdom and hidden treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (cf. Ecclus. 20:30).

What else is signified by the bag except the works of the world? And what else in this passage by sandals except examples of dead works? Therefore, whoever undertakes the office of preaching ought not to carry the burden of worldly affairs, lest, while this weighs down his shoulders, he fail to rise toward the preaching of heavenly things. Nor ought he to look upon examples of foolish works, lest he think that he must protect his own works as though with dead skins.

Everyone who greets on the road greets because of the opportunity presented by the journey, not from a desire to obtain that same salvation. Therefore, whoever preaches salvation to his hearers not out of love for the eternal homeland but from a desire for rewards greets as though on the road, because he wishes salvation for his hearers out of opportunity rather than intention.

“Into whatever house you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; otherwise it will return to you.” The peace offered from the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house, if a son of peace is in it, or returns to the same preacher. Either someone will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word that he hears, or, if no one wishes to hear, the preacher will not be without fruit, because peace returns to him: the Lord repays him for the labor of his work.

Behold, the one who forbade the carrying of a bag and purse grants expenses and food from that very preaching. For it follows:

“Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have.” If our peace is received, it is fitting that we remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have, so that we may receive earthly support from those to whom we offer the rewards of the heavenly homeland. Hence Paul, accepting these things as something small, says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9:11).

And it should be noted that he adds:

“For the worker is worthy of his wages.” The food that sustains him is already a wage for his work, so that here the reward begins from the labor of preaching, while there it is completed in the vision of truth. In this matter we should consider that two rewards are owed for one work of ours: one on the way and the other in the homeland; one sustains us in our labor, the other rewards us in the resurrection.

“And into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat what is set before you,” and so forth. Having described the hospitality of individual houses, he teaches what they should also do in the cities: namely, to share with the godly in all things, but to separate themselves entirely from the fellowship of the ungodly.

“And into whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say: ‘Even the dust that clung to us from your city, we wipe off against you.’” This may be either as a testimony to the earthly labor that they had undertaken for them in vain, or to show that they sought nothing earthly from them to such an extent that they would not even allow the dust of their land to cling to them.

Alternatively, the feet of the disciples signify the very work and progress of preaching. The dust with which they are sprinkled signifies the lightness of earthly thought, from which even the highest teachers cannot be free when, anxious for their hearers, they attend incessantly to salutary concerns and, as they travel through the paths of the world, scarcely gather the dust of the earth upon a single heel.

Those who receive the word turn the afflictions and anxieties of their teachers, which the teachers endured for their sake, into an argument for their own humility. But those who reject the teaching turn the labors, dangers, and weariness of the teachers’ concerns into evidence for their condemnation. This is the dust that is wiped off against those who despise the Gospel, and from which the feet of the evangelists are commanded to be washed by good hearers—or rather, which the Savior himself is said to have washed away.

“But I say to you that on that day it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for that city.” The Sodomites, amid all the sins of flesh and soul in which they burned insatiably, were also inhospitable, as Ezekiel testifies. Yet they had among them no guests such as the prophets among the Jews, or such as the apostles were. Lot was indeed righteous in sight and hearing, but he is not reported to have taught anything there or to have performed any signs. Therefore, “from the one to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12:48), and “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:6).

“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, as well as Tiberias, which John names, are cities of Galilee situated on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, which is formed by the flowing Jordan and is also called by the evangelists the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. The Lord therefore mourns the cities that did not repent after so many miracles and mighty works. He declares them worse than the Gentiles, who merely violated the natural law: after the promulgated law had been despised, these cities did not fear to trample upon the Son of God as well and to scorn grace with ingratitude.

“For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” We see the Savior’s saying fulfilled today, since Chorazin and Bethsaida were unwilling to believe while the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon, however, were once friendly to David and Solomon, and afterward believed through the disciples of Christ when they preached. They received the faith with such devotion that, when the apostle Paul departed from Tyre, all the citizens, with their wives and children, accompanied him outside the city. It was a most beautiful sight: so great a multitude of people escorted to the ships a very few guests, but guests illustrious for the faith of Christ, to bid them farewell.

But why the Gospel was not formerly preached to those who could have believed, but rather to the Jews who were unwilling to believe, is known by him whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10).

When the Lord says, “sitting in sackcloth and ashes” and repenting, by sackcloth—which is woven from goat hair—he signifies the harsh memory of the sin that pricks, with which the left side is to be clothed on the day of judgment; by ashes he demonstrates the consideration of death, through which the whole mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust. Moreover, by sitting he signifies the humiliation of one’s own conscience. Of this the Psalmist says: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. 126:2), which is to say: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5:6).

“And you, Capernaum, which are exalted to heaven, you will be brought down to hell.” There is a twofold meaning in this sentence. Either you will be brought down to hell because you resisted my preaching with the greatest pride; or because you were exalted to heaven through my lodging with you and, by my signs and mighty works, possessed such a privilege, you will be punished with greater torments than those to whom you refused to believe. And lest anyone think that this rebuke applies only to those cities or persons who despised the Lord while seeing him in the flesh, and not to all who even today scorn the words of the Gospel, he consequently added, saying:

“Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” Thus each person should learn that, in hearing or despising the preacher of the Gospel, he hears or despises not some insignificant persons but the Lord the Savior—or rather, the Father himself. For it follows:

“Whoever despises me despises him who sent me.” For without doubt the teacher is heard in the disciple, and the father is honored in the son.

This may also be understood as follows: “Whoever despises you despises me.” Whoever does not show mercy to one of my least brothers does not show mercy to me, because I too assumed for their sake the form of a servant and the condition of a poor man. “Whoever despises me,” unwilling to believe in God and trampling upon the Son of God, “despises him who sent me,” because “I and the Father are one.”

The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” They rightly confessed, offering honor to the name of Christ; but because, with faith still weak, they rejoiced in their mighty works, see what they hear:

And he said to them: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” “I see him now,” he says, “but I had already seen him when he fell.” When he says, “like lightning,” this either signifies his headlong fall from the heights to the depths, or that, though cast down, he still transforms himself into an angel of light. Since, therefore, he saw the disciples lifted up by the performance of signs, he terrifies them by this example and recalls them to the humility of the one who first fell through pride. Thus, remembering that he was cast out of heaven because of pride, they may recognize that they, though raised up from the earth, will be humbled if they become proud.

“Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over every power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you.” This means the power to cast every kind of unclean spirit out of possessed bodies, although it can also be understood quite literally. For Paul, attacked by a viper, suffered no harm; and John, as the story relates, drank poison and was not injured.

I think that serpents, which injure with their teeth, and scorpions, which injure with their tails, differ in this respect: serpents signify human beings or demons that rage openly, while scorpions signify those that lie in wait secretly. Serpents inject the poisons of evil persuasion into virtues as they begin; scorpions strive to corrupt virtues that have reached completion, at their end.

Nevertheless, “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you.” They are forbidden to rejoice in the subjection of the spirits, since they are flesh. For casting out spirits, like performing other miracles, is sometimes not the merit of the one who acts, but is accomplished through the invocation of Christ’s name—granted either for the condemnation of those who invoke it or for the benefit of those who see and hear—so that, although people may despise those who perform signs, they may nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation such great miracles take place. In the Acts of the Apostles, the sons of Sceva also appeared to cast out demons; and the apostle Judas is reported to have performed many signs among the other apostles, despite his traitorous intention.

“But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” “If Satan,” he says, “through pride lost the seat of heaven along with his companions, you ought to rejoice not in their humiliation but in your exaltation, so that, from the place where they fell after being raised up, you may ascend while remaining humble.”

This is not to be understood in a childish manner—as though God, to remedy forgetfulness, writes the good in heaven and the wicked on earth—for Jeremiah says: “All who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17:13). Rather, it should be understood in a salutary way: whether someone has performed heavenly or earthly works, through these he is, as though marked down in letters, eternally fixed in the memory of God.

At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” “Confession” does not always signify repentance but also thanksgiving, as we read very frequently in the Psalms. Let those who slander the Savior as not born but created hear that he calls his Father the Lord of heaven and earth. For if he too is a creature, and a creature can call its creator its father, it was foolish not to call him likewise both his own Father and the Lord, or Father, of heaven and earth.

“That you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.” He gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he has disclosed the mysteries of his coming to the apostles, which the scribes and Pharisees—who seem wise to themselves and prudent in their own sight—did not know; wisdom was justified by her children (Luke 7:35). Beautifully, he set little ones—that is, the humble—against the wise and prudent, to prove that he condemned swelling pride, not intelligence. This is the key of which he says elsewhere: “You have taken away the key of knowledge”—that is, the humility of faith in Christ, by which you could have arrived at recognition of his divinity; instead, you preferred to disdainfully cast it away.

“Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you.” From these words of the Lord we receive examples of humility, so that we may not rashly presume to scrutinize the heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. For after he had mentioned both, he did not immediately give the reason but said that it had pleased God thus. He thereby showed that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust.

Hence also, when he paid the laborers their wages in the vineyard, making certain workers equal in reward though unequal in labor, and when the one who had labored longer sought more in payment, he said: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius? I wish to give to this last one as well as to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” (Matt. 20:13–15). In everything, therefore, that is arranged outwardly, the evident cause is the hidden justice of the will.

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” When you read “all things,” you recognize the omnipotent one—not unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you read “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom all things properly belong by nature and by the right of one substance, not granted as a gift through grace.

The “all things” that he says have been handed over to him are not the elements of the world, which he himself created, but those to whom the Father revealed the mysteries of the Son as little ones in spirit, and whose salvation caused the same Son to rejoice in the Holy Spirit when he spoke these words. Concerning all these he says elsewhere: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37).

“And no one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” This should not be understood as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone, while the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son reveals him. Rather, what he says—“and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him”—must be referred to both, so that we understand both the Father and the Son himself to be revealed through the Son.

And turning to his disciples he said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see,” and so forth. They are not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, who saw only the Lord’s body, but those blessed eyes that are able to recognize his mysteries, concerning which it is said: “You have revealed them to little ones.” Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

“For I say to you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.” Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad. Isaiah too, and Micah, and many other prophets saw the glory of the Lord, and for this reason they were also called “Seers.” But all of them, looking from afar and greeting it [the source’s *salvantes* is evidently an OCR error for *salutantes*], saw through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12); the apostles, however, presently possessing the Lord, eating with him, and learning by questioning him whatever they wished, had no need to be taught through angels or various kinds of visions.

Those whom Luke calls “many prophets and kings,” Matthew calls more explicitly “prophets and righteous men.” For these are the great kings: they knew how not to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule over them and prevail.

And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and saying: “Teacher, by doing what shall I possess eternal life?” The lawyer who questions the Lord, testing him concerning eternal life, took, as I think, the opportunity for testing from the Lord’s own words, where he says: “Rejoice, however, that your names are written in heaven.” But by this very testing of his he shows how true is that confession of the Lord in which he speaks to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little children.”

[Col. 0468A] But he said to him: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” He answered and said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” In answering the lawyer, the Savior shows us the perfect path of heavenly life. When the lawyer first presents what is written in the Law concerning love of God and neighbor, he says:

“You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.” Then, after introducing the parable, when the lawyer answers that the one who showed mercy to the wounded man was his neighbor, he adds: “Go, and you do likewise”—that is, remember that you must love and support your neighbor in need with such zeal for mercy. He declares most clearly that love alone—and love not displayed merely in words, but proved by the accomplishment of deeds—is what leads to everlasting life.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: “And who is my neighbor?” What madness of empty glory! To win the favor of the crowd, so that he might boast of having answered wisely, the lawyer first professes that he does not know the commandment of the Law. Thus, truly, in accordance with the Savior’s judgment, he is wise and prudent in the Law; but because he desires not to humble himself with Christ’s little children, but to justify himself, he refuses to receive the blessed eyes of doves washed in the milk of innocence, by which he could see the mysteries of Christ. The Lord accordingly tempered his answer in such a way that he taught that everyone who shows mercy to anyone is a neighbor; yet this same parable also designated, in a particular sense, the Son of God himself, who graciously willed to become our neighbor through his humanity. Nor should we interpret “neighbor,” whom we are commanded to love as ourselves, concerning Christ in such a way that we try to diminish or remove the moral institutions of mutual brotherhood under the rules of allegory.

Taking up the question, Jesus said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood as Adam in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace, from whose blessedness he fell and came into this mortal and wretched life. How fittingly Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” signifies this life, always uncertain through various struggles and errors of waning.

[Col. 0468D] “And he fell among robbers.” Understand the robbers as the devil and his angels, into whom he fell because he was going down. For unless he had first become inwardly swollen with pride, he would not have fallen so easily when tempted outwardly. For this saying is entirely true: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Proverbs 16).

“They also stripped him.” That is, they deprived him of the garment of the glory of immortality and innocence. For this is the first robe with which, according to another parable, the extravagant son is adorned when he returns through repentance; and when the first-formed man had lost it, they realized that they were naked and put on tunics of skins, belonging to mortal nature.

“And after inflicting wounds on him, they went away, leaving him half-dead.” The wounds are sins, by which, violating the integrity of human nature, they implanted in its exhausted inward parts, so to speak, a kind of seedbed for increasing death. They went away, not by ceasing in any way from their ambushes, but by concealing the deceptions of those same ambushes. They left him half-dead because they were able to strip him of the blessedness of immortal life, but not to abolish the faculty of reason. In that part by which a human being can understand and know God, he is alive. But in that part by which he wastes away through sins and fails in misery, he is likewise dead and disfigured by a deadly wound.

Now it happened that a certain priest was going down the same road; and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed on. The priest and the Levite who, after seeing the wounded man, passed by signify the priesthood [Col. 0469B] and ministry of the Old Testament, in which, through the decrees of the Law, the wounds of the ailing world could be shown but not healed, because, as the Apostle says, it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of calves, lambs, and goats (Hebrews 9).

“But a certain Samaritan, traveling on his way, came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” The Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” signifies the Lord, to whom the prophet most rightly prays that he may not encounter these robbers: “Guard me,” he says, “from the trap which they have set for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Psalm 140). Descending from heaven for us human beings and for our salvation, he undertook the journey of the present life and came near the one who was wasting away from the wounds inflicted upon him—that is, having become in the likeness of human beings and having been found in appearance as a man (Philippians 2), he became kin through assuming our compassion and became near through the consolation of mercy.

“And approaching, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” The sins he found in human beings he restrained by reproving them, instilling hope of pardon in the penitent and fear of punishment in sinners. For he binds up wounds when he commands: “Repent”; he pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3). He also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (ibid.).

“And placing him on his own beast, he led him into an inn and took care of him.” His beast is his flesh, in which he graciously willed to come to us. He placed the wounded man upon it because he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree (1 Peter 2); and, according to another parable, when he found the sheep that had gone astray, he placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock (Luke 15). Thus, being placed upon the beast means believing in Christ’s Incarnation and being initiated into his mysteries, while also being protected from the enemy’s attack. The inn is the present Church, where travelers returning from this pilgrimage to their eternal homeland are refreshed. And fittingly he brought the man placed upon the beast into the inn, because no one will enter the Church unless baptized, unless joined to the body of Christ.

“And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, [Col. 0470A] and said: ‘Take care of him.’” The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection. For even before this, through the grace of his Gospel, he had illumined those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1); but after the resurrection had been celebrated, the splendor of perpetual light shone forth more powerfully. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. For “Christ is the end of the Law” (Romans 10). They are brought out and given to the innkeeper on the next day because then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). On the next day the innkeeper received the denarii, by whose value he was to heal the wounded man, because the Holy Spirit, coming upon them, taught the apostles all truth (John 16), so that they might apply themselves to instructing the nations and preaching the Gospel.

[Col. 0470B] “And whatever more you spend, when I return, I will repay you.” The innkeeper spends more than he received in the two denarii when the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Corinthians 7). Likewise: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 9). “But we did not use this authority, lest we burden any of you” (1 Thessalonians 2). When he returns, the Lord will repay the innkeeper what he promised, because the Lord, coming in judgment, says: “Because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?” He said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” According to the literal sense, the Lord’s [Col. 0470C] judgment is clear: no one is more our neighbor than the one who has mercy. For to the citizen of Jerusalem, neither the priest nor the Levite—though they belonged to the same people, indeed were born and raised in the same city—but a resident of a foreign nation became neighbor because he showed greater mercy. In a more sacred interpretation, since no one is more our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as the Lord our God; let us love him as our neighbor. For nothing is so near as the head is to its members. Let us also love the one who imitates Christ. For this is what follows:

“And Jesus said to him: ‘Go, and you do likewise.’” That is, so that you may show that you truly love your neighbor as yourself, devotedly perform whatever you are able to do in relieving his spiritual or bodily need.

Now it happened, while they were traveling, that he entered a certain village; and a certain woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary. This reading is connected with the preceding one by a most beautiful logic. For the former designates the love of God and neighbor in words and parables, while this one designates it in deeds themselves and in truth. These two sisters, beloved by the Lord, demonstrate the two spiritual lives by which the holy Church is exercised in the present age. Martha represents the active life, by which we join ourselves to our neighbor in charity; Mary, the contemplative life, by which we sigh in love for God. The active life is to give bread to the hungry, to teach the ignorant by the word of wisdom, to correct the one who has gone astray, to call back the proud neighbor to the way of humility, to care for the sick, to distribute what is suitable for each person, and to foresee how those entrusted to us may be able to endure. The contemplative life, on the other hand, is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, but to rest from external action and cling solely to the desire for the Creator, so that one no longer wishes to do anything, but, having trampled down every care, the spirit burns to see the face of its Creator. Thus it already knows how to bear the burden of corruptible flesh with sorrow and longs with all its desires to take part in those angelic choirs that sing hymns, to be mingled with the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption before God for ever.

She, sitting near the Lord’s feet, was listening to his word, while Martha was busy with much serving. [Col. 0471B] No one can doubt that these things correspond to both lives. The perfection of the contemplative life is uniform: to have the mind stripped of all earthly things and, as far as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ. How extensive the service of the active life is, the Teacher of the nations makes clear, recalling in the most frequent sayings of his Epistles his labors for Christ by land and sea and his dangers. In these passages, while also commending the Lord’s visions and revelations, he indicates that he was perfected no less in contemplative virtue, something imitable by very few. Hence he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are of sound mind, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

She stood and said: “Lord, is it no concern to you that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.” She speaks in the person of those who are still ignorant of divine contemplation and consider only the work of fraternal love, which they have learned, pleasing to God; therefore they suppose that all who wish to be devoted to Christ must be enslaved to this work. And fittingly Martha is described as standing, while Mary sits near the Lord’s feet, because the active life toils in strenuous struggle, whereas the contemplative life, when the disturbances of the vices have been calmed, already enjoys the desired repose of the mind in Christ.

And the Lord answered and said to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary.” Blessed David too, defining this one thing as necessary for human beings, desires to cling continually to God, saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm 72). And elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the will of the Lord and visit his holy temple” (Psalm 26). There is therefore one and only one theology—that is, contemplation of God—to which, deservedly, all merits of justification and every pursuit of virtue are subordinated.

“Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her.” Behold, Martha’s part is not condemned, but Mary’s is praised. For he does not say that Mary chose a good part, but the best part, so that Martha’s part also might be indicated as good. Why Mary’s part is best is added in the words: “which will not be taken away from her.” For the active life fails with the body. Who will offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? The active life is therefore taken away with the present age. The contemplative life, however, begins here so that it may be perfected in the heavenly homeland. For the fire of love, which begins to burn here, blazes more intensely in love when it sees the one whom it loves. The contemplative life is therefore not taken away, because when the light of the present age has been removed, it is brought to perfection.

# CHAPTER XI

And it happened that, while he was praying in a certain place, when he had ceased, one of his disciples said to him: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.” After the account of the sisters who signified the Church’s two lives, it is not without reason that the Lord is described both as having prayed himself and as having taught the disciples to pray. For the prayer he taught contains within itself the mystery of both lives, and the perfection of those lives is not to be attained by our strength but by prayers. And because Luke had often described the Savior as praying, he indicates what he accomplished by praying—for he was certainly pleading not for himself but for us—when, after the prayer had ended, he reports that the disciples asked how they ought to pray.

And he said to them: “When you pray, say: ‘Father, may your name be sanctified. May your kingdom come. Give us our daily bread today; and forgive us our sins, since we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not lead us into temptation.’” According to the evangelist Matthew, the Lord’s Prayer appears to contain seven petitions. In three of them eternal things are requested, [Col. 0472C] and in the remaining four temporal things, which nevertheless are necessary for attaining the eternal. For what we say—“May your name be sanctified; may your kingdom come; may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”—which some have not absurdly understood as referring to spirit and body, must be retained altogether without end. These things begin here and increase in us as we progress; but in their perfection—which is to be hoped for in the other life—they will always be possessed. But what we say—“Give us our daily bread today; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil”—who does not see that this pertains to the needs of the present life? In that eternal life, where we always hope to be, both the sanctification of God’s name and his kingdom will remain perfectly and immortally in our spirit and body. “Daily bread” is so called because it is necessary here in the measure in which it must be given to soul and flesh, whether it is understood spiritually, bodily, or in both ways. Here also is the forgiveness we ask for, where there is every remission of sins. Here are the temptations that either entice or drive us to sin. Here, finally, is the evil from which we desire to be delivered. In that life, however, none of these things exists.

The evangelist Luke, however, comprised not seven but five petitions in the Lord’s Prayer. He certainly did not differ from Matthew; rather, by the very brevity of his form he indicated how the seven are to be understood. God’s name is sanctified in the spirit, while God’s kingdom will come in the resurrection of the flesh. Thus Luke showed that the third petition is, in a certain way, a repetition of the two preceding ones; by omitting it, he made this understood more clearly. Then he adds the three petitions concerning daily bread, the remission of sins, and the avoidance of temptation. But what Matthew placed last—“but deliver us from evil”—Luke did not include, so that we might understand it as belonging to what was said above concerning temptation. For this reason he says, “but deliver,” not “and deliver,” as if demonstrating that it is one petition: “Do not do this, but do that,” so that each person may know that he is delivered from evil in the very fact that he is not led into temptation.

And he said to them: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because my friend has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’?” Asked by the disciples, the Savior teaches not only the form of prayer but also the persistence and frequency with which we should pray. The friend to whom one comes at midnight is understood to be God himself. In the midst of tribulation we must plead with him and earnestly request three loaves—that is, understanding of the Trinity, by which the struggles of the present life may be consoled. The friend who comes from a journey is our spirit, which departs from us whenever it wanders outward to pursue earthly and temporal things. It returns and desires to be refreshed with heavenly nourishment when, having returned to itself, it begins to meditate on what is above and spiritual. Beautifully, the one who had asked adds that he has nothing to set before him. For the soul sighing for God after the darkness of the world desires to think of nothing, speak of nothing, or look upon anything except him; it strives only to contemplate the joy of the supreme Trinity, which it has come to recognize, and to attain a fuller vision of it.

And the man inside may answer: “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.” The door of the divine friend is understanding of the word, which the Apostle prays may be opened to him for speaking the mystery of Christ. It is shut in a time of famine of the word, when understanding is not granted. And those who, distributing evangelical wisdom like bread, preached throughout the world are now the children of the master of the house, in secret repose with the Lord. Yet by praying the one who desires understanding is enabled to receive it from God himself, even when there is no human being through whom wisdom may be preached.

“And if he continues knocking, I say to you: Even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened to you.” This is a comparison from the lesser. If a human friend rises from bed and gives something, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more will God give, who without annoyance most generously bestows what is requested? Yet he wishes to be asked for this purpose: so that those who ask may become capable of his gifts. Therefore, lest the friend returning from his journey perish from hunger—that is, lest the spirit that has recently recovered from the vanity of its error waste away too long from lack of spiritual desire—let us ask for the banquets of the word by which it may be nourished; let us seek the friend who gives; let us knock at the door where hidden things are kept. For he has given great hope, and the one who promises does not deceive.

“For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” Therefore, in accordance with the preceding parable of the friend who asks, perseverance is necessary if we are to receive what we ask, find what we seek, and have opened what we knock upon. For if what is asked for is given, the seeker finds, and the door is opened to the one who knocks, then it is evident that the one who does not receive, the one who does not find, and the one for whom the door is not opened has not asked, sought, or knocked properly.

“And which of you fathers, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?” Bread is understood as charity, because of its greater desirability and because it is so necessary that without it all the rest is nothing, just as without bread a table is empty. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

“Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?” The fish is faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Since faith, though battered by the waves of this world, is not broken, it is rightly compared to a fish. In opposition to it he set the serpent, because of the poisons of deceit, which it also first sowed in the first man by giving him evil counsel.

“Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” The egg indicates hope. For an egg is not yet a fully formed offspring, but it is expected as it is kept warm. In opposition to it he set the scorpion, whose venomous sting is feared from behind, just as the opposite of hope is to look backward, since hope stretches toward the things that lie ahead.

“If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” How do the evil give good things? He called them evil because they were still lovers of this world and sinners. Yet the things they give are to be called good according to their understanding, because they regard them as good for us; indeed, they are good in the nature of things, but temporal and belonging to this frail life. Whoever is evil and gives them does not give from his own possession. “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness,” he who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them (Psalm 23). How much, then, should we hope that God will give good things to us when we ask, and that we cannot be deceived into receiving one thing instead of another when we ask him, since even though we are evil we know how to give what is requested! We do not deceive our children; and whatever good things we give, we give not from our own resources but from his.

Alternatively: The apostles, who by the excellence of their election had surpassed human goodness in many ways, are called evil in view of the supreme goodness, because nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, nothing good except the Godhead alone. All creatures, if they attain the blessedness of eternity or immutability, attain it not through their own nature but through participation in and grace from their Creator. But when it is said, “How much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”—for which Matthew wrote, “He will give good things to those who ask him” (Matthew 7)—it shows that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s good things, and that the things administered divinely do not subsist apart from him. For all benefits received from the grace of God’s gifts flow from this source.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0475]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0475A]

The Lord, exulting in the Holy Spirit—as was read above—said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little children.” This sentence, conscious of a hidden judgment, never ceases to repeat the effect of its power. For it continues to manifest itself both generally in the rejection of the Jews and the election of the nations, and specifically in each individual according to the differing qualities of their minds. Finally, to touch briefly upon what is near at hand: the lawyer, wishing to justify himself, approached the Lord in order to test him, but departed confounded; whereas Mary, humbly reclining at his feet, chose the better part of heavenly philosophy. Likewise, Christ’s little children, who have learned to place their hope not in their own righteousness but in the grace of their Redeemer, ask in what manner of prayers they should call upon that same grace. At once they hear both with what words they should pray, with what persistence they should persevere, and especially for what things they ought to supplicate: namely, faith, hope, and charity; and, by perfectly seeking their giver, they receive from the Father the good Spirit. In contrast, the wise and prudent, because they strive not only not to ask for, seek, and knock for the Spirit of grace, but even to blaspheme him, suffer here and in the future the unforgivable penalties of their obstinacy. And anyone who reads to the end of the Gospel—or rather, anyone who examines it wisely to the end of the age—will understand that “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5).

## INVOCATION
