Therefore, as I begin this fourth book of exposition of the Gospel with the reading in which the spirit of pride is cast out by the finger of God, I humbly implore your clemency, O Christ: may your good Spirit lead me in the right way and drive far from me the one who is from the North, so that, after the evil spirits have been cast out from me, I may search the commandments of my God, and, with the eyes of my mind revealed, may I, a devoted reader, enter upon the contemplation of the wonders of your most holy Law.

“And Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute. And when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled.” This demoniac is reported by Matthew to have been not only mute but also blind, and is said to have been healed by the Lord so that he both spoke and saw. Thus three signs were accomplished together in one man: the blind sees, the mute speaks, and the demon-possessed is liberated. This happened then in a bodily way, but it is also fulfilled daily in the conduct of believers: first, when the demon has been expelled, they behold the light of faith; then mouths that were previously silent are opened to the praises of God.

But some of them said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” These were not certain people from the crowd who made the accusation, but the Pharisees and scribes, as the other evangelists testify. For while the less educated crowds continually marveled at the Lord’s deeds, they, on the contrary, labored either to deny them or to distort by sinister interpretation what they could not deny, as though these were not works of divinity but of an unclean spirit—namely, Beelzebub, who was the god of Ekron. For Beel himself is Baal, while zebub means “fly.” And, contrary to certain corrupt copies, the name should not be read with the letter l or d at the end, but with b. Beelzebub is therefore interpreted as “Baal of flies,” that is, “man of flies,” or “one who has flies,” evidently because of the filth of the blood offered in sacrifice; from this most foul rite or name they called the prince of demons by that title.

“And others, testing him, were seeking a sign from heaven.” Either they wished fire to come down from above in the manner of Elijah, or, in imitation of Samuel, they wanted thunder to roar, lightning to flash, and rain to pour down in summertime, as though they could not slander those things as well and say that they had arisen from hidden and various disturbances of the air. But you who slander what you see with your eyes, hold in your hand, and experience as useful—what will you say about things that come from heaven? You will certainly answer that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven.

But he, seeing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.” He answered not their words but their thoughts, so that they might thereby be compelled to believe in the power of one who saw the hidden things of the heart. If, then, every kingdom divided against itself is desolated, the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not divided; it will not be desolated by any assault but will remain in eternal stability. If, however, the kingdom of the holy and undivided Trinity remains undivided—indeed, because it remains undivided—let the Arians cease to say that the Son is lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son. For those whose kingdom is one have one majesty also.

“But if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub.” By saying this, he wished it to be understood from their own confession that, by not believing in him, they had chosen to be in the devil’s kingdom; and that kingdom certainly could not stand if divided against itself. Let the Pharisees therefore choose whichever alternative they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they could find nothing to say against the Lord. [Col. 0477A] But if he can, let them take much greater care for themselves and withdraw from his kingdom, which cannot stand divided against itself. In what power the Lord Christ casts out demons, let them attend to what follows.

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.” He certainly said this concerning his disciples, the sons of that people, who were well aware that they had learned no evil arts from their good teacher by which they might cast out demons in the prince of demons. “Therefore,” he says, “they will be your judges”—those, he says, who are lowly and despised in this world, in whom not an artful malignity but the holy simplicity of my power appears; they, my witnesses, will be your judges.

Alternatively: He signifies the sons of the Jews, the exorcists of that nation according to its custom, who cast out demons by invocation. He constrains them by a prudent question to confess that this is the work of the Holy Spirit. If, he says, the expulsion of demons in your sons is attributed to God and not to demons, why should the same work in me not have the same cause? Therefore they will be your judges—not by authority but by comparison: they attribute the expulsion of demons to God, while you attribute it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

“But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” This is the finger that the magicians also confess, when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8); by this finger the stone tablets were also written on Mount Sinai. Therefore the Son is the hand and arm of God, and his finger is the Holy Spirit. The substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Let not the inequality of the members scandalize you, since the unity of the body builds. Alternatively: The Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the distribution of gifts given through him individually to human beings and angels. For in none of our members does division appear more clearly than in the fingers. But when he said, “The kingdom of God has come upon you,” he now calls the kingdom of God that by which the ungodly are condemned and separated from the faithful who are presently doing penance for their sins.

“When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace.” He calls the devil strong, and his courtyard the world that lies in evil. Until the Savior’s coming, the devil possessed it under a falsely peaceful dominion, because he rested without opposition in the hearts of unbelievers. Hence elsewhere he is also called the prince of the world, when the Lord says: “For the prince of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14). And again: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12). Concerning this expulsion he adds here:

“But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armor in which he trusted and distribute his spoils.” He speaks about himself: it was not through a deceitful, concordant operation, as they slandered, but through stronger power that he, the victor, freed human beings from the demon. The armor in which that falsely strong one trusted consists in the wickedness of spiritual cunning and deceit. His spoils are the human beings deceived by him. Christ the victor distributes them; this is the mark of a triumphator, because, leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings, appointing some apostles, others evangelists, these prophets, and those pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4).

“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Let no one think that this was said about heretics and schismatics, although it can also be understood in that way incidentally. Rather, from what follows and from the text of the speech, it refers to the devil and shows that the Savior’s works cannot be compared with the works of Beelzebub. The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The devil preaches idols; the Lord, knowledge of the one God. The devil draws them toward vices; the Lord calls them back to virtue. How, then, can those whose works are divided have harmony with one another?

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through waterless places.” Although it can be understood simply that the Lord added this to distinguish his works from Satan’s—that he always cleanses what has been polluted, while Satan hastens to stain what has been cleansed with more serious filth—it can also appropriately be understood of any heretic, schismatic, or even bad Catholic. At the time of baptism, the unclean spirit that had previously dwelt in a person is expelled through the confession of the catholic faith and renunciation of worldly conduct. It travels through waterless places: that is, the crafty ambusher examines the hearts of the faithful, cleansed of the fluidity of unstable thought, to see whether he might perhaps plant there the steps of his wickedness. But it is rightly said:

“Seeking rest and not finding it,” because, having fled chaste minds, the devil can find a repose pleasing to him only in the heart of the wicked. Hence the Lord says of him: “Under the shadow he sleeps in the secret place of the reed and in moist places” (Job 40). “In the shadow,” that is, darkened consciences; “in the reed,” hypocrites, since the reed is bright on the outside but empty within; “in moist places,” insinuating himself into wanton and soft-minded souls.

He says: “I will return to my house from which I came out.” This little verse is to be feared, not explained, lest the fault that we believed extinguished in us should, through our negligence while we are idle, overwhelm us again.

[Col. 0478D] “And when he comes, he finds it swept clean”—that is, cleansed from the stain of sins by the grace of baptism, but not enriched with any diligence in good works. Hence Matthew rightly says that he found this house empty, swept clean, and adorned: cleansed, that is, from former vices through baptism; empty of good deeds through negligence; and adorned with pretended virtues through hypocrisy.

And then he goes and takes seven other spirits worse than himself, and, entering, they dwell there. By the seven evil spirits he signifies all vices. For whoever, after baptism, is seized either by heretical depravity or by worldly desire, will immediately be cast down into the depths of all vices. Hence the spirits are rightly said to enter him then as worse spirits. For he will have not only those seven vices that are opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend, through hypocrisy, that he possesses the virtues themselves.

And the last state of that man is worse than the first. For it was better for him not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. We read that this was specifically fulfilled in Judas the betrayer, Simon Magus, and others of the same kind. But the Savior himself explained where this parable generally tends, according to Matthew, where, after bringing it to an end, he immediately added, saying: “So will it also be with this most wicked generation.” That is: what I have related as customarily happening particularly to any one person does not cease to happen generally to the whole nation of this people. For the unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law. And he went through dry places, seeking rest for himself. That is, having been driven out by the Jews, he wandered through the solitudes of the nations. When these later came to believe in the Lord, he, finding no place among the nations, said: “I will return to my former house, from which I came out. I shall have the Jews whom I had previously abandoned.” And when he came, he found it empty, swept clean. For the temple of the Jews was empty and did not have Christ as its guest, who said: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.” Therefore, because they did not have the protection of God and the angels, and were adorned with the superfluous observances of the Pharisees, the devil returns to them, adds to himself a sevenfold number of demons, inhabits his former house, and the latter state of that people becomes worse than the first. For they are now possessed by a far greater number of demons when they blaspheme Christ Jesus in their synagogues than they had been possessed in Egypt before the knowledge of the Law. For it is one thing not to believe that he will come, and another not to receive him who has come. Understand the number seven added to the devil either with reference to the Sabbath or with reference to the number of the Holy Spirit. Just as in Isaiah seven spirits of virtues are said to have descended upon the shoot from the root of Jesse and upon the flower that rises from the root, so, conversely, the number of vices has been consecrated in the devil.

And it happened that, while he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you suckled.” This woman is shown to possess great devotion and faith. While the scribes and Pharisees were testing the Lord and blaspheming him at the same time, she recognizes his incarnation with such sincerity above all others, and confesses it with such confidence, that she both shames the slander of the rulers present and confounds the faithlessness of future heretics. For just as the Jews at that time, by blaspheming the works of the Holy Spirit, denied the true Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, so heretics later, denying that Mary, ever virgin, had supplied the material of her flesh from her human members to the only-begotten God who was to be born through the working power of the Holy Spirit, said that one ought not to confess the Son of Man as true and consubstantial with his mother. But if the flesh of the Word of God born according to the flesh is declared foreign to the flesh of the virgin mother, then without reason are blessed the womb that bore him and the breasts that nursed him. For by what logic can he be believed to have been nourished by her milk if he is denied to have been conceived from her seed, when, according to the physicists, both fluids are shown to flow from the origin of one and the same source? Unless perhaps one should think that the virgin could supply the material of her flesh as seed to the Son of God in the flesh by nourishing him, but could not supply it by conception—as though that were the greater and more unusual miracle. But the Apostle opposes this opinion when he says: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. IV). Nor should those be heeded who think that one ought to read, “born from a woman, made under the Law,” but rather, “made from a woman.” For, conceived in the virgin’s womb, he drew flesh not from nothing and not from elsewhere, but from his mother’s flesh. Otherwise he would not truly be called the Son of Man, since he would have no origin from a human being. Let us, therefore, with these words against Eutyches, raise our voice with the catholic Church, whose type this woman represented; let us also raise our mind above the midst of the crowds, and say to the Savior: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you suckled” (Luke XI). Truly blessed is the mother who, as someone has said, in giving birth brought forth a king:

> He who holds heaven and earth throughout the ages,  
> whose divine power embraces all things in an eternal circle,  
> whose empire remains without end; she who, with blessed womb,  
> possessing a mother’s joys together with the honor of virginity,  
> was seen to have neither a predecessor like herself nor a successor.

But he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” Beautifully the Savior assents to the woman’s testimony, declaring blessed not only her who was worthy to give bodily birth to the Word of God, but also all who have striven to conceive that same Word spiritually through the hearing of faith, and to give birth to it through the keeping of good works, whether in their own heart or in that of their neighbors, and, as it were, to nourish it. For the same mother of God is blessed indeed because she became the temporal servant of the incarnate Word, but much more blessed because she remained eternally the guardian of that same Word, whom she must always love. By this saying he secretly strikes the wise men of the Jews, who sought not to hear and keep the Word of God but to deny and blaspheme it.

When the crowds were gathering in great numbers, he began to say: “This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah.” He had been pressed by a twofold question. Some were slandering him, alleging that he cast out demons by Beelzebub; this has been answered above. Others, testing him, were seeking a sign from heaven. He now begins to answer them, giving them not a sign from heaven, which they were unworthy to see, but one from the depths of hell—the kind that the prophet Jonah, shipwrecked and swallowed by the whale, both received and gave after being delivered from the abyss and the jaws of death: a sign of incarnation, not of divinity; of suffering, not of glorification. To his disciples, however, he gave a sign from heaven, showing them the glory of eternal blessedness, first figuratively when he was transformed on the mountain, and afterward truly when he was lifted up into heaven.

For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. He shows that the Jews, like the Ninevites, are entangled in grave sins and are near to destruction unless they repent. Yet just as punishment was announced to the Ninevites and a remedy was also shown to them, so the Jews too ought not to despair of pardon if they wish to repent. But see what follows:

“The queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them.” She will condemn them, certainly, not by the authority of judgment but by comparison with her better deed. If the queen of the South, who is undoubtedly understood to have been chosen, will rise at the judgment with the reprobate, it is shown that there will be one resurrection of all mortals, both good and evil, and that this will occur not, according to Jewish fables, a thousand years before the judgment, but at the judgment itself.

“For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” Here, in this passage, *hic* is not a pronoun but an adverb of place; that is, he is presently dwelling among you, and is incomparably superior to Solomon. Scripture relates how the queen of Sheba, abandoning her people and kingdom and overcoming so many difficulties, came to Judaea to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and, bringing him many gifts, received still more from him. She will therefore condemn the Jews at the judgment because she sought him from the farthest ends of the earth, having learned through the gift of wisdom that he was famous. But they, having among them one who was not wise from elsewhere but who himself is the wisdom and power of God, preferred not merely not to hear him but to blaspheme him and harass him with plots.

“The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.” Jonah preached for a few days; I have preached for so long. He preached to the unbelieving Assyrian nation; I to the people of God, the Jews. He to foreigners; I to citizens. He, speaking in a simple voice and performing no signs, was accepted; I, performing so many signs, endure the slander that I act by Beelzebub. Therefore, something greater than Jonah is here—that is, preaching in your midst. And for this reason, in the same way as the queen of the South, the men of Nineveh too will condemn the generation of the Jews; that is, they will convict it of unbelief. Alternatively: in the Ninevites and the queen of the South, the faith of the Church is preferred to Israel—a faith by which the Church is reconciled to the Lord no less through repentance for past folly than through diligence in learning wisdom. For the unity of the Church is gathered from two groups: those who do not know how to sin and those who cease from sinning. Repentance abolishes wrongdoing; wisdom guards against it.

“No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel.” The Lord speaks these words about himself, showing that, although he said above that no sign except the sign of Jonah would be given to the evil generation, nevertheless the brightness of his light was by no means to be hidden from the faithful. He himself lights the lamp, filling the earthen vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity. He certainly did not wish to hide this lamp from believers or place it under a bushel—that is, enclose it within the measure of the Law or confine it within the boundaries of the single Jewish nation.

“But upon the lampstand,” he says, “so that those who enter may see the light.” He calls the Church the lampstand, upon which he placed the lamp, because he fixed the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads, so that those who wish faithfully to enter the Church may openly behold the light of truth. By this saying he also condemns the rulers of the Jews, who, seeking signs externally, refused to enter through the open door of light by believing. Finally, he commands them to remember to cleanse and purify not only their works but also their thoughts and the very intentions of their hearts. For it follows:

“The lamp of your body is your eye.” By “body” he means the works that appear openly to everyone; by “eye” he means the intention of the mind that directs the work, by whose merit it is discerned whether those same works are works of light or of darkness, as he explained immediately afterward, saying:

“If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light. But if it is evil, your body too will be full of darkness.” If, he says, you strive to do whatever good you can with a pure and upright intention, the works you perform are certainly works of light, even if they appear to possess some imperfection before human beings. For “all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose as saints.” But if the intention that precedes the action is perverse, every work that follows is insignificant, however upright it may appear.

“See therefore that the light which is in you is not darkness.” That is, carefully and discerningly consider that the very intention of the heart, which is the light of the soul, not be darkened by the gloom of vices. In accordance with what is commanded elsewhere: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV).

“If therefore your whole body is full of light, having no part of darkness, it will be wholly luminous, and, like a lamp shining brightly, it will illuminate you.” By “our whole body” he means all our works, because the Apostle too calls certain works “our members”—works that he condemns and commands us to put to death, saying: “Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust” (Col. III), and other such things. If, therefore, you yourself have done a good deed with a good intention, having no part of dark thought in your conscience, then, even if it happens that one of your neighbors is harmed by your good action—for example, if he does or suffers something bad from money that he received from you when he was in need and asked for it, or if, through a word of exhortation by which you wished to correct someone who was in error, he should perhaps fall into more harmful error—you nevertheless, because of your simple and luminous heart, will be granted the grace of light both here and in the future. These words were spoken especially against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who craftily sought signs; according to their moral sense, they instruct us generally.

And while he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him; and he entered and reclined at table. Luke deliberately does not say, “And while he was saying these things,” but “While he was speaking,” to show that he was asked to dine with the Pharisee not immediately after finishing the words he had begun above, but after several intervening events. What those events were Matthew explains. After ending this discourse of the Lord—which he recalls partly more briefly and partly more fully than Luke—he immediately added: “While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him.” “While he was still speaking,” he says, so that you might understand that he was speaking the things indicated above. Mark too, after reporting what the Lord had said concerning the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, states: “And his mother and his brothers came.” Luke, however, did not preserve the chronological order of this event, but anticipated it and related it earlier from memory. Finally, he inserted it in such a way that it appears detached from the connection both with what precedes and with what follows. Therefore, after his mother and brothers had been announced to him as standing outside, he said: “Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark III). It is understood that he then entered the banquet when asked by the Pharisee.

But the Pharisee began, reasoning within himself, to say why he had not been baptized before the meal. The evangelist Mark disclosed the reason for the Pharisee’s thought when he said: “For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they frequently wash their hands, holding to the tradition of the elders; and they do not eat after returning from the marketplace unless they have been baptized” (Mark VII).

And the Lord said to him: “Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of plunder and wickedness.” Mark indeed reports that they customarily observed washings of cups, jugs, dishes, and bronze vessels. But, under the name of vessels, they are more truly accused of the deception of hypocrisy itself: they displayed one thing outwardly to people and did another at home, possessing the appearance of piety externally but disfigured within by the filth of vices. For the Lord wishes to explain more fully what he had stated above in brief about cleansing the eye of the heart.

[Folio/column 0483C] “Fools! Did not he who made what is outside also make what is inside?” He who made both aspects of human nature, he says, desires both to be cleansed. This is directed against the Manichaeans, who think that the soul alone was created by God, but the flesh by the devil. It is also directed against those who abhor bodily sins—namely, fornication, uncleanness, lust, theft, plunder, and other such things—as though they were the gravest offenses, but regard as trivial spiritual sins, which the Apostle condemns no less: bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, blasphemy, pride, and greed, which is the service of idols (Coloss. III).

“Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Give to the poor whatever remains after what is necessary for food and clothing. In accordance with this John too commands: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none” (Luke III). For he is not commanded to give alms in such a way that he exhausts himself in poverty, but, after caring for his own body, to support the needy as far as he is able.

Or this may be understood in another way: “what remains” means that, for those already overwhelmed by so much wickedness, the only remedy left is: give alms. This saying applies to everything done through beneficial compassion. For not only does the one who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the stranger, and other things of this kind give alms; the one who grants pardon to a sinner also gives alms. And the one who corrects with a blow a person over whom he has authority, or restrains him through some discipline, yet forgives from his heart the sin by which he was injured or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in rebuking and imposing some corrective punishment, because he shows mercy.

There are therefore many kinds of alms. When we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven us; but there is none greater than that by which from the heart we forgive whatever anyone has sinned against us. Or are we to understand what he said—“Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you”—in such a way that, even if they did not believe in Christ and were not reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, everything would be clean for Pharisees who lacked faith in Christ, provided only that they gave alms, as some think alms ought to be given, even though all those whom the faith of Christ does not cleanse are unclean? Concerning that faith it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV).

And yet what they had heard remains true: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner must begin with himself and give alms first to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been most truly said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX). For this reason we are reborn, so that we may please God, whom what we contracted by being born rightly displeases. This is the first alms that we have given ourselves, since through the mercy of the merciful God we sought out ourselves in our misery. On account of this order of love it was said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark XII).

Therefore, after he had rebuked them because they washed themselves outwardly while inwardly they were full of plunder and wickedness, reminding them of a certain alms that a person ought first to give himself, so that his inner parts might be cleansed, he said: “Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Then, to show what he had advised and what they themselves did not take care to do, lest they think that he was unaware of their alms:

“But woe to you Pharisees,” he says. It was as though he were saying: “I indeed warned you to give alms, through which everything might be clean for you; but woe to you,

“because you tithe mint and rue and every herb.” For these are the alms of yours that I know; do not suppose that I was now reminding you about them.

“And you pass over judgment and the love of God.” Through that alms you could be cleansed from every inner defilement, so that the bodies you wash would also be clean—for “everything” means both inner and outer things—as it is read elsewhere: “Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean also” (Matt. XXIII). But lest he appear to have rejected those alms that are made from the fruits of the earth, he said:

“But these things,” he says, “you ought to have done.” That is, judgment and the love of God: so that, truly judging our own misery and loving the love of God, which he himself has given, we may live piously and rightly, confessing his just judgment, of which the Apostle says: “Judgment indeed came from one offense to condemnation,” and giving thanks for his great love, concerning which the same herald of grace says: “But God commends his love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. V).

“These things you ought to have done, and not to omit those others,” that is, alms from the fruits of the earth. Therefore, let those who imagine that they can purchase impunity through whatever lavish alms of their produce or of their money, while remaining in the enormity of crimes and the wickedness of their offenses, not deceive themselves.

“Woe to you Pharisees, who love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace.” Woe to us wretched people, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed, who do not fear to burden ourselves with still more sins by proudly contending with one another for precedence during the brief and uncertain course of our life, in which we ought humbly to have mourned our sins.

“Woe to you, for you are like monuments that are not visible, and people walking over them do not know it.” This saying too rebukes the superstition of the Pharisees, who outwardly display the appearance of right teaching but conceal what ugliness they carry within, like monuments which, while presenting the common surface of the earth, are inwardly full of the stench of corpses breeding worms. Concerning these the Psalmist said: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. V); and immediately he disclosed what he had meant by adding: “With their tongues they acted deceitfully.”

But one of the lawyers answered and said to him: “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” What a wretched conscience—that, on hearing the word of God, thinks itself insulted, and, when the punishment of the faithless is recalled, continually understands itself to be condemned. Hence the one refuge left to me and those like me is to beseech the Lord with the prophet: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances. Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII).

But he said: “Woe to you lawyers also, because you load people with burdens that cannot be carried, and you yourselves do not touch the loads with one of your fingers.” The burdens of the Law could not be carried in the manner in which these lawyers imposed them upon people. Hence they rightly hear that they did not touch its loads with even one finger—that is, they did not fulfill it in the smallest matters—although, contrary to the custom of their fathers, without faith in and grace through Jesus Christ, they presumed both to observe it and to hand it down for observance. For this reason they attempted to cast far away and abolish the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and his burden, which is light, where there is rest for souls, although it is written: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I). The Apostle Peter also protested against those who were teaching believing Gentiles to be circumcised, saying: “And now why are you testing God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they too were” (Acts XV).

“Woe to you, who build the monuments of the prophets, while your fathers killed them.” It is not a crime to adorn the monuments of the prophets, but to imitate the killers of the prophets. Thus the Jews, by building monuments to the prophets, were accusing the deeds of their fathers who had killed them; but, by emulating their ancestral crimes while persecuting Christ and his apostles, they turned the sentence against themselves, themselves doing the very things that they condemned in their parents.

“Certainly you testify that you consent to the deeds of your fathers.” For they indeed killed them, while you build their tombs. They pretended, in order to win the favor of the crowd, to abhor the faithlessness of their fathers, magnificently adorning the memorials of the prophets who had been killed by them; but by the very work they testify how much they agree with their fathers’ wickedness, treating with insults the Lord who had been foretold by those same prophets. Thereby they declare themselves alike the sons of murderers and knowingly sinful, to the increase of their own condemnation. Hence it is rightly added:

“Therefore the Wisdom of God also said: I will send to them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute.” He calls himself the Wisdom of God. For he is the power of God and the wisdom of God, as the Apostle teaches (1 Cor. I). In Matthew, finally, we find it written in this way: “Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes.” But if the same Wisdom of God sent the prophets and the apostles, let heretics cease to give Christ a beginning from the Virgin; let them stop preaching one God of the Law and the Prophets and another God of the New Testament. The apostolic Scripture often calls prophets not only those who preached Christ’s future incarnation but also those who proclaim the future joys of the heavenly kingdom: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge.” Yet I would by no means believe that these are to be placed before the apostles in the order of the catalogue.

“So that the blood of all the prophets that has been shed from the foundation of the world may be required of this generation.” It is asked how the blood of all the prophets and righteous may be required from one generation of Jews, since many saints, both before the incarnation and after the Savior’s death and resurrection, were killed by other nations, and the Lord himself, although the Jews were shouting for it, was nevertheless crucified by a Roman governor and Roman soldiers. But it is the custom of Scripture often to reckon two generations of human beings: the good and the evil, namely, those “who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I), and those to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII). And elsewhere: “Serpents, brood of vipers” (Matt. XXIII).

“From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary.” Why it begins with the blood of Abel, who was the first to suffer martyrdom, is not surprising. But why it continues to the blood of Zechariah must be asked, since many others after him, up to the birth of Christ, and immediately after Christ was born, the innocent children in Bethlehem, were killed by this generation. Perhaps it is because Abel was a shepherd of sheep and Zechariah a priest, and because the one was killed in the field and the other in the temple court, that he wished to indicate under their names martyrs of both orders: laypeople, that is, and those devoted to the service of the altar.

“Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering.” The key of knowledge is the humility of Christ, which the lawyers neither wished to understand themselves in the Law and the Prophets nor to have understood by others. To enter means not to be content with the surface of the letter, but to penetrate as far as the secrets of the more sacred understanding. Alternatively: every teacher who scandalizes by his example those whom he builds up by his word neither enters the kingdom of God himself nor permits those who could enter to do so.

When he said these things to them, the Pharisees and lawyers began to press him vehemently and to overwhelm his speech, laying many traps for him and seeking to catch something from his mouth so that they might accuse him. How true were the charges of their faithlessness, hypocrisy, and impiety that they had heard, they themselves testify: while so great a storm was thundering around them, they did not come to their senses but attempted to attack the teacher of truth by treachery.

## CHAPTER XII

When many crowds had gathered, so that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Everything that he had discussed earlier while reclining at the Pharisee’s table belongs to this leaven. Concerning it the Apostle too commands: “Let us therefore celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. V). For just as a little leaven corrupts the whole mass of flour into which it is put and immediately stains the entire mixture with its flavor, so surely hypocrisy, once it has imbued the mind, deprives it of the whole sincerity and truth of the virtues.

“Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known.” But how does the hypocrisy of many remain hidden for a long time in the present age? Therefore this must be understood of the future time, when God will judge the hidden things of human beings. For, as one of the friends of blessed Job said most truly: “The praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite lasts but a moment. Though his pride rise to heaven and his head touch the clouds, in the end he will be destroyed like dung” (Job XX). “In the end,” he says, “he will be destroyed”—the one who seemed to flourish at the beginning. The meaning is therefore: Beware lest you imitate hypocrites, because the time will certainly come when your virtue will be revealed to everyone and their hypocrisy will be revealed.

“For whatever you have said in the darkness will be spoken in the light, and what you have said in the ear in private rooms will be proclaimed upon the housetops.” This may be fittingly understood not only of the future, when all the hidden things of hearts will be brought into the light, but also of the present time. For what the apostles once said or suffered amid the darkness of persecutions and the shadows of prisons is now publicly proclaimed throughout the world, with the Church glorified and their deeds read aloud. When he says, “It will be proclaimed upon the housetops,” he speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people commonly sit upon the roofs. Their roofs are not, as ours are, raised with pitched summits, but are made level and flat in form. Hence the Law commanded that whoever built a new house should place a parapet around the roof, so that innocent blood would not be shed if someone slipped and fell headlong. And in the construction of the temple we read: “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings, and built a floor above the entire house, five cubits high.” Therefore, “it will be proclaimed upon the housetops” means that it will be spoken openly, with everyone listening.

“But I say to you, my friends: Do not be frightened by those who kill the body and after this have nothing more that they can do.” If persecutors, after killing the bodies of the saints, have nothing further that they can do against them, then those who, in their senseless madness, throw the dead limbs of martyrs to be torn apart by wild beasts and birds, or cause them to be scattered into the air, dissolved in the waves, or reduced to ashes by flames, rage in vain. They can in no way resist the omnipotence of God, which will raise and restore them to life.

“Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna.” There are two kinds of persecutors: one openly raging, the other flattering in a feigned and deceitful manner. The Savior, wishing to fortify and instruct us against both, commands us above to beware of the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and here not to fear the slaughter inflicted by executioners, since after death neither the cruelty of the former nor the pretense of the latter can endure. Rather, we must please the Lord, who always sees; we must fear the Lord, who is always able to punish or to set free.

“Are not five sparrows sold for two asses, and not one of them is forgotten before God?” If God, he says, cannot forget the tiniest animals, or the flying creatures that are carried through the air, you who were made in the image of the Creator ought not to be frightened by those who kill the body. For he who governs irrational creatures does not cease to care for rational beings. The *dipondius*, for which five sparrows are sold—that is, for which they are exchanged—is a very small unit of weight, composed of two asses. Perhaps someone asks how the Apostle can say: “Is God concerned with oxen?” (1 Cor. IX), since an ox is certainly more valuable than a sparrow. But concern is one thing, and knowledge another. Finally, the number of hairs, of which he next says:

“But even the hairs of your head are all numbered.” This is understood not as an actual act of counting but as the capacity of knowledge. God does not devote the anxious vigilance of one who counts, but for him by whom all things are known, all things are, as it were, numbered. Yet they are rightly said to be numbered, because we number the things we wish to preserve. Here he shows the immense providence of God toward human beings and signifies his ineffable affection: nothing of ours is hidden from God, and even small and idle words do not escape his knowledge.

Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh ridicule ecclesiastical understanding at this point, as though we said that the very earthly matter of which our flesh consisted, after the soul departs and it becomes a corpse, must be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever dissolves and changes into the various forms and shapes of other things, although it returns to the body from which it dissolved, must necessarily return to the very same bodily parts where it had been. Otherwise, if the hair returns that frequent cutting removed, and the nails return that repeated trimming cut off, an excessive and indecorous deformity presents itself to those who think this way—and therefore do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.

But just as, if a statue made of any meltable metal were either liquefied by fire, crushed into dust, or melted into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it again from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference to its integrity which particle of the material was returned to which limb of the statue, provided that he recovered the whole from which it had been formed, so God, the wondrous and ineffable artisan, will restore our flesh with wondrous and ineffable speed from the whole substance of which it had consisted. It will not matter for its restoration whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and recalled into other parts of the body, since the providence of the artisan will ensure that nothing indecorous occurs.

“Therefore do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.” One should not read “you are more numerous,” which concerns comparison of number, but “you are worth more”—that is, you are of greater merit, dignity, and esteem before God than the countless bodies or kinds of sparrows that are counted.

“But I say to you: Everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, the Son of Man will acknowledge before the angels of God. But whoever denies me before human beings will be denied before the angels of God.” He refers back to what was said above, where it was stated that every covered and hidden thing would be revealed, concluding that this revelation will take place not in some insignificant gathering but in the presence of the heavenly city and of the eternal King and Judge. And lest, from his saying that those who denied him would be denied, the condition of all who deny—namely, both those who deny deliberately and those who deny through weakness or ignorance—be thought to be the same, he immediately added:

And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. Whoever takes offense at my flesh, thinking that I am merely a man because I have a son and brothers—James, Joseph, and Judas—and because I am a glutton and a wine-drinker: such an opinion and blasphemy, although it is not free from the guilt of error, nevertheless has forgiveness on account of the usefulness of the body. But whoever, clearly understanding the works of God and unable to deny their power, calumniates them, driven by envy, and says that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven, either in the present age or in the age to come. This is not because we deny that forgiveness could also be granted to him, if he were able to repent, by the one who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; rather, because we believe in the judge and giver of forgiveness, who says both that he will always receive repentance and that this blasphemy is nowhere said to be forgiven, we believe that this blasphemer, in accordance with the demands of his merits, will attain neither forgiveness nor even the fruits of worthy repentance. In accordance with this, the evangelist John wrote most truly concerning certain people blinded by the merit of their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and turn, and I may heal them’” (John XII).

Some, indeed, wish to say that the person who speaks a word against, or blasphemes, the Holy Spirit is one who resists with an unrepentant heart the unity of the Church, in which the forgiveness of sins takes place through the Holy Spirit. They say that the one safeguard against blasphemy’s becoming unforgivable is to guard against an unrepentant heart. The opinion of many of them, however, seems by no means sound, since anyone who resists the unity of the Church with an unrepentant heart—whether he is a Jew, a Gentile, or even a heretic—can certainly obtain forgiveness of sins in the Holy Spirit if he flees for refuge to the unity of the Church with a repentant heart. But they say that as long as someone resists the Spirit of grace with an unrepentant heart, so long he does not have forgiveness. Their opponents, however, object that this condition applies equally to all crimes. For as long as someone practices fornication, idolatry, adultery, intercourse with males, theft, and other crimes, he does not possess an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God; but once these crimes have been renounced, he can be washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. In the same way, they say, an unrepentant person cannot have forgiveness as long as he retains an unrepentant heart; but as soon as he repents, he will obtain forgiveness as well. No distinction can be found by which impenitence is more tightly bound to, or more incapable of forgiveness than, the other sins: remaining, like the other crimes, until repentance, it is erased as soon as repentance has been performed.

But the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit alone—by which someone, like the devil and his angels, does not shrink from attacking the majesty of the Godhead against his own conscience—does not have forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal offense. As the evangelist Mark clearly explains, after setting down this testimony of the Lord he added: “For they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” For neither those who believe that the Holy Spirit does not exist, nor those who believe and confess that he exists but is not God, nor those who believe that he is indeed God but is less than the Father and the Son, are held guilty of this charge of unforgivable blasphemy, because they do this not under the influence of diabolical envy but of human ignorance. Therefore the leaders of the Jews, and all who have been corrupted by a similar plague of envy and blaspheme the divine majesty, will perish without end. Read the first book of blessed Augustine’s *On the Sermon on the Mount*.

[Col. 0489D]

“But when they bring you into synagogues and before magistrates and authorities.” For above he had said: “I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute.”

“Do not be anxious about how or what you should answer, or what you should say. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what ought to be said.” Therefore, when we are brought before judges on account of Christ, we ought to offer only our will for Christ; as for the rest, Christ himself, who dwells in us, speaks on his own behalf, and the grace of the Holy Spirit will be supplied in our answering.

[Col. 0491A]

But someone from the crowd said to him: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” This brother is rightly rebuked: while the teacher was commending the joys of heavenly peace and unity, he wished to thrust upon him the trouble of earthly division. He is rightly designated by the term “man.” For, he says, when there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal? Are you not human beings, and walking according to human standards? The Lord denies that he is a divider among human beings, since he had come to reconcile them both with himself and with the angels. For “God is not a God of dissension but of peace.” And “the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one,” nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them (Acts IV). The sole divider of brotherhood and author of dissension is the one of whom it is said above: “The one who does not gather with me scatters.” And concerning his members: “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house” (Matthew XII).

[Col. 0491B]

And he said to them: “Take care and beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” Just as above the Lord had said many things against blasphemers and hypocrites, so here too, taking this foolish petitioner as his occasion, he strives to arm both the crowds and the disciples, by commands and examples alike, against the plague of greed, with which most mortals labor sufficiently—and more than sufficiently. It should be noted that he does not say, “Beware of greed,” but adds, “of all greed,” because some actions appear simple and innocent to human beings, but the inner judge sees and judges the intention with which they are performed. For who would regard it as a crime for someone to divide an inheritance with his brother, or to store the crops that have ripened in his own field in barns? Yet God himself is witness and judge, as it is written.

[Col. 0491C]

And he told them a parable, saying: “The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops, and he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do? For I have nowhere to store my crops.’ And he said: ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all that has been produced for me, and my goods.’” This rich man is not reproved because he cultivated the earth or gathered its produce into barns, but because he placed all his confidence for life in that abundance of possessions. Counting as his own crops and his own goods the produce that the earth had yielded more abundantly than usual, he did not intend to distribute it to the poor, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Give alms from what remains”; instead, after constructing larger storehouses, he strove to reserve it for his future luxury.

[Col. 0491D]

“‘My soul,’ he said, ‘you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast.’” A similar passage is read in Ecclesiasticus: “There is one who becomes rich by sparing, and this is his reward for what he says: ‘I have found rest for myself, and now I shall eat alone of my goods,’ and he does not know that time will pass and leave everything to others” (Ecclesiasticus XI).

[Col. 0492A]

But God said to him: “Fool! This very night they are demanding your soul from you. Whose, then, will the things you have prepared be?” You foolishly promised yourself many seasons of pleasures in life, but, seized by death on this coming night, you will leave to others what you have gathered. For God to say this to a human being is to restrain his wicked schemes by sudden punishment.

Alternatively: The soul is taken away in the night when it is in the darkness of the heart and in misery. It is taken away in the night because it did not wish to possess the light of reflection, so that it might foresee what it could suffer. Hence the apostle Paul rightly says to disciples who are thinking about the future: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may seize you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day. We are not of night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians V). For the day of departure seizes like a thief in the night when it drives out the souls of fools who have not previously considered the future.

[Col. 0492B]

“So is the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” If the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God is foolish and is to be snatched away in the night, then whoever wishes to be rich toward God should not store up treasure for himself, but distribute his possessions to the poor. For in this way he will deserve to be wise and a son of light. Hence the Psalmist, after saying of some greedy rich person: “But he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Psalm XXXVIII), immediately revealed where he had placed the treasure of his heart, saying: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0492C]

And he said to his disciples: “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear.” When he says, “Therefore I tell you,” he is referring to what came before: “For this reason I forbid anxiety about temporal things, lest you be found storing up treasure for yourselves with the rich of this age.” Thus we are entirely freed from concern for what nature has provided to all—to beasts of burden, wild animals, and human beings alike—and yet we are commanded not to be anxious about what we will eat. And because we prepare bread for ourselves in the sweat of our face, labor is to be undertaken, but anxiety is to be removed.

[Col. 0492D]

“Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.” He admonishes us to remember that God has given us far more by making and composing us from soul and body than he has given us in food and covering, so that we may understand that the one who gave the soul will much more easily give food. Similarly, the one who gave the body will much more easily give clothing.

At this point it is often asked whether this food reaches the soul, since the soul is incorporeal while this food is corporeal. But we should recognize that in this passage “soul” means this present life, whose support is this corporeal food. In accordance with this meaning, the following too was said: “Whoever loves his life will lose it” (Matthew X). If we do not understand this as referring to the present life—which must be lost for the kingdom of God, as the martyrs clearly demonstrated that it can be lost—this command will be contrary to the statement: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew XVI).

[Col. 0493A]

“Consider the ravens, because they neither sow nor reap. They have neither storeroom nor barn, and God feeds them.” If birds are nourished by God’s providence without care or hardship—birds that exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose soul is mortal, and which, once they cease to exist, will never exist again—how much more are human beings governed by God’s command, for whom eternity is promised!

[Col. 0493B]

“How much more valuable you are than they!” That is, you are worth more. For since the rational creature that is the human being has been ordered more sublimely in the nature of things than irrational creatures such as birds, you are certainly more precious.

“Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature? If, then, you cannot do even what is least, why are you anxious about the rest?” That is, the one by whose power and dominion it happened that your body was brought to this stature can also clothe it by his providence. That it was not by your own care that your body came to this stature can be understood from the fact that, even if you were to take care and wish to add one cubit to this stature, you could not. Leave, then, the care of clothing your body also to the one whose care you see brought it about that you possess a body of such stature.

“If, then,” he says, “you cannot do even what is least”—for this is a small thing, but it is God who works in bodies (so the text reads). A lesson concerning clothing was also to be given, just as one was given concerning food. Thus he continues and says:

[Col. 0493C]

“Consider the lilies, how they grow. They neither labor nor spin.” But these examples should not be examined allegorically, as though we were to ask what the ravens or the lilies signify. They have been set forth so that greater matters might be commended by means of lesser ones.

“I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” And indeed, what silk, what royal purple, what work of the weavers, can be compared with flowers? What is so red as the rose? What is so white as the lily? But that the purple of the violets is surpassed by no purple dye is more an indication for the eyes than for words.

[Col. 0493D]

“But if God so clothes the grass that is in the field today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?” In Scripture “tomorrow” signifies the future time, as Jacob says: “And tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Genesis XXX). And in the apparition of Samuel, the Pythoness speaks to Saul: “Tomorrow you will be with me” (1 Samuel XXVIII).

“And you, do not seek what you will eat or what you will drink.” It should be noted that he does not say, “Do not seek or be anxious about food, drink, or clothing,” but more explicitly, “What,” he says, “you will eat or what you will drink.” And above: “Nor for the body, what you will wear.” Here he seems to condemn those who, despising ordinary food or clothing, seek for themselves either more luxurious or more austere nourishment or garments than those with whom they lead their lives.

[Col. 0494A]

“And do not be lifted up on high.” Having forbidden anxiety about food, he consequently admonished them not to become proud. At first a person seeks these things to satisfy necessity. But when they have become abundant, he begins also to take pride in them. This is like someone who boasts, while wounded, that he has many plasters in his house, although it would be good for him to have no wounds and to need not even a single plaster.

“For all these things the nations of the world seek. But your Father knows that you need them. Nevertheless, seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.” Here he shows most clearly that these things are not to be desired as though they were our true goods, so that we ought to do good for their sake, if we do anything at all; nevertheless, they are necessary. For he made clear the difference between the good that is to be desired and the necessity that is to be taken up when he said: “Nevertheless, seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.”

The kingdom of God, then, is our good; it is what must be desired, and in it our end must be established, for the sake of which we do everything we do. But because in this life we serve as soldiers so that we may be able to reach that kingdom—and this life cannot be conducted without these necessities—“These things,” he says, “will be added to you, but you seek the kingdom of God.” For since he does not say, “They will be given,” but “They will be added,” he plainly indicates that one thing is given as primary and another is added. Since eternity should occupy our intention, while temporality belongs to our use, the former is given, and the latter is indeed added in abundance.

[Col. 0494B]

“Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.” He calls the flock of the elect “little,” either in comparison with the larger number of the reprobate, or rather because of the devotion of humility. For although he has already enlarged his Church to whatever extent of numbers, he nevertheless wishes it to grow until the end of the world and to reach the promised kingdom through humility. Therefore, gently consoling its labors, he promises with pleasing kindness that the kingdom is to be given to it by the Father, just as he commands it to seek only the kingdom of God.

“Sell what you possess and give alms.” “Do not fear,” he says, “that those who serve as soldiers for the kingdom of God will lack the necessities of this life; indeed, sell what you possess for the sake of almsgiving.” This is done worthily when someone, having once renounced all his possessions for the Lord, nevertheless afterward works with his hands so that he may both obtain his livelihood and give alms. Hence the Apostle boasts, saying: “I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing; you yourselves know that these hands ministered to the things that were necessary for me and for those who are with me. In everything I showed you that by laboring in this way it is necessary to support the weak” (Acts XX).

[Col. 0494D]

“Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old”—namely, by performing acts of almsgiving, whose reward remains forever. This command should not be understood to mean that the saints are to reserve no money for supplying either their own needs or those of the poor. For the Lord himself, whom angels served, is nevertheless recorded as having had a money box for the instruction of his Church, preserving what the faithful offered and distributing it for the needs of his own and of others in want. Rather, the command is that one should not serve God on account of these things, or abandon righteousness through fear of poverty.

[Col. 0495A]

“An unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth corrupts.” This may be understood simply: money that is stored up fails, either when treasures are seized by a thief or when the money itself is spoiled in the treasury by its own fragility; but money given for Christ confers in heaven an enduring fruit of mercy. Or it may certainly be understood in this way: the treasure of a good work, if it is amassed for the sake of earthly advantage, is easily corrupted and perishes; but if it is gathered solely with a heavenly intention, it cannot be corrupted externally by human favor or internally be stained by the blemish of empty glory [perhaps read: *maculari*, “be stained”]. For the thief snatches from outside, while the moth tears apart within.

The thief took away the riches of those to whom the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matthew VI). The moth corrupts the garments of those whom the Psalmist rebukes, saying: “For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves” (Psalm LII). By “bones” he means the strength of virtues.

[Col. 0495B]

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” This should be understood not only of money but of all the passions. The god of gluttons is their belly. Their heart, therefore, is where their treasure is. The treasures of the luxurious are banquets; those of the wanton, amusements; those of the lover, lust. Thus each person serves the one by whom he is conquered.

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands; and be like people waiting for their master.” Since he had shown that many are either wholly subject to the world or serve the Lord with an eye to worldly advantage, he teaches his own beautifully and concisely both to gird their loins, through restraint from love of worldly things, and to have burning lamps, so that they may do this with a true end and right intention.

Alternatively, we gird our loins when through continence we restrain the luxury of the flesh. We hold burning lamps in our hands when through good works we show our neighbors examples of light. For our Redeemer can in no way be pleased with one without the other: either a person who does good works but has not yet abandoned the defilements of luxury, or one who excels in chastity but does not yet exercise himself in good works. But even when both are practiced, it remains that whoever he is should strive toward the heavenly homeland in hope, restraining himself from vices not for the sake of this world’s honor, but placing his entire hope in the coming of his Redeemer. Hence he immediately adds:

[Col. 0495D]

“And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding.” The Lord went to the wedding because, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he joined to himself, as a new human being, the heavenly multitude of angels. He returns when he is manifested to us through judgment. And he fittingly adds concerning the servants who are waiting:

[Col. 0496A]

“So that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.” He comes when he hastens toward judgment; he knocks when, through the troubles of illness, he indicates that death is already near. We open to him immediately if we receive him with love. The one who trembles at leaving the body does not wish to open to the Judge who knocks, and he fears to see as judge the one whom he remembers having despised. But the person who is secure in his hope and conduct opens immediately to the one who knocks, because he joyfully endures the Judge; when he recognizes that the time of approaching death is near, he rejoices in the glory of the recompense. Hence it immediately follows:

“Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching.” The person watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open for the sight of the true light. The person watches who preserves through action what he has believed. The person watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence. Hence Paul says: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians XV). Again he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans XIII). But let us hear what the Lord, when he comes, displays to his watching servants.

[Col. 0496B]

“Amen I tell you: he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them.” He girds himself—that is, he prepares the recompense. He makes them recline—that is, he refreshes them in eternal rest. For our reclining means resting in the kingdom. Hence the Lord says again: “They will come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matthew VIII).

But the Lord ministers while passing by because he satisfies us with the illumination of his light. “He passes by” was said because he returns from judgment to the kingdom. Or certainly the Lord passes by for us after judgment because he raises us from the form of his humanity to the contemplation of his divinity. His passing by consists in leading us into the vision of his brightness: the one whom we see in his humanity at the judgment, we also see in his divinity after the judgment.

[Col. 0496C]

“And if he comes during the second watch, and if he comes during the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.” The first watch is the earliest period, that is, childhood. The second is adolescence or youth. These are one according to the authority of sacred speech, which says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ecclesiastes XI). The third is understood as old age.

Therefore, whoever did not wish to watch during the first watch should at least keep the second, so that whoever neglected to turn from his wicked ways in childhood may at least awaken to the paths of life in youth. And whoever did not wish to watch during the second watch should not lose the remedies of the third watch, so that whoever does not awaken to the paths of life in youth may at least come to his senses in old age.

To shake off the sluggishness of our mind, even external losses are introduced by way of comparison, so that through them the spirit may be roused to guard itself. For it is said:

[Col. 0496D]

“But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.” From this preceding comparison an exhortation is also added, when it is said:

“And you also must be ready, because at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man will come.” The thief breaks into the house while the master of the house is unaware, because while the spirit sleeps, neglecting its own watch, sudden death comes and breaks into the dwelling of our flesh. When it finds the master of the house sleeping, it kills him, because when the spirit does not foresee the coming losses at all, death carries it off unawares to punishment.

He would resist the thief if he were watching, because, anticipating the coming of the Judge who secretly takes away the soul, he would meet him through repentance, so that he might not perish unrepentant. Our Lord wished the final hour to be unknown to us for this reason: so that it might always be feared, and so that, since we cannot foresee it, we might prepare for it without interruption.

[Col. 0497A]

But Peter said to him: “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or also to everyone?” In the preceding parable the Lord had given two warnings: that he would come suddenly, and that they ought to await him prepared. But it is not readily apparent which of these Peter was asking about—or whether he was asking about both—or whom he was including with himself and his companions when he said, “Are you speaking to us, or also to everyone?”

Indeed, by “us” and “everyone” he should be understood to mean either the apostles and those like the apostles on the one hand and the other faithful on the other, or those who, dying individually each day, willingly or unwillingly receive the coming of their Judge, and those who, when the universal judgment comes, will be found alive in the flesh. But it is surprising if blessed Peter doubted either that the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God were to be awaited by all who wish to live soberly, justly, and piously, or that judgment—both of individuals and of all, of great and small, of faithful and unfaithful—would be future and unexpected.

[Col. 0497B]

It remains, therefore, to understand that, since these matters were already well known, he considered other matters that he might perhaps not know worthy of inquiry: namely, whether those sublime rules of heavenly life—which commanded them to sell their possessions, make purses that would not grow old, store up treasure in heaven, watch with girded loins and burning lamps, and await the Lord—applied only to the apostles and those like them, or also to all who are to be saved. That this was the meaning of his question is made clear, unless I am mistaken, by the Lord’s own response.

[Col. 0497C]

But the Lord said: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent steward whom the master will appoint over his household?” In responding to the questions, the Savior first teaches that judgment will come upon everyone, and that each person will receive rewards or punishments according to the merit of his work and the capacity of his understanding. Then, addressing what Peter had chiefly asked, he shows that the grace of virtues which he brought to the world must be pursued by each person to the extent of his ability.

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” The expression “Who, do you think, is...” indicates the difficulty, not the impossibility, of achieving virtue, as in the Psalmist: “Who is wise and will keep these things?” (Psalm CVI). This does not signify no one, but someone rare. Elsewhere the same expression is used not of what is difficult but of what is impossible: “What god is like you?” (Psalm LXXXII)—that is, none. “For you alone are Most High over all the earth” (ibid.).

[Col. 0497D]

“So that he may give them their measure of wheat at the proper time.” By the measure of wheat the proper measure of speech is expressed. For lofty matters ought to be concealed from many hearers and opened scarcely to a few, lest something beyond the capacity of a narrow heart be given and poured out beyond it.

Here Moses, coming forth from the secrecy of God, veils his shining face before the people, since he does not disclose to the crowds the inner mysteries of brightness. The speech of teachers, therefore, ought to be shaped according to the quality of their hearers, so that it may suit each person individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

[Col. 0498A]

“Blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he will find doing so. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses.” As great as the difference in merit is between good hearers and good teachers, so great is the difference in their rewards. When the Lord comes and finds the former watching, he will make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them. But when he finds the latter faithfully and prudently distributing the nourishment of the word to the household entrusted to them, he will appoint them over all that he possesses—that is, over all the heavenly joys of the kingdom. This does not mean that they alone will possess the Lord in these things, but that they will enjoy an eternal possession of them more abundantly than the other saints.

“For those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel XII). And the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching” (1 Timothy V).

[Col. 0498B]

“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the boys and the maidservants, and to eat, drink, and become drunk...” Just as the entire order of good rulers—how they should live and how they will be rewarded—is taught through the one faithful steward, so through this most wicked servant the work and eternal condemnation of all the evil leaders who are to be condemned are likewise described. Neglecting the fear of the Lord, they not only devote themselves to luxury but also incite their subordinates to acts of violence.

Nevertheless, it can also be understood typologically that he beats boys and maidservants when, by displaying the example of wicked conduct or speech, he corrupts the hearts of the weak, who have not yet been made firm in faith, hope, and charity. To eat, drink, and become drunk means to be occupied with every crime and enticement of the world that deranges the mind and causes it to wander.

It should certainly be noted that among the vices of the evil servant it is recorded that he thought his master’s return was delayed; but among the virtues of the good servant it is not counted that he hoped for his master’s speedy return. Rather, the good servant is praised only because, at the master’s command, whenever he might come, he gave his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, he displayed either the rule of the Lord’s word or the rule of his own example.

Indeed, we read that certain good servants were rebuked by the Apostle because, trembling and anxious, they believed that the day of the Lord was imminent, although he had promised that it would come unexpectedly.
