It is therefore proved to be best—even though we greatly desire, if possible, to know when the Desired One of all nations will come—that we patiently accept our ignorance of what it is not permitted to know, and, whether he is near or far, await and love his coming, ready as an example of a good servant.

[Col. 0498D]

“The master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will cut him in two and place his portion with the unbelievers.” He will cut him in two not by severing him with a sword, but by separating him from the company of the faithful and joining him to those who never belonged to the faith. For whoever does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever, as the Apostle says.

[Col. 0499A]

“But that servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare himself or act according to his will will be beaten with many blows.” Many misunderstand this statement and do not want to know what they should do, imagining that they will be beaten less if they do not know what they ought to have done. But it is one thing not to have known and another to have been unwilling to know. The person who wishes to understand but is unable to do so is ignorant; but the person who turns his ear away from the voice of truth so that he may not know is condemned not as one who is ignorant, but as one who despises.

[Col. 0499B]

“But the one who did not know and did things deserving of blows will be beaten with few. Everyone to whom much has been given, from him much will be demanded; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, they will ask more.”

Why, after saying “To whom much has been given,” did he add, “And to the one to whom much has been entrusted”—with divine judgments understood? Perhaps by the two expressions he wished to indicate both orders among the faithful: rulers and subjects. Much is often given even to private individuals, to whom both knowledge of the Lord’s will and the ability to carry out what they know are granted. But much is entrusted to the person to whom, along with his own salvation, the care of feeding the Lord’s flock is committed.

Thus the powerful suffer powerful torments, and a stronger torture awaits the stronger: that is, if those endowed with greater grace offend, a greater punishment will follow. The mildest punishment of all will be that of those who, apart from the sin they inherited originally, added no further sin. And among the other sins they added, each person will have a more tolerable condemnation there to the extent that he had less iniquity here.

[Col. 0499C]

“I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” This statement specifically answers the question of blessed Peter, who was asking whether the way of the stricter life was to be sought by everyone. By “fire” he means the fervor of the Holy Spirit, which illuminates the hidden places of the heart and, through continual movements, summons us to things above; it burns the vices of carnal desire like thorns and brambles; it improves the golden vessels of the Lord’s house by testing them; and it consumes wood, hay, and stubble.

Once sent upon the earth, this fire imbued those one hundred and twenty lamps that it found in the citadel of Zion with an inward sprinkling of its light. Concerning these, after saying above, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII), he added: “And your lamps burning.”

“Do you ask,” he says, “whether I am warning everyone to await the Lord’s coming with girded loins and burning lamps? But since I came forth for this very reason from the bosom of the Father and came into the world, to kindle human beings from earthly desires toward heavenly longings, what else do you think I desire than that the radiance of this fire illuminate every region of the world, that the flame of this devotion continually increase in the hearts of the faithful until the end of the age, and that it not be extinguished by any assault of unbelievers, whether by waves or by winds?”

[Col. 0499D]

“But I have a baptism with which I must be baptized.” “I must first,” he says, “be drenched in the immersion of my own blood, and thus set the hearts of believers aflame with the fire of the Spirit, by which they may be able both to despise—indeed, to hate—all earthly things and their own soul.”

“For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (the text cites *Thessalonians* III)—that is, the victory of the Passion. Concerning this he says elsewhere: “Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark X).

[Col. 0500A]

“And how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” Some manuscripts read: “And how I am distressed.” Such, then, is the Lord’s great condescension that he testifies to possessing a zeal for pouring devotion into us, bringing perfection to completion in us, and hastening the Passion for our sake. Although he himself had nothing that could cause him sorrow, he was nevertheless distressed—or constrained—by our hardships, and at the time of the Passion he displayed grief, which he had assumed not from fear of his own death but from the delay of our redemption.

In accordance with this he says: “And how I am distressed until it is accomplished!” Certainly, whoever is distressed until completion is secure concerning the completion.

Do you think that I came to bring peace upon the earth? No, I tell you, but division. He declares how, after the baptism of his passion and the coming of spiritual fire, the earth would be set ablaze. For the whole world was divided against itself on account of faith in Christ: each household contained both unbelievers and believers. Therefore a beneficial war was sent, so that evil peace might be broken. Isaiah also prophetically foretold this under the figure of Egypt, saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it, and I will set Egyptians against Egyptians” [Col. 0500C] (Isa. 19)—some fighting against the faith, others on behalf of the faith.

“For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three.” “Against two and against three” is what “into two and into three” signifies. It should be noted how he says that the five are divided, when he appears to have listed six persons: father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. We must understand that the same woman is designated by the name “mother” and “mother-in-law,” because the woman who is the son’s mother is also his wife’s mother-in-law; thus she is said to be divided both against her daughter and against her daughter-in-law.

If anyone also seeks to interpret these divisions allegorically, the three are divided against the two and the two against the three because the good think and act contrary to the evil, and the evil contrary to the good. No one doubts that the three pertain to those who preserve faith in the supreme Trinity. The two likewise correspond to those who dissent from the unity of faith; this is demonstrated in many places of Scripture, and especially by the fact that the unclean animals in the ark are retained under this number, while in Genesis it is said only of the works of the second day that God did not see them as good.

“Father against son, and son against his father.” Here the father is the devil, whose sons we once were—not because he created us, but because we imitated him, as the Lord says: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). But after we heard the voice of the one who admonished us, “Forget your people and the Lord [perhaps read ‘house’] of your father,” that fire came—that is, spiritual grace—and separated us from one another [Col. 0501A] and revealed another Father, to whom we might say, “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. 6).

“Mother against daughter, and daughter against mother.” The mother is the synagogue; the daughter is the primitive Church. The latter both endured persecution from the synagogue from which she derived her origin, and herself contradicted that same synagogue by the truth of the faith.

“Mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.” The mother-in-law is the synagogue; the daughter-in-law is the Church from the Gentiles, because Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, is the son of the synagogue, as the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh” (Rom. 9). Thus the mother-in-law—that is, the bridegroom’s mother—is divided, as we have said, both against her daughter-in-law and against her daughter, because the carnal synagogue, whether of circumcision or of uncircumcision, does not cease to persecute believers [Col. 0501B]. But those believers themselves are also divided against the mother-in-law and mother, refusing to receive carnal circumcision, as the Acts of the Apostles show.

And he said also to the crowds: “When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, ‘A cloud is coming,’ and so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say that there will be heat, and it happens.” The cloud rising from the west signifies his flesh rising from death. From it, rain—that is, the preaching of the Gospel—has been poured over all the lands. The south wind blowing before the heat signifies lighter tribulations before the judgment.

“Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of the earth and the sky. How is it that you do not interpret this time?” We have briefly touched upon what the cloud and the south wind mystically signify. But the literal meaning is also clear [Col. 0501C], because those who wished could very easily predict, from changes in the elements, the condition of the winds; so, if they wished, they could also understand this time—that is, either the first or the second coming of the Lord, for he had previously mentioned something about both—from the words of the prophets, who foretold both through very evident signs, either in the events themselves or in the course of the years.

And lest the crowd perhaps flatter itself on account of its ignorance, or claim that, being uneducated and unfamiliar with prophetic reading, it could not discern the course of the times, he adds attentively:

“And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” He shows that they, as rational creatures, even if they do not know letters, can nevertheless discern by natural intelligence either that the one who had performed such works in himself—works no one else had done—must be understood as being above humanity, and therefore believed to be God, or that, after so many injustices in this age, the just judgment of the Creator will come.

Therefore no one, because of what was said above about the servant who does not know his master’s will being struck with few blows, should presume, while sinning, upon the remedy of ignorance. For, to say nothing else, simply because he is human, he cannot be ignorant either of the evils he should avoid or of the goods he should desire.

“When you go with your adversary to the magistrate on the way, make an effort to be released from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison.” These words, like those above, teach that the enticements of the world must be trampled underfoot and that the coming of the dreadful [Col. 0502A] Judge must be awaited in continual expectation.

Our adversary on the way is the word of God, which is opposed to our carnal desires in the present life. The person who submits humbly to God’s commands is freed from him. Otherwise, the adversary will hand him over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, because the sinner will be held guilty in the judge’s examination on account of his contempt for the Lord’s word. The judge will hand him over to the officer because he will permit the evil spirit to drag him away for punishment, so that it may itself exact from the body the soul, forced forth for punishment—the soul that had willingly consented to it in guilt. The officer will throw him into prison because through the evil spirit he is thrust into hell until the day of judgment comes; from then on, the spirit itself will also be tormented with him in the fires of hell.

“I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last small coin” [Col. 0502B]. That is, until you have paid even for the smallest sins. Since you will always be able to pay them by suffering punishment, but never to discharge them by obtaining pardon—for there will be no place for pardon there—you will never come out from there, where you will pay the perpetual penalties of your deeds.

## CHAPTER XIII

At that very time some people came, telling him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. These Galileans, who were killed by the impious governor amid their sacrifices, paid the penalties for their own crimes by an impious and criminal death. Yet it was not death itself that harmed them—for the glory of the blessed martyrs shows that good people, too, can die in this way—but their wicked life, on account of which they were to be sent into the second death. Nevertheless, they were punished with such a death either for the correction of the living, so that when the pestilent man was scourged the fool might become wiser, or certainly as an example to those unwilling to be corrected and therefore destined to perish most miserably. Thus it follows:

And he answered and said to them: “Do you think that these Galileans were sinners above all the other Galileans because they suffered such things? I tell you, no; but unless you repent, you will all perish likewise.”

Indeed, those who did not repent perished in the same way, because in the fortieth year after the Lord’s passion the Romans came—those whom Pilate represented, since he belonged to their people and kingdom—and, beginning with Galilee, from which the Lord’s preaching had also begun, they destroyed the impious nation so completely that they defiled with human blood not only the courts of the temple, where sacrifices were customarily brought, but [Col. 0502D] even the inner chambers, into which the Galileans had no access.

Because, in a typological sense, Pilate—whose name is interpreted as “mouth of the hammerer”—signifies the devil, always ready to strike; because blood signifies sin; and because sacrifices signify good works, Pilate mingles the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices whenever the devil stains the almsgiving, prayers, fasting, and other good deeds of the faithful either with the deadly pleasure of flesh and blood, or with thoughts of hatred, or with the fury of envy, or with ambition for human praise, or with any other wicked plague. Thus, although these offerings appear to be presented to the Lord, the crafty adversary renders them useless to those who offer them. Would that we did not know how this happens among us every day.

“And likewise those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them. Do you think that they too were debtors above all the people dwelling in Jerusalem? I tell you, no; but unless you repent, you will all perish likewise.”

These inhabitants of Jerusalem, like those Galileans, were not the only sinners, but were punished as a warning to the rest. Crushed by the tower’s collapse, they foreshadow all the Jews who refused to repent, showing that they would perish together with their own walls.

The number eighteen is not without significance. Among the Greeks it is expressed by ι and η, that is, by the very letters with which the name Jesus begins. They indicate that these people especially deserved condemnation because they preferred to reject the name of the Savior when they heard it rather than accept it.

Mystically, the tower of Siloam is the one to which the Psalmist sings: “You have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Ps. 60). For the name Siloam itself, which is interpreted as “sent,” and the place where the man blind from birth received light, signify the one who said: “I have come as light into the world” (John 12), and again: “He who sent me is with me” (John 8).

Of his fall it is said elsewhere, under the metaphor of a stone: “Everyone who falls upon that stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will grind him to powder” (Luke 20).

Alternatively, each of us ought to build a tower of virtues, first calculating the expense, lest, when he cannot complete it, passersby ridicule him. This tower, well constructed, endures. But if, raised in pride, it does not have firm foundations, it will fall upon the one by whom it was built.

He also told this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard.” This fig tree can indeed signify the nature of the human race. It was well planted—that is, created according to the likeness of its author. But when God sought fruit from it for three years, it refused to produce, because before the Law, under the Law, and under grace it disdained obedience.

If you look back to what came before, however, you will notice that, although it bears the type of all humanity in general, it especially bears the type of the synagogue. For after that terrifying and dreadful sentence had been given—“Unless you repent, you will all perish likewise”—he immediately adds a parable about a barren tree destined to be uprooted. He teaches most plainly that those to whom he was speaking, like a fruitless fig tree, would be cut down if they did not repent.

The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel, as we learn from Isaiah’s song. The synagogue, established in that same house, is the fig tree in the vineyard. But the one who allowed his vineyard to be plundered by passersby also ordered the fig tree to be cut down.

“And he came seeking fruit on it, and found none.” The Lord, who had established the synagogue through Moses, appeared born in the flesh. Teaching frequently in the synagogue, he sought the fruit of faith but did not find it in the minds of the Pharisees.

Then he said to the vinedresser: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none.” The order of the apostles and teachers is expressed by the vinedresser; through their prayers and admonitions, constant care for the people of God is urged. For the Lord often complained to them about the fruitless nation of the Jews, which during the three years of his visitation—that is, in the legal decrees, the prophetic testimonies, and the very grace of the radiant Gospel—had remained negligent.

“Cut it down, then. Why should it even occupy the ground?” The Jewish nation was not cut down by the apostles but by the Romans, and it was expelled from the promised land. But by saying, “Cut it down,” he placed before it, by urging repentance, the calamity of the cutting down that was to come.

By a just judgment it lost both land and kingdom, for whose sake it had not feared to persecute the citizens of heaven and to kill the very King of heaven and earth, saying through its chief priests and Pharisees: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” [Col. 0504B].

The crowd of the Jewish people may also be represented by the soil occupied by the barren fig tree. Burdened by the harmful shadow of its leaders, so that it could not receive the light of truth, and prevented by the example of their perversity from being warmed by the sun of heavenly love, it corresponds to what the Savior says elsewhere to the same people: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter” (Matt. 23).

But he answered and said to him: “Lord, let it remain this year also, until I dig around it.” This is the voice of the apostles, who after the Lord’s passion prayed most earnestly for the Jews, asking that the vengeance of the Lord’s cross not be demanded from those who remained unrepentant.

“Until I dig around it”—that is, until I humble the root of its fruitless mind with the hoe of a two-edged rebuke, instilling fear both of present afflictions and of everlasting condemnation. Every ditch is lower at its bottom; and surely, while rebuke shows the mind what it is, it humbles it.

“And I will put manure on it.” That is, I will bring back to the mind the abomination of the evil deeds it has committed, and from the rottenness of manure I will stir up, as it were, the grace of compunction.

“And if indeed it bears fruit—otherwise, in the future you shall cut it down.” When he said, “And if indeed it bears fruit,” he added nothing, but left the sentence suspended. When he added, “Otherwise,” he immediately attached the judgment of future condemnation, saying, “In the future you shall cut it down,” because he saw that the synagogue was much more inclined to deny God than to confess him.

Therefore elsewhere also, acting out in deeds the same figure that he presents here in words, he condemned the barren fig tree to eternal sterility. He showed that even if the apostles dug around it by reproving it, and even if they brought manure by reproaching it for its sins, it would nevertheless not be enriched with the fruit of repentance, but would be removed by the severity of the strict double-edged axe.

Now he was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths, and behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years. After telling the parable of the fig tree, the Lord is said to have taught in the synagogue, so that it might be made clear that the parable was directed to no other matter, but that this was the fruit he sought in the fig tree and did not find: the word was offered to the synagogue, but not received.

Yet, lest you think that the whole synagogue was to be utterly destroyed because of the guilt of barrenness, but might know that remnants would be saved through the election of grace, the healing of the primitive Church immediately follows in the same place under the figure of the bent woman.

She had been bent over for eighteen years, a number completed by six times three. This shows that she who languished through weak works in the testimony of the Law, in the prophecy of the prophets, and in the revelation of grace was bent over. The number six, in which the creation of the world was completed, signifies the perfection of works. The three are, as I said, the three periods of the Lord’s visitation, during which Judea, because it had learned to perform earthly rather than heavenly things, was bent away from the uprightness of its mind, as though for eighteen years.

And she was bent over and could not look upward at all [Col. 0505B]. Because, thinking about earthly things and seeking what was weak, she did not yet attend to heavenly matters. She heard the prophet say: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” In contrast, the Apostle says to the members of the Church: “Think about the things that are above, not those that are upon the earth” (Col. 3).

When Jesus saw her, he called her to himself and said to her: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity.” And he laid his hands upon her, and immediately she was straightened, and she glorified God.

He saw her by predestining her through grace; he called her by enlightening her through teaching; he laid his hands upon her by assisting her with spiritual gifts; he raised her up to glorify God, advancing her in good works and making her steadfast to the end. “Those whom he predestined,” says the Apostle, “he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8).

But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, answered and said to the crowd: “There are six days on which one ought to work; on those days therefore come and be healed, and not on the Sabbath.”

Jesus healed on the Sabbath, showing that the time had already come for, according to the prophecy of the Song of Songs, the day to dawn and the shadows to be removed. But the ruler of the synagogue did not know either this or the far more excellent mystery that the Lord indicated by healing on the Sabbath: namely, that after the six ages of this world he would give the perpetual joys of immortal life.

As a figure of this, Moses commanded that the Sabbath be kept not from good activity but from servile—that is, harmful—activity, prefiguring the time when our worldly works would cease, but not religious works, that is, deeds of praising God [Col. 0505D]. Thus the ruler of the synagogue is both mistaken and misleading, because the Law prohibited on the Sabbath not healing a human being but carrying burdens—that is, being weighed down by sins.

But the Lord answered him: “Hypocrites! Does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to drink?”

He accuses the leaders of the synagogue of unbelief and rightly marks them with the name hypocrites, that is, pretenders. Although they desired to appear as teachers of the people, they were not ashamed to put the healing of a human being after the care of livestock.

In a deeper sense, however, by the terms “ox” and “donkey” he signifies the Jew and the Greek. Of their calling it is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.” Each of these, released from the bonds of sin, has laid aside the thirst and heat of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain.

And should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound—behold, for eighteen years—be released from this bond on the Sabbath?

The daughter of Abraham is every faithful soul; the daughter of Abraham is the Church gathered from both peoples into the unity of faith. When the time of the Law and of the Lord’s resurrection had been fulfilled, she broke through the bonds of her long captivity by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

For perhaps the mystery of the Sabbath and of the eighteen years can also be understood in this way, without impropriety. Mystically, then, the ox or donkey being released from the manger and led to drink is the same as the daughter of Abraham being raised from the bond of harmful inclination: the Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, is released from the snares of sins through the water of baptism and raised up to hope for heavenly things.

It should certainly be noted that a most unspeakable heresy attempts, from the Lord’s statement that the woman was bound by Satan, to assert that the defects of human bodies belong not to God as author but rather to the devil—as though, although the devil always desires to harm, he could harm anyone unless he had received power from the Almighty.

For what else is declared not only in the book of blessed Job, which that heresy, in its madness, rejects along with the other books of the Old Testament and with God himself who gave them, as though he were the evil ruler of the world, but also in the Gospel, where the demons did not enter even the swine unless he himself permitted it—as we also taught above?

When he had said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced in all the glorious things that were done by him. Those who are ashamed by the Savior’s words show that they deserve to be compared to the barren fig tree. Those who rejoice at his miracles declare that they belong, through the devotion of faith, to the daughter of Abraham—that is, to the Church glorifying God for her being raised up.

Therefore he said: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed.”

The kingdom of God is the preaching of the Gospel and knowledge of the Scriptures, which leads to life. Concerning it, he says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21).

This kingdom, then, is like a grain of mustard seed, both because of the fervor of faith and because mustard is said to drive out poisons. Hence elsewhere also we read that perfect faith is compared to a grain of mustard, because by its simplicity and humility it overcomes all doctrines of perversity.

Which a man took and put in his garden. The man is Christ; the garden is the Church, which is always to be cultivated by his teachings and endowed with gifts. He is rightly said to have received the seed that he sowed, because the gifts that he grants us with the Father through his divinity he received with us through his humanity. Hence it is said: “He received gifts among men.” And elsewhere Peter says: “Having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this one whom you see and hear.”

And it grew and became a tree. The preaching of the Gospel grew as it was spread throughout the whole world, and it grows in the mind of every believer, because no one suddenly becomes perfect. Rather, as it says, “He has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83), and below: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

For one ascends gradually from the valley of tears, so that the God of gods may be seen on the mountain of heavenly joys. As it grows, the mustard seed rises not like herbs, which quickly wither, but like a tree, one that rejoices in long years and abundant fruitfulness.

And note that while the barren fig tree is rebuked in the old vineyard, a mustard tree is soon produced anew in the garden of the Gospel.

And the birds of heaven rested in its branches. The branches of this tree are the various teachings. In them pure souls, which know how to strive upward on the wings of the virtues, rejoice to build nests and rest. “Who will give me wings like a dove’s?” it says; “I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54).

The humility of the Lord’s incarnation may also be understood in the grain of mustard: “which a man took and put in his garden,” because Joseph received the body of the crucified Savior and buried it in a garden. It grew and became a tree because he rose and ascended into heaven. It spread branches in which the birds of heaven might rest because he scattered preachers throughout the world, so that in their words and consolations the faithful might breathe again after the weariness of this life.

And again he said: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God, and to what is it like? It is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

A *satum* is a measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, containing one and a half *modii*. The leaven, then, signifies love, which makes the mind fervent and rouses it.

The woman signifies that daughter of Abraham upon whom he had laid his hands above and who was immediately straightened and glorified God—that is, she signifies the Church. We are her flour, all of us who are ground by the exercise of fear and hope, as though between an upper and a lower millstone, so that, according to the Apostle, we many may be one bread and one body in Christ.

Thus the woman hid the leaven of love in three measures of flour because the Church commands us to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. Under the figure of Sarah, Abraham is told: “Hasten three measures of fine flour, mix them, and make cakes baked under the ashes” (Gen. 18).

The three measures of flour may also signify the three fruits of the Lord’s seed: the thirtieth, the sixtieth, and the hundredfold—that is, the fruits of the married, the continent, and virgins.

It is beautifully said that the leaven was hidden in the flour until the whole was leavened, because love, stored within our mind, ought to grow until it transforms the entire mind into its own perfection, so that the soul can love, do, and remember nothing apart from love of its Creator.

Here this is begun, but there it is brought to perfection, where, since God is all in all, he warms everyone with the one and same fire of his love.

Someone said to him: “Lord, are those who are saved few?” But he said to them: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” [Col. 0508A].

One enters the hall of salvation through the narrow gate because the enticement of the deceptive world must necessarily be conquered through hardships and fasts. And he rightly said, “Strive to enter,” because unless the mind’s exertion burns fervently, the flood of the world cannot be overcome, through which the soul is continually dragged down to lower things.

“For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.” They seek to enter, summoned by love of salvation, but they will not be able, deterred by the roughness of the road. They seek it through desire for rewards, but soon recoil from fear of the labors.

This is not because the Lord’s yoke is harsh or his burden heavy, but because they do not wish to learn from him that he is gentle and humble in heart, so that they may find rest for their souls. Thus the gate by which one enters into life is narrow.

“But when the master of the house has entered and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us’” [Col. 0508B].

The master of the house is Christ, who in his divinity is wholly present everywhere. He is within for those whom his present vision gladdens in the heavenly homeland, but he is, as it were, outside for those who still struggle in this pilgrimage, aided by him as a hidden comforter, in accordance with his promise: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

He will enter and shut the door when, bringing his entire body, which is the Church, glorified by the glory of the resurrection, to the joy of contemplating him, he takes away from the rejected the opportunity for repentance that he now opens to all who piously knock.

To stand outside and knock at the door is to beg God in vain for the mercy they had neglected, excluded from the company of the blessed.

And answering, he will say to you: “I do not know where you are from.” How does he not know where they are from, when the Psalm says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Ps. 93), and elsewhere it is written: “He knows the deceiver and the one who is deceived”?

This is because “knowing” in God is sometimes said to mean recognizing and sometimes approving. “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous; but he who is unknown will be unknown” (2 Chron. 13). He does know the rejected, whom he judges by knowing them—for he would not judge those whom he did not know at all—and yet in a certain sense he does not know where they are from, because he does not approve in them the mark of faith and love for him.

Then you will begin to say: “We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.” This may be understood simply: the Jews, scorning the mysteries of faith, imagine that they are known to the Lord if they merely bring victims to the temple, feast before the Lord, and listen to the reading of the prophets, not knowing what the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14); and elsewhere: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3)—that is, in carnal circumcision.

Or it may be understood mystically: those eat and drink before the Lord who receive the nourishment of the word with worthy hunger. Hence those who say these things add, as if explaining them: “And you taught in our streets.”

For sacred Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink. In obscure passages it is food, because it is broken as though by explanation and swallowed by chewing. It is drink in clearer passages, because it is absorbed just as it is found.

Thus they testify that they understood both the hidden commands of sacred speech and its open ones, since they complain to the judge who rejects them that they ate and drank before him. But what follows must be feared greatly:

“And he will say to you: ‘I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’” “The feasting of legal festivals,” he says, does not help one whom the devotion of faith does not commend; knowledge of the Scriptures does not make known to God one whom the iniquity of his works shows to be unworthy in his sight.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Weeping is usually produced by heat, and gnashing of teeth by cold. Here a twofold Gehenna is indicated: one of excessive cold and one of unbearable heat. The statement of blessed Job agrees with this: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24).

Or certainly, the gnashing of teeth reveals the feeling of one who is indignant, because each person repents too late, groans too late, and too late becomes angry with himself for having sinned with such stubborn wickedness.

“And behold, there are last who will be first, and there are first who will be last.” The primary sense of this statement is clear from what came before: the peoples of the Gentiles, who had long lived without faith, would be called to faith, while the Jews, who had held the headship of faith and righteousness for so many ages, would become the tail.

It can also be understood in this way: some who are despised in this age will possess great glory in the future, while others who are glorious among human beings will be condemned by the strict Judge. It can also mean that many who come late to God’s service may excel through the great merits of their lives, while others who burn with spiritual zeal from early youth may finally grow weary, becoming torpid through idleness.

On that very day some Pharisees came and said to him: “Go out and depart from here, because Herod wants to kill you.” And he said to them: “Go and tell that fox.”

He calls Herod a fox because of his tricks and plots. The fox is an animal full of deceit, always wishing to hide in a den, foul-smelling with a dreadful odor, and never running along straight paths but through winding turns. All these traits apply to heretics, whose type Herod bears, and who strive to kill Christ—that is, to take away from believers the humility of Christian faith.

“Behold, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected.”

These words are understood as having been spoken by the Lord mystically and figuratively. For he did not suffer on that day which is the third from this day, since he immediately says:

“Nevertheless, I must walk today and tomorrow and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.”

Therefore what he says—“I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13)—must be referred to his body, which is the Church.

Demons are cast out when the Gentiles, abandoning the superstitions of their ancestors, believe in him. Healings are completed when life is lived according to his commands, after renunciation has been made of the devil and this age, until the end of the resurrection. At that time the Church will be perfected as though on the third day—that is, she will be brought to angelic fullness and perfected also through the immortality of the body.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children as a bird gathers its nest under its wings, and you were unwilling.”

By “Jerusalem” he calls not the city’s stones and buildings but its inhabitants. He laments over it with a father’s affection, just as we read elsewhere that he wept when he saw it.

When he says, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” he testifies that all the prophets sent previously had been sent by him. We also read in the song of Deuteronomy the comparison of a bird gathering its nest under its wings: “As an eagle protects its nest and longs for its young, spreading its wings, it took them up and carried them upon its pinions” (Deut. 28).

And appropriately, after calling Herod a fox because he was plotting his death, he compares himself to a bird. For the deceitful fox never ceases to lay snares for birds.

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” The city itself, which he had called his nest, he now calls the Jews’ house. It is not unjustly deprived of the Lord’s protection and left to its own power, because it not only disdained being protected by the wings of that almighty bird whom Matthew calls a hen, but also handed Christ over—the bird who wished to protect it—to be devoured by foxes, that is, to be crucified by Herod and Pilate [Col. 0510C].

Nor was there delay: it was given as plunder to those same foxes, that is, to the kingdom of the earth. For after the Lord had been killed, the Romans came and, as though plundering an empty nest, took away their place, their nation, and their kingdom.

“But I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

The crowds did say this to the Lord when he came to Jerusalem. But since Luke does not say where the Lord departed from there, so that he would not come until the time when this was already being said—for he continues on his journey until he comes to Jerusalem—this clearly compels us to understand the statement mystically, that is, of the coming when he will come in glory. This is especially so because Matthew testifies that the Lord said these words after the crowd had sung praises to him [Col. 0510D].

Alternatively, what he says means: “Unless you repent and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face.” The Jews have been given a time for repentance. Let them confess him blessed who comes in the name of the Lord, and they will behold the face of Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV

And it happened that, when he entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him, and behold, a certain man with dropsy was before him.

The disease of dropsy takes its name from watery fluid. For in Greek, ὕδωρ means “water.” It is a subcutaneous fluid arising from a disorder of the bladder, accompanied by swelling and distension and foul breath [Col. 0511A]. It is characteristic of the dropsical person that, the more abundant his disordered fluid becomes, the more intensely he thirsts.

Therefore he is rightly compared to one burdened by an overflowing discharge of carnal pleasures. He is also compared to a wealthy miser, who, the richer he becomes in wealth that he does not use well, thirsts all the more ardently for such things.

Jesus answered and said to the lawyers and Pharisees: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” But they were silent. The statement that Jesus “answered” refers to what was mentioned earlier: “And they were watching him.” For the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings. Yet rightly do those questioned remain silent, since they see that whatever they say will be turned against them. For if it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, why are they watching to see whether the Savior will heal? If it is not lawful, why do they themselves tend their animals on the Sabbath?

[Col. 0511B] But he took hold of him, healed him, and sent him away. By a deliberate dispensation the Lord heals the dropsical man in the presence of the lawyers and Pharisees, and soon afterward argues against avarice, so that through this bodily illness the sickness of their hearts might be represented. Indeed, after many of his exhortations in the course of the discussion, it is added: “But the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and mocked him.” The dropsical man, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. So too every avaricious person multiplies his thirst: once he has obtained what he desires, he yearns still more eagerly for other things to desire.

And answering them, he said: “Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath?” Thus he convicts the Pharisees, who were watching him, [Col. 0511C] and also condemns them for avarice. “If,” he says, “on the Sabbath you hasten to rescue a donkey or an ox, or any other animal that has fallen into a well—not caring for the animal but for your own avarice—how much more ought I to set free a human being, who is far better than an animal?” Appropriately, then, he compared the dropsical man with an animal that had fallen into a well, for he was suffering from an excess of fluid. Likewise, he compared the woman whom he said had been bound for eighteen years, and whom he released from that bondage, with an animal that is untied so that it may be led to water. And in both places he rightly mentioned an ox and a donkey, whether we understand them as signifying the wise and the foolish, or—as was said above—as signifying the two peoples. For the neck of one has been worn down by the yoke of the law, while another, whom any deceiver found like a brute animal incapable of retaining any rational understanding, he dragged away into whatever error he wished. The Savior, therefore, at his coming, found all bound by Satan’s chains and all submerged in the lowest well of desire. “For there is no distinction: all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. III).

He also told a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the places of honor, and saying to them: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.” Literally, this admonition of the Savior is clear: he teaches that humility is praiseworthy not only before God but also among human beings. Yet since the Evangelist does not call this a parable without reason, we should briefly consider what it also signifies mystically. [Col. 0512A] That “weddings” signify the union of Christ and the Church is evident in many passages. One of them is: “Can the children of the wedding feast fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark II). Another is: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding” (Matt. XXII). Whoever, then, comes to these wedding festivities after being invited—that is, whoever is joined to the members of the Church through faith—must not recline in the first place: he must not exalt himself above the others as though he were superior to them, boasting of his merits. Indeed, according to the parable in another passage, he should strive to appear clothed in a wedding garment—that is, radiant with the splendor of the virtues—but he should adorn the very habit of those virtues with devoted humility.

“Lest someone more honored than you be invited by him, and the one who invited both him and you come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place’; and then you begin, with shame, to occupy the lowest place.” The person who yields his place to one invited later who is more honored is the one who, made overconfident by reliance on his long way of life, is surpassed by the swift progress of those who have followed him in Christ. He occupies the lowest place with shame when, recognizing better things in others, he humbles whatever excellence he had thought belonged to his own conduct, saying with the Prophet: “I am needy and in labors from my youth; but, though exalted, I have been humbled and brought to shame” (Ps. LXXIII).

“But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place.” “The greater you are,” he says, “humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III). And the Psalmist exults: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; revive me according to your word” [Col. 0512C] (Ps. CXVIII). He plainly signifies that he can be revived by the Lord if he himself thinks humbly of his virtues.

“So that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’” When the Lord comes, he will bless the one whom he finds humble by calling him “friend,” and will command him to move up higher. “Whoever humbles himself like a little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”

“Then you will have glory in the presence of all those reclining with you.” It is beautifully said, “Then you will have glory,” so that you do not now begin to seek what is reserved for you at the end. For, as Solomon says, “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end.” This may also be understood as referring to the present life: one who is found reclining in the lowest place is exalted when the Lord comes. For every day the Lord enters his wedding feast; every day he judges the conduct, places, and bearing of those reclining at table. Often, looking down upon the proud, he grants the humble such abundant gifts of his Spirit that he rightly causes the assembly of those reclining together—that is, of those resting in faith—to glorify them with unanimous admiration. Astonished, it breaks forth into praise of its Creator, saying: “But to me your friends, O God, have been honored exceedingly; their dominion has been strengthened exceedingly.”

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” From this conclusion it is plainly evident that the Lord’s preceding discourse is to be understood figuratively. For it is not the case that everyone who exalts himself before human beings is immediately humbled, or that whoever humbles himself in the sight [Col. 0513A] of human beings is exalted by them. On the contrary, someone who raises himself either to the summit of dignity or to any other glory he seeks may continue to be exalted all the way to the end. Likewise, some humble and modest person may remain until the end of life in the modest condition with which he is content. And therefore, because according to the sentence of Truth everyone who carelessly elevates himself on account of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, while whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good works will be exalted by him, the Redeemer’s preceding discourse—by which he forbids the seeking of the chief places at weddings—plainly corresponds to this same meaning.

He also said to the one who had invited him: “When you give a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or your rich neighbors.” [Col. 0513B] He does not forbid brothers, friends, and rich people to hold banquets for one another as though this were a crime. Rather, just as with the other exchanges required by human necessity—where sinners lend to sinners so that they may receive equal things—he shows that such acts have no value for earning the rewards of heavenly life. Finally, he adds:

“Lest they also invite you in return, and repayment be made to you.” He does not say, “Lest sin be made for you,” but, “Let repayment,” he says, “be made to you.” The same is found in another passage: “If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you?” (Luke VI). Nor does he say there, “It is sin for you,” but, “What credit is that to you?” For even sinners do this. Nevertheless, there are certain banquets of brothers, friends, relatives, and rich neighbors that receive not only repayment in the present but also condemnation in the future. Indeed, they are counted by the Apostle among the works of darkness. “Let us walk honorably,” he says, “as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness” (Rom. XIII). Revelries are luxurious banquets, which are either celebrated by everyone contributing together or are customarily provided in turn by companions, so that no one is ashamed to say or do anything dishonorable, since they gather precisely so that disgraceful things may be done there: the abundance of wine stimulates them, and various pleasures of lust are aroused.

“But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” He calls it “the resurrection of the just” because, although all will rise, it is not improperly designated as though it were the peculiar resurrection of those who do not doubt that they will come to it blessed. Therefore, whoever invites the poor to a feast will receive a reward in the future. Whoever invites friends, brothers, and rich people receives his recompense. But even if he does this for God’s sake, following the example of the sons of blessed Job, as with the other duties of fraternal love, the one who commanded it himself grants the reward. Whoever invites gluttons and the lustful on account of wantonness will be punished with eternal punishment in the future.

When one of those reclining together had heard this, he said to him: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.” The bread eaten in the kingdom of God is not to be understood, as Cerinthus held, as bodily food, but rather as that which said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” [Col. 0514A] (John VI). That is: if anyone, having been perfectly incorporated into the sacrament of my Incarnation, is deemed worthy to enjoy the vision of my divine majesty, he will rejoice in the perpetual blessedness of immortal life. But because some receive this bread by faith alone, as though in adoration, while they disdain truly to reach its sweetness by tasting it, the Lord refutes in the following parable the torpor of such people as unworthy of the heavenly banquet. For it follows:

“But he said to him: ‘A certain man made a great dinner and invited many.’” Who is this man, if not the one of whom it is said through the Prophet: “And he is a man, and who knows him?” He made a great dinner because he prepared for us satisfaction from inward sweetness. He invited many, but few come, because sometimes even those who are subject to him through faith oppose his eternal banquet by living badly.

“And he sent his servant at the hour of dinner to say to those invited that they should come, because everything was now ready.” What is the hour of dinner except the end of the world? We are certainly in it, as Paul testified long ago, saying: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X). If, then, it is already the hour of dinner when we are called, we ought to make excuses for God’s banquet all the less, the more clearly we see that the end of the age has drawn near. This banquet of God is called not a luncheon but a dinner because dinner remains after luncheon, whereas after dinner no banquet remains. And because God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for us at the end, it was right for it to be called not a luncheon but a dinner. But who is signified by this servant sent by the master of the household to invite people, if not the order of preachers? To remove our weariness, everything is already prepared, because, to wipe away the tepidity of our minds at God’s dinner, that singular Lamb was sacrificed for us who took away the sins of the world.

“And they all began together to make excuses.” God offers what ought to have been requested; unasked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for. He announces the delights of eternal refreshment, offering them when asked, yet prepared and unrequested he is despised, and all together make excuses. But some say: “We do not wish to make excuses; for we rejoice that we are both invited to and will reach that banquet of heavenly refreshment.” They would certainly be speaking truly if they did not love earthly things more than heavenly ones, and if they were not more occupied with bodily matters than spiritual ones. Hence the very reason for the excuses is also supplied here, when it immediately continues:

“The first said to him: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it. I ask you to excuse me.’” What is signified by the farm except earthly possessions? He therefore goes out to see the farm who thinks only of external things for the sake of his possessions.

“And another said: ‘I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them. I ask you to excuse me.’” What do we understand by the five yokes of oxen except the five bodily senses? They are also rightly called yokes because they are doubled in the two sexes. Since these bodily senses cannot comprehend inward things but know only what is external, and, abandoning what is within, touch the things that are outside, curiosity is rightly signified by them. For curiosity is a grave vice: while it leads anyone’s mind outward to investigate the life of his neighbor, it always conceals from that person his own inner life. For this reason it is also said of those five yokes of oxen: “I am going to test them,” since testing sometimes properly pertains to curiosity. But it should be noted that both the one who excuses himself because of the farm and the one who excuses himself because he is going to test the yokes of oxen mingle words of humility with their excuses, saying:

“I ask you to excuse me.” For when he says “I ask,” yet refuses to come, humility sounds in his voice, but pride in his action. And behold, every perverse person recognizes this when he hears it, yet does not cease doing what he recognizes as wrong. For when we say to someone acting perversely, “Turn back, follow God, abandon the world,” where are we calling him except to the Lord’s dinner? But when he replies, “Pray for me, because I am a sinner; I cannot do this,” what else is he doing but asking and making excuses? By saying, “I am a sinner,” he suggests humility; but by adding, “I cannot turn back,” he displays pride.

“And another said: ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’” What is signified by the wife except carnal pleasure? Although marriage is good and was established by divine providence for the propagation of offspring, some people seek through it not the fruitfulness of children [Col. 0515C] but the satisfaction of pleasure. Thus an unjust matter can appropriately be signified by a just one. The supreme master of the household therefore invites us to the dinner of the eternal banquet. But while one person is occupied by earthly care, another is consumed by the shrewd consideration of another’s conduct, and the mind of yet another is defiled by carnal pleasure; every fastidious person fails to hasten to the banquet of eternal life.

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the household, angered, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.’” Behold: the person who devotes himself to earthly possessions more than is right refuses to come to the Lord’s dinner; the person who sweats over the labor of curiosity finds the nourishment of life prepared for him distasteful; the person who clings to carnal desires rejects the spiritual food of the banquet. Since the proud refuse to come, the poor are chosen. Why? Because, in Paul’s words, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. I). The poor and the weak are those who are weak in their own judgment before themselves. For there are poor people who are also, as it were, strong, since they grow proud even in poverty. The blind are those who possess no light of understanding. The lame are those who do not have straight steps in their conduct. But when vices of character are signified by bodily weakness, it is entirely clear that just as those who were called and refused to come were sinners, so too these who are invited and come are sinners. Yet proud sinners are rejected, while humble sinners are chosen. He chooses those whom the world despises, because often that very contempt brings a person back to himself. The poor and weak, the blind and lame, are said to come when they are called because the weak and despised of this world generally hear God’s voice more quickly precisely because in this world they have nothing in which to take delight. But when the poor have been led to the dinner, let us hear what the servant adds:

“Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” Many such people gathered from Judea have come to the Lord’s dinner, but the multitude that believed from the Israelite people did not fill the place of the heavenly banquet. A crowd of Jews has already entered, but room still remains in the kingdom where the multitude of the nations may be received. Hence the same servant is told:

“Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.” When the Lord invites people to the dinner from the alleys and streets, he designates that people who had learned to observe the law amid civic life. But when he commands that his guests be gathered from the roads and hedges, he plainly seeks to gather a rustic people—that is, the Gentiles. It should be noted, however, that in this third invitation he does not say, “Invite,” but, “Compel them to enter.” For there are some who understand that good things should be done but desist from doing them. As we said above, it often happens to such people that the adversity of this world strikes them amid their carnal desires. Frequently they waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under the burden of injuries, or are afflicted by heavier losses. Rebuking themselves for their own desires, they turn their hearts to the Lord. Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected away from the desires of the present life—what are they doing except being compelled to enter? But the sentence that immediately follows is greatly to be feared. For he says:

“But I say to you that none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.” Behold, he calls them personally; he calls them through angels; he calls them through the Fathers; he calls them through shepherds; often he calls them through miracles; often through scourges; sometimes through the prosperity of this world, sometimes through adversity. Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he should be unable to enter when he wishes.

Large crowds were traveling with him, and he turned and said to them: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, [Col. 0516D] and mother, and wife, and children, and brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple; and whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple either.” It is worth asking how we are commanded to hate our parents and our relatives according to the flesh, when we are also commanded to love our enemies. Certainly Truth says concerning a wife: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark X). And Paul says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. V). Behold, the disciple commands that a wife be loved, while the Master says, “Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple.” Does the judge announce one thing while the herald proclaims another? Or can we both hate and love at the same time? But if we weigh the force of the command, we must do both with discernment: we should love those joined to us by kinship of flesh, and whom we recognize as our neighbors, yet we should know how to hate and avoid them insofar as we suffer them as adversaries on the way of God. To show that this hatred toward our neighbors does not arise from lack of affection but from love, the Lord immediately added, saying: “And even his own life.” We hate our own life rightly when we do not yield to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. What is rejected and led to something better is loved, as it were, through hatred. So too we must show discernment in our hatred toward our neighbors, so that in them we love what they are and hate what obstructs us in the way of God. How this same hatred of one’s own life should be displayed, Truth reveals by adding:

“And whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” The cross takes its name from “torment” (*cruciatus*). We carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: either by afflicting the flesh through abstinence, or by considering the need of our neighbor as our own through compassion. Whoever feels pain at another’s need carries a cross in his mind. It must be understood, however, that there are some who practice abstinence from the flesh not for God but for empty glory; and there are many who show compassion to their neighbor not spiritually but carnally, favoring him not toward virtue but, as though out of pity, toward his faults. Such people appear indeed to carry the cross, but they do not follow the Lord. Hence Truth rightly says again: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” To carry the cross and go after the Lord is to practice either abstinence from the flesh or compassion toward one’s neighbor out of devotion to an eternal purpose. For whoever practices these things for a temporal purpose carries the cross but refuses to go after the Lord. Since sublime commands had been given, a comparison concerning the construction of something sublime is immediately added:

“For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost that is necessary, to see whether he has enough to complete it?” In everything we do, the end must be kept in view. We must precede every action with careful consideration. For behold, according to the word of Truth, the person who builds a tower prepares the expense required for the building. If, then, we wish to construct the tower of humility, we must first prepare ourselves for the adversities of this age. The difference between an earthly and a heavenly building is that the earthly building is constructed by gathering expenses, whereas the heavenly building is constructed by dispersing them. We incur expense for the former if we gather what we do not have; we incur expense for the latter if we also abandon what we possess. Consider also what is said:

“Lest, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to complete it, all who see it should begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’” For, in Paul’s words, “we have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings.” In everything we do, we must consider our hidden adversaries, who always watch our works and always rejoice at our failure. The Prophet, seeing them, says: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, nor shall my enemies mock me” (Ps. XXIV). While intent on good works, unless we watch carefully against evil spirits, we suffer as mockers the very ones whom we have as persuaders to evil. But since the comparison was given concerning the construction of a building, a likeness is now added, proceeding from the lesser to the greater, so that greater matters may be assessed from the smallest:

“Or what king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, sending a delegation, he asks for terms of peace.” A king comes against a king on equal terms for battle; yet, if he judges himself unable to prevail, he sends a delegation and requests terms of peace. With what tears, then, ought we to hope for pardon, since in that dreadful examination we do not come to judgment on equal terms with our King, being plainly shown to be inferior by our condition, weakness, and cause? But perhaps we have already cut away the sins of evil deeds and already avoided every outward wrong. Are we nevertheless sufficient to render an account of our thoughts? An army twice as large therefore comes against one half its size: the one who examines us, scarcely prepared in deed alone, examines us at once in deed and in thought. And therefore, while he is still far away, let us send a delegation and ask for terms of peace. He is said to be far away because he is not yet seen as present in judgment. Let us send our tears as a delegation; let us send works of mercy; let us sacrifice on his altar offerings of reconciliation. This is our delegation, which appeases the coming King.

“Thus, therefore, none of you who does not renounce all that he possesses can be my disciple.” By this conclusion the Lord most plainly teaches what it means to build a tower or to make peace with a stronger king: namely, to be his disciple. To prepare the expenses for completing the tower and to send a delegation to obtain peace means nothing other than to renounce everything we possess. Among these “all things” must necessarily be understood the love of our neighbors, which was mentioned above, and our very life, which some think is meant here in reference to this temporal life. We ought to possess it for a time in such a way that it does not hinder us from the eternal, even if someone threatens to take it away from us. There is, of course, a distinction between renouncing everything and abandoning everything. To abandon everything, put aside the cares of the world, and yearn only for eternal desires belongs to the few and the perfect. But it belongs to all the faithful to renounce everything they possess—that is, to hold worldly things in such a way that they are not themselves held by them in the world; to have temporal property for use and eternal things for desire; to conduct earthly affairs while directing their whole mind toward heavenly things.

“Salt is good. But if even salt has lost its savor, with what will it be seasoned?” This refers back to the preceding matters, where he had commanded that the tower of virtues should not merely be begun but also completed. It is good to hear the word of God and to season more frequently the hidden places of the heart with the salt of spiritual wisdom—or rather, to become salt of the earth together with the apostles, sufficient to imbue the minds even of those who still think according to earthly things. But if someone, once enlightened by the seasoning of truth, returns to apostasy, by what other teacher can he be corrected, having cast away the sweetness of wisdom that he himself had tasted, either frightened by the adversities of the age or enticed by its allurements? In accordance with what a certain wise man says: “Who will heal the enchanter who has been bitten by a serpent?” (Ecclus. XII). By this sentence Judas Iscariot and his associates may rightly be understood as being designated, since, overcome by love of money, he did not hesitate both to betray the rank of apostleship and to hand over the Lord.

[Col. 0519B] “It is fit neither for the earth nor for the dung heap; it will be thrown outside.” Just as salt that has lost its savor, once it has ceased to be useful for seasoning food and drying meat, will be useful for nothing—for it is not fit for the earth, since when spread upon it, it prevents plants from sprouting, nor for the dung heap, which would be useful to agriculture, since even when mixed with fertile clods it tends not to nourish the seeds of crops but to destroy them—so everyone who turns back after acknowledging the truth is able neither to bear the fruit of good works himself nor to cultivate others. He must be thrown outside, that is, separated from the unity of the Church, so that, in accordance with the preceding parable, his enemies may mock him, saying: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.” And therefore a very useful exhortation is added:

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” That is: whoever has ears of understanding by which he can receive the word of God must not despise it but hear it, obeying and doing what he has learned. For it is not the forgetful hearer but the doer of the work who will be blessed in his deed. Amen.

## CHAPTER XV

Now tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him in order to hear him; and the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying that he receives sinners and eats with them. Since not only can a righteous person sin through negligence, but a sinner also can come to his senses through diligence, after it has been related that savorless salt must be cast out, the company of penitents admitted within is immediately described. Drawing near to hear the word of God, they were received not only for conversation but also for eating together. When the Pharisees saw this, they were indignant, because true righteousness has compassion and false righteousness indignation—although righteous people too are accustomed rightly to be indignant with sinners. But one thing is done as a type of pride, another from zeal for discipline. Yet, because they were sick in such a way that they did not know themselves to be sick, the heavenly physician, so that they might recognize what they were, heals them with gentle fomentations, sets before them a kindly illustration, and restrains the swelling of the wound in their hearts. For he says:

“Which one of you who has a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it?” Behold, in a wonderful dispensation of mercy, Truth gave an analogy in which a human being might recognize himself, though it pertains especially to the very Maker of human beings. Since the number one hundred is perfect, he possessed a hundred sheep when he created the substance of angels and human beings. But one sheep was lost when, by sinning, man abandoned the pastures of life. He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the sublime choirs of angels in heaven. Why is heaven called a wilderness except because “wilderness” means “abandoned”? Man abandoned heaven when he sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness when the Lord was seeking the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely angels and human beings—created to see God had been diminished through the loss of man; and, in order that the perfect total of sheep might be restored in heaven, the lost man was sought on earth.

“And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” He laid the sheep upon his shoulders because, by assuming human nature, he himself bore our sins.

“And, coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’” Once the sheep was found, he returned home because our shepherd, having restored man, returned to the kingdom of heaven. There he finds friends and neighbors, namely those choirs of angels. They are his friends because they continuously preserve his will in their steadfastness. They are also his neighbors because, through the clarity of his vision, they enjoy him by their continual presence. And note that he does not say, “Rejoice for the sheep that has been found,” but, “Rejoice with me,” because our life is his joy, and when we are led back to heaven, we fulfill the solemnity of his gladness.

“I tell you that there will likewise be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance.” There will be greater joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous persons who stand firm, because those who know themselves not to be burdened with the weight of sins generally do indeed stand in the path of righteousness and commit no unlawful deeds, but they do not anxiously yearn for their heavenly homeland. They allow themselves so much liberty in lawful things as they remember having committed no unlawful ones; and they generally remain sluggish in performing outstanding good works, because they are very secure in having committed no graver evils. Conversely, those who remember having done some unlawful deeds sometimes, pierced by the pain of this very remembrance, burn with love for God and exercise themselves in great virtues. Therefore greater joy is made in heaven over a converted sinner than over a righteous person standing firm, just as a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, having returned after flight, presses the enemy bravely than the one who never turned his back and never did anything bravely. Yet amid these things it must be known that there are many righteous persons whose lives bring such joy that no penance of any sinner can at all be preferred to them. For many are conscious of no evils, yet exert themselves in affliction with such fervor as though they were oppressed by every sin: they reject even all lawful things, gird themselves nobly for contempt of the world, rejoice in lamentations, and humble themselves in all things. And as some lament sins of deeds, so they lament sins of thoughts. From this we must gather how much joy a righteous person, humbly mourning, gives God, if an unrighteous person gives joy in heaven when he condemns by penance what he has done wrongly.

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” He who is signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman. For he is God and also the wisdom of God. And because an image is impressed upon a drachma, the woman lost the drachma when man, who had been made in the image of God, departed by sinning from the likeness of his Creator. But the woman lit a lamp because the wisdom of God appeared in humanity. For a lamp is light in a vessel of clay; and light in a vessel of clay is divinity in flesh. Once the lamp was lit, she swept the house, because as soon as his divinity shone through flesh, our whole conscience was shaken. For the house is swept when the human conscience is disturbed by reflection upon its guilt; and, once the house has been swept, the drachma is found, because, while a human being’s conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the Creator is restored in that human being.

“And when she has found it, she calls together her women friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.’” Who are these women friends and neighbors except the heavenly powers mentioned above? They are so near to supreme wisdom as they draw near to it through the grace of continual vision. But we should consider why this woman is said to have had ten drachmas. For the Lord created the natures of angels and human beings to know him; and, because he wished them to endure for eternity, he undoubtedly created them in his likeness. The woman had ten drachmas because there are nine orders of angels, but, in order that the number of the elect might be completed, man was created as the tenth. Even after his sin, he did not perish from his Creator, because eternal Wisdom, shining with miracles through the flesh, restored him from the light in the vessel of clay.

Yes, I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents. To repent is both to grieve over the evils committed and not to commit again what must be grieved over. For whoever laments some sins while nevertheless committing others still either does not know how to repent or pretends not to. What good does it do if someone weeps over the sins of lust yet still pants with the fever of greed?
