Or what good does it do if he now mourns the faults of anger yet still wastes away in the fires of envy? But what we are saying is still far from sufficient: whoever laments sins must take the greatest care not to commit what should be lamented. For one must consider with the utmost seriousness that whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful ones, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator; whoever has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted.

But he said: “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me.’ And he divided the property between them.” When the scribes and Pharisees murmured about the reception of sinners, the Savior set forth three parables in succession. In the first two, which have been discussed above, he indicated how greatly he himself rejoices with the angels over the salvation of the repentant. But in the third, which follows, he demonstrates not merely his own joy and that of his companions, but also rebukes the murmur of those who are envious. The man, therefore, who is said to have had two sons is understood as God the Father, the father of two peoples and, so to speak, the author and creator of two branches of the human race. The elder son signifies those who remained in the worship of the one God; the younger, those who abandoned God in order to worship idols. The share of the property falling to the younger son is the rational faculty of perception in a human being. To live, understand, remember, and excel through a lively intelligence is a substance of divine gift. The younger son asks this of his father when, delighted with his own power, he sought to govern himself by free choice and to escape from the dominion of his Creator. And he divided the property between them: to the faithful, by granting them the protection of his grace, which they desired; to the unfaithful, by granting only the benefit of their natural intelligence, with which they were content.

And not many days later, when he had gathered everything together, the younger son departed for a distant region, and there squandered his property by living dissolutely. He went far away, not by changing his location but his mind. For the more someone transgresses in evil conduct, the farther he withdraws from God’s grace. He said that this happened “not many days” later, when he gathered everything together and departed for a distant region, because not long after the creation of the human race the soul, through free choice, decided to carry with it a certain power, as it were, of its own nature and to abandon the one by whom it had been created, relying on its own strength. It consumes those powers all the more quickly the more it abandons the one from whom they were given. Thus he calls this a prodigal life: one that loves to squander and to parade itself in outward displays, becoming inwardly empty, when a person follows whatever proceeds from that life and abandons the one who is inwardly present to him.

And after he had squandered everything, a severe famine arose in that region. “Everything he squandered” signifies the ornaments of nature that he consumed. The famine in the distant region is the lack of the word of truth through forgetfulness of the Creator. Concerning this it was said by the prophets: “For the Lord will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8).

And he himself began to be in need, and he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that region. He rightly began to be in need who had abandoned the treasures of God’s wisdom and the height of heavenly riches. The one citizen of that region to whom the needy man attached himself is certainly he who, because of his perversity, has been set over earthly desires and is called by the Lord “the prince of this world.” Concerning him the Apostle says: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 4).

And he sent him into his estate to feed pigs. To be sent into an estate means to be subjugated by desire for worldly substance. In another parable, someone who disdained the spiritual banquet to which he had been invited said: “I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it” (Luke 14). To feed pigs means to carry out the things in which unclean spirits rejoice.

And he desired to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating. The pods with which he fed the pigs are secular teachings, sounding with barren sweetness. In them, praises of idols and stories about the gods of the nations resound in varied speech and song, and demons take delight in them. Thus, when this man desired to be filled, he wanted to find in such things something solid and upright that pertained to blessed life, but he could not. This is what he says:

“And no one gave him anything.”

But when he came to himself—that is, when he redirected his attention inward, into the recesses of his conscience, away from those things that lure and deceive from outside in vain—he said:

“How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!”

How could he have known this, when he was sunk in such forgetfulness of God, as all idolaters were, unless this reflection already belonged to one who was recovering his senses, when the Gospel was being preached? The Father’s hired servants therefore have an abundance of bread because those who strive to perform worthy deeds with an eye to future reward are refreshed daily by the nourishment of heavenly grace. But those who, placed outside the Father’s house, desire to fill their stomachs with pods perish from hunger. That is, those who, living without end, seek blessed life through the studies of empty philosophy. For just as bread, which strengthens the human heart, is likened to the word of God, by which the mind is refreshed, so the pod—which is empty within and soft outside and does not nourish the body but fills it, so that it is more a burden than a benefit—is rightly compared with secular wisdom. Its speech is sonorous with the applause of eloquence but empty of the power of usefulness.

“I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.’”

How merciful and kind a father he knew him to be, since even though offended by his son, the father did not disdain to hear himself called “father.” “I will arise,” he says, because I have realized that I am lying down. “And I will go,” because I have withdrawn far away. “To my father,” because under the prince of pigs I am wasting away in miserable want. “I have sinned against heaven” signifies before the angelic spirits and holy souls, in whom God’s seat is found. “Before you” signifies in the inner chamber of conscience itself, which only God’s eyes could penetrate.

“And I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”

He does not presume at all to aspire to the affection of a son, who does not doubt that everything belonging to his father is his own, but desires the status of a hired servant, now intending to serve for wages. Yet he testifies that he cannot obtain even this except by his father’s gracious favor. Where, then, are the Pelagians, since they trust that they can be saved by their own power, contrary to the truth’s clearest declaration: “Without me you can do nothing”?

And he arose and came to his father. To come to the father is to be established in the Church through faith, where there can now be a lawful and fruitful confession of sins.

But while he was still far away—that is, before he understood God, yet already seeking him devoutly—

his father saw him. The impious and proud are appropriately said not to be seen, as though they were not held before one’s eyes. For only those who are loved are usually said to be held before the eyes.

And he was moved with compassion, and he ran to him and fell upon his neck. For the Father did not abandon the only-begotten Son, in whom he ran and descended even to our distant wandering. “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). And the Lord himself says: “The Father who remains in me performs his works” (John 14). What, then, is it to fall upon his neck except to bend down and humble his arm in an embrace of him? And “the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (John 12). This is certainly our Lord Jesus Christ.

And he kissed him. To be consoled by the word of God’s grace toward the hope of forgiveness of sins is, after remaining on a long journey, to receive from the father the kiss of love.

And the son said to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

Now, having been established in the Church, he begins to confess his sins. He does not say everything he had promised to say, but stops at: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” For he wishes by grace to become what, on the basis of his merits, he confesses himself unworthy to be. He does not add what he had said in his earlier reflection: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” When he had no bread, he desired even to be a hired servant. But after the father’s kiss, he now nobly disdains this. For he understands that there is no small difference between a son, a hired servant, and a slave.

A slave is one who still restrains himself from vices through fear of Gehenna or of present punishments. A hired servant is one who does so through hope and desire for the kingdom of heaven. A son is one who does so through affection for the good itself and love of virtue. In the perfection of these three virtues, the blessed Apostle gathers the entire sum of salvation, saying: “Now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. But the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13).

Faith is what makes us avoid the contagion of vices through fear of future judgment and punishments. Hope is what, drawing our mind away from present things, makes it disdain all bodily pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards. Love is what, setting us aflame with ardor of mind for Christ’s death and the fruit of spiritual virtues, makes us detest with complete hatred whatever is contrary to them. Thus, after this prodigal had come to himself and feared the punishments of dreadful hunger, he desired the status of a hired servant, already thinking of wages, as though he had become a slave. But his father, running to meet him, was not content to grant lesser things: passing over both stages without delay, he restored him to his former dignity as a son, and made him think not of the wage of an employer but of the inheritance of a father.

But the father said to his servants: “Quickly, bring out the finest robe and put it on him.”

The finest robe is the garment of innocence, which a human being received when well created but lost when badly deceived, when, after the transgression, he learned that he was naked and, having lost the glory of immortality, took a garment of skin—that is, a mortal garment. The servants who bring it out are the preachers of reconciliation. They bring out the finest robe when they affirm that mortal and earthly human beings are to be exalted, so that they will become not only citizens of the angels but also heirs of God and coheirs of Christ.

“And put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.”

The ring is either the seal of sincere faith, by which all the promises are marked with a firm impress upon the hearts of believers, or the pledge of the marriage by which the Church is espoused. And rightly the ring is placed on the hand, so that faith may shine forth through works and works may be strengthened through faith.

The shoes on the feet signify the ministry of proclaiming the Gospel, so that the course of the mind, directed toward heavenly things, may be preserved inviolate and clean from the contagion of earthly matters, and, fortified by the examples of those who came before, may walk securely over serpents and scorpions. Thus the hands and feet are adorned—that is, the work and the course. The work, so that we may live rightly; the course, so that we may hasten toward eternal joys. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13).

“And bring the fattened calf and kill it.”

The fattened calf is likewise the Lord himself, but according to the flesh. He is rightly called fattened because his flesh is so rich in spiritual power that, for the salvation of the whole world, it is sufficient to send to God the fragrance of sweetness—that is, the scent of sacrifice—and to intercede for all. To bring and kill the calf means to preach Christ and to make his death known. For he is, as it were, newly killed for each one of us when he believes that he was killed. His flesh is eaten when the sacrament of his passion is received by the mouth for cleansing and contemplated in the heart for imitation.

“And let us eat and feast, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

Not only the son who came to life and was found, but also his father and servants feast, refreshed by the flesh of the holy calf that was killed for the son, because the Father’s food is our salvation, and the Father’s joy is the remission of our sins. Nor is this true only of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For just as there is one will and one operation in the Godhead, so there is one delight of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Hence we read that blessed Abraham, receiving three angels as guests, killed a tender and choice calf and offered it to them to feast upon with milk, bread, and butter. For whoever desires to refresh—that is, gladden—the blessed Trinity through the duties of right devotion must also celebrate, with the sincerity of a devout confession, the death in the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, who is one person within that same Trinity.

And it should be noted that the finest robe is provided first, then the ring, then the shoes, and only afterward is the calf sacrificed. For unless someone has first put on the hope of immortality, unless he has fortified his works with the ring of faith, and unless he has proclaimed that faith through devout confession, he cannot participate in the heavenly sacraments.

And they began to feast. This banquet and festival are now celebrated, as the Church has spread and been extended throughout the world. For that calf, in the Lord’s body and blood, is both offered to the Father and nourishes the whole household.

Now his elder son was in the field. The elder son is the people of Israel. Although he did not go away to a distant land, he is nevertheless said to have remained not at home but in the field, because that people neither abandoned the Creator so far as to worship idols nor penetrated into the interior meaning of the law it had received. Content only with guarding the letter, it was accustomed both to perform and to hope for external and earthly things, hearing through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

And when he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. The son draws near to the house when that people, through any of the more discerning Israelites—for many such people were found and often still are found among them—rejecting the labor of servile works, considers from those same Scriptures the freedom of the Church. He hears music and dancing: those filled with the Spirit preaching the Gospel in harmonious voices, to whom it was said: “I urge you, brothers, that all of you say the same thing” (1 Corinthians 1), and that the soul and heart of those who live in concord may be one in the praises of God.

And he called one of the servants and asked what these things were. And he said to him:

“Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe.”

Your brother was at the ends of the earth, but because of him there is greater rejoicing among those singing a new song to the Lord, for “his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Psalm 47). And for the sake of the one who was absent, the one concerning whom it was said, “May your burnt offering be made fat” (Psalm 19), was killed.

But he became angry and was unwilling to go in. Therefore his father went out and began to plead with him. He is angry even now and still does not wish to enter. When, therefore, the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, his father will go out at the appropriate time, so that all Israel also may be saved, since blindness has come upon part of it. This blindness is like an absence in the field, until the fullness of the younger son—long established in the idolatry of the Gentiles—returns and enters to eat the calf. For at some time the Jews will receive an open calling into the salvation of the Gospel. He calls the manifestation of this calling the father’s going out to plead with the elder son.

But he answered and said to his father: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.”

It is asked how that people can be said never to have transgressed God’s command. The answer readily presents itself: it was not said of every command, but chiefly of the one most necessary command, by which it was ordered not to worship any other god. Nor should this son be understood as representing all Israelites, but those in whom he has his person who never turned from the one God to images. Although, as though placed in the field, this son desired earthly things, he nevertheless desired those goods from the one God. This is also confirmed by the testimony of his father himself, when he says: “You are always with me.” He does not rebuke him as though he were lying, but, approving his perseverance with him, invites him to enjoy a greater and more delightful rejoicing.

“And you have never given me a kid, so that I might feast with my friends.”

A sinner is certainly often signified by the name “kid,” but far be it from me to understand the Antichrist here. It would be exceedingly absurd to think that the one to whom it is said, “You are always with me,” wished from his father to believe in the Antichrist. Nor is it permissible to understand this son as one of those Jews who will believe in the Antichrist. For how could he feast upon that kid if he himself is the Antichrist and would not believe in him? Or if feasting upon the slaughter of the kid means rejoicing at the destruction of the Antichrist, how can the son say that this was not granted to him, when all the sons of God will rejoice at the condemnation of that adversary?

Clearly, then, he is complaining that the Lord himself was denied to him, since he considered him a sinner. For when he is a kid to that people—that is, when it regards him as a violator of the Sabbath and a profaner of the law—it did not deserve to enjoy his banquet. Thus when he says, “You have never given me a kid, so that I might feast with my friends,” it is as though he were saying: “You have never given me for feasting the one who appeared to me to be a kid,” denying me that very one because he appeared to me as a kid. When he says, “with my friends,” this may be understood either as the leaders speaking with the common people, or as the people of Jerusalem speaking with the other peoples of Judaea.

But when this son of yours, who has devoured his property with prostitutes, came, you killed the fattened calf for him.

The prostitutes are the superstitions of the Gentiles. To squander one’s property with them is, after abandoning the one marriage with the word of God, to commit fornication with the crowd of demons in the most shameful desire.

But he said to him: “Son, you are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

When he says, “Everything that is mine is yours,” it must not be understood as though those things did not also belong to his brother, as though you were suffering limitation in an earthly inheritance. How could everything belong to the elder son if the younger also has his share there? For the perfected, purified, and already immortal sons possess everything in such a way that each thing belongs to all and all things belong to each. For just as desire possesses nothing without distress, so love possesses nothing with distress.

When we have obtained that blessed state, the things above will be ours for living, equal things will be ours for sharing the banquet, and lower things will be ours for ruling.

If anyone is troubled by how the Truth, speaking to the Father in prayer, says, “Everything that is mine is yours, and yours is mine,” and thinks that this sounds very much like what is said to this son, “Everything that is mine is yours,” let him know that everything belonging to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son because he too is God and, born from the Father, is equal to the Father. For when, speaking of the Holy Spirit, he says, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, ‘He will take from what is mine and declare it to you,’” he was speaking of those things that belong to the very divinity of the Father, in which the Son is equal to him by possessing everything that the Father possesses. For the Holy Spirit was not going to take from creation, which is subject to the Father and the Son, what he says, “He will take from what is mine,” but certainly from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son was born.

Whether, then, one wishes to refer these two sons to the two peoples, or, as some prefer, to any two human beings—the repentant and the just, or one who appears just to himself—let the elder brother rejoice, because his younger brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.

# BOOK FIVE. READ HAPPILY.

[Col. 0527]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0527D]

After the Savior rebuked those who, considering themselves just, had murmured about the reception of sinners—or rather, of the repentant—through the three successive parables discussed above, teaching that the salvation of those who recover their senses is most pleasing to God and the angels but most grievous to envious human beings, he immediately adds a fourth and a fifth parable concerning the giving of alms and the practice of frugality. Through a devout and just discernment, he makes clear that those who have scattered their earthly goods and given them to the poor will be received by them into eternal dwellings. But those who desire to indulge themselves alone in such things will be buried in hell and will not obtain even the slightest drop of water capable of cooling, even for a moment, the enduring fires of their torments.

For the order of preaching is plainly most appropriate: after repentance, almsgiving—that is, the work of mercy—should be proposed. The repentant person rightly asks God to have mercy on him who himself does not delay to have mercy, as far as he can, on his needy neighbor. “But whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the poor, his prayer will be accursed.” Hence, when John the Baptist urged the crowds not to be cast into the fire because of the barrenness of their lives, but to produce fruits worthy of repentance, he immediately added counsel concerning their salvation to those who were asking, and said: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3).

Those same Pharisees and scribes, suffering no less from the plague of greed than from that of pride, refused to give money to the needy just as they refused forgiveness to the repentant. But the one who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2), now addressing them and now speaking to his disciples in their hearing, does not cease generously to bestow the gifts of his customary compassion. But let us come to the text.

## CHAPTER XVI

He also said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused before him as though he had squandered his property. And he called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’ But the steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do? For my master is taking the stewardship away from me. I am unable to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I know what I will do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.’”

In this steward whom the Lord was expelling from his stewardship and whom he praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as something to imitate. We must not commit fraud against our Lord in any way so that we may make almsgiving from that fraud. Nor may we understand those from whom we wish to be received into eternal dwellings as though they were debtors of God and our Lord, since in this passage the just and holy are signified—those who introduce into eternal dwellings those who have shared earthly goods with them in their needs.

Concerning such people he also says that if anyone gives one of them a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, he will not lose his reward (Matthew 10). But, conversely, these comparisons are also presented so that we may understand this: if the Lord was able to praise the man to whom he was committing fraud, how much more do those please the Lord God who perform such works according to his command.

Likewise, from the unjust judge who was importuned by a widow, he drew a comparison with God the Judge, to whom the unjust judge cannot be compared in any respect.

By the term “stewards,” then, we mean those who possess money but should be considered not masters of their own property, but rather stewards of what belongs to another. If, following the example of this servant, they carefully foresee the time when their stewardship and accounting will come to an end, they will easily be stripped both of the pleasure and love of all earthly things, and will take care to provide more for acquiring friends in the future than for accumulating riches in the present.

As he anxiously considered many things within himself, he said: “What shall I do? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” When the stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because once this life is finished—in which alone it is permitted to work—we can no longer seek the fruit of good conduct with the spade of devoted repentance.

To beg is a matter of shame, specifically that worst kind of begging in which those foolish virgins are reported to have begged. When the time of the wedding arrived and the oil of virtues had run out, they said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out” (Matthew 25). Solomon also speaks of this: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Proverbs 20).

Therefore, summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He replied: “A hundred measures of oil.” He said to him: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” Then he said to another: “And you, how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.” And he said to him: “Take your document and write eighty.”

A *cadus* is a Greek amphora containing three urns. A *corus* comprises thirty *modii*. As for the fact that he had the debtor write fifty instead of one hundred measures of oil, and eighty instead of one hundred measures of wheat, I think it serves no other purpose than this: each person in Christ’s Church should surpass the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees in what a Jew does for priests and Levites. Thus, while they gave tenths, these should give halves, as Zacchaeus did—not from the fruits but from his own goods.

Or perhaps one should understand it simply to mean that anyone who relieves the need of any poor person among the holy—whether from a half or indeed from a fifth, as twenty or fifty are in relation to one hundred—should be granted a sure reward for his mercy.

And the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. For the sons of this age are more prudent in their own generation than the sons of light. Let the wise of this age listen, so that they may abandon foolish wisdom and learn the wise foolishness of God. Let them learn how highly divine justice has valued their wisdom, since it does not call them truly prudent but prudent in their own generation. This accords with what is said elsewhere: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5).

Moreover, by calling lovers of eternal life “sons of light,” he rebukes those who are wise enough to do evil but do not know how to do good as being nothing other than sons of darkness. They are called sons of light and sons of this age just as others are called sons of the kingdom and sons of destruction. For each person is called the son of the one whose works he performs.

And I say to you: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.”

He calls the money that we possess for a time “the mammon of iniquity” because *mammon* is interpreted as “riches.” These are riches only for the unjust, who place in them the hope and abundance of their blessedness. When the just possess such money, it is indeed money, but it is not their riches; their riches are heavenly and spiritual. By spiritually supplying their need through these riches, and by excluding want from the wretched, they will be enriched by an abundance of blessedness.

If those who give alms from the mammon of iniquity make friends for themselves by whom they may be received into eternal dwellings, how much more ought those who distribute spiritual banquets—those who give their fellow servants food at the proper time—to be lifted up by the most certain hope of the highest reward?

Whoever is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much. And whoever is unjust in what is little is unjust also in much.

There are people who, though ignorant of the compassion and works of mercy owed to their neighbors, nevertheless truly consider themselves faithful on account of chastity, vigils, long prayer, complete faith, fasting, and the other virtues that the love of God usually produces. But the Judge himself bears witness that whoever is faithful in what is least—that is, in sharing money with the poor—is faithful also in what is greater, namely, in that action by which he especially desires to cling to the Creator and become one spirit with him.

But whoever neglects to administer rightly the temporal goods he possesses empties out for himself the glory of eternal things in which he takes pride. For “whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4). And as the same Apostle says: “Whoever has the substance of the world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 13).

If, therefore, you were not faithful in the mammon of iniquity, who will entrust to you what is yours?

It has already been explained above that the mammon of iniquity signifies the riches of the wicked. Referring to these, the Savior says elsewhere that “the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word” (Matthew 13). But he signifies true riches either as the joys of eternal life, concerning which it is written, “What are the riches of his inheritance among the saints?” (Ephesians 1), or as the abundance of spiritual virtues by which one reaches life. Concerning these Isaiah says: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is his treasure” (Isaiah 33).

And if you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?

The resources of this age are alien to us—that is, they lie outside our nature. For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing away. Our possession, however, is the kingdom of heaven. Our life is Christ. Our riches are the fruits of spiritual works. Concerning these Solomon says: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 13).

He therefore accuses the Pharisees of fraud and greed. Because they were not faithful with their possessions, preferring to hold privately the common goods of the Creator, they did not deserve to receive Christ. The tax collector Zacchaeus, whom I mentioned shortly before, offered half of his goods in order to acquire him.

No servant can serve two masters, because he cannot love both transitory and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not in affection.

For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other.

These words must be considered carefully. For he explains who the two masters are by saying:

[Col. 0532A] “You cannot serve God and mammon.”

Let the greedy person hear this; let the one who is counted by the Christian name hear that one cannot serve both mammon—that is, riches—and Christ. Yet he did not say, “the one who has riches,” but “the one who serves riches.” For the servant of riches guards riches like a slave. But whoever has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a master.

The one who serves mammon serves him who, because of his perversity, has been set over these earthly things and is called by the Lord the prince of this age. Therefore, “either he will hate the one and love the other,” as he ought: he will hate the devil and love God. “Or he will cling to the one and despise the other”: he will cling to the devil when he pursues temporal things as though they were the devil’s rewards. He will despise God—not, he says, “hate” him, but despise him, as those do who put God’s threats behind their desires and flatter themselves into impunity because of his goodness. To such people Solomon says: “My son, do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and mocked him. The Lord was warning the scribes and Pharisees not to be proudly minded, not to presume upon their own righteousness, but both to receive repentant sinners and tax collectors and to redeem their sins through alms if they happened to fall into them. But they mocked the teacher of mercy, humility, and frugality chiefly for two reasons: either because they supposed that he was imposing things of little use and that ought never to be done, as though he were dangerous; or because they regarded useful things as already accomplished by themselves and therefore considered his instruction superfluous.

And he said to them: “You are the ones who justify yourselves before human beings. But God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.”

They justify themselves before human beings who despise sinners as though they were weak and beyond hope, while considering themselves perfect in every respect and free from all frailty, and therefore believing that they have no need of the remedy of almsgiving. But the one who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts sees how justly this height of destructive arrogance must be condemned.

The Law and the Prophets lasted until John; from that time the kingdom of God is being proclaimed as good news, and everyone is pressing into it. The Pharisees, who were arguing with the Savior about avarice, mocked him, [Col. 0532D] as though he were prescribing things contrary to the Law and the Prophets, where they read that many people had been both wealthy and exceedingly rich, yet had pleased God. Moses himself had also foretold that the people he governed, if they followed the Law, would abound in all the good things produced by the earth, but if they neglected it, would be struck by pestilence, famine, poverty, and every evil. In response to them, he showed that there ought to be no small difference between the Law and the Gospel—not only in their promises but also in their commands—and that greater things are commanded for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, lesser things for the sake of the earthly kingdom, by the one and the same God who made heaven and earth. For there it is said: “If you are willing and obedient to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1). Here, however: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0533A] (Matthew 5). Therefore, when he said rightly that the kingdom of God is being proclaimed as good news, he added: “And everyone presses into it.” For great is the force, and immense the violence, by which we who are born from the earth seek the dwelling-place of heaven and desire to possess through virtue what we could not retain by nature—and not only despise earthly things, but also the tongues of those who mock us for despising them. This is what he added when, having spoken about despising riches, he was mocked by the Pharisees.

It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota of the Law to fall. Lest they suppose that, by saying, “The Law and the Prophets lasted until John,” he was proclaiming the destruction of the Law or the Prophets, he expressly declares that the greatest elements of the world will pass away more easily than the smallest words of the Law. And indeed: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7). And elsewhere: “According to his promises, we await new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3). But far be it that even the tip of a single letter—that is, any of the smallest details, even those that seem trivial or superstitious—should be free from spiritual mysteries; rather, all things are recapitulated in the Gospel. Nevertheless, the Law and the Prophets lasted until John, because what was to come could not be prophesied any further once it was clear through John’s proclamation that it had already come.

“Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced by her husband commits adultery.” What he had foretold about the Law’s never being violated, he confirms by taking one testimony from it as an example, so that from this one passage they might learn that, in the other matters as well, he had come not to abolish but to fulfill the decrees of the Law. Whoever wishes to see a fuller exposition of this testimony should examine not our writings but the records of our predecessors. For the blessed fathers Augustine, in the first book of *The Sermon on the Mount*, Jerome, and Ambrose, in their commentaries on the evangelists Matthew and Luke, as well as very many others in their respective works, have said enough and more about it.

“There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day.” That purple is the color of royal dress, dyed from marine shellfish, is something almost no one doubts. For shellfish, when cut around with iron, emit drops of purple color with which wool is dyed. Fine linen, *byssus*, is a certain kind [Col. 0533D] of linen, extremely white and very soft, which the Greeks call πάπατιν (*papatin*). The Lord had just urged them to make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we depart from this life, they may receive us into eternal dwellings; hearing this, the Pharisees mocked him. But by substantiating with examples what he had set forth, he showed that the rich man clothed in purple was tortured irredeemably in hell because he had neglected to make poor Lazarus his friend, by whom he could have been received into the dwellings of life.

Some people think that the commands of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New, but they are plainly deceived through careless consideration. In the former, it is not stinginess but robbery that is punished; there, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. Here, however, this rich man is reproved not for taking what belonged to another but for failing to give what belonged to himself; nor is it said that he oppressed anyone, but that he exalted himself in the possessions he had received. From this, then—from this above all—we must gather what punishment is due to the man who seizes what belongs to others, if the condemnation of hell strikes one who does not distribute what belongs to him.

There are also some who do not think that the wearing of fine and expensive clothing is a sin. Yet if it were not a fault, the word of God would certainly not so carefully point out that the rich man who is tormented in hell had been dressed in fine linen and purple. No one seeks distinguished clothing except for empty glory—that is, so that he may appear more honorable than others. We can gather the nature of this fault even more clearly from the opposite case: if the rejection of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the evangelist would not carefully have said of John: “He was clothed in camel’s hair” (Matthew 3). But we must pay the greatest attention to the order of the narrative in the mouth of Truth concerning the proud rich man and the humble poor man. For it says: “There was a certain rich man.” And immediately it adds:

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus.” Certainly, in society the names of the rich are usually better known than those of the poor. What, then, is the meaning of the Lord’s naming the poor man while speaking of the poor and the rich, but not naming the rich man, except that God knows and approves the humble, while he does not know the proud? Hence, to certain people who will be boasting at the end about the power of their miracles, he will say: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13). By contrast, Moses is told: “I know you by name” (Exodus 33).

Thus he says of the rich man: “A certain man.” Of the poor man he says: “A needy man named Lazarus.” It is as though he openly says: “I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I know the former through approval; I ignore the latter through the judgment of rejection.”

“He lay at his gate, full of sores, longing to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table; moreover, the dogs came and licked his sores.” The beggar Lazarus, full of sores, lies before the rich man’s gates. In this matter the Lord carried out two judgments at once. The rich man might perhaps have had some excuse if the poor and sore-covered Lazarus had not lain before his gate—if he had been far away, if his poverty had not been an unwelcome sight to his eyes. Conversely, if the rich man had been far from the poor man’s sore-covered eyes, the poor man would have endured a lesser temptation in his mind. But by placing the needy and ulcerated man before the gate of the rich man, who abounded in luxuries, he used one and the same circumstance both to heap condemnation upon the rich man, who showed no pity at the sight of the poor man, and also to test the poor man daily through the sight of the rich man.

Poverty alone could certainly have been enough for him as a punishment, even if he had been healthy. Illness, in turn, would have been enough, even if assistance had been available. But to test the poor man more fully, poverty and illness together consumed him, and in addition he saw the rich man going out, supported by attendant crowds, while no one visited him in his sickness and poverty. For that no one came to visit him is testified by the dogs, [Col. 0535A] who freely licked his wounds. Thus, from one circumstance, almighty God displayed two judgments when he allowed poor Lazarus to lie before the rich man’s gate: the wicked rich man increased the vengeance of his own condemnation, while the tested poor man grew toward his reward.

“It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.” Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs and into which they are received after this life. The burial of hell is the depth of punishments that, after this life, devours the proud and the merciless.

“Lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom; and, crying out, he said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and [Col. 0535B] send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this flame.’” O how subtle are the judgments of God! O how strictly the recompense of good and evil deeds is administered! It was certainly said above that in this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any. Now, concerning the rich man’s punishment, it is said that he longs to have water dripped into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger. Thus the man who refused to give even the smallest things from his table, placed in hell, came to seek even the smallest things.

But we must pay very close attention to what it means that the rich man, placed in the fire, asks for his tongue to be cooled. It is the custom of sacred speech sometimes to say one thing while implying another through the same statement. Above, the Lord had said that this proud rich man did not devote himself to loquacity but to excessive feasting. He did not describe him as sinning through talkativeness, but through gluttony, together with pride and stinginess. Yet because talkativeness commonly accompanies banquets, the man who is said here to have feasted badly is said to burn more severely in hell in his tongue. But what follows must be weighed with very great fear:

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted, while you are tormented.’” Behold: when it is said, “You received good things in your lifetime,” it is indicated that this rich man had possessed some good thing for which he received good things in this life. Again, when it is said of Lazarus that he received evil things, it is plainly shown that Lazarus too had possessed some evil that needed to be purified. But the fire of poverty purified Lazarus’s evils, while the happiness of passing life rewarded the rich man’s good things.

“And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.” In this matter it must be carefully asked how it can be said: “Those who wish to cross to you cannot.” For there is no doubt that those who are in hell wish to cross over to the lot of the blessed. But how is it said that those who have already been received into the lot of blessedness wish to cross over to those who are being tormented in hell?

But just as the reprobate desire to cross over to the elect—that is, to depart from the affliction of their punishments—so it belongs to the righteous to cross over to those who are afflicted and placed in torments by going to them in thought through mercy [Col. 0536A] and wishing to free them. Yet those who wish to cross from the seat of the blessed to those who are afflicted and placed in torments cannot do so, because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy according to the goodness of their nature, they are already joined to the justice of their Creator and constrained by such uprightness that they are not moved by any compassion toward the reprobate.

But after hope of himself is taken away from the rich man in the flames, his mind turns toward the relatives he had left behind, because punishment sometimes teaches the mind of the reprobate, though uselessly, to love, so that even then they may love their own spiritually—those whom, while they loved sins here, they did not love even themselves. Hence it now follows:

“And he said: ‘I beg you, therefore, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.’” In this matter it must be noted how many things are heaped upon the punishment of the rich man in the flames. For knowledge and memory are preserved for his punishment. He recognizes Lazarus, whom he had despised, and he remembers his brothers, whom he had left behind. His vengeance upon the poor man would not be complete if he did not recognize him in the retribution. Nor would his punishment in the fire be complete if he did not fear for his own what he himself suffers.

Thus, in order that sinners may be punished more severely in their torments, they see the glory of those whom they despised, and they are tormented by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly. It should be believed that, before the retribution of the final judgment, the unjust see certain righteous people in rest, so that, when they see them in joy, they may be tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the good fortune of the others. The righteous, however, always behold the unjust in their torments, so that their joy may increase from this: they see the evil from which they mercifully escaped, and they give greater thanks to their deliverer the more clearly they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been neglected. For those who see the glory of their Creator see nothing that is done in creation which they cannot see.

“And Abraham said to him: ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.’” But the rich man, who had despised the words of God, supposed that his followers could not listen to these words. Therefore the rich man replied:

“‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’” Immediately he is answered with a truthful judgment [Col. 0536D]:

“‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.’” For those who despise the words of the Law will all the less fulfill the commands of the Redeemer who rose from the dead, the more subtle those commands are. And it is plainly evident that those who refuse to fulfill his words certainly refuse to believe in him.

But whom does this rich man, according to the allegorical interpretation, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, signify except the Jewish people? They possessed an outwardly cultivated way of life and used the delights of the Law they had received for display, not for usefulness. Whom, however, does Lazarus, full of sores, figuratively express except the gentile people? When they turned to God, they were not ashamed to confess their sins, and thus they bore a wound in their skin [Col. 0537A]. For in a wound of the skin, poison is drawn from the inward parts and bursts outward. What, then, is the confession of sins except a kind of opening of wounds? The poison of sin, which lay hidden pestilentially in the mind, is beneficially opened in confession.

But wounded Lazarus longed to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any, because that proud people despised admitting any gentile to knowledge of the Law. Since that people possessed the teaching of the Law not for charity but for pride, it was as though they feared to give away their received riches; and because words flowed from its knowledge, they fell from the table like crumbs.

By contrast, dogs licked the wounds of the poor man who lay there. In sacred language, preachers are sometimes understood by dogs. A dog’s tongue heals a wound as it licks it, because holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of the mind with their tongue, so to speak. And because by speaking they rescue us from sins, they bring us back to salvation as though by touching our wounds. Hence Lazarus is aptly interpreted as “helped,” because those who heal his wounds through the correction of the tongue help him toward deliverance.

It happened that both men died: the rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, was buried in hell, while Lazarus was led by angels into Abraham’s bosom. What does Abraham’s bosom signify except the hidden rest of the Father, concerning which Truth says: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the children of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8)? The man who is said to have been clothed in purple is rightly called a child of the kingdom.

He lifts his eyes from far away to see Lazarus because, while unbelievers are below in the punishments of their condemnation, before the day of the final judgment they look upward toward the faithful who are in rest above them; after the faithful’s joys, they will in no way be able to contemplate them. What they see is far away because they cannot reach that place through merit.

He is shown to burn more intensely in his tongue when he says: “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this flame.” The unbelieving people held the words of the Law in their mouth, but refused to preserve them in practice. Therefore they will burn more intensely in the place where they show that they knew what they did not wish to do. He longs to be touched by the tip of the finger because, given over to eternal punishments, he desires to share even in the smallest work of the righteous [Col. 0537D].

He is answered that in this life he received good things because he regarded all his joy as passing happiness. The righteous too can possess good things here, and yet not receive them as recompense, because, while they desire better things—that is, eternal things—whatever good things are present seem to them no good at all while they burn with holy desires.

In this connection we must note that he is told: “Remember, son.” Behold, Abraham calls him son, yet does not free him from torment, because the faithful forefathers of this unbelieving people, when they see that many have strayed from their faith, do not rescue them from torments through any compassion, though they recognize them as sons according to the flesh.

The rich man, placed in torments, says that he has five brothers [Col. 0538A], because that same proud Jewish people, which has already been condemned in large part, knows that the followers it left on earth are devoted to the five bodily senses. He expresses the brothers he left behind by the number five because, placed in hell, he laments that they do not rise to spiritual understanding.

He asks that Lazarus be sent to them, and he is told that they have Moses and the Prophets. But he says that they will not believe unless someone rises from the dead. He is immediately answered: “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

Certainly Truth says concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5). Therefore what is said through Abraham’s reply is fulfilled. The Lord rose from the dead, but because the Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it also scorned believing in the one who rose from the dead. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not come to the one about whom Moses had spoken.

## CHAPTER XVII

“And he said to his disciples: ‘It is impossible that scandals should not come. But woe to the one through whom they come.’” The Apostle also says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.” In this world, so full of errors and hardships, it is therefore impossible that scandals should not come very frequently. But woe to the one who, through his own fault, causes what cannot fail to come to come through him.

Although, in a general sense, this may be understood either of some false brother or of Judas himself, who was preparing his mind for betrayal, nevertheless, according to the sequence of the discourse, this passage looks back to what came before, where the Lord spoke about giving alms and was mocked by the Pharisees. Whoever criticizes one who speaks rightly surely provides a scandal—that is, a stumbling-block and a downfall—to weak hearers, especially if he appears to possess knowledge of the Law in the eyes of the Pharisees. Rebuking such a person, the Apostle says: “And the weak brother for whom Christ died will perish through your knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8).

“It would be better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.” He speaks according to the custom of the province, in which, among the ancient Jews, this was the punishment for greater crimes: they were sunk into the depths with a stone tied to them. And indeed, it is better for an innocent person to end bodily life through a punishment, however savage yet temporary, than for one who harms his brother to earn the perpetual death of the soul.

A person who can be scandalized is rightly called a little one. For whoever is great does not depart from faith, whatever he may see or suffer. But whoever is little and small in spirit seeks opportunities for being scandalized. Therefore, above all, we must care for those who are little in faith, lest they be offended by an occasion provided by us, depart from the faith, and fall away from salvation.

It must certainly be noted that in our good works we must sometimes avoid scandalizing our neighbor, but at other times disregard it as nothing. Insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing scandal to our neighbors. [Col. 0539A] But if scandal is taken at the truth, it is better to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.

“Pay attention to yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.” We read something similar in Leviticus: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him” (Leviticus 19). Thus he indicates the order by which we can avoid scandals and escape perpetual woe: if we watch over ourselves so that we harm no one; if we correct the sinner out of zeal for justice; if we open the inner resources of mercy and compassion from our heart to the repentant.

Here we must carefully observe that we are not commanded to forgive every sinner indiscriminately, but to forgive the one who repents. First, we are to rebuke the sinner mercifully, so that afterward there may be someone whom we can justly forgive. Whoever sees his brother sinning and remains silent is no less a transgressor of the Lord’s command than one who refuses to grant forgiveness to that same repentant person. For the one who said, “If he repents, forgive him,” prefaced it with, “If he sins, rebuke him.”

Therefore forgiveness must be granted to a brother after rebuke, but certainly to one who, by repenting, has turned back from error, lest forgiveness be either harsh or indulgence too lax.

“And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times in the day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” The number seven does not set a limit on the forgiveness to be granted; rather, it commands that all sins be forgiven, or that forgiveness be granted always to the repentant. For it is often customary for totality—whether of a thing or of a period of time—to be indicated by seven. Hence what is sung in the psalm, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118), means nothing other than, “His praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

Elsewhere, when Peter asked how often he should forgive a brother who sinned against him—whether up to seven times—the Lord replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew 18), that is, four hundred and ninety times: he was to forgive a brother who sinned that many times in a day, as often as that brother could not sin.

Therefore, if your brother sins against you and repents, you have the power—indeed, the obligation—to forgive him, so that the Father in heaven may also forgive you when you repent and ask for pardon. But if, after being rebuked, he neglects to turn back and repent, observe what judgment Truth decrees concerning this: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him,” and so forth, until he says: “But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.” And rightly so, because under the name of a believer he has performed the works of unbelievers.

We are commanded to grant forgiveness in one way to a brother who asks for it, and in another way to an enemy who persecutes us. To the former, so that, having received remission for the sin by which he harmed us, though we were innocent, he may join us in shared charity; to the latter, so that when he wishes us evil and, if he can, does it, we may always wish him good and do whatever good we can. For David, though he mourned them mercifully, could not grant his persecutors, who had deprived themselves of the remedy of repentance, the same kind of forgiveness that Joseph is known graciously to have shown to his brothers, chastened by salutary contrition.

[Col. 0540A] “The apostles said to the Lord: ‘Increase our faith.’” Above, the Lord had said: “Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much. And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” Therefore the apostles, who had already been faithful in what belonged to another and in what was little—that is, in despising earthly things—ask that faith in what is their own and in what is greater be increased for them.

No one suddenly becomes fully mature; rather, in a good way of life, each person begins with small things in order to arrive at great ones. The beginnings of virtue are one thing, its outlook another, and its perfection another. Seeking these things with great earnestness, they say to the Lord: “Increase our faith.”

“The Lord said: ‘If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree: “Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,” and it would obey you.’” He compares perfect faith [Col. 0540B] to a grain of mustard seed: outwardly humble yet inwardly burning; insignificant to those who look upon it casually and apparently possessing no strength, but showing, when crushed by pressures, what perfection it contains within.

It should also be noted that mustard seed is extremely beneficial for cleansing the head. If it is thoroughly ground and sifted, mixed into warm, rich honeyed wine, and, while fasting, used as a gargle in the hot sun or in a bath, it cleanses the head of every harmful humor, even if it is thick, and also enables the dangers of impending weaknesses to be avoided.

Thus faith, tested by the pestle of temptations, disciplined by the sieve of discernment so that every superficial thought is removed, and sweetened with the honey of perfect love, drains from the heart—which is the head of our inner person—all the sewers of vice, not only for the present, but also taking precautions so that they cannot gather again in the future.

The mulberry tree, to be uprooted and transplanted into the sea, may be understood in a simple sense, because the sign of consummate faith is to command the elements by word, so that what is said specifically of one thing may be believed generally of all things. Elsewhere, when the disciples marveled at the fig tree dried up by his word, the Lord said: “If you have faith and do not doubt, you will do not only what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen” (Matthew 21).

Alternatively, through the mulberry tree, whose blood-red color causes its fruit and branches to be red—and for this reason it is called *rubus* by the Latins—the Gospel of the cross is expressed. Through the faith of the apostles, it was uprooted by the words of preaching from the Jewish people, in which it was held as though in the stock of its lineage, and was transplanted and planted in the sea of the nations.

The meaning of the parable that follows, which concerns ministers of the word, also supports this interpretation. It is helpful as well that leaves of the mulberry tree, placed upon a serpent, kill it, because the word of the cross, just as it brings all things beneficial, removes all things harmful.

“Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep—” This parable teaches that the more faith excels outwardly through virtues, the more humble it should become inwardly in the conscience. The servant who plows or tends sheep signifies any teacher of the Church. Concerning him the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” And to another who professed his love for him, he replied a third time: “Feed my sheep.”

“Who, when he returns from the field, will say to him at once, ‘Come over, recline,’ and will not say to him, ‘Prepare what I may eat?’” The servant returns from the field when the teacher, having temporarily interrupted the work of preaching, returns to his conscience and, coming back from public speech to the court of the heart, privately reviews with himself his deeds or words.

The Lord does not immediately say to him, “Come over, recline”—that is, cross over from this mortal life and rest in the blessed seat of eternal life. Before saying this later, he orders him, after the feeding and the farming, to prepare at home what he may eat: that is, to display the labor of open speech and also the humility of self-examination. The Lord deigns to enter the temple of such a conscience and desires most willingly to be nourished by such a supper. For, behold, he says: “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone rises and opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

“And gird yourself and minister to me until I eat and drink.” To gird oneself means to bind a humbled mind against all the wandering ends of thoughts by which the progress of one’s works is usually hindered. For the one who girds his clothing does so precisely so that, while walking, he will not become entangled and fall.

To minister to God is to profess oneself in every respect as least and to have no strength without his grace. The word “minister” derives from a lesser status—that is, subjection—just as “teacher” derives from a greater one. Therefore the person ministers to the Creator who, considering his nature and fearing his judgments, humbles himself with regard to his own virtues.

“And after this you will eat and drink.” “After,” he says, “I myself have delighted in the work of your preaching and have been refreshed by the feasts of your compunction, then at last you will cross over and recline, and you will be refreshed forever by the eternal banquets of my wisdom.”

“Does he thank that servant because he did what he had commanded? I do not think so. So you also, when you have done everything that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants.’” If, he says, one human being demands from a human servant not a single but a manifold service and nevertheless does not thank him, how much more should you, who can do nothing without me, not weigh the merits of your labors by the length of time, but continually increase your former efforts through love and willing service by ever-new dedication.

Therefore say: [Col. 0541D] “We are unprofitable servants.” Servants, indeed, because you were bought at a price; unprofitable, because the Lord has no need of your goods. If the one who has done everything is unprofitable, what should be said of the person who, through weakness, could not fulfill what was commanded, or—worse—despised it through pride?

Alternatively: “We are unprofitable servants,” because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory to come that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8). And elsewhere: “He crowns me with compassion and mercy” (Psalm 102). He does not say, “with your merits and works,” because we are anticipated by his mercy so that we may serve God humbly, and by his gift we are crowned so that we may reign sublimely with him.

“We have done what we were obliged to do.” Truly, we were obliged, because the one who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20) made us his debtors, so that, not trusting in our own works but always fearing his scrutiny, we may say with the prophet: “What shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us?” (Psalm 115).

To show that he had possessed a faith resembling a grain of mustard seed—humble, that is, and fervent—he began by saying: “I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was humbled exceedingly” (ibid.). To show how little he trusted in his own strength, he added, speaking in ecstasy: “Every human being is a liar” (ibid.). To signify that he was an unprofitable servant even after receiving the cup of precious death, he exclaimed: “O Lord, I am your servant, I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid; you have broken my bonds” (ibid.). He did not say, “I myself broke them; I am sufficient to save myself,” but, “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.).

This, then, is the sole perfection of faith in human beings: that, after fulfilling everything that has been commanded, they know themselves to be imperfect; and that, as long as they are exiles from the Lord, they always remember that there are evils within them which they must lament, and that good things are always lacking in them toward which, with his grace assisting, they may advance.

“And it happened, and so forth: ten leprous men met him.” Leprous people may not improperly be understood as those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, profess various doctrines of error. They do not conceal their ignorance; rather, they bring it into the light and display the boastfulness of their speech as though it were the highest expertise. Moreover, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truths. Thus truths mixed disorderly with falsehoods, appearing in a single human argument or narrative like different colors in one body, signify leprosy, which varies and stains human bodies with true and false patches of color.

Such people must be avoided by the Church, so that, if possible, they may stand at a greater distance and call out to Christ with a loud cry. Hence the text appropriately continues:

“They stood at a distance and raised their voice, saying: ‘Jesus, teacher, have mercy on us.’” They rightly name Jesus “teacher” so that they may be saved. By indicating that they had gone astray in his words, they humbly call him their teacher, asking to be saved; and when they return to knowledge of the teacher, they immediately return to the form of salvation. For it follows:

[Col. 0542D] When he saw them, he said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed. The Lord is found to have sent none of those to whom he granted such bodily benefits to the priests except lepers, because, evidently, the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the future royal priesthood that exists in the Church, through which all who belong to the body of Christ, the supreme and true high priest, are consecrated. And whoever, whether through heretical perversity, pagan superstition, Jewish faithlessness, or even fraternal schism, has been deprived by the Lord’s grace of his variegated color, as it were, must come to the Church and display the true color of faith that he has received. The remaining vices, like disorders of health and, as it were, of the soul’s members and senses, [Col. 0543A] the Lord himself heals and corrects inwardly in conscience and understanding.

Finally, Paul too, after hearing the Lord’s voice—“Why are you persecuting me?” and “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9)—was nevertheless sent to Ananias, so that through that priesthood he might receive the sacrament of the doctrine of faith established in the Church and his true color might be approved. This was not because the Lord cannot do everything by himself—for who else does these things even in the Church?—but so that the very fellowship of the gathered faithful, by mutually approving and sharing the doctrine of the true faith in all that is spoken in words or signified in sacraments, might overlay everything with one appearance of the true color.

Cornelius also, although an angel announced to him that his almsgiving had been accepted and his prayers heard, was nevertheless ordered, on account of the unity of doctrine and the sacraments, to send for Peter, as though this were said to him and his people: “Go, show yourselves to the priests”; for as they went, they were cleansed. Peter had already come to them, but they had not yet received the sacrament of baptism and had not yet reached the priests spiritually. Nevertheless, their cleansing was declared by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the wonder of languages.

But one of them, etc. This one, who returned glorifying God, signifies the devout humility of the one Church toward Christ. He rightly fell at the Lord’s feet and gave thanks. For that person truly gives thanks to God who, restraining the thoughts of his own presumption, humbly [Col. 0543C] sees how weak he is in himself; who attributes no virtue to himself; and who recognizes that the good he does comes from the mercy of the Creator. Hence it is rightly added:

And he was a Samaritan. “Samaritan,” in fact, is interpreted as “guardian.” By this name that people is most fittingly signified which, by giving thanks to the one from whom it has received, attributes everything it has received to him, singing in a manner the words of the psalm: “O my Strength, I will keep watch for you, for you, O God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58). He falls on his face because he is ashamed when he remembers the evils he has committed. For a person falls there where he is confounded. Hence Paul also said, as though to certain people lying on their faces: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). But concerning [Col. 0543D] the rider of a horse—that is, one who has been lifted up in the glory of this world—it is said: “His rider shall fall backward” (Gen. 49). Again, it is written of the Lord’s persecutors: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18).

What does it mean that the elect fall forward on their faces, while the reprobate fall backward, except that everyone who falls backward falls where he plainly does not see, whereas the one who falls forward falls where he sees? Thus the wicked, because they fall into invisible things, are said to fall backward, since they collapse where they cannot now see what will then follow them. The righteous, however, because they voluntarily cast themselves down from these visible things in order to be raised up in invisible things, fall, as it were, on their faces: pierced by fear, they see and humble themselves.

Then Jesus answered and said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” [Col. 0544A] If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed. In this way such a complete number is formed that it does not proceed farther unless it returns again to one, so that this rule is preserved through the infinity of number. Thus the nine need the one in order to be joined together in a certain form of unity and become ten. The one, however, does not need them in order to preserve unity. Therefore, just as the one who gave thanks was approved and praised as a sign of the one Church, so the nine who did not give thanks, having become reprobate, were excluded from fellowship in unity. Hence such people will remain in the number nine as imperfect. And rightly does the Savior inquire where they are, as though they were unknown. For God’s knowing means choosing; his not knowing means rejecting.

[Col. 0544B] “Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” In bodily terms, it is easy to see that a person may not have leprosy and yet may not be good in spirit. But according to the meaning of this miracle, it troubles the observer to consider how the cleansed person can be called ungrateful. Yet it is now easy to see that someone may attain a complete and true doctrine within the fellowship of the Church and discuss everything according to the Catholic rule, distinguish the creature from the Creator, and thereby appear, through the variety of his falsehoods, to have been freed from leprosy, while nevertheless remaining ungrateful to God and to the Lord who cleansed him. For, lifted up by pride, he is not brought low by the devout humility of giving thanks. He becomes like those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks.” In saying that they knew God, he shows that they had indeed been cleansed from leprosy; yet he immediately accuses them of ingratitude.

And he said to him: “Rise, go; your faith has saved you.” The man who devoutly fell before the Lord is commanded to rise and go, because the one who, carefully recognizing his own weakness, lies humbly prostrate is commanded, through the consolation of the divine word, to rise for strong works and to advance gradually toward more perfect things as his merits increase day by day. If faith saved the man whom it inclined to give thanks to his Savior and cleanser, then faithlessness destroyed those who neglected to give glory to God for the benefits they had received. Therefore this passage is rightly joined to the preceding one: there it was determined, through the parable, that faith must be increased by humility; here it is shown more clearly through the events themselves that it is not merely the acknowledged principle of faith, but the action carried out by faith, that saves the believer and gives glory to the Father who is in heaven.

When he was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation.” They ask about the time of the kingdom of God because, as Luke later explains, they supposed that when the Lord came to Jerusalem the kingdom of God would immediately be revealed. Thus even the apostles, led by this opinion, asked him after his resurrection: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1). And elsewhere Cleopas said: “But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). The kingdom of God, however, does not come with observation.

Nor will they say, “Look, here it is,” because its coming cannot be observed either by angels or by human beings. The time of the Lord’s Incarnation, although fixed with complete certainty by the prophecies of the prophets and announced by the proclamations of angels, was nevertheless declared by continuous signs, whether of angels, human beings, or certainly miracles, from the time he was conceived, born, and baptized, through his preaching, his death and resurrection, and his return to heaven.
