“For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.” He says that the kingdom of God is placed within them—that is, in their hearts—where they believe that he reigns. Hence it is written: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, “the word of faith that we preach” (Rom. 10).

And he said to the disciples: “The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.” This is the kingdom of God whose coming we hope for: to see the day of Christ. He rightly says “one day,” because in that glory of blessedness of which the prophet, sighing, said, “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83), there is no interruption by darkness, nor even any memory of misery or pain—those things that first passed away—to cloud the light of perpetual peace. It is good, therefore, to desire the presence of this day, yet not to imagine everything for ourselves merely because of the greatness of our desire, as though the day of the Lord were already at hand. Hence the Lord appropriately continued by foretelling what would come:

“And they will say to you, ‘Look there!’ Do not go out or pursue them.” This statement may be understood not only of a time but also of a person. Of a time, because there have been some who, calculating the cycles of the ages, claimed to have discovered the precise year, day, and hour of the world’s end, contrary to the Lord’s authority: “It is not for you to know the times or moments” (Acts 1). Of a person, because many heretics have come against the Church, and many will come, claiming to be christs. The first was Simon Magus, while the last, greater than the others, is the Antichrist. Therefore, if anyone says, “Look here,” or “Look there”—that is, that the kingdom of God has come or will come in this or that person or at this or that hour—do not follow them. They do not fear seeking what is too high for them and speaking unspeakable things.

“For as lightning flashing from beneath the sky shines upon the things that are beneath the sky, so will the Son of Man be in his day.” This is what the psalm says: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 49), because the Savior’s second coming will not be in humility, as before, but in glory and majesty. He beautifully says, “flashing from beneath the sky,” because the conflict will take place beneath the sky—that is, in the midst of the air—as the Apostle testifies: “We shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thess. 4). If the Lord will appear in judgment like lightning, no one will then be permitted to hide within his own [Col. 0546A] mind, because he will be penetrated by the very flash of the Judge. Mortals therefore cannot observe the time or place of his coming: like lightning, he will come flashing upon all, manifest and sudden.

The Lord’s answer may also appropriately be understood of that coming of his by which he comes daily in the Church. The kingdom of God is within us because the one who will one day come as Judge of all now also reigns, present in the hearts of the faithful. Heretics have so often troubled the Church by saying, each according to his own doctrine, that the faith of Christ remains in their teaching, that the faithful of those times desire the Lord to return to earth for even one day, if that were possible, and to declare in person what the truth of the faith is. “And you will not see it,” he says, because there is no need for the Lord to restore by bodily vision what he once manifested spiritually by the light of his Gospel spread throughout the whole world and established against every intrusion of the apocrypha by the undivided light of his love.

“But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.” While speaking much about the glory of his coming, the Lord also took care to insert a brief mention of the terror of his Passion, so that when they saw dying the one whom they had heard would be glorified, they might mitigate the pain of his Passion by hope in the promised glorification. At the same time, they would prepare themselves, if they loved the glory of the kingdom, not to fear the danger of death. He calls “this generation” not only the Jewish people but all the reprobate, by whom even now the Son of Man suffers and is rejected in his body—that is, in the Church. For although the head of this body, which is ourselves, has already raised itself free above all things, it nevertheless still feels, through the body that it retains below, the wounds of the reprobate.

“And as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the day of the Son of Man.” He confirms through many examples that the day of his coming will be sudden. For the one whom he had compared to lightning swiftly crossing all things, he likewise compares to the days of Noah and Lot, when sudden destruction overtook mortals.

“They were eating and drinking, marrying wives, and being given in marriage.” Here the Lord does not condemn marriages or food according to the insane doctrine of Marcion, Manichaeus, and Tatian, the founder of the Encratites, since the former contain the means of succession and the latter the supports of nature. Rather, in accordance with what the Apostle says—“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. 6)—the immoderate use of lawful things is condemned. They did not perish by water or fire because they devoted themselves entirely to these things and disregarded God’s judgments.

“Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.” Noah builds the ark when the Lord constructs the Church by joining together faithful men like smoothed pieces of wood. He enters it when it has been perfectly completed, when the eternal inhabitant illumines it on the day of judgment by the presence of his vision. But while the ark is being built, the wicked live in luxury; when it is entered, they perish, because those who here insult the saints while they struggle will there be punished with eternal damnation while the saints are crowned.

“Likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building.” Passing over the great and unspeakable crime of the Sodomites, the Lord recalls only those offenses that might seem trivial or even no offenses at all, so that you may understand what punishment awaits unlawful acts if lawful activities, without which this life cannot be lived, are punished with fire and sulfur when practiced immoderately.

Rightly, therefore, blessed Augustine, seeing the allurements of harmful custom and moved by righteous grief, exclaims: “Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unusual, but which, when customary, although they are so great that they entirely close the kingdom of God against those who commit them, we are often compelled to tolerate by seeing everything and sometimes even to do some of them by tolerating them—sins for the cleansing of which the blood of the Son of God was poured out. And would that, O Lord, we did not do everything that we could not prevent.”

“But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all.” Until this point Lot dwells in Sodom, that is, the people of the elect dwell among the reprobate as strangers. He is righteous both in sight and hearing and, in accordance with the interpretation of his name, Lot, avoids their crimes as far as he can. But when Lot goes out, Sodom will perish, because at the consummation of the age the angels will go out, separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire.

Here it should be noted that the fire and sulfur which he says rained from heaven signify not the very flame of eternal punishment but the sudden coming of that day. For the perpetual fire will not descend upon the wicked to punish them; rather, they themselves, cast out from the Judge’s presence, will be sent into eternal fire. Nevertheless, we do not doubt that sulfur is also present in that fire, as John testifies. Describing both fires—namely, the sudden fire of correction and the eternal fire of burning—he says: “And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them; and the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. 20).

“So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.” He rightly says “will be revealed,” because the one who meanwhile sees all things without appearing will then appear and judge all things. He will appear to judge especially at the time when he sees everyone forgetful of his judgments and enslaved to this age. For although the end of the world will come at the time long ago predetermined, yet because the love of many will grow cold near the end, human wickedness will increase so greatly that the world itself should rightly be destroyed along with the one who inhabits it.

Even now we see innumerable people so attached to feasting and drunkenness, buying and selling, and the other affairs of the world that it is plain they are provoking the anger of the stern Judge. Yet we fear that worse things are already about to come—things that no wise person can even contemplate without profound grief. What was once said concerning the destruction of one sinful people—“The iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. 15)—must plainly be understood as applying to the entire mass of the wicked that is destined for condemnation.

“In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his vessels in the house, must not come down to take them.” Thus far he has spoken of the fact that the kingdom of God—that is, Christ—comes not with observation but unexpectedly. Now he shows what sort of people should await this coming. The person on the housetop is one who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually in the open air. His vessels in the house are carnal desires, which he once loved too much but left behind in this world while seeking things above. As judgment approaches, he must not in any way return for them.

He speaks of that hour—not the hour when the Judge comes, but the hour when he will come; not the hour when fire descended upon Sodom, but the hour when Lot is compelled to depart, or rather when, while he delays, he is seized and dragged out by the angels. For when the Judge has already come and appeared, no one will be able to wish to descend into this world in order to seize anything from it. But this hour is also taking place today, while we await the Judge who will come with watchful vigilance, uncertain when he will arrive. Concerning it John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2).

“And whoever is in the field must likewise not turn back.” Whoever works in the Church and, like Paul and Apollos, plants and waters must not look back toward the worldly hope to which he has renounced.

“Remember Lot’s wife.” Lot’s wife signifies those who, in tribulation, look backward and turn themselves away from hope in the divine promise. Therefore she became a pillar of salt, so that, by warning human beings not to do this, she might, as it were, season their hearts and keep them from becoming foolish.

[Col. 0548C] “Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it.” This statement can rightly be understood in two ways, but both interpretations refer entirely to one end: that we should not fear suffering adversity for Christ, or even undergoing death itself. When a persecutor threatens death, the person who chooses to save his life temporarily by denying Christ rather than denying him undoubtedly prepares that life for eternal destruction. Likewise, whoever seeks the eternal salvation of his soul does not hesitate to lose it temporarily in the hands of persecutors—that is, to give it over to death.

Both interpretations are fittingly supported by what follows:

“And whoever loses it will give it life.” That is, whoever loses it here will give it life there. Whoever, for Christ’s sake, hands it over to death, considering it all day long as “a sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8), will then, when Christ rises and helps him, find it set free for the sake of Christ’s name.

“I tell you, on that night there will be two in one bed.” Earlier the Lord had said that the person in the field must not turn back, lest you think this was said only of those who would openly return from the field—that is, openly deny the Lord. He goes on to show that there are some who, although they seem to keep their face directed forward, nevertheless look backward in spirit and mind.

“On that night,” he says—on that night of tribulation so dark that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error (Matt. 24)—there will be two in one bed, namely, those who choose leisure and repose, occupied neither with worldly business nor with ecclesiastical affairs. Their repose is signified by the name “bed.”

“One will be taken, and the other will be left.” This is not spoken as though it concerned two individual people, but two kinds of disposition. Whoever devotes himself to continence, so that, living without anxiety, he may think about the things of God (1 Cor. 7), will be taken by God. But whoever, whether through love of human praise or through any other corruption of vices, damages the state of monastic life in which he has been formed will be left behind. Where such a person must be left, the Lamentations of Jeremiah suggest, when, describing under the figure of Judea the fall of any idle and sinful soul, he says: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1).

“There will be two grinding at the same mill.” He calls “grinding” those who, established among the peoples, are governed by teachers while engaging in the affairs of this age. He signified them by the name of women because, as I have said, it is fitting for them to be governed by the counsels of the experienced. He says “grinding” because of the circuit and rotation of temporal affairs. Yet he says that they are grinding at one mill insofar as, from those very affairs and occupations, they provide for the needs of the Church. Every activity of this world is a mill: while it piles up many cares, it turns human minds as though upon a wheel and casts out from itself something like flour, because it continually generates the tiniest thoughts in a restless heart.

“One will be taken, and the other will be left.” The part that has entered marriage solely for the sake of the propagation of the race and has distributed earthly substance in order to acquire heavenly things will be taken. The part that has served marriage for the allurements of the flesh will be left; and if it has offered earthly possessions to the Church or to the poor, it will have done so in order that, as though having redeemed the Lord, it might abound in these things still more.

“Two will be in the field; one will be taken, and the other will be left.” Just as above he placed two in one bed and two grinding at one mill, so here I think we should understand two in one field. He signifies those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in the field of God, concerning which its farmer said: “You are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3). The person who does not adulterate the word of God (2 Cor. 2), but speaks “as from God, in the presence of God, in Christ,” will be taken. But whoever proclaims Christ not sincerely, but from self-interest, will be left by him.

I do not think there are other classes of people from whom the Church consists than these three, each possessing two differences on account of being taken and left, although within each there may be many differences of pursuits and desires that nevertheless converge toward concord and unity. Hence the prophet Ezekiel saw three men delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job. In these three, preachers, continent persons, and married people are signified. Noah guided the ark upon the waters and therefore represented those who govern. Daniel was devoted to abstinence in the royal court and thus signified the life of the continent. Job, situated in marriage and attending to the care of his own household, was pleasing to God and fittingly represents the order of good married people.

They answered him: “Where, Lord?” He said to them: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather.” When the Savior is asked where the good will be taken and where the wicked will be left, he states one thing and leaves the other to be understood. By asserting that the saints will be with him, he implies that the reprobate will be separated from his vision and therefore condemned elsewhere only with the devil.

Wherever, then, the Lord is in his body, there the elect will gather—those who, by imitating his Passion and humility, are as though nourished by his flesh. Through the resurrection their youth will be renewed “like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102). This also agrees with the practices of those who thirst with their whole mind to contemplate the glory of heavenly majesty: the eagle, surpassing other birds in flight, delights to fix its eyes upon the very rays of the sun.

The following also accords with this: the eagle is accustomed, when it comes upon the stone aetites, to bring it to its nest as a defense, lest a serpent approach or dare to touch its young or eggs. Likewise, every wise person, in order to defend his actions and thoughts from the incursion of the ancient serpent, must always keep in his heart that stone which, “cut from the mountain without hands,” overthrew the kingdom of the devil (Dan. 2)—that is, the faith and love of Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII

He also told them a parable, because they ought always to pray and not grow weary. The Apostle likewise says: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing.” But who can pray always and persist in prayers without weariness or interruption, so that he has no time even to take nourishment or sleep?

Either, then, we must say that the person always prays and does not grow weary who, at the canonical hours each day, according to the rite of ecclesiastical tradition, does not cease to praise and entreat the Lord with the customary psalmody and prayers. This is what the Psalmist meant: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). Or certainly everything that the righteous person does and says according to God must be reckoned as prayer. For since the righteous person continually does what is just, through this he will pray without ceasing and will never stop praying unless he ceases to be righteous.

[Col. 0550D] “There was a certain judge in a certain city who did not fear God and did not respect human beings. And there was a widow in that city, and she kept coming to him, saying: ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ For a long time he was unwilling. But afterward he said within himself: ‘Although I do not fear God and do not respect human beings, nevertheless, because this widow is troublesome to me, I will vindicate her, lest by coming continually she finally wear me down.’”

The Lord presents parables either according to some similarity, as in the case of the man who had two sons, the elder near him in the field and the younger living riotously in a distant land; or he proves something from the very dissimilarity, as in the statement: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?” (Matt. 6).

Thus the former kind can be joined to these words: “As that is, so also is this.” The latter can be expressed: “If that is so, how much more is this?” or “If that is so, how much less is this?” Sometimes these things are stated obscurely and sometimes openly.

Here, therefore, the unjust judge is introduced not because of similarity but because of dissimilarity. That unjust judge in no way allegorically represents God. Nevertheless, the Lord wished it to be inferred from this that God, who is good and just, cares for those who entreat him, since even an unjust human being cannot despise those who assail him with continual prayers, if only to avoid their persistence becoming wearisome. For this is what he says: “Lest by coming she wear me down.” The widow herself may bear a likeness to the Church, which seems desolate until the Lord comes, although even now he secretly cares for her.

The Lord said: “Listen to what the unjust judge says. And will God not vindicate his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay on their behalf? I tell you, he will quickly vindicate them.”

If anyone is troubled by the question why God’s elect pray to be avenged—a prayer also mentioned in the Apocalypse of John—while we are explicitly instructed to pray for our enemies and persecutors, we must understand the vengeance of the righteous to be the destruction of all the wicked. They perish in two ways: either by turning to righteousness, or by losing through punishment the power by which they now have some temporary ability against the good, for as long as this is itself beneficial to the good. Although the righteous pray for their enemies, they may nevertheless, when they desire this end to come, rightly be said to desire vengeance.

“Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” Although the omnipotent Creator is always ready to vindicate his elect when they cry to him, on the day of judgment—something that must be held in a trembling heart—when the same Creator appears in the form of the Son of Man, the elect will be so rare that the ruin of the whole world will have to be hastened not so much because of the outcry of the faithful who have been unjustly condemned as because of the torpor of those who have been justly condemned.

When the Lord says, as though in doubt, “Do you suppose he will find faith?” he is not doubting but reproving. The word of doubt rebukes unbelief; divinity does not speculate. We too sometimes use a word of doubt in rebuke concerning matters of which we are certain in our hearts. For example, if you were angry with your servant and said, “You despise me? Consider that perhaps I am your master.” Or the Apostle said to certain people who despised him: “I suppose that I also have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7). One who says “I suppose” seems to doubt, but he was rebuking, not doubting. So also the Lord knows all things—through him all things were made—yet by speaking as though in doubt he rebukes the hearts of unbelievers.

He also told this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others. The Lord concluded the parable in which he taught them always to pray and not grow weary by saying that, when the Judge came, faith would scarcely be found on earth. Lest anyone flatter himself with empty faith, knowledge, or even confession, he immediately added this other parable to show more carefully that God examines not the words of faith but its works.

Among these works, humility holds the highest place. Hence above, when he compared faith to a mustard seed, small indeed but burning through contrition, he added by way of explanation: “When you have done all that is commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17). The proud, by contrast, although they do not do everything but only a small part of what is commanded, immediately presume upon their own righteousness and despise the weak. Therefore, as though empty of faith, they are not heard when they pray.

“Two men went up into the temple to pray.” [Col. 0552B] One was a Pharisee and the other a publican. The publican, praying humbly, belongs to those members of the aforementioned widow—that is, of the Church—of whom it was said above: “And will God not vindicate his elect, who cry to him?” The Pharisee, boasting of his merits, belongs to those concerning whom the terrifying conclusion follows: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?”

“The Pharisee stood and prayed this within himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican.’”

There are four forms in which every swelling of the arrogant is displayed: when they think that they possess good from themselves; or, if they believe that it has been given to them from above, when they think they received it on account of their own merits; or when they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or when, despising others, they desire to appear uniquely endowed with what they do possess. The Pharisee is found to have suffered from this plague of boasting. For he descended from the temple without justification because, attributing the merits of good works to himself as though uniquely his own, he set himself above the publican who was praying.

“I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.” The prophet Ezekiel writes concerning the living creatures shown to him from heaven: “The whole body of the four of them was full of eyes all around.” The bodies of the living creatures are described as full of eyes because the action of the saints is watchful on every side, providing desirably for good things and carefully avoiding evil things.

But we often become so intent on some matters that we neglect others. Wherever we neglect something, there we plainly have no eye. The Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, showing mercy, and giving thanks to God, but he had no eye for preserving humility. And what does it profit that nearly the whole city is carefully guarded against the enemy’s ambushes if one opening is left exposed through which the enemy may enter?

“But the publican, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes toward heaven, but beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.”

What confidence of forgiveness this fittingly offers to penitents: the publican, who fully recognized the guilt of his wickedness, wept and confessed; and although he came to the temple unjustified, he returned from the temple justified. In a symbolic interpretation, the Pharisee is the Jewish people, which exalts its merits through the justifications of the Law. The publican is the Gentile, who, placed far from God, confesses his sins. The one, departing in pride, went away humbled; the other, lamenting, merited to draw near and be exalted.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” This can rightly be understood both of the two peoples mentioned above and of every proud or humble person, just as can the statement we read elsewhere: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16).

Therefore, from the words of the exalted Pharisee—through which he merited to be humbled—we may derive, by contrast, a pattern of humility by which we may be exalted. Just as he, considering the vices of those worse than himself and his own virtues, was lifted up to ruin, so may we, considering not only our own sluggishness but also the virtues of those who are better, humble ourselves toward glory. Thus each of us should entreat as a suppliant and submissive person:

“Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the countless servants of yours who are exalted by contempt for the world, glorious through the merit of righteousness, angelic in the praise of chastity, or like the many among them who, after public crimes, have merited through repentance to become devoted to you. And even if, through the generosity of your grace, I have done some good, I do not know with what purpose I do it or with what severity you will weigh it.”

They were bringing infants to him also, so that he might touch them. When the disciples saw this, they rebuked those bringing them. [Col. 0553C] This passage shines forth as one full of instruction in humility: it demonstrates that the innocent and simple can attain the Lord’s grace. The disciples rebuked those who offered the children, not because they were unwilling for the infants to be blessed by the Savior’s hand and voice, but because, not yet possessing the fullest faith, they thought that he, like other human beings, might grow weary from the persistence of those bringing them.

But Jesus, calling them together, said: “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them. For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” He significantly said “such as these,” not “these,” to show that it is not age that reigns, but character, and that the reward is promised to those who possess a similar innocence and simplicity. The Apostle likewise agrees with this meaning: “Brothers, do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness. [Col. 0553D] Yet in understanding, be mature.”

“Amen I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.” Just as a child does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, is not captivated when he sees a beautiful woman, does not think one thing and say another, so you too will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven unless you possess such innocence and purity of heart. Alternatively: We are commanded to receive the kingdom of God—that is, the teaching of the Gospel—like a child, because in learning a child neither contradicts his teachers nor constructs arguments and words in resistance to them; rather, he faithfully accepts what is taught, and obeys and remains quiet with reverence.

And a certain ruler asked him, saying: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” [Col. 0554A] I think this ruler had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to be like a child would enter the kingdom of God. Therefore, anxious for a more certain instruction, he asks that it be explained to him not in parable but openly by what merits of conduct he might attain eternal life.

Jesus said to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.” Because he had called him “good teacher,” but had not confessed him as God or as the Son of God, he learns that no holy human being is good in comparison with God. Of this it is said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CVI). But when it says that God alone is good, this is not to be understood of the Father alone, but also of the Son, who says: “I am the good shepherd.” And likewise of the Holy Spirit, since “the Father from heaven will give the good [Col. 0554B] Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke XI). That is, the one and undivided Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is the one and only good God. The Lord therefore does not deny that he is good, but indicates that he is God. He does not testify that he is not a good teacher, but that no teacher apart from God is good.

“You know the commandments: You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother.” This is the chastity of childlike innocence, set before us for imitation if we wish to enter the kingdom of God. It should indeed be noted that, when the justice of the Law is observed in its proper time, it confers not only the good things of the earth but also eternal life.

He said: “I have kept all these things from my youth.” When Jesus heard this, he said to him: “You still lack one thing.” [Col. 0554C] We should not think that this ruler was lying when he said that he had kept the commandments of the Law; rather, he simply confessed how he had lived. For if he had been held guilty of the offense of lying, Mark the evangelist would certainly not have added, writing about him: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him: One thing you lack: Go, sell whatever you have” (Mark X), and so forth. The Lord loves those who keep the commandments of the Law, even though they are lesser commandments; nevertheless, he shows those who desire to be perfect what was lacking in the Law.

“Sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” Whoever wishes to be perfect must sell, as Ananias and Sapphira did—but he must sell everything; and [Col. 0554D] when he has sold it, he must give all of it to the poor, and thus prepare treasure for himself in the kingdom of heaven. Yet this is not sufficient for perfection unless, after despising wealth, he follows the Savior—that is, after abandoning evil, he does good. A purse is easier to despise than the will. Many abandon their riches but do not follow the Lord. He follows the Lord who imitates him and walks in his footsteps. For whoever says that he believes in Christ must walk as he walked.

When he heard these things, he became sorrowful, because he was very rich. This is the sorrow of the world, which produces death. These are the deceitful riches that, like thorns, have choked the Lord’s seed.

When Jesus saw that he had become sorrowful, he said: [Col. 0555A] “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” It is clear, certainly, that those who devote themselves here to multiplying riches disdain seeking the joys of the other life. Yet there is some difference between possessing money and loving money. Many possess it but do not love it. Many do not possess it but love it. Again, some both possess and love it, while others rejoice neither to possess nor to love the riches of the world. Their condition is safer, as they say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). Hence Solomon does not say, “Whoever possesses riches,” but, “Whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. V). And the Lord himself, according to Mark, after the disciples were astonished at these words, added by way of explanation: “Children, how difficult it is for those who trust in money to enter the kingdom of God!” (Mark X). [Col. 0555B] It should be noted that he did not say “Impossible,” but “Difficult”—that is, that it requires the greatest labor for those who possess money, or trust in money, to enter the court of the heavenly kingdom after stripping away the bonds of the love of money.

“For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” If it is easier for a camel, huge in its limbs and disproportionate in form, to penetrate the narrow opening of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, then no rich man will enter the kingdom of God. How, then, did Matthew in the Gospel—Zacchaeus and Joseph—or very many rich men in the Old Testament enter God’s kingdom? Perhaps because, through the Lord’s inspiration, they learned either to regard riches as nothing or to abandon them entirely. Was David trusting in the riches of his kingdom when he sings of himself [Col. 0555C]: “For I am solitary and poor” (Ps. XXIV)? And he exhorts others: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). I think he did not dare to say, “Do not accept them.” Could one believe that Abraham preferred his possessions to the Lord, for whose sake he did not hesitate to strike down his only heir?

In a deeper sense, it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. He wished himself to be understood by the name “camel,” because he voluntarily humbled himself and bore the burdens of our weakness. Where is this understood more clearly than in the very passage that says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III)? By the needle he signifies piercing; by piercing, the pains he endured in his Passion. The eye of the needle therefore signifies afflictions and sufferings. Once this was torn apart, he deigned in a certain manner to mend—​that is, to restore—the garments of our nature, so that, reformed for the better after the Fall, [Col. 0555D] we might rejoice in testimony to the Apostle, who says: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

And those who heard this said: “Who, then, can be saved?” What purpose does this response serve, since the crowd of the poor who might be saved after the rich have perished is incomparably greater? It serves because they understood that all who love riches, even if they are unable to obtain them, are counted among the rich.

He said to them: “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.” This should not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud, signified by the name of that rich man, will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride. Rather, it is possible for God, through the word—as we see has happened and happens daily—to convert people from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to saving humility.

[Col. 0556A] Peter said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” What great confidence! Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich. He sought his food by hand and by his craft, and yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because it is not enough merely to leave things, he adds what constitutes perfection: “And we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give us?

He said to them: “Amen I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or [Col. 0556B] children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this present time and, in the age to come, eternal life.” On the occasion of this saying, some construct the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the righteous, when everything that we have left for God will be repaid to us with multiplied interest, together with the gift of eternal life. They do not see how absurd it is that, even if the promise is worthy in other respects, it appears shameful with regard to wives according to the other evangelists—especially since the Lord testifies that there will be no marrying in the resurrection, and since, according to Mark the evangelist, he confirms that what has been left will be received in this present time together with persecutions. Yet those millenarians dogmatize that these persecutions, as well as the other contrary conditions, will be absent [Col. 0556C] during their thousand years.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever, for the sake of acquiring the kingdom of God, despises every affection and tramples underfoot all the delights and luxuries of the world will receive much more in the present, because from brothers and companions in his way of life, who are joined to him by a spiritual bond, he will receive a much more gracious love even in this life. The affection that joins parents and children, brothers and sisters, spouses and relatives—whether through the bond of intercourse or through the ties of blood—is plainly brief and fragile. Finally, it is sometimes torn apart even when an honorable cause intervenes. Only those who believe that everything belonging to their brothers is theirs, and everything belonging to them is their brothers’, retain the unity of perpetual union and possess all things indiscriminately. Read the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and soul,” and all things were common among them; none was needy among those who had left their possessions for the Lord. Of these Paul also says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing everything” [Col. 0556D] (II Cor. VI).

Certainly, from marital continence also, a much greater sweetness will be received than that which was previously provided by the mingling of the sexes. Formerly I possessed a wife in lustful desire; now I possess this same woman in the honor of sanctification and in true love of Christ. The woman is one, but the merit of chastity has grown a hundredfold. For what is said according to Mark—“He will receive a hundred times as much now in this present time, houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, with persecutions” (Mark X)—can be understood in a higher sense. The number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, though it appears to retain the same shape in the bending of the fingers, nevertheless increases immensely in magnitude. For all who despise temporal things for the sake of the kingdom of God taste, even in this life, by sure faith, even in this life, which is most full of persecutions, taste the joys of that same kingdom; and, in expectation [Col. 0557A] of the heavenly homeland, enjoy the most sincere love of all the elect together.

Jesus took the Twelve and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.” Foreseeing that [Col. 0557B] his disciples’ minds would be troubled by his Passion, the Savior foretells to them far in advance both the suffering of that Passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying as had been foretold, they would not doubt that he would also rise again. Foreseeing also that certain heretics would arise in the Church who would say that Christ had taught things contrary to the Law and the Prophets, and that the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New Testament must be believed to be different, he shows that the prophets’ predictions had no other purpose than the mystery of his own dispensation, which he temporarily assumed for us, so completely that the fulfillment of prophecy is the accomplished perfection celebrated in his Passion and subsequent glory. He also most openly refutes the madness of the pagans who mock his cross, since, as one foreseeing the future, he reveals the time of his approaching Passion and, [Col. 0557C] fearless of death, goes to the place where he will die.

And they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said. We read in the Gospel according to John that, when the Lord said, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everything to myself,” the crowd answered and said: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” (John XII). What, then, is the reason that the disciples cannot understand the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, repeated so many times, while the Jews understand from a single saying, and one expressed so obscurely that the Evangelist considers it worthy of explanation—“He said this,” he says, “signifying by what death he was going to die”—that the lifting up of the cross is meant? It is because the disciples, who especially desired to see his life, could not bear to hear of his death. They knew him not only as an innocent human being but also as true God, and they believed that he could in no way die. Moreover, because they were accustomed to hearing him speak frequently in parables, whenever he said something about his Passion they thought that it should not be understood as it sounded, but that, as love dictated, it referred allegorically to something else. The Jews, however, because they had conspired to kill him, understood whatever he said about his Passion or cross; for he was speaking of what they most eagerly desired to happen and were striving to accomplish. Thus, in a wondrous and unusual manner, the same mystery of the cross that love concealed from the faithful was disclosed to the unbelieving by envy. [Col. 0558A]

It happened that, as he approached Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. Allegorically, this blind man signifies the human race, which, expelled in its first parent from the joys of paradise and ignorant of the brightness of the heavenly light, suffers the darkness of its condemnation. But when Jesus is said to be approaching Jericho, the blind man is illuminated. Jericho is interpreted as “moon.” In sacred Scripture, the moon signifies the decline of the flesh, because, as it diminishes at monthly intervals, it represents the decline of our mortality. Therefore, when our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light, because when the Divinity assumes [Col. 0558B] the decline of our flesh, the human race receives the light it had lost.

This blind man is rightly described as sitting beside the road and as begging. For Truth itself said: “I am the way” (John XIV). Therefore, whoever does not know the brightness of eternal light is blind; but if he already believes in the Redeemer, he sits beside the road. If he believes but, in order to receive eternal light, neglects to ask and ceases from prayer, the blind man indeed sits beside the road, but he does not beg. If, however, he both believes and entreats, he is blind, sits beside the road, and begs.

And he cried out, saying: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” Those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” [Col. 0558C] What do those who precede the approaching Jesus signify, except the crowds of bodily desires and the tumult of vices? Before Jesus comes to our heart, these disperse our thoughts by their temptations and disturb the voices of our heart in prayer. Often, when we wish to turn to God after committing vices, when we try to implore forgiveness for the very vices we have committed, the images of the sins we have committed come before our heart, strike against the vision of our mind, confuse us, and suppress the spirit and voice of our supplication. But the one whom the crowd rebukes and tells to be silent cries out more and more, because the more violently we are oppressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more ardently we must persist in prayer.

[Col. 0558D] Jesus, standing still, ordered him to be brought to him. Behold, he stands who had previously been passing by, because while we still endure crowds of phantasms in prayer, we sense Jesus passing by to some extent. But when we persist vigorously in prayer, Jesus stands still and restores the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored.

When he had drawn near, he asked him, saying: “What do you want me to do for you?” He said: “Lord, that I may see.” Could the one who was able to restore light have been unaware of what the blind man wanted? Yet he wishes to be asked for what he already foreknows that we should ask and that he will grant. He urges us insistently to prayer, and yet he says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. VI). He asks, therefore, in order that the request may be made; he asks in order to stir the heart to prayer. [Col. 0559A] Hence the blind man immediately adds: “Lord, that I may see.” Behold, the blind man does not ask the Lord for gold but for light; he considers it of little value to ask for anything outside the light. For even if a blind man can possess anything whatsoever, without light he cannot see what he possesses. Let us therefore imitate the one whom we have heard was saved both in body and in mind. Let us ask the Lord not for false riches, not for earthly gifts, not for fleeting honors, but for light—the light that we can see together with the angels, which has neither a beginning to commence it nor an end to confine it. The way to that light is faith. Therefore, after the blind man has been illuminated, it is rightly added at once:

And Jesus said to him: “See; your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying [Col. 0559B] God. He sees and follows who does the good that he understands. He sees but does not follow who understands the good but scorns to do good. For he follows Jesus who imitates him. Hence he says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII). Let us therefore consider by what path he walks, so that we may deserve to follow. In this way it happens that not only does our own life advance toward God, but our very conversion also kindles others to the praise of God. Hence it is added there:

And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God. The people gave praise to God not only for the gift of light that had been obtained, but also for the merit of the faith that obtained it. They gave praise to God because they saw Jesus mercifully and powerfully restore light to the one who asked, and because they recognized that the cry of steadfast [Col. 0559C] faith, when it rightly seeks, can immediately obtain what it asks. Hence it should be noted that the Lord, appearing in the flesh, confirmed by his examples everything that he taught in words. For he commanded us: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V); and he himself, in all that he began to do and teach (Acts I), sought not his own glory among people but the glory of the Father (John VIII).

## CHAPTER XIX

And entering Jericho, he was passing through it; and behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, who was also chief among the tax collectors and himself rich. He was seeking to see Jesus, who he was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature. Running ahead, he climbed [Col. 0559D] a sycamore tree in order to see him, because he was going to pass that way. “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God” (Luke XVIII). Behold, the camel, having laid down the burden of its hump, passes through the eye of the needle (Matt. XIX): that is, the rich man and tax collector, having abandoned the burden of riches and rejected the disposition toward fraud, ascends the narrow gate and the confined way that leads to life (Matt. VII). With wondrous devotion to faith, in order to see the Savior, he makes up by climbing the tree for what nature had denied him. Therefore, although he himself does not dare to ask, he rightly receives the blessing of the Lord’s welcome that he desired.

Mystically, Zacchaeus, whose name is interpreted as “justified,” signifies the believing people from the Gentiles. The more occupied he was with worldly concerns, [Col. 0560A] the more humble he had been made by the sins that weighed him down. Yet he was washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. He sought to see the Savior entering Jericho, but he could not because of the crowd. He desired to share in the grace of faith that the Savior brought to the world, but his ingrained habit of vices prevented him from attaining his desire. The same crowd of harmful habit that above rebuked the blind man crying out lest he ask for light now also delays the tax collector who is looking upward, lest he see Jesus. But just as the blind man overcame the voices of the crowd by crying out more and more, so the short man must transcend the obstacle of the harmful crowd by seeking higher things. He must leave earthly matters behind and climb the tree of the cross. [Col. 0560B]

The sycamore, which is a tree similar in leaves to the mulberry but surpassing it in height, and hence is called by the Latins “the lofty tree,” is called the “foolish fig.” The Lord’s cross is likewise a tree that nourishes believers like a fig tree but is mocked by unbelievers as foolish. “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I). Zacchaeus, short in stature, climbed this tree so that he might be exalted by it, when any humble person conscious of his own weakness, trusting in the Lord, proclaims: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). Having climbed the sycamore, he sees the Lord passing nearby, because through this praiseworthy foolishness he directs his attention to the light of heavenly wisdom—​if not yet firmly, as it truly is, then at least swiftly and as though in passing. [Col. 0560C]

And when he came to the place, Jesus looked up and saw him. The Savior, passing through Jericho, came to the place where Zacchaeus had run ahead and climbed the sycamore, because, having sent throughout the world heralds of his word—in whom he himself both spoke and went—he came to the people of the nations. They, already exalted by faith in his Passion, longed to be blessed by the recognition of the face of his divinity. He looked up and saw him because he chose the one who had been raised by the grace of faith above earthly desires and who stood higher than unbelieving crowds. To see God means to choose or love. Hence the saying: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). We too hasten to turn our gaze away from what we detest, while we seek to see the things we love. [Col. 0560D] Jesus therefore saw the one who was looking at him, because he chose the one who chose him and loved the one who loved him.

The outstanding teacher shows this order of progress—that is, of reaching knowledge of the Divinity through faith in the Lord’s incarnation—as though from the sycamore to contemplate Jesus’ face, when he says: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II). Again, reproaching others, he says: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food” (Heb. V), calling the weak milk of the temporary dispensation and the difficult solid food of eternal majesty.

And he said to him: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today [Col. 0561A] I must remain in your house.” And he hurried down and welcomed him joyfully. At one time the Lord remained in the house of the ruler of the Pharisees—that is, he taught in the synagogue of the Jews. But because they attacked him with their poisonous tongue because he had not washed before the meal, because he healed on the Sabbath, because he received tax collectors and sinners, because he argued against greed, and because he did other things worthy of God, he grew weary of their crimes, departed, and fled, saying: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Today, however, he must remain in the house of the short Zacchaeus—that is, he must rest, as the grace of the new light shines forth, in the humble heart of the believing nations. As for the command that Zacchaeus come down from the sycamore and thus prepare a dwelling for Christ in his house, this is what the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, [Col. 0561B] yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Cor. V). For although he died through weakness, he lives through the power of God.

When they all saw this, they murmured, saying that he had gone in to a sinful man. It is evident that the Jews always hated the salvation of the nations. For it is written: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was spoken by Paul” (Acts XIII). And elsewhere: “The faithful brothers contended against the chief of the apostles, saying: Why did you enter uncircumcised men and eat with them?” (Acts XI).

Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor. [Col. 0561C] And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” While others accused him as a sinful man, Zacchaeus himself stood—that is, he persevered in the truth of the faith he had begun—not only proving that he had been converted from sin but also that he had conducted himself among the perfect.

When the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX), whoever lived innocently before conversion can, once converted, give everything to the poor. But one who has taken anything by fraud must first restore it according to the Law, and then give to the poor what remains to him. Thus he too, because he retains nothing for himself, scatters all his possessions and gives to the poor; “his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI). This is that wise foolishness which the tax collector had gathered from the sycamore, as though it were the fruit of life: to restore what had been taken, to abandon one’s own possessions, to despise visible things, to desire even to die for invisible things, to deny oneself, and to long to follow the footsteps of the Lord, whom one does not yet see. [Col. 0561D]

Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.” Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham not because he was born from Abraham’s line, but because he imitated Abraham’s faith. Just as Abraham, at the Lord’s command and in hope of a future inheritance, abandoned his land, his kindred, and his father’s house, so Zacchaeus left [Col. 0562A] his possessions to be distributed to the poor in order to acquire treasure in heaven. Beautifully, he says, “he too,” so that he might declare that not only those who persevere in righteousness but also those who turn back from injustice belong among the children of promise.

Alternatively: The salvation that formerly filled the house of the Jews has today shone upon the people of the nations, because this people too is a son of Abraham through belief in him. Of this the Apostle says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. III). And elsewhere he says that Abraham is “the father of circumcision,” not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised (Rom. IV).

“For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost.” This is what he says elsewhere: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX). Truly a merciful Teacher, who does not disdain to explain his mysteries to the murmuring crowds, showing so clearly that the repentance [Col. 0562B] of sinners is not to be rejected that the Son of God himself was sent to earth especially to seek it. To impress upon us the dispensation of his mercy, he very often calls himself the Son of Man, carefully commending to us what he graciously became for our sake.

While they were listening to these things, he added and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and because they thought that the kingdom of God would immediately appear. It is the Lord’s practice to affirm a preceding discourse by means of the parables that follow. Having therefore accepted and commended the repentance of the wealthy tax collector, he adds a parable to teach that he prefers the repentance of sinners to the righteousness of the proud, and that he will reign more broadly among the humble Gentiles in their ignorance of the Law than among the Jews exalted by the righteousness that comes from the Law. [Col. 0562C] And because the disciples, after hearing the Lord speak of his Passion and resurrection to be fulfilled in Jerusalem, did not understand what was being said and thought that the kingdom of God would come at once, he enlightens their ignorance and shows that he would first spread the faith of his kingdom throughout the whole world, and then, at the end of the world, come as judge and king of all ages.

He therefore said: “A certain nobleman went to a distant region to receive a kingdom for himself and then return.” That nobleman is the one to whom the blind man above cried: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Luke XVIII), and to whom, as he approached Jerusalem, they sang: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Matt. XXI). [Col. 0562D] The distant region is the Church from the Gentiles. Of this same nobleman, who says, “I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II), the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (ibid.). This inheritance and possession is called a distant region for two reasons: either because it cries out to the Lord from the ends of the earth, or because salvation is far from sinners (Ps. CCXVIII). Although God is present everywhere, the true God is nevertheless far from the understanding of those who worship idols. But those who were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. II).

Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas. The number ten pertains to the Law because of the Decalogue. Therefore the master of the household calls ten servants because he chooses disciples instructed in the letter of the Law. He gives them ten [Col. 0563A] minas because he reveals that the sayings of the Law are to be understood spiritually. For after his Passion and resurrection, he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures.

The mina, which the Greeks call *mna* (*mna*), is weighed at one hundred drachmas. Every word of Scripture, because it suggests the perfection of heavenly life, shines forth as though with the weight of the number one hundred.

And he said to them: “Trade until I come.” “Offer,” he says, “the words of the Law and the Prophets, examined through mystical interpretation, to the peoples, and receive from them a confession of faith and uprightness of conduct.” In accordance with this, the Psalmist commands his hearers, saying: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine” (Ps. LXXX). That is, [Col. 0563B] receive the praise of preaching in the intention of the heart, and return the devotion of action in the chastisement of the flesh. A tambourine is a hide stretched over wood. The hide stretched over wood is our flesh afflicted according to the example of the Lord’s cross.

But his citizens hated him. And they sent a delegation after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us.” By “citizens” he means the impious Jews. Of them he testifies elsewhere: “Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John XV). They hated him not only while he was present, even to the death of the cross, but also after his resurrection they sent persecution against the apostles and rejected the preaching of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0563C] And it happened that he returned after receiving the kingdom. This signifies the time when he who appeared to them in humility will come in the most manifest and exalted glory, when he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII).

And he ordered the servants to be called, to whom he had given the money, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading. He says “so that he might know,” not because anything can be hidden from him, to whom it is truly said: “Lord, you know all things.” Rather, “he might know” means that he might make everyone know. Then the works and thoughts of all will be openly displayed to all. Similarly, in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God tests you,” it says, “to know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII)—that is, to make it known.

No one should suppose that only those to whom the grace of preaching was given, and not also those to whom preaching was addressed, will then be summoned to judgment. They themselves are the money that the good servants acquired by trading. Indeed, those also to whom preaching was never given will be present there to be condemned; we shall speak of them below. [Col. 0563D]

The first came, saying: “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.” The first servant is the order of teachers sent to the circumcision. He received one mina in order to trade with it because he was commanded to preach one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God. But this same mina gained ten minas because by teaching he joined to himself the people established under the Law.

And he said to him: “Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.” [Col. 0564A] The servant is faithful in a little when he does not adulterate the word of God but speaks “as from God, in the presence of God, in Christ” (II Cor. II). For whatever gifts we receive in the present are very few and little in comparison with future things, because “we know in part and we prophesy in part.” But when the perfect comes, what is partial will be abolished (I Cor. XIII).

The ten cities are souls coming through the word of the Law to the grace of the Gospel. At that time, the one who has worthily lent them the money of the word to God will rightly be set over them in glory. Hence a certain outstanding trader, addressing the cities over which he presided—that is, the souls he had received to govern—says: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus [Col. 0564B]?” (I Thess. II).

And another came, saying: “Lord, your mina has made five minas.” This servant is the company of those who were sent to evangelize among the uncircumcised. To him, as he went forth to preach, the Lord had entrusted one mina—that is, one and the same faith, which had also been entrusted to the circumcision—but he made five minas of it, because he converted the nations, formerly enslaved to the senses of the body, to the grace of evangelical faith.

And he said to him: “And you, be over five cities.” That is, from the souls whom he had instructed in faith and conversion, shine forth as great and exalted. Concerning these Isaiah speaks mystically: “On that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan” (Isaiah XIX). For the five cities in the land of Egypt are the five bodily senses which we use in this world: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

“He who looks upon a woman in order to desire her” (Matthew V); he who turns away his ears so as not to hear the poor (Proverbs XXI); he who becomes drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery (Ephesians V); he who delights in crowning himself with roses before they wither (Wisdom II); he whose hands are full of blood and whose right hand is filled with gifts (Psalm XXV)—the five cities of such a man speak the language of Egypt, that is, all his senses perform the works of darkness. For Egypt signifies “darkness.”

But he who stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed and closes his eyes so as not to see evil (Isaiah XXXIII); he who tastes and sees how gracious the Lord is (Psalm XXXIII); he who chastises his body and brings it into subjection (I Corinthians IX); he who can say with the Apostle, “We are the good odor of Christ to God” (II Corinthians II)—the cities of such a man speak in a changed language, which is interpreted as “Canaan.” And he who had changed them from darkness by teaching is rightly said to be placed over five cities, because he is honored not only for his own progress but also for that of his hearers, whom he called to the light.

And another came, saying: “Lord, behold, your mina, which I kept stored away in a handkerchief. For I was afraid, because you are an austere man: you take up what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.”

The servant who, although commanded to trade, stored the money he had received from the Lord in a handkerchief, represents those who, being suited for preaching, refuse—at the Lord’s command—either to undertake the ministry of preaching through the Church, or at least to carry out worthily what they have undertaken. For to bind up money in a handkerchief is to hide the gifts received in the idleness of sluggish torpor.

There are people who flatter themselves with this perverse reasoning, saying: “It is enough for each person to give an account of himself. Why should anyone preach to others, so that each may also be compelled to give an account of them, when even those are without excuse before the Lord to whom the law was not given and who slept without hearing the Gospel, because through creation they could have recognized the Creator?” This is as though reaping where he did not sow—that is, also holding guilty of impiety those to whom the word of the law or of the Gospel was not ministered.

Avoiding what they regard as this danger of judgment, they rest in sluggish weakness from the ministry of the word; and this is as though binding in a handkerchief what they had received.

He says to him: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.” He is called a wicked servant because he is both idle and sluggish in carrying on the business, and insolent and proud in accusing the Lord’s judgment.

“You knew that I am an austere man, taking up what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow. Why, then, did you not give my money to the table?”

What he had thought he had said in his defense is turned into his own accusation. “If,” he says, “you knew me to be harsh and cruel, pursuing what belonged to others and reaping where I had not sown, why did such a thought not instill fear in you, so that you would know that I would seek my own more carefully, and would give my money, or silver, to the money-changers?” For the Greek word ἀργυρίῳ signifies both “money” and “silver.” “The words of the Lord,” he says, “are pure words, silver tested in the fire” (Psalm XI).

Therefore money and silver signify the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been given to the table—that is, to be impressed upon the ready and prepared hearts of the faithful. To this table, namely, the minds of the hearers, no money other than the Lord’s is to be brought, so that every word of the teacher follows the meaning of Scripture. For the fact that here the Lord says that not just any money, but his own, is to be lent out by the money-changers, the Apostle explains when he says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (I Peter IV).

“And when I came, I would certainly have collected it with interest.” Whoever receives the money of the word from a teacher and purchases it by believing must repay it with interest through action, so that he may carry out in deed what he learned by hearing. For with interest, even money that was not given is received back. Or certainly, he pays interest on the loan of the word he received who, from what he hears, also strives to understand other things that he has not yet learned from the preacher’s mouth.

And he says to those standing by: “Take the mina from him and give it to him who has ten minas.” And they said to him: “Lord, he has ten minas.”

Rightly does he lose the grace bestowed upon him, which he neglected to share by preaching to others, so that it may be increased in the one who labored through it. Accordingly, it is said to the angel of the church at Ephesus: “I will move your lampstand from its place unless you repent” (Revelation II).

And when Saul lost through pride the royal chrism which David obtained through obedience, he says: “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul and was directed to David from that day onward.” But the fact that the mina taken away from the wicked servant was commanded to be given to the one who had ten minas mystically indicates, as I think, that “when the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI), and that then the abundance of spiritual grace which we now suddenly exercise will be conferred upon the teachers of that people.

“But I say to you that to everyone who has, more will be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”

This sentence refers to what was said above, teaching that he too can lose the gift of God who, although he has, does not have—that is, does not use it—and that it is increased in the one who, having, possesses—that is, uses it well.

Since this exchange of graces ordinarily takes place in the present life, it should be noted that the examination of the returning Lord is even now partly carried out, but then will be fulfilled universally. For every day he returns after receiving the kingdom from the Father, because he observes the condition of the Church as it journeys on earth. Every day, among the great number of faithful servants, he lends money to one who will trade with it, examines in another the measure of completed work, bestows the gift of greater grace upon this one who labors faithfully and wisely, and deprives that one who pursues soft sloth and languid leisure in luxury of what he had given.

But when the universal judgment has been revealed—which is terrible even to say—many who seemed fit to teach will, because of the guilt of their negligence, be reckoned among the unlearned. Other brothers, however, simpler and wholly ignorant of the elementary subjects, will nevertheless, because of the devotion of their outstanding conduct, receive the highest rewards among the apostolic teachers. “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew X).

“Nevertheless, bring here my enemies, those who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them in my presence.”

This signifies the impiety of the Jews, or of all the reprobate who refuse to be converted to Christ, to be punished on the day of judgment. The two faithful servants signify the teachers of the two peoples; the ten and five minas, the peoples who believe the same faith; the wicked servant, bad Catholics; the enemies who did not want him to reign over them, the impiety of those who preferred either never to hear the word of faith or to corrupt it by misinterpretation; and the harvesting of the field that was not sown, the judgment of those also who did not happen to hear the word of God. These five persons express every kind of human being who will be present on the day of judgment.

And having said these things, he went before them, ascending toward Jerusalem.

When the parable was finished, he went up to Jerusalem to show that the parable had been prefaced chiefly on account of the fate of that very city, which, not long afterward, would both kill him and perish in a hostile disaster because of its hatred of his kingdom.

And it happened that, when he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples, saying: “Go into the village opposite you.”

Bethphage was a village of the priests on the Mount of Olives. Bethany also was a little village, or town, on the side of the same mountain, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as the evangelist John makes clear; there Lazarus was raised from the dead. The church now built there also points out his tomb.

Bethphage is called “house of the jaw,” and Bethany “house of obedience.” The Savior, as he was about to come to Jerusalem, exalted these places by the favor of his presence, because before his Passion he filled many, through teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and spiritual obedience.

These beautiful cities are described as situated on the Mount of Olives—that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us with the anointing of spiritual gifts and with the light of knowledge and piety. Hence, when elsewhere he said, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew V), he immediately added, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel” (ibid.), because this same Mount of Olives—that is, the supreme distributor of spiritual graces—which raises its city so that it may stand out, also kindles it with the oil of gladness so that it may be able to shine.

And because he did not wish this same light to be placed under a bushel, he sent the disciples into the village opposite them—that is, he arranged for teachers to penetrate by evangelizing the unlearned and barbarous shores of the whole world, as though they were the walls of a village set opposite them. It was right that two were sent, either on account of knowledge of the truth and purity of conduct, or on account of the mystery of the twofold commandment of love—love of God and of neighbor—which was to be preached throughout the whole world.

“When you enter it, you will find a colt of a donkey tied up, on which no human being has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here. And if anyone asks you why you are untying it, say this to him: ‘Because the Lord has need of it.’”

When the preachers entered the world, they found the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of unbelief. Each person was bound with the cords of his sins—not only among the nations but also among the Jews. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans III).

Thus Matthew rightly reports that the donkey also was found tied up with the colt. The donkey, which had been under the yoke and, being tamed, had carried the yoke of the law, signifies the synagogue. The colt of the donkey, wanton and free, represents the people of the nations.

“No human being had ever sat upon it”—that is, none of the rational teachers had ever imposed upon it the bridle of correction, by which it might either restrain its tongue from evil or be compelled to walk along the narrow way of life; nor had anyone, by useful exhortation, bestowed upon it the garments of salvation by which it might be warmed spiritually. A human being would have sat upon it if someone using reason had corrected it by suppressing its folly.

Therefore, not without reason, the two disciples sent to bring the animals to the Lord may be understood, following the example of the preceding parable, as the two orders of preachers: one sent to the nations, the other to the circumcision.

It should also be noted that the three evangelists who wrote in the Greek language mention only the colt; Matthew alone, who composed his Gospel for the Hebrews and in Hebrew speech, reports that the donkey as well was untied and brought to the Lord, to show that the salvation even of that Hebrew people, if it should repent, was not to be despaired of.

“Untie them,” he says, “and bring them here. Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

Those who had been sent went away and found the colt standing, just as he had told them.

Mark writes that the colt was found outside, before the door, at a crossroads. The door is he himself who says: “I am the door of the sheep; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John X).

The colt—that is, the people of the nations—lacked these pastures of life when it still stood tied outside this door, at a crossroads. It was rightly at a crossroads, because it did not hold to one certain way of life and faith, but wandered after the many uncertain paths of sects. Concerning these the text appropriately continues:

As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: “Why are you untying the colt?”

For it had many owners, since it was not devoted to one doctrine and superstition, but, according to the will of unclean spirits, was miserably dragged into various and different errors, proceeding toward mute idols as it was led.

Finally, in a certain vernacular usage of Scripture, what is unclean is called “common,” just as the voice from heaven says to Peter: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts XI). For whoever is holy belongs to God alone and is not common with anyone. But whoever is a sinner and unclean belongs to many. Many demons possess him, and therefore he is called common.

But they said: “Because the Lord desires its works.” And they led it to Jesus.
