Those who had opposed the untying of the colt fell silent when they heard the Lord’s name, because the teachers of error who resisted the teachers coming for the salvation of the nations defended their darkness only until, with miracles bearing witness, the power of the true possessor and lord shone forth. But after the power of the Lord’s faith had appeared, the complaints of the adversaries yielding everywhere, the free company of believers—bearing God in its heart—is brought forward.

And throwing their garments over the colt, they placed Jesus upon it.

The garments of the apostles may be understood either as the doctrine of virtues, the exposition of the Scriptures, or certainly the variety of ecclesiastical doctrines. With these they cover the hearts of human beings, previously naked and cold, so that they may become worthy of Christ as their rider.

As he went along, they spread their garments on the road.

While the donkey carried the Lord, the disciples spread their garments on the road, because, stripping themselves of the covering of their own bodies, they prepare the way for the simpler servants of God with their own blood, so that with the unhindered step of the mind they may walk toward the Jerusalem to which Jesus leads.

For Jesus goes toward Jerusalem sitting upon the colt whenever, governing the soul of any one of the faithful, he leads his own beast toward the vision of deepest peace, or whenever he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

But since, according to the other evangelists, not only the disciples but also many from the crowd spread their garments on the road, these may also signify those who, following the examples of the martyrs, subdue their bodies through abstinence, so that they may prepare a path for the Lord toward the mind or provide good examples for those who follow.

And when he was already drawing near to the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of those descending began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice.

As the Lord descended from the Mount of Olives, the rejoicing and praising crowds themselves also descended together with him, because when the author of mercy voluntarily humbled himself, those who greatly need mercy must imitate, as far as they are able, the traces of his humility.

We must, I say, look upon how Jesus descended from the Mount of Olives—that is, how, although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross—and we too must humble ourselves under his mighty hand, so that we may deserve to be exalted at the time of visitation.

[Col. 0569B] They said this concerning all the mighty works they had seen: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord.”

They had indeed seen many of the Lord’s mighty works, but they were especially astonished at the raising of Lazarus, which had recently taken place. The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead bore witness to it. For both the prophet and the crowd came out to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

It should be noted that the Savior did not now come for the first time from Galilee—that is, he did not first go up to Jerusalem five days before Passover—but that in the previous year, in the seventh month, he had come there for the feast of Tabernacles, as John records. From then onward, for six continuous months—that is, until the day of Passover on which he suffered—he had at times performed signs and taught in Jerusalem, at times ascended the Mount of Olives, at times, expelled from Judea, gone beyond the Jordan, and at times remained with his disciples in the desert city called Ephraim; yet during that period he had never returned to Galilee.

Therefore, concerning all the mighty works they had seen him perform during so long a time, the crowds praised God, saying:

“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest.”

“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord” should rather be understood to mean “in the name of the Lord,” that is, in the name of God the Father, although it may also be understood as in his own name, since he too is Lord. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord.”

But his words direct our understanding better, when he says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V).

For Christ is the teacher of humility, who humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians II). He does not therefore lose his divinity when he teaches us humility.

Christ is not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with iron, or visibly defeat enemies. He is King of Israel because he governs minds, provides for them eternally, and leads believers, hopers, and lovers into the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore the Son of God, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, who willed to be King of Israel, possesses this title by condescension, not promotion; it is a sign of compassion, not an increase of power. He who is called King of the Jews on earth is Lord of the angels in heaven.

But because Christ, in the flesh, shone forth as the propitiation of the whole world, both of human beings and of angels, heaven and earth beautifully join one another in his praise. For at his birth, when the ranks of the heavenly powers sang praise to God, they proclaimed: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” (Luke II). When he was about to triumph over the ruler of the world and soon return to heaven, mortals offer back a corresponding hymn of praise: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.”

And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to him: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”

What astonishing madness on the part of the envious! They do not hesitate to call him Teacher, because they knew that he taught the truth, yet they suppose that his disciples should be reproved by them as though they had been better instructed. They advise him to correct those whom he himself had educated, although they see him revealed as God by the signs that confirm him.

He answered them: “I tell you, if these become silent, the stones will cry out.”

When the Lord was crucified, all his acquaintances stood at a distance. They were afraid to confess as God the one whom they saw fixed to the wood. But while they were silent, stones and rocks proclaimed with a loud cry the King who comes in the name of the Lord.

For he gave up his spirit, and behold, the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened. The one whom human beings, whether through fear or unbelief, trembled to confess, even the hardest elements openly proclaimed as God and Lord of the world.

But in a deeper mystery he sometimes signifies the unbelieving and hard-hearted nations by the name of stones, to whom, after removing their heart of stone, he gave a heart of flesh (Ezekiel XI)—that is, a sensitive and human heart, by which they could believe in, praise, and behold God their Creator.

Therefore, even if the crowds of human beings are silent, the stones will cry out, because blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved (Romans XI).

And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had known.”

Everyone who has read the history of the city’s destruction knows that the overthrow of Jerusalem described here was carried out by Vespasian and Titus, Roman rulers. But we must first inquire what is meant by the words: “Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known.’”

The merciful Redeemer wept over the ruin of the faithless city, which did not know that this ruin was coming. Therefore the weeping Lord rightly says to it: “If you too had known”—understand: you would have wept now, because you do not know what is impending, yet you rejoice.

Hence it continues:

“And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace.”

Because it gave itself over to the pleasures of the flesh and did not foresee the evils that were to come, it possessed in its own day the things that could have been for its peace. Why it possessed present blessings for its peace is made clear when the text continues:

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.”

For if the evils that threatened had not been hidden from the eyes of its heart, it would not have rejoiced in its present prosperity.

The punishment that soon threatened it from the Roman rulers, as I have said, is then added:

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart. And they will surround you and hem you in on every side, and cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you. And they will not leave in you stone upon stone.”

The present migration of that same city also bears witness to this, because, although it is now built in the place outside the gate where the Lord had been crucified, the former Jerusalem was utterly destroyed.

The fault for which the punishment of its destruction was inflicted is then added:

“Because you did not know the time of your visitation.”

The Creator of all things graciously visited it through the mystery of the Incarnation, but it did not remember his fear and love. Hence, through the prophet, the birds of heaven are brought forward as witnesses in rebuke of the human heart: “The kite in heaven knows its time; the turtledove, swallow, and stork have observed the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord” (Jeremiah VIII).

And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling in it and those who were buying, saying to them: “It is written: ‘My house is a house of prayer.’”

The one who had foretold the evils to come and immediately entered the temple in order to drive out from it those who were selling and buying clearly revealed that the ruin of the people arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests. In describing the destruction, yet striking those who sold and bought in the temple, he showed through the very effect of his action from where the root of perdition had sprung.

[Col. 0571C] “But you have made it a den of thieves.”

It was beyond doubt that those who sat in the temple to receive gifts sought injuries against certain people when they did not give. Therefore the house of prayer had been made a den of thieves, because they knew how to remain in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give.

But because our Redeemer does not withhold the words of preaching even from the unworthy and ungrateful, after he had displayed the severity of discipline by driving out the perverse, he immediately showed the gift of grace; for it follows:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

We have passed briefly over these matters according to the historical sense; now let us return to examine the same things in their moral meaning.

“Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known.’”

He did this once when he announced that the city would perish. Our Redeemer never ceases to do this daily through his elect when he sees that some have fallen from a good life into depraved conduct.

He mourns for those who do not know why they are mourned, because, in the words of Solomon, “they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs II). If they had recognized the condemnation that threatens them, they would weep for themselves with tears of repentance over their sins.

“And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace.”

The perverse soul has its own day, in which it rejoices for a passing time. The things that are present are for its peace, because, while it rejoices in temporal goods, while it is exalted by honors, while it dissolves in the will of the flesh, and while it is frightened by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day—a day in which it will have a grave offense of condemnation in another’s day. For there it must be afflicted where the righteous will rejoice.

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.”

The perverse soul, devoted to present things and dissolved in earthly pleasures, hides the evils that follow from itself, because it refuses to foresee the future things that would disturb its present joy. And while it abandons itself to the delight of the present life, what else does it do than go toward the fire with closed eyes?

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.”

Who are ever greater enemies of the human soul than evil spirits? They besiege the soul as it leaves the body, although they nourish it with deceptive pleasures while it remains fixed in the love of the flesh.

They surround it with a rampart because, bringing back before the eyes of its mind the iniquities it committed, they hem it in while dragging it into fellowship with their own condemnation.

“And they will surround you and hem you in on every side.”

Evil spirits hem the soul in on every side when they recall to it not only the iniquities of its deeds but also those of its speech and, beyond these, of its thoughts, so that the soul which previously spread itself widely through many crimes is finally constricted by all of them in retribution.

“And they will cast you and your children who are within you down to the ground.”

Then the soul is cast down to the ground through knowledge of its guilt, when the flesh which it believed to be its life is compelled to return to dust. Then its children fall in death, when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the final punishment of life, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.”

These hard thoughts may also be understood through the symbolism of stones. For it follows:

“And they will not leave in you stone upon stone.”

When the perverse mind adds further perversity to a perverse thought, what else does it do than place stone upon stone? But in the destroyed city no stone is left upon stone, because when the soul is led to its punishment, every structure of its thoughts is scattered.

“Because you did not know the time of your visitation.”

Almighty God is also accustomed to visit the perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually through a commandment, sometimes through a scourge, sometimes through a miracle, so that it may hear truths of which it was ignorant and, although still proud and contemptuous, may either return, pierced by pain, or, overcome by benefits, blush for the evil it has done.

But because it does not recognize the time of its visitation, in the end it is handed over to those enemies with whom it is joined in the fellowship of its condemnation at the eternal judgment.

“And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling in it and those who were buying.”

Just as the temple is in the city, so the life of religious people is in the faithful community. Often some take up the habit of religion, but when they obtain a place among the sacred orders, they turn the office of holy religion into a commerce of earthly business.

Those who sell in the temple are those who bestow upon certain people what rightly belongs to a reward. For to sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward.

Those who buy in the temple are those who refuse to pay their neighbor what is just; while they disdain to do what is rightly owed, they purchase sin by giving a reward to their patrons.

To them it is rightly said: “My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves.” For when perverse people sometimes occupy a place of religion, they kill there with the swords of their wickedness where they ought to have given life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer.

The temple and house of God is also the very mind and conscience of the faithful. If it brings forth perverse thoughts that harm its neighbor, thieves sit there as in a den and kill those who walk innocently, when they drive into people who are guilty of nothing the swords of injury.

The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of thieves when, abandoning innocence and the simplicity of holiness, it attempts to do what may enable it to harm its neighbors.

But because we are constantly instructed against all these perversions by the words of our Redeemer throughout the sacred pages, what is now being done corresponds to what is said to have been done:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

For when he subtly teaches the minds of the faithful to avoid evils, Truth teaches daily in the temple.

The chief priests, the scribes, and the leaders of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they could not find what they should do to him.

Whether because he taught daily in the temple, because he had driven the thieves out of the temple, or because, coming as King and Lord, he received the praise of a heavenly hymn from so great a crowd of believers, the envious leaders sought to destroy him.

For all the people were hanging upon his words as they listened to him.

This can be understood in two ways: either they could not find what to do to Jesus, whom they had decided to destroy, because they feared an uprising of the people; or they sought to destroy Jesus because, neglecting their own teaching, they saw many flocking to hear him.

Meanwhile, it is pleasing to consider briefly how beautifully the legal shadow of Passover corresponds, both in its mystery and in its timing, to our Passover, in which Christ was sacrificed.

“On the tenth day,” he says, “of the first month, each person shall take a lamb for the household of his house. According to this ordinance you shall also take a kid, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month” (Exodus XII).

On the tenth day of the first month—that is, five days before Passover, as the evangelist John testifies—the whole people, going out to the Mount of Olives, took the Lord from there.

He is the lamb because he came to take away sins, and there is no sin in him; he is the kid because he was accused as a sinner.

They brought the lamb into the house, those who joyfully sang: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord.” They brought the kid, those who, in opposition and jealousy, said: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”

The whole people who hung upon his words as they listened to him were the lamb; the leaders who wanted to destroy him were the kid.

For five days before Passover, that is, from the tenth day of the moon until the fourteenth, they kept the lamb or kid that they were going to sacrifice. Although even then they thirsted for his blood, no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

They kept the lamb, those who willingly listened to his words; they kept the kid, those who lay in wait and sought to seize something from his mouth in order to accuse him.

But when the fourteenth day was complete—that is, when it had declined toward evening—after he had entrusted to his disciples the sacraments of his body and blood, which they were to celebrate, those who came to seize and bind him arrived, and what follows began to be fulfilled: “And the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice him at evening” (Exodus XII).

For not only the impious, who mocked his death, but also the holy, who mourned, stood near the cross of Jesus.

We have touched briefly upon these matters so that we might remind the reader that everything which follows from this point until the Passion of the Lord belongs figuratively to the lamb kept in the house and prepared for slaughter.

## CHAPTER XX

And it happened that, on one of the days when he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the Gospel, the chief priests and scribes came with the elders and said to him: “Tell us, by what authority are you doing these things?”

In various ways they construct the same accusation as before, when they said: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke XI). For when they say, “By what authority are you doing these things?” they doubt the authority of God and wish it to be understood that what he does belongs to the devil.

They add:

“Or who is it that gave you this authority?”

They most clearly deny that he is the Son of God, believing that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another.

But he answered and said to them: “I will also ask you one question. Answer me: Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men?”

The Lord could have refuted the accusation of those who were tempting him with an open answer, but he wisely questions them so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their own judgment.

But they reasoned among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say: ‘Why, then, did you not believe him?’”

The one whom they confess to have received his prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and you heard from him, therefore, by what authority I do these things.

“But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us.”

For they are certain that John is a prophet. They saw, therefore, that whichever of these they answered, they would fall into a snare. They feared being stoned, but they feared the confession of the truth even more.

And they answered that they did not know where it was from.

And Jesus said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

“I do not tell you what I know, because you do not wish to confess what you know.” Justly rejected, they withdrew in confusion, and what God the Father says through the prophet in the psalm was fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm CXXXI)—that is, John—“I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (ibid.).

It should be noted that, above all, knowledge of the truth is hidden from those who seek it for two reasons: when the one who asks is either less capable of understanding what he seeks, or is unworthy, through hatred or contempt of the truth itself, to have what he seeks revealed to him.

For the first reason the Lord says: “I have still many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI). For the other he commands his disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matthew VII).

He began to speak to the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and went abroad for a long time.” While the Lord was teaching the people and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and scribes came together with the elders and questioned him, testing him as to by what authority he performed signs. Having overcome them by his skill, the Lord carries out what he had begun. Indeed, while they were listening, he addresses the people all the more because they listened to his words more willingly. He introduces a parable by which he both reproves them for their impiety and teaches that the kingdom of God was to be transferred to the Gentiles.

The man, then, who planted the vineyard is the same one who, according to another parable, hired laborers for his vineyard (Matt. XX). “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). The tenants are the same as the laborers who are said to have been hired to cultivate the vineyard at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours. He went abroad—not by a change of place. For where can God be absent, who says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII), and elsewhere, “I am God who is near, and not far away,” says the Lord? But he is said to depart from the vineyard so that he might leave the cultivators free discretion to work. The same idea appears when, after leasing the vineyard to tenants, he says through Isaiah: “I waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” [Col. 0575C] (Isa. V).

And at the proper time he sent a servant to the cultivators, so that they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But after beating him, they sent him away empty-handed. He rightly says “the time of fruits,” not “of produce.” For no fruit arose from the Jews; no produce of this vineyard was found, although it was sought frequently and earnestly. The servant who was sent first is understood to be Moses the lawgiver, who for forty continuous years sought from the cultivators some fruit of the law he had given; but after beating him, they sent him away empty-handed. For they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. Moses was wearied because of them, because they embittered his spirit. This servant himself also openly declares in a song what he thinks of the fruit of the vineyard, saying: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is bitter to them. Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps” (Deut. XXXII).

And he added that he would send another servant. But after beating and insulting this one also, they sent him away empty-handed. The second servant signifies David, the prophet and king. He was sent after Moses so that, after the legal decrees, he might rouse the cultivators of the vineyard to the practice of good works through the melody of psalmody and the sweetness of the harp. David himself, in order to lift the heart of the people toward heavenly things, established that the Lord’s praises should be sung continually in pleasing melody amid the rites of the fleshly sacrifices. But after insulting him also, they sent him away empty-handed. For they said, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (1 Kings XII). They changed both David’s kingdom, through an ignoble lineage, and religion, through impiety. Nevertheless, on behalf of this vineyard—which, transplanted from Egypt, covered the mountains of Palestine with its shade—he pleads that it not be utterly destroyed: “Lord God of hosts, turn now; look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vineyard, and direct it, which your right hand planted” (Ps. LXXIX). Here he likewise explains who the man is who planted this vineyard: namely, the Lord, the God of hosts.

And he added that he would send a third, and after wounding him they cast him out. Understand the third servant as the chorus of the prophets, who repeatedly warned the people and foretold the evils that threatened this vineyard. But which of the prophets did they not persecute? “And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One” (Acts VII). These men also said much about the barrenness of this vineyard, but it is enough to cite the lament of one—Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed. How then have you been turned into bitterness, a foreign vine?” (Jer. II). To protect this vineyard—lest a vegetable crop of frail, feeble, and swiftly perishing sweetness should grow in it or for it—Naboth the Jezreelite was not merely wounded but, as we read, also killed. Even if we do not accept any prophetic saying from him, his deed was nevertheless prophetic, because by his own blood he prophesied that many martyrs would arise for this vineyard. That all teachers under the law can be included in these three ranks of servants, the Lord himself clearly reveals elsewhere, saying: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

But the lord of the vineyard said, “What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. Perhaps, when they see him, they will be afraid.” The fact that the lord of the vineyard is said to speak doubtfully, not deliberatively, does not arise from ignorance. For what could the lord of the vineyard—which here means God the Father—not know? Rather, God is always said to doubt so that human free will may be preserved. When the tenants saw him, they reasoned among themselves, saying, “This is the heir; let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.” The Lord most clearly proves that the leaders of the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy [Col. 0576D]. For they understood that he was the one to whom it had been said, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). Therefore, as though consulting among themselves, they said, “Behold, the whole world has gone after him, and if we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him” (John XII). The Son’s inheritance, then, is the Church, given to him from all the nations. The Father did not leave it to him when he died; rather, he wondrously acquired it through his own death, because by rising again he took possession of it. After killing him, the wicked tenants tried to seize it, since the Jews, by crucifying him, attempted to extinguish the faith that comes through him, to prefer their own righteousness, which comes from the law, and to implant it in the nations being instructed.

And they cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. The heir of the vineyard is slaughtered outside the vineyard because Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his blood. Or he was cast out of the vineyard and killed because he was first rejected from the hearts of unbelievers and then condemned to the cross. As a figure of this, Moses placed the altar of burnt offering, on which the blood of the victims was poured, not inside the tabernacle but at its entrance, mystically teaching that the altar of the Lord’s cross was likewise to be placed outside the gate of Jerusalem, and that Christ himself, the true offering of the Father, was not to be received in the innermost heart by the house of the Jews, which he had approached in order to sanctify it, but was to be stained outside with his own blood.

But when Mark says, with the order changed, “They seized him, killed him, and cast him out of the vineyard” (Mark XII), he indicates their obstinacy: even after the Lord had been crucified and raised from the dead, they refused to believe the apostles who preached him, but threw him away like a worthless corpse. For, insofar as it lay with them, they excluded him from their own borders and gave him to the Gentiles to receive.

“What, then, will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy these tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said to him, “May it never be!” They contradicted the Lord’s judgment because they recognized that it was directed against their own faithlessness. They understood the parable—not because they were already prepared by holiness to grasp the words of the mystery, but because they were inflamed by the fires of malice to carry out what was being said—and therefore were prepared to recognize what they had been contemplating for a long time, even though it was spoken in parables. Since the Jews denied that it would be just for the knowledge of the divine law, which they themselves despised, to be transferred to the Gentiles, observe what the Savior replied.

[Col. 0577C] But he looked at them and said, “What, then, is the meaning of what is written: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?” How, he says, will this prophecy be fulfilled, which says that the stone rejected by the builders is to be placed as the cornerstone, unless it is because Christ, rejected and killed by you, is to be preached to the Gentiles who will believe? Thus, as a cornerstone joining the two in himself, he might build for himself from both peoples one city of the faithful, one temple. The teachers of the Synagogue, whom he had previously called tenants, he now calls builders, because those who had been commanded to cultivate the people subject to them, as a vineyard, so that it might bear the fruits of life, were themselves commanded to construct and adorn it as a house worthy of God as its inhabitant. Hence the Apostle also writes to the faithful: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. III). But those who, as wicked cultivators, refused the fruit of God’s vineyard were the same who, as wicked masons, attempted to remove from God’s house the chosen, precious stone that was to be placed either in its foundations or at its corner—that is, they tried to rob their hearers of faith in Christ. Yet despite their unwillingness, that same stone was made the head of the corner, because he joined together in his faith as many as he wished from both peoples.

“Everyone who falls upon that stone will be shattered. But upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” It is one thing to stumble against Christ through evil works, another to deny him through impiety. Whoever is a sinner and yet believes in him falls upon the stone and is shattered, but is not utterly crushed, for he is preserved through wisdom for salvation. But upon whomever it falls—that is, upon whom the stone itself rushes—and whoever completely denies Christ, it will crush him, so that not even a fragment remains from which a little water might be drawn. Or he says this about those who fall upon him because they now despise him or inflict insults upon him. They do not yet perish utterly, but they are nevertheless shattered, so that they do not walk uprightly. But upon those over whom it falls, it will come from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction. Therefore he said that it would crush them, so that the ungodly might be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. I).

The chief priests and scribes sought at that hour to lay hands on him, but they feared the people. For they understood that he had spoken this parable against them. The chief priests and scribes sought to kill the Lord as though he were lying against them, but by seeking to do this they were themselves proving that what he said was true. He is indeed the heir whose unjust death he said must be avenged; they are the wicked tenants who were held back from killing the Son of God for a little while by human fear, until his hour came, but could never be restrained by divine love.

In a moral interpretation, whenever the mystery of baptism, to be exercised through works, is entrusted to any believer, it is as though a vineyard to cultivate is leased to him. One servant is sent, then another and a third, to receive fruit, when the Law, psalmody, and prophecy are read and their admonitions are followed through good conduct. But the servant sent is insulted or beaten and cast out when the word heard is either despised or, worse still, blasphemed. He kills the heir sent, insofar as it lies with him, who tramples on the Son of God and insults the Spirit of grace by whom he was sanctified. When the wicked cultivator is destroyed, the vineyard will be given to another, when a humble person is enriched with the gift of grace that the proud person despised.

What is also meant by the fact that the chief priests and scribes, seeking to lay hands on Jesus, are restrained by fear of the people occurs daily in the Church. Anyone who bears the name “brother” alone, yet does not love the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace, is ashamed or afraid to attack it because of the multitude of good brothers living alongside him. Yet, as the Lord says concerning the most foolish of birds, the ostrich, when the time comes he will raise his wings on high, because in persecuting the Church he will rejoice to hand the Lord over to the cross and to have him as a spectacle.

And watching him closely, they sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in his words and hand him over to the authority and power of the governor. The chief priests and scribes, seeking to arrest the Lord, feared the people. Therefore they tried to accomplish through the governor’s hands what they could not do themselves, so that they might appear to be free from responsibility for his death. For recently, under Caesar Augustus, when the census was celebrated throughout the whole world, Judea had been subjected to the Romans and made tributary. There was a great dissension among the people: some said that taxes ought to be paid for the sake of security and peace, since the Romans served as soldiers on behalf of everyone; but the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for their righteousness, opposed this, insisting that the people of God, who paid tithes, offered firstfruits, and observed the other things written in the law, ought not to be subject to human laws. The fire of this dissension grew so strong that after the Lord’s passion, when the Romans pressed them, they preferred to lose their country, nation, and kingdom, that famous temple with its religion—even the very light—rather than pay taxes.

And they questioned him, saying, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and do not show partiality, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” This flattering and fraudulent question was designed to provoke the respondent to fear God more than Caesar and to say that tribute ought not to be paid, so that the governor’s officers, who according to the other evangelists are said to have been present, might immediately arrest him as a leader of sedition against the Romans.

[Col. 0579B] But considering their deceit, he said to them, “Why are you testing me? Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?” Wisdom always acts wisely, so that those who test it may be refuted especially by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “a denarius.” This was a kind of coin reckoned as ten coins and bearing Caesar’s image. Those who think that the Savior’s question expressed ignorance rather than providential arrangement should learn from this passage that Jesus could certainly have known whose image was on the coin. But he asks in order to respond appropriately to their words.

They answered, “Caesar’s.” And he said to them, “Then give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” We should understand “Caesar” not as Augustus, but as his stepson Tiberius [Col. 0579C], who succeeded his stepfather and under whom the Lord also suffered. All the Roman kings, from the first Gaius Caesar, who seized imperial power, were called Caesars. When he says, “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” let us understand the coin, tribute, and money; and “the things that are God’s” as tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and sacrifices. In this way he himself pays tribute for himself and Peter, while giving to God the things that are God’s by doing the Father’s will.

Alternatively: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Just as Caesar demands from you the imprint of his image, so God demands it also, so that just as the coin is returned to Caesar, the soul, illuminated and stamped by the light of his countenance, may be returned to God. Hence the Psalmist says, “The light of your countenance has been stamped upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). This light is the whole of the human being and the true good, which is perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. He said “stamped upon us,” as a denarius is stamped with the king’s image. For the human being was made in the image and likeness of God, which he corrupted by sinning. His true and eternal good, therefore, is to be stamped anew through rebirth.

And they could not find fault with his word in the presence of the people; and, astonished at his answers, they kept silent. Those who ought to have believed because of such great wisdom were astonished that their cunning attempt at plotting had found no opening.

Some Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, then approached. There were two sects among the Jews, one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *deuterosis* (“second tradition”). Hence they were also called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “just,” claimed this title for themselves even though they were not just. Whereas the former believed in the resurrection of both body and soul and confessed angels and spirits, the latter, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, denied everything.

And they questioned him, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if someone’s brother dies, having a wife but being without children, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.” Observe the difference between letter and spirit. According to the letter, the living brother is compelled to marry so that he may raise up the dead man’s offspring; but the spirit is a teacher of chastity.

Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died without children [Col. 0580B]. The next took her, and he too died without a child. And the third took her. Likewise all seven; they left no offspring and died. Last of all the woman also died. Those who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies, judging that the soul perished with the body, rightly invent a story of this kind, which would expose as madness those who assert the resurrection of the dead. It may, however, be that something of this sort really happened among their people at some time.

“In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.” They oppose the shamefulness of the story in order to deny the truth of the resurrection. Mystically, however, these seven brothers who died without children correspond to all the reprobate, who throughout the whole course of this age—which revolves through seven days—remain barren of good works. When they have been taken away one by one by wretched death, worldly existence itself, which they passed without living works, will at last pass away like an infertile wife.

And Jesus said to them, “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage.” Although the Lord says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs” (Matt. VII), whenever he is found here to have spoken something about the glory of the resurrection, or elsewhere about the mystery of his dispensation or even of his divinity—things which many who were present did not receive, either by resisting or despising them—he should not be thought to have given what is holy to dogs or thrown pearls before pigs. For he did not give these things to those who were unable to receive them; yet they ought not to have been neglected because of the uncleanness of others. Indeed, when those who tested him questioned him, he answered them in such a way that they had nothing to contradict. Although they were wasting away in their poisons rather than being nourished by his food, others who were able to receive it heard many useful things because of the occasion provided by them.

But those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. This should not be understood as though only the worthy will either rise or live without marriage, while the unworthy—that is, sinners—are to be believed either not to rise at all or to rise for marriage. Rather, we should understand it in this way: everyone will rise, and everyone will remain in that age without marriage. But the Lord and Savior, in order to stir minds to seek the glory of the resurrection, wished to speak only about the elect.

If, then, in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, bodies capable of marrying and being given in marriage do rise—that is, the distinct members of women and men, differentiated according to their kinds—but they are not enslaved to any pleasure or necessity of intercourse. For no one says of a stone or a tree, or of those things that do not possess genital members, that they neither marry nor are given in marriage. Rather, this is said of those who, although they are able to marry, nevertheless do not marry for another reason.

For they can no longer die. Marriage exists for the sake of children; children for the sake of succession; succession because of death. Where, therefore, there is no death, there is no marriage.

For they are equal to the angels and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection. Those who are equal to the angels and are children of God, renewed in the glory of the resurrection, enjoy the perpetual vision of God without any fear of death, without any stain of corruption, and without any activity belonging to an earthly condition. Whoever desires then to rise to equality with the angelic dignity must now stoop to the least of his brothers.

But that the dead rise, Moses also showed at the bush, when he says that the Lord is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. To prove the truth of the resurrection, he could have used many other, clearer examples, including this one: “The dead will be raised, and those who are in the tombs will rise.” The question therefore arises as to what the Lord intended by presenting this testimony, which seems ambiguous or not sufficiently related to the truth of the resurrection. But the Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses and rejected the prophetic predictions. It would therefore have been foolish to bring forward testimonies whose authority they did not follow. To prove, moreover, the immortality of souls, he cites from Moses the example: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III). He immediately adds:

“God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” Since he thereby proved that souls remain after death—which they denied among other things—for it could not be that he was the God of those who in no way continued to exist, it follows that the resurrection of bodies, which did good or evil together with the souls, should also be introduced.

“For all live to him.” Clearly, all those whose God the Lord is live to him with the true life by which the righteous live even when they die in body. Concerning this the Lord says elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John XI). Believe, then, and even if you have died, you will live. But if you do not believe, you are dead even while you live. “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. V).

Some of the scribes answered and said, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” And they no longer dared to ask him anything. The chief priests, Sadducees, and scribes, seeking an opportunity for accusation and trying to find some word that could be exposed to attack, had been refuted in their arguments and therefore no longer questioned him. Instead, they openly handed him over to the Roman authorities. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but are slow to subside.

But he said to them, “How do they say that the Christ is the Son of David, while David himself says in the Book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’? David therefore calls him Lord; so how is he his son?” Jesus’ question remains useful to us even today against the Jews. For those among them who confess that the Christ is to come assert that he is a simple human being, a holy man descended from David. Let us therefore question them, instructed by the Lord: if he is a mere man and only David’s son, how does David call him his Lord? They are not reproved because they call him David’s son, but because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. For he is both Lord of David, remaining God before the ages, and appeared as David’s son, becoming human at the end of the ages. The fact that the enemies are subjected by the Father signifies not the Son’s weakness, but the unity of nature by which one acts in the other. For the Son also subjects the enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father upon the earth.

While all the people were listening, he said to his disciples, “Beware of the scribes, who wish to walk about in long robes, love greetings in the marketplace, the first seats in the synagogues, and the first places at banquets.” To walk about in long robes means to go out in public dressed in more elegant clothing. In this regard, the rich man who feasted splendidly every day is described as having sinned, among other things (Luke XVI). It should be noted that he does not forbid those to be greeted in the marketplace or to sit or recline in the first places to whom these things belong by the order of their office. Rather, he teaches the faithful to avoid as reprobate those who love such things improperly, whether they possess them or do not possess them, censuring the mind—not the rank—with just severity. Yet even this is not free from fault if the same men who desire to be called teachers of the Synagogue in the chair of Moses wish to be involved in lawsuits in the marketplace.

We are rightly commanded to beware of those who desire empty glory for two reasons: so that we may not be led astray by their hypocrisy, judging the things they do to be good, or be inflamed by rivalry, rejoicing vainly in the good things for which they pretend to be praised.

“They devour widows’ houses while making a show of lengthy prayer; they will receive a greater condemnation.” He does not merely say, “They will receive condemnation,” but adds “greater,” indicating that even those who pray standing in the corners so as to be seen by people (Matt. VI) deserve condemnation, but that those who perform these acts at greater length, as though they were more religious, seeking not only praise from people but also money, are to be punished with a more extensive condemnation. There are those who pretend to be righteous and highly meritorious before God and do not hesitate to accept money from the weak and from people troubled by the consciousness of their sins, as though they were going to be their patrons in judgment. And although an outstretched hand normally assists the poor with prayers, these men spend the night in prayer chiefly for the purpose of taking money from the poor. The curse of Judas rightly applies to them: “When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII). For the condemned man goes out when he is judged, and he turns his prayer into sin when, having been esteemed highly among people, he discovers in the divine examination that he cannot merely intercede for others, but cannot even rely on his own merits; indeed, he pays the penalty among his crimes for the very prayers by which he deceived human judgment.

## CHAPTER XXI

And looking up, he saw the rich putting their offerings into the treasury. Since in Greek φυλάσσειν means “to preserve,” and *gaza* in the Persian language means “riches,” the place where riches are kept is commonly called a *gazophylacium*, or treasury. It was a chest with an opening at the top, placed beside the altar on the right as one entered the house of the Lord. Into it the priests who guarded the doors deposited all the money brought to the temple of the Lord for the temple’s upkeep. Read the Book of Chronicles. Even now, whoever goes about the house of the Lord praying also looks upon those who bring gifts, praising the one whom he judges worthy and condemning the one whom he judges reprobate.

He also saw a certain poor widow putting in two small coins, and he said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others.” This passage teaches us morally how acceptable to God is whatever we offer with a good intention. For he weighs the heart, not the substance; he does not consider how much is present in the sacrifices, but from how much it is offered.

According to the laws of allegory, however, the rich who were putting offerings into the treasury signify the Jews lifted up by confidence in the righteousness of the law, while the poor widow signifies the simplicity of the Church. She is rightly called poor, because she has cast away either the spirit of pride or sins, as though they were the riches of the world. She is a widow because her husband suffered death for her and is now hidden from her eyes in the inner chambers of heaven, living as though in another region.

She puts two small coins into the treasury because she brings before the sight of the divine Majesty—where the offerings of our works are preserved as though recorded and sealed by a definite number—either the gifts of love of God and neighbor or the offerings of her faith and prayer. These are small when considered in light of her own weakness, but because of the merit of devoted piety they surpass all the works of the proud Jews.

“For all these put into the offerings of God from their abundance. But she, from what she lacks, put in all the living she had.” The Jew puts into God’s offerings from his abundance when, trusting in his own righteousness, he prays within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, and so forth” (Luke XVIII). But the Church puts all her living into God’s offerings, understanding that everything by which she lives is not the gift of her own merit but the gift of God, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I will keep my strength toward you, because you, God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me” [Col. 0584C] (Ps. LVIII).

## BOOK SIX. READ WITH GOOD FORTUNE

[Col. 0583]

[Col. 0583C] When Solomon, the wisest of kings, was building a temple for the Lord as a figure of Christ and the Church, among other things he also foreshadowed by fitting examples that, when the truth and light of those things which were then symbolically signified should finally arrive and appear, that whole shadowy—or, so to speak, imaginary—arrangement of types would immediately have to be entirely removed.

After constructing a house of incomparable workmanship from stone, wood, and gold, he sent for and, as a figure of the people from the Gentiles who would believe, brought Hiram of Tyre, the son of a widow (1 Kings VII)—clearly the son of the woman who, by putting two coins into the treasury, is praised as having put in more than all the others. “From the tribe of Naphtali,” he says, “with a Tyrian father, a craftsman in bronze, and full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge” (ibid.).

All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of brass. The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in clayey ground. For although he made all his vessels not by hammering but by casting, he first formed a clay model in the likeness of each vessel—a model necessary until the work of the vessel was completed, but afterward not only useless for any purpose, but also, so that the finished vessel might appear, certainly to be broken without hesitation.

Thus, as it were, forms made of clay precede the legal ceremonies, so that the vessels of evangelical truth, as though made of brass, might succeed them. The temporarily fashioned worthless clay vessel is worn away so that the splendor of the lasting ornament hidden within it may be revealed. The ashes of the heifer, which sanctified the unclean, are removed, and the cross of Christ, which redeems the world, is proclaimed.

As the time approaches when the bronze sea, whose life-giving water baptizes all who are to enter the Church; when the two pillars of the law, bearing lilies upon their capitals and securing on either side the entrance of the sheep devoted to Christ; when the ten lavers prepared for washing the victims; and, finally, when countless thousands of vessels of election are to be carried up to the mountain of the temple—all these things appear, the clayey ground that for so long concealed them in the plain is dissolved. That is, as the proclamation of the Lord’s passion approaches, through which the mysteries of the Church long hidden beneath the veil of the letter would be disclosed, that shadow which concealed the heavenly secrets gradually totters and begins to be destroyed [Col. 0585A].

Therefore, rightly after the offering of the poor widow—that is, after the faith of the Church had been praised by the Lord’s mouth—the Evangelist continues:

And when some were speaking about the temple, that it was adorned with beautiful stones and offerings, he said, “The days will come when not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.” Previously Jerusalem was that great royal city in which a most famous temple had been built for God. But after the one who was the true temple of God came and began to disclose the mysteries of the heavenly Jerusalem, that earthly city was destroyed, in which the heavenly one had appeared, and not one stone was left upon another in that temple.

Previously there was a high priest who purified the people with the blood of bulls and goats. But when the true High Priest came, who would purify believers with his own blood (Heb. XIII), that former priest was nowhere to be found, and no place was left for him. Previously there was an altar, and sacrifices were celebrated; but when the true Lamb came, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God (Heb. IX), all those things, established for a time, came to an end.

The divine dispensation therefore arranged that the city itself, the temple, and all those things should likewise be overthrown, lest someone who was still perhaps a child and nursing in the faith, seeing them remain, should be dazzled by the spectacle of their various forms while staring in astonishment at the rite of the sacrifices and the order of the ministries. But God, taking account of our weakness and wishing his Church to multiply, caused all those things to be overthrown and entirely removed, so that, once they had ceased without any hesitation, we might believe that these things are the true realities of which those former things had preceded as types.

They questioned him, saying, “Teacher, when will these things be? And what sign will there be when they are about to happen?” Because the Lord had openly answered those who praised the temple’s buildings that all these things would be destroyed, the disciples, while he was sitting privately on the Mount of Olives—as Matthew and Mark testify—asked about the time and signs of the destruction foretold.

He said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and ‘The time has drawn near.’ Do not go after them.” As the destruction of Jerusalem approached, many leaders arose who claimed to be christs and reported that the time of freedom was already at hand. In the Church itself, even during the times of the apostles, many leaders of heresies appeared who, among many other things contrary to the truth, proclaimed that the day of the Lord was imminent. The Apostle condemns them in his Epistle to the Thessalonians.

Many Antichrists came in the name of Christ. The first of these was Simon Magus, whom, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, everyone in Samaria obeyed, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God which is called Great” (Acts VIII), because for a long time he had driven them mad with his magic arts.

When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be terrified. These things must happen first, but the end will not come immediately. [Col. 0586A] “Wars” refers to enemies; “rebellions,” to fellow citizens. It is abundantly clear that both were rife among the Jewish people from the time of the Lord’s Passion onward—among that people which had chosen a rebellious robber in place of the Savior. Yet the apostles are warned not to be terrified when these things precede the end, and not to abandon Jerusalem and Judea. For the end was not to come immediately; rather, it was to be postponed for forty years, that is, until the desolation of the nation and the final destruction of the city and Temple.

Then he said to them: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines.” It is evident that these things literally occurred before the end of the Temple’s desolation, that is, during the Jewish revolt. But “kingdom against kingdom” may also be understood of the heretics, together with their pestilence—those whose “word spreads like gangrene” (2 Tim. 2)—and the famine of hearing the word of God (Amos 8), the shaking of the whole earth, and separation from the true faith. By fighting against one another, they bring victory to the Church.

“And there will be terrors from heaven and great signs.” Whoever reads Josephus’s history will find that these too were fulfilled at the same time. For, as he reports, a star resembling a sword hung above Jerusalem for an entire year and terrified the trembling citizens with its ill-omened portent. Chariots likewise, and armed horsemen, were seen rushing through the air and imitating the behavior of combatants for forty days. Moreover, a heifer brought to the sacrifices gave birth to a lamb among the hands of those performing the sacrifice. Why these events rightly occurred is immediately added, when it says:

[Col. 0586C] “But before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons, dragging you before kings and governors on account of my name.” This had been either the sole or the chief cause of the Jewish people’s destruction: after the killing of the Lord and Savior, they also persecuted the heralds and confessors of his name with impious cruelty.

“This will happen to you as an opportunity for testimony.” Testimony, clearly, of whom, if not of those who either inflict death by persecuting or fail to imitate the persecuted when they see them? The death of the righteous is a help to the good and a testimony against the wicked, so that the perverse perish without excuse through the very means by which the elect receive an example that enables them to live. Yet, after hearing of so many terrors, the hearts of the weak could be troubled; therefore consolation is added, as it immediately continues:

“Settle it therefore in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.” It is as though he were saying openly to his weakened members: “Do not be terrified; do not be afraid. You are approaching the contest, but I am the one who fights. You utter words, but I am the one who speaks.”

“But you will be handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name.” Evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain; but the torments we suffer from those whose affection we had relied upon wound us more deeply, because, along with the damage to the body, the loss of love also tortures us. Yet, because the things foretold concerning the affliction of death are severe, consolation concerning the joy of resurrection immediately follows:

“And not a hair of your head will perish.” We know that cut flesh hurts, whereas a cut hair does not hurt. He therefore says to his martyrs: “Not a hair of your head will perish,” plainly saying: “Why are you afraid that what hurts when cut may perish, when even that which does not hurt when cut cannot perish in you?” Alternatively: Not a hair of the heads of the Lord’s disciples will perish, because not only the brave deeds and words of the saints, of whom it is said, “The Lord keeps all their bones” (Ps. 33), but also the fleeting—as I may say—subtlest surface of the faithful’s thoughts, which emerges from the hidden root of the heart, as hair from the brain, will be preserved by the righteous Judge and rewarded with a worthy recompense.

Hence the Prophet rightly demonstrates how acceptable to the Lord are even the merits of good thoughts: “And the remnants of their thoughts will keep festival for you” (Ps. 75). For this reason, too, the Nazirite men in the Law are commanded to grow their hair during the time of consecration, and it is reported that no razor came upon Samuel’s head. Conversely, a captive woman, if she is to marry an Israelite man, and a person cleansed from leprosy, if he is to be worthy of communion with the Church, are commanded to shave all the hair of their bodies. For every thought of the wise that is good, pleasing, and perfect is saved forever, and its reward is with the Lord. But the thought of fools and wicked people, like a root unworthy of God’s sight, must be cut off through repentance.

“And by your endurance you will possess your souls.” Possession of the soul is assigned to the virtue of endurance because endurance is the root and guardian of all the virtues. Through endurance we possess our souls, because, when we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess precisely what we are. For we have been wonderfully constituted so that reason possesses the soul, and the soul possesses the body. But the soul’s right to possess the body is driven away if the soul is not first possessed by reason. The Lord therefore showed endurance to be the guardian of our condition, since through it he taught us to possess ourselves. True endurance is to bear the evils of others with equanimity and not to be moved by pain even against the person who inflicts the evil. For one who bears his neighbor’s wrongdoing in such a way that he nevertheless suffers silently and looks for the time of a fitting retribution does not practice endurance, but merely makes a display of it.

“When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near.” Up to this point the Lord has explained what would happen during the forty years before the end arrived; from here he sets forth, in his own words, the end of the desolation brought about by the Roman army.

“Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” Ecclesiastical history relates that, when the destruction of Jerusalem was imminent, all the Christians who were in Judea were warned by the Lord to depart from that place and live beyond the Jordan in a certain city called Pella until the desolation of Judea was completed.

“And let those who are in its midst depart; and let those who are in the regions not enter it. For these are days of vengeance, so that all things written may be fulfilled.” This seems to belong to a fitting warning: those who are outside should not enter it, but how could those who were within it depart once the city had already been surrounded by the army? Unless perhaps we say that the earlier statement, “Then let those who are in Judea flee”—that is, “then”—refers not to the time of the siege itself, but to the period immediately preceding the siege, when the Roman soldier first began to spread through the regions of Galilee and Samaria. Thus each person would hasten to flee while there was still time for flight. “These are days of vengeance,” namely, days demanding vengeance for the Lord’s blood.

“But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days.” Woe, in the presence of captivity, to pregnant women and nursing mothers, as some interpret it. The burden of their wombs or their arms, weighed down by their children, greatly impedes the necessity of flight. Read also the history of the Kings, where Jonathan’s wife, attempting to avoid the evil of captivity by a hasty flight, received her fallen son in her lap, leaving him permanently lame.

“For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.” This distress and wrath cling as an inseparable companion to that people, scattered among all nations even to this day; yet we must not believe that they will cling to it forever. For after the Lord has shown the course of that distress or wrath, saying:

[Col. 0588C] “And they will fall by the edge of the sword, and will be led captive among all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations,” he immediately added, in accordance with the prophecy that sings, “In wrath remember mercy”:

“Until the times of the nations are fulfilled.” The “times of the nations” are those which the Apostle mentions when he says: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved” (Rom. 11). Once Israel has obtained the promised salvation, it may perhaps not rashly be hoped that it will return to its ancestral soil and rejoice in the possession and habitation of its former capital, since it is said to be oppressed not forever, but only until the times of the nations are fulfilled.

[Col. 0588D] What will follow when the times of the nations have been fulfilled and all Israel has thus been saved, the Lord reveals in sequence. For according to Matthew, the disciples were asking not only about the time when the Temple would be overthrown, but also about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the age, as they sought to learn:

“And there will be signs in the sun, the moon, and the stars, and on the earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves.” Since, as the Lord intimates in what follows, at the appearance of the universal judgment heaven and earth will pass away, and since we read in John’s Apocalypse that “the sea will be no more,” it is fitting that, as that judgment draws near, the roaring of the sea and the waves is thrown into confusion. The inhabitants of the earth are afflicted as they press upon one another, while the greatest lights of heaven, their rays struck by a new terror, veil their troubled faces. And just as trees driven toward their fall customarily give advance indications through the crash and movement they make, so, as the end approaches, the elements tremble and sway as though in fear.

Thus what Matthew says—“The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven” (Matt. 24)—signifies the very presence of the judgment, when, with the glory of the true light appearing, all the lights of the world are compared with darkness and shadows. But when Luke says, “There will be signs in the sun, the moon, and the stars,” he indicates these as heralds and messengers preceding the same imminent judgment. Among them is also the Prophet’s statement: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). Likewise, what Luke says—“and on the earth distress among the nations”—I believe to be the same as what Matthew says in describing the time of the Antichrist: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be” (Matt. 24). But when Luke adds, “because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,” he heralds what John saw: that the sea would have no place among the other mutable things of the age.

“People fainting with fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken.” I believe this sentence designates the coming of the Judge, when, in accordance with the parable found elsewhere, all—that is, both the wise and foolish virgins—awakened by an unusual cry, trim their lamps, that is, reckon up the works they carry with them, for which they await with the greatest fear the outcome of the eternal judgment that already presses upon them. For until then almost the whole world will act without any fear of the Judge, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5).

Then, when fear and expectation of the strict judgment comes upon the whole world, many who seemed to flourish in this world will wither when they see themselves without fruit. Then the faith that flourished without works will dry up when tested by the just Judge. Nor is it surprising that human beings—that is, creatures earthly by nature and understanding—are troubled at his judgment, when even the powers of heaven themselves, that is, the angelic powers, tremble, as blessed Job also testifies when he says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command.” What, then, do boards do when pillars tremble? What does a slender twig of the wilderness suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” They will see in power and majesty the one whom they refused to hear when he was placed in humility, so that they may then feel his power all the more severely, the more they now refuse to bend the neck of their hearts to his patience. But because these words have been spoken against the reprobate, the discourse immediately turns to the consolation of the elect, for it continues:

“When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” When, he says, the scourges of the world multiply, when the terror of the judgment is displayed through the shaking of the powers, raise your heads—that is, gladden your hearts. For while the world, to which you are not friends, is coming to an end, the redemption that you seek is drawing near. In Sacred Scripture, the head is often used for the mind. As the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are directed by the mind. To raise our heads, therefore, is to lift our minds toward the joys of our heavenly homeland.

The Lord makes clear through a prudent comparison that the world ought to be trampled underfoot and despised. For it follows:

“And he told them a parable: ‘Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they produce fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.’” He therefore teaches openly that, just as the coming summer is recognized from the fruit of the trees, so the nearness of the kingdom of God is recognized from the world’s ruin. These words clearly show that the fruit of the world is ruin. It grows for the purpose of falling; it sprouts in order to consume in disasters whatever it has produced. The kingdom of God is rightly compared with summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away, and the days of eternal life shine with the brightness of the everlasting sun.

“Amen, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things have happened.” The Lord greatly emphasizes this by expressing it in such a way. In a certain sense, if one may say so, it is his oath: “Amen, I say to you.” For *Amen* means “true,” and yet it has not been translated, although one could have said, “I tell you the truth.” Neither the Greek translator dared to do this, nor the Latin one. Thus it remained untranslated, so that it might retain honor under a veil of secrecy—not that it should be denied, but lest, stripped bare, it should become commonplace.

Therefore “I tell you the truth” is spoken by the Truth, which, even if it did not say this, could in no way lie. Yet he emphasizes it, repeats it, in a manner awakens those who are sleeping, makes them attentive, and does not wish to be disregarded: “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all things have happened.” By “generation” he means either the entire human race or, specifically, the Jewish people.

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” The heaven that will pass away must be understood not as the ethereal or starry heaven, but as the aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven and the clouds of heaven receive their names. Peter bears witness to this when he says that “the heavens existed formerly, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed was destroyed.” But “the heavens that now exist and the earth have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people” (2 Pet. 3). He teaches plainly that the heavens destined to perish by fire are none other than those destroyed by water—that is, these empty, cloudy expanses of the windy air. For the water of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountaintops, cannot be believed to have reached beyond the boundaries of the air and the ether. Yet wherever the Flood could reach, there, according to the preceding statement of blessed Peter, the fire of judgment will likewise reach.

But if heaven and earth will pass away, it may be asked how Ecclesiastes can say: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. 1). The clear answer is that heaven and earth pass away in the form they now possess, yet subsist endlessly in their essence. “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7). And the angel says to John: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21). These will not be created as something different, but these very things will be renewed. Heaven and earth, therefore, will both pass away and remain, because they will be cleansed by fire from the form they now have, while they will always be preserved in their own nature.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. 101). They now announce this final transformation of themselves through the very changes by which they continually alternate for our use. The earth, abandoning its appearance in the dryness of winter, becomes green with the moisture of spring. The sky is daily covered by the darkness of night and renewed by the brightness of day. From this, then, let every believer learn that these things both perish and are nevertheless restored through renewal, since they are continually repaired as though from decay.

“Pay attention to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with drunkenness and debauchery and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth.” O foolish presumption of the human heart, which does not foresee the lamentable end of desire, drunkenness, and debauchery, even when the Judge himself gives warning, but, like a wicked servant, despises the decree of the eternal King after learning it.

Certainly, if some skilled and wise physician warned us, saying, “Take care lest someone, for example, drink too eagerly of the juice of this or that herb; for if he does so, sudden death will overtake him,” how carefully would each person observe the warning physician’s instructions, lest he perish by tasting what was forbidden? Yet now the Savior and Lord of souls and bodies commands that the herb of drunkenness and debauchery be avoided, and that the deadly juices of worldly cares likewise be shunned. Nevertheless, how many of us are not merely wounded by these things, but do not even fear being consumed by them? I believe there is no other reason than that they refuse to grant the Lord’s words the faith they grant to the words of physicians. For if they believed, they would certainly fear through believing; and by fearing, they would guard against the impending danger. But by growing numb, they prove how justly it has been said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18).
