[Col. 0591D] “Therefore stay awake at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are going to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” Whoever desires to stand before the Son of Man and, according to John’s Apocalypse, serve him day and night in his Temple, and not be cast away from his presence, accursed, into eternal fire, must be disciplined not only from worldly enticements, but also pray and keep watch—and do this not on certain days, but at all times, in accordance with the Psalm: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). Thus he will deserve to dwell in the house of the Lord and praise him forever and ever.

During the days he was teaching in the Temple, but at night he went out and stayed on the mountain called Olivet. And all the people would come to him in the Temple to hear him. What the Lord commands in words, he confirms through his own example. He who urges us, before the sudden coming of the universal judgment and before the uncertain departure of each of us, to neglect both the pleasures and cares of this life, and to keep watch and pray, himself, when the time of his Passion was approaching, devoted himself to vigilance in teaching and to prayer. At the same time, by his example he showed that truly keeping watch for God means, by word or deed, showing the way of truth to one’s neighbors: by word, calling those for whom he was about to suffer to faith, and by prayer, commending them to the Father.

We too, when we live soberly, justly, and devoutly amid prosperity, and amid adversity never despair of the heights of divine mercy, teach in the Temple throughout the days, because we offer believers a model of good works. At night we remain on Mount Olivet, because in the darkness of tribulations we breathe again through the consolation of spiritual joy, in accordance with the one who said: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God” (Ps. 51). That is: Just as one who bestows the fruit of mercy to the extent of his ability, I do not doubt that mercy is owed to me by the Lord.

And all the people also come to hear us when, having dispelled the works of darkness or, by God’s grace, overcome the clouds of afflictions, the children of light imitate us as those who walk honorably by day, not in revelries and drunkenness (Rom. 13).

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0592C] The feast of Unleavened Bread was approaching, which is called Passover. Passover, which in Hebrew is called *phase*, is named not from passion, as many suppose, but from passing over, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over them and did not strike them; or because the Lord himself, granting aid to his people, passed over them from above.

Seeking the higher sacramental meaning of this name, the evangelist John says: “Jesus knew that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). Here he plainly declares that the day of this festival is mystically called a “passing over” by the Law because the Lamb of God, who would take away the sins of the world, was either himself to pass from this world on that day, or was to lead us through a saving passage, as from Egyptian slavery.

Strictly speaking, according to the letter of the Old Testament, Passover differs from Unleavened Bread in this respect: Passover is the name given to the single day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. On the fifteenth day, when the exodus from Egypt took place, the feast of Unleavened Bread followed. Its solemn observance was established for seven days, that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month. Yet the Gospel regularly uses “day of Unleavened Bread” for Passover and “Passover” for the days of Unleavened Bread without distinction. Luke says: “The feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover.” Likewise John, when the matter took place on the first day of Unleavened Bread, that is, on the fifteenth day, says: “They did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover” (John 18).

For both the day of Passover was commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread, and we, as though making a perpetual Passover, are commanded always to pass from this world. For after the lamb is sacrificed in the evening on a single day, seven successive days of Unleavened Bread follow. Since Christ Jesus suffered once for us in the flesh at the fullness of time, he commands us to live throughout the entire period of this age—which is measured by seven days—in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. With all our effort he also urges us to flee the desires of the age as though they were the bonds of Egypt, and, as though withdrawing from worldly conduct, to enter among ourselves the secluded solitude of the virtues.

The chief priests and scribes were seeking how they might kill him, but they feared the people. Matthew attests that this occurred two days before Passover, when the chief priests, the elders of the people, and the scribes had assembled in the courtyard of Caiaphas. “They feared the people” not because they feared a rebellion, but because they were taking precautions lest the people’s support remove him from their hands.

Then Satan entered Judas, who is called Iscariot, one of the Twelve. John writes in his Gospel that, when the Lord had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot, and that after the morsel Satan entered him. But this is not contrary to Luke, who records that Judas had already been invaded by Satan before the morsel, because the one whom Satan now entered in order to deceive, he later entered so as to possess more fully once Judas had been handed over to him. He entered him now as though to tempt what was still alien; then as though to drag what had become his own toward whatever harmful actions he wished to undertake.

He went away and spoke with the chief priests and officers about how he might hand Jesus over to them, and they rejoiced. The statement “he went away and spoke” shows that Judas had been invited by the chief priests, not constrained by any necessity, but that he entered into the plot of his criminal mind of his own accord.

They agreed to give him money, and he promised them this. He sought an opportunity to hand him over without a crowd. Many people today abhor Judas’s crime as monstrous and wicked because he sold the Lord, his Teacher and God, for money, yet they do not guard against committing the same crime. For when they give false testimony against anyone for gifts, they plainly sell the Lord for money, because he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14). When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because “God is love.” Even if no one gives them money, they sell the Lord for silver, because they take the image of the prince of this age—that is, the example of the ancient enemy—while neglecting the image of the Creator, in whose image they were made.

For just as John the Baptist, who died not for confessing Christ but for defending the truth, nevertheless died for Christ because he accepted martyrdom for the truth, so, conversely, whoever despises the rights of love and truth certainly betrays Christ, who is truth and love—especially when he sins not through an encroaching weakness or ignorance, but, like Judas, seeks an opportunity to exchange truth for falsehood and virtue for crime while witnesses are absent.

The day of Unleavened Bread came, on which it was necessary to sacrifice the Passover. And he sent Peter and John, saying: “Go and prepare the Passover for us, so that we may eat.” He calls the day of Unleavened Bread the Passover of the fourteenth day of the first month, when, after the leaven had been discarded, the Passover—that is, the lamb—was customarily killed in the evening, as has already been said. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5).

This Passover then had to be sacrificed, that is, it had been sanctioned by the Father’s counsel and decree. Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day of the month, on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he both gave his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to celebrate and, when he was seized and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of that very sacrifice, namely, of his Passion.

But they said: “Where do you want us to prepare it?” “We have no dwelling; we have no tabernacle.” Let those who are concerned with building houses and planning the construction of imposing porticoes hear this; let those delighted by the display of costly marble and paneled ceilings adorned with gold recognize Christ, the Lord of all, who had no place to lay his head. For this reason the disciples ask him: “Where do you want us to prepare the Passover for you to eat?”

And he said to them: “Behold, as you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters.” This is indeed a sign of foreknowing divinity: while speaking with his disciples, he knows what will happen elsewhere. Fittingly, as the disciples prepare the Passover, a man carrying a jar of water meets them, to show that the mystery of this Passover is to be celebrated for the complete cleansing of the whole world. Water signifies the bath of grace; the jar signifies a perfect measure. They therefore prepare the Passover where a jar of water is brought in, because the time has come when, for the true worshipers of the Passover, the typical blood is removed from the threshold and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated for the removal of sins.

“And you shall say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’” The names of both the water-bearer and the Lord of the house have deliberately been omitted, so that it might be indicated that the opportunity is granted to all who wish to celebrate the Passover—that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments and to receive Christ as a guest in the lodging of their minds.

And he will show you a large upper room furnished; there prepare it. They went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. The large upper room is the spiritual Law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place. Whoever still observes the letter that kills, whoever understands nothing more in the lamb than an animal, performs the Passover in the depths, because he does not yet comprehend the majesty of the Spirit. But whoever follows the water-bearer—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, transcends the roof of the letter through the life-giving Spirit and prepares a dwelling for Christ in the elevated guest room of his mind, because he understands that all the mysteries of the Passover and all the other decrees of the Law were written concerning him.

When the hour came, he reclined at table, and the twelve apostles with him. He identifies the hour for eating the Passover which, as has often been emphasized, came at evening on the fourteenth day of the first month, when the fifteenth moon was already appearing over the earth, in accordance with the ordinances of the Law.

And he said to them: “I have desired with desire to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” First he desires to eat the typical Passover with his disciples, and then to reveal to the world the mysteries of his Passion, so that he might both prove himself the accomplisher of the ancient legal Passover and, by teaching that this Passover belonged to the figure of his dispensation, forbid its continued observance in a carnal manner. Rather, with the shadow having passed, he demonstrates that the light of the true Passover has now arrived.

The time and order of its fulfillment are beautifully prefigured in the days of Joshua, where it is written: “And they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, toward evening, in the plains of Jericho. And they ate of the produce of the land on the next day, unleavened bread and parched grain of that same year. And the manna ceased after they ate of the produce of the land, and the children of Israel no longer had that food” (Josh. 5).

For after Moses had died, Joshua, having received command of the people, nourished them for a time with the customary food of manna; he too was nourished by it, although he had once recognized and tasted the fruit of the land of promise. Then he crossed the Jordan, circumcised them with stone knives, and for three and a half years—that is, until the day of Passover—did not remove the customary manna. Moses having died, Joshua is appointed leader, because, when the Law has been corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, Christ is incarnated.

Joshua feeds and is fed with manna beyond the Jordan, because the Lord himself observes the ceremonies of the Law until the time of his baptism and desires them to be observed by all. Joshua circumcises the people brought across the Jordan with a stone, because, after the grace of baptism has been celebrated, the Savior precedes even the enticements of thought—which the Law could not overcome—with the severity of faith.

For three and a half years, as though nourished by the customary manna, he does not cease to observe the sacraments of the Law, although gradually calling them toward the heavenly promises, until, at the appointed time, he eats the desired Passover with his disciples. Then, as morning dawns, he consecrates the purest mysteries of his body and blood upon the altar of the cross, and offers them to the faithful who are to be imbued with them, like the unleavened produce of the land of promise. Finally, what follows is:

“For I tell you that from now on I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” How closely this agrees with Joshua’s words: “The children of Israel no longer had that food, but they ate of the produce of the land of Canaan” (Josh. 5). “I will not eat it,” he says, “until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”—that is, I will by no means celebrate the Mosaic Passover any longer, until it is fulfilled in the Church through spiritual understanding. For the Church itself is the kingdom of God. Concerning this kingdom he says elsewhere to the disciples: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). In this kingdom the Lord even today eats the fulfilled Old Passover, whenever he spiritually performs in his members, that is, in the Church itself, the things Moses commanded the untutored people to observe in a carnal manner.

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: “Take this and divide it among yourselves.” This cup also belongs to that ancient Passover to which he desired to bring an end. Having taken it, he gave thanks because all old things were destined to pass away and all things new were destined to come.

“For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” This verse may indeed be understood simply to mean that, from this hour of the supper until the time of the resurrection, when he was to come in the kingdom of God, he would not drink wine. For afterward the Apostle Peter testifies that he took food and drink, saying: “We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10).

But it is much more consistent to understand him as denying that he would taste again the typical drink of the Passover, just as above he denied that he would again eat the typical lamb, until the glory of his resurrection had been shown and manifested and the faith of the kingdom of God had come to the world. Thus, through the two greatest ordinances of the Law—the eating and drinking of the Passover, spiritually transformed—you might learn that all the sacraments of the Law, and all its commands that seemed to speak in a carnal manner, were now to be transferred to spiritual observance.

And having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” When the solemn rites of the old Passover, celebrated in remembrance of the ancient liberation from Egypt, had been completed, he passed over to the new Passover, which the Church desires to celebrate in remembrance of his redemption [Col. 0596C]. That is, substituting the sacrament of his flesh and blood in the figure of bread and wine for the flesh and blood of the lamb, he showed himself to be the one to whom the Lord swore and will not repent: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [110]). He himself breaks the bread that he offers, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will, but, as he says elsewhere, that he has authority to lay down his life and to take it up again.

And just as he had dealt with the ending of the old things, so also, in beginning the new, he gives thanks to the Father, giving us likewise an example that, at the beginning or completion of every good work, the Father who is in heaven is to be glorified. But when he says, “Do this in remembrance of me,” the apostle Paul explains it. After repeating his words—“Do this in remembrance of me; this is my body, which is broken for you”—and again, “This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood; do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me,” he added by way of explanation: “For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor. 11).

Likewise the cup, after supper, saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which will be poured out for you.” When he says, “Likewise the cup,” the words ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [by common construction] are understood: “he gave it to them,” so that the complete sentence is: “Likewise, after he had eaten, he gave them the cup.” Since bread confirms the flesh, while wine produces blood in the flesh, the one refers mystically to the body of Christ and the other to his blood. Yet because Christ must dwell in us and we in Christ, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup. For, as John testifies, “the waters are the peoples” (Rev. 15). No one is permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as a grain of wheat cannot be offered by itself without being mixed with water and made into bread. Such an offering would signify that the head ought to be separated from the members, and would falsely suggest either that Christ could suffer without the love of our redemption, or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without Christ’s passion.

If this troubles anyone—since the Savior, after supper, gave his body and blood to the apostles—so that they ask why, by the universal custom of the Church, we are taught to receive these same sacraments while fasting, let him hear briefly that the apostles then communicated after supper because it was necessary first to complete that typological Passover and thus pass over to the sacraments of the true Passover. Now, in honor of so great and so terrible a sacrament, it has pleased the teachers of the Church that we should first be fortified by participation in the Lord’s passion, first be inwardly and outwardly consecrated by spiritual feasts, and thereafter have our bodies refreshed by earthly food and ordinary nourishment.

When he says, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood,” he refers to the distinction from the Old Covenant, which was consecrated by the blood of goats and calves. As the lawgiver said while sprinkling it: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you” (Heb. 9). For it is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these sacrifices, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better sacrifices than these, as the Apostle explains throughout the Letter to the Hebrews, distinguishing the Law from the Gospel, with the most beautiful exposition and complete reasoning [Col. 0597C].

“Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table. And indeed the Son of Man goes as it has been determined; nevertheless, woe to that man by whom he will be betrayed.” He who had foretold his passion now foretells the betrayer, granting an opportunity for repentance, so that, when he understood that his thoughts and secret plans were known, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, being openly exposed, he become more shameless. He casts the crime into the general number, so that the guilty man might repent in awareness. He also foretells the punishment, so that the announced torments might correct one whom shame had not overcome [Col. 0597D].

Even today and forever, woe to the man who approaches the Lord’s table in wickedness, who, with plots concealed in his mind and with his inmost heart polluted by some crime, is not afraid to share in the secrets of Christ’s mysteries. For he betrays the Son of Man, after the example of Judas—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely, to his own members, whom he presumes to violate that immeasurable and inviolable body of the Lord. He sells the Lord who, neglecting love and fear of him, is shown to love and care more for earthly and perishable things, indeed even for criminal things. Woe, I say, to that man concerning whom Jesus—who is believed to be present at the sacred altars during the sacrifice, as the one about to consecrate what has been set before him, while heavenly ministers stand beside him—is forced to ask: “Behold,” he says, “the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” [Col. 0598A].

And they began to ask one another which of them it was who would do this. Certainly the eleven apostles knew that they were contemplating nothing of this kind against the Lord; nevertheless, they believed the teacher more than themselves. Fearing their own weakness, they sorrowfully asked about a sin of which they had no awareness. Judas too asked, shamelessly, as Matthew and Mark record, so that audacity might counterfeit a good conscience.

There arose also a dispute among them as to which of them seemed to be the greatest. Just as it is customary for the good, throughout Scripture, always to seek out examples of the Fathers who went before them, so that they may advance toward better things and, having recognized them, humble themselves concerning their own deeds, so conversely the reprobate, if they happen to find something blameworthy in the elect, eagerly embrace it, as though by this means they might conceal their own wickedness or defend it as righteous. Therefore they read with much greater eagerness that a dispute arose among Christ’s disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greatest than that “the heart and soul of the multitude of believers was one” (Acts 4). They recall much more tenaciously that dissension arose between Barnabas and Paul, so that they separated from one another, than what Paul himself says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal? Are you not human?”—as though the weakness of the saints were proposed for our imitation, rather than the fact that “they recovered from weakness and became strong in battle.” This is especially pertinent here, since the very cause of their dispute is unknown to us [Col. 0598B].

For it is not incredible that, in accordance with what is commanded elsewhere—“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13)—they may have competed by anticipating one another in honor. But whatever the cause for which they contended, let us consider not what the disciples, still carnal, did, but what the spiritual teacher commanded.

But he said to them: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But you must not be so. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves.” While the disciples were competing for precedence, the compassionate teacher did not rebuke them for the dispute they had begun; instead, with measured reasoning, he described the form of humility they were to follow. In attaining this form, however, the great and the leaders—that is, the teachers of the Church—need no small degree of discernment, lest, like the kings of the Gentiles, they rejoice in lording it over their subjects and in being raised up by their empty praises, but instead preside after the example of the King and become ministers.

For it is necessary that those who act in this way be companions of their subjects through humility, while standing firm against the vices of sinners through zeal for justice, so that they do not place themselves above the good in any respect, yet, when the guilt of the wicked requires it, immediately recognize the authority of their own precedence. Lest the mind of one who presides be carried away by delight in his power toward exaltation, it is rightly said by a certain wise man: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32). Hence Peter also says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming a model for the flock” (1 Pet. 5).

Nevertheless, sometimes a graver offense is committed if equality is maintained among the perverse more than discipline. Because Eli, overcome by a false compassion, was unwilling to strike his delinquent sons, he struck himself together with them by a cruel condemnation before the strict Judge. Therefore the ruler must present himself to his subjects as both a mother in compassion and a father in discipline. And amid all this, careful vigilance must ensure that neither strictness is harsh nor compassion lax [Col. 0598C–D].

“For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves.” To his words of exhortation he adds examples, which the evangelist John recalls more fully, writing among other things: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13).

The word “serves” may also be understood of everything that God accomplished in the flesh. For he signifies that he poured himself out to administer to us the sacrament of his own blood when he says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20). By this he also shows that this preeminent kind of service is to be imitated by the greater ones in the Church: we are to offer our brothers not only the services of mercy, almsgiving, salutary teaching, and spiritual example, but also, just as he laid down his life for us, to learn to lay down our lives for one another [Col. 0599A].

“But you are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you, just as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom.” It is not the beginning of endurance but perseverance that is granted the glory of the heavenly kingdom. For perseverance, which is also called constancy, is a certain strength and firmness of mind and, so to speak, the column of all the virtues. When it stands upright and firm, nothing is more certain or safer for good conduct. But if, struck by some storm, it is thrown down, it does not fall alone; all the goods of the soul collapse together.

Therefore, just as the Father appointed a kingdom for the Son, whom he exalted after he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross, and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. 2), so the Son will also lead those who remain with him in trials into the eternal kingdom [Col. 0599B]. “For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. 6).

The wretched Judas is excluded from the sublimity of this promise. For he must be believed to have gone out before the Lord said these things. He not only refused to remain with him in his trials, but even assisted the authors of his trials. Those who, after hearing the words of the incomprehensible sacrament, went away and no longer walked with him are excluded as well. For those who depart from the Lord cannot be saved unless they return through repentance.

“So that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.” This table, set before all the saints for their enjoyment, is the heavenly glory of life. That food and drink of which it is said elsewhere, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5), “for they shall be satisfied,” consists in enjoying the joy of the true and unshaken good, once desired and loved.

“And you shall sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” This is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High sung by the Psalm (Ps. 76 [77]): those who now gladly serve their fellow servants in humility will then be nourished by the exalted dishes of everlasting life at the Lord’s table; those who remain with the Lord here, unjustly judged in their trials, will there come with him as righteous judges over those who tested them; and the more greatly they are despised in this world with humility, the more greatly they will then increase in the height of power after receiving their seats [Col. 0600A].

But the Lord said: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you all, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.” Lest the eleven apostles should boast or attribute to their own strength the fact that they alone, among so many thousands of Jews, were said to have remained with the Lord in his trials, he showed that, unless they had been protected by the help of the Lord who aided them, they too could have been crushed by the same storm together with the others.

When Satan demands to test them and shake them as though winnowing wheat, he teaches that no one’s faith is tested by the devil except with God’s permission. For Satan’s demanding to sift the good means that he pants with the heat of his malice for their affliction. Insofar as he enviously seeks their testing, he perishes as though pleading for their proof. But when the Savior prays for Peter, asking not that he not be tested but that his faith not fail—that is, that after the fall of his denial he might rise again through repentance to his former state—he indicates that it is useful for the saints to be tested by the flames of trials. Thus they may either show that they are strong because they have been tested, or, having learned their weakness through trials, learn to become stronger; and when they have been proven, they too may receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him (Jas. 1) [Col. 0600B–C].

“And you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” “Just as,” he says, “I have protected your faith by praying that it not fail when Satan tests it, so you must remember to raise up and strengthen the weaker brothers by the example of your repentance, lest they perhaps despair of forgiveness.” After the resurrection he exhorts him in the same way: when Peter professed his love for him a third time—for it was fitting that the fear of a threefold denial should be washed away by the love of a threefold confession—he likewise entrusted his sheep to him to feed a third time [Col. 0600D].

He said to him: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” But he said: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you deny that you know me.” Because the Lord had said that he had prayed for Peter’s faith, Peter, conscious of his present affection and fervent faith but unaware of his future fall, did not believe that he could in any way fail him. But the one who alone knows what is in a person foretells, as God, the manner, time, and number of his denials, so that none of the faithful may either rashly trust in his own condition or rashly despair because of his fall; and, as the merciful one, he promises the assistance of his protection.

“When I sent you without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?” And they said: “Nothing.” Therefore he said to them: “But now, let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.” How rightly the Fathers define discernment as the mother and nurse of all the virtues is also proved by this saying of the Lord: he does not instruct his disciples according to the same rule of life in a time of persecution as in a time of peace.

There are virtues that must always be held firmly and earnestly; there are others that must be changed according to time and place by prudent discernment. For who does not know that compassion, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, chastity, faith, hope, love, and similar virtues must be preserved by the faithful without any interruption of time? But if anyone thinks that hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, reading, psalmody, prayer, labor, teaching, silence, and other things of this kind must always be practiced, he will not only deprive himself of their fruit but will also incur the reproach of indiscreet obstinacy, indeed of stubborn folly [Col. 0601A–B].

Therefore the Lord, the teacher and master of the virtues, to indicate the measure of discernment, commanded his disciples when sending them to preach to take nothing on the road, evidently ordering that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But when the danger of death was imminent, and the entire people was persecuting the shepherd together with the flock, he determined a rule appropriate to the time: he permitted them to take money necessary for their sustenance until the madness of the persecutors had subsided and the time for evangelizing returned.

Here he also gives us an example that, when a just cause occasionally arises, certain things may be interrupted without guilt from the strictness of our way of life. For example, when we travel through inhospitable regions, it is permissible to carry more provisions for the journey than we would have at home.

He also commands them either to take up a sword already possessed or, if they do not have one, to buy one, so that readers may know that it was not the disciples’ ability to resist that was lacking; rather, their teacher’s love of suffering was the greater. Even if there were no other reason for drawing the sword, this would have been sufficient: after the servant’s ear had been cut off, it was healed by the Lord’s touch, and the Savior’s power to do good admonished even his attackers, so that they might prefer not to endure the anger of the one who had been struck but to receive faith in the one who would rise again [Col. 0601C].

“For I tell you that what is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was reckoned among the unjust.’” For the things concerning me are reaching their fulfillment. Behold why the disciples are warned to take a purse, a bag, and a sword: because the Lord was to be reckoned among the unjust. Isaiah includes this among his descriptions of his passion (Isa. 53), signifying either the robbers among whom he was to be crucified, or the underworld to which he was to descend through death.

For he was reckoned among the unjust also when he descended to the underworld and recalled to the heights those of his own whom he found there. In accordance with this, another prophet sings to him: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9) [Col. 0601D].

And they said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” But he said to them: “It is enough.” Two swords suffice as testimony to the Savior’s willingly endured passion. One of them taught the apostles the boldness to fight for the Lord and, when his stroke tore off the servant’s ear, showed that the Lord, even though about to die, possessed both compassion and the power to heal. Alternatively, the sword, which was in no way drawn from its sheath, showed that they had not been permitted to do everything they could for his defense [Col. 0602A].

And going out, he proceeded according to his custom to the Mount of Olives. And the disciples followed him. Since the Lord was to be betrayed by a disciple, he went to the place of his customary retreat, where he could most easily be found. Where, then, are those who contend that he feared death and was crucified against his will?

Beautifully, he leads the disciples, imbued with the mysteries of his body and blood, up the Mount of Olives, indicating that all those baptized into his death are to be strengthened by the highest chrism of the Holy Spirit, so that they may say with the Psalmist: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4) [Col. 0602B]. And of them it is said earlier: “From the time of their grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied” (ibid.).

And when he reached the place, he said to them: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence, in the Lord’s Prayer, we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6): not rejecting temptation altogether, but praying for the strength to endure in temptations.

So here too he does not say, “Pray that you may not be tempted,” but “that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, that temptation may not finally overcome you or hold you within its snares. For example, the martyr who sheds his blood in confessing the Lord is indeed tested, but he is not bound in the nets of temptation; the one who denies, however, falls into the snares of temptation [Col. 0602C].

And he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw. And kneeling, he prayed, saying: After giving the apostles the command to pray, he himself withdrew from them and prayed alone for all, signifying that his prayer, like his passion, stands at a distance from ours; and he prays on his knees to show the humility of his mind through the posture of his body.

He withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, as though he were symbolically admonishing them to direct the stone toward him—that is, to bring it all the way to him in the temptation of the Law, which was written on stone. For that stone can reach as far as he, since Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes [Col. 0602D].

“Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.” He asks that the cup be taken from him, not out of fear of suffering but out of mercy toward the former people, lest that people drink the cup offered to it. Hence he pointedly did not say, “Take the cup from me,” but “this cup”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people, which cannot claim the excuse of ignorance if it kills me, since it has the Law and the Prophets, who daily prophesy about me. Yet, returning to himself, he confirms by the power of the Son of God what, speaking in the human person, he had held with trembling.

“Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.” “Let not,” he says, “what I speak in human affection be done, but that for which I descended to earth by your will. If it is possible for the multitude of the Gentiles to believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they must be blinded so that all the nations may see, then, Father, not my will but yours be done.”

Alternatively: As the Savior approached his passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak, saying, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me,” and he assumed their fear in order to remove it. Then again, displaying strength of mind through obedience, he said: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.” Thus, when what we do not wish to happen is imminent, we should ask in our weakness that it not happen, while through strength we remain prepared for the will of our Creator to be done even against our will [Col. 0603A].

And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him. Elsewhere we read that angels came and ministered to him. Thus, as evidence of both natures, he is described both as having been ministered to by angels and as having been strengthened by an angel, because the one who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages.

Before he was exalted by the glory of the resurrection, he was divine and above the angels; yet, as it is written, in his humanity he was made lower than the angels (Ps. 8), and in that humanity he was also subject to death. But after he trampled death by rising again, he placed his humanity above even the ranks of the archangels.

Certainly, if any heresy takes comfort from this, asserting that he was weak because he needed the assistance of an angel to strengthen him, let it remember that the Creator of angels did not need the protection of his creature. For, if he had wished, he could have led down from heaven twelve thousand legions of angels. Moreover, he necessarily was strengthened in the same way in which he was sorrowful. For if he is sorrowful for us—that is, if he is sorrowful on our account—then he must also have been strengthened for us and on our account [Col. 0603B–C].

And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. What could he, while in agony, be asking for himself, who, while placed on earth, bestowed heavenly things with authority? But, as death approached, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind, for we suffer a certain force of terror and fear when, through the dissolution of the flesh, we draw near to eternal judgment. For then the soul of anyone is not terrified without reason, when shortly afterward it encounters what it cannot change for eternity [Col. 0603D].

And his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. Let no one attribute this sweat to weakness, since sweating blood is contrary to nature. Nor can what benefits the case against the heresy that falsely asserts an apparition in opposition to bodily reality in any way be considered a matter of weakness: the sweat of blood supports the truth of his body.

Rather, one should understand that, through the earth watered and sanctified by his blood, it was made openly clear—not for him, who already knew it, but for us—that he had obtained the effect of his prayer: namely, that he would cleanse by his blood the faith of the disciples, which earthly weakness still impugned. Whatever scandal his death had brought upon it, he would wholly erase by dying; indeed, by his innocent death he would raise to heavenly life the entire world, dead in its sins [Col. 0604A].

And when he had risen from prayer and come to his disciples, he found them sleeping from sorrow. And he said to them: “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray, that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, lest the cup of my passion fall upon you. Here he clearly demonstrates that he had also prayed for those whom he diligently urges to become participants in his prayers by keeping watch and praying.

While he was still speaking, behold, a crowd appeared; and the one called Judas, one of the Twelve, was going before them. He approached Jesus to kiss him. The other evangelists make clear why he kissed him: namely, so that by this sign they might recognize the very man whom he was betraying. The Lord receives the kiss of the betrayer, not to teach us to pretend, but lest he appear to flee from betrayal, while also fulfilling the saying of David: “With those who hate peace I was peaceable” (Ps. 119 [120]) [Col. 0604B].

But Jesus said to him: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” “You betray,” he says, “the Son of Man,” because flesh, not divinity, is being seized. Yet what more strongly condemns the ungrateful man is that he betrayed the one who, although he was the Son of God, nevertheless for our sake wished to be the Son of Man. It is as though he were saying: “For your sake, ungrateful man, I assumed what you are betraying.”

I think the words should properly be pronounced as a question, as though he were reproving the betrayer with the affection of one who loves: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” That is: “Are you inflicting a wound by the pledge of love, shedding blood in the duty of charity, bringing death through the instrument of peace—a servant betraying his Lord, a disciple his teacher, one chosen betraying his author?” [Col. 0604C].

When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. Peter did this, as the evangelist John teaches, with the same ardor of mind with which he had done the other things. For he knew how Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious men, had received the reward of justice and an everlasting priesthood. What follows is:

But Jesus answered and said: “Let it be thus far.” This should not be understood as though he approved what had happened up to that point but did not want anything further to occur. Rather, in the words that Matthew records the Lord as having spoken—“Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26)—it is understood that the entire act in which Peter used the sword displeased the Lord.

It is more likely that, when they had asked him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” he then answered, “Let it be thus far”—that is, “Do not be disturbed by what is about to happen; they are to be permitted to proceed this far, namely, to seize me, so that the things written about me may be fulfilled.” But during the delay between the question of those asking the Lord and his response, Peter, eager to defend him and moved by an even greater zeal for the Lord, struck the servant.

Yet things that could happen simultaneously could not all be spoken simultaneously. For the evangelist would not say, “But Jesus answered,” unless he were answering their question. As for what judgment he passed on Peter’s deed, Matthew alone reports it. There too Matthew does not say, “Jesus answered Peter, ‘Put your sword back,’” but, “Then Jesus said to him, ‘Put your sword back,’” which makes it appear that the Lord said this after the deed [Col. 0604D–Col. 0605A].

And when he had touched his ear, he healed him. The Lord never forgets his compassion: he does not allow even his enemies to remain wounded. They inflict death upon the righteous man; he heals the wounds of his persecutors, mystically teaching that even those who have been wounded by consenting to his death can be healed if they turn back.

Allegorically, this servant is the Jewish people, enslaved to the priests by an improper obedience, so that at their urging they asked for Barabbas to be released and Jesus to be crucified—the one whom shortly before they had acclaimed with hosannas as the Son of David and King. In the Lord’s passion, this people lost its right ear, that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law, and remained content only with the left, that is, with the usefulness of the letter.

This ear is cut off by Peter’s sword—not because he removes the power of understanding from those who hear, but because he reveals that it has been taken away by divine judgment from the negligent. Yet this same right ear was restored by divine merciful favor to those from that same people who chose to believe, so that it might resume its former function.

Alternatively: the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signifies hearing renewed after the old condition has been removed, so that it may exist in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. To whoever this has been granted by Christ, it will also be granted to reign with Christ.

Hence Malchus, the name by which that servant was called, is appropriately interpreted as “king” or “one who will reign.” The fact that he was found to be a servant also pertains to that old condition which generates slavery, namely Hagar. But when healing came, freedom too was signified [Col. 0605B–C].

Jesus said to the chief priests, the officers of the temple, and the elders who had come to him. It is asked how Jesus is said to have addressed the chief priests, the officers of the temple, and the elders who had come to him, when the other evangelists report that they themselves did not come but sent ministers while waiting in the court of Caiaphas.

But because the high priests, Pharisees, and elders were arranging the Lord’s death in such a way that they seemed to be innocent of his blood—as though saying, “Let him not be handed over by us, but by his disciple; let him not be seized by us, but by the tribune and the crowds; let Barabbas not be chosen by us instead of him, but by the peoples; finally, let him not be condemned by us, but by the governor, and let him not be crucified by our hands but by those of the Roman army”—the evangelist, wishing to show especially those whose counsel directed everything to be guilty of his blood, says that the chief priests, the officers of the temple, and the elders came to seize the Savior.

From this it could be inferred that, just as they did not come in person but through those whom they sent to apprehend Christ, so, in the power of their command, they themselves came. Likewise, all who cried out with wicked voices that he should be crucified killed him—not indeed by their own hands, but nevertheless through the one whom their outcry drove to this crime [Col. 0605D].

“As against a robber have you come out with swords and clubs? When I was with you every day in the temple, you did not stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour and the power of darkness.” It is foolish, he says, to seek with swords and clubs one who willingly gives himself into your hands, and to investigate at night, as though he were hiding and avoiding your eyes, through a betrayer the one who taught every day in the temple. But you gather against me in darkness because your power—by which you arm yourselves against the light of the world—is in darkness [Col. 0606A].

And having seized him, they led him to the house of the high priest. “The high priest” signifies Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, as the evangelist John testifies.

But Peter followed from a distance. It was fitting that he followed from a distance, since he was already near to denying him. For he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Yet in this we must admire and venerate him greatly: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. His fear belonged to nature; his following, to devotion; his denial, to sudden weakness; his repentance, to faith.

Alternatively: the fact that Peter followed the Lord, who was going to his passion, from a distance signified that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s passions, but in a very different way. The Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffered for the Church [Col. 0606B].

After a fire had been lit in the middle of the courtyard, and they were sitting around it, Peter was in the midst of them. There is the fire of love, and there is also the fire of desire. Of the former it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it burn?” (Luke 12). Of the latter: “Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled” (Isa. 50).

The first fire, descending from heaven upon the believers in the upper room of Zion, taught them to praise God in various languages. The other, fed in the courtyard by Caiaphas with earthly fuel, inflamed the crowds with the flames of denying the Lord. With the former Moses consumed the golden head of the idol; with the latter Zedekiah consumed the writings of the prophesying Jeremiah.

Whoever extinguishes within himself a vicious and harmful fire can sing to the Lord: “For I have become like a leather bottle in the frost; I have not forgotten your statutes” (Ps. 118 [119]). But the one who has lost the flame of the virtues hears from the Lord: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24).

Numbed for a time by this cold, the apostle Peter wanted to warm himself at the coals of the persecutors, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage in the company of the faithless. But soon, when the Lord looked upon him, he abandoned both their fire with his body and his infidelity with his heart [Col. 0606C–D].

When a certain maidservant saw him sitting by the light and looked at him, she said: “This man too was with him.” What does it mean that a maidservant is the first to expose him, when men could surely have recognized him more readily, unless it was so that this sex too might appear to have sinned in the Lord’s death, and this sex might be redeemed through the Lord’s passion?

For this reason a woman was the first to receive the mystery of the resurrection and to preserve the commands, so that she might erase the ancient error of transgression.

But he denied him, saying: “Woman, I do not know him.” [Col. 0607A] Some, out of affection for the apostle Peter, interpret this passage as though he had rightly said that he did not know one whom the human mind cannot comprehend, since no one knows the Son except the Father (Matt. XI). Again, when questioned, he is said to have replied: “Man, I am not,” preferring to deny himself rather than Christ. But when questioned a third time, saying, “Man, I do not know what you are saying,” he is understood to have indicated that he did not know their sacrileges—that is, rejecting and condemning them with abhorrence. Yet how frivolous this interpretation is, both the Lord shows, who in a truthful prediction had foretold that Peter would deny him three times, and Peter himself makes clear: he demonstrates by his subsequent tears that he had spoken these words not deliberately but through sudden weakness.

And shortly afterward another person, seeing him, said: “You also are one of them.” [Col. 0607B] But Peter said: “Man, I am not.” In this denial of blessed Peter we learn that Christ is denied not only by the one who says that he is not the Christ, but also by the one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is one. The Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but “You will deny me.” He therefore denied Christ when he denied that he was Christ’s disciple.

After an interval of about an hour, another man insisted, saying: “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” This was not because the Galileans spoke one language and the people of Jerusalem another—for both were Hebrews—but because every province and region has its own distinctive features and cannot avoid the sound of its native speech. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles, when those upon whom the Holy Spirit had come were speaking in the languages of all nations, among the other people who had gathered from different regions of the world, even those who lived in Judaea are reported to have said in amazement: “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we each hear our own language in which we were born?”

And Peter said: “Man, I do not know what you are saying.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed. Sacred Scripture often designates the significance of events by the circumstances of time. Thus Peter, who denied the Lord at midnight, repented at the crowing of the cock. After the resurrection, in the light of day, he also professed three times that he loved the Lord whom he had denied three times, because what he had gone astray in amid the darkness of forgetfulness, he corrected by remembering the light that had now been hoped for; and, having attained the presence of that same true light, he fully restored everything that he had altered. I think that this cock signifies some teacher who, rousing us when we lie fallen and rebuking us when we are drowsy, says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. XV).

And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, as he had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And Peter went outside and wept bitterly. When the Lord looked upon him, Peter returned to his heart and wiped away the stain of denial with tears of repentance, because God’s mercy is necessary not only when repentance is being performed but also in order that it may be performed. For his looking upon someone means having mercy. Hence the Psalmist says: “How long,” he says, “will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God” (Ps. XII)—that is, “Have mercy and help me.” How harmful, indeed, is the company of the treacherous! Peter denied among the Jews that he knew as a man the one whom among his fellow disciples he had confessed to be the Son of God. But while he was being held in the courtyard of Caiaphas, could he repent? He went outside so that, separated from the council of the ungodly, he might wash away the filth of his fearful denial with unrestrained tears.

And the men who held him mocked him, beating him; and they covered him and struck his face. Here the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “They will strike the cheek of the judge of Israel with a rod” (Mic. V). But the one who was then beaten with the blows of the Jews is also beaten now by the blasphemies of false Christians. They covered him, not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that, as they had once done to Moses, they might hide his face from themselves. For if they believed Moses, they would perhaps believe the Lord as well. To this day that veil remains over their heart, unrevealed; but for us who believe in Christ it has been removed. For it was not without reason that, when he died, the veil of the temple was torn in two.

And they questioned him, saying: “Prophesy: who is it that struck you?” And they said many other blasphemous things against him. They did these things as an insult to the one who had wished to be regarded by the people as a prophet. But, by the dispensation of the one who suffers, everything is done for our sake, so that, as Peter exhorts us, since Christ suffered in the flesh, we may arm ourselves with the same intention. Heretics also, and the Jews to this day who deny that Jesus is God, as well as wicked Catholics who provoke him by their evil deeds and do not suppose that their thoughts and works of darkness are seen by him, mock him as though saying: “Prophesy: who is it that struck you?”

And when day came, the elders of the people, the chief priests, and the scribes assembled and led him into their council, saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us.” They did not desire the truth but were preparing an accusation. For, expecting Christ to come merely as a man from the line of David, just as on another occasion they themselves answered him when he questioned them, they asked him this as a matter of great importance, so that if he said, “I am the Christ”—understanding “Christ” only in their own sense, as one descended from David—they might accuse him of arrogating royal power to himself.

[Col. 0608D] And he said to them: “If I tell you, you will not believe me. And if I question you, you will not answer me, nor will you release me.” He had often told them that he was the Christ, as when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John X); and again: “The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me, but you do not believe” (ibid.), and other things of this kind. He had also asked how they could say that the Christ was the son of David when David himself, in the Spirit, called him his Lord, so that, challenged by this question, they might learn that he was not only truly human, because he was David’s son, but also truly God, because he was David’s Lord. But they neither wished to believe him when he spoke by following him, nor to answer him when he questioned them, nor to release him, though he had been proved innocent. Those who sought to accuse him as David’s descendant hear something greater.

“From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” If, therefore, in Christ, O Jew, pagan, and heretic, contempt, weakness, and the cross are an offense to you, see that through these things the Son of Man, born as a man from the womb of a virgin, will sit at the right hand of God the Father and will come in his majesty with the clouds of heaven. Hence the Apostle, after describing the degradation of the cross, added: “Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God” [Col. 0609B] (Phil. II).

And they all said: “Then you are the Son of God?” He said to them: “You say that I am.” He so tempers his answer that he both speaks the truth and does not expose himself to accusation through his words. For he preferred to prove himself to be Christ, the Son of God, rather than say it in such a way as to remove from those who condemned him the grounds for condemnation—for they themselves confessed what they alleged against him.

But they said: “Why do we still need testimony? We ourselves have heard it from his mouth.” They received the Lord’s testimony that he himself had declared that he was Christ and the Son of God in what he said: “The Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” And when they asked, “Then you are the Son of God?” he replied: “You say that I am.” Thus by their own judgment they condemn themselves, handing over to death the one whom, by the testimony of both their words and their deeds, they recognize as God. They also condemn the Arians, who refuse to understand the words announcing the divine majesty—words spoken after the Lord had already been glorified through death—which the executioners themselves, while he was still bound, scourged, and mocked, understood.

## CHAPTER XXIII

And the whole assembly of them rose and led him to Pilate. Thus the saying of Jesus was fulfilled, by which he foretold his death: “For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him” (Luke XVIII). By “the Gentiles” he means the Romans. Pilate was a Roman, and the Romans had sent him as governor to Judaea. The Jews handed the Lord over to him to be crucified, wishing in this way to make themselves appear as though strangers to his death, so that what would be revealed was not their innocence but their madness.

They began to accuse him, saying: “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” The Jews are convicted of impiety because, in accusing the Savior, they cannot find even something plausibly false to bring against him. Therefore, as Mark says, “their testimony did not agree” (Mark XIV). But he, to offer us an example of patience, remains silent and says nothing, just as he had earlier been beaten.

Pilate questioned him, saying: “Are you the king of the Jews?” But he answered: “You say so.” He responds to the governor with the same words with which he answered the chief priests, so that they might be condemned by their own judgment. It should be noted that, although two charges were brought against the Lord—namely, that he forbade the payment of tribute to Caesar and that he said he was Christ the king—Pilate thought he should question him about the single word “kingdom.” It could have happened that Pilate had also heard the Lord’s judgment: “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). Therefore, regarding this charge as an obvious lie born of envy and counting it as nothing, he may have considered only the matter he did not know worth investigating.

Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds: “I find no charge against this man.” This is what he himself had said to his disciples shortly before his passion: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV). But since the ruler of the world—that is, Pilate—acquits him in whom he has found no charge deserving condemnation, see what the Jews are doing: they do not seek the truth out of love of justice, but strive to condemn the just man, driven by the goad of envy.

But they grew more insistent, saying: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee even to this place.” This speech of the accusers teaches all the more clearly both that the one accused was innocent and that those who accused him were perverse. To have taught the people and to have stirred them from the sluggishness of former times by teaching, and by such activity to have passed from Galilee to Judaea—that is, through the whole promised land from one end to the other—is evidently not a crime but an indication of virtue. For a lover of the Lord could, as indeed he did, present the same statement as praise, saying to good hearers: “You know what took place throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.” Finally, Pilate did not think the Savior should be questioned about this; rather, taking the opportunity, he sought to free himself by freeing him. For what follows is:

When Pilate heard the word “Galilee,” he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him back to Herod, who himself was also in Jerusalem in those days. Pilate, so as not to be forced to pronounce judgment against one whom he knew to be innocent and handed over through envy, sent him to Herod to be heard, so that Herod, who was tetrarch of the man’s own region, might instead either acquit or punish him. But by divine providence, so that the Jews would have no excuse—as though it were not they but the Romans who had crucified Christ—Herod also, who was a Jew both by birth and by religion, was permitted to show, together with his army, what he thought about him. At the same time, the impiety of both regions is revealed: Judaea, where he was born, and Galilee, where he was raised and lived, conspiring in his death.

When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad. [Col. 0611A] For he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see him perform some sign. He questioned him at length, but he answered him nothing. He remained silent and did nothing because Herod’s cruelty did not deserve to see divine things, and the Lord was avoiding display. Perhaps Herod also signifies all the ungodly, who, if they do not believe the Law and the prophets, cannot see Christ’s wondrous works even in the Gospel.

The chief priests and the scribes were also standing there, persistently accusing him. While the chief priests and scribes accused him, the Lord answered briefly before Pilate and nothing before Herod, lest, by dispelling the charge, he be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be postponed. It was certainly just that he should give some answer to Pilate, who was pronouncing judgment almost unwillingly. But he considered Herod and the other leaders of the Jews entirely unworthy of his words, because they were condemning an innocent man contrary to the decrees of their own Law. For this reason, although he did not wish to answer, the likeness of a lamb was given, so that in his silence he might be regarded not as guilty but as innocent. When he was silent, like a lamb destined to be sacrificed for the whole flock, he displayed patience; when he answered, like the good shepherd, he fought on behalf of the sheep entrusted to him against the snares of wolves and robbers.

But Herod, with his army, despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment, and sent him back to Pilate. His being clothed in white gives an indication of an immaculate passion, since the immaculate Lamb of God was to take away the sins of the whole world. The one who was despised and mocked in a white garment suffered and was buried in chaste flesh. Alternatively: the fact that he is mocked here wearing white, but according to the other Evangelists a purple or scarlet garment, expresses the twofold kind of martyrdom by which the holy Church is adorned. She marvels at the innocent death of that same Lord and Bridegroom and says: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song V)—white in deed, ruddy in blood. He himself, flowering in the varied blossoms of his members, produces lilies in peace and roses in war.

And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other on that very day. Previously they had been enemies. This most wicked pact of Herod and Pilate, which they made in killing Christ, is preserved to this day by their successors, as though by hereditary right, whenever Gentiles and Jews, differing in race and religion and likewise in mind, nevertheless agree in persecuting Christians and destroying Christ’s faith in them.

Pilate, having summoned the chief priests, the magistrates, and the people, said to them: Pay attention to how earnestly Pilate sought to release Jesus. First, when the chief priests accused him, he said that he had found no charge in him. Then, when they persisted in their accusation, he sent him to Herod, to discover whether Herod might find some crime in him and perhaps decide that he should be released. Finally, after learning Herod’s will and finding no crime in Jesus, he sought the judgment of the people as well, to whom it was customary to release one prisoner at Passover. Again and a third time, wishing to release him, he questioned them. But the more eagerly he sought the assistance of one who could help release Jesus and did not find it, the more criminal he showed those whom he found unanimously desiring his death.

“You brought this man to me as one who was turning the people away; and behold, I, having questioned him in your presence, find no charge in this man concerning those matters of which you accuse him.” By saying this, Pilate indeed acquitted Jesus, whom he had proved innocent; but, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, he crucified by a mystery the one whom he acquitted by judgment.

“Nor did Herod. For I sent you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him.” Hear this, blind Jew; hear this, cruel pagan. Pilate himself confesses that neither he nor Herod found anything in Christ deserving death, but that, in killing or mocking the innocent man, they had merely yielded to the cries of another’s cruelty. Let the writings therefore perish which, composed so long afterward against Christ, show that it is not he who is accused before Pilate of magical arts, but that you are to be accused before the Lord of treachery and falsehood.

“I will therefore have him corrected [or: chastised] and release him. I will subject him to scourging and mockery, as much as you command, provided you do not thirst for innocent blood.”

Now he was obliged to release one prisoner for them at the feast—not by the sanction of an imperial law, but bound by the annual custom of the nation, which he was pleased to gratify in such matters.

But the whole crowd cried out together, saying: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas for us,” who had been imprisoned because of a certain uprising that had taken place in the city and because of murder. The Jews’ request remains with them to this day—the request they obtained with such effort. For when they were given a choice, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and a destroyer instead of the giver of life. Therefore they deservedly lost salvation and life, and they so immersed themselves in robberies and seditions that they lost both their homeland and kingdom, which they loved more than Christ, and to this day have not deserved to regain the freedom of soul or body that they sold.

Pilate spoke to them again, wishing to release Jesus. But they shouted back, saying: “Crucify him! Crucify him!” How great was the cruelty of the treacherous, who desired not only to kill the innocent man but to kill him by the worst kind of death—that is, by crucifixion! Those hanging on the wood, crucified and fastened by nails to the wood through hands and feet, were killed by a prolonged death and remained alive for a long time on the cross—not because a longer life was chosen, but because death itself was prolonged, so that the pain might not end too quickly. But he, through that most grievous death, destroyed every death. It was grievous only to the Jews who did not understand. For it had been chosen by the Lord. He was to have that very cross as his sign, and he was to set that cross, after conquering the devil, upon the foreheads of the faithful as a trophy, so that the Apostle might say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. V).

[Col. 0613A] But he said to them a third time: “What evil has this man done? I find no cause of death in him. I will therefore chastise him and release him.” By this chastisement Pilate sought with all his might to satisfy the people, so that they would not rage to the point of crucifying the Savior. He did not merely present him to them at their request, but also offered him to the desires of the wicked by mocking and scourging him. The words of the Evangelist John and the very pillar to which he was bound bear witness to this. He who is accustomed to loose those in chains subjected his limbs, filled with God, to the blows of scourges. That pillar, placed in the Church on Mount Zion, still displays to those who see it unmistakable traces of the Lord’s blood. But although Pilate does these things, observe what the insatiable fury of the sacrilegious desires.

But they persisted with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified, [Col. 0613B] and their voices grew stronger. They saw that the whole accusation they had brought against the Lord had been rendered void by Pilate’s repeated and careful questioning. At last, therefore, the shameless men turned to mere petitions, so that what they had been unable to accomplish by accusation and apparent argument they might now achieve by demands and shouting. Ecclesiastical history sufficiently demonstrates that the persecutors of the blessed martyrs afterward followed this same order of savagery.

And Pilate adjudged that their petition should be granted. He released for them the one who had been sent into prison because of murder and sedition, whom they had requested. But he handed Jesus over to their will. The seditious robber and author of murders was released to the Jewish people—that is, the devil, who long ago, because of the guilt of pride, had been driven from his homeland of light and sent into the prison of darkness. Therefore the Jews cannot have peace, because they preferred to choose the leader of seditions rather than the Lord. Since Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the father” or “son of the master,” he can bear the type of Antichrist, whom those to whom it is said, “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII), will prefer to the true Son of God. The Antichrist is called the son of the devil not because he is born from him, but because, like other sinners, he imitates him.

And as they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, coming from the countryside, and laid upon him the cross to carry behind Jesus. The Evangelist John relates that the Lord himself carried his cross. [Col. 0613D] Hence it is understood that the Lord first carried the cross, and afterward it was laid upon Simon, whom they perhaps encountered as they were going out—an arrangement entirely fitting the order of the mystery. For he suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps (1 Pet. II). Simon is rightly described as carrying the cross behind Jesus, in accordance with his command: “Let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matt. XVI). And because this Simon is said to have been not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian—and Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles—he rightly represents the peoples of the Gentiles. Once strangers and foreigners to the covenants, they are now, by obeying faith, citizens and members of God’s household. And, as it is said elsewhere: “Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII). Hence Simon is aptly interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.”

Nor should it be passed over that Simon is reported to have come from the countryside. In Greek, the countryside is called πάγος (*pagos*), from which the name “pagans” is derived, because they are alien from the city of God and, as it were, ignorant of urban conduct. But Simon, going out from the *pagus*, carries the cross behind Jesus when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s passion.

A great crowd of the people and of women who were weeping and lamenting him followed him. But Jesus turned to them and said: The great crowd followed the Lord’s cross, but not with one and the same mind. The people followed so that, since they had obtained his death, they might gaze joyfully upon him as he died; the women followed so that they might mourn the one whom they desired to live, now destined to die, dying, and dead. The lamentation was not attributed only to women because an innumerable company of believing men was not also deeply saddened by his passion, but because the female sex, as though regarded as more contemptible, could more freely display before the chief priests and magistrates present what it thought against them. But because the Lord knows those who are his, he passed over the crowd that was raging and turned his eyes and face toward the women who loved and lamented him, saying:

“Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” “Do not,” he says, “lament me as I die, for my swift resurrection can undo death, and my death will destroy both every death and the author of death itself. Rather, wash yourselves and your offspring with streams of fitting tears, lest, in vengeance for my cross, you be condemned with the treacherous to eternal death.” It should be noted that when he calls them daughters of Jerusalem, women not only from Galilee who had come with him but also citizens of that same city are shown to have adhered to him.

Even now, as though Jesus were being sacrificed, a twofold crowd follows him: some read, hear, and recall the history of his passion as though it were a story deserving laughter; others do so with eyes suitably filled with tears. Some receive the mysteries of his flesh and blood as though they were cheap and ordinary foods; others receive them with a breast worthy of so great a reality. But when the Lord looks upon a contrite and humbled heart, he immediately adds the grace of saving compunction, through which, as a more gracious, sweeter, and gentler consoler, he bestows comfort.

“For behold, the days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’” He signifies the days of the coming siege and captivity by the Romans.
