Concerning these, among other things, he had earlier said to the disciples: “Then let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains.” And shortly afterward: “But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing infants in those days” (Matt. XXIV). For it is natural, when captivity is imminent and hostile devastation rages through the fields and cities, that all who can escape seek out lofty or hidden places in which they may conceal themselves. Josephus specifically relates that, with the Romans pressing upon them, the Jews eagerly sought the caves of the mountains and the caverns of the hills. He even testifies that, when the fortification of the destroyed city of Jotapata was taken, he was betrayed, discovered, and captured by the enemy in a cave with forty companions.

It may also be understood additionally that by calling the barren and childless blessed he refers to those who have castrated themselves, in either sex, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. They say to the mountains and hills, “Fall upon us” and “Cover us,” when, remembering their own weakness at the onset of temptation, they seek protection through the examples, counsels, and prayers of the exalted—whether through virginity, martyrdom, or any other virtue of the saints.

“For if they do these things with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?” The green wood signifies himself and his elect; the dry signifies the ungodly and sinners. “If, therefore,” he says, “I who have committed no sin, who am rightly called the tree of life, and who produce the twelve fruits of grace each month, do not leave the world without the fire of suffering, what torment do you think awaits those who, empty of fruits, do not even fear to consign the tree of life itself to the flames? If judgment is now beginning with the household of God, and all who desire to live godly in Christ suffer persecution, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?”

Two others, evildoers, were also led with him to be put to death, so that what he said might be fulfilled: “And he was numbered with the transgressors.” But he was numbered with transgressors in death so that he might justify transgressors in the resurrection. Though he was in the form of God, he became human for the sake of human beings, so that he might give human beings the power to become children of God (John I).

And after they came to the place called Calvary, there they crucified him. Outside the city of Jerusalem and outside the gate were places where the heads of condemned persons were cut off, and they took their name, Calvary, from the decapitated. The Lord was crucified there so that where previously there had been a field of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised. And just as for the salvation of all he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so he was crucified as though guilty among the guilty, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more.

Sedulius beautifully expressed in verses how the Lord was placed upon the cross and what royal symbolism the position of that most sacred body contained:

> So that no one may fail to know that the form of the cross is worthy of worship,  
> Which, in glorious triumph, bore the Lord by a mighty design.  
> From it the four regions of the square world are gathered together.  
> The splendid East shines from the crown of its Author;  
> The stars of the West caress the soles of the sacred feet.  
> The right hand holds the North; the left raises the central axis;  
> And all nature lives from the limbs of the Creator,  
> While Christ, embraced by the cross, rules the whole world on every side.

The Apostle also describes the moral figure of the holy cross when he says: “Rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Eph. III). By breadth he signifies the good works of love; by length, perseverance in holy conduct to the end; by height, hope of heavenly rewards; and by depth, the inscrutable judgments of God, from which this grace comes to human beings.

These things are fitted to the mystery of the cross as follows. Breadth is understood as the transverse wood on which the hands are extended, signifying works. Length is understood from the transverse wood down to the ground, where the whole crucified body appears to stand, signifying persistence—that is, remaining with long-suffering endurance. Height is understood from the transverse wood upward to the part that projects toward the head, signifying expectation of heavenly things, so that those good works and perseverance in them may not be thought to be undertaken for the sake of earthly and temporal benefits from God, but rather for the sake of what faith, working through love, hopes for above: the eternal reward. Depth is that part of the wood which lies hidden, fixed deep in the earth, from which everything that projects upward rises, just as from God’s hidden will a person is called to participate in so great a grace—one in this way, another in that. The love of Christ that surpasses knowledge is found there where that peace exists which surpasses all understanding.

And there were robbers, one on his right and the other on his left. The robbers crucified on either side with the Lord signify those who, under faith in and confession of Christ, undertake either the contest of martyrdom or the disciplines of stricter continence. But all who undertake these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory are truly designated by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those, however, who renounce the world either with regard to human praise or from any less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and deeds of the blaspheming robber on the left. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body so that I may be burned, and give all my possessions to feed the poor, and do many other things, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). But blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).

But Jesus was saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Because Luke chose to write of Christ’s priesthood under the figure of the calf, it is fitting that in his Gospel the Lord, in the manner of a priest, intercedes for his persecutors and, by the same office, opens the gate of paradise to the confessing robber. For it must not be thought that he prayed these things to the Father in vain; rather, he obtained through his prayer what he prayed for in those who believed after his passion.

It should certainly be noted that he offered prayers to the Father not for those who, inflamed by the goads of envy and pride, preferred to crucify the one whom they understood to be the Son of God rather than confess him, but for those who, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge (Rom. X), did not know what they were doing (Luke XXIII). The apostle John also says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V). Imitate your Lord, therefore, and intercede for your enemies. If you cannot yet do so, at least beware of presuming to pray against them. Thus, strengthened by daily progress, you will eventually reach, with the Lord’s help, the point where you can intercede even for them.

[Col. 0617A] Dividing his garments, they cast lots. And the people stood watching. The Evangelist John explains this more fully: the soldiers divided the other things into four parts, according to their number, but for the tunic, which was seamless and woven from the top throughout, they cast lots. The Lord’s four-part garment signified his fourfold Church, spread throughout the entire world, which consists of four regions and is distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those regions. That tunic, assigned by lot, signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of love. For if love, according to the Apostle, has the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments (Eph. III), it is rightly said that the garment signifying it was woven from above. [Col. 0617B] And what else is commended by the casting of lots except the grace of God? Thus it comes to all through the one thing, when the lot is assigned to all, because God’s grace also comes to all in unity; and when the lot is cast, the matter is decided not by anyone’s person or merits but by God’s hidden judgment.

The rulers also mocked him, saying: “He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one.” Even unwillingly, the rulers and the people of the Jews confess that he saved others. Thus your own judgment condemns you. For the one who saved others could certainly have saved himself if he had wished. “Let him save himself,” they say, “if this is the Christ of God’s choice.” Rather, he did not wish to save himself by descending from the cross precisely because he is the Christ chosen by God. For he came to be crucified for us, and therefore neglected to save himself by descending from the cross, because by dying he undertook to save, together with the other sinners, even those who crucified him.

The soldiers also mocked him, coming near and offering him vinegar, saying: “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself.” The Jews themselves were vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. With this vinegar, so to speak, the soldiers gave the Lord to drink—the Lord whom they had handed over to death at the Jews’ instigation. It should be noted that the Jews, blaspheming the title of Christ and Son of God entrusted to them by the authority of Scripture, mock him. The soldiers, however, being ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not Christ, God’s chosen one, but the king of the Jews.

There was also an inscription written above him in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters [Col. 0617D]: “This is the King of the Jews.” Fittingly, the title testifying that Christ is king is placed not beneath but above the cross, because although on the cross he suffered for us in the weakness of his humanity, above the cross he nevertheless shone with the majesty of a king. Appropriately also, because he is both king and priest, when he offered to the Father the excellent sacrifice of his flesh upon the altar of the cross, he displayed as well the dignity of the royal title with which he was endowed, so that it might be known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross he did not lose his kingdom, but rather confirmed and strengthened it. Hence, after the Apostle had described the disgrace of the cross, he added: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every [Col. 0618A] name,” etc. (Philippians II). For the fact that this name was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin is what the same Apostle adds afterward: “And every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid.). As far as the literal sense is concerned, these three languages stood out there above the others: Hebrew on account of the Jews who gloried in the Law, Greek on account of the wise among the nations, and Latin on account of the Romans, who at that time ruled many, indeed almost all, nations. Whether they wish it or not, therefore, the whole kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of the divine Law testify that Jesus is the King of the Jews—that is, the ruler of those who believe in and confess God.

One of the criminals who were hanging there was blaspheming him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself [Col. 0618B] and us.” Some may perhaps wonder how the other Evangelists say that the criminals who were crucified with him reviled him. One of them indeed reviled him; according to Luke’s testimony, the other looked upon him and believed in God. But let us understand that, when briefly touching upon this passage, they used the plural number for the singular. Thus in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read in the plural: “They closed the mouths of lions” (Hebrews XI), although Daniel alone is understood to be meant. Likewise it says in the plural: “They were sawn asunder” (ibid.), although tradition relates this of Isaiah alone. In the Psalm also, where it says, “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together as one” (Psalm II), the plural number is used for the singular, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles. For they understood “kings” with reference to Herod and “rulers” [Col. 0618C] with reference to Pilate, who applied the testimony of that same Psalm. What, for example, is more usual than for someone to say, “The peasants insult me,” even if only one is insulting him?

But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.” And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Who would not marvel at this criminal’s mind? Rather, who could worthily marvel at it, or venerate it with fitting thanksgiving, when it was assisted by the Lord’s grace? Nails had fastened his hands and feet to the cross; nothing in him remained free from punishment except his heart and tongue. Under God’s inspiration, he offered him everything [Col. 0618D] that he found free within himself, so that, in accordance with what is written, “he might believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans X). The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: “But now abide faith, hope, and charity” (1 Corinthians XIII). Filled suddenly with grace, the criminal both received all these virtues and preserved them on the cross. He had faith, for he believed that the Lord would reign even though he saw him dying alongside himself. He had hope, for he requested entrance into his kingdom. He also vigorously maintained charity in his death, for he reproved his brother and fellow criminal, who was dying for a similar crime, for his wickedness, and proclaimed to him the life which he himself had come to know. He who came to the cross as such a man because of guilt—behold what sort of man he leaves the cross by grace. He confessed the Lord [Col. 0619A] whom he saw dying with him in human weakness, at the very time when the apostles were denying him, though they had seen him perform miracles by divine power.

And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise.” A most beautiful example for seeking conversion: forgiveness is released to the criminal so quickly, and grace is more abundant than the prayer. For the Lord always grants more than is requested. The man was asking that the Lord remember him when he came into his kingdom. But the Lord said: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” For to be with Christ is life, because where Christ is, there is the kingdom. Some people relate the two criminals crucified with the Lord to the two kinds of baptized people. For “all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized [Col. 0619B] into his death” (Romans VI). Both were similarly crucified, but one became worse through blasphemies on the cross, while the other became a martyr through his confession. Because through baptism, by which we are cleansed although we are sinners, some are crowned when they praise God, who suffered in the flesh, with faith, hope, and charity; others, when they refuse to possess either the faith or the works of baptism, are deprived of the gift they received.

Now it was about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour, and the sun was darkened. The brightest light of the world withdrew its rays, lest it either see the Lord hanging there or allow the impious blasphemers to enjoy its light. It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was withdrawing from the center of the world—but at dawn, that is, when the sun had already risen, he celebrated the mysteries of his resurrection. [Col. 0619C] By the time of day he signified what he displayed through the effect of his work: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Romans IV). For when Adam sinned, it is written that he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden “at the evening breeze” (Genesis III). “After midday,” therefore, refers to the light of faith having declined; “at the breeze,” to the fervor of charity having cooled; and he was heard walking because he had withdrawn from the sinful human being. The order of reason therefore required that, at the same hour of the day in which he had then closed paradise against the sinning Adam, the Lord should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant criminal.

And the veil of the temple was torn in the middle. This happened as the Lord expired, as Matthew and Mark testify, [Col. 0619D] but Luke narrated it in advance. For, wishing to join one miracle to another, after saying, “The sun was darkened,” he immediately considered it necessary to add: “And the veil of the temple was torn in the middle.” The veil of the temple is torn so that the secrets of the covenant and all the mysteries of the Law, which had previously been concealed, might appear and pass over to the people of the nations. For previously it had been said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm LXXV). But now: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and over all the earth,” he says, “is your glory” (Psalm LVI). And in the Gospel he had first said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew X). But after the Passion: “Go and teach all nations” (Matthew XXVIII).

And Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, said: “Father, into your [Col. 0620A] hands I commend my spirit”; and saying this, he expired. By invoking the Father, he declares that he is the Son of God. By commending his spirit, he indicates not a failure of his power but confidence in the same authority which he shares with the Father. For he loves to give glory to the Father, so that he may build us up to give glory to the Creator. Accordingly, he commends his spirit to the Father, in accordance with what he says in another Psalm with a joyful heart and lips exulting in the hope of rising again: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm XV).

When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying: “Truly this man was righteous.” It was not the centurion alone who glorified God, but also the soldiers who were with him guarding Jesus—as Matthew writes—who, [Col. 0620B] when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew XXVII). What blindness, then, among the Jews, who, despite so many deeds of power performed by the Lord and so many signs appearing at his death, refused to believe, and in their insensibility surpassed the Gentiles in scorning either to glorify or to fear God. Thus, rightly, the Church’s faith is represented by the centurion: when the veil of heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death, while the synagogue remained silent, the Church immediately affirmed Jesus as both truly a righteous man and truly the Son of God. For even the sum of one hundred, which—as was mentioned above—passes in the bending of the fingers from the left hand to the right, most fittingly corresponds to the mysteries and faith of the Church, to which the Gospel has been entrusted in place of the Law and the heavenly kingdom promised [Col. 0620C] in place of the riches of the earth.

And the whole crowd of those who had gathered together for this spectacle and saw what was happening returned, striking their breasts. The striking of their breasts, since it is a sign of repentance and mourning, can be understood in two ways. Either they were grieving that the one whose life they had loved had been unjustly killed, or they trembled because they remembered that they had brought about his death, while he was more greatly glorified in death. But whether this, or that, or both causes compelled different and dissenting persons in the crowd to beat their breasts, the distinction between nation and nation should be noted. For the Gentiles, fearing God as Christ died, glorify him with an open voice of confession; the Jews, merely striking their breasts, return home [Col. 0620D] in silence.

Now all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee were watching these things. This is what the Lord himself explains in the Psalm, recounting the sequence of his Passion and complaining to the Father: “You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery” (Psalm LXXXVII).

And behold, a man named Joseph, who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man. He had not consented to their plan and actions. He is called a member of the council because he belonged to the order of the curia and administered the office of the curia; he is also commonly called a *curialis*, because he carried out civic duties.

He was from the city of Arimathea in Judea, and he too was awaiting the kingdom of God. Arimathea is itself Ramathaim [Col. 0621A], the city of Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Thannitis, near Diospolis.

He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. This Joseph is praised as having been a man of great dignity in the world but of greater merit before God, so that through the justice of his merits he might be worthy to bury the Lord’s body, and through the nobility of his worldly power he might be able to receive that same body. For not just any unknown person could approach the governor and obtain the body of a crucified man.

And after taking it down, he wrapped it in a linen cloth and placed him in a tomb hewn out of rock, in which no one had yet been placed. From the simple burial of the Lord, the ambition of the rich is condemned: they cannot be without riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding [Col. 0621B], we can also perceive this: the one who receives Jesus with a pure mind wraps him in clean linen. He is placed in a new tomb so that, after the resurrection, while the other bodies remained there, no one might pretend that someone else had risen. The tomb is fittingly remembered as having been hewn from rock, so that, if it had been built from many stones, people might say that, after the foundations of the tomb had been undermined, the body had been secretly removed. Alternatively: the Lord alone is enclosed in the tomb, so that his distinctive burial—that is, one unlike ours—might signify a distinctive resurrection, just as the other mysteries of his dispensation differed from the frailty of our nature. For the old human being also appeared, but he was conceived and born of a virgin mother. He was tempted in every respect, but in likeness and without sin. He died, but in the manner [Col. 0621C] he himself willed. He was buried, but for as long as he willed. He was raised, but when he willed. This is therefore what he says: “I am alone until I pass over” (Psalm CXL). And elsewhere, concerning his distinctive burial: “In peace I will sleep and rest together, for you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope” (Psalm IV)—that is, while the resurrection of the other mortals is reserved for the end, you promised that I, by a unique gift, would rise from the dead on the third day.

It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was dawning. *Parasceve* is interpreted as “preparation.” The Jews who lived among the Greeks used this name for the sixth day of the week, which we now call Friday, because on that day they prepared what would be [Col. 0621D] necessary for the Sabbath. In accordance with the former command concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” etc. (Exodus XVI). But Jews who lived among the Romans more commonly called it in Latin *coenam puram* (“the pure supper”). Since, therefore, the human being was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—whence he also commanded that it be called the Sabbath, that is, rest—it was rightly on that same sixth day that the Lord, by being crucified, fulfilled the mystery of the restoration of humanity. Hence, when he had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished” (John XIX)—that is, the whole work of the sixth day, which I undertook for the resurrection of the world, is completed. But on the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. [Col. 0622A] Here an example of our devotion also shines before us: in this sixth age of the world, we must suffer for the Lord and be, as it were, crucified to the world; in the seventh age—that is, when one pays the debt of death—the bodies should remain in the tombs, but the souls should remain with the Lord in hidden peace, and after good works should rest, until at last, when the eighth age comes, the bodies themselves, purified by the resurrection, receive together with the souls the incorruption of the eternal inheritance. Hence, beautifully, the seventh day is not said in Genesis to have had an evening, because the rest of souls which now exists in that age is not to be consumed by any sorrow but is to be increased by the fuller joy of the future resurrection.

The women who had come with him from [Col. 0622B] Galilee followed, saw the tomb, and observed how his body had been placed. Above we read that all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him. When these acquaintances of Jesus returned to their homes after his corpse had been laid away, only the women who loved him more closely followed the funeral procession, wishing to see how he would be placed, so that at the appropriate time they might offer him the gift of their devotion. Even to this day holy women do the same on the day of Preparation: humble souls, aflame with a greater love for the Savior the more conscious they are of their own fragility, diligently attend in this age to the traces of his Passion, in which future rest must be prepared; and, if they are perhaps able to imitate it, they carefully consider in what manner that same Passion was completed.

[Col. 0622C] And returning, they prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they kept silence according to the commandment. The commandment was that the Sabbath rest should be observed from evening to evening. Therefore the devout women, after the Lord had been buried, remained occupied in preparing the ointments for as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset. They had done this not only on the day of Preparation; after the Sabbath had passed—that is, after the sun had set—as soon as permission to work returned, they bought spices so that, coming in the morning, they might anoint his body, as the Evangelist Mark testifies. For they did not wish to approach the tomb on the evening of the Sabbath, when night was already beginning. After inspecting the Lord’s burial, they return and prepare spices and ointments [Col. 0622D]; so those who have read, heard, and remembered the Lord’s Passion immediately turn to performing works of virtue with which Christ is pleased. On the Sabbath, having prepared the spices, they remain silent, coming after the Sabbath with gifts to the Lord, when, after the Preparation of the present life has ended, they joyfully await blessed rest, so that, when the time of the resurrection appears, they may meet Christ with the fragrance of spiritual actions, as though with spices.

## CHAPTER XXIV

But on the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came to the tomb, carrying the spices they had prepared. “One day after the Sabbath,” or “the first day after the Sabbath,” is the first day following the Sabbath; Christian usage calls this day the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection. The fact that the women came to the tomb very early in the morning shows, according to the [Col. 0623A] historical sense, the great fervor of their love in seeking and finding the Lord; according to the mystical sense, it gives us an example of approaching the Lord’s most holy body with an illuminated face and the darkness of vices cast away. For that venerable tomb also bore the figure of the Lord’s altar, on which the mysteries of his flesh and blood are customarily celebrated. Hence ecclesiastical tradition holds that these mysteries ought to be consecrated not in silk or dyed cloth but, after the manner of the linen cloth in which Joseph wrapped him, in pure linen. Just as he offered for us to death the true substance of an earthly and mortal nature, so we too, in remembrance of that fearful and venerable sacrament, should place upon the altar linen produced from the earth, white, and chastened by many kinds, as it were, of mortification. [Col. 0623B] The spices brought by the women signify the sweetness of the fragrance of virtues and prayers with which we ought to approach the altar. Hence, in his Apocalypse, when John had described golden bowls in the hands of angels—namely, pure consciences in the hearts of the elect—full of spices, he added an explanation, saying: “Which are the prayers of the saints.”

And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, and when they entered they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. Matthew sufficiently explained how the stone was rolled away by an angel. But the rolling away of the stone mystically indicates the disclosure of the mysteries that had been concealed under the veil of the letter. For the Law was written on stone. When its covering is removed, the dead body of the Lord is not found, but he is proclaimed alive. For even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way.

And while they were perplexed in mind about this, behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments. They were perplexed in mind because they were astonished that a stone of such immense size had been rolled away, and they grieved that a body worthy of such exceptional veneration had not been found. Just as, when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, angels immediately came to minister to him after victory had been completed, so, after the Savior had suffered in the flesh, angels came after the struggles of death had been overcome; they announced the glory of the triumphant one not only by words of consolation but also by their shining appearance. As angels are read to have stood beside the Savior’s body when it was placed in the tomb, [Col. 0623C] so they should also be believed [Col. 0623D] to stand beside the celebration of the mysteries of that most sacred body at the time of consecration, as the Apostle warns that women should have a veil in the church “because of the angels” (1 Corinthians XI).

As they were afraid and bowed their faces toward the ground, they said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen.” “Do not seek,” they say, “among the dead”—that is, in the tomb, which is properly a place of the dead—the one who has already risen from the dead to life. We too, following the example of women devoted to God, whenever we enter the church and approach the heavenly mysteries, whether because of the presence of the angelic power or because of reverence for the sacred offering, ought to enter with complete humility and fear. We bow our faces toward the ground in the sight of the angels [Col. 0624A] when, contemplating what the eternal joys of the citizens above are, we humbly remember that we are dust and earth. Thus blessed Abraham said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis XVIII). It should also be noted that the holy women are said not to have fallen to the ground in the presence of the angels, but to have bowed their faces toward the ground. We do not read that any of the saints, at the time of the Lord’s resurrection, prostrated himself on the ground in worship before either the Lord himself or the angels appearing to him. Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed: in memory of the Lord’s resurrection and in hope of our own, we pray on every Sunday and throughout the entire period of the Pentecost season not with knees bent but with faces bowed toward the ground.

[Col. 0624B] “Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying: ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and rise again on the third day.’” On the third day the Lord celebrated the triumph of his resurrection, as we learn from this passage, because he had foretold it among the disciples not only to the men but also to the women who followed him. For on the day of Preparation, giving up his spirit at the ninth hour and being buried in the evening, he rose in the morning of the first day after the Sabbath, as the Evangelist Mark clearly indicates. Therefore it was not without reason that he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, since he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. For he came to us, who were held by the death of spirit and flesh; he brought to us his one death—that is, the death of the flesh—and by receiving our two deaths [Col. 0624C], he dissolved them. If he himself had taken on both, he would have freed us from neither; but mercifully he accepted one and justly condemned both. He brought his single death to bear upon our double death, and by dying he subdued our double death.

And they remembered his words. The women who stood in the Lord’s tomb and remembered the words he had previously spoken about his dispensation provide us with a model, so that, while celebrating the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, we may always remember with worthy veneration not only that blessed Passion but also his resurrection from the dead and the glory of his ascension into heaven.

And leaving the tomb, they announced all these things to the eleven and to all the others. Just as at the beginning the woman was the author of guilt for the man, while the man [Col. 0624D] carried out the error, while the man carried out the error, so now she who had first tasted death first saw the resurrection; and, so that she might not bear among men the disgrace of perpetual condemnation, she who had transmitted guilt to the man also transmitted grace.

Now it was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary of James, and the other women who were with them who told these things to the apostles. Mary Magdalene is the sister of Lazarus, who anointed the Lord with ointment. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, concerning whom we read above. Mary of James was the mother of James the younger and Joseph, as the Evangelist Mark says; she was the sister of the Lord’s mother, and hence James himself deserved to be called the Lord’s brother.

And these words appeared before them like nonsense, and they did not believe them. The fact that the disciples were slow to believe the Lord’s resurrection was not so much [Col. 0625A] their weakness as our future firmness, if I may put it that way. For the resurrection itself was demonstrated to them, while they doubted, by many proofs. When we recognize these things as we read them, what else happens except that we are strengthened by their doubt?

But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; and stooping down, he saw only the linen cloths lying there, and he departed, wondering within himself at what had happened. Luke briefly mentions Peter’s running, but John explains more fully how it happened, saying that the disciple whom Jesus loved also ran with Peter, thereby indicating himself. Hence the question arises how Luke says of Peter, “And stooping down, he saw only the linen cloths lying there” (Luke XXIV), when John seems rather to indicate that he himself did this, while Peter, entering the tomb [Col. 0625B], saw not only the linen cloths but also the cloth that had been over his head. But it should be understood that Peter first, stooping down, saw what Luke mentions and John passes over; afterward he entered in order to examine the interior more carefully, entering before John himself went in.

And behold, two of them were going that same day to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus, and they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened. A *stadium*, by which the Greeks, according to what they say, measure the distances of roads, is one-eighth of a mile; therefore sixty stadia signify seven thousand five hundred paces. This distance of the journey appropriately suits those who, certain about the Savior’s death and burial but doubtful about his resurrection, were [Col. 0625C] walking. For who would doubt that the resurrection, which took place after the seventh day, corresponds to the number eight? The disciples, therefore, who were walking and speaking about the Lord completed the sixth mile of their journey because they grieved that he, who had lived without reproach, had reached the death which he suffered on the sixth day of the week. They also completed the seventh because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. But they traversed only half of the eighth, because they did not yet fully believe in the glory of the resurrection that had already been celebrated. Emmaus itself is the notable city of Nicopolis in Palestine, which, after Judea had been purged under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was restored and, along with its status, changed its name.

[Col. 0625D] And it happened that, while they were talking and questioning one another, Jesus himself approached and walked with them. As they spoke about him, the Lord approached and accompanied them, both to kindle faith in his resurrection in their minds and to show, by the hidden presence of his majesty, that he would always fulfill what he had promised. For “where two or three are gathered in my name, there,” he says, “I am in the midst of them.”

But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him. And he said to them: “What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?” The Lord did appear, but he did not show them an appearance by which they could recognize him. Thus the Lord effected outwardly in the eyes of the body what was taking place inwardly in the eyes of their hearts. For within themselves they both loved [Col. 0626A] and doubted; outwardly the Lord was present with them, yet did not reveal who he was. To those speaking about him he presented his presence, but to those doubting about him he concealed the appearance by which he could be recognized.

And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?” They thought him a stranger because they did not recognize his face. But in truth he was also a stranger to them, since the glory of the resurrection he had already received was far removed from the fragility of their nature. He was a stranger to them because he still remained outside their faith, since they did not yet know of his resurrection.

And he said to them: “What things?” And they said to him: “About Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.” They confess him to be a great [Col. 0626B] prophet, but they remain silent about the Son of God—either because they did not yet believe perfectly, or because they were concerned lest they fall into the hands of the Jews who were persecuting them. They did not know who the person was with whom they were speaking, and so they concealed what they had truly believed.

“And how the chief priests and our rulers handed him over to condemnation to death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” They were walking sadly with good reason, because in a certain sense they were accusing themselves: they had hoped for redemption in the one whom they had already seen dead, and they did not believe that he would rise. Above all, they grieved that he had been killed without guilt, because they knew him to be innocent.

“And now, in addition to all these things, today is the third day since [Col. 0626C] these things happened. But some women from among us also terrified us. They were at the tomb before daylight, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.” They are said rightly to have terrified those whose minds they could see were more filled with the grief caused by the Lord’s body not being found than with the joy by which they might have been refreshed through the angels’ announcement of his resurrection.

“And some of our people went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but they did not find him.” Although Luke said above that Peter ran to the tomb, and now represents Cleophas as saying that some of them ran to the tomb, it is understood that he is testifying that two went [Col. 0626D] to the tomb. He mentioned Peter alone at first because Mary had announced it first to him.

And he said to them: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. At this point we are compelled not by any need to interpret Scripture but by a twofold need to humble ourselves, since we have neither been instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought nor devoted ourselves as diligently as is fitting to fulfill what we may perhaps have learned. For if Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ, and of his entering into his glory through the narrow passage of the Passion, [Col. 0627A] how can those who, according to the measure of their strength, neither investigate how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor desire to reach the glory they wish to have with Christ through the passions of tribulations boast that they are Christians?

And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended to go farther. But they urged him, saying: “Stay with us, because it is toward evening, and the day is already declining.” And he entered with them. The simple truth did nothing deceitful; rather, in saying that “he pretended to go farther,” Scripture shows that he presented himself bodily to the disciples as he was in their minds. They were being tested to see whether those who did not yet love him as God could at least love him as a stranger. But because those with whom [Col. 0627B] the truth walked could not be strangers to charity, they invited him to their lodging as though he were a stranger. Why, however, do we say that they invited him, when it is written: “And they urged him”? From this example it is clearly gathered that strangers should not only be invited to lodging but also compelled to accept it.

And it happened that, as he reclined with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. They did not recognize him in the exposition of sacred Scripture, but they recognized him in the breaking of bread. They were not illuminated by hearing God’s commandments; they were illuminated by doing them. For it is written: “It is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified” (Romans II). Therefore, whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already been able to understand.

[Col. 0627C] And he vanished from their sight. And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” “I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). The Lord sent fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he set the hearts of flesh aflame. The earth burns when the heart of flesh, previously cold in its own pleasures, leaves behind the desires of the present age and is kindled with love of God. “Was not our heart burning within us,” they say, “while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” The soul catches fire from the word it hears; the coldness of the body withdraws; the mind becomes anxious with heavenly desire and alien to earthly cravings. True love, when it fills the soul, [Col. 0627D] torments it with tears. Yet while it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by the very torments it suffers; it delights to hear the heavenly commandments, and as it is instructed by each commandment, it is inflamed as though by an equal number of torches.

And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon. There was already a report that Jesus had risen, made by the women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had already appeared. This is what these two found them saying when they came to Jerusalem. It is therefore possible that, out of fear, they had previously been unwilling on the road to say that they had heard he had risen, since the women had said only that they had seen angels. Not knowing with whom they were speaking, they could rightly have been anxious lest, by spreading reports indiscriminately [Col. 0628A] about Christ’s resurrection, they should fall into the hands of the Jews. Among all the men, therefore, the Lord is understood to have appeared first to Peter, at least among all those whom the four Evangelists and the Apostle Paul mention. For Paul speaks to the Corinthians about the Lord: that he was buried, that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, and afterward to the eleven.

And they recounted what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. Besides the fact that, because of the condition of their minds—which still did not understand that Christ had to die and rise—their eyes suffered something similar, not because truth deceived them but because they were unable to perceive the truth and supposed something other than what was real, this also happened for the sake [Col. 0628B] of a certain mystery: it was done so that another likeness might be shown to them in him, and so that they would recognize him only in the breaking of bread. Thus no one might think that he had recognized Christ if he were not a participant in his body—that is, in the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: “One bread, one body, though we are many” (Romans XII). When he gave them the blessed bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him. They were opened, of course, for the recognition of him, when the impediment by which they were held, so that they could not recognize him, was removed. We may not implausibly understand this impediment in their eyes to have come from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized; nevertheless, Christ permitted it to remain until the sacrament of the bread, so that it might be understood that, when participation in his body had been received, the enemy’s impediment was removed, and Christ [Col. 0628C] could be recognized.

While they were saying these things, Jesus stood in the midst of them and said to them: “Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid.” John is understood to commemorate this appearance of the Lord after the resurrection, speaking as follows: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you,’” and so forth. But when John says that the apostle Thomas was not then with them, whereas according to Luke the two of them—one of whom was Cleopas—returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, with those who were with them, it must undoubtedly be understood that Thomas had gone out before the Lord appeared to them while they were saying these things.

[Col. 0628D] But they were troubled and terrified, and supposed that they saw a spirit. This first thought arose in the hearts of the apostles—the very thought that the Manichaean heretics suspect and believe concerning Christ: that he did not possess true flesh, but was a spirit. Those Manichaeans, indeed, never believe that Jesus was a man. The disciples, however, knew him as a man, having spent so long a time in his company. But after he died, when would they believe that what had been able to die could be resurrected? He therefore appeared to their eyes as one whom they knew. And since they did not believe that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day, they thought that they saw a spirit. This error of the apostles is the sect of the Manichaeans.

When these objections are brought against them, they usually answer in this way: “What evil do we believe? Because we believe Christ to be God, we believe him to have been a spirit; we do not believe him to have been flesh. Spirit is better than flesh. We believe what is better and refuse to believe what is worse.” If there is nothing evil in this statement, let Jesus leave his disciples in this error. What evil, too, did the disciples believe? They believed Christ to be a spirit. They did not think that he was nothing, but that he was a spirit. You suppose that you are endangered by a minor illness; hear the physician’s diagnosis.

And he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” What sort of thoughts, unless false, diseased, and harmful ones? Christ would have lost the fruit of his passion if there were no reality in the resurrection. “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” It is as though a good farmer were saying: “What I planted there, there I shall find—not thorns, which I did not plant.” Let it descend into your heart, because it is from above. But these thoughts did not descend from above; they rose up in the heart itself like harmful grass.

“See my hands and my feet, because it is I myself. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” He deigned to establish the certainty and reality of his resurrection by many and various proofs, in order to build up faith, drive unbelief from the heart, and remove every doubt concerning his resurrection. It would have been little merely to offer himself to their eyes to be seen, unless he also offered himself to their hands to be touched. When he displays his bones and flesh for the disciples to touch, he openly signifies the condition of the true resurrection that has taken place in him and is to take place in us.

For our body in the glory of that resurrection will not be, as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote, intangible and subtler than winds and air. In that glory of the resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the reality of its nature. Nor should the Apostle’s statement be thought to contradict this assertion: “For flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. XV). In this passage the Apostle means by the name “flesh and blood” not the substance of the true body, but the corruption of mortality. He himself subsequently explained this when he said: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (ibid.).

For in Sacred Scripture “flesh” is named in one way according to nature, in another according to guilt, and in another according to the corruption of mortality that resulted from guilt. It is according to nature when it is said: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II), and: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). It is according to guilt when it is said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). It is according to corruptibility when it is written: “And he remembered that they were flesh” (Ps. LXXVII), that is, fragile and mortal. The Psalmist himself makes clear that this is what he designated by the name “flesh,” immediately adding: “A spirit that goes and does not return” (ibid.).

Therefore flesh will not possess the kingdom of God—that is, flesh according to guilt or mortality. Yet flesh will possess the kingdom of God—that is, flesh according to nature. [Col. 0630A] The Lord displayed this flesh after his resurrection to the disciples, to be seen and touched. Concerning it blessed Job, when describing the glory of the resurrection, says: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX). Read the letter of Saint Augustine to Consentium concerning the Lord’s body after the resurrection.

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. Not only his hands and feet, on which the marks of the nails were clearly visible, but, as John attests, he also showed them his side, which had been pierced by the lance. By displaying the scars of his wounds, he might heal the wound of their doubt and unbelief. But just as after the resurrection he deigned to strengthen the disciples’ faith and hope by revealing the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will come displaying both these signs of his passion and the cross itself, thereby confounding the impiety and unbelief of the proud.

He will plainly show to all angels and human beings that he is the very one who died at the hands of the impious and for the impious. They will see—as it is written—“the one whom they pierced,” and “all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Rev. I).

It should certainly be noted that pagans commonly construct a charge at this point and ridicule with foolish chatter the resurrection we hope for. “If your God,” they say, “was unable to heal even the wounds inflicted on him by the Jews, but, as you claim, carried the marks of his scars with him into heaven, with what presumption do you suppose that he will restore your members from the dust intact?”

They should be answered that our God, who was able to raise from the tomb, whenever and however he wished, his flesh—already glorified with perpetual immortality—also raised it in whatever condition he wished. For it does not follow that one who is proved to have done greater things was unable to do lesser ones. Rather, for the sake of the divine economy, he who did the greater refrained from doing the lesser: that is, he who destroyed the kingdoms of death did not wish to erase the signs of death.

First, he did this so that through them he might establish the disciples’ faith in his resurrection. Second, so that, interceding for us with the Father, he might always show what kind of death he endured for the life of mortals. Third, so that, by continually presenting the signs of that death, he might renew for those redeemed by his death how mercifully they were helped, and so that they might never cease to sing the mercies of the Lord forever, but might say, “Those redeemed by the Lord say so, because he is good, because his mercy endures forever.” Finally, so that at the judgment he might declare to the faithless, among their other crimes, how justly they are condemned by displaying the scars of the wounds he received from them.

It is as though some exceptionally brave man, ordered by his king to labor in single combat for the safety of his whole people, were to receive many wounds but nevertheless kill the enemy, strip him of his spoils, and bring victory back to his people. When he was entrusted to a physician for treatment and asked whether he wished to be healed so that no trace of his wounds would remain, or rather so that the scars might remain while all disfigurement and ugliness disappeared entirely, he would answer that he preferred to be healed in such a way that, after recovering his former condition of health and beauty, he might carry with him forever the signs of so great a triumph.

Thus, assuredly, the Lord preferred to carry into heaven, as a perpetual sign of victory, not the wounds of his passion received for us, but their scars, rather than erase them. Yet none of this prejudices our faith in the resurrection, concerning which it is foretold in a true promise: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI).

But while they still did not believe and were marveling because of their joy, he said: “Have you anything here to eat?” To make known the truth of his resurrection, he deigns not only to be touched by the disciples but also to eat with them. He did this not because he needed food after the resurrection, nor to signify that we shall need food in the resurrection for which we hope, but in order by this means to establish the nature of the rising body, lest they should suppose that it was not a body but a spirit, and that he appeared to them not solidly but imaginatively. He ate by power, not by necessity. For the earth thirsting absorbs water in one way, while a burning ray of the sun absorbs it in another. The one does so from need; the other by power.

But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the remains and gave them to them. What are we to believe that the broiled fish signifies, except the Mediator between God and human beings, the man who suffered? He deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race; he wished to be caught in the snare of our death; and, as though by affliction, he was broiled in the time of his passion.

But he who deigned to become a broiled fish in his passion became a honeycomb for us in his resurrection. Or did he who wished the tribulations of his passion to be represented by the broiled fish wish the honeycomb to express both natures in his one person? A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax is divinity in humanity.

The Redeemer indicates this in such a way as to prepare for us who follow him the path of imitation. For behold, he wished to join the honeycomb to the broiled fish in his food, because he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while they experience tribulations here for God’s sake, do not withdraw from the love of inward sweetness. The honeycomb is taken with the broiled fish because those who receive affliction here for the sake of truth are there satisfied with true sweetness.

And he said to them: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you.” That is, when I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are. At that time he had been raised in the same flesh, but he was no longer with them in the same mortality. After he rose, he was with them for forty days—as we read—through the presentation of his bodily presence, but he was not with them in participation in human weakness.

“For it is necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms be fulfilled.” See how he removed every ambiguity. He was seen, he was touched, he ate; it was certainly he himself. Yet, lest he seem to have deceived the human senses in any way, he appealed to the Scriptures. Let the pagans say whatever they wish: “He was a magician; he was able to display himself in this way.” Could a magician, before he was born, have prophesied concerning himself? Produce the Scriptures, because what you see was foreseen; what you behold was foretold. “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. XLIV): hear what was foretold; see what has been fulfilled.

Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.” He offers himself to the eyes to be seen; he offers himself to the hands to be touched. It is little to establish this by the Law; he recalls the Scriptures. And even this is little: he opens their understanding, so that they may understand what they read. Then, after establishing the truth of his body, he establishes the unity of the Church.

“And repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” The rage of the heretics is not hidden in a corner; the Church is spread throughout the whole world. All nations have the Church. Let no one deceive us: she is the true Church, she is the catholic Church. She began at Jerusalem, she reached us, and she is both there and here. For she did not leave there in order to come here. She grew; she did not migrate.

And rightly is this written among the other mysteries of the Lord’s compassion: it was necessary that the ministers of the word, who were to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins in the name of Christ, crucified and raised from the dead, to all nations, should begin from Jerusalem. This was so not only because the utterances of God were entrusted to them, because theirs is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the legislation, and the worship, and the promises, because theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever (Rom. IX), but also so that the nations, entangled in various errors and crimes, might be drawn to hope for the obtaining of pardon by this supreme sign of divine compassion: that even those who crucified the Son of God should see that not merely forgiveness of guilt from the Father but also the joy of eternal life had been granted to them.

“But you are witnesses of these things, and I am sending upon you the promise of my Father.” That the grace of the Holy Spirit is called the Father’s promise is intimated more fully in the Gospel of John and more briefly here, when what follows says:

“But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” Concerning this power, that is, the Holy Spirit, the angel also says to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I). And the Lord himself says elsewhere: “For I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII).

Luke himself also speaks more plainly in the Acts of the Apostles about the promised power from on high and the command to remain in the city. “He commanded them,” he says, “not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which you have heard from my mouth. For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I). And shortly afterward: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses” (ibid.).

It should certainly be noted that there are some whom either lack of completion or age prevents from undertaking the office of preaching, yet haste drives them forward. They should be admonished to consider that the Truth itself, although it could suddenly have strengthened those whom it wished to strengthen, gave an example to those who would follow, so that the incomplete would not presume to preach. After fully instructing the disciples concerning the power of preaching, he immediately added: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

We remain seated in the city if we confine ourselves within the enclosures of our minds, lest by speaking we wander outward, so that when we are perfectly clothed with divine power, we may then go forth from ourselves, as it were, to instruct others also.

He led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it happened that while he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven. Passing over everything that may have been done by him with the disciples during the forty days, he silently joins the final day on which he ascended into heaven to the first day of his resurrection.

Beautifully, as he is about to ascend into heaven, he leads outside to Bethany the disciples whom he is going to bless. First, because of the name of the city, which means “house of obedience.” For he who descended because of the disobedience of the perverse undoubtedly ascended because of the obedience of the converted: “For he died,” as the Apostle says, “for our offenses, and rose again for our justification” (Rom. IV).

Then also because of the location of the same village, or small town, which is said to have been situated on the side of the Mount of Olives. For the house of the obedient Church, worthy of apostolic hospitality, placed the foundations of its faith, hope, and love nowhere other than in the side of that highest mountain, that is, Christ. From this side, opened by the lance, she rejoices that the mysteries of blood and water, by which she is born and nourished together, flowed forth for her. From its most fruitful summit, that is, from the height of his divinity, she longs for the gifts of spiritual anointing and eagerly awaits the promises of perpetual light and peace.

Third, because, as John writes, Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away (John XI). This number, consisting of seven and eight, is suited to the mysteries of the Scriptures and contains either the present and future life, or the Old and New Testaments, or the future Sabbath-rest of souls and the resurrection of the flesh, or certainly some other heavenly and spiritual mystery.

And therefore, rightly, he led those to whom he had opened the knowledge of both Testaments, and whom he had taught the entire rule of living and hoping, fifteen stadia to the place where he would bless them and give them the commandments of teaching. Rightly he separated by fifteen stadia the place of his glorious ascension from the place of his most victorious passion, so that all who desire either to live or to die for him might be strengthened alike by the desire and love both of resting after death and of being raised from the dead at the end.

And they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, worshiping him, and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. After the Lord had ascended into heaven, the disciples, worshiping in the place where his feet had last stood, immediately returned to Jerusalem, because there they had been commanded to await the Father’s promise, which they had heard from the Lord’s mouth. They brought back great joys, rejoicing that their God and Lord, after the triumph of the resurrection, had also entered the heavens.

They remained continually in the temple, praising and blessing God, so that in the place of prayer, amid devotions of praise, they might await the promised coming of the Holy Spirit with hearts ready and prepared in every way.

Let us also, following the example of the disciples, after celebrating at Jerusalem—the vision of peace—the solemnities of the Lord’s passion and resurrection, soon seek the fields of Bethany under Christ’s guidance, so that, with a quiet mind already pacified from every storm of discord, we may be imbued with the mysteries of his flesh and blood. Let us take care to become the house of obedience, following the footsteps of him who, in order to give us a pattern of life, “became obedient unto death” (Phil. II).

For thus we also deserve to be exalted by his daily blessing if, remembering daily his triumphant ascension into heaven, we rest, praising and blessing God, in Jerusalem—that is, in the hoped-for and long-desired vision of heavenly peace—like people waiting for their lord to return from the wedding feast (Luke XII).

Because blessed Luke the evangelist is understood to be represented among the four living creatures of heaven by the calf, by whose sacrifice those chosen for the priesthood were commanded to be initiated—for he undertook to expound the priesthood of Christ more fully than the others—he has most beautifully brought his Gospel, which he began with the ministry of the temple through the priesthood of Zechariah, to completion in the devotion of the temple. There he concluded with the apostles, who were to become ministers of the new priesthood, not in the blood of victims but in the praise and blessing of God. [Col. 0634D] Amen.

[Col. 0633]

# EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF SAINT JOHN (G, S)*

## Commendation of the Author

[Col. 0633D] This is John the evangelist, one of the disciples of God, who was chosen by God as a virgin. God called him away from a wedding, when he wished to marry. In the Gospel a double testimony to his virginity is given: he is said to have been loved by God more than the others, and the Lord commended his mother to him from the cross, so that a virgin might preserve a virgin.

Finally, this is shown more clearly in the Gospel: beginning the work of the incorruptible Word, he alone testifies that the Word became flesh and that the light was not comprehended by the darkness. He places first the sign that God performed at the wedding, so that, by showing what he was, he might demonstrate to readers that, wherever the Lord is invited, the wine of the wedding ought to fail, so that, when the old things have been changed, everything new instituted by Christ might appear.

He wrote this Gospel in Asia, after he had written the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos, so that, just as he set forth the incorruptible Beginning at the start of the canon, an incorruptible end might likewise be supplied through the virgin in the Apocalypse, when Christ says: “I am Alpha and Omega” (α and ω).

This is John who, knowing that the day of his departure had come, summoned his disciples and, revealing Christ in Ephesus through many demonstrations of signs, descended into the place dug out for his burial. After praying, he was laid with his fathers, as free from the sorrow of death as he is found to have been free from the corruption of the flesh.

Nevertheless, he wrote the Gospel after all the others; and this was owed to the Virgin. Yet neither the chronological arrangement of the writers nor the ordering of the books is explained by us one by one, so that, though the desire of the thirsty is deferred, the fruit of labor may be preserved for those who seek, and the doctrine of teaching reserved for God. Amen.

## Summary of the Gospel of Saint John

[Col. 0635]

[Col. 0635B] 1. The Levites of the Pharisees question John. Seeing Jesus, John calls him the Lamb of God, and Andrew says to Peter: “We have found the Messiah.”

2. At the supper Jesus changes water into wine; he drives the money-changers from the temple and says: “Destroy this temple.” He speaks with Nicodemus about baptism, and many other matters.

3. Jesus baptizes in Judea, and John at Aenon. John also says that Christ must increase, while he himself must decrease.

4. Jesus speaks with the Samaritan woman; he says that a prophet is without honor in his own country, and he raises the royal official’s son from death.

5. At the pool of Bethesda he heals a man’s illness of thirty-eight years, and says: “Search the Scriptures”; and: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also.”

[Col. 0635C] 6. Concerning the five loaves and two fish, and how they wished to make him king. Jesus walks upon the sea; he speaks about manna and the heavenly bread; and when disciples withdraw from him, he calls one of the Twelve a devil.

7. Going up into the temple in the middle of the feast of Booths, he teaches many. When some of the crowd have now believed, he cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” The rulers contend with the attendants and with Nicodemus. Concerning the adulterous woman. Jesus proclaims that he is the light of the world.

8. When questioned about himself, Jesus answers that he is the Beginning. That every sinner is a slave, and that Jesus existed before Abraham. He heals the man blind from birth.

9. Concerning the door and the sheepfold; walking in the temple during the feast of the Dedication, he says that he and the Father are one. Concerning the resurrection of Lazarus.

10. Mary anoints Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. Jesus sits upon a donkey; when the Greeks wish to see Jesus, he speaks about the grain of wheat that is cast into the earth. A voice comes from heaven to Jesus, and many of the rulers believe in Jesus but do not confess him because of the Pharisees.

11. He washes the disciples’ feet. He foretells Judas’s betrayal and Peter’s denial, and speaks about the love of the brothers; that he is in the Father and the Father in him; and about observing the commandments of the Spirit, the Paraclete.

12. Concerning the vine and the branches, love, and the promise of the Paraclete; that everything belonging to the Father is his; and the remaining commandments.

13. Jesus commends the disciples to the Father. Jesus is betrayed by Judas. Concerning Pilate’s address to the Jews about Jesus and Barabbas.

14. The passion of Christ, his burial, and his resurrection.

# THE EXPOSITION BEGINS

[Col. 0635]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0635D]

You should know that, among all the pages of divine Scripture, the authority of the Gospel rightly excels, because what the Law and the Prophets foretold as future is shown in the Gospel as given and fulfilled. Among the writers of the Gospels, the blessed John is especially eminent in the depth of divine mysteries. They also report—as is read in ecclesiastical history—that almost until the final period of his life he preached the Gospel in pure speech, without the aid of any written Scripture.

Indeed, from the time of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension until the final years of the reign of Domitian, approximately sixty-five years, he preached the word of God without any writing as an aid. But when he was sent into exile on Patmos by Domitian, who became the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, heretics, taking advantage of the absence of that devout father and bursting into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds deprived of their shepherd, Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists—who denied that Christ existed before Mary—stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse doctrine.

But after Domitian’s death, when John returned to Ephesus with the permission of the devout emperor Nerva, he was compelled by almost all the bishops of Asia at that time and by delegations from many churches to speak more profoundly about Christ’s coeternal divinity with the Father. For they thought that in the writings of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—they had sufficient testimony concerning his humanity and the things he did as a man.

He replied that he would not do this in any other way unless, after a fast had been proclaimed, they all prayed together to the Lord so that, with the Lord granting it, he might be able to write what was worthy. When this had been done, instructed by heavenly revelation and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he dispelled all the darkness of the heretics by the sudden disclosure of the light of truth, saying:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

And when knowledge of the three Gospels—namely, those of Matthew, Mark, and Luke—had reached him, he is said to have approved the faith and truth of what they had written. Yet he saw that certain things were lacking from the history of events, especially those things that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching.

For it is certain that the three earlier Gospels seem to contain only what happened after John the Baptist had been handed over and confined in prison. Since, as I have said, these matters appeared to have been omitted by them, the apostle John is said to have been asked to describe the deeds of the Savior that had been passed over by the earlier writers and had occurred before John’s imprisonment. Therefore he says in his Gospel: “This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs” (John II). And elsewhere he indicates the same thing by saying: “For John had not yet been sent into prison” (John III). From this it is clear that he described the deeds performed by Jesus before John was handed over.

But undoubtedly his chief intention was to declare the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he is equal to the Father, and he took particular care to commend this in his Gospel as far as he believed sufficient among human beings.

Thus he rose much more sublimely than the three earlier evangelists, so that one seems to see them, in a certain sense, conversing on earth with Christ as man, while he transcended the cloud by which the whole earth is covered [F., “through which the whole earth is covered”] and reached the clear light of heaven. From there, with the sharpest and most steadfast vision of the mind, he saw: “In the beginning the Word”; God from God, light from light, through whom all things were made; and he recognized that the Word himself became flesh in order to dwell among us—not that he was changed into flesh, but that he assumed flesh.

For unless the assumption of flesh had taken place while the divinity remained unchangeable, it would not be said: “I and the Father are one” (John X). For the Father and flesh are not one. This testimony of the Lord concerning himself was likewise recalled only by John: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV); and: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid.); and: “That they may be one, just as we are one” (John XVII); and: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same” (John V).

And if there are any other statements that properly disclose to those who understand the divinity of Christ, in which he is equal to the Father, John alone set them forth more fully in his Gospel. It is as though, from the breast of the Lord himself, upon which he was accustomed to recline at his meal, he had drunk the secret of his divinity more abundantly and, in a certain sense, more intimately.

Hence, if you pay careful attention, it may be understood that the three evangelists pursued more extensively the Lord’s temporal deeds and sayings, especially those useful for forming the conduct of the present life, and were concerned with the active life; whereas John, narrating far fewer of the Lord’s deeds but writing his sayings more carefully and abundantly, especially those that suggested the unity of the Trinity and the happiness of eternal life, directed his intention and preaching toward commending the contemplative life.

This is indeed John, one of Christ’s disciples, whom the Lord called as a virgin from the stormy, wave-tossed sea of marriage. In the Gospel a double testimony is given to his virginity: he is said to have been loved by God more than the others, and God commended his mother to him from the throne of the cross, so that a virgin might preserve a virgin.

By the singular privilege of chastity he deserved to grasp and disclose the mystery of the divine Majesty more profoundly than all the other writers of Christ’s miracles. For it is not without reason that he is said to have reclined upon Jesus’ breast at the mystical supper (John XIII, XXI), but by this it is taught most truly that he drank the draught of heavenly wisdom more excellently from the most holy fountain of that breast.

Hence, in the figure of the four living creatures, he is fittingly compared to a flying eagle.
