The eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and to fix its gaze more clearly than all living creatures upon the sun’s rays. Thus blessed John saw more sublimely the mysteries of Christ’s eternal birth.

Therefore the other evangelists describe Christ as born in time, while John testifies that he already existed in the beginning, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” This is understood in two ways. For the Father is the Beginning, as though he had said: “The Son is in the Father.” This evangelist called him the Word.

Nor should it trouble us that later in this Gospel, when the Jews asked who he was, God the Son himself answered: “The Beginning, who am also speaking to you” (John VIII). For if the Son is the Beginning, and has a Father, how much more easily should God the Father be understood as the Beginning, since he has a Son of whom he is Father? The Son is the Father’s Son, and the Father is certainly the Son’s Father; and the Father is God, but not God from God. The Son, however, is God from God. The Father is called light, but not light from light; the Son is called light, but light from light.

Thus the Father is Beginning, but not Beginning from Beginning; the Son is Beginning, but Beginning from Beginning. For what was in the beginning is not ended by time and is not preceded by a beginning.

But if you wish to refer the Beginning he mentions to creatures or to times, when he says: “In the beginning was the Word,” whatever creature had a beginning in order to exist, the Word of God, through whom all things exist, was then already present.

For this reason the evangelist says four times “was”: “was, was, was, was,” so that you might understand that the Word, coeternal with God the Father, preceded all times.

The other evangelists demonstrate that the Son of God suddenly appeared among human beings; blessed John declares that he had always been with God, saying: “And the Word was with God.” The others confirm him as a true man; John confirms that he himself is truly God, saying: “And the Word was God.” The others show him as a man dwelling among human beings temporally; John shows him as God remaining with God in the beginning, saying: “This was in the beginning with God.”

For if the earlier Beginning is gladly referred to the Father, and this later Beginning to creatures, it is understood that the Word—that is, the Son of God—is eternally in the Father and that, in his essence, he preceded every beginning of creatures.

The other evangelists testify to the mighty works he performed as a man; John teaches that God the Father made every visible creature through him, saying:

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

For if nothing among created things was made without him, it is plainly evident that he himself is not a creature, through whom every creature was made.

And lest anyone, hearing that a creature was made through the Son of God, should believe his will to be changeable—as though he suddenly wished to make a creature that he had never previously made from eternity—the evangelist clearly teaches that the creature was indeed made in time, but that in the eternal wisdom of the Creator it had always been determined when and what it would be when created. This is what he says:

“What was made, in him was life.”

That is, whatever appeared as something made in time, whether living or without life, had all of this perpetually lived, as it were, in the spiritual reasoning of the maker, and lives there—not because what he created is coeternal with the Creator, but because the reasoning of his will is coeternal with him. In that reasoning, from eternity, he had and has determined what to create and when, how to govern what he created so that it may remain, and to what end he should bring each thing he created.

Therefore it should be punctuated and continued as though in another voice: “In him was life,” because whatever was made through him also lives in him, just as an art lives in the mind of an artisan, although the chest or anything else made by him may perish.

[Col. 0639C] “And the life was the light of human beings.” By this statement it is plainly taught that the living reason through which all things have been ordered and are governed illuminates not every creature, but only the rational creature, so that it may be capable of understanding. Human beings, who were made in the image of God, can receive wisdom; animals cannot.

But no merely animal human being perceives the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Cor. V). Therefore, after saying, “And the life was the light of human beings,” he appropriately added something concerning those who, withdrawing far from the honor of human condition, “were compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII), and for that reason are deprived of the light of an upright will.

And, he says, the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. For Christ is the light of human beings, because by the presence of his knowledge he illumines all human hearts that deserve to be illuminated. The darkness, however, consists of the foolish and the wicked, whose blinded inner selves the light of eternal Wisdom clearly knows as they are, although they themselves are altogether unable, through understanding, to grasp the rays of that same light—just as a blind person might be surrounded by the sun’s radiance and yet not see the sun itself, whose light floods over him. Nevertheless, divine mercy provided such people with a way by which they might arrive at seeing that true light and become children of light, though they had been children of darkness; and the beginning of this knowledge was what follows.

There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He does not say, “So that all might believe in him.” For “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jeremiah XVII); rather, he says, “so that all might believe through him”—that is, so that through his testimony they might believe in the light, which they had not yet learned to see: namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who testifies about himself, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world. Holy people, indeed, are rightly called light, since the Lord says to them, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V), and the apostle Paul says, “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V). But there is a great difference between the light that is illuminated and the light that illuminates; between those who receive light through participation in the true light so that they may shine, and that perpetual light which is sufficient not only to shine in itself but also, by its presence, to illuminate whatever it touches. Compared with this true light, not only any lesser elect person, but John himself—“among those born of women no one has arisen greater than he” (Matthew XI)—is asserted not to be light, so that it might plainly be shown that John was not Christ, as people supposed. For he, as it is written, was “a burning and shining lamp” (John V): burning, that is, with faith and love; shining in word and action. But to pour the grace of light into hearts belongs only to him of whom it is said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” Every person, that is, who is illuminated, whether by natural intelligence or by divine wisdom. For just as no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, this comes from the one who illumines, of whom it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God.”

The evangelist then appropriately describes both his natures: his divine nature, by which he always remains wholly present everywhere, and his human nature, through which he was born in time and appeared confined to a place, saying:

He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to what was his own, and his own did not receive him. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, because he was God, because he was wholly everywhere, governing by the presence of his majesty without labor and sustaining without burden what he had made. And the world did not know him because the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

Here the evangelist calls “the world” human beings deceived by love of the world and, by clinging to the creature, turned away from knowing the majesty of their Creator. He came to what was his own because, although he had made the world through his divinity, he appeared born into it through his humanity. He came to what was his own because he deigned to become incarnate among the Jewish people, whom he had joined to himself by a special grace above all other nations. Thus he was in the world, and through the Incarnation he came into the world. To come or to depart belongs to humanity; to remain and to be belongs to divinity. Therefore, since he was in the world through his divinity and the world did not know him, he deigned to come into the world through his humanity, so that in this way the world might recognize him.

But let us see what follows: He came to what was his own, and his own did not receive him. The one whom they had not recognized creating and ruling all things in the power of his divinity, they did not wish to receive when he shone forth through miracles in the weakness of flesh. And what is more grievous, his own did not receive him—namely, the human beings whom he himself had created. The Jews, whom he had specially chosen for himself as a people, to whom he had revealed the secret of his knowledge, whom he had glorified through the wondrous deeds of their ancestors, to whom he had given the teaching of his law, and from whom he showed himself incarnate as he had promised—these people, for the most part, refused to receive him when he came. Not all of them refused; otherwise no one would have been saved, and his Incarnation would have been pointless. But now, while many from both peoples rejected him through unbelief, many received him through faith. The evangelist next makes this known, saying:

But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. Let us consider, dearly beloved brothers, how great is the grace of our Redeemer, how great is the abundance of his sweetness. He was born from the Father as the Only-Begotten, and he did not wish to remain alone. He descended to earth, where he might acquire brothers for himself to whom he could give his Father’s kingdom. He was born God from God, and he did not wish to remain only the Son of God; he deigned also to become the son of a human being—not losing what he was, but assuming what he was not—so that through this he might make human beings children of God and make them coheirs of his glory, so that they might receive by grace what he always possessed by nature.

Let us consider how great is the power of faith, by whose merit human beings are given the power to become children of God. Hence it is rightly written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk II). The righteous person lives by faith—not by that which is expressed only in a confession of the lips, but by that which works through love (Galatians V). Otherwise, “if faith has no works, it is dead in itself” (James II).

Let no one despise himself; let no one despair of his salvation. Let us all take care, each one of us take care, that though we were far away, we may deserve to be brought near through the blood of Christ. Let us see what is said: “To all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God.” “To all,” he says, who received him. For God is not a respecter of persons (Acts X), but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him.

The evangelist then indicates in what manner believers could become children of God and how greatly this generation differs from the carnal one:

Who were born, he says, not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God. Our individual carnal generation originated from bloods—that is, from the seed of male and female and from marital intercourse. Spiritual generation, however, is bestowed through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Distinguishing this from carnal generation, the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the Spirit is spirit” (John III).

But lest anyone doubt that a human being can be a child of God and become a coheir of Christ, the evangelist gives an example: the Son of God himself deigned to become human and dwell among human beings, so that by sharing in human weakness he might grant human beings a share in his divine power.

And the Word, he says, became flesh and dwelt among us. This means: The Son of God became human and lived among human beings. Scripture customarily designates the whole human being sometimes by the word “soul,” sometimes by the word “flesh.” By “soul,” for example, when it is written: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Deuteronomy X). By “flesh,” again, when it is written: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke III). Neither souls without bodies can descend into Egypt, nor can flesh without a soul see anything; rather, in the first passage the whole human being is signified by “soul,” and in the second by “flesh.”

Thus, in this passage, when it is said, “The Word became flesh,” nothing else should be understood than if it had been said, “God became human”: he put on flesh and a soul, so that just as each one of us is one human being consisting of flesh and soul, so from the time of the Incarnation Christ is one person consisting of divinity, flesh, and soul. He is God existing from eternity to eternity, true as he was, assuming in time a human being whom he had not possessed, into the unity of his person.

And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. Human beings could not see Christ’s glory before the Incarnation, but through the Incarnation they saw it, beholding his humanity rising through miracles and understanding the divinity hidden within. This was especially true of those who deserved to contemplate his love before his Passion, when he was transfigured on the holy mountain and a voice came down from God amid such magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew XVII). After his Passion, when they had seen the glory of his resurrection and ascension, they were wonderfully refreshed by the gift of his Spirit (Acts II). Through all these things they clearly understood that such glory belonged not to just any saint, but only to that human being who was the Only-Begotten from the Father in his divinity.

As for what follows—“full of grace and truth”—the man Christ Jesus was and is full of grace. By a unique gift, above all other mortals, he was granted that from the moment he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb he began to be truly God as he became human. Hence that same glorious ever-virgin Mary is rightly to be believed and confessed not only as the mother of Christ the human being, but also as the mother of God.

He was and is likewise full of truth: namely, through the very divinity of the Word, which deigned to assume that singularly chosen human being with whom there would be one person of Christ. It did not, as the heretics claim, change some part of its divine substance into the making of human nature; rather, while remaining with the Father all that it was, it assumed the whole true human nature from the seed of David, which it had not possessed.

John bears witness about him. The forerunner of our Redeemer, bearing witness about him, proclaims with a clear voice both the exaltedness of his humanity and the eternity of his divinity.

For he cries out, saying: This was he of whom I said to you, “He who comes after me was made before me, because he was before me.” In saying, “He who comes after me,” he indicates the order of the human dispensation: Christ was born after him, and after him was to preach, baptize, perform signs, and suffer death. But when he adds, “He was made before me,” he designates the excellence of that same humanity, which deservedly had to be preferred above all other creatures.

The words “before me” do not refer to the order of time, but to a difference of dignity, according to what is written concerning the sons of Joseph when Jacob blessed them: “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh” (Genesis XLVIII). There Manasseh could rightly have said: “He who came after me was made before me”—that is, he who was born after me yielded to me in power while I reigned. [Perhaps: “He preceded me in royal rank.”] In the same way John says of the Lord: “He who is to come after me was made before me”—that is, he who was to come after me to preach surpasses me in the height of an enduring kingdom and priesthood.

He then explains why the one who was to come after him would surpass him in dignity, adding: “Because he was before me”—that is, he was God, coeternal before the ages. Therefore, although he was born later than I, he will precede me in the glory of his majesty, even in the humanity he assumed.

After explaining the testimony of the Lord’s forerunner—what testimony he had borne about him—the evangelist immediately returns to the testimony of his own assertion, which he had begun to give. For it follows:

And from his fullness we all received, grace upon grace. Earlier he said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” After the forerunner had also confirmed this by his testimony, saying, “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who comes after me was made before me, because he was before me,’” the evangelist again continues what he had begun, saying: “And from his fullness we all received, grace upon grace.”

The Lord was full of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and truth, because, as the Apostle says, “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II). From his fullness we have all received according to the measure of our capacity, because grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephesians IV).

For of the one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, it could truly be said: “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah XI). All the saints, however, do not receive the fullness of his Spirit, but receive from his fullness as much as he gives. To one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills (1 Corinthians XII).

Since, therefore, from the fullness of our Creator we have received not merely some good thing but whatever good we possess, we must take the greatest care that no one, being careless, should exalt himself over his good action or thought. Otherwise, if he remains ungrateful to the giver, he may lose the good he received.

When the evangelist had said that we all received from Christ’s fullness, he immediately added: “Grace upon grace.” He thus testifies that we received a double grace: one in the present and another in the future. In the present, faith that works through love (Galatians V); in the future, eternal life.

Faith that works through love is the grace of God, because we received the ability to believe, to love, and to do the good things we know—not through any merits preceding our own, but from the one who gives, who says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and to receive life on account of faith, love, and good works” (John XV).

It is eternal grace, because we always need him as our guide so that we may not stray from the good path. To him it is said: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Psalm LXXXV).

It should be noted that some books read: “We all received from his fullness, and grace upon grace.” First we received something from his fullness, and afterward grace upon grace—that is, from his fullness we received the remission of sins, and grace, namely eternal life, in place of the grace of faith that works through love. It is entirely certain that all these things come to us from the one source, the fullness of Christ.

What, then, did we receive from the fullness of his goodness? Namely, the remission of sins, so that we might be justified by faith. What more? “And grace upon grace”—that is, in place of the grace in which we live by faith, we are to receive another grace. What is it, then, except grace—that is, eternal life?

It follows:

For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The law was indeed given through Moses, and in it heavenly law determines what should be done and what avoided. But what the law commanded is fulfilled only through the grace of Christ. The law was able to point out sin, teach righteousness, and show transgressors to be guilty before it. But the grace of Christ, poured through the spirit of love into the hearts of the faithful, causes what the law commanded to be fulfilled.

Thus the commandment “You shall not covet” (Exodus XX) belongs to the law through Moses because it is commanded; but it becomes grace through Christ when what is commanded is fulfilled.

Truth, however, came through Christ because the law had a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews X), not the very image of the realities; and, as the Apostle says elsewhere, “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Corinthians X). In place of the shadow, Christ displayed the light of truth; in place of the figure of the law, he displayed the very image of the realities prefigured, when the grace of the Spirit given by him opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV).

The law was given through Moses when the people were commanded to be cleansed by the sprinkling of the blood of a lamb. Grace and truth, which were figured in the light, came through Jesus Christ when, having suffered on the cross, he washed us from our sins in his blood.

The law was given through Moses because it instructed the people by saving commandments: if they kept them, they would enter the promised land and live in it forever; if not, it foretold that they would be struck down by the enemy. Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ because, by giving the gift of his Spirit, he also granted the ability to understand and observe the law spiritually; and he leads those who observe it into the true blessedness of heavenly life, which the promised land signified.

The evangelist makes clear what is the sum of the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ by adding:

No one has ever seen God; the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known. No greater grace can be given to human beings, and no higher truth can be known by them, than that about which the Only-Begotten Son of God speaks to his faithful: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew V); and about which, praying to the Father, he says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true and only God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII).

Since this most blessed perception of grace and truth cannot take place in the life of the present age, it is rightly said: “No one has ever seen God”—that is, no one still clothed in corruptible and mortal flesh can gaze upon the unbounded light of divinity. Hence the Apostle says more plainly: “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy VI). For no human being sees God: no one still burdened by a human condition or subject to the frailty of human life can do so.

That is why Moses, desiring to see God in his very nature—the God whom he saw in the angel—prayed: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me your glory” (Exodus XXXIII). He heard: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (ibid.).

The evangelist then explains how one must reach the vision of the immutable and eternal light, saying: “The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known.” To this corresponds what the Lord says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV), and elsewhere: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew XI).

Under his guidance we must come to the Father; through his teaching we must know the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as one God and Lord. For he himself, having become human for us and speaking to us in human form, clearly revealed what ought rightly to be believed about the unity of the Holy Trinity, how the faithful must hasten toward its contemplation, and by what actions it must be reached. He helps us come to it by instructing us in the sacraments of his Incarnation and sanctifying us with the gifts of his Spirit. After completing the final judgment in human form, he will exaltedly introduce us into the vision of the divine Majesty and wonderfully make known to us the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom.

Certainly, when he says, “who is in the bosom of the Father,” this should be understood proverbially as being in the Father’s secret. God is not to be thought of as having a bosom like the one we have in our garments, nor as being composed of human limbs and sitting as we do. Rather, because our bosom is within us, Scripture, speaking in our manner, says that he is in the bosom of the Father, intending us to understand that he always remains in the Father’s secret, to which human sight cannot reach.

The Only-Begotten Son will not make God known only then—that is, he will not manifest the glory of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, which is one God, only when, after the universal judgment, he brings all the elect together into the vision of his brightness. He also makes him known daily, whenever he begins to fulfill for each of the perfected faithful, as soon as they have been released from the corruption of the flesh, what he promised: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). “I will manifest myself,” he says, to those who love me, so that they who knew me as mortal in my humanity may now see me in my divine nature, equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This is John’s testimony, and so forth. These words commend John’s humility. Although he possessed such great virtue that Christ could have been believed to be him, he chose to remain firmly within himself, lest human opinion carry him vainly above himself.

For he confessed and did not deny; he confessed, “I am not the Christ.” But because he said “I am not,” he denied what he was, so that by speaking the truth he might become a member of the one whose name he would not deceitfully claim for himself. Thus, by refusing openly to claim the name of Christ, he became a member of Christ; because he humbly acknowledged his own weakness, he deserved truly to possess Christ’s exaltedness.

He immediately states who he is by adding:

I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness. You know that the Only-Begotten Son is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” From your own way of speaking you understand that a voice sounds first, so that afterward a word can be heard. John therefore asserts that he is a voice because he precedes the Word.

Since he goes before the Lord’s coming, he is called a voice because through his ministry the Word of the Father is heard by all. He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the Redeemer’s consolation to abandoned and desolate Judea. He indicates what he cries out when he adds:

Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said. The Lord’s way is made straight to the heart when life is prepared for the commandment. Hence it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Whoever, therefore, raises his mind in pride; whoever pants in the heat of greed; whoever pollutes himself with the filth of lust—such a person closes the door of his heart against the truth. By fastening the entrances of his mind with the bolts of vices, he bars the Lord from coming to him.

But those who had been sent continued to question him:

Why then do you baptize, if you are not Elijah, nor the Christ, nor the prophet? Because this was said not out of a desire to know the truth, but out of malicious rivalry, the evangelist quietly makes it known by adding:

And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. It is as if he said openly: Those who inquire about John’s actions are people who do not know how to seek instruction, but only how to envy.

Yet every holy person, even when questioned with a perverse mind, does not change from his pursuit of goodness. Thus John also answered words of envy with teachings of life. For he immediately adds:

I baptize in water, but one has stood among you whom you do not know. John washes the bodies of those baptized, not with the Spirit but with water; nevertheless, he does not wash them through the remission of sins.

Why, then, does he baptize, if he does not forgive sins through baptism? It is so that, maintaining the order of his forerunning—because by being born he had preceded the one who was to be born—he might also precede the Lord who was to baptize by baptizing first. And he who became Christ’s forerunner by preaching might also become his forerunner by baptizing, through an imitation of the sacrament.

Meanwhile, announcing the mystery of our Redeemer, he asserts that the Lord both stood among human beings and was unknown to them: appearing in the flesh, the Lord stood visibly in his body but invisibly in his majesty. Concerning him he also adds:

He who comes after me was made before me. This is said as though it meant, “He was placed before me.” He came after me because he was born later; but he was made before me because he was placed above me.

But when John said this a little earlier, he also explained the reasons for that precedence by adding: “Because he was before me.” It is as if he said openly: He surpasses me even though he was born later because the limits of time do not constrain the time of his birth. The one who is born in time from a mother was begotten timelessly by the Father.

He then makes clear how great the humility of reverence he owes him is by adding:

I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal. Among the ancients it was customary that if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who belonged to him, the man who came as bridegroom to her by right of kinship would remove his sandal.

What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be except the Bridegroom of the holy Church? John himself says of him: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). But because people thought John was the Christ, which John denies, he rightly declares himself unworthy to untie the strap of Christ’s sandal. It is as if he said openly: I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not claim for myself the name of bridegroom in terms of merit.

This can nevertheless be understood in another way as well. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? When the incarnate Lord came, he appeared, as it were, shod: in his divinity he assumed the death-bound condition of our corruptibility. But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this Incarnation. It cannot in any way investigate how the Word becomes embodied, how he is given life and animated by the Spirit within his mother’s womb, or how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived.

The strap of the sandal, therefore, is the bond of the mystery. John is unable to untie the strap of his sandal because even he, who recognized the Incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

What, then, does it mean to say, “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal,” except openly and humbly to confess his own ignorance? It is as if he said: What wonder if he has been placed above me, when I see that he was born after me but cannot comprehend the mystery of his birth?

These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. It is fitting that the forerunner of our Lord is said to have baptized in Bethany, for Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.” This shows that all must come to Christ’s baptism through the obedience of faith.

For just as the Magi were commanded to return to their homeland by another way (Matthew V), so we have been commanded to reach the joys of paradise by another way. Our parents were expelled from it through the guilt of disobedience; we, however, must reach the eternal paradise of blessedness through the good of obedience and through observance of God’s commandments.

The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him. John is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord.” The next day is the Christian people under grace, redeemed by the precious blood of Christ. The other day belonged to the earlier people under the law, who were redeemed from Egyptian slavery by the mystical blood of the lamb.

That lamb signified this Lamb whom the blessed Baptist, present at the time, pointed out with his finger, saying:

Behold the Lamb of God. Behold the innocent one, free from every sin, since he has bone from Adam’s bones and flesh from Adam’s flesh, but drew no stain of guilt from sinful flesh.

Behold the one who takes away the sins of the world. Behold the one who, righteous among sinners and gentle among the impious—that is, appearing like a lamb among wolves—also has the power to justify sinners and the impious.

The apostle Peter shows how he takes away the sins of the world and by what order he justifies the impious when he says: “You were not redeemed from your empty way of life inherited from your ancestors with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter I).

John continues his testimony about the Lord:

This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me. “After me comes a man”: he was born into the world after me and will begin to preach to the world after me. “He was made before me”: he surpasses me in the power of his majesty as much as a judge surpasses a herald, as the sun surpasses Lucifer, although he appears later. “Because he was before me”: because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

“After me comes a man” designates the time of his human birth, in which you should understand Christ as later than John. “He was made before me”: consider the primacy of royal power by which he presides even over the angels. “Because he was before me”: understand the majesty of divine eternity, by which he is equal to the Father.

“After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me.” He came after me in humanity, and for this reason surpasses me in dignity: because he was before me in dignity.

And I did not know him, he says. It is certain that John knew the Lord, the one whom he had been sent to bear witness to and whom he proclaimed as the judge who would come for all, saying: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Luke III). He testified that the Holy Spirit was to be given by him: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit,” he said (Matthew III). He desired to be cleansed by him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (ibid.).

How, then, does he say, “And I did not know him,” except that he recognized more perfectly, when Christ was baptized, the one whom he had already known? He knew him as the Savior and judge of the world, but he recognized more deeply the power of his majesty when the Holy Spirit descended upon him.

There is no doubt that when the blessed John saw the Holy Spirit, even in bodily form, and when he deserved to hear the Father’s voice, though it sounded bodily, he gained greatly from this sight and hearing. With the eyes of his mind opened, he received a great increase of knowledge concerning the excellence of divine compassion, so that, compared with the understanding with which he then began to be illumined, he seemed in every way to have previously been ignorant of how great Christ was.

Bearing diligent witness to the Lord concerning the testimony for which he had been sent, he adds:

But so that he might be revealed in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water. This is plainly to say: I did not come baptizing in water because I could remove the sins of the world by baptizing, but so that by baptizing and preaching I might reveal him to the people of Israel. He baptizes in the Holy Spirit and is capable of taking away the sins not only of Israel but of the whole world, if they are willing to believe in him. For this reason I came baptizing for repentance, so that by baptizing in this way I might prepare a path for the one who would baptize for the remission of sins.

And John bore witness, saying: I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him. The Spirit fittingly descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, so that the faithful might learn that they can become his members and be filled with his Spirit in no other way than by being simple and by having true peace with their brothers and sisters, which the kisses of doves signify.

Ravens also have kisses, but they tear apart; a dove does this not at all. They signify those who “speak peace with their neighbor, while evil is in their hearts” (Psalm XXVII). The nature of the dove, which is innocent of tearing, most appropriately corresponds to those who pursue peace with all and holiness, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians IV).

Therefore, by descending in the form of a dove, the Spirit signifies not only the innocence and simplicity of himself and of the one upon whom he descended, but equally the innocence and simplicity of those who think well of him and seek him in sincerity and simplicity of heart (Wisdom I).

And I did not know him, he says. Supply: “I did not know him so subtly and fully as I came to know him when the Spirit descended upon him.”

[Col. 0650A] “But he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’” The Lord baptizes in the Holy Spirit by forgiving sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit. For whether he himself first baptized some of his disciples with water, through whom the stream of baptism would flow to the other faithful, he also baptized those same people with the Spirit, releasing them from their sins and bestowing the gifts of the Holy Spirit; or whether his faithful, invoking his name, baptize the elect with water and anoint them with holy chrism, nevertheless he himself baptizes those same people with the Holy Spirit, because no one besides him can loose the bonds of sins or bestow the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

But we must observe more carefully that, when he had said, “upon whom you see the Spirit descending,” he added, “and remaining upon him.” The Spirit does indeed descend upon his saints; but because, as long as they are in the body, they cannot be free from sin—for they are not able always to direct the eye of the mind toward contemplation of heavenly things, but often bend it toward the concerns of earthly life—the Spirit unquestionably comes and departs from their hearts at different times. Hence it is said: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3). The Holy Spirit comes to the saints and departs from them, so that, since they are not capable of possessing him always, they may be refreshed by the frequent light of his return from time to time.

But in the one Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, the Spirit truly remains perpetually, finding in him no stain of foul thought from which he would recoil. He remained wholly in him, not only from the time when John saw him descend upon him, but from the moment when, beginning to become human, he was conceived through the ministry and work of the Spirit. Therefore he is shown descending upon him when he was baptized, although the Spirit had always remained in him, so that the Baptist himself might recognize more clearly whom he was to preach, and so that believers might receive the indication that they could in no way merit the baptism of the same Spirit unless they had first been baptized with water.

Meanwhile, we must ask how this could have been a distinctive sign by which to recognize the Son of God—namely, that the Spirit descended upon him and remained upon him—since he himself also promises his disciples the Spirit, saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14). And shortly afterward: “Because he will remain with you and will be in you” (ibid.). If the Spirit remains with God’s chosen servants and will be in them, what is so remarkable about asserting that the Spirit remains in the Son of God?

We must therefore note that the Holy Spirit always remained in the Lord; but in holy human beings, as long as they bear a mortal body, he partly remains forever and partly departs, to return again. He remains with them so that they may persist in good works, love voluntary poverty, pursue meekness, mourn for the desire of eternal things, hunger and thirst for righteousness, embrace mercy, purity of heart, and the tranquility of peace, and not fear suffering persecution for the observance of justice. [Col. 0651A] They desire to devote themselves to almsgiving, prayers, fasts, and the other fruits of the Spirit. He departs for a time, however, so that they may not always possess the power to heal the sick, cast out demons, or even prophesy. He remains always so that they may live wondrously; he comes for a time so that, through signs of miracles, they may also shine before others as the people they are inwardly.

“And I saw,” he says, “and bore witness that this is the Son of God.” Earlier he had said: “After me comes a man who was made before me.” Now he bears witness that “this is the Son of God,” clearly designating both natures—human and divine—in one and the same person of Christ. Let Manichaeus be ashamed when he hears, “A man came.” Let Photinus fall silent [Col. 0651B] when he hears, “This is the Son of God.” Let the meek hear and rejoice: a man came after John, stronger than John, who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; and this is the Son of God.

Because we had withdrawn from God through pride, the Son became human through mercy, so that the same one might correspond both to the Father through his divinity and to us through his humanity. Through a humanity like ours, he could fight the enemy on our behalf; through a divinity consubstantial with the Father, he could restore us worthily to the image and likeness of God, which we had lost through sin. Through the death of our frailty he could destroy the one who held the power of death, and through the impassible power of his divinity he could reconcile us to God the Father.

John was standing, and two of his disciples. John was standing because he believed in the Lord, and two of his disciples stood with him. For they immediately believed and followed him as he walked. We ought to examine each word of Scripture: why is John said to be standing, while the Lord is said to be walking?

“And looking at Jesus as he walked, he said: ‘Behold, the Lamb of God.’” The spotless Lamb, the year-old Lamb, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the Lamb who does not permit the destroyer in Egypt to strike the people of Israel. “Behold the Lamb of God.” His disciples heard him; why did he wish to say, “Behold”? When “behold” is said, the person indicated is in a certain way pointed out with a finger. He says to his disciples: “Why are you following me? Why do you suppose that you should have me as your teacher? Behold the Lamb of God; follow him. He must increase, but I must decrease.” No prudent person follows the one who is decreasing and abandons the one who is increasing.

“And the two disciples heard him speaking.” They followed the command of their teacher. John’s testimony was the faith of the disciples.

“And they followed Jesus.” In following Jesus, they left John; in following the Gospel, they lost the Law. Yet they followed the Gospel in such a way that they used the testimony of the Law.

“Jesus, turning and seeing them.” John’s disciples could not see Jesus closely and face-to-face as they followed behind him; they followed his back in order to see him. Thus those disciples could not see the Lord’s face. He turned around and, in a certain sense, descended from his majesty [Col. 0652A] so that the disciples could contemplate his face. He turned around so that he might be seen by the disciples from the Law. “Turning, then, and seeing them following him,

“He said: ‘What are you seeking?’” He does not ask as though he were ignorant, but he asks so that those who answer may receive a reward. “What are you seeking?” He did not say, “Whom are you seeking?” lest he appear to point to himself; instead he said, “What are you seeking?” He asks about the matter, so that they might identify the person. “What are you seeking?”

“They said to him: ‘Rabbi.’” The very form of address is an indication of their response and faith. For when they say “Rabbi,” which means “Teacher,” and follow him, they are clearly following a teacher, and they say:

“‘Where do you live?’ He says to them: ‘Come and see.’” They want to know Jesus’ dwelling; they want the Savior to show them what sort of dwelling he has, so that, when he has shown in whom Christ dwells, they may present themselves as people in whom the Lord can dwell. And he said to them: “Come and see.” Do you wish to see my dwelling? It cannot be explained in words; it is demonstrated by deeds. “Come and see.”

These men had come on the testimony of the Law, since they immediately confess in the very name they use and say “Rabbi,” which is interpreted as “Teacher.” Jesus, however, answered them and said: “You who are John’s disciples, who demonstrate your confession by the very name you use and say ‘Rabbi,’ come and see where I remain.”

“They came and saw where he remained, and they stayed with him that day.” Because they believed, they did not remain in the night but in the day. That night had no darkness, because the faith of the true light was there, and they stayed with him that day.

[Col. 0652C]

“It was about the tenth hour.” They were coming from the Law to the Gospel; the Decalogue of the Law was sending them toward faith in Christ.

“Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John and followed him.” In faith there is no order. Wherever there is a faithful soul, neither a multitude nor a small number of years is sought. Andrew was younger than Simon Peter, yet what is considered is not age but faith. He found Jesus first. “Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two.” Unless perhaps this too is Andrew’s distinction: that he is called Peter’s brother, upon whom the Church was later to be founded.

“They had heard from John and followed him.” [Col. 0652D] Here he first finds his own brother. O true devotion! As soon as he found Jesus, as soon as he found the pearl, as soon as he found the treasure, he announced it to his brother. He called his brother Simon—his brother not so much by blood as by the Spirit. He whom he had as a brother by kinship and blood, he wished also to have as a brother in faith; and he says to him:

“‘We have found the Messiah.’” No one finds him unless he seeks him. This man, who says that he has found him, shows that he had sought him for a long time.

“‘We have found the Messiah,’ which is translated ‘Christ.’” For a long time we sought Christ in Moses and in all the prophets; and the one whom we desired to find found us, and, having been found, we found him.

[Col. 0653A] “And he brought him to Jesus.” The elder does not disdain to follow the younger, because there was no order of age where there was the merit of faith.

“Jesus looked at him and said: ‘You are Simon, the son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas,’ which is translated ‘Peter.’” Peter had not yet done anything, and already he had earned a change of name. Had Andrew believed more? What greater thing had he done, so that he should receive more from his brother? What greater thing had he done? He followed his younger brother, and did not disdain to have as his teacher the one whom he had as his disciple.

“‘You are Simon, the son of Jonah.’” In our language, Jonah means “dove.” You are therefore the son of Jonah; you are the son of the Holy Spirit. He is called the son of the Spirit because he had received humility from the Holy Spirit.

“On the following day he wanted to depart for Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him: ‘Follow me.’” It is already clear from what precedes where Jesus wished to depart for Galilee—namely, from Judea, where John was baptizing and bearing witness to him that he was the Lamb of God. He urged two of his disciples to follow him, and one of them, Andrew, also brought his brother Peter to him.

According to the spiritual sense, it is already known to your fraternity through frequent exposition who it is who follows the Lord. For the one follows the Lord who imitates him. The one follows the Lord who, insofar as human frailty permits, does not abandon the examples of humility that the Son of God displayed in humanity. He earnestly desires to share in his sufferings and to attain participation in his resurrection and ascension.

But it is not without a definite sacramental reason [Col. 0653C] that the Gospel relates that, when Jesus was about to say to Philip, “Follow me,” he wished to depart for Galilee. Galilee is interpreted as “made migration” or “revelation.” In the sense of “made migration,” it designates the progress of the faithful: they strive either to migrate from vices to the heights of virtues, or to advance somewhat within the virtues themselves, continually moving from lesser things to greater ones, until, with the Lord’s help, they pass from this valley of tears to the citadel of heavenly joy.

In the sense that it signifies “revelation,” it intimates the blessedness of eternal life itself, for which the saints labor in the present. The Psalmist encompasses both interpretations of the name in one verse, where he says: “They will go from strength to strength; [Col. 0653D] the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Psalm 83).

This is the vision of which the Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3). Therefore, when Jesus was about to call a disciple to follow him, he rightly wished to depart for Galilee—that is, into “made migration” or “revelation”—so that, just as he himself, according to the Gospel, “advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2), and just as he suffered and rose again and thus entered into his glory, so also he might show that his followers must advance in virtues and, through passing sufferings, migrate toward the gifts of eternal joys.

[Col. 0654A] “Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.” We should not think that the Evangelist happened by chance and without mystical purpose to identify the city from which Philip came, and to show that it also belonged to Andrew and Peter. Rather, through the name of the city he intended figuratively to show what Philip already was in spirit and what he would be in his ministry, as well as what Peter and Andrew would be.

Bethsaida is called “House of Hunters.” They were indeed hunters who heard the Lord say: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4). He too was a hunter, for, before he was appointed by the Lord to the ministry of preaching, he soon demonstrated spontaneously through preaching how intent he was on capturing souls for life.

“For he found Nathanael and said to him: ‘We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets: Jesus, son of Joseph, [Col. 0654B] from Nazareth.’” What a net of faith, woven with the capacious bonds of devoted preaching, he casts around the brother he has found, whom, with prudent care, he wishes to capture for eternal salvation!

He says that the one whom Moses and the prophets marked out in their writings as the one who was to come has been found, so that all who follow may understand that he is the one whose coming all the ancient writings served to proclaim. He calls him Jesus, the name that the prophetic oracles sang beforehand as belonging to the future Christ. He calls him the son of Joseph, not to assert that he was born from the union of a man and a woman—he had learned from the prophets that he would be born of a Virgin—but to teach that, according to the prophecies of the prophets, he came from the house and family of David, from whom he knew Joseph to have descended.

Nor is it surprising if Philip calls him the son of Joseph, [Col. 0654C] since his own undefiled mother, Mary, ever a virgin and one who had not known a man, is also read to have spoken according to common usage: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2).

He adds the place of origin: “From Nazareth,” in order to identify him as the one of whom they had read in the prophets: “He shall be called a Nazaraean” (Matthew 2). It is therefore not surprising that Philip immediately sought to bring Nathanael to agreement in believing and coming to Christ, since he set before him on every side such great nets of truth.

“‘We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth.’” Nor is he without reason said to have originated from Bethsaida—that is, from the House of Hunters—for he is shown to have received from God an equally great concern for, and grace in, the hunt beloved by God. For what follows says:

[Col. 0654D] “And Nathanael said to him: ‘Something good can come from Nazareth.’” Nazareth is interpreted as “purity,” or “its flower,” or “separated.”

Thus Nathanael, agreeing with Philip’s words as he evangelized him, says: “Something good can arise from a city of such a name—namely, the Lord, Savior of the world, who is uniquely holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and who speaks in the Song of Songs: ‘I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys’ (Song of Songs 2); or of whom the prophet says: ‘A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean—that is, a flower—shall rise from his root’ (Isaiah 11).

Or indeed, an outstanding teacher may be sent from there, [Col. 0655A] one who is to preach to us the flower of virtues and the purity of holiness.

We can also rightly understand this passage in the following way: when Philip says, “Him of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets,” Nathanael responds:

“‘How do you know me?’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.’ Nathanael answered and said: ‘Rabbi, you are the Son of God.’” Nathanael recognized that the Lord had seen and known what was happening elsewhere—namely, how and where he had been called by Philip, although the Lord himself had not been bodily present there. Considering the vision of divine majesty, he immediately confessed him not only as Rabbi, that is, Teacher, but also as the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, Christ.

It is pleasing to observe how wisely the servant’s confession responds to the Lord’s praise. The Lord had declared him to be a true Israelite—that is, a man who could see God—because he possessed no deceit. [Col. 0655B] Nathanael confesses him not merely as a teacher who gives useful instructions, but also as the Son of God, who bestows heavenly gifts, and as the King of Israel, that is, of the people who see God. In religious devotion he thus signifies both that Christ is his king and that he is a soldier of Christ’s kingdom.

This saying of the Lord, by which he said that he had seen Nathanael under the fig tree before Philip called him, can also be understood mystically as referring to the election of spiritual Israel, that is, the Christian people. The Lord mercifully deigned to see them before they had yet been called to the grace of faith through his Apostles, while they were still hidden beneath the covering of oppressive sin.

The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and undefiled in his sight in love” (Ephesians 1).

Indeed, in Scripture the fig tree sometimes signifies the sweetness of heavenly love. Hence it is written: “Whoever guards the fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever is the guardian of his master will be honored” (Proverbs 27).

But because our first parents, confounded by the guilt of transgression, made themselves coverings from fig leaves (Genesis 3), this fig tree may not inappropriately signify to the human race the habit of sinning, rendered falsely sweet. While his elect still lie beneath it, not yet recognizing the grace of their election, the Lord sees Nathanael as one placed, so to speak, beneath the fig tree, [Col. 0655D] although Nathanael himself does not yet see the Lord.

“For the Lord knows those who are his” (1 Timothy 2). The name Nathanael itself most aptly corresponds to the salvation of these people. Nathanael is interpreted as “gift of God”; and unless each person is called by the gift of God, he will never escape the guilt of the first transgression or the shadows of sins that increase daily while falsely flattering him, nor will he merit to come to Christ to be saved.

Hence the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast.” The text continues:

[Col. 0656A] “Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Because I said to you, “I saw you under the fig tree,” you believe; you will see greater things than these.’” What he means by this he himself explains in what follows, promising believers the future opening of the kingdom of heaven and the proclamation to the world of both natures of his one person. This is truly a far more excellent mystery than the fact that, while we were still placed in the shadow of sin, he foresaw that we would be illuminated by him.

For it is greater that the Savior has filled us with knowledge of his grace, that he has opened to us the joys of heaven, and that he has dispersed throughout the world preachers of his faith, than that, by the power of his majesty, he foreknew us before the ages as those who would be saved.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.” We now see the effect of this promise fulfilled. For we see heaven opened, because, after the God-man entered heaven, we recognize that the entrance to the heavenly homeland has also been opened to us who believe in him.

We see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man, because we know that his preachers announce both the sublimity of Christ’s divinity and the weakness of his humanity. The angels ascend upon the Son of Man when preachers teach that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The angels descend upon the Son of Man when those same preachers add that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Nor are holy preachers without reason figuratively called angels; from angels they customarily receive the name “evangelists,” so that, just as angels are messengers, so they too, because of the same highest office of preaching, may be called bearers of good news.

It must also be noted that the Lord calls himself the Son of Man, [Col. 0656C] while Nathanael proclaims him to be the same Son of God. Something similar occurs when, according to the other Evangelists, he himself asks the disciples: “Who do they say that the Son of Man is?” And Peter replies: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Mark 8).

This occurred by a just and orderly dispensation: the two substances of the same Mediator, God and our Lord, were to be mentioned either by the Lord himself or by a mere human being. God the human being asserted the weakness of the humanity he had assumed, while a mere human being asserted in him the power of eternal divinity. He himself confessed his humility, while the other confessed his greatness.

It must be observed that the Lord, who calls blessed Nathanael a true Israelite, recalls in the words “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God [Col. 0656D] ascending upon the Son of Man” the vision of the patriarch Jacob, who was called Israel through the blessing.

When Jacob wished to rest in a certain place and placed a stone beneath his head, he saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, its top touching heaven; he also saw the angels of the Lord ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac” (Genesis 26).

Rising in the morning and rendering due praises to God with reverent fear, Jacob took the stone itself and set it up as a monument, pouring oil upon it. The Lord therefore makes mention of this place and most clearly testifies that it was figuratively a sign of himself and of his faithful.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0657A]

“On the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.” It is not without a mystery that the wedding is said to have taken place on the third day after the events described in the preceding passage of the Gospel. Rather, it signifies that, in the third age of the world, the Lord came to take the Church as his bride.

The first age of the world, before the Law, shone through the examples of the patriarchs; the second, under the Law, through the writings of the prophets; the third, under grace, through the proclamations of the Evangelists, like the light of the third day shining upon the world. In that age our Lord and Savior appeared, born in the flesh for the redemption of the human race.

The fact that this wedding is said to have taken place at Cana of Galilee—that is, in the heaven of accomplished migration—also announces figuratively that those above all are worthy of the grace of Christ who know how to burn with zeal for devout dedication, to strive for the better gifts, to advance from vices to virtues by doing good, and to migrate from earthly things to eternal things through hope and love.

While the Lord was reclining at the wedding, the wine ran out, so that, when better wine was miraculously made through him in a wondrous order, the glory of God hidden in the human being might be revealed and the faith of those who believed in him might grow stronger.

If we seek the mystery, then, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, that unmixed sweetness of the legal meaning had gradually begun to decline from its ancient strength because of the Pharisees’ carnal interpretation. He soon changed the outward surface of the legal letter through the power of the evangelical and heavenly grace. This is what it means to make wine from water.

But first let us see what the text says.

[Col. 0657C] “When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine.’ He answered: ‘What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.’” He did not dishonor his mother, since he commands us to honor father and mother (Exodus 20); nor did he deny that she was his mother, from whose virginal flesh he did not disdain to assume flesh, as the Apostle also bears witness when he says: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1).

For how could he be from the seed of David according to the flesh if he were not from the body of Mary according to the flesh, since she descended from David’s seed?

But when, about to perform a miracle, he says, “What is there between me and you, woman?” he signifies that he did not receive the divinity through which the miracle was to be performed from his mother in time, but had always possessed it eternally from the Father.

“What is there,” he says, [Col. 0657D] “between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” I do not share with your flesh, from which I assumed flesh, the divinity that I have always possessed from the Father. The hour has not yet come for me to demonstrate by dying the weakness of the humanity assumed from you. First it is necessary for me to reveal the power of eternal Deity by performing mighty works.

The hour did come when he showed what he shared with his mother, when, about to die on the cross, he entrusted the Virgin to the virgin disciple (John 19). Since he had suffered the weaknesses of the flesh, he piously entrusted to the disciple whom he loved most the mother from whom he had received that flesh.

But when he was about to perform divine works, he pretended not to know her, as though she were unknown, because he knew that she was not the author of his divine birth.

[Col. 0658A] While hanging on the cross and recalling this hour, the Lord said to his mother: “Mother, behold your son,” as though he had said: “Behold what I assumed from you. It is now shown by dying what it is, although this nature was later to be glorified in the glory of the resurrection.”

“His mother said to the servants: ‘Whatever he tells you, do it.’” His mother certainly knew the humanity of her son, although at this point he appears to deny what was being requested. Yet, knowing the piety of her son and trusting that he would not refuse what was being asked, she confidently instructed the servants to carry out the command of the son who was giving orders.

There were six stone water jars standing there, intended for the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. Water jars are vessels prepared to receive water. For in Greek, water is called *hydōr* (ὕδωρ). [Col. 0658B] Water, however, signifies the knowledge of Holy Scripture, which is accustomed both to wash its hearers clean from the filth of sins and to give them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge.

The six vessels in which it was held are the devoted hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life and faith was set before the human race as an example of right belief and conduct through the six ages of the world, that is, up to the time of the Lord’s preaching. And rightly are the vessels made of stone, because the hearts of the righteous are strong, being, as it were, made solid by faith in and love of that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands, made into a great mountain, and filling the whole earth (Dan. II). Of this stone Zechariah says: “In one stone are seven eyes,” that is, in Christ resides the whole fullness of spiritual knowledge. The apostle Peter also recalls it, [Col. 0658C] saying:

“Coming to him, the living stone, you yourselves also, like living stones, are built upon him” (I Pet. II).

The water jars were rightly placed for the purification of the Jews, because the law was given through Moses to the Jewish people alone. The grace and truth of the Gospel, however, was given through Jesus Christ no less to the Gentiles than to the Jews.

“Each holding,” he says, “two measures or three,” because the authors and ministers of Holy Scripture sometimes speak only of the Father and the Son, as in the passage: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). For Christ is the power and wisdom of God. At other times they also mention the Holy Spirit, according to the Psalmist’s words: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII). Understand “the Word,” “the Lord,” and “the Spirit” as the whole Trinity, which is one God. [Col. 0658D]

But as far as water is from wine, so far does the meaning in which the Scriptures were understood before the Savior’s coming differ from that which he himself, when he came, revealed to the apostles and left to their disciples to follow perpetually. Indeed, the Lord could have filled the empty water jars with wine, he who in the beginning of the world’s creation created all things from nothing. But he preferred to make wine from water, thereby teaching figuratively that he had come not to abolish or condemn the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them (Matt. V); and that through the grace of the Gospel he neither did nor taught anything other than what the legal and prophetic Scriptures had indicated that he would do and teach.

We therefore see the six water jars of the Scriptures [Col. 0659A] filled with saving water. Let us see that same water changed into the most pleasing fragrance and taste of wine.

In the first age of the world, Abel the righteous was killed by his envious brother (Gen. IV). For this reason Abel himself, blessed with the everlasting glory of martyrdom, received praise for his righteousness even in the Gospel and apostolic writings, while the impious fratricide suffered the punishments of eternal condemnation. Whoever, hearing this, fears being condemned with the wicked and desires to be blessed with the righteous, casts away every source of hatred and envy and strives to please God through the sacrifice of righteousness, the modesty of innocence, and the virtue of patience: such a person has surely found in Scripture a vessel of water from which he may rejoice to be healthfully washed and given drink.

But if he understands Cain’s murder as the faithlessness of the Jews, Abel’s killing as the passion of the Lord the Savior, and the earth that opened its mouth and received his blood from Cain’s hand [Col. 0659B] as the Church, which receives the blood of Christ poured out by the Jews as a mystery of her renewal, then he surely finds water changed into wine, because he understands the words of the sacred law in a more sacred sense.

At the beginning of the second age of the world, the earth was destroyed by the waters of the flood because of the magnitude of its sins (Gen. IV); but Noah alone, because of his righteousness, was rescued with his household in the ark. Whoever, hearing of the dreadful devastation of this punishment and the marvelous deliverance of the few, begins to live more correctly, desiring to be saved with the elect and fearing to be destroyed with the reprobate, has surely received a water jar by which he might be cleansed or refreshed.

But when he begins to understand more deeply, and recognizes the Church in the ark, Christ in Noah, baptismal water—which washes away sins—in the water that destroyed sinners, the various distinctions among those baptized in the human beings and animals contained in the ark, and the anointing of the Holy Spirit, with which the baptized are imbued, in the dove that brought an olive branch into the ark after the flood (Gen. VIII), then he marvels that wine has been made from water, because in the ancient account of the event he sees his own cleansing, sanctification, and justification prophetically announced.

In the third age of the world, God, testing Abraham’s obedience, commanded him to offer as a burnt offering his only son, the one whom he loved (Gen. XXII). Abraham did not delay doing what he was commanded, but a ram was sacrificed in place of the son. He himself, however, for the virtue of his obedience, was granted the distinguished and everlasting inheritance of blessing.

Behold, you have the third water jar. [Col. 0659D] Hearing how great is the power of obedience and with what reward it is honored, you too strive to learn and practice obedience. But if, in the sacrifice of the only beloved son, you understand his passion—of him of whom the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III)—then, because the divinity remained incapable of suffering while only the humanity underwent death and pain, the son is offered, as it were, but a ram is slaughtered. If you understand that the blessing promised to Abraham (Gen. XXII) was fulfilled in you, who believe from among the Gentiles, then surely he has made wine from water for you: he has opened a spiritual sense, by whose fragrance you are made drunk.

At the beginning of the fourth age, David received the kingdom of the Israelite people in place of Saul, a humble, innocent, [Col. 0660A] and gentle exile (Gen. XVIII). Saul, however, whose unjust persecution had tormented David, was rejected. Behold the fourth water jar, filled with a saving fountain. Whoever, hearing these things, begins to pursue humility and innocence and to drive pride and envy from his heart, has found, as it were, a draught of the clearest water by which he may be refreshed.

But if he recognizes that Saul signifies the Jews who persecute, and David Christ and the Church, and understands that their faithlessness and carnal kingdom were destroyed, while the kingdom of Christ and the Church would remain forever, then he not only perceives wine made from water because he knows that he is reading about himself, his own life, and his own kingdom; he also knows that he is reading about the king himself, where previously he had read an ancient history as though it concerned others.

In the fifth age of the world, the sinful people, when Nebuchadnezzar carried them away, were transported to Babylon (Ezra I). But after seventy years, having repented and been corrected, they were brought back to their homeland through Jesus the high priest; there they rebuilt the house of God, which had been burned, and the holy city, which had been destroyed (Ecclus. XLIX). Whoever reads or hears this and is seized by the fear of sinning and takes refuge in the remedy of repentance has been washed with the water of the cleansing jar.

But if he has learned to understand Jerusalem and the temple of God as the Church of Christ; Babylon as the confusion of sins; Nebuchadnezzar as the devil; Jesus the high priest as Jesus Christ, the true and eternal Pontiff; and the seventy years as the fullness of good works bestowed through the gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely, on account of the Decalogue and the sevenfold [Col. 0660C] grace of that same Spirit—and if he sees this happening daily, with some snatched from the Church by the devil through sinning and others reconciled through Jesus by the grace of the Holy Spirit, by recovering their senses and repenting, then he possesses wine made from water. Understanding that what is written pertains to him, he soon grows hot, as though with the new wine of great compunction, and whatever sin of captivity he discovers within himself, he asks to be freed from it through the grace of Christ.

At the beginning of the sixth age of the world, the Lord, appearing in the flesh, was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth according to the law (Luke I); and thirty-three days afterward he was brought to the temple, and the offerings prescribed by the law were presented for him (Luke II). Considering these events literally, we plainly learn with what great diligence we must undertake the mysteries of evangelical faith, since he himself who brought the blessing of grace, and who gave the law of the letter, first consecrated it through the ritual of its ceremonies—he who divinely established all things—and thus took care both to receive and to hand on the sacraments of the new grace.

Behold the sixth water jar, establishing a purer water than the others for washing away the contagion of sin and bearing the joys of life. But if in the circumcision on the eighth day you understand baptism, which redeemed us from the death of sins as a mystery of the divine resurrection; if in the bringing into the temple and the offering of the purifying victim you recognize it symbolized; then you also understand that the faithful, having come from the baptistery into the holy altar, ought to be consecrated by the singular sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. then you have indeed been endowed with wine made from water, and that too with the purest wine. [Col. 0661A]

But if you interpret the day of circumcision as referring to the general resurrection of the human race, when mortal offspring shall cease and mortality shall be changed wholly into immortality; and if you understand those who have been circumcised as being brought into the temple with the victim, when, after the resurrection and the completion of the universal judgment, the saints, now made incorruptible, will enter with the offerings of good works to contemplate forever the appearance of the divine majesty, then you will surely see wine made from water in such abundance that you may rightly proclaim to its creator and say: “How excellent is your cup, making one drunk!” (Ps. XXII).

Therefore the Lord did not wish to make wine for the joy of the wedding from nothing, but, commanding the six water jars to be filled with water, he wonderfully changed this into wine, because he bestowed the six ages of the world with the abundance of saving wisdom. Yet when he came, he enriched that wisdom with the power of a higher meaning. For carnal people understood only carnal things; he disclosed to spiritual people what must be understood spiritually.

Do you wish to know how he made wine from water? After his resurrection he appeared to two disciples walking on the road, and he went with them. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke XXIV). Do you wish again to hear how they were made drunk with that same wine? Later, when they recognized who it was that was offering them the word of life, they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid.).

Jesus therefore says: “Fill the water jars with water”; and they filled [Col. 0661C] them to the brim. What are the servants who did this meant to signify except the disciples of Christ?
