They filled the water jars with water—not by themselves filling the past ages of the world with legal and prophetic writings, but by prudently understanding and faithfully opening them, since the Scripture delivered through the prophets is both healthful for drinking the wisdom of heaven and useful for the correction of conduct.

They filled them to the brim because they correctly understood that no period of the world had been without holy teachers who, whether by words, examples, or writings, opened the way of life to mortals.

“And he says to them,” he continues, “Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast”; and they took it. The master of the feast is a learned interpreter of the law of that time, perhaps Nicodemus, or Gamaliel, [Col. 0661D] or his disciple Saul, now the teacher of the whole Church, the apostle Paul. When the word of the Gospel that lay hidden in the letter of the law and prophecy is entrusted to such men, wine made from water is indeed offered to the master of the feast.

And rightly is a dining room—*triclinium*, that is, three ranks of reclining guests distinguished by height—described as existing in the house of this wedding, which prefigured the mysteries of Christ and the Church, because there are plainly three orders of the faithful of whom the Church consists: married people, the continent, and teachers. The first rank of guests reclining at the wedding of the heavenly bridegroom—that is, in the Church, rejoicing in faith and works—is the rank of the faithful married; the second is that of the continent; the highest is that of preachers.

Accordingly, it is fittingly reported that the master of the feast, after calling the bridegroom, said:

“Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then what is worse. You have kept the good wine until now.”

For it belongs to teachers to recognize the difference between the law and the Gospel, between truth and shadow, and to prefer the new grace of evangelical faith and the gifts of the heavenly homeland that lasts forever to all ancient institutions and all promises of an earthly kingdom.

This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed in Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory. By this sign he showed that he was the King of glory and therefore the bridegroom of the Church: he came as an ordinary man to the wedding, but, as Lord of heaven and earth, he changed the elements as he wished.

There is a beautiful correspondence in this matter: at the beginning of the signs that he would show, once made immortal through the resurrection, to those who pursued only the practices of immortal life, he first imbued their carnal and, as it were, tasteless minds with the flavor of heavenly knowledge; afterward, he would fill them with the greater gift of spiritual grace, in the glory of refreshment.

The wonderful mystery of the sign just mentioned follows: how Jesus himself, with his mother and brothers, went up to Jerusalem, found buyers and sellers in the temple, and drove them out. The evangelist says:

“Jesus went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they remained there not many days. The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

The evangelist rightly [Col. 0662C] says that Jesus went down to Capernaum. Capernaum is interpreted as “a very beautiful village,” signifying this world, to which our Lord Jesus Christ is said to have descended for the salvation of the human race, never departing from his Father’s seat.

Some are accustomed to be troubled by what is read at the beginning of this Gospel passage: when the Lord descended to Capernaum, not only his mother and disciples but also his brothers followed him. Nor were there lacking heretics who thought that Joseph, the husband of the ever-blessed Virgin Mary, had fathered by another wife those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. Others, with even greater impiety, thought that he had fathered other children by Mary herself after the Lord’s birth.

But we, dearly beloved brothers, must know and confess without any hesitation that not only the blessed Mother of God but also the most blessed Joseph, the witness and guardian of her chastity, remained entirely free from every conjugal act; and that they are called the Savior’s brothers and sisters not because they were born as such, but because, according to the customary usage of Scripture, they were relatives.

Thus Abraham says to Lot: “Please let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Gen. XIII). And Laban says to Jacob: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing?” (Gen. XXXIX). It is established, of course, that Lot was the son of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and that Jacob was the son of Rebekah, Laban’s sister; yet because of their kinship they were called brothers.

According to this rule, therefore, which, as I have said, is extremely common in Holy Scripture, Mary’s and Joseph’s relatives too must be understood to have been called the Lord’s brothers. [Col. 0663A]

That Jesus went up to Jerusalem as the Passover approached certainly gives us an example of how vigilant we must be in submitting our minds to the Lord’s commands, since he himself, appearing in human weakness, observed the same decrees that he had established by the authority of his divinity. Lest servants should think that they could escape punishment or receive rewards without frequent sacrifices of prayer and good works, the Son of God himself went up among the servants to pray and offer sacrifice to God.

When he came to Jerusalem, let us see what he found them doing there and what he himself did.

“And he found,” he says, “in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money changers sitting. And when he had made a kind of whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well; and he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables.”

Oxen, sheep, and doves were bought in order to be offered in the temple. The money changers sat at tables so that the price of the sacrifices could readily be assessed between their buyers and sellers. Thus it seemed lawful to sell in the temple things that were bought for the purpose of being offered to the Lord in that same temple.

But the Lord himself, unwilling that anything belonging to earthly commerce—even anything thought honorable—should be displayed in his house, drove out the unjust traders and expelled them all together with the things in which they traded.

What, then, my brothers, what do we think the Lord would do if he found people quarrelling, occupied with idle stories, dissolved in laughter, or entangled in any other crime—he who saw people buying in the temple the sacrifices to be offered to him and hastened to drive them out? We have said this for the sake of those who, having entered the church, not only neglect the intention of praying but even increase the things for which they ought to have prayed; and who, in addition, pursue those who rebuke them for such folly with insults, hatred, or even slander, thereby adding sins to sins and, as it were, carelessly weaving for themselves an endless end by multiplying them, without fearing that they will be condemned by the examination of the strict Judge.

For we read twice in the Holy Gospel that the Lord, coming into the temple, drove out such traders: here, that is, in the third year before his passion, as we recognize from what follows in this evangelist’s writing, and in the very year in which he suffered, when five days before Passover he came to Jerusalem seated on an ass (Matt. XXI). But everyone who thinks rightly understands that he does this same thing in the temple of the holy Church through the examination of his daily visitation.

Therefore these things are greatly to be feared, dearly beloved, and to be dreaded with worthy fear; we must take diligent precautions lest, coming unexpectedly, he find something perverse in us for which we deserve to be scourged and driven from the Church. Above all, in that place which is specially called the house of prayer, we must take care not to do anything foolish, lest we hear from the Apostle, like the Corinthians: “Do you not have houses for doing or speaking about temporal things? Or do you despise the Church of God?” (I Cor. XI). And from the prophet, with the Jews: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI). [Col. 0664A]

Indeed, we should rejoice because in baptism we ourselves have been made the temple of God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III). We are the city of the great King, of which it is sung: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI)—that is, the foundation of the Church rests upon the solidity of the faith of the apostles and prophets.

But it is exceedingly dreadful because the Apostle added these words: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III); and the just Judge himself says: “I will destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (Ps. C).

We should rejoice because the solemnity of Passover is celebrated in us when we strive to pass from vices to virtues. For Passover is called “passage.” We should rejoice because the Lord deigns to visit our hearts—namely, his city—and because that same Passover deigns to illumine our good action with the presence of his mercy.

But we must fear greatly lest he find us doing something in his city other than what he loves, and lest, as a strict retributor, he show himself to us in a form we do not love. Let him not find money changers in us in the temple, nor sellers of oxen, sheep, or doves, and condemn us.

Oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life, sheep the works of purity and mercy, and doves the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because the field is ordinarily cultivated with the help of oxen. The field is the heart cultivated by heavenly teaching and properly prepared to receive the seeds of God’s word. Sheep provide their wool as clothing for human beings; and the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

Those sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel not out of divine love but with an eye to earthly profit, like those whom the Apostle rebukes because they do not proclaim Christ sincerely (Tit. I). Those sell sheep who perform works of mercy for the sake of human praise; of them the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI). Those sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit that they have received not freely, as commanded (Matt. X), but for a reward; who confer the laying on of hands, through which the Spirit is received, not necessarily for monetary profit but for the favor of the crowd. They grant sacred orders not for the merit of life but for favor.

Those lend money in the temple who serve not heavenly matters insincerely but earthly matters openly in the Church, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus [Col. 0664D] Christ.

The Lord shows what punishment awaits such fraudulent workers when, having made a whip from cords, he drives them all out of the temple. Those are driven out from the portion allotted to the saints who, placed among the saints, either hypocritically do good or openly do evil. He also drove out the sheep and oxen, because he showed that the lives of such people are rejected.

The cords with which he scourged the wicked and expelled them from the temple are the accumulations of evil actions, from which the Judge receives the material for condemning the reprobate. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. V); and Solomon says in Proverbs: “His own iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound with the cords of his sins” (Prov. V). For whoever accumulates and prolongs sins—on account of which [the reading “Arius” appears corrupt or uncertain] he will be condemned—also has the money changers’ coins, which the Lord had expelled, poured out, and their tables overturned, because, when the reprobate are condemned at the end, he will also remove the form of the very things they loved, according to what is written: “The world will pass away, and its desire” (I John II).

And to those who sold doves he said: “Take these things away from here; do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” He commands that the sale of doves be removed from the temple because the grace of the Spirit ought to be received freely and given freely. Hence Simon Magus, who wished to buy this grace with money in order to sell it at a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you for destruction. You have no part or share in this matter” (Acts VIII).

It must be noted that not only those who sell doves are sellers and make the house of God a house of commerce—those who, by conferring sacred orders, seek payment in money, praise, or even honor—but also those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they received through the Lord’s generosity, not with a pure intention but for the sake of some human recompense. This is contrary to the words of the apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, as the words of God; whoever ministers, as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.”

Therefore, whoever is such a person, if he does not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, must remove these things from his actions, lest he make the house of God a house of commerce.

Nor should it be passed over that Scripture carefully commends to us both natures of our Savior: his human nature, certainly, and his divine nature. [Col. 0665C] To understand that he was the true Son of God, let us hear what he himself says:

“Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.”

For he plainly shows himself to be the Son of God the Father when he calls the temple of God the house of his Father. To recognize in turn that he was the true Son of Man, let us recall that at the beginning of this passage he is said to have gone down to Capernaum with his mother.

It follows:

“His disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’”

Out of zeal for the Father’s house the Savior drove the wicked from the temple. Let us also be zealous for the house of God, dearly beloved brothers, and, as far as we can, let us insist that nothing perverse be done in it.

If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by lust, turbulent with anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to correct him and to set right what has been polluted and perverted. If we cannot amend anything in such people, let us nevertheless endure it with the sharpest anguish of heart. Above all, in the very house of prayer, where the body of God is consecrated and where the presence of angels is always believed to be present, let us act with all our strength so that nothing foolish is done and nothing hinders our own prayer or that of our brothers.

It follows:

“Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, since you do these things?’ Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three [Col. 0666A] days I will raise it up.’”

The evangelist later explained which temple he meant: namely, the temple of his body, which they destroyed in the passion and which he himself raised from the dead after three days. Since they were asking the Lord for a sign—why he should have driven the customary traders from the temple—he replied that he was entirely right to expel the wicked from the temple because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there was absolutely no stain of any sin. Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the symbolic temple of crimes, since he was able, by the power of his divine majesty, to raise from the dead the true temple of God, which human beings would destroy by death.

Then the Jews said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three [Col. 0666B] days?” They answered according to how they understood him. But lest we too understand the Lord’s spiritual statement carnally, the evangelist subsequently explained which temple he was speaking about.

When they say that the temple was built in forty-six years, they do not refer to its first construction but to its second. Solomon completed the first temple in the greatest peace of his reign through a splendid labor of seven years (III Kings VI). After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, it began to be rebuilt seventy years later, at the command of Cyrus the Persian, when the captivity was released (II Chron. XXXVI). But the descendants of the exiles, who were carrying out the work under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jesus, were unable to complete it for forty-six years because of opposition from the neighboring peoples (I Esdr. II, V). This number of years also corresponds most fittingly to the perfection of the Lord’s body.

For writers on natural matters report that the form of the human body is completed over that many days: during the first six days from conception it resembles milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; afterward it becomes solid over twelve days; during the remaining ten and eight days it is formed until all the members have acquired their complete features; and from then on, during the remaining time up to birth, it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, ten, and eight make forty-five. If we add one—namely, the day on which the body, now differentiated into its members, begins to increase—we find as many days in the building of the Lord’s body as years in the construction of the temple. [Col. 0666D] For that temple made by hands prefigured the Lord’s most sacred flesh, which he took from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage. It also signified his body, which is the Church, and the body and soul of each of the faithful, as we find in many passages of Scripture.

The first Adam, after his sin, heard: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III). The second Adam said of himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The first Adam was scattered throughout the whole world; in the second he was gathered together. This is signified by the name Adam, which is written with four letters, namely α, δ, again α, and μ. These four letters designate the four regions of the world into which Adam was scattered in his descendants. For this reason these four letters occur at the beginnings of the names of the regions of the world.

For ἄρκτος, which means “the north,” begins with α; δύσις, which means “the west,” begins with δ; ἀνατολὴ, which means “the east,” begins with α; and μεσημβρία, which means “the south,” begins with μ. These are the four regions of the world, beginning with those four letters. If these letters are considered according to Greek numerical values, they make forty-six: α is one, δ is four, another α is one, and μ is forty. Together they make forty-six, mystically signifying the forty-six days during which the temple of Christ’s body was built in the Virgin’s womb.

The flesh of Christ, which was taken from that same Virgin, was destroyed by the Jews and rebuilt by him according to the Scriptures of the prophets. Therefore the evangelist says:

[Col. 0667B] “For he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

When he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture—namely, the prophets who had foretold that Christ would rise on the third day.

And they believed the statement Jesus had made, that is: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”—that is, “On the third day I will raise from the dead what you will destroy on the cross.”

It follows:

“When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in him; but Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew what was in man.”

They did not believe in him in such a way as to be worthy for Christ to dwell in them. Their faith may be compared with that of catechumens, who believe in Christ, [Col. 0667C] but Christ does not entrust himself to them, because “unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). Christ entrusts himself to no one except one who is worthy to enter the kingdom of God. No one is worthy to enter the kingdom of God except one who has been born again of water and the Spirit.

For this reason ecclesiastical custom does not give catechumens communion in the body and blood of Christ, because they have not been born again of water and the Spirit; only to those who have been so reborn is participation in the body and blood of Christ entrusted.

Among these many who believed in Jesus was this Nicodemus. For that reason he came at night and not by day, because he had not yet been illumined by the light of heavenly grace.

## CHAPTER III

There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus at night. This ruler of the Jews came to Jesus at night, desiring to learn more fully, in a private conversation with him, the mysteries of faith, of which he had already received some rudiments through the open display of signs. Because he prudently asked him about what he did not know, he deserved to investigate and learn.

“Rabbi,” he said, “we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

He therefore confessed that Jesus had come from God to provide the world with heavenly instruction, and prudently understood from the miracles that God was with him. Yet he did not know that Jesus himself was God with God. But because he eagerly presented himself for instruction in the truth to the one whom he recognized as a teacher, he deserved to receive perfect instruction in the knowledge of his divinity. He deserved to learn the mysteries of both his births—namely, the divine and the human—as well as of his passion and ascension; and, with the Lord revealing them, he also learned the manner of the second birth, entry into the heavenly kingdom, and many other mysteries of doctrine.

Jesus answered and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

This statement shines more clearly for all the faithful insofar as it is evident that without its light they cannot be faithful. For who can obtain remission of sins and enter the kingdom of heaven without the bath of regeneration? But Nicodemus, who came to the Lord at night, did not yet know how to grasp the mysteries of the light. The night in which he came also signifies the ignorance by which he was oppressed.

For he had not yet been joined to the number of those to whom the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V). Rather, he remained among those to whom Isaiah says: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” (Isa. VI).

He therefore answered the Lord and said:

“How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born?”

Because he still did not understand the second birth, but had already become concerned about his salvation, he necessarily asked whether the one birth he knew could be repeated, or in what manner regeneration could be accomplished, lest, remaining without it, he be unable to share in heavenly life.

It must be noted, however, that what he said about the carnal birth must also be understood of spiritual regeneration: namely, that once it has been completed, it cannot in any way be repeated. Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in the confession of the Holy Trinity, one who has been baptized in this way cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

And because Nicodemus, troubled by the Lord’s first answer, carefully asks how it should be understood, he deserves to be instructed more plainly. Since the second birth is not carnal but spiritual, he is about to hear:

[Col. 0668D] For Jesus answered: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Explaining the manner of this birth afterward, and distinguishing it entirely from carnal birth, he said:

“What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” The nature of the spirit is invisible, while that of the flesh is visible; and therefore carnal generation is administered visibly—for the one who is born in the flesh advances through the stages of life by visible growth—whereas spiritual generation takes place entirely invisibly. For the one who is baptized is indeed seen to descend into the font, to be immersed in the waters, and to rise from the waters; but what the washing of regeneration has accomplished in him cannot be seen at all. The devotion of believers alone [Col. 0669A] knows that a sinner descended into the font but emerged purified; a son of death descended but a son of resurrection emerged; a son of transgression descended but a son of reconciliation emerged; a son of wrath descended but a son of mercy emerged; a son of the devil descended but a son of God emerged. The mother Church alone, which gives birth, knows this. To the eyes of the foolish, however, someone seems to emerge from the font just as he entered it, and everything being done appears to be mere play. Hence, at the end, when they see the glory of the saints, they will say, groaning in their torments: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. How, then, have they been counted among the sons of God?” (Wis. 5).

The apostle John says: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (John 3). “What is born [Col. 0669B] of the Spirit is spirit,” because the one who is regenerated by water and the Spirit is invisibly changed into a new person and from being carnal becomes spiritual. He is therefore rightly called not only spiritual but also spirit, because just as the substance of spirit is invisible to the eyes, so the one who is renewed by God’s grace becomes spiritual invisibly and becomes a son of God, although visibly he appears to everyone as flesh and as a son of man. It follows:

“Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

“The Spirit breathes where he wills,” because he has power over whose heart he will enlighten by the grace of his visitation. “And you hear his voice,” when, in your presence, someone who has been filled with the Holy Spirit speaks. “But you do not know [Col. 0669C] where he comes from or where he goes,” because even if the Spirit should fill someone for a time in your presence, you cannot see how he entered or how he departed, since his nature is invisible. “So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” For, while the Spirit acts invisibly, he too begins to be what he was not, so that unbelievers do not know where he comes from or where he goes—that is, that through the grace of regeneration he comes into the adoption of the sons of God and goes on to receive the heavenly kingdom.

But while Nicodemus was still asking how these things could happen, the Lord added, saying:

“You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?” He did not say this as though wishing to insult one who was called a teacher while ignorant of the heavenly mysteries, but to summon him to the way of humility, without which the heavenly door cannot be found.

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” He told them earthly things, as we found in the preceding reading, when he spoke of the passion and resurrection of his body, which he had taken from the earth, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Yet they did not believe the word he had spoken; nor could they even understand that he was speaking of any temple other than the temple of his body. If, then, they did not grasp earthly things when they heard them, how much less were they capable of grasping heavenly things—that is, the mysteries of divine generation?

The Lord continued to instruct him both about heavenly mysteries and about earthly things, because he saw him attending wisely and carefully [Col. 0670A] to what he heard. His ascent to eternal life is heavenly; his earthly exaltation, however, is to temporal death. He therefore speaks of heavenly things:

“And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

He then adds concerning earthly things:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

It is rightly asked how the Son of Man is said either to have descended from heaven or already to have been in heaven at the time when he was speaking these things on earth. The confession of the catholic faith is well known: the Son of God, descending from heaven, assumed the Son of Man in the Virgin’s womb; and, after completing the dispensation of his passion, he raised him from the dead and took him into heaven. Therefore Christ’s flesh [Col. 0670B] did not descend from heaven, nor was it in heaven before the time of the ascension, except because Christ is one person existing in two natures. For this reason the Son of Man is rightly said both to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before the passion, because what he could not have in his own nature he possessed in the Son of God by whom he was assumed.

For the same reason, because there is one Christ whose person exists in two natures, the Apostle says: “The Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20). God did not have blood in his own nature, but in the man he assumed he had blood to pour out for the Church. Hence the Psalmist says: “God has ascended amid jubilation” (Ps. 46). For how could God ascend except in man, since in the majesty of his own nature he is always present everywhere? [Col. 0670C]

It must also be asked how it was said: “And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” when all the elect truly trust that they will ascend into heaven, since the Lord promises them: “Where I am, there my servant will be also” (John 12). The clearest explanation of this question, however, is that Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, is the head of all the elect; likewise, all his elect are members of that same head. The Apostle says: “He gave him as head over the whole Church” (Eph. 1); and again: “You are the body of Christ, and individually members of it” (Eph. 5).

“No one, therefore, ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” No one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. In himself he ascended first, in the sight of the apostles, who were his more eminent members; and from that point onward he ascends daily in his members, gathering himself into heaven. Hence that same body, found amid the adversities of this world, glories and says: “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Ps. 29). It is as though it openly said:

“He who raised Christ, my head, whom the Jews killed, from the dead, and, frustrating all the plots of his enemies, lifted him into heaven—by rescuing me also from present dangers, I hope that he will join me to my head in the kingdom, because no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.”

Whoever desires to ascend into heaven should unite himself to the one who descended from heaven and is in heaven by true faith and love, clearly understanding that no one can ascend into heaven by any other way than through the one who descended from heaven. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). These things are said to all catechumens in the person of Nicodemus, so that they may learn to be incorporated by rebirth into the members of the one through whom they can ascend into the kingdom of God.

And because ascent or entrance into the kingdom cannot occur without faith and the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, it is rightly added:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

With wondrous heavenly teaching, the Lord leads the teacher of the Mosaic law toward the spiritual meaning of that same law, recalling the history of old and explaining that it was made a figure of his passion and of human salvation. The Book of Numbers relates that, weary of the long journey and labor in the wilderness, the people of Israel murmured against the Lord and Moses (Num. 23); and therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When, because of their bites and the deaths of many, they cried out to Moses and he prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. “Anyone who has been bitten,” he said, “who looks at it shall live”; and so it happened.

The wounds inflicted by the fiery serpents are therefore the poisons and stimuli of vices, which kill the soul they touch by spiritual death. It was fitting that the people who murmured against the Lord should be struck down by the bites of serpents, so that, through the order of the outward scourge, they might recognize how great a destruction they were suffering inwardly by their murmuring. The lifting up of the bronze serpent, by looking at which those who had been bitten were healed, signifies the passion of our Redeemer on the cross, by faith in whom alone the kingdom of death and sin is overcome.

Sins are rightly represented by serpents, sins that drag both soul and body to destruction—not only because the serpents were fiery, venomous, and cunning in killing, but also because our first parents were persuaded to sin by a serpent (Gen. 3) and, by sinning, were changed from immortal to mortal beings. The Lord is rightly shown by the bronze serpent because he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8). Just as the bronze serpent had an appearance like that of the fiery serpents but had absolutely none of the harmful heat of their venom in its members—and indeed healed those bitten by serpents through its being lifted up—so, precisely so, the Redeemer of the human race did not assume sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh, in which, by suffering the death of the cross, he would free those who believed in him from every sin and from death itself.

“Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so,” he says, “the Son of Man must be lifted up.” For just as those who looked at the bronze serpent lifted up as a sign were healed for a time from temporal death and from the wound inflicted by the serpents’ bites, so those who, by believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating, look upon the mystery of the Lord’s passion are saved forever from every death which, by sinning in soul and body alike, they had incurred. Hence it is rightly added:

“So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The meaning of this statement is clear: whoever believes in Jesus not only escapes the punishment of destruction but also receives eternal life. This is the difference between the figure and the reality: through the former, temporal life is prolonged; through the latter, life is given which will endure without end. Yet care must be taken that what the understanding rightly perceives may be fulfilled by corresponding action, so that, by living soberly according to our confession of the true faith, we may deserve to attain the life promised to us.

But because these things are said of the Son of Man—because he had to be lifted up on the cross, that is, to suffer death—lest Nicodemus think that he was only a son of man from whom perpetual life was to be expected, the Lord also took care to reveal to him the mystery of his divinity and to show that the same one was both Son of Man and Savior of the world. For it follows:

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

Here we should note that he repeats concerning the only-begotten Son of God the same words he had previously spoken concerning the Son of Man lifted up on the cross: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.” For the same Redeemer and Creator of ours, the Son of God existing before the ages, became the Son of Man at the end of the ages, so that the one who by the power of his divinity had created us to enjoy perpetual blessed life might himself, through the weakness of our humanity, restore us to receive the life we had lost. It follows:

“For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.”

Therefore, insofar as it depends on the physician, he came to heal the sick person. The one who does not wish to observe the physician’s instructions destroys himself. The Savior came into the world. Why is he called the Savior of the world, except because he came to save the world, not to judge the world? You do not wish to be saved by him? You will be judged by yourself. And what shall I say—“you will be judged”? See what he says:

“Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe …”

What did you expect him to say, except “is judged”? He says: “He has already been judged.” Judgment has appeared, but judgment has already taken place. For the Lord knows who are his (2 Tim. 2). He knows who will remain for the crown and who will remain for the flame. He knows his wheat on his threshing floor; he also knows the chaff. He knows the crop, and he knows the weeds.

“He has already been judged, whoever does not believe.” Why has he been judged? “Because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

“And this is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil.”

My brothers, whose works did the Lord find good? No one’s, for he found all their works evil. How, then, did some “do the truth” and come to the light? For this follows:

“But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.”

How, then, did some do a good work so that they might come to the light—that is, to Christ? And how did some love darkness, if he found all to be sinners and heals all from sin? The serpent in which the Lord’s death was represented healed those who had been bitten; and because of the bites of the serpents, the serpent was raised up—that is, the Lord’s death was raised up because of the mortal human beings whom he found unrighteous.

How is this judgment to be understood: “Light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil”? What does this mean? Whose works were good? Did you not come to justify the ungodly? Yet he says: “They loved darkness more than light.” There he placed the emphasis.

Many have loved their sins, because whoever confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting together with God. God accuses your sins; if you also accuse them, you are joined to God. There are, as it were, two things: the human being and the sinner. Insofar as you hear “human being,” God made that; insofar as you hear “sinner,” that the human being himself made. Destroy what you made, so that God may save what he made.

You must hate in yourself one work and love in yourself God’s work. When what you have done begins to displease you, then your good works begin, because you accuse your evil works. The beginning of good works is the confession of evil works. You do the truth and come to the light.

What does “you do the truth” mean? You do not flatter yourself, nor indulge yourself, nor deceive yourself. You do not say, “I am righteous,” when you are unrighteous; and so you begin to do the truth. You come to the light so that your works may be revealed, because they have been done in God. For the very fact that your sin displeased you would not have displeased you unless God had shone upon you and his truth had shown you to yourself.

But whoever, even after being admonished, loves his sins hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, so that his evil works, which he loves, may not be reproved. Whoever does the truth accuses his evil deeds in himself; he spares himself nothing and forgives himself nothing, so that God may forgive him. He acknowledges them himself and comes to the light, giving thanks to the one who showed him what he should hate in himself. He says to the Lord: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50). And with what confidence does he say this unless he again says: “For I acknowledge my transgression, and my sin is always before me” (ibid.)?

But if you place your sin behind you, God will turn it back before your eyes; and he will turn it back when there will no longer be any fruit of repentance. Run, lest the darkness overtake you.

It follows:

“After this Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he stayed with them, and there he was baptizing.”

The baptized one baptizes—not with the baptism with which he himself was baptized. The Lord, baptized by a servant, gives baptism, showing the way of humility and leading to the Lord’s baptism, that is, his own baptism, by offering in reality an example of humility. For he himself did not reject the servant’s baptism; and by the servant’s baptism a way was prepared for the Lord. The Lord was baptized and made himself the way for those coming to him. Let us hear him: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). If you seek the truth, hold to the way; for the one who is the way is himself the truth.

Let us hear John: “Jesus was baptizing.” We said that Jesus was baptizing—how could Jesus, how could the Lord, how could the Son of God, how could the Word do this? But “the Word became flesh.”

“Now John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim.” What is the place? Its name explains it, because there were many waters there. Aenon near Salim is the place where John was baptizing; the place is still shown today, at the eighth milestone south of Scythopolis, near Salim and the Jordan.

[Col. 0674B] “For John had not yet been cast into prison.”

Why was John baptizing? Because it was necessary that the Lord be baptized. Why was it necessary that the Lord be baptized? So that no one, however greatly endowed with grace or power, might disdain to be baptized. The Lord himself did not disdain the sacrament of baptism, although there was nothing in him to be cleansed by baptism, since he had no sin to be forgiven in the washing of baptism. The Lord was baptized by a servant so that the servant of the Lord would not disdain baptism.

“For John had not yet been cast into prison.” The evangelist says this so that it might be understood that the miracles he recounted earlier took place in the first year of the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, which began with his baptism; he understood that the other [evangelists] chiefly related the events of this year. [The syntax of the final clause is materially uncertain.]

A question arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification. John’s disciples were jealous of their teacher, because they heard that more people were flocking to Christ’s baptism and that the Jews preferred Christ’s baptism to John’s. Finally they came to John himself so that he might resolve the question they had had with the Jews concerning the distinction between Christ’s baptism and his.

“And they said to him: ‘Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him.’”

As though indignant that more people had come to Christ’s baptism, they said: “Everyone is coming to him, and they are leaving you. He was baptized with your baptism, yet now everyone is flocking to his baptism.”

He answered and said: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear witness to me that I said: ‘I am not the Christ.’ If you believe my testimony, know that I am not the Christ, but that his is the baptism in which there is forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit is given—not mine, in which only repentance and faith in the one about whom you now complain were given.

“A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. I am the herald; he is the judge. Therefore I am the servant; he is the Lord. He is the bridegroom; I am the friend of the bridegroom. He must increase, but I must decrease. I came to prepare his way, not to exalt myself. I am the voice of one crying out; he is the Father’s Word.

“The one who comes after me has been placed before me,” that is, he has been preferred to me in dignity. “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.” That is, I am not worthy to explain the mystery of his birth, by which he was born from the Virgin and came into the world.

“You have heard my testimony; believe my testimony; flock to the one in whose baptism there is forgiveness of sins.”

This John was held in such great authority that the people thought he was the Christ. But he rejected a false honor so that he might possess the solid truth. He did not wish to boast of being what he was not, lest he be without the one who always was.

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” I am not the bridegroom. But what am I? The friend of the bridegroom, rejoicing at the voice of the one who is the bridegroom, of whom it is said: “God is king of all the earth, and all the kings of the earth shall worship him” (Ps. 72); “all nations shall serve him.”

He is the true bridegroom. The bride is the holy Church, gathered from all nations, concerning which the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). She is a virgin and has a bridegroom; she gives birth daily and remains perpetually a virgin. This virginity is integrity of mind, perfection of love, unity of the catholic faith, harmony of peace, and chastity in body and soul, because bodily chastity is worthless without the integrity of the catholic faith.

The friends of this virgin—that is, of the universal Church—are the preachers of evangelical truth. Therefore this John says: “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” He stands who remains in the true faith and preaches what he believes.

Why does he stand? Because he does not fall. Why does he not fall? Because he is humble. This forerunner of the Lord stood upon the solid rock when he said: “I am not the Christ; I am not the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom.” Whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him rightly does not fall, rightly stands, rightly hears the bridegroom’s voice, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.

The bridegroom’s voice is therefore: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

John therefore confessed, as you heard above: “I am not the Christ.” When Jesus was making many disciples and this was reported to him, as though to provoke him—for they reported it as jealous people would: “Look, he is making more disciples than you”—John confessed what he was. By this he deserved to belong to Christ, because he did not dare to say that he was what Christ is.

This, then, is what John said: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” Christ gives, and a person receives. “You yourselves bear witness to me that I said: ‘I am not the Christ,’ but that I was sent before him.”

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice,” and does not make his joy arise from himself. For whoever wishes to rejoice in himself will be sad. Whoever wishes to rejoice in God will always rejoice, because God is eternal.

John described himself in this way: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice, he says, not because of his own voice; he stands and hears him. If, then, he falls, he does not hear him. For concerning the one who once fell it was said: “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8); this was said of the devil.

The friend of the bridegroom must therefore stand and hear. What does “stand” mean? To remain in the grace he has received. And he hears the voice at which he may rejoice.

Such was John. He knew the source of his joy and did not claim for himself what he was not. He knew that he had been enlightened, not that he was the enlightener. For the evangelist says: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). If every person, then John also, because he himself was one of the human beings.

It follows. And John says:

“Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”

What is his joy? That he should rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice. Many became foolish for this reason: they said that they were wise. The Apostle rebukes them in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1). Therefore God gives gifts to those who give thanks, but takes them away from those who do not give thanks.

John did not wish to be like this; he wished to be grateful. He confessed that he had received, said that he rejoiced because of the bridegroom’s voice, and said: “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”

“He must increase, but I must decrease.”

What does this mean: “He must be exalted, but I must be humbled”? This is a great mystery. Before the Lord Jesus came, people gloried in themselves. He came as a human being so that human glory might decrease and God’s glory increase. He came without sin and found everyone with sin. Since he came in order to forgive sins, God must bestow and the human being must confess. The human being’s confession is humility; God’s mercy is exaltation.

Since he came to forgive sins, then, let the human being acknowledge his humility, and God will show his mercy.

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” That is, he must give, but I must receive. He must be glorified, but I must confess. Let a human being recognize his place and confess to God, and let him hear the Apostle speaking to the proud and exalted person who wishes to raise himself up:

“What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4).

Let the person who has received understand, and let the one who wished to call his own what is not his decrease. For it is good for him that God be glorified in him, while he himself decreases in himself, so that he may increase in God (1 Cor. 4).

Christ and John signified these testimonies and this truth also by their deaths. John was beheaded, so that even there it might appear what is meant by “He must increase, but I must decrease.” That is, he must be exalted, but I must be humbled.

The very order of the lights in creation signifies this. Christ was born during the days when the light was increasing, while John was born during the days when it was decreasing, so that it might be shown what Christ is—that is, the true light—and what John is—that is, one enlightened by him.

Let us increase in him and through him, so that he may increase in us, until we reach the perfect day.

Let us hear further what John said about Christ, and what he said about himself. For he says:

“The one who comes from above is above all; and the one who is from the earth is earthly and speaks from the earth.”

“The one who comes from above is above all”—that is, Christ. “But the one who is from the earth is earth and speaks from the earth”—that is, John. Since every human being speaks from the earth, he is earthly; and while he speaks earthly things, he speaks from the earth.

But the one who has been enlightened by him who is the true light speaks of divine things. Grace comes from above; human nature is below. The carnal person judges carnally and suspects carnally. When God’s grace comes, enlightening the human being, he speaks of heavenly things, as it is said: “You who enlighten my lamp, Lord my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 18). This means: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

Therefore John, insofar as he is John, is from the earth and speaks from the earth. If you have heard anything divine from John, it comes from the one who enlightens, not from the one who receives. “The one who comes from heaven is above all, and he testifies to what he has seen and heard.”

“And no one accepts his testimony.”

The one who came from heaven, our Lord Jesus Christ, is above all. Concerning him it was said above: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” He is above all, and he speaks what he has seen and heard.

For that Son of God himself also has a Father, and he has heard from the Father. And what is it that he heard from the Father? Who can explain this? When can my tongue, when can my heart, be sufficient—my heart for understanding, or my tongue for expressing it? What is it that the Son heard from the Father? Perhaps, since he is the Son, he heard the Father’s Word. Rather, the Son is the Father’s Word.

Since the Word of God is the Son, and the Son spoke to us, he wished to speak to us not his own word but the Father’s Word, because he spoke the Father’s Word. In this way, as was fitting and necessary, John said:

“The one who comes from heaven is above all; and he testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony.”

“If no one accepts it,” he says, “why did Christ come?” Because there is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God, to be condemned with the devil. None of these accepts Christ’s testimony.

For if absolutely no one—if no human being—accepts it, what is the meaning of what follows?

“Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.”

Certainly, then, it is not absolutely no one; rather, as you yourself say, “Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” John perhaps answered when questioned, as though explaining to us whom he meant by “no one.” There is a certain people born for the wrath of God and foreknown for this purpose.

The Lord knows who will believe and who will not believe; God knows who will persevere in what they have believed and who will fall away. All who will exist for eternal life are numbered before God.

“No one accepts the testimony of the one who came from heaven. Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” “Certified” means that he sets this sign in his heart, as a singular and distinctive truth: that the one who was sent for the salvation of the human race is the true God.

What does “has certified that God is true” mean except that the human being is false and God is true? No human being can say what is true unless he is enlightened by the one who cannot lie. God, therefore, is true; Christ, however, is God. Do you wish to prove it? Accept his testimony, and you will find it: “Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” Who is this? The one who came from heaven and descended, who is above all: God is true.

“For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God.”

He is the true God; he is God and our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4).

“For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God.” He was speaking this about Christ in order to distinguish himself from him. For what of John? Did God not send John? Did he not himself say: “I was sent before him,” and: “The one who sent me to baptize with water” (John 1)? And it was said of him: “Behold, I send my angel before you, and he will prepare your way” (Mal. 3).

Does he himself not also speak the words of God, of whom it was even said that he is greater than a prophet (Matt. 12)? If, then, the Lord also sent John and he speaks the words of God, how are we to understand John’s statement about Christ as a distinction: “The one whom God sent speaks the words of God”? But see what he adds:

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

Hear the Apostle saying: “According to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4). To human beings he gives by measure; to the only Son he does not give by measure.

How does he give to human beings by measure? “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another gifts of healing” (1 Cor. 12).

Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? One has one gift, another has another; what one has, another does not have. There is a measure, a certain distribution of gifts.

Thus a measure is given to human beings, and harmony is produced, through which one body is formed. Just as one thing is given to the hand so that it may work, another to the eye so that it may see, another to the ear so that it may hear, and another to the foot so that it may walk—yet there is one soul that acts in all of them: in the hand so that it may work, in the foot so that it may walk, in the ear so that it may hear, and in the eye so that it may see—so there are also different gifts among the faithful, distributed to each according to measure, as to members.

But Christ, who gives, did not receive by measure. Hear what follows, for he had been speaking about the Son:

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son, and has given everything into his hand.”

Here too, note how distinctly it says: “The Father loves the Son.” Why? Does the Father not love John? Yet he did not give everything into John’s hand. Does the Father not love Paul? Yet he did not give everything into Paul’s hand.

The Father loves the Son, but as a Father loves the Son, not as a master loves a servant; as he loves the only Son, not as he loves an adopted son. Therefore he gave everything into his hand.

What does “everything” mean? It means that the Son should be as great as the Father.

## CHAPTER 4
Therefore, when Jesus heard that the Pharisees had heard, and so forth: Certainly, if the Lord had known that the Pharisees had understood these things about him in such a way that his making more disciples and baptizing more disciples would benefit their salvation—that they might follow him and themselves become disciples, and that they might desire all the more to be baptized by him—he would not have left the land of Judea but would have remained there for their sake. But because he recognized their knowledge, he recognized their envy at the same time: they had not learned this in order to follow him. Therefore he departed from there.

He could indeed have remained present without being seized by them, if he had wished. But because in everything he did as a man for human beings who would believe in him he offered an example—because a servant of God does not sin if he withdraws to another place when he sees the fierce rage of those pursuing him, or when they seek his life for evil purposes—it might have seemed that God’s servant sinned by doing this, unless the Lord had gone before him in doing it. Thus the good Teacher did this in order to teach, not because he was afraid.

Perhaps this also raises a question: why is it said, “Jesus was baptizing more people than John,” and then, after it has been said that he was baptizing, the qualification is added, “although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples”? What then? Was the statement false and corrected, or are both statements true, because Jesus both baptized and did not baptize? He baptized because he himself cleansed; he did not baptize because he himself did not immerse. The disciples supplied the ministry of the body; he supplied the assistance of his majesty.

For when would he cease baptizing, who does not cease cleansing? Of him the same John said, speaking through the person of John the Baptist: “This is he who baptizes” (John I). Therefore Jesus still baptizes. And for as long as those who are to be baptized are being baptized, Jesus baptizes. Let a human being approach the lower minister without fear, for he has a higher Teacher.

But perhaps someone may say: “Christ baptizes in the Spirit, not in the body.” As though anyone were immersed even in the sacrament of bodily and visible baptism by a gift belonging to anyone other than him! Do you wish to know that he himself baptizes not only with the Spirit but also with water? Hear the Apostle: “As Christ,” he says, “loved his Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind.” Cleansing her—how? “By the washing of water in the word” (Ephesians V). Take away the water: there is no baptism. Take away the word: there is no baptism.

It is often asked whether the Holy Spirit was given in this baptism of Christ’s disciples, on account of the words read later in this Gospel, where it is said: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII). Certainly the Holy Spirit was given in this baptism administered by Christ’s disciples, although not with that manifestation in which, after Christ’s ascension, on the tenth day, he was given in tongues of fire.

For the fact that God performs some things secretly and others visibly through a visible creature belongs to the governance of his wisdom, by which all divine actions are carried out with the most beautiful distinction according to the order of places and times. Just as the Lord himself certainly had the Holy Spirit with him in the very man whom he bore when he came to John to be baptized, and yet, after he had been baptized, the Holy Spirit was seen descending upon him in the form of a dove, so it should be understood that, before the Spirit’s manifest and visible coming, any holy persons could secretly possess him.

We say this in such a way as also to understand that through the visible manifestation itself of the Holy Spirit—which is called his coming—the fullness of the Spirit was poured into human hearts more abundantly, in an ineffable, indeed unimaginable, manner.

It follows:

“He left Judea and departed again into Galilee.”

What does “he left Judea” mean except that he left the unbelief of those who refused to receive him and rejected the stone which they ought to have built? And he went through the apostles into Galilee—that is, into the turning movement of this world—commanding the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII).

For it was necessary that he pass through Samaria. In the Gospel reading, the holy Evangelist has shown us most fully that the Lord Jesus Christ assumed the weakness of the human race. For after saying that the Lord had come to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph, in which estate Jacob’s well was located, he added:

“Jesus,” he says, “wearied from the journey, was sitting thus beside the well.”

The holy Jacob had left this estate to his son Joseph. I believe, however, that it was left not so much to Joseph as to Christ, whose figure the holy patriarch Joseph bore—he whom the sun truly worships, and the moon and all the stars bless.

The Lord came to this estate so that the Samaritans, who desired to claim for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch of Israel, might recognize their possessor and be converted to Christ, because he had become the legitimate heir of the patriarch.

The Evangelist says: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus beside the well.” The mysteries of the Gospel, signified in the words and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ, are not apparent to everyone. Some people, interpreting them less carefully and less soberly, frequently assert destruction instead of salvation and error instead of knowledge of the truth.

Among these mysteries is what is written: that the Lord came to Jacob’s well at the sixth hour of the day, weary from the journey, sat down, asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, and other matters written in that passage, which are said to require examination and discussion.

The first thing to be held concerning this matter is what must be guarded with the greatest vigilance throughout all the Scriptures: the exposition of the divine mystery must accord with the faith.

Our Lord therefore came to the well at the sixth hour of the day. I see in the well a dark depth; I am therefore urged to understand it as signifying the lower regions of this world (Ephesians IV), that is, earthly things, to which Jesus came at the sixth hour—that is, in the sixth age of the human race—as though in the old man’s old age. We are commanded to put off that old man in order to put on the new, who has been created according to God.

For the sixth age is old age: the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, and the fifth maturity. The life of the old man, therefore, which is lived according to the flesh under temporal conditions, is brought to its close in the sixth age, that is, in old age. For, as I have said, in the old age of the human race our Lord, its Creator and Restorer, came to us, so that, when the old man died, he might establish the new man in himself and, stripped of earthly clay, transfer him to the heavenly kingdoms.

Thus the well, as has been said, signifies by its dark depth the earthly toil and error of this world. The Apostle says: “Even if our outward man is being corrupted, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day” (II Corinthians IV). This is entirely correct, since all visible things belong to the outward man, to which Christian discipline bids us renounce. The Lord came at the sixth hour, that is, at midday, when this visible sun has already begun to decline toward sunset. For we too, called by Christ to the love of invisible things, return to the inner light that never sets, our inward man having been renewed. According to apostolic discipline, we seek not the things that are seen but those that are not seen. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Corinthians IV).

That he came to the well wearied signifies the weakness of the flesh; that he manifested humility signifies that he assumed for us the weakness of the flesh and deigned to appear so humbly as a man among human beings. Concerning this weakness of the flesh the prophet says: “A man set in suffering and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah LIII). Concerning humility the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians II).

Yet the fact that he sat—since teachers customarily sit—may be understood in another way, not as indicating the modesty of humility but the person of a teacher.

But it may be asked why he requested a drink from the Samaritan woman, who had come to be filled with grace, when he later proclaimed that he could give the abundance of the spiritual fountain to those who asked him. He certainly knew the faith of that woman, who, because she was a Samaritan, commonly represents the image of Samaritan idolatry. For they, having separated themselves from the Jewish people, had devoted the honor of their souls to images of dumb animals, that is, to golden calves.

Our Lord Jesus had come to lead the multitude of the nations, which had served images, to the unity of Christian faith and undefiled religion. For he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew IX). Therefore he thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood.

Then Jesus said to her:

“Woman, give me a drink.”

And our Lord knew what she thirsted for. Shortly afterward his disciples came; they had gone into the city to buy food, and they said to him:

“Rabbi, eat.”

But he said to them:

“I have food to eat which you do not know.”

His disciples therefore said to one another:

“Has anyone brought him something to eat?”

Jesus said to them:

“My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”

What else can the Father’s will be, and the work which he said he wished to complete, except that he should convert us from the destructive error of the world to faith in him? Therefore, just as his food is, so also is his drink: for this reason he thirsted in that woman, in order to do the Father’s will in her [Col. 0682A] and complete his work.

But understanding him carnally, she replied:

“You are a Jew; how can you ask a drink from me, though I am a Samaritan woman?” For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

Our Lord said to her:

“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

By this he showed her that he had not asked for such water as she had understood. But because he himself thirsted for her faith, he desired to give her the Spirit by which she might know. For we rightly understand this living water to be the gift of God, just as he himself says: “If you knew the gift of God”; and as the same John testifies elsewhere, saying that Jesus stood and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII). It follows entirely: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (ibid.).

For we first believe in order to deserve these gifts. This river of living water, therefore, which he wished to give that woman, is the reward of the faith for which he first thirsted in her.

Regarding the interpretation of this living water, he adds:

“But this he said concerning the Spirit whom those who were going to believe in him would receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid.).

This, then, is the gift of the Holy Spirit which, after his glorification, he gave to the Church, as another Scripture says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Psalm LXVII).

But the woman still thinks carnally, for she replied:

“Lord, you have neither a vessel for drawing, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, and his sons and his cattle?”

Now the Lord explains what he had said:

“Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give will never thirst. Rather, the water that I shall give will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

But the woman embraces the prudence of the flesh. What did she answer?

“Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw water.”

Jesus said to her:

“Go, call your husband, and come here.”

Although he knew that she had no husband, why did he say this? The question arises. For when the woman said:

“I have no husband,”

Jesus said to her:

“You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband.’ For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband; in this you have spoken truly.”

But these things must not be understood carnally, lest we seem to be like this same Samaritan woman even now. Rather, if we have already tasted something of that gift of God, let us treat the matter spiritually.

Some understand the five husbands as the five books administered through Moses. They understand the statement, “And the one whom you now have is not your husband,” as spoken by the Lord about himself, so that the sense is: “You served five husbands in the five books of Moses; but the one whom you now have—that is, the one whom you hear—is not your husband, because you have not yet believed in him.”

But since, before believing in Christ, she was still held in the union of those five husbands—that is, the five books—it may be asked how it could be said, “You have had five husbands,” as though she no longer had them, when she was still living subject to them.

Furthermore, since the five books of Moses preach nothing other than Christ, as he himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John III), how can it be understood that a person leaves those five books in order to pass over to Christ, when the person who believes in Christ does not abandon those five books but embraces them much more blessedly through spiritual understanding?

There is therefore another interpretation: the five husbands may be understood as the five bodily senses.

The first is the sense belonging to the eyes, by which we see this visible light and all sorts of colors, shapes, and forms of bodies. The second is that of the ears, by which we perceive the impressions of voices and every kind of sound. The third is that of the nostrils, by which we delight in the varied sweetness of odors. The fourth is taste in the mouth, which perceives sweet and bitter and tests every kind of flavor. The fifth judges throughout the whole body by touch—hot and cold, hard and soft, smooth and rough—and whatever else we perceive by touching.

The first age of human life is therefore imbued with these five bodily senses, by the necessity of mortal nature. For after the sin of the first man we were born in such a way that, before the light of the mind had been restored, we remained subject to bodily senses and passed through a bodily life without any understanding of the truth.

Infants and little children must necessarily be like this, since they are not yet able to receive reason. And because these senses are natural, governing the first age, and were bestowed upon us by God the Creator, they are rightly called men—that is, husbands—as though legitimate ones, since nature did not give them to us through its own error but through God the Creator.

But when someone reaches the age at which he can be capable of reason, if he is able immediately to grasp the truth, he will not use those senses as rulers. Instead, he will have as husband a rational spirit, to whom he will reduce those senses to service, subjecting his body to servitude.

Then the soul is no longer subject to five husbands—that is, the five bodily senses—but possesses the divine Word as its legitimate husband. Joined and clinging to him, and with the human spirit itself clinging to Christ—for “Christ is the head of the man” (I Corinthians XI)—the soul embraces spiritual things and enjoys eternal life without fear of separation.

For she was held by five husbands, signifying the multitude of the world subjected to vain superstitions. After that period of the five bodily senses, by which the first age is governed, the Word of God had not taken her in marriage; rather, the devil possessed her in an adulterous embrace.

Therefore the Lord says to her, seeing that she is carnal—that is, thinking carnally:

“Go, call your husband, and come here.”

That is: “Remove yourself from the carnal affection in which you are now established, because you cannot understand what I am saying; and call your husband”—that is, “Be present in the spirit of understanding.”

For the spirit of a human being is, in a certain sense, like the husband of the soul; it governs the animal affection as a spouse. This is not the Holy Spirit, who is given unchangeably with the Father and the Son, but the human spirit, of which the Apostle says: “No one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being” (I Corinthians II). For that Holy Spirit too is the Spirit of God, concerning whom he says again: “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (ibid.).

When this human spirit is present—that is, attentive—and submits itself to God in devotion, the human being understands what is spoken spiritually. But when the devil’s error dominates in the soul as though understanding were absent, he is an adulterer.

“Call your husband,” therefore, he says—that is, “the spirit which is in you, by which a human being can understand spiritual things.” For if the light of truth illuminates the husband, he is understood to be present. Call, therefore, “your husband,” so that he may be present when I speak to you and so that you may receive spiritual water.

To her who denied having a husband he says:

“You have spoken well. For you have had five husbands”—that is, “Five carnal senses ruled you in your first age; and the one whom you now have is not your husband, because there is not in you a spirit that understands God, with whom you can have a legitimate marriage. Rather, the devil’s error dominates and corrupts you with adulterous contamination.”

And perhaps, in order to indicate to those who understand that the five bodily senses are signified by the name of five husbands, after five carnal replies this woman names Christ in a sixth reply.

Her first reply was: “Since you are a Jew, how can you ask a drink from me?” The second: “Lord, you have no vessel with which to draw, and the well is deep.” The third: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or come here to draw.” The fourth: “I have no husband.” The fifth: “I see that you are a prophet; our fathers worshiped on this mountain.”

For this reply is carnal: a terrestrial place had been given to carnal people where they should pray, whereas the Lord said that spiritual people would worship in spirit and truth.

After he had spoken this, in the woman’s sixth reply she confesses that Christ will teach the history of everything.

For she says:

“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

But she still errs, because she does not see that the one whose coming she hopes for has already come. Nevertheless, by the Lord’s mercy, this error is now expelled like an adulterer.

For Jesus says to her:

“I am he, the one who is speaking with you.”

[Col. 0684D] When she heard this, she said nothing, but immediately left her water jar and hurried into the city, so that she might not only believe the Gospel and the Lord’s coming but also proclaim it.

Nor should the fact that she left the water jar and departed be passed over carelessly. For the water jar perhaps signifies love of this world, that is, desire: from the dark depth whose image the well bears—that is, from earthly conduct—people draw pleasure for themselves. Once they have tasted it, they burn again with desire for it, just as the one who drinks that water will thirst again.
