But once she had believed in Christ, it was necessary for her to renounce the world and, by leaving the water jar, to show that she had left worldly desire. Believing with the heart unto righteousness, she also confessed and proclaimed her faith unto salvation.

The woman said to him:

“Lord, I see that you are a prophet.”

The husband had begun to come; he had not yet come fully. She thought the Lord was a prophet. Indeed, he was a prophet, for he said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Luke IV). It was also said of him to Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deuteronomy XVIII)—like you, that is, in the form of the flesh, not in the excellence of majesty.

Therefore we find that the Lord Jesus was called a prophet, and thus this woman no longer errs greatly. “I see,” she says, “that you are a prophet.” She begins to exclude the adulterer: “I see that you are a prophet,” and she begins to ask about what had usually troubled her.

For there had been a dispute between the Samaritans and the Jews. The Jews worshiped God in the temple built by Solomon; the Samaritans, who lived far away, did not worship there. Therefore the Jews wanted to regard themselves as superior because they worshiped God in the temple.

For Jews do not associate with Samaritans. The Samaritans said to them: “Because you worship in the temple, you claim that you are superior to us in possessing what we do not have. But did our fathers, who pleased God, worship in that temple? Did they not worship on this mountain, where I now am? We therefore pray to God more properly on this mountain, where our fathers prayed.”

Both groups contended in ignorance. Since neither possessed a husband, the one group was inflamed against the other on behalf of the temple, the other on behalf of the mountain.

What, then, does the Lord now teach the woman, as though the husband who had been absent were beginning to be present? The woman says to him:

“Lord, I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that one must worship in Jerusalem.”

Jesus says to her:

“Woman, believe me.”

For the Church believes her bridegroom, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “Behold, my beloved speaks to me: Rise, hasten, my beloved, and come. For winter has passed, the rain has gone away, the flowers have appeared on the earth, the time of pruning has come, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs II).

Now that the husband is truly present, the woman rightly hears: “Believe me.” For the one who believes is already present in you, because your husband is present. You began to be present in understanding when you called me a prophet.

“Woman, believe me,” for “unless you believe, you will not understand.” Therefore, woman, believe me:

“The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when—”

What hour is this?

“When true worshipers will worship not on this mountain, not in the temple, but in spirit and truth. God is spirit. If God were a body, it would be necessary to worship him on a mountain, because a mountain too is bodily; it would be necessary to worship him in a temple, because a temple is bodily.

“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit. We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know, because salvation is from the Jews.”

He gave much to the Jews, but do not understand these people as rejected. Understand that wall to which another high wall has been joined, so that together they might be united in the cornerstone, which is Christ. One wall is from the Jews, one from the Gentiles. These walls are far apart from one another, but only until they are joined at the corner. The foreigners, however, were strangers and exiles from God’s covenants.

Accordingly, the statement “We worship what we know” was spoken from the person of the Jews. But it concerns those from whom the apostles came, those from whom the prophets came, and all those holy people who sold all they possessed and laid the proceeds of their property at the apostles’ feet (Acts IV). For God did not reject his people whom he foreknew (Psalm XCIII).

The woman heard this and added something. A little earlier she had called him a prophet. She saw that the one with whom she was speaking was saying things that showed him to be more than a prophet. Observe what she replied. The woman says to him:

“I know that the Messiah will come, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will show us everything.”

What does this mean? “At present,” she says, “the Jews contend about the temple and we contend about the mountain. When he comes, he will reject the mountain and overthrow the temple; he will teach everything, so that we may know how to worship in spirit and truth.”

She knew who could teach her, but she did not yet recognize him as the one who was already teaching. She was now worthy, therefore, that he should be revealed to her.

Messiah means “anointed”; in Greek, *Christos* (Χριστός), and in Hebrew, *Messiah* (מָשִׁיחַ). Therefore the woman says to him: “I know that the Messiah will come, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

Jesus says to her:

“I am he, the one who is speaking with you.”

She called her husband; the husband of the woman became her head; Christ became the head of the man. Now the woman is being ordered in faith and rightly governed for a life of goodness.

After she heard, “I am he, the one who is speaking with you,” what more could she say, when Christ the Lord wished to reveal himself to the woman to whom he had said, “Believe me”?

And immediately his disciples came, and they wondered that he was speaking with a woman. They wondered because he was seeking the lost, having come to seek what had perished (Luke XIX). Their wonder was at something good; they did not suspect anything evil.

Yet no one said: “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?”

The woman therefore left her water jar after hearing: “I am he, the one who is speaking with you.” And once Christ the Lord had been received into her heart, what could she do except leave the water jar and run to evangelize? She threw away desire and hastened to announce the truth.

Let those who wish to evangelize learn: let them throw the water jar down by the well. Recall what I said earlier about the water jar. It was a vessel with which water was drawn. In Greek it is called *hydria* (ὑδρία), because water in Greek is called *hydōr* (ὕδωρ)—as though it were called a “water-vessel.”

She therefore throws away the water jar, which was no longer useful but had become a burden. For she eagerly desired to be satisfied with that water so that she might announce Christ. Having cast off the burden, she ran into the city.

And she says to the people:

“Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Is he perhaps the Christ?”

They went out from the city and came to him.

And the disciples asked him, saying:

“Rabbi, eat.”

For they had gone to buy food and had returned. But he said:

“I have food to eat which you do not know.”

The disciples therefore said to one another:

“Has anyone brought him something to eat?”

What wonder is it if that woman did not understand the water? Behold, the disciples still do not understand the food. He heard their thoughts and now instructs them as a teacher—not indirectly, as he had instructed the woman, whose husband he was still seeking, but openly.

“My food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me.”

Therefore his drink too was in that woman: to do the will of him who sent him. That is why he said, “I thirst; give me a drink”—namely, so that he might work faith in her, drink her faith, and transfer her into his body. For his body is the Church.

“Therefore,” he says, “my food is to do the will of him who sent me.”

“Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes?”

He was fervent for the work and preparing to send workers. “You count four months until the harvest; I show you another harvest, white and ready.”

“Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see, because the fields are already white for the harvest.”

Therefore he is about to send reapers. “For in this the saying is true: one is he who sows, and another he who reaps, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice. I sent you to reap what you did not labor for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

Why, then, did he send reapers rather than sowers? Where were they to reap? Where others had already labored. For where the labor and sowing had already taken place, the crop had become ripe and was already calling for the sickle and the threshing floor.

Where, then, were the reapers to be sent? Where the prophets had already preached, for they were the sowers. For if they were not sowers, how had that woman come to say: “I know that the Messiah will come”? That woman was already ripe fruit; the harvests were white and were seeking the sickle.

“I sent you.” Where? “To reap what you did not sow. Others labored, and you entered into their labors.”

Who labored? Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob themselves. Read of their labors: in all their labors there is a prophecy of Christ. Therefore Moses, the other patriarchs, and all the prophets were sowers. How much they endured in that cold season when they were sowing!

Thus Judea was already a prepared harvest. It was rightly like a ripe crop there when so many thousands of people brought the proceeds of their possessions and laid them at the apostles’ feet (Acts IV), abandoning the burdens of their worldly possessions and following Christ the Lord. Truly, it was a ripe harvest.

What happened to that harvest? A few grains were cast out and sowed the whole world; and another harvest is arising, to be reaped at the end of the age.

Of this harvest it is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm XII). To this harvest, therefore, not the apostles but angels are sent. “The reapers,” he says, “are angels.”

This harvest grows among the weeds and awaits cleansing at the end. But that earlier harvest was already ripe, which is why the disciples were first sent where the prophets had labored.

Yet, brothers, observe what was said: “Let both he who sows and he who reaps rejoice together.” They had different temporal labors, but they will enjoy the same joy and receive their reward together: eternal life.

Many from that city believed in him because of his word, because of the testimony of the woman who said: “He told me everything I have done.”

When the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to remain with them; and he stayed there two days. Many more believed because of his word, and they said to the woman:

“We no longer believe because of what you have said. For we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

This too deserves brief attention, since the reading has ended. The woman first proclaimed; at the woman’s testimony the Samaritans believed and asked him to remain with them. He stayed there two days, and more believed. After they had believed, they said to the woman: “We no longer believe because of your word; we ourselves have come to know and understand that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

First through report, afterward through presence. This is what happens today with those who are outside and are not yet Christians: Christ is announced through Christian friends, only so that that woman—that is, the Church—may announce him and bring them to Christ. They believe through this report; he remains with them for two days—that is, he gives them the two commandments of love—and many more believe in him more firmly, because he truly is the Savior of the world.

After the two days he departed from there. For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.

After confirming the Samaritans—that is, the Gentiles—in faith and love, he returns in the last days of this age to his homeland, in which he had not yet received honor. Concerning it he himself testifies in this passage that a prophet has no honor in his own country.

In his homeland he performed miracles, and they did not believe in him. In Samaria he performed none, yet they believed the testimony of one woman. The Church believed in the Son of God through apostolic preaching, though that preaching was rejected by the Synagogue. Hence, in his earthly homeland, when Christ himself preached, only very few believed. This is what one Evangelist says elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV). The faith of the whole world through apostolic preaching was a greater work than Christ’s work, who in Judea saved only very few—so few that his disciples, apart from the Twelve, abandoned him, as it is said: “Many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him” (John VI).

The Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem on the feast day; they too had gone up for the feast. Perhaps they were stirred by curiosity about the miracles, not by a desire to hear his preaching.

Jesus therefore came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made water into wine. It was as though he were saying: “Although the house was full of those reclining at table, where Christ performed the miracle in their presence, nevertheless few believed in him,” as the Evangelist says: “And his disciples believed in him” [Col. 0689A].

Perhaps this was said to the shame of his fellow citizens and to the praise of foreigners. For the Galileans were Christ’s fellow citizens, while the Samaritans were foreigners.

It is read in the sacred history:

There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. “Royal official” is a diminutive form derived from “king”; and perhaps this man is called a royal official because he sought health for his son, yet did not possess complete faith—he had it, and he did not have it. Therefore he heard: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” For the man who sought health for his son plainly did believe. He would not have sought health from one whom he did not believe to be the Savior. Why, then, is it said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” when he believed before seeing the sign? But remember the man who asks, and you will clearly recognize that he doubted in faith. For he asked Jesus to come down and heal his son. Thus he sought the bodily presence of the Lord, although the Lord was nowhere absent in spirit. He therefore believed less in him, since he thought that he could not give health unless he were bodily present. For if he had believed perfectly, he would certainly have known that there is no place where God is not.

He was therefore divided in large part, because he did not give honor to the divine majesty but to bodily presence. He sought health for his son, and yet doubted in faith, because he believed that the one to whom he had come was powerful enough to heal, and yet supposed that God was absent from his dying son. But the Lord, when asked to go, indicated that he was not absent where he was invited: by a mere command he restored health, he who created all things by his will. In this matter we must carefully observe what we have learned from another Evangelist’s testimony: “The centurion said to the Lord: ‘Lord, my servant lies paralyzed in the house and is suffering terribly’” (Matt. VIII). Jesus immediately replied to him: “I will come and heal him.”

What does it mean that the royal official asks Jesus to come to his son, and yet Jesus refuses to go bodily, while the centurion does not invite him to come to his servant, and yet Jesus promises that he will go bodily? He does not deem it fitting to be present bodily for the royal official’s son, but does not disdain to visit the centurion’s servant. What does this mean, unless our pride is being checked? We honor in human beings, who were made in the image of God, not their nature but their honors and riches; and when we consider what surrounds them, we scarcely perceive their interior qualities. While we consider what is despised in their bodies, we neglect to weigh what they are.

Our Redeemer, however, to show that what is exalted among human beings is to be despised by the saints, and what is despised among human beings is not to be despised, did not wish to go to the royal official’s son but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant. Thus our pride was rebuked: it does not know how to value human beings for their humanity, but, as we have said, values only what surrounds them. It does not look upon nature or recognize God’s honor in human beings. Behold, the Son of God does not wish to go to the royal official’s son, and yet is ready to come for the salvation of a servant. This is what the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Cor. I).

[Col. 0690A] The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and went away. He was beginning to have faith in Jesus’ word, and therefore deserved the restoration of his son’s health. He who came doubtful in part departed faithful, and therefore deserved the restoration of his son’s health.

His servants now met him, announcing that his son was alive. So he asked at what hour he had begun to improve, and they said to him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” The number seven is sanctified in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in whom the health of believing human beings consists, because in the Holy Spirit, who is God’s gift, there is forgiveness of all sins for believers. The number seven, moreover, when divided into three and four, signifies the Holy Trinity in the number three, and the totality of all creatures in the number four: because of the four elements, the four living creatures, the four regions of the world, and the four seasons of the year. All these things were created from him, through him, and in him (Col. I), and subsist and are governed, since “in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII).

He himself believed, and his whole household. For the news had been brought to him that his son was well. Thus many Samaritans believed merely because of the word, whereas that household alone believed because of the miracle. This event foreshadows the faith of the Gentiles in their multitude and the faith of the Jews in their small number: the Gentiles believed through the word alone, that is, through apostolic preaching; but the Jews saw signs, and saw the Son of God himself performing them, and nevertheless only a few of them believed.

## CHAPTER V

The love of divine utterances, the sweetness of understanding Holy Scripture, and especially the humility of evangelical truth—in which an honorable simplicity of words is open to view, while a profound depth of meaning lies hidden—urge us to speak, with the Lord himself assisting, who gives sweetness so that our land may yield its fruit. They urge both us to speak and you to listen. Would that our ability to speak were as effective as the understanding eagerly given to you for listening, when I see you hear without weariness, with the tranquil joy of your hearts, from which what is wholesome is not rejected but received eagerly and retained profitably.

Let us therefore speak to you now also about the Gospel reading. Two miracles of human healing are recorded together: one invisibly accomplished through angelic ministry, the other visibly accomplished through the Lord’s presence. But we must briefly explain the mysteries of both, lest a lengthy explanation of a lengthy reading perhaps become burdensome to anyone.

The *probatica* pool, which was surrounded by five porticoes, represents the Jewish people, fortified on every side by the guardianship of the Law, so that they ought not to sin. For it is rightly represented by the number five, since the Law was written in the five books of Moses. The people who in some respects used to preserve purity of life, but in others were accustomed to be harassed by the temptations of unclean spirits, are rightly signified by the water of the pool, which at one time was accustomed to remain calm in the wind and at another to be disturbed when the winds rushed upon it.

The same pool is appropriately called *probatica*: in Greek, πρόβατα (*probata*) means “sheep,” because there were certainly people in that nation who could say to the Lord: “We are your people and the sheep of your flock; we will give thanks to you forever” (Ps. LXXVIII). In common usage, however, the pool is said to have been called *probatica*, that is, “the sheep pool,” because priests were accustomed to wash sacrificial victims in it.

The multitude of sick people lying in the porticoes just mentioned, awaiting the movement of the water, signifies the crowds of those who, hearing the words of the Law, grieved that they could not fulfill it by their own strength and therefore implored the help of the Lord’s grace with all the desires of their hearts. They were blind because they did not yet possess perfect faith; lame because they were unable to carry out in the steps of their conduct the good things they knew; withered because, although they possessed some measure of the eye of knowledge, they nevertheless lacked the richness of hope and love.

Such people lay in the five porticoes, but they were healed only when the angel came down into the pool, because through the Law there is knowledge of sin, while the grace of forgiveness came only through Jesus Christ (Rom. III). The angel who invisibly descended into the pool and, communicating the power of healing, moved the water represents him. The angel of the great counsel—namely, the messenger of the Father’s will—descended clothed in flesh among the Jewish people and moved sinners by his teaching. He became one destined to be killed, so that by his bodily death he might suffice not only to heal spiritually those who were sick but also to give life to the dead.

The movement of the water therefore indicates the Lord’s Passion, which took place when the Jewish people were moved and disturbed. And because through that same Passion believers were redeemed from the curse of the Law, those who had previously lain sick in the porticoes are healed as though they were descending into the water of the disturbed pool.

The letter of the Law taught those who were ignorant what should be done and what avoided, but did not help those who had been taught to fulfill its commands. Like people brought out from their former dwelling places of ignorance, it held them within its porticoes but did not heal the sick. The evangelical grace, however, through faith and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, heals all the sicknesses of our sins, from which we could not be justified by the Law of Moses. It sends the sick, as though cast out from the porticoes of the Law, into the troubled water of the pool so that they may be healed; through the water of baptism it washes them from the sins that the Law had revealed. The Apostle testifies that “all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death; we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

It is rightly said that whoever first entered after the water had been moved was healed of whatever sickness afflicted him, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God (Eph. IV), and whoever is instructed in the mysteries of Christ within Catholic unity is healed of whatever sickness of sin holds him. Whoever separates himself from unity, however, cannot attain the salvation that comes from the One.

This is what we have said about the first miracle of the Gospel reading, which the Spirit gave. Now let us speak to your fraternity about the second, which he himself gave. In it also a single healer is commended—not because the almighty compassion of the Savior could not heal all whom it found sick there, but to teach that outside the unity of the Catholic faith no place of salvation is open to anyone.

“There was,” he says, “a certain man there who had been in his illness for thirty-eight years.” This man, held by an illness of so many years, signifies any sinner weighed down by the enormity or multitude of his crimes. The length of time for which he suffered also corresponds symbolically to the guilt signified by him, for he had been ill for thirty-eight years. The number forty, which is made by multiplying ten by four, is customarily understood in Scripture as representing the perfection of upright conduct, because whoever conducts himself in perfect behavior fulfills the Decalogue of the Law through the four books of the holy Gospel. From this perfection the man who walks empty of love for God and neighbor—which love the Scripture of both Law and Gospel equally commends—falls short by two.

The Lord also taught this mystically when he healed the sick man, saying:

“Rise, take up your mat, and walk.”

“Rise” means: shake off the sluggishness of the vices in which you have long been lying sick, and rise to the practice of the virtues by which you may be saved forever.

“Take up your mat”: carry it—that is, love your neighbor, patiently bearing his weaknesses, since he patiently and for a long time supported you while you were still weighed down by the burden of temptations. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Rom. XII). And as he says elsewhere: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV).

“Walk”: love God with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole strength. And so that you may deserve to reach the vision of him, advance through daily steps of good works from virtue to virtue. Do not abandon the brother whom you lead by patiently bearing with him, for love of the one toward whom you are traveling; nor, for love of your brother, turn aside from the straight course by which you seek the one with whom you desire to remain.

But so that you may be saved perfectly, rise, take up your mat, and walk. That is: leave behind your former sins, assist your brothers in their needs, and in all that you do take care not to fix your mind upon this world, but hasten to see the face of your Redeemer. Rise by doing good; carry the mat by loving your neighbor; and walk while awaiting “the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Tit. II).

But what astonishing madness among the faithless! They ought to have believed and been spiritually healed at the unexpected healing of one who had long been sick. Instead, they were scandalized and devised accusations against both the healed man and the Savior: against the healed man because he had carried his mat on the Sabbath, and against the Savior because on the Sabbath he had commanded both that the man be healed and that he carry his mat. Who could know more about the Sabbath than such immense divine power?

“The Jews,” he says, “said to the man who had been healed: ‘It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat.’” They foolishly defended the letter of the Law, failing to understand the dispensation of the one who had once decreed the Law’s ordinances through a servant and who, now coming in person, would change the same Law by grace, so that what carnal people had long observed carnally according to the letter might henceforth be recognized by spiritual people as something to be observed spiritually.

On the carnal Sabbath, which they kept according to the Decalogue, the people were commanded to rest from every servile work on the seventh day. The spiritual Sabbath, however, is in the light of spiritual grace, which is understood as sevenfold: not on one day only, but every day we are to remain at rest from the disturbance of vices. For if, according to the Lord’s word, “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII), it is plainly evident that sins are rightly understood as servile works. From these we are commanded to remain free, as on the seventh day, in the reception of spiritual grace; and we are commanded not only to abstain from evil but also to devote ourselves to good works.

The Lord showed this figuratively in this reading as well, when he commanded the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, on the Sabbath day, not only to rise but also to take up his mat and walk. He indicated that those who waste away through a long sickness of vices and, empty of love for God and neighbor, fall short by two of the complete sum of virtues, can already rise from their ways through the gift of the Holy Spirit; and that, once their sluggishness has been shaken off, they ought to hasten toward the vision of their Creator with the honor of brotherly love.

The fact that the man who had been healed recognizes Jesus in the temple—not yet in the crowd, but afterward—teaches us mystically that if we truly desire to recognize the grace of our Creator, to be strengthened in his love, and to reach his vision, we must carefully flee the crowd: not only the disturbing thoughts and evil affections that trouble us, but also wicked people who may obstruct the purpose of our sincerity, either by displaying evil through their example or by mocking or even prohibiting our good works.

Let us diligently take refuge in the house of prayer, where, invoking the Lord in the secret freedom of our hearts, we may give thanks for the benefits we have received from him and humbly pray for those we are to receive. Indeed, let us take care to become the holy temple of God, into which he may deign to come and make his dwelling, hearing the Apostle: “Your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you” (1 Cor. VI).

Among these matters, my brothers, we must observe especially that when the Lord found in the temple the man whom he had healed, he said to him:

[Col. 0693D] “Behold, you have been healed; now do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you.”

These words plainly show that he had been ill because of his sins and could not be healed until those sins had been forgiven. The one who had healed him outwardly of his illness also saved him inwardly from his crime; hence he carefully warned him not to incur a more severe sentence of condemnation by sinning again.

This should not be understood as though everyone who becomes ill becomes ill because of sins. A person is often made ill so that he may not become proud of God’s gifts, as is read concerning the Apostle Paul (2 Cor. XII). A person is also often afflicted so that he may be tested, as blessed Job was afflicted and his patience tested. And illness is often given for correction: “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). To some, however, illness is given for the glory of God, as is read concerning the man born blind and concerning Lazarus (John IX, XI).

The Lord knows why he commands each person to be ill—often by a judgment hidden from human beings, but never an unjust one. Let us learn humbly to submit to the most merciful scourges of our Redeemer, judging that we suffer less than we deserve, always remembering that saying: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves” (Job V). And he himself says in the Apocalypse: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. III).

But when the man who had long been ill was healed inwardly and outwardly—that is, freed both from the scourges of open chastisement and from the sins by which he had deserved them—the Jews, who were themselves suffering inwardly from a worse illness, began to fall more grievously ill by persecuting Jesus because he had done these things on the Sabbath.

They persecuted him as though they were following both the authority of the Law and the examples of divine action, because the Lord completed the creation of the world in six days and rested on the seventh from all his works (Gen. II), and because he commanded the people to work for six days and rest on the seventh (Exod. XXXV). They did not understand that the carnal ordinances of the Law were gradually to be changed through spiritual interpretation, when the one who is not only the Lawgiver but also the end of the Law appeared—Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. X).

Nor did they notice that on the seventh day the Creator ceased not from the work of governing the world and from the annual—or rather daily—renewal of created things, but from the institution of new creatures. For when it is said, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Gen. II), this is to be understood as meaning that God ceased from creating new kinds of creatures.

But here Truth itself says:

[Col. 0694C] “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

The Father and the Son are working so that the diversity of the natures created in the world’s first formation may continue. The same thing is said in the Psalms: “He formed their hearts one by one” (Ps. XXXII). He does not create unknown kinds of souls, but reforms souls of the same substance that was created in the first human being.

Therefore, when the Psalmist referred not only the world’s original creation but also the daily governance of creation to the praise of the Creator, he said among other things: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). If we rightly confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, and if God made and governs all things in wisdom, it is plainly established that the Father is working until now, and so is the Son.

“My Father,” he says, therefore, “was not working only during the first six days, as you suppose, but is working until now—not by instituting a new kind of creature, but by propagating those which he created in the beginning, so that they may not perish. And I am working”—that is understood to mean, “until now, arranging, ruling, and increasing all things with him.”

It is as though he openly said: “Why are you jealous of me? Why do you blame me, teachers of the heavenly Law, because in the form of a human being I have worked the salvation of one person on the Sabbath, when in the nature of divinity, together with God the Father, I am always quietly working the whole human race—or rather, the entire structure of the world and all visible and invisible things?”

But they were too incapable of such a great and profound mystery. Therefore they sought all the more to kill him, because he not only violated the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. They were especially distressed because the one whom, on account of the weakness of his flesh, they had recognized as a true human being wished to be believed to be truly the Son of God—not adopted by grace, as are the other saints to whom the Prophet says, “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI), but in every respect equal by nature to the Father, differing not in substance but in person. They thought that Jesus Christ, by preaching, was making himself something he was not, rather than truthfully declaring what he was.

The Jews were therefore angered and indignant—and rightly so, in that a human being dared to make himself equal to God, but wrongly because they did not understand God in the human being. They saw the flesh but did not know God. They saw the dwelling but ignored its inhabitant. That flesh was a temple; God dwelt within it.

Jesus therefore did not make the flesh equal to the Father, nor did he compare the form of a servant with the Lord. He did not refer to what was made for our sake, but to what he was when he made us. I am speaking to Catholics about who Christ is. You who have believed rightly know that he is not merely the Word, but the Word made flesh, who dwelt among us (John I). In this flesh the Father is greater.

Thus the Father is both equal and greater: equal to the Word, greater than the flesh; equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for our sake.

But when the Jews were angered and disturbed because Christ had made himself equal to the Father—since they understood only a human being and not God, saw the flesh and did not believe in the divinity—he said to them:

[Col. 0695B] “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.”

The Father does not perform one set of works that the Son sees, while the Son performs another set after seeing the Father perform them. Rather, the Father and the Son perform the same works. For it follows:

“Whatever he does, the Son likewise does.”

It does not mean that when the Father has done one set of things, the Son likewise does another. If the Son does what the Father does, then the Father does not do one thing and the Son another; they are the same works of the Father and the Son. How, then, does the Son do them? He does the same things, and likewise, lest perhaps they should be the same but done differently.

“The same,” he says, “and likewise.” For everything that the Father does, he does through the Son, as it is said: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I). He said “likewise” because the Son does the same things that the Father does: because the substance and operation of the Father and the Son in divinity are one, their will and power are one, their life and essence are one. Everything in the Father and the Son is equal, except that the Father is Father and the Son is Son. There is distinction in persons, but unity in nature.

“The Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” We must not understand this statement carnally, as though it referred to two human beings, a father and a son, one showing and the other seeing, one speaking and the other hearing. All such notions are fantasies of the heart. Such a thought must be driven far from Christian minds.

Thus the example of the present reading teaches about the Son and the Father that there is no difference of divinity between the Father and the Son, but one majesty. When it says that the Son does nothing except what he has seen the Father doing, this is not to be understood bodily, because God does not see in bodily ways; all sight in him is the power of his nature. There can be no division in the simple nature of divinity. For the Son, seeing and being are the same. Therefore he added:

“For whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise.”

He shows the unity of one nature and one operation, because the operation of the Father and the Son is common, since they have one nature and therefore also one operation. Therefore he subsequently added:

“The Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does.”

He showed that all this revelation by the Father is instruction for our faith, so that the Father and the Son would not be confused for us, and so that no ignorance could be understood to exist either in the Son or in the Father—for the Father would show him all the works that he himself would perform. He immediately said:

[Col. 0696B] “And he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.”

For he says that the Father will show the Son things at which they may marvel. He soon explained what those same things were:

“For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.”

Power is equal through the unity of an indistinguishable nature; the revelation of the works provides instruction not about ignorance but about our faith. It does not bring knowledge of unknown things to the Son, but brings us the confession of unity. For the Father’s showing is his doing through the Son what he is going to do.

The greater works are the resurrection of the dead, which will take place on the last day—a greater work than the healing of this sick man, who was healed by Christ’s word and from whose healing this entire discourse arose. For he says, “so that you may marvel.” It is difficult to understand how the eternal Father could, as though in time, show anything to the coeternal Son, who knows everything that is with the Father.

Nevertheless, it is easy to understand what those greater works are. “Just as the Father,” he says, “raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” To raise the dead, then, is a greater work than to heal the sick.

But just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. Does the Father give life to some and the Son to others? No, but all things are through him. The Son therefore gives life to the same people as the Father, because the Father and the Son do not do different things or do them differently; the Son does these same things likewise. This must be understood and held firmly.

But remember that the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. Therefore recognize here not only the Son’s power but also his will. The Son gives life to whomever he wishes, and the Father gives life to whomever he wishes; the Son gives life to the same people as the Father. Accordingly, the Father and the Son have the same power and the same will. They also have the same life and the same giving of life to the dead.

Therefore he says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives life to whomever he wishes, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” The Son does not give life to some and the Father to others; one power brings about one giving of life. That power must also be honored with one voice. Therefore he subsequently added:

[Col. 0696D] “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

“The Father judges no one,” because the person of the Father did not assume humanity and will not be seen in the judgment. The person of the Son alone, in the form in which he was unjustly judged, will justly judge the living and the dead. For the Son will not be seen in the judgment in the nature in which he is consubstantial with God the Father, but in the nature in which he is of the same substance as his mother and became human.

This is to be understood as follows: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”—as though it were said: No one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but all will see the Son, because the Son is the Son of Man, so that he can be seen even by the impious, since they too will see the one whom they pierced (John XIX).

Lest we appear to be conjecturing this rather than demonstrating it clearly, let us bring forward the Lord’s own certain and manifest statement, by which we may show that this was the reason he said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”: because the judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man. This form is not the Father’s but the Son’s; nor is it that form of the Son in which he is equal to the Father, but that in which he is less than the Father, so that he may be visible in the judgment to the good and the wicked. Thus all will honor the Son just as they honor the Father, because no one honors the Father unless he has the Son.

For what does it mean to honor the Father except to acknowledge that he has the Son? It is one thing when God is commended to you because he is God, and another when God is commended to you because he is Father. When he is commended to you as God, the Creator is commended to you; the Almighty is commended to you; a certain supreme, eternal, invisible, unchangeable Spirit is commended to you. But when he is commended to you as Father, nothing other than the Son is commended to you, because he cannot be called Father if he does not have a Son, just as the Son cannot be called Son if he does not have a Father.

But perhaps you honor the Father as greater and the Son as lesser, saying to me: “I honor the Father; I know that he has a Son, and I do not err in calling him Father—for I do not understand the Father without the Son—but I also honor the Son as lesser.” The Son himself corrects and recalls you, saying: “So that all may honor the Son,” not less, “but just as they honor the Father.”

Therefore, whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. “I want,” you say, “to give greater honor to the Father and lesser honor to the Son.” You take honor from the Father precisely where you give less honor to the Son. For what else does this statement imply except that the Father either did not wish or was unable to beget a Son equal to himself? If he did not wish to, he was envious; if he was unable, he was deficient.

Do you not see, then, that this is how it must be understood? Where you wish to give greater honor to the Father, there you are insulting the Father. Therefore honor the Son as you honor the Father. If you wish, honor both the Son and the Father.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed over.” He does not pass over now, but has already passed from death into life.

And observe this: “Whoever hears my word and”—he did not say, “believes me,” but—“believes him who sent me.” Let him hear the Son’s word so that he may believe the Father. Why does he hear your word and believe another? When we hear someone’s word, do we not believe the one who speaks that word? Do we not place our trust in the one speaking to us?

What, then, did he mean by saying, “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me,” unless he meant: “Because the Word is in me”? And who is the one who hears my word, unless it is the one who hears me and believes me? He believes the one who sent me because when he believes him, he believes his Word. When he believes his Word, he believes me, because I am the Father’s Word.

He would not pass from death into life unless he had first been in death and had not been in life. When, therefore, he has passed into life, he will no longer be in death. He was dead and came to life; he had perished and was found (Luke XV). Thus a certain resurrection already takes place: people pass from one kind of death to one kind of life—from the death of unbelief to the life of faith, from the death of falsehood to the life of truth, from the death of iniquity to the life of righteousness.

This, then, is also a resurrection of the dead. Let him open it more fully and make it shine upon us, as he has begun:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.”

This is proper to the faithful: they hear about his Incarnation in such a way that they believe he is the Son of God. That is, they receive him as having been made for their sake, lesser than the Father in the form of a servant, while believing that he is equal to the Father in the form of God. Therefore it follows, and affirming this very point he says:

“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.”

When he says that he granted the Son to have life in himself, he means briefly: “He begot the Son as having life in himself.” For the Son was not without life and then received life; rather, by being begotten he is life. The Father is life without being begotten; the Son is life by being begotten. The Father is from no father; the Son is from God the Father. The Father is Father because of the Son, while the Son, both in being Son and in what he is, is so because of the Father; and what he is, he has from the Father.

He therefore said: “He granted the Son life, so that he might have it in himself,” as though he were saying: “The Father, who is life in himself, begot the Son, who is also life in himself.” For by “granted” he wished to be understood as having begotten, just as we might say to someone, “God granted you existence.”

Then he continues and says:

“And he granted him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

I think nothing could be clearer. Because he is the Son of God, equal to the Father, he does not receive this authority to exercise judgment; he possesses it with the Father in secret. But he receives it so that the good and the wicked may see him judging, because he is the Son of Man.

The vision of the Son of Man will be displayed also to the wicked. The vision of the form of God, however, will be displayed only to the pure in heart—for “they will see God” (Matt. V)—that is, only to the faithful. To their love he promises precisely this: that he will show himself to them.

Therefore see what follows: “Do not marvel at this,” he says. What prevents us from marveling except that which we truly marvel at? Anyone who understands, as I see it, would not say that the Father granted him authority to exercise judgment because he is the Son of Man, when one might rather expect it to be said, “because he is the Son of God.” But because the wicked cannot see the Son of God insofar as he is equal to the Father in the form of God, it is necessary that, when the living and the dead are judged and stand before the judgment seat, both the righteous and the wicked see the judge.

[Col. 0699A] “Do not marvel at this,” he says, “because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and they will come forth: those who have done good things, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil things, to the resurrection of judgment.”

It was therefore necessary that he receive this authority because he is the Son of Man, so that all who rise might see him in the form in which he can be seen by everyone—some for condemnation, others for eternal life.

What, then, is eternal life except that vision which is not granted to the impious? “That they may know you,” he says, “the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). This means that they may know him as the one true God who shows himself to them—not as he will show himself to those who are also to be punished.

In the form of the Son of Man, according to that vision, he is good—the vision that God, appearing, displays to the pure in heart: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart” (Ps. XXI). But when the wicked see him as judge, he will not appear good to them, because they will not rejoice in him in their hearts. Instead, “all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Matt. XXIV), meaning the number of wicked and unbelieving people.

For this reason also, when the man who had called him “Good Teacher” asked him for advice about obtaining eternal life, he answered: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God” (Mark X). Yet elsewhere the Lord himself calls a human being good: “The good person,” he says, “from the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and the evil person from the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil things” (Luke VI).

But because that man was seeking eternal life—and eternal life consists in that contemplation in which God is seen not for punishment but for everlasting joy—the Lord Christ shows us two resurrections in these words. The first is in faith, rising from sins, about which he says:

Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming—and now is—when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and the other, where he says: Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. The former is the resurrection of souls; the latter, which follows, will be the resurrection of bodies. Whoever rises in this first resurrection will rise in the second to glory. Whoever does not rise in this first will nevertheless rise in the second, [Col. 0699D] but to punishment. God accomplishes both through Christ. Whoever rises here through him will rise there to him; whoever does not rise here through him will not rise there to him either.

The hour is now, so that the dead may rise. The hour will come at the end of the age, so that the dead may rise; but let them rise now in mind, then in flesh. Let them rise now in mind through the Word of God the Son; then in flesh through the Word of God, the Son of Man, made flesh. For the Father himself will not come to judge the living and the dead, although the Father does not withdraw from the Son. How, then, will he not himself come? Because he himself will not be seen in the judgment. “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John XXIV). That form will be the judge which stood beneath the judge. That form will judge which was judged. For it was judged unjustly, and it will judge justly. Such [Col. 0700A] will the judge appear as can be seen both by those whom he is about to crown and by those whom he is about to condemn.

There is a distinction between the saying he uttered above, that the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and what he says here: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.” For there he adds, “and those who hear will live”; here, however, he simply says, “they will hear the voice of the Son of God.” Therefore that resurrection is unto life, whereas this future resurrection, of which he says, “They will hear the voice of the Son of God”—they will hear, I say, so that they may rise for judgment—does not here add “unto life,” because not all will rise to glory, but many to punishment. Therefore, speaking of the future resurrection, he added: “Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment,” that is, of condemnation, [Col. 0700B] because here he has used “judgment” for punishment.

Then will be the final winnowing, and he will separate the good from the wicked, the wheat from the chaff. Then the ungodly will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life. The text continues:

“I can do nothing of myself; but as I hear, I judge.”

Perhaps he said, “I can do nothing of myself,” as though he had said: “I am not from myself, but from the Father.” For the Father is from no other, whereas the Son is from the Father. Therefore he said, “As I hear, I judge,” because the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. As he hears, he judges; he hears, namely, through the unity of substance and the distinctiveness of knowledge. He does not judge from himself, because he is not from himself. The Father alone is not from another; the Son is begotten from the Father, as we have said. The Son hears from the one from whom he was begotten, because he is not from himself but from the one by whom he was begotten. From the one from whom he has understanding, from that same one, certainly, he has knowledge. Therefore, hearing from him is nothing other than knowledge.

The very words “As I hear, I judge” can also be understood of the nature of his humanity, which the Son of God assumed from the Virgin. When he was speaking of the resurrection of souls, he did not say, “I see,” but “I hear.” For “I hear” means, as it were, the command of the Father giving orders. Thus, now as a human being, as one of whom the Father is greater, now in the form of a servant and not in the form of God, he says, “As I hear, I judge.”

“And my judgment is just.”

From where does the judgment of a human being derive its justice? The text continues: “Because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” This [Col. 0700D] sending is the incarnation of Christ, which took place so that the Father’s will might be accomplished through him for the salvation of the human race. For in this passage, from these words of our Savior, he seems to wish to intimate to us that there are two natures in him, and that he truly possesses a soul, in which the will ordinarily resides. Yet this soul has been so closely joined and mingled with divinity that the whole will in it becomes spiritual rather than animal—that is, carnal.

For he continues:

“If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is not true” (and a little later): “The Father who sent me bears witness of me.”

At one moment he demonstrates in himself the nature of a human being; at another he signifies himself as equal to the Father in divine majesty. At one moment he claims for himself unity of divinity with God the Father; at another he shows the frailty [Col. 0701A] of human flesh. At one moment he indicates that he does not teach his own doctrine; at another that he does not seek his own will. At one moment he signifies that his testimony is not true; at another that it is true. For here he says: “If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is not true” (John VIII); and a little later: “If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is true” (ibid.).

How, then, is your testimony not true, Lord, except according to the frailty of the flesh? Likewise, what he said—“I have not come to do my own will” (John VI), and “The Son can do nothing of himself” (above, here), and many other statements of this kind—does not weaken the Son, disparage him, or separate him from the Father. Indeed, these things were stated so that his true incarnation might be recognized.

For when he says: “I came forth from the Father”; “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; “I and the Father are one”; and “Whoever sees me sees the Father also”; and “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills”—his true divinity is affirmed, because the will of the Father and of the Son is one operation, one grace, and, finally, one governance, as the teacher of the nations teaches when he writes: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (I Corinthians I).

“Another is he who bears witness of me.”

In what follows he shows who that other one is who bears witness concerning him, when he says: “The Father who sent me himself bears witness of me” (Matthew III). The Father’s testimony concerning the Son was given at the baptism, when a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” The Father also gave similar testimony on the holy mountain [Col. 0701C] concerning his Son in the hearing of the three disciples.

“And I know that his testimony is true” (John XIV).

Everything true is true from the truth. For God is truth, and whatever is true is true from God. He then stated what that testimony is:

“The works,” he says, “that I do bear witness of me” (and he added): “And the Father who sent me bears witness of me.”

He says that the works he performed he also received from the Father. The works, therefore, bear witness; the Father who sent him bears witness. John bore witness concerning Christ like a lamp—not to heal friends, but to confound enemies. For this had previously been foretold in the person of the Father: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with shame” [Col. 0701D] (Psalm CXXXI); “and upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

Imagine that you have been placed in the night: you have looked attentively at a lamp, admired the lamp, and rejoiced in the lamp’s light. But that lamp says that there is a Sun in which you ought to rejoice; and although it burns in the night, it commands you to await the day.

It is not, therefore, because that man’s testimony was unnecessary—for why would he have been sent if it were unnecessary—but so that a person might not remain with the lamp and suppose that the lamp’s light was sufficient for him. For this reason the Lord neither says that the lamp was superfluous nor declares that one ought to remain with the lamp. Another testimony is supplied by the Scripture of God, in which God himself bore witness to his Son, and in which the Jews had placed their hope—namely, in the law of God administered to them through Moses, God’s servant.

“Search the Scriptures,” he says, “in which you think you have eternal life; they themselves bear witness of me, and you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have eternal life.”

You who think that you have eternal life in the Scriptures, ask them concerning whom they bear witness, and understand what eternal life is. And because they seemed to reject Christ on account of Moses, as though he were opposed to the institutions and commandments Moses had handed down, he again convicts them, as it were, by reference to another lamp. For all human beings are lamps, since they can both be kindled and extinguished. Lamps shine when they possess wisdom and burn with the Spirit. But if they burned and have been extinguished, they already stink. [Col. 0702B]

The servants of God remained good lamps through the oil of his mercy, not through their own strength. For the free grace of God is the oil of the lamps. “I have labored more than all of them,” says one lamp; and, lest he seem to burn through his own strength, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Corinthians XV).

Every prophet, therefore, before the Lord’s coming, is a lamp. The apostle Peter says of him: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (II Peter I). The prophets are therefore lamps, and the whole of prophecy is one great lamp.

What of the apostles? Are they not also lamps? They certainly are lamps. For he alone is not a lamp. He is neither kindled nor extinguished, [Col. 0702C] but is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I). Of John it is said: “He was not that light, but came to bear witness to the light” (ibid.). Of Christ, however: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

What, then, is meant by the words that Truth himself spoke concerning the apostles: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew XV), and concerning John the Evangelist: “He was not that light” (John V)? Neither John by himself was a lamp, nor the apostles by themselves were light; rather, from the light, Christ, he was a lamp, and they were illuminated. He is the true Sun rising in the hearts of believers.

“But I have testimony greater than John’s.”

For the works that the Father gave me—the very works that I do—bear witness of me, because the Father sent me; and the Father who sent me himself bears witness of me.

Above he said: “I do not accept testimony from a human being.” Here he gives the reason why he did not accept testimony from a human being: because he has the testimony of the Father and the testimony of his works, and these are greater than human testimonies.

Therefore this sending is the incarnation of Christ; it is our redemption. Our redemption, moreover, is in the truth itself, which says: “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John X).

To this testimony of the Father he added concerning the Father himself that the Jews—or rather, all unbelievers, whose minds have been blinded—cannot receive the truth of his divinity, saying:

“For you have never heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you.” The Apostle says: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are justified, but the doers of the word of God” (Romans II). That is, the Son of God does not abide in the hearts of those who do not keep what they hear.

When he says, “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form,” he shows that the substance of divinity is incomprehensible and invisible, and that his voice could not be heard by carnal ears but could be understood or loved through spiritual understanding, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to what had been given to each person.

“Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they are the ones that bear witness of me; and you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have life.”

“You are unwilling to come,” that is, “you are unwilling to believe,” because “without faith it is impossible to please God” [Col. 0703B] (Hebrews XI). Our coming to Christ means believing that he is truly the Son of God and that through him we truly possess salvation.

For every holy Scripture bore witness to Christ, whether through figures, prophecies, or the ministries of angels. Moses, therefore, bore witness to Christ; John bore witness to Christ; and the other prophets and apostles bore witness to Christ. Above all these testimonies he places the testimony of his works, because through those others it was none but God who bore witness to his Son.

“I do not receive glory from human beings.”

That is, I do not seek human praise, because I did not come to be served but to serve (Matthew XX); that is, I did not come to receive carnal honor from human beings, but to give spiritual honor to all.

“But I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.”

They did not have the love of God because they did not believe in him who did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John VI). Therefore he added:

“I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me.”

That is, you did not believe in me, who came into the world for this reason: so that the name of the Father might be glorified.

“If another comes in his own name, him you will receive.”

Who is this one who comes in his own name, except the one who seeks his own glory and not the glory of the one who sent him? Whom were the Jews going to receive except Antichrist, who is to come seeking his own glory? And this will be the punishment for their sin, because they were unwilling to believe the truth and will believe a lie.

“How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?”

We must consider more attentively how great an evil boastfulness and ambition for human praise are, on account of which Truth himself declares that some cannot believe [Supplement: “he declares”], because they were devoted to worldly glory. What is the desire for human praise except the exaltation of a proud mind? A person wants to be esteemed for possessing what he does not strive to have within himself. He is one thing within, and desires to appear another outwardly.

Humility seeks glory from God alone; pride seeks it from human beings. Therefore John the Baptist was praised extraordinarily by Truth himself because he was not “a reed shaken by the wind” (Matthew XI). Since he was not pliable to the breeze of human praise or of hateful reproach, he had glory from God Christ, because he did not seek human glory.

“Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you chiefly place your hope.”

I do not accuse you because I did not come to condemn but to save. Moses, however, accuses you because you are unbelieving toward his voice. He wrote about me when he said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you would hear me” (Deuteronomy XVIII).

But pay attention to what follows: “Every soul that does not obey that prophet shall be cut off from the people of God.”

If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? Whatever the law or the prophets wrote, everything signified that Christ was to come. For if the Jews had believed the law or the prophets, they would certainly have believed Christ as well.

After these mystical and profoundly insightful words of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which he wished to reveal to those hearing him then, and to those reading him now, partly the hidden mysteries of his divinity and partly those of his humanity, the evangelist next added that by the miracle of the five loaves he wished to show who he was.

## CHAPTER VI

“After these things Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee,” etc.

Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is distinguished by many names according to the diversity of the surrounding regions. It is called the Sea of Tiberias only in those places where it displays the city of Tiberias, which, as they say, offers a healthful habitation through its warm waters. The Jordan flows through it; it extends eighteen thousand paces in length and five in breadth. Mystically, however, the sea signifies the turbulent and swelling revolutions of this present age, in which all sorts of wicked people, taking wrongful delight and devoted to the depths like fish, do not direct their minds toward the joys above.

Hence this same sea is rightly called Galilee, that is, “wheel,” because the love of the passing age casts hearts into a whirlpool and does not permit them to rise toward the desires of everlasting life. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “The ungodly walk in a circle” (Psalm XI).

But as Jesus departed across the Sea of Galilee, a very large crowd followed him, desiring to receive from him the great gifts of heavenly teaching, healing, and refreshment. The Jewish people alone followed him by believing. But after, through the dispensation of his incarnation, he approached, trod upon, and crossed the waves of corruptible life, a very large crowd of believing nations soon followed him, desiring to be spiritually instructed, healed, and satisfied. They said with the Psalmist: “Lord, I have taken refuge in you; teach me to do your will” (Psalm CXXIV); and again: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled” (Psalm VI); and again, trusting that they would receive from him the nourishment of perpetual life: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a pastureland” (Psalm XXII).

As for the fact that when Jesus went up onto the mountain he sat there with his disciples, but when the crowd came to him he went down and fed it in the lower places—the same crowd whom shortly before he had healed in the lower places—let us not believe that this happened without purpose. Rather, it mystically signifies that the Lord distributes his teaching and spiritual gifts according to the capacity of those receiving them. To minds that are still weak and spiritually childlike he entrusts simpler instructions and presents more open mysteries; to those who are higher and more perfect in understanding he discloses the more secret mysteries of his majesty, suggests loftier paths of devout conduct, and promises higher gifts of heavenly rewards.

Finally, when someone asked what he should do to possess eternal life, being as yet in a lower position, he bestowed the common gifts of his generosity, saying: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother” [Col. 0705B] (Matthew XIX). But when the man later sought greater things, wishing as it were to climb the mountain of virtues, he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (ibid.).

The Lord not only demonstrated this discernment and moderation while teaching in the flesh; even now he does not cease to demonstrate it through the ministers of his word. Thus, under the person of one good servant, he testifies that they ought to give their fellow servants a measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, to offer the banquets of the word suitably and in measured fashion, according to the capacity of their hearers.

As for the fact that, when Passover was approaching, the Lord taught, healed, and refreshed the crowds, we may interpret it mystically in this way: Passover is called a passage, and all those whom the Lord restores to the eternal sweetness of his gifts he prepares for a truly saving passage. They are to rise above carnal desires through the elevation of the mind, trample underfoot the weak desires and adversities of the world alike through hope in and love of the heavenly kingdom, and, if they are not yet able to reach the things above either in soul or in body—for this is plainly promised in the future—nevertheless despise as nothing, in comparison with eternal things, whatever they see the carnal embracing as something great. Thus did the one who, seeing the wicked “exalted exceedingly and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm XXXVI), passed beyond temporal things in contemplation and regarded as though already nonexistent the one whom he foresaw would soon be removed.

“When Jesus had lifted up his eyes.”

The fact that he is said to have seen the crowd coming toward him is an indication of divine compassion. For the grace of heavenly mercy is accustomed to meet all who seek to come to him, and, lest they go astray in their seeking, to open the light of his Spirit to those who hasten toward him.

That Jesus’ eyes mystically signify the gifts of his Spirit is attested by John in the Apocalypse. Speaking figuratively of him, he says: “And I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Revelation V)—which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.

When the Lord tested Philip, he said: “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?”

He does this with a provident dispensation, not so that he may learn what he himself did not know, but so that Philip, when tested, may recognize the slowness of his faith—a slowness which Philip himself did not know, though the Teacher knew it—and may be corrected by the miracle. For he ought not to have doubted in the presence of the Creator of all things, who brings forth bread from the earth and gladdens the human heart with wine (Psalm CIII), that bread worth a few denarii could suffice for many thousands of people, so that each might receive enough and depart already satisfied.

The five loaves with which he satisfied the multitude signify the five books of Moses. When these books are disclosed through spiritual understanding and multiplied through a richer sense, they daily refresh the hearts of believing hearers. They are rightly reported to have been barley loaves, on account of the harsher decrees of the law and the coarser coverings of the letter, which concealed, as it were, the marrow of the inner spiritual meaning.

The two fish that he added appropriately signify the writings of the psalmists and the prophets, since one group, by singing, and the other, by speaking, narrated to their hearers the future mysteries of Christ and of the Church. They are rightly represented by aquatic creatures, because the heralds of that age belong to the time in which the people of believers could in no way live without the waters of baptism.

There are some who think that the two fish, which gave the bread its pleasant taste, signify the two persons by whom that people was governed, so that through them it might receive the direction of counsel: namely, the royal and the priestly offices, to which that sacred anointing also belonged. Their duty was never to be broken or corrupted by the storms and waves of the people, and often to break apart the violent contradictions of the crowds like hostile waves; at times, while preserving their integrity, to yield to them; and altogether, like fish in a stormy sea, to conduct themselves amid the turbulent administration of the people.

Yet these two persons prefigured our Lord. He alone bore both offices, and he alone fulfilled them—not figuratively, but in reality.

The boy who had the five loaves and two fish, yet did not distribute them to the hungry crowds but offered them to the Lord for distribution, is the Jewish people, childlike in its understanding of the letter, which kept the words of the Scriptures closed within itself. When the Lord appeared in the flesh, however, he received them and showed what usefulness and sweetness they contained. He revealed how abundantly they overflowed with the manifold grace of the Spirit, although they had seemed few and contemptible, and through his apostles and their successors he presented them for distribution to all the nations.

Therefore other evangelists rightly report [Col. 0706D] that the Lord gave the loaves and fish to his disciples, while the disciples served them to the crowds (Matthew XIV; Mark XVI; Luke IX). For when the mystery of human salvation had been expounded through the Lord, it was confirmed to us by those who heard it.

He broke the five loaves and the two fish and distributed them to the disciples when he opened their understanding so that they might understand everything written about him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms (Luke XXIV). The disciples placed them before the crowds when they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed (Mark XVI).

The grass on which the crowd reclines and is refreshed signifies carnal desire. Everyone who wishes to be satisfied with spiritual nourishment must trample and suppress it. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah XL). Let him therefore recline upon the grass and crush the flower of the grass—that is, let him chastise his body and subject it to servitude, tame the pleasures of the flesh, and restrain the fleeting excesses of luxury—whoever desires to be refreshed by the sweetness of the living bread. Whoever desires to be renewed by the banquets of heavenly grace must abandon the weakness of old age.

The five thousand men who ate signify the refreshment of the life of those who are nourished by the word. In Scripture, the name “men” usually represents those who are more perfect, whom no feminine softness corrupts—such as the Apostle wishes those to be to whom he says: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strong” (I Corinthians XVI).

The number one thousand, beyond which our counting does not increase, is customarily used to indicate the fullness of the matters under discussion. By the number five, the five well-known senses of our body are expressed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. All those who strive to act manfully and to be strengthened in each of these senses, living soberly, justly, and devoutly so that they may deserve to be refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly wisdom, are represented by the five thousand men whom the Lord satisfied with mystical food.

Nor should it be passed over that, when he was about to refresh the multitude, he gave thanks. He gave thanks so that he might teach us also always to give thanks for gifts received from heaven, and so that he might make known how much he rejoices over our progress and delights in our spiritual refreshment.

Do you wish to know, brothers, how greatly our Savior rejoices in our salvation? The evangelist Luke relates that he gave the disciples authority over all the power of the enemy and indicated that their names were written in heaven. He immediately adds: “In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke X).

It is therefore clear that he rejoices in the salvation and life of the faithful, for he praises the Father with thanksgiving because he had revealed to the humble in spirit the mysteries he had hidden from the proud.
