As for the fact that, after the crowd had been satisfied, he commanded the disciples to gather what remained of the fragments so that nothing might perish, this certainly signifies that there are many mysteries in the divine utterances which the understanding of the common people does not grasp, and some which the less learned cannot attain by themselves. [Col. 0707D] Those who are able must therefore collect these things by searching them out more diligently and bring them, whether by word or in writing, to the instruction of their lesser brethren, lest the nourishment of the word perish through their negligence and be taken away from the people whom, by the Lord’s gift, they know how to gather it by interpretation.

“Therefore they gathered them,” he says, “and filled twelve baskets with the fragments.”

Since the number twelve is customarily used to represent the sum of any perfection, the twelve baskets full of fragments rightly express the entire chorus of spiritual teachers. They are commanded both to gather by meditation the obscure passages of Scripture, which the crowd cannot grasp by itself, and to preserve them in writing for their own use and that of the crowds.

The apostles and evangelists did this themselves by inserting into their little works many passages from the law and the prophets, with interpretation added. Their successors, the teachers of the Church throughout the world, have done the same by examining with more diligent explanation some even of the complete books of both Testaments. However despised these may be by human beings, they are fruitful in the bread of heavenly grace. For baskets are customarily used for servile work. Hence, concerning the people who served in clay and bricks in Egypt, the Psalmist says: “His hands served in the basket” (Psalm XX).

When those people had seen the sign he had performed, they said: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.”

They were right to call the Lord a great prophet, already the herald of great salvation that was to come into the world. For he himself also deigns to call himself a prophet when he says: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII). Yet they were not advancing in complete faith, since they did not know how to call him God as well.

Thus, seeing the sign Jesus had performed, they said: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.” Let us, seeing the world that Jesus made and the signs with which he filled it, with a more certain recognition of truth and faith say: “This is truly the Mediator between God and human beings, who was in the world in his divinity, and the world was made through him; who came in his own humanity to seek and save what had perished and to restore the world he had made; who, through the presence of his divinity, is with his faithful in the world every day, until the consummation of the age.”

But when Jesus knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled again to the mountain by himself.

It is therefore understood that, when the Lord sat on the mountain with his disciples and saw the crowds coming toward him, he had come down from the mountain and fed the crowds in the lower places. For how could he have fled there again unless he had previously descended from the mountain?

This signifies something: the Lord descended from on high to feed the crowds; he fed them and ascended. But why did he ascend when he knew that they wanted to seize him and make him king? What, then—was he not a king, that he feared becoming king? He certainly was, but not the kind of king who would be made by human beings; rather, the kind who would give a kingdom to human beings.

Perhaps Jesus signifies something to us here also, since his deeds are words. Therefore, in the fact that they wanted to seize him and make him king, and that for this reason he fled alone to the mountain, is what happened to him silent, without speech or significance? Or perhaps their attempt to seize him meant that they wished to anticipate the time of his kingdom?

For he had come at that time not yet to reign, as he will reign in the kingdom for which we say: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew VI; Luke VI). He always reigns with the Father insofar as he is the Son of God, the Word of God, the Word through whom all things were made.

The prophets, however, foretold his kingdom also according to the fact that Christ became human and made his faithful into Christians. There will therefore be a kingdom of Christians, which is now being gathered, now being prepared, now being purchased with the blood of Christ. At some point there will be a manifest kingdom, when the glory of his saints will be revealed on account of the judgment he will carry out—the judgment which he himself said above that the Son of Man would carry out. Concerning this kingdom the Apostle also says: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father” (I Corinthians XV).

Hence he himself also says: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

The disciples and the crowds who believed in him thought that he had come in such a way that he would already reign. This is what it means to wish to seize him and make him king: they wished to anticipate his appointed time. At that time he was concealing himself as the head, so that he might appear at the proper moment and reveal himself at the end of the age.

But why is it said that he fled? For if he had not wished it, he would not have been held; if he had not wished it, he would not have been seized; and if he had not wished it, he would not have been recognized. Yet this was done symbolically. He fled alone so that he might not reign carnally, because he alone ascended into heaven, from where he would reign spiritually in his saints.

He fled alone to the mountain, the firstborn from the dead, ascending above all the heavens and interceding for us. The priest prefigured him by entering the Holy of Holies once a year, not without blood, to intercede for the people: the Lamb placed above, alone on the mountain, entered within the veil, while the people remained outside (Colossians I; Psalm LXXI; Romans VIII; Leviticus XVI; Hebrews IX).

But let us see what the disciples were suffering in the little boat while he remained within the veil of heavenly exaltation. What is the little boat tossed by the waves except the Church, wearied by persecutions both outside and within? Outside, by open persecution from the pagans; within, by hidden sedition from false brothers. Therefore he added:

“When evening had come, his disciples went down to the sea; and when they had entered the boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum.”

He quickly stated what happened later. “They came across the sea to Capernaum,” and then he returns to explain how they came: they crossed by sailing across the lake. As they sailed toward the place to which he has already said they came, he explains retrospectively what happened.

The darkness had already fallen, and Jesus had not yet come to them. As the end of the world draws near, errors increase, terrors increase, iniquity increases, unbelief increases; finally, the light—which in John the Evangelist himself is shown clearly enough to be love, so that he says, “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2)—is very frequently extinguished. As love grows cold and iniquity abounds, these are the waves troubling the ship; the storms and winds are the cries of the accursed. From this love grows cold; from this the waves increase; from this the ship is tossed. As a great wind blew, the sea rose up, the darkness increased, understanding diminished, and iniquity grew. Yet amid all these things the ship continued on; it hastened toward land and sought the harbor. So amid every kind of temptation the Church advanced. It labors, but is not submerged. It awaits Christ, so that through him it may reach the harbor of tranquility. When, therefore, they had rowed twenty-five or thirty stadia, the waves grew, the darkness increased, and the storms raged; yet the ship proceeded. “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

Nor does the number of stadia itself seem to be without significance. For why would the Evangelist have said, “About twenty-five or thirty stadia”? It would have been enough to say “twenty-five” or “thirty.” The same Evangelist uttered these numbers as one estimating, not affirming. Let us ask what the number twenty-five consists of, and from what it is formed. It comes from five. That number five pertains to the Law: there are the five books of Moses; there are the five porticoes containing those who were sick; there are the five loaves feeding five thousand people. Thus the number twenty-five signifies the Law, because five multiplied by five—that is, five times five—makes twenty-five, the square of five. But before the Gospel came, this Law lacked perfection.

Perfection, however, is comprehended in the number six. For six is a perfect number, and is completed by its parts—that is, 1, 2, and 3. No other parts can be found in it, nor can those parts joined together produce anything other than the number six. Therefore God completed the world in six days (Genesis 2), and the five are multiplied by six so that the Law may be fulfilled through the Gospel, making six times five thirty.

Jesus therefore came to those who fulfill the Law, and he came walking upon the waves, with all the world’s swellings beneath his feet, pressing down all the heights of this age. Yet the tribulations are so great that even those who have believed in Jesus and who strive to persevere become afraid lest they fail Christ while walking upon the waves of the world. Why does the Christian fear while Christ says, “It is I; do not be afraid. Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16)?

They therefore wanted to take him into the boat, recognizing him and rejoicing, now made secure; and immediately the boat reached the land toward which they were going. An end was made at the land: from the watery to the solid, from the troubled to the firm, from the journey to faith—that is, to perfect tranquility, which will exist only in the harbor of eternal serenity, where there is complete love and no iniquity, complete happiness and no disturbance; where those who here labor courageously to the end of their lives will reign without end.

On the following day, the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had departed. Other boats, however, came from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread, giving thanks to the Lord. When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they boarded the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

Nevertheless, such a great miracle was suggested to them. For they had seen that the disciples alone had boarded the boat, and that the boat was no longer there. Other boats, however, had come from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread, in which the crowd had followed him with the disciples. Therefore he had not boarded; there was no other boat there. How, then, did Jesus suddenly come to the other side of the sea, unless he walked upon the sea in order to display the miracle?

And when the crowds had found him—behold, he presents himself to the crowds from whom he had feared being seized and had fled to the mountain. He confirms and reveals to us altogether that all those words and deeds were spoken and performed in a great sacrament, so that they might signify something. Behold, does not he who had fled from the crowds to the mountain now speak with those same crowds? Let them now seize him; let them now make him king.

And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?” After the sacramental sign of the miracle, he introduces a discourse, so that, if possible, those who had been fed might themselves be fed; and that he whose bread had filled their stomachs might satisfy their minds with words—but only if they understand. If they do not understand, let them take what they can understand, lest the fragments be lost. Let him speak, then, and let us listen.

Jesus answered and said, “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves.” You seek me for the sake of the flesh, not for the sake of the spirit. How many seek Jesus only so that he may prosper them in temporal matters! One has a business affair and seeks the intercession of the clergy; another is oppressed by someone more powerful and flees to the Church; another wants someone to intervene for him with a person before whom he has little influence. This one does this, that one does that. Every day the Church is filled with such people. Jesus is scarcely sought for Jesus’ sake. “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves.”

“Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life.” Do you seek me for the sake of that? Seek me for my own sake. He is indicating this food, which will shine forth in what follows.

“Which the Son of Man will give you.” I suppose he expected to eat bread again, to recline at table again, and to be filled again. But Jesus said, “Food not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life.” Earlier we said that the ship signifies the Church of Christ, which is tossed by the storms of this age and carries those who labor within it, so that they may labor courageously until Christ, restraining the waves of persecution, restores serenity. Here, however, he says:

“On the following day, the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there except one.” What is the crowd standing on the sea on the following day except, after Christ’s ascension, the crowd standing in good works—not lying amid earthly pleasures, but awaiting the place from which Jesus will come to them? Here too one boat is mentioned, just as previously there was one Church of Christ, in which he was bodily present. Now also there is one Church, which similarly awaits his coming in hope.

But what does it mean that other boats came from Tiberias, except the gatherings of heretics, who do not seek Jesus with sincere faith but, under the deceit of cunning, seek their own interests rather than the things of Jesus? Accordingly Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves and were filled” (Luke 6). Concerning those who have been filled, he says in another Gospel: “Woe to you who are filled” (ibid.). But concerning those who hunger for the bread of life and knowledge of righteousness, it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5). Christ immediately exhorted them toward this food in the following discourse, saying: “Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life.” Carnal food perishes; spiritual food endures—the food that the Son of Man will give you.

“For God the Father has sealed him.” Do not understand this Son of Man as though he were one of the other sons of men, of whom it is said: “The sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Psalm 35). This Son of Man, set apart by a certain grace, is a Son of Man excepted from the number of human beings; this Son of Man is the Son of God; this man is also God.

Therefore the Truth himself, who was then speaking to the Jews and now speaks to everyone through the words of evangelical proclamation, shows who he is—not what many then judged him, or even now judge him, to be. He added: “For God the Father has sealed him.”

What is “to seal” except to designate something as one’s own? To seal is to place something that will not be confused with other things. To seal is to place a mark upon a thing. Whenever you place a mark upon something, you place it there so that, since it is not confused with other things, it may be recognized by you. The Father therefore sealed him. What does “he sealed him” mean? He gave him something distinctive, so that he could not be compared with other human beings. Therefore it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

What, then, does “to seal” mean? To hold as excepted—as the text says, “above your companions.” Therefore, he says, do not despise me because I am the Son of Man; and seek from me food not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life. I am the Son of Man in such a way that I am not one of you; I am the Son of Man in such a way that God the Father has sealed me. What does “to seal” mean? To give me something distinctive, by which I would not be confused with the human race, but through whom the human race would be liberated.

They therefore said to him, “What shall we do, that we may perform the works of God?” For he had said to them: “Work for food not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life.” “What shall we do?” they said. “What must we observe in order to fulfill this command?”

Jesus answered and said to them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.” This, then, is to eat food not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life. Why do you prepare your tooth and your stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.

Faith is indeed distinguished from works, as the Apostle says: “We consider that a person is justified by faith without the works of the Law” (Romans 3). There are also works that appear good without faith in Christ, yet are not good because they are not directed toward the end from which they derive their goodness. “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10). Therefore he did not wish to separate faith from work, but said that faith itself is a work. For it is faith “which works through love” (Galatians 5).

Nor did he say, “This is your work,” but he said: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent”; so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1). Since he was inviting them to faith, they still sought signs by which they might believe. See whether the Jews are not asking for signs.

They therefore said to him, “What sign do you perform, then, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?” Was it not enough that they had been fed from the five loaves? They knew this, certainly, but they preferred manna from heaven to that food. The Lord Jesus, however, was declaring himself to be such that he should be placed above Moses.

For Moses had not dared to say of himself that he would give food not which perishes, but which has eternal life. Jesus was promising something greater than Moses. Through Moses, a kingdom was indeed promised, together with a land producing milk and honey, temporal peace, an abundance of children, bodily health, and all the other temporal things—yet these were spiritual in figure, because they were promised to the old human being in the Old Testament.

They were considering the promises made through Moses, and they were considering the promises made through Jesus. Moses promised a full belly in the land, but food that perishes; Jesus promised food not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life. They were considering that he promised more, yet they did not as yet see him doing greater things. They were considering what Moses had done, and still wanted something greater to be done by the one who made such great promises.

“What do you do,” they said, “so that we may believe you?” And so that you may know that they were comparing those miracles with this miracle, and therefore judging the things Jesus was doing as though they were smaller, listen to what follows.

“Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness.” But what manna was, perhaps you despise, as it is written: “He gave them manna to eat” (Exodus 16). Through Moses our fathers received bread from heaven, and Moses did not say to them, “Work for food that does not perish, but endures to eternal life.” Nor do you perform things such as Moses did. He did not give barley loaves, but manna from heaven.

Jesus therefore said to them, “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the true bread is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world.”

The true bread, then, is the one who gives life to the world; and he is the food of which I spoke shortly before: “Work for food that does not perish, but endures to eternal life.” Therefore that manna too signified this, and all those signs were signs of me. You loved my signs; what was signified by them you despise.

Therefore Moses did not give the bread from heaven. God gives the bread. But what bread? Perhaps manna? No, but the bread signified by manna—namely, the Lord Jesus himself. “My Father gives you the true bread.” For the bread is God who descended from heaven and gives life to the world.

They therefore said to him, “Lord, always give us this bread.” It was like the Samaritan woman to whom he said, “Whoever drinks of this water will never thirst” (John 4). Immediately she understood it bodily, yet did not wish to remain in want, and said: “Lord, give me this water.” So also these people said: “Lord, give us this bread, which may refresh us and never fail.”

Jesus therefore said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.” “Whoever comes to me” means the same as “whoever believes in me”; and where he said, “will not hunger,” this should also be understood as “will never thirst.” Both expressions signify eternal satisfaction, where there is no want.

Do you desire bread from heaven? You have it before you, and you do not eat.

“But I told you that you have both seen me and have not believed.” Yet I have not therefore destroyed the people. “For did your unbelief annul the faithfulness of God?” (Romans 3). See what follows.

“Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out.” What is that interior place from which no one is cast out? A great inner chamber, and a sweet secret place. O secret place without weariness, without the bitterness of evil thoughts, without the intrusion of temptations and sorrows! Is it not that secret place into which the one will enter to whom God will say: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25)?

“And whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Therefore I will not cast out the one who comes to me, because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.

It is a great sacrament that he says: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out.” Immediately adding the reason why he would not cast out the one who came to him—that is, the one who believed in him—he said: “Because I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

Who is cast out from that sweet and most pleasant secret place, into which the servant who does the will of his lord is commanded to enter, except the proud person? Except the soul that trusts in itself and seeks to be its own master? Otherwise the prophet would not say: “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Psalm 61).

But the soul subjected through humility to the grace of God is never cast out; rather, it enters into the joy of its Lord. Therefore, so that the cause of all diseases—namely, pride—might be cured, the Son of God descended and became humble.

Why are you proud, human being? God became humble for your sake. Perhaps you would be ashamed to imitate a humble human being; at least imitate the humble God. The Son of God came in a human being and became humble. You are commanded to be humble; you are not commanded to become an animal instead of a human being. He, God, became human; you, human being, recognize that you are human.

Your entire humility consists in recognizing yourself. Therefore, because God teaches humility, he said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). This is an affirmation of humility. Pride does its own will; humility does the will of God.

Therefore the one who comes to me will not be cast out. Why? Because I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. I came humble; I came to teach humility. I came as the teacher of humility. Whoever comes to me is incorporated into me; whoever comes to me becomes humble. Whoever clings to me will be humble, because he will not do his own will, but God’s; and therefore he will not be cast out.

Adam, because he was proud, was cast out (Genesis 3); but Christ, having become humble, was exalted above every name that is named either in heaven or on earth (Ephesians 1). The one who came as the teacher of humility came not to do his own will, but the will of him who sent him.

Let us come to him, let us enter into him, let us be incorporated into him, so that we too may not do our own will, but the will of God; and so that he may not cast us out, because we are his members, because he willed to be our head by teaching humility. No one can come to him except the humble; no one is cast out by him except the proud.

“This is the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of everything he has given me.” He is given to the one who preserves humility; he receives that person. Whoever does not preserve humility is far from the teacher of humility.

“That I should lose nothing of everything he has given me.” “It is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish” (Matthew 18). Something may perish from among the swollen and proud, but nothing perishes from among the little ones. For unless you become like this little one, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

“Everything that the Father has given me I will not lose, but I will raise it up on the last day” (John 6). See how here too he outlines that twofold resurrection. Whoever comes to me rises now, having become humble among my members; but I will raise him up on the last day according to the flesh.

“For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life; and I will raise him up on the last day.” Earlier he said: “He hears my word and believes him who sent me.” Now, however: “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him.” He did not say, “He sees the Son and believes in the Father.”

For to believe in the Son is the same as to believe in the Father, because, “just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself”; so that “everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John 5)—by believing and passing over into life, that is, into the first resurrection. And because this is not the only resurrection, he says, “I will raise him up on the last day.”

He continues:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” He is bread because he is life, and he is life because he came down from heaven, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). He is the supersubstantial bread, which we are commanded to request daily so that it may be given to us (Matthew 6). Our Lord Jesus Christ was saying that he was the bread who had come down from heaven.

The Jews murmured and said, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How, then, does he say that he has come down from heaven?”

They murmured because they did not understand this bread; they did not hunger for this bread; they did not love this bread. For if they had loved it, they certainly would not have murmured. Therefore they were far from the heavenly bread and did not know how to hunger for it, because they had languid throats of the heart. Their ears were open, yet they were deaf. They saw, yet they stood there blind.

This bread seeks the hunger of the inner person. Therefore he says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

They said, “Whose father and mother we know.” They knew an earthly mother; they did not know the heavenly Father, because they had not been drawn by the heavenly Father. The Lord himself soon made this known in the following words, saying:

“Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” The one comes whom the grace of God has anticipated; with the Prophet we say to him: “His mercy will anticipate me.” And again: “His mercy will follow me” (Psalm 22). It anticipates the willing; it follows in bringing the work to completion.

The Father draws to the Son those who believe in the Son for this reason: because they think that God is his Father. For God the Father begot a Son equal to himself; and whoever thinks, feels, and meditates in faith that the one in whom he has believed is equal to the Father, that person the Father draws to the Son.

Whoever says of Christ, “He is not the true God,” is not drawn by the Father; rather, a perverse thought draws him away from consenting to the truth. The one who has been drawn by the Father is the one who says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). The Lord said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). This revelation itself is the drawing.

When he said, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” he immediately added: “And I will raise him up on the last day.” I will give back what he hopes for; he will see what he has believed without yet seeing. He will eat what he hungers for; he will be satisfied with what he thirsts for. Where? In the resurrection of the dead, because “I will raise him up on the last day.”

For it is written in the prophets: “And they will all be taught by God.” Why did he say this? O Jews, has the Father not taught you, so that you can know me? All the people of that kingdom will be taught by God. They will not hear from human beings; and even if they hear from human beings, nevertheless what they understand is given within: within it flashes forth, within it is revealed.

Human beings can make the word sound outwardly, but they labor in vain unless God, teaching within, opens the senses. That person is taught by God whom God instructs inwardly in the recognition and love of truth.

“Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me.” How does the Father draw? By teaching and delighting, not by compelling through necessity, because no one believes by compulsion, but by willingness.

The Son was teaching; the Father was teaching. The human being who appeared was speaking, but God was teaching inwardly in the heart of the hearer. Therefore he added:

“Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” I am from the Father, and therefore I see the Father. What does it mean to be taught by the Father except to hear the word of the Father—that is, me?

Lest, then, when I say to you, “Everyone who hears from the Father and learns,” you say among yourselves, “But we have never seen the Father; how, then, could we learn from the Father?” Hear from me: “No one has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” I know the Father; I am from him. But how? I am the Word from him whose Word I am—not a word that sounds and passes away, but one that remains while he speaks and draws the hearer.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.” He wished to reveal what he was; for he could have said more briefly, “Whoever believes in me has me.” For Christ himself is the true God and eternal life.

Whoever believes in me, he says, comes to me; and whoever comes to me has me. But what does it mean to have me? To have eternal life.

Eternal life assumed death and wished to die—but from what belonged to you, human being, not from what belonged to it. It received from you that by which it would die for you. Life therefore assumed death so that life might kill death.

For “whoever believes,” he says, “has eternal life”—not what is apparent, but what is hidden. For eternal life, the Word, was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God, and the light was the life of human beings (John 1). He came to die, but on the third day he rose again.

“I am,” he says, “the bread of life.” And what was the source of their pride? “Your fathers ate manna and died.” Why did they eat and die? Because they believed what they saw, but did not understand what they did not see. Therefore he says “your fathers” because you are like them.

Moses and Aaron and the other saints who were among the people ate manna and did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually and hungered spiritually. Others, however, ate and remained in unbelief. So the Jews heard Christ speaking, but did not understand his words spiritually.

Therefore he said to them: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died.” By what death, except the death of unbelief? For the saints who were among them also died the common death. Thus the Lord Jesus by these words signified spiritual death, not bodily death.

Their fathers, then—that is, the evil fathers of evil people, the unbelieving fathers of unbelievers, the murmuring fathers of those who murmur—for that people is said to have offended God in nothing more than by murmuring against God. Therefore the Lord, wishing to show that these were their children, began with them here: “Why do you murmur among yourselves, you murmurers, children of murmurers? Your fathers ate manna and died—not because the manna was evil, but because they ate it evilly.”

“This is the bread that came down from heaven.” Manna signified this bread; the altar of God also signified this bread. Those sacraments existed in signs; the things signified are different, but what they signify is the same.

Hear the Apostle: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Corinthians 10). Spiritual, certainly, not bodily.

They had one kind, because it was manna; we have another. But the spiritual food was the same as ours—not the fathers of those who are like us, but our fathers, those to whom they were not like.

This, then, is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats from it, he will not die. This pertains to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: it is the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” He is living because he came down from heaven. Manna too came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

“If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”

When [perhaps: “how”] could flesh comprehend what he said—that the bread was flesh? What flesh cannot comprehend is called flesh; and for that very reason flesh comprehends it less, because it is called flesh. This is what they recoiled from; this they said was feigned; this is what they thought could not happen.

“My flesh,” he says, “is for the life of the world.” The faithful know the body of Christ, if they do not neglect to be the body of Christ. Let them become the body of Christ if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ except the body of Christ.

Whoever wishes to live, let him believe in Christ; let him eat spiritually the spiritual food. Let him be incorporated into the body of Christ, and let him not be a rotten member deserving to be cut off. Let him be beautiful, healthy, and suited to his head.

The Jews therefore argued among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” They argued among themselves because they did not understand the bread of concord, nor did they wish to receive it.

For those who eat such bread do not argue among themselves, because “we, though many, are one bread and one body” (1 Corinthians 10); and through this God caused such people to dwell in one house.

But when they argue among themselves and ask how the Lord can give them his flesh to eat, they do not yet eat. Rather, they are still told:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” You do not know how it is given, or what the manner of eating this bread is; nevertheless, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.

He was not speaking to corpses, but to the living. Therefore, lest they understand this life and continue to argue about the matter, he added immediately:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” Therefore the one who does not eat this bread and drink this blood does not have eternal life. For people who are not in his body through faith can possess temporal life in this age, however they may possess it; but they can never possess eternal life, which is promised to the saints.

And lest they think that, in this food and drink, eternal life was promised at the end only to those who receive them carnally and do not understand them spiritually, he immediately added and said:

“And I will raise him up on the last day.” Thus, in the meantime, he may have eternal life according to the spirit in rest, where the spirits of the saints are received. As for the body, it too is not deprived of eternal life; rather, on the last day, at the resurrection of the dead, the flesh will be raised.

“For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Since, in food and drink, people seek that they may not hunger or thirst, this is truly provided only by the food and drink that makes those by whom it is received immortal and incorruptible—that is, the fellowship itself of the saints, where there will be peace and complete and perfect unity.

For this reason, as people before us also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood in those things that are brought together into one from many: one thing is made into one from many grains, and another flows together into one from many grapes.

At last he now explains how what he is saying comes about, and what it means to eat his body and drink his blood.

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” To eat that food and drink that drink, then, is to remain in Christ and to have Christ remain in oneself.

Accordingly, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, certainly does not eat his flesh spiritually, even if carnally and visibly he presses the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood with his teeth. Rather, he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment, because an unclean person presumes to approach Christ’s sacraments. No one worthily receives them except the one who is clean; of such people it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5).

“As the living Father sent me,” he says, “and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” The Son does not become better through participation in the Father, since he was born equal to him; but our participation in the Son, through the unity of his body and blood—which that eating and drinking signifies—makes us better.

We therefore live because of him when we eat him—that is, when we receive from him the eternal life that we do not possess from ourselves. He lives because of the Father, having been sent by him, because “he emptied himself, becoming obedient even unto the wood of the cross” (Philippians 2).

“As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” It is as if he said: “I live because of the Father”—that is, I refer my life to him as to one greater, because of the self-emptying in which he sent me. But for each person to live because of me is effected through participation, by which he eats me.

Thus I, having been humbled, live because of the Father; he, having been exalted, lives because of me. He did not speak of the nature in which he is always equal to the Father, but of the nature in which he became less than the Father.

He also said earlier: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5)—that is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

“This is the bread that came down from heaven,” so that by eating it we may live, since we cannot possess eternal life from ourselves.

“Not as your fathers ate,” he says, “and died. Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” He said these things in the synagogue, teaching in Capernaum.

That they died, therefore, he wishes to be understood in the sense that they do not live forever. For certainly those who eat Christ will also die temporally; but they will live forever, because Christ is eternal life.

The sign that someone has eaten and drunk is this: if Christ remains in him and he remains in Christ; if he dwells in Christ and Christ dwells in him; thus he will not be abandoned.

This, then, he taught and admonished us in mystical words: that we should be in his body, under the head, among his members, eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity.

But many of those who were present were scandalized because they did not understand. When they heard these things, they thought only of flesh—the flesh that they themselves were.

But the Apostle speaks truly: “To think according to the flesh is death” (Romans 8). The Lord gives us his flesh to eat; yet to think according to the flesh is death, even though he says of his flesh that eternal life is found there.

Therefore we must not understand even the flesh according to the flesh, as in these words.

Many therefore, when they heard this—not from his enemies, but from his disciples—said: “This is a hard saying. Who can hear it?” If the disciples found this saying hard, what of his enemies?

Yet it was necessary that it should be said in such a way that it would not be understood by human beings. The secret of God should make attentive people intent, not turn them away.

These people, however, failed when the Lord Jesus spoke such things. They did not believe that he was saying something great, with a certain grace concealed beneath his words; rather, they understood as they wished, and like human beings for whom Jesus was not the head, they thought that Jesus intended to distribute among those who believed in him the flesh with which the Word had been clothed, as though it had been cut into pieces.

“This is a hard saying,” they said. “Who can hear it?”

But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were murmuring about him—for they said these things among themselves, so that he would not hear them—he, who knew them within themselves, heard what they said inwardly and answered, saying:

“This scandalizes you. Because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink’—this, surely, scandalizes you.”

If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? What does this mean? Here he resolves what had disturbed them; here he removes the stumbling block over which they had fallen; here, plainly, if they had understood, he draws them out of their error. For they had thought that he would distribute his body to them; but he said that he would ascend, whole and entire, into heaven. When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before, then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose. Surely then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by being eaten.

In these words it is clearly understood that Christ is one person, when he said that the Son of Man had previously been in heaven. He was speaking on earth [Col. 0720D], and he said that he was in heaven. To what else does this refer except that we should understand Christ to be one person, God and man, not two persons—lest our faith have not a Trinity but a Quaternity? Christ, therefore, is one: Word, soul, and flesh. One Christ, Son of God and Son of Man. One Christ, Son of God eternally, Son of Man in time; nevertheless, one Christ according to the unity of his person was in heaven when he was speaking on earth. The Son of Man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth. The Son of God was on earth after assuming flesh in the same way that the Son of Man was in heaven, in the unity of his person.

He explains this more fully at once, showing the difference between spirit and flesh, and between wishing to eat Christ carnally and receiving him spiritually. For he says:

[Col. 0721A] “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” A little earlier he had said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”; and now he says: “The flesh profits nothing.” That is: if you wish to understand carnally what I am saying, the flesh profits nothing; if you understand it carnally, as something to be eaten like other food, like the meat bought in butcher shops—for it is the Spirit who gives life. Through the Spirit, the flesh profits, although by itself it profits nothing, because “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. III).

For through the flesh the Spirit accomplished something for our salvation: the flesh was the vessel he possessed, through which the Spirit saved us, using the instrument of the flesh for the salvation of the human race, just as the devil used the serpent as an instrument for the overthrow of our first parent [Col. 0721B] (Gen. III). “It is the Spirit who gives life, but the flesh profits nothing.” I do not give my flesh to be eaten in the way they understood flesh.

Therefore:

“The words,” he says, “that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” For we have said, brothers, that in the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood the Lord commended this: that we should remain in him, and he in us. We remain in him when we are his members. He remains in us when we are his temple. But in order that we may be his members, unity binds us together. And what brings unity together except love? From where does the love of God come? Ask the Apostle. “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). [Col. 0721C] Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life. The Spirit makes the members living. Yet the Spirit does not make living members except those whom he finds in the body that he himself animates. For the spirit that is in you, O human being, by which you exist as a human being—does it give life to a member that it finds separated from your flesh? I mean your spirit, your soul. Your soul gives life only to the members that are in your flesh. If you remove one, it is no longer given life by your soul, because it is not joined to the unity of your body.

These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation. For a Christian ought to fear nothing so much as being separated from the body of Christ. If he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member; if he is not his member, he is not animated by his Spirit. “Whoever,” the Apostle says, “does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” What does “they are spirit and life” mean? They are to be understood spiritually. Have you understood them spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood them carnally? Even in that case they are spirit and life, but they are not so for you, O human being, who do not understand them spiritually and do not know how to venerate them by faith.

“For there are some among you who do not believe.” And for this reason they do not understand, because they do not believe. For the prophet said: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VI). Through faith we are joined together; through understanding we are given life. First we believe through faith, so that afterward we may be given life through understanding.

[Col. 0722A] For Jesus knew from the beginning who the believers were, and who would betray him. Judas, too, was among those who had been scandalized; Christ neither kept silent about him nor openly identified him, so that all might fear, even though one would perish. But after he had spoken of and distinguished believers from unbelievers, he stated the reason why they did not believe.

“Therefore,” he says, “I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father.” Faith is given by the Father to believers, so that no one may boast in his faith, as though it were his own and came from himself, but may recognize it as given by God, as grace.

“From that time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.” They went back—not after Christ, but after Satan. They returned in such a way that they were cut off from the body of Christ and did not return to him thereafter, because perhaps they had never truly been in his body in faith. And they were not few, but many. Let us therefore see what he said to the few who remained.

Then Jesus said to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” Judas did not leave either; but why he remained was already apparent to the Lord, and was revealed later. Peter answered on behalf of all: one on behalf of many, unity on behalf of everyone.

Simon Peter therefore answered him: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You are driving us away from yourself; give us another you. To whom shall we go if we depart from you? To whom shall we go?”

“You have the words of eternal life.” See how Peter, with the Lord giving and the Holy Spirit refreshing him, understood. From where did he understand, except because he believed the words of eternal life? For you have eternal life in the ministration of your body and blood, and we did not first know and then believe; rather, we believed and then came to know. We believed in order to know. For if we had wished first to know and afterward to believe, we would have been able neither to know nor to believe. What do we believe, and what have we come to know?

“That you are the Christ, the Son of God.” That is: you are eternal life itself, and in your flesh and blood you give nothing other than what you are.

Jesus answered: “Did I not choose you Twelve? And one of you is a devil.” He was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot; for he was going to betray him, although he was one of the Twelve. He was one of the Twelve not in faith but in number, not in truth but in pretense.

But how are we to understand “Did I not choose you Twelve?” when that one is said to be a son of the devil? Only because the eleven were chosen in one way, and that one in another. They were chosen to remain in Christ and for their sound to go out through the whole world (Ps. XVIII). That one was chosen so that through him the dispensation of divine mercy might be fulfilled in the salvation of the human race. Thus God’s goodness made good use of his wickedness, just as God made good use of the wickedness of Joseph’s brothers in selling him (Gen. XXXVII), so that from their evil deed God’s goodness might be revealed in the salvation of many.

Thus Judas’s evil was turned into our good. What the evil person does by making evil use of God’s good gifts harms himself; he will not be able to destroy God’s goodness.

Why did Christ choose twelve? [Col. 0723A] The number twelve is sacred. The honor of that number was not removed merely because one of them perished; another was appointed in the place of the one who perished, and the consecrated number remained—the number twelve—because they were to proclaim the Trinity throughout the whole world, that is, through the four quarters of the earth. Thus they were chosen in groups of four, so that the holy Trinity might be preached throughout the four parts of the world.

The year, too, runs according to the number twelve, and the order of the signs in the heavens, through which the sun and moon are known to move, is divided according to the number twelve. For this reason Christ sent the first preachers into the world according to this number. The number was not violated by Judas’s death; another was appointed in his place.

Regarding the most sacred significance of this number, Christ himself says in the Gospel, speaking of the highest glory of the saints: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

## CHAPTER VII

“After this,” he says, “Jesus was walking in Galilee. For he did not want to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.” In this he offered an example for our weakness. He had not lost his power, but was comforting our frailty. For it was destined, as I have said, that some of his faithful would hide themselves so as not to be found by their persecutors. And lest hiding be charged against them as a crime, he went before them as their head in what would be confirmed in his members.

Christ could have walked in Judea and not been killed, for he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X). He demonstrated this power when he wished to do so, when those who had come with weapons to seize him fell backward at his voice (John XVIII).

The Jewish feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), was near. *Scenopegia* is the feast during which the Jews were commanded, in the seventh month, to dwell for seven days in booths beneath the branches of trees (Lev. XXIII), in memory of their dwelling in the wilderness. This was the feast that the Jews celebrated with great solemnity, as though recalling the benefits of the Lord, who had led them out of the land of Egypt.

The Jewish Feast of Unleavened Bread is called not a single day, but, because of the customary observance of the entire festival, they were accustomed to call all the days belonging to that celebration one feast day.

His brothers therefore said to him: “Leave here and go to Judea.” The Lord’s brothers were called, according to the most familiar usage of holy Scripture, the relatives of holy Mary, ever-virgin. Abraham and Lot, and Laban and Jacob, are called brothers, although Laban was Jacob’s maternal uncle. Therefore, when you hear “the Lord’s brothers,” think of Mary’s blood relationship, not of her bearing any further offspring.

We have spoken of who these brothers were; let us hear what they said: “Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you are doing.” The Lord’s works were not hidden from his disciples, but they were hidden from these men. These brothers—that is, relatives—could have Christ as their relative; yet because of that very closeness they disdained to believe in him. Therefore the evangelist immediately continues:

“For even his brothers did not believe in him.” Why did they not believe in him? Because they were seeking human glory, saying to him:

“Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you are doing. For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be known publicly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.” These words show that they were seeking his glory in a carnal way, as though they had said: “You perform miracles, but secretly. Go into Judea, so that the leaders of the nation and the capital city of the kingdom may see your miracles. Make yourself known; appear before everyone, so that everyone may praise you.”

To this the Lord Jesus says:

[Col. 0724B] “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.” The Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV). The time of Christ’s glory had not yet come when he spoke these words.

What do those people seem to be seeking who were urging him to go into Judea, perform miracles, and make himself known to the world? They did not want him to remain hidden and be thought insignificant. But he wished humility to precede exaltation and to reach that very height by the way of humility.

“Your time,” that is, the glory of the world, “is always ready.” There will indeed be a time of glory. He who came in humility will come in exaltation. He who came to be judged will come to judge. He who came to be killed by the dead will come to judge the living and the dead.

“You go up to this feast.” What does “this” mean? The place where you seek human glory. What does “this” mean? The place where you wish to extend carnal joys and do not think about eternal ones.

“I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” At this feast you seek human glory; but my time—that is, the time of my glory—has not yet come. My feast will be not one that runs through and passes away over these days, but one that remains forever. That will be a festival: joy without end, eternity without stain, serenity without cloud.

After saying these things, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not openly but as if in secret. He did not go up to “this” feast because he was not seeking temporal glory, but was going to teach something salutary, correct human beings, remind them of the eternal feast, turn their love away from this age, and convert it toward God.

What does it mean that he went up to the feast as if secretly? This action of the Lord is not without significance. All the Jewish feasts existed in symbolic form. He therefore went up to them secretly because Christ was hidden in them: hidden from the earlier people, but now revealed to the better people; for what that people did in shadow, we now do in manifest light.

From this it is possible to understand that the Lord’s reply—“I am not going up to this feast”—also refers to his passion, because Christ did not ascend the cross at the feast of Booths but at the Paschal feast, when the lamb used to be killed.

The Jews were seeking him during the feast before he went up, for his brothers had gone up first. He did not go up at the time they thought and wished, so that what he had said might be fulfilled: “Not to this one,” that is, not on the first or second day to which you wish me to go. Later he went up, as the Gospel relates, midway through the feast—that is, when as many days of the feast had already passed as still remained. For, as we should understand, they celebrated the feast over many days.

They were saying: “Where is he?” And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. What caused the murmuring? Disagreement. What was the disagreement?

Some were saying: “He is good”; others: “No, but he misleads the crowds.” The same thing is said now about all his servants. Whenever someone excels in some grace, some say, “He is good,” while others say, “No, but he misleads the crowds.” Why does this happen? Because “our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III).

The body of Christ suffers from lovers of the world, until the end of the age, what it suffered then from the murmuring Jews. The grain has not yet been separated from the chaff, so that the wheat may be gathered into the barn and the chaff burned in eternal fire. Therefore what was said about the Lord serves for the consolation of whatever Christian this may be said about.

Yet no one spoke openly about him because of fear of the Jews. Those who said, “He is good,” spoke quietly; those who said, “He misleads the crowds,” made their noise heard like dry leaves. “He misleads the crowds”—they sounded more loudly. “He is good”—they whispered more softly.

But now, brothers, although that glory of Christ has not yet come which will make us eternal, his Church is nevertheless growing in such a way, and he has deigned to spread it throughout the world, that although it is whispered, “He misleads the crowds,” the cry “He is good” rings out more loudly. For a new heresy whispers secretly in corners, “Christ is adopted”; but the voice of the universal holy Church resounds more loudly: “Christ is the proper Son of God.”

They also hiss with a serpent’s mouth, “He is God only in name”; but the unanimous agreement of all the faithful cries out more distinctly and firmly, “Christ is good God,” as the outstanding preacher bears witness, saying: “From them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is over all, God blessed” (Rom. IX).

Jesus therefore went up to the temple midway through the feast [Col. 0725D] and was teaching. The Jews were amazed and said: “How does this man know letters, when he has not studied?” While he was hidden, he taught; while he spoke openly, he was not seized. The former—that he was hidden—was for an example; the latter was an exercise of power.

When he taught, the Jews were amazed. All of them, I think, were amazed, but not all were converted. Why were they amazed? Because many knew where he had been born and how he had been raised. They had never seen him studying letters, yet they heard him discussing the law and producing testimonies from the law—things no one could produce unless he had read them, and no one could read unless he had learned letters. Therefore they were amazed.

Their amazement, however, became for the Teacher an opportunity to introduce the truth more deeply. From their amazement and their words the Lord spoke something profound [Col. 0726A] and worthy of more careful examination. What, then, did the Lord answer those who were amazed at how he knew letters that he had not studied?

“My teaching,” he said, “is not mine, but his who sent me.” This is the depth of the matter. He appears to have spoken something contradictory in a few words. He did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but “My teaching is not mine.” How can it be mine and not mine? The question is how both can be true: mine and not mine.

If we carefully consider what the holy evangelist says at the beginning—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I)—the solution to this question depends upon it. What, then, is the Father’s teaching except the Father’s Word? Christ himself, therefore, is the Father’s teaching, if he is the Father’s Word. But because a word cannot be nobody’s word, but must be someone’s, he called himself his own teaching and yet not his own, because he is the Father’s Word.

The Lord Christ therefore seems to have said: “My teaching is not mine,” as though he were saying, “I am not from myself.” Although we say and believe that the Son is equal to the Father, that there is no difference of nature or substance between them, and that no interval existed between the one who begets and the one who is begotten, nevertheless, while preserving and safeguarding this truth, we say that one is the Father and the other the Son.

The Father is not Father if he does not have a Son; the Son is not Son if he does not have a Father. Yet the Son is God from the Father, while the Father is God but not God from the Son—not God from God. The Son, however, is God from God, light from light. The Father is light, the Son is light—not two lights, but one light. The Father is God, the Son is God—not two gods, but one God, Father and Son.

The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is also God. As the Father is God, as the Son is God, so also the Holy Spirit is God—not three gods, but one God, one light, one substance, one nature, one majesty, one eternity, one greatness, one power, and one goodness.

The Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, saw that not everyone would understand this profound mystery, and afterward gave instruction. Do you wish to understand? Believe. For God, speaking through the prophet, said: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VI). To this belongs what the Lord adds next:

“If anyone wishes to do his will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I speak from myself.” What does “if anyone wishes to do his will” mean? I had said, “If anyone believes,” and had given this counsel: “If you do not understand, believe.” Understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe; believe in order to understand, since “unless you believe, you will not understand.”

Since I had given obedience to believing as the means of attaining understanding, and had said that the Lord Jesus Christ himself joined these things together, we find him saying in the following statement: “If anyone wishes to do his will”—that is, to believe. But because “he will know,” that is, understand, is understood by everyone, while the phrase “if anyone wishes to do his will” refers to believing, we need our Lord himself as interpreter to show us whether doing the will of his Father truly refers to believing.

Who does not know that doing the will of God means performing his work, that is, what pleases him? The Lord himself openly says elsewhere: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John VI). “That you believe in him”—not merely “that you believe him.”

Nor does everyone who believes him immediately believe in him. The demons believed him, but did not believe in him (Matt. XVII; Jas. II; Rom. IV). Again, we can say of his apostles: “We believe Paul,” but not “We believe in Paul”; “We believe Peter,” but not “We believe in Peter.”

“Faith is reckoned as righteousness” for the one who believes in him who justifies. What does it mean to believe in him? It means, by believing, to love; by believing, to cherish; by believing, to go to him and be incorporated into his members. This, then, is the faith that God requires of us, the faith that “works through love” (Gal. V).

If you understand the words of God, understand that Christ is the Son of God and the Father’s teaching: he is not from himself, not from nothing, not from other subsisting beings, but from the Father alone, remaining in the Father and equal to the Father.

“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory.” This will be the one who is called Antichrist, exalting himself, as the Apostle says, “above everything that is called God or worshiped” (2 Thess. II).

The Lord, announcing that he would seek his own glory rather than the glory of the Father, said to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V). He indicated that they would receive the Antichrist, who will seek the glory of his own name—puffed up, not solid, and therefore unstable and destined to fall.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, gave us a great example of humility. He is indeed equal to the Father. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He himself said, and said most truly: “For so long I have been with you, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV). He himself said, and said most truly: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

If, then, he is one with the Father, equal to the Father, God from God, God eternally with God, immortal, equally unchangeable, equally beyond time, equally Creator and Dispenser of times—nevertheless, because he came in time, assumed the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II), he seeks the glory of the Father, not his own.

What, then, ought you to do, human being, who, when you do something good, seek your own glory, but when you do something evil, plot accusations against God? Pay attention to yourself. You are a creature. Recognize the Creator. You are a servant. Do not despise God. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you have this grace, you adopted human being; his glory was sought by the one who was uniquely born from him.

“But he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.” In the Antichrist there is injustice, and he is not true, because he will seek his own glory, not the glory of the one by whom he was sent. He was not sent, but came by permission.

Therefore, all who belong to the body of Christ, lest we be led into the snare of the Antichrist, let us not seek our own glory. If he sought the glory of the one who sent him, how much more should we seek the glory of the one who made us?

He continues:

“Did not Moses,” he says, “give you the law, and none of you keeps the law? Why are you seeking to kill me?” You seek to kill me because none of you keeps the law. For if you had kept the law, you would recognize Christ in the very writings, and you would not kill him who is present.

And they answered him. The crowd answered—as a crowd, not with order but with disturbance. Finally, see what the disturbed crowd replied:

“You have a demon. Who is seeking to kill you?” It was surely worse to say, “You have a demon,” than to kill him. For they said this to the one who was casting out demons. What else could a turbulent crowd say? What else could stirred-up filth smell like except something foul? The crowd was disturbed. By what? By the truth. The brightness of the light disturbed the crowd’s diseased vision. Eyes that are not healthy cannot bear the brightness of the light.

The Lord, however, was not truly disturbed. Tranquil in his truth, he did not return evil for evil or abuse for abuse. If he had said to them, “You have a demon,” he would have spoken truly. For how could they have said to the truth, “You have a demon,” unless the devil’s falsehood had provoked them?

Let us hear what the tranquil one answered, and let us live tranquilly.

“I did one work, and you are all amazed.” As though he were saying: “What would you do if you saw all my works?” The works they saw in the world were his works, but they did not see the one who made all things. He did one thing, and they were disturbed because he had made a man well on the Sabbath—not understanding that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, who established the Sabbath for man, not man for the Sabbath.

He did not destroy the Sabbath by making a man well on the Sabbath, because the observance of the Sabbath was given to human beings for the sake of human salvation.

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision.” It was rightly done that you received circumcision from Moses.

“Not because it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.” Abraham was the first to receive circumcision from the Lord.

[Col. 0728D] “And on the Sabbath you circumcise.” Moses convicts you in the law. You received the command to circumcise on the eighth day; you received the command in the law to rest on the seventh day (Lev. XII). If the eighth day of the one who has been born falls on the seventh day, the Sabbath, what will you do? Will you rest in order to keep the Sabbath, or will you circumcise in order to fulfill the sacrament of the eighth day?

“But I know,” he says, “what you do. You circumcise a man.” Why? Because circumcision belongs to a sign of salvation, and people ought not to rest from salvation on the Sabbath. Therefore, do not be angry with me either, because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath.

“If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath,” he says, “so that the law of Moses may not be broken”—for something salutary was instituted through Moses in that ordinance of circumcision—“why are you angry with me for making a man completely well on the Sabbath?”

Perhaps that circumcision signified the Lord himself, at whom they were angry because he was healing and restoring. It was commanded to be performed on the eighth day. And what is circumcision except the removal of flesh? This circumcision therefore signifies the removal from the heart of carnal desires.

It was not given without reason, nor was it commanded to be performed on that member, since through that member the human race is propagated: “Through one man, death; likewise through one man, the resurrection of the dead”; and “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death.”

Therefore everyone is born with a foreskin, because every human being is born with the defect inherited through descent. God cleanses us both from the defect with which we are born and from the defects we add by living badly only through the stone knife—that is, through our Lord Jesus Christ. For the rock was Christ.

They circumcised with stone knives, and by the name of the rock they represented Christ; yet they did not recognize him when he was present and, moreover, desired to kill him. But when you circumcise a man on the Sabbath, understand that this signifies a good work.

“What I did was to make the whole man well on the Sabbath.” For he was healed so that he might be healthy in body, and he believed so that he might be healthy in soul.

“Do not judge with partiality, but judge with righteous judgment.” What does this mean? If you circumcise on the Sabbath according to the law of Moses, you do not become angry with Moses; but because I made a man well on the Sabbath, you become angry with me. You show partiality. Attend to the truth and judge with righteous judgment.

If you judge according to the truth, you will condemn neither Moses nor me. And once you know the truth, you will know me, because I am the truth.

Brothers, escaping in this age the vice that the Lord pointed out here—showing partiality rather than maintaining right judgment—is a matter of great labor. The Lord warned the Jews, but he instructed us. He convicted them, but he taught us. He rebuked them, but he sharpened our understanding.

Let us not suppose that this was not said to us because we were not there at that time. Let us therefore hear the Gospel as though the Lord were present, and let us not say: “How fortunate were those who were able to see him!” Many among those who saw him physically killed him; many among us who have not seen him have believed.

Who is it who does not show partiality, except the one who loves equally? Whoever loves everyone equally judges equally concerning everyone. Nor should we think that this saying concerns those whom we honor differently because of their different ranks of dignity, but those whose cases we are commanded to discern.

The Lord Jesus therefore went up to the feast not openly but secretly—not because he feared being seized, since he had the power not to be seized, but to signify that even in the feast celebrated by the Jews the mystery was hidden and closed. Soon, however, the power that had been thought to be fear became evident. He was speaking openly during the feast, so that the crowds were amazed and said what we heard when the reading was read:

“Is this not the man whom they were seeking to kill? And look, he is speaking openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ?” Those who knew with what savagery he was being sought were amazed at the power by which he was not seized.

Because they did not fully understand his power, they thought that the rulers’ knowledge was the reason: they supposed that the rulers themselves had recognized him as the Christ and had therefore spared him at the time when they had sought to kill him.

Then those very people who had said to themselves, “Have the rulers recognized that this is the Christ?” raised for themselves the question by which it seemed to them that he was not the Christ. For they added:

“But we know where this man is from; when the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” What did the Jews mean by saying, “When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from” (Matt. II), when, in response to Herod’s question about the place of his birth, they indicated it according to the prophecy of the prophet Micah (Micah V), and it is therefore certain that they knew the place of his birth?

We must consider what they thought they knew and what they said they did not know. They knew the place of his birth through the words of the prophets, but because of the impiety of their hearts they did not know his divine birth, by which he was eternally born from God the Father. For Isaiah says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

The Lord therefore answered both points, speaking of the weakness of his humanity and the majesty of his divinity.

Jesus therefore cried out while teaching in the temple: “You know me, and you know where I am from.” He rightly said, “You know me, and you know where I am from”—that is, you know my birth according to the flesh, you know the nobility of my parents, and you know the appearance of my face. But according to my divinity you do not know:

“Because I have not come from myself, but the one who sent me is true, whom you do not know.” But in order that you may know him, believe in the one whom he sent. Then you will know that “no one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John I), and that “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X).

Finally, after he had said, “But the one who sent me is true, whom you do not know,” in order to show them how they could know what they did not know, he added:

“I know him.” Therefore ask me so that you may know him. Why do I know him? “Because I am from him, and he sent me.” He magnificently demonstrated both points. “I am from him,” he says, because the Son is from the Father, and whatever the Son is, he is from the one whose Son he is.

Therefore we call the Lord Jesus “God from God.” We do not call the Father “God from God,” but simply “God”; and we call the Lord Jesus “light from light.” We do not call the Father “light from light,” but simply “light.”

This, then, is what he meant when he said, “I am from him.” But when you hear, “He sent me,” referring to the fact that you see me in the flesh, do not understand a dissimilarity of nature, but the authority of the one who begets.

They therefore sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come. That is, because he did not wish it. For he who was born by his will also suffered by his will. Just as he had foreseen the hour of his birth, so he determined the hour of his passion.

If the hour of our death is subject to his will, how much more did the hour of his passion come according to his own will?

Great, therefore, is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: he was made in time for us, through whom the times were made. He was made among all things, through whom all things were made. He was made what he had made. He became human, although he had made humanity, so that what he had made would not perish.

According to this dispensation, the hour of his birth had already come, and he had been born; but the hour of his passion had not yet come. Therefore he had not yet suffered, because the hour had not yet come in which he wished to suffer.

For this reason it is written that on the cross, when all things had been completed according to the Scriptures of the prophets, he said: “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John XIX).
