When he wished it, the things written about him were completed; and once everything had been completed, he himself, by his own power, released his spirit.

Many of the crowd, however, believed in him. The Lord was saving the humble and the poor (Ps. 33); the rulers were raging, and therefore not only failed to recognize the physician but even wanted to kill him. There was a certain crowd that quickly saw its sickness and recognized his remedy without delay; moved by the miracles, it believed, while the rulers remained in unbelief. Therefore, when they heard of the faith of the multitude, they murmured because Christ was being glorified, and promptly sent officers to seize him. They were unable to seize him because he still did not wish to be seized; [Col. 0731C] but they heard him teaching—the very one whom they had come to seize.

Then Jesus said: “I am with you only a little while longer. What you now wish to do, you will do—but not now. What I do not wish to do now, why do I still not wish to do it now? Because I am with you only a little while longer.”

“And then I am going to him who sent me. I must fulfill my dispensation and thus arrive at my Passion.”

“You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” Here he already foretold his resurrection. They did not wish to recognize him while he was present, and afterward they sought him when they saw that the multitude already believed. Great signs had indeed been performed, and the Lord had already risen and ascended into heaven. Then great deeds were performed through the disciples, but it was he who performed them through them, just as he had performed them through himself. For he himself had said to them: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Why could they not come? Because they did not wish to believe; for no one can be saved without faith.

Then the Jews said, not to him but among themselves: “Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Surely he is going to the dispersion among the Gentiles and is going to teach the Gentiles?” They did not know what they were saying; but because he willed it, they prophesied. The Lord was indeed going to the Gentiles—not by the presence of his body, but by divine power in his disciples, concerning whom the prophet said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. 52). In these feet Christ was going to the Gentiles and was going to teach [Col. 0732A] those Gentiles who had received the faith [F. *acciperent*: “would receive”], the Gentiles whom the Jews despised. In their ignorance they prophesied truly, because they had failed to understand Christ’s saying: “And where I am, you cannot come.” Why can you not come? Because you do not wish to believe.

What does he mean by saying, “Where I am,” except: “I am in the bosom of the Father; I am coeternal with the Father”? He was speaking on earth, but he showed that he was in the Father’s bosom. Among the other dispensations of our Lord, the teachings of our salvation, and the doubts of the Jews concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—things that he said [sic], by which some would be confounded and others instructed—on the last day of that festival (for these events were then taking place), which is called *scenopegia*, that is, the construction of booths, concerning which your Charity already remembers that a discourse was delivered, the Lord Christ called out—not merely speaking, but crying aloud—so that whoever thirsted might come to him.

Are we thirsty? Let us come—not with our feet, but with our affections. Let us come not by moving away, but by loving. Yet the inner person, the one who loves, does move away; for moving away in the body is one thing, and moving away in the heart another. A person moves away in body who changes place by bodily motion; a person moves away in heart who changes affection by the movement of the heart. If you love one thing now and used to love another, you are not where you were.

The Lord was therefore crying out to us. He was standing and crying out:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

What this means, since the Evangelist explained it, we ought not to delay over. For concerning why the Lord said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” the Evangelist subsequently explained, saying:

“He said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John 7).

Let us know only this: the Lord Jesus cried out concerning charity. He cries out, then, and tells us to come and drink if we thirst within, because when we have drunk, rivers of living water will flow from our belly. The belly of the inner person is his heart’s conscience. Having drunk this liquid, the cleansed conscience revives; and, drawing from the spring, it will possess one—itself will also become a spring.

What is the spring, or what is the river, that flows from a person’s belly? Benevolence, by which he wishes to benefit his neighbor. For if he thinks that what he has drunk for himself is sufficient, he dries up, and living water does not flow from his belly. But if he hastens to benefit his neighbor, he does not dry up for this reason: he flows.

Let us see what those who believe in God drink. For certainly, if we are Christians and believe, we drink; and each person ought to know in himself whether he is drinking, so that, if he drinks, what he has drunk may flow from him. The spring will not abandon us if we do not abandon the spring. The Evangelist explained and said from what source the Lord had cried out, to what drink he had invited them, and what he had offered to those who drank, saying: “He said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. Which Spirit does he mean, except the Holy Spirit? Every human being has a spirit within himself, his own spirit—that is, his mind. For each person’s mind is his spirit, concerning which the Apostle Paul says: “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (1 Cor. 2).

But what does he mean by saying, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”? Surely the Spirit was in God’s holy prophets and patriarchs, who foretold many future things through the Holy Spirit? Elizabeth, too, is read to have been filled with the Holy Spirit, and likewise Zechariah, as the Evangelist says: “And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying” (Luke 1).

What, then, does he mean by saying that the Holy Spirit had not yet been given? We have many indications of the Spirit’s earlier presence before the Lord was glorified by the resurrection of his flesh. The prophets who foretold the coming Christ did not have another spirit. But a certain future mode of this gift was to appear, one that had not previously been manifested at all. It is of this that he speaks here. For nowhere do we previously read that people gathered together, after receiving the Holy Spirit, spoke in the languages of all nations (Acts 2).

After his resurrection, however, when he first appeared to his disciples, he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). Thus it was of this that he said: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” And he breathed upon their face—the breath by which he had first given life to the human being whom he made and raised from the clay, by which breath he had given a soul to his limbs (Gen. 2). He signified that the Spirit whom he breathed upon their face was the same Spirit, so that they might rise from the mud and renounce their works of clay.

Then, for the first time after his resurrection, the Lord gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples—the glorification of which the Evangelist speaks (John 20). Afterward, having remained with them for forty days, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates, he ascended into heaven while they watched and accompanied him with their gaze (Acts 1). Ten days having been completed there, on the day of Pentecost he sent the Holy Spirit from above. As I have said, they had been gathered together in one place; and after receiving him, they spoke in the languages of all nations (Acts 2).

Perhaps someone will ask why those who have been baptized in Christ and live according to the charity of his commandments do not speak in the languages of all nations, although it is certain that they have received the Holy Spirit. The reason is that the Church itself, which is the body of Christ, speaks in the languages of all nations. This was prefigured then in the primitive Church, which was founded in Judea among one nation only, but is now gathered from all nations. Just as one person then spoke in languages, so now the unity of the holy Church speaks in all languages.

We too receive the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together by charity, if we rejoice in the Catholic name and faith. Therefore, to the extent that each person loves the Church of Christ, to that extent he has the Holy Spirit. We have the Holy Spirit if we love the Church; and we love it if we remain in its bond and charity, which the Apostle confidently placed above all virtues (1 Cor. 13).

Whoever possesses this will possess every good, because without it whatever a person may be able to possess will profit him nothing. Concerning it the blessed Apostle James says: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2). Concerning this same matter the Truth himself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

While Christ was saying these things on the last day of the festival that we have just proposed and, as we were able, expounded, dissension arose among the crowd concerning him. Some thought that he was the Christ; others said that the Christ would not arise from Galilee. Those who had been sent to seize him returned free of guilt and filled with wonder. They even bore witness to his divine teaching when those who had sent them said:

“Why did you not bring him?”

For they replied that they had never heard a human being speak in this way. No human being speaks in this way; but he spoke in this way because he was God and human. The Pharisees, however, rejecting their testimony, said to them:

“Have you too been led astray? For we see that you have been delighted by his words.”

“Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.”

Those who did not know the law were the very ones who believed in him; and they who taught the law were despising the one who had given the law, so that what the Lord himself had said might be fulfilled: “I have come so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (Mark 4). The Pharisees, who were teachers, had become blind; the peoples who did not know the law were enlightened and believed in the author of the law.

Nevertheless, Nicodemus, one of the Pharisees, who had come to the Lord by night—and who was not himself unbelieving but timid (for this is why he had come by night to the light: because he wished to be enlightened but feared being known)—answered the Jews:

“Does our law judge a person unless it first hears him and learns what he does?”

For those wicked men wanted to be condemners before they were investigators. Nicodemus knew—or rather, believed—that if they were willing merely to hear him patiently, they might perhaps become like those who had been sent to seize him but had preferred to believe him rather than seize him.

They answered him, from the prejudice of their hearts, which they also directed against him:

“Are you too a Galilean?” That is, “As though you had been led astray by a Galilean?”

The Lord was called a Galilean because his parents were from the city of Nazareth. I speak of his parents according to Mary, not according to male seed. For he who already had a Father above sought on earth no one but a mother. Each of his births was marvelous: the divine birth without a mother, the human birth without a human father.

What, then, did those men say to Nicodemus as though they were teachers of the law?

“Search and see, because no prophet arises from Galilee.”

But the Lord of the prophets arose from there. “The Evangelist says, “They returned, each to his own home.”

## CHAPTER VIII

From there Jesus went on to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives signifies the height of the Lord’s compassion and mercy, since in Greek *ἔλεος* means “mercy,” while “oil” is called *ἔλαιον*; and the anointing of oil itself usually brings relief to weary and suffering limbs. Moreover, the fact that oil surpasses other liquids in both power and purity, and that whatever liquid one wishes to pour over it immediately sinks beneath it while the oil rises above it, fittingly suggests the grace of heavenly mercy, of which it is written: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144).

The time of dawn also signifies the rising of that same grace, because, once the shadow of the law had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed. Jesus therefore goes to the Mount of Olives to declare that the fortress of mercy is established in him. Again he comes at dawn [Col. 0735B] into the temple, to signify that this same mercy was to be disclosed and offered to the faithful—the temple, that is, of the New Testament, which was beginning to shine.

“And all the people,” he says, “came to him; and, sitting, he taught them.” The Lord’s sitting signifies the humility of the Incarnation, through which he deigned to have mercy on us. It is rightly said that, while Jesus was teaching seated, all the people came to him, because after he had drawn near to human beings through the humility of his Incarnation, his word was more willingly received by many.

By many, I say, his word was received, and by even more it was rejected in proud impiety. “The meek heard and rejoiced” (Ps. 33).

Finally, the Jews, testing him, brought a woman who had been caught in adultery. They asked what he commanded should be done with her, since Moses had commanded that such a woman be stoned (Lev. 20). Their intention was that, if he too decided that she should be stoned, they might mock him as having forgotten the mercy he always taught; but if he forbade her to be stoned, they would gnash their teeth against him and condemn him, supposedly with justification, as a supporter of crimes and an enemy of the law.

But Jesus, bending down, was writing with his finger on the ground. Through Jesus’ bending, humility is expressed; through the finger, which is flexible because of the articulation of its joints, the subtlety of discernment is expressed. Through the ground, moreover, the human heart is indicated, which is accustomed to produce the fruit of either good or evil actions.

When the Lord was asked to judge the sinful woman, he did not immediately give judgment. First he bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger; only afterward, when he was earnestly questioned, did he judge. In this he teaches us figuratively that, whenever we see the faults of our neighbors, we should not first judge them by reproving them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience and carefully examined it with the finger of discernment, determining through diligent investigation what pleases and what displeases the Creator. This agrees with the Apostle’s saying:

“Brothers, if a person is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6).

When they persisted in questioning him, he raised himself and said to them:

“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

Because the scribes and Pharisees were stretching the snares of their ambushes against the Lord from both sides, thinking that he would either prove merciless in judging or unjust, he foresaw their deceits. Like a thread passing through a spider’s web, he displayed in every respect the judgment of justice and the gentleness of compassion.

Behold the moderation of mercy: “Let the one among you who is without sin.” Behold again the justice of judgment: “Let him be the first to throw a stone at her.” It was as though he had said:

“If Moses commanded you to stone such a woman, see to it that he commanded this not to sinners but to the righteous. First fulfill the justice of the law yourselves, and then, with innocent hands and a pure heart, come together to stone the guilty woman. First perfect the spiritual commands of the law—faith, mercy, and charity—and then turn to judging carnal matters.”

After judgment had been given:

“But the Lord again bent down and wrote on the ground” [Col. 0736B].

According to ordinary human custom, it may be understood that the Lord wished to bend down before the shameless tempters and write on the ground so that, turning his face elsewhere, he might give them freedom to leave. He had foreseen that, struck by his answer, they would depart more quickly than they would ask further questions.

Finally, when they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders. But figuratively he admonishes us that, both before and after giving judgment, he bent down and wrote on the ground, so that both before we correct a sinning neighbor and after we have rendered him the ministry of deserved correction, we may examine ourselves with a worthy investigation of humility. We must ensure that we are not entangled either in the same offenses that we criticize in them or in other crimes.

For it might happen that someone who judges a murderer to be guilty and deserving of death may himself be found, before the eyes of the Creator, guilty in his own person through hatred of a brother’s death. Likewise, someone who accuses a brother of the crime of fornication may fail to see in himself the offense of pride (John 3). Therefore the judge of another’s crime is commanded to write it with the finger of discernment upon his own heart, lest he be found guilty in himself.

What remedy, then, remains for us amid such dangers? What remains for salvation? Nothing except that, when we see another person sinning, we immediately bend down—that is, humbly consider how cast down we are through the frailty of our condition if divine mercy does not sustain us. Let us write on the ground—that is, let us carefully weigh in our discernment whether we can say with blessed Job: “For our heart has not reproached us throughout all our life.”

Well does he who bent down write on the ground, while, standing upright, he brings forth words of mercy, because what he promised through participation in human weakness, he offers to human beings through the power of divine might as a dwelling of compassion.

“Jesus,” he says, “raising himself, said to her: ‘Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?’ She said: ‘No one, Lord.’”

No one dared to condemn the sinful woman, because each had begun to perceive in himself what he recognized as more deserving of condemnation. But since the crowd of accusers had been driven away by the presentation of the weight of justice, let us see with what gift of mercy he lifts up the accused woman. It follows:

“But Jesus said: ‘Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on do not sin.’”

Because he is merciful and compassionate, he releases past sins; because he is just and loves justice, he forbids her to sin any longer.

Yet because some might doubt whether Jesus, whom they knew to be truly human, could forgive sins, he himself deigned to show more openly what divinity is capable of. After repelling the wickedness of the tempters and removing the guilt of the sinful woman,

“Again he spoke: ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.’”

Here he clearly teaches not only by what authority he forgave the woman’s sins, but also that he himself is the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world. Human frailty could not have seen its perpetual splendor unless it had been covered by the cloud of flesh [Col. 0737B]. Through that flesh, as through a most luminous mirror, the brightness of the divine light might become known to human minds. Faith must cleanse them so that they may be made worthy of beholding so great a light.

Hence he continues: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Whoever now obeys my commands and examples will not fear the darkness of condemnation in the future, but will have the light of life, where he will never die at all.

Therefore, my brothers, let us follow Christ, the light of the world, lest we walk in darkness. The darkness to be feared concerns morals, not the eyes; and if it concerns the eyes, it concerns not the outward but the inward eyes, by which one distinguishes not white from black but what is just from what is unjust.

When our Lord Jesus Christ had said:

The Jews answered: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”

Before our Lord Jesus Christ came, he kindled and sent many prophetic lamps before him. Among these was John the Baptist, to whom the very great Light that is Christ bore witness—testimony such as he bore to no other human being. For he said: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11).

Yet this man, than whom no one born of women was greater, says concerning our Lord Jesus: “I indeed baptize you with water, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal I am not worthy to untie” (John 1). See how the lamp lowers itself before the day. The Lord himself testifies that John was a lamp. “He was,” he says, “a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for a time to rejoice in his light” (John 5).

Then the Jews answered: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 5). Let us see what they heard, and let us hear it too—but not as they did. They heard while despising; let us hear while believing. They wanted to kill Christ; we desire to live through Christ. In the meantime, let this distinction separate our ears and minds, and let us hear what the Lord answered the Jews.

Jesus answered and said to them:

“Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.”

Light reveals both other things and itself. Christ shows himself, shows the Father, and shows what was going to happen to the Jews. Therefore the Lord says—and he says truly:

“Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.”

He wanted the Father to be understood. The Son gave glory to the Father; the equal glorifies the one by whom he was sent. How much more ought a human being to glorify the one by whom he was created!

“I know where I came from and where I am going.” This one who is now speaking to you possesses what he did not abandon, and yet he came. By coming, he did not descend from there; by returning, he did not leave us. Why are you amazed? He is God. This can happen in the case of God [F. read *potest*, affirmatively], but it cannot happen in the case of a human being. The sun itself proceeds from the East to the West and abandons the East. Our Lord Jesus Christ is not in the East and then comes; he is there, he returned, and he is here.

Hear the Evangelist himself saying elsewhere—and if you can, grasp it; if you cannot, believe it: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1). He did not say, “He was in the bosom of the Father.” He was speaking here and said that he was there. And when he was going to depart from here, what did he say? “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Therefore the testimony of the light is true, whether it reveals itself or other things, because without light the light cannot be seen, and without light anything else that is not light cannot be seen. Thus light reveals itself and the things around it. So too Christ reveals himself and enlightens others—the things that are around him in charity and follow him, not with the steps of their feet but with acts of charity.

We read in the holy Scriptures that two comings of our Lord Jesus Christ were foretold by the prophets: one of mercy, which has already taken place; the other of judgment, which is to come. The first dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ is therefore medicinal, not judicial. For if he had come to judge first, he would have found no one to whom he could repay the rewards of justice. Since he saw that all were sinners and that absolutely no one was free from the death of sin, his mercy had first to be brought forward, and afterward judgment had to be exercised, because the Psalmist had sung concerning him: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100).

He did not say, “Judgment and mercy.” For if judgment came first, there would be no mercy; rather, mercy comes first, and afterward judgment.

What is the first mercy? The Creator of the human being deigned to become human: he was made what he had made, so that what he had made might not perish. What could be added to this mercy? Yet more was added: he was rejected by the human beings for whose salvation he had come into the world. He endured mockeries, scourges, spittle, the reproaches of enemies, and the most shameful death of the cross. He endured all these things because he willed to do so. He willed it in order to save the human being whom he had created.

No kind of death was more intolerable than the cross, because of its prolonged torments. Yet nothing is now more glorious than to carry the sign of the cross upon one’s forehead. Hence the Apostle, proclaiming the glory of the cross, says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

Because he came to judge no one, he accordingly answered the Jews:

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.”

He endured an unjust judgment in order to carry out a just one; but in enduring what was unjust, he acted mercifully. Finally, he was made so humble that he reached the cross. He deferred his power but made his mercy public.

How did he defer his power? Because he did not wish to descend from the cross, although he was able to rise from the tomb (Mark 15). How did he make his mercy public? Because, hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

Therefore, either because he had not come to judge the world but to save the world, he said, “I judge no one”; or, as I have mentioned, because he had said, “You judge according to the flesh,” he added, “I judge no one,” so that we might understand that Christ does not judge according to the flesh, as he was judged by human beings.

But so that you may now recognize Christ as judge as well, hear what follows:

“And even if I judge, my judgment is true.”

Behold, he also has judgment. But recognize the Savior, lest you experience the Judge. Why, then, did he say that his judgment was true?

“Because I am not alone,” he says, “but I and the Father who sent me.”

What is Christ’s being sent except his Incarnation? “Christ was sent” means the same as if you said, “Christ was incarnate.” He was sent by the Father and never departed from the Father; he was here through the Incarnation, and he is here now through divinity.

Therefore let faith cleanse our hearts, so that understanding may fill our hearts and we may understand the mystery of our salvation. It is lofty, deep, and secret. The substance of the Father and the Son is one; their divinity is one; their majesty is one. The Father did not suffer, but the Son alone.

Therefore let us understand that the Son’s being sent means the Son’s Incarnation. Do not believe that the Father was incarnate. How, then, is his judgment true except because he is the true Son of the Father? Therefore he said: “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

In another place the same one said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10): one in substance, two in persons. He said “one” because of the unity of substance; he said “are” because of the distinction of persons. Hear what he said: “I and the Father who sent me.” Distinguish the persons. Recognize that the Father is Father and that the Son is Son, lest you fall into the abyss of Sabellius. And do not say, “One thing and another thing,” but say, “One person and another person.” Not one thing in substance, but one person and another person; the Father is not greater, nor is the Son lesser, in the glory of divinity.

But believe: “We are one.” Therefore the Truth’s saying “one” frees you from Arius, while his saying “we are” frees you from Sabellius. If “one,” then they are not different; if “we are,” then he is not one person.

He had spoken of judgment when he said, “I judge no one.” Now he wishes to speak of testimony:

“In your law,” he says, “it is written.”

He said “in your law” as though he were saying: “In the law given to you by God,” just as we say “our daily bread,” which we ask God to give us.

What is written in your law?

“That the testimony of two human beings is true. I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.”

And so forth [Col. 0740A].

Do two human beings necessarily give true testimony by themselves? Did not two false witnesses give false testimony against Susanna? And when the Jews sought false testimony against Christ, the Evangelist says: “Finally two false witnesses came forward” (Matt. 26). Were they not false witnesses merely because there were two of them? What shall we say about two or three? The entire people lied against Christ. If the whole people, consisting of a great multitude of human beings, was found to give false testimony, how is it to be understood that “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand”? It is understood in this way because, through the mystery, the Trinity is commended, in which there is the perpetual stability of truth.

If you wish to have a good case, have two or three witnesses: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Finally, when Susanna, a chaste woman and faithful wife, was accused by two false witnesses, the Trinity supported her in her conscience and in secret. The Trinity raised up for her, from secrecy, one witness—Daniel—and convicted the two.

Therefore, because it is written in your law that the testimony of two human beings is true, accept our testimony, lest you experience judgment. “But I,” he says, “judge no one; I bear witness concerning myself; I defer judgment.”

Let us choose, brothers, the testimony of God, because God’s testimony is true. And since he is the witness of everything we do, he will be the judge of everything we have done. He seeks no other witness except himself, because he examines all the secrets of our hearts and asks from what source each thing proceeds. He is a witness because he does not seek another by whom to learn who you are or what kind of life you lead. He will repay each person according to his works.

Then the Jews answered the Lord, who was speaking about his Father, and said:

“Where is your father?”

They understood Christ’s Father carnally because they judged Christ’s words according to the flesh. The one who was speaking was flesh in what was visible and Word in what was hidden: a manifest human being, a hidden God.

Let us see, then, what the Lord answered them. “Where is your Father?” they said. “For we heard you say, ‘I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.’ We see only you; we do not see your father with you. How can you say that you are not alone but are with your father? Or show us that your father is with you.”

And the Lord said: “Do you see me and not see my Father?” This is what follows; he himself answered in these words. We have already offered the exposition of these words. See what he said:

“You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”

You say, then, “Where is your Father?” as though you already knew me, as though I were wholly what you see. Since you do not know me, therefore I do not show you my Father. You think I am a human being; therefore you seek a human father for me, because you judge according to the flesh.

But since, according to what you see, I am one thing, and according to what you do not see, I am another, I speak of my Father as hidden. First you must know me; then you will know my Father as well. “If you knew me, you would perhaps know my Father also.”

He who knows all things does not doubt when he says “perhaps,” but reproves. Observe how “perhaps,” which appears to be a word of doubt, is spoken as a reproach. It is a word of doubt when spoken by a human being, because a human being doubts through ignorance; but when a word of doubt is spoken by God, from whom nothing is hidden, that doubt reproves unbelief—it does not express uncertainty in the divinity.

Human beings sometimes doubt reproachfully concerning matters they know to be certain; that is, they use a word of doubt while not doubting in their hearts. For example, if you become angry with your servant and say: “Do you despise me? Consider that perhaps I am the Lord your God.” In the same way the Apostle, speaking to certain people who despised him, says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7).

By saying “I think,” he appears to doubt; but he is reproving, not doubting. Likewise, in another place, the Lord Christ, reproving the future unbelief of the human race, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18).

He therefore knows all things, through whom all things were made, and yet he reproves by means of doubt.

“If you knew me, you would perhaps know my Father also.”

He reproves unbelievers and admonishes the faithful, so that they may know that the Father and the Son have one knowledge—that insofar as they know the Son, they know the Father also.

Therefore, when the chosen disciple asked that the Father be shown to them, he answered: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). If the Son were unlike the Father, would he say to his disciples, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also”? Would he say to the Jews, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also”?

Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple. With great confidence, without fear—for he would not have suffered if he had not wished to, since he would not have been born if he had not wished to. What does it mean that Jesus spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple? The treasury is the place where treasures are stored. Jesus spoke to the Jews in the treasury, while he spoke in parables to the crowds. For the treasury was Christ, in whom all the mysteries lay hidden, to be opened at the proper time, when he himself—who had lain hidden in the letter—spoke not in proverbs but openly, explaining everything to his faithful. The treasuries also adjoined the temple, because Christ himself is the temple, of which he said, “Destroy this temple” (John II). All the mysteries of the ancient law adhered to him [Col. 0741D] and all looked toward him, until he came to open the individual treasuries of the mysteries, opening the understanding of his faithful so that they might understand what had lain hidden, as the Evangelist says: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV).

Finally, what follows? “No one seized him, because his hour had not yet come”—that is, the hour of his appointed purpose, the hour of his will. For he who was born by his will suffered by his will. Therefore, if he had not wished to suffer, he would not have suffered; that blood would not have been shed, and the world would not have been redeemed. Let us therefore give thanks both for the power of his divinity and for the compassion of his weakness, for the hidden suffering which the Jews did not know. Hence it was said to them a little earlier, “You know neither me nor [Col. 0742A] my Father”; and for the flesh he assumed, which the Jews did know, and whose homeland they knew, hence he said to them elsewhere, “You know both me and where I am from” (John VII). Let us recognize both in Christ: the manner in which he is equal to the Father, and the manner in which the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word, the other flesh; the one is God, the other man—but there is one Christ, God and man. Let us now hear what Christ said concerning his passion.

“I am going away,” he said, “and you will seek me.” Not with desire, but with hatred. For after he had withdrawn from human sight, both those who hated him and those who loved him sought him: the former by persecuting him, the latter by desiring to possess him. It is good to seek Christ’s soul, but consider how the disciples sought it; and it is evil to seek Christ’s soul, but consider how the Jews sought it. [Col. 0742B] The former sought it in order to possess it; the latter in order to destroy it. Finally, because they sought him in this way, they were to die with an evil and perverse heart, as he then added: “You will seek me; and lest you suppose that you seek me rightly: You will die in your sin.”

This is to seek Christ wrongly: to die in one’s sin. The one who remains in sin until death will die in his sin. He does not seek Christ who does not seek the salvation of his soul through repentance. To him the prophet cries: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isaiah LV). Whoever does not seek the merciful one while there is time will find him angry.

He said to the Jews, “You will die in your sin,” because he knew beforehand that they would remain in their sin. He used the singular, “in [Col. 0742C] sin,” and the plural, “your” (John XIII), because he knew that all those to whom he was speaking had one will and an equal wickedness: to destroy the one who had come to save them. Elsewhere, however, he said to his disciples:

“Where I am going, you cannot come now.” He did not take away their hope, but foretold a delay. When the Lord said this to his disciples, they could not then come where he was going, but afterward they were to come. Those others, however, would never come there, to whom he foretold, “You will die in your sin.”

After hearing these words, those who habitually thought in carnal terms, judged according to the flesh, and heard and understood everything carnally, said: “Will he perhaps kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot [Col. 0742D] come’?” Foolish words, altogether full of ignorance. For if he were to kill himself, why could they not go where he had gone? Were they not themselves going to die? What, then, does “Will he perhaps kill himself, since he said, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” mean? If he were speaking of a human death, what human being does not die? Therefore, when he said, “Where I am going,” he did not mean the place to which one goes in death, but the place to which he himself was going after death.

Since they did not understand these things, the Lord answered them, for they savored the things of earth. What did he say?

“He was saying to them, ‘You are from below.’” You savor earthly things because, like the serpent, you eat earth. What does “You eat earth” mean? You feed on earthly things, delight in earthly things, [Col. 0743A] gape after earthly things; you do not have your heart above. “You are from below.”

“I am from above. You are from this world; I am not of this world.” How, then, was he not of this world, through whom the world was made, who is always where he is, while all are of the world [sic]? But the world came first, and then man; Christ was before the world, and before Christ there was nothing, because “in the beginning was the Word,” and all things were made through him. Thus he was from above. From what above? Christ was from the Father himself. Nothing is above him, because he begot the Word, equal to himself, coeternal with himself, his only-begotten, outside time, through whom he established time. Therefore Christ is before all creatures and before all times, because he was begotten from the Father, coeternal with the Father. “I am from above; [Col. 0743B] you are from this world; I am not of this world.”

“I therefore told you that you will die in your sins.” He has explained to us, brothers, what he meant by “You are of this world.” He said, “You are of this world,” because they were sinners, because they were unrighteous, because they were unbelieving, because they savored earthly things. Were the apostles and the saints of God not of this world? They were, indeed, because they were born from Adam. But the Truth itself says of them: “I chose you from the world” (John XV)—that is, from the carnal manner of life which, in this passage, seems to be signified by the name “world.”

Those who were of the world were therefore made not of the world and began to belong to him through whom the world was made. But those to whom it was said, [Col. 0743C] “You will die in your sins,” remained in the world. Let no one say, “I am not of this world.” Whoever you are, O human being, you are of this world. But the one who made the world has come to you and delivered you from this world. If the world delights you, you always wish to remain unclean. But if this world no longer delights you, then you will be clean, and you will not hear what the Jews heard: “You will die in your sins.” Whoever sins more is more deeply in the world and more unclean; and the more a person cleanses himself from sin, the more he shows that he is not of the world.

The Jews rightly heard, “You will die in your sins,” because you cannot possibly be without sin, since you were born with sin. Nevertheless, if you believe in me, he says, although you were born with sin, you will not die in your sin. The whole misery, [Col. 0743D] therefore, consisted not in having sin, but in dying in sins. This is what every Christian ought to flee.

For this reason one hastens to baptism. For this reason, if someone is endangered by illness or by some other circumstance, he desires that help be brought to him. For this reason, too, when a little child rises from its mother’s arms, it is carried to the Church in pious hands, lest it depart this life without baptism and die in the sin in which it was born.

He added, saying: “If you do not believe, you will die in your sins.” Hope was restored to the despairing; an awakening came to sleeping hearts. They awoke, and many believed, as the continuation of the Gospel itself testifies when it says:

“While he was speaking these things, many believed in him.”

Among this people to whom the Lord was [Col. 0744A] speaking, therefore, there were those who would die in their sin, and those who would believe in the one who was speaking and be freed from every sin. Yet consider carefully what the Lord Christ said: “If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sin.”

What does “If you do not believe that I am” mean? By adding nothing, he expressed much. He said, “I am,” and did not add what he was: whether the Christ, or the Son of God, or the one whom the prophets had foretold, or the Savior of the world, or something else that is written about him in the Scriptures.

Great is what he said in the words “I am,” because God had said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exodus III). Here too, “Unless you believe that I am,” he used the same verb of eternal being before the Jewish people that he had then used with Moses through the angel in the bush of flame and fire, when he was about to send him to free [Col. 0744B] his people.

What else does “I am” mean here but this: “I am that very one who then came in the angel to send Moses, my servant, to free my people; I am now the very one who has come in person, incarnate and made man, to free [Col. 0744B] the human beings whom I created and to save those who had been lost”?

Whatever can in any way be changed, whether for the better or for the worse, in a certain sense dies with respect to what it previously was, when it begins to be something else or to be otherwise than it was. God alone is always the same: unchangeable truth, unchangeable goodness, unchangeable eternity, unchangeable nature, unchangeable substance. Whatever can be said of him is always the same as what was and what will be. Nothing seems more plainly to be understood in this [Col. 0744C] word spoken by the Lord, “I am,” than “I am God.”

“You will die in your sin.” But since they always savored earthly things, always heard according to the flesh, and answered in the same way, what did they say to him?

“Who are you?” For when you said, “Unless you believe that I am,” you did not add who you were. “Who are you, that we should believe?”

And he replied:

“The Beginning.” Behold what he is: to be the Beginning cannot be changed. The Beginning remains in itself and renews all things. He is the Beginning of whom it is said: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail.”

“The Beginning,” he said, “I who also speak to you.” Believe me to be the Beginning, lest you die in your sins. For, as though in their question “Who are you?” they had said [Col. 0744D] nothing other than “What are we to believe you to be?”, he answered: “Believe me to be the Beginning,” and added, “I who also speak to you”—that is, I who, for your sake, have become humble and descended to these words.

For if the Beginning had remained with the Father as he is, without taking the form of a servant and speaking as a human being to human beings, how could they have believed in him, since weak hearts could not see the intelligible Word without a voice, as they see sensible things? Therefore, he says, believe me to be the Beginning, because, so that you may believe, I not only am, but also speak to you.

These are the words of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Jews. He moderated his speech in such a way that the blind did not see, while the faithful opened their eyes. The Jews were therefore saying, “Who are you?” because the Lord had said above, “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your [Col. 0745A] sins.”

They asked, “Who are you?” as though seeking to know in whom they ought to believe, lest they die in their sin. He answered those who asked, “Who are you?” and said: “The Beginning, I who also speak to you” (Psalm CIII).

Why does the Lord Jesus call himself the Beginning? He is the Beginning because all things were made through him, as the Psalmist says: “You made all things in wisdom.” If, then, God made all things in Wisdom—that is, in his Son, coeternal and of one substance with him—the Son is certainly the Beginning of all things.

The Father is rightly called the Beginning, and the Son the Beginning; yet there are not two beginnings, just as the Father is God and the Son is God, yet there are not two gods, but one God. Thus the Father is the Beginning and the Son is the Beginning, yet there are not two beginnings; rather, we must confess one Beginning.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is also the Beginning. Yet there are not three [Col. 0745B] beginnings—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one Beginning; just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet there are not three gods, but one God. The Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Holy Spirit is almighty; yet there are not three almighty beings, but one Almighty.

For the Father, in relation to himself, is God; in relation to the Son, he is Father. The Son, in relation to himself, is God; in relation to the Father, he is Son. The Holy Spirit, in relation to himself, is God; in relation to the Father and the Son, he is the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, of one substance, power, and majesty with the Father and the Son.

Let us therefore hear what the Beginning says to us.

[Col. 0745C] “I have many things,” he said, “to say and judge concerning you.” Yet elsewhere he said, “I judge no one” (John VIII), indicating that his present coming was for the purpose of saving, not judging, because he had come to save the world, not to judge the world. But when he now says, “I have many things to say and judge concerning you,” he is speaking of the future judgment. For he ascended so that he might come to judge the living and the dead. No one will judge more justly than the one who was judged unjustly. “I have many things,” he says, “to say and judge concerning you.”

“But the one who sent me is truthful.” Observe how the equal Son gives glory to the Father. He provides us with an example: to give glory to God, to seek God’s glory rather than our own. It is as though he were saying: “O faithful human being, if I, the Son of the Father, equal to the Father, of one substance [Col. 0745D] with the Father, coeternal with the Father, give glory to the one from whom I am, how can you be proud before the one whose servant you are?”

“I have many things,” he says, “to say and judge concerning you; but the one who sent me is truthful.” He means, as it were: “I speak the truth because I am the Son of the truthful one, and I am the Truth.” The Father is Truth, and the Son is Truth. For the Lord himself says openly: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Therefore, if the Son is Truth, what is the Father except what he says—Truth? “The one who sent me is truthful.” The Son is Truth; the Father is truthful, but not by participating in truth. The Son is Truth, but from the Father, because the Son is from the Father, not from himself. Therefore he says elsewhere: “I did not come from myself” (John VIII)—that is, “I am not from myself.”

The Father is truthful, not by participating in truth, but by begetting Truth, because the Father begot the Son, who said of himself: “I am the way and the truth.” When the Lord Jesus had said, “The one who sent me is truthful,” they did not understand that he was speaking to them of the Father. They did not yet have the eyes of their hearts opened so that they could understand the equality of the truthful Father and the Truth [Col. 0746A] who is the Son.

He was saying to them:

“When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing from myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak.”

What does this mean? He seems to have said nothing other than that they would know who he was after his passion. Without doubt, therefore, he saw among them some whom he himself knew, whom he himself, together with all his saints, had chosen in foreknowledge before the foundation of the world, and who would believe after his passion.

These are the people whom we continually commend and set before others for imitation with earnest exhortation. After [Col. 0746B] the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, following the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, miracles were performed in the name of the one whom the Jews had persecuted as though he were dead and had despised. They were cut to the heart; those who had killed him in their fury were changed and believed; and the blood which they had shed in their rage they drank in faith—those three thousand and those five thousand Jews (Acts II and IV).

This is what he meant when he said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.” It was as though he were saying: “I postpone your knowledge so that I may complete my passion. In due course you will know who I am.” He did not mean that all those who were listening would then believe, that is, after the Lord’s passion. For a little earlier he had said: “While he was speaking these things, many believed in him,” and the Son of Man had not yet [Col. 0746C] been lifted up.

By “lifting up” he means the lifting up of the passion, not of glorification; of the cross, not of heaven. He was lifted up there, when he hung upon the wood. But that lifting up was a humiliation. For then he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, “for which reason God exalted him” (Philippians II).

There was one lifting up when he was raised upon the cross, and another when he ascended into heaven: the former was a humiliation, the latter a glorification. Yet the lifting up of the cross had to be accomplished through the hands of those who would afterward believe, to whom he says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John VIII).

Why was this said? So that no one would despair, however conscious he might be of evil in himself, when he saw that forgiveness was granted to [Col. 0746D] those who had killed Christ the Lord. He added: “Then you will know that I am.”

What does “I am” mean except that he is of one substance with the Father, just as we said above that he spoke to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus III), and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’”?

The Lord uses a word of substance concerning himself, so that it may be understood that the substance is eternal and that the substance of the Father and the Son is one. Yet, lest he himself be understood to be the Father, he immediately added: “And I do nothing from myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak.”

What does he mean by “I do nothing from myself”? It means, “I am not from myself.” But what he added—“As the Father taught me, so I speak”—has a very profound meaning. The heart must be cleansed, “for wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” ([Col. 0747A] Wisdom I), so that what he said, “As the Father taught me, so I speak,” may be understood correctly.

It is not to be understood as though a human father spoke to a human son, but in a more exalted and sacred way. The Evangelist’s words must be understood in one way—“In the beginning was the Word”—and in another way—“The Word became flesh.” We must think in one way about Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to God the Father, and in another way about his humanity, in which he is like us.

The Lord’s saying, “I and the Father are one” (John X), must not be understood in the same way as his saying, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV). Therefore, understand spiritually and incorporeally that the Father spoke the Son, because the Father incorporeally begot the Son.

He did not teach him as though he had begotten one who was ignorant; rather, “teaching” him means [Col. 0747B] begetting him knowing. “The Father taught me” means “The Father begot me knowing.” For if—as few understand—the nature of truth is simple, so that for the Son to be is the same as for him to know, then he received knowledge from the one from whom he received being. He did not first receive being from him and afterward knowledge; rather, just as the Father gave him being by begetting him, so he gave him knowledge. For, as has been said, in a simple nature being and knowing are not two different things, but one and the same.

He said these things to the Jews and added:

“And the one who sent me is with me.” He had already said this before, but he repeatedly emphasizes a great mystery: “He sent me, and he is with me.” If he is with you, O Lord, then one was not sent by another as though they were separate; both came. Yet although both are [Col. 0747C] together, one was sent and the other sent, because sending is incarnation, and the incarnation belongs to the Son alone, not to the Father.

The Father therefore sent the Son, but did not depart from the Son. “Therefore,” he says, “the one who sent me has not left me alone.” By whose authority, as by a father’s authority, I became incarnate; he is with me and has not abandoned me. Why has he not abandoned me?

“He has not left me alone,” he says, “because I always do what pleases him.” This is the equality that is always present—not from some beginning and thereafter, but without beginning and without end. For God’s generation has no beginning in time, because time itself was made through the Only-Begotten.

While he was speaking these things, many believed in him. The sound of them had not yet gone out into all the earth (Psalm XVIII); it had not yet been preached to everyone; it had not yet been [Col. 0747D] said, “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew XXVIII).

Therefore the Lord said to the Jews who had believed in him:

“If you remain in my word.” You will remain because you have been initiated, because you have begun to be there. If you remain in the faith which began to exist in you when you believed, where will you arrive? Consider what kind of beginning leads to what end. Have you loved the foundation? Look toward the summit, and from this humility seek another height.

Faith has humility; knowledge, immortality, and eternity do not have humility, but exaltation and elevation. They have no falling away, but eternal stability; no defeat by the enemy, and no fear of failing. It is great that one begins with faith, but greater still is the destination [Col. 0748A] reached through faith. Hear, then, where it leads, and see how great faith is.

“Therefore you also,” he says, “if you remain in my word in which you have believed,

“you will truly be my disciples.”

He also added:

“And you will know the truth.” Whoever knows the truth knows God, because God is truth, as the Lord himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Let us therefore believe so that we may know the truth, because no one can attain to knowledge of the truth without faith. What is it that we will know? That which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians II).

For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see. Truth is seeing what you have believed.

What is it that we are promised we will see? [Col. 0748B] In another place the Lord tells us what it is that we will see: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). This is the promise; this is the reward of faith, which works through love; this is the satisfaction for which the Psalmist prayed, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI).

O Lord, make us worthy to love you and not love the world, so that we may be able to reach that freedom which is attained through knowledge of the truth. Concerning this you added, saying:

“And the truth will set you free.” What does “set you free” mean? It means “will make you free.”

Finally, the carnal Jews, judging according to the flesh—not those who believed, but those in the crowd who did not believe—thought that an insult had been directed against them, because he said to them, “The truth will set you free.” [Col. 0748C] They were indignant, as though he had indicated that they were slaves. And in truth they were slaves.

He will explain to them what slavery is and what the future freedom is which he promises. For to say, “The truth will set you free,” means nothing other than “The truth will make you free,” just as “it saves” means nothing other than “it makes safe.”

We have heard what the free Truth said; let us hear what proud falsehood answers.

The Jews therefore said: “We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

The Lord had not said, “You will be free,” but “The truth will set you free.” Yet they understood nothing in this statement except carnal freedom. They exalted themselves because they were Abraham’s offspring and said: “We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

[Col. 0748D] O empty pride, O false boasting! How can you truthfully say, “We have never been slaves to anyone” (Genesis XXXVII)? Was Joseph not sold? Were the holy prophets not led into captivity? Finally, was this not the very people who made bricks in Egypt (Exodus I) and served under hard labor—not at least in silver and gold, but in mud?

If you have never served anyone, O ungrateful people, what does it mean that God continually reminds you how he freed you from the house of slavery? Or perhaps your fathers served, while you who are speaking have never served anyone? How, then, do you pay tribute to the Romans?

It was also from this circumstance that you proposed a trap to the Truth, as though seeking to ensnare him, when you said: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” If he had said, “It is lawful,” you would have held him as though he were willing to [Col. 0749A] oppress the freedom of Abraham’s offspring. But if he had said, “It is not lawful,” you would have accused him before the rulers of the earth of forbidding tribute to be paid to kings.

Then, when the coin was produced, you were defeated, and you yourselves were compelled to answer your own trap. For there you were told: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

When you yourselves had answered that the coin bore Caesar’s image, God likewise seeks his image in the human being. God does not seek something foreign from the human being, but what he himself formed in the human being. For this reason God became man: to restore in man what he had formed in man.

Let us therefore hear what the Lord answered the Jews who were lying and swelling with vain claims of freedom.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a [Col. 0749B] slave of sin.”

Who would not tremble at these words? If every human being is a sinner, every human being is a slave of sin. But let us listen more attentively to how we may be freed from this slavery. He strikes terror, but applies medicine, for the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you.”

What is “amen, amen” except “truly, truly I say to you”? Neither the Greek interpreter nor the Latin one dared to transfer this word into another language, so that it might retain the honor of a veiled, secret testimony to the truth in Christ.

The Truth says: “Truly, truly I say to you.” He doubles and repeats the word of truth in order to rouse those who were sleeping and make those who heard attentive, lest the one who said, “Amen, amen, I say to you,” be despised: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

O wretched slavery—to serve sin, to serve the devil, who [Col. 0749C] is the author of sin! Human beings often flee evil masters so as not to serve wicked men, yet they do not flee sin, whose slaves they are. How much happier it would be to flee sin and serve a human being with a free conscience!

Moreover, a human slave, sometimes exhausted by his master’s harsh commands, finds rest by fleeing. But wherever the slave of sin flees, he drags sin along with him. Wherever he flees, he cannot flee from himself. An evil conscience has nowhere to go: it follows itself; indeed, it does not depart from itself, because the sin it committed is within.

He committed sin in order to seize some bodily pleasure. The pleasure passes, but the sin remains. What delighted him goes away; what pricks him remains. Wretched slavery!

Sometimes people flee wicked masters, wishing to be rid of their masters, while they do not wish to be rid of [Col. 0749D] their sins. How much happier would a person be if he abandoned sin, fled to Christ, and called upon God the liberator!

The Lord alone frees from this slavery to sin, because he did not have that slavery. He alone came into the world without sin. He alone can free from sin who came without sin and became a sacrifice for sin.

Since everyone who commits sin is therefore a slave of sin, hear what hope of freedom we have:

“But a slave,” he says, “does not remain in the house forever.”

The Church is the house; the sinner is the slave. Let no one remain in sin, lest he be a slave of sin. In order to be able to remain in the house—that is, in the Church—let him remain in the body of his head, so that he may be a son, not a slave.

It is one thing to sin and another to remain in sin. Whoever remains in sin is a slave of sin; whoever flees from [Col. 0750A] sin will be a slave of righteousness. He struck terror into us so that we would not love sin; he gave us hope so that we would not despair of release from sin.

“Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is a slave of sin. But a slave does not remain in the house forever.”

What hope, then, is there for us, who are not without sin? Hear your hope:

“The Son remains forever.”

“If therefore the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.”

This is our hope, brothers: that we may be freed by the Free One, and that in freeing us he may make us his servants. We were slaves of desire; once freed, we become servants of love.

The first freedom is not to remain in sin but to serve righteousness, as the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness; but now you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Romans VI).

[Col. 0750B] Perfect freedom, however, is to serve God Christ: to love the one who truly freed us, who is the true Son of God and Lord in the form of a servant—not a servant, but Lord in the form of a servant.

That form of the flesh was indeed servile; but although he bore the likeness of sinful flesh, it was not sinful. He promised freedom to those who believed in him.

The Jews, however, as though proud of their own freedom, disdained to become free, although they were slaves of sin. They claimed to be free because they were Abraham’s offspring. What, then, did the Lord answer them? Let us hear.

“I know,” he said, “that you are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me.”

I acknowledge the origin of the flesh, not the faith of the heart. You are Abraham’s children, but according to the flesh. Therefore, he says, you seek to kill me.

[Col. 0750C] “For my word has no place in you.” That is, it is not received by you. If my word were received by you, it would surely receive you. What does “it has no place in you” mean? It means that it does not find a place in your heart, because your heart does not receive it.

You have certainly heard the Lord saying, “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Hear what he says next:

“I speak what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have seen with your father.”

What do they do? What he had said to them: “You seek to kill me.” They had never seen this in Abraham.

He says: “I speak what I have seen with my Father.” I saw the truth, and I speak the truth, because I am the Truth. If the Lord speaks the truth because he is the Father’s Truth, which he saw with the Father, then he says that he saw himself, because he is the Father’s Truth, [Col. 0750D] which he saw with the Father.

For he is the Word, the one who “was the Word with God.” Where, then, did they see the evil they were doing—the evil which the Lord reproves and rebukes? When we hear more clearly in what follows who their father is, then we will understand what sort of things they saw with such a father.

For as yet he does not name their father. A little earlier he mentioned Abraham, but with reference to the origin of the flesh, not to a likeness of life. There was another father of theirs, who had neither begotten them nor created them as human beings, yet they were his children insofar as they were evil, not insofar as they were human; they were his children in imitation, not in creation.

[Col. 0751A] They answered and said to him: “Our father is Abraham.”

It was as though they were saying: “What will you say against Abraham? If you can do anything, dare to criticize Abraham.” It was not that the Lord did not dare to criticize Abraham; rather, Abraham was such a man that he was not to be criticized by the Lord, but rather praised by him.

Yet they seemed to be testing him, so that if he said anything evil about Abraham, they would have an opportunity to do what they were contemplating. “Our father is Abraham,” they said.

Let us hear how the Lord answered them, praising Abraham while condemning them.

Jesus said to them: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.”

[Col. 0751B] There he is praised; here they are condemned. Abraham was not a murderer.

I do not say, he says, “I am the Lord of Abraham”—although if I said this, I would speak the truth. For elsewhere he said, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII), and then they wanted to stone him.

He did not say this. But meanwhile, what you see and behold, what you suppose to be all that I am: I am a man. Why do you wish to kill a man who tells you what he heard from God, unless you are not Abraham’s children?

And yet above he said: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” He did not deny their origin, but he condemned their deeds. Their flesh was from Abraham, but their life was not.

Therefore Christians have become Abraham’s offspring by the grace of God. They were not made co-heirs from Abraham’s flesh; God disinherited those people and adopted these. They are the ones of whom [Col. 0751C] John the Baptist said elsewhere: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew III).

Those are Abraham’s children who imitate Abraham’s faith. Therefore the Lord added: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham.” Prove your nobility by your deeds, not by your words.

“But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.”

“Do the works of your father.”

He still does not say who this father of theirs is. What did they answer now? They began, in some way, to understand that the Lord was not speaking about physical generation but about the conduct of life.

Since it is the custom of the Scriptures they were reading to call prostitution by a spiritual name, when the soul, as though prostituted, submits itself to many false gods, [Col. 0751D] they answered accordingly.

They therefore said to him: “We were not born of prostitution; we have one Father, God.”

Abraham had now become worthless in their eyes. They had rejected him in the way they wished to reject him with truthful speech, since Abraham was such a man whose deeds they did not imitate, although they boasted of belonging to his race.

They changed their answer, I think, saying among themselves: “Whenever we mention Abraham, he will say to us, ‘Why do you not imitate the one whose lineage you boast of?’ We cannot imitate such a holy, just, and innocent man. Let us call God our father; let us see what he will say to us.”

[Col. 0752A] Did falsehood find something to say while Truth could not find an answer? Let us hear what they said; let us hear what they heard.

“We have one Father,” they said, “God.”

Jesus therefore said to them: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me, for I proceeded from God and came; nor did I come from myself, but he sent me.”

You call God your Father; recognize at least your brother. Here he touched upon what he often says: “I did not come from myself, but he sent me; I proceeded from God and came.”

Christ’s mission, therefore, is his incarnation. But the Word’s procession from God the Father is an eternal procession, not having time as its condition, and through it time itself was made. He proceeded from him as God, as equal, as the only Son. The Father’s Word came to us because “the Word became flesh” in order to dwell in us. His coming is his humanity; his dwelling is his divinity.

[Col. 0752B] “Why,” he says, “do you not recognize my speech? Because you cannot understand my word.” They were therefore unable to understand because they were unable to hear. But why were they unable to hear, unless because they were unwilling to be corrected by believing? And this—from what cause?

“You are from your father the devil.” How long will you keep mentioning a father? How long will you keep changing fathers—now Abraham, now God? Hear from the Son of God whose children you are: “You are from your father the devil.” God, the Creator of all creatures, created the human being; how then does he say, “You are from your father the devil”? Whatever has been created by God is good; and every human being, insofar as he is God’s creature, is good. But insofar as he submits himself through free will to the devil, he is from the devil as father. Human nature is good, but it has been corrupted by an evil will; [Col. 0752C] and from this corruption he is from the devil as father. What God made cannot be evil, unless the human being himself is evil to himself.

For this reason the Jews are called children of the devil—not by being born, but by imitation. It is, in fact, the custom of Holy Scripture often to call people “children” on the basis of imitation or similarity in their deeds. Thus the prophet says to the Jews: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.” The Amorites were a certain people from whom the Jews did not derive their origin. The Hittites likewise had a people entirely foreign to the stock of the Jews. But because the Amorites and Hittites were impious, while the Jews imitated their impieties, they had found parents—not those from whom they were born, but those whose customs they followed and whose condemnation they shared.

[Col. 0752D]

But perhaps you ask where the devil himself came from. From the same source as the others, certainly. The angels remained steadfast in their obedience; that one, by disobeying and becoming proud, fell as an angel and became the devil. But now hear what the Lord says: “You are from your father the devil.”

“And you wish to do the desires of your father.” You seek to kill me, a man who tells you the truth. He envied the human being and killed the human being—for he is the devil. When the devil envied the human being, he clothed himself in the serpent, spoke to the woman, and through the woman poisoned the man. They died by listening to the devil (Genesis 3), whom they would not have listened to if they had wished to listen to God. For the human being was placed between God, who had created him, and the serpent, who was deceiving him. Whom ought he to obey? The Creator, not the deceiver.

Therefore he was a murderer from the beginning. Consider, brothers, the nature of murder. The devil is called a murderer, though he was not armed with a sword or girded with iron. He came to the human being, sowed an evil word, and killed him. Do not therefore think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to do evil. If you persuade your brother to do evil, you kill him. Hear the Psalmist: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56). Therefore you wish to do the desires of your father: this is why you rage against the flesh, because you cannot rage against the mind.

[Col. 0753A] “He was a murderer from the beginning.” Certainly, in the first human being: in him he was a murderer. From what point could murder have occurred? From the point at which the human being was made; for the human being could not have been killed unless the human being had first been made. He was therefore a murderer from the beginning. And from where was he a murderer?

[Col. 0753B] “And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.” Not in the way that truth is in Christ, so that Christ himself is the truth. If he had stood in the truth, he would have stood in Christ. But he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.

“When he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar, and its father.” What does this mean? You have heard the words of the Gospel; you received them attentively. Behold, I repeat them, so that you may recognize what you must understand. The Lord was speaking to him about the devil—things that deserved to be said by the Lord about the devil. “He was a murderer from the beginning”: this is true, for he killed the first human being. “And he did not stand in the truth,” because he fell away from the truth. When he speaks a lie, the devil himself speaks from what is his own. The devil himself speaks a lie from what is his own, [Col. 0753C] because he is a liar and its father.

The devil was a liar from himself, and himself generated his lie. He had first heard the lie from no one. Just as God the Father begot the Son, the truth, so the devil begot, as it were, the lie as his son. He begot the lie because he did not stand in the truth. For everyone who remains in God stands in the truth, because God is truth. But whoever withdraws from God will be a liar, as the Psalmist says: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115). To the extent that a human being withdraws from God, to that extent he will be a liar, insofar as he has turned away from the truth; and for this reason he will be a sinner. For every sin is not truth but a lie, because, by withdrawing from God, it does not possess the truth.

The devil, however, was created good, but became evil through himself, by turning away from the highest good. Therefore he spoke the lie from what was his own, because he found within himself the source of his becoming a liar. The human being, deceived by the devil, was made a liar by the devil, and therefore became the devil’s child not by nature but by imitation.

[Col. 0753D]

Let us therefore withdraw from the father of lies and run to the Father of truth. Let us embrace the truth, so that we may receive true freedom. The Jews had seen in their father what they were saying. What was it, except a lie? The Lord, however, had seen in his Father what he was saying. What was it, except himself? What was it, except the eternal Word of the Father, co-eternal with the Father? Therefore he added:

“I speak the truth to you, and you do not believe me.” For a liar speaks a lie, but the truth produces truth. The devil is a liar, whereas Christ is the truth and the defender of truth, because from the mouth of truth nothing other than truth can proceed. It follows, then:

[Col. 0754A]

“Which of you will convict me of sin?” Just as I convict you and your father of sin and falsehood. Behold the gentleness of Christ. He had come to release people from sins, and he said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” He does not disdain to show by reason that he is not a sinner—the one who, by the power of his divinity, was able to justify sinners. He asks them why they are unwilling to believe the truth, saying:

“If I have spoken the truth to you, why do you not believe me?” Unless it is because you are children of the devil and not of truth. Children of the devil not by nature but by imitation. And he gives the reason why they do not believe the truth when he says: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.”

[Col. 0754B] Again, do not consider nature, but vice. Thus they are from God, and they are not from God: from God by nature, not from God by vice.
