The good nature that is from God sinned by the will, believing what the devil persuaded it to believe, and was corrupted. Therefore it should seek a physician, because it is not healthy. Let nature be acknowledged, so that the Creator may be praised; let vice be acknowledged, so that the physician may be summoned.

Terrible is what follows:

“Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.” If the one who is from God hears God’s words, and whoever is not from him cannot hear his words, let each one of you ask himself whether he has received God’s words in the ear of his heart and understand from whom he is.

[Col. 0754C]

Truth commands us to desire the heavenly homeland, to crush the desires of the flesh, to turn away from the glory of the world, not to seize what belongs to another, and to give away what is one’s own. Let each one of you therefore weigh within himself whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart, and recognize that he is now from God. The Jews then said:

“Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Having received such an insult, let us hear what the Lord answered.

“I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.” Since “Samaritan” means “guardian,” and he is truly a guardian, of whom the Psalmist says, “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Psalm 126), and since through Isaiah he says, “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21), the Lord did not wish to answer, “I am not a Samaritan,” but rather, “I do not have a demon.”

[Col. 0754D]

For two things had been brought against him: he denied one and, by remaining silent, assented to the other. He had come as the guardian of the human race; and if he had said that he was not a Samaritan, he would have denied that he was a guardian. But he remained silent about what he recognized and patiently rejected what he heard falsely said, declaring: “I do not have a demon.”

Here the Lord offered us in himself an example of patience. If he had wished to answer the Jews, “You have a demon,” he would have spoken the truth, since unless they were filled with a demon they could not speak so perversely about God. But after receiving an insult, the truth did not wish to say even what was true, lest he seem not to have spoken the truth but, having been provoked, to have returned an insult.

[Col. 0755A]

What does this teach us, except that when we receive insults from our neighbors on the basis of falsehood, we should remain silent even about their true faults, lest the ministry of rightful correction be turned into weapons of rage? But he still teaches us by his example what we should do in such circumstances, when he adds:

“But I do not seek my glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.” We certainly know what is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Yet behold, the same Son, while receiving insults, does not seek his own glory. He reserves unlawful insults for the Father’s judgment, thereby showing us how patient we ought to be, while even the one who judges does not yet wish to avenge himself.

When the perversity of the wicked increases, preaching should not merely remain unbroken; it should also increase. He teaches us this by his example: after being called demon-possessed, he bestowed the benefits of his preaching still more abundantly, saying:

[Col. 0755B]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.” But just as it is necessary for the good to become better even through insults, so the reprobate always become worse through a benefit. For after receiving his preaching they say again:

“Now we know that you have a demon.” Since they had clung to eternal death, they did not see the very death to which they clung. While they looked only at the death of the flesh, they were blinded to the word of truth, saying:

[Col. 0755C]

“Abraham is dead, and the prophets; and you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death forever’?” Thus they place Abraham and the prophets before the truth itself, as though venerating them. But the reason is plainly shown to us: those who do not know God also falsely venerate God’s servants.

“You,” he says, “say, ‘You have a demon’; I call you to life. Keep my word, and you will not die.” They heard the words, “He will never see death,” concerning the one who kept his word, and they became angry because they were already dead with the death that had to be avoided. For they could not avoid the death by which Abraham and the prophets died—that is, the death of the flesh. Abraham was living in the Spirit; therefore the truth itself says of him elsewhere: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew 22).

[Col. 0755D]

What does he mean by “will never see death”? He means the death of condemnation with the devil and his angels. For this death of the body is, for the saints, a passage to a better life, but for the wicked, a passage to everlasting punishments. It is this that the truth wished to designate here by the name of death. But by this death, which the Lord wishes us to understand, neither Abraham died nor did the prophets die. They died, and they live; these were living, and they were dead.

“Whom do you make yourself,” they say, “that you say, ‘He will never see death forever who keeps my word,’ when you know that Abraham died and the prophets died?”

Jesus answered: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me.” He said this because of what they had asked: “Whom do you make yourself?” For he refers his glory to the Father, from whom he has his being as God. The Lord Jesus Christ calls him his Father—the one they called their Lord but did not know. For if they had known him, they would have received his Son.

[Col. 0756A] “But I,” he says, “know him.” To those judging according to the flesh he could for this reason also appear arrogant, because he said, “I know him.” But see what follows:

“If I say, ‘I do not know him,’ I will be like you, a liar.” Arrogance, then, is not avoided by abandoning the truth.

“But I do know him, and I keep his word.” He was speaking the word of the Father as the Son, and he himself was the Word of the Father speaking to human beings. It should be noted that the Lord saw them resisting him in open opposition, yet he did not cease to preach to them in repeated speech, saying:

[Col. 0756B] “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.” Abraham saw the Lord’s day when he received three angels as guests, in a representation of the supreme Trinity (Genesis 18). Having welcomed them, he spoke to the three as to one, because although there is a plurality of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in its nature.

But the fleshly minds of the hearers do not lift their eyes above the flesh. They consider only the age of his flesh, saying:

“You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Our gracious Redeemer draws them away from contemplation of his flesh and leads them to contemplation of his divinity, saying:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.” “Before” belongs to past time; “I am” to the present.

[Col. 0756C]

And because divinity has neither past nor future time but possesses eternal being, he did not say, “Before Abraham, I was,” but, “Before Abraham, I am.”

Hence it is also said to Moses, “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3). Before or after, Abraham had a being that could approach by the manifestation of his presence and depart through the course of life. The truth, however, possesses eternal being, because nothing begins for it in an earlier time and nothing ends in a later one.

But since the minds of unbelievers were unable to endure these words of eternity, they ran for stones and sought to overwhelm the one they could not understand. What the Lord did in the face of the rage of those throwing stones is shown when the text immediately continues:

[Col. 0756D] “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” It is very remarkable, dearest brothers, that the Lord avoided his persecutors by hiding himself, since, if he had wished to exercise the power of his divinity, he could have bound them in their own blows by a silent movement of his will or overwhelmed them with the punishment of sudden death.

But because he had come to suffer, he did not wish to exercise judgment. Certainly, at the very time of his Passion, he both demonstrated as much as he could and nevertheless endured what he had come to endure. For when he said to his persecutors, who were seeking him, “I am” (John 18), he struck down their pride by this one phrase and laid them all prostrate on the ground.

Therefore, if at this point he could have escaped the hands of those throwing stones without hiding himself, why did he hide himself? Because, as a human being among human beings and as our Redeemer, having been made so, he speaks one thing to us by word and another by example. What does he say to us by this example, except that even when we are able to resist, we should humbly avoid the anger of the proud?

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0757A]

After the Lord had gone out from the temple of the Jews, let us hear what he did among the Gentile people—indeed, among the whole human race. The Evangelist continues and says:

“Passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.” The things our Lord Jesus Christ did are both astonishing and wondrous, whether deeds or words. Deeds, because they were performed; words, because they are signs.

[Col. 0757B]

If, then, we consider what this event signifies, this blind man is the human race. This blindness occurred in the first human being through sin, from whom we all derive not only the origin of death but also the origin of iniquity.

If blindness is unbelief and illumination is faith, whom did Christ find faithful when he came? For this reason the Evangelist says of Christ, “And passing by.” Christ passes by in this way: he did not stand in the way of our sins, just as the Lord himself says in a certain parable, “A Samaritan came near the road” (Luke 10). He who comes to heal the wounded man who was half dead illuminates the blind man as he passes by. The one who is called wounded in the parable is illuminated as a blind man in the actual event.

He saw a man who was blind—not merely blind, but blind from birth. All human beings except the one who was born from a virgin were blind through original sin; that is, they were born with sin, which they drew from the sinful root of their first parent.

[Col. 0757C]

His disciples asked him, “Rabbi.” You know that “Rabbi” means “teacher.” They called him teacher because they desired to learn. They therefore put their question to the Lord as to a teacher:

“Who sinned, this man or his parents?” Jesus answered: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, that he should be born blind.”

What did he mean? If no human being is without sin, were the parents of this blind man without sin? Was he himself born without original sin, or had he added nothing through living? If both his parents had sin and he himself had sin, why did the Lord say, “Neither this man sinned nor his parents”? Unless he answered with reference to the matter about which he had been questioned: why was he born blind?

[Col. 0757D]

His parents had sin, but it was not through that sin that he was made blind. If, then, it was not through the sin of his parents that he was born blind, why was he born blind? Hear the teacher teaching. He seeks the believer in order to make him understand. He himself states the reason why that man was born blind: “Neither this man sinned,” he says, “nor his parents.”

“But so that the works of God might be revealed in him.” Not only what I am about to do in this one blind man, but so that what must be done through me in the blindness of the whole human race may be revealed. Then he continued and added:

[Col. 0758A]

“I must perform the works of him who sent me while it is day.” Remember how he gives all the glory to the one from whom he is, because the one who has a Son from him does not himself have one from whom he is.

What are the works of the Lord for which the Son of God came into the world, except to illuminate the blindness of the human race, heal whatever is wounded, seek what is lost, and restore what is disfigured? But what does he mean when he says, “I must perform the works of him who sent me while it is day”?

“Night is coming, when no one can work.” It is clear that in this passage the Lord mentioned a definite and specified day referring to himself—that is, the light of the world.

“As long as I am in the world,” he says, “I am the light of the world.” Therefore he himself is at work. But how long is he in the world? Do we suppose, brothers, that he was here then but is not here now? If we suppose this, then this night came after his ascension.

[Col. 0758B]

What does he say to his disciples as he ascends into heaven? “Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). The one who was then present in the world by bodily presence is now present everywhere in the world by divine power.

We have heard of the day; let us hear what this night is. What, then, shall we say about this night, when it will come and no one will be able to work? This night will belong to the impious; this night will belong to those to whom at the end it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

But it is also called night, not flame or fire. Hear that it is night as well: concerning a certain servant he says, “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness.” Let the human being work, then, lest that night overtake him, when no one can work.

Now is the time for faith to work through love. [Col. 0758C] And if we work now, this is the day; this is Christ. Hear him promising, and do not suppose that he is absent: “Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age.” There will be night there, where no one can work, but only receive what he has worked for.

The time of working is one thing; the time of receiving is another. For he will repay each one according to his works (Romans 2). Let us hear the Apostle exhorting us with vigilant minds to work while we have time. He says: “While we have time, let us do good” (Galatians 6).

We have heard what Christ said, admonishing the good and terrifying the wicked. But let us see what he did.

When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, made mud from the spittle, spread the mud over his eyes, and said to him:

[Col. 0758D] “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam”—which means “Sent.” What the Lord did is clear. Illumination was brought about in the blind man, but a great mystery is commended to us concerning the human race.

He spat on the ground and made mud from the saliva because “the Word became flesh.” He anointed the eyes of the blind man. He had been anointed, but he did not yet see. He sent him to the pool called Siloam.

It was appropriate for the Evangelist to commend to us the name of this pool, and he says that it means “Sent.” You recognize already who was sent. Unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity.

He therefore washed his eyes in the pool called “Sent” and was baptized in Christ. If, then, Christ baptized him in himself, so to speak, and at that moment illuminated him, when he anointed him he perhaps made him a catechumen.

The depth of so great a sacrament can indeed be explained and treated in other ways, but let this suffice for your charity. The catechumen is anointed—that is, he is taught to believe in Christ. He is sent to the pool of baptism so that he may be illuminated, recognize the true light, receive the forgiveness of sins, be made from a son of wrath a son of God, and, having been illuminated, come to preach Christ.

[Col. 0759A]

Accordingly, his neighbors and those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar, said: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” Some said, “It is he”; others said, “No, but he resembles him.” His opened eyes had changed his appearance.

[Col. 0759B]

He said, “It is I.” A welcome voice, lest he be condemned as ungrateful.

They therefore said to him: “How were your eyes opened?” He answered: “The man called Christ made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool and wash.’ I went, washed, and I see.”

Behold, he has become a messenger of grace. Behold, he evangelizes; seeing, he confesses. The blind man was confessing, while the hearts of the wicked were gnashing their teeth because they did not have in their hearts what he already had in his face.

They said to him: “Where is he?” He replied: “I do not know.” In these words his mind was still like that of one who had been anointed but did not yet see. But let us suppose, brothers, that he had that anointing in his mind: he preaches, yet does not know whom he preaches.

They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. [Col. 0759C] It was the Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. The Pharisees therefore questioned him again about how he had come to see. He said to them: “He put mud on my eyes; I washed, and I see.”

Some of the Pharisees said—not all, but some, for some were already being anointed. What then did those who neither saw nor had been anointed say? “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Rather, he was the one who kept it, because he was without sin. For this is the spiritual Sabbath: not to have sin.

Finally, brothers, this is what God teaches when he commends the Sabbath: “You shall do no servile work” (Leviticus 23). These are the words of God commending the Sabbath: “You shall do no servile work.” Ask the earlier readings what servile work is, and hear it from the Lord: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8).

But these men, as I said, neither seeing nor anointed, observed the Sabbath carnally and violated it spiritually.

[Col. 0759D]

Others said: “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Behold, these had been anointed.

And there was division among them. That day was divided between light and darkness.

They therefore said again to the blind man: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes?” What do you think about him? What do you suppose? What do you judge?

They were seeking a way to slander the man so that he might be expelled from the synagogue but found by Christ. But he steadfastly expressed what he thought. For he said:

[Col. 0760A] “He is a prophet.” He was still anointed in his heart and did not yet confess the Son of God, but he was not lying. The Lord himself says of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (John 4).

The Jews therefore did not believe that he had been blind and had come to see, until they summoned the parents of the man who had come to see and questioned them, saying:

“Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”

His parents answered them and said: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know. Ask him; he is of age. Let him speak for himself.”

We do know that he is our son. We would rightly be compelled to speak for an infant, because he could not speak for himself. He has long been able to speak; now he sees. [Col. 0760B]

We know him to have been blind from birth. We know that he spoke long ago; now we see that he sees. Ask him, so that you may be instructed.

His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue. It was no longer an evil to be outside the synagogue. They expelled him, but Christ received him. Therefore his parents said: “He is of age; ask him.”

They therefore summoned again the man who had been blind and said to him: “Give glory to God.” What does “Give glory to God” mean? Deny what you have received. This plainly is not giving glory to God but rather blaspheming God. “Give,” they say, “glory to God.”

“We know that this man is a sinner.” The man then said: [Col. 0760C] “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see.”

They said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” And the man, already becoming angry at the hardness of the Jews, was one who saw though he had come from blindness and could not endure the blind.

He answered them: “I told you already, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?” What does “Do you also?” mean except, “I already am one”? “Do you also want to?” I see now, but I do not see you seeing.

They cursed him and said: “You are his disciple.” Such a curse upon us and upon our children! For it is a curse if you examine the heart, not if you weigh the words.

“But we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses.” If only you knew that God spoke to Moses! You would know that God was foretold through Moses. For you have the Lord saying: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5).

[Col. 0760D]

Is this so? You follow the servant and turn your back on the Lord? But you do not even follow the servant, for through him you would be led to the Lord.

The man answered and said to them: “Here is what is astonishing: you do not know where he is from, yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, he hears him.”

He still speaks as one who has been anointed; for God also hears sinners. If God did not hear sinners, that tax collector would have prayed in vain, lowering his eyes to the ground

[Col. 0761A]

and striking his breast: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). By this confession he deserved justification, just as this blind man deserved illumination.

But sinners must wash their hearts with the tears of repentance, so that they may be heard. Then what took place in the face of this blind man will take place in their hearts, and they will perceive that God hears them—the one who came into this world to save sinners.

“From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” He freely and steadfastly confessed the truth. For these things were done by the Lord; by whom could they have been done except by the Lord? Or when could such things have been done by the disciples, unless the Lord dwelled in them?

They answered and said: “You were born entirely in sins.” [Col. 0761B] What does “entirely” mean? With your eyes closed—but the one who opened your eyes also saves the whole person. He will give resurrection in the heart, just as he gives illumination in the face. “You were born entirely in sins.”

“And you teach us?” And they cast him out.

They themselves had made him a teacher. They questioned him so many times in order to learn, and, after questioning him, they cast out the man who was teaching them. But what did I say earlier, brothers? They expel him; the Lord receives him. Indeed, because he was expelled, he became a Christian. Certainly, this man was cast out of the synagogue.

Jesus heard and came to him and said: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” And he replied: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

He saw, and he did not see. He saw with his eyes alone, but in his heart he did not yet see. The Lord said to him: “You see him”—that is, with your eyes—

[Col. 0761C]

“and the one speaking with you is he.”

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and when he found him, he said to him: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” Now he washes the face of his heart. He answered and said: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

And Jesus said to him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” Then he fell down and worshiped him. Now he washes the face of his heart.

Finally, with the face of his heart already washed and his conscience cleansed, recognizing him not merely as the Son of Man—which he had believed previously—but also as the Son of God, whom he now saw, he said: “I believe, Lord.”

But it is not enough to say, “I believe.” Do you want to see what kind of belief he had? Falling down, he worshiped him. If he had not believed the one he saw to be the Son of God, he would never have worshiped him.

[Col. 0761D] Therefore, sinners, devote yourselves to prayer. Confess your sins; pray that they may be blotted out; pray that they may be diminished; pray that, as you progress, they themselves may cease. Nevertheless, do not despair; pray even as sinners. For who has not sinned? Begin with the priests. It was said to the priests: “First offer sacrifices for your own sins, and then for the people” (Ezekiel 9; Hebrews 7).

It follows:

“For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

What does he mean when he says, “For judgment I came into this world,” whereas elsewhere he says, “I did not come to judge the world”? It means that one thing is the judgment of discernment and another the judgment of condemnation, concerning which the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever does not believe in me has already been judged” (John 3)—that is, condemned.

[Col. 0762A]

Here, as is clear from the words that follow, he signifies the judgment of discernment when he says: “So that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

What does “so that those who do not see may see” mean? It means: those who confess that they do not see and seek a physician, so that they may see. And what does “those who see may become blind” mean? It means: those who think they see and do not seek a physician, but remain in their blindness.

Therefore he called this discernment “judgment,” by which he distinguishes the humble from the proud, believers from unbelievers, and those who seek a physician from those who disdain to seek one.

O Lord, you came so that those who do not see may see—rightly, because you are light; rightly, because you are day; rightly, because you free human beings from darkness. Let every soul receive this; let every soul understand it, so that souls may not remain in darkness but be illuminated by the one who illuminates every human being coming into this world (John 1).

Some of the Pharisees were therefore stirred by these words:

[Col. 0762B] “And they said to him: ‘Are we also blind?’” Hear now what was disturbing them: “Those who see may become blind.”

Jesus said to them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin.” Since blindness itself is sin, if you were blind—that is, if you recognized yourselves as blind, called yourselves blind, and ran to the physician—you would not have sin.

“But now, because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains.” Why? Because by saying, “We see,” you do not seek the physician; you remain in your blindness.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0762C]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.” Up to the point where it says: “Jesus spoke this proverb to them.”

But they did not understand what he was saying to them. Because of the poisonous, proud, and incurable arrogance of the Pharisees—who boasted that they could see, although they were blind—the Lord Jesus composed the words that are read in this parable, which he himself graciously deigned to explain to those who understood it. In it he soundly admonished us, if we pay attention, not to glory in human wisdom or in moral distinction if the humility of Catholic faith in Christ is absent.

For there are many pagans who, according to a certain manner of life in this world, are called good and innocent people, and who seem to observe the commandments laid down in the law: they show honor to their parents, do not commit adultery, do not perpetrate murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness against anyone, and observe, as it were, the other things commanded in the law. Yet they are not Christians, and often boast, like those Pharisees, saying: “Are we blind too?” But they do all these things in vain, because they do not enter through the door; rather, in their swollen pride they seek to climb in by another way, as though by their own efforts.

Therefore the Lord set forth a likeness concerning his flock and the door by which one enters the fold. For what does the vain swelling of those who boast of living well profit them, when their life does not reach the goal of living well forever? This is the purpose for which living well ought to benefit each person: that he may be granted to live well forever. For if someone is not granted to live well forever, what does it profit him to live well? Thus those who either do not know the goal of living well because of blindness or despise it because of pride should not even be said to live well for a time.

No one has a true and certain hope of living well forever unless he acknowledges the life that is Christ and enters the fold through the door. For there are some people who glory in their own conduct and seek to draw others after them, not instructing their followers in Christ’s commandments but persuading them to live according to their own examples. Of such people Truth itself says elsewhere: “Teaching human doctrines and disregarding the commandments of God” (Matt. XV).

These seek to climb in by another way, to steal and kill, [Col. 0763B] rather than, like the shepherd, to save and preserve. Of such people it is said here: “But climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber.” Such teachers are found not only among those who are without the name of Christ, such as many philosophers who vaunted their wisdom with bombastic words and promised a blessed life to their followers, but also among very many who were reckoned by the Christian name and boasted that they had been enlightened by Christ, inventing for themselves various new names derived from Christ and contrary to the Catholic faith, as countless heretics did. They falsely imagined that they were entering through the door, which is Christ.

Sabellius says: “He who is the Son is himself the Father, but the Son is not the Father.” He does not enter through the door who calls the Son the Father. Arius says: “The Father is one thing, the Son another.” He would speak correctly if he said *alius*, “another person,” not *aliud*, “another thing.” For when he says “another thing,” he contradicts the one from whom he hears: “I and the Father are one” (here below). Therefore he too does not enter through the door. He preaches Christ as he pictures him to himself, not as Truth possesses him.

Photinus says: “Christ is man only, not God.” He too does not enter through the door, because Christ is both man and God. A new heresy that has arisen in our own times appears to agree with him, affirming and preaching: “Christ, like any of the saints, is God only by designation, and not truly.” Why go through many examples and enumerate the many vanities of heresies?

Hold fast to this: believe that the fold of Christ is the Catholic Church. Whoever wishes to enter the fold should enter through the door—that is, through Christ—and should preach Christ as true God and true Son of God. Nor should he preach Christ alone; he should also seek Christ’s glory, not his own. For many, while seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them.

Christ the Lord our God is a humble door, and he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Whoever enters through this door must humble himself, so that he may enter with a sound head. These are the ones who hear the voice of the true shepherd. These are the ones whom the true shepherd calls his own sheep by name. Of them it is said: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). Thus he calls them by name.

And who else sends them out except the one who forgives their sins, so that, freed from their harsh bonds, they can follow him? And who goes before them, so that they follow him, except the one who, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and over whom death will never again have dominion? He leads these sheep from faith to sight; he goes before them because he was the first of all to ascend into heaven. Those who are his sheep follow him because they know the voice of his teaching.

They do not follow alien guides but flee from them, because they do not know the voice—that is, the teaching—of strangers. But while the Lord Jesus was speaking, those who heard him did not understand, because they had fattened hearts and heard with difficulty (Isa. VI; Acts XXVIII). He names the door, names the fold, names the sheep, and commends all these things, but does not yet explain them. Let us therefore read on, because he will come to those words in which he deigns to explain some of what he has said; from his explanation, perhaps, he will also enable us to understand what he did not explain. He feeds us with what is clear and exercises us with what is obscure. Let us hear the one explaining whom we have heard making the proposition.

Then Jesus said to them again:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.”

Behold, he has opened the very door that he had presented as closed. He himself is the door. We have recognized it; let us enter, so that we may rejoice that we have entered.

“All who came are thieves and robbers.”

What is this, Lord? “All who came.” What do you mean? You came. But understand: he said, “All who came,” certainly meaning all except me. Let us recall the matter. Before his coming, the prophets came. Were they thieves and robbers? Far from it. They did not come apart from him, but came with him. I say, they came with him, because, while sending heralds of his coming, he possessed the hearts of those whom he sent. They therefore came with him because they came with the Word of God.

“I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John IV). He is the truth. They came with him because they were truthful and preached the truth. But all who came apart from him are thieves and robbers. They came on their own because they were not sent through him, as the Apostle says: “How will they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. X). And because they came on their own and were not sent by him, they are thieves and robbers.

Before Christ’s coming there were false prophets among the people of God and false teachers, just as after his coming there were very many false teachers under the Christian name—not teachers but seducers, not preachers but plunderers—practicing robbery, not adhering to sound doctrine but to false doctrine. Of them it is said: “They are thieves and robbers,” that is, they came to steal and kill.

But those who are truly sheep did not listen to them; they did not conceal a wolf’s heart beneath a sheep’s skin. Therefore those who preached before Christ’s coming preached in the same Spirit in which the Apostles and holy teachers preached after Christ’s coming, who showed the way of truth to the world.

But all who believed at that time—whether Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, or the other patriarchs and prophets who foretold Christ—were sheep, and they believed in Christ. They heard not a stranger’s voice but Christ’s own voice. For the judge was speaking through the herald, while the herald announced that the judge was to come.

There are others, therefore, whom the sheep did not hear, in whom Christ’s voice was not present: people who wandered, taught falsehood, babbled empty things, invented vanities, and led the wretched astray, such as the false prophets and the scribes and Pharisees in the time of the Lord himself. These are the ones who came on their own and were not sent by the judge.

With such people and their teachings driven far away, let us see whom the good Shepherd calls. For he says:

“I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.”

By this he clearly shows that not only the shepherd but also the sheep enter through the door. But what does “he will enter and go out and find pasture” mean?

To enter the Church through the door, Christ, is exceedingly good. But to go out of the Church, as John the Evangelist himself says in his Epistle, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John II), is certainly not good. Such an exit could not therefore be praised by the good Shepherd, so that he would say: “He will enter and go out and find pasture.” There is, then, a good and praiseworthy going out, as well as an entering, through the good door, which is Christ.

But what is this praiseworthy and blessed going out? I could perhaps say that we enter when we think something inwardly, but go out when we do something outwardly. And since, as the Apostle says, Christ dwells in our hearts through faith, to go out through Christ means, according to that same faith, to be outwardly present—that is, to act before human beings. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “Man goes forth to his work” (Ps. CIII); and the Lord himself says: “Let your works shine before human beings” (Matt. V).

But I am more pleased by what Truth itself, as the good Shepherd and therefore the good Teacher, in a certain way admonished us to understand concerning his words, “He will enter and go out and find pasture,” when he added:

“The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy; I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

He seems to have said that those entering should have life. Yet no one can go out through the door—that is, through Christ—to eternal life, which will be in sight, unless through that same door, Christ, he has entered into his Church, which is his fold, for temporal life, which exists in faith. Therefore he says: “I came so that they may have life”—that is, faith, which works through love. Through this faith they enter the fold so that they may live, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. II).

“And have it more abundantly”: those who persevere to the end go out through that door—that is, through faith in Christ—because true believers die, and they will have life more abundantly when they come to the place where that Shepherd has gone before them, where thereafter they will never die.

Although even here in the fold itself there is no lack of pasture—for we can understand the words “and find pasture” in relation both to entering and to going out—nevertheless, they will truly find pasture where those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied (Matt. XV). One found pasture to whom it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

The Lord’s discourse continues concerning the perfection of the good shepherd and the flight of the evil shepherd, whom he calls a hireling:

“I am,” he says, “the good Shepherd. The good Shepherd gives his life for his sheep; but the hireling flees, because he is a hireling and has no concern for the sheep.”

Speaking to his sheep, both those present and those yet to come—those who were already there because they were his sheep, and those who would become his sheep—speaking both to those then present and to those yet to come, to them and to us, and to all who would be his sheep after us, the Lord showed how much he loves his own.

All, therefore, will hear the voice of their shepherd saying: “I am the good Shepherd.” He would not have added “good” unless there were evil shepherds. But the evil shepherds are the thieves and robbers, or at least, to put it mildly, the hirelings.

Here we must recognize, distinguish, and understand all the persons whom he could have mentioned. The Lord has opened a way to two things that he had in a certain manner presented as closed. We already know that he himself is the door; we know that he himself is the shepherd. Who the thieves and robbers are was disclosed in the earlier statement. Now we have heard of the hireling; we have heard also of the wolf; and the doorkeeper has been named.

Among the good, therefore, there are the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the sheep; among the evil, there are thieves and robbers, the hireling, and the wolf. We understand the Lord Jesus Christ to be the door and the shepherd himself. He has left us to seek the doorkeeper. And what does he say concerning the doorkeeper?

“To him,” he says, “the doorkeeper opens.”

To whom does he open? To the shepherd. What does he open to the shepherd? The door. And who is the door itself? The shepherd also. These are different names signifying one thing: shepherd, door, and sheep. For a little earlier we heard the Lord’s own words: “I am the door.” And now we have read: “I am the shepherd,” who is also called the Lamb by the friend of the bridegroom, as we heard in this present Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). Of him the prophet had foretold long before: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII), although his entire body is understood as his sheep.

He too may be understood as the doorkeeper, because no one enters or goes out unless he opens, since he has the key of David: “He opens, and no one shuts; he shuts, and no one opens” (Rev. III). We should not, therefore, hesitate to understand, according to a certain likeness, the same person as both doorkeeper and door.

Who is the doorkeeper except the one who opens? And who opens except the one who reveals himself? For he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). If perhaps you wish to seek another person as the doorkeeper, it is the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord himself said to his disciples: “He will teach you all truth” (John XVI).

The door is Christ; Christ is the truth. Who opens the door except the one who teaches all truth?

When the Lord wished to show the work of the good shepherd, he set himself forth as an example, saying: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.” He did what he instructed; he displayed what he commanded. He laid down his life for his sheep.

The way of despising death, which we are to follow, has been shown to us; a pattern has been set before us, into which we are to be impressed. First, we must mercifully expend our outward possessions for his sheep; finally, if necessary, we must also devote our life to those same sheep. Whoever does not give his possessions for the sheep, when will he give his life for them?

We have explained—or rather, by the Lord’s teaching we have understood—who the shepherd is, who the door is, who the doorkeeper is, and who the sheep are; we have also learned who the thieves and robbers are. But now let us consider the hireling and the wolf, concerning whom the Lord himself said:

“But the hireling, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees.”

He is called not a shepherd but a hireling because he tends the Lord’s sheep not out of inward love but for temporal wages. A hireling is one who occupies the shepherd’s position but does not seek the profit of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of authority, feeds on temporal gains, and delights in the respect shown him by human beings.

These are the hireling’s wages: that for the very labor he undertakes in governing, he should find what he seeks, while remaining excluded in the future from the inheritance of the flock.

The wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and humble. But the one who seemed to be a shepherd and was not abandons the sheep and flees, because, fearing danger to himself from that person, he does not dare resist his injustice.

He flees—not by changing his location, but by withdrawing his assistance. He flees because he sees injustice and remains silent. He flees because he hides himself in silence.

But there is another wolf who every day, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, who prowls around, seeking an opening into the enclosures of the faithful and seeking the deaths of souls (1 Pet. V). Concerning this wolf it is immediately added:

“And the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.”

The wolf comes and the hireling flees, because the evil spirit tears apart the minds of the faithful in temptation, while the one who occupies the shepherd’s place has no concern for vigilant care. Souls perish, and he rejoices in earthly advantages.

The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into lust, inflames another with greed, raises another up in pride, divides another through anger, goads this one with envy, and trips that one through deceit. Thus the wolf scatters the flock when the devil kills the people of the faithful through temptations. But against these things the hireling is inflamed by no zeal and roused by no fervor of love, because, while he seeks only outward advantages, he negligently tolerates the inward losses of the flock. Hence it is immediately added:

“But the hireling flees, because he is a hireling and has no concern for the sheep.”

The sole reason for the hireling’s flight is that he is a hireling, as though it were openly said: He cannot stand in danger for the sheep who, while presiding over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit. While he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he is afraid to oppose himself to danger, lest he lose what he loves.

But because our Redeemer made known the faults of the false shepherd, he again showed the pattern into which we ought to be impressed, saying:

[Col. 0768A] “I am the good Shepherd.”

And he adds:

“And I know my own”—that is, I love them—“and my own know me.”

As though he plainly said: Those who love obey. Therefore he immediately added:

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep.”

As though he openly said: This is demonstrated by the fact that I know the Father and am known by the Father: I lay down my life for my sheep. That is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how much I love the Father.

But because he had come to redeem not only Judea but also the Gentiles, he adds:

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.”

The Lord had looked upon our redemption, since we come from the Gentile people, when he said that he must bring other sheep. You see this happening daily, brothers; today you see this accomplished in the reconciliation of the Gentiles.

He makes one fold out of two flocks because he joins the Jewish and Gentile people in his faith, as Paul attests when he says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). Choosing the simple from both nations for eternal life, he leads the sheep into his own fold. Concerning these sheep he again says:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.”

Of them he also said a little earlier: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.” He will enter into faith, but he will go out from faith to sight, from belief to contemplation. He will find pasture in eternal refreshment.

His sheep will therefore find pasture, because whoever follows him with a simple heart is nourished by the food of eternal verdure. And what is the pasture of these sheep except the eternal joys of the ever-green paradise? The pasture of the elect is the face of the God who is present. While it is contemplated without failing, the mind is satisfied forever with the food of life.

It follows:

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I will take it up again.”

What does he mean? “The Father loves me because I die in order to rise again.” The words “I” were spoken with great emphasis: “I,” he says, “lay down my life.” I lay it down. What does “I lay it down” mean? “I,” he says, “lay it down.”

Let the Jews not boast. They were able to rage, but they were not able to exercise power. Let them rage as much as they can. If I do not wish to lay down my life, what will they accomplish by raging? They were struck down by a single answer when they were asked: “Whom do you seek?” They said, “Jesus,” and he said to them, “I am he.” They drew back and fell (John XVIII).

Those who fell at one word of Christ, about to die, what will they do at the voice of the one who will judge? “I,” he says, “lay down my life.” Let the Jews not boast as though they had prevailed; he himself laid down his life.

Just as he had the power to lay it down, so he also had the power to take it up again. He showed this in other words in this same Gospel when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). The Evangelist then explained: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid.), and added that his disciples remembered these words when Jesus had risen from the dead.

What was raised was what had died. For the Word could not die, nor was that soul dead. Only the flesh died, and it rose on the third day.

But we must ask what he meant when he said: “I lay down my life.” Who laid it down? What did he lay down? Who is the one who laid it down?

What is Christ? The Word and man—not man in such a way that he is flesh alone, but because a human being consists of flesh and soul. The whole human being is in Christ. He would not have assumed the inferior part and abandoned the superior part, since the soul is the better part of a human being than the body.

Since, therefore, the whole human being is in Christ, what is Christ? The Word, I say, and man. “The Word became flesh” (John I), that is, God became man.

For he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.” Christ, however, laid it down for us; he laid it down when he wished, and when he wished he took up his life again.

To lay down one’s life, then, is to die. Thus the Apostle Peter also said to the Lord: “I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII), that is, “I will die in the flesh for you.”

The flesh laid down its life, and the flesh again took up its life—not, however, by the flesh’s own power, but by the power of the indwelling Word of God. The Word of God never laid down the life that it had assumed into the unity of its person. Rather, the life was laid down by the flesh and taken up again through the power of the divinity.

The flesh therefore laid down its life by expiring. See what the Lord himself said on the cross: “I thirst” (John XIX). Those who were present soaked a sponge in vinegar, fastened it to a reed, and applied it to his mouth. When he had received it, he said: “It is finished” (ibid.).

What is “It is finished”? All the things that had been prophesied as destined to occur before his death have been fulfilled. And because he had the power to lay down his life when he wished, after saying, “It is finished,” the Evangelist says: “And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.”

What is said there as “he gave up” is said here as “he lays down,” because to give up and to lay down are one thing. Who gave it up? What did he give up? He gave up the spirit; the flesh gave it up.

What does “the flesh gave it up” mean? The flesh sent it forth; the flesh exhaled it. For this is why one is said to “expire”—that is, to be made outside the spirit—just as one is said to be “exiled” by being made outside one’s soil.

What he says here, “I have power to lay down my life,” is said there as: “Bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.” The spirit is the soul. When the soul therefore departs from the flesh and the flesh remains without the soul, the human being is said to lay down his life.

When did Christ lay down his life? When the Word willed it. Sovereignty was in the Word; the power was there to determine when the flesh should lay down its life and when it should take it up.

For just as one human being consists of soul and body, so one Christ consists of the Word and man. Soul and body are two things, but one human being. The Word and man are two things, but one Christ.

Let no one waver in faith upon hearing the Lord say: “I have power to lay down my life.” The flesh lays it down, but by the power of the Word. The flesh takes it up, but by the power of the Word.

The Word, soul, and flesh are one Christ. When the flesh was killed, Christ was killed; when the flesh took up the soul again, Christ took up the soul again, because whatever was accomplished there in the dispensation of human salvation was accomplished entirely by one Christ, one proper and perfect Son of God, one true and almighty God: man because of the Word, God because of man; as it is said: “The Word became flesh” (John I).

But by the following words he shows how all these things were to be fulfilled:

“This commandment I received from my Father.”

The Word did not receive a commandment through a word; rather, in the only-begotten Word of the Father there is every commandment. When the Son is said to receive from the Father what he possesses substantially—as it is said, “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John V)—although the Son himself is life, his power is not diminished; rather, his generation is shown.

For the Father did not add something to the Son as though to one born imperfect, but by begetting he gave everything to the one whom he begot perfect. Thus he gave him his equality, whom he did not beget unequal.

But while the Lord was speaking these things, the light was shining in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

Dissension arose again among the Jews because of these words. Many of them were saying: “He has a demon and is insane; why do you listen to him?” These were the thickest darkness.

[Col. 0770C] Others were saying: “These words are not those of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” The eyes of these people had begun to be opened, and they were seeing something of the light and recognizing something of the truth.

We have heard the Lord’s patience and, amid the Jews’ insults, the preaching of salvation. But those people, hardened, began to test him rather than obey his words.

The Evangelist says:

“The Feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the temple in the portico of Solomon.”

The Dedication was the solemnity of the temple’s dedication, which the people of God, following the ancient tradition of their fathers, customarily celebrated every year. But it should be noted that the Dedication mentioned here does not refer to the temple’s first dedication but to its final one. This can readily be gathered from the fact that it is said to have occurred in winter.

The first dedication of that temple was carried out by Solomon in the autumn; the second, by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest, in the spring; and the third, by Judas Maccabaeus, in winter. At that time it is recorded that a special decree was established requiring the same dedication to be renewed every year by solemn ceremonies in remembrance (1 Kings VI, VIII; Isa. VI; 1 Macc. IV). It continued to be observed down to the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, as we have just heard while the Gospel was being read. This dedication is also known to be preserved in the Churches of Christ in our own time by a salutary custom.

We must consider why the Evangelist said that this Dedication took place in winter. It was entirely because of the Jews’ hardness and unbelief, which is often represented under the name of cold.

“And Jesus was walking in the portico of Solomon.”

If, then, the Son of God wished to walk in the temple where the flesh and blood of irrational animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit our house of prayer, where the mysteries of his own flesh and blood are celebrated?

If he did not disdain to walk through the portico in which a mortal and earthly king—although exceedingly powerful and wise—once used to stand in prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and enlighten the inner chambers of our hearts, provided that he perceives them to be Solomon’s portico—that is, provided that he sees that they possess his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom?

We must not think that only the house in which we assemble for prayer or for the celebration of the mysteries is the Lord’s temple. We ourselves, who assemble in the Lord’s name, are called and are his temple to a much greater degree, since the Apostle plainly says: “You are the temple of the living God, as God says: I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. VI).

The Evangelist therefore shows why he said that it took place in winter when he continues:

“The Jews surrounded him.”

They surrounded him, then, in order to test him, not out of a desire to recognize the truth, and they said:

“How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

They said this not while seeking the truth of faith, but while laying snares for the one whom they questioned and constructing an accusation, so that they might find an occasion on which to accuse him. They did not wish to believe that he was God, but only that he would be a mere man and come as a king exalted above other human beings.

In this madness their descendants have continued to err down to the present day and will continue until they receive the Antichrist in place of Christ. If the Lord Jesus Christ answered that he was the Christ, they were considering handing him over to the governor for punishment, as though, in opposition to Augustus, he were unlawfully claiming imperial power for himself.

But, concerned for our salvation—for whose sake these things were to be written—he tempered his answer in such a way that he both closed the mouths of his accusers and openly revealed to believers that he is the Christ.

They were asking about Christ as man, but he openly spoke of the mysteries of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father.

Let us therefore see what the Jews said while surrounding the Lord: “How long,” they say, “will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

Christ did not come to take away the soul of those who believe in him, but to give the soul life. But the Jews themselves took away their own soul through unbelief, because they had gathered to test Christ, not to believe in Christ.

Jesus answered them:

“I speak to you, and you do not believe.”

He showed specifically who he was when he said: “I speak to you”—that is, the Word of God coeternal with the Father. For the works that he does in the Father’s name bear witness that he is the Son of God, who did not seek his own glory but the glory of the one who sent him, because the glory of the Father and the Son is one.

But the hearts of unbelievers could not receive this faith. Of them he says:

“But you do not believe.”

And he gives the reason why they did not believe:

“Because you are not of my sheep.”

They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd; they are sheep by not despising the Redeemer; they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture.

How, then, did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep”? He saw that they were destined for eternal destruction, not for eternal life purchased by the price of his blood.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.”

For he says, “I know them.” It is the custom of Holy Scripture to say that the Lord knows whatever he chooses, as the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II), and to say that he does not know what he does not approve as worthy of eternal life. Therefore he will say to the impious: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII).

He continues concerning the sheep:

“And I give them eternal life.”

These are the pastures he promised earlier to his sheep: there no grass withers; everything is green, everything flourishes, everything remains whole, and whatever is received once is possessed forever.

“And they will never perish.”

Here we must understand the implied words: “But you will perish, because you are not of my sheep.”

“And no one will snatch them from my hand”—that is, from my power.

“My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all.”

What the Father gave to the Son is greater than all: that he should be his only-begotten Son, equal and consubstantial. What did he give? Certainly he gave by begetting, because he did not beget one inferior to himself, nor one later in time, but one coeternal with himself, always God, without a beginning in time.

It must not be said: “He did not exist before he was born.” For he was never not-born who was coeternal with the Father. Whoever understands, grasps this; whoever does not grasp it, let him believe. Let him be nourished by faith so that he may be able to grasp the Word of God, because the Word is the Son.

The Son is therefore always Son and always equal. He is not equal by growing but by being born: he is always the Son born from the Father, God from God, coeternal from the eternal.

The Father, however, is not God from the Son; the Son is God from the Father. Therefore by begetting, the Father gave him to be God; by begetting, he gave him to be equal. This is what is greater than all.

Therefore this John transcended all the heights of creatures, the thousands of angelic hosts, and all great things, and arrived at what is greater than all, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

This is what is greater than all: that I should be his Word, that I should be his only-begotten Son, that I should be the radiance of his light. Therefore no one snatches the sheep from my hand.

“And no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

The Father’s hand and the Son’s hand are one hand—that is, one power—because there is one divinity, one majesty, one eternity, and one equality.

This equality, which the Lord possessed in his divinity before the world existed, with the Father (John XVII), he received in humility from the time of the Incarnation. “And no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

He plainly makes it understood that his hand and the Father’s hand—that is, his power and the Father’s power—are one and indistinguishable. For this reason Christ must be believed to be one who, unlike the others, was not made through grace in time, but has always existed as the true Son of God. The following statement makes this even clearer, when he says:

I and the Father are one. “We are one,” he says: we have one substance, one divinity, one eternity, perfect equality, no dissimilarity. By these words he not only explained the Jews’ immediate question—whether he himself was the Christ—but also showed how detestable was the perfidy of the heretics whose coming he foresaw. Let Sabellius be silent when he hears, “I and the Father,” for his perverse teaching asserted that the Father and the Son are one person; but “I and the Father” indicates two persons. Let Arius likewise blush when he hears, “We are one,” for he maintains two natures in the Father and the Son, whereas “one” signifies one nature, just as “we are” signifies two persons. Let us follow the apostolic faith, which blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles, confessed: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

The Jews, hearing the Lord’s words, endured up to this point; but when he said, “I and the Father are one,” they could not bear it. Hard-hearted as usual, they ran to the stones, as the Evangelist says:

They took up stones to stone him. The Lord, because he did not suffer what he did not wish to suffer, and suffered nothing except what he wished to suffer, addressed them while they still desired to stone him. “The Jews took up stones to stone him.”

Jesus answered them: “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?” And they answered: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because, although you are a man, you make yourself God.” They answered this concerning what he had said: “I and the Father are one.” Behold: the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand. They were angry precisely because they perceived that “I and the Father are one” could be said only where there is equality between the Father and the Son. But see what the Lord answered the perverse men. He saw that they could not endure the splendor of truth, and he tested them in his words.

[Col. 0773D] Is it not written in your law—that is, the law given to you—“I said: You are gods”? God says through the prophet in the psalm to human beings, “I said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI). The Lord here called all those Scriptures “the law” in a general sense, although elsewhere he specifically calls the law by that name, distinguishing it from the prophets, as in: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. XI), and: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXVIII). At times, however, he divides these same Scriptures into three parts, when he says: “It was necessary that all things written about me in the law and the prophets and the psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV). Here, however, he also called the psalms by the name of the law, where it is written: “I said: You are gods.”

If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled, Scripture which the Father sanctified [Col. 0774A] and sent into the world—you say, “You blaspheme,” because I said, “I am the Son of God.” The word of God came to human beings so that they might be called gods; yet the Word of God himself, who is with God—if human beings become gods by sharing in him, can that in which they share not be God? If illuminated lights are gods, how is the light that illuminates not God? If those who have been warmed, as it were, by a saving fire become gods, is that from which they are warmed not God? You approach the light, are illuminated, and are numbered among the children of God. If you withdraw from the light, you grow dark and are counted among the darkness. Yet that light does not approach itself, because it does not withdraw from itself. If, then, the word of God makes you gods, how is the Word of God the Father not God?

Therefore the Father sanctified his Son and sent him into the world. Perhaps someone will say: If the Father sanctified him, was he at some time not holy? He sanctified him, then, in the same way as he begot him. In order that he might be holy, he gave this to him by begetting him, for he begot him holy. For if what is sanctified was previously not holy, how do we say to God the Father, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI)?

If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in him. How can human beings say: If we think rightly, we are in God; and if we live rightly, God is in us? The faithful, sharing in his grace and illuminated by him, are in him, and he is in them. But the only-begotten Son is not so. He is in the Father, [Col. 0774C] and the Father is in him, as an equal in the one to whom he is equal. Indeed, we can sometimes say: We are in God, and God is in us. Can we say, “I and God are one”? You are in God because God contains you. God is in you because you have become God’s temple. But merely because you are in God and God is in you, can you say, “Whoever sees me sees God”? How, then, did the Only-Begotten say, “Whoever sees me sees the Father”? “I and the Father are one.” Recognize what belongs properly to the Lord and what is the gift of the servant. The Lord’s own property is equality with the Father; the servant’s gift is participation in the Savior.

Therefore they sought to seize him. If only they had seized him—but by believing and understanding, not by raging and killing. “They sought to seize him.” [Col. 0774D] For when they wished to seize him, what did he do to them?

And he went out from their hands. They did not seize him because they had too little faith; and because he did not wish it—he who had the power to lay down his life—they did not seize him. But when he wished, he was seized by their hands of wickedness.

And he went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing; and he remained there. Many came to him and said: “John indeed performed no sign” (John V). You remember what was said about John: that he was a lamp and bore witness to the day. What, then, did these people say among themselves? “John,” they said, “showed no miracle; he did not drive out demons, he did not expel a fever, he did not give sight to the blind, he did not raise the dead, he did not feed so many thousands of people with five or seven loaves, he did not walk upon the sea, he did not command the winds and the waves. John did none of these things, and everything he said bore witness to this man.” Let us come to the day through the lamp. John performed no sign.

But everything John said about him was true. Behold: those who came to him seized him—not as the Jews wished to seize him while he was departing, but these seized him while he remained. What follows, finally? “And many believed in him.”

## CHAPTER XI

Now a certain man named Lazarus was ill, from Bethany, the village of Mary [Col. 0775B] and Martha. Many things are evident in this miracle of Lazarus. Let us not seek an explanation for every detail, so that we may deal more freely with what is necessary. In the preceding reading you remember that the Lord went out from the hands of those who wished to stone him and departed across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. While the Lord was there, Lazarus fell ill in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem. Mary was the woman who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill.

So his sisters sent to him, saying. We now understand that they sent to where the Lord was, since he was absent. They sent to the Lord across the Jordan, announcing that their brother was ill, so that, if he deemed it appropriate, he might come and free him from his illness. He delayed healing him so that he could raise him. What, then, did his sisters announce?

Lord, behold, the one you love is ill. They did not say, “Come”; it was enough simply to inform the one who loved him. They did not dare say, “Come and heal him.” They did not dare say, “Give the command there, and it will happen here.” Why should this man not do so as well, if the faith of that centurion is praised for it? For he said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Mark VIII). This man said none of these things, but only: “Lord, behold, the one you love is ill.” It is enough that you know; for you do not love and then abandon. Someone may say: How was a sinner signified by Lazarus, and yet loved so by the Lord? Let him hear the Lord saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark II). For if the Lord did not love sinners, he would not have assumed the likeness of sinful flesh.

When Jesus heard this, he said to them: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified.” This glorification of his did not increase him, but benefited us. Thus he said, “It is not unto death,” because that death itself is not unto death, but rather unto a miracle through which people would believe in Christ and avoid true death. Observe carefully how, as if indirectly, the Lord called himself God, because of those who deny it. There are heretics who deny that the Son of God is God; let them hear: “This illness,” he says, “is not unto death, but for the glory [Col. 0776A] of God.” What glory? The glory of which God? Hear what follows: “So that the Son of God may be glorified through it”—through what? Through that illness.

Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus. That sick man, all those beloved people, were sorrowful; yet the Savior of the sick, indeed the raiser of the dead and the consoler of the sorrowful, loved them.

When he heard that Lazarus was ill, he then remained in the same place for two days. They had announced it: “He remained there.” The time was prolonged until the four days were completed. This was not without reason, unless perhaps—indeed, certainly—the number of days itself intimates some mystery.

Then, after this, he said to his disciples: “Let us go again into Judea.” There he had nearly been stoned; and for that reason he appeared to have departed from there lest he be stoned. He departed as a human being; but on returning, as though he had forgotten the illness, he displayed his power. “Let us go,” he said, “into Judea.” When he had said this, observe how frightened the disciples became.

The disciples said to him: “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?” Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?” What does this answer mean? They said: “The Jews were just now wishing to stone you, and are you going there again so that they may stone you?” And the Lord replied: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?”

If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him. He was speaking about the day, but for our understanding it is as though it were still night. Let us invoke the day, so that it may drive away the night and illuminate the heart with light. What did the Lord wish to say? As far as I can see—as far as the height and depth of the saying extend—he wished to rebuke their hesitation and unbelief. They wished to give advice to the Lord, so that he would not die, although he had come to die, lest they themselves die. Likewise, in another place, holy Peter loved the Lord but did not yet fully understand why he had come; he feared that he would die and displeased Life itself—that is, the Lord himself (Matt. XVI). When human beings, then, wished to advise God—the disciples their teacher, servants their lord, the sick their physician—he rebuked them and said: “Are there not twelve [Col. 0776D] hours of daylight?” “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.” Follow me, if you do not wish to stumble. Do not give me advice when you ought to receive advice from me.

What, then, does “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?” signify? It signifies that, in order to show himself to be the day, he chose twelve disciples. “If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, do the hours give advice to the day? The hours follow the day; the day does not follow the hours.” If they were the hours, then, what about Judas, who was himself among the twelve hours? If he was an hour, he was shining. If he was shining, how was he handing the day over to death? But in this saying the Lord was foreseeing not Judas himself, but his successor. When Judas fell, Matthias succeeded him, and the number twelve remained. He did not choose twelve disciples without reason, except because he himself is the spiritual day. [Col. 0777A] Let the hours, then, follow the day; let the hours proclaim the day; let the hours be illumined by the day; let the hours be enlightened by the day; through the preaching of the hours, let the world believe in the day. Thus he said briefly: “Follow me, if you do not wish to go astray.” After this he said to them:

Lazarus, our friend, is asleep; but I am going to awaken him from sleep. He spoke truly: to his sisters he was dead, but to the Lord he was sleeping. To human beings he was dead, because they could not raise him. For the Lord raised him from the tomb with as much ease as you awaken a sleeping person from bed. Thus, according to his power, he called him sleeping, because other dead people are also often called sleeping in Scripture, as the Apostle says: “Concerning those who sleep, brothers, we do not want you to be ignorant, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope” (1 Thess. IV). He called them sleeping because he proclaimed that they would rise again. And elsewhere: “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all rise again” (1 Cor. XV), signifying our death under the name of sleep. For when the body is abandoned by the soul, it sleeps in the tomb, to be raised on the last day. But souls, when they leave their bodies, have different receptions: joy for the good, torments for the wicked. When the resurrection has taken place, however, the joy of the good will be greater, and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they are tormented together with their bodies. When the Lord told the disciples that his friend was sleeping, they answered, understanding it in this way:

Lord, if he is asleep, he will be safe. For dreams are commonly signs of recovery in the sick.

[Col. 0777C] Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he was speaking about the sleep of ordinary slumber. Then Jesus said to them plainly—he had spoken somewhat obscurely when he said that he was sleeping:

He said plainly: Lazarus is dead, and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there. He knew that he was dead, although the report had been only that he was ill. But what could be hidden from the one who had created him and into whose hands the soul of the dying man had gone forth? This is what he means by: “I rejoice for your sake, so that your faith may increase,” or be strengthened—that is, so that you may believe more fully and more firmly.

But let us go to him. Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: “Let us go also, so that we may die with him.” Jesus therefore came and found that he had already been four days in the tomb. Many things can indeed be said about the four days, as obscure passages of Scripture, according to the diversity of interpreters, produce many meanings. Let us also say what it seems to us that a dead man of four days signifies. Just as in the case of the blind man we understand, in a certain way, the human race, so perhaps in this dead man we shall likewise understand many things. For one thing can signify different things in different ways.

When a human being is born, he is born already with death, because he draws sin from Adam. Hence the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death spread to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V). Behold, you have one day of death, which a human being draws from the propagation of death. Then he grows and begins to approach the years of reason, so that he may understand the natural law, which all have fixed in their hearts: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV). Is this said only of pagans, and not read, in a certain way, in nature itself? Do you wish to suffer theft? Certainly not. Behold the law in your heart: “What you do not wish to suffer, do not do.” Yet people transgress this law: behold another day of death.
