The law given divinely through God’s servant Moses was also given, and it says there: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). Behold, the law has been written, and it too is despised. Add a third day of death. What remains? The Gospel also comes; the kingdom of heaven is preached; Christ is proclaimed everywhere; he threatens Gehenna and promises eternal life—and he too is despised. People transgress the Gospel: behold the fourth day of death. Rightly, then, one might think: Is mercy to be denied even to such people? Far from it. The Lord does not disdain to approach even such people in order to raise them.

Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. When Martha heard that Jesus had come, she went to meet him; but Mary remained at home. Martha therefore said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” She did not say: “Even now I ask you to raise my brother.” For how did she know whether it would be beneficial for her brother to rise? She said only: “I know [Col. 0778C] that you can. If you wish, you will do it. Whether you will do it, however, is your judgment, not something I presume to dictate.” “But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her:

Your brother will rise. Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.” I am certain about that resurrection; I am uncertain about this one.

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life.” You say: “My brother will rise on the last day.” It is true; but through whom he will rise then, he can rise now, because I am the resurrection and the life. He is the resurrection because he is the life, because whoever believes in me will never die. What does this mean? Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; just as Lazarus died and lives, because God is not the God of the dead, but of the living (Matt. XXII). [Col. 0778D] Concerning the fathers who died long ago—that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—he gave the Jews this answer: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; he is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark XII), for all of them live. Believe, then; and if you have died, you will live. But if you do not believe, even while you are living, you are dead. From what, then, does death exist in the soul? Because faith is not in it. From what does death exist in the body? Because the soul is not there. Therefore faith is the soul of your soul: just as the soul is the life of the body, so faith is the life of the soul. “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul until the flesh rises again, never afterward to die.” This is what he says: “Whoever believes in me, though he die, will live; and everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me, though he die for a time because of the death of the flesh, will not die eternally because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.” This is what he says:

And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this? She said to him: “Yes, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world. When I believed that you are the resurrection, I believed that you are the life. I believed that whoever believes in you, even if he dies, will live; and whoever lives and believes in you will never die.”

When she had said this, she went away and quietly called her sister Mary, saying: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” Notice how she called a subdued voice “silence.” For how was she silent when she said, [Col. 0779B] “The Teacher is here and is calling you”? Notice also how the Evangelist did not say where, when, or how the Lord called Mary, so that this might rather be understood from Martha’s words, while the truth of the narrative was preserved.

As soon as she heard, she rose quickly and came to him. Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. The Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary rise quickly and go out, followed her, saying that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Why did it concern the Evangelist to narrate this? So that we may see what occasion caused more people to be present when Lazarus was raised. The Jews thought that she was hurrying away to seek consolation for her grief through tears; they followed her so that the great miracle of a dead man of four days rising again would have many witnesses.

When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: “Where have you laid him?” By groaning in spirit and troubling himself he indicated something to us. Who could trouble him except himself? First, then, observe his power, and only afterward seek the meaning. You are troubled unwillingly; Christ is troubled because he wills it. Jesus hungered—it is true, but because he willed it. Jesus slept—it is true, but because he willed it. Jesus was sorrowful—it is true, [Col. 0779D] but because he willed it. Jesus died—it is true, but because he willed it. It was in his power to be affected in one way or another, or not to be affected. For he assumed a true soul and the flesh of the whole human being, joining it to himself in the nature of one person. The Apostle’s soul, too, was illumined by the Word, and the souls of the other apostles and holy prophets were illumined by the Word; but of none of them was it said, “The Word became flesh” (John I), and of none was it said, “I and the Father are one” (John X). The soul and flesh of Christ are one person with the Word of God; there is one Christ. Therefore, where supreme power is present, weakness is troubled at the prompting of the will. This is what is meant by: “He troubled himself.”

I have spoken of the power; attend now to the meaning. A great offender is signified by that four-day death [Col. 0780A] and by that burial. What, then, does Christ’s troubling himself signify, except that he wishes to show you how you ought to be troubled when you are weighed down and oppressed by such a mass of sin? You have looked at yourself and seen that you are guilty; you have reckoned up your deeds: “I did this, and God spared me; I committed that, and he delayed punishment; I heard the Gospel, and despised it.” Say—say it with tears: “I was baptized, and again returned to sin. What shall I do? Where shall I go? How shall I escape?” When you say these things, Christ already groans, because faith groans. In the voice of the one who groans, hope of resurrection appears. Where faith itself is within, there is Christ groaning. If faith is in us, Christ is in us. What else does the Apostle say than that Christ dwells in our hearts through faith (Eph. III)? If, then, your faith is in Christ, Christ is in your heart; therefore let Christ groan in your heart.

Christ wept for his dead friend, whom he had come to raise. Why did he weep, except to teach a human being to weep when oppressed by the weight of sins? Why did he groan and trouble himself, except because the faith of a person rightly displeased with himself ought in some way to groan in accusing evil works, so that the habit of sinning might yield to the force of repentance? And he said: “Where have you laid him?” You know that he was dead, and do you not know where he was buried? This too has a meaning. I dare not say, “He does not know.” For what does he not know? How do we prove this? Hear the Lord saying at the judgment: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII). I see you in my light, but I do not see you in that justice which I know. So here, as though not knowing such a sinner, he said: “Where have you laid him?” Such is the Lord’s voice in paradise after Adam sinned: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. XXIV). They said to him: “Lord, come and see.” What does “see” mean? Have mercy. For the Lord sees when he has mercy; hence it is said to him: “See my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. XXIV).

And Jesus wept. Then the Jews said: “See how he loved him.” What does “He loved him” mean? “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke V).

But some of them said: Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind, have caused this man not to die? What would it mean for him to have caused him not to die? What he is about to do is greater: he will raise him after death.

Jesus, groaning again within himself, came to the tomb. He groans in you as well, if you resolve to come back to life. [Col. 0780D] Every person who is oppressed by a very evil habit is told: “Come to the tomb.”

Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it. The dead man was beneath the stone; the guilty person is beneath the law. You know that the law given to the Jews was written on stone (Exod. XXXIV). All the guilty are beneath the law. Those who live rightly are not beneath the law. The law was not laid down for the righteous. What, then, does it mean to roll away the stone? It means to preach grace. For the Apostle Paul says that he is a minister of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. “The letter,” he says, “kills, but the Spirit gives life” (1 Cor. III). The killing letter is like a stone pressing down. “Remove the stone,” he says; remove the burden of the law; preach grace. Martha, the sister of the man who had died, said to him:

Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days. Jesus said: “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?” What does “You will see the glory of God” mean? It means that he raises even one who stinks and has been dead four days. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God; and where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Rom. III).

So they took away the stone. But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me, but I said this because of the people standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice, groaned, and wept. He cried out with a loud voice because a person whom the weight of an evil habit has thrust down rises with difficulty; nevertheless, he rises when inwardly given life by hidden grace. He rises after the loud voice. What happened? He cried out with a loud voice.

[Col. 0781B] Lazarus, come out! And immediately the one who had been dead came out, his feet and hands bound, and his face bound with a cloth. You marvel that he came out with his feet bound, yet do not marvel that one dead four days rose again? In both cases the Lord’s power was at work, not the dead man’s strength. He came out, still bound, still wrapped, yet he had already come outside. What does this signify? When you despise, you lie dead; and if you despise all that I have described, you lie buried. When you confess, you come out. For what is coming out except becoming manifest, as though emerging from hidden places? But God brings it about that you confess by crying out with a loud voice—that is, by calling with great grace. Therefore, when the dead man came out still bound, confessing and still guilty, so that his sins might be loosed, he said this to the attendants:

Release him and let him go. “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). He could have loosed the bonds, since he had raised the dead man; but for the sake of the unity of the holy Church of God and undivided charity, he says to the attendants, that is, to Christ’s disciples: “Release him,” because sins are not loosed without the unity of the Catholic faith and the ecclesial holiness of charity.

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus had done. Not all of the Jews who had gathered around Mary believed, but many did. Some of them—whether Jews who had gathered there or some of those who had believed—went to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus had done, either announcing it so that they too might believe, or rather betraying him so that they might rage against him. However it happened, and whoever brought this report to the Pharisees, what did they say?

The chief priests and Pharisees convened a council and said: “What are we to do?” Yet they did not say, “Let us believe.” These ruined men were more concerned with how they might harm him and destroy him than with how they might save themselves from perishing; nevertheless, they were afraid and were, as it were, seeking counsel. For they said:

“What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we leave him alone, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” They did not wish to lose temporal things, and they did not consider eternal life; thus they lost both. For after the Lord’s passion and glorification, the Romans did take away their place and nation, both by fighting and by transferring them elsewhere. And what was said elsewhere followed them: “The sons of this kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII). They feared that if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city of God and the temple against the Romans, because they thought that Christ’s teaching was directed against the temple itself and against their ancestral laws.

But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is better for us that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish.” He did not say this on his own, but, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied. Here he also taught that the Spirit of prophecy foretells future things even through wicked people. Yet the Evangelist attributed this to a divine mystery because he was high priest—that is, the chief priest.

It may be asked how he is called high priest “of that year,” when the Lord had established one high priest, with one succeeding him after his death. We should understand that, through ambitions and disputes among the Jews, it was later arranged that there would be several, serving in rotation from year to year. For this is said of Zechariah: “It happened, when he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood, that he was chosen by lot to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord” (Luke I). From this it is clear that there were several of them and that they had their turns. For only the high priest was permitted to offer incense; and by lot, several served during one year, with others succeeding them in another year, and from among them the one who would offer incense was chosen by lot. What, then, did Caiaphas prophesy?

That Jesus was going to die for the nation; and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad. The Evangelist added this. Caiaphas prophesied only concerning the Jewish nation, in which there were sheep of whom the Lord himself said: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). But the Evangelist knew that there were other sheep who were not of this fold, and that they too had to be brought in, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John X). These things were said according to predestination, because those who had not yet believed were not yet his sheep or the children of God.

From that day, therefore, they planned to kill him. Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples. This was not because his power had failed—for if he wished, he could have lived openly among the Jews and they could have done him no harm. But in the weakness of human life he gave his disciples an example, showing that it is not sinful for his faithful, who are his members, to withdraw from the eyes of their persecutors and to avoid the fury of criminals by hiding. Jesus knew that the time of his passion and of our redemption was drawing near. As the time approached in which he had determined to suffer, he also drew near to the place where he wished to complete the dispensation of that passion. [Col. 0783A] For the Evangelist says:

The Passover of the Jews was near. The Jews did not wish to have that festival stained with the Lord’s blood. On that festival the Lamb was slain who consecrated that same festival for you with his blood. There was a plot among the Jews to kill Jesus. He who had come from heaven to suffer wished to draw near to the place of his passion, because the hour of his passion was imminent.

Therefore many went up to Jerusalem from the surrounding region before the Passover, to purify themselves. The Jews did this according to the Lord’s command given through holy Moses in the law: on the festival that was the Passover, everyone was to gather from all around and be sanctified by celebrating that day. But that celebration was a shadow of things to come. [Col. 0783B] What is the “shadow of things to come”? It is the prophecy of Christ who was to come, the prophecy of the one who was to suffer for us on that day, so that the shadow might pass away and the light come; so that the sign might pass away and the reality be grasped. The Jews had the Passover in shadow; we have it in the light. Why else was it necessary for the Lord to command them, on that very festival, to slaughter a sheep (Exod. XII), unless it was because he was the one of whom it was prophesied: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII)? The doorposts of the Jews were marked with the blood of the slaughtered animal; our foreheads are marked with Christ’s blood. That sign—the sprinkling of the lamb’s blood—which kept the destroyer away from all those who were marked, was fulfilled in reality when Christ was killed for us, so that we need not fear the destroying devil if our heart receives the Savior.

[Col. 0783C] “They were looking for Jesus,” the Evangelist says, “and they spoke to one another as they stood in the temple: What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?” The Jews were looking for Jesus, but wrongly. They were looking for him so that they might kill him when he came to the festival. But let us seek him as we stand in the temple of God and persevere together in prayer; let us speak to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude, asking him to come to our festival, so that he may graciously enlighten us by his presence and himself sanctify us with his gifts.

The chief priests and Pharisees had also issued an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him. The Jews’ order, then, was sin. They sought to kill Christ, not to live in Christ. Let us seek to live in Christ, whom they sought to kill. They sought wrongly; let us seek rightly. For now is the time to seek the Lord, as the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. LV). Whoever wishes to find him merciful in judgment should seek him now in the service of humility and charity.

## CHAPTER XII
Knowing, therefore, that the Jews had conspired to kill him, the Lord did not flee the hands of those plotting against him. Rather, confident in the glory of the resurrection, he first came to Bethany, near the city of Jerusalem, where he had raised Lazarus from the dead; then also to Jerusalem, where he himself would suffer and rise from the dead. He came to Jerusalem so that he might die there; to Bethany, so that the raising of Lazarus might be more firmly impressed upon everyone’s memory, and so that the impious leaders, who did not fear to kill one who could raise the dead, might be confounded more and more and proved inexcusable—since they were moved neither by the benefits of the resurrection nor terrified by the divine power of him who raised the dead to withdraw their minds from their unjust slaughter.

Nor should we read casually why Jesus came to Bethany six days before Passover. The number six has great significance in the Holy Scriptures, and many works of our Lord are shown to have been accomplished in the perfect number six, because the number six, divided or combined according to its own proper parts, is evidently most perfect. It has three parts denominated within itself: one, two, and three. For its sixth part is one, its third part two, and its half three. One, two, and three are recognized as making six; and nothing else can be formed from these three parts joined together except six. Nor can the number six be divided into other parts than these three—one, two, and three.

It is well known that the Lord himself, the Creator of all things, completed the creatures of this world in six days, and that he made man on the sixth day (Gen. II). To liberate the man who had been ruined by the serpent’s deceit, the Son of God himself came to Bethany six days before Passover—the one through whom he had been created—so that the one who had been created on the sixth day might be liberated on the sixth day of the week. For I think no one is unaware that Christ suffered on the sixth day of the week.

Likewise, in the sixth month, when the archangel announced it, the holy Virgin is read to have conceived our same Redeemer through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (Luke I). Also at the sixth hour, in the fullness of his maturity, while sitting beside a well, he deigned to open to the Samaritan woman the streams of the divine fountain (John IV). It is also read that, in the sixth age of the world, the Creator himself came for the redemption of the world, according to the faith of sacred history.

These three parts—one, two, and three—from which, as we said, six is composed, likewise contain a certain mystery in the dispensation of human salvation. In the first period, under the law of nature, the holy fathers served God as though in a certain unity. In the second period, the law was added to nature, so that what evil habit had corrupted in nature, the law might reform in writing; and there were two: nature and law. In the third period, heavenly grace came through Jesus Christ, and there are three: nature, law, and grace.

Just as the law of nature did not destroy what was good, so grace did not abolish the law but fulfilled it, and restored nature to its former nobility. Yet nature and law could not be fulfilled without grace. Nor was free will given to man, or the commandment of the law given, in such a way that he would not need grace, as the Pelagian heresy maintains.

And lest the contrivers of accusations should say that Lazarus had been raised only in appearance, the Lord held a supper there, and Lazarus himself was one of those reclining with him. Thus, when they saw or heard him alive, speaking, eating, and familiarly conversing with his companions, they might at least recognize the power of the one who had raised him and receive grace.

Mystically, however, this supper of the Lord, at which Martha served and Lazarus reclined among the others, is the faith of the Church, which works through love. At this supper Martha serves when every faithful soul offers the Lord the service of its devotion. Lazarus becomes one of those reclining with the Lord when those who, after the death of their sins, have been raised to righteousness are nourished by the gifts of heavenly grace, rejoicing in the presence of the Truth together with those who have remained in their righteousness, penitents together with the innocent.

And appropriately this same supper is celebrated in Bethany, which is a city on the side of the Mount of Olives and is interpreted as “House of Obedience.” For the Church is the house of obedience, faithfully obeying the Lord’s commands. It is also the city set upon the mountain of mercy, which can never be hidden (Matt. V). Constructed from the side of its Redeemer—that is, imbued with the water of cleansing and the blood of sanctification that came forth from the side of him who died for it—it is founded from his side.

There also, Mary, Lazarus’s other sister, as a sign of great love, received a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard, as the following words of the Gospel show, and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair. This signifies not only an act of devotion but also the pious service rendered to God by other faithful souls.

Mary received a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard. What, then, is expressed by a pound of ointment except the perfection of righteousness? This ointment is said to have been made from genuine nard. What is suggested by ointment except the good fragrance of reputation? And this ointment was made from genuine nard—that is, faithful nard; for Greek *pistis* (πίστις) is called *fides* in Latin, “faith.” Without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI), nor can a good reputation exist without the Catholic faith.

O man, anoint Jesus’ feet by living well; follow the Lord’s footsteps, and wipe them with your hair. What is superfluous for you is necessary for the Lord’s feet—that is, for the least members of the Church, concerning whom the Lord will say at the end: “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV).

The house was filled with the fragrance—that is, the Church was filled with the good reputation of a religious life; for a good fragrance is a good life. Hear the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ,” he says, “in every place” (II Cor. II). And in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment.” Again: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave its fragrance” (Song I). Here it is plainly shown what Mary did once, and typologically what the whole Church and every perfect soul continually do.

Then one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” Woe to the impious betrayer! Woe to his accomplices in wickedness, who even now persecute Christ’s members and do not cease to envy their neighbors the reputation for virtue that they themselves do not deserve to possess.

Indeed, we might suppose that Judas had said this out of concern for the poor; but the truthful witness who knew his mind exposes him, saying:

“He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and, having the money box, he used to carry what was put into it” (John XII).

Judas did not perish at the moment when, corrupted by money, he betrayed the Lord. He was already lost when he followed the Lord. Having the Lord’s money box, he carried what was placed in it for the service of the poor, though with his faithless mind he was accustomed to steal it.

Seeing his heart already polluted by the filth of greed and foreseeing that it would be polluted by the worse filth of betrayal, the Lord entrusted to his keeping whatever they had in their purses. He allowed him to do with it whatever he wished, so that either the honor bestowed upon him or the memory of the money entrusted to him might recall his mind from selling the Lord.

But because the miser is always in want, and the wicked faithless man never remembers benefits, Judas, from the theft of the money he carried, proceeded to the betrayal of the Lord, who had entrusted money to him for safekeeping.

Then Jesus said: “Leave her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.”

As though Judas had asked innocently, the Lord explained simply and gently what Mary’s service concerned: namely, that he was going to die and would be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore Mary, who, although she greatly desired it, would not be able to reach the time of anointing his dead body, was granted the opportunity to offer while he was still alive the service that, after his death, she would be unable to offer because the resurrection would come swiftly.

Accordingly, Mark rightly bears witness that the Lord said of her: “She has done what she could; she has anticipated anointing my body” (Mark XIV). She could not touch him once he was dead; she did only what she could. She anticipated offering the service of burial while he was still alive.

[Col. 0786C] “For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.”

Here, too, with the restraint of great patience, the Lord does not accuse Judas of greed or of speaking about money without concern for the poor. Rather, he demonstrates by reason that those who, while he was living among human beings, ministered to him from their resources were not to be blamed, since he himself would remain bodily with the Church for only a short time, whereas the poor to whom alms could be given would always be present in it.

A large crowd of Jews therefore learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. Curiosity, not love, brought them to Jesus. But let us, dearest brothers, reverse the matter: if we know where Jesus is, where he makes his dwelling, where he finds a Bethany—that is, a house of the obedient soul—in which to dwell, let us come there through contemplation, not merely because of the man whom he raised from the death of the soul and granted spiritual life, but so that, by imitating the man’s good life, we may thereby deserve to reach the vision of Jesus, since we know with certainty where Jesus is.

For he rose after death and ascended into heaven, where he has an everlasting dwelling. This is the true Bethany, namely, the heavenly city, which no one can enter except the obedient.

But the chief priests devised plans to kill Lazarus as well, because many of the Jews were leaving on his account and believing in Jesus. O blind cunning of the blind—to wish to kill one who had been raised, as though the one who could raise the dead could not raise someone killed! Indeed, he taught that he could do both: he raised Lazarus, who was dead, and himself, who had been killed.

After the Lord had raised the four-day-old dead man while the Jews were astonished—some of them believing in envy, others perishing in envy—and after Jesus had reclined in the house, with Lazarus, who had been raised from the dead, also reclining, and after the ointment had been poured over his feet, so that the house was filled with its fragrance, matters concerning which we have discussed as much as we could above, we must now consider what happened before the Lord’s Passion. For the evangelist says:

“On the next day, the great crowd that had come for the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches and went out to meet him, crying: ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.’”

The palm branches signify praises and victory: the Lord was going to conquer death by dying and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the cross.

“Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” It should certainly be noted that “Hosanna” is a Hebrew compound word, partly altered and partly intact. Among them, “save,” or “make safe,” is called *hosi*; *anna* is an interjection of one making supplication, just as among the Latins *heu* is the interjection of one grieving and *papae* the interjection of one expressing wonder.

In the Psalm where the Seventy Translators rendered, “O Lord, save me” (Ps. CXVIII), the Hebrew is written: *hosanna anna Adonai*. Our translator Jerome, explaining it more carefully, rendered it: “I beseech you, Lord; save, I beseech you.” The word of supplication itself has the same meaning.

Thus *hosanna* signifies “Save, I beseech you.” The letter or vowel that terminates the first word is elided when it is joined to the following word, which begins with the vowel-letter aleph: the complete form is *hosi*, but through the force of the vowel-letter aleph, with which the following word *anna* begins, the two are joined. Poets call this *synaloepha* when scanning verses, although in scanning they pass over the written letter. In the word *hosanna*, however, the letter *yod* is not even written, but, while the sense of the speakers is preserved, it is entirely omitted.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” should be understood as meaning “in the name of the Lord God the Father,” although it can also be understood as “in his own name,” since he himself is also Lord. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord.” His own words direct our understanding better. He says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V).

Christ is the teacher of humility. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II). He therefore does not lose his divinity when he teaches us humility. In the former respect he is equal to the Father; in the latter he is like us. In that by which he is equal to the Father, he created us so that we might exist. In that by which he is like us, he redeemed us so that we might not perish.

The crowd addressed these praises to him: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” The leaders of the Jews could not endure this voice because such a great multitude was proclaiming Christ as its king. But what was it for the Lord to be King of Israel, when the King of the ages became King of human beings?

Christ is not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with iron, or defeat enemies. He is King of Israel because he rules the mind, provides for it eternally, and leads believers, those who hope and love, into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, for the Son of God, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, to will to be King of Israel is condescension, not promotion; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power. He who was called the King of the Jews is Lord of the angels in heaven.

And Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it. This is stated briefly here; how it happened is read in full in the other evangelists. A prophetic testimony is applied to this event, so that it might become clear that the great leaders of the Jews did not understand the one in whom what they read was being fulfilled. Jesus therefore found a young donkey and sat upon it.

As it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your King will come, sitting upon a donkey’s colt.”

This daughter of Zion, to whom these things are divinely spoken, was among those sheep who heard the shepherd’s voice. She was among that multitude which praised the Lord who was coming with such devotion and escorted him in such a great procession. To her it was said: “Do not fear. Recognize the one whom you praise, and do not tremble when he speaks, because that blood will be poured out through which your sin will be erased and your life redeemed.”

Understand the colt of the donkey, on which no one had sat—which is found in the other evangelists—to signify the Gentile people, who had not received the Lord’s law. The donkey itself, since both animals were brought to the Lord, signifies the people who came from the people of Israel—not untamed, but a people that recognized the Lord’s manger.

His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when he was glorified—that is, when he showed the power of his resurrection—they remembered that these things had been written about him. Recalling, in accordance with Scripture, what had been fulfilled before the Passion or during the Lord’s Passion, they found this also: that, according to the words of the prophets, he would sit upon a donkey’s colt.

The crowd that was with him testified that he had called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead. For this reason the crowd also went out to meet him: they had heard that he had performed this sign.

The Pharisees therefore said to one another: “You see that we are accomplishing nothing. Look, the whole world has gone after him.” One crowd troubled another. Why are you envious, blind crowd, because the world is following him through whom the world was made?

Now there were some Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship at the feast. These approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip then told Jesus.

Let us see what the Lord answered them. The Jews wanted to kill him; the Gentiles wanted to see him. Yet those who were crying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel,” were also Jews. Here are those from the circumcision, and these from the uncircumcision, like rams coming from opposite directions and converging in the one faith of Christ with the kiss of peace. Let us therefore hear the voice of the cornerstone.

Jesus, the evangelist says, answered them: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Someone might perhaps think that he called himself glorified for this reason: because the Gentiles wanted to see him. It is not so. Rather, he saw that these Gentiles would believe in him after his Passion and resurrection among all the nations, because, as the Apostle says, “blindness in part has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Rom. XI).

Taking occasion, therefore, from these Gentiles who desired to see him, he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles and declares that the hour of his glorification is already at hand—the glorification by which, once it had taken place in heaven, the Gentiles would believe. Hence it was foretold: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. LVI). This is the fullness of the Gentiles of which the Apostle says: “Blindness in part has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Rom. XI).

But the humility of the Passion had to precede the height of glorification. Therefore he continued:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

By this he was saying that he himself would be put to death and multiplied: put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, multiplied through the faith of all peoples.

Now, exhorting them to follow the footsteps of his Passion, he says:

“He who loves his life will lose it.”

This can be understood in two ways. “He who loves will lose”—that is, if you love, lose; if you desire to hold on to life in Christ, do not fear to die for Christ.

It can also be understood in another way: “He who loves his life will lose it.” Do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life. The latter seems more consistent with the Gospel sense. For it continues:

“And he who hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life.”

Therefore, in the earlier statement, “he who loves” is understood to mean “he who loves in this world,” and he will indeed lose it; but he who hates it—in this world—will preserve it for eternal life.

Great and astonishing is the statement: how a person’s love for his life causes him to perish, while hatred prevents him from perishing. If you have loved badly, then you have hated; if you have hated rightly, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving.

Here the word “soul” signifies the present life, or even the delight of this life. That delight must be lost so that you may joyfully find in the kingdom of God the will you have valiantly conquered in this world. For the holy martyrs hated this present life for Christ’s name, preferring to lose this present life rather than deny Christ. They fulfilled what follows:

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

What does “let him follow me” mean except “let him imitate me”? For the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). Behold what was said:

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

And with what result, what recompense, what reward?

“And where I am,” he says, “there also will my servant be.”

The reward of love, and the payment for the work by which Christ is served, is to be with the one whom one serves. For where can it be well without him? Or how can it be bad with him? Hear this more clearly:

“And if anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

With what honor, except that he may be with the Son? For what he said above—“Where I am, there also will my servant be”—he explains when he says, “My Father will honor him.” What greater honor can one adopted by God receive than to be where the Only-Begotten is—not made equal to the divinity, but joined to eternity?

What it means to serve Christ, for which such a great reward is promised, must be considered. “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” He wished this to be understood as though he had said: “If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me.”

Those therefore serve Jesus Christ who do not seek their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. For “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own, as it is written elsewhere: “He who says he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John II).

Even if someone offers bread to a hungry person, he ought to act from mercy, not ostentation, seeking nothing else there except the good work; his left hand should not know what his right hand is doing—that is, the intention of greed must be separated from the work of charity. To such a person it is said: “When you did it for one of my least ones, you did it for me.”

Nor are only those things that pertain to bodily mercy good. When someone performs every work for Christ’s sake, then the works are good, because “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” The believer is a servant of Christ even to that great work of love, which is to lay down one’s life for the brothers. For to lay down one’s life for them is also to lay it down for Christ, since he will say concerning his members: “When you did it for these, you did it for me” (Rom. X).

Concerning such a work he also deigned to make and call himself a servant, when he said: “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life for many” (Matt. XX). Therefore each person is a servant of Christ in the same respect in which Christ is a servant.

The Father honors one who serves Christ with that great honor: that he may be with his Son, and that his faith may never fail. In general he says of everyone: “If anyone serves me.” For whoever acts well serves Christ.

Therefore, according to his own measure, let each person serve Christ by living well, giving alms, and preaching his name and teaching to as many as he can. Whoever exhorts those living well to persevere in living well serves Christ. Whoever humbly obeys one who admonishes him serves Christ. And whoever faithfully serves Christ in this age will happily reign with Christ in the age to come.

When the Lord Jesus had foretold his Passion in the grain of mustard and urged his servants to follow him, he again adapted his feeling to our weakness and said:

“Now my soul is troubled.”

Why is your soul troubled, Lord Jesus? Did you not for this reason take a soul and become a complete human being, so that you might suffer in it? I see you, Lord, transferring our weakness into yourself and taking our cause upon yourself.

You are troubled because you wished to be troubled, just as you were born because you wished to be born. For shortly before, when you raised Lazarus, it was said of you: “He troubled himself.” By these words he seized us from our weakness and brought us to his strength.

It is the voice of the Lord’s strength when he says: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” It is the voice of our weakness when he says: “Now my soul is troubled.”

O Lord, mediator, God above us and human being for our sake, I recognize your mercy. For by your will, through your great love, you are troubled, and in doing so you console many members of your body who are troubled by the necessity of their weakness, so that they may not perish in despair.

Hear, therefore, soldier of Christ, what he adds next. Having said, “Now my soul is troubled,” he says:

“Father, save me from this hour; but for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

He taught you what to think, what to say, whom to invoke, in whom to hope, and whose certain and divine will you should place before your own weak human will. Do not therefore think that he has failed from on high because he wishes to look after you from below.

He also deigned to be tempted by the devil (Matt. IV), by whom he certainly would not have been tempted if he had not wished it. He answered the devil with the words that you ought to answer in temptations. He was tempted, but he was not endangered, so that he might teach you, when endangered in temptation, to answer the tempter and not follow after the tempter, but escape from the danger of temptation.

Just as he said here, “Now my soul is troubled,” so also he says there: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” And: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). He assumed the weakness of human beings in order to teach the sorrowful and troubled person to say what follows: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father.”

Thus the human being is directed from human things to divine things when the divine will is placed before the human will. What else is “Glorify your name” except “in his Passion and resurrection”? What else, then, does it mean except that the Father glorifies the Son, who also glorifies his name in the similar sufferings of his servants?

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

“I have glorified it” before I made the world; “and I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead and ascends into heaven.

It can also be understood in another way: “I have glorified it” when he was born of a virgin (Matt. I); when he was worshiped by the Magi, guided from heaven by a star; when he was recognized by the saints who were filled with the Holy Spirit (Matt. II); when he was declared by the Spirit descending in the form of a dove and manifested by the voice sounding from heaven (Matt. III); when he was transfigured on the mountain (Matt. XVII); when he performed many miracles; when he healed and cleansed many; when he fed such a great multitude from a few loaves (Matt. XIV); when he commanded the winds and waves; and when he raised the dead (Luke VIII).

“And I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead (John XI), when death will no longer rule over him (Rom. VI), and when “God will be exalted above the heavens and his glory over all the earth” (Ps. LVI).

The crowd that stood there and heard this said that thunder had occurred. Others said: “An angel has spoken to him.”

Jesus answered and said: “This voice came not for my sake but for yours.”

Here he shows that on that occasion what he already knew was not revealed to him, but to those to whom it was necessary that it be revealed. And just as that voice was made by divine action not for his sake but for theirs, so his soul was troubled by his will not for his sake but for the sake of others.

“Now is the judgment of the world.”

We do not think that this refers to the future judgment that will take place at the end of the world, when the good and the evil will be separated by an eternal division. Rather, it refers to the judgment that customarily takes place daily in the holy Church of God.

The devil possessed the human race and held the simple liable by the handwriting of sins; he ruled in the hearts of unbelievers. By abandoning the Creator, he deceived and dragged them captive to the worship of the creature.

But through faith in Christ, which was confirmed by his death and resurrection, and through his blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the devil’s dominion, joined to the body of Christ, and, under so great a head, his faithful members are given life by one Spirit.

This is what he called the judgment: this discrimination, this expulsion of the devil from those whom he had redeemed. Finally, observe what he says. As though we were asking what was meant by “Now is the judgment of the world,” he explains it, saying:

“Now the prince of this world will be cast out.”

We have heard what sort of judgment he said it was. It is therefore not the judgment that will come at the end, when the living and the dead will be judged, some separated to the left and others to the right. It is the judgment by which the prince of this world will be cast out.

How, then, was he inside, and where did he say he would be cast out? “Now,” he says, “the prince of this world will be cast out.” This must be understood as referring to what is now taking place, not merely to what he foresaw would happen afterward on the last day.

The Lord knew that after his Passion and glorification many peoples throughout the world would believe, and that the devil, who was inside their hearts, would be cast out when he was renounced through faith. Therefore he says: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.”

But someone may say: “Was he not cast out from the hearts of the patriarchs, prophets, and ancient righteous people?” Certainly he was cast out. How, then, was it said, “Now he will be cast out”? How can we understand it except in this way: what was then accomplished in a very few people was now foretold as about to be accomplished in many and great peoples?

The statement, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII), can present a similar question and receive a similar solution. The prophets did not foretell the future without the Holy Spirit (I Pet. I). Nor did the elder Simeon and the widow Anna recognize the infant Lord in the Holy Spirit (Luke II)? Nor did Zechariah and Elizabeth, through the Holy Spirit, prophesy such great things about him who had not yet been born but had already been conceived (Luke I)?

But “the Spirit had not yet been given” means that the abundance of spiritual grace had not yet been given by which the assembled believers would speak in all languages, and thus the future Church would be foretold in the languages of all nations; by which peoples would be gathered, sins would be forgiven far and wide, and thousands upon thousands would be reconciled to God.

What, then, someone may ask, since the devil is cast out from the hearts of believers, does he no longer tempt any of the faithful? On the contrary, he does not cease tempting them. But it is one thing to reign within and another to attack from outside. It is one thing to wound and another to kill.

Yet if he wounds, the one who heals is present. For just as it was said to those engaged in struggle, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin” (I John II), so those who are wounded hear what follows: “And if you sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (ibid.).

For what do we pray when we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI), except that our wounds may be healed? And what else do we ask when we say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” except that the one who lies in wait may not break in from outside—or indeed that no one may break in upon us from any side—nor deceive us by any fraud or overthrow us by any devices?

When he does not possess the place of the heart where faith dwells, he has been cast out. Yet “unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). Do not therefore presume on yourselves, if you do not wish to call the devil, once cast out, back inside.

Let us not imagine, however, that the devil is called “the prince of the world” in such a way that he can rule heaven and earth. Rather, the wicked people spread throughout the whole world are called “the world,” just as a house is named from those who inhabit it. We say that a house is good or a house is bad not when we criticize or praise the building of its walls and roof, but the conduct of the good or wicked people themselves.

Thus it is said: “The prince of this world,” that is, the prince of wicked people who dwell in the world. The good people who are likewise spread throughout the whole world are also called “the world.” Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. III). These are the people from whose hearts the prince of the world will be cast out.

When he had said, “Now the prince of this world will be cast out,” he continued:

“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things after me.”

What are “all things” except those from whom he is cast out? He did not say “all people” but “all things.” For not everyone has faith. He therefore did not refer this to the totality of human beings but to the integrity of the creature—that is, spirit, soul, and body; what we understand, what we see, and what we are as visible and tangible beings.

For the one who said, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI), draws all things after him.

Or, if “all things” is understood as human beings themselves, we may say that all those predestined for salvation are meant, of whom he said that nothing would perish when he spoke above about his sheep.

Or certainly “all kinds of human beings” may be intended: people of every language, every rank of honor, every variety of intelligence, every profession of lawful and useful arts, and whatever else can be named according to the countless differences by which human beings differ from one another through sins alone—from the highest to the lowest, from the king to the beggar. “I will draw all things after me,” he says, so that he may be their head and they his members.

But when he says, “If I am lifted up from the earth,” this means “when I have been lifted up.” He does not doubt that what he came to fulfill will happen.

Let this be related to what he said above: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” For what else did he call his exaltation than his Passion on the cross? The evangelist himself did not pass over this. He continued, saying: “He said this to indicate by what kind of death he was going to die.”

The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? Who is this?”

They had retained in memory that the Lord repeatedly said that he was the Son of Man. For in this passage he did not say, “If the Son of Man is lifted up from the earth,” but, as he had said above when the Gentiles who desired to see him were announced: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Keeping this in mind, and understanding his present statement—“When I am lifted up from the earth”—as referring to the death of the cross, they asked him and said:

We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever; and how then do you say, “The Son of Man must be lifted up”? For if he is the Christ, they say, he remains forever; if he remains forever, how will he be lifted up from the earth—that is, how will he die through the passion of the cross? [Col. 0794C] For they understood that he had said this, which they were planning to do. Thus it was not wisdom infused from above that opened to them the obscurity of these words, but a conscience goaded by them.

Therefore Jesus said to them: “The light is still with you for a little while. This is why you will understand that Christ remains forever.

“Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you. Walk; draw near; understand everything: both that Christ would die and that he would live forever, that he would pour out the blood by which he would redeem, and that he would ascend to the heights by which he would lead you there. Darkness will overtake you if you believe in Christ’s eternity in such a way that you deny in him the humility of death.

“And whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going.” Thus he can stumble against “the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense” (Rom. IX), which the Lord was to the blind Jews, just as, for believers, “the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Matt. XXI). For this reason they disdained believing in Christ: their impiety despised him as dead and mocked him as slain. Yet this was precisely the death of the grain that was to multiply, and the lifting up of him who draws all things after himself.

“While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.” When you hear something true, believe in the truth. It should be noted that he does not say, “See the light,” but “Believe in the light,” which is to be seen after the journey of this life. For, as has been said, he calls himself the light in which one must believe, thereby signifying his own divinity.

[Col. 0795A] Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them. He did not hide from those who had begun to believe and love, nor from those who had come to meet him with palm branches and praises, but from those who saw and envied, because they did not truly see, but, blinded against that stone, stumbled over it. When Jesus therefore hid himself from those who desired to kill him—a matter about which, because of your forgetfulness, you must often be reminded—he provided for our weakness; he did not detract from his own power. After the Lord Christ had foretold his passion in the lifting up of the cross, and the Jews, understanding this, had asked how he could say that he would die, when they had heard from the Law that Christ remains forever, the evangelist then continued and said:

“Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, when he said, ‘Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’”

He used “who” because of the rarity of believers: what the holy prophets heard from God and proclaimed among the people was believed by very few. In saying, “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” he sufficiently shows that the arm of the Lord is the name given to the Son of God—not because God the Father is defined by the form of human flesh, with the Son clinging to him as a bodily limb, but because all things were made through him; therefore he is called the arm of the Lord.

Just as your arm is that by which you work, so God’s Word is called the arm of God, because he worked the world through the Word. Why does a human being extend his arm in order to accomplish something, unless it is because what he has said does not immediately come to pass? But if he possessed such power that what he said came to be without that movement of the body, his word would be his arm. The Lord Jesus, however, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, is no member of the Father’s body; nor is he a word that can be conceived, uttered, or pass away. For when all things were made through him, “the Word was God” (John I).

The one whom the evangelist called the Word who was with God, the prophet called the arm of the Lord. When we hear “the arm of the Lord,” let us recognize Christ as the power and wisdom of God, through whom all things were made. “You have made all things in wisdom,” says the Psalmist (Ps. CIII). He is not the same person as the Father, but he and the Father are one; he is equal to the Father, wholly present everywhere.

[Col. 0795D] Here a difficult question arises: what evil had the Jews done, or what was their guilt, that they did not believe, if it was necessary that the word of the prophet Isaiah should be fulfilled, when he said, “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII)?

We answer that God, who foreknew the future, foretold through the prophet what would happen, but did not cause it to happen. God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows the future sins of human beings. He foreknew their sins—not his own, nor those of anyone else, but theirs. Therefore, if what he foreknew as theirs is not theirs, he did not truly foreknow it. But because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, those whom God foreknew would sin are undoubtedly not others but the very ones who sin.

Thus the Jews committed the sin which God did not compel them to commit—he who takes no pleasure in sin—but he foretold that they would commit it, because nothing is hidden from him. Yet the words of the Gospel that follow press the matter and make the question more profound. For it is said here as though the cause of their unbelief were that someone blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. This is said altogether of God, not of the devil.

We must therefore seek the reason why the prophet said that God had done this; and, with God granting it, we shall explain it as far as we can. They could not believe because the prophet had foretold it, because God had foreknown that it would happen. But if I am asked why they could not believe, I answer: because they were unwilling. God foresaw their evil will and foretold it through the prophet—he from whom the future cannot be hidden—and he foresaw that this blindness or hardening would be deserved by their evil will.

For God blinds and hardens in this way: by abandoning and not assisting. He does this according to a judgment hidden from us, but never unjust. When the Apostle Paul was treating this very difficult question, he said, “Is there injustice with God? Certainly not” (Rom. IX). If, then, there is no injustice with God—whether when he assists or when he does not assist—he acts justly, because he does everything not arbitrarily but by judgment. And if the judgments of the saints are just, how much more just are those of God, who sanctifies and justifies?

They are therefore just, but hidden. Consequently, when questions of this kind arise—why one person is judged in one way and another in another; why one is blinded when God abandons him, while another is enlightened when God assists him—let us not arrogate to ourselves judgment concerning the judgment of so great a Judge. Rather, trembling, let us cry out with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI).

Concerning such questions and judgments of God, let us listen to Scripture admonishing us and saying: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Eccli. III). Let us therefore enter upon the way of faith and hold to it with utmost perseverance. It leads to the king’s chamber, in which all the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Col. II).

For the Lord Jesus Christ did not envy his great and especially chosen disciples when he said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI). We must walk; we must advance; we must grow, so that our hearts may become capable of those things which we cannot yet contain. And if the final day finds us making progress, there we shall learn what we could not learn here.

It is therefore no wonder that those could not believe whose will was so proud that, “being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own” (Rom. X), as the Apostle says of them, they refused to submit to God’s righteousness. Since they were swollen with pride not from faith but as though from works, they were blinded by their very fear and stumbled against the stone of stumbling.

Thus it was said that they “could not,” where we must understand that they “were unwilling,” just as it is said of the Lord our God: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (II Tim. II). As it is a praise of the divine will that he wished them to be saved, so the fact that they could not believe is the fault of the human will.

God foreknew this concerning the Jews who were blinded and hardened, and the prophet foretold it in God’s spirit. But as for what he added, “And let them turn, and I will heal them,” whether this should be understood with the implied meaning “so that they may not turn,” the sentence connected with it above makes clear, where it says: “So that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart”; for here too the meaning is “so that they may not understand.”

For conversion itself comes from his grace, to whom it is said: “God of hosts, convert us” (Ps. LXXIX). Or should this too be understood as having been done through the mercy of heavenly medicine? They possessed a perverse and proud will and wished to establish their own righteousness; therefore they were abandoned and blinded for this purpose—blinded, I say, so that they would stumble against the stone of stumbling, and their faces would be filled with disgrace, and, thus humbled, they would seek the name of the Lord, seeking not their own righteousness, by which the proud person is puffed up, but the righteousness of God, by which the ungodly person is justified.

This benefited many of them, who, pierced by remorse for their crime, afterward believed in Christ. For them he himself had also prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

It follows:

“Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.”

Observe how the evangelist censured and condemned certain people whom he nevertheless said had believed in him. If they had advanced in this beginning of faith, they would, as they progressed, have overcome their love of human glory—just as the Apostle had overcome it, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

For this reason the Lord himself also fixed his cross—where the madness of proud impiety had mocked him—upon the foreheads of those who would believe in him, where the seat of shame is, in a certain sense, so that faith would not be ashamed of his name, and so that they would love the glory of God more than that of human beings.

While the Lord Jesus Christ was speaking among the Jews and performing so many miraculous signs, some believed, predestined to eternal life, whom he also called his sheep. Others did not believe and could not believe, because they had been blinded by God’s hidden, though not unjust, judgment. Others believed openly and came to meet him with palm branches; still others believed secretly but, because of the Pharisees, did not confess it. The evangelist censured these when he said: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.”

The glory of God is to confess Christ publicly, as the holy martyrs did. Concerning them the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father.” Whoever confesses Christ with a confession of praise will be confessed—that is, praised—by Christ before God the Father.

With these matters thus established, and with his passion already drawing near:

Jesus cried out and said: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.”

He had already said in another place: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John VII). There we understood that by “my teaching” he meant the word of the Father, which he himself is; and that by saying, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me,” he signified that he was not from himself but had one from whom he was.

The Son is God from God, the Father’s Son; but the Father is not God from God, but God, the Father of the Son. Now, when he says, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me,” how are we to understand this except that he appeared as a human being to human beings while God remained hidden? And lest they should think that he was merely what they saw, however great and excellent that might be, he wished to be believed to be such and so great as the Father is.

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “does not believe in me”—that is, merely in what he sees—but in him who sent me, that is, in the Father. Hence he must believe that the Father has a Son; and, while believing that the Father is eternal, he must also believe that he has a Son coeternal and consubstantial with him.

For this reason he said, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,” because he did not wish everything believed about Christ to be believed according to his humanity. He believes in me rightly who, according to what he sees of me, does not believe merely in me, but, according to what he believes in me, believes me to be equal to the Father.

And lest anyone should think that he wished the Father to be understood as the father of many sons regenerated by grace, rather than as the Father of the only Word who is equal to him, he immediately added:

“And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.”

So great is the unity between him and me that whoever sees me sees him who sent me. This vision must be understood as intellectual, not bodily. For now it belongs to the praise of the saints; after the day of the final resurrection it will exist in the reality of eternal blessedness, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

Let us attend to the rest. “I have come into the world as light, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.”

In another place he said to his disciples: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Yet he did not say, “You have come into the world as light, so that everyone who believes in you may not remain in darkness.” I affirm that this cannot be found anywhere in my reading. All the saints, therefore, are lights; but they are enlightened by believing in him. If anyone withdraws from him, that person will become darkened. The light that enlightens, however, cannot withdraw from itself, because it is altogether unchangeable.

When he says, “Everyone who believes in me will not remain in darkness,” he sufficiently makes clear that all have found themselves in darkness. But, so that they may not remain in the darkness in which they were found, they must believe in the light that came into this world, because through it the world was made.

“And if anyone hears my words,” he says, “and does not keep them, I do not judge him.” Hear how the Son says, “I do not judge him,” when elsewhere he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V)—unless we are to understand what follows:

[Col. 0799A] “For I did not come,” he says, “to judge the world, but to save the world.”

Now, therefore, is the time of mercy; afterward will be the time of judgment. For he says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C).

But concerning that final future judgment itself, see what he says:

“Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words has one who judges him. The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.”

He does not say, “Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words, I do not judge him on the last day.” For the Son of God came to save, not to judge. Therefore he said, “I do not judge him”—that is, now, in the present—but “I judge him on the last day.”

After saying, “Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words has one who judges him,” he added cautiously, as those who were waiting to learn who that judge would be: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.” He made it sufficiently clear that he himself would judge on the last day. For he spoke of himself, announced himself, and established himself as the door through which he himself, as shepherd, would enter to the sheep.

Those who did not hear will therefore be judged in one way, and those who heard and despised will be judged in another. “Those who have sinned without the law,” says the Apostle, “will also perish without the law; and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. II).

“For I,” he says, “have not spoken from myself.”

For this reason he says that he did not speak from himself. We have often said that the Son is not from himself but from the Father; therefore he added:

“But the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak.”

The Father does not speak to the Son through a spatial interval, or by the utterance of syllables, or by vocal sound, so that the Son might hear the Father’s command, as a human son ordinarily hears from a human father what his father commands him. Rather, the only-begotten Son is the Word of the Father and the Wisdom of the Father; in him are all the Father’s commandments.

The Son did not at some point fail to know the Father’s command, so that he would have needed to receive in time what he had not possessed—to receive it by being born, with the Father giving him by generation what he did not have. Rather, the Father begot him possessing life, as he said above: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V)—that is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

Here he says similarly: “As he gave me a commandment.” And because that eternal birth never was not, the Son, who is life, and who, just as he is eternal life, is eternal life by being born, likewise possesses the commandment—not that the Father gave what the Son did not have, but, as I have said, in the Father’s wisdom, which is the Father’s Word, all the Father’s commandments are present.

For he continues:

“And I know that his commandment is eternal life.”

If the Father’s commandment is eternal life, what else is meant than: “I am the Father’s commandment”? Accordingly, so too with what he adds and says:

“What I speak, therefore, I speak just as the Father has told me.”

We must not understand “he has told me” as though he spoke to the one Word through words, or as though God needed words in speaking to God. The Father spoke the Word to the Son, just as he gave life to the Son—not something the Son did not know or possess, but the Son himself was that Word.

What, then, does “As he has told me, so I speak” mean, except “I speak the Word”? The Father spoke as the Truthful One; the Son speaks as the Truth. The Truthful One begot Truth. What, then, would he say to the Truth? The Truth was not imperfect, so that something true could be added to it.

The one who begot Truth spoke to the Truth. The Truth itself therefore speaks as it was told, but to those who understand, in the manner in which it was born. Yet so that human beings might believe what they are not yet able to understand, words sounded from the mouth of flesh and passed away. The sounds, flying past, resounded after completing the brief periods of their temporal existence; but the realities of which those sounds were signs were, in a certain way, drawn into the memory of those who heard them and reached even us through written letters, which are visible signs.

The Truth does not speak in this way. It speaks inwardly to understanding minds; without sound it instructs; with an intelligible voice it fills them. Whoever, therefore, can see in it the eternity of its birth hears it speaking in the manner in which the Father told it what it should speak.

He has stirred us to a great desire for the inner sweetness of the Truth. Let us grasp it as we grow; let us grow as we walk; let us walk as we advance, so that we may be able to arrive through him himself at him himself, with him himself leading us and promising us: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV)—the way for those who seek, the truth for those who find, and the life for those who remain.

## CHAPTER XIII

When the evangelist John was about to write about that memorable ministry of the Lord, in which he graciously washed the feet of his disciples at Passover, before he went to his passion, he first took care to reveal what the name “Passover” mystically signified, beginning in this way:

“Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.”

Passover is interpreted as “passing over” or “transition.” The name is ancient, deriving from the fact that the Lord passed through Egypt at that time, striking down the firstborn of Egypt and liberating the children of Israel, and from the fact that the children of Israel themselves passed over that night from Egyptian slavery so that they might come to the land of the inheritance and peace formerly promised to them (Exod. XII).

Mystically, however, it signifies that at that time the Lord would pass from this world to the Father, and that the faithful, following his example, must abandon temporal desires and the slavery of vices and pass, through continual devotion to the virtues, toward the promise of the heavenly homeland.

The evangelist beautifully indicates how Jesus passed from this world to the Father when he says: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (I Cor. V)—that is, he loved them so greatly that, through that very love, he brought his bodily life to an end for a time, soon to pass from death to life, from this world to the Father.

“For no one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). Thus rightly both transitions—the legal and the evangelical—were consecrated by blood: the former by the blood of the paschal lamb, the latter by the blood of him concerning whom the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

The latter was accomplished by blood poured out upon the cross; the former by blood sprinkled in the form of a cross in the middle of the doorway, upon the lintel, and on the doorposts.

Passover is not, as some suppose, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one. Nevertheless, a very appropriate correspondence between the two languages appears in this name. Because he suffers, he is called πάσχη in Greek; therefore Passover has been thought to signify suffering, or the name has been understood as deriving from passion.

In its own language, that is, Hebrew, Passover means “passing over,” because the people of God first celebrated Passover when, fleeing from Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea.
