Thus this name, Passover, which in Latin, as I have said, is called “passing over,” is interpreted for us by the blessed evangelist: “Before the feast day of Passover,” he says, “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, so that he might pass from this world to the Father.”

There is Passover; there is passing over. From where, and to where? From this world, certainly, to the Father. Hope was given to the members in the Head that they would undoubtedly follow him as he passed over.

What, then, of unbelievers, who are alienated from this Head and from his body? Do they not also pass over, since they do not remain? They certainly pass over too. But it is one thing to pass from the world, another to pass along with the world; one thing to pass to the Father, another to pass to the enemy.

The Egyptians also passed over; they did not remain behind in their pursuit. Yet they did not pass through the sea to a kingdom, but through the sea to destruction (Exod. XIV).

Knowing, therefore, that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, Jesus, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end—that is, so that they too might pass from this world, where they were, to their Head, who had passed from it, through his love.

For what is “to the end” except “to Christ”? “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes,” says the Apostle (Rom. X). He is the end that perfects, not the end that destroys; the end toward which we go, not the end at which we perish.

The saying “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V) must be understood in precisely this way. He is our end; our passing over is toward him. “He loved them to the end” must be understood as “he loved them unto death,” because he loved them so greatly that he himself died for them.

“And supper having taken place,” he says, “when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him.”

“Supper having taken place” means that it had already been prepared and brought to the table of those dining, for their use. But when he says, “When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him,” if you ask what had been put into Judas’s heart, the answer is: that he should betray him.

This putting is a spiritual suggestion. It does not take place through the ear but through thought, and therefore not bodily but spiritually. Yet not everything called spiritual is to be understood as praise. The Apostle knows that there are “spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places,” against which he testifies that we struggle (Eph. VI). Nor would there be evil spiritual beings if there were not evil spirits; spiritual things receive their name from spirit.

Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God—since the Father had given all things into his hands, why did he wash not the hands but the feet of the disciples?

He knew that he had come forth from God through the humility of the Incarnation and would return to God through the victory of the resurrection, neither abandoning God when he came forth from him nor abandoning us when he returned. He knew all these things, and yet, as a sign of his own great humility and an example of our great humility, he rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and washed the feet of his disciples.

He fulfilled not the office of God and Lord but that of a human servant, humbly washing the feet even of the one whose hands he knew would be impudently defiled by his betrayal.

If we delight in examining this most humble mystery of our Savior with deeper investigation, this most sacred supper, at which the Lord reclined with his disciples, signifies the entire period during which he dwelt bodily in the Church. During that time he fed all people far and wide with the food of his saving word and the sweetness of his miracles, while he himself was nourished by the faith and love of those who heard him. For all whom he converted to the grace of truth he caused, through the Church, to increase as those who partake of food naturally increase.

He rose from supper and laid aside his garments. This signifies the time when, ceasing to dwell any longer among human beings in temporal fashion, he laid down upon the cross the limbs of the body he had assumed.

Having taken a towel, he girded himself. This signifies that, having received from the Father the command to suffer for us, he girded his limbs in the very exercise of his passion. A towel, which is produced through the labor of many kinds of torment, customarily signifies the affliction of sufferings. The Lord lays aside his garments and is girded with a towel to signify that he would lay down the bodily form he had assumed not without the pressure of suffering, but through the prolonged tribulation of the cross.

[Col. 0802C] He poured water into a basin, began to wash the disciples’ feet, and wiped them with the towel with which he was girded. This signifies the time when, having died on the cross, he poured water together with blood from his side upon the earth, by which he would cleanse the works of believers. He graciously chose not only to sanctify those works through the mysteries of his passion, but also to confirm them through those same examples.

Then he came to Simon Peter. It might seem that he had already washed the feet of some and afterward came to the first of them. For who does not know that the blessed Peter was the first of the apostles? But this should not be understood as though he came to Peter after some others; rather, it means that he began with him.

When he began to wash the disciples’ feet, he came to the one with whom he began—that is, to Peter. Then Peter was afraid, as any of them would have been afraid, and said:

“Lord, are you washing my feet? You, for me?” What is meant by “you”? What is meant by “for me”? These things should be pondered rather than spoken, lest perhaps what the soul conceives as somewhat worthy from these words cannot be fully expressed by the tongue.

But Jesus answered and said to him: “What I am doing you do not know now; afterward you will know.” Yet Peter, terrified by the greatness of the Lord’s action, does not permit what he does not know the reason for to be done. He still does not wish to see Christ humbled even to his feet; he cannot bear it.

“You shall never wash my feet,” he says.

What does “never” mean? “I shall never bear this; I shall never endure it; I shall never permit it.” For what is said to be done “never” is what is never done.

Then the Savior frightened the sick man who was resisting by warning him of the danger to his own salvation:

“If I do not wash you,” he says, “you will have no part with me.”

He says, “If I do not wash you,” although he was speaking only of the feet, just as one commonly says, “You are treading on me,” when only the sole of the foot is being trodden upon.

But Peter, disturbed by love and fear, and more afraid that Christ would deny him a share with himself than that Christ would humble himself to his feet, said:

“Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.”

“Since you threaten me in this way, when you wash my limbs, I do not withhold from you merely the lowest parts; I even place the highest parts beneath you. Do not deny me a share with you; I deny you no part of my body to wash.”

Jesus says to him: “Whoever has been bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.”

Entirely clean, certainly, except for the feet—or, rather, he needs only to wash his feet. But what does this mean? What is its significance? What necessity is there for us to investigate here? The Lord speaks; the Truth speaks: even the one who has been bathed needs to have his feet washed.

What do you think, my brothers, does this mean except that a human being is entirely washed in holy baptism—not excepting the feet, but wholly and completely? Nevertheless, when one afterward lives among human affairs, one inevitably treads upon the earth.

Human affections, therefore, without which one cannot live in this mortality, are like feet. They are the places where we are affected by human affairs. We are affected in such a way that, if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us (John I).

Therefore he who intercedes for us washes our feet daily. And we confess daily that we need to have our feet washed in the very prayer of the Lord, when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

For if we confess our sins, as it is written, then surely he who washed the feet of his disciples is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness (John I)—that is, even to the feet with which we walk upon the earth.

That washing of the feet signifies the forgiveness of sins—not, however, the forgiveness given once for all in baptism, but rather that by which the daily offenses of the faithful, without which one cannot live in this life, are cleansed by his daily grace.

The feet with which we walk and touch the earth, and which therefore we cannot keep free from the contamination of dust as we can the rest of the body, signify the necessity of dwelling on earth. Whoever has been bathed, therefore, needs only to wash his feet, but is entirely clean, because one who has been washed in the bath of baptism for the remission of all sins does not need to be washed again—indeed, cannot be washed again in the same way. Rather, only the daily contaminations of earthly conduct need to be cleansed by the daily forgiveness of the Redeemer.

A person is clean in the whole body of his actions, except only for those things that have clung to the mind through the necessity of temporal care. Because of their daily defilement, and likewise their daily cleansing, we say every day in prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

But this concerns the apostles and those like them. We, however, who often forget divine fear and walk along the left-hand path, cannot be freed from the filth of our errors by that light and daily solemnity of prayers. Rather, the greater defilement must necessarily be cleansed through a greater exercise of prayers, vigils, fasts, tears, and almsgiving.

After the Lord had washed the feet of the disciples, he took his garments and, when he had reclined again, he disclosed in word the mystery of the washing which he had shortly before presented to them through an action they did not yet understand.

After suffering on the cross he had consecrated for us the bath of forgiveness; he then took the limbs, now immortal, which he had laid down when they were mortal. After appearing to the disciples following the resurrection and dwelling familiarly with them, even eating with them, for forty days, he explained to them the benefit of his passion, whose outcome they had greatly feared until then because they did not know its mystical power.

“If I, then,” he says, “the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

This saying is rightly received and faithfully fulfilled both according to the literal sense and according to the mystical sense.

According to the literal sense, it means that through love we should serve one another—not merely by washing the feet of our brothers, but by assisting them in all their needs.

According to the mystical sense, it means that just as the Lord is accustomed to forgive us when we repent of our sins, so we should hasten to forgive our brothers when they sin against us. Just as he intercedes with the Father for us against our sins, so, if we know that our brother has committed a sin that is not unto death, we should ask that life be given to him who has committed a sin that is not unto death.

And, as the apostle James admonishes, “Let us confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, so that we may be saved” (I John V). Just as he laid down his life for us, so, when the moment requires it, let us lay down our lives for our brothers.

It follows:

You know what I have done for you.

Now the time has come for that promise to blessed Peter to be fulfilled. For the answer given to him when, terrified, he said, “You shall never wash my feet,” had been deferred: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you shall understand.” Behold, that “afterward” has now arrived, so that what had been deferred a little earlier may be stated. The Lord therefore remembered that he had long ago promised knowledge of what he had done—a deed so unexpected, so astonishing, and so terrifying that, unless he himself had powerfully frightened him, Peter would in no way have allowed the Master, not only of them but also of the angels, and the Lord, not only of them but of all things, to wash the feet of his disciples and servants. Since, then, he had promised knowledge of so great a deed by saying, “You shall understand afterward,” he now begins to teach what he did.

“You call me Teacher and Lord,” he says, “and you speak rightly, for so I am.” You speak rightly because you speak the truth: I am indeed what you call me. Human beings have been commanded: “Let not your own mouth praise you, but let the mouth of your neighbor praise you” (Prov. XXVII). For it is dangerous to please oneself when one must beware of becoming proud. But he who is exalted above all things is not lifted up by however much he praises himself. Nor can God rightly be called arrogant, for it is useful to us, not to him, that we should know him. No one knows him unless he himself makes himself known—he who knows all things. If, therefore, by refusing to praise himself he wished, as it were, to avoid arrogance, he would deny us wisdom.

No one would criticize him for saying that he is a teacher, even someone who believed that he was nothing other than a human being, since he would be professing what human beings themselves profess in every kind of art—indeed, so without arrogance that they are called “professors.” But that he also calls himself Lord of his disciples, although they are even, in worldly terms, freeborn men—who could tolerate that in a human being? Yet God is speaking here: there is no self-exaltation in such sublime majesty, and no falsehood in the truth. It is useful for us to be subject to that majesty. It is useful for us to serve the Truth. His saying that he is Lord is not a fault in him but a benefit to us. Let the one who is the Truth speak the truth, lest I fail to say what is useful while he remains silent about what is true.

The most blessed Paul—certainly not the only-begotten Son of God, but the servant and apostle of the only-begotten Son of God; not the Truth, but a participant in the Truth—says freely and confidently: “If I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I speak the truth” (II Cor. XII). He would boast humbly and truthfully, not in himself but in the Truth itself, which is higher than he, since he himself also commands that “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I). Was the lover of wisdom not afraid of foolishness if he wished to boast, while Wisdom herself would fear foolishness in her glory? He did not fear arrogance who said: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. XXXIII); and would the power of the Lord fear arrogance in its praise, when the soul of the servant shall be praised in the Lord?

“You call me,” he says, “Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” You speak rightly because I am what you call me. For if I were not what you call me, you would speak wrongly, even if you were praising me. “If I, therefore,” he says, “the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done for you, you also may do. This is what you did not know, blessed Peter, when you would not allow it to be done. This is what he promised you would afterward understand, when your Teacher, your Lord and God, frightened you into allowing him to wash your feet.

Among many people there is a custom of this humility, expressed even in an observable action. Thus the Apostle, when commending a widow of proven merit, says: “If she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints” (I Tim. V). And among the saints, wherever this custom does not exist, what they do not perform with their hands they perform in their hearts, if they belong to those who are addressed in the hymn of the three blessed youths: “Bless the Lord, holy and humble of heart” (Dan. III). Yet it is much better, and without dispute more truly, to do this also with the hands; nor should a Christian disdain to do what Christ did. For when the body bends down to the feet of a brother, the feeling of humility is either awakened in the heart itself or, if it was already present, strengthened.

But apart from this literal understanding, we remember that we have commended the depth of this deed of the Lord in this way: by washing the feet of disciples who had already been washed and cleansed, the Lord signified that, because of the human affections among which we live on earth, however far we may have progressed in attaining righteousness, we are not without sin. He continually washes us by interceding for us when we pray to the Father who is in heaven to forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

How, then, can this meaning apply to what he himself taught afterward, when he explained the reason for his action, saying: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done for you, you also may do”? Can we say that a brother can cleanse his brother from the thought of wrongdoing? Rather, let us recognize that in the depth of this deed of the Lord we have also been admonished to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, just as Christ intercedes for us.

We have heard the apostle James most clearly commanding this very thing and saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (James V), because for this purpose the Lord gave us an example. If he who has no sin, neither has had any nor will have any, prays for our sins, how much more ought we to pray for one another’s sins! And if he forgives us to whom we have nothing to forgive, how much more ought we to forgive one another, since we cannot live here without sin?

What else does the Lord seem to signify in this profound sacrament when he says, “For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done for you, you also may do,” except what the Apostle says most openly: “Forgiving one another, if anyone has a grievance against another; just as the Lord forgave you, so you also should forgive” (Eph. IV). Let us therefore forgive one another’s sins, pray for one another’s sins, and thus in a certain manner wash one another’s feet.

“Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him.” He said this because the Lord had washed the feet of servants, and he himself was the one who had sent those whom he sent. Ἀπόστολος (*apostolos*) in Greek is called *missus* in Latin, “one who is sent,” to show that what the Exalted One did humbly must be done much more by the humble and weak in a humble manner. But he also wished to suggest the spiritual meaning in this passage: if he who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found, intercedes for our transgressions (I Pet. II), then we ought much more to pray for one another. And if he forgives us to whom we have nothing to forgive, then we ought much more to forgive one another our debts. The Apostle likewise commands this, saying: “Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. IV).

“If you know these things,” he says, “you will be blessed if you do them.” This saving saying of our Savior must be considered carefully and continually, because we shall be blessed by knowing the heavenly commandments, provided that we pursue in action what we know. For the one who neglects to keep his commands once known cannot be blessed; and the one who disdains even to know them is excluded much farther from the lot of the blessed. When the Lord had said these things, he added:

“I do not speak of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But let Scripture be fulfilled: ‘He who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.’” What else does this mean but, “He will trample upon me”? It is known of whom he is speaking: that betrayer of his, Judas, is being indicated. Therefore he had not chosen Judas himself; by this saying he distinguishes him from those whom he chose.

“What I say,” he means, “that you will be blessed if you do these things, I do not say of all of you. There is one among you who will not be blessed and will not do them. I know whom I have chosen.” Whom, unless those who will be blessed by doing what he commanded and showed should be done—he who is able to make them blessed? Was Judas the betrayer, then, not chosen? What, therefore, does he mean elsewhere when he says: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John VI). Was he chosen for some purpose? Certainly—for a purpose for which he was necessary, but not for blessedness, of which he now says: “You will be blessed if you do these things.” He is not speaking of all of them. For he knows whom he has chosen for fellowship in this blessedness. Judas is not one of them, for he ate his bread in such a way as to lift his heel against him. They ate the Lord’s bread; he ate bread against the Lord. “Whoever eats unworthily,” the Apostle says, “eats judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI).

“From now on I tell you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe that I am he.” That is, I am the one of whom that earlier Scripture spoke, where it says: “He who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.”

Then he continues and says:

“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives anyone I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”

If we wish to understand the saying “Whoever receives me receives the one who sent me” as referring to the unity of nature between the Father and the Son, it will seem to follow, according to the same rule of these words, that “whoever receives anyone I send receives me” implies that the Son and the apostle are of one nature. This too could be understood without impropriety, since that giant is of a twofold substance, who rejoiced to run his course (Ps. XVIII). For “the Word became flesh” (John I), that is, God became man. Accordingly, he may seem to have said: “Whoever receives the one whom I send receives me according to my humanity. But whoever receives me according to my divinity receives the one who sent me.”

Yet when he said these things, he was commending not the unity of nature between the sender and the one sent, but the authority of the sender in the one who is sent. Thus let each person receive the one who has been sent in such a way that in him he regards the one who sent him. If you regard Christ in Peter, you find the teacher of the disciple. If you regard the Father in the Son, you find the begetter of the only-begotten. And so, in the one who has been sent, you receive the sender without any error.

When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, saying: “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” Was Jesus troubled here in spirit, not in the flesh, simply because he was about to say, “One of you will betray me”? Had this thought only then occurred to him, or had it only then suddenly been revealed to him, so that the sudden novelty of so great an evil troubled him? Had he not shortly before been saying: “He who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me”? Had he not already said above: “And you are clean, but not all”? There the evangelist added: “For he knew who would betray him”; and he had already indicated him earlier by saying: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?”

What, then, does it mean that he was now troubled in spirit when he testified and said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me”? Was it because he was now about to identify him explicitly, so that he would no longer remain hidden among the others but be distinguished from them, and because the betrayer himself had already gone out to bring the Jews, to whom the Lord was to be handed over by him? Did the approaching passion, the imminent danger, and the betrayer’s impending hand trouble him, although the betrayer’s intention had been known beforehand?

This is like the occasion when Jesus was troubled in spirit and said: “Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour” (John XII). Just as his soul was troubled there when the hour of his passion approached, so now he was troubled in spirit when Judas was about to depart, when the crime was about to come, and when the betrayer’s great deed was drawing near.

He is troubled, then, though he has the power to lay down his life and the power to take it up again. So great a power is troubled; the firmness of the rock is troubled—or rather, is our weakness troubled in him? Indeed, servants should believe nothing unworthy of their Lord, but recognize themselves as members in their Head. He who died for us was himself first troubled for us. Therefore he who died by his power was troubled by his power.

He who transfigured the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory (Phil. III), also transfigured in himself the feeling of our weakness, sympathizing with us through the feeling of his soul. Therefore, when the great, strong, steadfast, unconquered one is troubled, let us not fear as though he were failing. He does not perish, but seeks us. Us, I say—he seeks us altogether. Let us see ourselves in his disturbance, so that when we are troubled we may not perish through despair. For when the one who would not be troubled unless he wished to be is troubled, he consoles the one who is troubled unwillingly.

Let the Christian soul be troubled—not by misery but by mercy. Let it fear lest human beings perish from Christ. Let it grieve when someone perishes from Christ. Let it rejoice when human beings are gained for Christ. Let it desire that human beings be gained for Christ. Let it fear for itself, lest it perish from Christ. Let it grieve that it is a stranger to Christ; let it desire to reign with Christ. Let it rejoice while it hopes to be a stranger with Christ.

These are certainly the four things that are called disturbances: fear and sadness, love and joy. Christian souls possess them for just reasons. Christians are indeed very firm, if there are any who are not troubled by the approach of death. But are they firmer than Christ? Who could say this except someone utterly insane?

What, then, does it mean that he was troubled, except that he consoled the weak in his body—that is, in his Church—through the voluntary likeness of his own weakness? Thus, if any of his own are still troubled by the approach of death, they may look upon him, lest, thinking that this very fact proves them rejected, they be swallowed up by the worse death of despair.

How great a good, then, ought we to await and hope for from participation in his divinity, when his disturbance brings us tranquility and his weakness makes us strong? Whether, therefore, he was troubled here out of compassion for Judas as he perished, or troubled because his own death was approaching, there is nevertheless no doubt that he was troubled not through weakness of spirit but by his power, lest we despair of salvation when we are troubled not by power but by weakness.

He bore the weakness of the flesh, and that weakness was consumed by the resurrection. But because he was not only human but also God, by the ineffable difference between them he surpassed the entire human race in strength of soul. He was not therefore troubled by compulsion from another, but troubled himself. This is clearly expressed when he raised Lazarus. For it is written there that he troubled himself, so that this may also be understood where it is not written, though he is read to have been troubled.

When he judged it necessary, he stirred human feeling within himself by his power—he who by his power took up the whole human being. The Lord also graciously signified this to us by his disturbance: namely, that false brothers, the weeds in the Lord’s field, must necessarily be tolerated among the wheat until the time of the harvest (Matt. XIII), so that when urgent necessity compels some of them to be separated even before the harvest, this cannot happen without disturbance to the Church.

In a way foretelling the disturbance that would come upon his saints through schismatics and heretics, the Lord prefigured it in himself. When Judas, the evil man, was about to depart, leaving behind the clearest separation of the mixture of wheat in which he had long been tolerated, he was troubled not in the flesh but in the spirit.

[Note: To avoid syntactical harshness, *separatus* seems to require deletion, and the reading should be: *toler . . . separatione apertissima relicturo*—“about to leave the mixture in which he had long been tolerated, by a most evident separation.” EDIT.]

His spiritual servants are troubled by such scandals not through perversity but through charity, lest perhaps, in the separation of some weeds, some wheat also be uprooted. Jesus was therefore troubled in spirit, and testified and said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”

“One of you”—in number, not in merit; in outward appearance, not in virtue; by bodily association, not by spiritual bond; by the admiration of the flesh, not by complete unity of heart. Therefore he does not mean one who truly belongs to you, but one who is about to go out from you.

For how can what the Lord testified and said—“One of you”—be true if the same John, whose Gospel this is, says in his epistle: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II)? Judas, therefore, was not truly of them; for he would have remained with them if he had been of them.

What else, then, does “One of you will betray me” mean except: “One who is among you will go out and will betray me”? For the one who said, “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us,” had already said, “They went out from us.” Consequently both are true: they were from us, and they were not from us—according to one sense, from us; according to another, not from us. According to participation in the sacraments, from us; according to the particular character of their crimes, not from us.

The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain of whom he was speaking. Such holy love did they have toward their teacher, yet human weakness still prompted each of them to suspect the other. Each person’s conscience was known to himself; but because the conscience of his neighbor was unknown, each was so certain about himself that each was uncertain about the others, and the others about each one.

One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was therefore reclining at Jesus’ breast. What he had called “in his bosom,” he shortly afterward calls “upon the breast of Jesus.” This is John, whose Gospel this is, as he makes clear later.

It was the custom of those who ministered the sacred Scriptures to us that, when one of them was narrating a divine history and came to himself, he should speak as though of another person, inserting himself into the order of his narrative as a writer of events rather than as his own eulogist. Accordingly, when the blessed evangelist here also does not say, “I was reclining in the bosom of Jesus,” but says, “One of the disciples was reclining,” let us recognize rather than wonder at the custom of our authors.

What is lost to the truth when the event itself is stated while boasting is avoided through a certain manner of speech? For he was narrating something that contributed greatly to his praise. But what does “whom Jesus loved” mean? Does it imply that he did not love the others, of whom this same John had earlier said, “He loved them to the end” (John XIII), and the Lord himself: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV)?

Who could enumerate all the testimonies of the divine pages by which the Lord Jesus is shown to be the lover not only of that disciple, nor only of those who were present then, but also of the members who would come afterward and of his entire Church? Yet surely something is hidden here, and it relates to the bosom in which the speaker of these words was reclining. For what else is signified by the bosom than a secret?

Simon Peter therefore beckons to him and says to him. This expression deserves attention: something can be said not by sounding it aloud but merely by a gesture. “He beckons,” it says, “and speaks.” Certainly he speaks by beckoning. If something is said by thinking, as Scripture says, “They said among themselves” (John VII), how much more can something be said by a gesture, when what had been conceived in the heart is already expressed outwardly through signs of whatever kind?

What, then, did he say by beckoning? What, except what follows:

“What is he speaking about?” Peter indicated these words by a gesture, for he spoke not with the sound of his voice but by moving his body.

And so, when that disciple had reclined upon the breast of Jesus—this is surely the bosom of the breast, the secret place of wisdom—

he says to him, “Lord, who is it?”

Jesus answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the morsel after dipping it.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. And after the bread, Satan then entered into him.

The betrayer was identified; the hiding places of darkness were exposed. What Judas received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because the evil man received the good evilly. For it makes a great difference not what is received but who receives it, and not what is given but what kind of person the recipient is. Good things can harm, and bad things can benefit, depending on those to whom they are given.

“The sin,” says the Apostle, “in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (I Cor. XI). Behold, evil came through a good thing, when the good thing was received evilly. Why, then, are you surprised if Christ’s bread, given to Judas, harmed him by handing him over to the devil, when you see, conversely, that the devil’s angel, given to Paul, perfected him in Christ? Thus the good harmed the evil man, and the evil benefited the good man.

Remember where it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” The Apostle was speaking about such people when he said this, because they were taking the Lord’s body indiscriminately and carelessly, as though it were any ordinary food.

If, then, the person who does not judge—that is, does not distinguish—the Lord’s body from other foods is reproved, how is the enemy who pretends to be a friend and approaches his table condemned? If the negligence of a guest is touched by reproach, with what punishment is the seller struck—the one who betrays his host?

What was the bread given to the betrayer except a demonstration of the grace toward which he would prove ungrateful? Satan therefore entered into the Lord’s betrayer after this bread, so that he might possess more fully one who had already been handed over to him—one into whom he had previously entered in order to deceive him.

For Satan was not absent from him when he went to the Jews and agreed on the price for betraying the Lord, as the evangelist Luke most plainly testifies, saying: “Satan entered into Judas, who was surnamed Iscariot, one of the twelve, and he went away and spoke with the chief priests” (Luke XXII). Behold, this shows that Satan had already entered into Judas.

He had entered earlier by implanting in his heart the thought that he should betray Christ. Such was the man who had already come to dine. But now, after the bread, he entered into him not to tempt someone who was still alien to him, but to possess his own.

Some careless readers think that Judas then received Christ’s body. But it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed to all of them the sacrament of his body and blood, and Judas too was among them, as Saint Luke most clearly narrates. After that came the moment when, according to John’s account, the Lord most plainly identified his betrayer through the dipped and offered morsel—perhaps signifying by the dipping of the bread his pretence. For not everything that is dipped is washed; some things are dipped in order to be stained.

If the dipping signifies something good here, then the condemnation that followed was rightly suffered by one who was ungrateful toward that good. Yet Judas’s possession was still from the devil, not from the Lord: the bread had entered the ungrateful man’s belly, and the enemy had entered his mind.

Still, I say, the effect of so great an evil, already conceived in his heart, remained to be carried out, while the disposition deserving condemnation had already preceded it. And so, when the Lord, having given living bread to a dead man, had revealed the betrayer of the bread by giving him the bread—

“What you are going to do,” he says, “do quickly.”

He did not command the crime; he foretold it. It was evil for Judas, but good for us. For what was worse for Judas, and what better for us, than that Christ should be betrayed—by him, against Christ, but for us and apart from him?

“What you are going to do, do quickly.” O word spoken to one more willingly prepared than angrily compelled—not so much in rage hastening the destruction of the faithless man as hastening the salvation of the faithful, because Christ “was handed over for our transgressions,” and “loved the Church and gave himself for her” (Rom. IV; Eph. V). Hence the Apostle also says of this: “He loved me and gave himself for me” (Eph. V).

Unless Christ had handed himself over, no one would have handed Christ over. What does Judas have except sin? For in betraying Christ he did not consider our salvation, for the sake of which Christ was betrayed; he considered profit in money and found the loss of his soul.

“What you are going to do, do quickly”—not because you are able, but because the one who can do all things wills it.

None of those reclining at table knew why he had said this to him. Some thought that, because Judas kept the money box, Jesus was saying to him: “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.

The Lord therefore had a money box, preserving what the faithful offered both for the needs of his own followers and to distribute to other needy people. Here the pattern of ecclesiastical finances was first established. We understand from this that the command not to think about tomorrow (Matt. VI) was not given so that the saints should preserve no money, but so that they should not serve God for the sake of these things or abandon righteousness through fear of poverty.

The Apostle too, providing for the future, says: “If any believing woman has widows, let her provide for them sufficiently, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be able to provide for those who are truly widows” (I Tim. V).

When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night.

And the one who went out was night. When night had gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.”

“Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. XVIII)—that is, Christ to faithful disciples, so that they might hear him, love him, and follow him. “Night announces knowledge to night” (ibid.)—that is, Judas to unbelieving Jews, so that they might come to him and seize him in persecution.

What, then, did the Lord say after Judas went out to do more quickly what he was about to do—that is, to betray the Lord? What did Day say when Night had gone out? What did the Redeemer say when the seller had gone out?

“Now,” he says, “the Son of Man has been glorified.”

Why now? Was it because the betrayer had gone out, because those who would seize and kill him were approaching? Was he glorified now because he was close to being further humbled—because he was about to be bound, judged, condemned, mocked, crucified, and killed? Is this glorification, or rather humiliation?

Did not this same John say of him when he was performing miracles: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII)? He was not yet glorified when he was raising the dead, and he is glorified now when he is approaching death? He was not yet glorified while doing divine things, and he is glorified while about to suffer human things?

It would be strange if that divine Teacher meant and signified such a thing by these words. The saying of the Most High must be searched more deeply: he reveals himself somewhat so that we may find him, and then conceals himself again so that we may seek him, relying on what we have found as though on steps toward what remains to be found.

I see here something that prefigures a great reality. Judas went out, and Jesus was glorified. The son of perdition went out, and the Son of Man was glorified. For Judas was the one about whom he had said to them: “And you are clean, but not all” (above). When the unclean man went out, all the clean remained, and they remained with their cleanser.

Something similar will happen when this world, conquered by Christ, passes away, and no unclean person remains among Christ’s people—when, after the weeds have been separated from the wheat, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII).

Foreseeing this future and testifying that it was now signified, the Lord, when Judas departed like weeds separated from the wheat, while the holy apostles remained like wheat, said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” as though he were saying: Behold what will occur in that glorification of mine, where no evil person will remain and no good person will perish.

He did not say, “The glorification of the Son of Man has now been signified,” but, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” In the same way, Scripture does not say, “The rock signified Christ,” but, “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. XIX). Nor does it say, “The good seed signifies the sons of the kingdom,” or “The weeds signify the sons of the evil one,” but, “The good seed—these are the sons of the kingdom; the weeds are the sons of the evil one” (Matt. XIII).

Thus Scripture customarily names the things that signify as though they were the things signified. In the same way the Lord spoke when he said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” after the wicked man had been separated from him and the saints had remained with him; the glorification of Christ had been signified, when the wicked would be separated and he would remain in eternity with the saints.

When he had said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” he added:

“And God has been glorified in him.”

For the glorification of the Son of Man is itself the glorification of God in him. If God is glorified not in himself but in him, then God glorifies him in himself. Finally, as though explaining this, he adds and says:

“If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself.”

That is: if God has been glorified in him because he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him, then God also glorified him in himself, so that the human nature in which the Son of Man exists—the nature assumed by the eternal Word—might also be granted immortal eternity.

“And immediately,” he says, “he will glorify him,” predicting by this testimony that his resurrection would take place immediately—not like ours at the end of the world, but immediately. This is the glorification of which the evangelist had already spoken, as I recalled shortly before: the Spirit had not yet been given in that new manner in which he was to be given to those who believed after the resurrection, because Jesus had not yet been glorified—that is, mortality had not yet been clothed with immortality, and temporal weakness had not yet been changed into eternal power.

The saying “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” may also be understood as referring to this glorification, so that the word “now” is believed to refer not to the imminent passion but to the approaching resurrection, as though what was already so near to happening had actually happened.

“Little children, I am with you only a little longer.”

He did not want them to think that God would glorify him in such a way that he would no longer be joined to them in the manner of life by which he was present on earth. “I am with you only a little longer,” he says—as though he were saying: I shall indeed be glorified immediately through the resurrection, but I shall not immediately ascend into heaven; I am still with you for a little while.

For, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, “he was with them for forty days, entering and departing, eating and drinking” (Acts I). He did not have the need to hunger and thirst, but he thereby continued to demonstrate the truth of his flesh: he no longer had the necessity of eating and drinking, but he had the power to do so.

Did he signify these forty days when he said, “I am with you only a little longer,” or something else? The saying can also be understood in this way: “I am with you only a little longer; I am still, like you, in this weakness of the flesh”—until, namely, he should die and rise again. For after he rose, he was with them for those forty days, as has been said, by the display of bodily presence, but he was not with them in the fellowship of human weakness.

There is also another divine presence unknown to mortal senses, of which he likewise says: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). This certainly is not “I am with you only a little longer.” For the time extending to the end of the age is not a little while.

Or, if this too is a little while—for time flies, and in the eyes of God a thousand years are like one day, or like a watch in the night (Ps. LXXXIX)—we should nevertheless not believe that he intended to signify this here, since he immediately continued by adding:

You will seek me, and, as I said to the Jews, where I am going you cannot come. Certainly, after this “little while” during which I am with you, you will seek me, and where I am going you cannot come. Will they not be able to come, after the end of the age, to where he himself is going? And what of what he will say somewhat later in this very discourse: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17)? Therefore, when he said, “I am still with you a little while,” he was not speaking of that presence of his with his own by which he is with them until the end of the age; rather, he was speaking either of the mortal weakness by which he was with them until his passion, or of the bodily presence by which he was to be with them until his ascension. Whichever of these one chooses, one does not quarrel with the faith.

Lest this interpretation seem to anyone to depart from the truth—that is, that we say the Lord could have signified the sharing in mortal flesh in which he was with his disciples until his passion by saying, “I am still with you a little while”—let him also consider the words of another Evangelist after his resurrection, where he says: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke 24), although [or: even if?] at that time he was present with them as they stood together, saw him, touched him, and conversed with him. What does “while I was still with you” mean, then, except: “While I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are”? For at that time he was indeed in the same flesh, now raised up, but he was no longer with them in the same mortality. Therefore, just as there he truly said, while still in the mortality of the flesh, “while I was still with you,” where we can understand nothing else than “while I was still with you in the mortality of the flesh,” so here too he may reasonably be understood to have said, “I am still with you a little while,” as though he were saying: “For a little while longer, I am mortal as you are.”

Let us therefore examine what follows: “You will seek me; and, as I said to the Jews, where I am going you cannot come.” And to you I say this now—that is, now you cannot come. When he said this to the Jews, he did not add “now.” These disciples, therefore, could not at that time come to where he was going, but they could do so afterward. For shortly afterward he said this most plainly to the apostle Peter. When Peter had said, “Lord, where are you going?” he answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now, but afterward you will follow.”

Yet what this means must not be passed over carelessly. Where could the disciples not then follow the Lord, but could follow him afterward? If we say, “To death,” can there be found, for a human being who has been born, a time when he is not fit to die, since such is the lot of human beings in corruptible bodies that life is no easier than death? They were not, then, less fit to follow the Lord to death; rather, they were less fit to follow the Lord to the life that has no death. For the Lord was going to the place where, rising from the dead, he would die no more, and death would no longer have dominion over him (Romans 6). How could they, not yet mature for martyrdom, have followed the Lord who was to die for righteousness? Or how could they already have followed the Lord to the immortality of the flesh, when they were destined to die at some point and to rise again only at the end of the age? Or again, how could they already have followed the Lord to the bosom of the Father, while he would not leave them, just as he did not depart from the Father when he came to them, when no one can be in that blessedness except one who is perfect in love?

Therefore, teaching how they could become fit to go where he was going ahead of them, he says:

“I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.”

These are the steps by which Christ must be followed. Was this not already a commandment in the ancient law of God, where it is written, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19)? Why, then, is the Lord calling a commandment “new” which is plainly so old? Is it called a new commandment because, having stripped off the old person, he clothed us with the new? For it renews the hearer—or rather, the obedient person—not every kind of love, but that love which the Lord added in order to distinguish it from carnal love: “As I have loved you.”

For husbands and wives love one another, as do parents and children, and all the other human relationships by which people are bound together. I say nothing of the guilty and damnable love by which adulterers and adulteresses, fornicators and prostitutes, and all those whom not human relationship but the disgraceful corruption of human life joins together, love one another.

Christ therefore gave us a new commandment: that we love one another as he loved us. This love renews us, so that we may be new people, heirs of the new covenant, singers of the new song. This love renewed even the ancient righteous—the patriarchs and prophets at that time—as it later renewed the blessed apostles. It is this same love that now renews the nations and makes and gathers from the whole human race, spread throughout the entire world, a new people, the body of the new bride, the bride of the only-begotten Son of God. Of her it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up, made white?” (Song of Songs 3; 8). Made white, certainly, because renewed.

And from what else does this renewal come than from the new commandment, on account of which the members of this body care for one another? They hear and keep it: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”—not as those love one another who corrupt each other, nor merely as human beings love one another, but as those who love one another because they are gods and all sons of the Most High, so that they may be brothers to his only Son, loving one another with the love with which he loved them. By this love he will lead them to that end which is sufficient for them, where their desire will be satisfied with good things. For then nothing will be lacking to their desire, when God will be all in all.

Do not think, therefore, my brothers, that when the Lord says, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another,” he has omitted that great commandment which enjoins us to love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Matthew 22). For one who understands rightly finds both commandments contained in each. Whoever loves God cannot despise him when he commands that we love our neighbor; and whoever loves the neighbor in a holy and spiritual manner loves nothing in him except God.

This is the love distinguished from every worldly love, and in order to distinguish it the Lord added: “As I have loved you.” For what did he love in us except God—not what we already possessed, but so that we might possess him, in order that he might lead us, as I said shortly before, to where God is all in all (1 Corinthians 15)?

Thus a physician is rightly said to love the sick; and what does he love in them except health, which he certainly desires to restore—not the illness, which he has come to drive away? So let us also love one another, so that, insofar as we can, by the care of love we may draw one another toward possessing God within us.

He himself grants us this love, who says:

“As I have loved you, so you also should love one another.”

He loved us for this purpose: that we too might love one another. By loving us he bestowed on us the gift of being bound together by mutual love, so that, with our members joined by so sweet a bond, we may be the body of so great a Head.

“In this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

It is as though he were saying: Others who are not mine also possess my other gifts among you—not only nature, life, sensation, reason, and that salvation which human beings and sinners share in common, but also tongues, sacraments, prophecy, knowledge, faith, the distribution of their possessions to the poor, and the giving over of their bodies to be burned. Yet because they lack love, they clang like cymbals; they are nothing, and it profits them nothing (1 Corinthians 11).

Therefore, it is not by those good gifts of mine, which even those who are not my disciples may possess, that everyone will know that you are my disciples, but by this: if you have love for one another.

O bride of Christ, beautiful among women! O you who come up made white and lean upon your kinsman, because you are illumined by the light of him whose radiance makes you shine, and supported by his help lest you fall! How well it is sung to you in that Song of Songs, as in your wedding hymn: “Because love is in your delights” (Song of Songs 8)! Love does not destroy your soul with the ungodly. Love does not judge your cause; and, as death is strong, so love is in your delights. What an extraordinary kind of death this is, to which it was not enough merely not to be in punishments unless it was also in delights!

Simon Peter says to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Thus the disciple spoke to his teacher, and the servant to his Lord, as one ready to follow. Therefore the Lord, who saw why he had asked this question, answered him:

“Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.”

As though he were saying: “As to what you are asking, you cannot do so now.” He did not say, “You cannot,” but “You cannot now.” He introduced a delay, not a removal of hope; and the hope he did not remove, but rather granted, he confirmed in the words that followed, adding:

“But afterward you will follow.”

Why are you hurrying, Peter? The rock has not yet strengthened you by his Spirit. Do not exalt yourself through presumption: you cannot now. Do not cast yourself down through despair: you will follow afterward.

But what does he say next?

“Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”

He saw what desire was present in Peter’s heart, but Peter did not see what strength he possessed. The weak man boasted of his will, but the physician observed his condition. Peter was making a promise; Christ foresaw the future. The one who did not know was listening, while the one who foresaw was teaching how much Peter had taken upon himself: he looked at what he wanted but did not know what he could do. He had taken upon himself so much that, when the Lord came to lay down his life for his friends, and therefore also for Peter, Peter presumed to offer this to the Lord, promising, before Christ had laid down his life for him, that he would lay down his own life for Christ.

Jesus therefore answered:

“You will lay down your life for me?”

Is that so? Will you do for me what I have not yet done for you? “You will lay down your life for me”? Can you go ahead when you cannot follow? Why do you presume so greatly? What do you think of yourself? What do you believe yourself to be? Listen to what you are.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

See how quickly you will appear to yourself, you who speak grandly and do not know how small you are. You promise me your death; three times you will deny me, your life. You who now think that you can die for me, first live for yourself. For by fearing the death of your flesh, you will bring death upon your soul.

He did not say, “The cock will not crow until you deny the man,” or, as he customarily spoke in a manner more familiar to human beings, “The cock will not crow until you deny the Son of Man three times.” Rather, he said, “Until you deny me.” What is “me” except what he was? And what was he except Christ?

Whatever part of him Peter denied, he denied him himself. He denied Christ; he denied the Lord his God. For his fellow disciple Thomas, when he exclaimed, “My Lord and my God” (John 20), did not touch the Word but the flesh; he did not handle the incorporeal nature of God, but the body of a human being with inquisitive hands. He touched a human being, and yet he recognized God.

If, then, Peter denied what Thomas touched, Peter offended against what Thomas proclaimed. “The cock will not crow until you have denied me three times.” You may say, “I do not know the man”; you may say, “Man, I do not know what you are saying”; you may say, “I am not one of his disciples”: you will deny me.

If Christ said this—as it is impious to doubt—and foretold it truly, then without a doubt Peter denied Christ. Let us not accuse Christ when we defend Peter. Let weakness acknowledge its sin, for truth contains no lie. Peter’s weakness plainly acknowledged its sin—indeed, it acknowledged it fully—and by weeping he showed how great an evil he had committed by denying Christ.

He himself refuted his defenders and brought forth his tears as witnesses by which to convict them. Nor, when we say these things, do we take pleasure in accusing the first of the apostles. Rather, by looking at him, we ought to be warned that no human being should trust in human strength.

For what else was fitting for our Teacher and Savior than to demonstrate, in the person of the first of the apostles, that no one ought to presume upon himself? Thus what Peter was offering in his body occurred in his soul. Yet he did not go ahead of the Lord, as he rashly presumed to do; rather, it happened otherwise than he thought. Before the Lord’s death and resurrection, Peter died by denying him and came back to life by weeping.

He died because he presumptuously trusted in himself; but he came back to life because the Lord mercifully looked upon him.

## CHAPTER XIV

And he said to the disciples:

“Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.”

Lest they fear death in him as though he were merely a human being, and therefore become troubled, he consoles them while also declaring that he is God. “You believe,” he says, “in God; believe also in me.” For it follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me; this would not follow if Christ were not God.

“You believe in God; believe also in him who by nature, not by seizure, is equal to God.” For “he emptied himself” (Philippians 2), yet he did not lose the form of God; rather, he took the form of a servant. Do you fear death for this form of a servant? Let not your heart be troubled: God will raise up that form of God.

But what is the meaning of what follows?

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.”

Could it mean anything except that they were also afraid for themselves? Hence they ought to have heard, “Let not your heart be troubled.” For who among them would not be afraid when it had been said to Peter, who was more confident and ready than the others, “The cock will not crow until you have denied me three times”? Since they seemed destined to perish away from him, they were rightly troubled.

But when they hear, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,” and, “If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?” they are restored from their disturbance. They become certain and confident that, even after the dangers of temptations, they will remain with God and with Christ.

For even if one is stronger than another, one wiser than another, one more righteous than another, and one holier than another, “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” None of them will be excluded from that house, where each will receive a dwelling according to his merit.

That denarius, however, is equal for all, which the householder commands to be given to all who worked in the vineyard, without distinguishing between those who worked less and those who worked more (Matthew 20). By that denarius eternal life is signified, where no one lives more than another, since there is no different measure of living in eternity. But the many dwelling places signify different degrees of merit within the one eternal life.

“One glory is that of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars. For one star differs from another in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15). Like stars in heaven, the saints receive different dwelling places, corresponding to different measures of love, as their lot in the kingdom.

Yet because of the one denarius no one is separated from the kingdom. Thus God will be all in all: because God is love, love will bring it about that what each possesses will be shared by all. For each person possesses something when he loves in another what he does not also possess in himself.

There will therefore be no envy because of unequal brightness, since the unity of love will reign in all.

Accordingly, those who think that “there are many dwelling places” was said because there will be something outside the kingdom of heaven where innocent people may dwell in blessedness—those who departed this life without baptism because they could not enter the kingdom of heaven without it—must be rejected by the Christian heart.

This belief is not faith, because it is not true and catholic faith. The Lord did not say, “In the whole world,” or “In the whole creation,” or “In everlasting life or blessedness there are many dwelling places.” Rather, he said, “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (2 Corinthians 5).

Is this not the house in which we have “a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens”? Is this not the house of which we sing, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83)?

Will you dare to separate from the kingdom of heaven not the house of some baptized brother, but the house of God himself the Father, to whom all we brothers say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6)? Or will you dare to divide it in such a way that some of its dwelling places are in the kingdom of heaven and others outside the kingdom of heaven?

Far be it—far be it—from those who wish to dwell in the kingdom of heaven that they should wish to dwell with you in such folly. Far be it, I say, that when the entire house of the reigning sons is nowhere except in the kingdom of that royal house, some part of it should not be in the kingdom.

“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.”

How does he go and prepare a place if there are already so many dwelling places? If they did not exist, he would have said, “I go to prepare”; and if they still needed to be prepared, why would he not appropriately have said, “I go to prepare”?

Are these dwelling places both already present and still to be prepared? If they did not exist, he would have said, “I go to prepare”; yet because they exist in such a way as to require preparation, he does not go to prepare them as they already are. Rather, if he goes and prepares them as they are to be, he will come again and take his own to himself, so that where he is, they too may be.

How, then, are the dwelling places in the Father’s house not other places, but these very same places, already existing without doubt, and yet not already prepared? How can we understand this except in the manner in which the prophet also proclaims that God does what is still to come? For he does not say that God “will do what is to come,” but that he “did what is to come.” Therefore he both did these things and will do them. For they would not have been done if he had not done them, nor will they be future if he does not bring them about.

He did them by predestining them; he will do them by carrying them out. The Gospel clearly indicates this when it says that he chose the disciples (Matthew 4), namely, when he called them. Yet the Apostle says, “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1)—clearly by predestination, not by calling.

So also he prepared the dwelling places, and he prepares them—not other places, but the very ones he prepared, since he did what is to come. He prepared them by predestining them; he prepares them by carrying them out.

They therefore already exist in predestination. If he had said, “I will go and prepare,” that would mean, “I will predestine.” But because they do not yet exist in their actual realization, he says: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.”

He prepares the dwelling places by preparing those who will dwell in them. For when he says, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,” what should we understand the house of God to be except the temple of God? And what this is, let the Apostle be asked, and let him answer: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

This is also the kingdom of God which the Son will hand over to the Father. Hence the same Apostle says: “Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming, then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Corinthians 15)—that is, he will hand over to his Father, to be contemplated, those whom he redeemed by his blood.

Thomas says to him:

“Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?”

The Lord had said that they knew both: both the destination to which he was going and the way by which he was going. Thomas said that he knew neither—the place to which one goes nor the way by which one goes.

But he does not know how to lie. Therefore they did know, but did not know that they knew. Let him now convince them that they already know what they think they still do not know.

Jesus says to him:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

Could his apostles, with whom he was speaking, not have said to him, “We do not know you”? Therefore, if they knew him, and he is the way, they knew the way. If they knew him, and he is the truth, they knew the truth. If they knew him, and he is the life, they knew the life.

They are thus shown to know what they said they did not know. What, then, do we grasp from this discourse? What do you think, my brothers, except that he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way”?

And now we have learned that they knew the life and that they knew him who is the way. But the way is that by which one goes; is it also the destination to which one goes? Yet he had said that they knew both: where he was going and the way.

It was therefore necessary for him to say, “I am the way,” in order to show that, because they knew him to be the way, they knew the way, although they had thought that they did not know it.

But why was it necessary for him to say, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” when, once the way by which he was going had become known, it remained to learn where he was going? It was because he was going to the truth, he was going to the life.

He was therefore going to himself by way of himself. And where do we go except to him? And by what way do we go except by him? He, therefore, goes to himself by way of himself; we go to him by way of him—or rather, he himself goes to the Father, and he comes to us.

For elsewhere he says of himself, “I am going to the Father,” and in this passage he says it on our account.

“No one,” he says, “comes to the Father except through me.”

Thus he himself goes by himself, to himself, and to the Father; and we go through him, to him, and to the Father.

Tell me, Lord my God—tell me, I beg you—how do you go to yourself? Did you leave yourself in order to come to us, especially since you did not come from yourself, but the Father sent you?

I know that you emptied yourself; but you did so because you took the form of a servant, not because you abandoned the form of God, either to which you would return or which you would recover. You came, and you reached not only the eyes of flesh but also the hands of human beings. How, except in the flesh?

Through the flesh you came, while remaining where you were. Through the flesh you returned, without leaving the place from which you had come. If, then, through the flesh you came and returned, without doubt through the flesh you were not only the way for us by which we might come to you, but also the way for you by which you might come and return.

And when you went to the life that you yourself are, you surely led that same flesh of yours from death to life.

The Word of God is one thing, and the human being another; but “the Word became flesh,” that is, became human. Therefore the person of the Word is not one person and the person of the human being another, since both together are Christ, one person.

Accordingly, just as when the flesh died, Christ died, and when the flesh was buried, Christ was buried—for this is what we believe in our hearts for righteousness and confess with our mouths for salvation—so, when the flesh came from death to life, Christ came to life.

And because Christ is the Word of God, Christ is life. Thus, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, the one who never abandoned himself or lost himself came to himself.

As was said, God came to human beings through the flesh; truth came to liars. For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar. When he took his flesh away from human beings and raised it to that place where no one lies, the same one, because the Word became flesh, returned through himself, as through the flesh, to the truth that he himself is.

He preserved that truth even among liars and in death. Christ was dead for a time, but he was never false.

Receive an example that is different and far unequal, yet in some way helps us understand God from things more closely subject to God.

Look at me. As far as my soul is concerned, since I am what you also are, when I am silent I am with myself. But when I speak to you what you can understand, I somehow come forth to you. I do not leave myself, but I approach you without departing from where I come forth.

When I am silent, I somehow return to myself; and I somehow remain with you if you retain what you have heard in the discourse I deliver.

If an image made by God can do this, what can the Image of God do—an image not made by God, but born from God, and itself God?

That which came forth to us and by which he returned from us was his body. It did not pass away like my voice, but remains where it now no longer dies, and death will no longer have dominion over it.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “So that where I am, you also may be”? Where were they destined to be except in him? And therefore he too is in himself; so they are there where he is—that is, in him.

This is eternal life, in which we shall be when he has received us to himself; and this eternal life, which he himself is, is in him. Where he is, we too are to be—that is, in him—just as the Father has life in himself.

And surely the life he has is nothing other than the one who himself possesses it. So he granted the Son to have life in himself, although he himself is the very life that he has in himself.

But will we be the life that he is when we begin to be in that life—that is, in him? Certainly not. He, existing as life, possesses life, and he is what he possesses; and the life that is in him is himself in himself.

We, however, are not life itself, but partakers of his life. Thus we shall be there in such a way that we cannot be in ourselves what he is; rather, although we ourselves are not life, we shall have him as life—him who possesses life in himself because he himself is life.

In the end, he is both immutably in himself and inseparably in the Father. We, however, when we wished to be in ourselves, became troubled in ourselves. Hence the saying: “My soul is troubled within me” (Psalm 42). Changed for the worse, we could not remain even what we had been.

But when we come through him to the Father, as he says, “No one comes to the Father except through me,” by remaining in him no one will be able to separate us either from the Father or from him.

“If you had known me,” he says, “you would certainly have known my Father also.”

This is what he meant by saying, “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Then he adds:

“And from now on you know him, and you have seen him.”

But Philip, one of the apostles, not understanding what he had heard, says:

“Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

The Lord says to him:

“Have I been with you for such a long time, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

How can he now say, “I have been with you for such a long time, and you have not known me, Philip,” when they clearly knew both where he was going and the way, for no other reason than that they knew him?

The question is easily resolved if we say that some of them knew him and others did not, and that Philip was among those who did not know him. When he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way,” we should understand him to have addressed those who knew him, not Philip, to whom he said, “I have been with you for such a long time, and you have not known me, Philip?”

To those who already knew the Son, therefore, he also said concerning the Father, “From now on you know him, and you have seen him.” He said this because of the complete likeness that exists between the Son and the Father, so that those who knew the Son who is like the Father could now be said to know the Father.

They already knew the Son—if not all of them, at least some of those to whom he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way.” For he himself is the way.

But they did not know the Father. Therefore they hear: “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also”—through me, certainly, and him as well.

For I am one, and he is another. Yet lest they think him unlike the Son, he says, “From now on you know him.” They had seen the Son, who was completely like the Father.

They nevertheless needed to be taught that the Father, whom they did not yet see, was also such as the Son whom they saw. To this serves what is said afterward to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

This does not mean that the Son and the Father are the same person—a doctrine condemned by the catholic faith in the Sabellians, who are also called Patripassians—but that the Father and the Son are so alike that whoever knows one knows both.

We commonly speak in this way of two people who are very much alike. When someone sees one of them and wants to know what the other is like, we say, “You have seen this one? You have seen that one.”

Thus it is said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” not because the Son is the Father, but because the Son differs in absolutely nothing from the likeness of the Father.

For if the Father and the Son were not two, it would not have been said, “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also.” Since, then, he says, “No one comes to the Father except through me,” the meaning is: “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also, because I, through whom one comes to the Father, will lead you to him, so that you may know him also.”

But because I am altogether like him, “from now on you know him” when you know me; and “you have seen him” if you have seen me with the eyes of the heart.

What, then, is the meaning of what you say, Philip: “Show us the Father, and that is enough for us”?

“Have I been with you for such a long time,” he says, “and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

If this vision is too much for you, at least believe what you do not see.

“How can you say,” he asks, “Show us the Father?” If you have seen me, who am altogether like him, you have seen the one to whom I am like.

And if you cannot see this, can you at least not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?

Philip could have said here: “I do see you, and I believe that you are altogether like the Father. But is he to be blamed and rebuked because, when he sees one who is like him, he also wants to see the one to whom he is like? I know the likeness, but I still know the one without the other. I am not satisfied unless I also know the one to whom this one is like. Therefore, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

But the teacher rebuked the disciple because he saw what the petitioner’s heart was seeking. Philip desired to know the Father as though the Father were better than the Son, and for that reason he did not even know the Son, whom he believed to be inferior to something better.

To correct this understanding, it was said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” Why, then, do you say, “Show us the Father”? I understand what you are saying: you are not asking to see another who is like him, but you think that the other is better.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

Why do you want to see a distinction between those who are alike? Why do you desire to know separately those who are inseparable?
