“The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself. But the Father, who remains in me, himself does the works. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise …”

Therefore words too are works? Certainly they are. For whoever builds up his neighbor by speaking performs a good work.

But what does “I do not speak from myself” mean except “I am not, from myself, the one who speaks”? For he attributes what he does to the one from whom he himself is who does it.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.”

What does this mean? We did not find anyone who performed the works Christ performed; shall we find someone who will do even greater works?

But in the preceding discourse we said that it was a greater work when the sick were healed by the passing of Peter’s shadow—which the disciples accomplished—than by touching the Lord’s garment—which the Lord himself accomplished (Matthew 9). We also said that more people believed through the apostles than through the Lord himself preaching with his own mouth.

Thus these works should be understood as greater, not because the disciple was greater than the teacher, the servant greater than the master, the adopted child greater than the only-begotten Son, or a human being greater than God, but because he himself deigned to perform through them these greater works—the same one who says to them elsewhere, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

For he himself, to pass over countless other things, made them without them, made this world without them; and because he also deigned to become human, he made himself without them as well.

What, then, can they do without him except sin?

And here he immediately removed what might have troubled us concerning this matter. For after saying, “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these,” he immediately continued and added, “Because I am going to the Father.”

And whatever you ask in my name, I will do. He had said, “he will do”; afterward he says, “I will do.” Moreover, to do greater works through him than apart from him is not a deficiency but a condescension. For what can servants repay the Lord for all that he has repaid them? Since, among his other gifts, he deigned to grant them this also: that he should do greater works through them than apart from them.

Did not that rich and sorrowful man depart from his presence when he rejected the counsel concerning eternal life that he had sought and heard (Luke XVIII)? Yet afterward, when one person did not act upon what he had heard from him, many acted upon it when the good Teacher spoke through his disciples. Behold, greater works were done when he was preached by believers than when he spoke to hearers.

Yet this still raises a question: he did these greater works through the apostles. But he did not mean only them when he said, “The works that I do, you also will do, and you will do greater works than these”; rather, wishing all who belonged to his household to be understood, he says, “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these.” If, then, the one who believes will do them, certainly the one who does not do them does not believe. So it is with the saying, “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments” (Matthew VII): therefore, whoever does not keep them does not love.

Likewise, in another passage: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a prudent man who built his house upon rock.” Whoever, therefore, is not like this prudent man undoubtedly either hears these words of mine and does not do them, or does not hear and do them at all.

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even though he dies, will live.” Whoever, therefore, does not believe in me will certainly not live. The same applies here: “Whoever believes in me will do” (John XI). Therefore, the one who does not do them does not believe. [Col. 0825A]

What does this mean, brothers? Is one who has not done works greater than Christ not to be counted among those who believe in Christ? It is harsh, absurd, intolerable, impossible to accept unless it is understood. Let us therefore listen to the Apostle: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans IV).

In this work we do Christ’s works, because believing in Christ itself is Christ’s work. He works this in us, though certainly not without us. Listen, then, and understand: “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do.” First, therefore, I will do them; afterward he too will do them, because I cause him to do them. What works are these, except that the ungodly should become righteous?

“And he will do greater works than these.” Greater than which works, I ask? Does one who works out his own salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians II) do greater works than all Christ’s works, when Christ works this in him, though not without him? I would certainly say that this is greater than heaven and earth and whatever is seen in heaven and on earth. Heaven and earth will pass away, but the salvation and justification of the predestined will remain. In the former there are merely works of God; in the latter there is also the image of God.

But in heaven, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, archangels, and angels are Christ’s works. Does one who, with Christ working within him, cooperates in his own eternal salvation and justification do works greater even than these? I do not dare to rush to a judgment here. Let whoever can understand, understand; let whoever can judge, judge whether it is greater to create the righteous than to justify the ungodly. Certainly, if the two require equal power, this requires greater mercy.

This is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed on in the world, and was taken up in glory.

But no necessity compels us to understand all Christ’s works in the words, “He will do greater works than these.” For perhaps he meant the works that he himself was doing. At that time he was doing words of faith, and he had spoken beforehand of these works, saying: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father dwelling in me himself does the work.” At that time, therefore, his words were his works. And certainly it is less to preach words of righteousness—which he did apart from us—than to justify the ungodly, which he did in us in such a way that we too might do it.

“For I am going to the Father; and whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” [Col. 0825D] Thus he went to the Father without abandoning those in need, but hearing those who asked. Yet what does “whatever you ask” mean, when we often see his faithful ask and not receive? Is it perhaps because they ask wrongly? For the Apostle James reproved this, saying: “You ask, and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your passions” (James IV).

If, then, someone would use badly what he wishes to receive, in his mercy God does not grant it. Accordingly, if something is asked of him which, when granted, harms a person, one should fear more lest he give in anger what in his mercy he could have withheld.

Do we not see that the Israelites obtained something to their own harm? They had desired to eat meat, although manna was being rained down upon them from heaven (Numbers XI). Awake, therefore, faithful man, and listen attentively to what is written there: “In my name.” For he does not say merely, “Whatever you ask,” without qualification, but “in my name.”

Who, then, is the one who promised so great a benefit? Certainly, Christ Jesus. “Christ” signifies “king”; “Jesus” signifies “Savior.” Therefore, it is not just any king who will save us, but the King who is Savior. Consequently, whatever we ask against the benefit of salvation, we do not ask in the name of the Savior. Yet he is Savior not only when he does what we ask, but also when he does not do it, because when he sees that something is being asked against salvation, by not doing it he shows himself the Savior.

A physician knows what the sick person asks for his own health and what he asks against it. Therefore, he does not carry out the will of one who asks for harmful things, so that he may bring about health. Whenever, therefore, we wish him to do whatever we ask, let us ask not indiscriminately but in his name.

And if he does it, he does it as Savior, which is what his name means for his faithful. For he is also Judge to the ungodly, while he deigns to be Savior to the faithful. Whoever, therefore, believes in him: whatever that person asks in the name which he is for those who believe in him, he does, because he does it as Savior.

But if one who believes in him, through ignorance, asks for something against his own salvation, he does not ask in the name of the Savior, because the Savior will not be his Savior if he does what obstructs his salvation. Therefore, it is better for him not to do what he is invoked to do, so that by not doing it he may do what he is called.

For this reason, he is not only Savior but also the good Teacher. In the very prayer that he gave us, in order to do whatever we ask, he taught us what we should ask, so that we may understand also that when we ask contrary to the rule of his teaching, we are not asking in the Teacher’s name.

Certainly, even if we ask for certain things in his name—that is, according to the Teacher—he does not do them at the time we ask, and yet he does do them. For we ask that the kingdom of God may come (Matthew VI); nevertheless, he does not fail to do what we ask merely because we do not immediately reign with him in eternity. What we ask is postponed, not denied. Yet in our praying, like sowers, let us not grow weary (Galatians VI), for in due season we shall reap.

We must not listen carelessly to what the Lord says. Lest anyone suppose that he would do, without the Father, what he promised to do for those who asked, after saying, “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do,” he immediately added: [Col. 0826D]

“So that the Father may be glorified in the Son; if you ask anything in my name, I will do it.”

Therefore, he does nothing at all without the Father, since he does it precisely so that the Father may be glorified in him. The Father therefore acts in the Son, so that the Son may be glorified in the Father; and the Son acts in the Father, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son, because the Father and the Son are one.

Christ promised the apostles the Spirit, the Paraclete. Let us observe how he promised him:

“If you love me,” he says, “keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth.”

Since he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, without whom we can neither love God nor keep his commandments, how do we love in order to receive him, when, unless we have him, we cannot love? How do we keep the commandments in order to receive him, when, unless we have him, we cannot keep the commandments?

It remains, therefore, that we understand that the one who loves has the Holy Spirit; by having him, merits to have more; and by having more, loves more.

The disciples already had the Spirit whom the Lord promised, for without him they would not have called him Lord. Yet they did not yet have him in the manner in which the Lord promised him. Thus they both had him and did not have him: they did not yet have as much of him as they were destined to have. They had less; more was to be given them. They had him secretly; they were to receive him openly, since it also belonged to the greater gift of the Holy Spirit that what they had should be made known to them.

Speaking of this gift, the Apostle says: “We have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God” (1 Corinthians II).

The Lord brought about the manifest imparting of the Holy Spirit twice, not once only. Immediately after he rose from the dead, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). Did the one who gave him then therefore not also send afterward the one whom he had promised? Or is the Holy Spirit not the same Spirit who was then breathed forth from him and afterward sent by him from heaven?

Why, then, the gift of the Spirit that was visibly made was given twice is another question. Perhaps it was because of the two commandments of love, love of neighbor and love of God, so that it might be shown to belong to the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0827C]

But when he says, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” he shows that he himself is also the Paraclete. For *Paraclete* is called in Latin *advocatus*, “advocate”; and it is said of Christ: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John II).

He said that the world cannot receive the Holy Spirit in the same sense in which it is also said: “The prudence of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be”—as if we were to say, “Injustice cannot be justice.” Here, by “the world,” he means lovers of the world. This love is not from the Father, and therefore it is opposed to the love of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. We strive for the love of this world to be diminished and consumed in us. Therefore, the world cannot receive him, [Col. 0827D]

“because it does not see him or know him.”

For worldly love does not possess the invisible eyes by which the Holy Spirit can be seen, since he cannot be seen except invisibly.

“But you,” he says, “will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

He will be in them so that he may remain, not remain so that he may be in them. For being present to someone precedes remaining. Yet lest they think that “he will remain with you” had been spoken in the manner in which a guest ordinarily remains visibly with a person, he explained what he meant by “with you” when he added, “in you.”

Therefore, he is seen invisibly; and unless he is in us, his knowledge cannot be in us. Thus he is seen by us in us, just as our own consciousness is. We see another person’s face, but not our own; yet we see our own consciousness, though not another’s. Consciousness, however, exists only in us, whereas the Holy Spirit can exist even without us. He is given so that he may also be in us. But he cannot be seen and known by us in the manner in which he must be seen and known unless he is in us.

[Note: Delete *videndum* (“to be seen”), so that the syntax and sense may be satisfactory. EDIT.]

“I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.”

Orphans are the fatherless. The former is the Greek name for the same thing, the latter the Latin. For in the Psalm where we read, “You will be the helper of the fatherless” (Psalm IX), the Greek has *orphanō*.

Although, then, the Son of God has adopted us as sons for his own Father, and has willed that we should have as Father by grace the one who is his Father by nature, nevertheless he too shows toward us a fatherly affection of a kind when he says: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.”

Hence he also calls us the bridegroom’s children when he says: “The hour will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then the bridegroom’s children will fast” (Luke V). And who is the bridegroom except the Lord Christ?

Then he continues and says:

“A little while longer, and the world will no longer see me.”

What does this mean? Did the world not see him then, since by “the world” he wants those people to be understood of whom he also spoke above, saying of the Holy Spirit: “The world cannot receive him, because it does not see him or know him”?

The world certainly saw him with its eyes, visible in the flesh; but it did not see the Word hidden in the flesh. It saw a man; it did not see God. It saw the garment; it did not see the one clothed.

But since, after the resurrection, he showed his own flesh to his followers not only to be seen but also to be touched, and wished to show it to those who were not his, perhaps we should understand these words in this sense: “A little while longer, and the world will no longer see me. But you will see me, because I live, and you will live.”

Why did he say that he lives in the present, but that they would live in the future? Was it not because he also promised them the life of the flesh—the life, certainly, of the resurrection—which was to follow, of the kind that preceded in him? And because his resurrection was soon to occur, he used a verb in the present tense to signify its nearness; but because their resurrection is postponed until the end of the age, he did not say, “You live,” but “You will live.”

Thus, with two words, one in the present tense and one in the future, he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, which was soon to occur, and ours, which will come at the end of the age. “Because I live,” he says, “you will live.”

Because he lives, we too will live. Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians XV). No one comes to death except through him; no one comes to life except through Christ.

Because we lived for ourselves, we died. Because he lives, we will live. We died to him when we lived for ourselves. But because he died for us, he lives both for himself and for us. Because he lives, we will live.

For just as through ourselves we were able to have death, so we could not have life through ourselves.

“On that day,” he says, [Col. 0829A]

“you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.”

On what day, except the day of which he says, “You will live”? Then we shall be able to see what we believe. For even now he is in us, and we are in him. But now we believe this; then we shall also know it. Even now, by believing, we have knowledge of it, but then we shall know it by contemplation.

On that day, therefore, when we live by the life in which death is swallowed up, we shall know that he is in the Father, and we are in him, and he is in us. For then what has already been begun through him will be brought to perfection: that he may be in us and we in him.

“Whoever has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them, that is the one who loves me.”

The one who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or who has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—that one, he says, is the one who loves me.

Love must be demonstrated by works, lest the name be an unfruitful title.

“And whoever loves me,” he says, “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

What does “I will love him” mean? As though he were then going to love him and did not love him now? Far from it. How could the Father love us without the Son, or the Son without the Father? Since they work inseparably, how could they love separably?

He said, “I will love him,” with reference to what follows: “And I will manifest myself to him.” “I will love, and I will manifest”—that is, I will love for the purpose of manifesting.

For now he loved us so that we might believe and hold fast the commandment of faith; then he will love us so that we may see and receive the vision itself as the reward of faith. Now we love by believing what we shall see; then we shall love by seeing what we believe.

Since the Lord had said, “A little while longer, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me,” Judas questioned him about this—Judas not the betrayer, who was called Iscariot, but the one whose Epistle is read among the canonical Scriptures.

“Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?”

Let us be with those disciples as though we too were asking questions, and let us hear the common Teacher. For holy Judas, not unclean, not a persecutor of the Lord but a follower, asked why Jesus would manifest himself not to the world but to his own; why, after a little while, the world would not see him.

Jesus answered and said to him:

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

The reason is now explained why he will manifest himself to his own and not to strangers, whom he calls by the name “world”: the reason is that these love, whereas those do not love.

This is the reason proclaimed by the sacred Psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm XLII).

Those who are loved are loved because they love. But those who do not love—even if they speak in the tongues of men and of angels—become sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal; even if they have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have all faith so as to move mountains, they are nothing; even if they distribute all their possessions and hand over their body to be burned, it profits them nothing (1 Corinthians XIII). [Col. 0830A]

Love distinguishes the saints from the world; it makes them dwell together in unity in one house (Psalm LXVII).

In this house the Father and the Son make their dwelling, giving the very love by which they grant their manifestation in faith. Concerning this manifestation the disciple questioned the Teacher, so that not only those who were then hearing through his mouth but also we, through his Gospel, might know it.

He had asked about Christ’s manifestation and had heard about love and dwelling. There is therefore an inner manifestation of God, utterly unknown to the ungodly, for whom there is no manifestation of God the Father and the Holy Spirit. The manifestation of the Son could have existed for them, but in the flesh; and it is neither like that manifestation nor, whatever its character, can it remain with them always. It lasts only for a little while, and that for judgment, not joy; for punishment, not reward.

We must therefore understand, as far as he himself deigns to disclose it, how the words are to be understood: “A little while longer, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me.”

It is true that shortly afterward he was going to remove even his body, which the ungodly were able to see, from their eyes, since after the resurrection none of them saw him. But since it was said, with the angels bearing witness, “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts I), and we believe nothing other than that he will come in the same body to judge the living and the dead, certainly the world will then see him—the name by which those alienated from his kingdom are signified.

Consequently, it is far better understood that he intended the words, “A little while longer, and the world will no longer see me,” to signify another time: the time when, at the end of the age, he will be taken from the eyes of the condemned, so that thereafter they may see him among those in whom the Father and he himself make their dwelling by making them love him.

He said “a little while” because even what seems long to human beings is exceedingly brief before the eyes of God. Of this little while John the Evangelist says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II).

Moreover, lest anyone suppose that the Father and the Son alone, without the Holy Spirit, make their dwelling with those who love them, let him recall what was said above about the Holy Spirit: “The world cannot receive him, because it does not see him or know him; but you know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

Behold, the Holy Spirit also makes his dwelling in the saints with the Father and the Son, inwardly, certainly, like God in his temple. God the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—come to us as we come to them. They come by helping; we come by obeying. They come by enlightening; we come by contemplating. They come by filling; we come by receiving. Thus their vision in us is not external but inward, and their dwelling in us is not temporary but eternal.

This is how the Son does not manifest himself to the world. Here “world” refers to those of whom he immediately continued by saying: [Col. 0831A]

“Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

These are the people who never see the Father and the Holy Spirit, while they see the Son for a little while—not to be blessed but to be judged. They do not see him in the form of God, in which he is invisible with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in the form of a man, in which he willed to be in the world, contemptible in suffering and terrible in judgment.

As for what he added:

“And the word that you heard is not mine but the Father’s, who sent me,”

let us neither be surprised nor afraid. He is not less than the Father, but he is from the Father; he is not unequal to him, but he is not from himself.

For he did not lie when he said, “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” Behold, he said that the words were his. Is he contradicting himself when he later says, “And the word that you heard is not mine”?

Perhaps, because of a distinction, where he called them his own he used the plural, “words.” But where he said that the “word”—that is, the Word—was not his but the Father’s, he wished himself to be understood.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The Word is not his own, but the Father’s—just as he is not his own image but the Father’s, nor is he his own Son in the same way, but the Father’s.

Therefore, the equal agent rightly attributes to the one from whom he has this very equality whatever he does.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.”

That dwelling is different from the dwelling that he promised would come; this is different from the dwelling that he testifies is present. The former is spiritual and is bestowed inwardly upon minds; the latter is bodily and is presented outwardly to eyes and ears. The former blesses the liberated eternally; the latter visits those who are to be liberated in time.

According to the former, the Lord does not depart from those who love him; according to the latter, he goes and returns.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you”—that is, by the bodily presence in which he spoke visibly with them.

“But the Paraclete,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of everything that I have said to you.”

Does the Son speak and the Holy Spirit teach, so that we receive the words when the Son speaks but understand those same words when the Holy Spirit teaches? As if the Son could speak without the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit teach without the Son?

Or rather, does not the Son also teach, and the Holy Spirit also speak? When God speaks and teaches something, does not the Trinity itself speak and teach?

But because it is a Trinity, it was necessary to make its individual persons known, and for us to hear them distinctly while understanding them inseparably.

Hear the Father speaking where you read: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Psalm II). Hear him also teaching where you read: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John VI).

You have just heard the Son speaking; for he says of himself: “Whatever I have said to you.” If you wish to know him also as teacher, remember that he says: “One is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew XXIII).

As for the Holy Spirit, whom you have just heard teaching in the words, “He will teach you all things,” hear him also speaking where you read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit said to blessed Peter: “Go with them, because I sent them” (Acts X).

The entire Trinity, therefore, both speaks and teaches. But unless it were also commended individually, human weakness could in no way grasp it, however imperfectly. Since the Trinity is wholly inseparable, it would never be known as Trinity if it were always spoken of inseparably.

For when we say “the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” we do not, of course, say them simultaneously, even though they cannot exist otherwise than simultaneously.

When he added, “He will remind you,” we must understand that even what we are commanded not to forget—the most salutary admonitions—belongs to the grace by which Christ reminds us.

“Peace,” he says, “I leave with you; my peace I give you.”

This is what we read in the prophet: “Peace upon peace.” He leaves us peace as he departs; he will give us his peace when he comes at the end. He leaves us peace in this age; he will give us his peace in the age to come.

He leaves us peace in which, while remaining, we conquer the enemy; he will give us his peace when we shall reign without an enemy.

But what does he leave us as he ascends from us, except himself, since he does not depart from us? For he is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians II).

He himself, therefore, is our peace, both when we believe that he is and when we see him as he is.

But why, where he says, “I leave you peace,” does he not add “my,” whereas where he says, “I give you,” he says “my”?

Should “my” be understood even where it is not stated, because it is stated afterward and can be referred to both phrases—so that what is said once applies to both? Or perhaps something is hidden here that must be requested and sought, something that must be opened to those who knock.

What if he wanted his peace to be understood as the kind of peace that he himself possesses? The peace that he leaves us in this age should rather be called ours than his. Nothing conflicts with him within himself, because he has no sin at all. We, however, now possess a kind of peace in which we must still say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew VI).

We have some peace, therefore, because we delight in the law of God according to the inner person (Romans VII), but it is not complete, because we see another law in our members warring against the law of our mind.

Likewise, he himself is our peace among us, because we believe concerning one another that we love one another. But this peace too is not complete, because we do not see one another’s thoughts, and we form opinions about one another—whether for better or for worse—concerning things that are not in us.

Thus, even if this peace was left to us by him, it is ours. Unless it came from him, we would not have even such peace; but he himself does not possess such peace.

If we hold fast to the end the peace we have received, we shall have the peace that he possesses, in which nothing within us will oppose us and nothing in our hearts will be hidden from one another.

Nor am I unaware that these words of the Lord can also be understood so that the second phrase appears to repeat the same thought:

“I leave you peace; my peace I give you.”

That is, what he had said—“peace”—he repeated by saying “my peace,” and what he had said—“I leave you”—he repeated by saying, “I give you.”

Let each person receive the words as he wishes. Yet I am pleased—and I believe you are too, my beloved brothers—to hold fast to this peace in which we conquer the adversary in harmony, while longing for the peace in which we shall have no adversary.

But when the Lord added and said:

“Not as the world gives do I give to you,”

what else does this mean except: I do not give to you as human beings do who love the world? They give themselves peace so that, without the disturbance of quarrels and wars, they may enjoy not God but their friend, the world.

And when the righteous give peace so that they may not be persecuted, the peace cannot be true where there is no true harmony, because hearts are separated. For just as one who joins his lot to another’s is called a partner, so one who joins his heart to another should be called harmonious.

Therefore, beloved, since Christ has left us peace, and gives us his peace not as the world gives but as the one through whom the world was made gives it, let us be harmonious: let us join our hearts to one another, and let us have our heart raised up, lest it be corrupted on earth.

“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it fear. You heard that I said to you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.”

Their hearts could therefore be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he was to come to them, lest perhaps the wolf should attack the flock during the shepherd’s absence.

But from those whom the man was leaving, God was not departing: the same Christ, man and God. He was going away in respect of what he was as man, and remaining in respect of what he was as God. He was going away in respect of what was confined to one place, and remaining in respect of what was everywhere.

Why, then, should they be troubled and afraid, when he was leaving their eyes in such a way that he did not leave their hearts?

Yet even God, who is contained by no place, departs from the hearts of those who abandon him—not with their feet but in their conduct—and comes to those who turn toward him, not with their faces but with faith, and approach him in mind, not in the flesh.

But in order that they might understand that he was speaking according to what he was as man, after saying, “I am going away and coming to you,” he added:

“If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.”

In that respect, then, in which the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father, from whom he will also come to judge the living and the dead.

The same Christ, therefore, the Son of God, equal to the Father in the form of God, because he emptied himself—not by losing the form of God but by taking the form of a servant—is greater even than himself, because the form of God, which was not lost, is greater than the form of a servant, which was taken (Philippians II).

What is surprising or unworthy, then, if the Son of God, speaking according to this form of a servant, says, “The Father is greater than I”? And speaking according to the form of God, does not this same Son of God say, “I and the Father are one” (John X)?

They are one according to what he was as God, the Word; and the Father is greater according to what the Word became when he was made flesh.

According to this form of a servant, the child Christ was also less than his parents when, as a little one subject to his elders, he was obedient to them, as it is written (Luke II).

The Son, equal to the Father, through whom man was made so that he might be less than the Father, became man. Unless this happened, what is man?

Let the Lord and our Teacher say plainly:

“If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.”

Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: divine, in which he is equal to the Father; human, in which the Father is greater than he. Yet both together constitute not two but one Christ, lest God become a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

For just as one man consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ consists of God and man. Thus Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these elements, and Christ in each of them.

Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God.

Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant.

Again, considering each element of which man consists: who was not abandoned in the underworld? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone.

Who lay in the tomb for three days, destined to rise? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone.

Christ Jesus is therefore spoken of in each of these individual elements; yet all these together constitute not two or three but one Christ.

For this reason he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father.” Human nature should rejoice because it has been assumed by the only-begotten Word in such a way that it was established as immortal in heaven, and thus earth was exalted so that incorruptible dust might sit at the right hand of the Father.

This is the manner in which he said he would go to the Father. For certainly he was going to the one who was with him. But to go to him meant to depart from us, to transform and make immortal what he had assumed from us as mortal, and to raise to heaven that which, for our sake, had been on earth.

Who would not rejoice at this, if he loved Christ so much as to rejoice that his own nature is now immortal in Christ and to hope that this will come to pass through Christ?

And now I have told you this before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe. What does this mean, when a person ought rather to believe before that which is to be believed has happened? For this is the praise of faith: that what is believed is not seen. For what great thing is it if one believes what one sees? This accords with that saying of the same Lord, when he reproved the disciple, saying, “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who do not see and yet believe” (John 20).

And I do not know whether anyone should be said to believe what he sees. For faith itself is defined in the Epistle written to the Hebrews as follows: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11). Therefore, if faith concerns things that are believed, and that same faith concerns things that are not seen, what does the Lord’s saying mean: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe”? Should he not rather have said, “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may see”? For the one to whom it was said, “Because you have seen, you have believed,” did not believe the very thing that he saw; he saw one thing and believed another. He saw a human being; he believed him to be God.

But even if things that are seen are said to be believed—as when someone says that he has believed his own eyes—that is not the faith itself which is built up in us. Rather, from the things that are seen, we are led to believe those things that are not seen. Therefore, beloved, concerning the matter now before us, when the Lord says, “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe,” he is clearly speaking of what they were to see after his death: that he was living and ascending to the Father. When they saw this, they were to believe that he himself was the Christ, the Son of God, who had been able both to do this after predicting it and to predict it before doing it. Yet they were to believe this not with a new faith, but with a faith strengthened—or certainly with one that, when he died, had nearly failed, and that was restored when he rose again. For they had not failed to believe in him beforehand as the Son of God. But when what he had previously foretold had taken place in him, that faith which, while he was speaking to them, had been small, and when he was dying had almost entirely vanished, revived and grew. Then what does he say?

“I will no longer speak much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming.” Who is this, if not the devil?

“And he has nothing in me.” That is, absolutely no sin. Thus he shows that the devil is not the ruler of created things but of sinners, whom he now calls by the name “this world.” And whenever the name “world” is used in a bad sense, it indicates only the lovers of this world, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4).

Let it therefore be far from us to understand the devil as the ruler of the world as though he possessed dominion over the whole universe—that is, over heaven and earth and all that is in them. It is of such a world that it was said, when the discourse concerned Christ the Word: “The world was made through him” (John 1). The entire world, therefore, from the highest heavens to the lowest earth, is subject to the Creator, not to the deserter; to the Redeemer, not to the destroyer; to the liberator, not to the captor; to the teacher, not to the deceiver.

But the apostle Paul made clearer how the devil is to be understood as the ruler of the world. After saying, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—he added: “but against principalities and powers, and against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Ephesians 6). In the following word he explained what he meant by “world,” when he added, “of this darkness,” lest anyone should understand by “world” the whole creation, whose rulers the fallen angels certainly are not. “Of this darkness,” he says—that is, of the lovers of this world.

Yet some of these have been chosen—not through their own merit, but through the grace of God. To them it is said: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). All, therefore, were once under the rulers of this darkness—that is, of ungodly human beings—like darkness under darkness. But thanks be to God, who, as the same Apostle says, “has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1). In that kingdom the ruler of this world, that is, of this darkness, had nothing in Christ, because God had not come with sin, nor had the Virgin borne his flesh from the propagation of sin. And as though someone were to say to him, “Why then do you die, if you have no sin deserving the punishment of death?” he immediately added:

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that, just as the Father commanded me, so I do: rise, let us go from here.” He was speaking while reclining to those who were reclining. Yet he says, “Let us go.” Where, unless to the place where he was to be handed over to death—he who had no merit deserving death, but had the Father’s command that he should die, like the one of whom it had been foretold: “What I did not seize, then I repaid” (Psalm 68 [69])—without doubt intending to pay the debt of death and redeem us from the death we deserved.

## CHAPTER 15

“I am the true vine,” and so forth.

This Gospel passage, brothers, in which the Lord says that he is the vine and his disciples are the branches, is spoken according to the fact that he is the head of the Church and we are his members: “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” The vine and the branches are of one nature. Therefore, although he was God, whose nature we do not share, he became human, so that in him human nature might be the vine, whose branches we human beings can also be.

What, then, does “I am the true vine” mean? Did he add “true” in order to refer it to that vine from which this likeness was transferred? For he is called a vine by likeness, not by proper identity, just as he is called a sheep, a lamb, a lion, a rock, a cornerstone, and other such things. Rather, those things from which these likenesses are drawn are themselves more truly what they signify. But when he says, “I am the true vine,” he clearly distinguishes himself from the one to whom it is said: “How have you been turned into bitterness, O foreign vine?” (Jeremiah 2; Isaiah 5). For how can that be the true vine which was expected to produce grapes but produced thorns? “I am,” he says, “the true vine.”

“And my Father is the farmer. Every branch that does not bear fruit, he will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit.”

Are the farmer and the vine one and the same? Christ is the vine according to what he said: “The Father is greater than I.” But according to what he said, “I and the Father are one,” he too is the farmer. He is not like those who perform an external service by working from without; rather, he is such a farmer as also gives inward growth. For “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3). And Christ is certainly God, because “the Word was God” (John 1). Hence he and the Father are one; and although the Word became flesh, which he had not been, he remains what he was.

Finally, after saying of the Father, as of a farmer, that he takes away fruitless branches and cleanses fruitful ones so that they may bear more fruit, he immediately showed himself also to be the cleanser of the branches:

“Now you are clean,” he says, “because of the word which I have spoken to you.”

Behold, he too is the cleanser of the branches, which is the farmer’s work, not the vine’s. He also made the branches his fellow workers. For although they do not give growth, they nevertheless provide some assistance—but not from themselves, because he says, “Without me you can do nothing.” They are clean, of course, and are still to be cleansed. For unless they were clean, they could not bear fruit; and yet every branch that bears fruit the farmer cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit. It bears fruit because it is clean, and in order that it may bear more, it is cleansed further.

For who in this life is so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more? If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, “he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1). He cleanses the clean—that is, the fruitful—so that they may be more fruitful in proportion as they are cleaner.

“Now you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.” Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the baptism with which you have been washed,” but rather, “because of the word which I have spoken to you”? Is it not because the word also cleanses in the water? Take away the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself, as it were, a visible word.

For he was certainly speaking of this when he washed the disciples’ feet: “The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.” From where does water possess such great power that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless through the word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed. For even in the word itself, one thing is the passing sound and another thing is the enduring power.

“This is the word of faith which we preach,” says the Apostle: “because if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10). Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). And in his Epistle blessed Peter says: “In the same way baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience” (1 Peter 3).

This is the word of faith which we preach, through which baptism is undoubtedly consecrated so that it can cleanse. For Christ, the vine with us and the farmer with the Father, loved the Church and handed himself over for her. Read the Apostle and see what he adds: “So that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5). Cleansing, therefore, would by no means be attributed to the flowing and transitory element unless the word were added.

“Remain in me,” he says, “and I in you.” He is not in them in the same way that they are in him. Both are beneficial—not to him, but to them. For the branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the source of their life. The vine, however, is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment, rather than receiving anything from them.

Thus, for the disciples, both to have Christ remaining in them and to remain in Christ is beneficial—not to Christ. For when a branch has been cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root. Finally, he adds and says:

“As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.”

A great commendation of grace, my brothers! It enlightens the hearts of the humble and closes the mouths of the proud. Whether little or much, nothing can be done without him, without whom nothing can be done. For even if the branch has produced a little fruit, and the farmer cleanses it so that it may produce more, nevertheless, unless it remains in the vine and lives from the root, it cannot bear any amount of fruit by itself.

“If anyone does not remain in me,” he says, “he will be cast out like a branch and will wither; and they will gather him and throw him into the fire, and he will burn.”

The branches of the vine are therefore more contemptible if they do not remain in the vine, and more glorious if they do remain. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet Ezekiel that, once cut off, they are useful for none of the farmer’s purposes and are not assigned to any craftsman’s work (Ezekiel 15). One of two things awaits the branch: either the vine or the fire. If it is not in the vine, it will be in the fire. Therefore, if it is not to be in the fire, let it be in the vine.

“If you remain in me,” he says, “and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, ask, and it will be done for you.”

By remaining in Christ, what can they wish for except what accords with Christ? By remaining in the Savior, what can they wish for except what is not foreign to salvation? We wish for one thing because we are in Christ, and another because we are still in this world. From our remaining in this world, the desire sometimes steals upon us to ask for what we do not know is harmful to us. But far be it from this being done for us if we remain in Christ, who, when we ask, does nothing except what benefits us.

Therefore, while we remain in him and his words remain in us, whatever we wish we ask, and it will be done for us. For if we ask and it is not done, we are not asking for something that has a place in our remaining in him, nor for something contained in his words that remain in us. Rather, we are asking according to the desire and weakness of the flesh, which is not in him and in which his words do not remain.

The prayer he taught certainly belongs to his words—the prayer in which we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). Let us not depart from the words and meaning of this prayer in our petitions, and whatever we ask will be done for us. His words are said to remain in us when we do what he commanded and love what he promised. But when his words remain in the memory and are not found in one’s life, the branch does not remain in the vine, because it draws no life from the root.

Christ’s words do not remain in those who, as it were, touch them but do not cling to them. Therefore, they will be for such people not a benefit but a testimony; and because they are present in them without remaining in them, they are held by them so that they may be judged by them.

“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.”

The word *doxa* (δόξα), which is Greek, is *gloria* in Latin. I thought this should be mentioned because the Apostle says: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Romans 4). This is glory directed toward God—glory by which not the human being but God is glorified—if one is justified not by works but by faith, so that even the good works one performs come from God. For the branch could not bear fruit by itself.

Therefore, if God the Father is glorified in this, that we bear much fruit and become Christ’s disciples, let us not attribute this to our own glory, as though we possessed it from ourselves. This grace belongs to him; and therefore the glory is not ours but his. Hence elsewhere, after saying, “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works” (Matthew 5), he immediately added, lest they think their good works came from themselves: “and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Psalm 83 [84]).

For the Father is glorified in this: that we bear much fruit and become Christ’s disciples. By whom are we made so, if not by the one whose mercy goes before us? “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2).

But when he says, “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you,” he does not show an equality of nature between ours and his, as there is between the Father and himself. Rather, he shows the grace by which he is “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” He reveals himself as mediator when he says, “The Father loves me, and I love you.” For the Father certainly loves us also, but in him, because the Father is glorified in this: that we bear fruit in the vine—that is, in the Son—and become his disciples.

“Remain,” he says, “in my love.” How shall we remain? Listen to what follows: “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love.” He shows not how love is generated but how it is demonstrated, as though he were saying: “Do not think that you remain in my love if you do not keep my commandments.” For if you keep them, you will remain; that is, it will be evident that you remain in my love if you keep my commandments. Let no one deceive himself by saying that he loves him if he does not keep his commandments. For we love him in proportion as we keep his commandments; and in proportion as we keep them less, we love him less.

Although when he says, “Remain in my love,” it is not immediately apparent whether he means the love with which we love him or the love with which he himself loves us, the preceding words make this clear. For he had said, “And I have loved you,” and immediately added, “Remain in my love.” It is therefore the love with which he loved them.

What, then, does “Remain in my love” mean except “Remain in my grace”? And what does “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love” mean except this: “You will know that you remain in the love with which I love you if you keep my commandments”?

We do not therefore keep his commandments first so that he may love us; rather, unless he loves us, we cannot keep his commandments. This is the grace that is open to the humble but hidden from the proud.

But what is meant by the following?

“As I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.”

Here too he clearly wished the love of the Father to be understood as the love with which the Father loves him. For he had said, “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you,” and to these words he immediately added, “Remain in my love”—clearly, in the love with which I loved you. Therefore, when he also says of the Father, “I remain in his love,” this must be understood as the love with which the Father loved him.

But is grace also to be understood here as the means by which the Father loves the Son, just as the grace by which the Son loves us is grace, since we are sons by grace, not by nature, whereas the Only-Begotten is Son by nature, not by grace? Or is this also to be referred in the Son himself to his humanity?

Certainly it is. For by saying, “As the Father loved me, and I loved you,” he reveals the grace of the Mediator. The mediator between God and human beings is Christ Jesus not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human. And indeed, according to his humanity, it is written of him: “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2).

Accordingly, we can rightly say that, although human nature does not belong to the nature of God, it does, by grace, belong to the person of the Only-Begotten Son of God—and with such great grace that none is greater and none is equal to it. For no merits preceded that assumption of humanity; rather, all his merits began with that assumption.

The Son therefore remains in the love with which the Father loved him, and for that reason he kept his commandments. For what is that human being except the one whom God assumed? “The Word was God,” the Only-Begotten coeternal with the One who begot him. But so that he might be given to us as mediator, through ineffable grace “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

“I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.”

What is Christ’s joy in us except the joy with which he deigns to rejoice over us? And what is our joy, which he says is to be completed, except to have fellowship with him? For this reason he had said to blessed Peter: “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me.”

His joy in us is therefore the grace he has granted us. That grace is also our joy. Yet he had rejoiced in it from eternity, when he chose us before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1). We cannot rightly say that his joy was not complete. For God never rejoiced imperfectly. But that joy of his was not in us, because we did not yet exist, in whom it could be present; nor, when we began to exist, did we begin to exist with him.

Yet it was always in him, who rejoiced in us as destined to be his, with the most certain truth of his foreknowledge. His joy over our salvation, which was always in him when he foreknew and predestined us, began to be in us when he called us. And this joy we rightly call ours, by which we too shall be blessed. But our joy grows and advances, persevering toward its perfection.

It therefore begins in the faith of those being reborn and will be completed in the reward of those who rise again. This, I think, is the meaning of the saying: “I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.” Let mine be in you; let yours be completed. Mine was always complete, even before you were called, when you were foreknown as those who would be called by me. But let it also be in you, when you become what I foreknew concerning you. Let your joy be completed, because you will be blessed—something you are not yet, just as you have been created although you did not previously exist.

“This is my commandment,” he says, “that you love one another as I have loved you.”

Whether it is called a commandment or an order, both expressions translate the same Greek word, ἐντολή (*entolē*). Indeed, he had already spoken this saying: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you, so that you too may love one another” (John 13).

The repetition of this commandment commends it, except that there he says, “I give you a new commandment”; here, “This is my commandment.” There, it is as though such a commandment had not previously existed; here, as though he had no other commandment. But there it was called “new,” lest we remain in our old condition; here it is called “my,” lest we think it should be disregarded.

But when he says here, “This is my commandment,” as though there were no other, what are we to think, my brothers? Did God command us only to love one another, so that we need seek nothing else?

The Apostle certainly commends three things when he says: “Faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13). Although those two other things are included in love—that is, in charity—love is nevertheless said to be the greatest, not the only one.

How many commandments concerning faith have been given to us, and how many concerning hope? Who can gather them all together? Who can be sufficient to enumerate them? But let us consider what the same Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13). Where love is, what can be lacking? And where it is not, what can be of benefit?

The demon believes, but does not love (James 2). No one loves who does not believe. Someone who does not love may perhaps hope for forgiveness—in vain, certainly, but still he can hope. Yet no one who loves can despair. Therefore, where love is, faith and hope must also be present; and where there is love of neighbor, there must also be love of God.

For how does one who does not love God love one’s neighbor as oneself? Such a person is impious and unjust. But whoever loves iniquity plainly does not love, but hates his own soul (Tobit 12).

Let us therefore hold fast to this commandment of the Lord: that we love one another. Then we will do whatever else he commands, because whatever else there is, we possess here. This love is distinguished from the love by which human beings love one another merely as human beings. To distinguish it, the words were added: “as I have loved you.”

Why did Christ love us except so that we might be able to reign with Christ? For this purpose, then, let us also love one another, so that our love may be distinguished from that of others who do not love one another for this purpose—and therefore do not truly love.

The Lord defined the fullness of the love with which we ought to love one another, beloved brothers, when he said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

Since he had said earlier, “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you,” he added the words you have now heard: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” It follows from this, as the same evangelist John says in his Epistle (1 John 3), that just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers, loving one another as he loved us, who laid down his life for us.

This must not be understood as though we could be equal to the Lord Christ because we endured martyrdom for him even to the shedding of blood. He had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. We do not live as long as we wish, and we die even when we do not wish to die. He offered himself to us branches as the vine; apart from him we cannot possess life.

Finally, even if we die for our brothers, no martyr’s blood is poured out for the forgiveness of the sins of our brothers, as his blood was poured out for us. In this he gave us not something to imitate, but something for which to give thanks.

“You are my friends,” he says, “if you do what I command you.”

What great condescension! A good servant cannot be anything except one who has done the commands of his Lord; yet from the very standard by which good servants can be tested, the Lord wished his servants to be understood as his friends.

But, as I said, this is condescension: the Lord deigns to call those whom he knows as his servants his friends. To show that doing the commands of one’s Lord belongs to the duty of servants, he rebukes servants elsewhere, saying: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6). When you say, “Lord,” he says, show by doing his commands what you are saying.

Will he not say to an obedient servant: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25)? A person can therefore be both servant and friend, because he is a good servant. But let us attend to what follows:

“I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing.”

He established the name of friend in such a way as to remove that of servant—not so that both should remain in one person, but so that one should succeed the other when the other departs.

What does this mean? Will we not be servants even when we have done the commands of our Lord? Are we then not servants when we have been good servants? And who can contradict the Truth, which says, “I no longer call you servants”? He teaches why he said this: “because a servant,” he says, “does not know what his master is doing.”

Does a good and approved servant not also receive his master’s secrets? What, then, does he mean by saying, “A servant does not know what his master is doing”? Granted that he does not know what his master is doing: does he not even know what his master commands? For if he does not know this, how does he serve? Or how is he a servant who does not serve?

And yet God himself says: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants.” O astonishing matter! Since we cannot serve unless we do the commands of our Lord, how can we fail to be servants by doing those commands? If I am not a servant when I do the commands, and if I cannot serve unless I do them, then by serving I will not be a servant.

Just as there are two kinds of fear, which produce two kinds of people who fear, so there are two kinds of servitude, which produce two kinds of servants. There is the fear that perfect love casts out (1 John 4), and there is another fear, the holy fear that endures forever and ever (Psalm 18 [19]).

The Apostle had in mind the fear that is not in love when he said: “You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear” (Romans 8). But he had in mind the holy fear when he said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11).

In the fear that love casts out, there is also a servitude that must be cast out together with that fear. For the Apostle joined the two—servitude and fear—when he said: “You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear.”

The Lord was considering this servitude, the servitude belonging to a servant, when he said: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing.” He was not referring to the servant who belongs to holy fear, to whom it is said, “Well done, good servant, enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25), but to the servant who belongs to the fear that is to be cast out by love. Of this servant he says elsewhere: “A servant does not remain in the house forever; but the son remains forever” (John 8).

Since he has given us the power to become children of God (John 1), so that we may be not servants but children, we can, in a marvelous and ineffable yet true way, be servants and not be servants. We are servants in holy fear, to which belongs the servant who enters into his Lord’s joy; but we are not servants when we cast out the fear to which belongs the servant who does not remain in the house forever.

But to be such servants that we are not servants, we know that it is the Lord who acts. That servant does not know what his master is doing. When he does something good, he becomes proud as though he himself were doing it and not his master; and he boasts in himself rather than in the Lord. He has deceived himself, because he boasts as though he had not received.

But we, beloved, if we are to be able to be the Lord’s friends, must know what our Lord does. For he himself makes us not only human beings but also righteous; we do not make ourselves righteous. And who but he makes us know this?

“You are my friends,” he says, “because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.”

Who would dare to affirm or believe that any human being knows everything that the Only-Begotten Son heard from the Father, when no one can even grasp how he hears any word from the Father, since he himself is the Father’s one Word?

Moreover, a little later in this same discourse he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” How, then, are we to understand that he made known to his disciples everything that he heard from the Father, when for this very reason he does not say certain many things, because he knows that they cannot bear them now?

Without doubt, he says that he has done what he will do, because he has done the things that are still to come (Ecclesiastes 1). For just as he says through the Prophet, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 21 [22]), so here he says that he has made known to his disciples everything which he knows he will make known in that fullness of knowledge of which the Apostle says: “When the perfect has come, the partial will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13).

There he says: “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known. And now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face” (ibid.).

The Apostle himself also says that we have been saved through the washing of regeneration (Titus 3), yet elsewhere he says: “By hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8).

Hence his fellow apostle Peter also says: “Though you do not now see him, you believe in him; and when you see him, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorious joy, receiving the reward of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (1 Peter 1).

Therefore, just as we await the future immortality of the flesh and the salvation of our souls, although we are said already to have been saved after receiving the pledge, so we ought to hope for the future knowledge of everything that the Only-Begotten heard from the Father, although Christ has said that he has already done this.

“You did not choose me,” he says, “but I chose you.”

This is that ineffable glory. For what were we when we had not yet chosen Christ and therefore did not love him? For how can someone who does not choose him love him? Was what is sung in the psalm already in us: “I chose to be cast down in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Psalm 83 [84])? Certainly not.

What, then, were we except unrighteous and lost? We had not yet believed in him, so that he might choose us. For if he chose those who already believed, he chose people who had already been chosen. Why, then, would he say, “You did not choose me,” except because his mercy went before us (Psalm 58 [59])?

Do not say: “Before I believed, I was already doing good works; therefore I was chosen.” For what good work can there be before faith, when the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14)?

What, then, shall we say when we hear, “You did not choose me,” except that we were evil and were chosen so that, by the grace of the one who chose us, we might become good? For it would not be grace if merits had preceded it. But it is grace. Grace therefore does not find merits; it creates them. And observe, beloved, how he does not choose the good but makes good those whom he chooses.

“I,” he says, “chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

Is this not the fruit of which he had already said, “Without me you can do nothing”? He therefore chose us and appointed us to go and bear fruit. We had no fruit from which he might choose us. “That you may go,” he says, “and bear fruit.” We go in order to bear fruit, and he himself is the way by which we go—the way in which he appointed us so that we might go. Therefore, in all things, his mercy goes before us.

“And that your fruit,” he says, “should remain.”

“So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.”

Let love therefore remain; it is our fruit. At present it is in desire, not yet in satisfaction. And according to that desire, whatever we ask in the name of the Only-Begotten Son, the Father will give us.

But let us not suppose that we ask in the name of the Savior for what it is not beneficial for those being saved to receive. We ask in the name of the Savior when what we ask belongs to the prayer of salvation.

“These things I command you,” he says, “that you love one another.”

From this we must understand that this is the fruit of which he said: “I chose you so that you might go and bear fruit, and that your fruit might remain.” And when he added, “So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you,” he will give it to us if we love one another—since he himself will have given us this very love, he who chose us when we possessed no fruit, because we had not chosen him.

Therefore, commanding us concerning the fruit, he says: “These things I command you, that you love one another.” Hence the Apostle Paul, when he wished to commend the fruit of the Spirit over against the works of the flesh, placed this at the beginning: “The fruit of the Spirit is love” (Galatians 5). Then he connected the remaining things as though they had arisen from and been linked to this beginning.

Rightly, then, the good Teacher so often commends love as though it alone were to be commanded, without which the other good things cannot profit, and which cannot be possessed without the other good things by which a person is made good.

For the sake of this love, we must also patiently endure the world’s hatred. It is necessary that the world hate us when it sees that we do not want what it loves. But the Lord greatly consoles us concerning himself. After saying, “These things I command you, that you love one another,” he added:

“If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.”

Why, then, does the member raise itself above the head? You refuse to be in the body if you do not wish to endure the world’s hatred together with the head.

“If you were of the world,” he says, “the world would love what was its own.” Thus he says this to the whole Church, which he often also calls by the name “the world,” as in the passage: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). Likewise: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3). And in his Epistle John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2).

The whole world, therefore, is the Church, and the whole world hates the Church. The world thus hates the world: the enemy hates the reconciled, the condemned hates the saved, the defiled hates the cleansed. Yet this world whom God reconciles to himself in Christ, who is saved through Christ, and to whom every sin is forgiven through Christ, has been chosen out of the world that is hostile, condemned, and polluted. For from the same mass which wholly perished in Adam are made vessels of mercy, in which there is the world belonging to reconciliation; and this world is hated by the world belonging to the vessels of wrath, which have been perfected for destruction (Rom. 9).

Finally, after saying, “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own,” he immediately added:

“But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” They too, then, belonged to that from which they were chosen so as not to belong to it—not on account of their merits, since no good works had preceded them; not by nature, which through free choice had been wholly corrupted at its very root; but by a free gift, that is, by true grace. For he who chose the world out of the world made what he would choose; he did not find it already there, since “the remnant is saved according to the election of grace.” “But if it is by grace,” he says, “it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11).

If it is asked how the world of destruction loves itself, since it hates the world of redemption, it certainly loves itself with a false love, not a true one; consequently, it falsely loves itself and truly hates itself. “For he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). Yet it is said to love itself because it loves the iniquity by which it is wicked. And again it is said to hate itself because it loves what harms it. Thus it hates its nature and loves its vice. It hates what it was made by God’s goodness, and loves what was made in it through free will. Hence we are both forbidden and commanded to love it, if we understand correctly. We are forbidden where it is said to us, “Do not love the world” (1 John 2). But we are commanded where it is said to us, “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5). For these are the world that hates us.

Therefore we are forbidden to love in it what it itself loves in itself, and we are commanded to love in it what it itself hates in itself. We are forbidden to love vice in it, and commanded to love its nature, since it loves vice in itself and hates its nature. Thus we are rightly to love it and hate it, while it perversely loves and hates itself.

“Remember,” he says, “the word that I spoke to you: A servant is not greater than his lord. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.” It is therefore clear that the servant who does not remain in the house forever (John 8), the servant belonging to fear, which love casts out (1 John 4), is to be understood in the passage, “I no longer call you servants” (see above). But where it is said, “A servant is not greater than his lord; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you,” the servant belonging to chaste fear is signified—the fear that endures for ever and ever (Ps. 18). For this servant will hear: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25).

“But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.” What are “all these things” they will do, except those he has mentioned: they will hate, that is, and persecute the word they despise? For if they kept their word [the manuscript adds: “not”], and yet did not hate them or persecute them—or even if they hated them but did not persecute them—they would not do all things.

“But they will do all these things to you,” he says, “on account of my name.” What else does this mean than: “They will hate me in you; they will persecute me in you; and they will not keep your word because it is mine”? For they will do all these things to you on account of my name—not your name, but mine. The more wretched, therefore, are those who do such things on account of this name, and the more blessed are those who suffer such things on account of this name, as he himself says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5)—that is, for me, or on account of my name.

If we understand the words, “They will do all these things to you on account of my name,” in the first way, everything is referred to the righteous, as though he had said: “You will suffer all these things from them.” But if “on account of my name” is understood as though he were saying, “On account of my name, which they hate in you,” it may likewise be understood as “on account of the righteousness which they hate in you.” Accordingly, the good, when they persecute the wicked, may rightly be said to act both on account of righteousness, when they persecute the wicked out of love, and on account of the iniquity which they hate in the wicked. In the same way, the wicked may be said to suffer both on account of the iniquity that is punished in them and on account of the righteousness exercised in their punishment.

It may also be asked whether the wicked persecute the wicked—for example, when impious kings and judges, while persecuting the pious, punish murderers, adulterers, and every sort of criminal whom they know to have acted against the public laws. How then are we to understand what the Lord says: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own”?
