For the world does not love those whom it punishes, whereas we see the kinds of crimes mentioned above often punished by the world. The explanation is that the world exists both in those by whom such crimes are punished and in those by whom such crimes are loved. The world, therefore, understood as existing in the wicked and impious, hates what is its own insofar as it harms criminals, and loves what is its own insofar as it favors those very same people together with their fellow criminals.

Therefore, “They will do all these things to you on account of my name” means either “on account of which you suffer,” or “on account of which they themselves act,” because, while persecuting this in you, they hate it. And he added: “Because they do not know him who sent me.” This must be understood as referring to that kind of knowledge of which it is written elsewhere: “To know you is complete understanding” (Wis. 6). For those who know the Father by whom Christ was sent do not in any way persecute those whom Christ gathers, because they themselves too are gathered with them by Christ.

“If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” He points to the Jews more explicitly; so he was speaking of them also in the earlier passage. The Jews, then, persecuted Christ, as the Gospel most clearly indicates. Christ spoke to the Jews, not to the other nations. In them, therefore, he wanted the world to be understood—the world that hates Christ and his disciples. Indeed, it is not in them alone that he intended the world to be understood, but he also showed that they belonged to that same world.

What, then? “If I had not come, they would not have sin.” Were the Jews without sin before Christ came to them in the flesh? Who, even utterly foolish, would say that? Rather, he wishes a certain great sin—not every sin—to be understood under the general name. This is the sin by which all sins are held together, and if a person does not have it, all sins are forgiven him. It is this: that they did not believe in Christ, who came for the very purpose that people might believe in him. If he had not come, they certainly would not have had this sin. His coming became as saving for believers as it became destructive for unbelievers.

“But now they have no excuse for their sin.” Those who inquire may be troubled by the question whether those to whom Christ did not come and to whom he did not speak have an excuse for their sin. If they do not, why is it said that these have no excuse precisely because he came and spoke to them? If they do, is this excuse given so that they may be exempt from punishment, or so that they may be punished less severely?

To these questions I answer, as the Lord grants me understanding, that they have an excuse—not for every sin of theirs, but for this sin: that they did not believe in Christ, since he did not come to them and did not speak to them. But they are not included among those to whom he came in his disciples and to whom he spoke through his disciples. This is still what he does: he comes to the nations through his Church and speaks to the nations through his Church. To this belongs the saying: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). And the Apostle Paul says: “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13).

It remains to inquire whether those who died, or die, before Christ came to the nations through the Church and before they heard his Gospel can have this excuse. They certainly can, but for that reason they cannot escape condemnation. “For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. 3).

Certainly those to whom Christ came and to whom he spoke do not have that excuse for the great sin of unbelief by which they might say, “We did not see; we did not hear”—whether this excuse would be accepted by him whose judgments are inscrutable, or whether it would be accepted but would not free them from every condemnation. At any rate, they would be condemned somewhat more lightly.

You have heard the Lord saying:

“He who hates me hates my Father also.” Earlier he had said: “They will do these things to you because they do not know him who sent me.” If the Jews were asked whether they loved God, what else would they answer but that they loved him—not deliberately lying, but rather thinking so in their error? For how could they love the Father of truth when they hated the truth? They do not want their deeds to be condemned; but truth has this characteristic, that such deeds are condemned. Thus they hate the truth as much as they hate the punishments that truth inflicts upon such deeds. Yet they do not know that truth is the one that condemns those who are like them. Therefore they hate what they do not know; and when they hate it, they cannot but hate him from whom it was born. Accordingly, because they do not know that the Truth by whose judgment they are condemned was born from God the Father, they do not know him either—and they hate him.

“If I had not done among them works that no one else has done, they would not have sin.” This is that great sin of which he also said above: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin”—namely, the sin that they did not believe in him as he spoke and acted. This sin by which they did not believe in him is mentioned in this way because they are held by this sin and by the others as well. If they did not have this sin and believed in him, the others too would be forgiven them.

But what does this mean? After saying, “If I had not done works among them,” he immediately added, “that no one else has done.” For among Christ’s works, none seem greater than the raising of the dead, yet we know that the ancient prophets also did this. Elijah did so (1 Kings 17), and Elisha did so (2 Kings 4)—both while the person was living in the flesh and while he lay buried in his own tomb. Yet Christ did certain things that no one else did: he fed five thousand people with five loaves, and four thousand with seven loaves (Luke 9; Mark 8; Matt. 14); he walked upon the waters and enabled Peter to do the same; he changed water into wine (John 2); he opened the eyes of one born blind (John 9); and there are many other things that would take too long to recount.

But we reply that others also did things that he did not do, and that no one else did. Who but Moses struck the Egyptians with so many and such great plagues (Exod. 7–9 and following), led the people through the divided sea (Exod. 14), obtained manna from heaven for the hungry, and poured water from the rock for the thirsty (Exod. 16)? Who but Joshua son of Nun divided the waters of the Jordan for the people to cross, and by a prayer addressed to the Lord restrained and fixed the sun in its course (Josh. 3)? Who but Samson was satisfied in his thirst from the flowing jawbone of a dead ass (Judg. 15)? Who but Elijah was carried aloft in a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2)? Who but the three men—Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael—walked unharmed amid blazing flames that did not burn them (Dan. 3)?

I pass over the rest, since I think these examples are sufficient to show that other holy men also performed certain marvelous works that no one else performed. But no one among the ancients is read to have healed so many diseases, illnesses, and afflictions of mortals with such power. To say nothing of those whom he made well individually by commanding them as they came before him, the evangelist Mark says in one place:

“When evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons; and the whole city was gathered at the door. And he healed many who were afflicted with various diseases, and he cast out many demons” (Mark 1).

When Matthew recalled this, he also added prophetic testimony, saying: “So that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases’” (Matt. 8; Isa. 53).

Again, in another place Mark says: “Wherever he entered, into villages, towns, or cities, they placed the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched him were made well” (Mark 6). “No one else did these things among them.” For “among them” must be understood to mean not merely “in their presence” or “before them,” but truly “in them,” because he healed them. He intended these works to be understood as works that not only aroused admiration but also bestowed manifest salvation. For such benefits they ought to have returned love, not hatred.

Certainly, all the miracles of the others are surpassed by the fact that he was born of a virgin, and that he alone was able neither to violate his mother’s integrity by being conceived nor by being born. But this did not happen either before them or in them. The apostles reached knowledge of the truth of this miracle not by an observation shared with them, but through a discipleship set apart from them.

And then there is the fact that, on the third day, he restored himself alive from the tomb in the flesh in which he had been killed, and, never again to die, ascended with that flesh into heaven. This surpasses everything else that he did. But this too did not occur among the Jews or in their presence; and he had not yet done it when he said: “If I had not done among them works that no one else has done.”

Clearly, therefore, the works meant are those in which he displayed such great miracles of healing in their illnesses as no one had previously bestowed upon them. They saw these works, and, reproaching them for this, he added and said:

“But now they have seen and hated both me and my Father, so that the word written in their law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause.’” He calls it “their law,” not because they invented it, but because it was given to them, just as we say, “our daily bread” (Matt. 6), although we ask it from God by adding, “give us.”

He hates without cause who seeks no advantage from his hatred or seeks to avoid no disadvantage. Thus the impious hate God, and thus the righteous love him—that is, without ulterior motive, expecting no other good on his account, since he himself will be all things in all.

Whoever considers more deeply Christ’s words, “If I had not done among them works that no one else has done,” will find that he himself did them if any human being of God did anything of the kind. For he himself can do all things by himself, whereas no one can do anything without him. Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is not three gods but one God. Of him it is written: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders” (Ps. 71).

Therefore no one else did whatever works he performed among them, since whenever another human being did any of these things, he did them with Christ acting. But Christ performed these works himself, without their being the agents.

“But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

How does this relate to what he had said: “But now they have hated both me and my Father, so that the word written in their law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (see above)? Is it because, when the Paraclete came—the Spirit of truth—he convicted those who had seen and hated with a more manifest testimony? Indeed, did he not also turn some of those who had seen and still hated to faith, which works through love, by revealing himself to them?

To understand that this is what happened, let us recall the event. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the one hundred and twenty people gathered together, among whom were all the apostles. When they were filled with him and spoke in the languages of all the nations, many of those present were astonished by so great a miracle. They saw Peter give such a great and divine testimony about Christ that the one whom they had killed and counted among the dead was shown to have risen and to be alive. Cut to the heart, they were converted and received forgiveness for having shed so impiously and savagely so much blood, being themselves redeemed by the very blood they had shed (Acts 2).

For Christ’s blood was poured out for the remission of all sins in such a way that it could also blot out the very sin by which it was shed. Observing this, then, the Lord said: “They hated me without cause.” When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, he will bear witness about me—as though he were saying: “They hated me and killed me while seeing me; but the Paraclete will bear such testimony about me that he will make them believe in me without seeing me.”

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you too will bear witness. Because you have been with me from the beginning, you can preach what you know. But the fullness of that Spirit is not yet present with you, so that you may now do this. He, then, will bear witness about me so that you may bear witness.

For he will give you confidence to bear witness: the love of God poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who will be given to you (Rom. 5). This love was still lacking in Peter when, terrified by a servant girl’s questioning, he could not bear true witness, but, compelled by great fear contrary to his promise, denied him three times (John 18). “Fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4). “He will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness” (1 John 4).

Therefore, because he will bear witness, you too will bear witness: he in your hearts, you in your voices; he by inspiring, you by sounding forth, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18). It would have been too little for them to be encouraged by his example unless he also filled them with his Spirit.

Finally, the Apostle Peter had already heard the Lord’s words: “A servant is not greater than his lord; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (see above). He already saw these words fulfilled in the Lord. If example alone had been sufficient, he ought to have imitated the patience of his Lord; yet he gave way and denied him, unable to endure what he saw the Lord endure. But when he received the gift of the Holy Spirit, he preached the one whom he had denied, and he was not afraid to confess the one whom he had feared to acknowledge.

First, he had been instructed by example, so that he might know what was required. But he had not yet been strengthened by power, so that he might do what he knew. He had been taught to stand, but had not been made firm against falling. After this was accomplished through the Holy Spirit, he proclaimed it to the point of death. Therefore the Lord continues:

## CHAPTER XVI

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you so that you may not be scandalized.” For it is sung in the psalm: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them” (Ps. 118). Thus, having promised the Holy Spirit, through whose working in them they would become his witnesses, he appropriately added: “These things I have spoken to you so that you may not be scandalized.” For when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5), there is great peace for those who love God’s law, so that there is no scandal in them.

Then, expressing what they would have to suffer, he said:

“They will put you out of the synagogues.” But what harm was it for the apostles to be expelled from the Jewish synagogues, as though they would not have separated themselves from them even if no one had expelled them? Clearly, he wished to announce that the Jews would not receive Christ. Therefore those who did not wish to be in Christ would cast out with him those who could not exist without Christ.

For plainly, since there was no other people of God than that seed of Abraham, if they had recognized and received Christ, they would have remained as natural branches in the olive tree (Rom. 11), and there would not have been separate Churches of Christ and synagogues of the Jews. They would have been the same, if they had wished to remain in the same community. But since they did not wish this, what remained except that, remaining outside Christ, they should put outside the synagogues those who did not abandon Christ?

Once they had received the Holy Spirit and become his witnesses, they would certainly not be like those of whom it is said: “Many of the rulers of the Jews believed in him” (John 12), but, because of fear of the Jews lest they be expelled from the synagogues, they did not dare confess him. “For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (ibid.). They therefore believed in him, but not in the manner in which he wished them to believe—he who said: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John 5).

To disciples who believed in him in this way the prophecy applies, a prophecy that is found fulfilled in them: “Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and in your name they will rejoice all day, and in your righteousness they will be exalted, for you are the glory of their strength” (Ps. 88). It is rightly said to them: “They will put you out of the synagogues”—those, namely, who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10). And those who are expelled by human beings will not be ashamed, because God himself is the glory of their strength.

Finally, after saying this to them, he added:

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God. And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father, nor me.” That is, they have not known God, nor his Son, to whom they think they are offering service by killing you.

The Lord added these words as though they were intended to console those who would be expelled from the Jewish synagogues. Foretelling the evils they would suffer for bearing witness to him, he said: “They will put you out of the synagogues.” What, then, is the force here of the phrase “But the hour is coming”? He does not say, “And the hour is coming,” although he was predicting tribulation upon tribulation, not consolation after tribulation.

Or perhaps their separation from the synagogues would trouble them so greatly that they would prefer to die rather than remain in this life without the assemblies of the Jews? Far be it that those who sought the glory of God, not of human beings, should be so troubled.

What, then, does “They will put you out of the synagogues, but the hour is coming” mean, when it would seem more appropriate for him to say, “And the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God”? For it does not even say, “But the hour is coming when they will kill you,” as though death might come to them as a consolation for that separation. Rather, he says, “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

I do not think he intended this to signify anything other than that they should understand and rejoice that, when they were expelled from the assemblies of the Jews, they would gain so many people for Christ that the Jews would not be satisfied merely to expel them, but would prevent them from living, lest they convert everyone through their preaching to the name of Christ and turn them away from the observance of Judaism as though from divine truth.

We must understand this as spoken about the Jews, of whom he said: “They will put you out of the synagogues.” For even if the witnesses—that is, the martyrs—of Christ were killed by the nations, those nations did not think they were offering service to God, but to their false gods, when they did this. But among the Jews, everyone who killed the preachers of Christ thought he was offering service to God, believing that all who converted to Christ were abandoning the God of Israel.

For they were moved by this reasoning even to kill Christ himself. Their words concerning this matter have been recorded: “You see that the whole world has gone after him” (John 11); “If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (ibid.); and Caiaphas said: “It is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish” (ibid.).

In this too he sets his disciples apart through his example, when he had said to them: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” Just as they thought they were offering service to God by killing him, so they would think the same when killing them.

The meaning of these words, then, is this: “They will put you out of the synagogues; but do not fear solitude. Separated from their assembly, you will gather so many in my name that they, fearing that the temple among them and all the sacraments of the old law might be abandoned, will kill you. Thus they will shed your blood while thinking that they are offering service to God.”

This is what the Apostle said about them: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10). They thought they were offering service to God by killing God’s servants. O dreadful error! Is it so that you may please God that you strike one who pleases God? Do you overthrow the living temple of God by your blows, lest the stone temple of God be abandoned? O accursed blindness! Yet this happened in part in Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter (Rom. 11).

But while he was being killed for them, he was gathering those whom he had instructed beforehand concerning these future events, before he was killed, so that unexpected and unforeseen evils, although quickly passing, might not trouble minds that were ignorant and unprepared, but that such minds, forewarned and patiently accepting them, might be led to eternal goods.

That this was the reason he foretold these things to them, he himself also showed by adding:

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” Their hour: the dark hour, the nocturnal hour. But “by day the Lord commanded his mercy” (Ps. 41), and he declared it by night, when the night of the Jews darkened the day separated from them—the day of Christians—in that confusion, and when it was able to kill the flesh but was unable to darken the faith.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you; but now I am going to him who sent me.” First we must consider whether he had not foretold these future events before his passion. The other three evangelists clearly show that he did foretell them before they came to the supper which, according to John, he had finished when he spoke these words: “I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.”

Or is the question resolved by the fact that they too relate him as being near his passion when he said these things? Thus “from the beginning” does not mean the time when he was with them, since he spoke these words when he was already about to depart and go to the Father. Therefore, even according to those evangelists, what is said here is true: “I did not tell you these things from the beginning.”

But what are we to do concerning the testimony of the Gospel according to Matthew? He records that these things were announced to them by the Lord not only when Passover was already at hand and he was about to dine with the disciples in the imminence of his passion, but also from the beginning—when the twelve apostles are first named individually and sent out to perform divine works.

What, then, does he mean here by saying, “I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you”? It means that he had not from the beginning told them what he now says about the Holy Spirit: that he would come to them and bear witness when they were about to suffer these evils, because he was with them. The Consoler, or Advocate—for both meanings are given for the Greek word *paraklētos* (παράκλητος)—would be necessary when Christ had departed. For this reason he had not spoken of him from the beginning, when he was with them, because they were consoled by his presence.

But since he was about to depart, he had to tell them that the Spirit would come, through whom, with love poured into their hearts, they would preach the word of God with confidence. While the Spirit bore witness inwardly among them concerning Christ, they too would bear witness, and they would not be scandalized when the hostile Jews put them outside the synagogues and killed them, thinking that they were offering service to God. For love endures all things, and this love was to be poured into their hearts through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

This, then, is the whole meaning: he was going to make them his martyrs—that is, his witnesses—through the Holy Spirit, so that, while the Spirit worked in them, they would endure every hardship of persecution and would not grow cold in the love of preaching, being kindled by that divine fire.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.” I consoled you by my bodily presence, presented to your human senses, which you were able, as little ones, to comprehend.

“But now I am going to him who sent me,” and, he says, “none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” He indicates that he will go in such a way that none of them will ask where he is going, since the event would be openly visible to their bodily sight. Earlier they had asked him where he was going, and he had answered that he was going where they could not then come. Now he promises that he will go in such a way that none of them asks where he is going. For a cloud received him when he ascended from them, and as he went into heaven they did not ask with words but followed him with their eyes (Acts 1).

“But because I have spoken these things to you,” he says, “sorrow has filled your heart.” He saw what those words were doing in their hearts. They did not yet possess inwardly the spiritual consolation they would have through the Holy Spirit. They feared losing what they saw outwardly in Christ; and because they could not doubt that they would lose it, since he, who is truth, had announced this, human feeling was saddened because the sight of the flesh was being taken away.

But he knew what was more advantageous for them, since the inward sight is certainly better—the sight with which the Holy Spirit would console them. He would not place a human body before bodily eyes, but would pour himself into the hearts of believers.

Finally, he adds:

“But I tell you the truth: it is advantageous for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. But if I go away, I will send him to you.”

It is as though he were saying: “It is advantageous for you that this form of a servant be taken away from you. I, the Word made flesh, dwell among you, but I do not want you still to love me carnally and, content with this milk, always to wish to remain infants. It is advantageous for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. If I do not withdraw the tender nourishment with which I have fed you, you will not hunger for my solid food. If you cling to me carnally, you will not be capable of the Spirit.”

For what does “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” mean? Could he not send the Spirit while remaining here? Who would say that? The Spirit had not departed from where Christ was, nor had Christ come from the Father in such a way as to cease remaining in the Father. Finally, how could he not, even while present here, send the one whom we know came upon him at his baptism and remained upon him (John 1)—indeed, the one whom we know was never separable from him?

What, then, does “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” mean, except this: “You cannot receive the Holy Spirit as long as you persist in knowing Christ according to the flesh”? Hence the one who had already begun to possess the Spirit says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. 5). Whoever spiritually knows the Word made flesh knows the very flesh of Christ no longer according to the flesh.

This, surely, is what the good Teacher intended to signify when he said: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.” When Christ departed bodily, not only the Holy Spirit but also the Father and the Son were spiritually present with them.

For if Christ departed from them in such a way that, in his place, the Holy Spirit was with them but not with him, where is his promise: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28), and: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14)? He promised that he would send the Holy Spirit in such a way that the Spirit would be with them forever. Accordingly, when they passed from being fleshly or merely natural beings to becoming spiritual, they would possess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit more fully.

Therefore, the Father must in no way be believed to exist without the Son and the Holy Spirit. Wherever any one of them is, there is the one God, the Trinity. Yet the Trinity had to be presented in such a way that, although there is no difference of substances, the distinction of persons would nevertheless be commended individually.

And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.

What does this mean? Did not the Lord Christ convict the world concerning sin when he said, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15)? But lest someone perhaps say that this applies specifically to the Jews, not to the world, does he not say elsewhere, “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15)? Did he not convict concerning righteousness where he said, “Righteous Father, the world has not known you”? Did he not convict concerning judgment where he says that he will say to those on his left, “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25)? And many other passages are found in the holy Gospel where Christ will convict the world concerning these matters.

What, then, is the reason that he attributes this as something proper to the Holy Spirit? Or is it perhaps because Christ spoke to the Jewish nation and therefore does not seem to have convicted the world, so that the one who hears the convicting is understood to be convicted; whereas the Holy Spirit, in Christ’s disciples spread throughout the whole world, is understood to have convicted not one nation but the world? For as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to them: “It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority; but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1). This is what it means to convict the world. [Col. 0855D]

But who would dare say that the Holy Spirit convicts the world through Christ’s disciples and that Christ himself does not convict the world, when the Apostle cries out: “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13). Therefore, those whom the Holy Spirit convicts, Christ certainly convicts as well. But, as it seems to me, because love was to be poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit—love which drives out the fear that might have prevented them from daring to convict the world, which was raging with persecutions—he therefore said, “He will convict the world,” as though he were saying: “He will pour love into your hearts.” Thus, with fear driven away, you will have the freedom to convict.

We have often said that the works of the Trinity are inseparable, but that the persons had to be commended individually, so that both unity and Trinity might be understood not only without separation, but also without confusion.

“Concerning sin,” he says, “because they do not believe in me.” He placed this sin, as it were, alone before the others, because while it remains the others are retained, and when it departs the others are forgiven.

“But concerning righteousness,” he says, “because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

First, we must see whether anyone can rightly be convicted concerning sin, and how he can rightly be convicted concerning righteousness. For if a sinner is to be convicted because he is a sinner, will anyone think that a righteous person should be convicted because he is righteous? Far be it from us. For even if a righteous person is sometimes convicted, he is rightly convicted because, as it is written, “There is no one righteous on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7). Consequently, even when a righteous person is convicted, he is convicted concerning sin, not concerning righteousness. Likewise, in what we read as divinely spoken, “Do not become excessively righteous” (ibid.), it is not the righteousness of the wise person that is censured, but the pride of one who presumes. [Col. 0856A]

Whoever therefore becomes excessively righteous becomes unjust precisely through that excess. For the person who says that he has no sin, or who thinks that he is made righteous not by grace but by the sufficiency of his own will, makes himself excessively righteous. He is not righteous through sound vision, but rather puffed up, thinking himself to be what he is not.

How, then, is the world to be convicted concerning righteousness, unless concerning the righteousness of believers? For it is convicted concerning sin because it does not believe in Christ, and it is convicted concerning the righteousness of those who believe. The comparison itself of the faithful is the condemnation of the unfaithful.

The explanation itself also indicates this sufficiently. For, wishing to disclose what he had said—“But concerning righteousness,” he says, “because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me”—he did not say, “And they will no longer see me,” referring to those of whom he had said, “Because they do not believe in me.” Rather, when explaining what he called sin, he spoke of them, saying, “Because they do not believe in me.” But when explaining what righteousness he meant—the righteousness concerning which the world is convicted—he turned to those to whom he was speaking and said, “Because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

Therefore the world is convicted concerning its own sin, but concerning another’s righteousness, just as darkness is convicted by light. “For everything that is convicted,” says the Apostle, “is manifested by the light” (Ephesians 5). For how great the evil of those who do not believe was [perhaps read: *fuit*, “was”] can appear not only through itself but also through the good of those who believe. And because this is commonly the cry of the unfaithful—“How shall we believe what we do not see?”—the righteousness of believers had to be defined in this way: “Because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” [Col. 0856B]

For blessed are those who will not see and yet will believe (John 20). Even those who saw Christ were not praised for their faith because they believed what they saw—that is, the Son of Man—but because they believed what they did not see—that is, the Son of God. When, therefore, even the form of a servant had been removed from their sight, then in every respect was fulfilled: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1).

Faith is defined, as it is in the Epistle to the Hebrews, as “the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” But what does “You will no longer see me” mean?

He did not say, “I go to the Father, and you will not see me,” so that an interval of time during which he would not be seen might be understood—whether short or long, but in any case having an end. Rather, by saying, “You will no longer see,” the Truth seems to have declared that they would never thereafter see Christ. Is it an injustice to never see Christ and yet believe in him, when faith is praised precisely because the righteous person lives by it—because he believes that he will one day see Christ whom he does not now see?

Finally, according to this righteousness, are we going to say that the Apostle Paul was not righteous, although he confessed that he saw Christ after his ascension into heaven (1 Corinthians 15)—Christ of whom he had already said at that time, “You will no longer see me”? According to this righteousness, was the most glorious Stephen not righteous, when, as he was being stoned, he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7)? [Col. 0856C]

What, then, does “I go to the Father, and you will not see me” mean, except that now I am with you? At that time he was still mortal, “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8), able to hunger and thirst, to grow weary and to sleep. When this Christ—that is, Christ in such a condition—had passed from this world to the Father, they were no longer going to see him. This is the righteousness of faith concerning which the Apostle says: “And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Corinthians 5).

“Therefore,” he says, “your righteousness by which the world is convicted will be this: that I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” You will not see him in humility, but in exaltation. You will not see him mortal, but everlasting. You will not see him being judged, but judging. And by this faith of yours—that is, by your righteousness—the Holy Spirit will convict the unbelieving world. [Col. 0856D]

He will also convict it:

“Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.”

Who is this one, except the one of whom he says elsewhere, “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me”—that is, no right of his, nothing belonging to him, absolutely no sin? For this is why the devil is the ruler of the world.

The devil is not the ruler of heaven and earth and of everything in them, in the sense in which “world” is understood where it is said, “And the world was made through him” (John 1). Rather, the devil is the ruler of that world of which he immediately goes on to say: “And the world did not know him”—that is, the unbelieving human beings with whom the world throughout the whole earth is filled. Among them the faithful world groans—the world whom he chose out of the world, through whom the world was made. Of this world he himself says: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3). [Col. 0857A]

The world is condemned when he judges; the world is saved when he comes to its aid. For just as a tree is filled with leaves and fruits, and a threshing floor with chaff and grain, so the world is filled with unbelievers and believers.

Therefore the ruler of this world—that is, the ruler of these darknesses, namely, of the unbelievers from whom the world is rescued, of whom it is said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5)—the ruler of this world, of whom he said elsewhere, “Now the ruler of this world has been cast out” (Matthew 25), has certainly been judged, because he has been irrevocably destined for the punishment of eternal fire. [Col. 0857B]

Concerning this judgment, by which the ruler of the world has been judged, the world is convicted by the Holy Spirit, because it is judged together with its ruler, whom the proud and wicked person imitates. For if God, as the Apostle Peter says, “did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into the prisons of darkness and committed them to be kept for punishment in the judgment” (2 Peter 2), how can the world not be convicted by the Holy Spirit concerning this judgment, when the Apostle speaks these things in the Holy Spirit?

Let people therefore believe in Christ, so that they may not be convicted concerning the sin of their unbelief, by which sin all the other sins are held fast. Let them pass over into the number of the faithful, so that they may not be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom they do not imitate though they have been justified. Let them beware of the future judgment, so that they may not be judged together with the ruler of the world, whom they imitate though he has been judged. Indeed, lest the hard pride of mortals suppose that it will be spared, it must be frightened by the punishment of the proud angels. [Col. 0857C]

Thus the Lord says:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

What had to be added to them were things they did not know, not things they had learned that needed to be overturned. He could indeed say this in the following sense: even those things he had taught them, if he wished to disclose them to them as they are perceived in him by the angels, could not be borne by the human weakness in which they still remained.

But any spiritual person can teach another person what he knows, if, through progress, the Holy Spirit makes the other more capable; and in the same Spirit the teacher himself may be able to learn something more, so that both may be “taught by God” (John 6). [Col. 0857D]

Taking advantage of this statement, certain foolish people fabricated, with the most senseless presumption, an Apocalypse of Paul, which the sound judgment of the Church does not accept, filling it with I know not what fables. They claimed that this was the book from which Paul said that he had been caught up into the third heaven and had heard ineffable words “which it is not lawful for a human being to speak.” If he had said, “which it is not yet lawful for a human being to speak,” their audacity would at least have been somewhat tolerable. But since he said, “which it is not lawful for a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians 12), these are the people who impudently and disastrously dare to speak such things.

What does the Lord mean concerning the Holy Spirit when, promising that he would come and teach his disciples all truth—or lead them into all truth—he says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”? [Col. 0858A]

This is similar to what he said concerning himself: “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5). But when we were explaining that statement, we said that it could be understood according to his humanity, so that the Son might appear to have foretold his obedience—by which he became obedient unto death (Philippians 2)—also in the judgment by which he will judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4). For he will do this through that by which he is the Son of Man. Hence he said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

In the judgment it will not be the form of God, by which he is equal to the Father and cannot be seen by the wicked, that will appear, but the form of a human being, by which he was made lower even than the angels by a little (Psalm 8)—although he will come already in glory, not in his former humility, and will nevertheless be visible to both the good and the wicked. [Col. 0858B]

Hence he also says: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). In these words it is made clear that the form to be presented in the judgment is not the form in which, while possessing it, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but the form which he received when he emptied himself. “For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2).

In this statement he also seems to have commended his obedience for the execution of judgment, when he said: “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge.” For Adam, through whose one man’s disobedience many were constituted sinners, did not judge as he heard, because he transgressed what he heard and did evil from himself, since he did not do the will of God but his own. [Col. 0858C]

But this one, through whose one man’s obedience many are constituted righteous, was not only obedient unto the death of the cross, on which he was judged alive by the dead, but also promised that he would be obedient in that very judgment by which he will judge the living and the dead. “I cannot,” he says, “do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge.”

But concerning the Holy Spirit, when it is said, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak” (here above), will we dare to suppose that this was said according to his humanity, or according to the assumption of some creature? For only the Son in the Trinity took the form of a servant. That form was joined to him in the truth of his person, so that the Son of God and the Son of Man would be one Jesus Christ; otherwise we would proclaim not the Trinity but a quaternity—which God forbid. [Col. 0858D]

Because of this person, then, who consists as one person of two substances, divine and human, he sometimes speaks according to what he is as God, as in the statement, “I and the Father are one” (John 10); and sometimes according to what he is as a human being, as in the statement, “Because the Father is greater than I” (John 14). According to this understanding we take him to have spoken both that statement and the one I am now discussing: “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5).

But in the person of the Holy Spirit, how are we to understand what he says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak,” when in him there is not one substance of divinity and another of humanity, nor the substance of any other creature? A great difficulty arises here.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit did not become a human being by assuming a human being, nor an angel by assuming an angel, nor a creature by assuming any creature whatsoever, how are we to understand concerning him what the Lord says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”?

This is a difficult question—exceedingly difficult. May the Spirit himself be present, so that I may at least be able to express it as I can conceive it, and so that, according to the capacity of my small measure, it may reach your understanding.

First, you must know and understand, if you are able; and if you are not yet able to understand, you must believe that in that substance which is God, the senses are not distributed among their own locations as though through the mass of a body, as in mortal flesh, where among animals sight is in one place, hearing in another, smell in another, while touch is throughout the body. Far be it from us to believe this of that incorporeal and immutable nature. [Col. 0859A]

Therefore, in God, hearing and seeing are the same thing. For when God is said to know, all these are there: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching—without any alteration of the substance, without any mass that is conceived, in the childish understanding of the senses, as larger in one part and smaller in another.

When it is said concerning the Holy Spirit, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak,” this must be understood all the more in terms of the simple nature in which, most truly, simplicity must either be understood or believed—a nature that far surpasses the nature of our mind.

For our mind is changeable. By learning, it grasps what it did not know; by unlearning, it loses what it knew. It is deceived by likelihood, approving what is false in place of what is true; and through its own obscurity it is hindered, as though by certain darknesses, from reaching the truth. Therefore it is not that truly simple substance for which being and knowing are not the same. It can exist without knowing. [Col. 0859B]

But the divine nature cannot exist in this way, because what it has, it is. Consequently, it does not possess knowledge in such a way that knowledge by which it knows is one thing and essence by which it is another; rather, the two are one. Indeed, one should not even speak of “the two” where there is simple unity.

Thus the Father has life in himself and is not other than the life that is in him. “He gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5)—that is, he begot the Son, who himself would also be life.

We must therefore understand what is said concerning the Holy Spirit—“For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”—to mean that he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another: the Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father, however, was neither born from another nor proceeds from another.

But for this reason no inequality should enter the human mind’s thought concerning that supreme Trinity. The Son is equal to the one from whom he was born, and the Holy Spirit is equal to the one from whom he proceeds.

What difference there is between proceeding and being born would take a long time to investigate and explain, and it would be rash to define after explaining it. For it is difficult enough for the mind to grasp it in some fashion, and extraordinarily difficult for the tongue to express what the mind may perhaps have grasped—regardless of how great the teacher or how great the listener. [Col. 0859C]

He will not speak from himself, therefore, because he is not from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will hear from the one from whom he proceeds. For him, hearing is knowing, as was discussed above. Since, then, he is not from himself but from the one from whom he proceeds, and from whom he has his essence, from that same one he also has his knowledge. His hearing, therefore, comes from the one from whom his essence comes. Hearing is nothing other than essence.

Nor should it disturb us that the future tense is used. For it does not say, “Whatever he has heard,” or anything else, but, “Whatever he will hear, he will speak.” That hearing is eternal, because his knowledge is eternal.

In what is eternal—without beginning and without end—the verb of any tense, whether past, present, or future, is not used falsely. Although that immutable nature does not admit “was” and “will be,” but only “is”—for it truly is, because it cannot change, and therefore only this was properly said of it: “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3)—nevertheless, because of the mutability of the times in which our mortality and mutability move, we do not speak falsely when we say “was,” “is,” and “will be.” [Col. 0859D]

He was in past ages; he is in the present; he will be in the future. He was, because he was never absent; he will be, because he will never be absent; he is, because he always is. He does not pass away with the past as though he no longer existed, nor slip away with the present as though he did not remain, nor arise with the future as though he had not existed before.

Accordingly, because human speech varies according to the succession of times, and because he could not, cannot, and will not be absent from any time, verbs of any tense are truly spoken concerning him. [Col. 0860A]

The Holy Spirit, therefore, always hears because he always knows; hence he knew, knows, and will know. And consequently he has heard, hears, and will hear, because, as we have already said, for him hearing is knowing, and for him knowing is being. He therefore heard, hears, and will hear from the one from whom he is. He is from the one from whom he proceeds.

But what he adds—

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine, and he will announce it to you”—

must not be passed over carelessly.

When he says, “He will glorify me,” this can be understood to mean that, by pouring love into the hearts of believers and making them spiritual, he will show them how the Son was equal to the Father. Previously they had known him only according to the flesh and had thought of him as a human being, like other human beings.

Or certainly it may mean that, filled with confidence through that same love and having fear driven away, they announced Christ to people; thus his fame was spread throughout the whole world. In this sense he said, “He will glorify me,” as though he were saying: “He will take fear away from you and give you love. By proclaiming me more ardently through that love, you will spread the fragrance of my glory throughout the world and commend my honor.”

What they were going to do in the Holy Spirit, he said that the same Spirit would do. The same is true of the statement: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). [Col. 0860B]

The Greek word δοξάσει (*doxasei*)—which one Latin translator rendered as “he will clarify” (*clarificabit*) and another as “he will glorify” (*glorificabit*)—was rendered differently by the Latin translators in their respective versions because the Greek word δόξα (*doxa*), from which δοξάσει is derived, can be interpreted as both “clarity” and “glory.” For through glory someone becomes clear, and through clarity glorious; consequently, what is signified by the two words is the same thing.

As the distinguished ancient authors of the Latin language have defined it, glory is “frequent report about someone accompanied by praise.” When this has been produced concerning Christ in this world, it should not be thought to have conferred anything great upon Christ, but upon the world. Praising what is good benefits not the one who is praised, but those who praise.

Therefore, since nothing need be said here about those who disparage and blaspheme Christ—for he is speaking of the glory by which he has been glorified in the world—the Holy Spirit did not glorify him with true glory except in the holy Catholic Church. Elsewhere—that is, either among heretics or among certain pagans—there cannot be true glory on earth. And where frequent report about him accompanied by praise seems to exist, his true glory is sung in the Catholic Church through the Prophet: [Col. 0860C]

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Psalm 56).

Since, then, the Holy Spirit was going to come after Christ’s exaltation and glorify him, this is what the sacred psalm and the Only-Begotten himself promised would happen—and what we see fulfilled.

But when he says, “He will receive from what is mine, and he will announce it to you,” hear this with Catholic ears; receive it with Catholic minds. The Holy Spirit is not therefore, as certain heretics thought, inferior to the Son, as though the Son received from the Father and the Holy Spirit from the Son in certain gradations of natures. Far be it from us to believe this, far be it from us to say this, far be it from Christian hearts to think this.

Immediately afterward he himself resolves the question and explains why he said this: [Col. 0860D]

“All things whatsoever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

What more do you want? Therefore the Holy Spirit received from the Father what the Son received, because in this Trinity the Son was born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father alone was born from no one and proceeds from no one.

How the Only-Begotten Son said, “All things that the Father has are mine”—for this is certainly not to be understood in the same way as the statement addressed to the son who was not an only son but the elder of two: “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15)—will, if the Lord wills, be treated with careful consideration where the Only-Begotten says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine.”

“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father.”

These words were so obscure to the disciples before what he said had been fulfilled that, asking one another what he meant, they openly confessed that they did not know at all. For the Gospel continues:

“Then some of his disciples said to one another: ‘What is this that he says to us: “A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me,” and, “Because I go to the Father”?’ Therefore they said: ‘What is this that he says, “A little while”? We do not know what he is saying.’”

What troubled them was that he said, “A little while, and you will not see me.” For earlier, since he had not said “a little while,” but had said, “I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me,” he seemed to have spoken to them plainly, and they did not ask one another anything about it.

What was obscure to them then and soon afterward became clear is now entirely clear to us. For after a little while he suffered, and they did not see him. Again, after a little while he rose, and they saw him.

But the statement, “You will no longer see me,” since by the word “now” he wished it to be understood that they would not see him thereafter, we explained where he said, “The Holy Spirit will convict the world concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me”—namely, that they would no longer see Christ as a mortal. [Col. 0861A]

Jesus knew, as the Evangelist next says, that they wanted to question him, and he said to them:

“Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’? Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will become joy.”

This can be understood in the following way: the Lord’s disciples were saddened by the Lord’s death, and immediately rejoiced at his resurrection. The world—which is the name given to Christ’s enemies, by whom Christ was killed—then certainly rejoiced at Christ’s death, when the disciples were sorrowful.

By the name “world,” the friendship (*amicitia*) of this world can be understood, that is, of the people who are friends of this world. Hence the Apostle James says in his Epistle: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God” (James 4). It was among these enemies of God that it happened that even his Only-Begotten was not spared.

Then he adds and says:

“A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her distress, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. And so you too now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

This comparison does not seem difficult to understand, since he himself makes its meaning evident by explaining why it was given. Labor is compared with sorrow, and childbirth with joy—the joy that is usually greater when a boy rather than a girl is born.

But when he says, “No one will take your joy from you,” since their joy is Jesus himself, he signifies [perhaps read: *significat*, “he signifies”] what the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6). Up to this point, in the chapter of the Gospel on which we are discoursing today, everything has proceeded as though it were easy to understand. In what follows, keener attention is necessary. [Col. 0861B]

What does he mean when he says, “And on that day you will ask me nothing”? The word *rogare* (“to ask”) signifies not only “to request,” but also “to question.” The Greek Gospel from which this was translated has a word that can be understood in both senses, so that the ambiguity is not resolved even there. Yet even if it were resolved, that would not remove every question.

For after Christ rose, we read both that he was questioned and that he was asked. His disciples questioned him as he was about to ascend into heaven, asking when it would be made manifest and when the kingdom would belong to Israel (Acts 1). When he was already in heaven, holy Stephen asked him to receive his spirit (Acts 7). Who would dare either to think or to say that Christ seated in heaven should not be asked, while Christ remaining on earth should have been asked? That the immortal should not be asked, while the mortal ought to have been asked?

Rather, beloved, let us ask him to resolve the knot of this question himself, shining in our hearts so that we may see what he says.

For I think that the statement, “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you,” should not be referred to the time when he rose and showed them his flesh to see and touch, but rather to the time concerning which he had already said: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

For Christ had already risen, had already shown himself to them in the flesh, and was already seated at the right hand of the Father, when the same Apostle John, whose Gospel this is, said in his Epistle: “Now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet been manifested. We know that when it has been manifested, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). [Col. 0861C]

This vision does not belong to the present life but to the future one; not to what is temporal but to what is eternal. This is eternal life, as Life itself says: “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17).

Concerning this vision and knowledge the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13).

The Church now labors in childbirth by longing for the fruit of all her labor; then she will give birth by seeing it. She labors in groaning; she will give birth in rejoicing. She labors in prayer; she will give birth in praise. For this reason the child is male, since all the duties of action are directed toward this fruit of contemplation.

It alone is free, because it is desired for its own sake; action is directed toward it and serves it. Whatever is done well is directed toward it, because it is done for its sake. It itself, however, is not held and possessed for the sake of anything else, but for its own sake.

There, then, is the end that suffices for us; therefore it will be eternal. For no end suffices for us unless it is an end that has no end.

This was inspired in Philip when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14). In showing the Father, the Son also made this promise, saying: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (ibid.).

It is therefore better, I think, to understand the words discussed above in this sense: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” The whole span in which the present age flies past is a little while. Hence the Evangelist himself says in his Epistle: “It is the final hour” (1 John 2). [Col. 0861D]

For this reason he added, “Because I go to the Father,” which must be referred to the preceding statement, where he says: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” By going to the Father he was going to cause them not to see him. Consequently, this was not said because he was going to die and, until he rose again, withdraw from their sight, but because he was going to the Father—which he did after he rose and, having lived with them for forty days, ascended into heaven.

He therefore said to those who were then seeing him bodily: “A little while, and you will no longer see me,” because he was going to the Father and they were not thereafter going to see him as a mortal, such as they saw him when he spoke these words. [Col. 0862A]

But by adding, “And again a little while, and you will see me,” he made this promise to the universal Church, just as he made the promise to the universal Church: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

The Lord does not delay his promise. In a little while we shall see him, where we shall ask nothing and question nothing, because nothing will remain to be questioned and nothing sought will remain hidden. This little while seems long to us because it is still unfolding. When it has ended, then we shall perceive how brief it was.

Let our joy therefore not be like the joy of the world, concerning which it was said, “But the world will rejoice.” Yet let us not be sorrowful without joy during the labor of this longing. Rather, as the Apostle says, let us be “rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation” (Romans 12), because the woman in labor to whom we are compared rejoices more over the offspring that will soon come than she is saddened by her present pain.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.”

It has already been said in the preceding portions of this discourse of the Lord, concerning those who ask the Father for certain things in Christ’s name and do not receive them: whatever is requested contrary to the principle of salvation is not requested in the name of the Savior. [Col. 0862B]

For when he says “in my name,” this must be understood to refer not merely to letters and syllables, but to what the sound itself signifies and to what is rightly and truly understood by that sound. Therefore, whoever has an understanding of Christ that is not the understanding one ought to have of the only Son of God does not ask in his name, even if he does not omit the letters and syllables of the name “Christ,” because he asks in the name of the one whom he conceives when he asks.

But whoever has the understanding of Christ that ought to be held asks in his name. And he receives what he asks, provided that he does not ask contrary to eternal salvation. He receives it when he ought to receive it. For some things are not denied but postponed so that they may be given at the proper time.

The statement “He will give it to you” must therefore be understood so that these words are known to signify benefits that properly pertain to those who ask. All the saints are heard when they ask for themselves; but they are not heard on behalf of everyone—whether friends, enemies, or any others—because it was not said simply, “He will give,” but, “He will give to you.” [Col. 0862C]

“Up to now,” he says, “you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.”

When he says “complete joy,” it is certainly not bodily but spiritual joy. And when it becomes so great that nothing further can be added to it, then without doubt it will be complete. Whatever, therefore, is asked that pertains to attaining this joy—that is what must be asked in Christ’s name—if we understand [Col. 0866A] divine grace, if we truly seek the blessed life. Whatever else is asked is nothing—not because it is altogether no thing, but because, in comparison with so great a thing, whatever else is desired is nothing. For a human being is not altogether nothing, though the Apostle says: “Whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing.” In comparison with the spiritual person, however, who knows that by God’s grace he is what he is, even one who presumes upon empty things is nothing.

Thus the passage can rightly be understood in this way: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you”—so that “anything” is not understood to mean just anything whatsoever, but something that, in comparison with the blessed life, is not nothing. The words that follow, “Up to now you have asked nothing in my name,” can likewise be understood in two ways: either because you have not asked in my name, [Col. 0866B] since you have not known that name as it ought to be known; or because you have asked for nothing, since, in comparison with the thing you ought to have asked for, what you asked for must be regarded as nothing.

Therefore, so that they might ask in his name for not nothing but complete joy—for if they ask for anything else, that something is nothing—he exhorts them, saying: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” That is: ask this in my name, so that your joy may be complete, and you will receive it. For divine mercy will certainly not defraud his saints when they persevere rightly in asking.

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly.”

I could say that the hour of which he speaks ought to be understood as the future age, [Col. 0866C] where we shall see openly what blessed Paul says—“face to face” (I Cor. III)—so that “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs” would mean what the same Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in a riddle” (ibid.). And I will announce him to you because the Father will be seen through the Son, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke X).

But what follows seems to obstruct this interpretation:

“In that day you will ask in my name.”

For in the future age, when we have reached the kingdom where we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (I John III), what shall we ask for, when our desire shall be satisfied with good things (Ps. CII)? Hence it is also said in another psalm: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). [Col. 0866D] Petition belongs to some need, and there will be no need where this satisfaction exists.

It remains, therefore, as far as I am able to understand, that the Lord Jesus is to be understood as having promised to make his disciples spiritual instead of carnal or animal, although not yet such as we shall be when we also possess a spiritual body. Rather, they would become like the one who said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II); and: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (I Cor. III); and: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. But the animal person does [Col. 0867A] not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II).

The animal person, then, since he does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, hears whatever he hears about the nature of God in such a way that he cannot think of anything other than a body—however vast or immense, however luminous and beautiful that body may be. Nevertheless, all statements of wisdom about an incorporeal and unchanging substance are proverbs to him—not because he regards them as proverbs, but because he thinks in the manner of those who customarily hear proverbs without understanding them.

When, however, the spiritual person begins to judge everything, while he himself is judged by no one (I Cor. II)—even if in this life he still sees partially, as through a mirror—he perceives God openly, not through any bodily sense or imaginary thought by which he apprehends or fashions whatever likenesses of bodies he may imagine, but [Col. 0867B] through the mind’s most certain understanding. He understands that God is not a body but spirit. Thus, when the Son announces the Father openly, the one who announces is himself seen to be of the same substance.

Then they ask in his name, because in the sound of his name they understand nothing other than the reality itself that is called by that name. Such people can in some measure conceive of our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, interceding for us with the Father; but insofar as he is God, they can conceive of him hearing us together with the Father. I believe that he signified this when he said:

“And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you.”

[Col. 0867C] To contemplate how the Son does not ask the Father, but the Father and the Son together hear those who ask, the eye of the spiritual mind must rise.

“For the Father himself loves you,” he says, “because you have loved me.”

Does he love us because we love him? Or rather, do we love because he loves us? Let the Evangelist himself answer from his Epistle. “We love,” he says, “because he first loved us” (I John IV). It was therefore because we were loved that we came to love. To love God is altogether a gift of God. He gave himself to be loved, he who loved without being loved. We were loved while displeasing, so that there might arise in us something by which we could please him.

For we would not love the Son unless we also loved the Father. The Father loves us because we love the Son, even though we have received from the Father and the Son the gift of loving both the Father and the Son. The Spirit of both pours love into our hearts. Through that Spirit we love the Father and the Son, and [Col. 0867D] with the Father and the Son we love the Spirit himself.

God therefore made our devout love, by which we worship him, and he saw that it was good. He loves us for this reason: he loves in us what he himself has made. Yet he would not make in us something that he could love unless he had loved us before making it.

“And you believed,” he says, “that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into the world. Again I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”

We certainly believe this. It should not seem incredible that, in coming into the world, he came forth from the Father without abandoning the Father, and that, in leaving the world and going to the Father, he did not abandon the world. He came forth from the Father because he is from the Father; and he came into the world because he displayed to the world the body that he assumed from a virgin.

He left the world by bodily departure and proceeded to the Father by the ascent of his humanity; [Col. 0868A] yet he did not abandon the world in the governance of his presence. Such were Christ’s disciples when he spoke with them before the Passion: great things with little ones, but in such a way as was necessary for great things to be spoken to little ones. For, since they had not yet received the Holy Spirit—as they received him after Christ’s resurrection, either when he breathed upon them or from above—they understood human things more than divine things, as is made clear by many indications throughout the Gospel.

This, then, is what they said in the present passage. The Evangelist says:

“His disciples say to him: ‘Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.’”

A little earlier the Lord himself had said: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs.” [Col. 0868B] How, then, do they say: “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb”? Had the hour already come in which he had promised that he would no longer speak in proverbs?

The continuation of his words plainly shows that the hour had not yet come. He still promises an hour in which he will no longer speak in proverbs but will announce the Father openly to them. In that hour, he says, they will ask in his name, and he will not ask the Father concerning them, because the Father himself loves them, since they have loved Christ and have believed that he came forth from the Father, came into the world, and would again leave the world and go to the Father.

Since that hour in which he will speak without proverbs is still being promised, why do they say: “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb”? [Col. 0868C] It is because the things that he knows are proverbs to those who do not understand them—so much so that they do not even understand that they themselves do not understand.

They were little ones, not yet judging spiritually, and they were hearing about matters that pertained not to the body but to the Spirit. Finally, warning them about their still immature and weak condition according to the inner person, he says:

“Jesus answered them: ‘Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you will be scattered, each one to his own place, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.’”

A little earlier he had said: “I am leaving the world and going to the Father.” Now he says: “The Father is with me.” Who goes to one who is with him?

[Col. 0868D] To the person who understands, this is a statement; to the person who does not understand, it is a proverb. Yet even as it is not understood by little ones, it can somehow be endured and escaped. Although it does not offer them solid food, because they are not yet capable of taking it in, it does not deny them at least milk-like nourishment.

It is from this nourishment that they knew that he knew all things and had no need for anyone to question him. Why they said this can indeed be asked. It seems that they ought rather to have said: “You have no need to question anyone,” not “You have no need for anyone to question you.”

For they had said: “We know that you know all things.” Now someone who knows all things is ordinarily questioned by those who do not know, so that those asking may hear from the one who knows all things what they wish to know. It is not usually the one who knows all things who questions, as though he wished to learn something.

What, then, does it mean that, [Col. 0869A] although they knew that he knew all things, they thought they should say to him: “You have no need for anyone to question you,” when they seem to have ought to say: “You have no need to question anyone”?

And yet we read that both things happened: the Lord questioned others and was himself questioned. But the matter is quickly resolved. This was necessary not for him but for those whom he questioned or by whom he was questioned.

He did not question anyone in order to learn something from them, but rather in order to teach them. Those who questioned him wished to learn something from him, and it was certainly necessary for them to know something from the one who knew all things.

It was therefore not necessary for him that anyone question him, since, when we are questioned by those who wish to learn something from us, we discover [Col. 0869B] from their questions themselves what they wish to learn. It is necessary for us to be questioned by those whom we wish to teach something, so that we may know the questions to which we must respond.

But this was not necessary for him, who knew everything. He did not need to discover through someone’s question what that person wished to know, because he knew the questioner’s intention before he was questioned.
