He nevertheless allowed himself to be questioned so that he might show, both to those who were present at that time and to those who would hear these things spoken or read them written, what sort of people those were who questioned him. In this way we might know either by what frauds he could not be deceived or by what approaches progress could be made with him.

[Col. 0869C] To foresee human thoughts, and therefore not to need anyone to question him, was not a great thing for God; but it was a great thing for the little ones who said to him: “By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

Much greater, however, was the matter toward which he wished to stretch and enlarge their understanding. After they had said—and said truly—“You came forth from God,” he answered: “The Father is with me,” lest they should think that the Son had come forth from the Father in such a way that they supposed he had also departed from him.

Then, bringing this great and lengthy discourse to a close, he says:

“These things I have spoken to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”

The distress of which he had spoken earlier was to have this beginning. To show that they were little ones who, because they did not yet understand and were taking one thing [Col. 0869D] for another, treated as proverbs whatever great and divine things he said, he declared: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you will be scattered, each one of you to his own place.”

Behold the beginning of the distress, though it was not to continue in the same way. For when he added, “and you will leave me alone,” he did not mean that they would remain such during the subsequent distress that they would have in the world after his ascension. Rather, they would remain in him and have peace in him.

When he was arrested, they left not only his flesh but also, in their minds, the faith itself. This is what he means: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each one to his own place, and you will leave me.” It is as though he were saying: “Then you will be so disturbed that you will even abandon what you now believe.”

[Col. 0870A] They came to such despair and, so to speak, death of their former faith as was evident in Cleopas. After the Lord’s resurrection, without knowing that it was he with whom he was speaking, and while recounting what had happened to him, Cleopas said: “We were hoping that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV).

Behold how they had abandoned him, even abandoning the faith by which they had previously believed in him. But in the distress that they endured after his glorification, once they had received the Holy Spirit, they did not abandon him. Even though they fled from city to city, they did not flee from him. Having distress in the world so that they might hold peace in him, they were fugitives from him [Should it perhaps read: “they were not”?], but rather had him himself as their refuge.

When the Holy Spirit had been given, what is now said to them came to pass in them: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world.”

[Col. 0870B] They took courage, and they conquered. In whom, if not in him? The world would not have conquered him if the world had conquered his members. Hence the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory” (I Cor. XV), and immediately adds: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.), who had said to his own: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world.”

Before treating, with the Lord’s help, the matters we are now going to discuss, Jesus had said: “These things I have spoken to you so that you may have peace in me.” We must understand this not merely of the more recent things he had said shortly before, but of everything he spoke to them—whether everything he said to them from the time he began to have them as disciples, or certainly everything from the time after the supper when he began this remarkable and lengthy discourse.

For he recalled such a reason for speaking to them that everything he had said to them, or especially the things he said when he was about to die for them, like final words after the sacred meal, when the one who was going to betray him had gone out, [Col. 0870C] can most properly be referred to that end.

He commended this purpose of his discourse: that they should have peace in him. Everything that constitutes our being Christians is directed toward this. This peace will have no end in time, and it will itself be the end of all our hope, intention, and action.

For the sake of this peace we are imbued with his sacraments; for its sake we are instructed by his marvelous works and words; for its sake we believe and hope in him, and, insofar as he grants it, we are set aflame with love for him. In this peace we are consoled in every distress; through it we are delivered from every distress. [Col. 0870D] For its sake we endure every tribulation courageously, so that in it we may reign happily without any tribulation.

It was fitting that he should close with this the words that had been proverbs to the disciples who understood little. After he had said that he had spoken everything for this purpose—namely, that they should have peace in him while having distress in the world—and after he had exhorted them to take courage because he had conquered the world, he finished the discourse that he had directed to them. Then he turned his words to the Father and began to pray.

The Evangelist follows in this way:

## CHAPTER XVII

“Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.’”

The Lord, the only-begotten and coeternal Son of the Father, could, in the form of a servant and from the form of a servant, have prayed silently if that had been necessary. [Col. 0871A] But he wished to present himself to the Father as an intercessor in such a way that he would also remember that he was our teacher.

Therefore, the prayer that he made for us he made known also to us, because the discourse of so great a Teacher is directed not only to those who were present but also, on their behalf, to the Father—and if it was directed to those who were present to hear these words, then certainly also to us, who would have them written for reading.

Accordingly, when he says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” he shows that all time, and what he should do or permit to be done at each moment, had been ordered by him who is not subject to time. For future events in their several times have efficient causes in the wisdom of God, in which there are no times.

Let no one, therefore, believe that this hour came because fate compelled it, [Col. 0871B] or that a stellar necessity bound Christ to his Passion. Far be it from us to think that the stars compelled the Maker of the stars to die. Time did not force Christ to die; Christ chose the time at which he would die. He also established with the Father the time at which he would be born from a virgin, although he was born from the Father outside time.

In accordance with this true and sound teaching, the Apostle Paul says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV). And God says through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. LXIX); and again the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

He therefore says: “Father, the hour has come”—he who, together with the Father, arranged all hours—as though saying: “Father, the hour that we established together, [Col. 0871C] for the sake of human beings and among human beings, for my glorification has come. Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.”

Some understand the Son to have been glorified by the Father in this: that the Father did not spare him but handed him over for us all (Rom. VIII). But if he is said to have been glorified through his Passion, how much more through his resurrection? In the Passion, his humiliation rather than his glory is emphasized, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Then the Apostle continues concerning his glorification, saying: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory [Col. 0871D] of God the Father” (ibid.).

This is the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, which took its beginning from his resurrection. His humiliation begins in the Apostle’s discourse at the point where he says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (ibid.), and extends to the death of the cross. His glory begins where he says: “Therefore God exalted him,” and extends to the point where he is in the glory of God the Father.

Thus, in order that the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, might be glorified through his resurrection, he was first humbled through his Passion. He could not have risen from the dead if he had not died. Humiliation is the merit of glory; glory is the reward of humiliation.

But all this took place in the form of a servant. In the form of God, however, glory always was and always will be. Indeed, it was not—as though it might now no longer be—[Col. 0872A] nor will it be—as though it did not yet exist. Rather, glory always is, without beginning and without end.

When he says, therefore, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” this should be understood as though he had said: “The hour for sowing humiliation has come; do not delay the fruit of glory.”

But what does the following mean?

“So that your Son may glorify you.”

That the Son was glorified by the Father according to the form of a servant, which the Father raised from the dead and placed at his right hand, is shown by the fact itself, and no Christian doubts it. But since he did not merely say, “Father, glorify your Son,” but added, “so that your Son may glorify you,” it is rightly asked how the Son glorified the Father, since the Father’s eternal glory was neither diminished in human form nor capable of increase in its divine perfection.

[Col. 0872B] The Father’s glory in itself can neither be diminished nor increased. Among human beings, however, it was certainly less, when God was known only in Judea (Ps. LXXV), and when children did not yet praise the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. CXII).

But because this came about through the Gospel of Christ, so that through the Son the Father might become known among the nations, the Son certainly glorified both the Father and himself. If the Son had merely died and had not risen, he would certainly have been neither glorified by the Father nor one who glorified the Father.

But now, having been glorified by the Father through the resurrection, let him glorify the Father through the proclamation of his resurrection. The very order of the words makes this clear. “Glorify,” he says, “your Son, so that your Son may glorify you”—as though he were saying: “Raise me up, so that through me you may become known throughout the whole world.”

Then, explaining more fully how the Son glorifies the Father, he says:

[Col. 0872C] “As you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.”

He said “all flesh,” meaning “every soul,” signifying the whole by a part. In the same way, earlier, the whole human being was signified by a part, when the Apostle said: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities” (Rom. XIII). For what does “every soul” mean except “every human being”?

[Col. 0872D] This authority over all flesh that was given to Christ by the Father must be understood according to his humanity. For according to his divinity, all things were made through him, and all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created in him (Col. I).

“As you gave him authority over all flesh,” he says; “so let the Son glorify you”—that is, let him make you known to all flesh that you have given him. For you gave them to him in such a way that he might give eternal life to all whom you gave him.

“Now this is eternal life,” he says, “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

The order of the words is: “that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, as the only true God.” Consequently, the Holy Spirit is also understood, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the substantial and consubstantial love of both. For the Father and the Son are not two gods; nor are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit three gods. Rather, the Trinity itself is one and only true God.

Yet the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son, because there are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the Trinity itself is one God.

[Col. 0873A] If, therefore, the Son glorifies the Father in the way that the Father gave him authority over all flesh, and gave it in such a way that he might give eternal life to all whom he gave him, and if eternal life is this—that they should know the Father—then the Son glorifies the Father by making him known to all whom the Father gave him.

Furthermore, if the knowledge of God is eternal life, then the more we progress in this knowledge, the more we tend toward life. We shall not die in eternal life. The knowledge of God will therefore be perfect when there is no death at all. Then God’s glorification will be supreme, because his glory will be supreme.

Among the ancients, the glory by which glorious people are called glorious was defined in this way: “Glory is frequent report concerning someone, together with praise.” But if a human being is praised when people believe the report about him, how will God be praised when he himself will be seen?

[Col. 0873B] For this reason it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII). There God will be praised without end, where God will be known fully; and because he will be known fully, he will therefore be glorified.

But God is first glorified here, when, announced to human beings, he becomes known and is proclaimed through the faith of believers. Hence he says:

“I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do.”

He does not say “commanded” but “gave,” thereby emphasizing evident grace. For what does even human nature in the only-begotten Son possess that it has not received? Did it not receive the ability to do nothing evil but all things good when it was assumed into the unity of person by the Word through whom all things were made?

But how did he complete the work that he received to do, when the experience of the Passion still remained—through which he especially gave his martyrs an example to follow? Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II).

[Col. 0873C] The answer is that he says he has completed what he knew with absolute certainty he would complete. Long beforehand, in prophecy, he used verbs of the past tense for something that was to happen many years later. “They pierced,” he says, “my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. XXI). He does not say, “They will pierce” and “they will count.”

In this very Gospel he says: “I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John XV). Yet later he says to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI).

For he who predestined all future things by certain and unchangeable causes has done whatever he will do. [Col. 0873D] It is also said of him through the prophet: “He who made the things that are to be.”

In accordance with this, he continues:

“And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

Earlier he had said: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.” In that order of words he had shown that the Son would first be glorified by the Father, so that the Son might also glorify the Father.

Now, however, he says: “I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do; and now glorify me.” It is as though he had first glorified the Father, and then asked the Father to glorify him.

We must therefore understand that in both places he used the earlier verb [Col. 0874A] according to what was going to happen: “Glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify you.” But now he used the past tense for a future event when he said: “I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do.”

Then, by saying: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself,” as though he would be glorified later by the Father, although he had first glorified the Father, what does he show except that when he said above, “I glorified you on earth,” he spoke as though he had already done what he was going to do? Here, however, he asked the Father to do the thing through which the Son would accomplish that work—namely, for the Father to glorify the Son, through whose glorification the Son would also glorify the Father.

Finally, if we place a future-tense verb where he himself used the past tense for a future event, [Col. 0874B] no obscurity remains in the meaning, as though he had said: “I will glorify you on earth; I will complete the work that you gave me to do; and now glorify me, Father, with yourself.”

This is as clear as the earlier statement: “Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.” The meaning is entirely the same, except that here the manner of that glorification is stated, whereas there it is left unstated—as though the former statement were explained by this one for those who might be troubled about how the Father glorifies the Son and, especially, how the Son glorifies the Father.

By saying that he glorified the Father on earth, while he himself was glorified by the Father with the Father, he clearly shows the manner of both glorifications. He glorified the Father on earth by proclaiming him to the nations. [Col. 0874C] The Father, however, glorified him with himself by placing him at his right hand.

The Son subsequently preferred to use the past tense concerning the Father’s glorification when he said, “I glorified you,” in order to show that what was certainly going to happen had already taken place in predestination and was to be regarded as already accomplished: namely, that, having been glorified by the Father with the Father, the Son would glorify the Father on earth.

He made this predestination more plainly evident in his own glorification, by which the Father glorified him, when he added: “With the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

The order of the words is: “the glory that I had with you before the world existed.” This is the force of what he says: “And now glorify me.” It means: “As it was then, so let it be now. As then, by predestination, so now, by completion, accomplish in the world what had already taken place with you before the world existed. [Col. 0874D] Accomplish in its own time what you established before all times.”

Some have thought this should be understood as though the human nature assumed by the Word were converted into the Word and the human being were changed into God—or, if we consider their opinion more carefully, as though the human being perished in God.

No one, they would say, could claim from this transformation that the Word of God was either doubled or increased, so that what had been one became two, or what had been less became greater. But if human nature was changed and converted into the Word, what was the Word of God, in the measure and condition in which it existed? What would become of the human being, if he did not perish?

[Col. 0875A] Nothing compels us to accept this opinion, which I do not see as agreeing at all with the truth, if, when the Son says, “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed,” we understand him to be speaking of the predestination of the glorification of the human nature that exists in him—a nature that, from mortal, was to become immortal with the Father. This had already been accomplished by predestination before the world existed, although it was to be accomplished in the world over the course of time.

For if the Apostle said concerning us: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I), why should it be thought contrary to the truth that the Father glorified our head at the time when he chose us in him, so that we might be his members?

We were chosen in the same way that he was glorified, because, before the world existed, neither we nor the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, yet existed (Rom. IV). But the one who, insofar as he is the Word of God, also made the things that were to come, and [Col. 0875B] calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. IV), certainly glorified him, insofar as he is the human Mediator between God and human beings, before the foundation of the world, just as at that time he also chose us in him.

For what does the Apostle say? “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called.”

Perhaps we might hesitate to say that he himself was predestined, because the Apostle seems to have said this only about us—that we should be made conformed to his image. It is rightly said that he was not predestined according to what he is as the Word of God, God with God. For why would he be predestined, when he already was what he was, without beginning or end, eternal?

[Col. 0875C] But what did not yet exist had to be predestined, so that it might come to be in its own time in the manner in which it had been predestined to come to be before all times. Therefore, whoever denies that the Son of God was predestined denies that this same one is the Son of Man.

But, for the sake of those who are contentious, let us hear the Apostle at the beginning of his letters:

“Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection of the dead.”

[Col. 0875D] According to this predestination, therefore, he was also glorified before the world existed, so that his glory might be, through the resurrection of the dead, with the Father, at whose right hand he sits.

When he saw that the time had now come for his predestined glorification, so that what had already been accomplished in predestination might now be accomplished in its fulfillment, he prayed, saying:

“And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

It is as though he were saying: “It is time for me to possess, while living, at your right hand, that glory which I had with you in your predestination—that glory which I had with you before the world existed.”

I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. But if he says this only of those disciples with whom he supped, and to whom he spoke at such length before he began to pray, this does not pertain to that “clarification”—or, as others have interpreted it, “glorification”—of which he had spoken above, by which the Son clarifies or glorifies the Father. For how great, or of what kind, is the glory that twelve—or rather eleven—men should have become known to mortals? But if, when he says, “I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world,” he intended all to be understood here, including those who were going to believe in him and who would belong to his great Church, destined to come from all the nations, concerning which it is sung in the psalm, “In the great assembly I will confess you” (Ps. XXXIV), then this is plainly that clarification by which the Son clarifies the Father, when he makes his name known to all nations and to so many generations of human beings. And what he says here, “I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world,” is of the same kind as what he had said shortly before, “I have glorified you upon the earth”: in both places he uses the past tense with reference to the future, like one who knew that it had been predestined that this should happen, and therefore says that he has done what he was without any doubt going to do.

But that he spoke of those who were already his disciples, not of all who were going to believe in him, when he said, “I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world,” is shown more credibly by what follows. For when he had said this, he added:

“They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they have come to know that everything which you have given me is from you, because the words which you gave me I have given to them; and they received them and came to know truly that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.”

Although all these things could also have been said of all future believers in a completed form, while they were still destined to come, the stronger consideration for understanding him to be speaking here of those disciples whom he then had is what he says shortly afterward: “When I was with them, I was preserving them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled”—meaning Judas, who betrayed him. Of that number of twelve apostles, he alone perished.

Then he continues: “But now I am coming to you.” From this it is clear that he was speaking of his bodily presence when he said, “When I was with them, I was preserving them,” as though that presence were already no longer to be with them. In this way he wished to signify his ascension, which was soon to occur, when he said, “But now I am coming to you”—going, of course, to the right hand of the Father, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead, likewise according to bodily presence, in accordance with sound faith and doctrine. For by spiritual presence he was certainly going to be with them after his ascension, and with his whole Church in this world until the consummation of the age.

Therefore those of whom he said, “When I was with them, I was preserving them,” cannot rightly be understood as anyone other than those whom he had already begun to preserve as they believed in him, while he was bodily present, and whom he was going to leave by his bodily absence, so that he might preserve them with the Father by spiritual presence. After this he adds the rest of his own, when he says: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who are going to believe in me through their word.” Here he shows more clearly that above, from the place where he says, “I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me,” he was not speaking about all who belonged to him, but only about those who were hearing him say these things at that time.

From the very beginning of his prayer, then, when he raised his eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” up to what he says shortly afterward, “And now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed,” he intended all his own to be understood—those to whom he glorifies the Father by making him known. For when he had said, “So that your Son may glorify you,” he immediately showed how this would happen, saying, “Just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him.” And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.

For the Father cannot be glorified by the knowledge of human beings unless the one through whom he is glorified is also known—that is, the one through whom he becomes known to the peoples. This is the Father’s clarification, and it was not accomplished only among those apostles; it is accomplished among all human beings whose head Christ is, since they are his members. For the words, “Just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him,” cannot be understood of the apostles alone, but plainly of all those who, by believing in him, are granted eternal life.

Let us now see what he says about those disciples who were then hearing him: “I have manifested,” he says, “your name to the men whom you gave me.” Did they not, then, know the name of God when they were Jews? And what of the passage that is read: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV)? Therefore, “I have manifested your name to these men whom you gave me out of the world”—to those who hear me saying these things—not that name by which you are called “God,” but that by which you are called “my Father,” a name which could not be manifested without the manifestation of the Son himself.

For the fact that he is called “God” could not have made this name wholly unknown even to all the nations before they believed in Christ. The power of true divinity is such that it cannot be entirely and absolutely hidden from a rational creature that already makes use of reason. Except for the few in whom nature has been excessively corrupted, the entire human race confesses God to be the creator of this world. Insofar as he made this world visible through heaven and earth, he was known to all nations even before they were instructed in the faith of Christ.

But insofar as he is not to be worshiped with the insults offered to him or together with false gods, “God is known in Judah.” Yet insofar as he is the Father of this Christ through whom he takes away the sin of the world (John I), his name, previously hidden from all, he has now manifested to those whom the Father himself gave him out of the world.

But how did he manifest it, if the hour of which he had spoken above had not yet come—the hour when, as he said, “I will no longer speak to you in figures, but I will announce the Father to you openly”? Or is an announcement in figures to be considered open? Why, then, was it said, “I will announce openly,” unless what is in figures is not open? Whatever is not concealed in figures but is made manifest in words is, without doubt, said openly.

How, then, did he manifest what he had not yet spoken openly? Accordingly, the past tense must be understood as used with reference to the future, just as in the statement, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” although he had not yet done this, but spoke as though he had done what he knew had been immutably determined for him to do.

What, then, does “whom you gave me out of the world” mean? For it was said of them that they were not of the world. But regeneration, not generation, brought this about. What also does the following mean: “They were yours, and you gave them to me”? Were they ever the Father’s at a time when they were not the only-begotten Son’s? And did the Father ever possess anything without the Son? Certainly not. Nevertheless, God the Son once possessed something which that same Son as man did not yet possess: he had not yet become man from his mother, although at that time he possessed everything together with the Father. Therefore he said, “They were yours.”

God the Son did not separate himself from this possession, without whom the Father never possessed anything. But he is accustomed to attribute everything that can be done to the one from whom he himself is that which can act. From the one from whom he has being, he has the capacity to act; and he has always possessed both simultaneously, because he never existed without being able to act. Accordingly, whatever the Father could do was always with him and was possible for him, since he who never failed to exist and never failed to be able to act was never without the Father, and the Father was never without him.

Therefore, when he says, “And you gave them to me,” he shows that as man he received this power, so that he might possess them, since the one who was above all things was not always man. Thus, although he appears to have attributed to the Father the fact that he received them from him—because whatever he is is from him—he himself also gave them to himself, since whatever he is is from him. That is, Christ as God, together with the Father, gave human beings to Christ as man—something which Christ as man is not together with the Father.

Finally, the one who says here, “They were yours, and you gave them to me,” had already said to these same disciples above, “I chose you out of the world.” Let carnal thought be crushed here and perish. The Son says that the Father gave him human beings out of the world, while elsewhere he says to them, “I chose you out of the world.” As the same man, the Son received them from the Father, together with the Father. For the Father would not have given them to the Son unless he had chosen them.

Accordingly, just as the Son did not separate the Father from himself when he said, “I chose you out of the world,” because the Father also chose them together with him, so he did not separate himself from the Father when he said, “They were yours,” because the Father was also the Father of the Son himself. Now, as the same Son in his humanity, he received those who were not his, since he also received the form of a servant, that is, what was not his.

He continues and says: “And they have kept your word. Now they have come to know that everything which you have given me is from you”—that is, they have come to know that I am from you. The Father gave everything simultaneously when he begot the one who would possess everything. “For the words,” he says, “which you gave me I have given them; and they received them”—that is, they understood and retained them. For the word is received when it is grasped by the mind.

“And they came to know truly that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.” Here, too, “truly” must be understood. For by saying, “They came to know truly,” he wished to explain this by adding, “And they believed.” What they believed, therefore, they truly came to know; and what they truly came to know, they truly believed. “I came forth from you” means the same as “You sent me.”

When he said, “They came to know truly,” therefore, lest anyone think that this knowledge had already come through direct vision and not through faith, he explained it by adding, “And they believed,” so that we should supply “truly” and understand the statement to mean: “They came to know truly,” that is, “They believed truly.” This is not in the sense indicated shortly before, when he said, “Now you believe? Behold, the hour is coming, and indeed has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own, and you will leave me alone,” but they believed truly in the manner in which one must believe: without wavering, firmly, steadfastly, courageously—not about to return again to their own things and abandon Christ.

The disciples, then, were not yet such as he describes them by words in the past tense, as though they already were so; rather, he foretold what they would be after receiving the Holy Spirit, who, as had been promised, would teach them all things. Before they received him, how did they keep his word—as he spoke of them as though they had done so—when the first among them denied him three times, although he had heard from his mouth what would happen to the person who denied him before human beings?

He therefore gave them the words, as he says, which the Father gave him. But when they received those words spiritually, not outwardly in their ears but inwardly in their hearts, then they truly received them, because then they truly understood. And they truly understood because they truly believed.

But how the Father gave the Son himself those words—by what words can a human being explain it? The question certainly seems easier if it is believed that, insofar as he is the Son of man, he received those words from the Father. Yet who can recount when and how he learned them, though he was born of a virgin? And who can recount even his generation, which took place from a virgin (Isa. LIII)?

But if, insofar as he was begotten from the Father and coeternal with the Father, he is thought to have received these words from the Father, no temporal sequence should be imagined there—as though he once existed without possessing them and received what he had not possessed in order to possess it—for whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting him. For the Father gave the Son those things without which the Son could not be, just as he gave him being itself.

For how otherwise could the Word give words to the Word, in whom he ineffably spoke all things?

“I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me.” By “the world” he now wishes those to be understood who live according to the desire of the world and are not included in that distribution of grace by which they are chosen out of the world. Therefore he says that he does not pray for the world, but for those whom the Father gave him. For by the fact that the Father had already given them to him, it came about that they did not belong to that world for which he does not pray.

Then he adds:

“For they are yours.” For the Father did not lose those whom he gave to the Son, since the Son immediately continues and says:

“And all my things are yours, and your things are mine.”

Here it is sufficiently clear how everything belonging to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son: namely, because he too is God, born equal from the Father to the Father. This is not like what was said to one of the two sons, specifically the elder: “You are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours” (Luke XV). That statement concerned all those creatures which are beneath the holy rational creature, and which are certainly subject to the Church. In the whole Church, those two sons—the elder and the younger—are understood together with all the holy angels, to whom we shall be equal in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

But the statement, “All my things are yours, and your things are mine,” was made so that the rational creature itself might also be included here—the creature which is subject to God alone—in order that everything beneath it might be subject to it. Since this creature belongs to God the Father, it would not also belong to the Son unless the Son were equal to the Father. It was concerning this creature that he was speaking when he said: “I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me, who are yours; and all my things are yours, and your things are mine.”

Nor is it permissible that the holy ones of whom he spoke here should belong to anyone except the one by whom they were created and sanctified. Consequently, everything that belongs to them must belong to the one to whom they themselves belong. Therefore, since they belong both to the Father and to the Son, he demonstrates that the Father and the Son are equal, since the holy ones belong equally to both.

But when he said, speaking of the Holy Spirit, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you,” he spoke of those things which pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which the Son is equal to him by possessing everything that the Father possesses. For the Holy Spirit was not going to receive from the creature that is subject to the Father and the Son what is meant by “he will take from what is mine”; rather, he would receive from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son was born.

“And I have been glorified in them,” he says. He now speaks of his glorification as though it had already taken place, although it was still future; above, however, he was asking the Father that it should take place. But whether this is the same glorification of which he had said, “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed,” must certainly be investigated.

For if it was “with you,” how is it “in them”? Or, when this very fact is made known to them and, through them, to all who believe them as his witnesses, can we properly understand the Lord to have said of the apostles that he has been glorified in them? By saying that it had already happened, he showed that it had already been predestined, and he wished it to be regarded as certain that it would occur.

“And now,” he says, “I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world.” If you attend strictly to the hour at which he was speaking, both were still in the world—he himself, of course, and those of whom he was speaking. We cannot and should not understand this according to progress in heart and life, as though they were said still to be in the world because they continued to think worldly thoughts, while he was no longer in the world because he thought divine thoughts.

For one word is placed here which absolutely prevents us from understanding it in that way. He does not say, “I am not in the world,” but, “I am no longer in the world,” thereby showing that he had been in the world and was now no longer in it. Is it therefore permissible for us to believe that he had ever thought worldly thoughts and, having been freed from that error, no longer thought them? Who could clothe himself in so impious a meaning?

It remains, then, that according to the fact that he himself had previously been in the world, he said that he was now no longer in the world—plainly with reference to bodily presence—because his absence from the world was soon to occur, while theirs would occur later. In this way he showed that he was already saying that he was no longer here, while they were here, even though both he and they were still here.

Thus the man spoke in a manner suited to human beings, according to the human custom of speech. Do we not say every day of someone who is about to leave very soon, “He is no longer here”? This is especially said of those who are dying, although the Lord himself, as though foreseeing what might trouble those who would read his words, added:

“And I am coming to you.”

In this way he explained, in a sense, why he had said, “I am no longer in the world.” He therefore commends to the Father those whom he was going to leave by bodily absence, saying:

“Holy Father, preserve them in your name, those whom you gave me.”

Certainly, he is here asking God as man for his disciples whom he received from God. But attend to what follows:

“So that they may be one,” he says, “as we are.”

He does not say, “So that they may be one with us,” or, “So that we and they may be one, as we are one”; rather, he says, “So that they may be one, as we are.” They are to be one in their own nature, just as we are one in our own nature.

Without doubt he would not say this truly unless God were saying it—God who is of the same nature as the Father, as he said elsewhere, “I and the Father are one” (John X), not according to that in which he is also man. For according to this he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

“When I was with them, I was preserving them in your name.” “When I go to you,” he says, “preserve them in your name, in which I too preserved them when I was with them.” The Son, as man, preserved his disciples in the name of the Father while he was bodily present with them.

But the Father also preserved them in the name of the Son, answering those who asked in the name of the Son. For the same Son had said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.”

Nor should we understand this in such a carnal way as though the Father and the Son preserved us in turn, with their guardianship alternating in our preservation—as though one should take over when the other had departed. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is the one true and blessed God, preserve us together.

But Scripture does not lift us up unless it first descends to us, just as the Word became flesh and descended in order to lift us up, not falling in order to lie prostrate. If we have recognized him descending, let us rise with the one who lifts us up, and let us understand that, when he speaks in this way, he distinguishes the persons without separating the natures.

Therefore, when the Son was preserving his disciples by bodily presence, the Father was not waiting to take over the preservation when the departing Son had left; rather, both were preserving them by spiritual power. And when the departing Son removed his bodily presence, he retained spiritual guardianship together with the Father, because when the Son as man accepted those who were to be preserved, he did not remove them from the Father’s guardianship. And when the Father gave them to the Son to preserve, he did not give them without the one to whom he gave them, but gave them to the Son as man not apart from God—that is, to the same Son.

The Son therefore continues and says:

“Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.”

The betrayer of Christ was called the “son of perdition,” predestined to perdition according to Scripture, because it is especially of him that prophecy is made in the hundred-and-eighth psalm.

“But now,” he says, “I am coming to you; and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.”

Behold, he says that he is speaking in the world, although shortly before he had said, “I am no longer in the world.” We have explained why he said this there—or rather, we have shown that he himself explained it. Therefore, because he had not yet departed, he was still here; and because he was soon to depart, he was in a certain sense already no longer here.

What this joy is, of which he says, “So that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves,” was already expressed above, where he said, “So that they may be one, as we are.” He says that this joy of his—that is, the joy bestowed by him upon them—is to be fulfilled in them, and that this is why he said that he was speaking in the world.

This is that peace and blessedness in the future age, for the attainment of which one must live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this age.

While the Lord was still speaking to the Father and praying for his disciples, he said:

“I have given them your word, and the world has hated them.”

They had not yet experienced this through their own sufferings, which afterward followed them; but in his usual manner he says these things by foretelling future events in the words of the past tense. Then he supplies the reason why the world hated them:

“Because they are not of the world,” he says, “just as I am not of the world.”

This was bestowed upon them through regeneration. By generation they were of the world; for this reason he had already said to them, “I chose you out of the world.” It was therefore granted to them that, just as he was not of the world, neither should they be of the world, since he himself delivered them from the world.

But he was never of the world, because even according to the form of a servant he himself was born from the Holy Spirit, from whom they were reborn. For if they are now not of the world because they have been reborn from the Holy Spirit, he was never of the world because he was born from the Holy Spirit:

“I do not ask,” he says, “that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil.”

For although they were already not of the world, it was still necessary for them to be in the world. He repeats the same statement:

“They are not of the world,” he says, “just as I am not of the world.”

“Sanctify them in the truth.”

For in this way they are preserved from evil, which he had prayed above would happen. But it may be asked how they were already not of the world if they had not yet been sanctified in the truth; or, if they already were so, why does he ask that they should become so?

Or is it because, even after they have been sanctified, they progress in that same sanctity and become more holy—and this does not happen without the help of God’s grace, but through the one who sanctifies their progress, just as he sanctified their beginning? Therefore the Apostle also says: “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philipp. I).

The heirs of the new covenant are therefore sanctified in the truth, whereas the sanctifications of the old covenant were shadows of that truth. And when they are sanctified in the truth, they are certainly sanctified in Christ, who truly said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Likewise, when he says, “The truth will set you free” (John VIII), shortly afterward explaining what he had said, he adds: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (ibid.). Thus he showed that the one whom he had first called “the Truth” was afterward called “the Son.”

What else, then, did he say in this place by the words, “Sanctify them in the truth,” except, “Sanctify them in me”?

Finally, he continues and does not cease to make this clearer:

“Your word,” he says, “is truth.”

What else did he say than, “I am the truth”? For the Greek Gospel has **Λόγος** (*Logos*), the same word that is read where it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). And we know that this same Word is the only-begotten Son of God, who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

Therefore this reading may also be found here—and in some manuscripts it is found: “Your Word is truth”—just as in some manuscripts it is also written there, “In the beginning was the discourse” (*sermo*). In Greek, however, without any variation, **Λόγος** appears both there and here.

The Father therefore sanctifies his own heirs and his co-heirs in the truth—that is, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son. But he is still speaking about the apostles, for he adds:

“Just as you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world.”

Whom did he send, except his apostles? For the very name *apostle*, being Greek, means nothing other than “one who has been sent” in Latin.

God therefore sent his Son, not in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. VIII); and the Son sent those whom he sanctified from the stain of sin, although they had been born in sinful flesh.

But because, by becoming the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus became the head of the Church, while they are his members, he therefore says what follows:

“And for them I sanctify myself.”

For what does “And for them I sanctify myself” mean except, “I sanctify them in myself”? They themselves are also “I,” since, as I have said, those of whom he speaks are his members, and Christ is one—the head and the body—as the Apostle teaches when, speaking of the seed of Abraham, he says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. III).

For after saying above, “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (ibid.), what else was said to those to whom it was said, “Then you are Abraham’s seed,” except, “Then you belong to Christ”?

This is why the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Coloss. I). He did not say “of my afflictions,” but “of Christ’s,” because he was a member of Christ.

Immediately he adds:

“So that they themselves also may be sanctified in the truth.”

What else does this mean than “in me,” according to the fact that the Truth is that Word which was in the beginning, God? In him the Son of man himself was sanctified from the beginning of his creation, when the Word became flesh, because the Word and man became one person.

Then he sanctified himself in himself—that is, he sanctified himself as man in himself as the Word—because Christ is one, the Word and man, sanctifying man in the Word.

But on account of his members he says: “And for them I”—that is, I also promised this to them, because they too are I. It benefited me in myself, because I am man without them; and I sanctify myself—that is, I sanctify them in myself, as myself—because in me they too are I.

“So that they themselves also may be sanctified in the truth.” What does “they themselves also” mean except “just as I am in the Truth, which I am”? 

“I do not pray for these only”—that is, for the disciples who were then with him.

But also for those, he says, who are going to believe in me through their word. Here he intended all his own to be understood—not only those who were then present in the flesh, but also those who were to come. For all who afterward believed in him undoubtedly believed through the word of the apostles, and will continue to believe until he comes. To them he had said: “And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” Through them the Gospel was proclaimed, even before it was written down. And certainly whoever believes in Christ believes the Gospel.

Therefore, not only those are to be understood whom he says would believe in him through their word—those who, while the apostles themselves were living in the flesh, listened to them—but also those who believed in Christ after the apostles’ death, and we, born long afterward, believe in Christ through their word. For those who were then with him proclaimed to others what they had heard from him; and thus their word, so that we too might believe, has reached us wherever his Church exists, and will reach future generations—whoever, wherever they may be, will afterward believe in him.

Jesus might therefore appear in this prayer not to have prayed for certain of his own, unless we carefully examine his words in the same prayer. For if he first prayed for those who were then with him, as we have already shown, and afterward also for those who were to believe in him through their word, it may be said that he did not pray for those who were neither with him when he said these things nor afterward believed through their word, but had already believed in him, whether through them or by some other means.

For was Nathanael then with him? Was Joseph of Arimathea—the man who asked Pilate for his body, and whom this same evangelist John testifies had already been his disciple? Was Mary his mother, and the other women whom we learn from the Gospel had already been his disciples—were they then with him? Of them the same evangelist John often says: “Many believed.” For where did that multitude come from who, some going before and some following, accompanied him as he sat upon the animal, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm VIII)? And where did the children come from, of whom he says that it had been foretold: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (I Corinthians XV)? Where did the five hundred brothers come from, to whom he would not have appeared all at once after the resurrection unless they had already believed in him? Where did those one hundred and nine come from, who, together with these eleven, made one hundred and twenty when, gathered together after his ascension, they awaited and received the promised Holy Spirit (Acts I)? Where were all these people from, except from those of whom it was said: “Many believed in him” (John II)?

Did the Savior, then, not pray for these people at that time, because he prayed for those who were then with him and for others who had not yet believed in him through their word but were going to believe, whereas these people were neither then with him nor were going later to believe through their word, but had already believed in him?

I pass over the aged Simeon, who believed in him when he was an infant; Anna the prophetess (Luke II); Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke I), who prophesied about him before he was born of the Virgin; and their son John, his forerunner and the bridegroom’s friend, who recognized him in the Holy Spirit, proclaimed him while he was absent, and, when he was present, pointed him out to others so that they too might recognize him (John I). I pass over these because it may be answered that there was no need to pray for such people after their death, since they had departed this life with their great merits and, having been received, were at rest; the same answer is given regarding the ancient righteous.

For who among them could have been saved from the condemnation of the whole mass of perdition that came about through one man, unless, with the Spirit revealing it, he had believed in the one Mediator between God and human beings who was to come in the flesh? But was it necessary for him to pray for the apostles, while it was not necessary for him to pray for so many who were still in this life, though they were not then with him and had already believed? Who could say this?

It must therefore be understood that they had not yet believed in him in the manner in which he himself wished them to believe in him. For even Peter himself—although, when he confessed and said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI), the Lord had borne such a great testimony to him—preferred that Christ should not die rather than believe that, after dying, he would rise again. Hence he was immediately addressed by him as “Satan” (Mark VIII).

Those who had already died are therefore found to have been more faithful: they did not doubt, with the Spirit revealing it, that Christ would rise again. This was not true of those who had believed that he himself would redeem Israel, but, when they saw his death, lost all the hope they had placed in him.

We therefore believe nothing more reasonable than that, after his resurrection, once the apostles had received the Holy Spirit, been instructed and strengthened, and established as the first teachers in the Church, others believed through their word in the manner in which it was necessary to believe in Christ—that is, so that they might hold fast to faith in his resurrection. Consequently, all those who already appeared to have believed in him belonged to the number of those for whom he prayed when he said: “But I do not pray for these only, but also for those who are going to believe in me through their word.”

But blessed Paul the apostle and that thief—cruel in crime, faithful on the cross—still remain for us as a difficulty to be resolved. For the Apostle Paul says that he was made an apostle “not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ” (Galatians I); and, speaking of his own Gospel, he says: “For I neither received it from a human being, nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (ibid.). How, then, will he be among those of whom it was said: “They will believe in me through their word”?

That thief believed at the very moment when the faith that had existed, however imperfectly, among those teachers themselves had failed. He therefore did not believe in Christ Jesus through their word; yet he believed in such a way that, although he saw him crucified, he confessed that he would not only rise again but also reign, saying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII).

It therefore remains that, if the Lord Jesus is to be understood in this prayer as having prayed for all his own—whoever, whether then living in this life, which is a time of trial upon the earth (Job VII), or destined to live afterward—we should understand the expression “through their word” to signify the word of faith that they preached throughout the world. It is called their word because it was first and especially preached by them.

It was already being preached by them on earth when Paul received that same word through a revelation of Jesus Christ. For this reason he also laid the Gospel before them, lest he should have run, or be running, in vain (Galatians II); and they gave him the right hand of fellowship, because in him too they found—although it had not been given to him through them—their own word, which they were already preaching and upon which they had been founded. Concerning this word of Christ’s resurrection the same Apostle says: “Whether it was I or they, so we preach, and so you believed” (I Corinthians XV).

And again he says: “This is the word of faith that we preach: that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans X). In the Acts of the Apostles it is also written that God established faith for all in Christ, raising him from the dead.

Because this word of faith was principally and initially preached by the apostles who had adhered to him, it was therefore called “their word” (Acts XVII). It is not on that account not the word of God, because it is called their word, since the same Apostle says that the Thessalonians received from him not the word of human beings but, as he says, “as it truly is, the word of God” (I Thessalonians II). It is therefore God’s word because God gave it; it is called their word because God entrusted it to them first and especially to be preached.

Thus, in that prayer our Redeemer prayed for all whom he redeemed, whether then living in the flesh or destined to live afterward. While praying for the apostles who were then with him, he also included those who were to believe in him through their word.

When, therefore, the Lord Jesus had prayed for his disciples whom he then had with him, and had added his other disciples, saying: “But I do not pray for these only, but also for those who are going to believe in me through their word,” as though we were asking what or why he was praying for them, he immediately added:

“That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, so that they too may be one in us.” Earlier, when he was still praying only for the disciples whom he had with him, he had said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we also are.”

Now, therefore, he prayed this for us as well as for them: that all of us—that is, both we and they—might be one. Here we must carefully observe that the Lord did not say, “that we all may be one,” but “that they all may be one,” as in: “You, Father, are in me, and I in you”; “we are,” it is understood, “one.”

This is more appropriately said afterward, because earlier he had said of the disciples who were with him: “so that they may be one, as we also are.” Accordingly, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father in such a way that they are one, because they are of one substance.

We, however, can be in them, but we cannot be one with them, because we and they are not of one substance, insofar as the Son is God with the Father. For insofar as he is human, he is of the same substance as we are.

But here he wished rather to commend what he says elsewhere: “I and the Father are one.” There he signified that the Father and he have the same nature. Therefore, although the Father and the Son—and also the Holy Spirit—are in us, we must not suppose that they are of one nature with us.

Thus they are in us, or we in them, in such a way that they are one in their own nature, while we are one in ours. They themselves are in us as God is in his temple. We are in them as a creature is in its Creator.

Then, after saying “so that they too may be one in us,” he added:

“So that the world may believe that you sent me.”

What, then, does “that they all may be one, so that the world may believe” mean? Those “all” are the believing world. For the people who were one are not one group, and the world that is to believe another, since he plainly speaks of those concerning whom he had said: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who are going to believe in me through their word,” immediately adding: “that they all may be one.”

Who are all these people, if not the world—not the hostile world, certainly, but the faithful world? For behold, he who had said, “I do not pray for the world,” prays for the world, so that it may believe, since there is a world of which it is written: “So that we may not be condemned with this world” (I Corinthians XI).

He does not pray for that world, for he certainly knows the world that has been predestined to condemnation. There is also a world of which it is written: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John III). Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Corinthians V).

It is of this world that he says: “so that the world may believe that you sent me.” Through this faith the world is reconciled to God when it believes in Christ, who was sent by God.

How, then, are we to understand his words, “so that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me”? Surely not by supposing that he made the fact that the world would believe depend upon their being one—as though the world believed because it saw them to be one—since the world itself consists of all who, by believing, become one.

Rather, in praying he said: “so that the world may believe,” just as in praying he said: “that they all may be one,” and in praying he said: “that they too may be one in us.” For “that they all may be one” is the same as “that the world may believe”: by believing they become one, and they become perfectly one—although by nature they were one, they were not one because they had dissented from the One.

Finally, if we supply the word “I ask”—which is understood in his statement “I ask”—three times, or rather place it everywhere for greater fullness, the meaning of this sentence will become clearer:

“I ask that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you. I ask that they too may be one in us. I ask that the world may believe that you sent me.”

For this reason he added the words “in us”: so that we might know that the unity we attain through the most faithful love is to be attributed to God’s grace, not to ourselves. Thus the Apostle, after saying: “You were once darkness, but now light,” adds, “in the Lord” (Ephesians V), so that they would not attribute this to themselves.

Moreover, our Savior, by praying to the Father, demonstrated that he was human. Now, by demonstrating also that he himself, together with the Father, is God, he does what he prays for:

“And I,” he says, “have given them the glory that you gave me.”

What glory could this be except immortality, which human nature was destined to receive in him? For he himself had not yet received it; but, according to his customary manner, on account of the certainty of predestination, he signifies a future event by verbs in the past tense. He was soon to be glorified—that is, raised up—by the Father, and he himself was to raise us to that glory at the end.

This is similar to what he says elsewhere: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John V). And whom does he mean, except the very ones whom the Father raises? For whatever the Father does, the Son does not do something different but the same, and not in a different way but similarly; consequently, he also raised himself.

For where else do we find: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”? Therefore, although he does not say so, we must understand that he also gave himself the glory of immortality which he says was given to him by the Father.

For this reason he so often says that the Father alone does what he himself also does: so that, as Son with the Father, he may attribute whatever he is to the one from whom he is. But at other times, with the Father left unmentioned, he says that he does what he does with the Father. This is so that we may understand that the Son is not to be separated from the Father’s work when he says, with the Father unmentioned, that he himself performs some work, just as the Father is not separated from the Son’s work when the Son is said to perform, with the Father unmentioned, what the Father nevertheless performs.

When, therefore, the Son is silent about his own operation in the Father’s work, he commends his humility, so that he may be more salutary for us. But when, in turn, he is silent about the Father’s operation in his own work, he commends their equality, lest he be believed inferior.

In this way, therefore, in this passage he neither separated himself from the Father’s work, although he said: “the glory that you gave me,” since he himself also gave it to himself; nor did he separate the Father from his own work, although he said: “I have given them,” since the Father also gave it to them.

For the works of the Father and the Son are inseparable—not only those of the Father and the Son, but also those of the Holy Spirit. And just as, from the fact that he prayed to the Father for all his own, he intended that all should be one, so also through this benefit of his, expressed in the words “the glory that you gave me, I have given them,” he likewise intended that this unity should come about.

For he immediately added:

“So that they may be one, as we are one.” Then he added: “I in them, and you in me, so that they may be perfected in unity.”

Here he briefly indicated himself as Mediator between God and human beings. This was not said as though the Father were not in us, or we were not in the Father, since elsewhere he had said: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). Nor did he say here, as he had shortly before: “I in them, and you in me,” what he had said earlier: “They in me, and I in you”; instead he said: “You in me, and I in you, and they in us.”

What he now says, “I in them, and you in me,” is spoken from the person of the Mediator, just as the Apostle says: “You are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (II Corinthians III).

When he adds, “so that they may be perfected in unity,” he shows that the reconciliation accomplished through the Mediator is brought to this point: that we may enjoy perfect blessedness, to which nothing can be added.

Therefore, I do not think that what follows—“so that the world may know that you sent me”—should be understood as though he had again said: “so that the world may believe.” For “to know” is sometimes used in the sense of “to believe,” as in what he said somewhat earlier: “They truly knew that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.” Later he said “they believed,” whereas earlier he had said “they knew.”

But here, since he is speaking of perfection, the knowledge must be understood as the kind that will come through sight, not the kind that now comes through faith. For the order seems to have been preserved in what he said shortly before: “so that the world may believe,” whereas here he says: “so that the world may know.”

There, although he said “that they all may be one” and “that they may be one in us,” he did not say “that they may be perfected in unity”; and so he added: “so that the world may believe that you sent me.”

Here, however, he says: “so that they may be perfected in unity”; and then he does not add “so that the world may believe,” but “so that the world may know that you sent me.”

For as long as we believe what we do not see, we are not yet perfected in the way we will be when we are worthy to see what we believe. Thus he most rightly says there, “so that the world may believe,” and here, “so that the world may know.”

Nevertheless, both there and here, in the words “that you sent me,” we are to understand how far this belongs to the inseparable love of the Father and the Son: at present we believe this in the manner by which, through believing, we are moving toward knowledge.

If he had said, “so that they may know that you sent me,” it would have had the same meaning as what he says, “so that the world may know.” For they are the world—not the world that remains hostile, such as the world predestined to condemnation, but the world that has been made a friend from an enemy, for whose sake God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (II Corinthians V).

Therefore he said: “I in them, and you in me,” as though he were saying: “I in them to whom you sent me, and you in me, reconciling the world to yourself through me.”

For this reason he also adds:

“And you loved them, as you loved me.”

The Father loves us in the Son, because he chose us in him before the foundation of the world. For whoever loves the Only-Begotten certainly loves his members also, whom he adopted in him and through him.

Nor are we therefore equal to the Only-Begotten Son, through whom we were created and recreated, because it is said: “You loved them, as you loved me.” For one who says, “As this is, so that is,” does not always signify equality. Sometimes he means only that, because one thing exists, another also exists; or that, because one thing exists, another may come to exist.

For who would say that the apostles were sent by Christ into the world in precisely the same way that he himself was sent by the Father? To pass over other differences, which would take too long to enumerate, they were certainly sent when they were already human beings, whereas he was sent so that he might become human. Yet earlier he said: “As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world,” as though he were saying: “Because you sent me, I sent them.”

So also here: “You loved them,” he says, “as you loved me.” This means nothing other than: “You loved them because you also loved me.” For one who loves the Son would not fail to love his members. Is there any other reason for loving his members except that he loves him?

He loves the Son according to his divinity because he begot him equal to himself. He also loves him according to that in which he is human, because the Only-Begotten Word itself became flesh (John I), and because of the Word the flesh of the Word is dear to him.

But he loves us because we are members of the one whom he loves; and he loved us for the purpose of our becoming such members before we existed.

Therefore the love with which God loves is incomprehensible and unchangeable. He did not begin to love us from the time when we were reconciled to him through the blood of his Son. Rather, he loved us before the foundation of the world, so that we too might be his children together with his Only-Begotten, before we were anything at all.

When, therefore, we are reconciled to God through the death of his Son, this must not be heard or understood as though the Son reconciled us to him so that he might then begin to love those whom he hated—as an enemy is reconciled to an enemy so that afterward they become friends and love one another, though previously they hated one another.

Rather, we were reconciled to the one who already loved us, although on account of sin we were enemies of him.

Whether I speak truly, let the Apostle testify: “God commends his love toward us,” he says, “because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” He therefore had love toward us even when, acting in hostility toward him, we were committing iniquity. Yet it was also most truly said to him: “You hate all who work iniquity.”

Thus, in a marvelous and divine manner, even when he hated us, he loved us. For he hated us as what he himself had not made; and because our iniquity had not entirely destroyed the work of his hands, he knew that in each one of us there was both something to hate—that which we had done—and something to love—that which he had made.

This may indeed be understood of all human beings, in accordance with the true statement made to him: “You hate nothing of what you have made” (Wisdom XI). For he would not have willed what he hated to exist; indeed, it would not exist if the Almighty had not willed it to exist, unless even in what he hates there were something he loved.

He rightly hates, as though by the standard of his own art, the vice that is foreign to him; yet he loves what is his own even in the midst of vice, whether on account of his benefits by which it is healed or on account of his judgment by which it is condemned.

Thus God hates nothing of what he has made. He is the creator of natures, not of vices. The evils that he hates he did not make; and, with regard to those same evils, whether by healing them through mercy or ordering them through judgment, the good things he made are themselves present.

Since, therefore, he hates nothing that he has made, who could worthily express how greatly he loves the members of his Only-Begotten, and how much more he loves the Only-Begotten himself, in whom all things visible and invisible were created—things which, ordered in their several kinds, he loves most perfectly?

He brings the members of the Only-Begotten, by the generosity of his grace, to equality with the holy angels. But the Only-Begotten, since he is Lord of all, is undoubtedly Lord of the angels according to the nature by which he is God—not equal to the angels, but rather equal to the Father. According to the grace by which he is human, how could he not surpass the excellence of every angel, since flesh and Word are one person?

The Lord Jesus lifts his own to a great hope, than which there can be no greater. Listen, and be joyful in hope, because of which this life is not to be loved but endured, so that you may be patient in its tribulation.

Listen, I say, and attend, so that our hope may be raised up. Christ Jesus speaks—the Only-Begotten Son of God, coeternal and equal with the Father, speaks; he who became human for our sake, yet did not become what every human being is, a liar, speaks. The Way, the Life, and the Truth speaks. He who has not yet conquered speaks of those whom he has conquered.

Listen, believe, hope, and desire what he says:

“Father,” he says, “I will that those whom you have given me should be where I am, and that they also should be with me.”

Who are these whom he says were given to him by the Father? Are they not those of whom he says elsewhere: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI)?

How the things that he says are done by the Father are also done by him together with the Father, we know if we have made progress in this Gospel. These, then, are those whom he received from the Father, and whom he himself chose from the world.

For what did he choose them?
