So that they would no longer be of the world, just as he himself is not of the world, and yet so that they too would be the believing world, recognizing that Christ was sent by God the Father, so that the world might be liberated from the world and the world to be reconciled to God might not be condemned with the most hostile world.

For, as he said at the beginning of this prayer, the Father gave him authority over all flesh—that is, over every human being—so that he might free whomever he wished and condemn whomever he wished, since he will judge the living and the dead. But he says that those were given to him to whom he gives eternal life.

For he says: “So that he may give eternal life to all that you have given him.” Therefore those to whom he will not give eternal life were not given to him, although authority over them also was given to him when authority over all flesh—that is, over every human being—was given to him.

Thus the world to be reconciled is liberated from the hostile world, when he exercises his authority over that hostile world in sending it into eternal death; but he makes the former world his own, granting it eternal life.

Accordingly, the good Shepherd promised this reward to all his sheep without exception, and the great Head to all his members: that where he is, we too should be with him. What the almighty Son said he willed from the almighty Father cannot fail to happen.

There too is the Holy Spirit, equally eternal and equally God, the one Spirit of the two, and the substance of their will.

For that which is said to have been spoken as the Passion drew near—“Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matthew XXVI)—does not mean that the Father has one will and the Son another, or that they ever had different wills. It is the voice of our weakness, although a faithful weakness, which our Head transformed into himself when he also bore our sins.

That the Father and the Son have one will, whose Spirit is also one—the Spirit who, when added to them, enables us to recognize the Trinity—let piety believe, even if weakness does not yet permit us to understand it.

But since, in the brevity demanded by our discourse, we have already said to whom he made the promise and how firm that promise is, let us now consider, as far as we can, what it is that he deigned to promise:

“Those whom you have given me,” he says, “I will that they also should be where I am, and that they should be with me.”

As far as concerns the creature in which he was made from David’s seed according to the flesh, he himself was not yet where he was destined to be. Yet he could say, “Where I am,” in the sense that we should understand him to have been shortly going to ascend into heaven, so that he could already say that he was where he was soon to be.

He could also say it in the manner in which he had earlier spoken to Nicodemus: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). There too he did not say “will be,” but “is,” on account of the unity of the person in which God and man are one, and man is God.

He therefore promised that we would be in heaven. For the form of a servant, which he assumed from the Virgin, was lifted up and placed at the right hand of the Father.

On account of the hope of this great good the Apostle also says: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace we have been saved—and raised us up together and seated us in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians II).

This, then, can be understood as what the Lord said: “That where I am, they also may be with me.” He himself said of himself that he was already there; concerning us, he said that he willed us to be there with him, not showing that we were already there.

The Apostle, however, spoke of what the Lord said he willed to happen as though it had already happened. For he did not say: “He will raise us up and make us sit in the heavenly places,” but: “He raised us up and made us sit in the heavenly places,” because he does not vainly but faithfully reckon as accomplished what he does not doubt will happen.

As far as concerns the form of God, in which he is equal and coeternal with the Father, if we wish to understand according to it what was said—“I will that where I am, they also may be with me”—let every thought of bodily images withdraw from the mind.

Whatever presents itself to the mind as long, broad, thick, colored by any bodily light, and extended through spaces of place, whether finite or infinite: let the mind turn the eye of its contemplation or attention away from all such things as far as it can.

Let it not inquire where the Son, equal to the Father, is, since no one finds where he is not. Rather, whoever wishes to seek should seek to be with him—not everywhere as he is, but wherever it is possible for him to be.

For when he said to the man hanging in punishment but making a saving confession, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII), his soul, according to the fact that he was human, was to be in the underworld that very day, and his flesh in the tomb. But according to the fact that he was God, he was certainly also in paradise.

Thus the thief’s soul, freed from its former crimes and already blessed by his gift, although it could not be everywhere as he could, nevertheless could be with him in paradise on that very day, from which he who is everywhere had not departed.

For this reason it was not enough for him to say: “I will that where I am, they also may be”; he added: “with me.” To be with him is a great good.

For even the wretched may be where he is, since wherever they may be, he is also there. But only the blessed are with him, because they cannot be blessed except through him.

Is it not truly said to God: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Psalm CXXXVIII)? Or is Christ not the Wisdom of God, which reaches everywhere because of its purity?

But “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John II). Therefore, to take some sort of example from a visible thing, although it is very dissimilar: just as a blind person, even if he is where the light is, is not himself with the light but is absent from what is present, so the unbeliever and impious person—or even the faithful and devout person who is not yet fit to behold the light of wisdom—even though he cannot be anywhere where Christ is not, is nevertheless not with Christ, at least not through sight.

For a faithful person who believes devoutly is undoubtedly with Christ through faith. Hence he says: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke XI).

But when he said to God the Father: “Those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me,” he was speaking entirely of that sight in which we will see him as he is (I John III).

Let no one disturb the serene meaning with a cloudy contradiction. Let what follows bear witness to what precedes. For after saying, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me,” he immediately added:

“So that they may see my glory, which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.”

He said, “So that they may see,” not “so that they may believe.” This is the reward of faith, not faith itself. For if faith is rightly defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews as “the conviction of things that are not seen” (Hebrews XI), why should the vision of the things that were believed and hoped for not rightly be defined as the reward of faith?

When we see the glory that the Father gave the Son—even if in this passage we understand it not as the glory that the Father gave him by begetting him as equal to himself, but as the glory that he gave to the Son made human after the death of the cross—then, when we see the glory of the Son, the judgment of the living and the dead will certainly take place.

Then the impious will be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord (Isaiah XXVI). Which glory could this be except that by which he is God? For “blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God” (Matthew XXV). The impious are not pure in heart; therefore they will not see him.

Then they will go into eternal punishment—for this is what it means that the impious will be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord—while the righteous will go into eternal life (Matthew XXVI).

And what is eternal life? “That they may know you,” he says, “the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

This does not mean that they will know him in the manner in which those who were not pure in heart nevertheless saw him judging in the glorified form of a servant. Rather, they will know him as the only true God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit: the Son, because the Trinity itself is the only true God.

If, therefore, we understand the statement “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” according to the fact that the Son of God is God, equal and coeternal with the Father, then we will be in the Father with Christ—but he as he is, and we as we are, wherever we may be bodily.

For if places are to be spoken of even with respect to things that do not contain bodies, and if each thing has a place where it is, the eternal place of Christ, where he always is, is the Father; and the place of the Father is the Son, because he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and in this prayer: “You, Father, are in me, and I in you.”

They themselves are also our place, because he continues: “so that they too may be one in us.” And we are God’s place, because we are his temple, as the one who died for us and lives for us prays on our behalf.

We are one in them, because “his place was made in peace, and his dwelling place in Zion” (Psalm LXXV), which we are.

But who is capable of thinking about these places, or about what is in these places, without spacious capacities and bodily movements? Nevertheless, some progress is made if at least whatever of this kind presents itself to the eye of the heart is denied, rejected, and repudiated, while that light in which these things are seen as things to be denied, rejected, and repudiated is contemplated as far as possible, and its certainty is recognized and loved, so that from there we may rise and advance toward what is within.

When the feeble mind, less pure than those things are, is unable to penetrate them, let it be driven away from there, not without a groan of love and tears of longing; let it patiently endure as long as it is purified by faith, and let it prepare itself through holy conduct so that it may be able to dwell there.

How, then, will we not be with Christ where he is, when we will be with him in the Father, in whom he is? The Apostle did not keep silent about this for us, although we do not yet possess the reality but do possess hope.

For he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians III).

Behold, for the present, through faith and hope, our life is where Christ is; it is with him because it is with Christ in God. Behold, it is as though what he prayed would happen has already happened, when he said: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me.” But when will it happen through sight?

“When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” (ibid.). Then we will appear as what we will be, because then it will be apparent that we did not believe and hope in vain before we were what we will be.

He will accomplish this—the one to whom the Son, after saying, “so that they may see my glory, which you have given me,” immediately added: “because you loved me before the foundation of the world.”

For in him he also loved us before the foundation of the world; and then he predestined what he will accomplish at the end of the world.

Father, he says, righteous Father, the world has not known you. Because you are righteous, therefore it has not known you. For that world predestined for condemnation did not know you deservedly; but the world whom he reconciled to himself through Christ knew you, not by merit but by grace. For what does it mean to know him except to possess eternal life, which he certainly did not give to the condemned world but gave to the reconciled world? Therefore the world did not know you because you are righteous, and you repaid it according to its merits, so that it would not know you. And therefore the reconciled world knew you because you are merciful, and you came to its aid, so that it might know you, not according to merit but by grace. Finally, he continues:

“But I have known you.” He himself is the fountain of grace: God by nature, but man through the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, by ineffable grace. Finally, it is on his account, because the grace of God is through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. VII).

“And these have known,” he says, “that you sent me.” This is the reconciled world. But because you sent me, they have known; therefore they have known by grace.

“And I have made your name known to them,” he says, “and I will make it known.” I have made it known through faith; I will make it known through sight. I have made it known to those journeying by faith; I will make it known to those reigning without end.

“So that the love,” he says, “with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” The expression *dilectio quam dilexisti me* (“the love with which you loved me”) is not customary. In ordinary usage one would say *dilectione qua dilexisti me* (“with the love with which you loved me”). This has been translated from the Greek; but there are similar expressions in Latin, as when we say, “He served a faithful service” and “He served an energetic military service,” whereas it would seem that one ought to say, “He served with faithful service” and “He served in an energetic military campaign.” But what sort of expression is “the love with which you loved me”? The Apostle likewise used one of the same kind: “I have fought the good fight” (II Tim. IV); he did not say, “with a good fight,” which would be more customary and apparently more correct.

But how is the love with which the Father loved the Son also in us, except because we are his members and are loved in him, since he himself is loved in his entirety—that is, the head and the body? For this reason he added, “And I in them,” as if he were saying, “Since I am also in them.” For he is in us in one way as in his temple, but in another way because we ourselves are he, since, according to the fact that he became man in order to be our head, we are his body.

The Savior’s prayer is ended. The Passion begins.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0895C]

“When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples,” etc. The evangelist’s account of the Lord’s entering the garden with his disciples did not take place immediately after he had finished that prayer, of whose words he says, “When Jesus had said these things.” Rather, certain other events intervened, which this evangelist passes over but which are read in the accounts of the other evangelists, just as there are many things found in this evangelist which they likewise omitted in their narratives. Whoever wishes to know how they all agree with one another, and how one does not contradict the truth proclaimed by another, should seek the answer not in these discourses but in other more laborious writings.

Let us therefore not understand the words, “When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the torrent Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he himself entered, and his disciples,” as though he entered that garden immediately after those words. Rather, what was said, “When Jesus had said these things,” should serve to prevent us from supposing that he entered before he had finished those words.

“But Judas also,” he says, “who betrayed him, knew the place.” The order of the words is: “The one who betrayed him knew the place,” because, he says, Jesus often met there with his disciples. There, then, the wolf covered with sheep’s clothing, and tolerated among the sheep by the household master’s profound counsel, learned where he might briefly scatter the flock by lying in wait for the shepherd (Zech. XIII).

“Therefore Judas,” he says, “having received a cohort, and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.” The cohort was not a Jewish cohort but a military one. It should therefore be understood to have been received from the governor, as for the purpose of holding an accused man, with the lawful order of authority preserved, so that no one would dare resist those who were taking him. Yet such a large and heavily armed force had also been assembled that it came either to frighten or even to resist, if anyone should dare defend Christ. Thus his power was concealed and weakness was put forward, so that these things might seem necessary to his enemies against one whom they could have accomplished nothing without his own will—he, the good one, making good use of evil things, making good things out of evil things, in order to make good people out of the evil and distinguish them from the evil.

Then Jesus, as the evangelist continues, [Col. 0896B] “knowing all that was to come upon him, went forth and said to them, ‘Whom do you seek?’ They answered him, ‘Jesus the Nazarene.’ Jesus said to them, ‘I am he.’ Judas, who betrayed him, was also standing with them. When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.”

Where now is the cohort of soldiers and the officers of the chief priests and Pharisees? Where are the terror and the protection of weapons? One voice saying, “I am he,” struck, drove back, and cast to the ground without any weapon that entire crowd, fierce with hatred and terrible with arms. For God was hidden in the flesh, and eternal day was so concealed in human limbs that he was sought with lanterns and torches. He was to be killed by darkness, yet he says, “I am he,” and cast down the ungodly. What will he do when he comes to judge, who did this when he himself was to be judged? What will he be able to do when he reigns, who was able to do this when he was about to die? And now Christ says everywhere through the Gospel, “I am he,” while the Antichrist is awaited by the Jews, so that they may go backward and fall to the ground, because, abandoning heavenly things, they desire earthly things.

Certainly the persecutors came with the traitor to seize Jesus; they found the one they were seeking. They heard, “I am he.” Why did they not seize him, but go backward and fall, unless it was because he willed this—he who could do whatever he willed? Yet if he had never allowed himself to be seized by them, they would indeed not have done what they came to do; but would he himself have done what he came to do? They sought to kill him in their rage; but he too sought us by dying. Therefore, because he rashly displayed his power to those who desired but could not act, let them now seize him, so that he may accomplish his will through those who do not know it.

Again, therefore, he asked them, “Whom do you seek?” They said, “Jesus the Nazarene.” Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these men go,” so that the saying might be fulfilled which he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me, I have not lost any one.”

“If you seek me,” he says, “let these men go.” He sees enemies, and they do what he commands. They allow those whom he does not wish to perish to go away. But were they not destined to die later? Why would he lose them if they died then, except because they did not yet believe in him in the manner in which all who do not perish believe?

Simon Peter, therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the chief priest and cut off his right ear. [Col. 0897A] The servant’s name was Malchus. This evangelist alone also gives the servant’s name, just as Luke alone records that the Lord touched his ear and healed him (Luke XXII). Malchus is interpreted as “the one who will reign.” What, then, does the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signify, except hearing cut off by old age and renewed so that it may exist in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter? When this has been granted by Christ, who would doubt that he will reign with Christ? And that he was found to be a servant also belongs to that oldness which generates slavery, which is Hagar (Gal. III). But when healing came, freedom was represented.

Nevertheless, the Lord disapproved of Peter’s action and forbade him to go further, saying:

“Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” In his own deed that disciple wished to defend his master; he did not consider what had been signified. He therefore had to be instructed in patience, and the event had to be recorded for our understanding. When he says that the cup of suffering was given to him by the Father, this is surely what the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). Yet the author of this cup is also the one who drank it. Hence the same Apostle says again: “Christ loved us and delivered himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Eph. V).

Then the cohort, the tribune, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus [Col. 0897C] and bound him. They seized the one to whom they did not draw near, because that day remained with him, while they remained darkness; nor did they hear, “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). For if they had been enlightened in this way, they would have seized him not with hands to kill him but with their hearts to receive him. But when they seized him in that manner, they moved farther away from him and bound the one whom they ought rather to have wished to be freed. Perhaps there were among them some who then placed their bonds upon Christ and were later freed by him and said, “You broke my bonds.”

Let this suffice for today. God willing, what follows will be treated in another discourse.

After the persecutors, through Judas’s betrayal, had seized and bound the Lord—who, as the Apostle says, “loved us and delivered himself up” (Eph. V), and “delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII)—it should be understood that Judas is not praiseworthy because of the usefulness of this betrayal, but condemnable because of the criminal intention behind it,

they brought him, as the evangelist John narrates here, first to Annas. He does not fail to state why this was done:

“For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.” But he says, “Caiaphas was the one who had given the counsel to the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.” Matthew, wishing to narrate this more briefly, appropriately recalls that he was to be led to Caiaphas, because he was first led to Annas precisely because Annas was Caiaphas’s father-in-law. Here it should be understood that Matthew intended this to refer to that same Caiaphas.

“Simon Peter was following Jesus,” he says, “and another disciple.” Who this disciple was should not be rashly asserted, since it is not stated. John commonly indicates himself in this way and adds, “whom Jesus loved.” Perhaps, then, this was he. Whoever he may have been, let us examine what follows.

“That disciple,” he says, “was known to the high priest, and Peter was standing outside at the door. Therefore the disciple who was known to the high priest went out and spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. The maidservant who kept the door said to Peter, ‘Are you not also one of this man’s disciples?’ He said, ‘I am not.’”

Here is the boldness of the man making promises and placing excessive confidence in himself. Where are those words he spoke when he said, “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII)? Is this following the master—to deny that one is his disciple? Is one laying down his life for the Lord in such a way that he fears the voice of a maidservant lest this happen?

But what wonder is it if God foretold the truth while a man presumptuously declared what was false? Certainly, in this denial of the Apostle Peter, which had now begun, we must observe not only that Christ is denied by the one who says that he is not the Christ, but also that he is denied by the one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is a Christian. For the Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but, “You will deny me.” He therefore denied Christ when he denied that he was his disciple. What else did he thereby deny than that he was a Christian? Although Christ’s disciples were not yet called by this name—for the disciples first began to be called Christians at Antioch after his ascension—the reality already existed, and was later to receive that name. They were already disciples, who were later called Christians, and they transmitted this common name, like the common faith, to those who came after them.

Therefore, the one who denied that he was Christ’s disciple denied the reality whose name is “to be called a Christian.” How many later accomplished what he could not—not only old men and old women, in whom the weariness of this life could more readily lead them to despise death for confessing Christ, nor only young people of both sexes, from whom courage might appropriately be demanded because of their age, but even boys and girls? An innumerable company of holy martyrs entered the kingdom of heaven bravely and forcefully. How then could this man not do so, he who had received the keys of that kingdom?

This is why it was said, “Let these men go,” when he delivered himself up for us, who redeemed us by his blood, so that the saying he had spoken might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me, I have not lost any one.” For surely, if Peter had gone away from there after denying Christ, what else would have happened to him than that he would have perished?

The servants and officers were standing beside a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves. It was not winter, but it was cold, as can sometimes happen even at the spring equinox.

Peter was also with them, standing and warming himself. The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching. Jesus answered him: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gather, and I have spoken nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.”

A question naturally arises which must not be passed over: how did the Lord Jesus say, “I have spoken openly to the world,” especially when he said, “I have spoken nothing in secret”? Did he not say in this very discourse, which he delivered to the disciples after the supper, “I have spoken these things to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures but will announce the Father openly”? If, then, he did not speak openly even to his more intimate disciples, but promised an hour when he would speak openly, how did he speak openly to the world?

Furthermore, as the authority of the other evangelists also testifies (Matt. IV; Luke VIII), he spoke much more clearly to those same disciples, in comparison with those who were not his disciples, when he was apart from the crowds with them. For then he explained to them the parables which he presented to others in concealed form.

What, then, does “I have spoken nothing in secret” mean? We should understand him to have said this: “I have spoken openly to the world,” as if he had said, “Many have heard me.” But “openly” was, in one respect, openly, and in another respect, not openly. It was openly, because many heard; and again it was not openly, because they did not understand. And when he spoke apart to the disciples, he certainly was not speaking in secret. For who speaks in secret when he speaks in the presence of so many people? It is written, “Every word shall stand upon the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII), especially when he tells a few people what he wishes to become known through them to many, as the Lord himself said to those who were still few in number: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. X).

Therefore, even what seemed to be spoken secretly by him was, in a certain sense, not spoken in secret, because it was not spoken to those to whom it had been said in such a way that they should keep silent about it, but rather in such a way that it should be preached everywhere. If, then, something can be both openly and not openly, or both in secret and not in secret, how is it written that “those who see may see and not see” (Mark IV)? How do they see, except because it is openly and not in secret? And how, again, do these same people not see, except because it is not openly but in secret?

Yet the very things they had heard but had not understood were such that they could not justly and truthfully accuse him. Whenever they tried to find, by questioning him, grounds for accusing him, he answered them in such a way that all their deceits were blunted and their accusations frustrated. Therefore he said, “Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.”

When he had said these things, one of the officers standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” Jesus answered, “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?”

What could be truer, gentler, or more just than this response? It belongs to the one of whom the prophetic voice had gone before: “Direct your course prosperously, advance and reign, for the sake of truth and gentleness and justice” (Ps. XLIV).

If we consider who it was that received the blow, would we not wish that the one who struck him might be consumed by heavenly fire, swallowed up by the opening earth, seized by a demon and made to roll about, or punished by some similar penalty, even a more severe one? What of these things could he not have commanded by his power, through whom the world was made, if he had not preferred to teach us the patience by which the world is conquered?

Someone may say: “Why did he not do what he himself commanded? For he ought not to have answered the one who struck him in this way, but to have offered the other cheek” (Matt. V). What then? He answered truthfully, gently, and justly, and he prepared not only the other cheek for one who would strike it again, but his entire body to be fastened to the wood. [Col. 0900B] In this way he demonstrated more clearly what had to be demonstrated: that his great commands concerning patience are to be fulfilled not by bodily display but by preparation of the heart. For it is possible for someone to offer the other cheek visibly while remaining angry. How much better, then, that he answered with truth while at peace and was prepared in a tranquil spirit to endure more grievous things?

Blessed is the one who can truthfully say, concerning all the unjust things he suffers for justice, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. CVII). From this comes what follows: “I will sing and make melody” (ibid.), which Paul and Barnabas were also able to do in the harshest imprisonment (Acts XVI). But let us return to what follows in the Gospel narrative.

“And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.” According to Matthew, he was being led to him from the beginning, since he himself was the chief priest of that year (Matt. XXVI). The two high priests—Annas and Caiaphas, who were in office at that time—should be understood to have customarily held office in alternate years. The evangelist Luke mentions them when he relates the time at which the Lord began to preach the kingdom of heaven through his forerunner John and to gather disciples. For he says: “Under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness” (Luke III), etc.

These two high priests therefore held office in alternate years, and it was Caiaphas’s year when Christ suffered. Consequently, according to Matthew, after he had been seized he was led to Caiaphas; but first, according to John, they came with him to Annas, not because Annas was his colleague but because he was his father-in-law. It should be believed that this was done according to Caiaphas’s wishes, or perhaps that their houses were situated in such a way that Annas could not be passed by those going through. But after the evangelist had said that Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, he returned to the point in the narrative where he had left Peter, in order to explain what had happened in Annas’s house concerning Peter’s threefold denial.

“Simon Peter was standing,” he says, “and warming himself.” This repeats what he had already said; then he joins to it what followed. They therefore said to him, “Are you also one of his disciples?” He denied it and said, “I am not.” He had already denied him once; here is the second time.

Then, to complete the third denial, one of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?” Peter therefore denied him again, and immediately the cock crowed. Behold, the physician’s prediction was fulfilled and the patient’s presumption was confuted. What Peter had predicted did not happen: “I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII); but what Christ had predicted happened: “You will deny me three times” (Matt. XXVI).

“They therefore bring Jesus,” he says, “to Caiaphas, into the praetorium.” For he had said that Annas, his colleague and father-in-law, sent him to Caiaphas. But if he was taken to Caiaphas, why was he taken into the praetorium, which can mean nothing other than the place where the governor Pilate lived? Either, because some urgent matter required it, Caiaphas had gone from Annas’s house to the governor’s praetorium, where both had assembled to hear Jesus, and had left Jesus with his father-in-law to be heard; or Pilate had taken possession of a praetorium in Caiaphas’s house, and the house was so large that it could accommodate the Lord dwelling in one part and the judge in another.

“It was morning, and they”—that is, those who were leading Jesus—“did not enter the praetorium.” This means the part of the house occupied by Pilate. It was Caiaphas’s house. Explaining why they did not enter the praetorium, he says: “So that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.” They had begun to observe the days of Unleavened Bread, during which they considered it a defilement to enter the dwelling of a foreigner.

O impious blindness! They feared being defiled, so they said, by entering the dwelling of another, yet they were not defiled by their own crime. They feared defilement in the praetorium of a foreign judge, but did not fear the blood of an innocent brother—let me say this for the moment—because their conscience was held guilty of evils. But that the Lord himself was being led to death by their impiety, and that the giver of life was being killed, should be attributed not to their conscience but to their ignorance.

Pilate therefore went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered him, “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” Let those freed from unclean spirits, the sick who were healed, the lepers who were cleansed, the deaf who heard, the mute who spoke, the blind who saw, the dead who rose again—and, surpassing all these, the foolish who became wise—be questioned and answer whether Jesus is a criminal. But they said this of the kind of men concerning whom he himself had already said in prophecy: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. XXXIV).

Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews then said to him, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.”

What is this mad cruelty saying? Did they not kill the one whom they brought forward to be killed? Or does a cross perhaps not kill? This is how those who do not follow wisdom but persecute it behave foolishly. What does “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” mean (Exod. XXII)? If he is a criminal, why is it not lawful? Does the law not command them not to spare evildoers, especially those who, as they supposed, lead people away from their own God?

But it should be understood that they meant that it was not lawful for them to kill anyone during the festival of Passover, which they had already begun to celebrate, and on account of which they also feared being defiled by entering the praetorium. Have you become so hardened, false Israelites? Have you lost all understanding through excessive wickedness, so that you think yourselves undefiled by the blood of an innocent man merely because you hand him over to another to shed it? Will Pilate also kill with his own hands the one whom you thrust upon his authority to be killed? If you did not want him killed, if you did not plot against him, if you did not secure his betrayal by money, if you did not seize him, bind him, bring him, hate him, if you did not offer him to be killed by Gentile hands and demand his death with your voices, then do not boast that he was killed by you.

But if, in addition to all those preceding actions of yours, you also cried out, “Crucify, crucify,” hear what the Prophet cries against you: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). Behold with what weapons, with what arrows, with what sword you killed the righteous man, when you said that it was not lawful for you to kill anyone.

This is why, when the chief priests themselves did not come to seize Jesus but sent others, the evangelist Luke nevertheless says at the same point in his narrative: “Jesus said to those who had come out against him, the chief priests and magistrates of the temple and elders, ‘Have you come out as against a robber?’” etc. (Luke XXII). Just as the chief priests came not personally but through those whom they sent to seize Christ—and in what sense did they come except through the authority of their command?—so the crowd that shouted with impious voices for Christ to be crucified killed him not personally, but nevertheless killed him through the one who was driven to this crime by their shouting.

But when the evangelist John adds, “So that the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, signifying by what death he was to die,” he does not mean the death of the cross. Rather, he means that the Jews would hand him over to the Gentiles, that is, to the Romans. For Pilate was a Roman, sent as governor over Judea by the Romans.

Thus, so that this saying of Jesus might be fulfilled—that is, so that the Gentiles might kill him after he had been handed over to them, as Jesus had foretold—Pilate, who was a Roman judge, wished to return him to the Jews so that they might judge him according to their law. But they refused to accept him, saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” In this way the saying of Jesus concerning his death was fulfilled: the Gentiles killed him after he had been handed over by the Jews. Their crime was less than that of the Jews, who wished in this way to make themselves appear strangers to his killing—not so that their innocence might be shown, but their madness.

Pilate therefore entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others tell you about me?” The Lord certainly knew both what he himself was asking and what the other would answer. Yet he wished it to be said, not so that he himself might know, but so that what he wished us to know might be recorded.

[Col. 0903A]

Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?” Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.”

This is what the good Teacher wished us to know. But first the opinion of human beings concerning his kingdom had to be shown, whether that opinion belonged to the Gentiles or to the Jews, from whom Pilate had heard it—as though he were being sentenced to death because he had unlawfully aspired to kingship, or because rulers commonly envy those who are destined to rule. It had to be made clear that his kingdom was not hostile either to the Romans or to the Jews.

The Lord could have answered Pilate’s first question—“Are you the king of the Jews?”—by saying immediately, “My kingdom is not of this world,” and so forth. But by asking in return whether Pilate said this of his own accord or had heard it from others, and by wishing to show through Pilate’s answer that this had been presented to him by the Jews as a crime, he disclosed to us the thoughts of human beings, which he knew to be empty (Ps. XCIII).

Then, after Pilate’s answer, he more appropriately and suitably replied to both Jews and Gentiles: “My kingdom is not of this world.” If he had answered immediately when Pilate questioned him, he might have seemed to have replied about himself only to the Gentiles, who held this opinion about him, and not also to the Jews. But since Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me; what have you done?” he removed from himself the suspicion that he had said on his own initiative that Jesus was king of the Jews, showing that he had heard this from the Jews.

Then, by saying, “What have you done?” he sufficiently showed that this had been brought against him as a crime, as though he were saying: “If you deny that you are a king, what have you done to be handed over to me?” It would not be surprising if one who said that he was a king were handed over to a judge for punishment. But if he did not say this, Pilate would have to ask what else he had done that made him worthy to be handed over to a judge.

Hear, then, Jews and Gentiles. Hear, circumcision; hear, uncircumcision. Hear, all the kingdoms of the earth. I do not hinder your dominion in this world. “My kingdom is not of this world.” Do not fear that utterly vain fear which seized that Herod when Christ’s birth was announced and led him to kill so many infants in order to reach him, becoming more cruel through fear than through anger (Matt. II).

“My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world.” What more do you want? Come to the kingdom that is not of this world. Come by believing, and do not rage through fear.

The prophecy does indeed say of God the Father: “Yet I have been established as king by him upon his holy mountain, Zion” (Ps. II). But that Zion and that mountain are not of this world. For what is his kingdom except those who believe in him, concerning whom he says, “They are not of this world, just as I am not of the world,” although he wished them to be in the world? For this reason he said concerning them to the Father: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John XVII).

Therefore here too he does not say, “My kingdom is not in this world,” but, “It is not of this world.” And when he proves this by saying, “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews,” he does not say, “But now my kingdom is not here,” but, “It is not from here.”

His kingdom is here until the end of the age, having tares mixed within it until the harvest. For the harvest is the end of the age, when the reapers will come—that is, the angels—and gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin (Matt. XIII). This would certainly not happen if his kingdom were not here. Yet it is not from here, because it is a pilgrim in the world (II Cor. V). To his kingdom he says, “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John XV).

They were therefore of the world when they were not his kingdom, but belonged to the ruler of the world. Everything human is of the world: created, indeed, by the true God, but generated from Adam’s corrupted and condemned stock. But whatever from that stock has been reborn in Christ has become a kingdom no longer of the world. For thus God rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. I), concerning which he says, “My kingdom is not of this world,” or, “My kingdom is not from here.”

Pilate therefore said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king.” He did not fear to confess that he was a king. But the words “You say that I am a king” are so balanced that he neither denies that he is a king—for he is a king whose kingdom is not of this world—nor admits that he is such a king as would be thought to have a kingdom of this world.

That is the kind of king the one who had said, “So you are a king?” understood him to be. The answer given was, “You say that I am a king.” It is as though he had said, “You say this in a carnal way, as a carnal man.”

Then he adds: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.” The syllable of the pronoun in the expression “For this I was born” should be prolonged, as though he had said, “I was born for this matter”; but it should be shortened, as though he had said, “I was born for this purpose,” or “For this I was born,” just as he says, “For this I came into the world.” In the Greek Gospel there is no ambiguity in this expression. It is therefore clear that here he recalled his temporal birth, because he came into the world incarnate—not that birth without beginning by which he was God, through whom the Father created the world.

Thus he said that he was born for this, that is, for this purpose, and that he came into the world for this purpose, namely, by being born of a virgin, to bear witness to the truth. But because faith does not belong to everyone, he added: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” He hears with his inner faculties—that is, he obeys my voice—which would amount to saying, “He believes me.”

Since Christ therefore bears witness to the truth, he certainly bears witness to himself. For his voice is, “I am the Truth” (John XIV). And in another place he said, “I bear witness concerning myself” (John VIII).

When he says, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” he commends the grace by which he calls us according to his purpose. Concerning this purpose the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Rom. VIII). The purpose, namely, of the one who calls, not of those who are called. Elsewhere this is stated more clearly: “Share in the Gospel according to the power of God, who saves us and calls us with his own calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace” (II Tim. I).

For if we consider the nature in which we were created—since the Truth created everyone—who is not of the Truth? But not everyone has been given the ability to hear the Truth, that is, to obey the Truth and believe in the Truth, because this is granted by the Truth itself, with no preceding merits whatever, lest grace cease to be grace.

For if he had said, “Everyone who hears my voice is of the truth,” one might think that he is said to be of the truth because he obeys the truth. But he did not say this. He said, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Accordingly, he is not of the Truth because he hears its voice; rather, he hears because he is of the Truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed on him by the Truth.

And what else is this than believing in Christ through Christ’s gift?

Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” (He did not wait to hear the answer.) But when he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them, “I find no case against him. It is customary for me to release one man for you at Passover. Do you want me, then, to release the king of the Jews?” I believe that, when Pilate said, “What is truth?” the custom of the Jews immediately came to his mind—the custom by which one man was ordinarily released to them at Passover. For this reason he did not wait for Jesus to answer him, “What is truth?”, lest there be delay, since he had remembered the practice by which someone could be released to them at Passover—a release which it is clear he greatly desired. Yet he could not remove from his heart the thought that Jesus was the king of the Jews, as though Truth itself, about which he had asked what it was, had fixed this upon him in the title.

But when they heard this, they all cried out again, saying:

“Not this man, but Barabbas.” Now Barabbas was a robber.

We do not reproach you, O Jews, for releasing a guilty man at Passover, but for killing an innocent man. Yet unless this had happened, the true Passover would not have taken place. The Jews, though in error, were holding the shadow of the truth; and, by the wondrous ordering of divine wisdom, the truth signified by that same shadow was fulfilled through deceitful men, because, for the true Passover to take place, Christ was sacrificed like a sheep.

## CHAPTER XIX

When the Jews had cried out that they did not want Jesus released to them by Pilate at Passover, but rather Barabbas the robber—not the savior, but the killer; not the giver of life, but its taker—

Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him. We should believe that Pilate did this for no other reason than that, once the Jews had been satisfied by these outrages, they might think it enough for them and desist from raging against him to the point of death. This also explains why the same governor allowed his cohort to do what follows; or perhaps he even ordered it, although the evangelist has been silent about that. [Col. 0906A] For he says what the soldiers did next, but does not say that Pilate ordered it.

“And the soldiers,” he says, “plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, and clothed him in a purple garment. They came up to him and said, ‘Hail, king of the Jews!’ and struck him with blows.”

Thus were fulfilled the things Christ had foretold about himself. Thus the martyrs were instructed to endure everything their persecutors might wish to inflict. Thus, for a little while, his dreadful power was hidden. Thus the kingdom that was not of this world conquered the proud world, not by the violence of fighting, but by the humility of suffering. Thus the grain that was to be multiplied was sown amid horrible disgrace, so that it might spring forth in wondrous glory.

Pilate went out again and said to them, “Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no case against him.” Then Jesus came out, carrying the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he said to them, “Behold the man.”

It is clear from this that Pilate was not unaware of what the soldiers had done, whether he ordered it or permitted it—namely, for the reason we mentioned above: so that his enemies might drink in his mockery with complete satisfaction and no longer thirst for blood. Jesus comes out to them wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment—not glorious in authority, but full of disgrace—and he is presented to them: “Behold the man.” If you are jealous of a king, spare him now, because you see him cast down. He has been scourged, crowned with thorns, dressed in a mocking garment, insulted with the bitterest abuse, and struck with blows. Shame is burning; let jealousy grow cold. But it does not grow cold; rather, it burns more fiercely [Col. 0906C] and increases.

For when the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him.”

The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

Behold another and greater jealousy. The former had seemed small, as though it concerned an unlawful attempt to claim royal power; and yet Jesus falsely claimed neither title. Both are true: he is the only-begotten Son of God, and he is the king appointed by God over Zion, his holy mountain (Ps. II). He would now demonstrate both, except that the more powerful he was, the more he preferred to be patient.

[Col. 0906D] When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.

When the accounts of all the evangelists are compared, this silence of the Lord Jesus Christ is found to have occurred not only before the chief priests, but also before Herod, to whom Pilate had sent him, as Luke indicates, to be heard (Luke XXIII), and before Pilate himself. Thus the prophecy concerning him had not gone before in vain: “Like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII)—that is, whenever those questioning him received no answer.

Although he often answered certain questions, the likeness to a lamb was given because of those questions to which he did not wish to respond, so that in his silence he might be regarded not as guilty, but as innocent. [Col. 0907A] Whenever he was being judged, wherever he did not open his mouth, he did not open it just as a lamb does not: not like one conscious of evil, who was being convicted of his own sins, but like the gentle one who was being sacrificed for the sins of others.

Pilate therefore said to him, “Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?”

Jesus answered, “You would have no authority against me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

Behold, he answered; yet wherever he did not answer, he did not open his mouth like a guilty or deceitful man, but like a lamb—that is, like one simple and innocent. Therefore, where he did not answer, he was silent like a sheep; where he answered, he taught like a shepherd.

Let us learn, then, what he said, which he also taught through the Apostle: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII). And let us learn that the one who, out of jealousy, hands an innocent man over to a governing authority for execution sins more than the authority itself if that authority kills him through fear of another and greater authority.

For God had given Pilate an authority that was itself subject to Caesar’s authority. Therefore he says, “You would have no authority against me at all”—that is, whatever limited authority you possess—unless this very authority, whatever it is, had been given you from above. But because I know how great it is—for it is not so great that you are altogether free to use it—therefore “the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

He handed me over to your authority out of jealousy; you are about to exercise that same authority against me out of fear. Even when a man is afraid, he ought not to kill an innocent man, but doing so out of zeal or jealousy is a much greater evil than doing so out of fear. For this reason the truthful Teacher did not say, “The one who hands me over to you has sin,” as though the other had none; rather, he said, “He has the greater sin,” so that Pilate would understand that he too had sin. For the lesser sin does not thereby become no sin at all.

From that point Pilate sought to release him. What does the phrase “from that point” mean, as though he had not already been seeking to release him? Read what comes before, and you will find that he had long been seeking to release Jesus.

“From that point,” then, must be understood as meaning “because of this,” that is, “for this reason”: so that he would not incur the sin of killing an innocent man handed over to him, although he was less guilty than the Jews, who had handed him over to be killed. “From that point,” therefore—that is, for this reason, so that he might not commit this sin—he was seeking to release him not now for the first time, but from the beginning.

The Jews, however, cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

They thought that, by frightening Pilate with the name of Caesar, they had inflicted upon him a greater fear in order to make him kill Christ than earlier, when they had said, “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” Pilate had not feared their law enough to kill him; rather, he had feared the Son of God lest he kill him. Now, however, he could not disregard Caesar, the source of his authority, as he had disregarded the law of a foreign people.

The evangelist continues and says:

So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside [Col. 0908A] and sat down on the tribunal at the place called the Stone Pavement, but in Hebrew, Gabbatha. Now it was the Preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour.

The hour at which the Lord was crucified will be discussed, if the Lord wills, when we reach the very passage where his crucifixion is narrated, because a major dispute commonly arises over this question on account of the testimony of the other evangelist, who said, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark XV).

When Pilate had therefore sat down on the tribunal, he said to the Jews, “Behold your king.”

But they cried out, “Away with him, away with him; crucify him!”

Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?”

He is still attempting to overcome the terror they had inspired by invoking Caesar. He wants to break them through their disgrace, saying, “Shall I crucify your king?” He could not soften them by reminding them of Christ’s disgrace; instead, he is quickly overcome by fear.

For the chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”

Then he handed him over to them to be crucified.

It would have seemed most plainly that he was acting against Caesar if, when they professed to have no king but Caesar, he wished to impose another king upon them by releasing him unpunished—the very man they had handed over to him to be killed on account of these claims.

So he handed him over to them to be crucified. But had they wanted anything else earlier, when he said, “Take him yourselves and crucify him”? Or even before that: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law”?

Why, then, had they insisted so strongly, saying, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” and pressing in every way that he should be killed not by them but by the governor? Why had they refused to accept him for execution, if they now accepted him to be executed?

Or, if this is not the meaning, why is it said, “Then he handed him over to them to be crucified”? Is there a distinction? There certainly is. For it does not say, “Then he handed him over to them so that they might crucify him,” but “so that he might be crucified”—that is, so that he might be crucified by the judgment and authority of the governor.

The evangelist nevertheless says that he was handed over to them in order to show that they had been entangled in the crime from which they were trying to distance themselves. Pilate would not have done this unless he intended to fulfill what he saw them eagerly desiring.

What follows, then, is this:

They took Jesus and led him out.

This may refer to the soldiers, the governor’s attendants. For later it is stated more explicitly: “The soldiers, therefore, when they had crucified him.” Yet even if the evangelist attributes the whole action to the Jews, he does so deservedly. They themselves accepted what they had demanded most eagerly, and they themselves did whatever they had extorted others into doing.

While Pilate was judging and condemning him from the tribunal, they took our Lord Jesus Christ and led him out at about the sixth hour.

And carrying his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him.

What, then, does the evangelist Mark mean when he says, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark XV)? The Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, and at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers. We should understand that the fifth hour had already passed and that something of the sixth had begun when Pilate sat down on the tribunal—the time John called “about the sixth hour.” [Col. 0909A]

When he was led out to be fastened to the wood with two robbers, and the events narrated as taking place beside his cross were occurring, the full sixth hour was completed. From that hour until the ninth, while the sun was darkened, darkness came, as the testimony of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—confirms.

There is another solution to this question: perhaps the sixth hour here does not refer to the sixth hour of the day. John does not say, “It was about the sixth hour of the day,” but, “It was the Preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour.”

“Preparation” is the Latin meaning of the Greek word *parasceve* (παρασκευή). The Jews readily use this Greek word in such observances, even those who speak Latin more than Greek. Thus it means: “It was the preparation of Passover.”

But our Passover, as the Apostle says, is Christ, who was sacrificed (1 Cor. V). If we calculate the preparation for this Passover from the ninth hour of the night—for it was then, apparently, that the chief priests foretold the Lord’s sacrifice, saying, “He is deserving of death,” while he was still being heard in the high priest’s house—then it is appropriately understood that the preparation of the true Passover began at that point. The Jewish Passover was its shadow: the sacrifice of Christ, who had been foretold by the priests as destined to be sacrificed.

Accordingly, from that hour of the night, which is shown to have been the ninth, to the third hour of the day, when the evangelist Mark testifies that Christ was crucified, there are six hours: three of the night and three of the day.

Therefore, during this Preparation of Passover—that is, the preparation for Christ’s sacrifice, which had begun at the ninth hour of the night—it was about the sixth hour. In other words, the fifth hour had ended and the sixth had already begun when Pilate ascended the tribunal. [Col. 0909C]

For the preparation itself, which had begun at the ninth hour of the night, was still underway until the sacrifice of Christ, which was being prepared, took place. That sacrifice occurred, according to Mark, at the third hour—not the third hour of the preparation, but the third hour of the day. The same sixth hour, therefore, was the sixth hour not of the day but of the preparation, six hours being counted from the ninth hour of the night to the third hour of the day.

Let each person choose whichever of these two solutions to this difficult question he prefers. The better choice will be judged by the one who reads what has been most carefully argued concerning the agreement of the evangelists.

“They took Jesus and led him out; and carrying his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him.”

Jesus was going to the place where he was to be crucified, carrying his own cross. [Col. 0909D]

It was a great spectacle—but if impiety was watching, a great mockery; if piety, a great mystery. If impiety was watching, it was a great lesson in disgrace; if piety, a great monument of faith.

If impiety was watching, it laughed at the king carrying the wood of his punishment instead of the scepter of his kingdom. If piety was watching, it saw the king carrying the wood on which he was to be fastened—the wood that he would also fix upon the foreheads of kings. In that very thing he was to be despised by the eyes of the impious, in which the hearts of the saints were to glory.

For when Paul was about to say, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI), Christ, carrying that very cross on his shoulder, commended it to us. And he was carrying the lamp that was destined to burn and was not to be placed under a bushel, but on a lampstand.

Carrying his own cross, therefore, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him; and with him two others, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle.

These two were robbers, as we learn from the narratives of the other evangelists (Mark XV; Luke XXIII). Christ was crucified with them and placed between them, concerning whom the preceding prophecy had said: “And he was reckoned among the transgressors” (Isa. LIV).

Pilate also wrote a title and placed it above the cross. It was written: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.”

Many of the Jews read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “King of the Jews.”

These three languages stood out there above the others: Hebrew because of the Jews, who gloried in the law of God; [Col. 0910B] Greek because of the wise men among the nations; Latin because of the Romans, who at that time ruled many—indeed, almost all—nations.

The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but rather, ‘He said, I am the king of the Jews.’”

Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

O ineffable power of divine action, even in the hearts of those who are ignorant! Was not some hidden voice sounding inwardly in Pilate, in a certain—if one may say so—loud silence, what had been prophesied so long before in the words of the Psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title”? Behold, he does not corrupt the inscription of the title. What he has written, he has written.

But the chief priests, who wanted it corrupted, said: “Do not write ‘King of the Jews,’” they said, “but, ‘He said, I am the king of the Jews.’”

What are you saying, madmen? Why do you oppose something that you cannot alter by a single stroke? Will it not be true simply because Jesus said, “I am the king of the Jews”? If what Pilate wrote cannot be corrupted, can what Truth said be corrupted?

But is Christ the king of the Jews alone, or also of the nations? He is also king of the nations. For after the prophecy had said, “Yet I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the Lord’s command” (Ps. II), so that no one might say that he had been appointed king on account of Mount Zion only for the Jews, it immediately added: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (ibid.).

Accordingly, he himself, speaking through his own mouth to the Jews, says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

Why, then, do we want a great mystery to be understood in this title, in which was written “King of the Jews,” if Christ is king also of the nations? Because, of course, the wild olive has been made a sharer in the richness of the olive tree (Rom. XI). For the olive tree has not become a sharer in the bitterness of the wild olive.

In the one concerning whom the title “King of the Jews” has been truthfully written, who are to be understood as Jews except the seed of Abraham, the children of promise, who are also children of God? For not all who are children of the flesh are counted as seed, but the children of promise are counted as seed (Rom. IX). These also included the nations, to whom he said: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III).

Christ, therefore, is king of the Jews—but of Jews by the circumcision of the heart, in spirit and not in letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God; of those who belong to Jerusalem above, our free mother, eternal in the heavens, the spiritual Sarah who casts out the slave woman and her children from the house of freedom (Rom. II).

For this reason Pilate wrote what he wrote, because the Lord said what he said.

When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier, and also his tunic. The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout.

They said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be,” so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

What the Jews wanted happened. It was not they themselves, but the soldiers who obeyed Pilate, while he was the judge, who crucified Jesus. Yet if we consider their intentions, their plots, their actions, their handing him over, and finally their clamors by which they extorted the deed, then the Jews certainly crucified Jesus more truly.

But we must not pass over in silence the division and casting of lots for his garments. Although all four evangelists remember this event, the others speak more briefly than John. John, however, speaks with complete clarity and says into how many parts they divided his garments—namely, four—so that they might take one part each.

From this it appears that there were four soldiers who obeyed the governor in crucifying him. For he plainly says: “When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier, and also the tunic.”

The wording must be understood as follows: “They took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier. They also took the tunic.” Thus the meaning is that no lot was cast over the other garments, but over the tunic, which they took together with the others but did not divide in the same way.

Explaining this, he continues: “The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout.” And narrating why they cast lots for it, he says: “They said to one another, ‘Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be.’”

It is therefore clear that they had equal portions in the other garments, so that there was no need to cast lots. In the case of that one garment, however, they could not each have a portion unless it were torn, and then they would take its pieces uselessly. To avoid this, they preferred by lot that it should come to one of them.

The prophetic testimony also agrees with this account of the evangelist. John immediately adds: “So that the Scripture might be fulfilled,” saying, “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

For the Scripture does not say, “They cast lots,” but “They divided.” Nor does it say, “Casting lots, they divided the other garments”; without mentioning the lot at all, it later says, “And for my clothing they cast lots,” on account of that remaining tunic.

On this matter I will say what he himself has granted, after first refuting the accusation that might arise—as though the evangelists disagreed among themselves—and demonstrating that the words of none of the others contradict John’s account.

Matthew, by saying, “They divided his garments, casting lots” (Matt. XXVII), intended the entire division of the garments to include that tunic for which they cast lots. For, in dividing all the garments, among which the tunic was included, they certainly cast lots for that garment.

Luke likewise says, “Dividing his garments, they cast lots” (Luke XXIII). In dividing them, they came to the tunic for which the lot was cast, so that the entire division of his garments among them might be completed.

What difference is there between Luke’s “Dividing them, they cast lots” and Matthew’s “They divided them, casting lots”? None, except that Luke used the plural “lots” for the singular number. This kind of expression is not unusual in the Holy Scriptures, although some manuscripts are found to read “lot” rather than “lots.”

Mark alone therefore seems to introduce a difficulty. For by saying, “Casting lots over them, to determine what each should take” (Mark XV), he appears to speak as though the lot had been cast over all the garments, not over the tunic alone.

But here too brevity creates obscurity. “Casting lots over them” means as though one had said, “Casting lots while they were being divided.” And this is what happened. The division of all his garments would not have been complete unless the lot had determined who would also take the tunic, so that the contention among those dividing them might be ended—or, rather, might not arise at all.

What Mark says, “To determine what each should take,” since this is assigned to the lot, must not be referred to all the garments that were divided. The lot was cast to determine who would take the tunic, which he omitted to describe—what kind of tunic it was and how, after equal portions had been made, it alone remained and came to the lot so that it would not be torn.

In place of this, he says, “To determine what each should take,” that is, “Who would take it,” as though the whole sentence were: “They divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine who would take the tunic that had remained after equal portions had been made.”

Someone may perhaps ask what the division of the garments into so many parts and the casting of lots for that tunic signify.

The four-part garment of our Lord Jesus Christ represented his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world—which consists, of course, of four regions—and distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, among all those regions.

For this reason he says elsewhere that he will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds (Mark XIII). What does this mean except from the four parts of the world: east, west, north, and south?

That tunic, for which the lot was cast, signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity.

Speaking of charity, the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (Eph. IV). Elsewhere he says: “To know also the charity of Christ, which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. III). And again elsewhere: “Above all these things, charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. III).

If charity has a more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments, then the garment it signifies is rightly said to have been woven from above. It is seamless so that it may never be torn apart, and it comes to one person because it gathers all into one.

The same thing is seen among the apostles. Although their number was twelve—that is, fourfold in its distribution among them—and although all were questioned, Peter alone answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. VI). And to him it is said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.), as though he alone had received the power of binding and loosing, even though he spoke the former on behalf of all and received the latter together with all, representing the unity itself.

He spoke on behalf of all because unity exists in all.

Thus, when John had said, “Woven from above,” he added, “throughout.” What if we refer this to what it signifies? No one is excluded from the whole, whoever is found to belong to that whole from which, as the Greek language indicates, the Catholic Church receives its name.

And what is commended by the lot except the grace of God? Thus, through one person, it reaches all, when the lot pleases everyone, because the grace of God also reaches all in unity. When the lot is cast, the decision is made not according to anyone’s person or merits, but according to the hidden judgment of God.

Nor should anyone say that this signified nothing good because it was done by evil men—not by those who followed Christ, but by those who persecuted him.

What, then, shall we say about the cross itself, which was likewise made and imposed upon Christ by enemies and impious men? Yet it is rightly understood to signify what the Apostle says: “What is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. III).

Finally, what do all people recognize as the sign of Christ except the cross of Christ? If this sign is not applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water in which they are reborn, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is properly accomplished.

How, then, can nothing good be signified through what evil men do, when through the cross of Christ, which evil men made, every good thing is signified to us in the celebration of his sacraments?

“And the soldiers,” he says, “did these things.”

Now there stood beside the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son.” Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own household.

This is surely the hour of which Jesus had said to his mother, when he was about to turn water into wine, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John II).

He had foretold this hour, which had not yet come then: the hour in which, as he was dying, he would acknowledge her from whom he had been born as a mortal. At that time, when he was about to perform divine works, he rejected his mother as though unknown—not in respect of his divinity, but of his human weakness. Now, however, while suffering human things, he commended her with human affection, since from her he had become human.

Then the one who had created Mary was making himself known through power; now what Mary had borne was hanging upon the cross.

A moral lesson is therefore being conveyed here. He does what he urges others to do. By his own example the good Teacher instructs children to provide care for their parents, as though the wood on which the limbs of the dying man were fixed had also become the teacher’s chair.

From this teaching the Apostle Paul had learned what he taught when he said: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for the members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. V).

What is as much a part of one’s household as parents are to children, or children to parents?

The Teacher of the saints himself therefore established an example of this most salutary commandment. He did so not as God providing for the servant whom he had created and governed, but as a human being providing another son, in a certain sense, for the mother from whom he had been created as a human being and whom he was leaving.

The reason why he did this is indicated by what follows. The evangelist says: “From that hour the disciple took her into his own household,” speaking of himself.
