He customarily referred to himself in this way as the disciple whom Jesus loved. Jesus certainly loved them all, but he loved this one above the others and with greater familiarity, so that he made him recline upon his breast at the meal.

I believe that, through this, he intended to commend more profoundly the divine excellence of the Gospel that he was to preach through him.

But what possessions did John receive the Lord’s mother into? Surely he was one of those who had said to him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you”; but he had also heard there: “Whoever has left these things for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age” (Matt. XIX).

That disciple therefore possessed a hundred times more than he had left—possessions into which he could receive the mother of the one who had given him those possessions.

But blessed John had received the hundredfold in that society where no one called anything his own, but everything was held in common, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II). Thus the apostles were “as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. VI), and distribution was made to each according to each person’s need (Acts II).

From this it must be understood that what was necessary was distributed to this disciple in such a way that a portion was also assigned there to blessed Mary as his mother.

Rather, we should understand the statement “From that hour the disciple took her into his own household” to mean that whatever was necessary for her care came under his responsibility.

He took her into his household—not into estates, which he did not personally possess, but into duties, which he undertook to administer in his own charge.

Then he continues:

After this, Jesus, knowing that everything had been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I thirst.”

A vessel full of vinegar had been placed there. They put a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and offered it to his mouth.

When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is accomplished.” And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

Who can arrange events as this man arranged them—this man who suffered? Yet he was the Mediator between God and human beings, the man of whom it was foretold: “He is also a man, and who recognizes him?” For all through whom these things were being done did not recognize the man who was God.

He appeared as a man, while God was hidden within him. The one who appeared was suffering all these things, and the very one who was hidden was arranging them all.

He therefore saw that everything that had to happen before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit had been accomplished. And, so that this too might be accomplished, which Scripture had foretold—“In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXIII)—he said, “I thirst,” as though he were saying: “You have left this undone; give me what you are.”

The Jews themselves were degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. They were like a vessel full of the iniquity of this world, and their hearts were like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and tortuous hiding places.

They placed the sponge full of vinegar around hyssop. Since hyssop is a lowly herb and cleanses the breast, we appropriately understand it as signifying the humility of Christ, which they surrounded and which they thought they had circumvented.

Hence the words in the fiftieth Psalm: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, Lord, and I shall be clean.”

We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II), his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

Nor should we be troubled about how they could bring the sponge to his mouth when he had been lifted above the ground on the cross. As we read in the other evangelists—something John omitted—it was done on a reed (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV), so that the drink in the sponge might be raised to the heights of the cross.

The reed signified Scripture, which was being fulfilled by this deed. Just as one speaks of a tongue—Greek, Latin, or any other—as the meaningful sound produced by that tongue, so one may call the written letter a reed because it is written with a reed.

We customarily call the meaningful sounds of human speech “tongues.” To call Scripture a “reed” is less customary, and therefore it is all the more mystically signified.

The impious people were doing these things; merciful Christ was suffering them. The one who was doing them did not know what he was doing. But the one who was suffering not only knew what was happening and why it was happening; he was also himself doing good through those who were doing evil.

When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is accomplished” (John X). What else could this mean except what prophecy had foretold so long before?

Then, because nothing remained that still had to be done before he died, like one who had authority to lay down his life and take it up again, after completing everything for which he had been waiting to be accomplished, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

Who sleeps in this way, when he wishes, as Christ died when he wished? Who departs in this way, whenever he wishes, as he departed when he wished?

How great a power must be hoped for or feared in the one who will judge, if such power appeared in the one who was dying!

John is silent about the words he spoke when he gave up his spirit: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” He says “spirit” because spirit is the name of something so incorporeal that it is also independent of the body, in accordance with what was said above: “God is spirit.”

The Jews, therefore, because it was the Preparation, asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away, so that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day.

It was not the legs that were to be taken away, but those whose legs were broken so that they might die and be removed from the wood, lest, while hanging on the crosses, they defile the great festival with the horror of their prolonged suffering.

The soldiers therefore came and broke the legs of the first man, and then of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.

The evangelist used a watchful expression: he did not say, “He struck his side,” or “wounded it,” or anything similar, but “opened it,” so that there might somehow be opened there the door of life, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed, without which one does not enter into the life that is true life. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins. That water tempers the saving cup. It provides both a bath and a drink. This was prefigured by what [Col. 0916B] Noah was commanded to make a door in the side of the ark, so that the animals that were not destined to perish in the Flood might enter—animals by which the Church was prefigured. For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man, and she was called “Life,” and “mother of the living.” For she signified a great good before the great evil of transgression. Here too the second Adam, with his head bowed, slept on the cross, so that from his side there might be formed his bride, who flowed forth from the side of the sleeping one. O death, from which the dead are brought back to life! What is purer than this blood? What is more healing than this wound?

“And he who saw it,” he says, “has borne witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that [Col. 0916C] you also may believe.” He did not say, “So that you also may know,” but “so that you may believe.” For the one who saw knows, and the one who did not see believes his testimony. Believing pertains more to faith than seeing does. For what else is believing than to entrust oneself to faith?

“For these things happened,” he says, “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: You shall not break a bone of him.” And again another Scripture says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” He supplied two testimonies from Scripture, one for each of the events he narrated as having taken place. Since he had said, “But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs,” the testimony “You shall not break a bone of him” (Exod. XII) pertains to this. This was commanded to those who were ordered to celebrate the Passover by sacrificing a sheep under the old law, which had gone before as a shadow of the Lord’s Passion; hence, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). Concerning him the prophet Isaiah had also [Col. 0916D] foretold: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII). Likewise, because he had added, “One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance,” the other testimony pertains to this: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. XII), where Christ was promised as one who would come in the flesh in which he was crucified.

After these things Joseph of Arimathea, because he was a disciple of Jesus, asked Pilate to remove the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came—the man who had first come to Jesus by night—bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds’ weight. The sentence should not be punctuated as though we were to say, “First bringing a mixture of myrrh,” or as though the word “first” belonged to what follows. Rather, Nicodemus had come to Jesus “first by night,” [Col. 0917A] as John himself related earlier in his Gospel (John III). Thus Nicodemus should be understood to have come to Jesus not only at that time, but at that time for the first time; afterward he kept coming, so that by listening he might become a disciple. This is certainly made known to nearly all peoples now in the revelation of the body of the blessed Stephen.

They therefore took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the custom of the Jews in burying. It does not seem to me that the evangelist wished to say without reason, “as is the custom of the Jews in burying.” In this way, unless I am mistaken, he admonished us that in such services as are performed for the dead, the custom of each people should be observed.

Now there was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet [Col. 0917B] been placed. Just as no one before him and no one after him was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary, so no one before him and no one after him was buried in this tomb.

Because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there on account of the Jews’ Parasceve. He wishes it to be understood that the burial was hastened, lest it grow dark, when, because of the Parasceve—which the Jews more commonly call among us in Latin a “pure meal”—no one was permitted to do such a thing.

## CHAPTER XX

Now on the first day of the week, which Christian custom already calls the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0917C], Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. Of the evangelists, Matthew alone called this day “the first of the Sabbath.”

She therefore ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have placed him.” Some Greek manuscripts also have: “They have taken my Lord,” which may be understood as spoken with a more fervent affection of love or service. But we did not find this reading in the greater number of the manuscripts available to us.

Peter therefore went out, together with that other disciple, and they came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and that other disciple outran Peter and came first to the tomb. Here one should notice and commend [Col. 0917D] the recapitulation: how the narrative returns to what had been passed over, and yet adds it as though it followed directly. For after he had already said, “They came to the tomb,” he went back in order to tell how they had come, and said: “Now the two were running together,” and so forth. Here he shows that the other disciple, who represents himself but narrates everything as though about someone else, outran Peter and arrived at the tomb first.

“And when he had bent down,” he says, “he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.” Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but wrapped separately in one place. Do we suppose that these details signify nothing? I would by no means think so. But we are hastening to other matters in which [Col. 0918A] we are compelled by some necessity of inquiry or obscurity to linger. To seek what each of these things may signify in themselves, though they are manifest in themselves, is indeed a holy delight, but it belongs to those who have leisure, which we do not have.

Then that other disciple, who had come first to the tomb, entered as well. He came first; he entered later. This too is certainly not without significance, but I have no leisure for it here.

“And he saw,” he says, “and believed.” Some, paying insufficient attention, think that John believed that Jesus had risen. But what follows does not indicate this. What, then, does the statement immediately added mean?

“For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.” He therefore did not believe that he had risen who did not know that he had to rise. What, then, did he see? What did he believe? [Col. 0918B] Clearly, he saw that the tomb was empty, and believed what the woman had said: that he had been taken away from the tomb. For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead. And therefore, when they heard this from the Lord himself, although it was stated most plainly, because they were accustomed to hearing him speak in parables, they did not understand and believed that he was signifying something else. Mary Magdalene had announced to Peter and John, the Lord’s disciples, that the Lord had been taken away from the tomb. When they came, they found only the linen cloths in which the body had been wrapped. What else could they believe except what she had said—and what she herself had believed?

Then the disciples went away again to their own place—that is, where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb) [Col. 0918C]. But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping. When the men had returned, the stronger affection held the weaker sex fixed in the same place; and the eyes that had sought the Lord and had not found him now gave themselves over to tears, grieving more that he had been taken away from the tomb than that he had been killed on the wood, since not even the memory remained of so great a teacher, whose life had been taken from them. Thus this grief held the woman at the tomb.

While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb. Why she did this, I do not know. For she did not fail to know that the one she was seeking was no longer there, since she herself had announced to the disciples that he had been taken away; they had come to the tomb and had sought the Lord’s body not only by looking but also by entering, and had not found it. [Col. 0918D] What, then, does it mean that, while she was weeping, she again bent down and looked into the tomb? Was it because she was grieving so intensely that she could hardly believe what her own eyes and theirs had seen? Or rather, was it brought about in her mind by divine inspiration that she should look? For she looked:

“And she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.” Why was one sitting at the head and the other at the feet? Could it be because those who are called *angeli* in Greek are called *nuntii*, “messengers,” in Latin, and in this way they signified that Christ’s Gospel was to be proclaimed from head to foot, from beginning to end?

They said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them: “Because [Col. 0919A] they have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.” The angels were restraining her tears; what else were they announcing, in a certain way, than future joy? For they said, “Why are you weeping?” as though they were saying, “Do not weep.” But she, thinking that they had asked because they did not know, disclosed the reason for her tears: “Because they have taken away,” she said, “my Lord.” Calling him her Lord, she signified the lifeless body of her Lord by the whole for the part, just as all confess Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our one Lord. He is at once Word, soul, and flesh; yet it was only his flesh that was crucified and buried. “And I do not know,” she said, “where they have placed him.” This was the chief cause of her grief, because she did not know where to go to find consolation for her sorrow. But the hour had now come when the joy that had somehow been announced by the angels who forbade her to weep [Col. 0919B] would succeed her tears.

Finally, when she had said these things, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away.” Jesus said to her: “Mary.” She turned and said to him: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”

Let no one accuse the woman because she called the Lord a gardener and Jesus a teacher. In the first case she was asking; in the second she was recognizing. There she honored the man from whom she was requesting a favor: she called him “lord,” although she was not his servant, so that through him she might reach the Lord whose servant she was. Thus [Col. 0919C] she used “Lord” in one sense when she said, “They have taken my Lord,” and in another when she said, “Lord, if you have taken him away.” The prophets too called men who were human beings “lords,” but in a different sense from the one of whom it is written: “The Lord is his name” (Amos IX).

But this woman, who had already turned back in order to see Jesus when she thought he was the gardener—and was certainly speaking with him—how is she said to have turned again when she said to him, “Rabboni,” unless it is because she had then turned physically, although she thought that he was not what he was, and now had turned in her heart and recognized what he was?

Jesus said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.”

There is [Col. 0919D] something in these words that we must examine briefly, but with careful attention. When the woman recognized and called him “Teacher,” Jesus was teaching her faith as she responded to him; and that gardener was sowing in her heart, as in his own garden, the mustard seed. What, then, does “Do not touch me” mean? As though the reason for this prohibition were being sought, he added: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.” What does this mean? If he cannot be touched while standing on earth, how could he be touched by a human being while seated in heaven? Yet before he ascended, he offered himself to the disciples to be touched, saying—as the evangelist Luke testifies: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see me having” (Luke XXIV). Or when he said to the disciple Thomas: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; [Col. 0920A] and bring your hand and put it into my side.”

Who could be so absurd as to say that he wished to be touched by the disciples before he ascended to the Father, but did not wish to be touched by women until after he had ascended to the Father? But lest anyone be permitted to be foolish in this way, women too are read to have touched Christ after the resurrection and before he ascended to the Father. Mary Magdalene herself was among them, since Matthew relates that Jesus met them and said: “Hail.” “They came up,” he says, “and held his feet, and worshiped him” (Matt. XXVIII). John omitted this, but Matthew truly reported it.

It remains, therefore, that some sacramental meaning is concealed in these words. Whether we find it or are wholly unable to find it, we must nevertheless have no [Col. 0920B] doubt that some meaning is present. Either, then, he said, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” so that in that woman the Church from the Gentiles might be represented, which did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father; or Jesus wished to be believed in this way, namely, to be touched spiritually in such a way that he and the Father are one. For he somehow ascends to the Father in the innermost understanding of the person who makes such progress in him that he recognizes him as equal to the Father. Otherwise he is not rightly touched—that is, otherwise one does not rightly believe in him.

Mary could, however, believe in such a way as to think him inferior to the Father. This is forbidden when he says to her: “Do not touch me”—that is, “Do not believe in me in the way you still understand me. [Col. 0920C] Do not extend your thought only as far as what I became for you, without passing on to that through which you were made.” For how could she not yet believe in him in a merely carnal way, when she wept for him as for a human being? “For I have not yet ascended,” he says, “to my Father. There you will touch me, when you believe that, as God, I am not inferior to the Father.”

“But go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father.” He did not say, “Our Father.” Therefore, he is my Father in one way and your Father in another: my Father by nature, your Father by grace. “And my God and your God.” Here too he did not say, “Our God.” Therefore, he is my God in one way and your God in another: my God, under whom I am also human; your God, among whom I am also mediator.

Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her.

When it was evening [Col. 0920D] on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Nails had pierced his hands, and a lance had opened his side. To heal the hearts of those who doubted, the traces of his wounds were preserved. But the mass of his body, in which divinity was present, was not hindered by closed doors. For he was able to enter without their being opened, just as at his birth virginity remained inviolate.

The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Then he said to them again: “Peace be with you.” The repetition is a confirmation. For he himself promised through the Prophet “peace upon peace.”

“As the Father sent me,” he said, “I also send you.” We know the Son as equal to the Father, but here we recognize the words of the Mediator [Col. 0921A]. He shows himself to be the intermediary when he says: “He sent me, and I send you.”

When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” By breathing on them he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but also his own.

“Whose sins you forgive,” he said, “are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained.” The love of the Church, which is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, forgives the sins of those who share in it. But it retains the sins of those who do not share in it. Therefore, after saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added the teaching concerning the remission of sins.

But Thomas, one of the Twelve, who is called Didymus [Col. 0921B], was not with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, although the doors were closed, and stood in the midst and said: “Peace be with you.” Then he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side,” and so forth. He saw and touched the human being, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched. But through what he saw and touched, he now believed without hesitation in what he did not see or touch. Jesus said to him:

“Because you have seen me, you have believed.” He did not say, “Because you have touched me,” [Col. 0921C] but “Because you have seen me,” since sight is, in a certain sense, a general term for perception. For the other four senses too are sometimes named in this way, as when we say: “Hear and see how well it sounds”; “Smell and see how fragrant it is”; “Taste and see how good it is”; “Touch and see how warm it is.” In every case “see” is used, although sight in the strict sense is understood to belong to the eyes.

Hence the Lord himself also says here: “Put your finger here and see my hands.” What else does he say than “Touch and see”? Yet the disciple did not have eyes in his finger. Therefore, whether by looking or even by touching: “Because you have seen me,” he says, “you have believed.” It could, however, be said that the disciple did not dare to touch him when he offered himself to be touched. For it is not written: “And Thomas touched.” Whether, therefore, he saw and believed merely by looking, or also by touching, what follows more fully proclaims and commends the faith of the Gentiles.

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” He used verbs in the past tense [Col. 0921D], as though the one who knew in his predestination what was future already regarded it as accomplished.

Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.

This chapter indicates the end of this book. But afterward it narrates how the Lord manifested himself at the Sea of Tiberias and commended, through the catching of fish, the sacramental meaning of the Church [Col. 0922A] as it will be at the final resurrection of the dead. I therefore think that this serves to commend that matter: the chapter has been inserted as though it were the end of the book, while also functioning as a kind of prologue to the narrative that follows and somehow giving it a more prominent place.

## The Apostles’ Fishing

## CHAPTER XXI

It is customary to ask about this fishing of the disciples whether Peter and the sons of Zebedee returned to what they had been before they were called by the Lord. For they were fishermen when he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. XIV). At that time they followed him so that, having left everything, they might cling to his teaching [Col. 0922B]. They did so to such an extent that when that rich man went away sadly—the man to whom he had said, “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX)—Peter said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (ibid.).

What, then, does it mean that now, as though they had abandoned their apostleship, they become what they had been and take up again what they had left, as though they had forgotten what they had heard: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX)?

If they had done this after Jesus’ death, before he rose from the dead—which indeed they could not have done, since the day on which he was crucified held them all intent until his burial, which took place before evening; the following day was the Sabbath, when, as they observed their ancestral custom, they were certainly permitted to work; but on the third day the Lord rose [Col. 0922C] and restored them to the hope that they had already begun to lose concerning him—we would nevertheless think that they had done it because of the despair that had occupied their hearts.

But now, after he had been returned to them alive from the tomb; after the evident reality of his restored flesh had been offered to their eyes and hands, not only to be seen but also to be touched and handled; after they had examined the places of his wounds, even up to the confession of the apostle Thomas, who had declared that he would not believe otherwise; after they had received the Holy Spirit through his breathing; after hearing from his mouth the words: “As the Father sent me, I also send you: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained”—they suddenly [Col. 0922D] become, as they had been, not fishers of men but fishers of fish.

To those whom this troubles, then, we must respond that they were not forbidden, while preserving the integrity of their apostleship, to seek their necessary livelihood through their trade, a lawful and permitted one, if at some time they had no other means of living. Unless perhaps someone will dare to think or say that the apostle Paul did not belong to the perfection of those who, having left everything, followed Christ, because, in order not to burden anyone to whom he preached the Gospel, he supported himself by the work of his own hands (II Thess. II).

In this respect what he says was fulfilled even more fully: “I labored more than all of them” (I Cor. XV); and he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.). This too should be attributed to the grace of God: that in both mind and body he was able [Col. 0923A] to labor so much more than all of them that he neither ceased preaching the Gospel nor, like them, supported this life from the Gospel, even though he was sowing the name of Christ much more widely and fruitfully among so many peoples among whom the name of Christ had not been proclaimed by the prophets.

Here he showed that the apostles were not placed under an obligation to live from the Gospel—that is, to receive their livelihood from it—but were given the authority to do so. The same Apostle recalls this authority when he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If others share in your authority, should not we do so even more?” But, he says, “we have not used this authority” (I Cor. IX).

And a little later: “Those who serve at the altar,” he says, “share in the altar. So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. [Col. 0923B] But I have used none of these things” (ibid.).

It is therefore sufficiently clear that it was not commanded to the apostles, but placed within their authority, that they should live from nowhere else except the Gospel, and that from those to whom they sowed spiritual things by preaching the Gospel they should reap material things—that is, receive support for this bodily life and, like soldiers of Christ, accept the pay owed to them, as from the provinces belonging to Christ.

Hence that same outstanding soldier had said a little earlier concerning this matter: “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense?” (I Cor. IX). Yet he himself did this because he labored more than all of them.

If, therefore, the blessed Paul chose not to use with the other preachers of the Gospel the authority that he certainly possessed together with them, but served as a soldier at his own expense, so that his teaching would not offend peoples wholly alien to the name of Christ [Col. 0923C] as though it were being sold; and if, having been brought up otherwise, he learned a trade he had not known, so that, while the teacher supported himself by his own hands, no hearer would be burdened—how much more could the blessed Peter, who had already been a fisherman, practice what he knew if at that particular time he had found no other means of living?

Someone may reply: “Why did he not find another means, since the Lord had promised, saying: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’?” (Matt. VI).

Indeed, even in this way the Lord fulfilled what he promised. For who else supplied the fish to be caught? We must believe that he brought them to them for no other reason than that, by the want which compelled them to go fishing, he intended to display a miracle that had been arranged in advance, so that he might both feed the preachers of his Gospel and enhance the Gospel itself through the great sacramental meaning [Col. 0923D] represented by the number of the fish.

Simon Peter therefore says, “I am going fishing.” Those who were with him say to him, “We are coming with you.” And they went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing, up to the point where, although there were so many, the net was not torn.

This is a great mystery in the great Gospel of John, and, so that it might be commended all the more forcefully, it was written in the final place. The fact, then, that seven disciples were present at this fishing—Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the two sons of Zebedee, and two others whose names are not given—by that number seven signifies the course of time. For all time revolves through seven days.

To this belongs the fact that, when morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore, because the shore is also the end of the sea, and therefore signifies the end of the age. The same end of the age is also shown by the fact that Peter drew the net onto the land, that is, onto the shore. The Lord himself disclosed this when elsewhere he gave a parable about a net cast into the sea, saying that they draw it to the shore. Explaining what the shore was, he said: “So it will be at the consummation of the age” (Matt. XIII). But that is a parable in words, not an event actually performed.

By an event actually performed, as in this passage, the Lord signified how things will be at the end of the age; by the other fishing he signified what the Church is like now. The fact that he performed the former at the beginning of his preaching, but this one after his resurrection, shows that the former catch of fish signifies the good and the wicked whom the Church now contains, while this one signifies only the good whom it will possess eternally, when the resurrection of the dead has been completed at the end of this age.

Finally, in that episode the Lord did not stand on the shore as he did here when he ordered the fish to be caught. Rather, he got into one boat, which belonged to Simon, and asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting in it, he taught the crowds. When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch” (Luke V). There too the fish that were caught were in the boats, not, as here, drawn onto the land.

By these signs, and by whatever other signs may be found, the Church in this age is represented there, but here at the end of the age. Therefore that event took place before, and this one after the Lord’s resurrection, because there Christ signified us as called, while here he signified us as resurrected.

There the nets are not cast to the right, lest they signify only the good; nor to the left, lest they signify only the wicked, but indiscriminately: “Let down your nets,” he says, “for a catch,” so that we may understand the good and the wicked mixed together. Here, however, he says: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat,” signifying that those who were standing on the right were only the good.

There the net was torn, to signify schisms. Here, however, since at that time there were no schisms in that supreme peace of the saints, it was appropriate for the Evangelist to say: “Although there were so many”—that is, so large a number—“the net was not torn,” as though he were looking back to the place where it had been torn and, by comparison with that evil, commending this good.

There such a great multitude of fish was caught that the two boats were filled and began to sink—that is, they were pressed down toward submersion. They did not actually sink, but they were nevertheless endangered. From what else do such things arise in the Church, which we lament, unless it is because such a great multitude cannot be resisted, entering almost to submerge discipline with its ways wholly alien to the path of the saints? [Col. 0924D]

Here, however, they cast the net on the right side, and now they were unable to draw it in because of the multitude of fish. What does “they were now unable to draw it in” mean except that those who belong to the resurrection of life—that is, to the right—and who die within the nets of the Christian name will not appear until the shore, that is, the end of the age, when they have risen?

Therefore they were unable to draw the nets in such a way as to pour the fish they had caught into the boat, as happened with those among whom the net was torn and the boats were pressed down. The Church has these “right-hand” ones after the end of this life, lying hidden in the sleep of peace as though in the deep, [Col. 0925A] until the net reaches the shore—the net that was being drawn as though for about two hundred cubits.

I think that the two boats there, because of circumcision and uncircumcision, were represented here by the two hundred cubits, on account of the elect of both kinds, of circumcision and of uncircumcision—as one hundred and one hundred—because in the sum represented by one hundred the number has passed to the right.

Finally, in that fishing the number is not stated, as though what had been foretold through the Prophet were being fulfilled there: “I have proclaimed and spoken; they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). Here, however, there are none beyond the number, but the number is definite: one hundred fifty-three. Its meaning must be explained, with the Lord’s help.

If we establish a number that signifies the Law, what will it be except ten? For it is most certain to us that the Decalogue of the Law—that is, those well-known ten commandments—was first written by the finger of God on two stone tablets (Exod. XXXI). But when the Law is not assisted by grace, it makes transgressors, and exists only in the letter. For this reason the Apostle says most emphatically: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (I Cor. III).

Let the Spirit, then, be added to the letter, lest the letter kill because the Spirit does not give it life; but let us carry out the commandments of the Law not by our own strength, but by the grace of the Savior. When grace is added to the Law—that is, when the Spirit is added to the letter—the number seven is, in a certain sense, added to the number ten.

The testimony of the sacred writings shows that the Holy Spirit is signified by this number, namely, seven. For holiness, or sanctification, properly pertains to the Holy Spirit. Thus, although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, since “God is spirit” (John IV), and although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, the Spirit is nevertheless called “the Holy Spirit” by the proper name of both.

Where, then, did sanctification first sound forth in the Law except on the seventh day? God did not sanctify the first day, on which he made the light; nor the second, on which he made the firmament; nor the third, on which he separated the sea from the land, and the land produced grass and trees; nor the fourth, on which the stars were created; nor the fifth, on which he made the animals that live in the waters and fly in the air; nor the sixth, on which he made the living creature of the earth and humanity itself. Rather, he sanctified the seventh day, on which he rested from his works (Gen. II). [Col. 0925D]

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit is fittingly signified by the number seven. The Prophet Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. XI), and then, commending him through a sevenfold work or gift, he says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (ibid.).

What of the Apocalypse? Are not seven spirits of God spoken of there (Apoc. I), although there is one and the same Spirit, distributing his own gifts to each as he wills (I Cor. XII)? But the sevenfold operation of the one Spirit was named in this way by the same Spirit who was present with the writer, so that seven spirits would be spoken of.

When, therefore, the Holy Spirit is added to the ten of the Law through the number seven, the result is seventeen. This number, when all the numbers from one up to itself are counted and added together, reaches one hundred fifty-three.

For if you add two to one, the result is three; if you add three and four to these, the total is ten. Then, if you add all the succeeding numbers up to seventeen, the total reaches the number mentioned above. That is, if to the ten which you had reached by counting from one through four you add five, the result is fifteen; if to this you add six, the result is twenty-one; if to this you add seven, the result is twenty-eight; if to this you add eight, nine, and ten, the result is fifty-five; if to this you add eleven, twelve, and thirteen, the result is ninety-one; if to this you add fourteen, fifteen, and sixteen, the result is one hundred thirty-six; and to this number add the one that remains, the number under discussion, namely seventeen, and that number of fish is completed. [Col. 0926B]

Thus not merely one hundred fifty-three saints are signified as destined to rise to eternal life, but also the fact that this number contains three times the number fifty, with three added in addition, on account of the mystery of the Trinity.

The number fifty is completed by multiplying seven by seven and adding one. For seven times seven is forty-nine. One is added, so that it may signify that there is one who is demonstrated through the seven because of the sevenfold operation.

We know also that the Holy Spirit was sent on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s ascension; the disciples had been commanded to await this promise (Acts I, II; Luke XXIV).

It is therefore not without reason that these fish are said to be so many and so great—that is, one hundred fifty-three and large. For it is written: “They drew the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three.”

When the Lord had said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V)—since he was certainly going to give the Spirit through whom the Law could be fulfilled—he added, as though he were going to add seven to ten, after only a few intervening words: “Therefore whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

This person, then, may belong to the number of the large fish. But that least one who loosens by his deeds what he teaches in words can exist in the sort of Church signified by that first catch of fish, which contains good and wicked people, because it too is called the kingdom of heaven. For this reason he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. XIII), where he wishes the good and the wicked to be understood as well, those whom he says will be separated on the shore, or at the end of the age.

Finally, to show that these least ones are reprobate—those who teach good things in speech but undo them by living wickedly, and who will not be least in eternal life but will not be there at all—after saying, “He shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V), he immediately added: “But I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

It follows, therefore, that the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven as it is now, namely the Church, will not enter the kingdom of heaven as the Church will then be. By teaching what he loosens, he will not belong to the company of those who do what they teach. And for this reason he will not be among the number of the large fish, because “whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Since this person will be great here, that least one will not be there.

Indeed, the great will be so great there that the one who is least there will be greater than the one than whom no one is greater here. Yet those who are great here—that is, those who, in this kingdom of heaven where the net gathers good and wicked people, do the good things they teach—will themselves be greater in that eternal kingdom of heaven. These are signified by the fish belonging to the right and to the resurrection of life.

This number may also suggest the holiness of the Church, which was brought about through our Lord Jesus Christ. Since creation is constituted by the number seven—when the threefold number is assigned to the soul and the fourfold number to the body—the assumption of humanity itself is signified. Let three be multiplied by seven, because the Father sent the Son, and the Father is in the Son, and the Son was born of a virgin through the gift of the Holy Spirit. These are the three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The human being himself was assumed sevenfold through the temporal dispensation, so that he might become eternal.

The total is therefore twenty-one, or three times seven. This assumption of humanity was effective for the liberation of the Church, of which he is the head. The Church itself, on account of soul and body, is also found in this same number seven.

Let twenty-one likewise be multiplied by seven, on account of those who are liberated through the man who is the Lord, and the result is one hundred forty-seven. To this is added the number six, a sign of perfection, because it is constituted by its own parts that measure it, so that nothing less and nothing more is found. For one, which you have, measures it six times; two, which it has three times; and three, which it has twice. Taken together, one, two, and three make six.

Perhaps this also relates to the mystery that God completed all his works on the sixth day (Gen. II). When six, therefore, which is a sign of perfection, is added to one hundred forty-seven, the result is one hundred fifty-three. This is the number of fish found after, at the Lord’s command, the nets were cast on the right side, where sinners belonging to the left are not found.

After the Lord had spent forty days with his disciples following his resurrection—thereby commending to them what had been accomplished temporally for our sake—he ascended into heaven. After another forty days he sent the Holy Spirit, by whom those who had believed in visible and temporal things might be spiritually perfected for the apprehension of invisible things. He indicated this same perfection, which is conferred through the Holy Spirit, by the ten days after which he sent the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0927D]

Therefore, since the perfection that comes through the Holy Spirit, while we still walk in the flesh, even though we do not live according to the flesh, is joined to the temporal dispensation, the number fifty rightly seems to belong to the Church—but to the Church already purified and perfected, which embraces by charity the faith of the temporal dispensation and the hope of the future eternity; that is, it joins, as it were, the number forty to the number ten.

This Church, to which the number fifty belongs, reaches the number one hundred fifty and three because it is chosen from three kinds of people: Jews, Gentiles, and carnal Christians—or because it is imbued with the sacrament of the Trinity. For fifty multiplied by three is one hundred fifty. When the three themselves are added, because what is washed in the bath of regeneration in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit ought to be distinguished and eminent, the result is one hundred fifty-three.

This is the number of fish found because the nets were cast on the right side. Therefore it contains large fish—that is, perfect people suited to the kingdom of heaven—where, once the dispensation signified by the number forty has come to rest, the number ten remains as the reward that the saints who labor in the vineyard will receive. [Col. 0928B]

When that fishing had been completed, Jesus said to them:

“Come, have breakfast.”

And no one of those reclining dared ask him, “Who are you?” because they knew that he was the Lord.

If they knew, what need was there for them to ask? But if there was no need, why is it said, “They did not dare,” as though there were a need, but they did not dare because of some fear?

The meaning, therefore, is this: so great was the evidence of the truth by which Jesus appeared to those disciples that none of them dared not only to deny but even to doubt it. For if anyone had doubted, he would certainly have had to ask. Thus it is said: “No one dared to ask him, ‘Who are you?’”—as though it were said, “No one dared to doubt that it was he.”

[Col. 0928C]

Then Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.

Here it is also stated what they ate for breakfast. We too shall say something pleasant and salutary about that breakfast, if it feeds us as well.

Earlier it was narrated that when these disciples came down onto the land, they saw a charcoal fire laid there, with a fish placed on it, and bread. This should not be understood to mean that the bread too had been placed on the coals. Rather, the verb “they saw” is to be understood only with the first two items. If we repeat that verb where it must be supplied, the whole statement may be expressed as follows: “They saw a charcoal fire laid there, and a fish placed upon it, and they saw bread.” Or, better: “They saw a charcoal fire laid there and a fish placed upon it; they also saw bread.”

At the Lord’s command they also brought some of the fish they themselves had caught. Although the narrator does not explicitly state that they did this, he does not fail to state that the Lord commanded it. For he says: “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.” Who, with him commanding, would believe that they did not do it?

The Lord therefore made breakfast for those seven disciples of his from the fish they had seen placed upon the coals, adding to it some of the fish they had caught. It is likewise narrated that they saw bread.

The roasted fish is Christ who suffered; he is also the bread that came down from heaven. The Church is incorporated into him in order to share in eternal blessedness. For this reason it was said: “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught,” so that all of us who bear this hope might understand that, through that number seven of the disciples—by which our universal company can be understood as symbolized in this passage—we share in so great a mystery and are joined to the same blessedness. [Col. 0929A]

This is the Lord’s breakfast with his disciples, with which John concludes his Gospel, although he had many other great things to say about Christ, as I think, with a profound contemplation of great realities.

Here the Church as it will be among the good alone is signified by the catch of one hundred fifty-three fish; and for those who believe, hope for, and love these things, participation in such great blessedness is signified by this breakfast.

“This is now the third time,” he says, “that Jesus was manifested to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

We must refer this not to the manifestations themselves but to the days: first, on the day when he rose; then after eight days, when the disciple Thomas saw and believed; and today, when he performed this act concerning the fish.

After how many days he did this is not stated. For on that first day he was seen more than once, as the combined testimony of all the Evangelists demonstrates. But, as has been said, his manifestations must be counted so that this may be the third.

The first manifestation must be considered one and the same because it occurred on one day, whenever and to whomever he showed himself on the day on which he rose; the second occurred after eight days; and this is the third. After that, he appeared whenever he wished, until the fortieth day on which he ascended into heaven, although not everything has been written down.

When they had eaten, he says to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” and so forth.

This was the outcome of the denier and lover—lifted up by presumption, cast down by denial, cleansed by weeping, tested by confession, and crowned by suffering. This was the outcome: that he should die for his name with perfect love, together with whom he had rashly promised that he would die.

Strengthened by Christ’s resurrection, he would do what he had prematurely promised when he was weak. For this was necessary: first Christ had to die for Peter’s salvation, and then Peter for the preaching of Christ. What human rashness had begun to dare was out of order, since the truth had established this sequence.

Peter thought that he would lay down his life for Christ, needing to be delivered for the sake of his deliverer, when Christ had come to lay down his life for all his own, among whom Peter also was. And behold, this has now happened.

Now, with the Lord himself granting it, let true steadfastness of heart for accepting death for the Lord’s name be acquired, rather than false confidence being presumed by us in our error. Now we should not fear the destruction of this life, because, when the Lord rose, an example of the other life went before us.

Now, Peter, you should not fear death: the one whom you grieved as dead is alive. You dared to anticipate the Teacher whom, out of a carnal love, you tried to prevent from dying for us; you feared his persecutor. Now that the price has been poured out for you, you should follow the purchaser (Matt. XVI), and you will follow him all the way to the death of the cross.

You heard the words of the one whom you have already proved truthful. He himself foretold that you would suffer, the one who had foretold that you would deny him.

But first the Lord asks what he knew—not once, but a second and a third time—whether Peter loved him. Each time he hears from Peter no answer other than that he is loved, and each time he commends nothing else to Peter than that his sheep be fed.

A threefold confession is given in response to the threefold denial, so that the tongue may serve love no less than fear, and so that approaching death may not appear to have drawn more words from him than present life.

Thus the duty of love is to feed the Lord’s flock, just as denying the shepherd was an indication of fear. Those who feed Christ’s sheep with the intention that they should be their own rather than Christ’s prove that they love themselves, not Christ—out of a desire either for glory, domination, or gain, rather than out of a love of obedience, assistance, and pleasing God.

Against this, then, the voice of Christ, repeated so many times, keeps watch: the Apostle laments those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. II).

Is “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” anything other than if he had said: “If you love me, do not think of feeding yourself, but my sheep. Feed them as mine, not as yours. Seek my glory in them, not your own; me as Lord, not yourself; my gains, not yours. Do not belong to the company of those who belong to the perilous times, lovers of themselves, and the other vices joined to this beginning of evils” (II Tim. III).

This is the fault that must be guarded against most carefully by those who feed Christ’s sheep: that they seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and devote to the uses of their own desires those for whom Christ’s blood was shed.

The love of Christ in the one who feeds his sheep must grow into so great a spiritual fervor that it conquers even the natural fear of death, by which we do not wish to die, even when we desire to live with Christ.

For the Apostle Paul also says that he has a desire to depart and be with Christ. Yet he groans under his burden and does not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (Phil. I). [Col. 0930C]

And to this lover of his the Lord says:

“When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

He said this to him, signifying by what death he would glorify God. “You will stretch out your hands,” he says—that is, you will be crucified. But, in order for you to reach this, “another will gird you and lead you not where you wish, but where you do not wish.”

First he said what would happen, and then how it would happen. For he was led where he did not wish, not after he had been crucified, but precisely in order to be crucified. Once crucified, he did not go where he did not wish, but rather where he wished.

Released from the body, he wished to be with Christ. Yet, if it had been possible, apart from the distress of death, he desired eternal life. He was led unwillingly to that distress, but he was led out of it willingly. He came to it unwillingly, but overcame it willingly, and he retained this weakness of feeling, by which no one wishes to die, to such an extent that even old age could not take it away from blessed Peter, to whom it was said: “You will be led where you do not wish.”

For the sake of comforting us, the Savior himself also assumed this feeling in another form when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). He had certainly come to die, and possessed the necessity of death, but by voluntary power he was going to lay down his life and by the same power take it up again.

Nevertheless, however great the distress of death may be, the force of love by which we love the one who, although he is our life, also wished to endure death for us ought to conquer it. For if death had no distress, or only a slight distress, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great.

But if the good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, made so many martyrs out of those very sheep, how much more ought those to strive for the truth even to death and against sin even to the shedding of blood, to whom he entrusts the sheep themselves to be fed—that is, to be taught and governed?

Accordingly, when his example of suffering has gone before, who does not see that pastors ought all the more to cling in imitation to the Shepherd, since many sheep also imitated him? Under this one Shepherd, in one flock, the pastors themselves are sheep.

For he made all of them his sheep, for all of whom he suffered, because he himself also became a sheep in order to suffer for us.

When, therefore, the Lord had foretold by what death Peter would glorify God, he said to him: “Follow me,” and so forth, up to the point where he says: “But if I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?” [Col. 0931B]

For why is Peter told, “Follow me,” while it is not said to the others who were present with him, even though the disciples certainly followed him as their teacher? And if this is to be understood of suffering, was Peter the only one who suffered for Christian truth? Was not another of those seven there—the son of Zebedee, the brother of John—who, after Christ’s ascension, is reported to have been killed by Herod?

Someone might answer that it was said appropriately to Peter, “Follow me,” because James was not crucified, whereas Peter experienced not only death but also death on a cross, like Christ.

If this, and nothing else more appropriate, can be found, why then was it said concerning John: “If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?” And why was it repeated, “You follow me,” as though John would not follow because Christ had willed that he remain until he came?

Who could readily believe that something other than what the brothers who were present at the time believed had been said—namely, that this disciple would not die, but would remain alive until Jesus came?

But John himself removed this opinion, clearly declaring that the Lord had not said this. For why would he add:

Did Jesus not say, “He does not die,” unless it was so that what was false might not cling to people’s hearts? But let anyone who wishes still resist, and say that what John says is true: that the Lord did not say that this disciple would not die, but that this was nevertheless signified by the kind of words John reported him to have spoken. Let him assert that the apostle John is alive and contend that, in his tomb near Ephesus, he is sleeping rather than lying dead; let him take as evidence the report that the earth there gradually rises and seems to boil up, and let him maintain, whether steadfastly or obstinately, that this happens because of John’s breathing. For there can be no shortage of people who believe this, if there are not lacking those who even assert that Moses is alive, because it is written that his grave was not found (Gen. XXXIV), and that he appeared with the Lord on the mountain where Elijah also was (Matt. XVII)—although we read that Elijah did not die but was taken away (2 Kings II). As though Moses’ body could not have been hidden somewhere in such a way that people were altogether unaware where it was, and then divinely awakened for an hour when he appeared with Christ together with Elijah, just as many bodies of the saints rose for an hour when Christ suffered and appeared to many in the holy city after his resurrection, as it is written (Matt. XXVII).

But is this immense question thereby resolved, if, by a great miracle of the sort that the Almighty can perform, a living body remains asleep beneath the earth for so long, until the end of the age? On the contrary, the question becomes greater and more difficult: why would Jesus, as a great gift, have granted a long bodily sleep to the disciple whom he loved more than the others, so that he was worthy to recline upon his breast, when he freed blessed Peter from the burden of that very body through the immense glory of martyrdom and granted him what the apostle Paul said and wrote that he desired—to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I)?

But if—as is more generally believed—the reason Saint John says that the Lord did not say “He does not die” is that no one might suppose from those words that he meant this, and if John’s lifeless body lies in his tomb like the bodies of other dead people, it remains that, if what rumor has spread about the earth that is periodically removed and then grows again is really true, this happens either so that his precious death may be commended in this manner, since martyrdom does not commend it—for no persecutor killed him for the faith of Christ—or for some other reason hidden from us. Yet the question remains: why did the Lord say of a man who was going to die, “If I will that he remain until I come”?

Among these two apostles, Peter and John, who would not also be moved to ask why the Lord loved John more, when Peter loved the Lord more? Whenever John mentions himself, so that he may be understood without naming himself, he adds that Jesus loved him, as though Jesus loved him alone, so that by this sign he might be distinguished from the others, whom he certainly loved all. What else, then, did John want understood by saying this, except that he was loved more? Far be it from us to suppose that he said this falsely. What greater indication of his own greater love could Jesus have given him than that, while this man was a fellow member of the company of his fellow disciples and shared in so great a salvation, he alone reclined upon the breast of the Savior himself?

That the apostle Peter loved Christ more than the others can indeed be demonstrated by many proofs. But, without going far afield, it appears clearly in the reading immediately preceding this one, concerning the Lord’s third manifestation, where he asked Peter: “Do you love me more than these?” He certainly knew this, yet he asked so that we too, who read the Gospel, might know of Peter’s love for the Lord, both from the Lord’s question and from Peter’s answer. But when Peter replied, “I love you,” he did not add “more than these,” because he answered according to what he knew about himself. He could not know how much he was loved by anyone else, since he could not see another person’s heart. Nevertheless, by saying in his earlier words, “Yes, Lord, you know,” he himself sufficiently declared that the Lord, who knew, had asked what he asked.

The Lord therefore knew not only that Peter loved him, but also that Peter loved him more than the others. Yet if we put the question and ask which of the two is better—the one who loves Christ more, or the one who loves him less—who would hesitate to answer that the one who loves him more is better? Likewise, if we ask which of the two is better—the one whom Christ loves less, or the one whom he loves more—we shall undoubtedly answer that the one who is loved more by Christ is better.

In the first comparison I proposed, therefore, Peter is preferred to John; in this second one, John is preferred to Peter. Let us consequently formulate a third question: Which of the two disciples is better—the one who loves Christ less than his fellow disciple does but is loved more by Christ than his fellow disciple, or the one whom Christ loves less than his fellow disciple? [The printed Latin wording is syntactically defective.] Here the answer plainly hesitates, and the question grows greater.

As far as I myself understand, I would readily answer that the one who loves Christ more is better, and that the one whom Christ loves more is happier, if I could discern how I might defend the justice of our Liberator, who loves less the one who loves him more and loves more the one who loves him less. Nevertheless, I shall attempt to discuss the resolution of so great a question, according to the strength he himself grants. Until now it has been proposed, not explained. Let this be the beginning of its explanation: we must remember that, in this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wis. IX), we live a wretched life; but since we have already been redeemed through the Mediator and received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, we possess a blessed life in hope, even though we do not yet possess it in reality. “Hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII).

This life, then, about which it is written, “Is not human life upon earth a temptation?” (Job VII), in which we cry out daily to God, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI), a person is compelled to endure even after sins have been forgiven, although sin was originally the cause of his entering into such misery. The punishment is longer than the guilt, lest the guilt be considered small if the punishment ended together with it. This is the evil of the days that we spend in this mortality, although in them we love to see good days—a condition to be mourned, indeed, but not censured (Ps. XXXIII).

For it comes from the just anger of God, concerning which Scripture says: “A man born of a woman, short-lived and full of anger” (Job XIV). While containing his mercies within this anger, as it is written (Ps. LXXVI), God, besides the other consolations for the wretched that he never ceases to provide for the human race, sent his only-begotten Son, through whom he created all things, so that, while remaining God, he might become man, and so that the man Christ Jesus might be the mediator between God and human beings. Those who believe in him, with the guilt of all sins released through the washing of regeneration, would be freed from eternal condemnation and would live in faith, hope, and charity.

And because even those who walk in him are not without sins—sins that creep in through the weakness of this life—he gave the salutary remedies of almsgiving, by which their prayer might be assisted. He taught them there to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

This is what the Church does in this sorrowful life, with blessed hope. The apostle Peter represented this Church in a symbolic universality because of the primacy of his apostleship. In what properly pertained to himself, he was one human being by nature, one Christian by grace, and, by an even greater grace, one and the same chief apostle. But when he was told, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI), he signified the whole Church.

In this world the Church, amid various temptations—like rains, rivers, and storms by which it is shaken [F. “by which it is battered”]—does not fall, because it is founded upon the rock, from which Peter receives his name. For Peter is not named from the rock; rather, Peter is named from the Rock, just as the Christian is named not from Christ, but the Christian from Christ. This is why the Lord said, “Upon this rock I will build my Church”: Peter had said, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God”; “upon this rock,” therefore, he said, “which he has confessed, I will build my Church.”

For the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. X), and upon this foundation Peter himself was also built. “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III). The Church, then, which is founded in Christ, received from him the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter—that is, the power to loose and bind sins. What the Church is properly in Christ, Peter is by representation in the Rock: by this representation Christ is understood as the Rock and Peter as the Church.

This Church, which Peter represented, so long as it dwells amid evils, is freed from evils by loving and following Christ. It follows him more closely in those who struggle for the truth even unto death. But the whole Church is told, “Follow me”; and on behalf of this whole Church Christ suffered. Of him the same Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. II). This, then, is why he was told, “Follow me.”

There is another life, immortal and free from evils. There we shall see face to face what here is seen through a mirror and in a riddle (1 Cor. XIII), when progress has been made to a great degree in desiring the truth. The Church therefore knows two lives divinely proclaimed and commended to it: one in faith, the other in sight; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of dwelling; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation; one turns away from evil and does good, the other has no evil from which to turn and possesses a great good in which to rejoice; one fights with an enemy, the other reigns without an enemy; one restrains carnal desires, the other is free for spiritual delights; one assists the needy, the other is where it finds no needy person; one forgives the sins of others so that its own may be forgiven, the other neither suffers anything that it might forgive nor does anything for which it asks forgiveness; one distinguishes good and evil, the other beholds what is good.

Thus one is good, but still wretched; the other is better and blessed. The former was signified by the apostle Peter, the latter by John. The former is carried on here until the end of this age, and there it finds its end; the latter is postponed until after the end of this age, but in the future age it has no end.

Therefore one is told, “Follow me”; but of the other: “If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.” For what else is this, as far as I understand and comprehend it, except: “Follow me by imitating the endurance of temporal evils; let him remain until I come to repay eternal goods”? It can be expressed more clearly in this way: “Let perfected action follow me, shaped by the example of my passion; but let begun contemplation remain until I come, to be perfected when I come.”

For a devout fullness of patience follows Christ, reaching even unto death; but a fullness of knowledge remains until Christ comes, when it will be revealed. Here the evils of this world are endured in the land of the dying; there the goods of the Lord will be seen in the land of the living.

When he said, “I will that he remain until I come,” this should not be understood as though he had said “remain” or “continue to remain,” but “await.” For what is signified by him will not be fulfilled now, but when Christ comes. But what is signified by the one to whom it was said, “You follow me,” unless it is enacted now, will never reach what is awaited.

In this active life, the more we love Christ, the more easily we are freed from evil. Yet he loves us less as we now are, and for this reason he frees us, so that we may not always remain as we are. There he loves us more, because we shall not possess what displeases him and what he removes from us. Nor does he love us here for any other reason than to heal us and transfer us from the things he does not love.

Here, therefore, we are loved less, where he does not wish us to remain; there, more, to which he wishes us to pass, and from which he does not wish us to perish. Let Peter therefore love him so that we may be freed from this mortality; let John be loved by him so that we may be preserved in that immortality.

But this interpretation shows why Christ loved John more than Peter, not why Peter loved Christ more than John. For Christ does not love us more in the future age—where we shall live with him without end—than in this age, from which he rescues us so that we may remain there; and therefore we shall not love him less then, when we are better, since we cannot be better in any way except by loving him more.

Why, then, did John love him less than Peter, if he signified that life in which he is to be loved much more? It is because the words “I will that he remain,” that is, await, “until I come,” were spoken for this reason: we do not yet possess the love that will then be greater, but await it as something future, so that when he himself comes, we may possess it.

For, as the same apostle says in his Epistle: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III). Then, therefore, we shall love more greatly what we shall see. The Lord himself, knowing by predestination what our future life will be like in us, loves it more, so that by loving us he may bring us to it.

Accordingly, since “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV), we know our present misery because we experience it. Therefore we love more the Lord’s mercy, which we desire to be shown in order to free us from misery, and each day we seek and receive it above all through the forgiveness of sins. This was signified by Peter, who loves more but is loved less, because Christ loves us less as wretched than as blessed.

We love contemplation of the truth, such as it will be then, less because we do not yet know or possess it. This was signified by John, who loves less and therefore awaits, until the Lord comes, both that life itself and the fulfillment in us of the love owed to it. Yet John is loved more, because what is represented through him makes a person blessed.

Nevertheless, no one should separate these two distinguished apostles. Both were destined to exist in what John signified. By representation, the one followed and the other remained. By faith, however, both endured the present evils of this misery. Both awaited the future goods of that blessedness.

Nor did they alone do this; the whole holy Church, the bride of Christ, does so—destined to be rescued from these temptations and preserved in that happiness. Peter and John represented these two lives, each one representing one; yet both walked temporally in this present life by faith, and both will enjoy the other eternally by sight.

Therefore, for all the saints who belong inseparably to the body of Christ, the first of the apostles, Peter, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for the governance of this stormiest life, so that sins might be bound and loosed. And for all those same saints, because of the most sacred and utterly tranquil harbor of that life, John the evangelist reclined upon the breast of Christ. For it was not John alone, but the whole Church, that binds and looses sins.

Nor did John alone drink from the spring of the Lord’s breast what he might proclaim concerning the divinity of Christ and the Trinity and unity of the entire Godhead—truths that are to be contemplated face to face in that kingdom, but now, until the Lord comes, are to be regarded in a mirror and in a riddle—rather, the Lord himself spread the Gospel throughout the whole world for all his people to drink, according to each person’s capacity.

There are some who have thought—and these are by no means contemptible interpreters of sacred Scripture—that the apostle John was loved more by Christ for this reason: that he never took a wife and lived most chastely from early childhood. This does not appear clearly in the canonical Scriptures; nevertheless, it too greatly supports the appropriateness of this interpretation, since he signified that life in which there will be no marriages.

This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true. “There are also,” he says, “many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.”

The world should not be understood as unable to contain them because of the size of its physical spaces, as though the things that could be written in it could not fit there; rather, they might perhaps be impossible to grasp because of the capacity of the readers. Nevertheless, without compromising the truth of the events, words often seem to exceed the facts. This does not happen when something obscure or doubtful is explained by supplying its cause and reason, but when something clear is either magnified or diminished, while the path of signifying the truth is not abandoned.

Words thus exceed the thing being indicated in such a way that the speaker’s intention remains apparent and does not deceive—an intention that knows how far belief extends, and from which something may be diminished or enlarged in speech beyond what ought to be believed. The Greeks call this mode of speech hyperbole. This mode, as here, is found in several other passages of the divine writings, as in: “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. LXXII), and: “The crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Ps.
