LXVII), and many things of this kind, which are not lacking in the holy Scriptures, just as other tropes—that is, modes of expression—are not lacking. I would discuss these at greater length if, with the evangelist bringing his Gospel to an end, I were not also compelled to bring my discourse to an end.

[EXPOSITION OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.]

[Col. 0937]

[NOTICE.]

There follow the excellent expositions of the same venerable Bede, presbyter and servant of Christ, on the Acts of the Apostles, arranged in fitting order and measured sequence—not only because they were written by the same evangelist Luke whose Gospel was expounded immediately before, but also because they agree most closely of all with the Gospel’s style, and further because, perhaps for these reasons, after the Gospels and the Epistles of Paul, for which the same author separately compiled explanations, they are customarily cited in the commonly used Bibles. After these, following the order mentioned above, we shall add his explanations of the Catholic Epistles and finally of the Apocalypse of Saint John, bringing this volume, not without hope and not unfaithfully, to a close.

[Col. 0937]

EXPOSITION OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. (C)

LETTER OF Bede TO ACCA, BISHOP, FOR THE EXPOSITION OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.

[Col. 0937B] To Acca, the most dearly desired and truly most blessed lord in Christ, bishop: Bede wishes perpetual salvation in the Lord.

I have received your very frequent letters, in which your Blessedness has deigned to admonish me not to allow the keenness of my mind to grow sluggish and fall asleep in idle leisure, but to devote myself daily, wakeful and tireless, to meditating upon and examining the Scriptures. You also urged me, after the exposition of the Apocalypse of the holy evangelist John—which, at the request of our brother Eusebius, I composed in three books and have now arranged to have transcribed and sent to you—to devote whatever labor I could to an explanation of the blessed evangelist Luke, following the footsteps of the Fathers.

Because I have not yet been able to do this—both frightened by the immensity of the work and hindered by the necessity of pressing circumstances, which you know better than I do—yet, lest the authority of your request be disregarded, I did what I could in the meantime. For I sent a little work on the Acts of the Apostles, which, having been completed only a few days ago, I had written onto parchment sheets after correcting it as quickly as the time allowed, so that your sacred desire might not be delayed.

In it I attempted, as far as I could, to clarify those matters that seemed either to have taken place mystically or to have been expressed obscurely. In this little work I was helped by many other writers of the Catholic faith, but especially by Arator, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church. He went through the book itself in order in heroic verse and mingled in the same meter several flowers of allegory, giving me the opportunity either to gather other things from them or to explain the same things more clearly.

The Acts of the Apostles, then, as blessed Jerome says, seem indeed to sound forth a bare history and to weave the infancy of the nascent Church. But if we know that its author Luke was a physician, whose praise is in the Gospel, we perceive at the same time that all his words are medicine for the sick soul.

As we shall explain some matters according to the measure of our small ability, we shall first take care to point out that the evangelist Luke, as has been said, was, according to the tradition of the ancient interpreters of the Church, highly skilled in the medical art and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Hence his style, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, is more polished and has the flavor of secular eloquence; he also makes greater use of Greek testimonies than of Hebrew ones.

From this there arises something that I find especially astonishing and that, because of my slowness of understanding, strikes me with the greatest bewilderment: I do not know how to investigate the reason why, although in the Hebrew text ten generations are found from the Flood to Abraham, Luke himself—who, with the Holy Spirit guiding his pen, could not have written anything false—preferred to place eleven generations in the Gospel according to the Septuagint interpreters, adding Cainan.

In the Prologue to his Gospel he says that he seemed good to him to write carefully and in order, because many had attempted to do so. But we must understand him to mean those whose authority in the Church is considerable, because those who attempted it were entirely unable to complete what they had undertaken. Luke, however, not only carried his narrative through the resurrection and ascension of the Lord, so that it might have a place worthy of his labor among the four authors of the Gospel Scriptures; he also subsequently wrote what was done through the apostles, insofar as he judged it sufficient for building up the faith of readers and hearers.

Thus his book alone came to be regarded in the Church as trustworthy in recounting the acts of the apostles, while all those who dared to write the apostles’ deeds and sayings without the requisite fidelity were rejected.

For Mark and Luke wrote at a time when they could be approved not only by the Church of Christ but also by the apostles themselves, who were still living in the flesh. For by the Lord’s will it was arranged that not only the apostles who had seen Christ, but also the disciples who had learned through hearing, should record Christ’s deeds and sayings, so that the teachers who followed in the Church might receive both the confidence and the authority to preach and write about what they had not seen.

The Acts of the Apostles, however, especially those of blessed Paul, whose constant companion on his journeys blessed Luke was, he composed as one who had himself seen them.

The whole course of these events, as far as we have been able to observe from the histories of others, covers twenty-eight years: six years of Tiberius Caesar, four of Gaius, and fourteen of Claudius. Under this emperor the apostle Peter came to Rome; in his fourth year there was a famine, and in his eighth year the Jews were expelled from Rome. Then there were four years of Nero, during the final two of which blessed Paul remained at Rome in unrestricted custody. From this we understand that the book was composed in that same city.

To distinguish the same period also by the kings of the Jews: Herod, Philip, and Lysanias ruled as tetrarchs for six years. Herod the king, also called Agrippa, who died at Caesarea, ruled for seven years. Agrippa, his son, under whom Paul was sent to Rome, ruled for fifteen years. Twelve years remain from his time until the overthrow of Jerusalem.

I have set these matters out more distinctly so that, when you review the history of the same little book, you may clearly recognize what happened under each period.

I also sent a brief explanation of the Epistle of the most blessed evangelist John. I extracted most of it, in a concise abridgment, from the homilies of Saint Augustine, which are spread out with the greatest richness and sweetness. At the end I added some material composed through my own labor.

If you find anything useful in either work, ascribe it to the gifts of God; if anything superfluous, show compassion for my weakness. May the almighty Lord preserve your Blessedness, who intercedes for us, safe forever for the governance of the Church.

BEGINNING OF THE EXPOSITION.

[Col. 0939]

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0939C]

“I made the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began to do and to teach.”

He says that he wrote in the Gospel about all Christ’s deeds and sayings—not because he was able to comprehend everything, lest he contradict John, who says: “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book” (John XX), but because he selected from everything material on which to speak, judging that what was suitable and appropriate would suffice for the purpose of his ministry.

Theophilus is interpreted as “lover of God” or “loved by God.” Therefore, whoever is a lover of God should believe that this was written for him and, since Luke the physician wrote it, should find here healing for his own soul. We should also note that he says: “What Jesus began to do and to teach”—first to do, and afterward to teach. For in establishing a good teacher, Jesus taught nothing except what he did.

“Until the day on which, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.”

Because of a hyperbaton, this should be read as: “Until the day on which he was taken up,” with “giving commands” understood as preceding the ascension—that is, giving the apostles the commands that are read either here or in the Gospels. The meaning, then, is: “I wrote about Jesus from the time when he began to perform signs and teach until the day when, having completed these things, he returned to the place from which he had come.”

“Appearing to them for forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God, and eating with them,” and so forth.

To establish faith in his resurrection, the Lord appeared alive to the apostles repeatedly after his passion, took food, and offered his flesh—the same flesh he had raised from the dead—to be touched. But through the deeper mystery of this forty-day association with the disciples, he signifies that he will fulfill by his hidden presence what he had promised: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

This number signifies this temporal and earthly life, either because of the four seasons of the year or because of the four winds of heaven. For after we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, as though having crossed by way of the Red Sea, we need the Lord’s guidance in this wilderness to lead us to heavenly things. He rewards us with the denarius of his image and blesses us with the presence of the Holy Spirit as with the true rest of the jubilee.

“But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

The apostles had not yet been baptized—not with water, however, but with the Holy Spirit. We understand that they had already been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some believe, or—with greater probability—with Christ’s baptism. For Christ did not need to have baptized servants who had themselves been baptized so that through them he might baptize others, since he did not lack the ministry of that memorable humility when he washed their feet.

Thus, when the Lord said, “John indeed baptized with water,” he did not add, “But you will baptize”; rather, he said, “But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” For neither the apostles nor their successors, who baptize in the Church to this day, are able to baptize in any other way than John did—that is, in water. But when Christ’s name has been invoked, the inward power of the Holy Spirit is present, cleansing at once the souls and bodies of those baptized while a human being supplies the water. This did not happen in John’s baptism. “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

“Therefore, when they had assembled, they asked him, saying: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?”

Since he had appeared to them and spoken about the kingdom of God, and had also promised that the Holy Spirit would come not many days later, they consequently ask him about that same kingdom—namely, whether they should believe that it was to be restored immediately with the coming of the Holy Spirit, or reserved for the saints in the future.

For they were still carnal disciples and, once Christ’s resurrection had been completed, believed that the kingdom of Israel would come immediately. In accordance with this, Cleopas says: “But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” The evangelist also stated earlier that, when the Lord was coming to Jerusalem, they supposed that the kingdom of God would immediately appear.

But the prophecy had to be fulfilled in which the Psalmist sings to the Father: “But you have rejected, despised, and delayed your Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII). The Father rejected and despised the Son when, in his passion, he abandoned him as he cried out: “My God, my God, why have you rejected me?” (Matt. XXVII). But he delayed him so that the one whom the saints of that time thought would reign might be awaited as coming in his majesty on the day of judgment.

Therefore, the Lord himself, indicating that the spiritual Israel and the heavenly kingdom had been promised by the prophets, says:

“It is not for you to know the times or moments that the Father has placed in his own authority.”

The time of that kingdom is so secret, he says, that it is disclosed only to the Father’s knowledge. And when he says, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows it, since everything that belongs to the Father belongs to him; but it is not expedient for mortals to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged the next.

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you. And you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem,” and so forth.

“When the Holy Spirit comes upon you,” he says, “he will not bring the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, as you suppose; rather, he will give you power to bear witness concerning me.”

The time of that kingdom is so far off that before it comes the fame of the Gospel must first pass through not only this city of Jerusalem, but also all the borders of Judea, then the neighboring nation of Samaria, and finally the farthest regions around the circuit of the world.

“And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up.”

Mark, recalling another saying of the Lord, states: “And indeed, after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven” (Mark XVI). But because Luke more significantly adds, “When he had said these things, he was lifted up,” he clearly shows that, when the discourses he had mentioned were completed, the Lord ascended into heaven.

“And a cloud received him from their eyes.”

Everywhere creation offers service to its Creator. The stars announce him at his birth; clouds cover him in his passion; clouds receive him as he ascends; and they will accompany him when he returns for judgment.

“And behold, two men stood beside them in white garments.”

White garments are more appropriate to exaltation than to humiliation. Therefore, when the Lord ascends, angels appear in white garments. They are not said to have appeared in white garments when the Lord was born, because at his birth he appeared as humble God, whereas at his ascension he was shown as exalted man. The place also corresponds: the man who was born in a humble little town returned to heaven from a lofty mountain.

[Col. 0942B] “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven.”

The angels appear to them for two reasons: to console them for the sadness of the ascension by recalling his return, and to show that he truly went into heaven, not merely as Elijah seemed to go into heaven.

“He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

That is, he will come to judge in the same form and substance of flesh in which he came to be judged. He gave that flesh immortality; he did not remove its nature. His divine glory also, which once appeared to three disciples on the mountain, will be seen by all the saints after the judgment, when the wicked will be removed so that he may not see the glory of God.

“Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet.”

Our Lord and Savior, after conquering the prince of darkness, leads the faithful into a place of peace and light. Fittingly, he ascended the mountain of chrism, promising the Holy Spirit, whose anointing teaches us about everything.

“Which is near Jerusalem, having a Sabbath day’s journey.”

According to the historical sense, this indicates that the Mount of Olives was separated from the city of Jerusalem by the distance of a mile. According to the law, on the Sabbath it was not permitted to walk more than a thousand paces.

According to the allegorical sense, whoever is worthy inwardly to contemplate the glory of the Lord ascending to the Father and to be enriched by the promise of the Holy Spirit enters the city of perpetual peace by a Sabbath journey. For him, according to Isaiah, Sabbath will follow Sabbath, because whoever has ceased from wicked work here will rest there in heavenly reward.

But, on the other hand, whoever in this world, as though during the six-day period, has neglected to work for salvation will be excluded at the time of perpetual rest from the boundaries of blessed Jerusalem, despising the Gospel command: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.”

“And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room where they were staying.”

He indicates a place above, because they had already ascended from earthly association on the Sabbath to the higher things of knowledge and virtue.

James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas of James. Some think that there were two apostles named James: namely, James the son of Zebedee and James the son of Alphaeus, while a third James, the brother of the Lord, was not an apostle but the bishop of Jerusalem. This is by no means true. Rather, in accordance with the testimony of the Gospels, it must be understood that the same James, the apostle son of Alphaeus, presided over Jerusalem who is called the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt, whom John the Evangelist mentions: “They were standing beside the cross of Jesus—his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas” (John 19). He calls this Mary “of Clopas” by her father’s name or by that of her family.

For how can the brother of the Lord be said to be not an apostle but a third James, when Paul too calls him an apostle: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord” (Galatians 1)? And the Evangelist Mark calls the same man not the third but the other James, saying: “There were also women looking on from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome” (Mark 15). Since “greater” and “lesser” ordinarily establish a distinction not among three but between two, James the younger is called the son of Alphaeus, to distinguish him from the greater, who was the son of Zebedee. Read the book of blessed Jerome Against Helvidius.

Simon the Zealot is the man who is called “the Cananaean” in the Gospels. For *Cana* is interpreted as “zeal.” He was from the Galilean village of Cana, where the Lord changed water into wine; after his brother James, he governed the Church of Jerusalem, and at the age of one hundred and twenty, under Trajan, he ascended the cross. He is shown to have been the Savior’s cousin according to the flesh, because Hegesippus testifies that his father, Clopas, was the brother of Joseph.

Judas of James—that is, the brother of James—is the same man who is called Thaddeus in the Gospels. According to ecclesiastical history, he was sent to Edessa, to Abgar, king of Osroene. The text continues:

> All these were persevering with one accord in prayer.

Those who await the coming of the Holy Spirit persevere with one accord in prayer. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful person” (Wisdom 1). Therefore whoever desires to receive the gifts promised by him must persist in prayers founded upon fraternal charity.

> Now the company of persons was about one hundred and twenty.

These one hundred and twenty, rising gradually and by increments from one to fifteen, produce the number fifteen, the fifteen degrees that are mystically contained in the Psalter because of the perfection of both Testaments, and in which the Chosen Vessel dwells with Peter at Jerusalem. For it was necessary that the mystery which the lawgiver displayed in the number of years should be indicated by their number by the preachers of the new grace.

> Brothers, it is necessary that the Scripture be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold, and so forth.

The apostle Peter fears remaining with the number eleven. For every sin is “eleven,” because in acting perversely it passes beyond the precepts of the Decalogue. Hence, because none of our righteousness is innocent in itself, the tabernacle that contained the Ark of the Lord was covered above with eleven curtains of goats’ hair.

He restores the number of the apostles to twelve, so that through the two parts of the number seven—for three times four makes the dignity of the double— they might preserve with their number the grace that they preached by their word; and that those who were about to preach faith in the Holy Trinity to the fourfold world might already confirm the perfection of their work by the mystery of the number, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

According to the higher sense, however, the loss suffered by the Church through false brothers continues to this point, for the greater part unrepaired. But when, at the end of the world, the Jewish people who crucified the Lord are believed to be reconciled to the Church, as though the fiftieth day were approaching, the number of the apostles is restored.

> And this man indeed acquired a field from the reward of iniquity.

He who sold the Lord of life, having lost the land of the living, possesses a field of blood and eternal death, a memorial of his crime and his name. Otherwise, it was not Judas himself who deserved to possess the field of the potter bought with the price of blood: after returning the thirty pieces of silver, he immediately punished the crime of his betrayal by a still more criminal death. But, in the manner of sacred language, it is said that he “possessed” what he caused to be possessed. Thus blessed Job says: “My garments abhor me”—that is, my corruptible members will make me abominable.

> And, being hanged, he burst open in the middle.

The deranged betrayer found a punishment worthy of himself, so that the throat from which the voice of betrayal had gone forth might be strangled by the knot of the noose. He also sought a fitting place for his destruction: he who had handed over the Lord of human beings and angels to death, hated by heaven and earth, perished in mid-air, as though destined to be associated only with the spirits of the air, following the example of Ahithophel and Absalom, who persecuted King David.

A death itself entirely appropriate to him followed, so that the entrails that had conceived the deceit of betrayal might burst and fall, spilling out into the empty air. A death very similar to this is reported to have condemned Arius, the arch-heretic: because Judas attempted to extinguish Christ’s humanity while Arius attempted to extinguish his divinity, both of them, having lived empty in understanding, likewise perished empty-bellied.

> Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in it, and let another receive his bishopric.

These verses are straightforward and were openly explained by blessed Peter in his interpretation: Judas received the deserved punishment of his transgression, and, departing to his own place—namely, the infernal Gehenna—he abandoned the dwelling common to human society by an untimely and impious death. Nevertheless, when blessed Matthias received the place of his ministry and apostleship, the most sacred totality of apostolic perfection was restored.

It should be noted, however, that according to the Vulgate Edition the whole testimony is by no means taken from Psalm 108. Only the final part is from that psalm; the earlier part is from Psalm 68, where it is said concerning the Jews: “Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in their tents.” Since blessed Peter wished to establish both the rejection of Judas and the election of Matthias by prophetic testimonies, he joined together the testimony specifically concerning Matthias’s bishopric and the testimony stated generally concerning the rejection of the Jews, among whom Judas too belonged.

I do not know which unskilled first editor added this to Psalm 108. When he saw that these verses had likewise been cited by blessed Peter, but that his Psalter did not likewise contain them, he began to think that he possessed a corrupted codex and rashly added what it had not contained. In the same way, eight verses from Paul’s Epistle to the Romans were added to Psalm 13; Paul himself had woven them together from all the psalms and from the prophet Isaiah. The first of these is: “Their throat is an open tomb.” The last is: “There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

For what I have said is confirmed not only by the Hebrew truth and the more carefully corrected Edition of the Septuagint translators, but also by evident reasoning: in that same Psalm 108, apart from these verses, there are thirty curses pronounced against Judas Iscariot, corresponding to the number of silver pieces for which he did not fear to sell the Lord. The first of these is: “Appoint a sinner over him.” The last is: “And let them be clothed with shame as with a double cloak.”

> Joseph who is called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.

Barsabbas is interpreted as “son of quiet,” while Matthias means “little one of God.” Concerning him Arator writes:

> … O how greatly human judgments  
> Differ from those above! He who was just  
> Is deservedly surpassed in human praise by the Little One.

> And they cast lots for them, and so forth.

This example—or the fact that the prophet Jonah was discovered by lot—does not mean that lots should be trusted indiscriminately, “since the privileges of individuals,” as Jerome says, “cannot by any means be made a common law.” There, gentile sailors, compelled by the storm, sought by lot the cause of the danger; here, Matthias is chosen by lot, lest the apostles’ election appear to diverge from the command of the ancient law, where the high priest was ordered to be sought by lot, as is said concerning Zechariah: “According to the custom of the priesthood, he went out by lot to offer incense” (Luke 1).

He was chosen by lot then, as I believe, so that it might be foreshadowed that the priest was always to be sought until the one should come for whom it had been reserved—he who entered the holy places not with the blood of victims but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9). His sacrifice was offered at the time of Passover, but truly consumed on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit appeared in fire. For it was the ancient custom that victims accepted by God should be consumed by heavenly fire. Therefore, until the truth was fulfilled, it was permitted to enact the figure.

This is why Matthias, who was ordained before Pentecost, was selected by lot. The seven deacons, however, were afterward ordained not by the casting of lots but solely by the election of the disciples and by the prayer and laying on of hands of the apostles. If some, compelled by necessity, think that God should be consulted by lots on the apostles’ example, let them observe that the apostles themselves did this only after gathering an assembly of the brothers and pouring out prayers to God.

## CHAPTER II

> When the days of Pentecost were being completed, they were all together in the same place.

This was the upper room, into which they are said above to have ascended. For all who desire to be filled with the Holy Spirit must transcend the dwelling of the flesh through contemplation of the mind.

Just as the forty days during which the Lord, after his resurrection, lived with his disciples signify the Church, rising together with Christ, as a pilgrim in this present life, so the fiftieth day, on which the Holy Spirit is received, appropriately expresses the perfection of blessed rest, by which the Church’s temporal labor will be rewarded with an eternal denarius.

For the number forty itself, calculated through its aliquot parts, adds to itself the denary and makes fifty. Half of forty is twenty; a quarter is ten; a fifth, eight; an eighth, five; a tenth, four; a twentieth, two; and a fortieth, one. Twenty, ten, eight, five, four, two, and one make fifty.

The figure of this calculation is very easily evident, since the present struggle secretly generates for us the eternal joy of the jubilee, as though in the womb, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure” (2 Corinthians 4).

Our true blessedness consists in this: that we, glorying in the immortality of body and soul, are satisfied by the eternal vision of the supreme and blessed Trinity. For we consist in the body’s four most familiar qualities. In the inner person, however, we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. This is the perfect denarius of life: that we rejoice in the present vision of divine glory.

It should also be noted, according to the historical sense, that among the ancients the day of Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day, on which the law was given—was reckoned from the slaughter of the lamb. Here, however, the fiftieth day on which the Holy Spirit was sent is counted not from the Lord’s passion but, as blessed Augustine explains, from his resurrection. By returning to the example of the ancient sign, that day most clearly consecrated the Lord’s Day by his coming. At that same point in time, he showed that the true Passover was to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.

For just as here, so there too God appeared in a vision of fire, as Exodus says: “The whole mountain of Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire” (Exodus 19).

> And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing Spirit, and so forth.

The Lord appeared through fire, as blessed Pope Gregory explains, but through himself he produced speech inwardly. Neither was the fire God nor was that sound God; rather, by what he displayed outwardly he expressed what he accomplished inwardly. He who made the disciples inwardly burning with zeal and instructed by the word displayed fiery tongues outwardly. Thus the elements were brought forward as signs: bodies were to perceive fire and sound, while hearts were to be taught by invisible fire and a voice without sound.

> And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire.

The Holy Spirit appeared in fire and in tongues because he makes all whom he fills at once burning and speaking—burning from him and speaking about him. At the same time, this indicated that the holy Church, spread throughout the boundaries of the world, was to speak in the voice of all nations.

> And it sat upon each of them.

The statement that it “sat” is an indication of royal power. Or certainly it signifies that his rest is in the saints.

> And they began to speak in various tongues.

The humility of the Church gathers together again the unity of languages that the pride of Babylon had scattered. Spiritually, however, the variety of tongues signifies the gifts of diverse graces.

It is also not inappropriate to understand that the Holy Spirit first gave the gift of tongues to human beings, by whom human wisdom is both learned and taught externally, in order to show how easily he can make them wise through the wisdom of God that is within them.

> Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven.

I think it appropriate to inquire who these people were and from what captivity the Jews had come. The captivity that had taken place in Egypt or Babylon had already ended. The Jews had not yet fallen into captivity to the Romans, although that captivity too was already impending as vengeance for the crime committed against the Savior. It remains, therefore, that the captivity under Antiochus is intended; this had occurred not very long before.

> For each one heard them speaking in his own language.

Here the question arises how each person heard them speaking the mighty deeds of God in his own language. Was it that those who spoke in different languages uttered what was being said in each person’s language—that is, that each apostle spoke now in one language and now in another, passing through them all? Or was the miracle rather that, whatever language the speech of those who spoke had been pronounced in, it was understood by each hearer according to his own language?

For example, when a single apostle was teaching in the Church—for it was necessary that, while the others were silent, one should speak and that one speech should reach the hearing of all—did that one speech itself possess such power that, although the hearers were from different nations, each received the sound and grasped the meaning of that same single speech pronounced by the apostle according to his own language? Unless perhaps, on this interpretation, the miracle appeared to belong more to the hearers than to the speakers.

> And those who dwelt in Mesopotamia, and Judea, and Cappadocia.

Here “Judea” signifies not the entire nation but a part of it, namely the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, the Decapolis, and the other regions of the same province. Although all these regions spoke one Hebrew language, each nevertheless possessed its own distinct local manner of speech. Hence, during the Lord’s passion, Peter is revealed by his speech to be a Galilean.

> Jews also and proselytes.

They called proselytes—that is, newcomers—those who, tracing their origin to the gentiles, preferred to choose circumcision and Judaism, as Achior is said to have done in the book of Judith. Thus, they say, not only Jews by birth had gathered from different parts of the world, but also those who had been born uncircumcised and had joined themselves to their ritual.

> But others, mocking, said: These men are full of new wine.

Although they spoke mockingly, they nevertheless testify mystically to the truth. These men were filled not with the old wine that failed at the wedding of the Church, but with the new wine of spiritual grace. For the new wine had already come into new wineskins, when the apostles were proclaiming the mighty deeds of God not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit (Romans 7).

> For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.

The Holy Spirit, about to proclaim the glory of the undivided Trinity, appropriately descended at the third hour. And because it is said above, “They persevered in prayer,” they rightly receive the Holy Spirit at the hour of prayer, so that readers may understand that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not easily received unless the mind is lifted above carnal things by attention to heavenly realities.

The Church understands the three times at which Daniel is said to bend his knees during the day and worship—the third, sixth, and ninth hours—in this way. The Lord, sending the Holy Spirit at the third hour, ascending the cross himself at the sixth, and surrendering his soul at the ninth, graciously chose to make those hours known and holy to us above all others.

> I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh.

The word “pouring out” demonstrates the generosity of the gift: the grace of the Holy Spirit was to be bestowed not, as formerly, only upon prophets and priests, but freely upon all conditions and persons of both sexes. The prophet goes on to explain what “all flesh” means.

> And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and so forth. And I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on the earth below.

Wonders in heaven occurred when a new star appeared at the Lord’s birth; when he ascended the cross, the sun was darkened and heaven itself was covered with darkness. Signs on earth occurred when, as the Lord gave up the Spirit, the earth trembled, opened the tombs, split the rocks, and brought forth again many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep.

> Blood and fire and vapor of smoke.

The blood of the Lord’s side, the fire of the Holy Spirit, and the vapor of compunction and weeping. For just as smoke arises from fire, so compunction is born from the burning of the Holy Spirit.

It remains to believe that blood flowing from dead flesh in a living stream—something contrary to the nature of our bodies—was made a sign. A sign of what, indeed, except our salvation and life, which certainly arose from his death? The fire may also be understood as the illumination of the faithful, and the vapor of smoke as the blindness of the Jews who did not believe.

Hence, when he was about to give the law, the Lord descended in fire and smoke: he illuminates the humble through the brightness of his manifestation and darkens the eyes of the proud through the murkiness of error.

> The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood.

This is believed to have been partly fulfilled in the Lord’s passion and partly to lie in the future before the great day, that is, the day of judgment. At that time the sun was darkened, but the moon could not visibly appear to human beings as changed into blood, since then—being the fifteenth day, as was appropriate at Passover—it had been hidden during the day from mortal sight by the interposition of the earth.

> And it shall be: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

This is what Peter says elsewhere: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

> Jesus the Nazarene, a man attested by God, and so forth, up to “by afflicting him, you killed him.”

Like a learned teacher, he first admonishes the unbelievers whom he pities, so that after they have been pierced by proper fear he may afterward offer them the counsel of salvation at the fitting time.

Because he is speaking to people who know the law, he shows that Christ is the one promised by the prophets. Yet he does not first call him the Son of God on his own authority, but a man approved, a righteous man, a man raised from the dead—not by the customary and common resurrection delayed until the end of the world, but by one celebrated on the third day—so that the assertion of his singular and glorious resurrection might obtain testimony to his eternal divinity.

Since he showed that the bodies of others underwent corruption after death, he demonstrates that this one, of whom it is said, “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15), was free from human frailty. He also proves that he surpassed the merits of the human condition and therefore was to be attributed more to God than to human beings.

What kind of opening the apostles used in their preaching among the gentiles may be learned from the account of Cornelius the centurion and from the speech of the apostle Paul delivered at Athens.

> I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.

“Coming,” he says, “into that which passes away, I did not remove my eye from him who always remains. I arranged this in advance, so that after temporal things had been completed I might return to him, because he favors me, so that I may remain steadfastly in him. And I will attribute the fact that I committed no sin, and that deceit was not found in my mouth” (1 Peter 2), not to his humanity but to his divinity. Therefore there was joy in my thoughts and exultation in my words, on account of the resurrection, clearly, because through it the world was set free.

> Moreover, my flesh also will not fail in death, but will sleep in the hope of the resurrection.

For you will not abandon my soul to be possessed by the underworld, nor will you permit the consecrated body—through which others too are to be sanctified—to undergo corruption.

> You have made known to me the paths of life, by which one goes to eternity.

On those paths, after the sorrow of the passion, “you will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15). And to him who ascends into heaven you will give the delights of your right hand forever.

> For he was not abandoned in the underworld.

Thus Christ descended according to his soul to the underworld, so that he might assist those whom it was necessary to assist; but he was not abandoned in the underworld, because by his swift return he sought the body that was to rise again.

> Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God,

because the psalm had said, “For he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken,” and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this Spirit, whom you see and hear. You see him in the fiery tongues; you hear him in our speech.

By saying that he received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father and poured him out, he makes both natures of the same Christ evident: he received as a human being, and he poured out as God.

> For David did not ascend into the heavens.

He himself says: “For, as these final words show, blessed David foretold not his own ascent but that of his Lord. He was to be sent from Zion—that is, he was to come from the royal stock of that same David—and was to rule in the midst of his enemies. In the same way, understand that the things he stated earlier concern not David but Christ’s death and resurrection.”

> The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.

The first occurrence of the name “Lord” among the Hebrews is the Tetragrammaton, which is properly applied to God. The second is common among mortals, by which kings and other human beings are also called.

If the Arian heresy should wish to use this difference to argue that the Son is lesser and the Father greater, we shall answer that the lower name belongs to the one who is commanded to sit. As blessed Peter consequently explained: “God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.”

For it was not divinity that was crucified, but flesh. And that can indeed happen which was able to be crucified.

> Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.

This is what Peter says elsewhere concerning the Lord: “Whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things” (Acts 3). Then, when all the times of refreshment have come from the presence of the Lord, he will send Jesus Christ, who has been proclaimed to us from the royal seats, to judge the living and the dead (Wisdom 18).

> When they heard these things, they were pierced in heart, and so forth.

Observe the prophecy of Joel fulfilled: after the fire of the Holy Spirit comes the vapor of compunction. For smoke commonly brings forth tears. Those who had laughed begin to weep; they beat their breasts and offer their prayer to God as a sacrifice, so that they may be able to taste the blood which is to save them, the blood that, while condemned, they had called down upon themselves and their children. The text continues:

> Repent, he said, and let each one of you be baptized.

Before mentioning baptism, he first set forth the laments of repentance, so that, following the custom of the Church, they might first pour over themselves the water of their affliction and afterward be washed by the sacrament of baptism.

> And about three thousand souls were added on that day.

When the baptism of the Church was first celebrated, divine mercy, in its providential ordering, gathered an equal number of souls for the confession of the Holy Trinity. Moses, on the fiftieth day from Passover, on which the law was given, commanded the solemnity of the firstfruits to begin. Now, however, with the Holy Spirit coming upon them, not sheaves of grain but souls were consecrated to the Lord as firstfruits.

> And they held all things in common, and so forth.

If the love of God is poured into our hearts, it immediately produces love of our neighbor as well. Therefore, because of the twofold burning of charity, the Holy Spirit is read to have been given to the apostles twice. It is a great sign of fraternal love to possess all things in common and to have nothing as one’s own.

## CHAPTER III

> Now Peter and John were going up into the temple, and so forth.

At the ninth hour, as they are about to enter the temple, the apostles first heal a lame man who had long been disabled; then, laboring until evening, they instruct many thousands of people in the word of faith. For the teachers of the Church, coming at the end of the world, preach first to Israel in its sickness and afterward also to the gentiles. These are the laborers whom the master of the household brings into the vineyard at the ninth and eleventh hours (Matthew 20).

> And a certain man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried.

Because the people of Israel proved rebellious not only against the Lord incarnate but also from the earliest times of the law, it was as though they had been lame from their mother’s womb. This is well prefigured by Jacob, who wrestled with the angel and was indeed blessed but nevertheless limped (Genesis 32): the same people prevailed against the Lord in his passion, being blessed in some respects through faith but lame in others through unbelief.

> Whom they placed daily at the temple gate called Beautiful.

The Beautiful Gate of the temple is the Lord, through whom whoever enters will be saved. Israel, weakened and unable to go to this gate, is brought there by the voices of the law and the prophets, so that by hearing the wisdom of faith from those entering within, it may ask for help.

The prophets, by their predictions of future things, place their hearers, as it were, at the gate; but it belongs to Peter to lead them into the temple. To him, because of his strong confession, were given both the name “rock” and the keys of heaven.

> Silver and gold I do not have, and so forth.

The old tabernacle did indeed possess the ordinances of ritual worship, and the holy secular sanctuary was decorated with gold and silver. But the blood of the Gospel shines forth more precious than the metals of the law, because that people, which had previously lain in weakness of mind before gilded doors, enters the temple of the heavenly kingdom after being healed in the name of the Crucified.

Otherwise, blessed Peter, remembering the Lord’s command—“Do not possess gold and silver” (Matthew 10)—was accustomed not to store away for himself the money placed at the apostles’ feet, but to preserve it for the use of the poor who had abandoned their own patrimonies.

> And taking him by his right hand, he lifted him up.

Whoever he raises, he also strengthens with his right hand. For the speech of a teacher has less effect in the hearts of hearers if it is not also commended by examples of his own conduct.

> And leaping up, he stood and walked. And he entered the temple with them.

An excellent order of perfection: first the man who had lain down rises; then he seizes strength; and thus he enters the gate of the kingdom with the apostles.

> And they were all filled with wonder and amazement.

He calls amazement “fear.” In another sense, however, *ecstasy* means being out of one’s mind—not alienated through fear but taken up by some inspiration of revelation.

> All the people ran together to them, to the portico called Solomon’s.

After Israel was saved through the apostles, the whole world runs together to the thresholds of the true and peaceful Solomon, of whom it is said: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9). He is the stone cut from the mountain which, when the earthly kingdom hostile to faith has fallen, alone holds peaceful dominion throughout the world (Daniel 2).

> Every soul that will not hear that Prophet shall be destroyed.

Briefly and clearly, by the testimony of the prophets and the law, he teaches that the Lord is to be heard by all nations: he will condemn unbelievers but grant eternal blessing to the faithful.

> And all the prophets from Samuel onward.

Although the patriarchs and holy men of earlier times prophesied about Christ in words and deeds, I call “the prophets” properly those who wrote openly about Christ and the mystery of the Church. Their period began with Samuel, under whom the age of the kings in Judea also began, and continued until the release from the Babylonian captivity.

> And in your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed.

The seed of Abraham is Christ, in whose faith blessing was promised to all the families of the earth, both Jews and gentiles. The apostle gently wins the minds of the Jews in order to make them more ready to believe, saying that the Healer of the whole world chose to visit and bless them first.

> To you first, he says, God, having raised up his Son.

Here we must also observe that he refers to the same Son of God whom he has called the seed of Abraham, because of the two natures of that same Christ, lest they should believe Christ to be merely human or should believe one Son to belong to humanity and another to God. The insane Manes and Nestorius were deceived by this snare of heresy.

## CHAPTER IV

> While they were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them, and so forth.

The priests and the captain—or, as another Edition says, the prefect—of the temple, who appeared to be the teachers and judges of the people, were distressed because the crowd had gathered to listen to the apostles. The Sadducees were distressed because the apostles preached the resurrection. Both groups were distressed because they affirmed that Jesus, whom they knew to have been killed by them as a man, had been glorified by God the Father.

> And the number of the men became five thousand.

If the five thousand men whom the Lord fed in the wilderness (Matthew 14) are understood as the people established under the law but refreshed by Christ’s gift, then these five thousand too, instructed by the apostles’ teaching, can signify the people of the gentiles, following spiritually the mysteries of that same law.

It is fitting that both groups are granted a heavenly gift in the evening, because “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians 4).

> This is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

The builders were the Jews. While all the gentiles dwelt in the desolation of idols, they alone read the law and the prophets daily for the purpose of building. As they built, they came to the cornerstone that would embrace two walls: that is, in the prophetic Scriptures they found Christ, who was to come in the flesh and to establish two peoples in himself.

Because they preferred to stand in one wall—that is, to be saved alone—they rejected the stone that was not fitted for one wall but for two. Yet God, although they were unwilling, himself placed this stone as the cornerstone, so that from the two Testaments and the two peoples an edifice of one and the same faith might arise.

> And there is salvation in no one else.

If salvation belongs to no one else but Christ alone, then the fathers of the Old Testament too were saved through the incarnation and passion of that same Redeemer, in whom we believe and hope to be saved. Though the sacraments differ according to the circumstances of the times, the faith nevertheless remains one and the same.

For they learned through the prophets that the same dispensation of Christ which we have learned was accomplished through the apostles was to come. There is no redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a ransom for all.

> When they saw that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they were astonished.

The unlettered are sent to preach so that the faith of believers might not be thought to have been produced by human eloquence and learning rather than by the power of God, as the Apostle says: “Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (1 Corinthians 1).

They were called *idiotae*, “ordinary” or “uneducated men,” because they were content with their own language and natural knowledge and were unfamiliar with literary studies. Indeed, the Greeks call what is private or one’s own *ἴδιον* (*idion*).

> For the man on whom this sign of healing had been performed was more than forty years old.

According to the historical sense, the man’s mature age shows the miracle to be beyond dispute for obstinate detractors. Allegorically, however, the people of Israel did not seek only for forty years in the wilderness the filth of Egypt while scorning the manna; even in the promised land it continued to limp between the rites of the Lord and of idols.

Or, if the number forty signifies the twofold fullness of the law—for four times ten makes forty—then its transgressor, weak and lying down, passes beyond the perfection of forty.

> Lord, you who made heaven and earth, and so forth.

After hearing the threats of their persecutors, they ask for confidence to resist through signs of power.

> Against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed.

They explain literally the name “Christ,” concerning which it was said, “And against his Christ” (Psalm 2). For Christ received his name from *chrisma*, that is, from anointing. In accordance with the saying, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 24)—that is, with the Holy Spirit.

And when they had prayed, the place in which they were assembled was shaken. Those who sought the strength of steadfast hearts against the deceit of their enemies received, through the earthquake, a sign that their prayer had already been heard, so that they might recognize that earthly hearts would yield to them, since, when the Holy Spirit came, the earth itself was shaken with fear beneath their feet. Yet it may also be understood as the joyful fear of those who, by believing, were destined to submit to the apostles: once their earthly heaviness had been shaken off, they learned to rise again with Christ and to set their minds on heavenly things.

[Col. 0954A] Now the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul. Those who had wholly abandoned the world did not, boasting of noble birth, put themselves before one another; rather, as though born from the womb of one and the same mother, the Church, they all rejoiced in the same love of brotherhood.

And with great power the apostles gave witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord. He carefully distinguishes the order of teachers and hearers. For the multitude of believers, having scorned their possessions, was joined together by the bond of mutual charity. The apostles, however, shining with powers, disclosed the mysteries of Christ to all.

Now Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles. I think this is the Barnabas who is later read to have been ordained an apostle of the Gentiles together with Paul. Hence, because he was a Cypriot by birth, later departing from Paul, he returned to his native island. Some, however, think that he was rather Paul’s colleague who, above, was chosen by lot with Matthias for the apostleship. They pay insufficient attention to the fact that, according to more accurate copies, this man is called Barnabas, while the other, with a changed letter, is called Barsabas; and in the book of Hebrew names this one is interpreted as “son of consolation,” while the other is “son of quiet.”

Which is translated, “SON OF CONSOLATION.” Whenever Sacred Scripture gives the names of things or persons together with their interpretation, it certainly indicates that a more sacred meaning is contained in them. He is therefore rightly called “son of consolation,” since, despising present things, he is consoled by hope of the future. For the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete precisely because, for those who suffer oppression in the world, through the inward infusion of his gift he grants *paraklēsis* (παράκλησις), that is, the consolation of heavenly joys. Thus blessed Peter, by the grace of the same Spirit, is called Bar-Jona, that is, “son of a dove.” It follows:

And he brought the price and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Arator says of this:

> They prove that what they avoid touching must be abandoned,  
> and teach that the gold they place beneath their feet  
> must be trampled.  
> From it earthly cares come to human hearts;  
> it is scattered upon the same earth.

## CHAPTER V

Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart? In another Translation, according to the Greek exemplar, it is read thus: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?” Here it should be noted that no creature can fill the soul and mind of a human being according to their substance; only the creating Trinity can do so. For the mind is filled by created things only according to their activity and the impulse of the will. Satan fills someone’s mind, and the ruling power of the heart, not by actually entering into him and into his understanding, or—as I might put it—entering through the heart’s entrance, since this power belongs to divinity alone, but like a certain crafty, wicked, deceitful, and fraudulent deceiver, drawing the human soul toward an affection for evil through thoughts and incentives to vice, with which he himself is filled. Satan therefore filled Ananias’s heart, not by entering into him personally, but by inserting the poison of his wickedness.

You have not lied to men but to God. [Col. 0955A] Above he had said that Ananias had lied to the Holy Spirit. Thus he declares the Holy Spirit to be God and condemns the error of Macedonius before Macedonius had been born.

When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and died. He did not inflict so severe a sentence on the transgressor out of any desire for gain, but, foreseeing in the Spirit the tares that would later adulterate the Church’s simplicity by corrupt practices—for from these, it is said, the exceedingly wicked class of Sarabaites arose, who, without abandoning their possessions at all, pretend to observe apostolic strictness—he did not allow the guilty to be healed by any repentance. Rather, he took care to cut out the harmful growth at its roots, so as to instill fear in those who came afterward. Accordingly, it follows:

[Col. 0955B] And great fear came upon the whole Church and upon all who heard these things. But none of the others dared to join them. The punishment of the two who had deceitfully attempted to join them provided an example for the rest.

So that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them, and they might be delivered. At that time Peter visibly lifted up the sick by the shadow of his body; even now he does not cease to strengthen the infirm among the faithful by the invisible shelter of his intercession. And because Peter is a type of the Church, he himself rightly walks upright, while, with his accompanying shadow, he raises those lying down: for the Church, directing its mind and love toward heavenly things, passes through the earth as though in shadow, and here renews through temporal sacraments and figures of heavenly realities those whom there it rewards with everlasting gifts. Some connect with this passage what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV).

Then the high priest rose, and all who were with him—the sect of the Sadducees, and so forth. In Greek, “heresy” is named from *hairesis* (αἵρεσις), “choice,” because each person, rejecting the statements of others, chose what he thought ought to be followed. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “just”—for they claimed for themselves what they were not, as we read below—denied altogether the resurrection of the body and said that the soul perishes with the flesh. They did not even believe that an angel or spirit existed, and, accepting only the five books of Moses, rejected the proclamations of the prophets. For this reason above all they supported the rulers in persecuting the apostles, evidently moved by jealousy because the apostles, with great power and miraculous signs, bore witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord.

But an angel of the Lord, opening the prison doors during the night, and so forth. So that Thomas would not doubt that the Lord possessed flesh and bones when he saw him enter through closed doors, behold, the Lord himself, still clothed in mortal flesh together with his companions, comes out through closed doors.

We found the prison securely locked, with the guards standing before the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one. Why, profane Jew, are you goaded by blind madness, saying that the apostles stole the Lord from the tomb? Tell me, I ask: by what theft do you think those same apostles were taken from your locked prison?

They were perplexed about what would happen to them. Even then they were unwilling to entrust themselves to faith. Innate wickedness hardens the faithless heart even in the face of manifest signs.

And you wish to bring this man’s blood upon us. The high priest forgot the debt he had invoked upon himself and his people when he said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

But a Pharisee named Gamaliel rose in the council. This Gamaliel, as Clement indicates, was a companion of the apostles in faith; yet, remaining among the Jews at their counsel, he was able, amid such a storm, to calm their fury.

For before these days Theudas arose, and so forth. According to Josephus, this Theudas persuaded many, after removing their possessions from the city, to occupy the banks of the Jordan. Since he was a magician, he claimed to be a prophet and said that, by his command, he could divide the river’s current and provide a passage across it. By order of the procurator Fadus, a troop of cavalry came upon him; after many had been killed or captured, they carried his head back to Jerusalem.

After him Judas the Galilean arose. Josephus also writes that this man was a Gamalite, from the city of Gamala. Having taken a certain Pharisee named Sadducus as an accomplice in his undertaking, he compelled the populace not to lose their liberty by paying tribute to the Romans. He cited the Law’s command to serve the Lord alone and argued that those who brought tithes to the Temple ought not to pay tribute to Caesar. This heresy grew so far that it disturbed even the Pharisees and a large part of the people, so that they thought the Lord Christ should be asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not.

## CHAPTER VI

There arose a complaint by the Hellenists against the Hebrews. The cause of the complaint was that the Hebrews, as being more educated, preferred their own widows in the ministry to the widows of the Hellenists.

It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables. Arator says of this:

> This passage shows  
> that dishes of the mind are better for the unlearned people  
> than banquets spread over the limbs.

Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, and so forth. From this point the apostles—or the successors of the apostles—decreed that throughout all the churches there should be seven deacons, who would hold a higher rank than the others and stand near the altar, like the columns of the altar, and not without some mystery attached to the number seven.

Now Stephen, full of grace and power, performed wonders and great signs among the people. But some members of the synagogue called the Synagogue of the Libertines rose up, and so forth. Stephen is called *Coronatus* in Latin, “Crowned.” In a most beautiful manner, by a kind of presage contained in his name, he anticipated in name what he was destined to receive in reality: humbly stoned, but sublimely crowned. In Hebrew his name is interpreted as “your standard.” Whose? The standard, namely, of the martyrs who followed, for whom he became the first example of dying for Christ through suffering.

And they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by whom he spoke. This is what the Lord himself says to his martyrs: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict.” It was fitting that, in the protomartyr, he should confirm what he had deigned to promise to all who were handed over for his name.

## CHAPTER VII

The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, and so forth. It should be noted, according to Stephen’s words, that God did not speak to Abraham, as Genesis seems to say, after his father’s death—for his father certainly died at Harran, where Abraham himself, his son, also lived with him—but before he lived in that city, when he was still in the region of Mesopotamia, of which Harran itself is a city.

[Col. 0957B] Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you. Then he went out from the land, and so forth. He calls the land and kindred of Abraham the homeland and race of the Chaldeans, from which Abraham had already departed and in which he was now living in Mesopotamia. But because, for whatever reasons, he had left while still held by the hope and desire of returning, he hears from the Lord: “Go out from your land.” This does not mean that he should move his body from there, which he had already done, but that he should tear away the love of his heart. Therefore what follows—“Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans”—signifies not a departure of the body but of the mind, by which he separated himself forever from the society and people of the Chaldeans. For, according to the chronology of the *Chronicles*, in the same year he left Chaldea, entered Mesopotamia, stayed at Harran, and was led into the promised land.

[Col. 0957C] Because his offspring will be an alien in a foreign land, and they will enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years. This should not be understood as though he said that this offspring would be mistreated or enslaved for four hundred years. Rather, it should be read by hyperbaton: his offspring will be foreigners for four hundred years, during part of which period slavery will also occur. Since it is written, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI), and from the year of Isaac’s birth to the year of the exodus from Egypt there are four hundred and five years—which Scripture, in its customary manner, calls four hundred—the offspring was to be foreign during those years, whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt. It may also be understood in this way: from Isaac’s fifth year, when he began to be afflicted through the son of the slave woman, the labor of four hundred years is reckoned.

Joseph summoned his father Jacob and all his kindred, numbering seventy-five persons. He follows the Seventy Translators in saying this; in the Hebrew text, however, only seventy persons are found. But even if you wish to calculate the list of persons in Genesis itself, after adding Jacob himself and Joseph with his two sons, who were in Egypt, you will find only seventy persons.

And he himself died, and so did our fathers, and they were transferred to Shechem. Scripture reports concerning Joseph alone that his bones were carried up from Egypt and buried at Shechem. Yet from these words of blessed Stephen, and from the writings of Saint Jerome, who was a resident of those regions, it should also be understood that the other patriarchs were buried there, although Joseph’s memory is rightly more celebrated: he himself commanded that this be done with his bones, and the city belonged to his tribe. For Jerome reports in his *Life of the Blessed Paula*:

> “He crossed through Shechem”—he says—“not, as most people mistakenly read, Sichar, which is now called Neapolis; and, entering the church built on the side of Mount Gerizim near Jacob’s well, where the Lord sat, he saw it.”

A little later he says:

> “And turning aside from there, he saw the tombs of the twelve patriarchs.”

Likewise, in his book *On the Best Kind of Interpreting*:

> “The twelve patriarchs were not buried at Arbes, but at Shechem.”

But what follows rightly raises a difficulty:

[Col. 0958B] And they were placed in the tomb that Abraham bought for silver from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem. Genesis teaches that Abraham bought from Ephron, son of Seor the Hittite, at Kiriath-arba, a burial place for four hundred silver shekels; there Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam the first-formed man were buried. It also says that Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia, received from Hamor, the father of Shechem, a parcel of land near the city of Shechem on which to pitch his tents, for one hundred lambs. Abraham therefore did not buy a tomb from Hamor the Shechemite, but from Ephron the Hittite; and the twelve patriarchs were not buried in that tomb, but at Shechem, as we have said. Yet blessed Stephen, speaking according to common usage, follows the common opinion in his speech. Joining two accounts together, he attends not so much to the order of the surrounding history as to the issue under discussion. Since he was accused of speaking against the holy place and the Law, he proceeds to show how Jesus Christ is demonstrated by the Law to have been promised, and that they had preferred to serve neither Moses then nor the Lord now. I have said this as best I could, without prejudging a better judgment, if one exists. Moreover, where it says “from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem,” the Greek exemplar reads: “from the sons of Hamor, who was in Shechem.” This seems more consistent with the history in Genesis, although it could have happened that the same Hamor had a father and a son named Shechem.

As the time of the promise drew near, which God had confessed to Abraham. Namely, the promise of which it was said: “And after this they will go out and serve me in this place.”

Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Throughout his whole speech he rebukes them for having already been opposed to the Law and to Moses.

This is the Moses who said to the children of Israel: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.” “Like me”: visible in the flesh, but more wondrous and terrifying than I in majesty. “Let no one say,” he means, “that Christ’s teaching is new and adventitious. Moses himself, whom your fathers refused to obey, proclaims that he would come in the form of a man and give the precepts of life to all souls.”

Did you offer me victims or sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness? Although they offered sacrifices because they were obliged to serve the Lord, they are rightly said to have served idols in their hearts from the time when they transformed gold into the head of a calf. For although we later read that they offered certain things to the Lord, they did so not willingly but, as we learn from this passage, out of fear of punishment and of the death of those who fell because of the idols. The Lord, however, regards not what is offered but the will of those who offer it. Accordingly, whenever opportunity arose, they always returned in their hearts to Egypt.

And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch. “Although,” he says, “you appeared to bring victims and sacrifices to the Lord’s tabernacle, with the full intention of your minds you embraced the shrine of Moloch.” Moloch, or Melchom, as it is also frequently written, is the idol of the Ammonites; its name is interpreted as “your king.”

[Col. 0959B] And the star of your god Remphan. “You abandoned,” he says, “the true and living God and accepted the star Remphan—that is, your own creation—as your god.” It signifies Lucifer, whose worship the people of the Saracens had embraced in honor of Venus. And because Remphan, as I said, is interpreted as “your creation,” or “your rest,” the prophet consequently added:

The images that you made, to worship them. The omitted construction is to be supplied by common usage (*apo koinou*, ἀπὸ κοινοῦ).

And I will carry you beyond Babylon. “Because of these sacrileges,” he says, “you will be led captive not only into Babylon but also beyond Babylon.” The first martyr should not be thought to have erred because, instead of “beyond Damascus,” which is written in the prophet (Amos V), he said “beyond Babylon.” He put the meaning rather than the word, for they were led beyond Damascus into Babylon, just as they were led beyond Babylon.

The tabernacle of the testimony was with our fathers in the wilderness. Because they accused him of acting against the holy place, he shows here that the Lord does not value an ornamented stone but desires the splendor of souls directed toward heaven. He wishes it to be understood that, just as the tabernacle was abandoned when the Temple was built, so the Temple itself should be understood as destined to be destroyed when a better order succeeded it. In accordance with this, Jeremiah once foretold, saying: “Do not trust in words of falsehood, saying, ‘The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord is this’” (Jerem. VII). And a little later: “I will do to this house, in which my name has been invoked and in which you trust, as I did to Shiloh, where my name dwelt from the beginning, and I will cast you out from my presence” (ibid.).

[Col. 0959D] Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. This should not be understood carnally, as though God had limbs placed in heaven and on earth in the manner in which we sit. Rather, to show that he is within and above all things, he declared heaven to be his throne and earth the footstool of his feet. To show that he also surrounds all things, elsewhere he says that he measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful. Spiritually, heaven signifies the saints and earth sinners, because God dwells as ruler over the former, while he casts down the latter in condemnation.

[Col. 0960A] Or what is the place of my rest? Certainly not a golden or marble place of an earthly dwelling, but the one the prophet adds: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI).

You received the Law through the disposition of angels. For the Law was ordained through angels, by the hand of a mediator.

Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Since the Lord Christ is the perfect Son both of God and of man, why did blessed Stephen prefer to call him the Son of Man rather than the Son of God? He would evidently have attributed greater glory to him if he had chosen to call him the Son of God rather than the Son of Man—unless it was so that, by this testimony, the unbelief of the Jews might be confounded, since they remembered having crucified a man and refused to believe that he was God. To strengthen the blessed martyr’s endurance, therefore, the door of the heavenly kingdom is opened; and so that an innocent man, being stoned, would not stumble on earth, the crucified God-man appears crowned in heaven. Since standing signifies one who fights or helps, he rightly saw him standing at God’s right hand, because among the men who persecuted him he had him as his helper. Nor does it seem discordant that Mark describes him as sitting at God’s right hand, since sitting is the posture of one who judges: even now he judges all things invisibly, and at the end he will come visibly as judge of all.

And they drove him outside the city and stoned him. The Lord also suffered outside the gate; he chose us from the world for his heavenly kingdom and glory, and Stephen, as a stranger to the world, is stoned outside the city. For here he had no abiding city but sought the one to come with his whole mind. In a fitting reversal of things, the martyr directs the gaze of his heart from the world to the heavens, while the persecutor of stiff neck stretches out his hands toward stones. Hence Arator says:

> The rebellious Jewish people, crazed,  
> seize stones and rush upon Stephen;  
> by your hardened crime you will always be stony.

But kneeling down, he cried out with a loud voice, saying: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. He prayed standing for himself, but knelt for his enemies, because their greater wickedness demanded a greater remedy of supplication. Wonderful was the virtue of the blessed martyr: he burned with zeal so that he openly reproached those who held him for the faults of their unbelief, yet he burned with love so that even in death he prayed for those by whom he was being killed.

## CHAPTER VIII

And all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria. This is what the Lord himself commanded: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. X). It happened by his will, so that the occasion of tribulation might become the seedbed of the Gospel.

The crowds paid attention to what was said by Philip. Both from the present chapter and from the story of the Samaritan woman, it is proved that this people was ready to believe.

Then Simon himself also believed. Either, overcome by the words and power of blessed Philip, he truly believed in the Lord; or, as is more credible, he pretended to believe until he received baptism, so that, being exceedingly desirous of praise and wishing to be believed a Christ himself, as the histories relate, he might learn from Philip the arts by which he performed miracles. His successors are also said to have done this: instructed by their founder in his wicked arts, they entered the Church through every kind of deceit and made a habit of stealing baptism.

They sent Peter and John to them. Arator beautifully explains this:

> Peter often makes John his companion,  
> because the virgin is pleasing to the Church.

It should be noted, however, that Philip, who was evangelizing Samaria, was one of the seven. If he had been an Apostle, he himself could certainly have laid hands on them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For this belongs only to bishops. Presbyters may baptize, whether without a bishop or in the bishop’s presence, and they may anoint the baptized with chrism; but they may not sign the forehead with the same oil consecrated by a bishop. This belongs only to bishops when they confer the Spirit, the Paraclete, upon the baptized.

May your money be with you for destruction, and so forth. When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it does not burst forth from a desire formed by their own will, but from the justice of judgment. Within themselves they perceive God’s subtle judgment and recognize that the evils which rise outwardly deserve to be struck by a curse. They do not sin in cursing, since their curse does not disagree with the inward judgment. For when the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even to destruction, the outcome of both parties shows that the sentence against the guilty has been hurled by one and the same inward judge. Thus Simon, who received a curse from Peter, perished by eternal condemnation. Likewise, later, Bar-Jesus, rebuked by Paul, was immediately deprived of the common light.

For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.
