For this reason the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, to teach those who wished to receive him that they should be innocent. Whoever stores the gall of bitterness in his heart, however baptized he may appear, has not been released from the bonds of his iniquity; rather, after being cleansed for the brief moment of the hour of baptism, he is soon oppressed by a more ferocious demon sevenfold. He therefore tries in vain to purchase the grace of the Spirit who has not cleansed himself in his mind of the raven’s nature.

Rise and go toward the south. He is rightly sought, found, and washed at noon who, burning with devotion of heart, deserved to be consecrated to God as a kind of firstfruits of the nations. In him that saying of the Psalmist was especially fulfilled: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God.”

To the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza—this is desert. It is not the road but Gaza that is called desert. For that ancient Gaza, which was once the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt, was destroyed down to its foundations, and another city was built elsewhere in its place. Allegorically, it signifies the people of the Gentiles, formerly deserted by the worship of God and cultivated by the preaching of none of the prophets. The road that descends to it from Jerusalem and opens the fountain of salvation is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He descended from the Jerusalem above to our weakness and whitened the blackness of our guilt with the water of baptism.

And behold, an Ethiopian eunuch, a powerful man. He is called a man because of the strength and integrity of his mind; and not undeservedly, since he had such zeal for the Scriptures that he did not cease reading them even while traveling, and such love for religion that, abandoning the royal court, he came from the remotest parts of the world to the Lord’s Temple. Therefore, while rightly seeking an interpreter of his reading, he found the Christ whom he was seeking; and, as Jerome says, he found more at the Church’s fountain in the wilderness than he sought again in the synagogue’s gilded Temple. There was fulfilled what Jeremiah says in wonder: “The Ethiopian has changed his skin”; that is, after the filth of sins had been washed away, he came up from Jesus’ bath made white.

Of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. In the Book of Kings we also read that the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. It was customary for that nation always to be ruled by women, and to call them Candaces.

Who was over all her treasures. By sending the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians to Jerusalem, he signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which would offer to the Lord the gifts of virtues and faith. The etymology of the name also agrees with this. “Candace” can be interpreted as a Hebrew-derived form meaning “the one who changes.” She is the one to whom, in the psalm entitled “For those who will be changed,” it is said: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV), and so forth.

But the Spirit said to Philip. The Spirit spoke to Philip in his heart. To say that the Spirit of God spoke words to us is to say that, by a hidden power, he imitates in us the things that ought to be done.

He was led like a sheep to slaughter. As a sheep, when it is led to the sacrifice, does not resist, so he suffered of his own will. Or, in a higher sense, just as a lamb used to be sacrificed at Passover, so Christ our Passover was sacrificed (I Cor. V).

And like a lamb before its shearer is silent. He not only redeemed us with his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm those chilled by their unbelief with his garment, and so that we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.” Thus he did not open his mouth when, in his Passion, he wished to give only a few answers to Pilate and the chief priests and none at all to Herod.

In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him. Since the judge of all found no truth in the judgment, he was condemned without any guilt by the riotous demand of the Jews and the voice of Pilate.

Who will recount his generation? This may be understood of his divinity: it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of divine birth, of which the Father says, “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX). Or it may refer to the Virgin’s childbirth, which can scarcely be explained. When Mary asks its manner, she is told through the angel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” Thus the mysteries of his birth are spoken of only by the angel or by the evangelist, whose account of it is exceedingly brief.

Because his life will be taken from the earth. So that he might live not on earth but in heaven.

Then Philip opened his mouth, and so forth. Philip is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp,” and the meaning is beautiful: the mouth of the lamp opened its mouth when it brought the obscurities of prophecy into the light of knowledge. Yet, according to the historical sense, this circumlocution may also indicate that his speech at that time would be somewhat longer.

They came to a certain water. Even today there is a village called Bethsoro in the tribe of Judah, twenty miles from Elia as one travels toward Hebron. Near it, a spring wells up at the foot of the mountain and is swallowed by the same earth from which it arises. At this place the eunuch was baptized by Philip.

What prevents me from being baptized? And he ordered the chariot to stop, and so forth. Another Translation, according to the Greek exemplar, has several additional verses here, where it is written: “Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?” Philip said to him: “If you believe with all your heart, you will be saved.” He answered: “I believe in Christ, the Son of God.” And he ordered the chariot to stop, and so forth. I therefore believe that our translator also originally translated these verses, but that they were later removed through the negligence of scribes.

The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away. Some testify that an angel did this through the Holy Spirit, as Jerome reports.

He evangelized all the cities until he came to Caesarea. He means Caesarea of Palestine, where he is later described as having a house, which is still shown today, together with the chamber of his four virgin daughters who prophesied.

## CHAPTER IX

Now Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord. That is, afflicting those present with murders and terrifying those absent with threats.

Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my members?” but “Why are you persecuting me?” For he himself, in his body, which is the Church, still suffers from the wicked. He declares that benefits bestowed upon the members of that body have been bestowed upon him when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV). Explaining this, he adds: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (ibid.).

I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. He did not say, “I am God” or “I am the Son of God,” but, he means: “Receive the weakness of my humility and lay aside the scales of your pride.”

Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do. He did not immediately show him what had to be done, but foretold that he would hear it later in the city, so that he might stand more firmly in goodness afterward, having first been utterly overthrown and fallen from his former error.

And when his eyes had been opened, he saw nothing. He could not have seen well again unless he had first been well blinded, excluding the personal wisdom by which he was disturbed and committing himself in all things to faith.

And for three days he was unable to see. Because he had not believed that the Lord had conquered death by rising on the third day, he is now instructed by his own example, changing three days of darkness into light restored.

For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name. “He must not,” he says, “be feared as a persecutor but rather embraced as a brother, since he is ready to endure with the saints the adversities that he had inflicted upon them.”

And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes. The entire body of a dragon is said to be covered with scales. Since the Jews were called serpents and offspring of vipers, the one who followed their unbelief had, as it were, covered the eyes of his heart with a serpent’s skin. But when the scales fell from his eyes at the hand of Ananias, it was shown outwardly on his face that he had already received the true light in his mind.

His disciples took him by night. That is, the disciples of Christ. In Greek, the word “his” is not added, but only “disciples,” so that they may be understood generally as the disciples of Christ or of the Church. For Paul is not yet read to have made disciples; he had only confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus.

They let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket. This mode of escape is still preserved in the Church when someone, surrounded by the snares of the ancient enemy or by the traps of this age, is saved by the bulwark of his own hope and faith. For the wall of Damascus—which is interpreted as “drinking blood”—is the adversity of the world. King Aretas, whose name is interpreted as “descent,” signifies the devil. The basket, which is customarily made from reeds and palm branches, signifies the union of faith and hope. The reed signifies the greenness of faith; the palm, hope of eternal life. Whoever therefore sees himself surrounded by the wall of adversity should hasten to climb into the basket of virtues by which he may escape.

When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join himself to the disciples. We should not suppose that, immediately after being baptized, he came to the apostles in Jerusalem. Rather, as he himself wrote to the Galatians, he first went to Arabia and then returned again to Damascus. Afterward, coming to Jerusalem three years later, he saw Peter and stayed with him for fifteen days. He saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. Then, as Luke also relates, he came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. Whether he endured the ambushes at Damascus on his first or second visit is not easily clear. The second visit can also be understood from the statement that, after many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him. Luke seems to omit Arabia because Paul did not preach there, in accordance with what he himself says later when speaking to King Agrippa: “In Damascus first, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I preached.”

But Barnabas took him and led him to the apostles. This is that Barnabas, a Cypriot by birth and a Levite, who above is remembered as having brought the price of his field and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

[Col. 0965A] He also spoke and disputed with the Greeks. Note that he taught Greeks in Jerusalem and Jews in Damascus, which is a Gentile city, lest this perhaps signify that the Gentiles would be assisted into the city of God, while the Jews would fall into the faithlessness of the Gentiles. In accordance with what Isaiah says: “Lebanon shall be turned into Carmel, and Carmel shall be reckoned as a forest” (Isa. XXIX).

Now he found there a certain man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a pallet for eight years. This Aeneas signifies the human race, formerly languishing in the delight of the weak, but healed through the apostles’ work and word. For since the world itself is raised up by four regions, and the course of the age is varied by the year’s four seasons, whoever embraces present and passing pleasures is laid out, as though on a pallet, weakened by the number eight years [that is, twice four]. The pallet itself is slothfulness, where the sick and infirm soul rests—that is, in bodily pleasure and every worldly delight.

“Aeneas, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you. Rise and make your bed.” The one whom he had cured of paralysis he immediately commanded to rise and make his bed, signifying spiritually that whoever has received the firm foundation of faith in his heart should not merely shake off the torpor in which he had lain exhausted, but should also prepare good works in which he may be able to rest.

Now in Joppa there was a certain female disciple named Tabitha, which is translated as Dorcas—that is, “doe” or “she-goat.” She signifies souls exalted by their devotion to virtue, but despised in human opinion. [Col. 0965C] For blessed Luke would not have added the interpretation of the name unless he recognized that a great mystery lay within it. A doe and a she-goat are animals similar in nature but different in size; they dwell on lofty mountains and, although from far away, nevertheless see all who come. Hence in Greek they are called *dorkades* (δορκάδες), from their sharpness of sight. In the same way, the saints, dwelling on high through the merits of their works, attentively direct their minds toward heavenly things and constantly keep watch over themselves with careful circumspection. For since these animals are clean according to the Law, but timid and unarmed—expressing their nature, Martial says:

> The boar is feared for its tusk; the stag is defended by its antlers;  
> What are timid does but prey?

Does this not plainly signify those who strive to live simply and to walk with a disciplined step in their conduct, as though with a divided hoof, and to ruminate on the word of God through continual meditation? If through ignorance or weakness they should incur spiritual death, they nevertheless deserve to be restored to life because of the integrity of their right intention, as is shown to have happened to Peter himself, to whom what is written about Dorcas may most appropriately be applied.

Now it happened in those days that she became ill and died. For when the saints commit some offense through the frailty of mortal nature, they perish, as it were, in the days of their good works, through the cause of a sudden illness. But when they immediately devote themselves to tears, ascend toward the hope of recovering virtue, invoke the aid of the saints, and recall the good deeds they had interrupted, they certainly do what follows.

“After washing her, they placed her in the upper room.” And the rest, in which Peter’s summons and the display of Dorcas’s alms are related.

“And all the widows stood around him, weeping.” The widows are the devout thoughts of the penitent soul, which for a time had laid aside the vigor of their former understanding, as though the governance of a husband, and which must earnestly intercede for the sinful soul.

“And showing him the tunics and garments that Dorcas made for them.” They pleaded not with their own words for the dead woman, but through her works, because almsgiving liberates not only from the second death but also from the first.

“He said: ‘Tabitha, arise.’ She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.” The order of the one rising is most fitting: first she opens the eyes of the mind, and then, recognizing Peter’s voice, sits up; she recovers the light of her vigilance, which she had lost, and lives according to the teaching of those who had helped her.

“Giving her his hand, he raised her up.” Tabitha rises when Peter’s hand touches her, because the soul weakened by sins recovers in no better way than through the examples of the saints.

## CHAPTER X

“Now there was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius,” etc. Faith is reached not through virtues, but virtues through faith, as blessed Pope Gregory explains. “For Cornelius,” he says, “whose alms were praised before baptism with an angel as witness, came not through works to faith, but through faith to works. For if he had not previously believed in the true God, whom was he praying to? Or how could almighty God have heard him if he did not show that he was being perfected in good things by him? He therefore knew God, the Creator of all, but did not know that his almighty Son had become incarnate. He possessed the faith by which his prayers and alms could please God. By good action he merited to know God perfectly and to believe in the mystery of the Incarnation of his Only-Begotten, so that he might reach the sacrament of baptism. Through faith, therefore, he came to works, but through works he was made firm in faith.”

“He clearly saw in a vision, about the ninth hour of the day,” etc. He appropriately receives the oracle concerning the seeking of baptism at the ninth hour, because he was to be baptized in the death of the one who surrendered his spirit at the ninth hour.

“And now send men to Joppa.” Since, after his alms and prayers had been received, he is immediately commanded to summon a teacher of salvation, it is plainly indicated that through those alms and prayers he had sought from the Lord a complete knowledge of his salvation.

“He called two of his household servants and a soldier who feared the Lord.” Cornelius sent three men to Peter, because the Gentile world, which was to believe, subjected Europe, Asia, and Africa to the apostolic faith, to be won partly by military pursuits—that is, the urgency of preaching—and partly by household occupations. Note that one soldier and two household servants are sent. For the stronger they are, the fewer you will find among the members of the Church; there are more who know how to hear the word than who know how to speak it.

“Peter went up to the upper parts.” This signifies the Church, which, having abandoned earthly desires, is to have its way of life in heaven.

“To pray about the sixth hour.” At the sixth hour Peter becomes hungry in the midst of his prayers—specifically, for the salvation of the world, which the Lord had come to seek and save at the sixth age of the world. He also wished to indicate this when, at that same hour of the day, he thirsted beside the Samaritan woman’s well.

“And a certain vessel like a great linen cloth descended.” That vessel signifies the Church, endowed with incorruptible faith. For the linen moth does not consume linen, although it corrupts other garments. Therefore whoever wishes to belong to the mystery of the Catholic Church should expel corruption from his heart—that is, evil thoughts—and should be so firmly established in incorruptibility of faith that his mind is not gnawed by wicked thoughts as by moths. Alternatively: The moth is the heretic, wishing to corrupt the Lord’s garment but unable to do so because the Lord orders otherwise. This was also represented in that garment of the Lord which the soldiers did not dare to tear.

“To be lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners.” The four corners by which the linen cloth hung designate the four regions of the world, across which the Church is extended. For she is “the city of our God, on his holy mountain,” spreading joy throughout the whole earth. That it is lowered from heaven indicates that it is preserved and increased solely by the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon it. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God” (Rev. XXI). The four corners may also represent the four evangelists, through whom the Church is nourished and exalted by a heavenly gift.

“In it were all the four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth and the birds of heaven.” Those animals are all the nations, unclean through their errors but cleansed by a threefold immersion—that is, through the mystery of the Holy Trinity in baptism. They abandon the image of man and have taken on the forms of beasts and serpents. Hence, because of his deceitful wickedness, Herod is told: “Go, tell that fox” (Luke XIII). And to the Pharisees: “Broods of vipers” (Luke III). And of the lustful: “They became raging horses toward women” (Jer. V). And of the shameless: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII). And of the pleasure-loving: “Nor cast your pearls before swine” (ibid.). And of the proud and deceitful together: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests” (Matt. VIII). And generally of all: “Though man was in honor”—that is, made in the image of God—“he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII). But Solomon points out the true, that is, incorrupt, man when he says: “Fear God and observe his commandments. For this is every man” (Eccl. XII).

“Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” “Rise,” he says, “prepare yourself to evangelize. Kill in the Gentiles what they were, and make them what you are. For whoever eats food set outside transfers it into his own body. He therefore commands that the nations, previously placed outside through unbelief, be joined to the society of the Church, which Peter signifies, after their former life has been killed. In accordance with what the apostle Paul says of himself: “For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God and for Christ.” And again: “I live, yet now it is not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). But those who are surrounded by heretics are devoured as though alive by death.

“For I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” The Jewish people, boasting that it is God’s portion, calls “common” the foods used by all human beings—for example, pork, oysters, hares, and animals of this sort that do not divide the hoof or chew the cud, as well as fish without scales. “Unclean foods,” however, are called the flesh of beasts or reptiles, inedible to any mortal.

[Col. 0968B] “This happened three times.” Because the mystery of the Holy Trinity was to be preached by the twelve apostles throughout the four regions of the world, the four lines were lowered from heaven a third time. Or, as blessed Ambrose interprets it, the figure repeated three times expressed the work of the Trinity. Therefore in the mysteries the questioning is threefold, the confirmation is celebrated threefold, and no one can be cleansed except by a threefold confession. Hence in the Gospel Peter himself is asked three times whether he loves the Lord, so that by a threefold reply he might release the bonds with which he had bound the Lord by denying him. These things were appropriately shown to Peter when the Gentile Cornelius sent for him, so that he would not hesitate to hand on the Christian faith to the uncircumcised. For Cornelius belonged to those animals displayed in the Gospel vessel. [Col. 0968C] Hence he is also confirmed by the Holy Spirit in doing this very thing.

“And immediately the vessel was taken up into heaven.” After the threefold lowering, the linen cloth is received into heaven, because after the Church’s life in this age—during which, cleansed through faith and baptism, she journeys as an exile—there follows a blessed and eternal heavenly dwelling.

“The Spirit said to him: ‘Behold, three men are seeking you.’” He heard this in his mind from the Spirit, not in the ear of the flesh.

“Rise, therefore, go down, and go with them.” He is commanded to descend from the roof and go to preach, so that the Church may not merely contemplate the Lord by ascending to lofty things, but may also return to active life and preach him to the weak and to those still situated, as it were, outside, yet knocking at the door of Simon—that is, at obedience—like one rising from bed. In accordance with what the Lord says: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John I).

His house is appropriately said to have been situated beside the sea. The sea signifies the tumult and fury of the world, tossed by waves, where wicked people, like extremely greedy fish, pursue and devour one another. But “the citizenship of the saints is in heaven” (Phil. III). Even if the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, they have a building from God, “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V).

“Behold, I am the one whom you seek. What is the reason for which you have come?” The Spirit told him that the soldiers were present, but kept silent about why they had come, because, to preserve the humility of the human mind, the Spirit of prophecy sometimes touches one part and does not touch another.

“And it happened that when Peter had entered, Cornelius came to meet him, and falling at his feet, worshiped.” By the gesture of his body Cornelius displays in advance the devotion he possessed within his heart. The hearer comes to meet his teacher when he receives the word of faith with a pure heart, a diligent and attentive ear, and eager desire. For one who is dragged slowly toward belief is raised up, as it were, by the teacher from a lying position. But one who, ashamed of the stains of his life, falls on his face and thereby displays signs alike of humility and shame, rightly merits being raised by his instructor.

“But Peter lifted him up, saying: ‘Rise; I myself am also a man.’” The holiness of his conduct earned the fellowship of equality. For in the fault of Ananias and Sapphira, zeal for vengeance displayed the right of power.

“And God showed me not to call any man common or unclean.” He showed this at the time when the angelic voice sounded: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”

“Four days ago, up to this hour, I was praying at the ninth hour in my house,” and so forth. In the Greek and in certain Latin manuscripts it is written as follows: “Four days ago, up to this hour, I was fasting, and praying from the sixth hour until the ninth, and behold, a man,” and so forth. It was very fitting that he should be heard who, continuing his earnest prayer for three hours, extended it from the sixth hour to the ninth. At that time the Lord himself, whom he was entreating, was praying for the salvation of the whole world with his hands extended on the cross.

“He sent the word to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all.” In this, he says, it is evident that God is not a respecter of persons, because he sent his Only-Begotten Son, who is both Lord and Creator of all, to make peace with the human race. In his name, with the prophets bearing witness, not only Jews but all who believe receive the forgiveness of sins.

“You know what took place throughout all Judea,” and so forth. He briefly gathered together everything said in the Creed: that Jesus is the Christ; that he is Lord of all; that he was sent to reconcile the world to God; that he was heralded by the voice of John; that he was anointed by the Holy Spirit; that, with God dwelling in him, he was manifested through miracles; that he was crucified, raised from the dead, and manifested to his own; that he will come as judge of all at the end; and that he will also spread his Church throughout the whole world by faith.

“How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power.” Another edition reads: “As God anointed him.” John therefore preached Jesus as one whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit, specifically when he said: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. III). And again: “Because I saw the Spirit descending like a dove upon him” (John I). Jesus was therefore anointed not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized. Yet he was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit when the Spirit descended upon him after his baptism in the likeness of a dove. At that time he graciously chose to prefigure his body—that is, his Church—in which chiefly those who are baptized receive the Holy Spirit. Rather, he is to be understood as having been anointed with that mystical and invisible anointing when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person. For this reason we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

“Because God was with him.” That is, the Father was with the Son. It is better to understand it in this way than to signify that the Son’s divinity was dwelling with the man whom he assumed, lest we appear to divide Christ into two persons and fall into the doctrine of Nestorius.

“To us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.” Here blessed Peter explains what is not recited in the Gospel: namely, that after the resurrection he drank with the Lord. Unless perhaps we believe that it was indicated there where he says: “Until I drink it anew with you in my Father’s house.”

“While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were hearing the word.” Then they asked him to remain with them for several days. So that there might be no doubt about baptism being given to the Gentiles, this is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who anticipates in a new order the very waters of the bath that he usually sanctifies. This is found to have happened once as a testimony to the faith of the Gentiles, but never among the Jews.

[Col. 0970C] “And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. And the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the gift of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations,” and so forth. Since the Church’s rule is that the faithful be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, the question arises how Luke, throughout the text of this entire little book, testifies that baptism was given only in the name of Jesus Christ. Blessed Ambrose resolves this by saying that the mystery was fulfilled through the unity of the name. For whether you say “Christ,” and thereby designate God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed, the Son himself, who was anointed, and the Spirit with whom he was anointed—for it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit”—or whether you say “Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth, provided you also comprehend this in your heart; or whether you say “Spirit,” you have named God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit also belongs to the Son. Hence, so that authority may be joined to reason, Scripture also indicates that we may rightly be baptized in the Spirit, when the Lord says: “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts I). And the Apostle says: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (I Cor. XII). Alternatively: It is especially fitting that we be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, because, as the Apostle says: “All who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death,” and so forth (Rom. VI).

## CHAPTER XI

“And I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, and beasts, and reptiles, and birds of heaven,” etc. I am amazed that these things are interpreted as referring to certain foods forbidden by the old Law but now permitted to be eaten, since neither snakes nor reptiles can be eaten, nor did Peter himself understand it in this way. Rather, he understood that all human beings alike are summoned to Christ’s Gospel and that no one is by nature polluted. For he was not rebuked for eating beasts, but for associating with Gentiles; and he explained the mystery of this vision.

“Now these six brothers also came with me.” Beautifully, by the witness of the seven brothers, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is shown to have been poured out. Alternatively: Because this world was formed in six days, the six brothers signify perfected works. They appropriately accompany the teacher when, amid words of exhortation, they display to their hearers examples of perfected action.

“And they glorified God, saying: ‘Then God has also granted repentance leading to life to the Gentiles.’” This is what we read in the book of blessed Job: “Gold shall come from the north, and praise fearful to God” (Job XXXVII). For first, from the cold heart of the Gentiles, the splendor of faith arose, and because of this unexpected faith Judea glorifies God with trembling.

“They traveled as far as Phoenice, Cyprus, and Antioch,” etc. From this point, after the revelation of the evangelical linen cloth, upon which the holy animals might rest softly in heavenly hope, the affairs of the Church began to grow, as the Gospel was preached through foreign provinces, islands, and cities, not only to Jews but also to Gentiles.

“He departed for Tarsus to seek Saul.” For it was said above that Saul was secretly sent from Jerusalem to Tarsus.

“And one of them named Agabus rose up and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was to come.” Agabus may be interpreted as “messenger of tribulation.” In accordance with his name, he prophesies here a general famine and below chains for the apostle Paul.

“They resolved to send a contribution to the brothers dwelling in Judea.” They knew that famine would rage most severely in Judea, and especially in Jerusalem. There the poor among the saints were those who, after selling their possessions, houses, and fields and bringing the proceeds to the apostles, had little time left for acquiring money. Moreover, some were deprived of their own property by unbelieving Jews because of their confession of faith. To them the Apostle says: “You joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions” (Heb. X). Among those who gave alms, the religious deed of Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, is remembered. After purchasing grain from Egypt, she supplied the needs of the inhabitants of Jerusalem with the greatest generosity. Hence she also merited an honorable burial before the gates of that city.

## CHAPTER XII

“Now at that same time King Herod laid hands [the source breaks off].” This was evidently not during the time of the famine, which histories report as having occurred in the fourth year of Claudius, since Herod died in the third year of that emperor, but at the time when offerings were being brought to Jerusalem. We should not suppose that the Herod who had been tetrarch and was later made king is meant in this chapter. For Josephus reports that Caius, after assuming power, immediately handed the principate of the Jews to this Herod, the son of Aristobulus, whom he nevertheless calls Agrippa, and likewise gave tetrarchies to Philip and Lysanias. In the fourth—that is, the final—year of his reign, he also bestowed them upon that same Herod. But Herod himself, who had either been responsible for John’s death or had been present at the Lord’s Passion, he condemned to perpetual exile after torturing him with many diseases. Furthermore, this Herod, or Agrippa, was struck by an angel in the third year of Claudius and the seventh of his own reign, and left the kingdom to his son Agrippa. Aristobulus, whom Josephus mentioned, was the one who, with his brother Alexander, had been killed by his treacherous father, the elder Herod, under whom the Lord was born.

“He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.” Concerning this James, Clement of Alexandria relates a memorable story. “The man,” he says, “who had brought him before the judge for execution—James, that is—was himself moved and confessed that he was a Christian. Both were led together to punishment. As they were being taken along the road, he asked James to grant him forgiveness. After a brief deliberation, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded together.”

“Delivering him to four squads of soldiers.” Just as a centurion had a hundred men under him, so a squad of four soldiers had soldiers under its command.

“And striking Peter’s side, he awakened him.” The striking of his side recalls the Passion of Christ, from whose wound our salvation flowed. To us also, held fast by the chain of afflictions, the apostle Peter himself offers such consolation, saying: “Since Christ therefore suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought” (I Pet. IV).

“Gird yourself and put on your sandals.” We read that prophets and apostles used belts; because of the severity of the prison, Peter had loosened his bindings for a time, allowing his tunic to fall around his feet and thereby tempering the cold of the night to some extent. He thus gives an example to the weak: when we are tested either by bodily hardship or by human injury, we may relax something of the strictness of our chosen way of life. And because it is said, “Let your loins be girded, and your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace,” he is spiritually commanded to resume the insignia of virtue and of preaching the word.

[Col. 0972D] “They came to the iron gate that leads to the city.” Narrow—indeed, iron—was the gate that leads to the heavenly Jerusalem, but it has already been made passable for us by the apostles’ footsteps, who conquered the iron door with their own blood. Concerning this, Arator writes:

> Iron gates—what wonder if they yield to Peter,  
> whom God appoints guardian of the heavenly court,  
> making him retain the summit of his Church  
> and commanding him to overcome hell?

“And Peter, coming to himself.” That is, he returned from the summit of contemplation to what had previously been present in ordinary understanding.

“The girl came forward to listen.” The first woman announced to the disciples that the Lord had emerged from the enclosure of the tomb, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.

[Col. 0973A] “But they were saying: ‘It is his angel.’” That each one of us has an angel is found in the *Shepherd* and in many passages of Holy Scripture. The Lord also says concerning little ones: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII). Jacob says of himself: “The angel who rescued me from all evils.” Here too the disciples believed that Peter’s angel had come.

“Coming down from Judea to Caesarea.” Although, according to the location of the places, this may seem to refer to Caesarea Philippi, since it, like Tyre and Sidon, is a city of Phoenicia, nevertheless, as Josephus explains, we learn that these events took place in Caesarea of Palestine, formerly called Strato’s Tower. It lies on the border of Phoenicia and Palestine, situated on the shore of the Great Sea.

[Col. 0973B] “They were asking for peace, because their region was nourished by him.” They needed the friendship of their neighboring king because their territory was very narrow and hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and Damascus. Hence even their metropolis, Tyre, did not possess from its own land such wealth as would allow it to be the marketplace of the whole world; it possessed such wealth from the mooring of ships. It is especially rich in purple dye and shellfish.

“But immediately the angel of the Lord struck him.” Josephus likewise agrees: “Because,” he says, “he did not shrink from the impiety of unlawful flattery, he looked up and soon saw an angel threatening and standing over his head; and he immediately recognized him as the minister of his destruction, whom previously he had known as the provider of good things.” And shortly afterward: “But, tormented by continual abdominal pains for five days, he violently ended his life.”

## CHAPTER XIII

“Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have taken them.” According to the order of the history, Saul appears to have received the apostleship with Barnabas and the name Paul in the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion. In the fourteenth year, in accordance with the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, he set out to teach the Gentiles. Nor does ecclesiastical history contradict this when it says that the apostles were commanded to preach in Judea for twelve years.

“They were preaching the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews.” [Col. 0973D] For the sake of those unfamiliar with the places, I thought it should be noted once: wherever you see a synagogue of the Jews, know that the events being described took place in a city.

“Whose name was Barjeu.” It is read corruptly as *Barjesu*, whereas it should be read *Barjeu*, that is, “sorcerer,” or “in evil.” I believe this is because the name *Jesu* is written with the same letters, but with a mark placed above it. For it is not appropriate to call a wicked and magical man the son of Jesus—that is, of the Savior—when Paul, on the contrary, calls him the son of the devil.

“But Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit.” He received the name Paul from the proconsul Sergius Paulus, because he had brought him under the faith of Christ. The following sections of this little book deal with Paul’s miracles. It was fitting that he should bring apostolic acts to completion, the one whom the Lord had chosen after he had long kicked against the goads.

“Behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind.” The Apostle, mindful of his own example, knew that one could rise from the darkness of the eyes of the mind into the light. For he did not deserve to have the eyes of the flesh who was striving to take away the eyes of the mind from others.

“They came to Antioch of Pisidia.” There are two cities called Antioch: one in Coele Syria, founded by King Seleucus, formerly called Rebla, near which they say the spring Daphne is located and whose waters it enjoys in great abundance; in that city the disciples were first called Christians. The other is the Antioch of which the text now speaks, in the province of Pisidia.

“He distributed their land to them by lot, as if after four hundred and fifty years.” God had said to Abraham that his offspring would be an inhabitant in a foreign land for four hundred years. And again he said: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” From the birth of the offspring, therefore, until Israel’s departure from Egypt, there were—as Exodus records—four hundred and five years. Add to these forty years in the wilderness and five in the land of Canaan, after which the land appears to have rested from battles and the lot to have been cast, and you will find four hundred and fifty years.

“And God gave them Saul for forty years.” I believe that, because the Book of Kings does not plainly state how many years Saul reigned, the Apostle wished to say what the more common report held. But when we investigate the matter more carefully there, as the Books of Chronicles also attest, we find that Samuel and Saul governed Israel for forty years. For it says: “In the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, Solomon began to build the temple of the Lord, in the fourth year of his reign.” When you add to the three hundred and ninety-six years during which the judges ruled, as their book indicates, forty years of David and four of Solomon, forty remain; during these, as Josephus testifies, Samuel spent twenty years and Saul another twenty in governance.

“Because God has fulfilled this promise to your children by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” We should not think that this Psalm passage refers to Christ’s resurrection, which he has just mentioned, but rather to his Incarnation, about which he spoke above. For the following verse bears unmistakable witness to the resurrection. Since he had spoken above of Christ’s Incarnation, Passion, and resurrection, he wished to support both together by testimonies from the Psalm. Therefore, he says: “Although you are the eternal Son, before the ages, now you will appear as one born in time.” Some manuscripts have: “As it is written in the first Psalm.” This is explained by taking the first and second Psalms as composed together: the first begins with blessedness and the second ends in blessedness.

“For I will give you the holy and faithful things of David”—that is, whatever I promised David, I, the faithful guarantor, will most certainly fulfill for you: namely, that Christ would be born from his line. Thus Isaiah, anticipating the mysteries of the New Testament, says: “I will establish with you an everlasting covenant, the holy and faithful things of David” (Isa. LV). In the Hebrew truth it is read: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.”

“Many Jews and devout proselytes followed them.” It is better read: “And worshipers of God,” as we saw in the Greek. This signifies those who were Gentiles by nature but Jews by religion, whom the Greeks call *proselytes* (προσήλυτοι).

“For thus the Lord commanded us: ‘I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles.’” What was said specifically to the Lord Christ, the apostles now consider to have been said to themselves, remembering that they are his members, just as he himself said because of the unity of that same body: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

“But they shook the dust from their feet against them and came to Iconium.” In accordance with the Gospel’s command, the dust is shaken from their feet as testimony to their labor: they entered their city, and the apostolic preaching reached them. Or the dust is shaken off so that they receive nothing from them—not even what is necessary for food—because they rejected the Gospel.

“And the disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.” The Greek has: “But the disciples,” so that we may understand that while the Jews were persecuting the faith, the disciples, by contrast, were enriched with spiritual joy.

## CHAPTER XIV

“They stirred up the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers.” The Greek continues: “But God made peace”; certain Latin manuscripts lack this. It also reads there: “They were evangelizing,” followed in the Greek by: “And the whole multitude was moved by their teaching.”

“But Paul and Barnabas remained in Lystra.” These verses too are absent from some of our manuscripts.

“And a certain man in Lystra, who was infirm in his feet, was sitting,” etc. Just as the lame man whom Peter and John healed at the temple gate prefigures the salvation of the Jews, so this sick Lycaonian signifies the people of the Gentiles, far removed from observance of the Law and the temple but gathered through the preaching of the apostle Paul. “They gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship,” he says, “so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision.” The circumstances also suit the interpretation. The former occurred at the beginning of the faith, when the word was not yet believed among the Gentiles; this one, however, occurred after the Jews had been expelled because of their faithlessness and sprinkled with the dust of condemnation, while the Gentiles were being converted and rejoicing.

“And seeing that he had faith to be saved.” The former seeks money from the apostles according to Jewish custom, but this man seeks salvation through faith.

“He said in a loud voice: ‘Stand upright on your feet.’” In a Greek manuscript it is read: “He said in a loud voice: ‘I say to you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, stand upright on your feet.’” We have included this from the translation so that, bewildered by the manuscripts’ variation, you will not be unaware of which reading is the more authentic.

[Col. 0976A] “The gods, made like men, have come down to us.” The foolish error of the Gentiles, who think that everything they see above themselves is a god.

“And they called Barnabas Jupiter,” evidently because he seemed to be their chief. For they believed Jupiter to be the father of the gods and king of men.

“But Paul they called Mercury, because he was the leader of the word,” since they believed Mercury granted eloquence and speech to mortals. Hence the Latins called him Mercury, as though he ran in the middle—that is, between the ears and tongues. The Greeks called him *Hermes* (Ἑρμῆς), that is, “interpreter.”

Bringing bulls and garlands before the gates. [Col. 0976B] Bulls for sacrifices, but garlands either to adorn the façade of the temple according to the Gentile rite, or to place upon them as though he were about to sacrifice them to the gods.

They leapt into the crowd after tearing their garments, and so forth. Terrified, they tear their clothing because they were being honored with the worship due to gods. For this is customary among the Jews whenever they hear something blasphemous and seemingly directed against God. Herod, however, because he did not give honor to God but yielded to the people’s excessive acclamation, was immediately struck by an angel.

## CHAPTER XV

They determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain others from among them, should go up to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem, and so forth. Concerning this journey of his Paul himself writes to the Galatians: “Then, after fourteen years, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also, and I conferred with them about the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles” [Col. 0976C] (Gal. II). The number of years that he gives there must be examined. For we know that the apostles Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion, that is, in the last year of Nero, and that blessed Peter occupied the episcopal chair at Rome for twenty-five years. But twenty-five and fourteen make not thirty-eight, but thirty-nine. We must therefore believe that blessed Peter came to Rome in the fourth year of Claudius Caesar, the same fourteenth year after the Lord’s Passion in which Paul addressed him at Jerusalem. At the same time, unless I am mistaken, this calculation proves that the blessed apostle Paul came to the faith in the very year in which the Lord suffered and rose again.

[Col. 0976D] Saying that it is necessary to circumcise them. The Galatians had been deceived by this error, believing that circumcision and the ceremonies of the Law had to be combined with the grace of baptism.

Purifying their hearts by faith. It is therefore not necessary to cleanse by circumcision of the flesh those whose hearts are so purified by faith that they are deemed worthy to receive the Holy Spirit even before baptism.

But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they do. If they too—that is, the fathers, unable to bear the yoke of the old Law—believed themselves to be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, it is clear that this was the grace that enabled the righteous of ancient times to live. Since “the righteous lives by faith,” [Col. 0977A] the sacraments could be different according to the diversity of times, yet they returned in complete harmony to the unity of the same faith.

“After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen,” and so forth. The tabernacle of David signifies the shadow of the Law. Corrupted and torn apart by the traditions of the Pharisees, it was raised up by God’s spiritual grace when the Lord returned—that is, when he appeared in the flesh—so that not only the Jews but also all the nations of the Gentiles might seek his name.

And from things strangled and from blood—that is, from shedding blood or from eating meat with the blood. These provisions were granted to those coming from Gentile life as elementary beginnings of faith and because of their long-established Gentile custom. But lest they think that the same things were sufficient even for the more perfect, [Col. 0977B] he vigilantly added and said:

“For Moses from ancient times has in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues.” That is: even if we do not now burden them with the severity of the commandments, nevertheless, as time proceeds, when they gather more frequently for the reading of the Law and the Prophets, they will gradually take up the rules of conduct and the obligations of mutual love. For it is understood that the primitive Church, still practicing Judaism, observed these things on the Sabbaths.

“For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” That is, it pleased the Holy Spirit, who, possessing authority over himself, breathes where he wills and speaks what he wills.

“It has seemed good to us also”: not by our will alone, but [Col. 0977C] by the prompting of that same Spirit.

Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch. During these days what the apostle Paul says was fulfilled: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face” (Gal. II).

But Paul was insisting that he should not be accepted. Because he had placed himself directly at the forefront of the battle yet had stood there with excessive lukewarmness, Paul rightly rejected him, lest the strength of the others be corrupted as though by his contagion.

But disagreement arose. Do not consider this a fault. For to be moved is not evil; what is evil is to be moved irrationally and without any just matter demanding it.

And Barnabas, taking Mark with him, sailed to Cyprus. [Col. 0977D] Because of his affection for a brother dear to him and related by blood—for they are said to have been cousins—Barnabas, separated from Paul, returned to his native island, and nevertheless carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER XVI

He circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. This was not because he thought the figures of the Law could provide any benefit once the truth of the Gospel had shone forth, but so that the Jews might not withdraw from the faith on account of the Gentiles. Yet the ancient shadow was to be removed gradually, just as the depravity of the ancient customs of the Gentiles, as stated above. These legal shadows, having once been established by the Lord, were sometimes employed by the Apostles in those times to avert the [Col. 0978A] unbelief of the Jews. The institution of the Gentiles, however, as truly discovered by Satan, was never touched by the saints.

They were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia, and so forth, up to “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.” Truly, the Lord is dreadful in his counsels concerning the sons of men. One promises to follow him as teacher in all things, yet is not permitted to do so; another is ordered to follow, yet is not granted the delay he requested for burying his father. Saul is drawn along, unconquered and resisting. To Cornelius, who persisted in prayers and almsgiving, the way of salvation is shown as a kind of recompense; and God, who knows hearts, removed the Teacher from Asia by the grace of his favor, lest, if what is holy were given to dogs, the wickedness of the heart should be judged more severely for having despised the preaching. Again, while the apostle was attending to other matters, [Col. 0978B] a Macedonian envoy—whom we believe to be the angel of that people—asks that crumbs of the Lord’s bread be offered to him.

Which is the chief city of Macedonia, a colony. A colony is a place filled with new inhabitants because of a shortage of native ones. Hence it is called a colony from the cultivation of the land.

A certain girl who had a spirit of Python. What sort of art Pythonic divination involved we find in the Book of Kings, where, at Saul’s request, the Pythoness summoned from the underworld either Samuel’s soul or, rather, an unclean spirit in his place. They say that this kind of magical apparition was discovered by Apollo Pythius and was thus named from his title. The Hebrew name also agrees with this, [Col. 0978C] for they call Python “the mouth of the abyss.”

“These men are servants of the Most High God.” This is not a confession proceeding from the will, followed by the reward of confessing; rather, compelled by fear of the Holy Spirit, the lying spirit speaks the truth, not daring, in the presence of the light, to conceal its darkness any longer. But to the sinner God says: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?”

Lest we be corrupted by bitter

“Honey of deceit, if he sings truly who provides false things,” as Arator says.

“I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” He blinded Barjesus, who was an opponent of the faith, both through the affliction of his art and through the loss of his eyes. But this woman, who, although perverse in mind, nevertheless spoke the truth, he took care only to deprive of her wicked art. Since it was unworthy for an unclean spirit to announce the word of the Gospel, he commanded it to depart and be silent, because demons ought to confess the Lord with trembling, not praise him with joy.

“And they proclaim a custom which it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.” They are speaking of faith in Jesus Christ, in whose name the spirit of Python had gone out. For the Romans had already decreed that no god should be accepted unless approved by the senate.

At midnight Paul and Silas, worshiping God, were singing a hymn, and so forth. Here both the devotion of the apostolic heart and the power of prayer are expressed: they sang hymns in the innermost prison; their praise shook the prison floor and its foundations, opened the doors, and finally loosened the chains of those bound. [Col. 0979A] Alternatively: whoever among the faithful considers it complete joy when he falls into various trials (Jas. I), and willingly glories in his weaknesses so that the power of Christ may dwell in him (II Cor. XII), certainly sings hymns with Paul and Silas amid the darkness of the prison and chants to the Lord with the Psalmist: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me; you are my exultation” (Ps. XXXI).

He washed their wounds, and he himself was baptized. A beautiful reversal of circumstances: the man whose wounds he washed through them himself lost his wounds through them.

## CHAPTER XVII

Opening and explaining that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that this is Christ Jesus. [Col. 0979B] From the Scriptures Paul was demonstrating both points: that Christ had to suffer and rise again, and that this suffering and resurrection belonged to no one other than Jesus of Nazareth. For there were, and still are today, certain Jews so faithless that, although they cannot deny that Christ’s suffering and resurrection are contained in the Scriptures, they nevertheless altogether deny that these things apply to Jesus and prefer to await the Antichrist rather than believe in Jesus Christ. Therefore Paul not only preached the mysteries of Christ, but also taught that they had been accomplished in Christ Jesus.

And a great multitude both of worshipers and of Gentiles; that is, many came to Christ both from those who had exchanged the Gentile rite for Judaism and from those who had remained wholly Gentile.

[Col. 0979C] Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica. He speaks of nobility of soul, by which they had formed themselves through hearing and examining the word.

But certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers disputed with him. The Epicureans, following the slowness of their teacher, placed human happiness solely in bodily pleasure; the Stoics placed it solely in the virtue of the soul. Although they disagreed with one another, they unanimously opposed the Apostle because he taught that, just as a human being subsists from soul and body, so he ought to be blessed in both; but that this is to be perfected neither in the present age nor by human virtue, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ in the glory of the resurrection.

“What does this babbler wish to say?” He is rightly called a babbler—Greek σπερμόλογος—because the word of God is seed. The Apostle Paul himself says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you,” and so forth (I Cor. IX).

[Col. 0979D] “I found an altar on which was written: To an unknown god.” God was known in Judea, but not received. In Achaia God was unknown, although sought in many ways. Therefore, “the one who is ignorant will be ignored, and the one who transgresses will be condemned.” Neither group is free from guilt, but those who did not offer faith to Christ, whom they did not know, are more excusable than those who laid hands upon Christ, whom they knew.

“God, who made the world and everything in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands,” and so forth. The order of the Apostle’s argument must be carefully observed. Addressing the Gentiles, he arranges his discourse in such a way that he first teaches that there is one God, the author of the world and of all things, [Col. 0980A] in whom “we live and move and are,” and whose offspring we are. Thus he shows that God should be loved not only because of the gifts of light and life, but also because of a certain kinship of origin. Next, by clear reasoning he overthrows the opinion concerning idols: the Creator and Lord of the whole world cannot be enclosed in temples of stone; the giver of every benefit does not need the blood of victims; the creator of human beings and governor of all things cannot be created by human hands; and finally, God, in whose image human beings were made, should not be thought similar to metals. He teaches that the remedy for error is the practice of repentance. For if he had first wanted to destroy the rites of idols, the ears of the Gentiles would have rejected him. Once, therefore, [Col. 0980B] he had persuaded them that there is one God, he then established by his judgment that salvation had been given to us through Christ. Yet he called him a human being rather than God, beginning with the things he had done in the body and describing them as divine, so that he might appear to have been more than human: death conquered by the power of one [perhaps: of him], and a dead man raised from the underworld. For faith grows gradually. When he had appeared to be above humanity, he was then believed to be God. What difference does it make in what order someone believes? Perfection is not sought at the beginnings; one arrives at perfected things from the starting points.

“For in him we live and move and are.” Since this verse is difficult to understand, it should be explained in the words of blessed Augustine. [Col. 0980C] “The Apostle,” he says, “shows that God works unceasingly in the things he has created. We are not in him as though we were his substance, in the way it is said that he has life in himself; rather, since we are something other than he is, we are in him for no other reason than that he works this. And this is his work by which he contains all things, and which his wisdom extends powerfully from end to end and orders all things sweetly. Through this ordering we live and move and are in him. Hence it follows that, if he were to withdraw this work of his from created things, we would neither live, nor move, nor exist.” A little later he says: “For neither heaven and earth, nor all the things that are in them—that is, the whole spiritual and bodily creation—remain in themselves; rather, they are in him of whom it is said: ‘For in him we live and move and are.’ [Col. 0980D] For although each part can exist in the whole of which it is a part, the whole itself exists only in him by whom it was created.” Elsewhere the same blessed Augustine says: “If the Apostle had said this according to the body, it could also be understood of this bodily world. For in it, according to the body, we live and move and are.” Therefore this should be understood according to the mind, which was made in his image, in a certain higher manner—one that is likewise not visible but intelligible. For what is not in him, of whom it is divinely written: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. XI)?

“As some of your own poets have said.” This is what he says elsewhere: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ crucified.” [Col. 0981A] To those who did not accept the authority of the prophets, he speaks not through Moses, Isaiah, or any other prophet, but through the testimony of their own authors, reciting, namely, a verse of Aratus and confirming his own truths by means of their falsehoods, which they could not contradict. For it is a mark of great knowledge to give one’s fellow servants their food at the proper time and to consider the character of one’s hearers.

“For we are indeed his offspring.” We are rightly called God’s offspring, not because we were produced from his nature, but because we were created voluntarily through his Spirit and recreated by adoption.

“Among them also was Dionysius the Areopagite.” This is the Dionysius who later gloriously governed the Church of Corinth as bishop and left volumes of his own genius concerning many matters useful to the Church, which remain to this day. [Col. 0981B] He received his surname from the place over which he presided. For the Areopagus is the council-house of Athens, deriving its name from Mars. In Greek, Mars is called Ἄρης, and a hill is called πάγος.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to depart from Rome. Josephus relates that this happened in the ninth year of Claudius. The historian Suetonius reports it as follows: “Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, who were continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus.” It is by no means clear whether he ordered the Jews, who were then rioting against Christ, to be restrained and suppressed, or whether he also wished Christians to be expelled at the same time, as people belonging to a related religion.

[Col. 0981C] For they were practitioners of the tentmaking trade. Like exiles and foreigners on earth, they build tents for themselves to use on the road. In Greek, tents are called σκῆναι, a word deriving its etymology from providing shade; among them shade is called σκία, while σκῆναι or σκηνώματα means, as it were, “shade shelters.” The ancients fashioned these from woolen cloths, wood, or goats’ hair, or from the leaves and branches of trees. Mystically, however, just as Peter draws us from the waves of the world by fishing with the nets of faith, so Paul, raising shelters of protection, defends us by word and deed from the rain of sins, the heat of temptations, and the winds of ambushes. Two verses in Greek follow at this point, but they are absent from some of our manuscripts.

He disputed in the synagogue every Sabbath, [Col. 0981D] persuading both Jews and Greeks. Then the reading found in both texts is added:

“When Silas and Timothy had come from Macedonia,” and so forth. “He had his head shaved at Cenchreae, for he had a vow.” Cenchreae is the harbor of Corinth, where, about to board a ship, he shaved his head in fulfillment of a vow. For according to the Law of Moses, those who had vowed themselves to God were commanded to grow their hair for as long as they wished to be Nazirites, and afterward to cut it and consign it to the fire. Paul therefore did this—not because he had forgotten what he had decided with the other apostles at Jerusalem concerning the abolition of the Law, but so that those who had believed from among the Jews might not be scandalized. He pretended to be a Jew in order to win Jews. Some manuscripts have the plural: “They shaved their heads, and they had a vow,” that is, Priscilla and Aquila. But the distinguished teachers [Col. 0982A] of the Church, Jerome and Augustine, each in his own letters, use the singular and interpret the passage as referring to Paul. Jerome presents it as follows: “Bidding farewell to the brothers, he sailed for Syria, and with him were Priscilla and Aquila; and he had his head shaved at Cenchreae, for he had a vow.”

He departed from Ephesus and, going down, went up to Caesarea and greeted the Church. He means Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia. For he had not yet arrived in Syrian Phoenicia. It was once called Mosacha, after Mosoc, the son of Japheth; later it received the name Caesarea from Caesar Augustus.

When he arrived, he greatly benefited those who had believed. For he powerfully refuted the Jews. Another translation reads: “He benefited the believers greatly through grace.” [Col. 0982B] This is therefore what the Apostle writes to those same Achaeans: “I planted, Apollos watered” (I Cor. III).

## CHAPTER XIX

And he said to them: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” That is: “After baptism, did you receive the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is customarily given?”

“John baptized with a baptism of repentance.” This baptism, he says, was not able to grant the forgiveness of sins, but could teach repentance alone. For just as the sign of circumcision had existed among the patriarchs as a seal of the faith they possessed, so this washing was received by the penitent people as a distinctive seal of their devotion. Yet even this, figuratively, pointed forward to the baptism of Christ, through which forgiveness would be given.

[Col. 0982C] When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. The question is frequently debated whether those who, perhaps through ignorance, were baptized by unbaptized persons who nevertheless held the right faith ought to be baptized again. I think this chapter explains the matter. For what difference is there between someone’s being baptized then, before the beginning of Christ’s baptism, and someone’s being baptized now without continuity with that same baptism, since John himself proclaimed that those whom he had baptized in faith and in the name of Christ, although Christ was still to come, had to be baptized again, saying: “I baptize you with water; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. III)? For if, as some teach, the mere reception of Christ’s body and blood could now suffice as a remedy for such people, it could have sufficed then as well. There would have been no need for Christ’s disciples to baptize those whom John had baptized with water, but only to confirm them through participation in the blood.

There were about twelve men in all, and so forth. Truly, the judgments of God are a great abyss. Behold: Asia, recently deemed unworthy even of the apostles’ visitation, is now consecrated by the apostolic number and exalted by the prophetic office. It should also be noted that the Holy Spirit displayed the signs of his coming here among twelve disciples, and earlier among one hundred and twenty, which is the number twelve multiplied by ten: the former occurrence in Jerusalem, the latter in Ephesus, which is a Greek city. I believe this was to show that, whether someone believes from among Jews or Gentiles, the Spirit fills only those who share in the unity of the catholic and apostolic Church.

[Col. 0983A] But some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name over them, and so forth. Josephus reports that King Solomon devised and taught his people methods of exorcism—that is, adjuration—by which unclean spirits, once expelled from a person, would not dare to return. This sometimes occurs even through the reprobate, either for the condemnation of those who perform such acts or for the benefit of those who see and hear them, so that, although people may despise those who perform signs, they may nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation such miracles take place.

There were seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who were doing this. It is better read according to the Greek: “There were some of the sons of Sceva.” Since Satan himself “transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI), [Col. 0983B] he is not afraid to cloak his servants in the same disguise. Therefore, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is usually signified by the number seven—in this figure the Lord also dines with seven disciples after the resurrection, and seven brothers come to Cornelius to evangelize him for baptism in the Holy Spirit—the sons of Sceva are counted as seven because they supposedly intended to expel evil spirits. But because they invoke the name of Christ and the apostles not in belief but in an attempt, they are rightly condemned for their deceitful falsehood not only by God but also by the demons themselves. They are appropriately called the sons of Sceva, whose name is interpreted as “the shouting little fox.” This animal, exceedingly clever in deceit and cunning, represents the Jews, Gentiles, and heretics who are always plotting against the Church of God [Col. 0983C] and making a din with something like a chattering voice. Concerning them the guardians of that same Church are commanded: “Seize for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.”

“I know Jesus, and I know Paul.” Concerning this verse Arator says:

“Recognize your fury,

hostile nation: the demon confesses that the one whom

you deny has come reigns—and by this very fact you are convicted,

for, when he goads you, you fall.”

Many of those who had practiced curious arts brought their books, and so forth. By “curious arts” he means the practice of magic, whose adherents rightly burn their books, even though they had been valued at a great price, when they see the very demons whom they had served honoring the Lord Jesus Christ and his apostles.

[Col. 0983D] They found the sum of fifty thousand denarii. In the Gospel, debts are cancelled under the number fifty denarii. I believe this is because, existing through the five bodily senses in this life, we transgress the precepts of the Decalogue. Here, because of the enormity of the magical crime, the number one thousand has also been added. Alternatively: the number fifty is often related to repentance and the forgiveness of sins; hence there is both the fiftieth Psalm of repentance and the fiftieth year of remission.

Sending two of those who ministered to him into Macedonia, and so forth. He sent disciples ahead to prepare the alms that he was going to take to Jerusalem, so that, when he himself arrived, the collection would not then have to be made.

For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, and so forth. [Col. 0984A] This Demetrius, who attempts to disrupt the way of the Lord, fulfills through his actions the meaning of his own name. For it is interpreted as “pursuing excessively.” Accordingly, he builds the temples he makes for Diana from no other material than silver. In Scripture, silver commonly signifies eloquence, just as gold signifies understanding. Gentile cunning likewise customarily supports its religion not by any rational understanding, but by the bare brilliance of speech.

“Not only is this trade of ours in danger of being brought into disrepute, but also the temple of the great Diana will be counted as nothing and destroyed,” and so forth. That is: not only will our works be exposed as vain and unworthy of payment, but our religion too will be dishonored if Paul’s teaching prevails—that idols are not gods. What remarkable folly among the Gentiles: [Col. 0984B] they are not ashamed to worship those whom they know can be built or destroyed by human beings.

And they cried out, saying: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians.” Demetrius had said that Diana was going to perish; they, on the contrary, marvel that she is great.

And they rushed with one accord into the theater. The theater is a place shaped like a semicircle, where the assembled people, standing, watched dramatic performances within. Thus it received its name from the spectacle; in Greek, the word for theater derives from viewing. Therefore, as Arator says:

“It was fitting that Diana’s cause and worth

should be handled in no other forum by the lascivious;

the arena holds the ugly work of a deformed assembly.”

## CHAPTER XX

And he departed to go to Macedonia. After he had passed through those regions [Col. 0984C] and encouraged them with much discourse, he came to Greece. Greece is the province of Achaia, which the Greeks call ἑλλάς. Accordingly, wherever the Latin manuscripts have “Greeks,” or “Gentiles” to distinguish them from Jews, the Greek exemplar has ἕλληνας and ἑλληνιστάς. Paul therefore came there after Macedonia because, as stated above, he had decided to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem.

On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, and so forth; that is, on the Lord’s Day, which is the first day after the Sabbath, when we had assembled to celebrate the mysteries.

And he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room. [Col. 0984D] Allegorically, we may say here that the upper room is the height of spiritual gifts; the night, the obscurity of the Scriptures; the abundance of lamps, the exposition of their more hidden sayings; and the Lord’s Day, the remembrance of either the Lord’s resurrection or our own. The spiritual teacher should thus be admonished that, whenever he has drawn his hearers, enticed by the sweetness of the resurrection and the joys of the life to come, toward the heights of the virtues, and has touched upon any hidden matters of Scripture by discoursing at length, he should immediately illuminate those same matters for weaker hearers with the lamp of a plain exposition. Thus, when the Apostle said that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman, he immediately added by way of explanation: “Now these things are two covenants,” and so forth.

[Col. 0985A] A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the window, and so forth. Eutychus means “mad” in Hebrew, but “fortunate” in Greek. The first meaning suits the person who has fallen from the summit of the virtues through the pleasure of youth; the second suits the person who, through the preacher’s condescension, has returned to the heights of the virtues.

Overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third-story upper room, and so forth. Amid the words of preaching an opportunity for healing arose, so that the discourse might be confirmed by the sweetness of the miracle and teaching, the labor of keeping watch might be restrained, and the memory of the teacher, already about to depart, might be more firmly fixed in their minds. The three upper rooms, the highest of which Paul occupies to preach, are faith, hope, and charity. “The greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII). If anyone abandons it through indolence and is not afraid to fall asleep amid the Apostle’s words, [Col. 0985B] he will already be counted among the dead. For “whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II).

When Paul had descended to him, he bent over him. That he descends, bends over, and embraces him is what he himself says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” The restoration of those who sin through negligence is more difficult than that of those who sin through weakness. The former is represented by Eutychus, the latter by Tabitha, whom Peter raised. Therefore Tabitha falls ill and dies during the day, while this young man falls and dies at midnight. After her death Tabitha is washed and placed in an upper room; here the young man, having fallen from the third upper room, is mourned below as dead. Paul is present and teaching in the one case; [Col. 0985C] in the other, the teacher is absent. Paul descends to this young man; Peter ascends to raise Tabitha. She sits up as soon as she sees Peter; this young man, having died at midnight, finally rises in the morning and is brought back to life when the sun of righteousness breathes upon him.

For he was hurrying, if possible, to celebrate Pentecost at Jerusalem. The Law had indeed commanded that all Jews assemble in Jerusalem three times a year—that is, at Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths—but the Apostle hastens to celebrate the fiftieth day, that is, the day of remission and of the Holy Spirit, having broken the bonds of the world.

He summoned the elders of the Church. In Greek, πρεσβυτέρους—“presbyters”—is found instead of “elders.”

[Col. 0985D] Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city.
