By saying “in the cities,” he plainly shows that he learned what was going to happen to him not from himself, but because it had been revealed to others concerning him. Among these was the prophet Agabus, as well as those disciples who, while he was staying at Tyre, warned him through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem.

Saying that bonds and tribulations await me in Jerusalem. So that where he had once persecuted the Church, there he might now contend for the peace of the Church.

Nor do I consider my life more precious than myself. By “life” he means temporal life in the body, which the person who awaits eternal joy in another life considers of little worth.

Because I am clean from the blood of all of you. [Col. 0986A] He believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors because he had not spared their vices when they needed to be struck down.

In which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops. Above, he had said that the presbyters of Ephesus had been summoned to Miletus; now he calls these same men bishops, that is, overseers. For one city could not have several bishops, but he signifies the same presbyters—truly priests—under the name “bishops.” The rank is shared, and in many respects the terms are almost equivalent.

To shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. He does not hesitate to call it the blood of God, because of the union of person in the two natures of that same Jesus Christ. On account of this union it was also said: “The Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). Let Nestorius therefore cease separating the Son of Man from the Son of God and making two Christs for himself. [Col. 0986B]

And from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things. John speaks of the same people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II).

For over three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears. Arator explains this beautifully and briefly:

“He who sings the Church’s three teachings repeatedly produces

a historical volume, one sounding morally, and one typological;

hence Judea, left vacant, called a barren tree,

did not yield the fruit expected for three years.”

I have shown you everything. That is: one must persist not only in teaching amid pressures and tears, but also in working with one’s hands, so that none of the weak may be burdened. This is what is meant by: “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke X), [Col. 0986C] namely, to preach the Gospel and not seek one’s expenses from the Gospel.

It is more blessed to give than to receive. He does not place rich almsgivers above those who, having abandoned everything, followed the Lord. Rather, he especially glorifies those who, after renouncing once and for all everything they possess, nevertheless labor with their hands at what is good, so that they may have something with which to give to the person suffering need.

## CHAPTER XXI

We set out, while they escorted us with their wives and children, and so forth. The prophecy was fulfilled that sings concerning the Church: “The daughters of Tyre will entreat your face with gifts; all the rich among the people…” (Ps. XLIV), and so forth, up to the end of the psalm. For no city received, detained, or sent away the Apostle with greater affection. Indeed, to this day the place where they prayed together is shown in the sands.

A certain prophet came from Judea. He says “from Judea” because Caesarea, where they were staying, belongs to the region of Samaria and lies on the border of Phoenicia and Palestine.

“Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews will bind in Jerusalem the man whose belt this is.” He imitates the ancient prophets, who used to say: “Thus says the Lord God.” For the Holy Spirit is Lord and God just as the Father and the Son are, and their operation cannot be separated, since their nature and will are one. Hence we also read above: “The Holy Spirit says: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” [Col. 0987A] (Acts XIII), that is, for the apostolate. Paul himself writes: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. I). We have said this so that no one, like Macedonius, might believe that the Holy Spirit is a creature or that he possesses lesser authority than the Father or the Son.

On the following day Paul entered with us to see James. This James, the brother of the Lord—that is, the son of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother, whom the evangelist John mentions—was her son. Immediately after the Lord’s Passion he was ordained bishop by the apostles and governed the Church at Jerusalem for thirty years, that is, until the seventh year of Nero. Since the Jews were unable to kill Paul, which was their chief desire, as soon as Festus died [Col. 0987B] and before Albinus had arrived in the province, they turned their hands against James. He was buried beside the temple, where he had been thrown down.

They have heard about you that you teach defection from Moses among all the Jews who live among the nations, etc.; that is, that through the teaching of Christ you declare that the practices handed down through Moses to the fathers should be condemned as sacrilegious and not commanded by God. This is what they had spread about Paul—not those who understood the intention with which these practices ought then to have been preserved by faithful Jews, namely, to commend the divine authority and the prophetic holiness of those sacraments, not to obtain the salvation that had already been revealed in Christ and bestowed through the sacrament of baptism [Col. 0987C]—but those who wanted them observed as though the salvation of believers could not exist in the Gospel without them. For they had recognized him as an exceedingly zealous preacher of grace, teaching what was most opposed to their purpose: that a person is not justified through those practices, but through the grace of Christ, for whose announcement those shadows were commanded in the Law. Therefore, while trying to stir up envy and persecution against him, they accused him as an enemy of the Law and of the divine commandments. He could not more suitably avoid the odium of this false accusation than by himself observing what he was thought to condemn as sacrilegious, and thus showing that Jews at that time were not to be forbidden these practices as wicked, nor Gentiles compelled to them as necessary [Col. 0987D]. For if he truly rejected them in the way that had been reported about him, and accepted their observance only so that by a simulated action he could conceal his real opinion, James would not have said to him:

“And everyone will know that what they have heard about you is false”; rather, he would have said, “Everyone will think so”—especially since in Jerusalem itself the apostles had already decreed that no one should compel the Gentiles to judaize. They had not, however, decreed that anyone should then prevent Jews from judaizing, although Christian teaching no longer compelled even the Jews themselves to do so.

When the seven days were being completed. These days had not yet been completed; their course was in progress, and their completion was anticipated. Hence the Greek says more explicitly: “When the seven days were beginning to be completed.” Otherwise the statement cannot be reconciled with what he himself said to the governor five days after his arrival in Caesarea: “There are no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.” For if, in addition to these seven days and those five days, you count the day of that council on which he divided the Pharisees and Sadducees among themselves, and the day on which the Jews had sworn to kill him, it is beyond doubt that more than twelve days would be found to have elapsed there.

“This is the man who everywhere teaches everyone against the people, the Law, and this place.” Because they saw that the followers of the new grace were attending the ceremonies of the Law and the rites of the Temple less frequently, they feared—as it is written in the Gospel—that the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation [Col. 0988B].

He said: “Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian?” etc. For a certain Egyptian had come to Judaea who, by magically fabricating a claim to prophetic authority, gathered thirty thousand Jews. Leading them through the desert, he reached the Mount of Olives, prepared from there to attack Jerusalem and bring the city under his control. Felix, however, forestalled his attempt by immediately confronting him with armed forces. The Egyptian fled with a few companions, while others were also killed, and Felix easily checked the rash undertaking.

“Four thousand men who were assassins.” There is no need to create a dispute over this number of followers between the tribune who spoke these words and Josephus, who wrote about the Egyptian. It could have happened that the Egyptian first arrived with only a few men, operating secretly as they pursued their tyranny, and later joined more people to himself through open deception [Col. 0988C]. We read that in the time of Felix this kind of brigand arose. They did not lie in wait in hidden places or at concealed times; instead, carrying *sicae*, that is, short swords held in the hand, they mingled with the people in broad daylight and wounded those beside them with a concealed stroke, so that death preceded any outcry and the attacker remained hidden. If anyone became enraged because such things were happening in the middle of the city, he too was killed. Thus, through fear of danger or concealment of the crime, the assassin was not detected.

“A citizen of Tarsus in Cilicia, a city not unknown.” The Apostle was indeed born in the town of Giscala in Galilee. When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. They sent him to Jerusalem for the study of the Law, and, as he himself recounts below, he was instructed by Gamaliel, a most learned man [Col. 0988D]. He does not call himself a citizen but a *municipalis*, from the *municipium*, that is, from the territory of that city in which he was brought up. It is called a *municipium* because it renders only its duties—namely, the taxes or services owed. For liberal privileges, the most famous rights, and those proceeding from the emperor belong to the dignity of cities. Nor is it surprising that he calls himself a Tarsian rather than a Giscalite, since the Lord himself, although born in Bethlehem, was called a Nazarene, not a Bethlehemite.

## CHAPTER XXII

“But they did not hear the voice of him who was speaking with me.” Above, the narrative of this vision says that his companions stood terrified, hearing the voice but seeing no one. From this it follows that they heard the sound of an indistinct voice, but did not hear the articulation of the words [Col. 0989A].

“While they were shouting, throwing off their garments, and scattering dust into the air.” At the Lord’s passion, only the priest leapt from his throne and tore his garments, because at that time the old priesthood was to be replaced by the new. But now, because after the apostles’ death the whole nation was soon to be stripped of the glory of its kingdom, they all throw off their garments and raise to heaven a cry mingled with dust. As the Psalmist says: “The pride of those who hate you has continually risen” (Psalm 73).

“I obtained this citizenship at great expense.” Another Edition makes clearer what he said. The tribune said: “You say so readily that you are a Roman citizen? I know at what price I acquired this citizenship” [Col. 0989B].

And Paul said: “But I was even born a citizen.” That is: “In this respect I am more Roman than you: I did not purchase the Roman name after being born elsewhere, but was born within the very city whose citizenship I possess.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

“God will strike you, whitewashed wall.” He did not say this because his mind was disturbed, but certainly spoke prophetically. For that figurative high priesthood, constructed in the likeness of a whitewashed wall, was destined to be struck and destroyed when the true priesthood of Christ had arrived through the apostles’ preaching of the Gospel. Hence he says: “God will strike you.” He did not say, “May God strike you”; by using the indicative [Col. 0989C] mood he signifies that this would in fact happen, rather than cursing him in the optative mood. That he spoke these words with a calm mind he shows in his next reply, saying:

“I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest.” For although he truly knew that in the New Testament this man was not the chief of the priests, nevertheless, while instructing others and urging those in authority to conduct themselves with greater moderation, he himself also wished to act temperately here.

“Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee,” etc. Just as the unity of the good is always beneficial, so the unity of the wicked is always harmful to the good. Therefore the Apostle now strives to divide his persecutors, so that those who had encircled him while united might, once divided, release their grip. Thus the Red Sea, which had hemmed in the children of Israel as a solid barrier, when divided liberated them from Egypt [Col. 0989D]. As for his testimony that he is a son of the Pharisees—or, according to the Greek, a son of a Pharisee—this means what he boasts above: that he learned the prophets and the Law at the feet of Gamaliel, who is recorded as a Pharisee.

“They bound themselves under oath, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.” Since the Lord says, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5), these men, by contrast, hunger for wickedness and thirst for blood so intensely that they renounce even food for their bodies until they are sated by this man’s death. But there is no wisdom, prudence, or counsel against God. For although Paul above offered sacrifices, shaved his head, practiced barefoot observances, and became a Jew to the Jews, he nevertheless did not escape the chains that had been foretold [Col. 0990A]. Here too, although these men form plans, bind themselves under oath, and lay ambushes, the Apostle is preserved, so that at Rome also he may bear witness to Christ, as he had been told.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“And the leader of the sedition of the sect of the Nazarenes.” At that time Christians were called Nazarenes as a term of reproach. Later, however, a heresy arose among the Jews called that of the Nazarenes. They believe in Christ as the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, and say that he is the one who both suffered under Pontius Pilate and rose again—the one in whom we too believe. But because they want to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor [Col. 0990B] Christians.

“Whom we also seized.” From him you yourself, by judging all these matters, will be able to learn. In this place some of our manuscripts contain several verses, which read as follows in the Greek: “Whom we also seized and wished to judge according to our Law. But Lysias the tribune came with great force and removed him from our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you, so that by judging you yourself may learn about all these matters,” etc.

“But I confess this to you: according to the sect which they call a heresy, so I serve my ancestral God.” The Greek reads better: “According to the Way which they call a heresy, so I serve the ancestral God.” For what consistency would there be in someone speaking Greek saying, “According to the sect which they call a heresy,” when the Latin *secta* and the Greek *hairesis* mean the same thing? Rather, he says: “So I serve the ancestral God according to that Way which unbelievers now call a heresy”—that is, a sect—as though the term suggested more stubborn pursuit of something than diligence in discerning what is right [Col. 0990C].

“Certain Jews from Asia.” Join this to what precedes: that is, “These are the men who found me in the Temple.”

“When two years had been completed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus.” The two years refer to Paul’s residence in Caesarea, not to the duration of Felix’s governorship. For it was said above that he had been judge of that people for many years. This is especially clear since historical accounts state that the Apostle was sent to Rome in Nero’s second year, while Claudius Caesar was emperor when he appointed Herod Agrippa—the son of the Herod whom the angel struck in Caesarea—king of the Jews, and also sent Felix as procurator of the entire province, including Samaria and Galilee and the region called Transjordan [Col. 0990D].

## CHAPTER XXV

“No one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar.” He appeals to Caesar and hastens to go to Rome so that he may devote himself longer to preaching and, accompanied by many believers gained here, go to Christ crowned with them.

“King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea.” This Agrippa, who came to Caesarea with his sister, is the son—as I have said—of Herod Agrippa, whom we read above was killed by an angel. He held the kingdom of Judaea until the destruction of Jerusalem, always friendly to the Romans and entirely secure from that Jewish revolt [Col. 0991A].

## CHAPTER XXVI

“Concerning all the matters of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed that I am to defend myself before you today.” Another Edition translated this verse as follows: “I consider myself especially blessed to begin giving my defense before you today.” Saint Jerome placed it somewhere with his own exposition in this form:

“Concerning all the matters of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed that today I am to be defended before you, who especially know all the customs and controversies that exist among the Jews. For he had read the words of Isaiah: ‘Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of one who listens,’ and he knew that words of speech achieve as much as the judge’s understanding has grasped” [Col. 0991B].

“And when they were being killed, I gave my vote.” Another Edition says: “And when they were to be killed, I gave my vote against them,” that is, I myself gave the decision as to how they should be killed.

Festus said in a loud voice: “You are mad, Paul.” He attributed it to madness that a man in chains, having been given the opportunity to defend himself, should speak not about the external slander by which he was oppressed, but about the conscience in which he gloried; that he should recount all the miracles of the revelation by which he had been changed from a persecutor into an apostle; and that, preaching about the resurrection of the dead, he should expound with the force and fervor of a public speaker the dispensation revealed by our Redeemer. Yet, in truth, just as it is foolish insanity when the prodigal son leaves his father and feeds pigs, so there is also a spiritual—that is, true—madness, about which the Apostle says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.” In reference to this the Psalmist sings: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and false madnesses” (Psalm 39) [Col. 0991C].

“Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.” He did not say this as flattery, as some think, but truly foretold it. For Agrippa, being instructed in the Jewish rite and laws, believed that the prophets had spoken truthfully; but, as an unbeliever, he did not know to whom that same truth led—namely, the Lord Christ. Nevertheless, it is recorded that in an address delivered to the Jews he said: “But you presume upon the assistance of religion, although the disciples of Jesus have already filled the Roman world; or do we suppose that this religion is growing without the will of God?” [Col. 0991D]

## CHAPTER XXVII

“When we had been sailing slowly for many days and had scarcely reached a position opposite Chios.” It is better read, “opposite Cnidus,” which is an island opposite Asia.

“But the centurion believed the pilot and the shipowner more.” The Greek *naukleros* is called *navicularius* in Latin.

“The Typhonic wind drove against it.” Another translation says in Latin: “A stormy wind.” For Greek *typhos* means “swelling” or “inflation” in Latin.

“When the ship was seized and could not make headway against the wind,” etc. Another translation expresses this more clearly: “When the ship was seized and they could not meet the wind, they surrendered the ship to the blasts and began to take in the sails” [Col. 0992A].

“Then we sailed past the island called Clauda, which they could not occupy, but the boats sent out began to assist the ship by encircling it. They also dragged the anchors, fearing that they might run aground on the Syrtes.” This shows that they fastened the anchors to ropes lowered from both sides of the ship’s middle section around its forward part, so that the anchors could be dragged. In our own sea, that is, the British Sea, people likewise customarily attach heavy millstones behind a ship to restrain it. They did this to slow the vessel, lest its excessively rapid movement carry it onto the Syrtes, terrifying even by hearsay because they draw everything toward themselves. Hence Sallustius says that their name was given to them from their dragging action [Col. 0992B].

“We could scarcely secure the boat.” Once it had been lifted out, they used it for assistance. A *scapha*, or *catascopos*, is a light boat made of wickerwork and covered with raw hide. In Greek it is named from observing, because sailors or pirates customarily use such a vessel to survey lands and shores. After they had lowered it into the sea to assist the larger ship, they could scarcely secure it amid the boiling waves so that it would not slip away.

“Having lowered the vessel, they were carried along in this manner.” Another translation reads: “Fearing that they might fall into the Syrtis, they loosened the masts and were carried along in this manner.”

“For an angel of God stood beside me this night.” He did not say this to boast about himself, but to summon them to faith. For this reason the sea was permitted to become turbulent: so that through what was not heard and through what was heard, the spiritual grace in Paul might be revealed [Col. 0992C].

“Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved,” etc. Because in the danger of shipwreck the skill of the sailors, who knew the sea, could be more useful than the soldiers’ weapons, they therefore regarded the loss of the boat as less serious than allowing the sailors to leave.

“When it began to grow light, Paul urged everyone to take food.” A very beautiful allegorical meaning appears here, since Paul urged those whom he had promised would be saved from the shipwreck to take food. Because in the middle of the night they were held amid the breakers by four anchors, at daybreak they make for the shelter of the land; for no one escapes the storms of this world unless he is nourished by the bread of life. Whoever, during the night of present tribulations, relies with all his strength upon wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice soon reaches, with the Lord’s help shining upon him, the harbor of salvation that he has sought—provided only that, freed from worldly affairs, he seeks the flame of love by which to warm his breast [Col. 0992D].

“After raising the foresail, they headed toward the shore according to the direction of the breeze.” The *artemon* is a small sail designed more for steering the ship than for speed.

“When we had come upon a place between two seas, they drove the ship onto it.” *Bithalassum* means “between two seas,” because the Greeks call the sea *thalassa* (θάλασσα). It signifies a shore extending into the sea and surrounded on both sides by the same sea, which divides there.

“The bow remained fixed and immovable, but the stern was being broken apart by the force of the sea,” etc. This ship perished because it did not glide over the waves in a gentle course, but was violently driven into the very seabed: part of it was held fast by the ground, while the remainder was battered by the waves and broken apart. Such indeed is the downfall of a mind devoted to this world. When it neglects to trample upon worldly desires, it fixes the bow of its intention deep in the earth and loosens the entire structure of its subsequent works through the waves of anxiety. But those who escape by the fragments of this little ship make for land, because others conduct themselves more cautiously by the examples of those who perish.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“When Paul had gathered a quantity of brushwood and placed it on the fire.” The Apostle came out of the sea and lit a fire because of the cold; by the warmth of love he heats the hearts of those whom, through teaching, he has drawn out from the waves of storms [Col. 0993B]. The pieces of brushwood signify various exhortations. They are effective for kindling charity and, having been cut from the wholeness of Scripture, are as though branches had been stripped of their leaves.

“When the viper came out because of the heat, it fastened upon his hand.” The unclean spirit, driven away from the hearts of the faithful by the flame of virtues, tries to pour the poisons of persecution into teachers of truth, so that it may wound the hand—that is, hinder the work of spiritual teaching.

“But he shook the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.” By the same fire with which he warms his people, he burns the creature, because through the same virtues the saints make progress while the wicked, together with their instigator, perish through envy, as the prophet says: “Zeal has seized an uneducated people, and now fire has consumed their adversaries” [Col. 0993C].

“It happened that Publius’s father was lying sick with fever and dysentery,” etc. Why does Paul heal an unbelieving sick man through prayer, while he restores Timothy, a faithful man, by medical skill, and leaves Trophimus, also faithful, entirely ill? It is because the former had to be healed outwardly by a miracle, since inwardly he was not alive; those who were living healthily within did not need this.

“We sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island, whose sign was the Castors.” I believe the original reading was “whose sign was the Castors,” but that a letter was added through the error of scribes, just as we often find *frustra panis* written instead of *frusta panis*, and *appropriat* instead of *appropiat*, in very ancient manuscripts [Col. 0993D]. For in the Greek, instead of “with the sign of the Castors,” we find written *parasēmō Dioskourois* (παρασήμῳ διοσκούροις). The *Dioskouroi* (διόσκουροι) are the twin Castors, that is, Castor and Pollux, as they are called in Greek. The city of the Colchi bears witness to this: founded by Amphitus and Circius, the twin charioteers, it was named Dioscurias after them. For this reason the pagans invoke them as gods of the sea: when, as omens for sailors, single stars appear on a ship or its masts, they are dangerous; but when twin stars appear, they announce a favorable voyage. At their arrival, they are said to drive away that dreadful phenomenon called Helen.

In another translation we found written, instead of *parasēmō Dioskourois*, “whose sign was the sons of Jupiter.” For the myths say that Jupiter transformed himself into a swan, violated Leda, the wife of Theseus, and that Helen was born from this [Col. 0994A]. Hence the verse: “This melodious bird sought the embraces of Leda’s offspring”; and they also say that he changed her into a star and begot the twins Castor and Pollux.

“For the Holy Spirit spoke well through the prophet Isaiah to your fathers, saying: ‘Go to this people and say: You will hear with the ear,’” etc. The prophecy that the Apostle affirms was spoken by the Holy Spirit, the prophet’s own book recalls as having been spoken by the Lord. From this it is plainly shown that the Lord and the Holy Spirit have one will and one nature, and that in the designation “Spirit” the name “Lord” is also understood. Paul did not write these things about some other Holy Spirit who had been different in the prophets before the Lord’s coming, but about the one of whom he himself was also a participant, as were all who were carried forward in the faith of perfected virtue. Hence, when he mentions him with the article, he seems to testify that he is solitary and one. He says not simply *Pneuma hagion* (Πνεῦμα ἅγιον), “Holy Spirit,” but, with the addition of the article, *to Pneuma to hagion* (τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον), “this Holy Spirit.” He also recalls that Isaiah prophesied with the articulated expression *to hagion to Pneuma* (τὸ ἅγιον τὸ Πνεῦμα), “the Holy Spirit.”

Peter likewise, in the speech by which he persuaded those present, said: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold” (that is, *to Pneuma to hagion*, “the Holy Spirit”) “through the mouth of David concerning Judas” (Acts 1). He too shows that the same Spirit worked in the prophets and in the apostles. These excerpts from the books of blessed Didymus may occupy this place in our own little works [Col. 0994B].

“For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears.” We must not think that the fatness of the heart and the heaviness of the ears belong to nature rather than to the will. He adds the fault of free choice and says:

“And they have closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes.” That is, by their preceding merits they themselves became the cause for God to close their eyes. Or this should be joined to what precedes, where the Lord says to the prophet: “Go to this people, and reproach them for the sins by which they deserved blindness, if perhaps even in this way they may consent to hear and turn to me” (Isaiah 6).

“He remained for two full years in his own rented lodging,” that is, in the lodging that he had rented for himself, preaching Christ to everyone—not only to the Jews [Col. 0994D], but also to the Gentiles, whom, after the Jews’ rejection, he had said would be saved.

“And preaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with confidence, without hindrance.” He was not only not forbidden to preach at Rome, but, before Nero’s rule had grown stronger and before such great crimes had erupted as the histories relate about him, Paul was released so that he might preach the Gospel of Christ also in the regions of the West, as he himself says to the Romans: “Now, therefore, I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints.” And shortly afterward: “When I have completed this, I shall depart by way of you for Spain.” Later, that is, in Nero’s final year, he was detained by him and crowned with martyrdom. He explains both matters in the Second Epistle to Timothy, which he dictated while suffering imprisonment: “At my first defense,” he says, “no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (2 Timothy 4) [Col. 0995A]. He very clearly signifies Nero by the lion, on account of his cruelty. And below: “The Lord saved me and will save me for his heavenly kingdom” (ibid.), since he sensed that the martyrdom awaiting him was at hand. Hence, in the same Epistle, he had prefaced these words: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith” (ibid.).

[Col. 0995]

# BOOK OF RETRACTATIONS ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES (C)

## THE BOOK BEGINS

### PREFACE

[Col. 0995B]

We know that the distinguished teacher and bishop Augustine, when he was an old man, composed books of *Retractations* concerning certain works that he had written in his youth. He did so so that what he had learned over time through repeated reading and through the gift of heavenly generosity might be committed to the monuments of literature and left for posterity to read—not as one ashamed of his former ignorance, but rather as one rejoicing in his own progress. We too have decided, according to our modest ability, to imitate his diligence. After the exposition of the Acts of the Apostles that we wrote several years ago, at the request of the venerable bishop Acca, with all the care we could exert, we now compose in the same volume a brief little book of *Retractations*, chiefly with the aim either of adding what had been said too briefly or correcting what seemed to have been said otherwise than we wished. In it we have also taken care briefly to mention certain passages that we saw placed differently in the Greek, or with additions or omissions. Whether these were omitted or expressed differently through the translator’s negligence, or corrupted or left aside through the carelessness of copyists, we have not yet been able to determine. For I do not dare to suspect that the Greek exemplar itself was falsified. Therefore I warn the reader that wherever we have done this, he should read it for the sake of learning, but should not insert it into his own copy as though correcting it, unless he should happen to find such a rendering preserved from ancient times in the Latin manuscript of his edition.

For Jerome also explains many testimonies from the Old Testament according to the Hebrew truth; nevertheless, neither did he himself wish to interpret these passages in this way in our manuscripts, nor have we wished to correct them. For example: “I shall not look upon man any more, and the inhabitant; my generation has ceased” (Isaiah 38). And: “His tomb will be glorious” (Isaiah 11); and: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises” (Isaiah 24); and: “Everyone who kills Cain will be punished sevenfold” (Genesis 4). He says that the Hebrew has: “He will release seven acts of vengeance”; and: “From the wings of the earth”; and: “His resting place is glorious”; and: “The inhabitant of rest: my generation has been removed.” He wished the reader to know that these are the forms found among the Hebrews, solely for the sake of learning, not for the sake of correction [Col. 0995D].

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0996B]

“I made the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach.” The words “the first account” do not constitute an adverb of order, as in the Apostle’s statement, “First of all, I give thanks to my God” (Romans 1). Rather, as is very easily evident from the Greek, “first” is a noun that should be joined to the word that follows, “account,” so that the meaning is that the first account was the Gospel, written concerning Jesus, while the second is what he is now going to produce by adding the Acts of the Apostles. He completes his reference to the first account when he adds: “Until the day on which, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.” Then he begins the second account when he continues: “To whom he also showed himself alive after his passion by many proofs over forty days,” etc. For although in the Gospel he testified that Jesus ascended into heaven and that the disciples returned from Bethany to Jerusalem, he did not say there that for forty days after his passion Jesus frequently appeared to them, that they asked him about the restoration of the kingdom of Israel, or that, as he was ascending to heaven, angels stood beside them and foretold that he would return in the same manner, along with other matters of this kind [Col. 0996C].

“For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” *Baptisma* is Greek; in Latin it is called *tinctio*, “immersion” or “dipping.” Hence in certain manuscripts we find it translated in this way: “John indeed dipped with water, but you will be dipped in the Holy Spirit.” Here we see a remarkable agreement between the words of the Lord and those of his forerunner. John said to those whom he baptized concerning the Lord: “I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Mark 8). The Lord himself said: “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

It should also be noted that the Lord’s baptism in the Holy Spirit, which John had foretold, refers not only to the time when the apostles and the other believers of that period were baptized with water for the remission of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit given them by the Lord, but also to the time when, at the Lord’s own sending, they received the gifts of that same Spirit more fully from heaven. Even now, whoever receives baptism for the remission of sins is baptized in the Holy Spirit, through whose gift people are both cleansed from all sins and helped to advance in good works [Col. 0996D].

“Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” It means not, “the kingdom of this Israel,” but “the kingdom to this Israel”; and this is clear in the Greek, where *tō Israel* (τῷ Israel) is written, not *hou Israel* (οῦ Israel). The meaning would be understood more easily if one word were added: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to the people of Israel?” [Col. 0997A]

“While they were looking intently into heaven as he went.” The Greek has: “And while they were gazing into heaven as he went”; that is, they were gazing into heaven, where he himself was going. Hence the angels also say to them: “Why do you stand looking into heaven?” But that they were also looking at the one who was going into heaven is demonstrated by the angels’ following words: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” [Col. 0997B].

“When they had entered the upper room, they went up to the place where they were staying.” The order of the words is likewise given in the Greek: “When they had entered the upper room, they went up to where they were staying: Peter and John, and Andrew and James.” In the Greek the order of the names is as follows: “Peter and Andrew, and James and John, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas of James.”

Histories in which the sufferings of the apostles are recorded—and which many regard as apocryphal—report that these men preached in Persia and were killed there by the chief priests of the temples in the city of Suanir, suffering a glorious martyrdom. The book of the *Martyrology* also supports this account. It is entitled under the name and with a preface attributed to blessed Jerome, although Jerome himself is said not to have been the author of that book but its translator, while Eusebius was its author [Col. 0997C].

Isidore, moreover, thinks that this Simon was the one who governed the Church of Jerusalem after James, the brother of the Lord, and was crowned with the martyrdom of the cross under Trajan when he was one hundred and twenty years old. We too once followed him in the first book of our *Acts of the Apostles*, not examining more scrupulously what he had written, but simply accepting his statements, thinking that he had learned these things from reliable ancient histories. Even now we do not dare to deny this, especially since the man who wrote the aforementioned sufferings of the apostles has himself most clearly revealed that he wrote uncertain and false things.

For he says that the eunuch of Candace, whom Philip baptized in Judaea, was in Ethiopia at the time when Matthew was teaching there and assisted him in his teaching. Yet it is clear that Candace is not the name of a man but of a woman: not the eunuch’s name, but that of his mistress, namely, the queen of the Ethiopians. As we have learned from the records of the ancients, all their queens customarily bore this name in antiquity [Col. 0997D].

In the same work, following Jerome’s commentary, I also wrote concerning Judas, the brother of James, who was likewise called Thaddeus, that he had been sent to Abgar, king of Osroene, as ecclesiastical history had handed down. But later, examining the ecclesiastical history itself more carefully, I found that it was not written there that the apostle Thaddeus, one of the Twelve, had been sent to heal the king mentioned above. Rather, it was Thaddeus, one of the Seventy disciples, who was sent to heal the king mentioned above [Col. 0998A]. I do not think that this error should be charged against me, since, following the authority of great teachers, I believed without hesitation that what I found in their little works ought to be accepted.

“With the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.” He says “the brothers of Jesus,” not “the brothers of Mary.” For the distinction is clear in the Greek, where *autēs* (αὐτῆς) is not written, but *autou* (αὐτοῦ), which without any doubt is the pronoun of the masculine gender among them. Blessed Luke took care to make clear to his readers that the Lord’s brothers were participants in his faith at that time. Of them it had previously been said: “Even his brothers did not believe in him.”

“And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Haceldama” [Col. 0998B]. He says “in their language,” referring to those who lived in Jerusalem. Although both groups certainly spoke Hebrew, the distinctive speech of the Jerusalemites nevertheless differed from that of the Galileans, from whom the apostles came. We learn this in the account of the Lord’s passion, where Peter himself, even against his will, was betrayed by his speech as a Galilean.

“And they appointed two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus.” The Greek contains more: “And after these words they appointed two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.” Where we read *Justus* in this sentence, *Justus* also appears in the Greek itself. If we believe that it is a Latin name, it seems that this man possessed such great virtue that even the Romans who might have known him gave him the name of righteousness. But if it is a Hebrew name, it can be interpreted as “sparing” or “he himself has been lifted up,” as Jerome teaches in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. What is called *Justus* in Latin is called *Sadoch* in Hebrew and *dikaios* (δίκαιος), “righteous,” in Greek.

Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, a man learned in every respect, reports that both of these men who were appointed to the apostolic lot belonged to the number of the seventy disciples.

## CHAPTER II
And when the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. Some manuscripts incorrectly read *Pentecosten*. For *Pentecoste* in the nominative case means “the fiftieth day”; *Pentecostes* in the genitive means “of the fiftieth day”; *Pentecosten* in the accusative means “the fiftieth day” as object. No proper usage permits us to say *Pentecosten*, when we ought to say, “When the day of the fiftieth day was being fulfilled,” or certainly, as it is read in Greek in the singular: “And when the day of the fiftieth day was being fulfilled.” But in the prayers of that same day one should say: “And celebrating the most sacred *Pentecosten*,” that is, “the fiftieth day.” From the customary use of this word, some who do not know Greek have thought that this solemnity of the day should also be called *Pentecosten* in the nominative case.

And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a powerful wind arriving, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting, and so forth. In the very giving of the Law and of grace, the clearest distinction between the Old and New Testaments appears. There the people stood far away; there was fear, but there was no love. Indeed, they were so afraid that they said to Moses: “Speak to us yourself, and let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die” (Exod. XX). Therefore God descended, as it is written, upon Sinai in fire, terrifying the people who stood far away; he wrote the law with his finger on stone, not with his Spirit in the heart. Here, however, when the Holy Spirit came, the faithful had gathered together in one place; he did not terrify them on a mountain, but entered the house. From heaven a sound suddenly arose, and it sounded as though a powerful blast were being carried along; yet no one was frightened. You have heard the sound: see the fire, since on the mountain also there were both fire and sound—but there there was smoke as well, whereas here there was fire: tongues divided as if of fire. Was he terrifying them from afar? Certainly not. For he settled upon each one of them, and they began to speak in tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Hear the tongue speaking, and understand that the Spirit was writing not on stone but in the heart.

And there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them, and so forth. This means “of this fire,” not “this fire.” For in Greek one finds *πυρὸς* rather than *πῦρ*. The distinction would be clearer if, with a verb added, it were said: “There appeared divided tongues like burning fire,” or “like shining fire,” so that it might be understood that the tongues were divided in the appearance of fire.

And they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation, and so forth. In Greek, at this point, “in various tongues” is not found, but rather “in other tongues.” For Isaiah had said: “In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Accordingly, blessed Luke, wishing to indicate that this prophecy had been fulfilled by the giving of the Spirit, took care to place in this sacred history the same word that he had seen in the prophecy.

Because each one heard them speaking in his own language. But all were amazed and astonished, saying: “Behold, are not all these who are speaking Galileans?” and so forth. I know that some have reproached me because I said that this sentence could be understood in two ways, or rather because I asked how it ought to be understood. I answer them briefly: everything that I wrote about this sentence in my earlier volume I did not put forward from my own judgment, but took from the words of a holy and altogether irreproachable teacher, namely Gregory of Nazianzus.

It is indeed certain that the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in all languages, and no believer may doubt this. But it is rightly asked how they spoke: whether the apostles’ speech had such power that it could be heard and understood equally by all who knew different languages; or whether, whenever one of them spoke—for it was necessary that one person in an assembly of such great multitude should deliver the teaching while the others remained silent—he first addressed the Hebrews in Hebrew, while the others did not know what he was saying; then the Greeks in Greek, while the others were ignorant of it and waiting; then the Parthians; after them the Medes; and likewise the Elamites and the other nations listed in order, speaking to each in its own language while each group waited and remained silent until its turn came, so that they might understand what was said and thus assent in faith to the words of the teachers.

Luke reports Peter speaking to the crowds, but he does not report that he repeated a second or third time the same things he had said; rather, he simply reports that they were consecrated through the mysteries of the Christian faith after receiving the counsel of salvation. I do not think he would have been in error if someone believes that both things could have occurred: that the apostles, in the Holy Spirit, were able both to understand and speak the languages of all nations, and that their words also, by a greater miracle, could have been understood equally by all who heard them, whatever language in which they were uttered.

[Col. 1000B] And those who dwell in Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia. All these provinces named after Judea indeed speak Greek, but if they made no sound different according to their native customs, they would certainly not be mentioned with such careful distinction of languages. Hence the marvelous grace of the Spirit in the apostles is to be contemplated: it not only taught them the diversity of all languages, but also caused the differences of local usage within each language, corresponding to the number of provinces that used it, to be recognized in their speech.

And Roman newcomers. The Greek is more correctly rendered: “And Roman travelers,” that is, Jews who were living abroad in Rome, just as others lived abroad elsewhere, as was said above. For that there were converts there—called in Greek *proselytes*, that is, those who had come from the nations to Judaism after abandoning the rites of paganism—is made clear by the following verse, where it says: “Jews as well as proselytes.”

Blood, fire, and vapor of smoke. Fire and smoke were discussed in the preceding book. By blood he means not only the blood of the Lord’s wound but also the Lord’s sweat, when, as he prayed before his betrayal, his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground. This is counted among signs wrought by divine power because it is proved not to occur at all in the ordinary course of human nature. It is therefore a sign, because it signified that the whole world was to be washed in the Lord’s blood: just as once the tabernacle or temple was consecrated to the Lord by the blood of victims, so now throughout the world the people of the faithful were to be dedicated as his holy house by his blood. Nor was the place of prayer to be only Jerusalem; rather, in every place of his dominion, the elect would lift pure hands to the Lord in prayer.

The sun will be turned into darkness. In Greek the word for darkness is read in the singular, namely *σκότος* (*skotos*), which the Latin translator, because he could not express it in the singular, necessarily rendered in the plural as *tenebras*, “darknesses.” I thought this should be mentioned so that anyone of the English nation who reads this may know that, because of the authority of the Latin language, it is not necessary for him to render *tenebras* in his own speech in the plural; he may instead use the singular, since this is equally possible on the authority of the Greek from which it was transferred into Latin writing.

This man, delivered up according to the determined plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by the hands of the wicked after afflicting him. In Greek there is one additional word, which nevertheless bears greatly upon the matter: “Receiving him who had been delivered up according to the foreknowledge of God.” For he was delivered by the governor into their power on the condition that they should choose either him or the robber. Having received this option, they granted life to the robber, but killed Jesus through the hands of the soldiers, though by their own cries and pleas.

Whom God raised, having loosed the pains, since it was impossible for him to be held by it. The sense of this sentence appears to be that, when the Lord descended to the realms below, the pains of punishment were loosed—that is, they were utterly unable to touch him. Yet if we examine the Greek text, where it is written, “Whom God raised on the third day, loosing through him the pains of death, since it was not possible for him to be held by it,” it becomes entirely clear that he says the pains of hell, or of death, were loosed by the Lord—that is, that through his descent to the realms below the holy were liberated from the places beneath. Although they were held in Abraham’s bosom, that is, in the consolation of secret rest, they were nevertheless not wholly free from the pain of death or hell. They did not yet deserve to see and enter the heavenly joys above until what was spoken by the prophet to the Lord came to pass: “You also, by the blood of the covenant, brought out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. IX). For if the saints in the pit of the infernal places were entirely free from the pain of death, why does he call them prisoners until they were brought out by the blood of Christ? Through him, therefore, he loosed the pains of death, since it was impossible for him to be held by it. For just as he himself was immune from the power of death, so he was also powerful to rescue from death’s dominion whomever he wished.

For David says concerning him, that is, concerning his person: “I always saw the Lord before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.” In explaining what the Mediator between God and human beings himself did, he gives us, who are merely human, counsel by which we may avoid sins. For whoever continually beholds the presence of his Creator with the eye of the mind is not turned toward wrongdoing. He also states the reason why he was not shaken. When the Lord gives assistance at the right hand, the left-hand powers do not prevail; rather, the mind whom he guards remains more firmly established in him. He appropriately said that the Lord was at his right hand, because if he does not hold that side, the devil, lying in wait, will immediately seize it, as it is written concerning Judas: “And the devil stood at his right hand” (Ps. CVIII).

Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted. He says “therefore,” namely because the Lord stood at his right hand, and he testifies that gladness arose in his thoughts and exultation in his tongue. Indeed, as the Passion approached, he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and he began to be afraid and distressed (Mark XIV). But he was sorrowful in order to show that he was truly human in soul and body and genuinely capable of suffering; his soul and tongue, however, exulted because he knew that the human race would be saved through his Passion.

Moreover, my flesh will rest in hope. He rejoiced because he could neither be shaken nor overcome by his enemies; but he says that, beyond this joy, his gladness increased still further because in his flesh—by whose death he saved us—he would also provide an example of resurrection.

For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption. It is certain that the Lord’s soul was not abandoned among the dead: after removing those for whose sake he had descended there, it soon returned to the realms above. It is likewise certain that his flesh did not undergo corruption, since it was glorified by a swift resurrection.

But it must be asked how, in another psalm, reproaching the impenitent and obstinate, he says of the labor of his Passion: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Ps. XXIX). The matter is resolved as follows: there he says that he descends into corruption when his body is pierced by the violence of the nails and the lance, since the piercing of a solid body may rightly be called a kind of corruption. Here, however, he rightly denies that corruption—that is, putrefaction—occurred, the corruption that generally ravages human flesh but was utterly unable to affect his most holy body.

You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence. These words are rightly understood not only of the Lord, who needed no other guide to overcome the kingdom of death but, having once received the fullness of divine power and wisdom, was able by himself to destroy death, rise to life, and ascend to the right hand of the Father; they are also understood of his elect, who, by his gift, find the way of truth by which they may return to the life they lost in the first-formed human being. They too will be filled with joy in the presence of God the Father, because this is our perfect blessedness: to deserve to see him face to face, as Philip understood very well when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough” (John XIV). That joy of seeing the Lord’s face is sufficient; nothing else is required, nor will anything further be required when he who is above all has been seen. These are also the words that follow in the psalm: “Pleasures are at your right hand forever” (Ps. XV).

Since he was therefore a prophet, and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that one from the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne, he spoke with foresight about the resurrection of Christ, and so forth. In Greek there is additional wording: “To raise up Christ from the fruit of his loins and to seat him upon his throne.” But where the text continues, “With foresight he spoke about the resurrection of his Christ, because neither was he abandoned in hell,” the Greek more consistently reads: “Because neither was his soul abandoned in hell.” And blessed Fulgentius, writing to Trasamund, presents it in this way: “For immediately he added concerning the raising of his body from the dead, saying: ‘Nor did his flesh see corruption.’” In accordance with this, the prophet embraced both matters when he said: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV).

And having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he poured out this which you see and hear. In Greek it reads as follows: “He poured out this gift, which you now see and hear.” First he had taught that Jesus, whom the Jews crucified and whom God raised, was the Christ; now, gradually calling the faith of his hearers toward higher things, he also indicates that this man is truly God, when he affirms that he poured out the gift of the Holy Spirit—a gift that every wise person recognizes as belonging solely to divine power. Beautifully, he uses the same word, “pouring out,” which the prophetic statement mentioned above had already said the Lord would use, so that from this too his hearers might infer that the Lord Jesus Christ himself was the one who, even before assuming flesh, had been accustomed to speak through the prophets; who arranged the future ages of the world as he wished; who would give signs and wonders in heaven and on earth; who would save all who called upon his name; and who would fulfill the other things described in prophetic speech as the Son of God and true God.

For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” [Col. 1003C] Some manuscripts read, “The Lord says,” but the Greek exemplars, both in this book and in the Psalter, read: “The Lord said.” Most clearly, blessed Peter explains through this psalm how what he had earlier taken from another psalm is to be understood: that the Lord swore to David to raise up Christ from the fruit of his loins and seat him upon his throne. For this throne of the kingdom was to be understood not as an earthly throne in Jerusalem, where David reigned, but as the throne at the right hand of his majesty in heaven.

Here he plainly established from the prophetic Scriptures both natures of our one and same Redeemer: the human, namely, which arose from the fruit of David’s loins through the Virgin; and the divine, on account of which, after ascending into heaven, the human being was taken up to the Father’s right hand. In the one nature he truly became David’s son; in the other, David’s Lord. Therefore he appropriately added:

Therefore let the whole house of Israel know with complete certainty that God made him both Lord and Christ. He proved him to be Lord by David’s word: “The Lord said to my Lord”; and by what the prophet Joel said: “And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II), declaring that he truly accomplished this on that very day. He taught him to be Christ by the word of the same David, in which the Lord said to him: “Sit at my right hand”; and likewise by the prophet’s declaration that the Holy Spirit is his Spirit and that he was able, by his own power, to give this Spirit to human beings. Who but an unbeliever could doubt that this belongs to no human being except the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ? For how could he rightly be believed to be not truly Christ—that is, anointed with the entire fullness of the Holy Spirit—if he was shown to give that same Spirit powerfully to whomever he wished?

He therefore says that God made him both Lord and Christ. Is the Lord Christ both God and human, one person existing in two natures? In his divinity he was eternally begotten by the Father; in his humanity he was made by the Father in time, when, through the working of the Holy Spirit, he ordained that he should become incarnate in the Virgin’s womb.

“And Lord,” he says, “God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” Jesus is the proper name of the man whom the Jews crucified, just as Aaron and David are proper names of men. “Lord,” however, is a title of power and majesty, to which every creature ought rightly to be subject. Concerning this, he said to the disciples after his resurrection: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Moreover, “Christ” is the designation of royal or priestly dignity. For priests and kings were accustomed, under the Law, to be anointed with holy oil and therefore to be called *christs*, as a figure of him who, anointed by God with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—above his companions, graciously became our king and great priest: priest, so that by the sacrifice of his Passion he might cleanse us from every sin and, placed at God’s right hand, might even now intercede for us; king, so that, after conquering all our adversaries, he might lead us into the immortal kingdom.

What shall we do, brothers? In Greek there is additional wording: “Show us.” We frequently find this verb added to this sentence in the works of those who interpreted the Holy Scriptures.

And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy” (Joel II). What he added—“and for all who are far away, whomever the Lord our God will call”—refers to the testimony that he had placed last from the prophet: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (ibid.). This refers especially to the calling of the nations, which had been separated far away from the fellowship, kinship, and merit of the children of Israel, yet, through calling upon the Lord’s name, were to be saved from their error according to the prophet’s promise.

Therefore those who received his word were baptized. Another translation, following the precise character of the Greek, reads: “Those who gladly received his word were baptized.” This rendering expresses more clearly that not merely some of those who had heard Peter’s word, but all who had gathered to hear it were baptized after hearing it gladly.

But the Lord added daily to those who were being saved to the same fellowship. In Greek it is read as follows: “But the Lord added to the Church those who were being saved”; and then another narrative begins.

CHAPTER III

Now Peter and John were going up together into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. This can be connected with the preceding sentence as follows: While the Lord was daily adding believers to his Church through the preaching of the apostles, the foremost of the apostles went up into the temple to pray to God together—that is, that he might always provide increase for his Church.

And immediately his bases and soles were strengthened. *Bases* is a Greek word, and it is placed in the Greek text itself; in Latin it means “supports.” By this term he indicates that the man’s steps were strengthened, as some have also translated it in Latin. But it must be known that among the Greeks steps are properly called *διαβήματα* (*diabēmata*) or *πορίαι* (*poriai*).

And they were filled with astonishment and ecstasy. Another edition has “admiration” instead of *ecstasy*, that is, “an excess of mind,” but this is not strictly correct; for greater admiration can sometimes lead the mind into an excess and carry it beyond its customary mode of thought toward higher things.

The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up, and so forth. In Greek it is more consistently rendered: “The God of our fathers glorified his servant Jesus.” It was fitting that, when addressing those who had killed the Lord, the wise teacher should first recall his humanity, which could be delivered up and killed; then, as the glory of his resurrection was gradually disclosed, he should also declare that he was God and the Son of God. Finally, a little later, he calls him the Author of life. At the close of the speech he says more openly: “To you first, God, raising up his Son, sent him to bless you, so that your sins may be blotted out, so that when the times of refreshment come from the presence of the Lord, then your sins may be blotted out.”

By “the times of refreshment” he means the distinction made at the universal judgment and the redemption of the righteous. Concerning this, they themselves, having suffered tribulations but been saved in hope, say to the Lord in the psalm: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV). For our sins will then be fully blotted out when, through the power of the resurrection, death—the last enemy—has been destroyed (I Cor. XV). In one translation we find this verse set down for the clarification of its meaning as follows: “So that when the times of refreshment come, they may come to you also from the presence of the Lord.” Indeed, this is how it is written in Greek, with the pronoun added: “So that the times of refreshment may come to you from the presence of the Lord.”

Whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things, which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from the beginning of the world. This is what the Psalmist testifies was said by God the Father to the same Lord Jesus Christ: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX). He was taken up into heaven and sits at God’s right hand. In that seat of the Father’s majesty he always remains divinely, nor was he ever absent from it; but in the humanity he assumed he will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead, when all his enemies will be placed beneath his feet and all things spoken by God through all the prophets from the beginning of the world will be restored.

For when all the saints enter eternal life with the Lord, the wicked, together with the devil, will undergo everlasting punishments, and nothing at all will remain for the prophets to promise us as still to be hoped for, since both parties—the good and the wicked—will have received from the just Judge an irrevocable sentence at the final judgment. Origen is greatly deceived and greatly deceives others, for he thinks that after this judgment, even after an interval separated by a very long span of time, he will be liberated with the other sinners who will have been sent with the devil from the judge’s left hand into Gehenna and brought into the heavenly kingdom. He takes this to be promised to them by the prophet who says: “And they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited” (Isa. XXIV). Yet the prophet’s meaning is clear according to sound interpretation: he foretold that the enemies and persecutors of the holy Church would each be carried into Gehenna on the day of his death, but foresaw that all would be released from there for a short time on the day of judgment, when, having received immortal bodies, they would again be plunged into the twofold punishment of eternal death. The prophet’s following words also show that this is what he intended in this passage. After saying, “And after many days they will be visited,” he immediately added: “And the moon will be ashamed, and the sun will be confounded” (ibid.), which both prophecy and the Gospel words declare will occur on the day of judgment.

[Col. 1006C] Moses indeed said: “For the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to all that he will speak to you,” and so forth. The beginning of this passage contains additional wording in Greek: “Moses indeed said to your fathers: ‘For the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet.’”

The force of the statement is clear: our Lord took the truth of flesh from the people of Israel, appearing in the likeness of Moses, so that just as Moses led carnal Israel, instructed and purified by ceremonies and legal rites, into the promised land, so the Lord, gathering spiritual Israel from the whole world through the grace of the Gospel, might lead it into the heavenly kingdoms. And just as those who despised the law of Moses were expelled from the promised land by hostile nations, so those who have scorned the teaching of evangelical grace will be driven out from the assembly of the saints by avenging spirits. For this is what follows:

But every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be exterminated from the people. It must be noted, however, that blessed Peter took care here to preserve not the words of the Mosaic statement but its meaning. For it is written in Deuteronomy, where Moses says to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb” (Deut. XVIII). A little later: “And the Lord God said to me: ‘They have spoken well in all things. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth; he will speak to them everything that I command him. But whoever does not wish to listen to his words, which he will speak in my name, I will be his avenger’” (ibid.).

In place of this, Peter wrote, “He will be exterminated from the people,” more clearly indicating that this is the form of divine vengeance: those who despise the heavenly commandments are made strangers to the lot of the elect. Here, then, as in many other passages where the apostles and evangelists provide examples from the Old Testament, it is evident that they sought the meaning of the Scriptures rather than the words, and did not take great care over the order or phrasing of the discourse, so long as the matter became clear to the understanding.

Saying to Abraham: “And in your seed all the families of the earth will be blessed.” From both testimonies—from the one proclaimed by the Lord to Moses and from the one proclaimed to Abraham—his severity and his goodness are revealed. His goodness is revealed in those who, having received faith in Christ, deserve to be blessed by him; his severity in those who, because of their deserved contempt and disobedience, are exterminated from the people of the blessed, that is, cast outside the boundaries of eternal blessedness.

The statement “In your seed all the families of the earth will be blessed” is to be understood in the same way as the Gospel statement: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into the world” (John I). For not all the families of the earth are blessed in Christ, nor is every human being coming into the world enlightened by Christ, since many more are condemned eternally while spending their lives in the darkness and curse in which they were born, or even adding worse things to it. Rather, it must be understood that all the families of the earth that are to be blessed are blessed in Abraham’s seed—that is, in Christ—and that every human being who belongs to the lot of the saints, which is in the light, is enlightened by his grace. Nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved (Acts IV).

It may also rightly be understood in this way: there is no kindred or family of the earth in which some do not receive the blessing of the heavenly inheritance. I am speaking of those families or kindreds—seventy-two in number—into which, after the Flood, we read that the human race was divided during the building of the tower. Thus, in Abraham’s seed—namely, in the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ—all the elect will be blessed: not only those who believed in him after his Incarnation, but also those who preceded the time of his Incarnation by being born in the flesh. For, by ascending into heaven, that same God-man opened the doors of the heavenly kingdom for all; on the day of judgment he will say to all: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV).

CHAPTER IV

The priests and the magistrate of the temple came upon them. *Magistratus* must be read in the singular, as is readily clear from the Greek, where *στρατηγός* (*strategos*) is written in the singular. In some Latin manuscripts we find “the superintendent of the temple,” but more correctly in others “the praetor of the temple.” In Greek, *praetor* is *στρατηγός* (*strategos*), whereas “magistrate” or “ruler” is *ἄρχων* (*archon*).

He said to them: “Rulers of the people and elders.” In Greek there is additional wording: “And elders of Israel, hear.” Similarly, in what follows, where it is said: “In this matter he stands before you healthy,” the Greek reads: “Healthy before you today,” and nothing else.

But when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and discovered that they were uneducated and ordinary men, they were astonished. “Uneducated” does not mean that they did not know letters, but that they did not possess expertise in the grammatical arts. For in Greek, more clearly, instead of this word, *ἀγράμματοι* (*agrammatoi*) is found, that is, “illiterate”; while *idiotae* properly means “unskilled” or “inexperienced.” Indeed, in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where it is written, “And if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (II Cor. XI), the Greek has *ἰδιώτης* (*idiōtēs*) for “unskilled.”

Because everyone was glorifying what had happened. [Col. 1008B] The Greek text is better: “For everyone was glorifying God in what had happened.” The addition found in our manuscripts, “in what had occurred,” is not found in Greek. In fact, *glorificabant* and *clarificabant* are commonly translated indifferently into Latin from the one Greek word *ἐδόξαζον* (*edoxazon*), but there is a difference between an event being made famous and God being glorified or honored in an event.

For events or statements to be made famous means that they are brought to the notice of many by the spreading of their reputation; this can also happen with remarkable human deeds. But for God to be made glorious or glorified in human deeds is proper to Christian piety and humility, since he himself commands and says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

[Col. 1008C] Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things? The prophet does not ask as one who is ignorant; rather, in amazement at the madness of the wicked, he rebukes those who rose up against the Lord the Savior, though he had harmed them in nothing and had instead assisted them with many benefits. He used “nations” for the Roman soldiers and “peoples” for the Jews. Hence it is appropriately said that the nations raged, while the peoples meditated on vain things against God.

The leaders of the Jews carefully deliberated how they might hand the Lord over to death; the soldiers, however, are found to have inflicted nothing upon him and laid no ambush, but merely to have obeyed the governor’s orders in his humiliation and death. Thus they are said to have raged, being driven by an ignorant and disorderly impulse; and because raging is properly the behavior of wild beasts, they are rightly said to have raged, since, setting reason aside, they were inflamed by beastlike fury.

The statement that the peoples meditated on vain things refers to what is said of the blessed man in the preceding psalm: “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. I). For just as blessed is the person who spends all his time meditating on the divine law, so that people is rightly assigned to perpetual misery which, in its pride, not only turned away from meditating on God’s law but also, in its madness, repeatedly exercised itself against God and Lord, the author of the law.

The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. [Col. 1009A] He means the Jewish rulers and Pilate himself. He uses “kings” in the plural because of Herod the tetrarch, as the apostles’ following words testify. Yet the plural designation “kings” may also rightly refer to Herod the tetrarch himself, who joined Pilate in consenting to the Lord’s death, and to the other Herod of the same name and wickedness, who, in persecuting the newly born Lord, killed the children in Bethlehem. Although they did not act at the same time, they stood and gathered together with the Jewish rulers against the Lord with the same hatred and wickedness of mind.

It must also be noted that these verses are so interwoven that the first receives from the second the concluding phrase, “against the Lord and against his Christ,” while the second receives from the first the adverb “why,” so that the complete arrangement of both is:

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things against the Lord and against his Christ? Why did the kings of the earth stand by, and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against his Christ?”

He says “kings of the earth” to distinguish them from those for whom, while they are pilgrims on earth, a kingdom is preserved in heaven.

When you stretch out your hand, healings and signs and wonders may be performed through the name of your holy Son Jesus. In Greek it reads, “Through the name of your holy Servant [or Child] Jesus,” which seems more consistent with the apostles’ prayers, since they strove in every way that the man whom the Jews had crucified, having been taken up into heaven, might be recognized as God’s Son when the signs of miracles became conspicuous through his name.

[Col. 1009C] “And they spoke the word of God with confidence.” In Greek there is an addition: “To everyone willing to believe.” Likewise, in the following reading, where it says, “Now the multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul,” Greek copies also have—though our manuscripts do not—the addition: “And there was no division at all among them.” Then follows what is also contained in our manuscripts: “Nor did any of them say that anything of what they possessed was his own.” Blessed Cyprian likewise expressed this sentence in the third book of his *Testimonies*, saying: “The crowd of those who believed was moved by one soul and one mind; nor was there any distinction among them, nor did anyone consider his own any of the possessions they had.”

This passage also agrees and most fittingly corresponds [Col. 1009D] with what was said above: those who received the Holy Spirit on the holy day of Pentecost, although they were all Galileans, spoke in the languages of all the Jews and proselytes who were present from different parts of the world.
