For there, through the uniting of differing languages, it was beautifully foreshadowed that the holy Church, through the gift of that same Spirit, would have one heart and one soul among the various nations and languages throughout the world. Not all believers speak in every language; rather, the uniting of different languages in the faith of Christ was a sign that there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Eph. 4).

“But everything was common to them.” In Latin, *communia* (“common”) is called in Greek *koiná* (κοινά). From this word it is clear that perfect servants of God are called in Greek *koinobítai* (κοινοβῖται), that is, “those living in common,” and that their dwellings are called *koinóbia* (κοινόβια). For *bíos* (βίος) is plainly their word for “life”—not the life that is opposed to death, but the manner of life by which someone lives: in military service, agriculture, or any honorable or dishonorable occupation; whether he is a monk, layman, or cleric. The life by which we are distinguished from the dead, however, is called by the Greeks *zōḗ* (ζωή). Those, therefore, who live in such a way that everything is common to them in the Lord are rightly called *koinobítai*, a single name properly formed from two words. This life is happier than all other ways of living in this world to the extent that it already imitates the condition of the future age, where all blessed goods are common to all who behold the glory of the one from whom all good things come. And because there the highest grace of peace and security reigns, the city in which the pattern of this life first appeared was rightly called Jerusalem, that is, “Vision of Peace.”

Hence one should note the difference both of things and of places. In the work of pride, the tower, when the language and mind of the human race were one, they were deservedly divided because of their iniquity, so that although the people there spoke in all languages, no one could understand the will or words of his neighbor. But in Jerusalem those same languages were united because of humility, and although there was one language for all, their will and soul were also one. This is enacted even today throughout the world, while the elect, amid manifold divisions of speech, serve the Lord with one undivided heart and purpose. But the reprobate all serve the devil in such a way that the same slavery is often carried on among them with one mind and with contentious zeal and strife. For this reason their city is rightly called Babylon, that is, “confusion.”

“Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles—which is interpreted ‘son of consolation’—a Levite, a Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it, and so forth.” It is remarkable that Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, considers this Barnabas—who was later ordained an apostle of the Gentiles together with Paul and, after their long companionship, returned again to Cyprus, from which he had originated, to preach—to have belonged to the number of the Lord and Savior’s seventy disciples. Yet blessed Luke expressly writes that he came into the apostles’ discipleship after the Lord’s ascension. Unless perhaps we should suppose that he had previously followed Christ’s discipleship in such a way that he had not yet renounced all that he possessed. Whether that accorded with evangelical teaching is readily evident to anyone.

## CHAPTER V

“Now the high priest arose, and all who were with him,” and so forth. In Greek this reading begins by referring back to what precedes: “And seeing these things, the high priest arose.”

“But when the officers of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were perplexed about them, wondering what this might become.” Here too *officer* should be read in the singular, as also in what follows, where it says: “Then the officer went to the temple with the attendants.” For the Greek copy has the singular *strategós* (στρατηγός), that is, “praetor,” in both places. It should be known, however, that the Greek has more at this point, for it reads: “But when the priests, the officer of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were astonished and perplexed about them, asking, ‘What does this mean?’”

“And the high priest questioned them, saying: ‘We strictly charged you,’” and so forth. In Greek it is more logically expressed: “Did we not strictly charge you?” For this manner of speaking is more appropriate to one who is asking a question.

“We must obey God rather than human beings.” In Greek it is read interrogatively: “Must we obey God rather, or human beings?” The apostles appropriately refuted the pontiff’s foolish and rash question with a firm and prudent answer.

“The God of our fathers raised up Jesus.” In Greek it has, “His Servant [or Child] Jesus,” in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Give power to your servant; save the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 85).

“And we are witnesses of these words, and so is the Holy Spirit whom God has given to those who obey him.” We are witnesses because we saw the glory of his resurrection and followed him with our eyes as he ascended into heaven.

The Holy Spirit also bears witness, because, so that we might proclaim the mighty works of God to you with unwavering boldness, even while you resound with opposition, he himself strengthened us by his presence; speaking in us, he himself formed these words as well. This is what the Lord promised them when he said: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me, and you also will bear witness” (John 15)—that is, he will inspire you to speak, while you will bear witness concerning me by speaking outwardly.

“But a certain Pharisee named Gamaliel rose in the council, a teacher of the law,” and so forth. Concerning this Gamaliel we also read in the book of Saint Clement that he was secretly a disciple of the apostles, but that, at their counsel, he was ordered to remain among the Jews in order to mitigate their fury whenever necessity arose. That this truly happened became completely known throughout the Church of Christ today through the discovery of the relics of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, which took place by divine arrangement through that same man. For it appeared in a vision to the holy servant of God and presbyter Lucian—as Lucian the presbyter later wrote to all the churches—and he revealed with a most pleasing manifestation where Saint Stephen had been buried, together with Nicodemus, who had buried the Lord with Joseph, and with Gamaliel himself and his son Abibas.

“After him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the census.” In Greek it reads, “In the days of the *apographḗ* (ἀπογραφή),” that is, “in the days of the registration for the census,” as we likewise find it translated into Latin in the *Ecclesiastical History*.

“And now therefore I say to you: Withdraw from these men and let them go.” In Greek there is an addition: “Without defiling your hands.”

“But if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them.” In Greek there is also an addition here: “Neither you nor your rulers.”

“Lest perhaps you be found opposing God.” Where our text has “opposing God,” or, as some have translated it, “opposing God,” Greek has a single word, *theomákhoi* (θεομάχοι), “God-fighters” or “those who fight against God.” I thought this worth mentioning so that, whenever we encounter *theomákhos* or *theomachía* in histories, we may know the force of the word more precisely.

## CHAPTER VI

“They set them before the apostles, and, after praying, laid hands on them.” It was not those who appointed them, but the apostles, who laid hands on them. The common administration of affairs indeed required that men be chosen as ministers for the widows. But once those who appeared worthy of this ministry had been found, as the providence of saving counsel gradually increased, as it usually does, it pleased them to ordain these same men as ministers not only of reading but also of the sacred altar, the Lord’s blood, and the common nourishment and table of the multitude of believers. This is demonstrated by the words: “And, after praying, they laid hands on them.” For this is proper to those who are promoted from the common number of the faithful to the office of the most holy altar.

“Now Stephen, full of grace and strength, performed great wonders and signs among the people.” In Greek there is an addition: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” In the preceding book I wrote that *Stephen* means “crowned,” and what I wrote is not far from the truth. But, on investigating more carefully, I discovered that in Greek *Stephen* does not mean “crowned,” but “crown.” For among them this is a masculine noun, and therefore it suits a man; “crowned,” however, is called *stephanēphóros* (στεφανηφόρος), as though “bearing a crown.” Thus, in the psalm where we sing, “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness” (Ps. 64), the verse begins in Greek: “You will bless the crown” (*eulogḗseis tò stéphanon*, εὐλογήσεις τὸν στέφανον). Eusebius beautifully explains the mystery of this name, saying: “Immediately after his ordination, he was stoned by those who had also killed the Lord, and through this a crown was given by Christ to Stephen, in keeping with his name.” Among the Greeks, “crown” is also called by the neuter noun *stémma* (στέμμα). I thought this worth mentioning because we often find this name bestowed in Latin books as well.

[Col. 1012D] “But some of the synagogue arose, which is called that of the Libertines and Cyrenians,” and so forth. In the Greek text itself the name “Libertines” is written. Libertines are called the children of freedmen—that is, of those who, after slavery, were manumitted and granted freedom. It is therefore clear that they were born from a servile stock, those who first rebelled against the faith of Christ. Although they had been emancipated by human masters, they did not cease to be slaves of sin. In their person the most wicked heretical persecutors of the faith and of all holiness are fittingly represented. Concerning them Peter says: “For, speaking arrogant words of vanity, they entice through the desires of the flesh and dissipation those who have scarcely escaped from those who live in error, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption” (2 Pet. 2). [Col. 1013A] Opposed to this slavery is the freedom of the Spirit, which the Beroeans possessed. In their praise, Paul and Silas are said to have preached: “Now these were nobler than those in Thessalonica, for they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily.”

“And they could not resist the wisdom and the Holy Spirit who spoke.” In Greek there is an addition: “And they could not resist the wisdom that was in him and the Holy Spirit who spoke; for this reason they were rebuked by him with all confidence.” Since, therefore, they could not contradict the truth, they secretly induced men to say, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VII

“Now the high priest said.” In Greek “to Stephen” is added; and then follows: “If these things are so.”

“He said: ‘Men, brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham.’” Because blessed Stephen was accused of having spoken blasphemous words against Moses and God, at the very beginning of his speech he most carefully countered their slander by saying that the God who spoke to the fathers and prophets is the God of majesty and glory. When he later reached the time of Moses in his speech, he indeed exalted Moses with worthy praises, but he proved that the people had been rebellious and always disobedient to his words. It should be noted, however, what an art of speaking he employs. He began to address his persecutors as though he feared them: “Men, brothers and fathers, listen.” What could have reconciled the listener more gently or mercifully than praising the Savior? [Col. 1013C] He began pleasantly, so that he might be heard for a long time. And because he had been accused of speaking against God and the law, just as at the beginning of his address he showed that he was proclaiming the true God, so also he expounded the giving of the law to them, presenting himself as the preacher of the very law whose destroyer he had been accused of being. But as his speech proceeded, when he reproved both their new and their ancient errors, he made entirely clear how authoritative a spirit he possessed and how free his soul was from fear of the enemy.

“And they were placed in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price of silver.” In Greek it reads, “Our father Abraham.” Blessed Stephen added this to please his listeners, so that he might be heard longer and more willingly.

“But as the time of deliverance approached, which God had pledged to Abraham.” In Greek it is better expressed: “Which God had promised to Abraham.”

“And as he approached to examine it, the voice of the Lord came: ‘I am the God of your fathers.’” In Greek it is written: “A voice came from heaven, saying to him: ‘I am the God of your brothers. Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.’” According to the moral sense, this passage admonishes us that, standing in the Church—which is rightly called holy ground—we should renounce dead works.

“And he handed them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the Prophets.” He uses the singular because among the Hebrews the Twelve Prophets constitute one book, not twelve books corresponding to the number of those prophets. The host of heaven is sometimes called the army of angels. In this passage, however, it seems more fitting that he called the stars the host of heaven, since he immediately adds the prophet’s testimony, in which they are accused of having received the star of their god in place of God, and the tent of Moloch in place of the tent of the true God.

“Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit.” He shows them that the circumcision of the foreskin, about which they gloried against the grace of the Gospel, has no value for salvation, since they were proved to possess an impure mind and hearing. At the same time, in speaking this way, he interprets and explains to them what the angel signified when he appeared to Moses in the fire of the flame of the bush, so that the bush burned but was not consumed. Fire signifies the Holy Spirit; [Col. 1014B] the bush, which is a kind of thorn plant, figuratively proclaimed the sins of that people. The Lord therefore appeared to Moses in a bush containing fire but not consumed by it, to indicate that he himself would come with the illumination and ardor of the Holy Spirit to instruct the people, yet would not consume the sins of that same people. Rather, despite his merciful benefits, that people would continually resist him with the thickest thorns of their wickedness.

“Behold, I see the heavens opened.” What we say in Latin as *video* (“I see”) is expressed in Greek by *theōrō* (θεωρῶ), from which the name *theōría* (“theoria,” that is, the contemplative life) is derived. Through this contemplation some of the elect, while still held in this life, have been divinely exalted and deemed worthy, after more diligently cleansing the eye of the heart, of beholding the joys of the future life—as happened in the present case to Saint Stephen, and to Paul when he was caught up to the third heaven, and to many others on other occasions. Hence God is also called *Theós* (Θεός) in Greek, because he sees everything and all things are naked and open to his eyes.

“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, “he fell asleep.” He says beautifully “he fell asleep,” rather than “he died.” For he offered the sacrifice of love and fell asleep in the hope of resurrection.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Now on that day a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.” If the Church was scattered while the apostles remained in Jerusalem, as Luke says, it is clear that the man who, writing under the name of Melito, bishop of Asia, composed a book concerning the death of the blessed Mother of God, wrote falsely when he said that in the second year after the Lord’s ascension all the apostles had been divided throughout the whole world, each to preach in his own province. He says that, as the death of blessed Mary approached, all of them were lifted from the places where they were preaching the word of God and carried on clouds to Jerusalem, being set down before the door of her house. Among them was Paul, recently converted from persecutor to the faith of Christ, who had been appointed with Barnabas to the ministry among the Gentiles. That writing also specifically states concerning the apostle John that at that time he was preaching in Ephesus.

All of this plainly contradicts the words of blessed Luke, who relates that, after the other believers had been driven out of Jerusalem, the apostles remained there and preached everywhere until the Church had peace throughout Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. No one doubts that this could not have been accomplished in a single year. Luke also clearly indicates that Paul was appointed to the ministry among the Gentiles with Barnabas not in the second year after the Lord’s ascension, but after a long interval. Let us certainly not believe that the blessed apostle John—to whom the Lord, on the cross, entrusted his virgin mother to a virgin—departed after one year and left her alone, so abandoned for so long that, when she died, she feared that even her body would be burned by her enemies; and that, after being carried on clouds, he returned to her as though forgetful or neglectful of her, while she anxiously prayed to him, saying:

“I beg you, my son John, to remember the word of your teacher, my Lord Jesus Christ, who entrusted me to you. [Col. 1015B] Behold, having been called, I shall enter upon the way of all the earth. But I have heard the plans of the Jews, who say: ‘Let us wait for the day when she who bore Jesus of Nazareth dies, and let us burn her body.’ Therefore now, my son, take care of my funeral rites.”

I have taken care to mention these things because I know that some people, through careless rashness, assent to the aforementioned volume against the authority of blessed Luke.

“But devout men took care of Stephen and made great lamentation over him.” The book recounting the discovery of his relics, which we mentioned above, remembers this lamentation and the killing of blessed Stephen. It reports that, among other things, Gamaliel said in a vision to the presbyter Lucian:

“I am Gamaliel, who brought up Paul, the apostle of Christ, and taught him the law in Jerusalem. Here beside me, in the eastern part of the monument, lies my lord Stephen, who was stoned by the Jews and the chief priests in Jerusalem for the faith of Christ, outside the gate that is toward the north and leads to Cedar. There he lay cast out day and night, so that no burial might be given him, according to the command of the wicked rulers, and so that his body might be consumed by wild beasts. But by God’s will not one of these touched him—not a beast, bird, or dog.

“I, Gamaliel, taking pity on the ministry of Christ and hastening to receive a reward and a share with the holy man in the faith, sent by night as many devout people and believers in Christ Jesus as I knew, who lived in Jerusalem among the Jews. I encouraged them, [Col. 1015D] supplied what was necessary for their expenses, and secretly persuaded them to go and carry his body in my vehicle to my estate, that is, Caphar Gamalan—interpreted ‘the village of Gamaliel’—which is twenty miles from the city. There I had lamentation made for him for forty-five days, and placed him in my new monument, in the eastern chamber. I ordered them to provide from my resources whatever was necessary for his mourning.”

“Those who had been scattered therefore passed through the country, proclaiming the word of God.” For “scattered,” Greek has “disseminated,” that is, dispersed.

[Note: [Col. 1015] Perhaps *diasparentes* should be written; the Greek copy reads *diasparéntes* (διασπαρέντες), which means “disseminated” in Latin. EDITOR.]

For they were the ones of whom Isaiah said: “All who see them will recognize them, because these are the offspring whom the Lord has blessed,” and of whom the Lord says in the Gospel parable: “The good seed, these are the children of the kingdom” (Matt. 13). This seed was therefore disseminated throughout the regions so that the harvest of faith, which began in Jerusalem, might first fill Judea and Samaria and then the entire world. Finally, concerning these same scattered—or rather disseminated—people, we read below that they spoke the word not only to Jews but also to Greeks, and that through them the foundations of the Church arising in Antioch were most nobly laid.

“Now Philip had gone down to a city of Samaria and was preaching Christ to them.” He too belonged to the number of those disseminators, and was the first to preach Christ in Samaria. Through the deacon was begun what Christ said to the apostles: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria” (Acts 1).

“But there was a certain man who had previously been a magician in the city, deceiving the people of Samaria.” For “deceiving,” Greek has *exístōn* (ἐξιστῶν), which means “bringing into ecstasy,” that is, converting them to mental derangement, or astonishment and amazement, evidently through the display of his magical deceptions.

“To whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying: ‘This is the power of God.’” “This” (*hic*) is not an adverb of place but a pronoun, as though it said: “This man is the power of God.”

“May your money be with you for destruction.” It is more correctly written “for destruction” (*in perditionem*), in accordance with the Greek authority, than “in destruction” (*in perditione*). For his money was not going to be with him in that destruction to which the wicked man was to be condemned. Rather, because the apostles refused to accept the money he was offering for his sacrilegious bargain, he was ordered to keep it with him, for his own destruction, so that he might pay eternal penalties because of this money, which he had gathered for an unjust purchase.

## CHAPTER IX

“For behold, he is praying, and he sees a man named Ananias entering and laying hands on him.” In Greek it reads: “And he saw in a vision a man”—that is, *en horámati* (ἐν ὁράματι), a word which the presbyter Juvencus also used in his Gospel poem, saying:

“Make all unacquainted with this vision.”

It is therefore evident that during those three days in which, having been blinded, he awaited the future grace of light, he was by no means languid in idleness. Rather, having been exalted by divine illumination, he was searching out heavenly mysteries. And, unless I am mistaken, it is credible that during that time he was taught the mystery of the Gospel dispensation, concerning which he himself boasts in his letter to the Galatians: “For I neither received it from a human being nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1). A little later he says: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem,” and so forth (ibid.).

The text of this little book also confirms this when it continues: “He was with the disciples who were in Damascus for some days, and immediately in the synagogues he preached Jesus to them, that he is the Son of God” (Acts 9). It in no way asserts that he learned anything from human beings, but confirms that immediately after his baptism he undertook the ministry of an outstanding teacher. He should indeed be compared with the one of whom it is written: “Because the utterance of the Lord set him ablaze” (Ps. 104).

“The Jews made a plan to kill him.” Their plot against Paul became known; they were guarding the gates of the city day and night in order to kill him. It was not the Jews who guarded them, but the citizens themselves together with their king, Aretas, as the apostle himself, who was besieged and escaped, writes to the Galatians. For Gentiles and Jews, although they disagree among themselves, are always united in persecuting Christians.

“But when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples.” In the Greek text Paul’s name is added in this verse: “When Paul had come to Jerusalem.” This does not mean that at that time he was already called by that name, before converting Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus, to the faith of Christ. Rather, Luke anticipates the name and appropriately indicates beforehand that he would be called Paul at the point where he first narrates his coming to Jerusalem after his conversion and his joining the apostles. Thus, from the place where shortly before he had departed as a proud persecutor of the Church, he might now enter as the Church’s humble defender.

Since *paulum* in Latin means “a little” or “somewhat,” that man rightly preferred to be called Paul, who, amid the greatest works of virtue, did not cease to remain humble. Nor should we suppose that Paul or Peter are Hebrew rather than Latin or Greek names, since it is clear that the Hebrews do not possess the letter *p* in any form.

“But Barnabas took him and led him to the apostles, and told them how on the road he had seen the Lord,” and so forth. Paul himself shows when these things happened and to which apostles Barnabas brought him, writing to the Galatians: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me,” and so forth, until he says: “Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I stayed with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother” (Gal. 1).

Therefore, when Luke subsequently says: “He was with them, coming in and going out in Jerusalem,” it is credible that this took place during the fifteen days in which he says he stayed with Peter and James. And what follows in the Epistle—“Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (Gal. 1)—Luke indicates how this happened when he continues: “He also spoke and disputed with the Greeks, but they sought to kill him. When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.” Tarsus is a city of Cilicia, while Caesarea Philippi is a city of Syria.

When he adds, “He was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they had only heard that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once attacked” (ibid.), this is what Luke stated earlier: he attempted to join the disciples, and they all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple, until they learned it through Barnabas’s account. Since it is therefore clear that Paul came to Jerusalem three years after his conversion and was associated with the number of the apostles, while, as he himself writes, he was still unknown by face to the churches of Judea that were in Christ, those who, by following apocryphal books, think that he had already been ordained with Barnabas to the apostolate of the Gentiles in the second year after the Lord’s passion are greatly mistaken.

“The Church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace.” Where Latin says “throughout all,” Greek has *kath’ holēs* (καθ’ ὅλης), “through the whole.” Hence it should be noted that the Church is called catholic from the fact that, spread throughout the whole world, it exists in one peace.

[Col. 1018B] “And it was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit,” or “was multiplied,” as it is written in Greek. For what we call “consolation,” Greek has *paraklḗsei* (παρακλήσει). Hence it is plainly evident that the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete because, illuminating the hearts of the faithful, he multiplies the Church throughout the whole world and fills it with his grace.

## CHAPTER X

“And send for Simon, who is called Peter; he is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is beside the sea.” Everything in Holy Scripture is full of spiritual figures, including names and the locations of places. Peter lodges in the house of Simon, that is, of one who obeys; and this Simon is a tanner because he is a teacher of the Church. Peter finds a welcome and beloved lodging there wherever he finds obedient hearers—those who chastise their body and bring it into subjection (1 Cor. 9), who, protected by God, stand firm in the citadel of virtues, so that, having crossed beyond all the waves of this passing world, they may look down upon them with tranquil freedom of mind.

This is what it means for Simon the tanner to have a house in which he receives Peter in one part of the city that is beside the sea: perfect hearers of the word maintain in the holy Church a way of life that despises, with the single steadfastness of an unfeigned faith, either the fleeting glory of the world or its temporal and shifting terrors.

“An ecstasy came upon him, and he saw heaven opened.” The opening of heaven signifies the revelation, now soon to be made to the Gentiles, of the heavenly mysteries, and also the entrance into the heavenly kingdom itself, which was to be opened.

“Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” What is said in Latin as “kill” is expressed in Greek here by *thýson* (θῦσον). This is not the general word for killing, but the specific word for the killing by which victims are sacrificed to God. For a victim or sacrifice is called in Greek *thysía* (θυσία), and an altar *thysiastḗrion* (θυσιαστήριον). In the psalm where we sing, “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. 4), Greek has *thýsate thysían* (θύσατε θυσίαν); and for “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.), it has *thýson tō Theō thysían* (θῦσον τῷ Θεῷ θυσίαν).

According to this meaning, Peter is told, “*Thýson* and eat,” which our translator rendered, “Kill and eat.” It could equally have been translated, “Offer in sacrifice and eat,” so that he might understand that animals of various kinds had been offered to him from heaven for this purpose: that by preaching he might make those represented by such animals into an offering of the Lord—rescued, that is, from the harmful life of ancestral tradition and transferred, through the sacraments of the Lord’s passion, into the new life of divine service.

“What God has purified, you must not call common.” The meaning of this divine utterance is readily apparent: the Gentiles, whom Peter still considered unclean, the inward providence of their Creator was already counting among the clean. But one should note the custom of Holy Scripture, which is accustomed to call the unclean “common,” because the person who wishes to serve various enticements cannot be clean, as Scripture says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6). And again: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Luke 4). Whoever therefore desires to be clean should not divide his mind among various and manifold thoughts, but should bind himself to following solely the will of his Creator.

“And Cornelius said: ‘From the fourth day until this hour I was praying at the ninth hour in my house.’” In Greek it is written more fully and clearly: “From the fourth day until this hour I was fasting and worshiping, from the sixth hour until the ninth.” This plainly shows that, on the fourth day before he spoke these things with Peter, he remained fasting until the ninth hour; and, so that his fasting might be acceptable to God, from the sixth hour of the day until the ninth he devoted himself to earnest prayers. Therefore he deserved to obtain what he sought with such persistence in fasting and prayer.

“He is lodging in the house of Simon the tanner beside the sea.” “Immediately, therefore, I sent for you, and you did well to come.” In Greek it continues: “When he arrives, he will speak to you.”

“Now therefore we are all present in your sight to hear everything that has been commanded you by the Lord.” In Greek it reads: “We are present in the sight of God.” This was rightly said by one who had a mind ready to obey the divine will as soon as he learned it and believed that God’s majesty was present everywhere.

To us who ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead. In Greek, “for forty days” has been added; and Saint Augustine declared that this was how it stood in his manuscript, adding in explanation:

> “Not that they had eaten and drunk with him every day for forty days. For that would conflict with John, who inserted those eight days during which he was not seen by them, so that he might appear for the third time by the Sea of Tiberias.” [Col. 1019D]

Elsewhere, explaining the sacramental significance of both his eating and his fasting for the same number of days, he says:

> “He fasted when he was tempted before his death, still needing food; but he ate and drank when he was glorified, no longer needing food. There he was displaying in himself our labor; here, in us, his consolation, determining both by forty days. For he fasted forty days when he was tempted in the wilderness, as it is written in the Gospel, before the death of his flesh; and again he was with his disciples for forty days, entering and departing, eating and drinking after the resurrection of his flesh.”

By this number forty, the course of this age seems to be signified [Col. 1020A] in those who are called by grace to him who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. For the Law has ten commandments, now spread throughout the world by the grace of Christ; and the world is divided into four parts, while ten multiplied by four makes forty, since the Lord gathered those redeemed by him from the regions—from the east and the west, from the north and the sea (Ps. 106).

Thus, fasting forty days before the death of his flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Abstain from the desires of this age” (1 Pet. 2). But eating and drinking forty days after the resurrection of his flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.” Fasting belongs to the tribulation of struggle, since one who is engaged in combat abstains from everything; but food belongs to the hope of peace, which will not be perfected until our body, whose redemption we await, has put on immortality. We do not yet glory in having attained it, but already feed upon it through hope. The Apostle shows that we do both at once when he says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation,” as though the former belonged to food and the latter to fasting. For while we travel along the Lord’s way, we both fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future—here not setting our heart upon earthly things, there feeding upon things above.

And the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished because the gift of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues, etc. This resembles the passage concerning the same apostle Peter when he gave the Jews an account of why he had entrusted the Gentiles with the sacraments of baptism. [Col. 1020C]

“If therefore,” he said, “God gave them an equal gift, just as he gave us,” etc. There are also many other testimonies of Scripture that unanimously attest that the Spirit is God’s gift insofar as he is given to those who love God through him. He is therefore God’s gift insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given; but he is God in himself, even if he is given to no one, because he was coeternal with the Father and the Son before he was given to anyone. Nor, because they give him, is he for that reason inferior to them. For he is given as God’s gift in such a way that, as God, he also gives himself. “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XI

But the disciples, according to what each possessed, determined to send supplies for the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending them to the elders through the hands of Barnabas and Paul. To those who misunderstand, the disciples here seem not to have kept the Lord’s command: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6); nor does Paul seem to have imitated the birds of the air and the lilies of the field in accordance with the Lord’s command, since he often testifies concerning himself that he worked with his own hands so as not to burden anyone. Yet these and similar passages of Scripture make it sufficiently clear that our Lord does not disapprove when someone provides for such things in a human manner; rather, he disapproves when someone serves God for the sake of such things, so that in his works he looks not to the kingdom of God but to acquiring them. The whole command, therefore, is reduced to this rule: even when providing for these things, we must think of the kingdom of God, but in the service of the kingdom of God we must not think of these things. [Col. 1021A]

## CHAPTER XII

Gird yourself and put on your sandals. Instead of “little shoes,” or “boots,” as some manuscripts read, the Greek has *sandalia*, “sandals.” In the Gospel we read that this kind of footwear was permitted to the apostles, certainly not without a figurative, mystical meaning. For the apostles’ foot was neither covered nor bare against the ground, so that they might be admonished neither to conceal the Gospel nor to devote it to earthly advantages, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who proclaim good things!”

And he sat on the tribunal and addressed them. Instead of “on the tribunal,” he says “in the tribunal.” It is a feature of Latin usage [Col. 1021B] that in this expression *pro* is used to mean “in.”

## CHAPTER XIII

The Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them. This seems to have happened after Herod’s death. He died in the third year of Claudius’s reign, which, according to the reliable testimony of the chronicles, was the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion. Since it is therefore established that Paul was set apart for the apostleship with Barnabas only after so much time had elapsed since the Lord’s Passion, it is plainly evident that those who composed or accepted the book mentioned above concerning the death of holy Mary are greatly mistaken. For, as we have often recalled, that same fabrication says that in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension, when the same most blessed Mother of God was about to die, the apostles, already scattered throughout the world for preaching, were suddenly snatched together in a cloud to visit her; among them was Paul, recently converted to the faith and immediately made, with Barnabas, an apostle of the Gentiles. Anyone who believes blessed Luke understands that this happened quite differently: Paul was ordained an apostle not in the second year after the Lord’s Passion but in the thirteenth. Consequently, he recognizes that the aforementioned little book concerning blessed Mary’s death, since it is manifestly mistaken about the chronology, is also of suspect reliability in its other matters. [Col. 1021C]

They found a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet, whose name was Bar-Jesus. In Greek there is an addition: “who is interpreted as Elymas.” [Col. 1021D]

But Elymas the magician resisted them—for that is how his name is interpreted—seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Here too the Greek has an addition: “because he gladly listened to them.”

But Saul, who is Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, and so forth. Just as Barnabas’s name was changed immediately after his renunciation, so that, instead of Joseph, he was called Barnabas—that is, instead of “increased [one],” “son of consolation”—so, after he had been increased and added to the number of the elect, he immediately deserved, through the grace received from the Spirit, both to be called and to be a son of *paraklēsis*, that is, of consolation. In the same way Saul, after receiving the rank of apostle, took the name Paul. Since he had been made humble from being proud, he was rightly called Paul instead of Saul. Saul is named after Saul, the wicked and persecuting king; Paul is named from a humble and small spirit. For *paulum* means “a little.” Thus, interpreting his own name in a manner of speaking, he himself said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15). [Col. 1022A]

And immediately a mist and darkness fell upon him. In Greek, the word for “darkness” is in the singular, *skotos* (σκότος). The Latin translator did not follow this because Latin does not have this noun in the singular—a point that we likewise explained above.

And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them by lot, as though after four hundred [Col. 1022B] and fifty years, and after this he gave them judges. We explained in the preceding book of our exposition how this number can be understood. But it should be known that the Greek is written differently:

> And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them by lot. And after this, after approximately four hundred and fifty years, he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

How this agrees with the statement contained in the Book of Kings—that from Israel’s departure from Egypt until the building of the Temple there were four hundred and ninety years—it is beyond our ability to explain, unless perhaps he followed the common report in his speech, as blessed Stephen is shown to have done in his address to the Jews concerning the burial of the twelve patriarchs. [Col. 1022C]

And God gave them Saul, son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. Here too, concerning Saul’s reign, the Apostle seems to have followed popular opinion, as we already said in the preceding book. Yet, concerning what I said there—that Eusebius, following Josephus, assigned forty years to the reigns of Samuel and Saul, dividing the number equally between them—afterward, examining Josephus’s histories more carefully and chronologically, I saw that he did not himself write that forty years belonged to the aforementioned period, but assigned only twelve years to Samuel and twenty years to Saul.

Moreover, after rereading the books of the Chronicles more attentively, I noticed why Eusebius did not wish to follow Josephus’s authority here, just as he did not follow him concerning the years of Joshua. Josephus assigned Joshua twenty-six years, whereas Eusebius thought that twenty-seven should instead be recorded. [Col. 1022D] This, then, was the reason: if he followed Josephus, he could by no means have the prescribed total of four hundred and eighty years from Israel’s departure from Egypt until the Temple began to be built; rather, in his manuscripts he would find ten years missing from that period. He allowed this to happen because, following the Septuagint interpreters, he omitted from his Chronicles the judge Ahialon, who ruled the people for ten years after Abessa. But when he discovered that, according to the sacred history and the edition he followed, ten years were missing from the prescribed reckoning, he took care to add them from his own material wherever it seemed convenient and least contrary to sacred history. Thus he adds one year to Joshua’s period [Col. 1023A], eight years to the period of Samuel and Saul, and, to complete the number ten, he counts the fourth year itself of Solomon’s reign, in which the Temple began to be built. Anyone who follows the Hebrew truth finds that this ought not to be done. As for what I myself wrote in the preceding book—that the judges ruled the people from Moses to Samuel for three hundred and ninety-six years—I followed the authority of the Chronicles, not yet noticing that its reckoning of the years does not agree with the Hebrew truth.

He said: Whom do you suppose me to be? I am not he. In Greek it is stated more fully: “I am not the Christ.”

Men, brothers, sons of Abraham’s race, and those among you who fear God. In Greek there is an addition: “Hear.”

And we announce to you the promise made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled it for our children. The Greek reads more consistently: “That God has fulfilled it for their children.” It continues:

Raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm. Saint Father Hilary refers to this passage as follows:

> “But that which now appears in the psalm—‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ (Ps. 2)—belongs not to the Virgin’s childbirth, nor to the regeneration of baptism, but to the Firstborn from the dead: this is established by apostolic authority. For in the Book of Acts of the Apostles it is said: ‘We proclaim to you the promise made to our fathers; God has fulfilled this for our children, raising up our Lord Jesus Christ, as it is also written in the psalm: You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’ when he raised him from the dead, never again to return to destruction (Acts 13). This, then, is the voice of God the Father, according to the Apostle, uttered on the day of the resurrection.”

A little later, after recalling the Apostle’s statement concerning him—“Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2), and so forth—he says:

> “And in the glory of God the Father, he says, he is born today as one begotten: that is, the assumption of the servant’s form is honored by the reward of death, in the form of God that he had previously retained; and a new, yet not unfamiliar, birth occurs in time, when the Firstborn from the dead is born to resume the glory of God the Father, he who had been found in the form of a servant after having been in the form of God.” [Col. 1023C]

Look, you despisers, and wonder, and perish. In Greek it is written thus: “Hear, you despisers, and wonder; look, and perish.” [Col. 1023D]

As they spoke, they persuaded them to remain in the grace of God. At this point the Greek has a verse that our manuscripts do not contain: “And the word was reported throughout the entire city.” Then what we also have is added: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city assembled to hear the word of God.”

## CHAPTER XIV

The priest of Jupiter, who was before the city, bringing bulls and garlands before the gates, etc. It was the custom of the pagans, as Pliny testifies, when sacrificing in honor of their gods, to take garlands for victims that had themselves also been crowned. [Col. 1024A]

But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium arrived. In Greek this narrative begins as follows: “While they were staying there and teaching, some Jews from Antioch and Iconium arrived.”

## CHAPTER XV

Now therefore, why are you testing God by placing upon the disciples’ necks a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? It is evident that the statement “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Matt. 4) must be understood in various ways. That person, therefore, tests God who strives to serve and please him in a manner different from what God himself has commanded, and who trusts that he can keep his commandments without the help of his grace. Blessed Peter, however, wishes to remove the exceedingly heavy yoke [Col. 1024B] of observance of the Law from the disciples’ necks, so that he may place upon them the easy yoke of evangelical freedom. Concerning this, Paul says to those who share the same grace: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8).

That they abstain from the pollutions of idols, from immolation, from what has been strangled, and from blood. “What has been strangled” means carrion, concerning which Ezekiel writes: “The priests shall not eat any carrion or anything caught by a beast, whether of birds or cattle” (Ezek. 44). Explaining this, Jerome says:

> “And according to the literal sense, these precepts apply to every chosen royal and priestly race, which properly refers to Christians, who have been anointed with spiritual oil, concerning which it is written: ‘God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.’ They are commanded not to eat carrion, whether of birds or cattle, whose blood has not been poured out—what is called ‘strangled’ in the Acts of the Apostles—and which the letter of the apostles from Jerusalem urges must necessarily be observed; nor anything caught by a beast, because it too has similarly been strangled. It condemns priests who, out of greedy appetite, preserve such things in thrushes, fig-peckers, dormice, and other creatures of this kind.” [Col. 1024C]

They have troubled you, overturning your souls, with commands that we did not give them. In Greek there is an addition: “Overturning your souls by saying, ‘It is necessary to be circumcised and to observe the Law,’ although we did not command them.”

Who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In Greek there is an addition: “Into every temptation.” [Col. 1024D]

For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. In Greek it is written: “For it has pleased the Holy Spirit and us.”

They were dismissed in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. Instead of “to those who had sent them,” the Greek has “to the apostles.”

## CHAPTER XVI

And taking him, he circumcised him because of the Jews. It is reasonably asked why the Apostle, who circumcised Timothy, did not wish to circumcise Titus, as he himself writes to the Galatians. The explanation must be that he circumcised Timothy because of the Jews’ potential scandal, in order to show through him that he did not condemn the sacraments of the Mosaic Law, but did not impose them upon the Gentiles as necessary for salvation.

But after he circumcised Timothy, certain Jews who wanted the Gentiles circumcised because they claimed that the Gentiles could not be saved without those sacraments began to boast and say: “Paul also holds what we say: that salvation is impossible without these sacraments. For if he does not believe this, why did he circumcise Timothy?” When Paul heard this—having done it in freedom, not from necessity, because of the Jews’ scandal and not for Timothy’s salvation—he saw that they had gained an opportunity for another kind of preaching and for stirring up suspicion against Paul, and he did not wish to circumcise Titus. It is therefore clear why he wished to circumcise the one [Col. 1025A] and did not wish to circumcise the other: he wished to circumcise the former because of the Jews’ scandal, but refused to circumcise the latter because of the opportunity it would give to those who believed wrongly.

And a woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, from the city of the Thyatirans, a worshiper of God, heard, etc. “Seller of purple” means a seller of purple cloth, as we also find it rendered in another translation; in Greek she is called *porphyropōlis* (πορφυρόπωλις). It is fitting that the woman who was the first to believe in Illyricum through the Apostle’s preaching is said to have been a seller of purple. For she signifies the Church, which is accustomed, as it were, to sell purple because she does not hesitate to give her blood for Christ, so that through this she may purchase eternal life. Purple properly signifies the shedding and color of blood by the very property of its nature, since it is made from the blood of shellfish. [Col. 1025B]

Lydia compelled the Apostle and his companions to enter her house and remain there because the Church, having been rejected by the Jews, received the preaching of the Gospel with inward devotion of heart.

And it happened, as we were going to prayer, that a certain girl possessing a spirit of Python met us, etc. The one who mercifully joined the believing seller of purple to the members of the holy Church soon deprived the pythoness, who was proclaiming God’s greatness with an unclean mouth, of her wicked art through strict judgment. This is that power which the holy apostles received from the Lord when he said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18). [Col. 1025C]

As for what I wrote in the earlier book—that *python* could mean “mouth of the abyss” in Hebrew—I wrote what I found in the Book of Hebrew Names. But the reader should know that this name is Greek and has been violently interpreted according to the Hebrew language. Jerome himself, the interpreter of the Hebrew names, did not conceal this, as though it were pronounced *Fythona*: the Hebrews do not have the letter *p*, but in foreign words they use *f* in its place.

It should also be noted that in this reading, where it is written in Latin that the girl “met us,” the Greek has *hypantēsai* (ὑπαντῆσαι), which I thought worth mentioning so that the reader might observe that the Lord’s feast called *Hypantē of the Lord* received its Greek name from this: Simeon and Anna, together with the other faithful and elect who were there, came to meet the Lord with devoted heart and service when he was brought into the Temple. [Col. 1026A]

And when day had come, the magistrates sent lictors. Lictors were those assigned to punish defendants. Hence in Greek they are called *rhabdouchoi* (ῥαβδοῦχοι), from the rod. For the Greeks call a rod *rhabdos* (ῥάβδος). Hilary recalls this office in his exposition of the Apostle’s statement: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4). He asks: “Surely Paul did not possess praetorian authority, so that he could threaten with a rod and come to the Church of Christ with the office of a lictor?”

## CHAPTER XVII

And when they did not find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city. In Greek it is written [Col. 1026B]: “And certain other brothers.” Hence it must be understood that Jason too was a brother, that is, a believer in Christ.

Many of them believed, as did many honorable women among the Gentiles and not a few men. Some manuscripts, more accurately and consistently following the Greek exemplar, read: “And not a few men.”

And some were saying: What does this babbler want to say? Concerning this name Saint Augustine says:

> “We read that the Apostle Paul was called a sower of words. It was said by those who mocked him, but should not be rejected by believers. For he truly was a sower of words, but a reaper of conduct. And we, although so very small and in no way comparable with his excellence, sow the word of God in God’s field, which is your heart, and await an abundant harvest from your conduct.” [Col. 1026C]

And he made from one every race of humankind. When he says “from one,” it is clear that he means “from one human being.” But the Greek has the fuller reading: “He made from one blood,” which undoubtedly means the same thing. For by the name “blood” he designates the propagation of the flesh; and by “flesh,” according to the customary usage of Scripture, he intends a human being, in accordance with the Psalmist’s statement: “To you all flesh shall come” (Ps. 65).

## CHAPTER XVIII

And departing from there, he entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus. The name “Justus” is also written in Greek, either because this was the man’s proper name or because the Romans who knew him gave him this surname on account of his merit in righteousness. [Col. 1026D] It should not, however, be thought that this was Titus, the disciple of the Apostle Paul, to whom Paul himself wrote an Epistle and whom he ordained bishop of the Cretans. That Titus had been with him long before this time, when he came from Antioch to Jerusalem concerning the question of circumcision, with Barnabas still accompanying him. For Paul himself says to the Galatians: “Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also, and I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles.” He laid before them the Gospel he preached, carefully inquiring in the council of the apostles whether he was right to preach that Gentiles could attain salvation through the baptism of faith without circumcision—not because he himself had any doubt about this matter, but so that the minds of those who doubted might be strengthened by the authority of the apostolic synod. [Col. 1027A]

But Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his household, etc. This is believed to be the Crispus whom Paul indicates, writing to the Corinthians, that he himself baptized him: “I give thanks to God,” he says, “that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius.”

But all the Greeks, having seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, were beating him before the tribunal. In Greek it is written more accurately: “But all the Greeks, having seized Sosthenes.” After the Jews had been disgracefully expelled from the tribunal, the Gentiles inflicted an even greater insult by beating their ruler.

And bidding farewell to the brothers, he departed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila accompanying him; he had shaved his head at Cenchreae, etc. The wording is ambiguous as to whether Paul or Aquila shaved his head at Cenchreae. But Jerome the presbyter plainly understands this, as we explained more fully in the preceding book, to have been said of Paul. For after stating this opinion in a letter to Augustine, he immediately added:

> “Suppose that there he was compelled, through fear of the Jews, to do in the matter of Timothy’s circumcision what was permissible. Why then did he grow his hair under a vow, and afterward, in accordance with the Law, cut it off at Cenchreae?”

If we wish to follow Jerome’s interpretation here, we nowhere read at all that Aquila was shorn. If we say that Aquila was shorn at this point, there remains at the end of this little book a passage where we also read that Paul was shorn, or shaved. Those who say that Aquila was shorn together with Priscilla his wife are misled by a corrupt manuscript. In Greek the reading is clearly *keiramenos* (κειράμενος), that is, “having been shorn,” in the singular; and it says “he had a vow,” not “they had a vow,” whether the reference is understood to be to Paul or to Aquila. [Col. 1027B–C]

For he vehemently refuted the Jews, publicly demonstrating through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. In Greek it is written thus: “Demonstrating publicly and in the houses.” This is characteristic of an excellent teacher: to teach many people in general while not ceasing to exhort individuals courageously.

## CHAPTER XIX

He separated the disciples, disputing every day in the school of a certain Tyrannus; this continued for three years, etc. During this period, while Paul was staying in Ephesus, he is said to have written the First Epistle to the Corinthians. In it he also mentions Priscilla and Aquila, saying: “Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their house” (1 Cor. 16). These words also show that they not only served Christ faithfully but maintained a congregation of the faithful in their house. He is said to have written the Second Epistle while he was in Troas. The reasoning of the matter shows that the Epistle to the Romans was written afterward. For Paul himself testifies that he wrote it while setting out for Jerusalem. [Col. 1027D]

So that even handkerchiefs or aprons from his body were carried to the sick. Many among us do not know what “aprons” signify. But Gregory, who is now bishop of the apostolic see, while he was still archdeacon, replied to a friend in Britain who had asked him about this, among other matters, that it was a kind of handkerchief used by the Hebrews on the head. [Col. 1028A]

## CHAPTER XX

Sosipater of Beroea, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him. Here the reading is “a Beroean,” not “of this Beroea.” The Greek has an addition: “He accompanied him as far as Asia.”

When he had been roused from sleep, he fell from the third story. Instead of “third story,” the Greek has *tristegon* (τρίστεγον), which I wished to mention so that the reader might know what is meant in Genesis by the command concerning the construction of the ark: “You shall make chambers and triple roofs in it” (Gen. 6). For *stegē* (στέγη) means “roof” in Greek, and *tristega* (τρίστεγα) means “triple roofs.”

Taking him with us, we came to Mytilene. In the first book, following Pliny Secundus, we wrote that Mytilene was an island opposite Asia. But the same Pliny writes elsewhere that Mytilene was a city on the island of Cyprus. Both statements should be believed true; nevertheless, Paul and his companions did not now come to a city of Cyprus but to an island of Asia. For it is reported that much later, after traveling through many regions, he appeared in Cyprus, but did not enter this place. [Col. 1028B]

For he was hurrying, if it were possible for him, to celebrate the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem. In Greek it is written “the day of Pentecost,” that is, “the fiftieth day.” Note, therefore, that the times of both Passover and Pentecost were celebrated even in the days of the apostles. But whether they were celebrated among the Jewish adherents of the Law on the day when the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt and the Law was given on Mount Sinai, or rather on the day of the Lord’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, let those who know say. It is nevertheless established that the Apostle Peter celebrated Passover at Rome on the Lord’s day of Christ’s resurrection; and it is established that the evangelist Mark, sent by him, taught this in Egypt. [Col. 1028C]

## CHAPTER XXI

And entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him, etc. He deserved to be called an evangelist because of the primacy of his preaching office, although all of them performed this work. His house and his daughters remained in that same city for a long time thereafter. Finally, Jerome also mentions him in the Life of Saint Paula, when he describes her coming to Caesarea:

> “In that city,” he says, “she saw the house of Cornelius, now a church of Christ, and the little house and chamber of Philip’s four virgin prophetesses.” [Col. 1028D]

Concerning those who believed from among the Gentiles, we have written, judging that they should abstain from idols, from immolation, etc. In Greek the statement is more clearly distinguished: “Concerning those who believed among the nations, we have written, judging that they should observe none of these things except that they should keep themselves from sacrificial offerings to idols,” etc.

The Jews who believed in Christ were not, therefore, at that time prohibited from entering according to the custom of the Law, while the Temple and their religion still stood, although they were to possess salvation only in the sacraments of the New Testament. Rather, those who had believed from among the Gentiles and had been instructed in the sacraments of the Gospel were prohibited from turning to receive the sacraments of the Law. They were nevertheless commanded to observe carefully those commandments of the Law that pertain to the formation of conduct and the cleansing of the heart, such as: “You shall not covet” (Rom. 7).

This was the fourth apostolic synod held at Jerusalem. The first concerned the election of the twelfth apostle in place of Judas; the second, the election of the seven deacons; the third, circumcision, so that it would not be imposed upon believers from among the Gentiles; and this fourth concerned those who had believed from among the Jews at that time, so that they would not be prohibited, wherever necessity required, from being initiated even into the legal ceremonies. This was done, of course, to avoid the scandal of those who thought that they had condemned the Mosaic decrees as though they were doctrines of idolatry—a practice they had also previously been accustomed to follow, as Timothy’s circumcision in particular proved. [Col. 1029A]

He ordered him to be taken into the barracks. Here, and throughout this entire narrative, wherever the word “barracks” occurs, it should be explained that in Greek it is singular. The Latin translator preferred to put it in the plural so that, if he rendered it in the singular, he would send the reader’s understanding in a wholly different direction and cause a fortified place to be understood instead of an assembly of an army and soldiers. Likewise in the psalm where it says, “And they fell in the midst of their barracks,” the Greek has *parembolē* (παρεμβολή) in the singular. [Col. 1029B]

When he had come to the steps, it happened that he was carried, and so forth. “Steps” signifies not a descent from the Temple but an ascent into the barracks. This is clear from the Greek, where *anabathmos* (ἀναβαθμός), meaning “ascent,” is written, not *katabathmos* (καταβαθμός), meaning “descent.”

I am indeed a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. Instead of “citizen,” some manuscripts have “municipal inhabitant,” which is translated from the single Greek word *politēs* (πολίτης), a noun derived from *polis* (πόλις), meaning “city.” Hence, when the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3), some have translated: “Our municipal citizenship is in heaven.” Jerome likewise wrote to Heliodorus:

> “He wished no other municipal citizenship to be understood than civic conduct, which in Greek is called *politeuma* (πολίτευμα).” [Col. 1029C]

## CHAPTER XXII

Educated according to the truth, being a zealous adherent of the ancestral Law. In Greek there is an addition: “Being a zealot for God,” in accordance with the statement to the Romans: “For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” [Col. 1029D]

Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? In Greek, at this point too, there is an addition: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

And those who were with me saw the light. In Greek there is an addition: “And they became afraid.”

But it happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the Temple, that I fell into a state of mental astonishment and saw him. Instead of “mental astonishment,” some manuscripts have “ecstasy of mind,” others “fear,” and others “alienation.” For the Greek word *ekstasis* (ἔκστασις) is translated into Latin in different ways. The same word was also used above in Peter’s vision, when he was summoned to instruct Cornelius. [Col. 1030A] “For an ecstasy fell upon him, and he saw heaven opened.” The minds of the praying apostles were indeed carried away, but from what is below to what is above—not so that they might go astray, but so that they might see.

I acquired this citizenship at great expense. Instead of “citizenship,” the Greek has *politeia* (πολιτεία), which signifies more properly civic life—that is, social intercourse among citizens—or the administration of the commonwealth, rather than the city itself. For the tribune had not purchased the city of Rome, of which he would have been the possessor, but participation in Roman citizenship, of which he was a member. Paul, however, was all the more a Roman citizen because he possessed this not by purchase but by birth.

The tribune was also afraid after he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen. In place of “citizen,” the same Greek word is used here as above for “municipal inhabitant,” namely *politēs* (πολίτης). [Col. 1030B]

## CHAPTER XXIII

And they bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. “They bound themselves under a curse” means “they cursed themselves.” For the Greek has *anethematísan* (ἀνεθεμάτισαν) for this verb; but later, where they said, “With a curse we have bound ourselves to taste nothing,” the Greek has *anathemati anethematisamen* (ἀναθέματι ἀνεθεματίσαμεν). Those who are alienated from the fellowship of Christ and the Church by a priestly anathema know how severe this word is.

## CHAPTER XXIV

After many years I came to my nation to bring alms and offerings and to make vows. [Col. 1030C] The alms refer to what he had brought for the needs of the saints, of which he frequently speaks in his Epistles. The offerings and vows refer to what, at the urging of James and the elders, he had offered to God in the Temple. In Greek, however, “vows” has not been added. Although Luke did not say in the chronological order of his history that Paul came from Greece to Jerusalem with the alms for Christ’s poor, the words that he reports Paul himself to have spoken nevertheless show that he did so.

## CHAPTER XXV
Festus, however, replied that Paul was being kept in Caesarea, while he himself would depart sooner. “Shortly” here certainly means “more quickly,” although sometimes “to act shortly” is said of something done later and with mature deliberation. For in Greek it is written ἐν τάχει, that is, “with speed.”

[Col. 1030D] When Agrippa and Bernice had arrived with great display, etc. In Greek, φαντασία is written for “display”; by this word is designated elaborate preparation and the pomp of royal office, with which he, encompassing himself on every side, was attended.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Since I lived according to the most certain sect of our religion, as a Pharisee. For “sect,” the Greek has αἵρεσιν, “heresy” or “sect.” Hence it is proved that at that time this word also denoted a good sect among the Greeks, whereas now among us it is accustomed to denote only an evil one.

## CHAPTER XXVII

When it was decided that he should sail to Italy and that Paul, with the other prisoners, should be handed over to a centurion. [Col. 1031A] The Greek reads more coherently: “When it was decided that we should sail to Italy, they handed Paul and certain other prisoners over to a centurion.”

And, sailing across the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Lystra, which is in Lycia. In Greek, Smyrna is written for Lystra; for this Jerome, in the book of Hebrew Names, gives Myrrha. I think that this is found in certain manuscripts because μύρρα (“myrrh”) is called Smyrna in Greek. Accordingly, in the psalm where we sing, “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia” (Psalm 44), the Greek is written thus: “Smyrna, and stacte, and cassia.”

We came to a certain place called Good Harbors. It is “the Good Harbors,” not “this Good Harbor.”

[Col. 1031B] And he trusted the shipmaster more. Ναύκληρος is the Greek word for “master of a ship.”

If somehow they could reach Phoenix to winter there, a harbor of Crete facing toward the southwest wind and the northwest wind. The southwest wind, called λίψ in Greek, blows between the southern quarter and the west, inclining toward the west; the northwest wind, however, lies toward the north and west, but bends more toward the west. It is therefore clear that the province of Phoenix lay west of Crete, and for that reason its harbor looked from some of its places toward the southwest wind, and from others toward the northwest wind. Consequently, if either the southwest or the northwest wind blew, they could loose their cable from Crete and reach Phoenix. But even if the south wind itself, that is, the meridional wind, were blowing, they could nevertheless, by the twofold direction of the rudders and the curving of the sails, sail toward Phoenix, had not divine judgments opposed them. Hence what follows is added:

But when the south wind began to blow, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, etc., we were scarcely able to secure the boat. In the first book, following Isidore, we wrote that a boat was a light little vessel woven from willow and covered with raw hide. But afterward, examining the writings of others, we found that scaphae also meant little boats hollowed from a single tree, which the Greeks call μονόξυλα.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

For, having kindled a fire, they refreshed us all. The Greek reads: “They received us all.” We too think that this was first translated into Latin in that form, but was altered through the negligence of copyists.

Now it happened that the father of Publius lay afflicted with fever and dysentery. Dysentery is a disease of the intestines, a disorder accompanied by ulceration, because a bloody or bilious discharge, or some other alteration of the humors, is expelled. The ancient authorities, however, judge it harmful when it has shown a black discharge from the beginning. For Hippocrates says in the Aphorisms: “Dysentery beginning from black bile is fatal.”

Those suffering from it then experience continual discharge from the lower abdomen, sometimes green, sometimes mucous; they also pass shavings or scraps with drops of blood, together with intestinal and umbilical pain. They suffer sleeplessness and loss of appetite, and often a slight fever—the fever which the father of Publius is reported here to have suffered. Sometimes there is also an [uncertain: extalis] evacuation, especially in infants. It is sometimes caused by chilling or by the corruption of sharper humors.

[Col. 1032B]

Gregory also mentions this disease in the fifth book of his Histories, saying:

“In the time of the emperor Tiberius, a dysenteric illness seized almost all Gaul. Those who suffered had a severe fever accompanied by vomiting, excessive pain in the kidneys, heaviness of the head or neck, and the substances discharged from the mouth were saffron-colored or, at any rate, green. Many asserted that a hidden poison was present; but herbs that cure poisons, taken as a drink, brought help to many.”

He remained for a full two years in his rented lodging and received all who came to him, preaching [Col. 1032C] the kingdom of God. Jerome refers to this passage in his letter to Lucinius:

“Paul enters Rome in chains so that he may set free those bound by the errors of superstition; he remains in rented lodgings for two years, in order to give us the eternal gift of both Testaments.”

By this exposition he taught that the other things written in this volume, whether about the apostle Paul himself or about various other persons, do not merely display for us, on the surface of the letter, the fruit of ecclesiastical teaching; rather, whoever understands them perfectly will find that the marrow of their spiritual meaning is pregnant with power.

[Col. 1032A]

**END OF THE BOOK OF RETRACTION.**

[Col. 1031]

# FIVE QUESTIONS ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES  
(C, S)*

## QUESTION ONE

[Col. 1031D]

**QUESTION.** What does the statement we read mean: “Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, having a Sabbath-day’s journey,” that is, one thousand paces?

**ANSWER.** For on the Sabbath the Jews were permitted to go as far as the Mount of Olives; or, if they happened to be somewhere else, they assumed the liberty of walking that distance.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 1032D]

**QUESTION.** How is the Holy Spirit breathed upon the apostles by the Savior before the Ascension, according to the evangelist John, when according to the Acts of the Apostles he was sent upon the apostles after the tenth day following the Ascension?

**ANSWER.** There are many gifts of grace from the Holy Spirit, according to what the Apostle says: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit,” etc. (1 Corinthians 12).

Therefore, before the Ascension they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they could forgive sins, baptize, and pour the spirit of adoption into believers, according to what had also been said at that time when the Savior breathed the Spirit upon them: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained.”

After the Ascension, however, they received a much greater grace of the Holy Spirit in the working of miracles, in the grace of healings, and in the reception of different languages, in accordance with what had been promised to them on that same day: that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power, by which they could preach the Gospel of Christ to all nations.

Thus, in this reception of the Holy Spirit, the progress of the apostles is demonstrated according to the distribution of the Lord’s grace; the Scriptures are not in conflict with one another. A certain distinguished teacher also explained admirably why the Holy Spirit was given twice, saying:

“Concerning the one whom the Savior first gave here through himself, and whom he afterward sent from heaven, it was signified that the love of neighbor and the love of God are poured into the hearts of the saints through the Holy Spirit, who was given to them for proclaiming the word of God.”

Through this gift the apostles carried themselves into the regions of the world. As far as history relates, Bartholomew went to the Indians; Thomas traveled to the Parthians; Matthew softened the Ethiopians by preaching; Andrew corrected the Scythians; John instructed Asia with divine speech; Peter traveled through Cappadocia [Col. 1033C] and Galatia, Bithynia likewise and Pontus, and the neighboring provinces, preaching to the Jews, and finally came to Rome to enlighten it. Paul filled innumerable and diverse nations with the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and subdued them victoriously by his commands as by weapons.

## QUESTION III

**QUESTION.** Since it is first read in the Acts of the Apostles: [Col. 1034A] “The men who accompanied him,” that is, the Apostle, “stood amazed, hearing indeed the voice but seeing no one,” how does the Apostle later say: “Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of him who was speaking with me”?

**ANSWER.** Above, where they are said to have heard a voice, they received from God not an articulated voice but an unformed sound of a voice. Thus he later says that they did not hear the voice—that is, the distinct meaning of the words, by which they could understand what was being uttered. Accordingly, they are reported both to have heard and not to have heard in different respects because, insofar as sound is concerned, they heard it, but insofar as words are concerned, they did not hear it.

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 1034B]

**QUESTION.** Why was what was thought to be unclean previously called common food?

**ANSWER.** Because what was then prohibited by God was open in common to the other peoples, who did not observe the law’s distinctions among foods, by which the Jews boasted that they were God’s portion. It was purified, however, when the Lord also said to Peter: “What God has purified, you must not call common” (Acts 10).

## QUESTION V

**QUESTION.** What is meant by the passage in the Acts of the Apostles where the twelve who had been baptized with John’s baptism are baptized by Paul?

**ANSWER.** This was because they had not been baptized in the name of the Trinity. [Col. 1034C] For although John’s baptism baptized people into the one who was to come, it was properly called John’s baptism.
