Hence those who come from heretics are not rebaptized by us if it is established that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity; only the imposition of hands is applied to those converted to the true faith,

so that through this the infusion of the Holy Spirit

may be received.

[Col. 1033]

# EXPOSITION OF THE NAMES OF THE PLACES AND CITIES READ IN THE BOOK OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES  
(C, S)

## A

[Col. 1033D]

**Acheldemach**, that is, “field of blood,” which is still shown today in the district of Helia, on the southern side of Mount Zion. To this day, in accordance with Jewish custom, it covers some of the bodies of the ignoble with earth and leaves others to decay in the open air.

**Egypt** has the Great Sea and the Arabian Gulf to the north, the Red Sea to the east, the Ocean to the south, and Libya to the west. The lower part of it is divided and bounded by the Nile, which embraces it on the right and left, with the Canopic mouth at the African side and the Pelusiac mouth at the Asian side, separated by one hundred and sixty thousand paces. For this reason some have counted Egypt among the islands, since the Nile divides it in such a way that it forms the shape of the Greek letter Δ, and many have therefore called Egypt by the name of that Greek letter, Delta. The distance from the point where the channel first divides toward the sides to the Canopic mouth is one hundred and sixty thousand paces; to the Pelusiac mouth, two hundred and fifty-six thousand.

The region of the **Ethiopians**, rising near the river Indus beside Egypt, lies between the Nile and the Ocean in the south, close beneath the sun. Its peoples are three: the Hesperians of the west, the Garamantes of Tripoli, and the Indians of the east.

[Col. 1035A]

**Alexandria**, a city of Egypt, once called No, lies like a barrier between Egypt, Africa, and the sea. There the tomb of the blessed evangelist Mark is still venerated in the church.

**Amphipolis**, a city of Macedonia. There is another of the same name in Syria.

**Antioch**, a city of Coele-Syria, in which the apostles Barnabas and Paul were ordained. There is another in the province of Pisidia in Asia, where the same men, preaching to the Jews, said: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, but since you rejected it,” etc. (Acts 13).

**Antipatris**, a city of Palestine, now ruined, which Herod, king of Judaea, named after his father.

**Appius’ Forum**, the name of a marketplace in Rome derived from Appius, formerly consul; the Appian Way also received its name from him.

[Col. 1035B]

**Apollonia**, a city of Macedonia. There is another in the province of Africa called Pentapolis.

**Areopagus**, the council of Athens, interpreted as “the court of Mars,” because Mars was once judged there by the twelve gods.

**Arabia**, the region between the gulf of the sea called the Persian Gulf and that called the Arabian Gulf. It contains many peoples: Moabites, Ammonites, Idumaeans, Saracens, and very many others. Arabia is said to be interpreted as “sacred,” because it is a frankincense-bearing region that produces fragrant substances. Hence the Greeks called it Eudaemon, and our people called it “Blessed.”

[Col. 1035C]

**Asia**, the region called Asia Minor, except on the eastern side where it extends toward Cappadocia and Syria, is surrounded on every side by sea. Its provinces are Phrygia, Pamphylia, Cilicia, Chaonia, Galatia, and many others. But especially where the city of Ephesus is, the name Asia is used.

**Assos**, a coastal city of Asia, also called Apollonia.

**Athens**, a city in Achaia devoted to the study of philosophy. Although it is one city, it is always customarily called by a plural name. Its harbor, Piraeus, is described as once having been fortified by a wall with sevenfold defenses.

**Attalia**, a coastal city of Pamphylia.

**Azotus**, a notable town of Palestine, called Esdod in Hebrew; it is one of the five cities formerly belonging to the Philistines.

## B

[Col. 1035D]

**Babylon**, the metropolis of the kingdom of the Chaldaeans, where those who built the tower and whose language was divided lived; the surrounding region is therefore called Babylonia. Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that it was extremely powerful and situated on a plain in the form of a square, with twelve thousand paces from corner to corner of its walls—that is, sixty-four thousand paces around its entire circuit. Its citadel, that is, the Capitol of the city, is a tower said to have been four thousand paces in extent, built after the Flood. After its destruction, only so many brick walls are said to have remained, and these were recovered in order to capture the wild animals that abound there.

**Beroea**, a city in Macedonia, which nobly received the word of the Lord.

[Col. 1036A]

**Bithynia**, a province of Asia Minor, formerly called Bebrycia and afterward Mygdonia. It is also Greater Phrygia, separated from Galatia by the river Hiera. It has a city of the same name.

## C

There are two cities called **Caesarea** in the land of promise. One is Caesarea of Palestine, situated on the shore of the Great Sea. Formerly called Pyrgos, that is, “tower,” it was better, more beautifully, and much more usefully equipped against the force of the sea by Herod, king of Judaea. It was called Caesarea in honor of Caesar Augustus. He also built there a temple of white marble. There his grandson Herod was struck by an angel, the centurion Cornelius was baptized, and the prophet Agabus bound himself with Paul’s belt.

The other is **Caesarea Philippi**, mentioned in the Scripture of the Gospel, at the foot of Mount Lebanon, where the sources of the Jordan are. It was founded by Philip the tetrarch of that region and named in honor of Tiberius Caesar.

There is also a third **Caesarea**, the metropolis of Cappadocia, which Luke mentions as follows: “Departing from Ephesus and going down to Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church.”

**Cappadocia**, a region at the head of Syria, that is, toward the north.

**Carrhae**, a city of Mesopotamia, famous among the Romans for the disaster of Crassus, but among us famous for the hospitality shown to the patriarch Abraham and for the death of his father.

**Cenchreae**, the harbor of the very famous city of Corinth.

The region of the **Chaldaeans** lies between Babylonia and Arabia, and between the Tigris and Euphrates.

**Canaan**, son of Ham, possessed the land from Sidon to Gaza, which the Jews afterward occupied after expelling the Canaanites.

**Chios**, an island before Bithynia. Its name in the Syrian language signifies mastic, because mastic grows there. Some have called it Chia, after the nymph Chione.

**Cilicia**, a province of Asia crossed by the river Cydnus and separated from Coele-Syria by Mount Amanus, which Solomon mentions.

**Cyprus**, an island in the Pamphylian Sea, formerly notable for fifteen towns and famous for its wealth, especially its copper. There the first discovery and use of this metal took place. Nearby, on the coast of Cilicia, are a promontory and a town of Venus.

[Col. 1036D]

**Cyrene**, a city in Libya; its region is also called Pentapolis because it shines especially through five cities: Berenice, Arsinoe, Ptolemais, Apollonia, and Cyrene itself.

**Cnidus**, an island opposite Asia.

**Cos**, a very famous island opposite Asia, adjoining the province of Attica. There is also a town of the same name on the island of Calamna.

**Corinth**, a coastal city of Achaia.

**Crete**, an island of Greece formerly famous for one hundred cities, whence it was called Hecatopolis.

## D

[Col. 1037A]

**Damascus**, a noble city of Phoenicia, which once held primacy throughout Syria and is now said to be the metropolis of the Saracens. Their king Maumas dedicated to himself and his people a famous basilica there, while Christian citizens throughout the surrounding area frequent the church of the blessed John the Baptist.

**Derbe**, a city of the province of Lycaonia.

## E

The **Elamites**, princes of Persia, were named from Elam, son of Shem.

**Ephesus**, the work of the Amazons, is a city in Asia where the blessed evangelist John rests.

## F

There are no names beginning with F, but these two begin with Φ.

[Col. 1037B]

**Phrygia**, a province of Asia lying above the Troad, bordering Galatia on its northern side, Lycaonia, Pisidia, and Mygdonia on its southern side, and reaching Cappadocia to the east. There are two Phrygias: Greater Phrygia contains Smyrna, while Lesser Phrygia contains Ilium.

**Phoenicia**, a province of Syria, whose parts include Samaria, Galilee, and many other regions.

## G

There are two **Galilees**. One is Galilee of the nations, near the borders of Tyre in the tribe of Naphtali. The other lies around Tiberias and the Lake of Gennesaret in the tribe of Zebulun.

**Galatia**, a province of Asia, deriving its name from the Gauls. These, summoned by the king of Bithynia as auxiliaries, divided the kingdom with him after achieving victory. Later, mingling with the Greeks, they were first called Gallograeci and afterward Galatians.

[Col. 1037C]

**Gaza**, a notable city of Palestine, which among the ancients was the southern boundary of the Canaanites. The site of ancient Gaza is now scarcely indicated except by traces of foundations. The city now visible was built in another place in place of the one that collapsed.

**Greece**, a certain province of Achaia, called Hellas by Greek writers. In it lies the city of Athens, once called Attica.

## H

**Hadrumetum**, a city in the region of Africa called Byzacium.

**Hadria**, or Adria, is the name of the sea opposite Ravenna, entered through the mouths of the river Po. It took its name from the nearby city of Hadria, which also gave that sea the name Adriatic.

[Col. 1037D]

**Jerusalem**, once the metropolis of all Judaea, is now called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian Caesar, because he restored it on a broader site after Titus had destroyed it. Through his work it came about that the holy places—the sites of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, and also of the discovery of the holy Cross—which once lay outside the city are now enclosed within the northern wall of that same city.

## I

**Iconium**, a very celebrated city of Lycaonia; there is another in Cilicia.

**Joppa**, a maritime town of Palestine in the tribe of Dan, where rocks are still shown on the shore on which Andromeda is said to have been fastened and freed through the aid of Perseus, once her husband.

[Col. 1038A]

**Italy**, a region in the homeland of the Romans, deriving its name from King Italus. It is enclosed by the Great Sea from the southwest wind and the north wind, while the Alps block its remaining approaches.

**Judaea** sometimes denotes the entire land of the twelve tribes; sometimes only the two tribes once called Juda, to distinguish them from Galilee, Samaria, and the other regions of the land of promise. Historians should be noted here: Judaea belongs to Palestine, while Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia.

## L

**Lasea**, a coastal city of the island of Crete, near the place called Good Harbors, as Luke himself explains. For it some corruptly read Thalassa.

[Col. 1038B]

There are two provinces of **Libya**. One is Libya Cyrenaica, of which it is said: “And the part of Libya that is around Cyrene” (Acts 2). This is the first region of Africa after Egypt and gave its name to the Libyan Sea. After it comes the Libya of the Ethiopians, extending as far as the southern Ocean.

**Lycaonia**, a province of Asia.

There is also a city of the same name in Lesser Phrygia.

**Lycia**, a province of Asia.

**Lydda**, a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea, now called Diospolis.

**Lystra**, a city of Lycaonia.

## M

**Macedonia**, the most renowned province of Greece, made still more famous by the courage of Alexander the Great.

[Col. 1038C]

**Madian**, a city near Armon and Areopolis, of which only ruins are visible; there Moses lived in exile with Jethro, his father-in-law.

The **Medes** were named from Madai, son of Japheth. These regions lie between the river Indus and the river Tigris, extending from Mount Caucasus to the Red Sea: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persia, and Media. Sacred Scripture often calls all of them by the name Media.

**Mesopotamia**, the region between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, is shown by its Greek name itself to lie “in the midst of the rivers.” To its south comes Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and finally Arabia Eudaemon.

**Miletus**, a city in coastal Asia, separated by ten stadia from the mouth of the river Maeander, where Paul addressed the elders of Ephesus. There is also an obscure island of the same name in the Aegean or Ionian Sea.

**Mysia**, a province of Asia, now called Aeolis. There is another of the same name near the river Danube. Some authorities say that the Moschi, Bryges, and Thyni crossed over from Europe; from them the peoples in Asia are called Mysians, Phrygians, and Bithynians.

[Col. 1038D]

**Mytilene**, an island opposite Asia, seven thousand five hundred paces from the nearest mainland.

## N

**Nazareth**, a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor, from which our Lord Jesus Christ was called a Nazarene. It has a church at the place where the angel entered to announce the Gospel to the blessed Mary, and another where the Lord was raised.

[Col. 1039]

**Neapolis**, a city of Caria, which is a province of Asia.

## O

The **Mount of Olives** lies east of Jerusalem, with the brook Kidron flowing between them. There the final footprints of the Lord are still shown impressed in the ground. Although believers daily take away earth from that place, the same holy footprints nevertheless continually return to their former condition. Finally, when the church in whose center they are was built in a circular form and with very beautiful workmanship, only the highest point, as they say, could not in any way be covered or vaulted, because of the passage of the Lord’s body; rather, its path remains open all the way to heaven.

## P

**Pamphylia** is a province of Asia.

**Paphos**, a coastal city on the island of Cyprus, once famous for the rites of Venus and the songs of poets. Having collapsed through frequent earthquakes, it now shows what it formerly was only by traces of its ruins.

The **Parthians** are situated between the river Indus to the east and the river Tigris to the west, as stated above.

**Patara**, a city of the province of Lycia in Asia.

**Perge**, a city of the province of Pamphylia.

**Philippi**, a city in the first part of Macedonia.

**Pisidia**, a province of Asia.

**Pontus**, a region of many peoples beside the Pontic Sea, which separates Asia and Europe and is known to be sweeter than other seas because of the very great inflow of the mouths of the Danube.

**Ptolemais**, a coastal city of Judaea near Mount Carmel, formerly called Acho. There is another Ptolemais in the province of Africa called Pentapolis, which I mentioned above.

**Puteoli**, a city and colony of Campania, also called Dicaearchia.

## R

**Rhegium**, a coastal city of Sicily, separated by twenty thousand paces from the promontory of Pelorus. Its name is interpreted in Greek as “breach,” because this part of Sicily, once joined to the Italian territory of Bruttium, was afterward torn away by the intervening sea. The strait is fifteen thousand paces long and one thousand five hundred wide near the Royal Column. In this strait are the rock Scylla and also Charybdis, a swirling sea; both are famous for their savagery.

**Rhodes**, the most famous of the Cyclades and the first toward the east, was once called Ophiusa. It contained a city of the same name, famous for a bronze colossus seventy cubits high. It is twenty thousand paces from the harbor of Asia.

**Rome**, a city in Italy, once mistress of the whole world, was so called from the name of its founder Romulus. Because of its exceptional excellence, many writers preferred to call it “the City,” as though it alone existed.

## S

**Salamis**, a city on the island of Cyprus, now called Constantia. In the time of the emperor Trajan, the Jews destroyed it after killing all its inhabitants.

**Salomon**, a coastal city of the island of Crete.

**Samaria**, a royal city in Israel situated on the summit of Mount Somer. The entire surrounding region also once received its name from the city, lying between Judaea and Galilee. Herod, son of Antipater, called it Σεβαστή in Greek, that is, “Augusta,” in honor of Caesar Augustus.

**Samos**, an island in the Aegean Sea, where earthen vessels are said to have first been discovered. Hence such vessels were called Samian.

[Col. 1040]

**Samothrace**, an island in the Carpathian Gulf.

**Sharon**, which means “level” or “plain,” is a region extending from Caesarea of Palestine to the town of Joppa. It is still a place suitable for grazing flocks, and in accordance with the character of its soil it continually produced the fruit of faith when Peter preached. The region between Mount Tabor and the Lake of Tiberias is also called Sharon.

**Seleucia**, a famous city of Syria, situated on the promontory of Antioch in Syria.

**Shechem**, the city of Jacob, now called Neapolis, near the tomb of Joseph. It took its name from the son of its king, Hamor. Near it the Lord spoke to the Samaritan woman at the well, where a church has now been built out of the side of Mount Gerizim.

**Sicily** is marked out by three promontories, and was therefore once called Trinacria, from its triangular shape; afterward it was called Sicily from its king Siculus. The first promontory is called Pelorus and faces north. The city of Messana lies nearby, while the promontory of Caenys in Italy is twelve stadia away. The second is called Pachynus and faces toward the southeast wind. The third is called Lilybaeum; it has a city of the same name and points toward the west.

**Sidon**, a notable city of Phoenicia, once the boundary of the Canaanites, situated to the north near the rising of Mount Lebanon. It is itself also a maker of glass.

**Sinai**, a mountain in the region of Madian above Arabia, in the desert, also called Horeb by another name. Hence it is said: “And they made a calf in Horeb” (Psalm 105), although Moses wrote that this was done at Sinai.

**Syracuse**, the metropolis of Sicily beneath the promontory of Pachynus.

**Syria**, called Aram in Hebrew, is the region between the river Euphrates and the Great Sea, extending as far as Egypt. It contains very large provinces: Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, apart from the Saracens and Nabataeans, whose peoples number twelve.

The **Syrtes** are sandy places in the Great Sea, very terrifying and dreadful because they habitually drag everything toward themselves and hold fast whatever approaches in their shallow waters. They are near the Egyptian Sea and merge with it.

**Smyrna**, a city of the province of Lycia in Asia, which Luke mentions as follows: “And sailing across the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Smyrna of Lycia” (Acts 27). For this some manuscripts read: “We came to Lystra, which is in Cilicia.” Jerome, moreover, in the book of Hebrew Names, gives Myrrha and interprets it as “bitter.”

## T

**Tarsus**, the metropolitan city of the province of Cilicia, made glorious by the apostle Paul.

**Theater**, a place that takes its name from spectacle, because there the people watched theatrical performances from above.

**Thessalonica**, a city of Macedonia.

**Thyatira**, a city of Lydia, which is a province of Asia, formerly famous for the temple of Aesculapius. The Lydia who was a citizen of this city was a seller of purple, that is, a dealer in purple cloth, and she received the faith of Christ at Philippi.

**Tyre**, the metropolis of Phoenicia in the tribe of Naphtali, nearly twenty miles from Caesarea Philippi. Formerly it was an island, separated from the mainland by deep sea for seven hundred paces; Alexander made it part of the mainland by bringing many embankments into the narrow strait in order to conquer it. Its chief fame rests on purple dye and the murex shell.

**Troas**, a coastal city of Asia, also called Antigonia.

Volume back matter

[Col. 1039]
